improvements</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 1 provides definitions for key terms that appear in the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30 (“the <ital>Act</ital>”). Going back as far as 1874, the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> contained definitions for “contractor”, “subcontractor”, and “owner”. The definitions for “contractor”, “Crown”, “subcontractor”, “wages” and “workman” [later “worker”] have remained consistent throughout the over 125-year history of lien legislation in this Province. The definition of “material” was added by amendment in 1896 and the definition of “wages” was added in 1897. A definition for “workman” was introduced in the amendments of 1968–69. Definitions for “Crown”, “estate or interest in land”, and “public work” were added by <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1975</ital>. The <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 introduced numerous new definitions. Definitions of “home” and “home buyer” were added in 1990 to accompany the reform of the priority sections in that regard.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The 1983 <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> introduced several key definitions and modified others. The key definitions are as follows:</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>1)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Contract” and “subcontract”; “subcontractor” and “contractor”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Mechanic's Lien Act</ital> contained no definition of “contract”. As noted in the Attorney General's Committee Report (see Appendix), courts had interpreted the word “contract” to include subcontracts, with unanticipated consequences such as the application of the doctrine of substantial completion to subcontracts. As a result, the 1983 Act drew a clear distinction between contracts and subcontracts. Contracts are made between the owner and contractor, while subcontracts relate to any other contract concerning the improvement. Whereas the statutes of Manitoba and Saskatchewan include definitions for “contract”, “subcontract”, as well as for “contractor” and “subcontractor”, the other provinces define only for “contractor” and “subcontractor”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Because of the importance of the distinction between contractors and subcontractors, courts have not allowed the lines between these concepts to become blurred. Courts have dismissed arguments that contractors are agents of the owners, thereby rendering the subcontractors “contractors” for the purposes of the Act. Such a position, it has been held, would prejudice subcontractors who could have no knowledge of this arrangement and would pursue their remedies as “subcontractors”; (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Sheet Metal Dominion & Roofing Works" p2="Di Iorio" post.rptr="295" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I9089e3d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Sheet Metal Dominion & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio">Sheet Metal Dominion & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 295 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I908a0ae0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at [1996] O.J. No. 270, 1996 CarswellOnt 297 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Main Line Construction Ltd." p2="Nicolini" post.rptr="2815" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I55a6f040fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini">Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 2815 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>2)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Home buyer”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Construction Lien Amendment Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 77 amended the <ital>Construction Lien Act 1983</ital>, to exclude “home buyers” from the statutory definition of “owner”. This permits home buyers to purchase free of subsisting but unregistered liens. Courts have generously enforced this definition (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc." p2="Denamer Homes Inc." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63bda9205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc.">L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Paola's Painting & Decorating Ltd." p2="Villa Nova Construction Inc." post.rptr="227" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63bda9215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paola's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc.">Paola's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc. (1989), 33 C.L.R. 227 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>). On the other hand courts have also strictly observed the statutory threshold of a 30 per cent deposit before the “home buyer” definition applies (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Di Mario" p2="Schuster" post.rptr="140" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63bdd0305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Mario v. Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Florida Drywall Co." p2="Graham" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63bdd0315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Florida Drywall Co. v. Graham">Florida Drywall Co. v. Graham (1986), 20 C.L.R. 235 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The definition of “home buyer” was amended effective October 25, 2010 by S.O. 2010, c. 16 to reflect changes to the Condominium Act, 1998.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>3)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Improvement”, “land”, and “premises”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Attorney General's Committee Report recommended a definition of “improvement” that more clearly stated that the lien created by the Act applies only in the case of the construction and building repair industries. The result was s. 1(1) of the Act. The lien statutes of Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan have similar definitions of “improvement”. Only Saskatchewan and Manitoba include specific provisions for demolition work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">“Improvement” is defined to refer to actual construction work on the premises and if actual construction has not commenced, there must be proof of some enhancement to the value of the land for there to be an “improvement” under the Act (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd." p2="Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd." post.rptr="1325" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I908aa720f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd.">Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 1325, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 184 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). On the other hand, if construction has commenced, an “improvement” will be found even if there is a diminution in the value of the land.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">“Land” is defined to refer to both the land and all buildings affixed to the land, but it excludes the “improvement”. The precursor of this definition, s. 6(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, required that the services and materials giving rise to a lien be provided to “any land, building, structure or works or the appurtenance to any of them”. New Brunswick's definition of “land” includes improvements. Nova Scotia's definition refers to the specific types of land mentioned in the section creating a lien itself. Yukon defines land as including “fixtures within the meaning of the <ital>Personal Property Security Act</ital>.” None of the other common law provinces have a definition for “land”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">“Premises” is the most comprehensive definition, including both “land” and “improvement”. This definition derives from s. 6(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. The most interesting aspect of the definition of “premises” has been its extension not just to the land “occupied” by the improvement, but to land “enjoyed therewith”. To qualify as “land enjoyed therewith”, both proximity of location and a use for a common purpose are required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The definition of “improvement” was amended effective October 25, 2010 by S.O. 2010, c. 16 as a legislative response to the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in <ital>Kennedy Electric Ltd. v. Rumble Automation Inc.</ital> Presumably, under the new definition, the work held not to be lienable in <ital>Kennedy Electric</ital> would be lienable under the new definition.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>4)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Materials” and the supply of materials:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Since 1896, “materials” have been defined to include “every kind of movable property”. Subsection 6(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 further indicated that, to be the subject matter of a lien, “material” had to be “plac[ed] or furnish[ed] … to be used” in an improvement. Courts sought some <ital>nexus</ital> between the materials and the improvement, but often did so in a contradictory manner. The definition of “materials” in the 1983 Act was expanded to make it clear that one could lien for materials that had become, or were intended to become, a part of the improvement, or were used directly in making the improvement (<ital>i.e.</ital>, consumed material), or were used to facilitate directly the making of the improvement (<ital>i.e.</ital>, tools). The definition was expanded to refer to rented equipment without an operator used in the making of the improvement. Appliances and air cooling systems have been found not to be materials according to this definition. A product may also be found to be a “material” if it is used by a subcontractor or contractor to create another product that is supplied to the improvement (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I55a801b0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>). The Acts of Alberta, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories do not define “materials”. Saskatchewan does not include rented equipment or consumed materials in its definition.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The original definitions of “supply” date back to 1923. Section 6 incorporated the 1952 statute, stating that the placing or furnishing of material on the land under construction or on land in the vicinity, designated by the owner or its agent was “good and sufficient delivery” for purposes of the Act. These provisions were carried forward into the 1983 Act and into s. 1(2) of the current statute. Prior to the 1952 amendments, the courts had excluded materials that were not supplied to the property itself even if they were supplied under the direction of the contractor or subcontractor (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1918" p1="Milton Pressed Brick Co." p2="Whalley" post.rptr="369" pre.rptr="42" ref.id="I63be6c705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Milton Pressed Brick Co. v. Whalley">Milton Pressed Brick Co. v. Whalley (1918), 42 O.L.R. 369 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1915" p1="Kalbfleisch" p2="Hurley" post.rptr="268" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63be6c715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kalbfleisch v. Hurley">Kalbfleisch v. Hurley (1915), 34 O.L.R. 268 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). In general, courts no longer require that the supplier have a general knowledge of the improvement being supplied at the time of the sale and delivery. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2010" p1="Sunview Doors Ltd." p2="Academy Doors & Windows Ltd." post.rptr="163" pre.rptr="87" ref.id="I63be93805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sunview Doors Ltd. v. Academy Doors & Windows Ltd.">Sunview Doors Ltd. v. Academy Doors & Windows Ltd. (2010), 87 C.L.R. (3d) 163, 2010 CarswellOnt 1450 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>5)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Owner”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The statute has broadened the definition of “owner” to include individuals other than the registered owner. It was established in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="Ownix Developments Ltd." post.rptr="242" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I63beba905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. Ownix Developments Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. Ownix Developments Ltd. (1984), 8 C.L.R. 242 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, that the statutory “owner” need not be the party contractually liable to pay the general contractor. The definition of “owner” dates from <ital>The Mechanic's Lien Act of 1874</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.), and is comprised of three essential elements: that the owner have an “interest in the premises”; that the owner make a “request” for the work; and that the work be supplied on the credit or behalf of or with the privity or consent of, or for the direct benefit of the owner. Although all three elements are necessary, the third is easily established after the first two have been proven (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1981" p1="Muzzo Brothers Ltd." p2="Cadillac Fairview Corp." post.rptr="529" pre.rptr="1981" ref.id="I55a876e0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Muzzo Brothers Ltd. v. Cadillac Fairview Corp.">Muzzo Brothers Ltd. v. Cadillac Fairview Corp. (1981), 1981 CarswellOnt 529, 34 O.R. (2d) 461 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>). The 1983 Act eliminated the explicit reference to municipal corporations and railway companies and deleted reference to “persons claiming under [the owner] whose rights are acquired after the work in respect of which the lien is claimed is commenced or the materials placed or furnished have been commenced to be placed or furnished”, as being inconsistent with the priority provisions of the statute. In addition, the definition of “owner” was phrased to be comprehensive, not inclusive, as had been the case under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>6)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Interest in the Premises”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">“Interest in the premises” is a separately defined term. This definition was introduced in 1975 along with amendments that made the Crown subject to the Act. The initial definition included the Crown's statutory right of entry on land. The 1983 Act made the definition comprehensive and referred to “an estate or interest of any nature”. This definition has been broadly interpreted to include the interests of mortgagees, mortgagors, vendors, tenants and purchasers. A mere license or right to use the premises or a reversionary interest in respect of a determinable or conditional estate have been held not to constitute an “interest in the premises” (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="52" ref.id="I63bf2fc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>); <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Graham Mining Ltd." p2="Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc." post.rptr="279" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I63bf56d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc.">Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc. (2000), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed in the Court of Appeal at (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 1549, 2002 CarswellOnt 1502 (C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The requirement for a “request” has been a contentious issue. No direct dealing between the lien claimant and the owner is necessary as long as the court can infer from the circumstances that a request has been made for the work to be done. Mere knowledge of or acquiescence in the work being done will usually not be construed as a “request” (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1916" p1="John A. Marshall Brick Co." p2="York Farmers Colonization Co." post.rptr="542" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63bf56d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="John A. Marshall Brick Co. v. York Farmers Colonization Co.">John A. Marshall Brick Co. v. York Farmers Colonization Co. (1916), 35 O.L.R. 542 (Ont. C.A.); affirmed (1917), 54 S.C.R. 569 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Andre Knight Ltd." p2="Presement" post.rptr="289" pre.rptr="[1967] 2" ref.id="I63bf7de05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andre Knight Ltd. v. Presement">Andre Knight Ltd. v. Presement, [1967] 2 O.R. 289 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Di Mario" p2="Schuster" post.rptr="140" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63bf7de15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Mario v. Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). The older cases had required some degree of direct dealing (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1917" p1="John A. Marshall Brick Co." p2="York Farmers Colonization Co." post.rptr="569" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I63bfa4f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="John A. Marshall Brick Co. v. York Farmers Colonization Co.">John A. Marshall Brick Co. v. York Farmers Colonization Co. (1917), 54 S.C.R. 569 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>7)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Supply of services”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Under s. 6(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 lien rights were extended to “any work upon or in respect of” a construction project. Subsection 1(2) of that statute made it clear that “the doing of work” included the performance of services. The 1983 Act adopted s. 6(1) of the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> of “any work done or service performed upon or in respect of an improvement”. Much of the case law that predates the 1983 Act may still apply. The definition in the 1983 Act expressly included the services of rented equipment with an operator and, where construction had not commenced, the making of a design, plan, drawing or specification that added value to the land.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Saskatchewan's definition of the “services” most closely parallels that of Ontario but does not refer to the work of architects and engineers. British Columbia defines “services” to include services of an architect or engineer before or after commencement of construction and the services of rented equipment with an operator. Manitoba's definition expressly includes contract administration, contract inspection or supervision and architectural and engineering work, but specifically excludes the services of an architect or engineer who does not work for the contractor or subcontractor. Most of the other common law provinces have not included a definition of “supply of services” or “services” in their statutes. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island do refer to “work”, which is defined as “the doing of work and the performance of services upon or in respect of an improvement”. Not all services extended to an owner, contractor or subcontractor give rise to a lien. Courts have held that there must be some <ital>nexus</ital> between the service and the construction project. Supervision has been a source of controversy in many cases. It has been held that off site construction management services do not give rise to a lien (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I2d0b6750f65111ee9732e3e835885970" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tamma Construction Co." p2="Brault" post.rptr="953" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I908d6640f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault">Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 953, 25 O.R. (3d) 472, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 124 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). On the other hand, the services of estimating and site supervision have been found to be lienable (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Edward Stephens Associates Ltd." p2="G.L. Trenching Ltd." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63bfcc025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edward Stephens Associates Ltd. v. G.L. Trenching Ltd.">Edward Stephens Associates Ltd. v. G.L. Trenching Ltd. (1989), 40 C.L.R. 161, 73 O.R. (2d) 112 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Another historical area of controversy had been the work of architects and engineers. Cases decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> made it clear that the preparation of drawings, plans and specifications was work that would give rise to a lien only if the construction actually commenced and the architect or engineer was retained to superintend or direct the construction (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1919" p1="Read" p2="Whitney" post.rptr="377" pre.rptr="45" ref.id="I63bff3105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Read v. Whitney">Read v. Whitney (1919), 45 O.L.R. 377 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). Where the planned project was abandoned, the situation was not as clear. The 1983 Act added the provisions concerning the supply of a design, plans, drawings or specifications if they enhanced the value of the owner's interest in the land. What is meant by “enhancing the value” in this context is not entirely clear. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1975" p1="Armbro Materials & Construction Ltd." p2="230056 Investments Ltd." post.rptr="226" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I63bff3115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Armbro Materials & Construction Ltd. v. 230056 Investments Ltd.">Armbro Materials & Construction Ltd. v. 230056 Investments Ltd. (1975), 9 O.R. (2d) 226 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite> the court held that, even though no construction had commenced, the engineer's plans could be sold with the land and therefore added value to the land. Note: The <ital>Government Process Simplification Act (Ministry of the Attorney General), 1997</ital>, S.O. 1997, c. 23, s. 4, repealed s. 3(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, extending lien rights to architects, holders of certificates of practice and their employees with respect to rights arising after November 28, 1997.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>8)</bold></designator><name date.updated="0"><bold>“Written notice of a lien”:</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This definition was introduced with the 1983 Act, although the concept was a hold-over from the <ital>Mechanic's Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. Where a payer has received “written notice of a lien”, it is obligated under s. 24(2) of the Act to hold back funds, in addition to the basic holdback, sufficient to satisfy the lien. “Written notice of lien” has been interpreted to mean the actual physical delivery of a written notice. The definition includes a “claim for lien” and any written notice that identifies the payer and the premises and gives a statement of the outstanding account, but does not include the mere registration of a claim for lien (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Hal Mann Tiles Inc." p2="Palmer" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63c01a205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer">Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer (1995), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 61 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (1995), 24 O.R. (3d) 93 <point>at 96</point> (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>; and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="28" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I63c041305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at [1996] O.J. No. 270, 1996 CarswellOnt 297 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). The definition is not exhaustive. Courts have required that the notice have four elements: an indication of the supply of services or materials to the contractor and the premises; a statement that there is an account owed to the subcontractor by the contractor; a statement that the subcontractor is claiming a lien and will preserve it unless payment is made; and a statement as to the amount that the lien will claim (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I908eece0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd." p2="Shell Canada Products Ltd." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63c068415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd.">Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). The written notice must include some statement that a lien is claimed as opposed to a simple demand in debt (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anglin & Co." p2="Simmons" post.rptr="136" pre.rptr="[1933]" ref.id="I63c068425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anglin & Co. v. Simmons">Anglin & Co. v. Simmons, [1933] O.W.N. 136, [1933] 2 D.L.R. 794 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1923" p1="Sanderson Pearcy & Co." p2="Foster" post.rptr="519" pre.rptr="53" ref.id="I63c08f505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sanderson Pearcy & Co. v. Foster">Sanderson Pearcy & Co. v. Foster (1923), 53 O.L.R. 519 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General Principles Relating to the Act</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pryers Construction Ltd." p2="MVMB Holdings Inc." post.rptr="7605" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63c0b6605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pryers Construction Ltd. v. MVMB Holdings Inc.">Pryers Construction Ltd. v. MVMB Holdings Inc., 2018 ONSC 7605, 2018 CarswellOnt 21480, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 201 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed on other grounds 2019 ONSC 6135, 2019 CarswellOnt 17424, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 226 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, which was in force at the time the improvements were made by the plaintiff and the contract was entered into with the defendant, was the governing legislation for the parties. The new <ital>Construction Act</ital> came into effect as of July 1st, 2018, but the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> prevailed where the contract for improvement was entered into prior to July 1, 2018. There is nothing expressly stated in the new legislation that it was to be retroactive. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Section 87.3 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> explicitly provides that the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> continue to apply if: the contract for the subject improvement was entered into prior to July 1, 2018; a procurement process for the improvement was commenced before July 1, 2018 by the owner of the premises; or in the case of a premises that is subject to a leasehold interest that was first entered into before July 1, 2018, a contract for the improvement was entered into or a procurement process for the improvement was commenced on or after July 1, 2018 and before the day subsection 19 (1) of Schedule 8 to the <ital>Restoring Trust, Transparency and Accountability Act, 2018</ital> came into force. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 8, s. 19 (1).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63c0b6615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Divisional Court opined that the <ital>Report of the Attorney General's Advisory Committee on the Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> has little, if any, probative value in interpreting the Act. Rather, it is the words of the statute that govern its interpretation. When the Act is read as a whole, it is clear that the Report enshrines no underlying policy proposition directed solely to protecting lien claimants. Like most remedial legislation, the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> balances a series of competing values, and there is nothing in the Act that suggests any overarching intention to favour lien claimants above the interests of mortgagees beyond the value of the holdbacks the legislation requires.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90909a90f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The broad purpose of the legislation is to provide an efficient means of dealing with trade claimants that would otherwise be left behind without security if unpaid on a building project where payments typically flow from above and follow performance. On a failing or failed project, there may be many such claimants. In setting down the rules, the Act does not go so far as to restrict claims thereunder to lien claims. Contract claims by the plaintiff and counterclaims of any kind are permitted, presumably to avoid duplication of proceedings. Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings is the element of the Act that provides the direction for the interpretation of s. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d). Howland J.A., in <ital>A.J. (Archie) Goodale Ltd.</ital> set the tone for interpretation by observing that the Act should not be available as a subterfuge for pursuing an ordinary action by summary procedure; but where all the steps have been taken and a conclusion reached at a hearing, the court should not dismiss the action for lack of a lien claim and thus compel a further proceeding concerning the same issue. The same reasoning suggests that the court has available the discretion to dismiss or to permit the action to proceed without the claim, as the circumstances dictate.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63c104805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1, 1998 CarswellOnt 3970 (Ont. C.A.); affirming (1996), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 71 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Ontario Court of Appeal applied <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarkson Co." p2="Ace Lumber Ltd." post.rptr="110" pre.rptr="[1963]" ref.id="I63c104815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkson Co. v. Ace Lumber Ltd.">Clarkson Co. v. Ace Lumber Ltd., [1963] S.C.R. 110, 36 D.L.R. (2d) 554 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Oliver" p2="Muer Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63c12b905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd.">Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd. (1985), 12 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="George Wimpey Canada Ltd." p2="Peelton Hills Ltd." post.rptr="787" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I55ad7ff0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="George Wimpey Canada Ltd. v. Peelton Hills Ltd.">George Wimpey Canada Ltd. v. Peelton Hills Ltd. (1982), 35 O.R. (2d) 787 (C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I909184f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> to the strict interpretation of the trust sections of the lien Act, Part II, affirming in doing so a line of cases prohibiting the deduction of overhead expenses from trust monies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarkson Co." p2="Ace Lumber Ltd." post.rptr="110" pre.rptr="[1963]" ref.id="I63c152a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkson Co. v. Ace Lumber Ltd.">Clarkson Co. v. Ace Lumber Ltd., [1963] S.C.R. 110, 36 D.L.R. (2d) 554 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> [R.S.O. 1960, c. 233] must be given a strict interpretation in determining whether any lien claimant is entitled to a lien but, if a person passes that threshold and is found to be entitled to claim a lien, then the statute should be liberally interpreted with respect to the right it confers upon the lien claimant. This principle has been consistently and repeatedly affirmed at all levels (see, for example, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Gillies Lumber Inc." p2="Kubassek Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="334" pre.rptr="176" ref.id="I63c152a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd.">Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd. (1999), 176 D.L.R. (4th) 334, 47 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.A.) <point>at 339</point> [D.L.R.]</ref></cite> (Laskin J.A. in dissent, but not on this point), and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re" post.rptr="262" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I63c179b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re">A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 262, 2002 CarswellOnt 210, 21 C.L.R. (3d) 50 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc." p2="Lombardo" post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63c179b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo">Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo (1991), 49 C.L.R. 141 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The purposes of the Act are twofold. It provides security for work done and materials supplied. It allows workers and suppliers to proceed to trial in an expeditious and cheap manner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Carpet-Trend (Eastern) Inc." p2="519583 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="307" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63c1a0c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carpet-Trend (Eastern) Inc. v. 519583 Ontario Inc.">Carpet-Trend (Eastern) Inc. v. 519583 Ontario Inc. (1986), 43 C.L.R. 307 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is designed to assist contractors, workmen, suppliers, <ital>etc.</ital>, not grantees. It has provided a procedure by which grantees are placed on alert as to the possibility of there being unpaid contractors, workmen, and suppliers, other than those who have registered liens. The registration of a single lien opens the door to an enquiry as to the existence of other unpaid and registered lien claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Oliver" p2="Muer Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63c1a0c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd.">Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd. (1985), 12 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The lien law is strictly statute law unknown both at common law and in equity. Courts have taken a strict approach in interpretation in determining whether a party has a right to enforce its rights under the statute. The onus is upon the claimant to show that he is a person entitled to the protection of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63c1c7d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In a construction lien matter, the subtrades know they have extraordinary rights given to them by statute against the owner. There is consequently a heavy evidentiary burden on a lien claimant to show that the owner's degree of control should deprive the owner of a statutory holdback defence, where, on a balance of probabilities, it has been established that the owner set up and managed its own general contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Hussey Seating Co. (Canada) Ltd." p2="City of Ottawa" post.rptr="262" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63c1c7d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hussey Seating Co. (Canada) Ltd. v. City of Ottawa">Hussey Seating Co. (Canada) Ltd. v. City of Ottawa (1997), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 262, 32 O.R. (3d) 633 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1997), 145 D.L.R. (4th) 493 <point>at 499</point>, 33 C.L.R. (2d) 262 (note) (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 41 O.R. (3d) 254 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was enacted in order to provide an orderly system whereby contractors and subcontractors, workmen and others, would be reimbursed for goods and services provided for the benefit of an owner. Where the plaintiff had not filed a claim for lien within the time frame as set out in the Act, any claim under that Act is unenforceable. To allow a claim in restitution would be to circumvent the provisions of the Act and would result in the indirect enforcement of a transaction contemplated by the Act even though that transaction was invalid because of the plaintiff's failure to adhere to the provisions of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Action</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="1067833 Ontario Ltd." p2="1274123 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="325" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63c215f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1067833 Ontario Ltd. v. 1274123 Ontario Ltd.">1067833 Ontario Ltd. v. 1274123 Ontario Ltd. (2001), 31 C.L.R. (3d) 325, 2001 CarswellOnt 5901 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The word “action” is defined to mean an action under Part VIII, which restricts its meaning to lien claims. Rule 76.01(1) is intended to prevent claims, which are enforceable under Part VIII from being brought under the simplified procedure. Here, the defendant was permitted to amend the defence and file a counterclaim, which could be brought under the simplified procedures, because the counterclaim was not an action within the meaning of R. 76.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Eurocor Ltd." p2="Vernich" post.rptr="631" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I63c215f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich">Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich (1992), 9 O.R. (3d) 631, 2 C.L.R. (2d) 208 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Neither s. 1(1) nor s. 50 of the Act confines an action commenced under the Act to lien claims.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Construction trade newspaper</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Kappeler Masonry Corp." p2="Winston Hall Nursing Homes Ltd." post.rptr="65" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63c23d005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kappeler Masonry Corp. v. Winston Hall Nursing Homes Ltd.">Kappeler Masonry Corp. v. Winston Hall Nursing Homes Ltd. (2001), 12 C.L.R. (3d) 65 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—When working on a project that has a payment certifier in place, contractors and subcontractors know, or ought to know, that they should be reading the Daily Commercial News regularly to determine whether a certificate of substantial performance has been issued with respect to the project on which they are owed money.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Contract</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DNR Restoration Inc." p2="Trac Developments Inc." post.rptr="3680" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8d692470ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc.">DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 3680, 2023 ONSC 1849 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—“Contract” is defined in CA section 1 to be the contract between an owner and a “contractor.” The <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not confine the concept of “contract” to the provision of “services and materials.” The court rejected the argument that the contract between the owner and the “pure” construction manager was not “a contract for the improvement” under section 87.3(1)(a) as it concerned the provision of services only. If construction managers with contracts with the owner, such as here, have lien rights, they surely are “contractors” with “contracts” for the purpose of section 87.3(1)(a). A “contract” can encompass the entire improvement or, such as in this case, a part of it. Where a contract is narrower than the scope of the improvement, and there are other contracts for the improvement, the only logical interpretation to be given to section 87.3(1)(a) is that the first contract will determine which version of the Act will apply to all contracts for the improvement, subject to any evidence of procurement if all the contracts are dated after July 1, 2018.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="The Fifth Wall Corp." p2="Tonelli" post.rptr="6590" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63c264105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="The Fifth Wall Corp. v. Tonelli">The Fifth Wall Corp. v. Tonelli, 2022 ONSC 6590, 2022 CarswellOnt 16879 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants moved for partial summary judgment seeking a determination on whether the (ON) <ital>Consumer Protection Act, 2002</ital> applied to their residential construction contract, and if so, an order requiring the plaintiff to pay damages under that Act equal to the amounts paid in excess of the listed amounts for various items in Schedule B to the construction contract. Nothing in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> expressly excludes the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital> from applying to the supply of services and materials that give rise to lien and other rights under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There was also no proper basis to hold, as a general proposition, that the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital> cannot and does not apply to costs-plus contracts concerning residential construction and renovation of premises. In this case, the plaintiff was constructing a custom residential house for use by the defendants' family, and not for any commercial or industrial purpose. The plaintiff's operations and supply of services fit within the definition of “supplier” in the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital>. The construction contract was an agreement between the parties in which the plaintiff agreed to supply services and materials for the construction work at the premises for payment. The parties' contract was accordingly a “consumer agreement” within the meaning of the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital>. There were, however, triable issues on whether the Schedule B items were “estimates” within the meaning of the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital> and, if so, whether changes to the scope of work were agreed, expressly or impliedly.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="13245" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6703a2703b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The trial judge found that there were two separate contracts, one for structural steel and one for miscellaneous metals, and hence, each contract had to be liened separately. The work was separately tendered, separately quoted on by the plaintiff, and the contracts were awarded separately and reflected in two separate written agreements executed on different dates. On appeal, the trial judge was held to have erred in law in finding that separate claims for lien must be registered in respect to separate subcontracts between the same parties for the same improvement. Absent certification of substantial performance or completion, it did not matter whether a subcontractor provided its services or materials under one subcontract or multiple subcontracts. [<ital>Authors' Note:</ital> This decision was decided under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Khalimov" p2="Hogarth" post.rptr="6244" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63c28b205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khalimov v. Hogarth">Khalimov v. Hogarth, 2015 ONSC 6244, 2015 CarswellOnt 15551, 56 C.L.R. (4th) 167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After a dispute over payments and scope of work, work on the project stopped for several months, after the contractor and plaintiff subcontractor left the site. The contractor advised the owners by email that the contract had been terminated “some time ago” and informed them that they could pay out the holdback after 45 days. Subsequently, there was a brief attendance by the subcontractor to retrieve tools and equipment. The subcontractor's first lien was registered and then subsequently discharged following execution of a document titled “Amendment to Contract”, which provided a scope of work, a method of verifying that the work was performed, and a contract price. Work under the amending document began and then subsequently stopped, and the owners terminated the contract. The master held that, on the evidence, the contractor abandoned the contract prior to its email, and the retrieval of tools by the subcontractor was an act that was consistent with the original contract having been terminated or abandoned. The document that the parties titled “Amendment to Contract” was in reality a new contract that did not form part of the original agreement. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dieleman Planer Co." p2="Elizabeth Townhouses Ltd." post.rptr="8" pre.rptr="1974" ref.id="I63c2b2305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dieleman Planer Co. v. Elizabeth Townhouses Ltd.">Dieleman Planer Co. v. Elizabeth Townhouses Ltd., 1974 CarswellBC 8, 1974 CarswellBC 352, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 449, 20 C.B.R. (N.S.) 81 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, differentiated here, where the Court indicated that cessation of work is abandonment only if it is permanent, with no intention to return and complete the project.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works" p2="Di Iorio" post.rptr="295" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63c2b2315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio">Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 295 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Master was not in error in concluding that a new contract was created between the owners and the subcontractor which embraced the obligation of the owner to pay past debts of the general contractors to the subcontractor, as an incentive for the subcontractor to complete the project. This incentive constituted valid consideration to include these additional amounts.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I55b1c5b0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Act takes great pains to differentiate between a “contract” and “sub-contract”. In fact, they are mutually exclusive terms.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:6: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Contractor</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DNR Restoration Inc." p2="Trac Developments Inc." post.rptr="3680" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8d6ad220ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc.">DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 3680, 2023 ONSC 1849 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—“Contractor” is defined in section 1 of the CA to be the one who contracts with the owner for the supply of “services or materials”. The <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not confine the concept of “contract” to the provision of “services and materials.” The court rejected the argument that the contract between the owner and the “pure” construction manager was not “a contract for the improvement” under section 87.3(1)(a) as it concerned the provision of services only. If construction managers with contracts with the owner, such as here, have lien rights, they surely are “contractors” with “contracts” for the purpose of section 87.3(1)(a). A “contract” can encompass the entire improvement or, such as in this case, a part of it. Where a contract is narrower than the scope of the improvement, and there are other contracts for the improvement, the only logical interpretation to be given to section 87.3(1)(a) is that the first contract will determine which version of the Act will apply to all contracts for the improvement, subject to any evidence of procurement if all the contracts are dated after July 1, 2018.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Mahendran" p2="9660143 Canada Inc. et al" post.rptr="6678" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63c300505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mahendran v. 9660143 Canada Inc. et al">Mahendran v. 9660143 Canada Inc. et al, 2021 ONSC 6678, 2021 CarswellOnt 13812 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Mahendran v. Singh et al.</ital>, 2022 CarswellOnt 9268 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was never a contractor within the definition of the Act and was in fact an owner of the property and therefore not entitled to a lien. The plaintiff's cross-examination demonstrated that the parties agreed to keep title in the defendant's name and share the profits when the property was sold. The plaintiff was a partner in the construction of the residence and not exclusively a contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cohen" p2="Brin" post.rptr="1302" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63c300515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cohen v. Brin">Cohen v. Brin, 2013 ONSC 1302, 2013 CarswellOnt 2307 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff architect, defendant and third party decided to acquire, renovate and sell older residential properties. The plaintiff contended that he was hired as a contractor for a fixed monthly fee plus a share in the profits upon sale of the property. On the totality of the evidence, the court held that the relationship at its inception was that of three equal partners, each of whom was to contribute a skill, talent or financing in exchange for an equal share of the profits. The plaintiff architect's contribution of design and project management services did not transform him from a partner into a contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pegah Construction Ltd." p2="Panterra Mansions Joint Venture Corp." post.rptr="3226" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63c300525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pegah Construction Ltd. v. Panterra Mansions Joint Venture Corp.">Pegah Construction Ltd. v. Panterra Mansions Joint Venture Corp., 2013 ONSC 3226, 2013 CarswellOnt 7268, 21 C.L.R. (4th) 175 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 ONSC 6719, 2013 CarswellOnt 14956, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 227 (Ont. S.C.J.); motion to oppose conformation dismissed 2014 ONSC 3966, 2014 CarswellOnt 8889, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 58 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The use of the label “construction manager” in a written contract is not determinative of the structure of the relationship of the parties. Rather, the court must interpret the written contract by considering the contract in its entirety and objective evidence of intention. Here, the plaintiff was found to be the owner's general contractor. No cases were provided where a construction manager who took on the risk of cost overruns and payment to trades was not treated as a general contractor for purposes of holdback, priority, obligation to pay trades and liability to an owner for cost overruns. The liability for payment to the trades was sufficient to determine the structure of the relationship.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Centrum Renovations & Repair Inc." p2="Ditta" post.rptr="7390" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63c327605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Centrum Renovations & Repair Inc. v. Ditta">Centrum Renovations & Repair Inc. v. Ditta (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 7390, 65 C.L.R. (3d) 270 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 2992, 67 C.L.R. (3d) 137 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 8700 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 6650 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The court was satisfied that the plaintiff was a “contractor” rather than a construction manager because the plaintiff:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(i)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">had always acted as a general contractor in the past and had never undertaken any project as a “construction manager”;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(ii)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">negotiated with virtually all of the subtrades in the manner of a general contractor;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(iii)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">in the vast majority of cases had received the quotes of the subcontractors;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(iv)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">was asked by a subcontractor to pay its account because the defendant's financial arrangements for the project had not been completed; and</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(v)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">directly paid a subcontractor on account of its work on excavation and fill.</para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd." p2="One Shaftesbury Community Assn." post.rptr="5995" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63c375805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn.">Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5995, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 184 (Ont. Master); additional reasons as to costs at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 3684, 72 C.L.R. (3d) 71 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A project for a residential retirement community utilized a right-to-occupy or life-lease legal structure. The property in question was purchased and the title was transferred to a non-profit community association, which entered into a construction and development agreement with a for-profit numbered company that was to assume the role of construction manager, and to negotiate, execute and monitor all contracts necessary to market, plan, construct and administer the project until the building was completed and delivered to the Association. When construction costs escalated, and some units did not sell or could not be sold because of title problems, there was shortfall in the mortgage money required to pay the general contractor and five trades. The Master found that the numbered company was not a “contractor” within the definition of that term in s. 1(1) of the Act. It did not contract with the owner to supply services or materials to the improvement. Rather, it was an “owner” or, at worst, the agent of the owner. Its responsibilities vis-à-vis its joint venturer or principal, the Association, were defined by agreement between the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Coldstream Concrete Ltd." p2="Dacosta Realty Inc." post.rptr="2585" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63c39c905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Coldstream Concrete Ltd. v. Dacosta Realty Inc.">Coldstream Concrete Ltd. v. Dacosta Realty Inc. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2585, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 150 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied concrete and engaged a subcontractor to do work in connection with the construction of foundations on lands owned by the defendant H Inc., although the quotation was requested and approved by, and the invoice for the work was sent to, the president of the defendant D Inc. The plaintiff filed a construction lien against the property and successfully brought an action for judgment for concrete supplied and work done. However, neither H Inc. nor its president knew that an agreement had been entered into with the plaintiff, and although offers had been exchanged and the sale of property by H Inc. to D Inc. had been discussed, there was never a meeting of the minds and no binding and enforceable agreement of purchase and sale. There was no privity of contract between the plaintiff and H Inc. or its president. On the balance of probabilities, H Inc. did not give D Inc. permission either expressly, indirectly or by implication to enter onto the property to do work in the absence of a binding and unconditional agreement of sale. The plaintiff was therefore not a “contractor” within definition in s. 1 of the Act because it was never employed by and never contracted with the owner or its agent to supply materials or services to the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Van Ryssen" p2="Lagare" post.rptr="858" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I55b40fa0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Van Ryssen v. Lagare">Van Ryssen v. Lagare (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 858 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Although a worker's activities reflected a level of responsible involvement greater than some—if not all—of the other workers on the crew, he was found not to be a partner of the contractor. He did not participate in the negotiations with respect to the contract, he was not a signatory to the contract and his name did not appear endorsed on any of the cheques made payable to the contractor. As a worker, he was entitled to put forward a lien claim. This was so even though he was paid more than the other workers, his duties included ensuring the employees got to the site on time, he went to the bank with the contractor's principal, he would be present when the hours of work and pay were settled with the crew, and his handwritten notes included a reference to a problem with an NSF cheque written to the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="182" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63c3c3a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1994), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 182, 1994 CarswellOnt 1108 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The court rejected the argument that if the general contractor was found to be an undisclosed agent of the owners of the land, the subcontractor would become in effect the general contractor and different lien rights and obligations would apply. A subcontractor cannot have its lien rights prejudiced by a relationship that it knew nothing about, with which it was not in agreement, and without having been given the opportunity at the time to determine the correct procedure for establishing its lien rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63c3c3a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In a construction lien matter, the subtrades know they have extraordinary rights given to them by statute against the owner, whoever that may be, rights which are independent of any consideration of agency. The subtrades must know that the owner is, in varying degrees, involved in his own project. There is consequently a heavy evidentiary burden on a lien claimant to show that the owner's relationship and degree of control with respect to the lien claimants themselves is such that it surpasses all acceptable and reasonable involvement by an owner and slips into what, on the balance of probabilities, can only be described as an owner contracting for himself through the guise of an alter ego, someone presented to the claimants as a general contractor. In the present case, although the contractor was authorized to act as agent for the owner and there was some overlap between the owner and the contractor, the burden was not met by the lien claimants and the owner was not liable on the contract as an undisclosed principal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Main Line Construction Ltd." p2="Nicolini" post.rptr="2815" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I63c3eab05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini">Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 2815 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A contractor, N, was found to be the general contractor of a project based on the following facts: the owner always dealt with him when decisions regarding the job were to be made; N was at the job site about half the time; most of the subtrades were of the view that he was the general contractor; N received the down payment for the job and in the end, sent out an invoice on his own letterhead which showed the monies as having been received; N asked another contractor to do the estimate for the job, worked with him to revise the original estimate and finally reached an agreement with the owner on what the base price would be.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:7: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Court</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Savoia" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63c411c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia">Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia (2006), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 235, 207 O.A.C. 1, 2006 CarswellOnt 340 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—“Court” in s. 50(2) of the Act means the Superior Court of Justice, and the Small Claims Court is a branch of the Superior Court of Justice. Therefore, as the Small Claims Court is a “court of competent jurisdiction”, the only limiting factor in a trust claim is the amount involved. Where a trust claim is heard in Small Claims Court, the court is constrained by its monetary jurisdiction.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:8: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:8</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Holdback</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63c438d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The definition of “holdback” in s. 1(1) does not refer to 10 per cent of the “improvement” or to 10 per cent of the “project.” It refers specifically to 10 per cent of the “value of services or materials under a contract” and not “contracts.”</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:9: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:9</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Home</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Kostolnik" p2="Vanbots Construction Corp." post.rptr="151" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I63c45fe05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kostolnik v. Vanbots Construction Corp.">Kostolnik v. Vanbots Construction Corp. (2000), 6 C.L.R. (3d) 151 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—There is nothing in the statutory definition of “home” that requires the purchaser of a “home” under the Act to actually live in the property.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:10: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:10</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Home buyer</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Kostolnik" p2="Vanbots Construction Corp." post.rptr="151" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I63c45fe15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kostolnik v. Vanbots Construction Corp.">Kostolnik v. Vanbots Construction Corp. (2000), 6 C.L.R. (3d) 151 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Although the onus was on the applicants to prove that the premises were “ready for occupancy” (see subs. (2)), the production of the municipal permit authorizing occupancy issued by the municipality, and the issuance of a certificate of completion and possession under the Ontario <ital>New Home Warranties Plan Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.31, was sufficient to shift the onus to the lien claimants to prove that the homes were not ready for occupancy. In this case, the lien holders were unable to discharge that onus. The Master found that the units were ready for occupancy and that the applicants were “home buyers” under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and were entitled to an order discharging the relevant lien claims and certificates of action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="595997 Ontario Inc." p2="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I63c486f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="595997 Ontario Inc. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)">595997 Ontario Inc. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 61 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A landscape contractor registered a general lien for the full amount of its claim on each of several lots in a townhouse development, even though the contract provided that liens would arise and expire on a lot-by-lot basis and would be apportioned to reflect the actual services and materials provided to each lot. The landscape contractor brought an action against the developer and the purchasers of one of the townhouses. The purchasers of the townhouse paid the full amount of the general lien into trust and successfully moved to dismiss the lien action against them, by obtaining a declaration that they were “home buyers” under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The trust funds were paid out to them. The orders were upheld on appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Ottawa Air Design Ltd." p2="Zietak" post.rptr="106" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63c4ae005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ottawa Air Design Ltd. v. Zietak">Ottawa Air Design Ltd. v. Zietak (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 106 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Purchasers were found to be home buyers even though they did not sign the certificate of completion and possession until long after the deed was registered. The new home in question was ready for occupancy when conveyed and the date of the issuance of the Ontario <ital>New Home Warranties Plan Act</ital> certificate was held to be the date when it was signed by the vendor, particularly where the purchaser closed the transaction on that date. That being the case, there was no obligation on the purchasers to retain any holdback for liens that they were not aware of when the transaction closed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc." p2="Denamer Homes Inc." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63c4ae015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc.">L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A “home buyer” is not a person whose interests can be the subject of a lien. The answer to the question of whether or not a “home buyer” has an interest in which a lien can be created cannot be different when the “home buyer” acquires title after a lien is registered. As well, a Certificate of Completion and Possession that did not have inserted therein the date of possession is nevertheless valid for the purposes of s. 1(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Di Mario" p2="Schuster" post.rptr="140" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63c4d5105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Mario v.
