Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The purchasers entered into an agreement for the purchase of a new home to be constructed by L Inc. The agreement provided for the purchasers to pay a sum of $25,000 upon acceptance of the offer, a further $25,000 at the rough framing stage and a further $25,000 at the drywall boarding stage. Although the agreement between the purchasers and L. Inc. indicated that the sum of $75,000 was a deposit, both of the parties anticipated that the monies would be used to fund the purchase of the lot and construction of the house. Accordingly, the purchasers were not home buyers within the meaning of the Act because they “paid” more than 30 per cent of the purchase price prior to the conveyance.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="898446 Ontario Inc." p2="Greyrock Building Corp." post.rptr="222" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63c4d5115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="898446 Ontario Inc. v. Greyrock Building Corp.">898446 Ontario Inc. v. Greyrock Building Corp. (1991), 49 C.L.R. 222 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor entered into an agreement with the builder to do work on homes now owned by the three personal defendants (the “movers”). The movers had entered into agreements of purchase and sale with the builder for their respective premises. None paid more than 30 per cent of the purchase price prior to closing and, in two of the three cases, the purchases were financed, in part, by second mortgages to J. Ltd. After non-payment, the plaintiff filed liens against the properties and commenced construction lien actions. The movers applied for summary judgment dimissing the actions against them and discharging the liens on the grounds that they were “home buyers” as defined in the Act. The material filed by the movers was inaccurate and misleading, and the movers' counsel required an opportunity to file further material to establish that his clients came within the definition of “home buyer.” Therefore, since the movers had not made out a case in which there was no doubt as to the result, their application for summary judgment was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd." p2="Villa Nova Construction Inc." post.rptr="690" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I55b7e030fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc.">Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 690, 33 C.L.R. 227 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The priorities addressed in s. 80 do not apply in the case of a purchaser who is a “home buyer” and who is thereby not an “owner” under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Florida Drywall Co." p2="Graham" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63c4fc215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Florida Drywall Co. v. Graham">Florida Drywall Co. v. Graham (1986), 20 C.L.R. 235 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendants G entered into a purchase and sale agreement with the defendant T Ltd., pursuant to which T Ltd. was to construct a house for G. The purchase price of the land and completed house was $245,000, and G paid $5,000 to T Ltd. upon execution of the agreement and an additional $80,000 one month later; $60,000 of the latter amount was a loan to the defendants L and T Ltd. secured by a promissory note. The transaction closed June 12, 1984 when G paid the balance of $265,000, being the original purchase price plus $20,000 for extras. G took possession without a municipal occupancy permit or certificate of completion under the Ontario <ital>New Home Warranties Plan Act</ital>. The plaintiffs registered claims for lien brought actions against G in support of their respective lien claims. The issue turned on whether the defendants G were “owners” within the meaning of the Act, and the court found that they were. The payment of $80,000 by G to T Ltd. was considered and calculated as a payment on account of the purchase price. The total sum paid prior to conveyance was $85,000, which constituted 32 per cent of the total purchase price of $265,000. It therefore followed that the defendants G could not meet either of the provisos essential to the application of s. 1(1), and that at all material times they were “owners”, and not “home buyers”, and were not exempt from lien claims under the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

AND OTHERS">IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS, 2024 CarswellOnt 12454, 2024 ONSC 4625 (Ont. S.C.J. [Comm. List])</ref></cite>—The definition of “improvement” in the Act does not include language showing that services or materials supplied under separate contracts in relation to the same project must be treated as having been supplied in respect of separate improvements.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Atlas Dewatering Corporation" p2="Harvie Construction Inc." post.rptr="4294" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I670bdfd03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Atlas Dewatering Corporation v. Harvie Construction Inc.">Atlas Dewatering Corporation v. Harvie Construction Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 4294, 2024 ONSC 1775, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1427 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 6605 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 7440 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor lien claimant provided “de-watering” services to a project involving the reconstruction and realignment of a municipal roadway. The work consisted of the installation of a system of well points, pumps and pipes to assist in lowering the groundwater table on the construction site, and subsequent removal of that equipment. The definitions of “improvement”, “premises” and “supply of services” in the Act were broad enough to capture this work. The dewatering services were by design done on or in respect of the same premises which were the subject of the project. The work done by the claimant was integral to its alteration and restoration.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="On Point Ltd." p2="Conseil des Écoles Catholiques du Centre Est et al." post.rptr="7206" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8d6fdb30ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="On Point Ltd. v. Conseil des Écoles Catholiques du Centre Est et al.">On Point Ltd. v. Conseil des Écoles Catholiques du Centre Est et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 7206, 2023 ONSC 2812 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The portable school classrooms built by the plaintiff were “improvements” within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, and therefore engaged the lien provisions of the Act. The concept of the lien was rooted in adding value or utility to the land, and there was a direct connection/attachment between the work performed to construct and erect/install the portables and enhancing the utility of the school.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1140676 Ontario Inc." p2="2650997 Ontario Inc. et al" post.rptr="8176" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I63c523305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al">1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al, 2020 ONSC 8176, 2020 CarswellOnt 19368, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 352 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 143, 2021 CarswellOnt 89, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 359 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An agreement allowing the plaintiff to extract aggregate and wood from the defendant's land was not an agreement to improve the defendant's lands, and therefore not lienable. Any improvements to the defendant's lands were entirely incidental to the agreement, and while the defendant may have benefitted by the construction of a road on to the lands and the stripping back of topsoil to access aggregate, whatever construction was done was wholly for the benefit of the plaintiff's extraction operation. There was no payment made to the plaintiff, and the only consideration flowing from the agreement was payment to the defendant of a percentage of the sale proceeds of the material that was extracted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Keen Landscaping Inc." p2="Stewart" post.rptr="2001" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63c54a405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Keen Landscaping Inc. v. Stewart">Keen Landscaping Inc. v. Stewart, 2017 ONSC 2001, 2017 CarswellOnt 5110, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 140 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It is unreasonable to interpret an “improvement” under the <ital>Act</ital> to include construction on the property that brings a property into noncompliance with the drainage and grading by-laws. In these circumstances, where conformance with the by-law after the project is unknown, a determination of whether the rectification efforts have affected the grade of the property is a relevant consideration.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="U.S. Steel Canada Inc., Re" post.rptr="12275" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63c54a415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="U.S. Steel Canada Inc., Re">U.S. Steel Canada Inc., Re, 2016 CarswellOnt 12275 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the materials and services provided were provided to an “improvement” within the definition of the Act, and whether they could therefore be the subject of a lien. The court found the following to be lienable supply of goods or services to an improvement: (i) supply and installation of garden soil and 15 flower plants (if intended to alter and/or add to the land by planting flowers the nursery's supply of flowers would amount to a supply of materials for the improvement and give rise to a lien in no different manner than the supply of lumber for the construction of a building on the land); (ii) labour and material to spray for vegetation control; (iii) labour and material to remove vegetation inside compounds, remove and clean dirt and debris and install landscape cloth and spread gravel; (iv) grounds keeping (the court differentiated a service such as snow ploughing, and addressing vegetation and accumulation of dirt. Although snow would melt of its own accord, vegetation and dirt would not). [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I9099c250f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 138 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3385 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3338, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 5 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5779, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5521, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Inside Outside Home Services Inc." p2="Einstein Design" post.rptr="1039" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63c571515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Inside Outside Home Services Inc. v. Einstein Design">Inside Outside Home Services Inc. v. Einstein Design, 2013 ONSC 1039, 2013 CarswellOnt 3056 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 5946 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant challenged whether the Act applied to leased premises, but, in the absence of evidence that the tenant was required to return the premises to the landlord in a base building condition, and given that the scope of the work performed by the plaintiff appeared to be an “improvement” to the property within the meaning of the Act, the lien was found to be valid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="DST Consulting Engineers Inc." p2="Towanda Timber Ltd." post.rptr="5884" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I63c598605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="DST Consulting Engineers Inc. v. Towanda Timber Ltd.">DST Consulting Engineers Inc. v. Towanda Timber Ltd. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 5884 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6983 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While transportation services alone will not give rise to a lien, the contractors in this case did more than merely transport aggregates to the construction project. They located and selected the aggregates, excavated the material, ensured that the aggregates met specifications and quality control, loaded the aggregates into their trucks and transported the aggregates from the pits to the construction site. Quality control was an essential part of the contract and if quality control specifications were not met, the aggregates would be rejected under the contractual terms. The subcontractor was subcontracted by the defendants to do the required sampling and quality control analysis, and said quality control went to the core of the construction project. It was not plain and obvious that the services of the subcontractor were of minor importance, and it should be left to the trial judge to determine whether the plaintiff could establish whether its services came within the provisions of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Kennedy Electric Ltd." p2="Rumble Automation Inc." post.rptr="6120" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I9099e960f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Kennedy Electric Ltd. v. Rumble Automation Inc.">Kennedy Electric Ltd. v. Rumble Automation Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6120, 2007 ONCA 664, 64 C.L.R. (3d) 33, 229 O.A.C. 156, 285 D.L.R. (4th) 466, 2007 CarswellOnt 6120 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1079, 2008 CarswellOnt 1080 (S.C.C.); affirming (2006), 265 D.L.R. (4th) 20, 208 O.A.C. 156, 50 C.L.R. (3d) 283, 2006 CarswellOnt 1491, [2006] O.J. No. 972 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming (2004), 73 O.R. (3d) 530, 2004 CarswellOnt 5301, [2004] O.J. No. 5091 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Whether or not a service falls within the definition of “improvement” is essentially a fact-finding exercise. While a trial judge must apply the statutory definition of “improvement” to the evidence and is therefore engaged in deciding a question of mixed fact and law, the factual determination is by far the more significant element in the exercise. While every case depends upon its facts, the installation or repair of machinery used in a business operated in a building, particularly where the machinery is portable, will in most cases not give rise to lien rights under the Act. On the other hand, where machinery is installed in a building for the use of a business and is completely and permanently integrated into the building, a lien claim will arise. In this case, the installation of an assembly line for truck frames which consisted of 100 mezzanine platforms and 165 robots, which was bolted into a building especially built to house it, weighed 500,000 tons and covered 100,000 square feet, was held not to give rise to a lien. The trial judge did not commit a palpable and overriding error in finding that the assembly line was portable and that the building addition and the assembly line were not part of a single project.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Note: The definition of “improvement” was amended effective October 25, 2010 by S.O. 2010, c. 16. Presumably, under the new definition, the work held not to be lienable in <ital>Kennedy Electric</ital> would be lienable under the new definition.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="520271 Ontario Inc." p2="Guest" post.rptr="8868" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63c5bf705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="520271 Ontario Inc. v. Guest">520271 Ontario Inc. v. Guest (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 8868 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An improvement must result in an increase to the value of the land. The electrical work done here, while benefiting the lease-hold interest by making the premises more conducive to a veterinary practice, was not of benefit by way of increasing the value of the property. Such work did not qualify as an improvement and was hence not a lienable interest. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: the statutory definition of “improvement” does not require an increase in value, so that the court's insistence on such an increase as a necessary component of an improvement seems questionable.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="1353025 Ontario Inc." p2="Walden Group Canada Ltd." post.rptr="2583" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I909a3780f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd.">1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2583, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant provided financial consulting services for the owner for the purpose of preparation, presentation and liaison with brokers and lenders in order to obtain a construction loan. The owner moved under s. 47 for an order vacating the claim for lien. The court dismissed the motion, holding that “though on the facts of this case I tend towards a view that the type of services rendered by the Respondent should not be entitled to lien, the appropriate place for decision is at Trial where the truth and reliability of the allegations can be tested for trustworthiness and the witnesses' credibility may be properly evaluated.”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="940691 Ontario Inc." p2="Philip Services Inc." post.rptr="204" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63c5e6815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="940691 Ontario Inc. v. Philip Services Inc.">940691 Ontario Inc. v. Philip Services Inc. (2006), 50 C.L.R. (3d) 204, 2006 CarswellOnt 2046 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 7061, 59 C.L.R. (3d) 223 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The transportation of waste materials from various construction sites to designated transfer stations does not constitute services to an “improvement” for the purposes of creating a lien pursuant to the provisions of s. 14 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Services must be provided in the context of an alteration, addition or repair to, or the construction, erection or installation on, or the demolition or removal of building structures or works on the property liened.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="3726843 Canada Inc." p2="879115 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1386" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63c60d905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="3726843 Canada Inc. v. 879115 Ontario Ltd.">3726843 Canada Inc. v. 879115 Ontario Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1386, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 220 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 2275, 43 C.L.R. (3d) 307 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A moveable walls/furniture system which the defendant intended to be a portable piece of its business office and not a part of the building did not constitute a lienable improvement. Although the plaintiff stressed the effort and expense that would be required to disassemble and move it, the system was sold in part based on those features.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="2615" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I909a85a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2615, 71 O.R. (3d) 732, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 96 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 6441, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 32, [2005] O.J. No. 4831 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5521, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Remediation work performed on the cleanup of an illegal tire dump constituted an alteration and repair of the land, and as such, it was supplied to an improvement with the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and supported the registration of a lien. The removal of hundreds of thousands of tires which had been declared a contaminant within the meaning of the <ital>Environmental Protection Act</ital> could be distinguished from activity such as snow removal from a shopping plaza parking lot, which had previously been held to not give rise to a lien. While the presence of snow was transitory and would take care of itself in due course, the tires in the present case could not be considered transitory. See, however, the decision of Mazer J., unreported, April 29, 2004, which decided on similar facts, that the removal of tires did not give rise to a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Wolfedale Electric Ltd." p2="R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc." post.rptr="4663" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63c634a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wolfedale Electric Ltd. v. R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc.">Wolfedale Electric Ltd. v. R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 4663, 2004 CarswellOnt 2956, 47 B.L.R. (3d) 1 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A portion of the work done on a shuttle car operation related to modifications and installations in respect of additional cables. The components supplied by the plaintiff were held to be an integral part of the system, as the shuttle car operation would have had no purpose and could not have functioned were it not for the work performed by the plaintiff. The work constituted an improvement and the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Hunter Douglas Canada Inc." p2="Skyline Interiors Corp." post.rptr="80" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63c634a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hunter Douglas Canada Inc. v. Skyline Interiors Corp.">Hunter Douglas Canada Inc. v. Skyline Interiors Corp. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 80, 2004 CarswellOnt 68, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 120 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant's installation of window blinds in customers' homes did not constitute an improvement within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Rather, such blinds, attached by a few screws, were for the convenience of the occupant and not an enhancement of the value of the building. The simple fact that something is attached to a building does not make it an “installation on any land” within the meaning of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re" post.rptr="262" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I63c65bb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re">A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 262, 2002 CarswellOnt 210, 21 C.L.R. (3d) 50 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion to discharge a lien allegedly arising from the supply and installation of an assembly line for manufacturing automotive parts was dismissed as the issue of lienability was a genuine issue for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd." p2="Modern Tile Supply Co." post.rptr="783" pre.rptr="55" ref.id="I909afad0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co.">Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co. (2001), 55 O.R. (3d) 783, 11 C.L.R. (3d) 1, 2001 CarswellOnt 3138 (Ont. C.A.); affirming (1998), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 216, 1998 CarswellOnt 4637 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The purpose of the definition of “improvement”, as set out in the Report of the Attorney General's Advisory Committee on the Draft <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (see Appendix), was “to protect those who contribute their services or materials towards the making of an improvement to a premises”. The report also stressed that while the definition of “improvement” was a broad one, it was drafted to make it clear that the lien created by the Act applied “only in the case of the construction and building repair industries”. The supplier supplied floor coverings, wall coverings and curtains to a retail store. The store's owners requested that the supplier place the name of the store's customer on the order, but the supplier billed the store. The supplier brought an action against the store for outstanding sales accounts, and an action against the store owners personally, pursuant to the trust provisions of ss. 8(1) and 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. A judgment against the store was entered on consent. The action against the store owners personally was dismissed. The supplier appealed. The appeal was dismissed as the trust provisions of the Act created a trust only for the benefit of persons who supplied services or materials to a specific improvement, not for the benefit generally of persons who supply contractors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Desourdy 1949 Paving Inc. (Trustee of), Re" post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63c682c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Desourdy 1949 Paving Inc. (Trustee of), Re">Desourdy 1949 Paving Inc. (Trustee of), Re (2000), 17 C.B.R. (4th) 66 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor demolished the building and had the rubbish from the demolition delivered to the subcontractor. The subcontractor, while it did not itself haul the rubbish away from the construction site, removed iron bars from the concrete portion of the material before crushing and disposing of it. In the circumstances, the disposal services provided by the subcontractor constituted an “improvement” as defined by the Act, entitling the plaintiff to the trust benefits of the Act. The services were directly related to the demolition activity performed by the contractor, and while they were at the end of the contractual chain, they provided a direct and essential contribution to the construction of an improvement on the site, namely the disposal of the demolition rubbish. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court distinguished the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Slack Transport Ltd." p2="General Concrete Ltd." post.rptr="640" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I909b21e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Slack Transport Ltd. v. General Concrete Ltd.">Slack Transport Ltd. v. General Concrete Ltd. (1983), 9 D.L.R. (4th) 640, 46 O.R. (2d) 255, 1983 CarswellOnt 1432 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1983), 46 O.R. (2d) 255 (note) (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, “Supply of Services”, below, on the facts. In <ital>Slack</ital>, the contractor had a contract to supply and install concrete slabs on various construction sites. The subcontractor, a trucker, supplied truck drivers and some of the trucking equipment and delivered the contractor's slabs to the constructions sites but did not load or unload them.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd." p2="Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd." post.rptr="1325" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I63c6a9d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd.">Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 1325, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 184 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Four plaintiffs sought payment for equipment supplied and delivered to a remote mining location in Northwestern Ontario. The mining program was to have proceeded in a series of stages, but a cessation of work halted the program indefinitely. Some of the equipment actually supplied to the site was intended to be used at a later stage in the program but, due to the cessation of work, the equipment was either not used or not installed. The defendant argued that the value of the land was not enhanced by the presence of the equipment, and there was no “improvement” within the meaning of the Act. The court found that there was an improvement in fact and that the presence of the equipment supplied by the plaintiffs added to the ability of the mining program to be moved forward. This was so even in respect of equipment not yet installed or actually put into use when, due to an ostensibly temporary interruption of the project's financing, the work was halted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I55bb89b0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The term “<ital>improvement</ital>” is meant to be a term of art under this definition. It is the project designed and to be undertaken as between the owner and general contractor, whether it be a new building or some mere alteration, addition or repair. It cannot be seriously said to embrace subcontracts as such.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Moffatt & Powell Ltd." p2="682901 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63c6d0e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Moffatt & Powell Ltd. v. 682901 Ontario Ltd.">Moffatt & Powell Ltd. v. 682901 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 205 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the owner undertook the erection of a three-storey residence for the elderly that contained 66 separate suites, and all 16 lien claimants contracted with the owner to perform work or services or to supply materials for that “construction”, all the claimants performed work or services in respect of the same improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="IBL Industries Ltd., Re" post.rptr="20" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I63c6f7f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="IBL Industries Ltd., Re">IBL Industries Ltd., Re (1990), 80 C.B.R. (N.S.) 20, 43 C.L.R. 192 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—The manufacture and supply by a subcontractor of parts of an emissions control system were “improvements” within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The components were an integral part of the system, and the fact that some part of the work could be removed from the structure of which it was an essential part was not determinative of the issue.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I909b9710f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—The addition of foam insulation to a building constituted an “improvement”, as defined in s. 1(1) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63c71f005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re">Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re (1986), 20 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—Portable schoolrooms which, in the normal course of business, were built at one location and delivered completely finished to the site and were installed on cement blocks which rested on cement pads were not “improvements” within the meaning of s. 1(1). The portable rooms had no water or sewage facilities and were self-contained units that could be moved from place to place like a mobile home. The portable classrooms were chattels, and not affixed to the land.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:12: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:12</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Interest in the premises</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Graham Mining Ltd." p2="Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc." post.rptr="291" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I63c71f015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc.">Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc. (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 291 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 3774 (Div. Ct.); affirmed in the Court of Appeal at (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 1549, 2002 CarswellOnt 1502 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—This case concerned an attempt to lien a limited partnership's contingent future interest in a provincial water power lease. A reading of the definition sections of the Act, together with a reading of s. 76, supports the conclusion that the interest of an owner which is lienable by virtue of s. 14 of the Act is, has always been and will remain an “interest in land”. An interest in personalty, or an interest in an improvement by itself without an attached “interest in land” cannot constitute a lienable interest. The long standing authority to this effect of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pankka" p2="Butchart" post.rptr="837" pre.rptr="[1956]" ref.id="I63c746105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pankka v. Butchart">Pankka v. Butchart, [1956] O.R. 837 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, decided under the former <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>, remains good law, as does the authority of the Divisional Court decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63c746115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, decided under the present <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63c76d205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207, 52 O.A.C. 107 (Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Reversionary provisions that may be described as a “fee simple upon condition subsequent” or as “a determinable fee simple” do not, in either case, amount to an interest in the premises as required by the statute, but are rather mere rights which may be exercised should the circumstances permit. Neither amounts to an interest in land.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:13: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:13</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Lien claimant</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Triple “R” Demolition Inc." p2="1186468 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="125" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63c794305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Triple “R” Demolition Inc. v. 1186468 Ontario Ltd.">Triple “R” Demolition Inc. v. 1186468 Ontario Ltd. (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 125 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An entity incorporated after the date of the contract and after performing much, if not all of the contract work, was not permitted to rely on s. 21(2) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. B.16, nor could the lien claimant avail itself of s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The contract was void <ital>ab initio</ital>, and a lien claim based on such a contract could not be saved by s.  6.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="EMCO Supply" p2="Anduhyaun Inc." post.rptr="91" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I63c794315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc.">EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc. (1998), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 91 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The definition of “lien claimant” in s. 1(1) only requires the person to have what purports to be a preserved lien, that is, a form of claim for lien that has been registered. It does not require that the lien be validly or properly preserved.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="George & Asmussen Ltd." p2="MCM Projects Inc." post.rptr="254" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63c7bb405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Projects Inc.">George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Projects Inc. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 254, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Holdings Inc.)</ital> 6 O.R. (3d) 645 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A bank which had issued a letter of credit to a municipality to secure the obligations of the owner of the property, under a site plan control agreement with the municipality, was not entitled to step into the shoes of the municipality and claim priority over the lien claimants. The definition of “lien claimant” is considered in this context.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:14: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:14</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Materials</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc." p2="Momat Developments Inc." post.rptr="270" pre.rptr="59" ref.id="I63c7e2505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc.">Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc. (2002), 59 O.R. (3d) 270, 2002 CarswellOnt 2284, 19 C.L.R. (3d) 40 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Appliances bought before the making of an improvement is commenced, but later installed are “materials” within the meaning of s. 1 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd." p2="Modern Tile Supply Co." post.rptr="783" pre.rptr="55" ref.id="I909ca880f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co.">Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co. (2001), 55 O.R. (3d) 783, 11 C.L.R. (3d) 1, 2001 CarswellOnt 3138 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The definition of “material” in the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> makes reference to an “improvement”, with the result that the earlier cases based on the former definition in the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> should not be relied upon. The decisions in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1979" p1="Schulz Concrete Pipe Ltd., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="32" ref.id="I63c809605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schulz Concrete Pipe Ltd., Re">Schulz Concrete Pipe Ltd., Re (1979), 32 C.B.R. (N.S.) 157, 1979 CarswellOnt 256 (S.C.)</ref></cite> <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc." p2="Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd." post.rptr="6" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63c809615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd.">Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 6, 1989 CarswellOnt 692 (H.C.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I909ccf90f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite> were therefore not followed. Here, the supplier supplied floor coverings wall coverings and curtains to a retail store. The store's owners requested that the supplier place the name of the store's customer on the order, but the supplier billed the store. The supplier brought an action against the store for outstanding sales accounts, and a construction lien action against the store owners personally, pursuant to the trust provisions of ss. 8(1) and 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. A judgment against the store was entered on consent. The action against the storeowners personally was dismissed. The supplier appealed. The appeal was dismissed. The trust provisions of the Act created a trust only for the benefit of persons who supplied services or materials to a specific improvement, not for the benefit generally of persons who supply contractors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Arborform Countertops Inc." p2="Stellato" post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63c830715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato">Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 25, 29 O.R. (3d) 129 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied countertops for the sole purpose of improvements to be made to commercial and residential properties by the defendants. The countertops required no change to their character save and except there may have been the need to do some cutting and sanding, as might be required with a new door or window. For the purposes of determining whether the plaintiff was a “materialman” supplying “materials” within the meaning of the Act, it was irrelevant that the countertops were installed in project “A” rather than “B” given that they were purchased from the plaintiff for installation in project “A” and “B”. If a contractor building a new subdivision consisting of twenty-four units orders and has delivered twenty four doors from a supplier, the fact that each door is not identified for a specific unit will not, ordinarily, make that supplier any less a materialman.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Markborough Properties Inc." p2="841202 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="77" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63c857805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Markborough Properties Inc. v. 841202 Ontario Inc.">Markborough Properties Inc. v. 841202 Ontario Inc. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 77 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien for supply of a sprinkler system was disallowed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Southdale Towers Ltd." p2="Carlton Management Group Inc." post.rptr="233" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I63c857815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southdale Towers Ltd. v. Carlton Management Group Inc.">Southdale Towers Ltd. v. Carlton Management Group Inc. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 233 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The applicant and the respondent entered into a property management contract pursuant to which the applicant authorized the respondent to lease, manage, repair and maintain the respondent's premises, and appointed the respondent “a sole and exclusive agent.” In the circumstances, the supply of appliances to the unit could not be considered the supply of “materials” within the definition of that term in the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc." p2="Process Cooling Systems Inc." post.rptr="324" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63c87e905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. Process Cooling Systems Inc.">Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. Process Cooling Systems Inc. (1993), 16 O.R. (3d) 324, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 86 (Gen. Div.); appeal allowed (1996), 30 O.R. (3d) 159 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A water cooling system in a manufacturing plant did not fall within the definition of “material” under the Act. Although the equipment supplied became attached in many ways to the system of which it was part for the purpose of cooling water and regenerating water and although it was attached electrically and from a plumbing and drainage point of view, it was not and did not become a part of the building and was not incorporated into the building. An appeal was allowed on an issue of alleged fraudulent misrepresentation against a personal defendant. As a result, all issues were sent back for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I909d44c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—Despite the fact that the chemicals purchased from a supplier were not supplied by a contractor in their raw state, but were combined to form an insulation product, they were “materials”, which became part of an improvement. It is not necessary that a supplier know or intend that its materials will end up in a specific improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Homebuilder Inc." p2="Man-Sonic Industries Inc." post.rptr="18" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63c8a5a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Homebuilder Inc. v. Man-Sonic Industries Inc.">Homebuilder Inc. v. Man-Sonic Industries Inc. (1987), 28 C.L.R. 18 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff, a builder and vendor of new homes, utilized certain artists' sketches in connection with certain types of its homes. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant appropriated those sketches for their own use in the construction and sale of new homes by them. The court held that the fact that the plaintiff might have had a claim to a construction lien under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> if there had been an agreement was of no relevance. There was no basis for imposing a construction lien or a constructive trust parallel thereto in the absence of a contract to provide services.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63c8a5a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re">Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re (1986), 20 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—Portable schoolrooms which, in the normal course of business were built at one location and delivered completely finished to the site and were installed on cement blocks which rested on cement pads were “materials”, but the installation was not an improvement.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:15: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:15</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Owner</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dalren Limited" p2="Loadstar Trailers Inc." post.rptr="19768" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6715cae03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Dalren Limited v. Loadstar Trailers Inc.">Dalren Limited v. Loadstar Trailers Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 19768, 2024 ONSC 7144 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant was an “owner” under the Act, because the manufacturing facility - the improvement - was built at the location “at the request of” the defendant and on its behalf and for its direct benefit. It did not matter that the defendant was not the registered owner of the property when the procurement process began, or even when the contract was signed almost 3 years later. At the time the improvement was made, the defendant had a lienable “interest in the premises” upon which the improvement was made and was an owner under the Act and for the purposes of s. 87.3.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc." p2="Global HVAC & Automation Inc." post.rptr="16009" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6715f1f03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc. v. Global HVAC & Automation Inc.">HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc. v. Global HVAC & Automation Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 16009, 2024 ONSC 5752 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused <ital>KCL Group Limited v. HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc.</ital>, 2025 CarswellOnt 6184 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimants registered their respective claims for lien against title to the property on the 56th day following their last supply to the project, rendering the liens timely under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, but out of time under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The corporate entities who initiated the purchase of the land in question, and sought a preliminary proposal and quote for the project design prior to July 1, 2018, had nothing more than an interest in the shares of the subsidiaries or closely held corporations that ultimately obtained ownership of the land. They were legally distinct and separate corporate entities, and they had no rights or interest in the assets of the ultimate corporate owner. While the shareholding corporate entities maintained an interest in the project and in the improvement through its contractual dealings, at no time before July 1, 2018 did they have any interest in the premises, even though one of them entered into an agreement for the purchase of the premises.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Walsh Construction" p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="7974" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I671619003b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Walsh Construction v. The cheques were issued by the plaintiff because of complications arising from RM's divorce proceedings.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cohen" p2="Brin" post.rptr="1302" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63ca2c405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cohen v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It cannot be assumed that a registered owner of a property is an “owner” within the meaning of the Act where the contract for work or services is made between a tenant and a contractor. Here, under the lease, the defendant plaza owner/landlord was responsible for the exterior of the property while the defendant tenant was responsible for the interior, with a Leasehold Improvement Allowance (LIA) provided to the tenant to subsidize the cost of the tenant's work. The tenant hired the plaintiff company to complete work on the leased premises, and the latter submitted its invoices to the tenant, which paid them directly. The plaintiff subsequently brought an action against both the tenant and landlord for payment under the contract, alleging that the landlord was an “owner” of the premises within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and that a portion of the LIA that had been held back constituted a trust fund pursuant to s. 7. Relying on <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pinehurst Woodworking Co." p2="Rocco" post.rptr="669" pre.rptr="1986" ref.id="I63ca53515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pinehurst Woodworking Co. v. Rocco">Pinehurst Woodworking Co. v. Rocco, 1986 CarswellOnt 669, 38 R.P.R. 116, 13 O.A.C. 121 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the court held that it could not reasonably be inferred from the circumstances that there was an implied request from the landlord to the plaintiff for work to be done. The advances on the LIA were not designed to flow through to the plaintiff contractor in the sense that the plaintiff did not have an interest in the advances made by the landlord to the tenant. The fact that the tenant received reimbursement in part from the landlord was not important to the plaintiff, and there was no evidence that the landlord actually exercised its right under the lease to be heavily involved in the tenant's work. As a result, the landlord did not fall within the definition of an “owner” as set out in the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chris Nash Building Inc." p2="Buckland" post.rptr="5395" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63ca53525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Chris Nash Building Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The definition of “owner” makes it clear that a required element of being an “owner” is to have “an interest” in the property. An owner's solicitor, who merely holds insurance monies before giving them to the actual “owner”, is not liable as an owner for the purposes of s. 7 of the Act. To be an owner, it is necessary that a person have “an interest in a premises”, is likely to benefit from the improvements, and has some say in the nature of the improvement, and the progress of the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="78" ref.id="I63ca7a605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. (3d) 259, 2007 CarswellOnt 9547, 74 R.P.R. (4th) 296 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (2006), 54 C.L.R. (3d) 142, 2006 CarswellOnt 2801 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. The trial judge found that the mortgagee which sought priority over the lien claimants acted in a commercially irresponsible manner by engaging in acts such as continuously advancing funds to an owner which made no payments and which did not have fire insurance in place. Its failure in this regard was a decision of an “owner” and the judge pierced the corporate veil to give the lienholders priority over the second mortgage. In upholding the trial judge's reasoning, the Court of Appeal noted that the absence of direct dealings between the person said to be an owner under the Act and construction suppliers was not determinative, and was only one factor to consider in examining the relationship between the parties. Otherwise, a developer could easily escape its obligations to suppliers by the simple device of arranging for an associated or related company to directly engage suppliers for the provision of services or materials, which would defeat the intended protection provided to lienholders under the Act. For this reason, a “request” for work to be done may be inferred from the totality of the circumstances, viewed in light of the substance of the relationship between the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Ravenda Homes Ltd." p2="1372708 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2372" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I63caa1705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc.">Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 2372 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the defendant was an “owner” or “payer” within the meaning of the Act, and hence liable to have its property liened. The plaintiff agreed to become the homebuilder for the defendant's development property under an agreement that provided the plaintiff lien claimant with an option to purchase developed lots without deposit to the defendant. The plaintiff constructed three model homes, performed renovations on the defendant's home on a separate lot to convert it to a sales office, and marketed the lots on the development property. Differences arose which resulted in the registration of construction liens on the defendant's home, and the model homes. The defendant's motion to dismiss the liens was dismissed. Although under s. 1(1), an owner was a person “who is liable to pay under a contract” and no specific agreement existed for a direct payment for the model homes between the plaintiff and defendant, the agreement when read as a whole provided that the plaintiff would pay the defendant when it sold the relevant homes to a third party purchaser. Although this would create liability from the plaintiff to the defendant and not <ital>vice versa</ital>, the defendant still had an obligation to convey the property when so requested. In the event that it failed to do so, and breached the terms of its contract, it would only be logical for the plaintiff to seek repayment of its investment on a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> basis. Thus the owner would be “liable to pay” within the meaning of s. 1(1). Master)</ref></cite>—A project for a residential retirement community utilized a right-to-occupy or life-lease legal structure. The property in question was purchased and the title was transferred to a non-profit community association, which entered into a construction and development agreement with a for-profit numbered company that was to assume the role of construction manager. When construction costs escalated, and some units did not sell or could not be sold because of title problems, there was a shortfall in the mortgage money required to pay the general contractor and five trades. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In order to have a valid and enforceable lien, a lien claimant must show that the person sought to be charged as “owner” requested the work, service or material to be supplied, either directly or impliedly. Here, the plaintiff builder alleged the existence of an oral agreement with the defendant developer which authorized the builder to erect houses on lots owned by the developer and defer the payment of purchase monies for each lot until construction was completed and each house was sold. There was neither an express request or a request by implication on the part of the developer derived from the circumstances in order to give rise to lien rights against the latter's interests sought to be charged. The evidence clearly established that the plaintiff, on its own version of the alleged oral agreement, had complete control over how the houses were built, designed, constructed or sold. The developer was therefore not an owner within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Haas Homes Ltd." p2="March Road Gym & Health Club Inc." post.rptr="2847" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I909fb5c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Haas Homes Ltd. v. (3d) 243 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A mere request for an improvement to be made to the property was insufficient ground for a finding that someone was a statutory owner, but had to be accompanied by one or more of the other elements set out in the definition of an owner in s. 1(1) of the Act: (a) upon the credit; on behalf of; with the privity or consent of; or for the direct benefit of the alleged owner. Here, an offer to lease set out the respective scope of the landlord's and the tenant's work required to renovate the upper floor of the property as a health club. The lien claimant quoted to the tenants, never entered into a written contract, and dealt with the tenants only for payment, claims for extras and credits for approval. During the performance of the contract, representatives of the landlord were on the scene, in addition to those of the claimant and the tenants, exercising a general supervisory function over all contractors engaged in the work, including its own general contractor and sub-trades, as well as the contractors for new tenants who were fitting up their own premises. On motion to oppose confirmation of the Master's report, the Master was held to have made a reversible in law in concluding on the evidence that the landlord was a statutory owner within the meaning of s. 1(1). (3d) 107 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff produced geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering reports in respect of certain property for the defendant developer, as part of efforts to develop the land. Subsequently and separately, the defendant purchaser retained the plaintiff for a major investigation project on the lands, but failed to pay the plaintiff's invoices. The accounts were never copied to the developer, the plaintiff made no demand for payment to the developer at the time, and the developer had no input or control over the nature or extent of the work. While the developer was aware that a study was ongoing it showed no interest in it. The plaintiff placed a lien against the premises when payment for its services was not forthcoming, and sought a judgment against the defendant, which had no legal interest in the property. As an alternative, the plaintiff sought an order requiring the registered titleholder of the lands, the second defendant, to sell the lands and apply the proceeds of sale towards payment of the judgment. The Court concluded that the developer was not an owner at law, and the fact that the developer was the registered titleholder did not make it so. Although it was well within the scope of the law to imply or infer a request from the surrounding circumstances even if the parties did not deal directly about the request, more than mere knowledge or awareness of the work was needed. The developer engaged in preliminary preparation for construction on the land using the general contractor and subcontractors, including some excavation and the partial delivery of a pre-fabricated building. Subsequently, after the developer failed to obtain necessary zoning changes, the project was cancelled and the agreement of purchase and sale was terminated by mutual consent. In the circumstances, the developer had an equitable interest in the lands which could be liened. Case law held that an agreement of purchase and sale provided the purchaser with an equitable interest in the property under s. 1(1)(b) of the Act, the developer was an owner having an interest in a premises on whose behalf an improvement was made. Despite the fact that title to the land was held by them, the mall owners did not request that this work be done, and accordingly the Act did not create a lien against their interest in the land. P was held to be an owner within the meaning of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, where, the object of the entire construction program was to establish a head office for the Canadian subsidiary; P was entitled to approve the building plans and to supervise construction throughout, and had the authority to make alteration to the plans of the building as construction proceeded. The security afforded by the Act is a claim against the interest of the person requesting the work and whose interest is to be thereby enhanced.
