Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The purchasers entered into an agreement for the purchase of a new home to be constructed by L Inc. The agreement provided for the purchasers to pay a sum of $25,000 upon acceptance of the offer, a further 25,000 at the rough framing stage and a further $25,000 at the drywall boarding stage. After executing the agreement, the purchasers realized that the original lot on which the home was to be constructed was too narrow for the model home which they had selected. As a result, the purchasers put L Inc. in contact with S Ltd. who owned a larger lot. S Ltd. then agreed to sell the larger lot to L Inc. Since the purchasers had an interest in the “premises” being the “improvement” or home being built and the improvements were made on behalf of the purchasers, with their consent and for their direct benefit, the purchasers were statutory “owners” under the Act. S. Ltd. was an owner under the Act. In addition, S Ltd. was the registered owner of the land, was aware that L Inc. was building a home on the land and that the land was to be transferred to the purchasers. S Ltd. made no attempt to stop construction of the home. Accordingly, the inaction of S Ltd. could be considered a “request” by S Ltd. to L Inc. for the construction of the home in order that the sale could be completed to the purchasers and the sale of the land could be completed from S Ltd. to L Inc. In the result, S Ltd. was also a statutory owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Riverside Glass Ltd." p2="Charron's Quality Market Ltd." post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63cbd9f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd.">Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor entered into an agreement with the defendant M. Ltd., which was owned by the defendant RQ and his brother, to supply labour and materials for a building to be erected on Lot 111. Title to Lot 111 resided in RQ and his brother, and the adjoining lot, Lot 112, was owned by M. Ltd. The plaintiff had instructed its former solicitor to file a lien against the market. The solicitor subsequently registered a lien and a certificate of action against Lot 112. The defendants claimed that the lien and certificate of action were registered against the wrong lot. As the market owned one lot, and its owners owned the adjoining lot, the market was within the meaning of “owner” under the Act. Therefore, the lien registered against Lot 112 was valid against the same owner's interest in Lot 111.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Big Creek Construction Ltd." p2="York-Trillium Development Group Ltd." post.rptr="285" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63cbd9f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd.">Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd. (1993), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 285, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 331 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 138 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The rationale behind the definition of “owner” and the issues relevant to piercing of the corporate veil are to be distinguished.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="J.P. Lariviere Construction Ltd." p2="TFP Future Properties Inc." post.rptr="112" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63cbd9f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J.P. Lariviere Construction Ltd. v. TFP Future Properties Inc.">J.P. Lariviere Construction Ltd. v. TFP Future Properties Inc. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 112 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In an action arising out of the construction of an automotive centre and gas bar, the lessee and its petroleum distributor were held not to be “owners” as defined by the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63cc01005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207, 52 O.A.C. 107 (Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A party that grants land in “fee simple upon condition subsequent” or as “a determinable fee simple” does not, in either case, retain an interest in the premises so as to qualify as an owner under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Lark Manufacturing Inc." post.rptr="113" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63cc01015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Lark Manufacturing Inc.">D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Lark Manufacturing Inc. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 113 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A benefit obtained by a landlord as a reversionary is not a direct benefit as referred to under the definition of “owner” in s. 1(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Florida Drywall Co." p2="Graham" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63cc01025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Florida Drywall Co. v. Graham">Florida Drywall Co. v. Graham (1986), 20 C.L.R. 235 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendants G entered into a purchase and sale agreement with the defendant T Ltd., pursuant to which T Ltd. was to construct a house for G. The purchase price of the land and completed house was $245,000, and G paid $5,000 to T Ltd. upon execution of the agreement and an additional $80,000 one month later. $60,000 of the latter amount was a loan to the defendants L and T Ltd., secured by a promissory note. The transaction closed when G paid the balance of $265,000, being the original purchase price plus $20,000 for extras. G took possession without a municipal occupancy permit or certificate of completion under the Ontario <ital>New Home Warranties Plan Act</ital>. The plaintiffs registered claims for lien and brought actions against G in support of their respective lien claims. In granting judgment to the plaintiffs, the court held that the defendants G were owners. The payment of $80,000 by G to T Ltd. was considered and calculated as a payment on account of the purchase price. The total sum paid prior to conveyance was $85,000, which constituted 32 per cent of the total purchase price of $265,000. It therefore followed that the defendants G could not meet either of the provisos essential to the application of s. 1(1), and that at all material times they were “owners”, and not “home buyers”, and were not exempt from lien claims under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Leyburn Electric Ltd." p2="Merton Development Corp." post.rptr="2428" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63cc28105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Leyburn Electric Ltd. v. Merton Development Corp.">Leyburn Electric Ltd. v. Merton Development Corp. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2428 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The relevant time for determination of whether a person is an “owner” within the meaning of s. 1 of the Act is the date on which the lien claimant supplied services or materials to the improvement. Where a plaintiff worked on a residential condominium development and registered a lien before the condominium corporation was registered, the corporation was not an “owner”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc." p2="Denamer Homes Inc." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63cc4f205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc.">L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The exclusion of “home buyer” from the definition of “owner” in s. 1(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> reflects the fact that a purchaser who pays less than 30 per cent of the purchase price prior to closing is clearly not financing the construction of the home. In essence, therefore, those who supply services or materials to the building are forced to look to the vendor for payment and cannot create lien rights in the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Southern Plumbing Ltd." p2="Quality Craft Interiors Ltd." post.rptr="195" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63cc4f215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southern Plumbing Ltd. v. Quality Craft Interiors Ltd.">Southern Plumbing Ltd. v. Quality Craft Interiors Ltd. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 195 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The evidence disclosed that the landlord had provided the tenant with $400,000 to use for the renovations. In addition, the landlord tried to help the trades and also had people present to ensure that the job was done correctly and that the building was not damaged. By simply contributing to the cost of the renovations through “tenant inducements,” the landlord did not become as an “owner” so as to attract liability for a construction lien. The evidence amounted to nothing more than the landlord's employees expressing their understandable concerns about where and how work was being done at their head office building. There was nothing in the evidence to show that the landlord inserted itself as an “owner” in the construction program. The landlord was entitled to protect the integrity of its building without fear of being held liable as an “owner.”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Venneri Engineering Ltd." p2="Zonenward Leasex Management Inc." post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63cc4f225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc.">Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 141 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The landlord was not an “owner” within the meaning under the Act because the lien claimants failed to show that the landlord had requested the work. The significant element of direct contractual dealing between the landlord and the lien claimants required to prove such a request was missing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd." p2="Villa Nova Construction Inc." post.rptr="227" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63cc76305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc.">Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc. (1989), 33 C.L.R. 227, 1989 CarswellOnt 690 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The priorities addressed in s. 80 do not apply in the case of a purchaser who is a “home buyer” and who is thereby not an “owner” under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Roboak Developments Ltd." p2="Lehndorff Corp." post.rptr="194" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I63cc76315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Roboak Developments Ltd. v. Lehndorff Corp.">Roboak Developments Ltd. v. Lehndorff Corp. (1986), 39 R.P.R. 194, 18 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—AC Inc. purchased land for a residential development from L Corp., which took back a vendor mortgage to be repaid incrementally as the houses were sold. AC Inc. subsequently obtained a construction mortgage from SM, began construction on four model homes and soon became insolvent. At a meeting, L Corp., SM and AC Ltd. tentatively agreed with R that R would take over the project from AC Ltd. by assuming A's two mortgages. However, before a written agreement was executed, R, at SM's urging, started work on the understanding that R would recover all his costs if no firm agreement was ever reached. Subsequently, with no written agreement reached, L Corp. refused to pay R's invoices for costs incurred and stated that R should look to AC Inc. for reimbursement. L Corp. then took an assignment of S's construction mortgage through its subsidiary B. R filed a lien and commenced an action against L Corp. and B for reimbursement of its costs, and L counterclaimed for losses suffered on two lots plus costs incurred during construction for which R had allegedly agreed to reimburse L. The court awarded R a lien judgment against both L and B for the amount expended in construction together with costs, and a personal judgment for interest. L's counterclaim was dismissed. R performed the work, in the absence of an agreement, on the representation of S that R would be paid its costs until the homes were sold. SM expressly requested and consented to R completing the construction commenced by A. It was to be inferred that R performed the work at the request and with the consent of L Corp. Both SM and L thus became “owners” pursuant to the definition set out in s. 1(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. B assumed the liability of SM and became an owner to the same measure as SM when it took the assignment of the mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Regional Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Ann-Rob Properties Ltd." post.rptr="300" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63cc9d405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Regional Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Ann-Rob Properties Ltd.">Regional Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Ann-Rob Properties Ltd. (1986), 22 C.L.R. 300 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant AR Ltd., of which LH Ltd. and GB were shareholders, owned land on which it intended to construct a strip plaza. LH Ltd. was hired as the construction manager, and the defendant GB was engaged as design consultant to prepare the plans. GB was also the principal of LV Ltd. The plaintiff was a plumbing contractor who gave plumbing advice to AR Ltd. and that advice was incorporated by GB into the plans for the plaza. When tenants leased part of the plaza from LV Ltd., which had acquired the lease from AR Ltd., they contracted with the plaintiff to perform the plumbing work for which they were liable under the lease as tenant improvements. The work to be performed for the tenants was shown on the plans prepared by GB for the plaza. When the tenants failed to pay the plaintiff, it registered a lien and commenced an action, claiming the moneys unpaid under its contract with the tenants. The plaintiff also claimed against AB Ltd. and LV Ltd. on the basis that each of them was an owner as defined in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. In the result, the court allowed the action as against AR Ltd. and LV Ltd. In the circumstances it was to be inferred that LV Ltd. and AR Ltd. had each requested the plaintiff to do the leasehold improvements ordered by the tenants. Although AR Ltd. had no direct dealings with the plaintiff, it had provided plans to the plaintiff which indicated work that it knew would be done by a tenant. In addition, there was an inter-connection between AR Ltd., LV Ltd., GB and LH Ltd., the details of which would not be appreciated by the plaintiff. AR Ltd. in effect consented to the things done by GB in whatever capacity he acted, either personal or corporate. GB wanted the plaintiff to do the work, and at no time told the plaintiff not to do it or that AR Ltd. would not pay for such work. In interpretating the definition of “owner”, there is no doubt that a request does not have to be direct, and may be inferred. The substance and not merely the form of the relationship between the parties must be considered.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

(2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 2372 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the defendant was an “owner” or “payer” within the meaning of the Act, and hence liable to have its property liened. The plaintiff agreed to become the homebuilder for the defendant's development property under an agreement that provided the plaintiff lien claimant with an option to purchase developed lots without deposit to the defendant. The plaintiff constructed three model homes, performed renovations on the defendant's home on a separate lot to convert it to a sales office, and marketed the lots on the development property. Differences arose which resulted in the registration of construction liens on the defendant's home, and the model homes. The defendant's motion to dismiss the liens was dismissed. Although under s. 1(1), an owner was a person “who is liable to pay under a contract” and no specific agreement existed for a direct payment for the model homes between the plaintiff and defendant, the agreement when read as a whole provided that the plaintiff would pay the defendant when it sold the relevant homes to a third party purchaser. Although this would create liability from the plaintiff to the defendant and not <ital>vice versa</ital>, the defendant still had an obligation to convey the property when so requested. In the event that it failed to do so, and breached the terms of its contract, it would only be logical for the plaintiff to seek repayment of its investment on a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> basis. Thus the owner would be “liable to pay” within the meaning of s. 1(1). Such an interpretation was analogous to the landlord and tenant provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, whereby landlords are occasionally considered “owners” under the Act even though they are clearly not liable to pay cash for the materials or services provided to the leased premises.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Vecero" p2="C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc." post.rptr="903" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90a1b190f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc.">Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 903, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 74 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A mortgagee of a bankrupt developer was held not to be a “payer” as defined by this subsection.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="J.P. Lariviere Construction Ltd." p2="TFP Future Properties Inc." post.rptr="112" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63ccc4525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J.P. Lariviere Construction Ltd. v. TFP Future Properties Inc.">J.P. Lariviere Construction Ltd. v. TFP Future Properties Inc. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 112 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In an action arising out of the construction of an automotive centre and gas bar, the lessee and its petroleum distributor were held not to be “payers” as defined by the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Cedar Rent All Ltd." p2="Canada Packers Inc." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="59" ref.id="I63cceb605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cedar Rent All Ltd. v. Canada Packers Inc.">Cedar Rent All Ltd. v. Canada Packers Inc. (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 523, 27 C.L.R. 49 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The meaning of the words “pay” and “payment” was not limited to the delivery of money from a debtor to a creditor, but included also delivery of goods and other valuable things tendered. There is still a place in society for transactions by barter and not currency. It would be contrary to the intention of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to allow an otherwise valid claim for lien to be defeated before trial because the value of services rendered was in dispute.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

(1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 125 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An entity incorporated after the date of the contract and after performing much, if not all of the contract work, was not permitted to rely on s. 21(2) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. B.16, nor could the lien claimant avail itself of s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. ARC Productions Ltd.">Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd., 2018 ONSC 5366, 2018 CarswellOnt 15345, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 38 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant general contractor performed renovations for the tenant renting two physically connected but separate properties owned by separate holding corporations, who were in turn owned by a parent company. The tenant subsequently went bankrupt. The contractor registered a claim for lien only against one of the municipal addresses, and the Master ruled that the second property constituted lands “enjoyed with” the first, liened property, such as to extend the lien registration to the second property. That was a question of fact, with relevant factors including commonality of officers and directors, whether separate legal owners were related, whether there was a visible separation or property line and whether there was an integrated or common use. Here, the registered owners were related, had common officers and directors and the two addresses were operated as a single development. The properties were physically adjacent and there was an access door linking the two buildings through the atrium. The fact that an access fob was required did not detract from the connecting link between the buildings, which shared electrical and mechanical services and facilities. The two separate municipal addresses formed a single complex that was marketed under a single name.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Croatia (Republic)" p2="Ru-Ko lnc." post.rptr="133" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63cd39805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Croatia (Republic) v. Ru-Ko lnc.">Croatia (Republic) v. Ru-Ko lnc. (1998), 37 O.R. (3d) 133 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Work was done to convert an existing structure into a foreign mission. Prior to completion of the work, the contract was terminated and the lands and premises listed for sale by the foreign government. An application was brought to vacate the contractor's lien based on the <ital>Foreign Missions and International Organizations Act</ital>, S.C. 1991, c. 41 and Article 1 and 22 of the <ital>“Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations”</ital>. As the premises in question had never actually been occupied by the foreign mission, they did not fall within the definition of “premises of the mission” and the motion to vacate was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd." p2="Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd." post.rptr="1325" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I63cd39815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd.">Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 1325, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 184 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Four plaintiffs sought payment for equipment supplied and delivered to a remote mining location in Northwestern Ontario. In addition to materials supplied to the main mining site, one of the plaintiffs supplied electrical equipment to a nearby camp site that served as the headquarters for the mining program, and which was also used to board workers who were employed at the main mining site. In ruling that the camp was not land “enjoyed therewith” for the purposes of the definition of premises, the court pointed out that it had a long-standing and separate history of being independently operated as a tourist resort. As well, the camp's location was geographically removed from the mining sites by several kilometres, and its uses were both separate and severable from the mining location.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Riverside Glass Ltd." p2="Charron's Quality Market Ltd." post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63cd39825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd.">Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor entered into an agreement with the defendant M. Ltd., which was owned by the defendant R.Q. and his brother, to supply labour and materials for a building to be erected on Lot 111. Title to Lot 111 resided in RQ and his brother, and the adjoining lot, Lot 112, was owned by M. Ltd. The plaintiff had instructed its former solicitor to file a lien against the market. The solicitor subsequently registered a lien and a certificate of action against Lot 112. The defendants claimed that the lien and certificate of action were registered against the wrong lot. The building on Lot 112 was to be torn down and used as a parking lot for the market on Lot 111. Therefore, Lot 111 came within the meaning of “enjoyed therewith” as set out in the definition of “premises” in s. 1(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Alarm Group Ltd." p2="Bloor-Madison Realty Inc." post.rptr="1784" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63cd60905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alarm Group Ltd. v. Bloor-Madison Realty Inc.">Alarm Group Ltd. v. Bloor-Madison Realty Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 1784 (Master)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Alarm Group Ltd." p2="Bloor-Madison Realty Inc." post.rptr="3613" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63cd60915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alarm Group Ltd. v. Bloor-Madison Realty Inc.">Alarm Group Ltd. v. Bloor-Madison Realty Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 3613 (Ont. Gen. Div.); varying (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 3075 (Ont. Gen. Div.); settling and varying (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 1784 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In the course of considering the existence and extent of a settlement of a lien proceeding, the Master had to consider the sheltering of a lien, which, in turn, required the Master to consider whether or not both the sheltered and sheltering liens had affected the same “premises”. A review of the authorities and consideration of the essential factual issue of “used or enjoyed therewith” was conducted, the result of which was the inclusion of the sheltered lien in the settlement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Lunardo" p2="Psihogios" post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63cd87a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lunardo v. Psihogios">Lunardo v. Psihogios (1989), 43 C.L.R. 302 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendants brought a motion for an order dismissing the plaintiff's lien action and striking out the plaintiff's lien registered against their lands on the basis that the property described in the lien was the backyard of their premises and not land on which the building alleged to have been supplied services and materials was situate. The court held that the defendants had failed to establish that the plaintiff's claim for lien was defective. The land described in the lien claim, although not the land on which the building rested, was part of the “premises” under s. 1(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Furthermore, the land description appearing in the lien claim, although incomplete, was sufficient to identify the land on which the lien was claimed. The plaintiff was entitled to have the legal description of the lands to which his lien applied correctly amended.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Phoenix Drywall" p2="Mississauga Rest Home Two Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63cd87a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Phoenix Drywall v. Mississauga Rest Home Two Inc.">Phoenix Drywall v. Mississauga Rest Home Two Inc. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 1, 1988 CarswellOnt 766 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff registered a lien on property adjacent to the actual lienable property. The liened property was vacant but embraced a parking lot intended to service the adjoining rest home. Ownership in the parcels had some overlapping uniformity but the management and directorship of both corporations owning the adjacent parcels was uniform. The defendants brought a motion for an order vacating the registered lien because no services or materials were supplied to the liened land. The plaintiff brought a cross-motion seeking leave to amend its claim for lien. The motion was dismissed and the cross-motion was allowed. The specific use for each parcel demonstrated an obvious and vital integration of uses for a common purpose and as such were to be deemed lienable premises as they represented land “enjoyed therewith” within the definition of “premises” in the Act. The plaintiff was, therefore, permitted to amend its claim for lien without assistance of the curative provisions of s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:19</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Price</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RJ Concrete" p2="Eco Depot LTD." post.rptr="1759" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63cdaeb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RJ Concrete v. Eco Depot LTD.">RJ Concrete v. Eco Depot LTD., 2022 ONSC 1759, 2022 CarswellOnt 3636 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The price of contract work is measured by the stipulated price contract, not by the contractor's costs. It is only where there is no agreement on price that the actual value of the services that have been supplied to the improvement becomes relevant. Where there is a fixed price contract, it may be necessary to determine the actual value of the services and materials supplied if work ended before the completion of an identifiable task or milestone, but otherwise, the price of the work is measured by the contract price. The proper calculation for claims for extras may be made in different ways, depending on the nature of those claims and the terms of the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Haas Homes Ltd." p2="March Road Gym & Health Club Inc." post.rptr="2847" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I90a274e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc.">Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2847, 2003 CarswellOnt 2687, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 243 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim may arise as a result of the definition of “price” in s. 1(1), which, in the alternative, means the “agreed price” or the “actual value” of the services or materials supplied to the improvement under the contract. Such a claim is usually allowed only where one person had supplied goods or services to another person outside the scope of their contract as to price, and the claimant asks the court to establish a reasonable value for the goods and services.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63cdaeb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The starting point in determining the owner's holdback liability as mandated by s. 22 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is “the price of the services or materials as they are actually supplied under the contract or subcontract”. Price includes GST.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:20: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:20</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Subcontract</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Infinite Construction Development Ltd." p2="Chen" post.rptr="3929" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I671d1de03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Infinite Construction Development Ltd. v. Chen">Infinite Construction Development Ltd. v. Chen, 2022 ONSC 3929, 2022 CarswellOnt 9316, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 386 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2023 CarswellOnt 8169, 2023 ONSC 2627, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 409 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 5721, 2022 CarswellOnt 14512 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The lien claimant subcontractor alleged that it, not the original contractor, had performed all of the work required under a renovation contract, and that the contract was equitably assigned to it by the contractor through an oral agreement. No written assignment agreement was executed until over two years later after the claimant had registered both of its claims for lien against the property. Whether the claimant was a “contractor” or a “subcontractor” under the Act bore directly on whether its lien rights had expired by the time the claims for lien were registered. If the claimant was a “subcontractor”, its lien was preserved out of time based on the time of last supply. If it was a “contractor”, then there was a triable issue on the timeliness of its lien based on when the contract was terminated. Nothing in the Act prevented a general contractor, who has been contracted by the owner, from subcontracting with a second general contractor to perform the full scope of the first general contractor's work. While the functional role of the second general contractor would demonstrate all the indicia of a typical general contractor, and it could even be the “constructor” for the purposes of the (ON) <ital>Occupational Health and Safety Act</ital>, absent a contract with the owner or its agent, the second general contractor would still fall within the definition of a “subcontractor” under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Its services and materials would be supplied under an agreement with the first general contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Ravell Investments Ltd." p2="DCLC Developments Ltd." post.rptr="863" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I63cdfcd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravell Investments Ltd. v. DCLC Developments Ltd.">Ravell Investments Ltd. v. DCLC Developments Ltd. (1995), 24 O.R. (3d) 863, 1995 CarswellOnt 833, 23 C.L.R. (2d) 304 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the main subcontract had been augmented by a contract for extras, both involving the same kind of work, the subcontracts were held to have melded into one another for the purposes of calculating the last day on which work was done. A different result might have been reached had the work performed under the two subcontracts been of a dissimilar nature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I55c43c40fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Act takes great pains to differentiate between a “contract” and “subcontract”. In fact, they are mutually exclusive terms.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:21</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Supply of Services</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Northridge Homes Ltd." p2="Sandhu" post.rptr="5689" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63ce23e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northridge Homes Ltd. v. Sandhu">Northridge Homes Ltd. v. Sandhu, 2018 ONSC 5689, 2018 CarswellOnt 16294, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 265 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 2658 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Both supervision and clean-up were set out in the contract and as per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="2615" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I2d23f860f65111ee9732e3e835885970" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2615, 71 O.R. (3d) 732, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 96 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 6441, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 32, [2005] O.J. No. 4831 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5521, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, clean-up services are a supply to an improvement as required by the <ital>Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Toronto Dominion Bank" p2="450477 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4908" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63ce23e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Dominion Bank v. 450477 Ontario Ltd.">Toronto Dominion Bank v. 450477 Ontario Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4908, 2016 CarswellOnt 12434, 65 C.L.R. (4th) 329 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—After an extensive review of the Canadian case law, the master concluded that no authority required a conclusion that equipment repair services are <ital>per se</ital> not lienable. Rather, the most appropriate test for determining whether the subject services are lienable is the functional “nexus” test signaled by the court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd." p2="Valley Ridge Inc." post.rptr="139" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I63ce4af05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc.">M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc. (1993), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 139 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. This test focused on the importance of the work's function to the project, namely whether the construction parties, particularly the owner, considered the subject services necessary for the completion of the project and whether the services benefitted the majority of the contractors and subcontractors. Applied to the facts in issue, repair materials and services, including giant tire repair and replacement services, were held to be lienable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Parma General Contractors Inc." p2="Pulcini" post.rptr="528" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63ce4af15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini">Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini, 2012 ONSC 528, 2012 CarswellOnt 1445, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 145 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—There was a genuine issue for trial relating to whether “site supervision” claimed by the plaintiff fell within the definition of “supply of services” in subsection 1(1) of the <ital>Act</ital>, and the moving defendant failed to discharge its burden to demonstrate otherwise.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dean Construction Co." p2="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4629" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63ce4af25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd.">Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd., 2011 ONSC 4629, 2011 CarswellOnt 8977, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 240 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2011 CarswellOnt 8862 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A claim for standby charges for men and equipment required to be kept on the site as a consequence of the differences in soil conditions from that represented by the owner is no different than charges for the supply of materials, men and equipment for actual work necessitated by the differences in soil conditions or rental equipment kept on site, and can be recovered in a lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gokdenz Construction Ltd." p2="Dalakis" post.rptr="7135" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63ce72005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gokdenz Construction Ltd. v. Dalakis">Gokdenz Construction Ltd. v. Dalakis, 2011 ONSC 7135, 2011 CarswellOnt 13395 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—It is settled law that a claim for tools is not lienable. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The Master referenced <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Fibre Free Technology Co." p2="1062869 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3147" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63ce72015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Fibre Free Technology Co. v. 1062869 Ontario Ltd.">Fibre Free Technology Co. v. 1062869 Ontario Ltd., 1995 CarswellOnt 3147 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, in support of this proposition.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Hugomark Services Inc." p2="Ontario" post.rptr="7033" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63ce72025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hugomark Services Inc. v. Ontario">Hugomark Services Inc. v. Ontario, 2010 ONSC 7033, 2010 CarswellOnt 9777, 99 C.L.R. (3d) 60 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 1147 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Attendance by a lien claimant at two meetings with the defendants to resolve outstanding claims under the contract did not preserve or revive the liens, and did not constitute the supply of services. The attendance did not constitute a direct supply of services to the site or towards an improvement of the site, and had nothing to do with the actual construction, performance of work, or the improvement of the premises that were the subject of the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lewis Builds Corp." p2="Printing Factory Lofts Inc." post.rptr="9436" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I63ce72035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lewis Builds Corp. v. Printing Factory Lofts Inc.">Lewis Builds Corp. v. Printing Factory Lofts Inc., 2008 CarswellOnt 9436 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The claimant provided pre-construction management services including attending design coordination meetings; maintaining a status report on the construction estimate tendering progresses; developing and maintaining a budget control log; developing and maintaining a pre-construction/construction schedule; meeting with consultants, subcontractors and suppliers to assist in developing the design; conducting document reviews at completion of design development and construction documents; site logistics planning; developing Requests for Proposals (RFP's) for elements of the work which would be pre-purchased to assist in design development and/or to ensure that the construction schedule would be met. These pre-construction management services did not meet the definition of the “supply of services” in the Act, which only recognizes intellectual property services as lienable in circumstances where the planned improvement does not proceed to construction. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc." p2="Project 801 Inc." post.rptr="4169" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63ce99105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc.">B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc., 2011 ONSC 4169, 2011 CarswellOnt 6581, 6 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, and related cases discussed under s. 14(1) for a different view of the lienability of construction management services.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="JV Mechanical Ltd." p2="Brewers' Warehousing Stores Ltd." post.rptr="1619" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63ce99115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="JV Mechanical Ltd. v. Brewers' Warehousing Stores Ltd.">JV Mechanical Ltd. v. Brewers' Warehousing Stores Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 1619, 53 C.L.R. (3d) 299 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Collection of monies alleged to be owed does not amount to a supply of services or material to an improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="MHA Contracting Inc." p2="Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="713" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63cec0205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MHA Contracting Inc. v. Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd.">MHA Contracting Inc. v. Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 713, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The services performed by the plaintiff consisted primarily of (1) review of tender documents and calculation of bids; (2) review of blueprints to assess material and labour requirements; (3) communications with suppliers to solicit quotes and coordination of the responses; (4) maintenance of binders at the office containing key project information; (5) preparation of progress billing statements. Occasionally, he signed to accept delivery of parts, or delivered a small part, and once attended the job site to take measurements and to help unload pipes. He often dropped off cheques to a site supervisor on his way home. These latter services represented less than 1 per cent of his time. The court concluded that the work done by the plaintiff was not lienable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353" p2="779857 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2528" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I63cec0215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 v. 779857 Ontario Inc.">I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 v. 779857 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2528, 36 C.L.R. (3d) 48 (Master)</ref></cite>—Where workers attended to hear their foreman assign the work for the day, readied their tools and equipment for the day's work, and cleaned up and packed up their tools and equipment and job boxes, this amounted to “work done” and, was therefore, a “supply of services”. As a result, the lien was preserved in a timely manner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams" p2="AXA Pacific Insurance Co." post.rptr="1443" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63cec0225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Williams v. AXA Pacific Insurance Co.">Williams v. AXA Pacific Insurance Co. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 1443, 2003 CarswellOnt 1263, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 310 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant issued a labour and materials payment bond for the use and benefit of “claimants” in respect of the construction of a mining facility. The plaintiff provided food and services to the employees of the contractor, who was the principal named in the bond. The issue for determination in the action was whether the plaintiff was a “claimant” within the meaning of the bond, although it was not resolved on the basis of whether the plaintiff was entitled to a claim for lien. The bond defined a claimant as one having a direct contract with the principal for labour, material, or both, used or reasonably required for use in the performance of the contract. In fixing its unit prices in its tender the contractor considered as a factor, the estimated cost to provide meals to its personnel together with other factors, such as salary and wages, fuel, equipment lease or finance costs, equipment repair and depreciation, tool acquisitions, administration, overhead, statutory remittances and a margin for profit. There was a specific obligation in the contract to provide accommodation and meals for the contractor's employees in order to assure the ready availability of a work force sufficient to complete the contract on time. The court considered whether the requirement for meals and sleeping accommodation were too remote from what is reasonably required for use in the performance of the contract, and concluded it was not. Meals and incidental services which the contractor was required to provide to its employees were obligations arising under the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="GeoCor Engineering Inc." p2="Kingston 2000 Developments Ltd." post.rptr="5101" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63cee7305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="GeoCor Engineering Inc. v. Kingston 2000 Developments Ltd.">GeoCor Engineering Inc. v. Kingston 2000 Developments Ltd. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 5101, 2003 CarswellOnt 4996, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 107 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Geotechnical reports qualify as a supply of services or improvements under the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re" post.rptr="262" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I63cee7315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re">A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 262, 2002 CarswellOnt 210, 21 C.L.R. (3d) 50 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion to discharge a lien allegedly arising from the supply and installation of an assembly line for manufacturing automotive parts was dismissed as the issue was a genuine issue for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Kreuchen" p2="Parc Savannah Development Ltd." post.rptr="377" pre.rptr="171" ref.id="I63cf0e405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kreuchen v. Parc Savannah Development Ltd.">Kreuchen v. Parc Savannah Development Ltd. (1999), 171 D.L.R. (4th) 377 (B.C. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The lien of a land use consultant, where the development did not proceed to construction, was disallowed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90a3ad60f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 69 O.R. (2d) 334, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Construction management services could not give rise to a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tamma Construction Co." p2="Brault" post.rptr="953" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90a3ad61f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault">Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 953, 25 O.R. (3d) 472, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 124 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The portion of a lien claim found to be attributable to management fees was held not to be the proper subject of a lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Fibre Free Technology Co." p2="1062869 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3799" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63cf35505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Fibre Free Technology Co. v. 1062869 Ontario Ltd.">Fibre Free Technology Co. v. 1062869 Ontario Ltd. (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 3799 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The portion of a lien claim for demolition work relating to “recyclables”, such as wood, steel and kitchen equipment, was held to be not the proper subject of a Claim for Lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Southdale Towers Ltd." p2="Carlton Management Group Inc." post.rptr="233" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I63cf35515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southdale Towers Ltd. v. Carlton Management Group Inc.">Southdale Towers Ltd. v. Carlton Management Group Inc. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 233 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The applicant and the respondent entered into a property management contract pursuant to which the applicant authorized the respondent to lease, manage, repair and maintain the respondent's premises, and appointed the respondent “a sole and exclusive agent.” In the circumstances, the respondent's services in renting units, enforcing leases and purchasing and supplying appliances for the units could not be categorized as services to an improvement for the applicant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd." p2="Valley Ridge Inc." post.rptr="139" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I63cf35525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc.">M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc. (1993), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 139 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A claimant who provided security services for a building project was entitled to a lien against the premises as the work qualified as a “supply of services” under the Act. The services were for the benefit of the project as a whole, and the general contractor derived a benefit as it carried out its contract of construction.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd." p2="Preston Heights Estates Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I63cf5c605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd.">G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd. (1992), 1 C.L.R. (2d) 157 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The claim of a company that provided security services on a construction site was properly the subject of a lien under the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. The claim was allowed because the services were provided entirely on the subject premises during the period of construction, and were therefore of benefit to the contractor, by protecting the site from vandalism. They also protected the interests of lien claimants whose security by way of a lien would be diminished if loss occurred due to vandalism.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Edward Stephens Associates Ltd." p2="G.L. Trenching Ltd." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63cf5c615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edward Stephens Associates Ltd. v. G.L. Trenching Ltd.">Edward Stephens Associates Ltd. v. G.L. Trenching Ltd. (1989), 40 C.L.R. 161, 73 O.R. (2d) 112 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The services of estimating and job supervision fall within the requirements of s. 1(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90a3fb80f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—This definition is broad enough to cover an indirect supplier of services, and applies to a company supplying chemicals to a contractor in their raw state, which chemicals were later combined by that contractor to form an insulation product.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Canario Development Corp." p2="Fitzsimmons, MacFarlane" post.rptr="36" pre.rptr="60" ref.id="I63cf83715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canario Development Corp. v. Fitzsimmons, MacFarlane">Canario Development Corp. v. Fitzsimmons, MacFarlane (1987), 60 O.R. (2d) 36, 48 R.P.R. 311 (S.C.)</ref></cite>—The “services” referred to in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> do not include legal services, which are covered by the <ital>Solicitors Act</ital> and which cannot be the subject of a claim for lien. See also <ital>Instrument No. 309056</ital>—<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Halton, (Re)" post.rptr="1308" pre.rptr="[1987]" ref.id="I63cf83725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Halton, (Re)">Halton, (Re) (1987), [1987] O.J. No. 1308 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>, to the same effect.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Oliver" p2="Muer Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63cf83735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd.">Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd. (1985), 12 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff solicitor was retained to pursue four severance applications and to appear before the Ontario Municipal Board. As a result of his efforts, four lots were created with a residential zoning from one parcel previously zoned open parkland, and the plaintiff registered a claim for lien in respect of the services rendered. The court held that no lien existed. The services performed by the plaintiff did not entitle him to a construction lien. The supply of services must be upon or in respect of an improvement and, in the present case, the legal services were too remote and there was no evidence of any particular planned improvement. They did not have the degree of nexus with an improvement required to fall within the scope of the definition.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Slack Transport Ltd." p2="General Concrete Ltd." post.rptr="640" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I63cfaa805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Slack Transport Ltd. v. General Concrete Ltd.">Slack Transport Ltd. v. General Concrete Ltd. (1983), 9 D.L.R. (4th) 640, 46 O.R. (2d) 255, 1983 CarswellOnt 1432 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1983), 46 O.R. (2d) 255 (note) (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—While the Act creates a lien in favour of a person who performs any service “upon or in respect of” a construction activity being carried out on a work site, the connection that must exist with the construction activity itself is too tenuous and insufficiently direct where the only service performed by the person claiming to be entitled to such a lien is the transportation by that person of construction materials to the work site. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Muscillo Transport Ltd." p2="Bank of Nova Scotia" post.rptr="3239" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I63cfaa815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Muscillo Transport Ltd. v. Bank of Nova Scotia">Muscillo Transport Ltd. v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 3239, [1997] O.J. No. 3584 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1998), 112 O.A.C. 398 (note), 227 N.R. 145 (note), [1997] S.C.C.A. No. 568 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, where the Court of Appeal held that because the language of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was in substance identical to the language of its predecessor, the <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital> [in so far as the supply of services to an improvement was concerned], the court's judgment in <ital>Slack Transport Ltd. v. General Concrete Ltd.</ital> remained definitive.]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:22: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:22</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Wages</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="S.E. Rozell & Sons Inc." p2="Groff" post.rptr="695" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90a449a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="S.E. Rozell & Sons Inc. v. Groff">S.E. Rozell & Sons Inc. v. Groff (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 695, [2000] O.J. No. 707, 2 C.L.R. (3d) 58 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Employer Health Tax contributions, Workers' Compensation assessments, unemployment insurance premiums and the employer's Canada Pension Plan contributions, while monetary contributions, are not “wages” within the meaning of the Act. Such payments are to be characterized as overhead. “Wages” includes vacation pay above the statutory minimum, so long as the payments are reasonable.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:23: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:23</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(1)—Written Notice of a Lien</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Construction Inc." p2="Unimac-United Management Corp." post.rptr="6136" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63cfd1915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp.">Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp., 2016 ONSC 6136, 2016 CarswellOnt 15025, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 17928, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 1(1) establishes four required elements for a “written notice of lien”. It must be given by a person having a lien and it must identify the payer, the premises, and the amount owed by the payer to the person having a lien. The court found that a written notice of lien must also contain a warning to the payer that the dispute has reached the “lien stage”, which was defined by the master as “the stage where the lien claimant is not satisfied with the <ital>status quo</ital> flow of funds and wants it interrupted”. This fifth element, while not contained in the wording of s. 1(1), stems from the master's reading of the word “notice” and the purpose of a written notice of lien. The master found that the primary purpose of a written notice of lien is to stop payment until the lien is satisfied. As such, a written notice of lien must convey the notice giver's intention to preserve the lien and interrupt the existing flow of payment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Hal Mann Tiles Inc." p2="Palmer" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63cff8a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer">Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer (1995), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 61 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The constructive notice rising from the registration on title of a claim for lien does not satisfy the requirement that “written notice of a lien” be “received”. The plain meaning of the word “received”, is actual, physical receipt. While some statutes and rules of practice expand the meaning of “received” by deeming that a document has been received in certain circumstances, that is not the case with s. 24(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd." p2="Shell Canada Products Ltd." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63cff8a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd.">Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A letter from the plaintiff subcontractor to the defendant contractor, allegedly faxed to the owner, stating that the plaintiff intended to proceed with a lien registration, but giving the contractor a further deadline within which to resolve the dispute did not amount to notice for the purposes of s. 24(2). The omission of the amount owed to the Plaintiff was fatal to the written notice. There can be no deviation from the requirement that however and by whatever means notice is given, it must, at a minimum, contain: (a) an identification of the payer and the premises, and (b) the amount that the person has not been paid and is owed to the person by the payer. The decision of Master Saunders is <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I90a497c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> is referred to for the “four ingredients” of notice in writing of a claim for lien. However, the Court in <ital>Andrew Paving</ital> noted that, if anything, the definition of “written notice of a lien” in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is less onerous than the judicial definition of “notice in writing of the lien” as discussed in <ital>Mutic</ital> under <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63d01fb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Here a group of lien claimants argued that registration of the first claim for lien operated as “written notice of a lien” within the meaning of this subsection. The court found the reasoning of the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Town-N-Country Plumbing and Heating (1985) Ltd." p2="Schmidt" post.rptr="716" pre.rptr="86" ref.id="I63d01fb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Town-N-Country Plumbing and Heating (1985) Ltd. v. Schmidt">Town-N-Country Plumbing and Heating (1985) Ltd. v. Schmidt (1991), 86 D.L.R. (4th) 716</ref></cite> to be persuasive and noted a similar result in the Ontario case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Hal Mann Tiles Inc." p2="Palmer" post.rptr="93" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I63d01fb35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer">Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer (1995), 24 O.R. (3d) 93, Master</ref></cite>, in coming to its conclusion that only written notice served on the owner in advance of payment will satisfy the subsection, and then only to the extent of the amount claimed in the notice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I90a4bed0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A drywall subcontractor wrote to a mortgagee to block a final advance. The premises and the parties were identified and the amount owing was stated. No lien was claimed. The mortgagee responded requiring a written direction from the mortgagor. The court followed <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1969" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="Mountview Construction Ltd." post.rptr="515" pre.rptr="67" ref.id="I63d046c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. Mountview Construction Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. Mountview Construction Ltd. (1969), 67 W.W.R. 515, 4 D.L.R. (3d) 203 (Alta. T.D.)</ref></cite> in holding that the notice should contain at least the following four ingredients: an indication of the supply of services or materials to the contractor; a statement that there is an account owed to the subcontractor by the contractor; a statement that the subcontractor is claiming a lien and perhaps will register it unless payment is made; and, a statement as to the amount that the lien will claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The requirement to actually claim a lien in the written notice is supported by <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anglin & Co." p2="Simmons" post.rptr="136" pre.rptr="[1933]" ref.id="I63d06dd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anglin & Co. v. Simmons">Anglin & Co. v. Simmons, [1933] O.W.N. 136, [1933] 2 D.L.R. 794 (C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1923" p1="Sanderson Pearcy & Co." p2="Foster" post.rptr="519" pre.rptr="53" ref.id="I63d06dd15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sanderson Pearcy & Co. v. Foster">Sanderson Pearcy & Co. v. Foster (1923), 53 O.L.R. 519 (C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1900" p1="Craig" p2="Cromwell" post.rptr="585" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I63d06dd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Craig v. Cromwell">Craig v. Cromwell (1900), 27 O.A.R. 585</ref></cite>; and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1943" p1="Dziadus" p2="Sloan" post.rptr="449" pre.rptr="[1943] 3" ref.id="I63d06dd35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dziadus v. Sloan">Dziadus v. Sloan (1943), [1943] 3 W.W.R. 449, 51 Man. R. 236, [1944] 1 D.L.R. 65 (C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:24: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:24</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(2)(a)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19950331" p1="469804 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Royal Plumbing & Heating)" p2="Ontario Hospital Association" ref.id="I63d094e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="469804 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Royal Plumbing & Heating) v. Ontario Hospital Association">469804 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Royal Plumbing & Heating) v. Ontario Hospital Association (March 31, 1995), Court File No. CLA73421/91Q, Master Clark (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The full purchase price of an ice melter, delivered to the site and partially installed prior to the registration of the lien, was held to be lienable. The materials could be liened for before actual installation, but the cost of labour could not be.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:25: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:25</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(2)(b)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd." p2="Schleiss Development Co." post.rptr="5504" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I63d0bbf05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd. v. Schleiss Development Co.">Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd. v. Schleiss Development Co. (2001), [2001] O.J. No. 5504, 2001 CarswellOnt 4906, 15 C.L.R. (3d) 10 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor and supplier delivered portions of the components of a pre-fabricated building to be used to house an ice rink complex. The balance of the building components were never delivered to the lands and remained within the supplier's compound, approximately 100 kilometers from the lands. Although the deliveries of the building components were intended improvements, the purpose of s. 1(2)(b) was to protect against liens for materials warehoused at the controlled locations of suppliers and contractors, and was not applicable to supplies not yet shipped.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
1:26: <editorial.commentary.section date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">1:26</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 1(4)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dalren Limited" p2="Loadstar Trailers Inc." post.rptr="19768" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67202b203b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Dalren Limited v. Loadstar Trailers Inc.">Dalren Limited v. Loadstar Trailers Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 19768, 2024 ONSC 7144 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although the contract to build a manufacturing facility was not signed until December 11, 2020, the procurement process was held to have begun by December 11, 2017, when the plaintiff provided the principal of the defendants with a written “preliminary proposal” to build the facility. The fact that the final location of the proposed facility changed subsequent to delivery of the proposal did not mean that there was more than one improvement. The location of the proposed improvement was inchoate until the final decision was made to build it on its final location, but it was one process for one improvement.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
2:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 2.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">2:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">thresholds at which a contract is considered “substantially performed” increased</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">thresholds at which a contract is deemed to be completed increased</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">new subsection (4) sets out the circumstances in which multiple improvements under a single contract should be treated, for the purposes of the section, as if they were made under separate contracts</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(1) defines “substantial performance” of a “contract” and relates only to the prime contract (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="486" pre.rptr="162" ref.id="I63d1cd605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 486, 39 C.L.R. (2d) 132, 110 O.A.C. 177 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). The precursor of s. 2(1) was the similarly worded s. 1(3) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65. The differences between the present s. 2(1) and the old s. 1(3) are the requirement of a “known defect” in the case of a “correction”, the numerical components of the formula itself and the removal of a “deeming” provision.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(2) permits the determination of substantial performance of a completed portion of the improvement where the completed portion is a “substantial part” of the improvement and is ready for use or is actually being used, and where the remainder of the improvement cannot be completed expeditiously for reasons beyond the contractor's control or by agreement between the owner and the contractor. This subsection was intended to prevent delay in the release of holdback where parts of the works were deferred for good reason. The precursor of this subsection appeared for the first time as s. 1(4) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65.
