The only significant difference between the old s. 1(4) and the present s. 2(2) is the addition in s. 2(2) of the provision allowing the owner and contractor to agree to defer a portion of the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(3) defines “completion” of a “contract” and “last supply” of services and materials. This subsection was first introduced with the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The previous <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> had created some difficulty with its definition of substantial performance by virtue of the fact that it had not defined “contract”. Courts had held that the definition applied to subcontracts as well as contracts (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1975" p1="Union Electric Supply Co." p2="Joice Sweanor—Electric Ltd." post.rptr="227" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I63d1cd615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Union Electric Supply Co. v. Joice Sweanor—Electric Ltd.">Union Electric Supply Co. v. Joice Sweanor—Electric Ltd. (1975), 7 O.R. (2d) 227 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). The Advisory Committee confined the definition to prime contracts so that the release of holdback funds would be expedited. The Committee also revised the amounts in the definition to reflect the depreciation in the value of the dollar and removed the “deeming” provision in order to avoid potential confusion. The Committee included the reference to “known defect”, in order to make it clear that the owner could not delay release of holdback on account of hidden defects.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section describes substantial performance of a construction contract for the purposes of the Act. As a result of the definition of “contract” in s. 1(1), the doctrine of substantial completion only applies to contracts between the owner and the contractor. It does not pertain to subcontracts. To apply the doctrine in that way could hinder the lien claims of suppliers and workers who, unlike the main contractor, often have no way of knowing when a subcontract has been substantially performed. In determining whether substantial completion has been achieved, only “known” defects are to be taken into consideration.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2, including s. 2(3), pertains only to the prime contract; see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="486" pre.rptr="162" ref.id="I63d1f4705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 486, 39 C.L.R. (2d) 132, 110 O.A.C. 177 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. Determination of whether an improvement is “substantially performed” is a factual question in view of the reference to “intention”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(2) permits the determination of substantial performance of the completed portion of an improvement where the completed part is ready for use, or is being used, and the remainder cannot be completed expeditiously for reasons beyond the control of the contractor or by agreement between the owner and contractor. This provision prevents a substantial hold up in the release of the holdback where part of the works are deferred for some good reason.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The question of whether a portion of the improvement is a “substantial part” of the improvement for the purpose of s. 2(2) was dealt with by the Ontario Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Co." p2="JJ's Hospitality Ltd." post.rptr="96" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I63d21b805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd.">Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd. (1996), 30 O.R. (3d) 96, 93 O.A.C. 159 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(3) deals with “completion” as opposed to “substantial performance” of a contract and deems the completion of a contract and the last supply of services and materials to take place when the price of completion, correction of a known defect, or last supply is not more than the lesser of 1 per cent of the contract or $1,000. The scale of modern construction renders this definition almost meaningless.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Interborough Electric Inc." p2="724352 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="5591" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63d21b815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Interborough Electric Inc. v. 724352 Ontario Ltd.">Interborough Electric Inc. v. 724352 Ontario Ltd., 2015 ONSC 5591, 2015 CarswellOnt 14676, 53 C.L.R. (4th) 214 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 2440 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not provide for substantial performance of a subcontract, and therefore the concept of substantial performance applies only to a contractor, not a subcontractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3161" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63d242905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 3161, 2012 CarswellOnt 6816, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 67 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2013 CarswellOnt 7357, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 9258, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Work last performed by the plaintiff was work that had to be completed after all the other trades had finished their work, and was not thereby reduced to mere touch-ups or rectification of deficiencies. The latter would be relevant to the plaintiff's completion date only if it pertained to rectifying its own work, but here it was rectifying deficiencies caused by other trades. The value of the work performed exceeded 1 percent of the contract price, and the contract was therefore not substantially complete at the time of the work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="711121 Ontario Inc." p2="Simkins Homes Ltd." post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I63d242915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="711121 Ontario Inc. v. Simkins Homes Ltd.">711121 Ontario Inc. v. Simkins Homes Ltd. (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 171, 2001 CarswellOnt 573 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a case dealing primarily with implied terms, the Court found insufficient evidence to find an implied term in a subcontract in the siding and home construction industry to the effect that a subcontractor was not to be paid until its work had been completed to the satisfaction of the retail purchaser. The Court held that such a term would also be difficult to reconcile with the “substantial compliance” provisions under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Banca Commerciale Italiana of Canada" p2="Finestkind Homes (Sousa) Inc." post.rptr="2926" pre.rptr="[1996]" ref.id="I63d242925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Banca Commerciale Italiana of Canada v. Finestkind Homes (Sousa) Inc.">Banca Commerciale Italiana of Canada v. Finestkind Homes (Sousa) Inc. (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 2926 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 5143 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 1533 (Ont. C.A.); affirmed (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 161 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In finding that the evidence pointed towards meeting the definition of “substantial performance”, the court noted that (i) the construction costs of the dwelling at issue exceeded the original contract price by approximately $110,000; (ii) the substantial portion of the work that remained to be done on the dwelling was not included in the original contract obligations of the builder; (iii) there were no major items outstanding on the building, and (iv) the amount for which a deficiency claim by a subsequent purchaser was settled strongly suggested that the amount of work outstanding was modest.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="729806 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Tri-Star)" p2="796105 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1436" pre.rptr="[1994]" ref.id="I63d242935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="729806 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Tri-Star) v. 796105 Ontario Ltd.">729806 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Tri-Star) v. 796105 Ontario Ltd. (1994), [1994] O.J. No. 1436, Master</ref></cite>—One of the issues in this case concerned a judicial interpretation of “substantial completion” in the context of an apartment building renovation project where defects in workmanship were evident. When considering the question of “substantial completion” and whether defects bar payment for work, a court can consider, <ital>inter alia</ital>, whether a job is a personal residence or a structure of some special use (<ital>e.g.</ital>, up-scale restaurant, theatre, gallery, museum, or up-scale hotel) that should be accorded recognition by the court or whether the job is ordinary, in this case a multi-unit low income apartment building and the conduct of the parties. An extensive review of the authorities is conducted and payment ordered despite defects that might otherwise have prevented the finding of “substantial completion” necessary for payment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd." p2="F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma)" post.rptr="162" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63d269a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd. v. F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma)">Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd. v. F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma) (1992), 3 C.L.R. (2d) 162 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The contractor entered into a contract with an old age home to add a new wing to the existing complex and to renovate the remaining wings. The contract price was for $3,447,508, with the work being performed in three phases. When the new wing was finished, the architect issued a certificate of substantial completion, and thereafter, approximately $2,700,000 was paid to the contractor and others. After work was finished on some of the remaining wings, a second certificate of substantial completion was issued and $19,827.33 was released for payment. When the contractor was unable to complete the work, several liens were filed, and an action was brought to enforce them. The plaintiffs claimed that the payments made following the issue of the two certificates of substantial completion did not comply with the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and their action was allowed in part. The new wing was being used at the time when the architect's certificate was issued. The remainder of the improvement could not be completed expeditiously for reasons beyond the control of the contractor, not only because the contract provided for three phases but because the release of the wings in phases 2 and 3 to the contractor depended on the speed with which the owner completed the moves and made the vacated wings available. Further, the evidence supported a finding that the parties agreed not to complete the improvements expeditiously. Accordingly, the release of the money after the first certificate of substantial completion was made in accordance with the conditions of s. 2. Moreover, although the certificate did not strictly comply with the rules set out in s. 32, any errors therein were cured by virtue of s. 6 of the Act. The situation was, however, different with respect to the second certificate of substantial completion, since the work on the remaining wings could not be said to be a substantial part of the improvement. Accordingly, the payment made subsequent to the second certificate of substantial completion did not comply with the provisions of s. 2, and the action had to be allowed with respect to the second holdback payment of $19,827.33.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 2(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Beta & Associates" p2="Toronto (City)" post.rptr="328" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63d290b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beta & Associates v. Toronto (City)">Beta & Associates v. Toronto (City), 2015 ONSC 328, 2015 CarswellOnt 354, 42 C.L.R. (4th) 134 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was granted a declaration that the contract for repair of a fountain had been substantially performed, and for payment of a portion of amount claimed in the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sentinel Polymers Canada Inc." p2="Tender Choice Foods Inc." post.rptr="5110" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63d290b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sentinel Polymers Canada Inc. v. Tender Choice Foods Inc.">Sentinel Polymers Canada Inc. v. Tender Choice Foods Inc., 2010 ONSC 5110, 2010 CarswellOnt 7096, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 125 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the cost of rectifying the defects in the resurfacing of a floor exceeded three percent of the contract price, there was not substantial performance of the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90a6baa0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 2(1) does not apply to a subcontractor. See also, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="486" pre.rptr="162" ref.id="I63d2b7c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 486, 40 O.R. (3d) 543, 1998 CarswellOnt 2653 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> for a review of individual definitions and confirming the result in <ital>Canadian Rogers</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 2(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vestacon Limited" p2="ARC Productions Ltd." post.rptr="5366" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63d2b7c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd.">Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd., 2018 ONSC 5366, 2018 CarswellOnt 15345, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 38 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The purpose of section 2(2) of the Act is to expedite release of holdback in extraordinary cases where completion of a contract is delayed beyond the control of the contractor seeking release of holdback. In that event, if the portion of the contract that has been completed can be severed, then a certificate of substantial performance for the completed portion of the contract may be issued and published. If subsection 2(2) of the Act is invoked the total contract price would be reduced by the portion of the contract that cannot be completed expeditiously and then the test for substantial performance would be applied to the balance. However, in the absence of consent of the contracting parties or an inability to complete the contract expeditiously, section 2(2) does not apply. Here, the lien claimant general contractor performed renovations for a tenant renting two properties owned by separate holding corporations, who were in turn owned by a parent company. The tenant subsequently went bankrupt. The contractor sought declarations that three issued certificates of substantial performance were invalid, in order to extend the time period for expiration of the lien. In applying s. 2(2), the Master found that the reason for delay was beyond the contractor's control, but the length of the delay did not constitute an inability to complete the contract work expeditiously. There was no evidence of an agreement between the tenant and contractor to treat the two properties separately for purposes of determining substantial performance.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Echafauds Plus (Laval) Inc." p2="RBG Environmental Inc." post.rptr="4744" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63d2b7c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Echafauds Plus (Laval) Inc. v. RBG Environmental Inc.">Echafauds Plus (Laval) Inc. v. RBG Environmental Inc., 2014 ONSC 4744, 2014 CarswellOnt 11117 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The owner initiated default proceedings under a construction contract after the contractor failed to complete its work by the specified deadline. The parties subsequently reached a new agreement to bring the original contract to an end, to have the holdback and other retained funds paid to the contractor for payment to its trades, and to have the contractor complete the balance of the work for the unearned portion of the original contract price. (The owner determined that using other contractors to finish the work would cost significantly more than the unearned balance of the original contract price.) A “transition agreement” changed the contract price to the value of the work that had been done to that date, stated that the original contract was “completed and terminated”, set the substantial performance date provided for partial payment of the holdback to the contractor. It provided that declarations from the subtrades and suppliers would be obtained giving the same date as the last day of supply. A second construction contract, with the specified scope of work being the unfinished portion of the original contract, was executed. A Certificate of Substantial Performance (“CSP”) was issued using the completion date in the transition agreement. After the owner later terminated the second contract for delays in completion, the subcontractors registered lien claims, which were challenged by the owner as registered too late after issuance of the CSP. The motion was dismissed and the lien claims were allowed. The transition agreement and CSP were not consistent with s. 2(2). There was no credible evidence that any part of the contractor's work was being used or was ready for use for the purpose intended, nor that the purpose of the transition agreement was to delay the uncompleted portion of the original contract. In fact, the purpose of the transition agreement was the commercial convenience of the owner and the contractor. The clear intention of s. 2 was to create certainty for all parties affected by the Act, not only for the basic formula for determining substantial performance in s. 2(1), but also for the exception to the basic formula in s. 2(2). Therefore, pursuant to s. 5(1), a contract amendment to a construction agreement that deletes the unearned portion of the contract price, thereby deeming the contract as substantially completed and triggering the early release of holdback, is not valid unless authorized under s. 2(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Torbear Contracting Inc." p2="Haldimand (County)" post.rptr="5785" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63d2ded05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Torbear Contracting Inc. v. Haldimand (County)">Torbear Contracting Inc. v. Haldimand (County) (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5785, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 273 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6206, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor entered into a contract with the county for the redevelopment of a long-term care facility, with the work to occur in four phases so that existing services could be maintained. The contractor completed the first two phases in April 2006, which represented 92 per cent of the total work, with the last two phases expected to be completed by December 2006. In May 2006, the contractor asked the consultant to issue the certificate of substantial performance and requested release of the holdback. When the consultant denied the request on the grounds that substantial performance of the entire project had not been achieved, the contractor unsuccessfully applied for an order declaring that a portion of work was substantially performed to allow release of holdback. The agreed upon scheduling by phases could not be interpreted as an agreement not to complete the work expeditiously, and had that been their intention, the parties could have specifically addressed certificates of substantial performance with each phase. Section 2(2) refers to an inability to complete the work expeditiously, and while the phrase is not defined in the Act, it must refer to meaningful delay, not something minor or of little significance. There was no evidence to support a finding that the work could not be completed expeditiously, either by reference to the contract, external factors or conduct of the owner. While a liberal interpretation of the statute is warranted, compliance with the provisions in s. 2 is mandatory. This statutory provision cannot be loosely applied as a means to renegotiate the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Carmichael Engineering Ltd." p2="United Colour & Chemicals Ltd." post.rptr="111" pre.rptr="[1997]" ref.id="I63d2ded15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carmichael Engineering Ltd. v. United Colour & Chemicals Ltd.">Carmichael Engineering Ltd. v. United Colour & Chemicals Ltd. (1997), [1997] O.J. No. 111, 1997 CarswellOnt 275 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An ammonia recovery system was deemed to be substantially complete within the meaning of s. 2(2) on or before the date that testing of system was undertaken.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Co." p2="JJ's Hospitality Ltd." post.rptr="4471" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90a708c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd.">Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 4471, 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101, [1993] O.J. No. 1171, 12 O.R. (3d) 351; additional reasons at (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101 <point>at 122</point> (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1995), 19 C.L.R. (2d) 47 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (1996), 30 O.R. (3d) 96, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. J.J.'s Hospitality Ltd.)</ital> 93 O.A.C. 159 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The contractor and owner entered into a stipulated price construction contract, with the work to be performed in stages so that the owner's hotel, and its bar and restaurant, could remain in operation as the construction progressed. Work was commenced on the Pavilion first, but delays were experienced which were largely beyond the control of the contractor. Prior to completion of the work, the municipality issued an occupancy permit authorizing use of the Pavilion, and the Pavilion was turned over to the owner for its intended use six weeks after the latest date called for in the contract. After determining that the remainder of the work could not be expeditiously completed, the contractor applied for certification of substantial perfomance of the Pavilion area, and following inspection the architect signed a certificate of substantial performance with respect to the Pavilion area. The architect then issued the owner a certificate for payment of the holdback for the work certified. The owner paid that amount to the contractor. In late August 1989, the contractor became insolvent and abandoned the contract. The owner then retained another builder to finish the work. A second certificate of substantial performance was subsequently issued with respect to the whole improvement. Several lien claimants questioned the validity of the first certificate of substantial performance, claiming that the first certificate should not have been granted and that the owner was required to holdback not just the amount due with respect to the second certificate of substantial performance, but also an additional amount equal to holdback under the earlier certificate of substantial performance. The court rejected the lien claimants' argument. The value of the work and materials comprising the Pavilion represented 57.2 per cent of the total contract price. The Pavilion was therefore a “substantial part” of the improvement. Moreover, the Pavilion had been turned over to the owner and was being used as intended when the contractor applied for certification of substantial performance. Accordingly, the preconditions to the application of s. 2(2) were properly met. Moreover, since the words “the price of services or materials remaining to be supplied and required to complete the improvement” in s. 2(2) referred to the price of the services or materials necessary to complete the remainder of the entire improvement, whether supplied in whole, in part, or not at all, the architect and the contractor were correct in their computation of the amount of the holdback. In the result, the first certificate of substantial performance was proper and the plaintiffs were entitled to judgment for payment of holdbacks retained by the owner with respect to the second certificate of substantial performance.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Soo Mill</ital> was cited and not followed by the Nova Scotia Supreme Court: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gateway" p2="B.H. Fancy" post.rptr="128" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63d305e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gateway v. B.H. Fancy">Gateway v. B.H. Fancy (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 128, 133 N.S.R. (2d) 70, 380 A.P.R. 70 (S.C.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90a756e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 2(2) does not apply to a subcontractor.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 2(3)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jamrik" p2="2688126 Ont. Inc." post.rptr="2854" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67224e003b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc.">Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 11019, 2024 ONSC 2854, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3654 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The definition of contract “completion” in s. 2(3) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> applies to the entire Act, and not just to the adjudication provisions of the Act. It does not mean different things for the purposes of construction lien claims and adjudication claims. The adjudicator erred in finding that the contract was not “completed” within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> because more than 1% of the contract price was owing and unpaid. The “price of completion” in s. 2(3) of the Act refers to the value of uncompleted work, and not the quantum of disputed payment claims. In coming to a contrary conclusion, the adjudicator misconstrued the plain meaning of the Act, failed to apply settled and longstanding jurisprudence on the meaning of deemed “contract completion” under the Act, and misconceived the scheme of the prompt payment and adjudication provisions of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Scepter Industries Ltd." p2="Georgian Custom Renovations Inc." post.rptr="988" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63d32cf05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Georgian Custom Renovations Inc.">Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Georgian Custom Renovations Inc., 2018 ONSC 988, 2018 CarswellOnt 1901, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 174 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed on other grounds 2019 CarswellOnt 20917 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The “correction of a known defect”, for which the price exceeds $1,000 or 1 percent of the contract, will prevent a contract from being “deemed” complete. When the shortcomings or defects are more substantial in nature, they constitute part of what it means to complete the “contract”. It is not merely a question of whether something is characterized as a “repair” or “deficiency”. The assessment is more contextual and must be assessed having regard to the contract as a whole. If the deficiencies or defects are more substantial in nature, and go to the core of what it means to “complete” the contract, the contract is not complete. In this case, where the owner was holding back more than 60 percent of the contract price for non-compliance, it could not suggest that the contract was complete.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Provincial Partitions Ltd." p2="Toronto (City)" post.rptr="2839" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63d354005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Provincial Partitions Ltd. v. Toronto (City)">Provincial Partitions Ltd. v. Toronto (City), 2015 ONSC 2839, 2015 CarswellOnt 6264, 48 C.L.R. (4th) 158 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—For the reasons given by Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90a756e1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the threshold calculation in s. 2(3) of the Act applies to contractors' liens but not to subcontractors' liens.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Martin Creek Construction Ltd." p2="Emelko" post.rptr="485" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63d354025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Martin Creek Construction Ltd. v. Emelko">Martin Creek Construction Ltd. v. Emelko, 2014 ONSC 485, 2014 CarswellOnt 947, 30 C.L.R. (4th) 272 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Attendance by a subcontractor's technician at the work site for three hours to install an exhaust hood and to talk to homeowners, billed out at less than $1,000, did not operate to extend the time for completion of the contract. The contract was deemed complete pursuant to s. 2(3) prior to the attendance, and the plaintiff's claim for lien was not preserved within the time required by the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Micon Interiors General Contractors Inc." p2="D'Abbondanza Enterprises Inc." post.rptr="6156" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I90a77df0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Micon Interiors General Contractors Inc. v. D'Abbondanza Enterprises Inc.">Micon Interiors General Contractors Inc. v. D'Abbondanza Enterprises Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 6156, 76 C.L.R. (3d) 289, [2008] O.J. No. 4132 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The law is clear that work required to be done by a contractor to repair a defect in its work, or in that of any of its sub-trades, cannot be relied on to extend the time for registering a lien. Such work cannot be considered “completion work” under s. 2(3). The reference in s. 2(3) to the supply of services or materials required for the “correction of a known defect” does not include work required to correct a defect or deficiency in the contractor's own work or the work of his sub-contractors but rather, refers to the correction of work done by others for whom he is not legally responsible but which correction work is done at the request of the owner as an extra to its own contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Riddell Contracting Ltd." p2="2004778 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3819" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I63d37b105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Riddell Contracting Ltd. v. 2004778 Ontario Inc.">Riddell Contracting Ltd. v. 2004778 Ontario Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 3819, 31 C.L.R. (3d) 209, [2003] O.J. No. 3916 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor undertook the installation of a boiler system, refrigeration repairs and sheet metal work services on the property, and argued that its arrangement with the owner was a prevenient arrangement and therefore, the “deemed completion” rule under s. 2(3) of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not apply. The court was not persuaded. There was one contract that related to the boiler installation, and the plaintiff also provided ongoing service and maintenance. It could not be concluded that the minor service work the plaintiff provided subsequently constituted separate contracts linking that work to the original and substantial work done previously. The bulk of the plaintiff's lien claim was not within the 45-day time limit.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Eng" post.rptr="2839" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I90a77df1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd. v. Eng">Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd. v. Eng (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 2839, 48 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 45 O.R. (3d) 795, [1999] O.J. No. 3404 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The deeming provisions of s. 2(3) of the Act do not apply to prevenient arrangements. The law of prevenient arrangements, enunciated by the Supreme Court of Canada in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1954" p1="Menzies & Herbert Ltd." p2="Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590" post.rptr="74" pre.rptr="1954" ref.id="I90a7a500f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590">Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590 (1954), 1954 CarswellAlta 74, [1955] 1 D.L.R. 161, [1954] S.C.R. 589 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, was not repealed, altered or varied by the enactment of s. 2(3) in 1983, nor has there been any derogation from the <ital>Rocky Mountain</ital> decision since 1983. As a result, in the <ital>Wood Lumber</ital> case, the time periods set out in s. 31 and s. 36 of the Act do not commence until the last materials were supplied to the project.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="486" pre.rptr="162" ref.id="I63d3a2205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 486, 40 O.R. (3d) 543, 1998 CarswellOnt 2653 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—For the purposes of s. 2(3) the word “contract” can only refer to the contract between the contractor and the owner. Thus, the “deeming” provisions of s. 2(3) cannot be said to apply to subcontracts.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd." p2="Redesco Inc." post.rptr="148" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63d3a2215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd. v. Redesco Inc.">Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd. v. Redesco Inc. (1993), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 148 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Having regard to the presence of the phrase “to supply services or materials to an improvement” in the definition of “contractor” and of the phrase “for services or materials supplied to an improvement” in s. 31(2)(a) and (b), it was clear that s. 2(3) was to be interpreted as being limited to contracts or dealings between the owner and the contractor. Accordingly, s. 2(3) did not apply to subcontractors, and there was no basis upon which to find that the subcontractors' claims were out of time.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I55c9ba80fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The term “<ital>improvement</ital>” is meant to be a term of art under this definition. It is the project designed and to be undertaken as between the owner and general contractor, whether it be a new building or some mere alteration, addition or repair. It cannot be seriously said to embrace subcontracts as such. Thus, the use of this term of art, “improvement,” in both s. 2(1) and s. 2(3) is a strong indicator that s. 2, in each of its subsections, was only intended to deal with and control the general contract and not subcontracts.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90a7cc11f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 2(3) does not apply to a subcontractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="R.T. Grant Construction Ltd." p2="Ross" post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63d3f0405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R.T. Grant Construction Ltd. v. Ross">R.T. Grant Construction Ltd. v. Ross (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 302 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In ruling that the registration of the plaintiff's claim for lien was timely, the court accepted the plaintiff's evidence as to the date that he returned to complete his contract, and found the plaintiff to be well within the required time period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Extender Products Ltd." p2="Patrick Harrison & Co." post.rptr="8" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63d3f0415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Extender Products Ltd. v. Patrick Harrison & Co.">Extender Products Ltd. v. Patrick Harrison & Co. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 8 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Section 2(3) does not refer to third persons who supply materials to a contractor. The deeming provision would therefore only apply to materials and services supplied by the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Smith" p2="Angus" post.rptr="113" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63d3f0425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Smith v. Angus">Smith v. Angus (1988), 31 C.L.R. 113 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—When a contract is over 99 per cent performed, the period in which a lien may be filed to protect a contractor must start to run. To allow the contractor to have extended protection by virtue of a claim being made against him for alleged deficiencies is contrary to the purpose and intent behind s. 2 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Trane Canada Inc." p2="George Evans Co." post.rptr="18" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63d3f0435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trane Canada Inc. v. George Evans Co.">Trane Canada Inc. v. George Evans Co. (1986), 22 C.L.R. 18 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The reading of this subsection may refer both to the completion of the contract and to all other persons who last supply services and/or materials, and may include the subcontractors who supply services and/or materials. This subsection can be construed in two parts; namely, when a contract shall be deemed to be completed, specifically relating to the owner and contractor, and situations relating to all other persons who last supply sevices and/or materials. The word “and” within the subsection may be interpreted to be disjunctive as opposed to conjunctive, so that services and/or materials need not necessarily complement the word “contract” within the subsection.</para.text></para><head align="l" date.trace="20250528" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 2(4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Caledon (Town)" p2="2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction" post.rptr="4555" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I672338603b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Caledon (Town) v. 2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction">Caledon (Town) v. 2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction, 2024 ONSC 4555, 2024 CarswellOnt 12799 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 2(4) presupposes that more than one improvement may be the subject matter of a contract, but it does not state, or imply, that a contract is presumed to be in respect of a single improvement. Nor does it state, or imply, that there is such a presumption unless it is displaced by contract. Unlike all the other subsections of this provision, it does not apply “for the purposes of this Act” but rather “for the purposes of this section” and addresses a particular problem that arises where a contract is in respect to more than one improvement: establishing the date of substantial completion of the contract. In this subsection, the Legislature has provided that substantial completion will arise on an improvement-by-improvement basis if the parties to the contract have so agreed by their contract. By necessary implication, substantial completion of the contract will be determined by reference to all improvements that are the subject of the contract if the parties have not agreed to the contrary in the contract. The provision does not change or modify the nature of what an “improvement” is under the Act, and it does not provide that “improvement” is co-extensive with “contract”.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
3:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 3.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">3:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 3(1) specifies that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> binds the provincial Crown. By virtue of s. 3(2), the Act does not apply to provincial road construction contracts as defined by the <ital>Ministry of Transportation and Communications Creditors Payment Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 290 (“the MTCCP”). Section 3(3) excludes from the Act the notice requirements of any action against the provincial Crown specified under the <ital>Proceedings Against the Crown Act</ital>. These provisions were first introduced by <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1975</ital>, S.O. 1975, c. 43, on July 3, 1975. Until that date, the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> did not bind the provincial Crown.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 3, which must be read in conjunction with s. 16 (liens that do not attach to the land), defines the applicability of the Act to Crown interests. The application of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is specifically extended to the Crown in right of Ontario, but as it is provincial legislation, it cannot and does not bind the federal Crown. This Act's provisions with respect to the limitations of a contractor's liability to non-privies are, however, incorporated by reference into the federal Crown's standard form labour and material payment bond.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Pursuant to s. 3(2), the Act does not apply to provincial road construction contracts as defined in the <ital>Ministry of Transportation and Communications Creditors Payment Act</ital>. In addition, pursuant to s. 3(3), s. 7 of the <ital>Proceedings against the Crown Act</ital>, which requires notice to the Crown of any pending action, does not apply to actions brought under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> with respect to the limited number of actions against the provincial Crown contemplated by the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 3 at one time contained a prohibition against liens by architects and holders of certificates of practice under the <ital>Architects Act</ital>. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Carruthers & Wallace Ltd." p2="Mathers & Haldenby Inc." post.rptr="275" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I63d465705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carruthers & Wallace Ltd. v. Mathers & Haldenby Inc.">Carruthers & Wallace Ltd. v. Mathers & Haldenby Inc. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 275, 26 O.R. (3d) 593 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd." p2="Carleton University" post.rptr="120" pre.rptr="23" ref.id="I63d465715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Carleton University">H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Carleton University (1995), 23 O.R. (3d) 120, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 129 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, the courts held that engineer “subcontractors” of architects had lien rights even though their payer may not, but only for services that were not “architectural” in nature. As a result, by a statute entitled the <ital>Government Process Simplification Act (Ministry of the Attorney General), 1997</ital>, S.O. 1997, c. 23, s. 4, the government extended lien rights to architects, holders of certificates of practice under the <ital>Architects Act</ital> and their employees. These rights arose in relation to contracts made after royal assent, which occurred on November 28, 1997.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Snowmont Investments Corp." p2="Elliott" post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="153" ref.id="I63d465725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott">Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott (1997), 153 D.L.R. (4th) 305, 1997 CarswellOnt 4333, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 240 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The history of the statute and, particularly, the court's jurisdiction over liens and lien actions is carefully considered in this case.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 3(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Comstock Canada Ltd." p2="Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd." post.rptr="112" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I63d48c805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Comstock Canada Ltd. v. Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd.">Comstock Canada Ltd. v. Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 112 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It is not permissible to file a lien under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> against lands that house nuclear facilities. To do so would affect a vital part of a federally regulated enterprise. The ownership of the lands subject to the lien is an essential and integral part of the nuclear facility enterprise.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Standard Industries" p2="Toronto-Dominion Bank" post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63d48c815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Standard Industries v. Toronto-Dominion Bank">Standard Industries v. Toronto-Dominion Bank (1989), 34 C.L.R. 66, 68 O.R. (2d) 303 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs received 75 per cent of their valid claims through the procedures set out in the <ital>Ministry of Transportation and Communications Creditors Payment Act</ital>, and sought to obtain the remainder of the claim under the trust fund established pursuant to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The court dismissed their action. If the plaintiffs were entitled to claim pursuant to the <ital>MTCCP Act</ital> and the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, two procedures would be in operation at the same time creating confusion, expense and possible unfairness. Secondly, the general contractor could avoid the obligations which he had assumed by contracting out all of the work to be performed.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
4:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 4.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">4:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 4 specifies that no one can contract out of the applicability or remedies of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Such “agreements” are rendered “void”. This section was first introduced in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. Section 6 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 had allowed parties to expressly agree not to have lien rights. This provision was of long standing, originating in the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> of 1873. Even as early as 1896, however, the <ital>Act</ital> rendered void any agreement by a “workman” making less than $50 a day that the Act did not apply. As a result, “waivers of lien” are neither stipulated for nor sought by owners settling up contract balances.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Courts have been careful not to void partially performed agreements that contravene s. 4 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. For instance, “pay when paid” would appear to undermine a person's right to register a claim for lien within the time periods given by the Act. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Kor-Ban Inc." p2="Pigott Construction Ltd." post.rptr="160" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I55caa4e0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Kor-Ban Inc. v. Pigott Construction Ltd.">Kor-Ban Inc. v. Pigott Construction Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 160 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (September 29, 1995), Doc. 11819/89 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, the court held that a “pay when paid” clause rendered non-payment by the owner a true condition precedent to the subcontractor's entitlement. The court held that there was no contravention of the Act since the subcontractor still had the right to file a lien. Another example is the mandatory arbitration, choice of jurisdiction and choice of law languages, which may have the effect of denying lien claimants full access to the procedures and remedies of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Courts have consistently avoided applying s. 4 to render such agreements void (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="Bracknell Corp." post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63d4daa15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp. (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 171 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1993), 12 B.L.R. (2d) 113, 110 D.L.R. (4th) 390 (Ont. Gen. Div. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="E.S. Fox Ltd." post.rptr="35" pre.rptr="19" ref.id="I63d4daa25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. E.S. Fox Ltd.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. E.S. Fox Ltd. (1995), 19 C.L.R. (2d) 35 (Ont. Gen. Div. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="KEB Hana as Trustee" p2="Mizrahi Commercial (THE ONE) LP et al." post.rptr="3928" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6723fbb03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="KEB Hana as Trustee v. Mizrahi Commercial (THE ONE) LP et al.">KEB Hana as Trustee v. Mizrahi Commercial (THE ONE) LP et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 3928, 2024 ONSC 1678, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1128 (Ont. S.C.J. [Comm List])</ref></cite>—The Receiver successfully moved under the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> for a lien regularization order and a construction continuance order. The order was fair and reasonable since the rights granted to lien claimants were substantively consistent with those granted under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, with the result that they were not prejudiced by the order. No element of the provincial lien legislation regime was being circumvented or compromised, but was being complied with, or deemed to have been complied with, on a streamlined basis. The lien regularization order had the effect of removing the requirement for each lien of bringing a motion to lift the stay, filing, perfecting, and registering that lien and then vacating that lien upon the posting of security. It maximized value for the benefit of all stakeholders and, in a way, that did not prejudice the rights of any lien claimant. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: A “lien regularization order” is a tool used in bankruptcy and <ital>Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act</ital> proceedings to provide a mechanism for managing statutory lien rights in the insolvency context by creating a streamlined scheme that replaces the <ital>Construction Act</ital>'s requirements in favour of an alternative framework overseen by the courts. Such an order will generally provide for a stay of lien registration, preservation or perfection, and provide rights equivalent to protections mandated under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. A construction continuance order is designed, in cases of insolvency and receivership, to promote a smooth transition of construction management and ensure that the project continues without significant interruption.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd." p2="OHL Construction Canada" post.rptr="7505" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63d501b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada">Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada, 2013 ONSC 7505, 2013 CarswellOnt 18456, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 213 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 3763, 2014 CarswellOnt 8361, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 223 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In complex litigation related to construction of a subway extension to York University, the plaintiff subcontractor successfully sought to stay its own lien action after delivering a notice of arbitration to the defendant contractor. A claimant should not have to forego its lien rights simply because the dispute is subject to an arbitration agreement. A plaintiff can, in appropriate circumstances, effectively move for the interim stay of a portion of a construction lien action, and can move to have its own lien action stayed to permit a contractual arbitration to take place. The arbitral issues incorporated into the lien proceeding can be stayed until the completion of the arbitration. Although s. 7(2)4 of the <ital>Arbitration Act</ital> (ON) permitted a Court to refuse to implement arbitration proceedings where it could be demonstrated that there was “undue delay” on the part of the party seeking to invoke the arbitration clause, the Master was satisfied that the litigious steps taken by the lien claimant were in response to the defendant contractor's attack on the claimant's statutory lien rights prior to delivery of the notice of mediation and arbitration. These steps were necessary and justified to preserve its lien rights and avoid any attempt at a summary dismissal. Despite the complexity of the litigation, and the possibility of a multiplicity of actions involving parties not involved in the arbitration, the Master determined that arbitration was the most efficient route to narrow the issues and that that the parties necessary for a timely resolution of the construction lien claim would be at the table. The stay expressly allowed the plaintiff to obtain an order referring the matter to the Master at Toronto for trial, or to otherwise set the matter down for trial, in order to avoid the expiry of the lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Varcon Construction Co." p2="1554098 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="43" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63d501b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Varcon Construction Co. v. 1554098 Ontario Inc.">Varcon Construction Co. v. 1554098 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONCA 43, 2012 CarswellOnt 476, 11 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirming 2011 ONSC 1649, 2011 CarswellOnt 1720, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 162 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor negotiated two construction contracts with the numbered company. After the plaintiff experienced difficulties in obtaining payment, the parties eventually negotiated a settlement agreement designed to guarantee payment by way, <ital>inter alia</ital>, of an additional guarantee by one of the corporate defendants and consent to judgment. The trial court found that the construction agreements were merged into the settlement agreement, that the plaintiff no longer had a claim in breach of contract, and that, consistent with the remedial purpose of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and with sections 4 and 5 of the Act that prevent parties from contracting out of its provisions, the statutory trust created by s. 7(1) of the Act survived the settlement agreement. The defendant's appeal on the issue of breach of trust was dismissed, but the Court of Appeal held that the trial judge erred in finding that the effect of the settlement agreement was to extinguish the defendant's liability to the plaintiff, and allowed the plaintiff's cross-appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tricin Electric Ltd." p2="York Region District School Board" post.rptr="2452" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I63d501b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tricin Electric Ltd. v. York Region District School Board">Tricin Electric Ltd. v. York Region District School Board, 2009 CarswellOnt 2452, 82 C.L.R. (3d) 237 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The negotiation, mediation and arbitration protocol under a construction contract was invoked for the first time after lien litigation involving three actions was commenced, but the litigation raised several issues outside of those contemplated by the terms of the contract and, therefore, the ambit of the arbitration clause. In the circumstances, s. 106 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> favoured allowing the litigation to proceed, rather than imposing a stay in favour of arbitration of only one or two issues in one of three actions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd." p2="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." post.rptr="892" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63d528c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc.">H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 892, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 305 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was the amount of the holdback properly retained by the owner hospital, which claimed payments made to the contractor in trust to be paid to other contractors should have been deducted from its holdback liability and that the plaintiff was estopped from arguing that the hospital should not be given any credit towards the holdback. Estoppel could not arise in circumstances where a statute provided mandatory terms. The legal relationship in matters involving construction contracts was governed not only by the contract between the parties, but also by operation of statute. While estoppel might apply on those parts of the contract, which were not effected by the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, they could not apply to permit waiver out of the statutory provisions. The payments made, while they could certainly be applied towards any amount outstanding between the parties, could not be considered to be a reduction in the amount of holdback required. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Gencon Construction Ltd. (Trustee of)" p2="M & Y Construction Ltd." post.rptr="148" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63d528c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gencon Construction Ltd. (Trustee of) v. M & Y Construction Ltd.">Gencon Construction Ltd. (Trustee of) v. M & Y Construction Ltd. (1988), 48 R.P.R. 148 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, did not apply as the Master specifically noted that he based his decision there on other grounds and noted “…I do not wish to decide whether such estoppel by representation can be effected where a party is asserting rights given by statute.”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Monaco Electric Ltd." p2="Empire Myers Road Inc." post.rptr="713" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63d54fd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Monaco Electric Ltd. v. Empire Myers Road Inc.">Monaco Electric Ltd. v. Empire Myers Road Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 713, 2004 CarswellOnt 773, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 270 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contracts stated that any liens that might arise under the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> were to arise on a lot-by-lot basis. The clauses were not exclusionary clauses. S. 20(2) was applicable. The contract only determined the manner in which the lien(s) were to be registered, and did not deprive the claimant of a right to a construction lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Downsview Contracting Ltd." p2="768068 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Kinwood Homes)" post.rptr="2819" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63d54fd15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Downsview Contracting Ltd. v. 768068 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Kinwood Homes)">Downsview Contracting Ltd. v. 768068 Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Kinwood Homes) (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2819, 1998 CarswellOnt 2656 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The court considered the case of an alleged partnership for the development of a parcel of land. Section 4 was relied on in part, to defeat the allegation of partnership.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="E.S. Fox Ltd." post.rptr="35" pre.rptr="19" ref.id="I63d54fd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. E.S. Fox Ltd.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. E.S. Fox Ltd. (1995), 19 C.L.R. (2d) 35 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A subcontractor supplying electrical services and materials brought an action against the contractor relating to extra materials and labour provided to the contractor in the course of performing the contract. It was a term of the printed form subcontract that arbitration was to be the exclusive mechanism for the resolution of claims not settled by the contractor and the court action and referring the matter to arbitration. The dispute constituted a claim within the meaning of the subcontract, and the arbitration obligation survived the completion of the subcontract as well as its fundamental breach.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Applied Insulation Co." p2="Megatech Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="251" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63d576e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Applied Insulation Co. v. Megatech Contracting Ltd.">Applied Insulation Co. v. Megatech Contracting Ltd. (1994), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 251 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A “pay when paid” defence, as provided for in a subcontract, did not apply where the defendant contractor was in default and the plaintiff subcontractor had not caused or contributed in any way to the defendants' inability to meet its financial obligations.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="Bracknell Corp." post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63d576e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp. (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 171 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1993), 12 B.L.R. (2d) 113, 110 D.L.R. (4th) 390 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where an agreement between a contractor and subcontractor provided that any claims arising under it would be arbitrated and that such arbitration would be held in Missouri in accordance with Missouri law, the parties should be held to their agreement and the courts should defer to the arbitrators.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Kor-Ban Inc." p2="Pigott Construction Ltd." post.rptr="160" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63d576e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kor-Ban Inc. v. Pigott Construction Ltd.">Kor-Ban Inc. v. Pigott Construction Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 160 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A clause in a subcontract stating that the general contractor is not required to pay a subcontractor until payment from the owner is received by the general contractor, specifies the condition governing the contractor's legal entitlement to payment, and not merely the time of payment. Where such a payment clause existed, payment to the general contractor by the owner was a condition precedent to the contractor's obligation to pay the subcontractor, and until such payment had been made, the subcontractor did not have a cause of action against the general contractor. However, because the payment clause did not affect the subcontractor's right to file a lien, it did not contravene the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="H.H. Robertson Inc." p2="861330 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3085" pre.rptr="[1992]" ref.id="I63d576e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.H. Robertson Inc. v. 861330 Ontario Inc.">H.H. Robertson Inc. v. 861330 Ontario Inc. (1992), [1992] O.J. No. 3085 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A contractor's “pay when paid” clause does not mean that money paid into court by the owner must be paid out to the contractor before any amount could be lienable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Gencon Construction Ltd. (Trustee of)" p2="M & Y Construction Ltd." post.rptr="148" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63d59df05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gencon Construction Ltd. (Trustee of) v. M & Y Construction Ltd.">Gencon Construction Ltd. (Trustee of) v. M & Y Construction Ltd. (1988), 48 R.P.R. 148 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The general contractor of a project made a voluntary assignment in bankruptcy, and the trustee in bankruptcy sought to complete the project. It contacted the subcontractors and, with their approval, drafted an order providing for a scheme of payment for the subcontractors to finish the project. Each of the subcontractors was requested not to file any construction liens against the project and, to this end, two subcontractors released liens they had previously filed. The respondent, however, alleged that s. 4 of the Act prohibited it from waiving its lien rights under the Act. The Master held that the purpose of s. 4 is to prevent those in a position to offer employment from extracting a waiver of lien rights from those in an inferior bargaining position. In this case, the mischief the provision sought to prevent was not present as there was a group of persons all agreeing to relinquish their lien rights. The respondent initially agreed with the order and relied upon and benefited from it. In doing so, the respondent induced the other subcontractors to enter into the agreement. Furthermore, the trustee, as an officer of the court is under a duty to hold and distribute money on an equitable basis. The conflict between his duty and the legislation must be resolved by the paramountcy of the trustee's duty to act in an honest, fair and moral manner.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
5:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 5.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">5:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 5 is a companion to s. 4 and deems contracts to be amended insofar as is necessary to be in conformity with the Act. Section 5(1) dates from the 1983 Act. The previous <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> did not contain such a blanket amending provision. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 54, s. 6 introduced for the first time a provision that deemed every contract to be amended so as to conform to the holdback provisions, but no more. Section 5(2) dates from the <ital>Construction Lien Amendment Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 77, s. 3.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Advisory Committee deemed s. 5(1) necessary to avoid the result that an entire agreement would be rendered unenforceable on the grounds of illegality. This provision was included to ensure that the compliant portions of agreements continued. Section 5(1) has indeed been used by courts to avoid the severe result of rendering “void” an entire contract that may undermine remedies provided by the Act. Section 5(2) concerns the specific case of an agreement of purchase and sale deeming it to be amended to allow the purchaser to retain holdback.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Echafauds Plus (Laval) Inc." p2="RBG Environmental Inc." post.rptr="4744" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63d5c5005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Echafauds Plus (Laval) Inc. v. RBG Environmental Inc.">Echafauds Plus (Laval) Inc. v. RBG Environmental Inc., 2014 ONSC 4744, 2014 CarswellOnt 11117 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 5(1) applies to all construction contracts, and is a clear restriction on the freedom to contract in a way that is not in conformity with the Act. Therefore, pursuant to s. 5(1), a contract amendment to a construction agreement that deletes the unearned portion of the contract price, thereby deeming the contract as substantially completed and triggering the early release of holdback, is not valid unless authorized under s. 2(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bradhill Masonry Inc." p2="Simcoe County District School Board" post.rptr="4708" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63d5ec105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bradhill Masonry Inc. v. Simcoe County District School Board">Bradhill Masonry Inc. v. Simcoe County District School Board, 2013 ONSC 4708, 2013 CarswellOnt 9684, 24 C.L.R. (4th) 253 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 12638, 24 C.L.R. (4th) 277 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2015 ONSC 2963, 2015 CarswellOnt 8852, 47 C.L.R. (4th) 300 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—When a sub-trade has done work for which it had not been paid, it has a potential lien for “the price of those services or material” under s. 14 of the Act, regardless if whether, under a technical interpretation of the contract, nothing was owing and payable to the sub-trade as of the date the lien was registered. To hold otherwise would mean that the contract terms regarding timing of payment would take precedence over the legislation, and that if a sub-trade filed a claim for lien at the wrong time, its lien would be worthless even though the tradesperson had not been fully paid for their work and materials supplied to the job.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Kor-Ban Inc." p2="Pigott Construction Ltd." post.rptr="160" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63d5ec115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kor-Ban Inc. v. Pigott Construction Ltd.">Kor-Ban Inc. v. Pigott Construction Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 160 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A clause in a subcontract, stating that the general contractor is not required to pay a subcontractor until payment from the owner is received by the general contractor, did not contravene the Act, because the payment clause did not affect the subcontractor's right to file a lien.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">section 32(5) (manner of publication of certificate of substantial performance) was removed from the scope of section 6</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">new section 6(2) lists examples of curable minor errors or irregularities</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The scheme of this so-called “curative” section was radically altered by the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. The previous provision, s. 19 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, had required only “substantial compliance” with the statutory requirements of the claim for lien and the procedural aspects of a lien action. Furthermore, s. 19 specified that no lien would be invalidated by reason of a failure to substantially comply with those provisions, unless prejudice could be proven and then only to the extent of the proven prejudice. This liberal curative provision had been introduced as early as 1896 and had remained virtually unchanged until 1983. The case law gave courts a broad curative discretion. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1980" p1="North York Steel Fabricators Ltd." p2="Hamilton (City)" post.rptr="456" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I63d63a305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="North York Steel Fabricators Ltd. v. Hamilton (City)">North York Steel Fabricators Ltd. v. Hamilton (City) (1980), 27 O.R. (3d) 456 (Ont.
