C.A.)</ref></cite>, for instance, the Ontario Court of Appeal held that the section gave the court a discretion to uphold a claim for lien even when there was no substantial compliance with the statutory requirements. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1979" p1="Nor-Min Supplies Ltd." p2="Canadian National Railway" post.rptr="390" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I63d661405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nor-Min Supplies Ltd. v. Canadian National Railway">Nor-Min Supplies Ltd. v. Canadian National Railway (1979), 27 O.R. (2d) 390 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> the Court of Appeal used this <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> section to uphold a claim for lien that had been registered on the wrong property. The Attorney General's Committee Report found that such a broad discretion conflicted with the technical and complex nature of the statutory remedy and recommended that the court's discretion be limited to minor irregularities only. As a result, s. 6 adopts no general standard of statutory interpretation or judicial discretion and operates in specific circumstances only, and even then only where there has been a failure to strictly comply. Read properly, the section actually limits the court's general power to cure defects.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In the early years of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, courts were inclined to view that s. 6 reserved to the courts a general curative power where no prejudice was established (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19861120" p1="Allied Fasteners & Supplies Ltd." p2="Ferris (No. 1)" ref.id="I63d661415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Allied Fasteners & Supplies Ltd. v. Ferris (No. 1)">Allied Fasteners & Supplies Ltd. v. Ferris (No. 1) (November 20, 1986), Galligan J. (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> Kirsh's Construction Case Finder, No. 6.6). Now s. 6 is rigidly limited and does not grant a general curative power, even where no prejudice is found (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Guillevin International Inc." p2="Enertech Lighting Systems Inc." post.rptr="245" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I55cc2b80fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc.">Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 245, 19 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The claim for lien of a corporation that did not exist at the time of the contract was held invalid and no relief was granted under s. 6 (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Triple “R” Demolition Inc." p2="1186468 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="125" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63d688505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Triple “R” Demolition Inc. v. 1186468 Ontario Ltd.">Triple “R” Demolition Inc. v. 1186468 Ontario Ltd. (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 125 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). Even where it applies, there is no discretion in s. 6 to grant relief from other than minor irregularities (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-City Flooring Co." p2="Quatrosense Environmental Ltd." post.rptr="744" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63d688515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd.">Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd. (1991), 3 O.R. (3d) 744, 49 C.L.R. 319 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). What is found to be a minor irregularity varies from case to case. For instance, a claim for lien on the wrong premises has been held to be both curable and non-curable under s. 6 (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Ambler-Courtney Inc." p2="CAAG Land Development Ltd." post.rptr="58" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I63d688525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ambler-Courtney Inc. v. CAAG Land Development Ltd.">Ambler-Courtney Inc. v. CAAG Land Development Ltd. (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 58 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1593095 Ontario Ltd. (Northwood Window and Door Centre)" p2="McCann" post.rptr="163" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I672582503b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="1593095 Ontario Ltd. (Northwood Window and Door Centre) v. McCann">1593095 Ontario Ltd. (Northwood Window and Door Centre) v. McCann, 2024 CarswellOnt 207, 2024 ONSC 163, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3229 (Ont.S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Whether the last day of supply was several days later than the date set out in the claim for lien was held to be of no practical consequence. The lien was properly registered within 45 days of either of the relevant days and the lien was perfected within 90 days of any of the dates. The defendants were not prejudiced by this slight inaccuracy, and the lien was not void for this irregularity.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gandhi" p2="Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="5490" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I4a1eb6e05c3e11f0930ac66992ce991e" title="Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd.">Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 5490, 2024 ONSC 2184, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3698 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 8126, 2024 ONSC 3095 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The claim for lien appeared to erroneously set out an earlier date for last supply, such that the lien was held by the motion judge to be expired. Screenshots of a WhatsApp discussion confirmed a later date that would render the lien valid. The appeal was allowed and the motion to strike the claim for lien and to return the lien bond was dismissed. With respect to the earlier date set out in the claim for lien, absent a formal judicial admission and an applicable special standard, like Rule 51, the date in a claim for lien form had no special status requiring especially “powerful evidence” to rebut it. In the absence of prejudice, s. 6 provided that a claim for lien is not defeated by reason only that there has not been strict compliance with the requirement to disclose the dates of supply of services.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="3458" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6725a9613b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 266 (Ont. S.C.J.); varied 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The court found that there were two separate subcontracts, one for supply and installation of structural steel and one for supply and installation of miscellaneous metals, that the expiration of lien rights was on a contract-by-contract basis, and that the plaintiff's subcontractor's lien claim for the steel contract was registered out of time. However, the miscellaneous metals lien did not expressly mention the services or materials supplied with respect to the miscellaneous metals contract, but only referred to “structural steel and related materials.” The court concluded that, although the lien was poorly worded and the phrase “related materials” was equivocal, the lien included the supply of services and materials under the miscellaneous metals contract. The brief description of the services or materials supplied found in s. 34(5) attracted the benefit of the curative proviso in s. 6, and the poorly-worded description of the services and materials supplied was a relatively minor error that did not prejudice the defendant in any way, as the latter could not have been under any misapprehension that the lien, as registered, related only to the structural steel contract. On appeal, the trial judge was held to have erred in law in finding that separate claims for lien must be registered in respect to separate subcontracts between the same parties for the same improvement. However, the trial judge exercised his discretion to apply the curative provision in s. 6(1) of the Act “to the extent necessary” to address the “poorly worded” description of services in the claim for lien, and there was no error in principle in this exercise of discretion. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990 c. C.30].</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9585800 Canada Inc." p2="JP Gravel Construction Inc." post.rptr="19773" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63d6af615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction Inc.">9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction Inc., 2019 CarswellOnt 19773, 2019 ONSC 7022, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 38 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 8917, 2019 ONSC 3396, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 29 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor registered and then discharged a construction lien against the construction project, and then immediately registered a second construction lien after that discharge, for the same amount and using substantially the same information as contained in the first lien. The first lien was allegedly discharged due to an error in the time of delivery of services which listed the incorrect year, an error corrected in the second lien, and the plaintiff denied any intention of discharging its entitlement to a lien against the defendant contractor. The motions judge refused to vacate the lien, because the time frame in the first lien was clearly incorrect, and found it to be a nullity since it was a lien for non-existent work. She then found the second lien was appropriate and valid, with the result that s. 48 of the Act did not apply. On appeal, the motions judge was held to have erred in failing to give effect to s. 48. As well, the argument concerning nullity of the first lien was not raised by the parties, and it was therefore a denial of procedural fairness to decide the motion on that basis without giving the parties notice and a chance to make submissions on the issue. Counsel would have been able to raise the significance of s. 6, which stated that a claim for lien was not invalidated because of a failure to comply with certain subsections, including s. 34(5). Subsection 34(5) specified the content of a claim for lien and referred to “the time within which the services or materials were supplied.” Reading s. 34(5) with s. 6, it appeared that an error made with respect to the time within which the services or materials were supplied was a minor irregularity within the meaning of s. 6, and a court could refuse to declare the claim for lien invalid or vacate the lien after the court determined the issue of prejudice to the other parties. The defendant would not have suffered any prejudice had the plaintiff sought an order to correct its error with respect to the timing of the services.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Stubbe's Precast Commerical Ltd." p2="King & Columbia Inc." post.rptr="995" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63d6d6705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Stubbe's Precast Commerical Ltd. v. King & Columbia Inc.">Stubbe's Precast Commerical Ltd. v. King & Columbia Inc., 2018 ONSC 995, 2018 CarswellOnt 2163, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 270 (Ont. S.C.J.); appeal quashed <ital>Stubbes Precast v. King & Columbia</ital>, 2018 ONSC 6539, 2018 CarswellOnt 18402, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In filing two separate construction liens against the defendant's property, the plaintiff's lawyer incorrectly set out a portion of the plaintiff's corporate name as <ital>Ltd.</ital> instead of the correct <ital>Inc.</ital> The court held that this misnomer was not a reason to discharge the liens, exercised its discretion under the curative provision of s. 6 and amended the style of cause accordingly. There was no evidence that the defendant was misled, prejudiced or acted to its detriment because of the mistake. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="G.C. Rentals Ltd." p2="Falco Steel Fabricators Inc." post.rptr="70" pre.rptr="132" ref.id="I90aa8b30f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="G.C. Rentals Ltd. v. Falco Steel Fabricators Inc.">G.C. Rentals Ltd. v. Falco Steel Fabricators Inc. (2000), 132 O.A.C. 70, 2000 CarswellOnt 1040 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> was held to be a complete answer to the defendant's motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Environmental Building Solutions Corporation" p2="2420124 Ontario Limited et al." post.rptr="6202" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63d6d6725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Environmental Building Solutions Corporation v. 2420124 Ontario Limited et al.">Environmental Building Solutions Corporation v. 2420124 Ontario Limited et al., 2017 ONSC 6202, 2017 CarswellOnt 16035, 83 C.L.R. (4th) 81 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2017 ONSC 6769, 2017 CarswellOnt 18562, 83 C.L.R. (4th) 89 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 6 applies only where the issue is one of strict compliance with the legislation, meaning compliance with minor, procedural, relatively unimportant and/or technical matters. A material misstatement as to the amount of the lien could not be characterized as technical, minor or procedural so as to attract the saving power of the section. Here, the amount claimed exceeded by approximately 25% the alleged value of the improvement to the land, and s. 6 was not available to the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc." p2="Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd." post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63d6fd805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc. v. Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd.">Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc. v. Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd., 2016 ONCA 305, 2016 CarswellOnt 6411, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 1, 398 D.L.R. (4th) 251 (Ont. C.A.); affirming 2014 ONSC 5655, 2014 CarswellOnt 15009, 45 C.L.R. (4th) 275, 328 O.A.C. 189 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 6825, 2014 CarswellOnt 16757, 45 C.L.R. (4th) 287 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Applying <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd." p2="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="575" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90aab240f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)">Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 575, 38 C.B.R. (3d) 250 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1996), 206 N.R. 315 (note), [1996] S.C.C.A. No. 214 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, the Court confirmed that s. 6 cannot be used to correct the improper registration of a general lien claim contrary to s. 20(2) of the Act. Here, the appellant subcontractor had the ability to learn of the restriction in the contracts between the owner and the contractor by asking for information using s. 39, but it did not do so.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Beta Construction Inc." p2="Chiu" post.rptr="5288" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63d724905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beta Construction Inc. v. Chiu">Beta Construction Inc. v. Chiu, 2015 ONSC 5288, 2015 CarswellOnt 12694, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 100 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 ONSC 5353, 2015 CarswellOnt 12959, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 133 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the lien claimant was the contracting party. The master did not allow the defendants to rely on a technicality to avoid paying the contractor that supplied services and materials to their home renovation, in the face of clear evidence that they were dealing with the corporate plaintiff throughout the renovation, rather than another unincorporated business owned by the corporate plaintiff's principal. Although the written contracts identified the contractor on the first page and the signing page as the unincorporated entity, the defendants believed that they had contracted with the principal's incorporated entity, and the intention of the parties was that the contracting party be the corporate defendant. Unlike in <ital>Juddav Designs Inc. v. Cosgriffe</ital> (see ss. 51 and 55, below), where the corporate entity took no part in the supply of services and materials, the corporate plaintiff here was identified in the contract, was the payee of payments made by cheque, was the bank account holder of deposits made by direct transfer from the defendants' account and was the entity that wrote receipts out to the defendants for payments made on the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Govan Brown & Associates Ltd." p2="Equinox 199 Bay Street Co." post.rptr="3924" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63d724915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Govan Brown & Associates Ltd. v. Equinox 199 Bay Street Co.">Govan Brown & Associates Ltd. v. Equinox 199 Bay Street Co., 2014 ONSC 3924, 2014 CarswellOnt 8856, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 78 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 6 is not a <ital>carte blanche</ital> curative provision to correct all defects in a registered construction lien. It is narrower than the predecessor test of “substantial compliance” under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, and is designed as a curative provision to protect lien claimants from losing their lien rights if they fail to comply strictly with the form and content requirements of registration under the Act, absent prejudice to other parties. Its application should not be limited to technical, trivial or minor matters. Where electronically filed liens name the defendant in the wrong part of the statements on the form registered or name the wrong entity in the claim for lien, it is a failure to “strictly” comply with the requirements of s. 34(5) of the Act, but not so serious an error as to take it outside of the application of s. 6 of the Act. The failure of the defendant to register various business names and to contract with the plaintiff in its correct corporate name was the source of the lien claimants' confusion as to the identity of the leasehold owner. The defendant ought not be permitted to benefit from a “corporate name shell game”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="S & L Mechanical Plumbing & Heating" p2="6176666 Canada Ltée" post.rptr="1701" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63d724925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S & L Mechanical Plumbing & Heating v. 6176666 Canada Ltée">S & L Mechanical Plumbing & Heating v. 6176666 Canada Ltée, 2011 ONSC 1701, 2011 CarswellOnt 2307 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 2878, 2 C.L.R. (4th) 90 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—During the hearing of a motion to correct the name of the lien claimant, the defendant submitted evidence, which the plaintiff accepted, that the plaintiff was not registered under the (Ont) <ital>Business Names Act</ital>, and that as a result, could not sustain its lien action. Further investigation at the request of the judge revealed that the plaintiff had in fact registered under the <ital>Business Names Act</ital>, but the defendant then objected to the introduction of the new evidence after the motion was heard. While evidence of the registration should have been obtained by due diligence on the part of the solicitor for the plaintiff before the motion was heard, the defendant had provided inaccurate evidence that the plaintiff relied on. In the circumstances, the court exercised its discretion to allow the admission of the evidence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="David J. Cupido Construction Ltd." p2="Humphrey Funeral Home & Chapel Ltd." post.rptr="238" pre.rptr="73" ref.id="I63d74ba05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="David J. Cupido Construction Ltd. v. Humphrey Funeral Home & Chapel Ltd.">David J. Cupido Construction Ltd. v. Humphrey Funeral Home & Chapel Ltd. (2008), 73 C.L.R. (3d) 238, 2008 CarswellOnt 4382 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Notwithstanding that the claim for lien stated that the date of last supply was earlier than it may in fact have been, the lien claim could be amended at trial if the court was satisfied that the evidence proved that materials or services were supplied on or after the date referenced in the claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Bayan Construction Ltd." p2="Cusimano" post.rptr="2210" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I2d2bc090f65111ee9732e3e835885970" title="Bayan Construction Ltd. v. Cusimano">Bayan Construction Ltd. v. Cusimano (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2210, 70 C.L.R. (3d) 123 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the owners contracted with the corporate plaintiff or with its principal in a personal capacity and, therefore, whether the corporate plaintiff was the proper party to issue the lien claim, and the proper defendant to the owner's counterclaim. Quotes for this job were made, invoices written and accounting statements issued under the non-corporate business name, and the cheques were made payable to the business name or to the principal's personal name. There was no reason for the owners to believe, and no basis upon which they ought to have known, that they were doing business with an incorporated entity. There was no agreement with the lien claimant's corporate persona, nor did the company provide services on the project. Rather, the owners hired the corporate principal personally. The claim for payment ought to have been made by him personally and the claim for damages for deficiency ought to have been made against him personally, and both were dismissed. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The Master considered the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="G.C. Rentals Ltd." p2="Falco Steel Fabricators Inc." post.rptr="70" pre.rptr="132" ref.id="I63d772b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. Rentals Ltd. v. Falco Steel Fabricators Inc.">G.C. Rentals Ltd. v. Falco Steel Fabricators Inc. (2000), 132 O.A.C. 70, 2000 CarswellOnt 1040 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, but noted that in this case the lien claimant had not sought leave to add the principal as a plaintiff and the defendants had not asked to add him as a defendant by counterclaim.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Engineered Construction Ltd." p2="Arena Entertainment Corp." post.rptr="8685" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63d772b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Engineered Construction Ltd. v. Arena Entertainment Corp.">Engineered Construction Ltd. v. Arena Entertainment Corp. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 8685 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The failure to name an “owner” in the claim for lien did not amount to a minor or technical irregularity. It was a fundamental error in the assertion of a valid claim for lien, as was a significant understating of the amount claimed for lien. It was not a case of transposing figures or misplacing a decimal, rather it was a substantial and real error on the part of the plaintiff. As a result, a plaintiff could not rely on s. 6 to permit it to amend the claim for lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Braun" p2="974850 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="6257" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63d772b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Braun v. 974850 Ontario Inc.">Braun v. 974850 Ontario Inc. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6257, 60 C.L.R. (3d) 121 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A variance in the monetary amount contained in the lien claim filed on title and the statement of claim was not significant or fatal to the claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Kuch Stephenson Gibson Malo Architects & Engineers" p2="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." post.rptr="892" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I63d772b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kuch Stephenson Gibson Malo Architects & Engineers v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc.">Kuch Stephenson Gibson Malo Architects & Engineers v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 892, 2005 CarswellOnt 894, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 258 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff preserved a lien in a lesser amount and then commenced an action to enforce a lien in a larger amount, s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> permitted the lien to be declared valid. The amount initially registered was in essence “overperfected” in registering a statement of claim in which the claim exceeded the amount of the lien claim. The Court relied on the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="City Acoustics Ltd." p2="Waterloo Region Roman Catholic Separate School Board" post.rptr="416" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63d799c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="City Acoustics Ltd. v. Waterloo Region Roman Catholic Separate School Board">City Acoustics Ltd. v. Waterloo Region Roman Catholic Separate School Board (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 416, 20 C.L.R. (2d) 156 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, where s. 6 was held to permit a lien being declared valid despite a larger amount being in the statement of claim. Further, the defendant acknowledged that there was no prejudice. The amount claimed in excess of the lien claim was to proceed as an action seeking personal judgment for breach of contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="G.C. Rentals Ltd." p2="Falco Steel Fabricators Inc." post.rptr="70" pre.rptr="132" ref.id="I63d799c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. Rentals Ltd. v. Falco Steel Fabricators Inc.">G.C. Rentals Ltd. v. Falco Steel Fabricators Inc. (2000), 132 O.A.C. 70 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Although a contract was signed, and liens were filed, in the name G.C. Rentals Ltd., and the contractor was actually registered in the business name of “G.C. Rentals & Repairs”, this error amounted to a misnomer, not a nullity. “G.C. Rentals & Repairs” was a legal entity that was capable of suing or being sued, and was not a “nonentity”. The amendment sought by the lien claimant did not involve substituting a new party but merely correcting the plaintiff's name. The defendants were not misled nor prejudiced by the error, and knew that claims were being made against them by the “other party” to the contract. What occurred was a misdescription of the lien claimant's name, and the lien claimant was entitled to the relief provided by s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Gillies Lumber Inc." p2="Kubassek Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="2692" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I63d7c0d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd.">Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 2692, 1999 CarswellOnt 2160 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1997), 32 O.R. (3d) 475 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There were four separate projects and technically four separate owners at the time of registration of a general lien covering all four projects. The general lien was disallowed. The Divisional Court had converted the general lien into a specific lien on each of the respective properties, following <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1910" p1="Ontario Lime Assn." p2="Grimwood" post.rptr="17" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63d7c0d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Lime Assn. v. Grimwood">Ontario Lime Assn. v. Grimwood (1910), 22 O.L.R. 17 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Rockwell Electric Ltd." p2="Welsford Development Corp." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63d7c0d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rockwell Electric Ltd. v. Welsford Development Corp.">Rockwell Electric Ltd. v. Welsford Development Corp. (1989), 33 C.L.R. 1, 89 N.S.R. (2d) 159 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. The Court of Appeal reversed (Laskin J. dissenting), wiping out all of the plaintiff's lien rights. Section 6 does not enable the court to amend or rectify a claim for a general lien that is otherwise not available to a lien claimant under s. 20(1). Section 6 is remedial, but applies only to minor or technical irregularities. The defects in the general lien in this case were too significant to be considered minor or technical in nature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd." p2="Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board" post.rptr="1228" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I55cd6400fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd. v. Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board">Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd. v. Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 1228, 28 O.R. (3d) 380, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 296 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The omission of s. 53(1) from the curative provision of s. 6 means nothing more than that the details of the action were left to Part VIII and the rules of court. Section 6 addresses only defects in the claim for lien, not the proceedings to enforce lien rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="City Acoustics Ltd." p2="Waterloo Region Roman Catholic Separate School Board" post.rptr="416" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90ab7590f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="City Acoustics Ltd. v. Waterloo Region Roman Catholic Separate School Board">City Acoustics Ltd. v. Waterloo Region Roman Catholic Separate School Board (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 416, 20 C.L.R. (2d) 156 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The curative provision of s. 6 was applied to validate two lien claims. In the first claim, although the wrong party was identified as the party to whom services or materials were supplied, all defendants in the action were fully identified and it had been known to all parties for some time which company was the correct one. With respect to the second claim, although the amount owing was incorrectly stated, all parties to the litigation were taken to have been aware of the proper amount of the claim. No lien claimant or other party to the litigation had been prejudiced by the errors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19861120" p1="Allied Fasteners & Supplies Ltd." p2="Ferris (No. 1)" ref.id="I63d80ef05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Allied Fasteners & Supplies Ltd. v. Ferris (No. 1)">Allied Fasteners & Supplies Ltd. v. Ferris (No. 1) (November 20, 1986), Kirsh's Construction Case Finder No. 6.6 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—As stated by the Master in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Guillevin International Inc." p2="Enertech Lighting Systems Inc." post.rptr="245" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I55cd8b10fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc.">Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 245, 19 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, <ital>Allied Fasteners</ital> is the highest authority on the general thrust of s. 6. In <ital>Allied Fasteners</ital>, the Divisional Court stated that s. 6 gives the court a curative discretion where there has been a failure of strict compliance with s. 34(5) of the Act, a discretion the limits of which were not to be defined by that case. In <ital>Guillevin</ital>, the Master held that s. 6 has a curative effect only if the court finds no prejudice. Where prejudice is found, and to the extent it is found, s. 6 does not cure a failure of strict compliance. The converse is also true. Section 6 does not give the court power to cure any defect, it merely allows the court to enforce strict compliance to the extent that it finds prejudice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Michelin Group Inc." p2="Forsan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I63d80ef25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd.">Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 523, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 202 (Gen. Div.); affirmed (1995), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 215 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 6, which provides that a claim for lien is not invalidated for failure to strictly comply with the specified sections of the Act, does not apply where the issue is not the lien's validity, but rather the failure of a party to perfect a lien by bringing an action within the required time frame. It has been said about this case that although the Divisional Court concurred in the result, and therefore dismissed the appeal, they were of the view that the lien could have been amended by the trial judge if there had been evidence before him sufficient to prove the amended lien's validity. To the extent that reasoning is available from the brief endorsement of the Divisional Court, it is difficult to agree with. If correct, it means that the date given on the face of the registered lien as the “date of last supply” is irrelevant if work has been done after that date, but only until the date the affidavit of verification was sworn. The decision of the trial judge is thoroughly reasoned and does not lead to this apparent anomaly.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd." p2="Redesco Inc." post.rptr="148" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63d80ef35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd. v. Redesco Inc.">Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd. v. Redesco Inc. (1993), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 148 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where there was not even imperfect compliance with s. 33, s. 6 could not be applied to cure the defect. In any event, s. 6 was not applicable because the subcontractors were deprived of the knowledge that the majority of the holdback moneys were to be paid out. The time period involved, the 45 days following the alleged substantial completion date, was the time when the subcontractors were performing the bulk of their work. Since the subcontractors were unaware that a payout of a large portion of the holdback was being made, they were unable to consider their position and determine whether to file liens at that time. Accordingly, the subcontractors were prejudiced by the failure to comply with s. 33, and s. 6 could not be applied to assist the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="AFG Glass Inc." p2="Glaxo Canada Inc." post.rptr="215" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63d836005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="AFG Glass Inc. v. Glaxo Canada Inc.">AFG Glass Inc. v. Glaxo Canada Inc. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 215 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Due to a faulty fax communication, the solicitor for the plaintiff subcontractor filed and registered a lien for $25,000, when in fact the amount owing was $118,045.22. There were seven lien claimants in total and the owner offered to pay each 72 per cent of its claim out of the holdback. Four lien claimants accepted the offer, but when the plaintiff was about to accept the offer, the error was discovered, and the plaintiff brought a motion to amend the statement of claim and the claim for lien to increase the claim from $25,000 to $118,045.22. The motion was opposed by the owner and the two lien claimants who had not yet accepted the owner's offer. The Master dismissed the motion to amend the actual lien, although the motion to amend the statement of claim was allowed in part. Section 6 only provides that no claim for lien is “invalidated” because of any failure to comply strictly with the requirements of certain sections. It was not argued that the plaintiff's claim for lien was “invalidated” because the lesser amount was mistakenly inserted in the claim for lien, but rather that the “claim for lien” should be limited to the amount claimed therein, and that the plaintiff should not be allowed to increase the amount of its claim for lien. The wording of s. 6 did not authorize a court to make the order sought. In addition, s. 6 is more restrictive to lien claimants than former s. 19 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 which spoke about “substantial compliance”. This section was designed to relieve only against minor errors and omissions in the preparation of documents and forms, and that substantial compliance is no longer sufficient. The mistake made here in understating the amount claimed in the claim for lien by $93,000, was not a minor error or omission.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Corporate Status of Lien Claimants</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brock Contracting" p2="Kozikowski" post.rptr="7618" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63d836015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brock Contracting v. Kozikowski">Brock Contracting v. Kozikowski, 2018 ONSC 7618, 2018 CarswellOnt 21555, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor carried on business as a sole proprietorship using the original business name. She later incorporated a numbered company, and, after the last supply of services and materials to the defendant's property, registered the subsequent business name, and cancelled the original business name's registration. The new corporation then commenced a lien action under the subsequent business name. Pursuant to s. 73, the corporation did not have the right to register a lien, since it was not a party to the contract and supplied no services or materials to the project. Section 6 could not be used to cure the invalid lien in this case. This is not a case in which a minor, inconsequential error in the name of the corporation was used to describe the lien claimant. In this case, the wrong entity registered the lien. Section 6 does not apply to a failure to comply with s. 14 of the Act. Thus, an error with respect to the identity of “the person who supplies services or materials to an improvement for an owner” cannot be cured by recourse to the section. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court noted that the absence of the words “minor irregularities” in the previous version of s. 6 was rectified in the 2017 amendments with the addition of ss. 6(2), which, confirms that ss. 6(1) is intended to apply only to “minor errors or irregularities”.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Vinpat Construction Ltd." p2="Henze Holdings Inc." post.rptr="2274" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I90abeac0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Vinpat Construction Ltd. v. Henze Holdings Inc.">Vinpat Construction Ltd. v. Henze Holdings Inc. (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 2274, 18 C.L.R. (3d) 307 (Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff corporation did not exist at the time of the entering into the building contract, and the contract was originally with its principal, personally. The plaintiff corporation relied on s. 21(2) of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital> to argue that it had adopted the contract and was entitled to its benefits and that the principal ceased to be bound by it and ceased to be entitled to its benefits personally. The Master found that s. 21(1) of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital> did not apply, as it had not been agreed between the principal and defendant, as part of their bargain, that the principal was entering into this contract on behalf of a corporation later to be incorporated. There was no adoption of the contract under s. 21(2). The corporate plaintiff therefore had no status to maintain the action. As the principal did not want to be substituted as a plaintiff in order to maintain the action as a lien action or a personal non-lien action under s. 63 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the action was dismissed, the lien discharged and the claim for lien and certificate of action vacated from title.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Skyaramic Development Inc." p2="Zotalis" post.rptr="323" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63d85d115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Skyaramic Development Inc. v. Zotalis">Skyaramic Development Inc. v. Zotalis (1996), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 323 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—If a company is dissolved and not revived under s. 241(5) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. B-16, at the time lien rights expire, a subsequent revival will not save the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Triple “R” Demolition Inc." p2="1186468 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="125" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63d884205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Triple “R” Demolition Inc. v. 1186468 Ontario Ltd.">Triple “R” Demolition Inc. v. 1186468 Ontario Ltd. (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 125 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An entity incorporated after the date of the contract and after performing much, if not all of the contract work was not permitted to rely on s. 21(2) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. B-16, nor could the lien claimant avail itself of s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The case contains a detailed and useful summary of authorities on s. 6. In order to apply s. 6, the errors or omissions must be of a minor nature and there must be no prejudice to those against whom a lien is claimed. In this case the contract was void <ital>ab initio</ital>, and a lien claim based on such a contract could not be saved by s. 6. In terms of prejudice, the developer had laboured under the constant belief that the individuals who had executed the agreement represented a legitimate corporate entity, and the lien claimant knowingly adopted misleading letterhead to further that false impression. The developer therefore advanced substantial amounts of money to a non-existent entity, and relied for performance on a non-existent corporation, the consequences of which could have proved disastrous.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Affidavit of Verification</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Petroff Partnership Architects" p2="Mobius Corp." post.rptr="2260" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I63d8ab305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp.">Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2260, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 277, 65 O.R. (3d) 118 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—An electronically registered lien is valid in the absence of a sworn paper affidavit of verification. The plaintiff registered a construction lien electronically and followed the electronic registration requirements which did not include an affidavit of verification as contemplated by s. 34(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and Form 9 under Reg. 175, R.R.O. 1990. Section 24 of the <ital>Land Registration Reform Act</ital> provides in subsection (1) that: “If a document is submitted in an electronic format and is required under any Act to include an affidavit, a declaration, a statement or other written evidence, the evidence shall be in an electronic format approved by the Director and shall be included in a manner approved by the Director”. Subsection (2) of s. 24 provides that: “If an electronic document includes evidence in an electronic format in accordance with this section, the evidence shall be deemed to comply with the requirement to submit the affidavit, declaration, statement or other written evidence under the applicable Act despite the fact that the evidence is not in writing and has not been signed by the parties required to provide the evidence.” The defendants moved for an order discharging the lien and vacating its registration, arguing that the affidavit of verification should have been electronically scanned into the claim for lien. Master Sandler dismissed the motion, holding that “in my view, s. 24(1) requires the ‘evidence’ […] to be in an electronic format, as was done in this case, and s. 24(2) ‘deems’ that ‘evidence’ to comply with the requirement to submit an affidavit of verification under the C.L.A. No additional paper affidavit is required. Mr. Gillott's suggestion (noted in para. 10 above) was based on an ‘abundance of caution’ so as to avoid the very issue that arose in this case. Now that it has [been] raised, and rejected by a court ruling, perhaps those in the profession who have adopted this practice will use slightly less caution. (But probably, some will await the ruling of an appellate court before changing their practice)”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="573521 Ontario Inc." p2="Waldman" post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63d8ab315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="573521 Ontario Inc. v. Waldman">573521 Ontario Inc. v. Waldman (1996), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 305 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An individual dealt with an owner, but substituted a numbered company in the contract, alleging that, as an individual, he became a mere project manager at that point. The company's lien was struck, following <ital>Venditti v. Petriglia</ital> as the affidavit was in the form for an individual (Form B) when it should have been sworn in the corporate form (Form A).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Edgecon Construction Inc." p2="All Saints Church Homes For Tomorrow Society" post.rptr="3501" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90ac38e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Edgecon Construction Inc. v. All Saints Church Homes For Tomorrow Society">Edgecon Construction Inc. v. All Saints Church Homes For Tomorrow Society (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 3501, [1995] O.J. No. 2209, 18 C.L.R. (3d) 254 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—As long as the essential averments are stated, it does not matter how they are expressed. Improper use of Form A of the Affidavit was acceptable if, on all the facts, the necessary averments could be gleaned from the deponent's evidence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Accent Design Inc." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="33" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I90ac5ff0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1994), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 33 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The deponent swore that the lien claimant was D. Inc. The lien claimant was actually an unincorporated partnership. As there was no valid affidavit, the lien was fatally flawed from the start and the defendant's motion to discharge the lien was allowed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Venditti" p2="Petriglia" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63d8d2425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venditti v. Petriglia">Venditti v. Petriglia (1989), 33 C.L.R. 1, 33 O.A.C. 76 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The curative provisions of s. 6 provide no relief to persons who neglect to verify their claims for lien with an affidavit of verification which complies with the requirements of s. 34(6).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Sefri Construction International Ltd." p2="Jaltas Inc." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I63d8d2435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sefri Construction International Ltd. v. Jaltas Inc.">Sefri Construction International Ltd. v. Jaltas Inc. (1990), 38 C.L.R. 15 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Following <ital>Venditti v. Petriglia</ital>, a lien verified by an affidavit containing no signature of a commissioner of oaths was struck as failing to strictly comply with the statutory requirement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Irving Oil Ltd." p2="M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63d8f9505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Irving Oil Ltd. v. M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd.">Irving Oil Ltd. v. M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd. (1985), 20 C.L.R. 26 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Although s. 6 relieves against failure to comply strictly with s. 34(5), there is no similar provision relating to s. 34(6). Hence, where there was no verifying affidavit as required by s. 34(6), s. 6 cannot be used to correct the deficit.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Gallaway" p2="Gary Eddie Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="14" ref.id="I63d8f9515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gallaway v. Gary Eddie Construction Ltd.">Gallaway v. Gary Eddie Construction Ltd. (1985), 14 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The failure to file the affidavit of verification was a mere slip or inadvertence which the court had discretion to relieve against where no prejudice was alleged or proven. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court, in reaching its conclusion in this case, relied in part upon an earlier decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. Subsequent cases have held that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not permit the court to relieve against the failure to file the affidavit of verification under s. 34(6).]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Certificate of Substantial Performance</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Villa Nicolini Inc." post.rptr="5444" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63d920605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc.">Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc., 2012 ONSC 5444, 2012 CarswellOnt 12496, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 36 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 ONSC 6616, 2012 CarswellOnt 15361, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 37 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Failure of the architect to set out the dates of the sub-contracts certified as complete, where no actual prejudice was involved, did not invalidate the impugned Certificates of Completion at issue, and the default could be cured by s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="For-Con Construction Ltd." p2="1120062 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3824" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63d920615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="For-Con Construction Ltd. v. 1120062 Ontario Inc.">For-Con Construction Ltd. v. 1120062 Ontario Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3824, 1998 CarswellOnt 3644 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—It is envisaged by the drafter of the Act that minor mistakes might be made in complying or attempting to comply with the ten “Rules” in s. 32(1), that is why s. 32(2) and 32(5) are expressly referred to in s. 6. Failure to give a copy to the contractor, Rule 4, is not so mentioned where, as in this case, the certificate was eventually published and either did or ought to have come to the attention of the contractor as a result, failure to comply with Rule 4 is not fatal to the validity of the Certificate.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of)" p2="Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality)" post.rptr="191" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63d920625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of) v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality)">I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of) v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality) (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 191 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 6 can be applied to cure defect, errors or omissions in certificates of substantial performance, subject to a consideration by the court of actual prejudice. The omission of the legal description of the lienable property in both the certificate and the publication is “a failure to comply strictly with s. 32(2)”, and falls within the ambit of s. 6. The lien in this case stated only a municipal address. Both <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-City Flooring Co." p2="Quatrosense Environmental Ltd." post.rptr="744" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63d947705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd.">Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd. (1991), 3 O.R. (3d) 744, 49 C.L.R. 319 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd." p2="951034 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2064" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63d947715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc.">L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. 2064 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> are reviewed in detail. To the extent that either of these cases holds that s. 6 cannot apply because of s. 32(2) of the <ital>Act</ital> and s. 2(6) of Regulation 175 (Form 6) in order to protect the integrity of the system, they are disagreed with. Subsection 28(d) of the <ital>Interpretation Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. I-11 is relied upon.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd." p2="951034 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2064" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63d96e805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc.">L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. 2064 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Defects in a legal description in a published certificate of substantial performance were not minor or clerical irregularities that could be cured by s. 6 of the <ital>Act</ital>. This case is given a close reading in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of)" p2="Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality)" post.rptr="191" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63d96e815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of) v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality)">I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of) v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality) (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 191</ref></cite> at 202 <ital>et seq.</ital></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Advice Pipelines Ltd." p2="Barrie" post.rptr="64" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I63d96e825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Advice Pipelines Ltd. v. Barrie">Advice Pipelines Ltd. v. Barrie (1994), 1 C.L.C.F. 64 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial performance giving the address of the owner as “City Center” was declared valid using s. 6.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63d96e835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial performance issued by the project architect stated that “the contract for the following improvement: Princess Gardens, Phase I, basic shell to the above premises was substantially performed”, even though the architect acknowledged there was no such improvement as a basic shell. As well, the certificate was further deficient in that the name of the contractor was shown as “c/o owner”, and the address for service was left blank. The court found that these irregularities were significant, and not minor ones curable under s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd." p2="F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma)" post.rptr="162" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63d995905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd. v. F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma)">Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd. v. F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma) (1992), 3 C.L.R. (2d) 162 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial completion as published failed to comply with the following statutory requirements under s. 32(2): the name of the owner was present but his address for service was not included; the name of the contractor was present but there was no address for service; it did not describe the payment certifier; it did not state the date on which the contract was substantially performed; and there was no legal description of the property upon which the construction was done. Nevertheless, the defects were curable pursuant to s. 6, as there was no evidence that anyone was prejudiced by these deficiencies or omissions. The architect, contractor and the owner and their addresses were well known.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-City Flooring Co." p2="Quatrosense Environmental Ltd." post.rptr="744" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63d995915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd.">Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd. (1991), 3 O.R. (3d) 744, 49 C.L.R. 319 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A contractor's claim for lien was disputed because more than 45 days had elapsed between the publishing of the certificate of substantial performance and the filing of the lien. However, the certificate did not use Form 6 as required by the regulations to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and omitted the names and addresses of the owner and contractor and the street address and legal description of the premises. As well, notification of the substantial completion was not by publication of a copy of the actual certificate, as required by the Act, but by publication of a certificate which included the missing details except for the legal description of the premises. On application by the contractor, the certificate of substantial performance and publication thereof were held to be invalid. The omissions were not minor or clerical irregularities to be cured by s. 6 of the Act. The contractor had not published a copy of the actual certificate but had created a largely different one by adding most of the missing details. Consequently, the contractor was entitled to judgment in the amount of the lien.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:6: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Persons Referred to in Lien</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="One Oak Construction Inc." p2="1850168 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4090" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63d9bca05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="One Oak Construction Inc. v. 1850168 Ontario Inc.">One Oak Construction Inc. v. 1850168 Ontario Inc., 2022 ONSC 4090, 2022 CarswellOnt 9821, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 10 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff successfully moved for an order correcting a misnomer of its name in the title of proceedings and directing the Land Registrar to certify the new certificate of action registered on title and withdraw the misnamed one. The claim for lien was registered with the correct plaintiff's name and the motion was brought reasonably promptly following the misnomer being identified. There was no requirement in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> that the certificate of action bear the correct party name, and it followed that amendment of the certificate of action ought not to impact the validity of perfection, which turned on the timing of registration of the issued certificate of action in the correct form. It was appropriate to direct that the certificate of action (and statement of claim) be amended <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> to correct the misnomer. As the court had the authority and discretion to amend the statement of claim, it also had the authority and discretion to amend the certificate of action, which is a document issued by the court evidencing the issuance of the statement of claim with the same title of proceedings.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:7: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Registering Against Wrong Premises</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Ambler-Courtney Inc." p2="CAAG Land Development Ltd." post.rptr="58" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I63d9e3b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ambler-Courtney Inc. v. CAAG Land Development Ltd.">Ambler-Courtney Inc. v. CAAG Land Development Ltd. (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 58 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant inadvertently registered its lien in the Land Registry system, when the premises had previously been transferred into Land Titles. There were also irregularities in the legal description itself, both in the Claim for Lien, the Document General, and in the Certificate of Action, apparently contrary to s. 34(5). The defendant owner moved under ss. 45 and 47 to discharge and vacate the lien. The issue of the proper registry office was resolved in favour of the lien claimant, as in the relevant jurisdiction the two offices, Land Titles and Land Registry, were in the same building hence each was a “proper land registry office”. The other irregularities in the legal description were cured using s. 6.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Electrical Equipment Co." p2="General Motors of Canada" post.rptr="2630" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63d9e3b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Electrical Equipment Co. v. General Motors of Canada">Electrical Equipment Co. v. General Motors of Canada (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2630, 1998 CarswellOnt 2603 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was registered against the defendant's head office rather than its truck plant, and accordingly the lien was vacated and the certificate of action dismissed. The plaintiff sought to have the defendant's statutory holdback paid into court pending the plaintiff's review and accounting of funds as between the contractor and the sub-contractor with whom the plaintiff had contracted. The court found that since the lien was registered on the wrong land, there was no holdback, and while allegations of breach of trust and responsibility remained open, those obligations did not support an application for payment into court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Riverside Glass Ltd." p2="Charron's Quality Market Ltd." post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63da0ac05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd.">Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owned two adjacent lots. The plaintiff delivered materials to one lot and registered its lien on that lot. The materials were incorporated into an improvement on the adjacent lot. Although the lien claimant relied in argument on the “enjoyed therewith” portion of the definition of “supply” in s. 1 of the Act, the court also invoked s. 6 in “curing” the defect. A similar result was reached for similar reasons in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Phoenix Drywall" p2="Mississauga Rest Home Two Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63da0ac15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Phoenix Drywall v. Mississauga Rest Home Two Inc.">Phoenix Drywall v. Mississauga Rest Home Two Inc. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 1, 1988 CarswellOnt 766 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63da0ac25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207, 52 O.A.C. 107 (Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The curative provisions of s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> clearly narrowed the court's authority to correct defects in the process employed by a lien claimant in complying with s. 34(5). The discretionary power of the court under s. 6 does not extend to permit a court to validate a claim for lien where wrong lands are named. The setting out of the wrong lands is a fatal flaw which a court is not empowered to correct.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Ottawa Air Design Ltd." p2="Wesmar Construction Co." post.rptr="159" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63da0ac35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ottawa Air Design Ltd. v. Wesmar Construction Co.">Ottawa Air Design Ltd. v. Wesmar Construction Co. (1990), 40 C.L.R. 159 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The applicant registered a claim for lien within the time provided by the Act, but the claim was registered against the wrong part lot. In allowing the applicant to amend the description of the land in the claim, the court stated that the rights of the applicant would be extinguished at trial if the error was not rectified at the interlocutory stage, because the owners of the two part lots in question were in no way connected. Since the Act was meant to deal with these problems in a summary way, liberal interpretation was necessary. Since no prejudice was shown to any party, the applicant was granted its relief and the description of the land in the lien claim was changed <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Lunardo" p2="Psihogios" post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63da31d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lunardo v. Psihogios">Lunardo v. Psihogios (1989), 43 C.L.R. 302 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendants brought a motion for an order dismissing the plaintiff's lien action and striking out the plaintiff's lien registered against their lands on the basis that the plaintiff did not supply any labour or services to the lands specified in the lien claim. The evidence revealed that the plaintiff's claim for lien was not presented in registrable form and changes were made to facilitate registration. The court held, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that the land description appearing in the lien claim, although incomplete, was sufficient to identify the land on which the lien was claimed. The plaintiff was entitled to have the legal description of the lands to which his lien applied correctly amended.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Twin Windows Inc." p2="Holiday Construction Ltd." post.rptr="311" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I63da31d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Twin Windows Inc. v. Holiday Construction Ltd.">Twin Windows Inc. v. Holiday Construction Ltd. (1985), 15 C.L.R. 311 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff's solicitor discovered that a claim for lien which he had registered was registered against the wrong property, he brought a motion for an order allowing registration of the claim for lien and certificate of action <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> against the defendant owner's lands. The jurisdiction of the court to provide relief against mistakes is not as broad under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> as it was under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. Section 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not allow the provision of the relief requested.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6:8: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6:8</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Persons Referred to in Lien</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="3925308 Manitoba Inc." p2="Hoffer" post.rptr="5098" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63da58e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="3925308 Manitoba Inc. v. Hoffer">3925308 Manitoba Inc. v. Hoffer, 2010 ONSC 5098, 2010 CarswellOnt 8403, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 246 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 9205, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 260 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The original lien was filed with a typographical error that set out an incorrect digit in the plaintiff's corporate name. After the time to file a lien had expired, an application was made to amend the lien to the correct corporate name, and an amended statement of claim with the correct corporate name was issued with the consent of the defendants. In their statement of defence and counterclaim, the defendants acknowledged that it was the numbered company with whom they had contracted. There was no prejudice to the defendants by the failure of the plaintiff to comply strictly with the provisions of the Act and the defendants did not seek to have the lien vacated and the action dismissed prior to trial and did not plead the issue. The plaintiff was entitled to rely upon the consent of the defendants when the claim was amended and should not have to defend claims that had not been properly put before the court. If the defendants had taken issue with the irregularities, it would have been open to them to amend their pleadings accordingly and to bring a motion to vacate the lien and dismiss the claim at an early stage of the proceedings. The lien was therefore not invalidated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Petroff Partnership Architects" p2="Mobius Corp." post.rptr="2260" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I63da58e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp.">Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2260, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 277, 65 O.R. (3d) 118 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The failure of the lien claimant to include the tenant's name as an “owner” in the first Statement, “Name and Address of Owner” of an electronic lien claim, was, taking into account all the other words used in the claim for lien, a minor or technical irregularity to which s. 6 applied. There was no prejudice to the tenant since the latter hired the lien claimant to do the work for which the lien was claimed. A careful reading of the “Statements” section of the electronic lien claim made it clear that the claimant was claiming a lien against the interest of both the owner and tenant in the identified premises, thus distinguishing it from <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams & Prior Ltd." p2="Taskon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="474" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90adbf80f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd.">Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 474, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2003] O.J. No. 498 (Master)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams & Prior Ltd." p2="Taskon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="474" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90adbf81f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd.">Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 474, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2003] O.J. No. 498 (Master)</ref></cite>—Where the subtenant against whose interest liens were being asserted was not mentioned in any way anywhere in either of two claims for lien, contrary to the requirements of s. 34(5)(a) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, this was fatal and could not be “cured” by s. 6. The first question to ask in such cases is not whether there is prejudice caused by non-compliance with s. 34(5), but rather whether such non-compliance is a minor or technical irregularity or not. If it is a minor or technical irregularity and s. 6 applies, then the court will go on to consider prejudice. If it is more than a minor or technical irregularity, s. 6 has no application whatsoever. In the event that a lien is claimed against a leasehold interest, it is fundamental to the survival of the lien that the name of the tenant against whom the lien is claimed be named in the claim for lien itself. The total omission to do so is a fundamental error in the assertion of a valid claim for lien against the subtenant's interest in the premises. In reaching this decision, the Master chose not to follow the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Guillevin International Inc." p2="Enertech Lighting Systems Inc." post.rptr="245" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I55cf86e0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc.">Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 245, 19 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and preferred the approach taken by the Court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Gillies Lumber Inc." p2="Kubassek Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I63daa7005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd.">Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd. (1999), 47 C.L.R. (2d) 1, 1999 CarswellOnt 2160 (C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Guillevin International Inc." p2="Enertech Lighting Systems Inc." post.rptr="245" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I55cfadf0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc.">Guillevin International Inc. v. Enertech Lighting Systems Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 245, 19 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. Not followed by Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams & Prior Ltd." p2="Taskon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="474" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90ade690f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd.">Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 474, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2003] O.J. No. 498 (Master)</ref></cite>—The owner named in the claim for lien appeared, <ital>prima facie</ital>, not to be the owner contemplated in s. 34(5).
