As the Act requires only that the “owner” be named, as opposed to the holder of the fee simple, it was difficult to imagine what sort of prejudice the holder of the fee simple might raise if it was otherwise a proper, but unnamed party. In the result, s. 6 did not apply to invalidate the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19891114" p1="713059 Ontario Ltd." p2="729372 Ontario Ltd." ref.id="I63daa7035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="713059 Ontario Ltd. v. 729372 Ontario Ltd.">713059 Ontario Ltd. v. 729372 Ontario Ltd. (November 14, 1989), Doc. No. 3679/89, Dunlop L.J.S.C.</ref></cite>—The wrong numbered company was named as owner in the claim for lien. After the time for preservation of its lien expired, the claimant discovered the error and moved to amend <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>; the defendant cross-moved to dismiss. The lien was declared invalid for failing to strictly comply with s. 34(5)(a).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6.1:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6.1:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jamrik" p2="2688126 Ont. Inc." post.rptr="2854" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6729c8103b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc.">Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 11019, 2024 ONSC 2854, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3654 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The prompt payment provisions of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> are a recent innovation that exist because of a recognition that money should continue to flow, and work continue to be done, pending final determination of claims through the litigation process. The principled basis for interim payment determinations through adjudication disappears once a contract is completed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Arcamm" p2="Avison et al." post.rptr="2232" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6729c8113b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Arcamm v. Avison et al.">Arcamm v. Avison et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 2232, 2023 ONSC 1151, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 72 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2023 CarswellOnt 10831, 2023 ONSC 4193 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed in part <ital>Arcamm Electrical Services Ltd. v. Avison Young Real Estate Management Services LP</ital>, 2024 CarswellOnt 19788 (Ont. C.A.); additional reasons 2025 CarswellOnt 1133 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite></trace>—The prompt payment provisions of 6.1 did not apply where the plaintiff's invoices failed to (a) clearly set out the period during which services or materials were supplied, but only provided an end date; (b) identify the authority, whether in the contract or otherwise, under which the services or materials were supplied; (c) specify the name, title, telephone number and mailing address of the person to whom payment was to be sent.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
6.3:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 6.3.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">6.3:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ledore Investments" p2="Dixin Construction" post.rptr="931" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I672a3d403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Ledore Investments v. Dixin Construction">Ledore Investments v. Dixin Construction, 2024 CarswellOnt 931, 2024 ONSC 598 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The adjudicator concluded that the contractor was not required to pay the subcontractor's invoices pursuant to the prompt payment provisions of the Act, but his reasoning turned on a point neither party had raised. He found that, because the subcontractor had not delivered to the owner a “proper invoice” as defined in the Act, the Act's prompt payment provisions did not apply. The adjudicator's decision breached procedural fairness and was set aside under s. 13.18(5)5. The subcontractor was not given an opportunity to be heard on the key issue that determined the outcome. Although the Act contemplates a speedy and targeted adjudication process, fundamental procedural fairness demanded an opportunity for the parties to provide at least written submissions on the key issue that would determine the adjudication. The matter was remitted to the adjudicator so he would have the opportunity to make a determination on that issue after having received the parties' submissions.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

October 1, 2019, the Act applies a prompt payment regime to all public and private sector construction contracts requiring payment within 28 days between the owner and general contractor from the date of submission of a “proper invoice”.</para.text></para><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Obligation to pay within 28 days of receipt of the invoice</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Obligation to pay is subject to owner giving contractor a notice of non-payment in prescribed form</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Obligation to pay continues to apply to any amount payable under the proper invoice that is not the subject of that notice</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Upon receiving full payment from the owner, the general contractor has seven days to pay subcontractor(s) included in the invoice submitted to the owner for the services included in that invoice</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Upon receiving partial date.updated="0">Where money withheld by the owner relates to the work of a specific subcontractor, the money paid will be distributed among the other subcontractors rateably</para.text></para></list.item></list><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See Conduct of Lien, Trust and Adjudication Proceedings, chapter 10 for details</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
7:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">7:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Statutory trusts were first introduced into lien legislation in this Province by <ital>Statute Law Amendment Act, 1942</ital>, S.O. 1942, c. 34, s. 21. In 1950, s. 2a became s. 3 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1950, c. 227. This section imposed a trust obligation on a “builder or contractor or a subcontractor” concerning “[a]ll sums received… on account of the contract price”. The beneficiaries of the trust were the “proprietor, builder or contractor, sub-contractors, Workmen's Compensation Board, workmen and persons who have supplied material on account of the contract”. The owner was not subject to the statutory trust obligation at that time. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 54, added the criminal sanction of a $5,000.00 fine or two years imprisonment for a breach of the trust obligation by either the statutory trustee or “every director or officer of a corporation who knowingly assents to or acquiesces in any such offence by the corporation”, and exempted monies retained by the statutory trustee in repayment of his own funds used for work or material on a project. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, introduced the owner's trusts concerning sums payable on certificates and sums received by the owner for the financing of the project. The 1968–69 legislation also permitted the application of trust monies to repay funds lent to a statutory trustee to pay for work and materials on the project. The Advisory Committee noted that the broad trust provisions of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> did not give guidance as to the administration of the fund. As a result, the flow of funds through a project could be interrupted by notices from subcontractors and suppliers to the owner that the release of trust funds to the contractor could lead to a breach of trust by the contractor (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1975" p1="Bre-Aar Excavating Ltd." p2="D'Angela Construction (Ontario) Ltd." post.rptr="654" pre.rptr="58" ref.id="I63dcf0f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bre-Aar Excavating Ltd. v. D'Angela Construction (Ontario) Ltd.">Bre-Aar Excavating Ltd. v. D'Angela Construction (Ontario) Ltd. (1975), 58 D.L.R. (3d) 654, 8 O.R. (2d) 598 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>). It was decided not to allow such notices to impede the flow of funds.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Act contains a complete code of trust provisions. The trust remedy is powerful and well established. It is useful in tracing monies through many hands and has the effect of protecting construction claims against a bankrupt payer. These sections keep construction funds within the “construction pyramid” but, with the exception of overhead payments, do not otherwise change the manner in which persons in the construction industry try to do business.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">There are several key concepts engrafted upon the statute by case law. The phrase, “[a]ll amounts received by an owner … that are to be used in the financing of the improvement”, in ss. 7(1) has been an issue in several cases. “Received” has been interpreted to include “receivable” see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co." p2="Empire Brass Manufacturing Co." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="1955" ref.id="I55d15ba0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.">Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co. (1955), 1955 CarswellBC 177, [1955] 3 D.L.R. 561, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.)</ital> [1955] S.C.R. 694 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>. In the case of monies certified by a payment certifier as being due from an owner to a contractor, the Ontario Court of Appeal has applied the owner's trust section literally, to impose a trust on revenues even before the deduction of the expenses incurred to earn them (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Structural Contracting Ltd." p2="Westcola Holdings Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63dd18015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc.">Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc. (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 417, 2 C.L.R. (3d) 165 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (2001), 147 O.A.C. 399 (note) (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 7(2) creates a second owner's trust obligation that applies even when the money is not borrowed or acquired for the purposes of financing the improvement. This sub-section is aimed at those situations where the owner is financing the improvement out of general revenues. The trust arises when a payment certifier certifies that an amount is payable under the construction contract, and attaches to an amount in the owner's hands or which the owner receives subsequently that is equal to the amount so certified.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 7(3) establishes a third owner's trust obligation, imposing a trust on those monies in an owner's hands or received, after a certificate of substantial performance has been issued or a declaration of substantial performance has been made by the courts. This provision may assist where certification or declaration has occurred but no draw has been made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 7(4) should be read in conjunction with ss. 10, 11, and 12. It prohibits appropriation or conversion of trust funds by an owner.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
7:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">7:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Tremblar" p2="1839563 Ontario" post.rptr="15015" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90afe260f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario">Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15015, 2020 ONSC 1316, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 275 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15163, 2020 ONSC 6302 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 20127 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Master allowed the owner defendant's motion for summary judgment and dismissed the plaintiff subcontractor's claim against it for breach of trust and unjust enrichment. The Master applied both <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd." p2="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc." post.rptr="3671" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63dd3f115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd. v. King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc.">Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd. v. King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc., 2019 ONSC 3671, 2019 CarswellOnt 9651, 71 C.B.R. (6th) 187, 100 C.L.R. (4th) 169, 47 E.T.R. (4th) 177, 10 P.P.S.A.C. (4th) 165 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2021 CarswellOnt 7769 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Robert Nicholson Construction Co." p2="Edgecon Construction Inc." post.rptr="3107" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63dd66205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Robert Nicholson Construction Co. v. Edgecon Construction Inc.">Robert Nicholson Construction Co. v. Edgecon Construction Inc., 2016 ONSC 3107, 2016 CarswellOnt 8345, 36 C.B.R. (6th) 224, 51 C.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> in concluding that there could be no trust established in the absence of privity of contract between the owner and subcontractor. While monies paid to the contractor are impressed with a trust for the benefit of subcontractors to the exclusion of others until the subcontractors are fully satisfied, the tentacles of those trust provisions do not extend back to an owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Van Geel" p2="Pennha" post.rptr="16833" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I63dd66215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Van Geel v. Pennha">Van Geel v. Pennha, 2020 CarswellOnt 16833, 2020 ONSC 6975, 4 C.L.R. (5th) 189 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor performed renovations at the defendants' cottage property before a dispute ended the project. The plaintiff did not avail itself of the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, or invoice the defendants for many months. After the defendants subsequently sold the cottage and used the proceeds to purchase a new residence, the plaintiff commenced an action asserting entitlement to an interest in the defendant's new home based on constructive trust principles or an equitable mortgage. He alleged that his work had enhanced the value of the cottage property and thereby permitted purchase of the new residence. The defendants successfully moved to set aside the <ital>ex parte</ital> order registering a Certificate of Pending Litigation (“CPL”) against the title to their current residence. Referencing the decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Rafat General Contractor Inc." p2="1015734 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="7519" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90b00970f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.">Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 7519, 81 O.R. (3d) 798, 52 C.L.R. (3d) 63, [2005] O.T.C. 1107, [2005] O.J. No. 5526 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="992426 Ontario Inc." p2="Koenpack Canada Inc." post.rptr="4769" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63dd8d305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="992426 Ontario Inc. v. Koenpack Canada Inc.">992426 Ontario Inc. v. Koenpack Canada Inc., 2018 ONSC 4769, 2018 CarswellOnt 16362, 94 C.L.R. (4th) 80, 40 C.P.C. (8th) 211, [2018] O.J. No. 5102 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the court found that it would be even more subversive of the statutory scheme than in <ital>Rafat</ital> to allow the plaintiff to transmogrify its unperfected statutory lien under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> into an interest in the defendant's subsequently acquired property. Any contractor having failed to perfect its security under the Act could tie up title to any subsequently purchased property simply on the strength of the ability to trace some part of the proceeds of sale of the original property to that second property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vision Air Conditioning and Heating Corporation" p2="Golden Dragon Ho Inc." post.rptr="3520" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63dd8d315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vision Air Conditioning and Heating Corporation v. Golden Dragon Ho Inc.">Vision Air Conditioning and Heating Corporation v. Golden Dragon Ho Inc., 2018 ONSC 3520, 2018 CarswellOnt 8981, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 314 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The corporate defendant, which was controlled by the individual defendant, ordered but did not pay for services and was found to owe the amount set out in the judgment. The corporation did not borrow funds to finance the construction projects, intending to pay the invoices out of its own resources, including income from rental properties, but it fell into financial difficulties. The contractor unsuccessfully pursued summary judgment against the individual defendant for statutory breach of trust. Section 7(1) is broad enough to capture any funds specifically earmarked for financing a construction project or improvement such as insurance proceeds, funds advanced by landlords, guarantees or inter-company transfers provided they are funds received (or receivable) by the owner for the specific purpose. However, general revenues of a corporation, self-financing through rental income or even general borrowing on a line of credit are not funds impressed with a trust even if the owner originally intended to use those funds to pay for the construction. The section requires that there is a distinct fund which is identifiably for the purpose of completing the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Simpson" p2="Bridgewater Bank" post.rptr="714" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63dd8d325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simpson v. Bridgewater Bank">Simpson v. Bridgewater Bank, 2012 ONSC 714, 2012 CarswellOnt 1420, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 243 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 5054, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff general contractor entered into construction contract with the owner for construction of a home, and the defendant bank provided mortgage financing. The bank's solicitor held back 10 per cent from each of construction advances, and, after the contractor eventually obtained judgment in its lien action against the owner, the bank completed a sale of the property under power of sale pursuant to the mortgage. The contractor successfully brought action for a declaration that the monies held back by the bank were trust funds held for his benefit. Although the bank was not obligated to retain a holdback under ss. 22(1) or 78 of the Act, the mortgage funds had been advanced to the owner, and she was charged interest on the entire sum, inclusive of the funds held back by the bank's solicitor. Those monies were held in trust for the owner, and the bank had no right to them <ital>vis-à-vis</ital> the owner. Even if the owner did not actually receive the monies, notwithstanding it was being held in trust for her, she was deemed to have received them, and it was appropriate, in the circumstances of this case, to interpret “received” as including receivable. Furthermore, the matter was not <ital>res judicata</ital> because the contractor did not raise the trust issue in the lien action against the owner. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co." p2="Irvine & Reeves Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="1955" ref.id="I55d1a9c0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd.">Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd. (1955), 1955 CarswellBC 177, [1955] 3 D.L.R. 561, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.)</ital> [1955] S.C.R. 694 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Andrea Schmidt Construction Ltd." p2="Glatt" post.rptr="791" pre.rptr="1979" ref.id="I63ddb4415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andrea Schmidt Construction Ltd. v. Glatt">Andrea Schmidt Construction Ltd. v. Glatt, 1979 CarswellOnt 791, 25 O.R. (2d) 567 (Ont. H.C.); affirmed 1980 CarswellOnt 1365, 28 O.R. (2d) 672 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, cited under the Commentary, above, which establish the principle of “deemed receipt” in order to give a meaning to the word “received” that would not render the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> nugatory.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Man-Shield (Now) Construction Inc." p2="Rainy River District School Board" post.rptr="323" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63dddb505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Man-Shield (Now) Construction Inc. v. Rainy River District School Board">Man-Shield (Now) Construction Inc. v. Rainy River District School Board, 2012 ONSC 323, 2012 CarswellOnt 1405, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 117 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 2150, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 126 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where a defendant holds trust monies for the benefit of a plaintiff pursuant to the provisions of s. 7(1), the provisions of s. 7(3) and (4) do not entitle a contractor to immediate payment of those monies in circumstances where there is a claim for set off by a statutory trustee. The quantum of the trust amount cannot be determined without a determination of the value of the set-off claim. Section 7 cannot be read in isolation when the provisions of section 12 clearly give a trustee a right to set off against monies held in trust, subject to the provisions of Part IV regarding holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Placha" p2="Limotta" post.rptr="6779" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63dddb515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Placha v. Limotta">Placha v. Limotta, 2011 ONSC 6779, 2011 CarswellOnt 12848, 6 C.L.R. (4th) 169 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff was held to be the beneficiary of a trust under s. 8(1) and the individual and corporate defendants trustees of those funds, the onus shifted to the defendants to demonstrate that payments made from the trust funds were to proper beneficiaries of the trust. In the absence of such evidence, the individual named defendants were jointly and severally liable with the corporate defendants based on their positions as officers or directors of those corporations. The facts did not reveal aspects of misconduct, misappropriation or defalcation that would bring into operation provisions of s. 178 of <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>. The fact that there was money owed by an individual bankrupt defendant to the plaintiff and that the trust existed by virtue of <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, without more, was not sufficient to conclude that the judgment survived the insolvency process.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chris Nash Building Inc." p2="Buckland" post.rptr="5395" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63dddb525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Chris Nash Building Inc. v. Buckland">Chris Nash Building Inc. v. Buckland, 2010 ONSC 5395, 2010 CarswellOnt 7962, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 10009, 98 C.L.R. (3d) 157 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The definition of “owner” makes it clear that a required element of being an owner is to have “an interest” in the property. Section 7 does not impose liability on a person, such as an owner's solicitor, who merely holds insurance monies before giving them to the “owner”, but only imposes strict liability upon a person who has “an interest in a premises”, is likely to benefit from the improvements, and has some say in the nature of the improvement, and the progress of the improvement. Assuming that most, if not all of insurance funds received by a solicitor in trust were impressed by a trust in the hands of the owner, the solicitor was not liable for any breach of that trust unless the court concluded on the evidence that he participated in the breach of trust by the owner or that he had a duty to inquire. Here, there was no evidence as to any other circumstances that would have placed any obligation on the solicitor to make any further inquiry.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Structural Contracting Ltd." p2="Westcola Holdings Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63de02605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc.">Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc. (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 417 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—When a contractor working on a commercial property is unpaid, rents received by the owner/landlord are trust funds under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and remain so until the contractor is paid. To exclude rent from the trust in the case of a landlord would be to exclude the landlord from the application of s. 7.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Elmford Construction Company Limited" p2="South Winston Properties Inc." post.rptr="588" pre.rptr="45" ref.id="I63de02615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elmford Construction Company Limited v. South Winston Properties Inc.">Elmford Construction Company Limited v. South Winston Properties Inc. (1999), 45 O.R. (3d) 588 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2001), 59 O.R. (3d) 111 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—A real estate developer provided letters of credit as security for the performance of its obligation to provide services under a subdivision agreement with the town and municipality, to be drawn upon by the town or municipality if the services were not constructed. When the developer failed to pay the plaintiff contractor hired to construct the services, the plaintiff unsuccessfully argued that the letters of credit, which the municipality had drawn upon but not used to pay the plaintiff, constituted a trust fund. The plaintiff, who did not register a lien, did not have any contractual or beneficial entitlement to the proceeds of the letters of credit. It was not a party to the letters or to the subdivision agreements, and had no contractual relationship with the town. There was nothing in the letters of credit or in the subdivision agreements that obliged the town to use any proceeds drawn from the letters to pay the claims of third parties like the plaintiff nor was there anything that created a trust. The trust provisions in s. 7 of the CLA exclude amounts received by a municipality from the statutory trust. Subsection 7(2) applies “where amounts become payable under a contract to a contractor by the owner on a certificate of a payment certifier”. Here there was never a contract between the plaintiff and the town, nor a certificate of a payment certifier.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="University Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Dynasty Executive Suites Ltd." post.rptr="4707" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63de02625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="University Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Dynasty Executive Suites Ltd.">University Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Dynasty Executive Suites Ltd. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4707, 1998 CarswellOnt 4398 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The proceeds of a trust action are trust funds for the benefit of all lien claimants, not just those who contributed to the legal costs of the trust action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co." p2="Windigo Community Development Corp." post.rptr="22" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63de29705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp.">D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp. (1998), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 22 (Ont. Gen. Div.); denying leave to appeal from (1998), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 14 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The first named defendant allegedly remitted progress payments to a passive intermediary company, with knowledge that the funds were not being paid to the plaintiff contractor. These allegations, if proved, were sufficient to give rise to an obligation pursuant to an implied or resulting trust quite apart from, and in addition to, the statutory trust scheme of the Act. The defendant's motion for leave to appeal the dismissal of its motion to strike the plaintiff's claim was therefore denied. The thrust of trust provisions is to provide, in addition to the lien, a remedy to subcontractors and suppliers who, because of the lack of direct privity with the owner, struggled under the disadvantage of being deprived of a personal claim against the owner based upon contract. But those trust provisions were not intended to displace or curtail a breach of trust remedy held by persons who otherwise stood in a direct relation with the owner in circumstances that would give rise to a trust obligation. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In the original motion to strike, the court applied the “plain and obvious test” in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Hunt" p2="T&N plc" post.rptr="959" pre.rptr="[1990] 2" ref.id="I63de29715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hunt v. T&N plc">Hunt v. T&N plc (1990), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, as adopted by the Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Nash" p2="Ontario" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I63de50805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nash v. Ontario">Nash v. Ontario (1995), 27 O.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> in finding that the plaintiff's trust action against a non-privy survived a R. 21 challenge.] The case marks a potentially radical re-reading of the current state of trust law in this province.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Tampa Hall Ltd." p2="Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce" post.rptr="274" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63de50815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tampa Hall Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce">Tampa Hall Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 274, 37 O.R. (3d) 150 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A motion to certify a series of breach of trust claims as a class proceeding under s. 5 of the <ital>Class Proceedings Act, 1992</ital>, S.O. 1992, C-6, failed in this case. There was a disclosed cause of action (s. 5(1)(a)), there was an identifiable class of two or more persons (s. 5(1)(b)), however the Court could not conclude that there was sufficient commonality of issues (s. 5(1)(c)) or that the balance of convenience favoured a class proceeding (s. 5(1)(d)).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Batoni Construction Inc." p2="Anthomax Mechanical Ltd." post.rptr="134" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63de50825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Batoni Construction Inc. v. Anthomax Mechanical Ltd.">Batoni Construction Inc. v. Anthomax Mechanical Ltd. (1997), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 134, 146 D.L.R. (4th) 243, 33 O.R. (3d) 647, 100 O.A.C. 225 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The trust sections of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> apply only to land within the Province of Ontario and have no extra-territorial effect. While the claims for lien and trust claims are severable, the Act is restricted in its application to lands located in this province.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Opec Acoustics & Drywall Ltd." p2="Kascon Corp." post.rptr="75" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63de50835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Opec Acoustics & Drywall Ltd. v. Kascon Corp.">Opec Acoustics & Drywall Ltd. v. Kascon Corp. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 75 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where a breach of trust allegation is based on malfeasance such as fraud, misrepresentation, malice or malicious intent, it is clear that R. 25.06(8) of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> applies to such pleadings. However, the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> creates a category of “breach of trust” that is independent of the “condition of mind” applicable under R. 25.06(8), and that is not a lower standard of pleading than that contemplated by R. 25.06(8). Because all amounts owing to a contractor or subcontractor whether or not due or payable, or received by a contractor or subcontractor on account of any contract or subcontract, are within the knowledge of the contractor or subcontractor, it is sufficient in the pleadings under the Act to allege a breach of contract where no accounting has been made of those funds to any subcontractors or other persons who have supplied services or materials to the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Vecero" p2="C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc." post.rptr="903" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90b0f3d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc.">Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 903, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 74 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A mortgagee gave one mortgage to the owner to purchase the land. It was fully advanced on purchase. Seven separate mortgages were registered as building mortgages and were 90 per cent advanced. The project failed, the owner was bankrupted and the lands were sold and the proceeds paid into court. It was held that as the mortgagee was neither an “owner” nor a “payer” in these circumstances, the unadvanced moneys could not be trust moneys and the lien claimants were entitled only to their s. 78 remedy.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Canadian Asbestos Services Ltd." p2="Bank of Montreal" post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63de77915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canadian Asbestos Services Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal">Canadian Asbestos Services Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 54 (Ont. Gen. Div.); supplementary reasons at (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 204 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—None of the proceeds from holdbacks and moneys held in trust pursuant to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> could form part of the assets or estate of a company which would be available for general distribution to all classes of creditors under the federal <ital>Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">These contractors or subcontractors who performed work or supplied materials to the project in compliance with ss. 7(1) and 8(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had a first charge upon the funds in question.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
7:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">7:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 7(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rassaun Services Inc." p2="Sle-Co Plastics Inc." post.rptr="2912" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63de9ea05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rassaun Services Inc. v. Sle-Co Plastics Inc.">Rassaun Services Inc. v. Sle-Co Plastics Inc., 2019 ONSC 2912, 2019 CarswellOnt 7313, 99 C.L.R. (4th) 301 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff removed equipment from “L facility” owned by one company and installed it in a second facility owned by another company. When its accounts were not paid, it sought a remedy against the second facility, and the defendant, but not the L facility or original company, claiming that the defendant promised payment after the sale of the L facility was completed. In a motion by the plaintiff to renew or extend a certificate of pending litigation, the court ruled that identification of a source of payment of an outstanding unsecured debt was simply a “reasonable expectation” of the place from which the creditor would be paid and was insufficient to establish a statutory trust under s. 7.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lacroix" p2="Dompierre" post.rptr="3873" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63de9ea15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lacroix v. Dompierre">Lacroix v. Dompierre, 2016 ONSC 3873, 2016 CarswellOnt 9637, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2016 CarswellOnt 17664, 2016 ONSC 6931, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The evidence was clear that the plaintiff sub-subcontractor knew he was not going to be paid once he received certain correspondence from the subcontractor, and that he knew he had suffered damages at that time. Nevertheless, he did not commence the breach of trust of claim until four years later, and the court concluded that it was commenced out of time.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1088812 Ontario Ltd." p2="Carlo" post.rptr="18655" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63dec5b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1088812 Ontario Ltd. v. Carlo">1088812 Ontario Ltd. v. Carlo, 2014 CarswellOnt 18655 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff had the onus to prove that a trust was created and that the defendants had breached any such trust. From the evidence as a whole on a balance of probabilities, the court was unable to find that a trust fund was created, and consequently there was no breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Terradyne Construction Management Ltd." p2="6832458 Canada Inc." post.rptr="1495" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63dec5b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Terradyne Construction Management Ltd. v. 6832458 Canada Inc.">Terradyne Construction Management Ltd. v. 6832458 Canada Inc., 2015 ONSC 1495, 2015 CarswellOnt 3658, 46 C.L.R. (4th) 213 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The motion judge correctly stated and applied the applicable law, that there was an initial onus on the plaintiff to prove the existence of a statutory trust. The motion judge then looked at the facts before him and decided that the plaintiff had not satisfied its initial onus with respect to the funds in question.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Kamnik Electric Ltd." p2="Friedman" post.rptr="8589" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63dec5b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kamnik Electric Ltd. v. Friedman">Kamnik Electric Ltd. v. Friedman, 2015 CarswellOnt 8589 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After obtaining judgment in Small Claims Court against the corporate contractor, and waiving any excess over $25,000 to come within the monetary jurisdiction of that court, the plaintiff issued a subsequent claim for breach of trust and fraud against the principal of the contractor. Because it was not clear as to when the applicable limitation period had commenced to run, and whether it had expired, the matter needed to be examined through the rigours of a trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Varcon Construction Co." p2="1554098 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1649" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63dec5b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Varcon Construction Co. v. 1554098 Ontario Inc.">Varcon Construction Co. v. 1554098 Ontario Inc., 2011 ONSC 1649, 2011 CarswellOnt 1720, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 162 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed on other grounds 2012 ONCA 43, 2012 CarswellOnt 476, 11 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor negotiated two construction contracts with the related defendants to build two shell buildings that the defendants would later finish on the interior as fitness centres. After the plaintiff experienced difficulties in obtaining payment, the parties eventually negotiated a settlement agreement designed to guarantee payment by way, <ital>inter alia</ital>, of an additional guarantee by one of the corporate defendants and consent to judgment. The court found that the construction agreements were merged into the settlement agreement, and that the plaintiff no longer has a claim in breach of contract. However, the statutory trust created by s. 7(1) of the Act survived the settlement agreement, a conclusion consistent with the remedial purpose of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and with sections of the Act that prevent parties from contracting out of its provisions. In the absence of evidence that the defendants complied with their obligations as trustee, they failed to discharge the onus on them and were liable for breach of trust. There was sufficient evidence that the personal defendant had effective control over the activities of the defendant companies, and was therefore liable for the breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Fulton Homes Ltd." p2="D'Elia" post.rptr="735" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63deecc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Fulton Homes Ltd. v. D'Elia">Fulton Homes Ltd. v. D'Elia (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 735, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 290 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 4255 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While there was clear evidence that the defendant's general operating revenues and operating account were in fact used to pay the trades, it did not mean that these funds were therefore impressed with a s. 7 trust. There was no evidence that the funds were meant “to be used in the financing of the improvement.” In reaching this conclusion, the court adopted the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Andcur Building Corp." p2="756203 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4894" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I63deecc15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andcur Building Corp. v. 756203 Ontario Ltd.">Andcur Building Corp. v. 756203 Ontario Ltd. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 4894, 35 C.L.R. (2d) 252 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd." p2="846539 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="230" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63deecc25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd.">Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 230 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4717 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The trust provisions of s. 7(1) expressly exclude from the statutory trust amounts received by a municipality. Contractors had installed roads, lighting and sewers on road allowances in a subdivision project, and the roads were dedicated to the local municipalities. Standard bank letters of credit had been provided to the municipalities by the developer to guarantee the performance of the works on the road allowances and payments by the developer. The developer became bankrupt. The bank sold the subdivision lots and paid down the loan with the proceeds. The proceeds were held not to be subject to a statutory trust. The trust provisions in s. 7 excluded amounts received by a municipality from the statutory trust, and, further, the contractors had no expectation that they would be paid by the municipalities beyond their lien rights under s. 17(4). There was no privity of contract between the lien claimants and the municipality and there was no possible claim for unjust enrichment as the contractors knew that the intention of the development agreement was that the municipalities would get the improved road allowances at no cost. The letters of credit were simply a contract by the bank, at the developer's request and cost, to indemnify the municipalities to the extent of their obligations under the Act. They were not intended to secure the contractors against non-payment by the developer.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Andcur Building Corp." p2="756203 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4894" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I63df13d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andcur Building Corp. v. 756203 Ontario Ltd.">Andcur Building Corp. v. 756203 Ontario Ltd. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 4894, 35 C.L.R. (2d) 252 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Unless it is expressly constituted a “specific fund” within the meaning of the Rules, neither the general revenues of a corporation nor its operating loan or line of credit constitute a trust fund within the meaning of this subsection. The mere fact that a corporation intends to pay a contractor from its general revenues is not alone sufficient to impress those revenues with a trust. Where none of the money that was received was sought or received for the purpose of financing or in any way paying for the contractor's work, cash flow generated from general operating revenues, or from an operating loan or line of credit obtained to finance a business's general operations did not fall under the application of s. 7. Otherwise any corporation in the same situation would be prevented from paying its creditors without exposing its directors to liability under s. 13 of the Act. The decision of Justice Feldman in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Van Arnhem" p2="Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc." post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63df13d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Van Arnhem v. Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc.">Van Arnhem v. Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 54</ref></cite> was distinguished in this case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Trans Eastern Lumber Corp. (Receiver of)" p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="306" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I63df3ae05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trans Eastern Lumber Corp. (Receiver of) v. Kinalea Development Corp.">Trans Eastern Lumber Corp. (Receiver of) v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1996), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 306 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Trans Eastern registered a claim for lien against lands owned by Kinalea which lien was preserved and perfected in timely fashion. The mortgagee vacated this lien by posting a bond. Subsequently, monies were transferred by Kinalea to Trans Eastern's general account, which Trans Eastern chose to apply to a debt that bore no relation to the lands in question. At the time the said funds were received by Kinalea, there were amounts owing to contractors for services or materials supplied to the lands so that the funds in question were trust funds. The court held that the monies were impressed with a trust by s. 7 of the Act and neither Kinalea nor Trans Eastern had any power to appropriate it except for the express purposes of the trust. The test is not who the parties are, that is whether they are creditor, debtor or innocent third parties, but rather the test is what is it that is involved. A creditor is not permitted to use the <ital>Rule in Clayton's Case</ital> so as to allocate funds to a purpose outside the trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Anand" p2="Medjuck" post.rptr="2571" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63df3ae15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anand v. Medjuck">Anand v. Medjuck (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 2571 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A trust company obtained summary judgment dismissing a Plaintiff's claim based, <ital>inter alia</ital>, on principles of constructive trust and transmitted fiduciary duty. Following the decision of Bayda J.A. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1976" p1="MacDonald" p2="Hauer" post.rptr="110" pre.rptr="72" ref.id="I63df3ae25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MacDonald v. Hauer">MacDonald v. Hauer (1976), 72 D.L.R. (3d) 110 (Sask. C.A.)</ref></cite>, the court held that there were three essential elements for a constructive trust: first, assistance by a stranger of a nominated trustee; second, knowledge; and third, a dishonest and fraudulent design on the part of the nominated trustee. As to the second element, knowledge, the degree of knowledge was only that which would put a reasonable man on enquiry.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Van Arnhem" p2="Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc." post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63df3ae35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Van Arnhem v. Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc.">Van Arnhem v. Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 54 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The contractor was hired by S to design a system that would give adequate heating and cooling to a tanning salon. The contractor asked S if he had funds set aside for the project. S replied that he did. The contractor asked which of S's companies would be paying for the work. S said that he did not know yet. The contractor completed a substantial amount of the work, including the rough-in and unit installation. The contractor then had to stop for the drywaller to do its work. The contractor was never called back to complete its work. The contractor subsequently made efforts to have its bill paid, but such efforts were unsuccessful. The contractor brought an action against the company that owned the salon for breach of statutory trust and against S as president of the company for assenting to or acquiescing in the breach of trust. In the circumstances, it was appropriate to interpret the word “received” in s. 7(1) as including “receivable.” Where the principal of the company controlled both the finance of the project and its ownership and construction, including when, if ever, the designated funds would be “received” by the owner, it was necessary to protect the beneficiaries of the trust funds from such an unscrupulous principal. The trust existed, and it was a breach of trust to fail to fund the owner in order to allow the proper payments to be made from the trust to the beneficiaries. Moreover, it was clear that S assented to and acquiesced in the breach. He was the person whose statement formed the evidence that the fund existed. He advised the contractor that cheques had been drawn up to pay the invoices and then failed to make the cheques available. Further, he told the contractor that the funds had been diverted to other uses until the project in question was completed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Kasper Land Drainage Inc." p2="Spectrum Realty Inc." post.rptr="44" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I63df61f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kasper Land Drainage Inc. v. Spectrum Realty Inc.">Kasper Land Drainage Inc. v. Spectrum Realty Inc. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 44 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's construction lien action was vacated on account of its failure to obtain a trial date, the security which the defendant had posted was cancelled, and the action for recovery of payment continued as provided by s. 38. When the letter of credit was cancelled, the guaranteed investment certificate supporting it as collateral was cashed, and the proceeds were disbursed to various creditors of the defendant. The plaintiff obtained a <ital>Mareva</ital> injunction on the basis that the funds paid out were imposed with a trust pursuant to s. 7(1), and subsequently moved to continue the injuntion. Held, the injunction was continued, although it was far from clear that proceeds from the release of the posted security were impressed by a trust under s. 7. It was clear on the evidence that the defendant had not complied with the trust provisions of the Act. The plaintiff had more than a strong prima facie case that it would succeed at trial and had met the conditions required to entitle it to a <ital>Mareva</ital> injunction.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Salazar" p2="Bond Towers Ltd." post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I63df61f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Salazar v. Bond Towers Ltd.">Salazar v. Bond Towers Ltd. (1990), 44 C.L.R. 207 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner gave to a trust company a mortgage on two properties on which construction work was being done. The owner's loan submission document referred to renovation at one of the premises as one of the purposes for which the mortgage was sought. However, funds under the mortgage for one property were advanced by way of a single advance, and for the second property the disbursements were timed to be used for the purchase of that property. The trust company made no payments which related to the progress of renovations on the premises. The plaintiffs performed some of the renovation work on the first property, for which they filed a construction lien, and registered a certificate of pending litigation with respect to the second property, alleging the mortgage to be a construction mortgage which would permit them to trace the mortgage funds used to purchase that property. The defendants applied to discharge the certificate of pending litigation, and the discharge was granted. There was no triable issue regarding the matter. The legally binding documentation, the disbursement of the funds received from the mortgage and the single advance of all the funds went to supporting the proposition that the mortgage was not a construction mortgage. The mortgage application was a preliminary document which did not in itself present a triable issue.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
7:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">7:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 7(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Feltz Design Build Ltd." p2="Larson et al." post.rptr="2469" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63df89005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Feltz Design Build Ltd. v. Larson et al.">Feltz Design Build Ltd. v. Larson et al., 2021 ONSC 2469, 2021 CarswellOnt 4450 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Feltz Design Build Ltd. v. Larson</ital>, 2022 CarswellOnt 1775 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The trusts established by subs. 7(2) extend to all amounts received by the owner after the stipulated event has occurred, even if from sources entirely unrelated to the property that has been improved. A breach of trust was established where the proceeds of the sale by the defendant owner of another piece of real estate exceeded the amount owing to the claimant and were used to satisfy amounts owing on account of mortgages registered against the parcel.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Robert Nicholson Construction Co." p2="Edgecon Construction Inc." post.rptr="3107" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63df89015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Robert Nicholson Construction Co. v. Edgecon Construction Inc.">Robert Nicholson Construction Co. v. Edgecon Construction Inc., 2016 ONSC 3107, 2016 CarswellOnt 8345, 36 C.B.R. (6th) 224, 51 C.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2015 ONSC 1237, 2015 CarswellOnt 3975, 125 O.R. (3d) 373, 48 C.L.R. (4th) 168 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motions judge erred in law when he found that a subcontractor could be a beneficiary of the statutory trust fund created under s. 7(1) of the Act, as the wording of that section is clear; the owner's trust fund exists “for the benefit of the contractor”. Under s. 8 of the Act, a separate and distinct trust obligation is imposed on contractors and subcontractors, the beneficiaries of which are other subcontractors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re" post.rptr="3326" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63dfb0105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re">Veltri Metal Products Co., Re (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3326, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The owner's lenders held a general security interest in all or substantially all of its assets. A sale order provided that the sale proceeds were to “stand in place and stead” of the owner's assets without prejudice to any claim being advanced against them as could have been advanced against the assets. In effect, the sale proceeds were substituted for the owner's assets and were subject to the claims of the secured creditors. The court approved sale of the insolvent owner's assets included the sale of its leasehold interest in the premises upon which the appellant lien claimants' work was performed. The asset sale could not have taken place in the face of the claims of the owner's secured creditors without the consent of those creditors and court approval, and the sale was subject to the terms imposed by the court. Under these terms, the gross proceeds of sale were applied in payment of specific items and, thereafter, the net sale proceeds, which stood in substitution for the owner's fully secured assets, were paid to the Monitor. Thus, the owner had no interest in or right to any of the net sale proceeds ultimately paid to and held by the Monitor. At best, the owner was a conduit for the receipt by the Monitor of the sale proceeds. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: It appears that <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co." p2="Irvine & Reeves Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="1955" ref.id="I55d37e80fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd.">Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd. (1955), 1955 CarswellBC 177, [1955] 3 D.L.R. 561, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.)</ital> [1955] S.C.R. 694 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, was neither raised in the facta nor argued in the appeal.] Accordingly, the sale, proceeds were not trust monies in the owner's hands or received by it as owner, as required to trigger the trust provisions of s. 7(2) and (3) of the Act. This distinguished this case from <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Structural Contracting Ltd." p2="Westcola Holdings Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63dfb0125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc.">Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc. (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 417, 2000 CarswellOnt 2018, 2 C.L.R. (3d) 165 (C.A.); leave to appeal to S.C.C. dismissed (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 709, 2001 CarswellOnt 710 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> and similar cases. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also the earlier related request by the Monitor for advice and directions in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re" post.rptr="3211" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63dfd7205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re">Veltri Metal Products Co., Re (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 3211, 2004 CarswellOnt 3153 (S.C.J. [Commercial List]); leave to appeal allowed (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 5526 (C.A.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re" post.rptr="3211" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63dfd7215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re">Veltri Metal Products Co., Re (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 3211, 2004 CarswellOnt 3153 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3326, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—This was a motion by the monitor in CCAA proceedings for advice and directions regarding the validity, scope, and priority of certain claims under s. 7 and s. 9 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Property in which Veltri had an interest had been sold by court order, which contained provisions for the distribution of the net proceeds of sale. This distribution conflicted with the distribution scheme of s. 7(2) and the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Structural Contracting Ltd." p2="Westcola Holdings Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63dffe305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc.">Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc. (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 417, 2000 CarswellOnt 2018, 2 C.L.R. (3d) 165 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 709, 2001 CarswellOnt 710 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>. The court read and applied <ital>Structural</ital> as contemplating the existence of “different trusts”, including the prior trust established by the sale order in this case, thus defeating the claim of the s. 7(2) trust claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Elmford Construction Co." p2="South Winston Properties Inc." post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63dffe315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elmford Construction Co. v. South Winston Properties Inc.">Elmford Construction Co. v. South Winston Properties Inc. (2002), 20 C.L.R. (3d) 302, 2002 CarswellOnt 1117 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor performed work on the owner's land, certified by a payment certifier, and received judgment for a substantial unpaid balance. Subsequently, pursuant to the <ital>Creditor's Relief Act</ital>, the sheriff distributed monies received from an escrow agent to the plaintiff contractor and to another party, who, while not a contractor, had been owed monies by the owner pursuant to another judgment. On appeal, the plaintiff contractor successfully challenged the sheriff's distribution to the non-construction judgment creditor. The fact that funds released from escrow had no direct connection with contractor's work did not prevent those funds from becoming trust funds. Subsection 7(2) is very broadly worded and should be contrasted with the more restrictive s. 7(1). Subsection 7(2) does not deal with the source of the funds, it designates that funds attributable to the owner are designated trust funds for the benefit of the contractor who has had its work certified. Accordingly, here, the contractor was not required to share them pursuant to the distribution scheme of s. 32 of the <ital>Creditors' Relief Act</ital>. The fact that the owner did not take physical possession of the monies released from escrow did not prevent them from “being in the owner's hands or received by the owner.” The fact that the monies were detoured by the garnishment to the Sheriff did not change their character. It was appropriate in the circumstances to interpret the word “received” as including receivable or payable.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
7:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">7:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 7(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Bank" p2="Penex Metropolis Ltd." post.rptr="464" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63e025405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Bank v. Penex Metropolis Ltd.">Royal Bank v. Penex Metropolis Ltd., 2010 CarswellOnt 464, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 199 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The s. 7(3) trust applies to completed contracts as well as substantially completed contracts, and there is nothing limiting the time for a motion to the court under s. 32 to declare a contract substantially complete. If any amount remains unpaid under the contract, the contract is outstanding, and if there is completion, there must have been a prior substantial completion. The owner or trustee cannot avoid s. 7(3) by refusing to certify substantial completion. The contractor must be free to apply to the court for a declaration, whether the lien rights have expired or not.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Structural Contracting Ltd." p2="Westcola Holdings Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63e025415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc.">Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc. (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 417 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Section 7(3) is not restricted to profits in the hands of an owner. As a practical matter, such a limitation would turn actions to enforce the trust sections of the Act into accounting exercises.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="University Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Dynasty Executive Suites Ltd." post.rptr="4707" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63e025425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="University Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Dynasty Executive Suites Ltd.">University Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Dynasty Executive Suites Ltd. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4707, 1998 CarswellOnt 4398 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In a combined action <ital>in rem</ital> and <ital>in personam</ital> the plaintiff moved upon the unreported authority of Gray J. in <ital>Geist Construction Ltd. v. Ruten Construction Limited et al.</ital> for an order excluding those beneficiaries who would not contribute to the costs of the action. The motion was dismissed. The trustee was required to proceed on behalf of all statutory beneficiaries.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
7:6: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">7:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 7(4)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1022403 Ontario Ltd." p2="Man-Shield (NWO) et al." post.rptr="19032" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8d8c15c0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="1022403 Ontario Ltd. v. Man-Shield (NWO) et al.">1022403 Ontario Ltd. v. Man-Shield (NWO) et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 19032, 2023 ONSC 6695 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Garnished funds paid into Court are not trust funds under the provisions of s. 7 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and the action by a municipality in responding to a garnishment order was not a breach of the statutory trust. A garnishment is a mechanism to allow creditors to seize property belonging to their debtors, and the municipality in responding to the garnishment was not appropriating or converting trust monies to itself. The fact that the debtor contractor had the right to contest the garnishment here was evidence that its entitlement to ownership either by contract or by statutory trust was preserved and recognized. However, that ownership interest was not of a nature that immunized the funds from garnishment. Neither was the act of responding to a garnishment a breach of trust by a payor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clearwater Structures" p2="614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction" post.rptr="5601" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63e04c505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clearwater Structures v. 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction">Clearwater Structures v. 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction, 2021 ONSC 5601, 2021 CarswellOnt 12375, 70 E.T.R. (4th) 202 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 7565, 2021 CarswellOnt 16601 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The suggestion that the failure to release trust funds when they become due and owing cannot constitute a breach of trust would serve to completely undermine the purpose and effect of the trust provisions of the Act. The decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Susin" p2="Genstar Development Co." post.rptr="4650" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I90b2c890f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Susin v. Genstar Development Co.">Susin v. Genstar Development Co. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 4650, 14 C.L.R. (3d) 292 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 4980, 27 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, does not stand for the immutable proposition that a failure to pay out trust funds received and owing on a sub-contract can never constitute a breach of trust. Allowing the contractor to conduct its business in this way would lead to the absurd situation wherein a contractor could retain funds owing to a subcontractor arbitrarily and indefinitely without concern for its obligations under the Act. Such conduct would create commercial chaos and allow a contractor to hold off paying a subcontractor for any number of bogus or flimsy reasons or for any number of ulterior purposes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Susin" p2="Genstar Development Co." post.rptr="4650" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I90b2efa0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Susin v. Genstar Development Co.">Susin v. Genstar Development Co. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 4650, 14 C.L.R. (3d) 292 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 4980, 27 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Failure to pay the holdback did not, in itself, amount to a breach of trust, even if the holdback itself constituted a trust fund. Here, the plaintiff claimed monies due under a contract for a construction project completed in 1974 made between the plaintiff's bankrupt predecessor and a predecessor of the defendant. The monies included the outstanding balance of the holdback and extras allegedly due and owing to the plaintiff's predecessor. The plaintiff unsuccessfully argued that the defendant's predecessor breached the trust provisions of the Ontario former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, by failing to pay the balance of the holdback, and that the defendant was answerable for the breach. Due to the passage of time, the defendant was no longer in a position to discharge its onus respecting the status or disposition of the holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Di-Mar Construction Ltd." p2="Wellington Business Centre Inc." post.rptr="68" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63e073615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di-Mar Construction Ltd. v. Wellington Business Centre Inc.">Di-Mar Construction Ltd. v. Wellington Business Centre Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 68 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—W. Inc. constructed a building with financing obtained from P. Ltd. After initial construction, it was decided to enclose the ground floor area, and a new mortgage agreed to provide a mortgage to W. Inc. to pay off the P. Ltd. mortgage, to assist with the cost of enclosure, and to allow the balance to be used by W. Inc. for investment purposes. The mortgagee advanced the entire sum to W. Inc., part of which was deposited into an interest-bearing money market fund held in trust for W. Inc. The balance of the mortgage proceeds were used to pay off P. Ltd.'s mortgage, rather than to complete the enclosure. Two liens were subsequently registered against the property, and the moneys in the money market fund were seized by the mortgagee and applied to reduce the outstanding balance of the mortgage. The court found that the liens had priority over this assignment, and that the lien claimants were entitled to recover the amount of their respective liens from the mortgagee. The increase in the new mortgage was obtained to pay for the enclosure of the ground floor. When the mortgagee appropriated the trust funds in the bank account held for W. Inc., there was nothing left to pay the subtrades. The reassignment of those funds to the mortgagee was made to deprive lien claimants from recovering sums owed to them.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
8:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Ontario's first trust provisions were instituted as part of the <ital>Statute Law Amendment Act, 1942</ital>, S.O. 1942, c. 34. The trust obligation introduced that that statute was imposed on “all sums received” by a “builder or contractor or a sub-contractor” and was specified to benefit “the proprietor, builder or contractor, sub-contractors, Workmen's Compensation Board, workmen and persons who have supplied material on account of the contract”. It is interesting to note that the “proprietor” was a beneficiary of this early contractor's trust. The contractor's trust section of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, s. 8(1)(b) incorporated the concept of “receipt”, extended the trust obligation from amounts “received” to amounts “owing to a contractor or subcontractor, whether or not due or payable” and narrowed the class of beneficiaries by deleting the “owner” and “the Workman's Compensation Board”. The Advisory Committee introduced s. 8(1)(a) in order to incorporate the principle of deemed receipt established in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co." p2="Empire Brass Manufacturing Co." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="1955" ref.id="I55d48ff0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.">Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.
