(1955), 1955 CarswellBC 177, [1955] 3 D.L.R. 561, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.)</ital> [1955] S.C.R. 694 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>. The Committee saw no reason to include payers (“owners”) in the class of beneficiary. As with s. 7, the Committee had initially favoured a mandated procedure for the interruption of funds when a payer had received notice that the payment would or could lead to a breach of trust. Again, after careful consideration, the Committee decided against such a provision.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The payment of overhead costs from progress draws was a constant source of litigation until 1998, when the Ontario Court of Appeal put this issue to rest in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63e0c1815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. No overhead expenses may be paid until all trust beneficiaries have been paid for the work and material they supplied to the project. Another common practice had been the commingling of trust funds with non-trust funds, usually as a banking convenience. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="St. Mary's Cement Corp." p2="Construc Ltd." post.rptr="939" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I55d48ff1fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Construc Ltd.">St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Construc Ltd. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 939, 32 O.R. (3d) 595, 33 C.L.R. (2d) 234 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, the court made it clear that while commingling of accounts is not prohibited by the Act, the Act contemplates a separate trust fund for every project in which the contractor is involved and separate accounting for every trust fund. Failure to maintain discrete trust accounts will make the defence of an action in breach of trust more difficult. (See also: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19990927" p1="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates" p2="Bradsil (1967) Ltd." post.rptr="273" pre.rptr="45" ref.id="I63e0e8905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. Bradsil (1967) Ltd.">Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. Bradsil (1967) Ltd. (1999), 45 C.L.R. (2d) 273 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (September 27, 1999), Doc. CA C31530 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="S.E. Rozell & Sons Inc." p2="Groff" post.rptr="695" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I63e0e8915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S.E. Rozell & Sons Inc. v. Groff">S.E. Rozell & Sons Inc. v. Groff (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 695, [2000] O.J. No. 707, 2 C.L.R. (3d) 58 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">There is also a line of cases that deals with the issue of whether third parties, particularly banks, can be impressed with trust obligations even though they are strangers to the trust. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Gold" p2="Rosenberg" post.rptr="385" pre.rptr="152" ref.id="I63e0e8925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gold v. Rosenberg">Gold v. Rosenberg (1997), 152 D.L.R. (4th) 385 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Citadel General Assurance Co." p2="Lloyds Bank Canada" post.rptr="411" pre.rptr="152" ref.id="I63e0e8935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Citadel General Assurance Co. v. Lloyds Bank Canada">Citadel General Assurance Co. v. Lloyds Bank Canada (1997), 152 D.L.R. (4th) 411 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> the Supreme Court of Canada clarified this issue. When a stranger to the trust benefits by breach of the trust and has knowledge sufficient to put a reasonable person on inquiry the stranger will be liable for “knowing receipt”. Where the stranger to the trust does not benefit from the breach of trust, it will be held liable for the breach of trust only if it actually knew of the breach or was wilfully blind or reckless in not knowing. This is “knowing assistance”.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
8:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Waygar Capital Inc." p2="Quality Rugs of Canada Limited" post.rptr="10363" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I672fbb803b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Waygar Capital Inc. v. Quality Rugs of Canada Limited">Waygar Capital Inc. v. Quality Rugs of Canada Limited, 2024 CarswellOnt 10363, 2024 ONSC 2486, 14 C.B.R. (7th) 304, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3706 (Ont. S.C.J. [Comm. List]</ref></cite>—Section 8 trusts do not necessarily trump super-priorities granted under s. 11.2 of the <ital>Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act</ital>. While it is true that s. 8 trusts survive insolvency proceedings, it is equally clear that priorities created by provincial legislation may conflict with the court-ordered priority of a “debtor in possession” (DIP) charge under s. 11.2. In that circumstance, there is an operational conflict and the court-ordered priority under the CCAA prevails to the extent of the conflict. Here, the insolvent and then the Receiver found it necessary to use funds received through payment of accounts receivable to fund ongoing operations. Thus, funds that were otherwise potentially impressed with a statutory trust were used during the CCAA and receivership proceedings to fund the insolvent's ongoing operations with a view to maximizing benefit for creditors generally. The suppliers' motion for super-priority of trust and lien charges was dismissed given the constitutional paramountcy of the CCAA priorities</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Pylon Paving (1996) Inc." p2="Beaucon Building Services Inc." post.rptr="3282" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I672fbb813b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pylon Paving (1996) Inc. v. Beaucon Building Services Inc.">Pylon Paving (1996) Inc. v. Beaucon Building Services Inc., 2022 ONSC 3282, 2022 CarswellOnt 7605, 35 C.L.R. (5th) 273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—In an action to which the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applied, the plaintiff moved before an associate judge to, <ital>inter alia</ital>, strike the statement of defence, note the defendants in default, and obtain default judgment on its breach of trust claim against them under (ON) rule 19.05. While the statement of claim set out the essential elements of the breach of trust claim, it did not plead the extent of the trust nor the extent of the alleged breach of trust under s. 8, such as alleging that the defendants received and appropriated or converted an amount equal to or greater than the indebtedness to the plaintiff. The extent of any breach of trust was a matter requiring judicial determination as an unliquidated claim, which was not a claim for which an associate judge had jurisdiction to grant default judgment. However, the associate judge did grant the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment against both the corporate and individual defendants for breach of trust. While it might seem inconsistent for an associate judge to be precluded from granting default judgment for an unliquidated sum, yet still be entitled to grant summary judgment on the same record, R. 20 permitted summary judgment motions to be brought before an associate judge and contained no similar restriction to that found in r. 19.04(3.1)(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clearwater Structures" p2="614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction" post.rptr="5601" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63e10fa15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clearwater Structures v. 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction">Clearwater Structures v. 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction, 2021 ONSC 5601, 2021 CarswellOnt 12375, 70 E.T.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, does not stand for the immutable proposition that a failure to pay out trust funds received and owing on a sub-contract can never constitute a breach of trust. With respect to the issue of unjust enrichment, the master noted that the remedy required an absence of juristic reason for the enrichment, and a contract between an owner and a contractor constituted a juristic reason. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In an elaborate scheme, the defendant homeowner obscured his identity in dealings with the plaintiff subcontractor that provided lumber for the construction of his home, in order to evade payment. The subcontractor dealt only with an individual, determined to be the owner, who acted on behalf of a shell company contractor set up by the owner and which the latter controlled. The owner drew on his own funds to prepare a bank draft that he faxed to the subcontractor under the contractor's name as evidence to the subcontractor that payment had been received from the owner, and deposited those funds with a paralegal firm, and then directed payment of those funds, at least in part, back to his own numbered company. The court found that the funds provided to the paralegal for deposit in his trust account constituted monies received by the shell company on account of its contract price related to the construction of the owner's home, and were trust funds under s. 8(1)(a) the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. A trust could result under s. 8 with respect to a payment from the individual defendant homeowner <ital>qua</ital> owner to the individual defendant homeowner <ital>qua</ital> controlling person at the contractor. The court rejected the argument that the shell company did not “receive” the monies, as required by the statute, since the funds were always the funds of the owner and not of any contractor. Debts for a project subject to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> are choses in action that supply the required certainty of subject matter. At issue was whether the funds held by the receiver met the three certainties of a trust: certainty of intent, object and subject matter. Counsel for the general contractor subsequently sought a charging order pursuant to s. 34 of the <ital>Solicitors Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c.S.15, for fees incurred on behalf of certain plaintiffs in the earlier action. The motion was opposed by GN, a related plaintiff in an action that was heard together with that earlier action. GN disputed that the charging order held priority over the amount owed by the plaintiffs to GN, arguing that it had priority over any money paid by the owners to the plaintiffs. The trial court erroneously concluded that the funds that were subject to the solicitor's charging order were not trust funds for the benefit of GN under the Act, and that the portion of the monies sought to be charged constituted the plaintiff's pro rata share of its lien claim, and as such were expressly trust funds for the benefit of the plaintiffs, not GN. However, this latter conclusion was reversed on appeal to the Divisional Court, which noted that all monies paid to a contractor by an owner “on account of the contract price” are trust funds “for the benefit of the subcontractors”. Section 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> creates one trust fund for a contractor under its contract with an owner in respect to all of its subcontractors under that contract. All of the unpaid subcontractors and suppliers in “privity of trust” with the contractor are beneficiaries of that trust. All are entitled to assert their trust claims against the entirety of trust proceeds until their trust claims have been paid in full or until trust funds are exhausted. The status of interest payments on monies owed reflects the status of the principal sums on which interest accrued. Costs are not trust funds and so interest on those costs is not trust funds. Here, in a case involving charges of criminal fraud, the defendant's scheme was found to have intrinsically breached his trust obligations to the suppliers and subcontractors by failing to abide by the pay when paid principle. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although it was not possible to link the plaintiff's supply of roofing materials to a particular improvement, the contractor did not have other suppliers. There was a clear link between the materials supplied and the projects completed for which payment was received. A s. 8 statutory trust in favour of the plaintiff existed, and the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment for the amounts owing was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="F.D.M. Contracting Co." p2="FTD Construction Inc." post.rptr="5528" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63e26f315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="F.D.M. Contracting Co. v. FTD Construction Inc.">F.D.M. Contracting Co. v. FTD Construction Inc., 2010 ONSC 5528, 2010 CarswellOnt 7743, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 234 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff and the defendant were construction companies that undertook construction projects, and they agreed that since the defendant had the requisite bonding facility necessary to obtain contracts and the plaintiff the necessary experience to perform the work, the defendant would bid on the contracts and would employ the plaintiff to carry out the work. The court found that the plaintiff was not a subcontractor to the defendant on the construction contracts and that no trust obligations arose against the latter under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. It was clearly contrary to the agreement between the parties which described the arrangement as a partnership with partners of co-equal status, and while there may have been fiduciary responsibilities that flowed from the partnership, they did not involve the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Colautti Construction Ltd." p2="Ashcroft Development Inc." post.rptr="359" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63e26f325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Colautti Construction Ltd. v. Ashcroft Development Inc.">Colautti Construction Ltd. v. Ashcroft Development Inc., 2011 ONCA 359, 2011 CarswellOnt 2993, 1 C.L.R. (4th) 138 (Ont. C.A.); reversing in part on other grounds 2009 CarswellOnt 6744, 91 C.L.R. (3d) 218 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At trial, the individual defendant developer was found liable for breach of trust. The judge held that as long as there were monies outstanding to the plaintiff, there was a breach of trust where: (1) there was no proper system in place to receive, monitor and disburse these trust funds; (2) the individual defendant admitted that he did not maintain a separate trust account for each project and that one account was used for expenses other than those related to contractors and that other account may have been used to pay his wife's salary. Here, the individual defendant also admitted that he did not keep record of what was paid to contractors from advances received, as opposed to what was paid out for other purposes. On appeal, the Court affirmed the finding on this point, as well as the finding that, as the plaintiff contractor had made reasonable inquiries as to the source and intended allocations of various advances, it was entitled to allocate those advances to payment of older debts outside the contracts, provided that debt was still outstanding. As well, it was held that there was no authority for the proposition that the owner of an improvement is entitled to defend a debt action brought by a contractor on the basis of the contractor's alleged failure to fulfill its own trust obligations to subcontractors. Standing to complain of a s. 8 breach of trust is limited to those in direct privity with the contractor and who are owed monies by the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2010" p1="Sunview Doors Ltd." p2="Academy Doors & Windows Ltd." post.rptr="163" pre.rptr="87" ref.id="I63e296405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sunview Doors Ltd. v. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The Court of Appeal sought to resolve the conflicting jurisprudence concerning the interpretation of s. 8(1) of the Act, as previously applied in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd." p2="Modern Tile Supply Co." post.rptr="783" pre.rptr="55" ref.id="I90b587b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co.">Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co. (2001), 55 O.R. (3d) 783, 11 C.L.R. (3d) 1, 2001 CarswellOnt 3138 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. Here, the plaintiff supplied custom sliding patio doors to the corporate defendant, which failed to pay for the goods and went out of business. While the plaintiff knew that the doors the corporate defendant ordered were for specific improvements because of the information provided respecting dimensions, colour and door opening direction, it did not know the location of the improvements where the doors were being installed. Neither the orders placed by the corporate defendant nor the corresponding invoices issued by the plaintiff identified where the doors would be installed. The Divisional Court had distinguished <ital>Central Supply</ital> on the facts, but also exercised its coordinate jurisdiction to the panel in <ital>Central Supply</ital>, and disagreed with the ruling in the latter “that the supplier must have intended that its materials be incorporated into a specific and identifiable improvement in order to attract a trust remedy.” The Court of Appeal held that the reference in s. 8(1) to the creation of a trust fund for the benefit of “persons who have supplied services or materials to the improvement” generally requires that a link be made between the materials supplied and the improvement. However, nothing in the wording of the section requires that the supplier intend that the material be incorporated into a known and specific improvement at the time of sale or supply and this requirement should not be read in into s. 8(1). Provided that the supplier is able to link the material to the improvement for which the subcontractor was owed money or has been paid, the supplier will be entitled to the benefit of s. 8.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Patene Building Supplies Ltd." p2="Niagara Home Builders Inc." post.rptr="8157" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I63e296425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Patene Building Supplies Ltd. v. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2010 CarswellOnt 752, 96 C.L.R. (3d) 209 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Sale or rent proceeds from constructed homes received by the defendant company were clearly trust funds as defined in the Act and should have been used to pay the supplier.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Cast-Con Group Inc." p2="Alterra (Spencer Creek) Ltd." post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="71" ref.id="I63e296435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cast-Con Group Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff sought to add five defendants to the proceeding, and to amend the statement of claim so as to assert a breach of trust against certain defendants, the Judge dismissed the motion on the grounds that adding new causes of action to the existing contract claim would effectively circumvent the two year limitation period and therefore result in the existing and proposed defendants suffering prejudice that could not be repaired by costs or an adjournment. The Motions Court refrained from comment on whether a claim could be amended to include a trust claim where a lien claim had previously been removed from the same pleading, but the Divisional Court noted that since the plaintiff had performed part of the work to which the novel claim related before the amendments to the <ital>Limitations Act</ital>, there would be no prejudice to the defendants if that part of the trust claim proceeded. The Divisional Court otherwise upheld the motions ruling.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1463150 Ontario Ltd." p2="11 Christie Street Inc." post.rptr="6937" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I63e2bd505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1463150 Ontario Ltd. v. 11 Christie Street Inc.">1463150 Ontario Ltd. v. 11 Christie Street Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6937 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—An order was made on consent vacating the claims for lien and certificates of action on payment of money into court by the defendant owner. By subsequent order, a portion of this money was paid to the plaintiff contractor and the lien action was dismissed. Two subcontractors had commenced separate actions against the contractor for amounts remaining payable to them and for declarations that all monies payable by the owner to the contractor constituted a trust fund for their benefit. The two subcontractors sought an order that any monies paid to the contractor by the owner to or on account of the settlement be paid into court in amount sufficient to protect claims of the subcontractors. Rule 45.02 provided that where the right of a party to a specific fund is in question, the court may order the fund to be paid into court or otherwise secured on such terms as are just. The Master held that the moving parties had satisfied the three-pronged test under R. 45.02 and ordered an amount equal to the amount they could have claimed if they had asserted a claim for lien to be paid into court. Given its source and in the circumstances the whole payment received by the plaintiff was impressed with a trust based on s. 8(1) of the Act. Paying the funds into court would favour the balance of convenience in that the statutory regime respecting trust funds set out in the Act and the trust imposed thereby would be maintained. The plaintiff demonstrated that it had treated the funds as its own to disperse and to keep contrary to the intent and provisions of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1977" p1="Iori (Litigation Administrator of)" p2="Village Building Supplies (1977) Ltd." post.rptr="1365" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I63e2bd515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Iori (Litigation Administrator of) v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant supplier agreed to release its liens in exchange for a mortgage on a home owed by the plaintiff wife. The mortgage in favour of the supplier was subsequently declared to be null and void because the wife's signature on the mortgage had been forged and the mortgage had been registered without her knowledge or consent. Although the supplier was found to be innocent, had it or its advisors exercised due diligence, the fraud would probably have been prevented. The admitted forgery was also held to invalidate the defendant supplier's counterclaim for unjust enrichment and breach of constructive trust. It did not appear from the record that the wife had sufficient knowledge of circumstances such that it would be open to find that an honest person would have been on inquiry. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A claim for breach of trust under the Act was held not to be statute-barred under the <ital>Limitations Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Emco Corp." p2="Ontario Trenchless Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3628" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I63e2e4615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Corp. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the defendant did not provide details of how the payments were used but instead simply denied that it breached the Act, it had not shown a defence on the merits. As per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="St. Mary's Cement Corp." p2="Construc Ltd." post.rptr="939" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I55d68bc0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A trust claim under the Act is not a truly declaratory remedy, and orders under s. 8 and s. 13 are not truly declaratory in nature. They do not involve a declaration of duty or of rights in the necessary sense, and any declaration is incidental to the substantive remedy of damages.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada" p2="Matthews" post.rptr="1629" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63e30b705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada v. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were officers and directors of the general contractor, to which labour and material payment bonds were issued by the plaintiff insurer to guarantee payment in respect of any default by the company in paying its subcontractors. After the general contractor was petitioned into bankruptcy, the plaintiff's bonds were called upon, and the plaintiff became subrogated to the subcontractors' rights against the general contractor. Based on those subrogated rights, the plaintiff commenced an action against the appellants for breach of the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. For the purposes of the subrogated action, the plaintiff stood in the shoes of the subcontractors. Accordingly, the defendants' claim of improvident underwriting was not a tenable defence at law to the subrogated action for breach of trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Central Supply Co. Div.)</ref></cite>—Part II of the Act deals with trusts and Part III deals with liens. Under Part III, if the supply of services or materials is not made “upon or with respect to” the improvement to which the supply is made, no lien entitlement is created. Although liens and trusts represent discrete remedies under the Act, the scheme and purpose of the Act argues for a consistent approach between Parts II and III. The similarity in wording between s. 8(1), which delineates when a trust arises under Part II, and in ss. 14 and 15, which create the lien under Part III, also supports a consistent requirement that there be an identifiable improvement before either a lien or trust can be established. Where invoices from the supplier did not refer to a specific work site, improvement or premises, no trust was created. In reaching this result, the court did not follow the decisions in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1979" p1="Schulz Concrete Pipe Ltd., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="32" ref.id="I63e30b725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schulz Concrete Pipe Ltd., Re">Schulz Concrete Pipe Ltd., Re (1979), 32 C.B.R. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 6, 1989 CarswellOnt 692 (H.C.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90b623f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Failure to pay the holdback did not, in itself, amount to a breach of trust, even if the holdback itself constituted a trust fund. Here, the plaintiff claimed monies due under a contract for a construction project completed in 1974 made between the plaintiff's bankrupt predecessor and a predecessor of the defendant. The monies included the outstanding balance of the holdback and extras allegedly due and owing to the plaintiff's predecessor. The plaintiff unsuccessfully argued that the defendant's predecessor breached the trust provisions of the Ontario former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> by failing to pay the balance of the holdback, and that the defendant was answerable for the breach. Due to the passage of time, the defendant was no longer in a position to discharge its onus respecting the status or disposition of the holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="S.E. Groff (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 695, [2000] O.J. No. 707, 2 C.L.R. (3d) 58 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To be a s. 8 trust fund beneficiary, one must have (or at least have been entitled to) lien rights under s. 14(1). While it is true that s. 8 does not prohibit the commingling of trust funds with other funds, the weight of the case law seems to be to the effect that commingling places the trust funds at risk, and merely exposing them to that unnecessary risk is an act which is inconsistent with the high standards expected of a trustee. The fact that, in the end, the risk is not realized is immaterial—good luck should not be a defence to a breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63e359925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Act contemplates a separate trust fund for every project in which the contractor is involved and separate accounting for every trust fund. It is only by separately accounting for the moneys held in trust that a contractor can ensure that trust moneys are not in fact applied to other purposes. The fact that the Act does not expressly require that trust funds be kept separate from the general accounts of the contractor is not determinative of whether a failure to do so constitutes a breach of trust. A trustee has an obligation to protect the trust funds, and the practice of intermingling trust funds with other moneys and using them for general purposes is inconsistent with the trustee's duty to maintain proper control of the trust funds. This is so regardless of whether the total amount paid to trades and suppliers on a project is equal to or greater than the trust moneys received by the contractor. (See also: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction Co." p2="S.I. Guttman Ltd." post.rptr="232" pre.rptr="104" ref.id="I63e3a7b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd.">Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I.
