C.A.)</ref></cite>, affirming the principle that losses cannot be passed down to trades in breach of trust.)</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Alta Surety Co." p2="Toronto-Dominion Bank" post.rptr="221" pre.rptr="23" ref.id="I63e3a7b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alta Surety Co. v. Toronto-Dominion Bank">Alta Surety Co. v. Toronto-Dominion Bank (1995), 23 C.L.R. (2d) 221 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant Bank, as banker for a group of related construction companies, utilized a mirror accounting system, to avoid dealing with the separate account balances of each company. Only the net balance of all companies on the system was considered, and as long as that amount was positive, individual company overdrafts were not considered problematic. The group of companies eventually ran into financial problems and the bank was sued. The bank was held, in the parallel case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Arthur Andersen Inc." p2="Toronto Dominion Bank" post.rptr="363" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63e3a7b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arthur Andersen Inc. v. Toronto Dominion Bank">Arthur Andersen Inc. v. Toronto Dominion Bank (1994), 17 O.R. (3d) 363 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1994), 14 B.C.L.R. (2d) 1 <point>at 49</point> (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 207 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, to be a constructive trustee liable for a breach of trust. In ruling on motions for summary judgment in the present case, the court rejected the bank's argument that it could only be liable for breach of trust if it had received a benefit and that it had not done so, because it had not appropriated the money for itself. The court found that the Bank did in fact derive a benefit, as the mirror account system was a product which was “sold” to its customers in appropriate circumstances. This brought benefit to the Bank in the way of more customers, continuing customers and the various changes which any account brings. Such a benefit was sufficient to meet the test set out by the Court of Appeal in <ital>Arthur Andersen Inc.</ital>, s. 10, below.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co." p2="Irvine & Reeves Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="1955" ref.id="I55d77620fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd.">Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd. (1955), 1955 CarswellBC 177, [1955] 3 D.L.R. 561, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.)</ital> [1955] S.C.R. 694 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—A subcontractor retained by the general contractor to install heating plants in four schools, hired the appellant to supply and install the automatic heating controls. The respondent was the subcontractor's principal supplier of materials for both the present contract and earlier contracts. Before completion of its school contract, the subcontractor assigned to the respondent its present and future book accounts as security for its debts on those supplies. The general contractor subsequently made payments by cheques jointly to the subcontractor and the respondent, who would jointly decide which of the subcontractor's accounts should be paid, and the remaining moneys were applied on account of the debt of the respondent. The appellant, after losing its right to a mechanic's lien against the schools by failing to file within the prescribed time, obtained judgment against the subcontractor for the balance of moneys owed it, and the subcontractor subsequently went into liquidation. The trial judge found that the subcontractor was a subcontractor within the meaning of s. 19 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.B.C. 1948, c. 205; that the assignment secured only the specific debt; that the debt had been extinguished, and the subsequent monies subject to the trust had been received by the respondent. The Court of Appeal overturned the trial judgment. The Supreme Court of Canada, in allowing the appeal, held that the word “received” in s. 19 included money paid to an assignee. Otherwise, the purpose of s. 19 could be evaded by an assignment contemporaneous with the contract. However, although no assignment could obliterate the rights created by s. 19 in the monies paid, those monies were not required to be distributed on a <ital>pro rata</ital> basis. Rather, the subcontractor had some discretion, and his duty was fulfilled when the monies were paid to beneficiaries of the trust, whatever the division. The respondent was in breach of trust in so far as trust moneys received beyond the debts arising out of the contracts were applied to other debts. It was liable to the appellant for any balance owing to it on the same contract. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.B.C. 1948, c. 205, but its principle is illustrative for the purposes of interpreting the Ontario legislation.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarkson Co." p2="Canadian Bank of Commerce" post.rptr="513" pre.rptr="[1966]" ref.id="I63e3cec15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkson Co. v. Canadian Bank of Commerce">Clarkson Co. v. Canadian Bank of Commerce, [1966] S.C.R. 513</ref></cite>—The plaintiff trustee brought an action against the defendant bank and the defendant construction company, alleging that, by using trust funds received by the company to allow the bank to pay off an overdraft, the parties were in breach of trust. At trial, the funds received by the company and deposited to its credit in the defendant bank were found to constitute a trust fund under s. 3 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> [analogous to R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8] and judgment was granted against the bank for the amount found due, together with interest and costs. The judgment provided that the declaration of the trust fund should be binding on the company, but that otherwise the action against it should be dismissed. On appeal, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and dismissed the action. The Supreme Court of Canada, in restoring the trial judgment, held that with the company in the possession of trust funds and with unpaid subcontractors who were <ital>prima facie</ital> entitled to the trust fund, the onus of proving the facts, if they existed, which would bring the case within the exception created by subs. (5) lay upon the bank and that in the present case, that onus had not been satisfied. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.B.C. 1948, c. 205, but its principle is illustrative for the purposes of interpreting the Ontario legislation.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Di Mario" p2="Schuster" post.rptr="140" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63e3cec25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Mario v. Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 8 of the Act creates a trust where the contractor, as trustee, holds all money owing to or actually received by it in trust for the benefit of its subcontractors who have supplied services or material. In addition, s. 8 creates a trust where a subcontractor, as trustee, holds all money owing to or actually received by it in trust for the benefit of its subcontractors, who would be sub-subcontractors of the general contractor. The trust created pursuant to s. 8 continues to be created at each level of the “pyramid” for the benefit of each class of subcontractors supplying services or materials to the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Toronto Dominion Bank" p2="General Glass & Aluminum Co." post.rptr="31" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63e3f5d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Dominion Bank v. General Glass & Aluminum Co.">Toronto Dominion Bank v. General Glass & Aluminum Co. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 31 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor deposited a cheque from the general contractor at its bank, and the bank applied the funds to eliminate the subcontractor's indebtedness to the bank. The trust claimants obtained a declaration that the funds were impressed with a trust in their favour pursuant to s. 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The bank had intimate knowledge of the nature of the subcontractor's business since it had a banking relationship with the subcontractor for 15 years, and was also aware that the subcontractor's accounts receivable were subject to holdbacks. The bank was therefore under a duty to inquire as to whether the cheque was subject to a trust in favour of the trust claimants. Furthermore, a trust arises on the date that funds are received by the bank for subcontractor obligations that commenced prior to receipt of the funds but were completed afterwards. Therefore, the entire amount was subject to a trust in favour of the trust claimants. That portion of the total funds representing payment for the Goods and Services Tax was to be held in trust by the bank in favour of Revenue Canada, if it chose to advance such a claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="George & Asmussen Ltd." p2="MCM Projects Inc." post.rptr="204" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63e3f5d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Projects Inc.">George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Projects Inc. (1992), 3 C.L.R. (2d) 204 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A charging order entitled a law firm who had represented a lien claimant to a charge on moneys for their fees and disbursements in priority to the lien claimant. A creditor of the lien claimant was unable to prove that its materials were supplied to the property that was the subject of the construction lien action and accordingly the court was unable to determine what portion of the creditor's claim was impressed with a trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd." p2="Preston Heights Estates Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I63e41ce05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd.">G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd. (1992), 1 C.L.R. (2d) 157 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee made several mortgage advances, but on two of them, it deducted certain amounts and reimbursed itself to cover interest owing on mortgages it held on unrelated properties, which were also controlled by the owner. The owner provided the bank with a statutory declaration that all contractors and subcontractors had been paid. A number of lien claims were registered against the property. The mortgagee was held liable for breach of trust because it failed to make reasonable enquiries about whether the workers on the project might not be paid before diverting funds to other mortgage accounts which it held. Moreover, a reasonable person would not have relied on the very sketchy and misleading declaration of the owner, which had no statutory effect in any event. The lien claimants for whom judgment had been granted were entitled to share <ital>pro rata</ital> in the proceeds held in lieu of the trust funds as well as in the holdback funds. Notwithstanding its breach of trust, the mortgagee was entitled to be next in priority to the extent of its mortgage in priority of G Ltd., a second mortgagee, since the parties had executed a postponement agreement, and the mortgagee's breach of trust should not overturn that agreement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Anron Mechanical Ltd." p2="L'Abbé Construction (Ontario) Ltd. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="133" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63e41ce15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anron Mechanical Ltd. v. L'Abbé Construction (Ontario) Ltd. (Trustee of)">Anron Mechanical Ltd. v. L'Abbé Construction (Ontario) Ltd. (Trustee of) (1991), 5 C.B.R. (3d) 133, 46 C.L.R. 49 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—L Ltd., a construction company, made an assignment in bankruptcy while involved in three separate projects, with all moneys received or paid out on those projects being mingled in one account. The trustee in bankruptcy subsequently recovered the payment of a fraudulent preference, and three parties claimed entitlement to it. The trustee claimed entitlement to the moneys recovered on the basis that he had recovered them. The bank, as intervenor, claimed entitlement, alleging that it held a security interest on them. An unpaid subcontractor claimed entitlement on the basis that it was one of a class of beneficiaries of a trust impressed on the moneys under s. 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and claimed payment in full to the exclusion of the other beneficiaries because it alone had pursued its remedies. With respect to the trustee in bankruptcy, the court found that although it is the general rule that property received by the trustee as a result of a fraudulent preference is the property of the trustee and available for the general benefit of all creditors, this is not so where, as here, the moneys were originally impressed with a trust and are still directly traceable and identifiable with that trust. Otherwise, a general contractor could then easily divert moneys, defeat the rights of the unpaid subcontractors, and thwart the whole purpose of s. 8. With respect to the bank's claim, although there was an agreement between the bank and L Ltd. assigning to the bank all moneys received in L Ltd.'s account, this agreement specifically excluded amounts subject to a trust in favour of others. The moneys in question were subject to a trust under s. 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, being moneys received by contrators from owners for the benefit of subcontractors. Although the moneys had been mingled in the one account, they were not so mingled as to have the trust impressed upon them, and this therefore gave the subcontractors a preferential lien prior to that of the bank. Lastly, although the subcontractor worked on the project and had a right to a share in the recovered moneys, it did not have a right to payment in full over the other beneficiaries in the same class merely because it was the only one to pursue its remedies. The trust created by the Act was for the benefit of all unpaid contractors. Once bankruptcy occurred, a <ital>pro rata</ital> distribution was required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="313" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63e41ce25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd. (1990), 40 C.L.R. 313 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's first construction lien action was dismissed for failure to comply with s. 37, and the court ordered the letter of credit lodged by the defendant delivered up for cancellation. Subsequently, the plaintiff commenced a second action against the contractor, seeking virtually the same relief, but adding a trust fund claim pursuant to s. 8. The plaintiff then moved under R. 45.02 for an order requiring the defendant pay into court the amount of the claim. The court dismissed the motion. Apart from the sum of 25 per cent of the lien required by s. 44(1)(d), the plaintiff would, if such motion were successful, be in the same position as if the order declaring the lien to have expired and ordering the delivery up of the security furnished had not been given.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Edward Stephens Associates Ltd." p2="G.L. Trenching Ltd." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63e443f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edward Stephens Associates Ltd. v. G.L. Trenching Ltd.">Edward Stephens Associates Ltd. v. G.L. Trenching Ltd. (1989), 40 C.L.R. 161, 73 O.R. (2d) 112 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—Section 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> restricted claims made against the trust funds held under the Act to those where there existed privity of contract. Similar legislation in other provinces indicated, and the case law interpreting it suggested, that the trustee and the beneficiary of a lien trust fund must be connected by privity of contract for a valid claim to be made and accepted. But see: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co." p2="Windigo Community Development Corp." post.rptr="14" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63e443f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp.">D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp. (1998), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 14 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc." p2="Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd." post.rptr="6" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63e443f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd.">Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 6 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs were suppliers of windows, doors and other building materials to the defendants. The defendants used the materials in the manufacture of products which they supplied under contract directly to owners as improvements in the construction of homes. The plaintiffs did not know to whom the products were sold. The defendants alleged that the materials supplied to them were done so in the ordinary course of business and that the plaintiffs had no entitlement to a trust fund under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The plaintiffs commenced an action to enforce their rights and brought a motion, <ital>inter alia</ital>, for an interim injunction restraining the defendants from dealing with or distributing their assets. The plaintiffs were suppliers of materials used in making the various improvements by the defendants to the owners' properties. As suppliers of such materials, the plaintiffs were entitled to the benefit of the trust fund provisions in s. 8 of the Act, and the trustee in bankruptcy of the defendants was estopped from dealing with or distributing the assets of the defendants until the action had been concluded.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
8:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Overheads</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Varco Pruden Buildings" p2="Thom Win Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1190" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63e46b005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Varco Pruden Buildings v. Thom Win Construction Ltd.">Varco Pruden Buildings v. Thom Win Construction Ltd., 2013 ONSC 1190, 2013 CarswellOnt 2293 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.—Payments out of trust funds were found to be in respect of overhead and operational costs, which constituted a breach of the trust provisions under s. 8.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20020529" p1="Marino" p2="Bay-Walsh Ltd." post.rptr="2211" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I63e46b015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd.">Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd. (May 29, 2002), Doc. 98-0469, [2002] O.J. No. 2211 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A trustee cannot, directly or indirectly, exhaust or reduce the trust fund until the beneficiaries of that trust lower in the pyramid are paid “all amounts related to the improvement owed to them.” The trustee cannot directly or indirectly pay himself first. To use the fund to satisfy the overhead costs of the trustee, directly or indirectly, is to appropriate or convert part of the fund to the contractor's or subcontractor's own use or to a use inconsistent with the trust. The test has very little to do with whether the payments out of the trust are overhead or otherwise, but rather whether those persons paid are <ital>bona fide</ital> statutory beneficiaries of the trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Dietrich Steel Ltd." p2="Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd." post.rptr="475" pre.rptr="170" ref.id="I63e492105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dietrich Steel Ltd. v. Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd.">Dietrich Steel Ltd. v. Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd. (1999), 170 D.L.R. (4th) 475 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Although the individual directors and officers had used their operating company for a single project, using a specific single purpose bank account, and although it was admitted that the only payments made out of this single purpose bank account were for direct project expenses, and that all holdbacks and other monies received from sale of the completed premises were distributed by court appointed trustee, it was held that unless all payments were for services or materials which were or could have been lienable, they were paid in breach of trust. Personal judgment was awarded against the officers and directors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Court of Appeal held that the trusts under Part II of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> are unique in that the costs of administering the trust are not a proper charge on the trust property. The Court held that a segregated account did not necessarily preclude either a breach of trust by the corporation or the personal liability of its directors, officers or persons in control. The Court held that the change in the statute from the former “not <ital>authorized</ital> by” to “<ital>inconsistent</ital> with” may have made the section more liberal, but not so as to permit payment for services that were otherwise non-lienable. It was argued that as every payment to every lien claimant includes some component of overhead and profit, it should not be inconsistent for the overhead component to be paid to the party who was actually entitled to the funds. This argument was rejected. Finally, the appellant submitted that the Act should not be “read up” so as to unnecessarily restrict entry into the marketplace. Only independently wealthy businesses can afford to pay all of their overheads out of non-project receipts, until all trade payables have been satisfied. This argument was rejected. The finding of personal liability was reversed, as the case had been argued on an agreed statement of fact that merely stated that the personal defendants were officers and directors of the corporate defendant. This alone was held not to be sufficient to satisfy the requirements of s. 13(1)(b) (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63e492115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1, 1998 CarswellOnt 3970 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction Co." p2="S.I. Guttman Ltd." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I63e492125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd.">Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd. (1996), 29 C.L.R. (2d) 146, 16 E.T.R. (2d) 41 (Ont. Gen. Div.); appeal dismissed (1997), 104 O.A.C. 232 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The principle that overheads cannot be paid out of trust funds is referred to and approved.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63e4b9205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1, 1998 CarswellOnt 3970 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A contractor cannot pay overhead expenses such as wages, office expenses, rent, legal and accounting fees in reduction of its trust obligations to trades and suppliers. Lawyers, accountants and landlords are not “other persons” who supplied services or materials to the improvement within the meaning of s. 8. The contractor argued that but for the payment of overhead expenses, no work would have been done “upon” the project and therefore such payments must be “in respect of” an improvement. The Court of Appeal disagreed, reasoning that as ss. 8(1) and 14(1) provide for a preference of one class of creditor over another that did not exist at common law, these sections of the Act must be strictly interpreted. The Court also observed that if the recipients of overhead payments were included in the class of beneficiaries, the benefits to the group clearly intended to be within the class would be reduced proportionately and significantly. Consequently the payment of overhead expenses for wages, office expenses, rent, legal and accounting fees did not reduce trust obligations. This decision should be read together with the Court of Appeal's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Dietrich Steel Ltd." p2="Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd." post.rptr="475" pre.rptr="170" ref.id="I63e4b9215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dietrich Steel Ltd. v. Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd.">Dietrich Steel Ltd. v. Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd. (1999), 170 D.L.R. (4th) 475 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Heritage Masonry Ltd." p2="Building Team Ltd." post.rptr="1226" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63e4b9225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Building Team Ltd.">Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Building Team Ltd. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 1226, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 101 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Overheads cannot be paid with trust funds. No special <ital>mens rea</ital> is required for officers and directors to be found liable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref court="Ont. Gen. Div." fjur="Ontario" jur="Canada" norm.rptr="carsont" p1="Home Depot Inc." p2="Fieder Painting Inc." post.rptr="4514" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I267753f001a911efa7fea76a6b7cbe8e" title="Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc.">Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 4514 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In this action for breach of trust, the plaintiff had judgment against the corporate defendant and proceeded against the defendant's two officers. Approximately one-fifth of the cash paid through the defendant corporation was challenged and much of it had been spent on rent, credit card debt, vehicle leases, vehicle maintenance, employee hotel bills, two-way radios, general office expenses, membership fees, professional fees, employee benefits, shareholder repayments, loan interest and service charges. The judge considered <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="BPCO Inc." p2="Deelstra" post.rptr="958" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I63e4e0315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="BPCO Inc. v. Deelstra">BPCO Inc. v. Deelstra, 1994 CarswellOnt 958, and Emco Supply v. Gueguen, 1987 CarswellOnt 772</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Emco Supply" p2="Gueguen" post.rptr="229" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I63e4e0325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Supply v. Gueguen">Emco Supply v. Gueguen (1987), 25 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>, and the commentary of Raymond Barnard, relied upon by the court in <ital>BPCO</ital>. The court concluded, with <ital>Emco</ital>, that s. 8 was “crystal clear” in that overhead expenses could not be paid out of trust funds.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Datasphere Sales Ltd." p2="Universal Light & Power Corp." post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63e4e0335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp.">Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff obtained a declaration that funds received by the defendant under s. 8(1)(b) of the Act were held in trust. The Act specifically describes situations in which money may be paid out by the trustee in power and legitimate diminution of his or her contractual and trust obligations. The intent was to allow retention, but not expenditure, outside the very narrow scope of the words of ss. 10, 11 and 12, of the trust funds. There was no right in the defendant to put some or all of the funds to general use because in its view, in the light of claims it had or proposed to assert against the beneficiary-contractor, the ultimate arithmetical calculations would demonstrate that the trust moneys owing netted out at a balance less than the gross total of the funds retained.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Emco Supply" p2="Gueguen" post.rptr="229" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I63e507405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Supply v. Gueguen">Emco Supply v. Gueguen (1987), 25 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied materials and services to a number of projects for the defendant E Ltd. for which the defendant G was the sole officer, director and shareholder. E Ltd. became insolvent and the plaintiff commenced an action against E Ltd. and G personally claiming payment of amounts owing on all projects and claiming that E Ltd. breached the trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> by appropriating project funds for its own and other uses inconsistent with the Act. From a court ordered accounting, it was shown that the plaintiff was owed money by E Ltd. on all projects, and E Ltd. did not maintain a separate trust account for each project but placed all funds received in its general account from which it paid subcontractors, suppliers and its own overhead. The action was allowed. The court found that the defendant was not entitled to consider, in determining whether or not there had been a breach of trust, that an overpayment to subcontractors and suppliers on one project could be used to cancel out underpayments on the other projects. This finding was supported on two grounds. Firstly, s. 8 contemplated that there should be a separate and distinct trust for each contract. Any other interpretation would entitle a contractor who was carrying on several projects to pay that contractor or supplier who provided services or materials at the earliest stage of the project, thereby jeopardizing the claims of those who provided services or materials at the end. Secondly, the general contractor was not entitled to deduct from trust moneys for the cost of its overhead. If the amount claimed for overhead was deducted from funds disbursed, the corporate defendant was in breach of trust.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
8:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Jurisdictional Issues</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Northwest Angle 33 First Nation" p2="Razar Contracting Services Ltd. et al." post.rptr="3819" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I673401403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Northwest Angle 33 First Nation v. Razar Contracting Services Ltd. et al.">Northwest Angle 33 First Nation v. Razar Contracting Services Ltd. et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 3819, 2023 ONSC 1233 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2023 ONSC 6891, 2023 CarswellOnt 19913 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Skukowski" p2="James Conci Holdings Inc." post.rptr="4343" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I90b7f8b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Skukowski v. James Conci Holdings Inc.">Skukowski v. James Conci Holdings Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4343, 1998 CarswellOnt 4119 (Ont. Gen. Div.); varied (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4511, 1998 CarswellOnt 4297 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 87 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> remains good law. Section 8 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> was provincial legislation of general application and therefore applicable on First Nations territory pursuant to s. 88 of the <ital>Indian Act</ital>. A trust claim could be advanced in relation to an improvement on federal land, including land reserved for First Nations. Here, the First Nation successfully sought an interpleader order pursuant to Ont. r. 43.02(1) ordering it to pay into court an amount held, as the result of construction work carried out on the First Nation by the contractor and various subcontractors. The parties intended the monies to be a contractual holdback and not the property of the contractor or a debt payable to the contractor pending substantial completion. The monies were a trust fund for the benefit of the unpaid subcontractors and suppliers of the contractor, pursuant to s. 8(1). Neither the Canada Revenue Agency (on account of unremitted source deductions) nor an individual subcontractor (on account of a garnishment order obtained and served on the First Nation) could claim priority over the monies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Matthews Equipment Limited" p2="YALDA CONTRACTING INC." post.rptr="1823" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63e507415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Matthews Equipment Limited v. YALDA CONTRACTING INC.">Matthews Equipment Limited v. YALDA CONTRACTING INC., 2021 ONSC 1823, 2021 CarswellOnt 3579, 88 C.B.R. (6th) 142, 11 C.L.R. (5th) 33 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While the court found, on motion for default judgment, that the corporate defendant and its directors breached their trust obligations under ss. 8 and 13 of the Act, the admitted facts and affidavit evidence were not sufficient to find that the breach of trust constituted fraud or misappropriation for the purpose of s. 178(1)(d) of the (Can) <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, or that the breach of trust was the result of something other than inadvertence, negligence or incompetence. The question of whether it was appropriate to issue a declaration that the judgment would survive any claim for bankruptcy that might be made by the defendants should be adjudicated if and when it arose.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Savoia" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63e52e505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia">Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia (2006), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 235, 207 O.A.C. 1, 2006 CarswellOnt 340 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Small Claims Court has jurisdiction to consider a trust claim under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provided that the amount involved is within the monetary jurisdiction of that court. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Bradbury" p2="Nu-Life Builders Ltd." post.rptr="296" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I63e52e515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bradbury v. Nu-Life Builders Ltd.">Bradbury v. Nu-Life Builders Ltd. (1986), 24 C.L.R. 296, 1986 CarswellOnt 789 (Ont. Prov. Ct.)</ref></cite> was wrongly decided.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Harold Stecho Electric Ltd." p2="Van-Con General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="429" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63e52e525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Harold Stecho Electric Ltd. v. Van-Con General Contractors Ltd.">Harold Stecho Electric Ltd. v. Van-Con General Contractors Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 429, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 88 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—This defendant, a discharged bankrupt, moved to dismiss the claim of the plaintiff, which included a claim for damages for breach of the fiduciary duty of a trustee under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. While s. 178 of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> stated that the fiduciary's liability under a statutory trust is not released by a discharge order, that section did not deal with a stay of proceedings imposed by s. 69 of that Act and R. 11.01. Rule 11.01 mandated the stay of the proceeding against the defendant until an order to continue was obtained.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Commdoor Aluminum" p2="Solar Sunrooms Inc." post.rptr="131" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I63e555605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Commdoor Aluminum v. Solar Sunrooms Inc.">Commdoor Aluminum v. Solar Sunrooms Inc. (2004), 2 C.B.R. (5th) 131, (2004) 41 C.L.R. (3d) 217, 2004 CarswellOnt 2387 (C.A.); affirming (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2173, 2003 CarswellOnt 2023, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 179 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 178(1)(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, a discharge from bankruptcy does not release an individual from his personal obligation as trustee under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> where he acted in a fiduciary capacity.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Wolfedale Electric Ltd." p2="R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc." post.rptr="4663" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63e555615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wolfedale Electric Ltd. v. R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc.">Wolfedale Electric Ltd. v. R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 4663, 2004 CarswellOnt 2956, 47 B.L.R. (3d) 1 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff alleged breach of the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> by the individual defendant, who subsequent to judgment entered into bankruptcy. The plaintiff did not specifically plead fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation or defalcation by the individual defendant. The court had no difficulty in finding that both the corporate entities and the individual defendant breached a duty of care and negligently allowed the plaintiff to enter into a contract with a non-existing entity and that the individual defendant breached the trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and acted personally in a fiduciary capacity as a trustee under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. While accepting the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Commdoor Aluminum" p2="Solar Sunrooms Inc." post.rptr="131" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I63e555625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Commdoor Aluminum v. Solar Sunrooms Inc.">Commdoor Aluminum v. Solar Sunrooms Inc. (2004), 2 C.B.R. (5th) 131, (2004) 41 C.L.R. (3d) 217, 2004 CarswellOnt 2387 (C.A.); affirming (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2173, 2003 CarswellOnt 2023, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 179 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the court was reluctant to grant the relief that was sought in submissions when it was not specifically pleaded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co." p2="Caravaggio" post.rptr="178" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63e555635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co. v. Caravaggio">Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co. v. Caravaggio (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 178, 2002 CarswellOnt 2379 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although the defendant was a fiduciary of the plaintiff by operation of s. 8 of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the issue as to whether or not the judgment to which the plaintiff would be entitled survived the defendant's personal bankruptcy ought properly to be brought in the Bankruptcy Court pursuant to the provisions of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Skukowski" p2="James Conci Holdings Inc." post.rptr="4343" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63e57c705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Skukowski v. James Conci Holdings Inc.">Skukowski v. James Conci Holdings Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4343, 1998 CarswellOnt 4119 (Ont. Gen. Div.); varied (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4511, 1998 CarswellOnt 4297 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 87 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—It is not clear that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> has no application to claims arising from work on First Nation reserves. The Act creates two remedies: the right to file a lien and sell the land in question to satisfy the lien, which procedure does not lie against lands owned by the Federal Crown; and a trust on amounts owing to contractors or sub-contractors or received by contractors or sub-contractors for the benefit of persons who have supplied services or materials to the improvement. This trust cannot impose a duty upon the Federal Crown to ensure the proper disposition of funds on such a project, but it does not necessarily mean that persons other than the Federal Crown are free of trust obligations. These trust provisions are part of the general law of the land preserved by s. 88 of the <ital>Indian Act</ital>, and no legitimate Federal interest is affected by the imposition of a trust on funds which have flowed to contractors and sub-contractors. Without determining whether the Act applied to the First Nation in this case, the court found that the First Nation had constituted itself a trustee of all the project funds paid to it by the Federal Crown. Amounts remaining in the account were ordered paid to a receiver.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd." p2="Stowe Nut & Bolt Co." post.rptr="115" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63e57c715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Stowe Nut & Bolt Co.">Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Stowe Nut & Bolt Co. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 115, 1988 CarswellOnt 770 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The trust provisions imposed upon a payer are inapplicable to the Crown.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Bradbury" p2="Nu-Life Builders Ltd." post.rptr="296" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I63e5a3805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bradbury v. Nu-Life Builders Ltd.">Bradbury v. Nu-Life Builders Ltd. (1986), 24 C.L.R. 296 (Ont. Prov. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A plaintiff cannot prove its right under s. 8 of the Act in the Ontario Provincial Court because the Act creates no jurisdiction in the Provincial Court to hear a trust action. In addition, a breach of trust is a serious allegation, requiring strong proof. The onus was on the plaintiff in this action to prove his case, which he failed to do.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
8:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 8(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="20/20 Management Limited" p2="Concord Adex Inc." post.rptr="3119" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63e5a3815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="20/20 Management Limited v. Concord Adex Inc.">20/20 Management Limited v. Concord Adex Inc., 2022 ONSC 3119, 2022 CarswellOnt 7244 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were granted a stay of proceedings pursuant to s. 106 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> of the plaintiff's breach of trust claims upon payment into court of the admitted amount of the claims. The court adopted the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ramco Installation Ltd." p2="Mometal Structures Inc." post.rptr="6807" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63e5a3825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ramco Installation Ltd. v. Mometal Structures Inc.">Ramco Installation Ltd. v. Mometal Structures Inc., 2014 ONSC 6807, 2014 CarswellOnt 16561 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Symtech Innovations Ltd." p2="Fit Ergonomics Inc." post.rptr="4766" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63e5a3835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Symtech Innovations Ltd. v. Fit Ergonomics Inc.">Symtech Innovations Ltd. v. Fit Ergonomics Inc., 2021 ONSC 4766, 2021 CarswellOnt 9721 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 6936, 2021 CarswellOnt 14398 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, supporting the conclusion that the trust claims would be moot once the full, admitted amount of the claims were paid into court. The stay would result in material efficiencies for the balance of these proceedings, particularly at trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Airex Inc." p2="Ben Air System Inc." post.rptr="390" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63e5ca905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Airex Inc. v. Ben Air System Inc.">Airex Inc. v. Ben Air System Inc., 2017 ONCA 390, 2017 CarswellOnt 7269, 48 C.B.R. (6th) 200, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 179 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The main issue on appeal was whether the motions judge erred in failing to find a genuine issue requiring a trial concerning whether the defendants breached s. 8 of the Act. The defendant argued that they filed evidence on the motion, which, at a minimum, raised an issue that the corporate defendant paid out more money on account of equipment purchases, payments to sub-contractors and wages and salaries for the project than it received from the owner, including payments made to itself from trust funds to reimburse itself for payments made in relation to the project. They relied on the application of ss. 10 and 11 of the Act. The Court of Appeal found that the defendants failed to file evidence on the motion that carried sufficient weight to support its position.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="S.G.J. Northland Steel Manufacturing Inc." p2="Local Decor Designs Inc." post.rptr="3262" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63e5ca915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S.G.J. Northland Steel Manufacturing Inc. v. Local Decor Designs Inc.">S.G.J. Northland Steel Manufacturing Inc. v. Local Decor Designs Inc., 2017 ONSC 3262, 2017 CarswellOnt 7983, 79 C.L.R. (4th) 280 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor's obvious non-payment of sub-contractors at the time of abandonment of the construction contract was a breach of trust under s. 8.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="International Assn. of Insulators Local 95" p2="Vella" post.rptr="4146" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63e5ca925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="International Assn. of Insulators Local 95 v. Vella">International Assn. of Insulators Local 95 v. Vella, 2016 ONSC 4146, 2016 CarswellOnt 10215, 69 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs obtained a default judgment against the director of the defendant employer for unpaid wages owed to the plaintiffs, and a declaration that the director had breached the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The defendant corporation hired union members to perform work but failed to pay the wages and benefits owing. Individual employees were “persons who supplied services” as part of “improvements” for which the defendant was paid. As a director of the corporate defendant, the individual defendant was liable under s. 13.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Bank of Canada" p2="Atlas Block Co." post.rptr="3062" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63e5ca935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Bank of Canada v. Atlas Block Co.">Royal Bank of Canada v. Atlas Block Co., 2014 ONSC 3062, 2014 CarswellOnt 8345, 15 C.B.R. (6th) 272, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Paragraph 67(1)(a) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> excludes from estate property divisible among the creditors of the bankrupt “any property held by the bankrupt in trust for any other person.” However, case law is clear that this does not extend to assets subject to a deemed trust created by provincial statute where such deemed trust does not otherwise have all the attributes of a valid trust at common law. For the purposes of this paragraph, there was no apparent reason why a deemed trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> should be treated differently than any other provincial statutory deemed trust. Here, the insolvent respondent was both a retailer and a supplier of construction goods to construction projects, and the supplier supplied various locations of the respondent with cement powder. The supplier sought to establish the existence of a s. 8 trust impressed on monies collected from construction project customers. However, those monies did not meet the test for a trust at common law and could not meet the test of certainty of subject matter because they were co-mingled with other funds which were clearly, and admittedly, not subject to a trust. The Receiver was under no obligation to segregate funds received from construction projects even if it had the capacity to do so. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court also held that, apart from the operation of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, the supplier's hypothetical right to assert trust claims was not barred under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. See the treatment of this case under subs. 8, <ital>General</ital>, above.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ramco Installation Ltd." p2="Mometal Structures Inc." post.rptr="6807" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63e5f1a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ramco Installation Ltd. v. Mometal Structures Inc.">Ramco Installation Ltd. v. Mometal Structures Inc., 2014 ONSC 6807, 2014 CarswellOnt 16561 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Funds sufficient to cover the breach of trust claim were conceded, and the issue was not that the funds had been inappropriately spent, but that the balance was not owed for the reasons pleaded. A condition precedent to the declaration of the breach of trust was proof that there was an encroachment of funds <ital>actually</ital> owed. If the funds were not owed or due for an established reason, the use of the funds was not necessarily a breach, and the evidentiary burden shifted to the defendants to establish why the plaintiff should not receive the full contract price. In the circumstances, on a motion for partial summary judgment, a declaration of a breach was premature, until a determination of entitlement to the outstanding monies was made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Forest City Fire Protection Ltd." p2="1099516 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2346" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63e5f1a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forest City Fire Protection Ltd. v. 1099516 Ontario Inc.">Forest City Fire Protection Ltd. v. 1099516 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2346, 2015 CarswellOnt 6364, 49 C.L.R. (4th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was a beneficiary of the trust monies received by the defendant, who was unable to demonstrate that payments made from the trust monies were made to proper beneficiaries under the trust. By failing to provide any accounting as to what was done with the monies received, the burden of proof on the defendants was not discharged, and a breach of trust was found.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ambassador Electric Inc." p2="Fernwood Builders (London) Ltd." post.rptr="3738" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63e618b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ambassador Electric Inc. v. Fernwood Builders (London) Ltd.">Ambassador Electric Inc. v. Fernwood Builders (London) Ltd., 2014 ONSC 3738, 2014 CarswellOnt 9397, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 106 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were found to be in breach of the Act's trust provisions. In denying a motion by the defendants for an order discharging a certificate of pending litigation (“CPL”) and authorizing the release of the net proceeds of the sale of land, the court held that the principles expressed in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Rafat General Contractor Inc." p2="1015734 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="7519" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90b90a20f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.">Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 7519, 81 O.R. (3d) 798, 52 C.L.R. (3d) 63, [2005] O.T.C. 1107, [2005] O.J. No. 5526 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Firenze Exteriors Inc." p2="Westwing Construction Group Inc." post.rptr="934" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I63e618b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Westwing Construction Group Inc.">Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Westwing Construction Group Inc. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 934, 2005 CarswellOnt 917, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 129 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, respectively, were not inconsistent. The court in <ital>Rafat</ital> distinguished <ital>Firenze</ital>, on the basis that it dealt with an alleged breach of trust and diversion of funds from a construction project to construction of a personal residence. It was not a case where lien rights arose, were allowed to expire, and then an interest in the same land was later asserted. Here the land subject to the CPL was not that to which services were supplied for the purposes of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Furrow Systems International Ltd." p2="Island Pools & Landscaping Ltd." post.rptr="1428" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63e618b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Furrow Systems International Ltd. v. Island Pools & Landscaping Ltd.">Furrow Systems International Ltd. v. Island Pools & Landscaping Ltd., 2014 ONSC 1428, 2014 CarswellOnt 12763, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 169 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the evidence with respect to the diversion of trust funds under the Act was nothing more than an assertion based on a belief, supported only by the fact that there was a “for sale” sign on the property, such evidence was not sufficient to support the granting of a mareva injunction. A plaintiff seeking a mareva injunction must satisfy the normal criteria for an injunction as well as the additional criteria for a mareva injunction.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pat Noble Lumber & Building Supplies Ltd." p2="Bailey" post.rptr="4278" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63e63fc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pat Noble Lumber & Building Supplies Ltd. v. Bailey">Pat Noble Lumber & Building Supplies Ltd. v. Bailey, 2012 ONSC 4278, 2012 CarswellOnt 9205, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 151 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied construction materials to the defendants, which were used by the defendants in the renovation of certain premises. Applying <ital>Sunview Doors Ltd. v. Academy Doors & Windows Ltd.</ital>, the court found that the plaintiff had established that 1) the defendants were a contractor or subcontractor; 2) the plaintiff supplied materials to the projects on which the defendants were a contractor; 3) the defendants received or were owed monies on account of its contract price for those contracts; and 4) the defendants owed the plaintiff money for those materials. As a result, the plaintiff had succeeded in establishing that it was a beneficiary of a trust pursuant to s. 8(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Sirron Systems Inc." p2="North America Construction (1993) Ltd." post.rptr="8865" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63e63fc15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sirron Systems Inc. v. North America Construction (1993) Ltd.">Sirron Systems Inc. v. North America Construction (1993) Ltd., 2011 CarswellOnt 8865, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 11 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 CarswellOnt 2500 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Prior to the project's completion, the defendant contractor contentiously terminated its subcontract with the plaintiff and directly or indirectly finished the work. The plaintiff sued for wrongful termination of the subcontract and sought a declaration that monies received by the defendant constituted statutory trust funds for the plaintiff's benefit. The plaintiff also sought punitive damages. The defendant's motion for an order under r. 45.02 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> paying the alleged trust funds into court, and for summary judgment on the breach of trust claims was granted. Having regard to payment into court, there was no genuine issue requiring trial of breach of trust claims, nor was there a genuine issue requiring the trial of the punitive damages claim. The facts did not support such award, particularly in light of the dispute regarding termination, the existence of a clause in the subcontract that required the plaintiff to indemnify the defendant on termination in certain circumstances, and the payment into court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Genrep Ltd./Ltée" p2="Industrial Light & Electric Inc." post.rptr="7013" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63e666d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Genrep Ltd./Ltée v. Industrial Light & Electric Inc.">Genrep Ltd./Ltée v. Industrial Light & Electric Inc., 2010 ONSC 7013, 2010 CarswellOnt 9750, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 264 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 825, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff elected not to file a lien claim against the project site for payment for supply of a generator, but instead took the position that progress payments were funds impressed with a trust pursuant to s. 8, and subsequently sought a certificate of pending litigation against the property. The defendants unsuccessfully argued that the plaintiff, having failed to register a lien, ought not to be able to tie up the land at a late stage. The plaintiff had a right to choose its remedies and consider its risks, and chose to proceed without a lien. While that took away its lien rights, it did not affect its rights in the trust action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Lancorp Construction Co." p2="Royal Vista Homes (Weston) Ltd." post.rptr="301" pre.rptr="77" ref.id="I63e666d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lancorp Construction Co. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff received payment for its work and voluntarily discharged its lien, it lost its right to assert an interest in the land, and could not do so pursuant to the trust provisions of the Act. The court relied on <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Rafat General Contractor Inc." p2="1015734 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="7519" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90b97f50f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.">Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Carosi Construction Ltd." p2="Niagara (Regional Municipality)" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63e666d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carosi Construction Ltd. v. Niagara (Regional Municipality)">Carosi Construction Ltd. v. Niagara (Regional Municipality) (2006), 50 C.L.R. (3d) 157, 2006 CarswellOnt 453 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A subcontractor carried out work for the judgment debtor contractor at a construction site. The bank claimed priority under its general security agreement with respect to monies seized by the sheriff from the contractor, while the subcontractor disputed the claim and moved for a declaration that the amount owed to it was held in trust for its benefit pursuant to s. 8 of the Act. The subcontractor's claim was based on an assignment and direction from the contractor which irrevocably assigned all debts and money owed as a result of the settlement of certain lien actions, to the subcontractor. The court ruled that the assignment and direction could not create or delineate the order in which trust money was to be disbursed, and that the contractor's trust established by s. 8(1) was limited to funds on account of the same improvement. There was no evidence that the funds referred to in the assignment were in relation to the relevant construction project. Section 8 simply preserves the money flowing in to the project for persons ultimately entitled to the money concerned, as is clear from the wording of the section, “on account of the contract or subcontract price of an improvement”. However, that portion of the monies in court that was seized on account of a garnishment that was connected to the construction project was subject to the statutory trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="1379691 Ontario Ltd." p2="Appugliesi" post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63e68de05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1379691 Ontario Ltd. v. Appugliesi">1379691 Ontario Ltd. v. Appugliesi (2005), 46 C.L.R. (3d) 302, 2005 CarswellOnt 4684 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 9210 (Ont. S.C.J.); varied (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6580 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Settlement funds released by a contractor to the solicitor of the lien claimant subcontractor to be held in trust in settlement of the subcontractor's lien action, were held to be trust monies under s. 8. The subcontractor, as a trustee, had a duty to preserve the trust fund for the benefit of its subcontractors and suppliers until all of them were paid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Rafat General Contractor Inc." p2="1015734 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="7519" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90b9a660f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.">Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.
