S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Distinguishing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Firenze Exteriors Inc." p2="Westwing Construction Group Inc." post.rptr="934" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I63e68de25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Westwing Construction Group Inc.">Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Westwing Construction Group Inc. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 934, 2005 CarswellOnt 917, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 129 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the court held that to obtain a Certificate of Pending Litigation a party must have a reasonable claim to an interest in land pursuant to s. 103 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides a comprehensive code as to how liens are to be preserved, and by supplying labour and material, a lien arose in favour of the contractor pursuant to the Act. Having failed to preserve its lien, the plaintiff could not then look to the trust provisions in the Act to later assert an interest in the same land. The scheme of the Act, and the fact that the trust provisions give rise to personal rights only, led to the conclusion that the contractor had no tenable claim to an interest in the owner's land.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Forest Trim & Doors" p2="Azor Woodworking Ltd." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I63e68de35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forest Trim & Doors v. Azor Woodworking Ltd.">Forest Trim & Doors v. Azor Woodworking Ltd. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 26, 2005 CarswellOnt 50 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The parties entered into a barter agreement, whereby the defendant subcontractor would supply labourers to a construction company that was related to the plaintiff supplier (“the related company”), and the related company would pay the labour costs to the plaintiff to reduce the defendant's existing debt for construction materials. In consideration of this arrangement, the plaintiff agreed to continue to supply the defendant with construction materials. When the defendant was unable to pay in full the plaintiff's subsequent invoices, the plaintiff obtained summary judgment against the corporate defendant for the debt, and against the corporate defendant's sole officer, director, and controlling mind, for breach of trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There was no agreement that the wages of the labourers working on the related company's projects could be paid from the funds the defendant received from its new projects. There was no evidence of either a waiver or direction from the plaintiff to pay labourers working on the related company's projects from the trust funds. Section 8(1) of the Act specified that amounts received by a contractor on account of an improvement constituted trust funds for the people who supplied the materials for the improvement. Section 8 created a separate trust when a contractor received monies for a project to protect its suppliers and sub contractors. The trust created by s. 8 was limited to the payment of labourers working on the defendant's new projects and did not include labourers working on the related company's projects.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Firenze Exteriors Inc." p2="Westwing Construction Group Inc." post.rptr="934" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I63e6b4f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Westwing Construction Group Inc.">Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Westwing Construction Group Inc. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 934, 2005 CarswellOnt 917, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 129 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractors provided construction materials and services to the defendant general contractor and claimed breach of trust against both it and its principals. The plaintiffs sought an accounting and a tracing order, and obtained an interim certificate of pending litigation against the principals' residence. The Master held that if the plaintiffs could prove at trial that trust funds owing to them were converted to the principals' own use before the subcontractors were paid in full for the project, then they would succeed at trial. They had raised a triable issue, which if successful, entitled them to an equitable interest in the residence based on the statutory trust created by the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Tri-Tec Drywall Services Ltd." p2="Wilson Memorial General Hospital" post.rptr="3550" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63e6b4f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Tec Drywall Services Ltd. v. Wilson Memorial General Hospital">Tri-Tec Drywall Services Ltd. v. Wilson Memorial General Hospital (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3550, 45 C.L.R. (3d) 314 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant unsuccessfully moved for an accounting of the trust funds required to be retained by the general contractor. This was a lien action, not a trust action, and the order for an accounting ought not to be made except in the context of a trust action where this specific relief has been pleaded. Money received by a contractor is not properly characterized as trust money within the meaning of s. 8 and does not constitute a trust fund for the benefit of persons who are not owed money directly by the contractor but are owed money by a subcontractor. The creation of a s. 8 trust is premised upon privity of contract as a condition precedent for a trustee beneficiary relationship. To hold otherwise would require all contractors to retain money received from an owner in trust until all persons in the construction chain were paid. Clearly, this is not what was intended by the legislature in creating a scheme to allow the speedy resolution of construction related disputes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pre-Con Inc." p2="Carosi Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4431" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I63e6dc005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pre-Con Inc. v. Carosi Construction Ltd.">Pre-Con Inc. v. Carosi Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4431, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 65 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor rendered its invoice for supply and installation of pre-cast concrete double tees, less 10 per cent statutory holdback required under the Act. The contractor submitted its application for payment to the owner municipality, which included monies for the double tees but not the full amount of the subcontractor's invoice. A payment certificate was issued to the contractor, and the subcontractor brought an action for damages with respect to its unpaid invoice. Pursuant to minutes of settlement, the parties agreed that if the court found that the contractor received funds from the municipality, which were owing to the subcontractor, the subcontractor was entitled to judgment, including a declaration against the contractor for breach of trust under the Act. The subcontractor's action was allowed. The contractor's liability for breach of trust extended to the full amount of the invoice, and not only the amount allocated in the contractor's application for payment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="802798 Ontario Ltd." p2="McConnery" post.rptr="3282" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63e6dc015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="802798 Ontario Ltd. v. McConnery">802798 Ontario Ltd. v. McConnery (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 3282, 2003 CarswellOnt 3212, 31 C.L.R. (3d) 316 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A standard construction management contract was signed by the corporate defendant builder, as owner, and the construction manager. The corporate defendant did not have an office or employees and the construction manager agreed to provide all of the overhead, administration, accounting, supplies and management for the project. The agreement was, in substance, a “contracting out the overhead”. However, as the personal defendant was a director of both corporate bodies, the management contract was not entered in an arm's length transaction, since both companies were related. In the circumstances, the payment of monies towards the management contract was a breach of the trust provisions of the Act. Section 8(1) of the Act made it clear that trust funds cannot be used by the contractor in order to satisfy general business expenses, nor finance overhead expenses.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Commdoor Aluminum" p2="Solar Sunrooms Inc." post.rptr="2173" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63e6dc025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Commdoor Aluminum v. Solar Sunrooms Inc.">Commdoor Aluminum v. Solar Sunrooms Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2173, 2003 CarswellOnt 2023, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 179 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2387 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The case deals with onus in a trust action. Where the corporate and individual defendants provided no accounts with respect to the company generally, or with respect to each job, and provided only the company's bank statements and guessed at the various bid prices and actual costs of each job, their initial onus was not discharged and it did not fall to the plaintiff to re-construct such accounting. The plaintiff need only show, as it did, that the defendant received monies from a particular job for which the plaintiff supplied materials and that the defendant owed the plaintiff for those materials. Both defendants breached the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> by failing to account for money received on each job and failing to ensure that the persons supplying the materials and services were paid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Decaro Glass Ltd." p2="921560 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1333" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63e6dc035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Decaro Glass Ltd. v. 921560 Ontario Ltd.">Decaro Glass Ltd. v. 921560 Ontario Ltd. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 1333, 2003 CarswellOnt 1201, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 257 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants failed to use a segregated bank account for the project, employed inadequate accounting and were found liable for breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="1150402 Ontario Inc." p2="Delfino" post.rptr="768" pre.rptr="62" ref.id="I63e703105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1150402 Ontario Inc. v. Delfino">1150402 Ontario Inc. v. Delfino (2003), 62 O.R. (3d) 768, 2003 CarswellOnt 87, 23 C.L.R. (3d) 277 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Monies received by a contractor constitute a trust fund for the benefit of direct subcontractors to that contractor only and not to sub-subcontractors. A beneficiary must have privity of contract with the alleged trustee. Otherwise, a contractor who received money from an owner would be required to continue to hold that money in trust, subject to the payments permitted by s. 10 and s. 11, until every person down the construction chain had received all sums owing to them from all intermediate parties. Such an interpretation would disrupt the flow of funds through the construction pyramid. Moreover, it would likely prevent a contractor from recovering its overhead expenses and profit on a project indefinitely, notwithstanding it had paid all amounts owing by it to those parties with whom it stood in privity of contract. Subsection 8(1) must be read in light of s. 10, which requires privity of contract between payor and payee for the payment by the trustee to qualify as a payment in discharge of the trust under s. 10. If the beneficiaries of the s. 8(1) trust were intended to include persons who did not have privity with the contractor, it would not make sense to exclude payments to them from the scope of s. 10. Had the legislature intended to impose a broad trust obligation on a contractor in favour of all persons known and unknown who supplied services or material to a project, it would have done so with express language. This interpretation was consistent with the considerations that were articulated in the <ital>Report of the Attorney General's Advisory Committee on the Draft Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc." p2="Momat Developments Inc." post.rptr="270" pre.rptr="59" ref.id="I63e703115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc.">Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc. (2002), 59 O.R. (3d) 270, 2002 CarswellOnt 2284, 19 C.L.R. (3d) 40 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff entered into a contract with the defendant contractor to supply and install heating and air conditioning systems in seven townhouses being built by the defendant owner. One individual defendant was the president of the owner, while his brother, the second individual defendant, was both its general manager and the president of the defendant contractor. All sums paid for the project were paid by cheques drawn on the owner's bank account. The plaintiff successfully alleged breach of the statutory trust under s. 8 on the part of the owner. With respect to this project, the owner was both the owner and the general contractor, and the normal privity rule did not apply. In ordinary circumstances, the plaintiff would have to demonstrate what part of all the money coming into the owner's hands was trust money that came from the lender or was otherwise earmarked for the project. Only after that was done would the duty fall upon the trustee to demonstrate that the disbursements made benefited subcontractors or other persons who have supplied services or materials to the improvement. Here, however, no attempt by the owner was made to segregate trust funds, no serious attempt was made to ascertain if disbursements of trust monies were consistent with the statutory objects of the trust and hardly any effort was made to keep a record, by vouchers, invoices or otherwise, of the reason for making payments. In such circumstances, even to place the onus on the <ital>cestui que trust</ital> to identify the trust money effectively enabled any unscrupulous owner-contractor to defeat the purpose of the Act by the simple expedient of blending funds and keeping shoddy records. Because of this, the owner bore the double onus of demonstrating i) that the money found in its account was not trust money, and ii) that the monies it disbursed from that account benefited the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="STO Industries Canada Inc." p2="L.A. Architectural Coatings Inc." post.rptr="281" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63e72a205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="STO Industries Canada Inc. v. L.A. Architectural Coatings Inc.">STO Industries Canada Inc. v. L.A. Architectural Coatings Inc. (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 281, 2002 CarswellOnt 1131 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To successfully assert a breach of trust claim, the supplier must first prove that material supplied went to a specific project. Upon receipt of payment, the supplier must seek information about the source of the fund and allocate the payment to the particular account outstanding. If the supplier fails to make reasonable inquiry and chooses, in the words of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Ross Gibson Industries Ltd." p2="Greater Vancouver Housing Corp." post.rptr="481" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63e72a215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ross Gibson Industries Ltd. v. Greater Vancouver Housing Corp.">Ross Gibson Industries Ltd. v. Greater Vancouver Housing Corp. (1985), 21 D.L.R. (4th) 481, 1985 CarswellBC 293, 16 C.L.R. 136 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, to “turn Nelson's blind eye” to the source of funds, it does not create a situation of breach of trust, but it may provide a valid defence to the supplier's trustee. While a supplier did not commit a breach of trust by applying incoming payments to the oldest outstanding accounts, the supplier could not, in these circumstances, rely upon the trust provisions of the Act and take the position that the project account remained unpaid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="B.A.C., Local 6" p2="Marathon-Delco Inc." post.rptr="201" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63e72a225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B.A.C., Local 6 v. Marathon-Delco Inc.">B.A.C., Local 6 v. Marathon-Delco Inc. (2001), 12 C.L.R. (3d) 201 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor entered into a construction contract with the owner hospital. Subsequently, the union obtained judgment against the contractor and served the hospital with a garnishment. The existence of the garnishment proceedings against the debtor contractor did not change the fundamental character of the funds owed to it by the hospital, which were impressed with dual statutory trusts, first as between the owner and contractor, and, second, as between the contractor and lien claimants. This case can be usefully compared and contrasted with the <ital>Elmford Construction</ital> case, under s. 7 of the Act (above).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Progress Doors Ltd." p2="Toronto Dominion Bank" post.rptr="2071" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I63e72a235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Progress Doors Ltd. v. No. 414, 2002 CarswellOnt 985, 2002 CarswellOnt 986</ref></cite>—The plaintiff alleged that the defendant bank improperly withdrew funds from the account of one of its customers, a contractor, to which a statutory trust attached, and claimed from the bank the amount owing by the contractor. The bank's motion for summary dismissal of this action was granted. The defendant was entitled to the monies paid in by the contractor unless the defendant had notice that the payment of funds constituted a breach of trust. Neither the structure of the financial arrangement nor the nature of the customer's business nor the conduct of the banking relationship would have put a reasonable person on inquiry as to whether the customer was observing its trust obligations. The motions judge rejected the plaintiff's submission that the following circumstances should have put the defendant on notice: (i) the fact that the defendant did not disclose its instructions to its staff with respect to clients in the construction business; (ii) that the bank's deponent on the matter was the supervisor of the bank employees who dealt directly with the contractor's account and not the actual account manager; (iii) that in the year that the contractor changed its year end, the defendant did not ask for any financial information, even unaudited statements; and (iv) that the contractor's operating line of credit was used more extensively than originally contemplated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="ABCO Construction Inc." post.rptr="294" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63e751305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. ABCO Construction Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. ABCO Construction Inc. (2000), 5 C.L.R. (3d) 294 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Supervisory and management functions performed by one of the defendant's principals fell within the kind of services found by the Ontario Court of Appeal to be “overhead”. However, manual labour performed by the same man was held to be “directly related to the improvement” and thus lienable. Law firms are not eligible recipients of trust funds under ss. 8 or 10 of the Act. The Act contemplates that the payment out of trust funds should only be to beneficiaries of the trust. It cannot be said that the services of the law firms were performed upon or in respect of the improvement itself. On the contrary, such services are more in the nature of the kinds of services that have been held to be overhead and not eligible for payment out of trust funds.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3424, 1998 CarswellOnt 3379 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 3998 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a remarkable, perhaps unique case on its facts, involving the self interested 100 per cent prepayment of a 2,239,759 contract price, and the subsequent expenditure of that sum by the non-arm's length contractor so as to defeat, for all practical purposes, a mason's lien, the Court held that where an owner has prepaid a contractor to the foreseeable prejudice of the trades, equity demands no less than that the owner's obligations be not limited to the 10 per cent holdback and the full liens should be recoverable against the owner. The statutory frame of reference for such an order is found in ss. 8 and 13, the trust sections of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="G.V.B.S. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd.">Maple Leaf Homes and Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 6</ref></cite> and agreeing with the policy expressed by Granger J. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Re Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc." p1.pp="Re " post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90bb2d00f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Re Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc.">Re Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Tam-Kal Ltd." p2="Stock Mechanical Inc." post.rptr="4577" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63e79f505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tam-Kal Ltd. v. Stock Mechanical Inc.">Tam-Kal Ltd. v. Stock Mechanical Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4577, 1998 CarswellOnt 4346 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1999), 50 C.L.R. (2d) 224 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Prior to the release of the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63e79f515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirming (1996), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 71 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> this case was argued on, <ital>inter alia</ital>, ss. 10 and 13 issues. Trailer purchases, plan copying, permits, moving expenses, heating, and small petty cash items were permissible expenses under s. 10, whereas payments to a bookkeeper, estimator and management were disallowed. The court was unable to conclude that s. 8 required the establishment of a separate trust fund for each project. It is sufficient if, on a particular project it is proven that more was paid out to beneficiaries overall than was received. This case must be read with care in view of the Court of Appeal's <ital>Rudco</ital> decision.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Colella Excavating Ltd." p2="All Types Excavating & Grading Inc." post.rptr="3142" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I63e79f525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Colella Excavating Ltd. v. All Types Excavating & Grading Inc.">Colella Excavating Ltd. v. All Types Excavating & Grading Inc. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 3142, 34 C.L.R. (2d) 132 (Ont. Gen. Div.); reversed (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 6423 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Colella Excavating Ltd." p2="All Types Excavating & Grading Inc." post.rptr="3142" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I90bb5410f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Colella Excavating Ltd. v. All Types Excavating & Grading Inc.">Colella Excavating Ltd. v. All Types Excavating & Grading Inc. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 3142, 34 C.L.R. (2d) 132 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The onus is on the plaintiff to prove that the defendant received trust funds. The relevant information was in the hands of the defendants, but could have been obtained by the plaintiff under s. 39 or by aggressive use of the production provisions of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. The plaintiff did neither and failed to prove its case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Electrical Equipment Co." p2="General Motors of Canada" post.rptr="2630" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63e7c6605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Electrical Equipment Co. v. General Motors of Canada">Electrical Equipment Co. v. General Motors of Canada (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2630, 1998 CarswellOnt 2603 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was registered against the defendant's head office rather than its truck plant, and accordingly the lien was vacated and the certificate of action dismissed. The plaintiff sought to have the defendant's statutory holdback paid into court pending the plaintiff's review and accounting of funds as between the contractor and the sub-contractor with whom the plaintiff had contracted. The court found that since the lien was registered on the wrong land, there was no holdback, and while allegations of breach of trust and responsibility remained open, those obligations did not support an application for payment into court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Opec Acoustics & Drywall Ltd." p2="Kascon Corp." post.rptr="75" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63e7c6615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Opec Acoustics & Drywall Ltd. v. Kascon Corp.">Opec Acoustics & Drywall Ltd. v. Kascon Corp. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 75 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where a breach of trust allegation is based on malfeasance such as fraud, misrepresentation, malice or malicious intent, it is clear that R. 25.06(8) of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> applies to such pleadings. However, the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> creates a category of “breach of trust” that is independent of the “condition of mind” applicable under R. 25.06(8), and that is not a lower standard of pleading than that which is contemplated by R. 25.06(8). Because all amounts owing to a contractor or subcontractor whether or not due or payable, or received by a contractor or subcontractor on account of any contract or subcontract, are within the knowledge of the contractor or subcontractor, it is sufficient in the pleadings under the Act to allege a breach of contract where no accounting has been made of those funds to any subcontractors or other persons who have supplied services or materials to the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="St. Mary's Cement Corp." p2="Construc Ltd." post.rptr="939" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I55dbbbe0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Construc Ltd.">St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Construc Ltd. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 939, 32 O.R. (3d) 595, 33 C.L.R. (2d) 234 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—It is the clear intention of the statute that trust funds be used only to pay the claims of beneficiaries until such time as all of them have been paid in full. There is no justification for a contractor paying for any portion of its overhead expenses out of trust funds. Payment out of trust funds for items such as payroll, insurance, rent, membership fees, interest payments on loans, legal and accounting expenses, advertising, entertainment expenses and the like is improper and constitutes a breach of the trust provisions of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="977724 Ontario Inc." p2="Godard" post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63e7ed715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="977724 Ontario Inc. v. Godard">977724 Ontario Inc. v. Godard (1997), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 54 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The onus is on the person alleging a breach of trust under the Act to establish a <ital>prima facie</ital> case that a breach has taken place or exists. The burden would then shift to the defendant to account for all the proceeds. It was inappropriate to grant a motion for summary judgment where the defendant's business records had been seized, he was therefore unable to offer an accounting, and had stated in his affidavit that all trust monies had been dispersed to the sub-contractors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd." p2="Fahuki Construction Inc." post.rptr="3286" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I55dbbbe1fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd. v. Fahuki Construction Inc.">Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd. v. Fahuki Construction Inc. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 3286, 30 C.L.R. (2d) 156 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The weight of authority in Ontario is to the effect that a general contractor is not entitled to pay any of its own overhead or expenses out of funds received pursuant to a general contract until all subcontractors and suppliers are paid in full. Accordingly, the distribution by a contractor of all of the funds received by it from the owner of a project, and the application of a part of those funds to the contractor's own overhead and expenses constituted a breach of trust pursuant to s. 8 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Heritage Masonry Ltd." p2="Building Team Ltd." post.rptr="1226" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63e7ed735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Building Team Ltd.">Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Building Team Ltd. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 1226, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 101 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—If the Act were interpreted so as to permit contractors to deduct their own overhead expenses from funds held in trust for the subcontractors, such an interpretation would defeat the purpose of the hold back provisions in the Act, namely to protect subcontractors. Accordingly, overhead expenses cannot be deducted from trust funds.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Main Line Construction Ltd." p2="Nicolini" post.rptr="2815" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I63e814805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini">Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 2815 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant N Ltd., which disputed the allegation that it was the general contractor, received $25,000.00 on account of a renovation project, with $5,000.00 received as a deposit and the balance by way of Minutes of Settlement. In finding N Ltd. to be the general contractor, the court held that the $25,000 constituted a trust fund pursuant to s. 8(1), and that N Ltd. was a trustee of the monies pursuant to s. 8(2). Accordingly, it was improper for N Ltd. to keep the balance of the monies received.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc." p2="Process Cooling Systems Inc." post.rptr="324" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63e814815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. Process Cooling Systems Inc.">Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. Process Cooling Systems Inc. (1993), 16 O.R. (3d) 324, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 86 (Gen. Div.); appeal allowed on other grounds (1996), 30 O.R. (3d) 159 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not apply to the supply of a water cooling system in a manufacturing plant and the purchaser/contractor was not liable for breach of trust under the Act. Although the equipment supplied became attached in many ways to the system which it was part for the purpose of cooling water and regenerating water and although it was attached electrically and from a plumbing and drainage point of view, it was not and did not become a part of the building and was not incorporated into the building.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="IBL Industries Ltd., Re" post.rptr="20" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I63e814825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="IBL Industries Ltd., Re">IBL Industries Ltd., Re (1990), 80 C.B.R. (N.S.) 20 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—The manufacture and supply by a subcontractor of parts of an emissions control system were “improvements” within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The components were an integral part of the system, and the fact that some part of the work could be removed from the structure of which it was an essential part was not determinative of the issue. The trustee was entitled to collect the funds, which were impressed with a trust in favour of the subcontractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re" post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90bbf050f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re">Richmond Brothers Insulation Inc., Re (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 157, 69 O.R. (2d) 22, 73 C.B.R. (N.S.) 284, 34 C.L.R. 29 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—R, an installer of urethane foam insulation, bought two chemicals to create the insulation in raw form from C, which shipped the chemicals in bulk to R on a general credit basis. R then stored the chemicals in tanks on its property. At the date of bankruptcy, R owed approximately $89,300 to C but was owed approximately $61,000 for completed foam insulation contracts. Approximately 50 per cent of the contract price represented the cost of the chemicals. The trustee in bankruptcy brought an application to determine whether 50 per cent of the accounts receivable of R constituted a trust fund for C's benefit under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The court found that C was entitled to 50 per cent of the amounts received by the trustee in bankruptcy on account of the improvements incorporating C's chemicals. The Act's trust provisions are intended to protect persons who supply raw materials which are subsequently incorporated into an improvement, whether the materials were supplied directly to the improvement or indirectly in bulk to a contractor working on the improvement. Accordingly, the amount of $30,478 constituted a trust fund for C's benefit.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I63e83b915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re">Inseco Ltd. (Trustee of), Re (1986), 20 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—The debtor built portable schoolrooms which, in the normal course of business were built at one location and delivered completely finished to the site and were installed on cement blocks which rested on cement pads. The debtor was notified of the delivery site by the School Board prior to installation. The portable rooms had no water or sewage facilities and were self-contained units that could be moved from place to place like a mobile home. It was argued that due to the cement pads and foundation, upon which the portable rooms rested, the schoolrooms were not moveable property or chattels, and therefore were part of an improvement to the land, and therefore created a lienable interest. The court disagreed. The portable classrooms were chattels, and did not create an interest in land. As such, the work performed did not constitute an improvement pursuant to the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to which the trust provisions applied.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
8:6: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 8(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="San Remo Lighting" p2="Am-Tech" post.rptr="176" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63e83b925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="San Remo Lighting v. Am-Tech">San Remo Lighting v. Am-Tech, 2019 ONSC 176, 2019 CarswellOnt 425 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The monies received by the defendant subcontractor from the contractor were deposited into a single general account from which the defendant paid all of its ongoing expenses and costs including wages, dividends, bonuses, rent, equipment, supplies and subcontractors. It did not retain or segregate monies pursuant to the trust requirements of the Act. The defendant pleaded a set-off as against the plaintiff for defaults including the delivery of incorrect material, materials not delivered and delays. The defendant subsequently deposited monies into its lawyer's trust account to retroactively satisfy its trust obligations to the plaintiff. The court found that despite the alleged set off claim, there was still a trust obligation on the defendant's part to retain the monies. There was an absolute obligation under ss. 8 and 12 to retain the funds in trust, and the trust provisions of the Act do not permit the trustee to disburse the trust fund by reason of having a claim which it wishes to assert by way of set-off against the beneficiary.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1705371 Ontario Ltd." p2="Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc." post.rptr="7423" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63e862a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1705371 Ontario Ltd. v. Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc.">1705371 Ontario Ltd. v. Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc., 2018 ONSC 7423, 2018 CarswellOnt 21112, 85 C.L.R. (4th) 132, 27 C.P.C. (8th) 34 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 480 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After a noting in default, the factual allegations in the statement of claim were deemed to be true and, together with additional evidence provided by the plaintiff, demonstrated that the corporate defendant breached the trust created by s. 8 by refusing to pay the plaintiff for the supply of masonry services out of the payments that it had received as a statutory trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Monro Ltd." p2="Faga Group Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4968" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63e862a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Monro Ltd. v. Faga Group Construction Ltd.">Monro Ltd. v. Faga Group Construction Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4968, 2016 CarswellOnt 12595, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 329 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The corporate defendant received monies in respect of various construction projects for which the plaintiff had supplied materials. The corporate defendant was noted in default and failed to prove that it properly distributed the monies received in respect of the various construction projects. It was therefore liable for breach of trust pursuant to s. 8. Pursuant to s. 13, the individual defendants were jointly and severally liable along with the corporate defendant for breach of trust. As directors, officers and controlling minds of the corporate defendant, they acquiesced in or assented to the corporate defendant's breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="S&R Flooring Concepts Inc." p2="RLC Stratford LP" post.rptr="5288" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63e862a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S&R Flooring Concepts Inc. v. RLC Stratford LP">S&R Flooring Concepts Inc. v. RLC Stratford LP, 2013 ONSC 5288, 2013 CarswellOnt 12254, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 89 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To show a breach of trust under s. 8(2), it was not necessary to show that, even if funds were received, the defendant paid the trust funds to a person who did not supply labour or material to the project. Where there was evidence that the general contractor received the funds and the plaintiff did not, a trier of fact could reasonably infer that the general contractor appropriated or converted those funds to a use “inconsistent with the trust.”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="690536 Ontario Inc." p2="Trimark Homes Ltd." post.rptr="894" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63e889b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="690536 Ontario Inc. v. Trimark Homes Ltd.">690536 Ontario Inc. v. Trimark Homes Ltd., 2012 ONSC 894, 2012 CarswellOnt 4188, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 130 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 10745, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 143 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff having proved the existence of the statutory trust, the defendant did not satisfy the onus of proving that it has complied with its obligations as trustee by establishing that payments made out of trust funds were to beneficiaries of the trust or within the exceptions enumerated by the Act. Rather, it used proceeds from one contract to satisfy liabilities owed the trades on others, and was therefore liable for breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Belmont Concrete Finishing Co." p2="Marshall" post.rptr="1560" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63e889b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmont Concrete Finishing Co. v. Marshall">Belmont Concrete Finishing Co. v. Marshall, 2011 ONSC 1560, 2011 CarswellOnt 6942, 7 C.L.R. (4th) 147 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2011 CarswellOnt 11115, 7 C.L.R. (4th) 158 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2012 CarswellOnt 11103, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Once a breach of trust has occurred under s. 8, the corporation's liability for the breach of trust is not discharged until the trust beneficiaries are paid (as set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Andrea Schmidt Construction Ltd." p2="Glatt" post.rptr="791" pre.rptr="1979" ref.id="I63e889b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andrea Schmidt Construction Ltd. v. Glatt">Andrea Schmidt Construction Ltd. v. Glatt, 1979 CarswellOnt 791, 25 O.R. (2d) 567 (Ont. H.C.); affirmed 1980 CarswellOnt 1365, 28 O.R. (2d) 672 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). However, the failure to remedy pre-existing breaches of trust under s. 8 does not create continuing breaches of trust under that provision. A breach of trust under s. 8 of the Act is a discrete event that occurs at a point in time when monies in a trust fund are appropriated or converted. Moreover, s. 8 requires a plaintiff to prove conduct that constitutes appropriation or conversion of moneys received in respect of any particular project for purposes inconsistent with the trust fund in respect of such project. The failure to pay a subcontractor does not, by itself, establish a breach of trust. If a particular project proves to be unprofitable, the failure to pay a subcontractor, in whole or in part, will not constitute a breach of trust if all of the monies received in respect of the project are used to pay other subcontractors. In the case of contractors or subcontractors having an involvement in more than one project, s. 8 treats monies from each project separately. The circumstances pertaining to any particular project must therefore be considered individually to determine whether the contractor or subcontractor appropriated or converted trust monies paid to such contractor or subcontractor on account of such project.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Komatsu Canada Ltd." p2="Medway Contracting Group Ltd." post.rptr="4801" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I63e8b0c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Komatsu Canada Ltd. v. Medway Contracting Group Ltd.">Komatsu Canada Ltd. v. Medway Contracting Group Ltd., 2009 CarswellOnt 4801 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Payments made to non-eligible recipients while eligible suppliers remain unpaid constitutes a breach of trust. Here, the defendants made payments to various non-eligible third parties while monies were still owing to the plaintiff, which constituted a breach of s. 8. The loss sustained by the plaintiff was held to be the total amount that the defendant paid out to non-eligible third party creditors while monies were owing to the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Genrep Ltd./Ltée" p2="Industrial Light & Electric Inc." post.rptr="236" pre.rptr="68" ref.id="I63e8b0c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Genrep Ltd./Ltée v. Industrial Light & Electric Inc.">Genrep Ltd./Ltée v. Industrial Light & Electric Inc. (2008), 68 C.L.R. (3d) 236, 2008 CarswellOnt 2112 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Monies paid by the general contractor to the defendant subcontractor, made in regard to the supply of a generator by the plaintiff supplier, were allegedly used to pay down debt on the home of the subcontractor's officers. The officers subsequently filed proposals into bankruptcy, and the subcontractor filed an assignment into bankruptcy. The plaintiff supplier commenced an action against the subcontractor for breach of trust and brought a motion seeking a tracing order with respect to the officer's home and for a certificate of pending litigation against the home. In holding that the plaintiff's claim was stayed by virtue of s. 69.1 of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, the court distinguished <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Wormald Fire Systems Inc." p2="Coopers & Lybrand Ltd." post.rptr="77" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63e8b0c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wormald Fire Systems Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand Ltd.">Wormald Fire Systems Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand Ltd. (1985), 11 C.L.R. 77 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>, on the basis that the defendant there had actually made an assignment in bankruptcy and on the basis that in that case there had been no issue of competing interests of other creditors to the trust fund property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Savoia" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63e8b0c35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia">Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia (2006), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 235, 207 O.A.C. 1, 2006 CarswellOnt 340 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In the Small Claims Court, a liberal, non-technical approach should be taken to pleadings. Relief that is not pleaded may be granted so long as supporting evidence is not needed beyond what was adduced at trial, provided that, in all of the circumstances, it is not unfair to grant such relief. The trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> place a burden upon a defendant to prove compliance with the trust provisions once a plaintiff establishes the existence of a trust, and it was unfair to a defendant to award judgment against him upon a trust claim that was not pleaded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc." p2="Mississauga (City)" post.rptr="235" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63e8d7d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Mississauga (City)">Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Mississauga (City) (2003), [2004] O.J. No. 235, 2004 CarswellOnt 222, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 169 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After termination of the plaintiff's contract by the defendant City for delay, the plaintiff sued the City for, <ital>inter alia</ital>, punitive damages and breach of trust. On the evidence, the court concluded that the defendant City had paid its obligations under the construction contract pursuant to the certificates issued by the architect and that sufficient funds were available to pay the sub-trades, but that the plaintiff contractor was fully responsible for financial problems which developed. Instead of paying those sub-trades, the plaintiff's principal improperly paid himself or his companies in contravention of the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and had commingled trust funds. Having met its obligations under the contract, the City was justified in terminating the contract on the basis that the work had not been completed in accordance with the many extensions provided by the City with respect to the completion date.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="STO Industries Canada Inc." p2="L.A. Architectural Coatings Inc." post.rptr="281" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63e8d7d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="STO Industries Canada Inc. v. L.A. Architectural Coatings Inc.">STO Industries Canada Inc. v. L.A. Architectural Coatings Inc. (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 281, 2002 CarswellOnt 1131 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The principal subcontractor of a small company, who was also the president, and hence a trustee under the Act, was the master plasterer on various projects, and reported his income received from the company as an independent subcontractor. The reasonable payments made to the principal by the corporation were payments made in breach of s. 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and not payments for “services rendered”. Although technically the subcontractor may stand as an independent contractor with respect to work performed on the project, his obligations as trustee stipulated in s. 8(2) of the Act superseded any rights that he might acquire under s. 8(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Draft Masonry (York) Co." p2="P.A. Restoration Inc." post.rptr="231" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63e8d7d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Draft Masonry (York) Co. v. P.A. Restoration Inc.">Draft Masonry (York) Co. v. P.A. Restoration Inc. (1988), 48 R.P.R. 231, 29 C.L.R. 256 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—This was an action for an alleged breach of trust arising out of an escrow arrangement gone wrong. The lien claimant plaintiff, through its solicitor, delivered to solicitors for the defendant a Discharge of Lien in registerable form to be held in escrow until they were “in a position to deliver” a certified cheque for a specified amount and on Direction upon the owner for the balance, among other things. A solicitor's trust cheque was delivered, cashed, and the Discharge registered. No irrevocable direction was delivered and there were other less serious deficiencies in compliance. In this action, the defendant defaulted and judgment went against the balance of the defendants, including the defendant's solicitors involved in the breach of escrow.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Wormald Fire Systems Inc." p2="Coopers & Lybrand Ltd." post.rptr="77" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63e8fee05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wormald Fire Systems Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand Ltd.">Wormald Fire Systems Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand Ltd. (1985), 11 C.L.R. 77 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff claimed for construction work which it performed for the defendant M Ltd., which filed a proposal pursuant to the provisions of the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital>. The defendant CL Ltd. was named trustee under the proposal, and interim receiver and manager of M Ltd. The plaintiff then instituted an action for an accounting of trust monies and for damages pursuant to the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. CL Ltd. and M Ltd. moved to strike out the statement of claim on the ground that it disclosed no reasonable cause of action and on the further ground that leave to proceed ought to have been applied for pursuant to ss. 49 and 186 of the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital>. The motion was dismissed. Section 47 of the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital> excluded from the property of a bankrupt any property held in trust for any other person. This claim was to monies held in trust, and the plaintiff was therefore not obliged nor entitled to prove its claim in the bankruptcy. As a result, there was no stay of proceedings under that Act and leave to proceed was not required.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">8.1:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This is a new section introduced in 2018 to set out how the trustee of a contractor's or subcontractor's trust must handle the trust funds.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Expert Review identified concern about the former trust provisions with respect to their enforceability in the event of the insolvency and/or bankruptcy of a payer</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Given the doctrine of constitutional paramountcy, in the case of an operational conflict between provincial legislation, i.e. the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, and federal legislation, including the <ital>BIA</ital>, the federal legislation will prevail</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 67 <ital>BIA</ital> provides that property of a bankrupt divisible among his creditors shall not comprise property held by the bankrupt in trust for any other person</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Supreme Court of Canada has held that exception set out in section 67(1) applies to statutory trusts established by provincial legislation only if such trusts bear the attributes of a common law trust</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Establishment of trust account meant to prevent trust funds from losing their common law trust certainties by becoming untraceable</para.text></para></list.item></list></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
9:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 9.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">9:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 9 was enacted for the first time as part of the remedial <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. It preserves trust claims in the event of sale of the property.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 9 prevents the avoidance of lien claims by means of the sale of the property by the original owner while there are subsisting but unpreserved lien rights. Section 9(1) constitutes the net consideration received by the owner on such a sale as trust funds for the benefit of the contractor, and is of particular interest in residential subdivision construction.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">“Mortgage indebtedness” and “reasonable expenses arising from the sale” are the only items that can be deducted from the gross proceeds of the sale, however under standard charge terms, these become rather expansive exclusions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 9(2) describes the trust obligation in relation to the “former” owner and states that he or she must hold the net proceeds of the sale until the contractor is paid in full. Of note is the reference to “the” former owner, implying that there is only one. If this is interpreted as referring to only one owner, the section may not apply to situations where the property is “flipped” from owner to owner.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbancorp Cumberland 2 GP Inc. (Re)" post.rptr="3403" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I63e974105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbancorp Cumberland 2 GP Inc. (Re)">Urbancorp Cumberland 2 GP Inc. (Re), 2020 CarswellOnt 3403, 2020 ONCA 197, 11 C.L.R. (5th) 225, 444 D.L.R. (4th) 273, 77 C.B.R. (6th) 196 (Ont. C.A.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 4921 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The developer was granted insolvency protection continued under the (Can.) <ital>Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act</ital>. It owned unsold condominium units in a project it constructed, and owed significant unpaid sums to various appellant suppliers and contractors. The condominium units were ultimately sold during the insolvency proceedings. As a result of the sale, the appellants claimed that a trust arose over the proceeds to the extent of the amounts owing to them, which would give them an effective priority for those amounts. The Court of Appeal found that a trust created by s. 9(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> can be effective in a CCAA sales process. It would only be displaced under the doctrine of paramountcy if it conflicted with a specific priority created under the CCAA. In this case, nothing displaced the operation of the s. 9(1) trust over the proceeds to the extent of the amounts owed to the claimant appellants. The Court did not interpret <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re" post.rptr="3211" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I90be1330f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re">Veltri Metal Products Co., Re (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 3211, 2004 CarswellOnt 3153 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List]); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3326, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, as standing for the proposition that the substantial involvement of the CCAA Monitor in the sales process prevents a s. 9(1) trust from arising. <ital>Veltri</ital> was correctly decided on its facts, which were very different from this case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Roni Excavating Ltd." p2="Sedona Development Group (Lorne Park) Inc." post.rptr="389" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63e99b205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Roni Excavating Ltd. v. Sedona Development Group (Lorne Park) Inc.">Roni Excavating Ltd. v. Sedona Development Group (Lorne Park) Inc., 2015 ONSC 389, 2015 CarswellOnt 826, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 278 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2015 CarswellOnt 16117, 55 C.L.R. (4th) 63 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The corporate defendants C/C were in joint venture with the SDG to develop lands for townhomes, with C/C serving as financier and developer, and SDG as builder. Both were found to be owners under the Act. The proceeds of sale of the lands, which were paid into court, were trust funds for the benefit of the lien claimants. Even though no one contracted directly with C/C, SDG, as an owner, could not be considered the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Avium Corp." p2="1353025 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1826" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63e99b215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Avium Corp. v. 1353025 Ontario Inc.">Avium Corp. v. 1353025 Ontario Inc., 2010 ONSC 1826, 2010 CarswellOnt 9135, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 111 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After dismissal of the plaintiff's lien claim, the plaintiff unsuccessfully moved to amend the statement of claim to declare that the proceeds of the sale of the relevant premises constituted a trust fund for the benefit of the plaintiff in accordance with s. 9. To attempt to assert a trust claim following the dismissal of the lien action simply added time, expense and additional complexity and issues to a lien claim that had been capable of being resolved under the Act. As well, the proposed amendment was not legally tenable, as the s. 9 trust fund is an amount equal to the value of consideration received by the owner as result of the sale <ital>less</ital> the reasonable expenses arising from the sale and the amount, if any, paid by the vendor to discharge any existing mortgage indebtedness on the premises.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vance" p2="337737 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="5226" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63e9c2305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vance v. 337737 Ontario Ltd.">Vance v. 337737 Ontario Ltd., 2010 ONSC 5226, 2010 CarswellOnt 9314, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 274 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 299, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 405, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 287 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant company agreed to sell the property in question to one of the individual defendants, and agreed that the latter was authorized to proceed with renovations to the premises while the former was still the owner and that the individual defendant would be responsible to pay for the costs of any renovations. As a result of the work, the plaintiff registered a lien against the property. The president and sole shareholder, another personal defendant, sold the property in question while it continued to be subject to the plaintiff's lien. As a result, the mortgage back for received as consideration by the corporate defendant on the sale of the premises, constituted a trust fund for the benefit of the plaintiff until all amounts owing to him were paid. In the absence of evidence as to whether the mortgage payments received were held in a separate trust account, the court was unable to determine whether or not the corporate defendant or its principal had breached the terms of this trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="2039503 Ontario Ltd." p2="Turner" post.rptr="3470" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I63e9c2315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2039503 Ontario Ltd. v. Turner">2039503 Ontario Ltd. v. Turner (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3470 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A real estate commission is among the “reasonable expenses arising from the sale” contemplated by s. 9(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re" post.rptr="3326" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63e9c2325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Veltri Metal Products Co., Re">Veltri Metal Products Co., Re (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3326, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The owner's lenders held a general security interest in all or substantially all of its assets. A sale order provided that the sale proceeds were to “stand in place and stead” of the owner's assets without prejudice to any claim being advanced against them as could have been advanced against the assets. In effect, the sale proceeds were substituted for the owner's assets and were subject to the claims of the secured creditors. The court-approved sale of the insolvent owner's assets included the sale of its leasehold interest in the premises upon which the appellant lien claimants' work was performed. The asset sale could not have taken place in the face of the claims of the owner's secured creditors without the consent of those creditors and court approval, and the sale was subject to the terms imposed by the court. Under these terms, the gross proceeds of sale were applied in payment of specific items and, thereafter, the net sale proceeds, which stood in substitution for the owner's fully secured assets, were paid to the Monitor. Thus, the owner had no interest in or right to any of the net sale proceeds ultimately paid to and held by the Monitor. At best, the owner was a conduit for the receipt by the Monitor of the sale proceeds. Section 9(1)(a) of the Act provides that where an “owner's interest in a premises” is sold by the owner, an amount equal to “the value of the consideration received by the owner as a result of the sale”, less enumerated deductions, constitutes a trust fund for the benefit of the claiming contractor. In this case, contrary to the requirements of s. 9(1)(a), there was no showing that the owner's leasehold interest in the premises had any value; nor was an allocation of any part of the sale proceeds to that leasehold interest established. Moreover, under the terms of the sale order the proceeds of sale realized on the asset sale were not “received” by the vendor as owner of the property sold. Accordingly, the sale proceeds were not “consideration received by the owner as a result of the sale”, within the meaning of s. 9(1)(a) of the Act. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: It appears that <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co." p2="Irvine & Reeves Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="1955" ref.id="I55ddb7b0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd.">Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Irvine & Reeves Ltd. (1955), 1955 CarswellBC 177, [1955] 3 D.L.R. 561, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co. v. Empire Brass Manufacturing Co.)</ital> [1955] S.C.R. 694 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, was neither raised in the facta nor argued in the appeal.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works" p2="4701 Steeles Holdings Inc." post.rptr="250" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63e9e9415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. 4701 Steeles Holdings Inc.">Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. 4701 Steeles Holdings Inc. (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 250, 2002 CarswellOnt 1268 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contractor incorporated separate companies for each residential development, and owed the plaintiff roofing subcontractor monies for work and materials provided in the installation of roofs on homes sold by these separate companies. There was no dispute about the installation of the residential roofs, but there was a dispute over the quality of a roof built by the plaintiff for unrelated commercial offices and warehouse facilities. After the housing projects were completed, the funds owing were transferred to the general account, which held the “profits” for the jobs. At various times, the funds in issue were held by two related corporations and used for other projects, such as deposits on land for new developments. Pursuant to s. 9 of the Act, the funds received from such sales should have been held in trust, subject to payments of reasonable sales expenses and discharge of any mortgages. The transfer of the funds to separate corporations constituted a breach of trust. This was not a case where the owner was accused of breach of trust because it commingled funds from several projects of a business in one account. It was a case where the owner had paid the money which it owed to the subcontractor to another corporate entity instead of holding it in trust, as it should have.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="561861 Ontario Ltd." p2="1085043 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63e9e9425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc.">561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc. (1999), 49 C.L.R. (2d) 143, 1999 CarswellOnt 2227 (Ont. Bktcy.)</ref></cite>—Where land was sold in a bankruptcy setting under a proposal and in accordance with the provisions of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, the land was not sold by an “owner” and the proceeds did not constitute trust funds in accordance with s. 9(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Co-Fo Concrete Forming Construction Ltd." p2="344602 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="178" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63ea10505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Co-Fo Concrete Forming Construction Ltd. v. 344602 Ontario Ltd.">Co-Fo Concrete Forming Construction Ltd. v. 344602 Ontario Ltd. (1999), 50 C.L.R. (2d) 178 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4717 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were the owners of the lots on which the plaintiff built the foundations. When those lots were sold, the defendants failed to retain part of the proceeds in trust in accordance with s. 9 of the Act. The defence of acquiescence failed, as the defendants did not show that the plaintiff was aware of its rights under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and had acquiesced in not enforcing those rights. The defence of laches also failed, as it required an inordinate delay and acts or omissions on the part of the plaintiff, which prejudiced the defendants by lulling them into a false sense of security. In this case, the plaintiff had billed the defendants for the amount owing on a regular basis, met with the defendants in an effort to settle the account, sent the defendants a copy of their ledger card to explain how the balance due was calculated, and, through their lawyer, demanded payment of the account.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd." p2="846539 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="230" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63ea10515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd.">Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 230 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner and bank moved successfully to dismiss various claims by summary judgment, including claims for breach of trust. The trust claims were made with respect to the uncashed proceeds of certain letters of credit filed with the municipality by the developer to support subdivision agreements with the municipality. No call whatsoever had been made on these letters of credit at the time of the motion. The work to which the subdivision agreements related was work on the municipal road allowance, which the court rejected as an “improvement” within the meaning of s. 1(1) (referring to <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="George Wimpey Canada Ltd." p2="Peelton Hills Ltd." post.rptr="787" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63ea10525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="George Wimpey Canada Ltd. v. Peelton Hills Ltd.">George Wimpey Canada Ltd. v. Peelton Hills Ltd. (1982), 35 O.R. (2d) 787 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1982), 23 R.P.R. 123 (note) (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>), the plaintiff was not a “contractor” and the bank was not an “owner” (see also comment on this case under s. 7(1), above).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Budinsky" p2="Breakers East Inc." post.rptr="243" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63ea10535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Budinsky v. Breakers East Inc.">Budinsky v. Breakers East Inc. (1993), 12 C.L.R. (2d) 243, 15 O.R. (3d) 198, 18 C.P.C. (3d) 166, 106 D.L.R. (4th) 370 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A law firm successfully defended, on appeal, against an application brought by numerous purchasers of condominium units who sought rescission of their agreements of purchase and sale and the return of their deposits. The law firm rendered its accounts to its client, the owner of the units, and a number of lien claimants filed claims with respect to the condominium pursuant to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The law firm applied for an order that it was entitled to a charge on: (a) the costs awarded by the lower court and by the Court of Appeal; (b) the deposits paid by the purchasers to the respondent in connection with the purchase of the condominium units; and (c) the proceeds from the closings of the sales of the condominium units. The issue was whether any charge granted in favour of the law firm on the deposits and proceeds was subject to the trust in favour of the lien claimants created by s. 9(1) of the Act. It was held that the legal accounts did not represent “reasonable expenses arising from the sale” within the meaning of s. 9(1)(b). The fees were incurred in defending applications brought for rescission of the agreements of purchase and sale and in no way arose from the sale by the respondent of its interests in the premises. Accordingly, the general principle should apply, namely, to the extent that funds held by the respondent were subject to a trust established pursuant to s. 9, the charging order granted to the law firm would not apply to such funds.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
10:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 10.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 10 was first introduced as part of the remedial <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital> to clarify the trustee's obligations and confirm that the trust obligations are shaped by contract. A trustee can discharge its obligations to “all beneficiaries of the trust” by paying “a person” for services and materials supplied to the improvement. This section underscores the need for privity of contract between payor and payee, <ital>i.e.</ital>, between trustee and beneficiary. Section 10 became the focus of a debate over the effect of notice of a potential breach of trust prior to payment. The Committee originally favoured a statutory procedure to interrupt the flow of trust funds in such circumstances. The Committee decided against such a procedure as it would unduly interfere in the flow of funds on a construction project. The Committee here affirmed its basic philosophy that: “every effort should be made to minimize the disruption of the flow of funds through the construction pyramid”.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 10 allows a trustee to discharge, on a dollar for dollar basis, its obligations to “all beneficiaries” of the trust by paying “a person” who the trustee is liable to pay for services or materials supplied to the improvement. This section, however, must be read together with s. 85 which requires a rateable distribution in the case of an insolvent payer. It makes clear that a trustee's obligation is, in its simplest terms, to pay to the person it owes the amount owing on the improvement, and that if that is done without any actual notice of a possible breach of trust by the payee, the trustee will have discharged its duties.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Robert Nicholson Construction Co." p2="Edgecon Construction Inc." post.rptr="3107" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63ea5e705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Robert Nicholson Construction Co. v. Edgecon Construction Inc.">Robert Nicholson Construction Co. v. Edgecon Construction Inc., 2016 ONSC 3107, 2016 CarswellOnt 8345, 36 C.B.R. (6th) 224, 51 C.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2015 ONSC 1237, 2015 CarswellOnt 3975, 125 O.R. (3d) 373, 48 C.L.R. (4th) 168 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motions judge erred in law when he found that a subcontractor could be a beneficiary of the statutory trust fund created under s. 7(1) of the Act, as the wording of that section is clear; the owner's trust fund exists “for the benefit of the contractor”. Under s. 8 of the Act, a separate and distinct trust obligation is imposed on contractors and subcontractors, the beneficiaries of which are other subcontractors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1000728 Ontario Ltd." p2="Corbar Contracting Inc." post.rptr="11095" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63ea5e715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1000728 Ontario Ltd. v. Corbar Contracting Inc.">1000728 Ontario Ltd. v. Corbar Contracting Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 11095 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 1742, 2012 CarswellOnt 3463, 17 C.L.R. (4th) 251 (Ont. Div.
