Ct.)</ref></cite>—Funds impressed with a statutory trust were held to be used for purposes that were permitted pursuant to s. 10 and the trustee was discharged to the extent of the payments made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Langille" p2="Venetsanakos" post.rptr="291" pre.rptr="19" ref.id="I63ea85805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Langille v. Venetsanakos">Langille v. Venetsanakos (2002), 19 C.L.R. (3d) 291, 2002 CarswellOnt 2641 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Following flood damage, the defendant fitness centre applied insurance proceeds towards the costs of re-construction. The plaintiff had provided clean-up and other work at two related centres on several occasions following floods. The defendant did not use any of the insurance money to cover its day-to-day operating expenses, and the director of the companies did not receive any of the insurance money for his personal use. The defendant established that payments made out of the trust fund were to beneficiaries of the trust, and that the company chose to apply the insurance funds it received towards the costs of construction as opposed to applying them towards the plaintiff's bill. The payments to other beneficiaries did not constitute an improper preference.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Desourdy 1949 Paving Inc. (Trustee of), Re" post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63ea85815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Desourdy 1949 Paving Inc. (Trustee of), Re">Desourdy 1949 Paving Inc. (Trustee of), Re (2000), 17 C.B.R. (4th) 66 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A secured creditor of the bankrupt contractor unsuccessfully argued that statutory holdback funds paid by the owner into court were not imposed with a trust because the funds belonged by contract to the contractor which had paid out much more than the total sum it received from the owner. Sections 10 and 11, by their express terms, provide a defence to the trustee in bankruptcy for the contractor, not to other creditors of the bankrupt's estate. To allow a secured creditor to claim the court funds and to rely on the protection of those sections would defeat the trust protection and the resulting financial preference accorded to trust claimants by s. 8(1) of the Act and s. 67(1)(a) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63ea85825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirming (1996), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 71 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—After a thorough review of the cases, the Court of Appeal adopted the reasoning of Killeen J. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref court="Ont. Gen. Div." fjur="Ontario" jur="Canada" norm.rptr="carsont" p1="Home Depot Inc." p2="Fieder Painting Inc." post.rptr="4514" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I267fb86001a911efa7fea76a6b7cbe8e" title="Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc.">Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 4514 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> that these trusts reflect the pyramid's nature of the payment scheme devised under the <ital>Act</ital> and are aimed at creating, as it were, a fortress of impregnability against deductions by either an owner or a contractor from the trusts imposed in favor of the respective beneficiaries down the line.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Tam-Kal Ltd." p2="Stock Mechanical Inc." post.rptr="4577" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63eaac915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tam-Kal Ltd. v. Stock Mechanical Inc.">Tam-Kal Ltd. v. Stock Mechanical Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4577, 1998 CarswellOnt 4346 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1999), 50 C.L.R. (2d) 224 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Prior to the release of the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Rudco Insulation Ltd." p2="Toronto Sanitary Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I63eaac925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc.">Rudco Insulation Ltd. v. Toronto Sanitary Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirming (1996), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 71 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> this case was argued on, <ital>inter alia</ital>, ss. 10 and 13 issues. Trailer purchases, plan copying, permits, moving expenses, heating, and small petty cash items were permissible expenses under s. 10, whereas payments to a bookkeeper, estimator and management were disallowed. The Court was unable to conclude that s. 8 required the establishment of a separate trust fund for each project. It is sufficient if, on a particular project it is proven that more was paid out to beneficiaries overall than was received. This case must be read with care in view of the Court of Appeal's <ital>Rudco</ital> decision.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Arthur Andersen Inc." p2="Toronto Dominion Bank" post.rptr="363" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63eaac935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arthur Andersen Inc. v. Toronto Dominion Bank">Arthur Andersen Inc. v. Toronto Dominion Bank (1994), 17 O.R. (3d) 363 (C.A.); additional reasons (1994), 14 B.C.L.R. (2d) 1 <point>at 49</point> (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 207 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant bank, as banker for a group of related construction companies, utilized a mirror accounting system, to avoid dealing with the separate account balances of each company. Only the net balance of all companies on the system was considered, and as long as that amount was positive, individual company overdrafts were not considered problematic. The group of companies eventually ran into financial problems and the bank was sued. The bank was held, on appeal, to be a constructive trustee liable for a breach of trust. Although the bank knew that the business of construction group involved the deposit of trust funds, and that through the mirror system unorthodox use of construction draws was being made to retire overdrafts, there was wilful blindness to the possible results. However, although the bank was wilfully blind to these facts from the commencement of his involvement with the group, its wilful blindness only became important when the bank knew, or should have known that it was likely that trade accounts of the group would not be paid. It was incumbent on the bank to make further inquiries at that time and the bank should also have ceased to transfer funds to the concentration account through the mirror system after it became aware of the situation.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
11:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 11.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">11:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">By virtue s. 1 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, contractors and subcontractors were permitted under that statute to retain from trust funds an amount they had used to pay for “materials supplied” on account of the contract and for “workmen or subcontractors” who had performed “work or services or placed or furnished any material” in respect of the contract. These provisions were included in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital> as s. 2(2). Section 2(5) of that statute extended the same exemption to owners in relation to construction financing and an exemption for “money [that] is lent to a person upon whom a trust is imposed” and that was used to pay “in whole or in part” for work done or materials placed or furnished or for any rented equipment concerning the contract. Subs. 2(2), (5) and (6) later became s. 3(2), (5) and (6) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. All of these sections were carried forward into s. 11 of the 1983 and 1990 versions of the statute. The Advisory Committee initially contemplated using a single comprehensive clause to capture the essence of s. 11, but chose the two clauses that now appear in order to preserve the substance of the predecessor sections of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 11(1) allows a trustee to “retain” out of trust funds an amount equal to any non-trust monies that the trustee has borrowed or otherwise used to pay for services or materials supplied to the improvement. Subsection 11(2) goes further and allows a trustee not only to “retain” but also to “apply” trust funds to repay borrowed money otherwise used to pay beneficiaries. The courts have made it clear that the loan must be specifically to the project and must be repaid by the statutory trustee, not the creditor (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction Co." p2="S.I. Guttman Ltd." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I63eafab05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd.">Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd. (1996), 29 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.); appeal dismissed (1997), 104 O.A.C. 232 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd." p2="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc." post.rptr="367" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63eafab15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd. v. King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc.">Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd. v. King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc., 2021 ONCA 367, 2021 CarswellOnt 7769, 156 O.R. (3d) 1, 89 C.B.R. (6th) 167, 67 E.T.R. (4th) 28 (Ont. C.A.); affirming 2019 ONSC 3671, 2019 CarswellOnt 9651, 71 C.B.R. (6th) 187, 100 C.L.R. (4th) 169, 47 E.T.R. (4th) 177, 10 P.P.S.A.C. (4th) 165 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In a lien matter in which the contractor and two subcontractors sought payment on the project, the contractor settled the claim of one of its subcontractors and took an assignment of the latter's lien. This arrangement did not permit the contractor to “stand in the shoes” of that subcontractor when it came to the distribution of the trust funds. That result would only be the case if the contractor had used non-trust funds to pay the subcontractor and receive an assignment of its lien. That conclusion followed from the express language of s. 11(1) of the Act. If the contractor used monies impressed with a trust in favour of the subcontractor, then that subcontractor's claim to the trust funds was gone, leaving only the second subcontractor with the right to claim against the trust funds. The contractor did not acquire any right to claim against those trust funds. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also the summary of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc." p2="Plati" post.rptr="557" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63eafab25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati">King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati, 2017 ONSC 557, 2017 CarswellOnt 1712, 64 C.L.R. (4th) 102 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> under subsection 24(2), and the discussion of <ital>Great Northern Insulation Services Ltd. v. King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc.</ital> under s. 8.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Paragon Building Ltd." p2="Bleta Estate" post.rptr="383" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63eb21c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paragon Building Ltd. v. Bleta Estate">Paragon Building Ltd. v. Bleta Estate, 2014 ONSC 383, 2014 CarswellOnt 689, 9 C.B.R. (6th) 25, 29 C.L.R. (4th) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 CarswellOnt 2376, 32 C.L.R. (4th) 139 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sub-subcontractor was retained by the subcontractor to perform renovation work, and after being terminated by the subcontractor registered a lien and commenced an action against the owner and subcontractor. The defendants claimed it was inappropriate for the plaintiff to allocate the subcontractor's payments first to outstanding accounts it had with it on four other projects. The Master held that while the payments were trust monies under Part II of the Act, the trust obligations were owed to those “subcontractors” in privity of contract with the trustee and that the trust obligations were discharged by paying those subcontractors. Where all subcontractors of a trustee have been paid trust monies under the Act, any residue belongs to the trustee without restriction. As the plaintiff had fully paid its only subcontractor, the allocation did not violate the statutory scheme.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Bernard" p2="JDS Uniphase Corp." post.rptr="309" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63eb21c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bernard v. JDS Uniphase Corp.">Bernard v. JDS Uniphase Corp. (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 309, 2002 CarswellOnt 3274 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff lent money to the general contractor to provide interim financing for the latter's various construction projects, and received an assignment of the security, including accounts receivable, held by the contractor's primary source of operational funding, a bank. The owner was a commercial tenant of the premises in which construction projects at issue were situated. Because of financial difficulties, the contractor was unable to pay its sub-trades. The holdback in the owner's hands was insufficient to pay the amount due the subcontractors, and the unpaid balance on the projects by the owner was $19,461.43. At no time was there any relevant contractual relationship between the plaintiff and the owner, or the plaintiff and any subcontractor. The plaintiff advised the owner of its security position as a result of the bank assignment and demanded payment of the contractor's “outstanding account”, and claimed priority over all other creditors of the contractor. The owner argued that its liability amounted to $19,461.43 and that the subcontractors, whose claims greatly exceeded $19,461.43, had claims against this sum in priority to that of the plaintiff, pursuant to the trust provisions of the Act. The court ruled that the security held by the plaintiff, as assignee from the bank, did not attach to the trust fund. The plaintiff, as a lender of his own funds and as assignee of the rights of the bank, was a lender within the meaning of s. 11(2) of the Act. The contractor was a trustee within the meaning of s. 8 of the Act. However, the plaintiff failed to demonstrate that he had an entitlement to the trust fund in priority to the claims of the subcontractors and his request for a partial summary judgment was dismissed. The amount of $19,461.43 was an amount “owing to a contractor” on account of the contract and, therefore, constituted, under s. 8, a trust fund for the benefit of the subcontractors. Under s. 11 of the Ontario Act, it did not matter whether the lender was secured or unsecured, and the security held by the plaintiff, as assignee from the bank, did not attach to the trust fund.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="LeBrun Northern Contracting Ltd., Re" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I63eb48d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="LeBrun Northern Contracting Ltd., Re">LeBrun Northern Contracting Ltd., Re (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 150 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As the result of rapid progress of a contractor which temporarily outstripped the owner's financing arrangements, the owner, with the knowledge and approval of the plaintiff subcontractor, sought and obtained interim financing from a bank to satisfy certified progress payments due to the contractor in respect of the work. The owner provided its government funding authority with a notice of assignment and form of irrevocable letter of direction in favour of the bank. When a dispute arose as to the application of funds to be received from the government funding authority, the contractor applied to the court to have the advance of funds declared a specific fund for its benefit under Ontario R. 45.02 and Part II of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There was some evidence that not all of the interim bridge loan had been used to pay for the supply of services or materials to the improvement. The Court rejected the plaintiff's argument that the repayment of the bridge financing loan in such circumstances did, or could constitute a breach of the statutory trust. Accordingly, s. 11(2) of the Act permitted repayment of the bank's interim financing loan.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction Co." p2="S.I. Guttman Ltd." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I63eb48d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd.">Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd. (1996), 29 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.); appeal dismissed (1997), 104 O.A.C. 232 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 11(2) will not apply if the loans repaid were not advanced specifically for the project which was the subject of the litigation, but for the general operation of a the debtor. Additionally, the trustee, rather than the creditor, must exercise the discretion to pay the lender. The exemption from liability for a trustee who acts reasonably, as set out in s. 35 of the <ital>Trustee Act</ital> (Ont.), does not apply to a trust created by the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
12:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 12.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">12:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Set-off must now be related to the improvement unless contractor or subcontractor becomes insolvent, in which case set-off continues to be possible whether or not related to the improvement (see also s. 17(3))</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 12 was first introduced as part of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. Subject to its holdback obligations, a statutory trustee may “retain” trust funds in an amount equal to the balance in the trustee's favour of all “outstanding debts, claims or damages” owed to the trustee by the trustee's payee. These debts, claims or damages need not be related to the improvement in question. This underscores the fundamental concept of privity of contract that underlies Part II of the Act. The previous <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> had not included an express set-off provision, however, several cases had read this set-off right into the statute. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Trust Co." p2="Universal Sheet Metals Ltd." post.rptr="374" pre.rptr="[1970] 1" ref.id="I63eb6fe05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Trust Co. v. Universal Sheet Metals Ltd.">Royal Trust Co. v. Universal Sheet Metals Ltd., [1970] 1 O.R. 374 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> the Ontario Court of Appeal held that the trustee of a bankrupt contractor could set-off against trust monies all debts owed to the contractor by a subcontractor concerning a separate contract. The Court of Appeal relied upon s. 129(1) of the <ital>Judicature Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, c. 197 which provided for a set-off of mutual debts notwithstanding the fact that the debts were deemed in law to be of a different nature. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1968" p1="S.I. Guttman Ltd." p2="James D. Mokry Ltd." post.rptr="7" pre.rptr="[1969] 1" ref.id="I63eb96f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S.I. Guttman Ltd. v. James D. Mokry Ltd.">S.I. Guttman Ltd. v. James D. Mokry Ltd. (1968), [1969] 1 O.R. 7 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, the Ontario Court of Appeal quoted with approval the principle that damages incurred by the owner on account of the contractor's failure to complete the specific project upon which the trust arose may be set off by the owner against the trust fund. A similar result was obtained in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1976" p1="Standard Industries Ltd." p2="Treasury Trails Holding Ltd." post.rptr="8" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I63eb96f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Standard Industries Ltd. v. Treasury Trails Holding Ltd.">Standard Industries Ltd. v. Treasury Trails Holding Ltd. (1976), 24 C.B.R. (N.S.) 8; affirmed (1977), 23 C.B.R. (N.S.) 244 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. The present s. 12 incorporates this line of authority.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The effect of s. 12 is that the value of any trust claim by a payee will be limited to the net amount owing by the payer after all set-offs have been exercised. Subsection 17(3) of the Act places a similar restriction on the amount of a person's lien. Jurisprudence under s. 12 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> of 1983 has been limited and has followed precedents set under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Blundell" p2="Frederick Fortune Operating as Home-Works et al." post.rptr="1722" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ebbe005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Blundell v. Frederick Fortune Operating as Home-Works et al.">Blundell v. Frederick Fortune Operating as Home-Works et al., 2019 ONSC 1722, 2019 CarswellOnt 4727, 99 C.L.R. (4th) 7 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The claimant sub-subcontractor registered a lien as the result of unpaid invoices by the subcontractor. The subcontractor alleged the unpaid amounts were set-offs to address deficiencies in the lien claimant's work. The correspondence from the subcontractor's lawyer enclosing a trust payment to the claimant's lawyer, equal to the lien amount, did not make it clear that the funds were intended to function as a payment of security, nor did it set out any conditions on the trust. However, an agreement by the sub-subcontractor to discharge the lien after receipt of the payment into trust was more consistent with the expectation that the funds would be released to satisfy the unpaid invoices unless a claim in respect of the deficiencies was brought by the subcontractor. The subcontractor could have brought a claim against the lien claimant alleging that deficiencies in the latter's work justified a set-off of funds equal or greater to the money paid into trust, or attached conditions to its initial payment of the funds in trust. However, they did not do so within the limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bisquip Leasing Corporation" p2="Coco Paving Inc. et al" post.rptr="341" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ebbe015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bisquip Leasing Corporation v. Coco Paving Inc. et al">Bisquip Leasing Corporation v. Coco Paving Inc. et al, 2019 ONSC 341, 2019 CarswellOnt 599, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 366 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Working with the plaintiff on multiple projects, the defendant withheld monies equal to the sum of a third-party invoice as a back charge against the plaintiff on a different project. The plaintiff argued that s. 12 expressly permitted it to do so without being in breach of trust. In granting the plaintiff summary judgment, the court held that the amount still held in trust was available to pay the judgment. Simply because the defendant could claim a set off under s. 12, it was not an answer to the plaintiff's outstanding claim as a result of the judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="San Remo Lighting" p2="Am-Tech" post.rptr="176" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ebbe025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="San Remo Lighting v. Am-Tech">San Remo Lighting v. Am-Tech, 2019 ONSC 176, 2019 CarswellOnt 425 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The monies received by the defendant subcontractor from the contractor were deposited into a single general account from which the defendant paid all of its ongoing expenses and costs including wages, dividends, bonuses, rent, equipment, supplies and subcontractors. It did not retain or segregate monies pursuant to the trust requirements of the Act. The defendant pleaded a set-off as against the plaintiff for defaults including the delivery of incorrect material, materials not delivered and delays. The defendant subsequently deposited monies into its lawyer's trust account to retroactively satisfy its trust obligations to the plaintiff. The court found that despite the alleged set off claim, there was still a trust obligation on the defendant's part to retain the monies. There was an absolute obligation under ss. 8 and 12 to retain the funds in trust, and the trust provisions of the Act do not permit the trustee to disburse the trust fund by reason of having a claim which it wishes to assert by way of set-off against the beneficiary.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1587855 Ontario Inc." p2="Contract Glaziers Corp." post.rptr="7934" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63ebe5105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1587855 Ontario Inc. v. Contract Glaziers Corp.">1587855 Ontario Inc. v. Contract Glaziers Corp., 2016 ONSC 7934, 2016 CarswellOnt 19971, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 53 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The overall purpose of the Act is to provide parties with an efficient means of resolving construction disputes, and owners, contractors and sub-contractors all have both rights and obligations under the legislation. Therefore, a defendant has the procedural right under the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> to advance a claim under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> even if the plaintiff chooses not to proceed under the Act. Here, the plaintiff was admittedly owed monies by the defendant for the supply of services and materials on one construction project, and commenced an ordinary breach of contract action. The defendant claimed that s. 12 gave it the right to hold monies owing to the plaintiff on that project to cover the defendant's asserted but unproven claims against the plaintiff on a second project. The fact that the plaintiff did not advance a claim under the Act did not void the rights and protections that the defendant had under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Architectural Millwork & Door Installations Inc." p2="Provincial Store Fixtures Ltd." post.rptr="320" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63ebe5115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Architectural Millwork & Door Installations Inc. v. Provincial Store Fixtures Ltd.">Architectural Millwork & Door Installations Inc. v. Provincial Store Fixtures Ltd., 2016 ONCA 320, 2016 CarswellOnt 6796, 51 C.L.R. (4th) 42 (Ont. C.A.); affirming 2015 ONSC 4913, 2015 CarswellOnt 11730, 51 C.L.R. (4th) 25, [2015] O.J. No. 4083 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2017 ONSC 1134, 2017 CarswellOnt 1931, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 161 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The availability of the right of set-off under s. 12 requires the party seeking to exercise it to prove the existence of trust funds against which set-off can be applied. If no trust funds are retained or all the monies are spent, the purpose of the trust provisions is defeated and any right of set-off is extinguished. In the present case, neither party pleaded the existence or breach of a trust fund. The respondent subcontractor did not assert any claim to trust funds, and the appellant contractor did not allege there was a trust fund under the Act, or at all. Rather, the appellant pleaded that it had not been paid by the owner for the work performed by the respondent and therefore had no obligation to pay the respondent's invoices, negating the existence of a trust fund. As a result, the appellant had no right under s. 12 to setoff against the monies that it admitted were owed to the respondent.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Man-Shield (Now) Construction Inc." p2="Rainy River District School Board" post.rptr="323" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63ec0c205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Man-Shield (Now) Construction Inc. v. Rainy River District School Board">Man-Shield (Now) Construction Inc. v. Rainy River District School Board, 2012 ONSC 323, 2012 CarswellOnt 1405, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 117 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 2150, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 126 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As long as there is an obligation by a trustee to retain holdback, there can be no set-off against those amounts. However, the inviolate nature of holdback ends when the amounts being held back are no longer needed because the liens which they are designed to benefit have expired, been satisfied or at least protected by other means. Holdback is maintained for the benefit of those lower on the lien tree. If the lien rights of those lower on the tree change, the obligation on those higher on the lien tree changes as well. Trust funds cease to be capable of being additionally characterized as holdback when the lien rights of any person claiming against the contractor expire as provided in Part V or the lien rights have been satisfied, discharged or provided for under s. 44.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Bestdoor Co." p2="Toronto Economic Development Corp." post.rptr="1708" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63ec0c215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bestdoor Co. v. Toronto Economic Development Corp.">Bestdoor Co. v. Toronto Economic Development Corp. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1708, 43 C.L.R. (3d) 315 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Master made no error in principle in concluding that the owner of the property, after receiving written notice of the lien, was entitled to apply the amount by which the general contractor's invoice exceeded the statutory holdback in satisfaction of amounts owed to the owner by the general contractor on account of rent on an unrelated property. The arrears of rent had accrued before the notice of lien was given. While the satisfaction by A of an obligation to pay money to B by the discharge of a debt owing by B to A appears to constitute a payment within the ordinary sense of the word, the Court relied on the decisions in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1968" p1="S.I. Guttman Ltd." p2="James D. Mokry Ltd." post.rptr="7" pre.rptr="[1969] 1" ref.id="I63ec0c225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S.I. Guttman Ltd. v. James D. Mokry Ltd.">S.I. Guttman Ltd. v. James D. Mokry Ltd. (1968), [1969] 1 O.R. 7, 1968 CarswellOnt 330 (C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1969" p1="Canadian Comstock Co." p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="[1970]" ref.id="I63ec0c235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canadian Comstock Co. v. Toronto Transit Commission">Canadian Comstock Co. v. Toronto Transit Commission (1969), [1970] S.C.R. 205, 1969 CarswellOnt 141, 1969 CarswellOnt 141F</ref></cite>, which held that, for purposes of the previous Act, a set-off did not constitute a “payment” and concluded that there was no reason that a different interpretation should prevail under the current Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Essroc Canada Inc." p2="Towne Concrete Forming Ltd." post.rptr="2460" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63ec0c245fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Essroc Canada Inc. v. Towne Concrete Forming Ltd.">Essroc Canada Inc. v. Towne Concrete Forming Ltd. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 2460, 2004 CarswellOnt 6647 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants conceded breach of trust but sought to set off an amount based on the fact that the defendant had not been paid by various of its own customers. However, there were no records kept regarding the costs incurred per project. The court rejected the argument that if a percentage of the defendant's concrete was supplied by the plaintiff, then that percentage of its unpaid accounts must therefore be deducted from the amounts owing to the plaintiff in respect of the trust claim. The court found that if the defendant could show that it was not itself paid for the projects in respect of which the plaintiff's concrete had been provided, that a credit would properly be allowed to the extent of such non-payment. The trust provisions of the Act did not create a penalty. A lesser amount was set off.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="West York Construction (1984) Ltd." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="32" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63ec33305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="West York Construction (1984) Ltd. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">West York Construction (1984) Ltd. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 32 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 12 gives the trustee of funds a right to set-off for “outstanding debts, claims and damages”. A claim for delay in performance of a contract falls within that section. Where a contractor was entitled to immediate payment of the holdback, but the owner retained a portion of the funds on account of a claim for delay, the funds remained trust funds, and were no longer technically holdback funds, since liens had not been registered. Pursuant to s. 12, the owner was entitled to refuse payment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Arborform Countertops Inc." p2="Stellato" post.rptr="129" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I63ec33315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato">Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato (1996), 29 O.R. (3d) 129 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The intention of s. 12 is to allow a contractor to “retain” money alleged to be for set-off, but not to spend them. Where trust funds are spent and not “retained”, the contractor is precluded from a defence of set-off.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Majestic Contractors Ltd." p2="N.C.L. Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="213" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63ec33325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Majestic Contractors Ltd. v. N.C.L. Contracting Ltd.">Majestic Contractors Ltd. v. N.C.L. Contracting Ltd. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 213 (Sask. Q.B.)</ref></cite>—A payer under a construction contract in Ontario may take advantage of the Ontario <ital>Judicature Act</ital> [now <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43], which permits procedural set-offs to set off against a debt due to the payee, notwithstanding that the debt and the set-off arise under entirely different contracts.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Datasphere Sales Ltd." p2="Universal Light & Power Corp." post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63ec5a405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp.">Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—There is no right in a trustee to put some or all of the trust funds to general use because, in its view, in light of claims it has or proposes to assert against the beneficiary-contractor, the ultimate arithmetical calculations will demonstrate that the trust moneys owing net out a balance less than the gross total of the funds retained. The word used in s. 12 is “retain”, not “spend”. Trust funds can be retained, they cannot be spent.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Trust Co." p2="Universal Sheet Metals Ltd." post.rptr="374" pre.rptr="[1970] 1" ref.id="I63ec5a415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Trust Co. v. Universal Sheet Metals Ltd.">Royal Trust Co. v. Universal Sheet Metals Ltd., [1970] 1 O.R. 374 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Section 3(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, c. 233 was enacted to ensure that the benefit of the trust thereby created would not be diverted from the subcontractor entitled to such benefit. The fact that a debt claimed by the builder was of a different nature from the debt due to the subcontractor was not material because of the provisions of s. 129(1) of the <ital>Judicature Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, c. 197. In setting off the debt due by the claimant to the builder, the trustee was not diverting from the claimant the benefit to which it is entitled under the provisions of s. 3 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="P. Nicholls Enterprises Ltd., Re" post.rptr="470" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63ec81505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="P. Nicholls Enterprises Ltd., Re">P. Nicholls Enterprises Ltd., Re (1985), 50 O.R. (2d) 470 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Two contractors, W Ltd. and N Ltd., worked together on different projects, with W Ltd. serving as contractor on several projects and N Ltd. as contractor on others. As a result, W. Ltd. owed monies to N. Ltd. for some projects and N. Ltd. owed monies to W. Ltd. for other projects. After N. Ltd. became bankrupt, the question arose as to whether W. Ltd. could set off from the amounts owing to N Ltd. the amounts owed to it by N Ltd. The trustee in bankruptcy argued that the amounts owing by W Ltd. to N Ltd. constituted a trust fund under s. 3(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, ss. 8–12] which provides that “all sums received by a … subcontractor constitute a trust fund”, and that consequently they were not amenable to set-off, an argument that was accepted by the motions court judge. On appeal, it was held that the debts could be set off under the general power of set-off under s. 135(1) of the <ital>Judicature Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 223, made applicable to bankruptcy proceedings by s. 75(3) of the <ital>Banruptcy Act</ital>, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3. The trust established by the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> did not come into effect until receipt of the funds by the trustee, and since no funds were payable, because of the set-off, no trust came into existence.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, s. 1 had imposed criminal sanctions against “every director or officer of a corporation who knowingly assents to or acquiesces in any such offence by the corporation”. This was a summary conviction offence and a fine of not more than $5,000.00 or no more than two years imprisonment was prescribed. This provision was carried forward with very little change into <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, s. 2(7) and later into the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, s. 3(7). The criminal sanctions of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> were rarely used. The Advisory Committee in 1982 recommended that they be abandoned. The Committee believed that the <ital>Criminal Code</ital> s. 296 (now 336) concerning “Offences Resembling Theft” would be enough to deter the conversion of trust funds with the intent to defraud. This is an indictable offence punishable by up to 14 years of imprisonment. The Committee believed that civil liability for breach of trust would be sufficient to deter other types of breaches of trust, particularly with the added statutory provisions in s. 13 concerning the potential liability of those with “effective control,” and the mandatory joint and several liability of and equal contribution between those found liable or who have admitted liability for breaches of trust. The 1983 Act removed the criminal sanction and imposed a civil liability on any “director or officer of a corporation who assents or acquiesces in conduct that he or she knows or reasonably ought to know amounts to a breach of trust by the corporation”. In addition, s. 13(1) extended the remedy to include “any person, including an employee or agent of the corporation, who has effective control of a corporation or its relevant activities”. Under s. 13(2) of the Act, the court is permitted to pierce the corporate veil in order to determine whether a person has “effective control” of a corporation. Subsection 13(3) and (4) provide for mandatory joint and several liability.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 13 prevents the use of a shell corporation or resignation from corporate office as a device for avoiding obligations under the Act, by providing for the personal liability of a corporation's directing minds for a breach of trust by that corporation. Only those who have the power to prevent such a breach of trust are intended to be captured by this section. Section 13 provides a civil remedy only. The quasi-criminal remedy in the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> has been repealed. Section 336 of the <ital>Criminal Code</ital> makes breach of trust with intent to defraud a criminal offence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 13(2) allows the court to “pierce the corporate veil” by permitting the court to disregard the form of any transaction and the separate corporate existence of any participant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsections 13(3) and (4) provide for mandatory joint and several liability, and for equal contribution between liable parties, unless the court considers equal contribution to be unfair.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Some basic principles have been established. No special <ital>mens rea</ital>, or intent, is required to establish personal liability under this section. The standard is one of reasonableness and whether the defendant knew or “ought reasonably to have known” of a breach of trust (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Heritage Masonry Ltd." p2="Building Team Ltd." post.rptr="1226" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90c0f960f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Building Team Ltd.">Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Building Team Ltd. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 1226, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 101 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, and see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Home Depot Inc." p2="Fieder Painting Inc." post.rptr="4514" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I2c7f8240019a11ef8bb0a9f7b9b79c2b" title="Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc.">Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 4514 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). It appears that personal defendants sued under s. 13 may not avail themselves of the discretionary protection of the protection of s. 35 of the <ital>Trustee Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. T.23 which states that the court may relieve the trustee from personal liability where the trustee has otherwise “acted honestly and reasonably, and ought fairly to be excused for the breach of trust”; see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction Co." p2="S.I. Guttman Ltd." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I63eccf725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd.">Ontario Electrical Construction Co. v. S.I. Guttman Ltd. (1996), 29 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.); appeal dismissed (1997), 104 O.A.C. 232 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. Although, s. 13 does not impose strict liability evidence of direct dealing by the officers and directors with the trust property is not required in order to establish liability. The test is subjective. The level of sophistication of the officers and directors is relevant; see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd." p2="Fahuki Construction Inc." post.rptr="3286" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I55e0c4f0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd. v. Fahuki Construction Inc.">Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd. v. Fahuki Construction Inc. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 3286, 30 C.L.R. (2d) 156 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. Any knowing personal benefit derived from the breach of trust will be conclusive against a defendant.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Muralis Architectural Products Inc." p2="Envelope Inc." post.rptr="7793" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63ecf6815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Muralis Architectural Products Inc. v. Envelope Inc.">Muralis Architectural Products Inc. v. Envelope Inc., 2021 ONSC 7793, 2021 CarswellOnt 17400 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court concluded that the three individual defendants were liable for breach of trust under s. 13 where C was the sole director of the corporate defendant; wrote the deposit cheque and lived with D; D was intimately involved in the acceptance by the corporate defendant of the plaintiff's purchase order and in the three invoices that gave rise to the claim; B was intimately involved during the process, and signed the quotation and cut-list issued by the plaintiff as being correct.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Feltz Design Build Ltd." p2="Larson et al." post.rptr="2469" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63ed1d905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Feltz Design Build Ltd. v. Larson et al.">Feltz Design Build Ltd. v. Larson et al., 2021 ONSC 2469, 2021 CarswellOnt 4450 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Feltz Design Build Ltd. v. Larson</ital>, 2022 CarswellOnt 1775 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendant principal of the corporate defendant was an experienced businessperson who had participated in many construction projects. It was clear that he knew or ought to have known that after the consultant issued payment certificates, monies received by the corporate defendant from whatever source were impressed with a trust and that their use for any other purpose was contrary to the Act. He was jointly liable with his company for breach of trust to the full extent of the amount owing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Yanic Dufresne Excavation Inc." p2="Saint Joseph Developments Ltd. et al." post.rptr="6633" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I63ed1d915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yanic Dufresne Excavation Inc. v. Saint Joseph Developments Ltd. et al.">Yanic Dufresne Excavation Inc. v. Saint Joseph Developments Ltd. et al., 2021 ONSC 6633, 2021 CarswellOnt 14651, 16 C.L.R. (5th) 229 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 CarswellOnt 8077 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Yanic Dufresne Excavation Inc. v. Saint Joseph Developments Ltd.</ital>, 2022 CarswellOnt 10499, 22 C.L.R. (5th) 185 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In order for a breach of fiduciary duty by a bankrupt to constitute “misappropriation or defalcation” within the meaning of s. 178(1)(d) of the BIA so as to give rise to a judgment debt that survives the bankrupt's discharge, there must be some improper dealing with property entrusted to the fiduciary and some element of moral turpitude in the sense of dishonesty, wrongdoing or misconduct. Here, the court found the defendant bankrupt real estate broker to be a sophisticated businessman who had signing authority on the corporate defendant's account and signed a significant number of cheques. The bankrupt did not satisfy his obligation to ensure that the funds were spent on paying the trades, even though he was aware that the trust account had to be set up properly, that the appropriate funds were to go into the appropriate accounts, that the appropriate bills were to be paid from the appropriate accounts, and that the directors had to comply with their fiduciary duties under the Act. The debt fell under section 178(1)(d) of the BIA and survived the bankrupt's discharge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Steel Tree Structures Ltd." p2="Gemco Solar Inc." post.rptr="1309" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ed1d925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Steel Tree Structures Ltd. v. Gemco Solar Inc.">Steel Tree Structures Ltd. v. Gemco Solar Inc., 2019 ONSC 1309, 2019 CarswellOnt 2926, 98 C.L.R. (4th) 275 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An action for breach of trust, whether at common law or under s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, does not run concurrently with a claim for breach of a construction contract but rather when the circumstances that support those causes of action should have been discovered by the Plaintiff. Here, the defendant failed to show that the plaintiff ought to have known at an earlier date that its losses were caused or contributed to by the acts or omissions of the defendants, and the plaintiff's claim was not barred by statute.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="620369 Ontario Inc." p2="El Badry" post.rptr="5534" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63ed44a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="620369 Ontario Inc. v. El Badry">620369 Ontario Inc. v. El Badry, 2018 ONSC 5534, 2018 CarswellOnt 15472, 93 C.L.R. (4th) 356 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 18194 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While a lack of particulars regarding breach of trust would create a difficulty for the plaintiff if a default judgment was sought, this difficulty does not exist with respect to a consent judgment. If a plaintiff in the pleadings makes a general allegation of breach of trust pursuant to s. 8 and s. 13, it is open to a defendant to admit to this allegation without defining the particulars of the breach. Therefore, the lack of particulars of the alleged breach of trust was not a reason to set aside a consent judgment in this case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sound Solutions" p2="Cladit Siding Solutions Inc. et al" post.rptr="4892" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63ed44a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sound Solutions v. Cladit Siding Solutions Inc. et al">Sound Solutions v. Cladit Siding Solutions Inc. et al, 2018 ONSC 4892, 2018 CarswellOnt 14600, 92 C.L.R. (4th) 328 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where allegations of breach of trust and issues raised in the counterclaim were readily bifurcated from issues in the main action, partial summary judgment in regard to the issues in the main action was a cost-effective manner to deal with those claims of breach of contract and equitable set-off. There was no reason why adjudication of its claim for breach of contract, subject to equitable set-off, should be delayed to schedule a trial dealing with the separate issues of breach of trust and conduct of the parties raised in the counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Firstonsite Restoration Limited" p2="4049 River Road GP Inc." post.rptr="4485" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63ed44a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Firstonsite Restoration Limited v. 4049 River Road GP Inc.">Firstonsite Restoration Limited v. 4049 River Road GP Inc., 2018 ONSC 4485, 2018 CarswellOnt 12052, 93 C.L.R. (4th) 109 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2019 CarswellOnt 20682 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff provided demolition and clean-up work required as a result of fire damage to the defendant's hotel, but as the defendant was under-insured, the plaintiff was not paid in respect of this work. The defendant submitted uncontroverted evidence that the entire insurance payout was used to pay other suppliers and contractors in the remediation and rebuilding of the hotel. There was no evidence establishing that any of the insurance proceeds were earmarked especially for the plaintiff. The plaintiff accordingly failed to meet the test under s. 13.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Employment Professionals Canada Inc." p2="Steel Design and Fabricators (SDF) Ltd." post.rptr="1722" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63ed6bb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Employment Professionals Canada Inc. v. Steel Design and Fabricators (SDF) Ltd.">Employment Professionals Canada Inc. v. Steel Design and Fabricators (SDF) Ltd., 2016 ONSC 1722, 2016 CarswellOnt 3930, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 64 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2016 ONSC 4230, 2016 CarswellOnt 15858, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 78 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The determination of when a limitation period commences for an action under s. 13 is governed by ss. 4 and 5 of the <ital>(Ont.) Limitations Act, 2002</ital>. Accordingly, the limitation period for an action under s. 13 against the officers of a contractor does not commence when payment is due pursuant to the terms of the agreement between a supplier and a contractor, but rather when the breach of trust was discoverable. Here, applying the discoverability principle in light of the available evidence, defendants did not demonstrate that the action was commenced after the expiry of the limitation period for any of the invoices issued by the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Delco Automation Inc." p2="Carlo's Electric Ltd." post.rptr="7157" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63ed6bb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Delco Automation Inc. v. Carlo's Electric Ltd.">Delco Automation Inc. v. Carlo's Electric Ltd., 2014 ONSC 7157, 2014 CarswellOnt 17794, 46 C.L.R. (4th) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 2932, 46 C.L.R. (4th) 324 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed in part 2016 ONCA 591, 2016 CarswellOnt 12792, 62 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The trial judge concluded that the funds in question were impressed with a trust, and it was not reasonable to believe that the experienced principal of the defendant was not aware of his personal responsibility to protect and pay the plaintiff and other subcontractors. However, the evidence did not demonstrate that the requirements of s. 178(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> had been met, namely that the debt owing arose from his fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation or defalcation while acting in a fiduciary capacity. Accordingly, the request for an order that both judgments for breach of trust survive the bankruptcy was denied. On appeal, the evidence was held not to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal had assented to, or acquiesced in, conduct that he knew, or reasonably ought to have known, amounted to a breach of trust by his company. His appeal in respect of his personal liability was allowed, while the remainder of the judgment was affirmed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Toro Aluminum" p2="Sampogna" post.rptr="5345" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63ed6bb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toro Aluminum v. Sampogna">Toro Aluminum v. Sampogna, 2013 ONSC 5345, 2013 CarswellOnt 11635, 5 C.B.R. (6th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The applicant obtained a declaratory order pursuant to Section 178(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> that its judgment against the respondent for breach of trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was not released upon the respondent's discharge from bankruptcy. The applicant held a default judgment based on a statement of claim which set out facts, all deemed to be admitted, which disclosed a breach of trust for which the respondent was liable. The respondent was in a very good position to produce evidence accounting for the funds and provide more than a brief statement in an affidavit that there was no wrongdoing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Belmont Concrete Finishing Co." p2="Marshall" post.rptr="1560" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63ed92c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmont Concrete Finishing Co. v. Marshall">Belmont Concrete Finishing Co. v. Marshall, 2011 ONSC 1560, 2011 CarswellOnt 6942, 7 C.L.R. (4th) 147 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2011 CarswellOnt 11115, 7 C.L.R. (4th) 158 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2012 CarswellOnt 11103, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—While s. 13 does not refer to s. 8, it is clear from the introductory clause that the breach of trust of the corporation contemplated by s. 13 is the action of appropriation or conversion of project trust monies in s. 8. The Legislature did not intend s. 13 to impose liability on the individuals named therein for every breach of trust by a corporation. The breach of trust contemplated by s. 8 is the action of appropriation or conversion. It is not the action of failing to remedy the breach of trust after an appropriation or conversion has occurred—for example, by failing to repay the trust fund or by failing to pay the beneficiaries directly.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc." p2="Country Cottage Living Inc." post.rptr="2289" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63ed92c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc. v. Country Cottage Living Inc.">Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc. v. Country Cottage Living Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 2289, 93 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 2783, 93 C.L.R. (3d) 166 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 178(1)(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, an order of discharge does not release the bankrupt from any debt or liability arising out of fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation or defalcation while acting in a fiduciary capacity. If a debt under s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is to survive bankruptcy pursuant to s. 178(1)(d), there must be some element of dishonesty, wrongdoing, or misconduct on the part of the debtor sufficient to exclude the debtor from the relief granted by the Act; see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Simone" p2="Daley" post.rptr="551" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I63ed92c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simone v. Daley">Simone v. Daley (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 551 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Superior Crane (Canada) Inc." p2="Justan Consulting Ltd." post.rptr="4591" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90c1e3c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Superior Crane (Canada) Inc. v. Justan Consulting Ltd.">Superior Crane (Canada) Inc. v. Justan Consulting Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 4591, [2003] O.J. No. 4717, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 21, 49 C.B.R. (4th) 295 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 169, 40 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.)</ref></cite>. Here, the court found no misconduct, and therefore the debt did not survive the bankruptcy.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vicor Mechanical Ltd." p2="Pegah Construction Ltd." post.rptr="154" pre.rptr="86" ref.id="I63edb9d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vicor Mechanical Ltd. v. Pegah Construction Ltd.">Vicor Mechanical Ltd. v. Pegah Construction Ltd., 86 C.L.R. (3d) 154, 2009 CarswellOnt 7682 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Cases under s. 178 of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> that hold that construction lien trust debts are not discharged in a bankruptcy situation do not render a statutory trust claim under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> a de facto fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation such that the elements of those torts need not be pleaded, and pleaded properly. This is particularly so where the plaintiff desires a judgment or finding of liability on these specific grounds, in addition to a judgment or finding of liability under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. If the plaintiff wishes to obtain a finding on these alternative grounds, the plaintiff must plead the constituent elements of those claims. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: But see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HC Matcon Inc." p2="Aspden Developments Inc." post.rptr="9970" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I63edb9d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="HC Matcon Inc. v. Aspden Developments Inc.">HC Matcon Inc. v. Aspden Developments Inc., 2007 CarswellOnt 9970, 96 C.L.R. (3d) 199 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2009 ONCA 695, 2009 CarswellOnt 5849, 96 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, where the court held that trust debts not involving misconduct do not survive bankruptcy.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of)" p2="Acro Capital Inc." post.rptr="1038" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63edb9d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc.">700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1038, 2004 CarswellOnt 986, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 47 (S.C.J. [Commercial List]); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 1796 (S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The defendant solicitors acted for the developer owner, and after the sale of certain condominiums was completed, the proceeds were received by the solicitors and a sum paid out of them to the defendant company. The plaintiff was subsequently appointed trustee under s. 68 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to act as receiver and manager of the developer owner's assets, property and undertakings. The Plaintiff claimed against the defendants on the basis that the payment out of the proceeds was a breach of trust for which the solicitors were liable. The latter unsuccessfully moved under Ont. R. 21 to strike out the Statement of Claim against them and dismiss the action as showing no reasonable cause of action. A construction lien trustee had the authority to claim against the defendant solicitors for alleged breaches of the Act's trust provisions when it was not the bankrupt, but the contractor, who was the beneficiary of those trusts. Part II of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> declared how the trusts came into effect and were discharged by payment and declared who are the beneficiaries, but did nothing to alter the law as to the general nature of the trust and the normal right and duties of the trustee. The Act contained no definition of “trust” or “trustee” and it was to be assumed that these terms were to be read in their normal meaning in law, that is, as carrying the rights and obligations of a trustee under the common law. Under ordinary trust law, the trustee was the legal owner of the <ital>corpus</ital> of the trust and had the right to sue any one who deprived the trust of its property or who damages the trust property in any way. The trustee could sell the <ital>corpus</ital> and give good title to it to a <ital>bona fide</ital> purchaser for value without notice, even though he lacked an actual power to sell. Equity took the view that one with title, who contracted in his own name, had full capacity to act. The right of the beneficiary was generally a personal one, to compel the Trustee to properly discharge his duties as trustee. In addition, the trustee may also bring an action on behalf of the trust to recover the trust property, except as against a <ital>bona fide</ital> purchaser for value. This may be regarded as a beneficiary's remedy, or as a trustee's remedy, which the beneficiary is permitted to bring on behalf of the trust in particular circumstances. But the evolution of this remedy has not deprived the trustee of the rights of ownership.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 13(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Learmont Roofing Ltd." p2="Learmont Construction Ltd." post.rptr="894" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I673cb3d03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Learmont Roofing Ltd. v. Learmont Construction Ltd.">Learmont Roofing Ltd. v. Learmont Construction Ltd., 2022 ONCA 894, 2022 CarswellOnt 18557, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 309 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite></trace>—It was clear that the personal defendant was liable for the breach of the defendants' trust obligations as he failed to remit the amount owed to the plaintiff. His explanation for cancelling the payment cheque was obviously disingenuous, and the motion judge found that the funds were diverted for his personal benefit, or to protect investment in the corporate defendant. The defendants were held severally and jointly liable for the amount owing to the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Convoy Supply" p2="Elite Construction" post.rptr="5353" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I673cb3d13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Convoy Supply v. Elite Construction">Convoy Supply v. Elite Construction, 2022 ONSC 5353, 2022 CarswellOnt 13480, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 270 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2023 ONCA 373, 2023 CarswellOnt 7851, 30 C.L.R. (5th) 193 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite></trace>—The plaintiff commenced a claim against the defendants seeking, <ital>inter alia</ital>, damages for breach of trust. The defendants were noted in default and judgment was granted. The personal defendant, the directing mind of the corporate defendant, was deemed to admit the alleged facts, which included that he assented to and acquiesced in the diversion of trust funds established under the Act for purposes inconsistent with the trust. Directing trust funds for a purpose inconsistent with the trust was sufficient to trigger s. 178(1)(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, with such diversion considered dishonest. The judgement therefore survived the defendant's bankruptcy. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bibico Electric Inc." p2="Battlefield Electrical Services Inc." post.rptr="16003" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63ee07f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bibico Electric Inc. v. Battlefield Electrical Services Inc.">Bibico Electric Inc. v. Battlefield Electrical Services Inc., 2011 CarswellOnt 16003 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONCA 676, 2012 CarswellOnt 12372 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, which held that a pleading, successful on default judgment, that the personal defendant “caused and assented to and acquiesced in the diversion of trust funds established under the Construction Lien Act for purposes inconsistent with the trust, and that the appellants had failed to account for the trust funds” was sufficient to meet the threshold for the type of “wrongdoing, improper conduct or improper accounting” contemplated by s. 178(1)(d).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Pylon Paving (1996) Inc." p2="Beaucon Building Services Inc." post.rptr="7605" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I673cdae03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pylon Paving (1996) Inc. v. Beaucon Building Services Inc.">Pylon Paving (1996) Inc. v. Beaucon Building Services Inc., 2022 ONSC 3282, 2022 CarswellOnt 7605, 35 C.L.R. (5th) 273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—In an action to which the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applied, the plaintiff moved before an associate judge to, <ital>inter alia</ital>, strike the statement of defence, note the corporate and individual defendants in default, and obtain default judgment on its breach of trust claim against them under (ON) rule 19.05. While the statement of claim set out the essential elements of the breach of trust claim, it did not plead the extent of the trust nor the extent of the alleged breach of trust under s. 8, such as alleging that the defendants received and appropriated or converted an amount equal to or greater than the indebtedness to the plaintiff. The extent of any breach of trust was a matter requiring judicial determination as an unliquidated claim, which was not a claim for which an associate judge had jurisdiction to grant default judgment. However, the associate judge did grant the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment against both the corporate and individual defendants for breach of trust. While it might seem inconsistent for an associate judge to be precluded from granting default judgment for an unliquidated sum, yet still be entitled to grant summary judgment on the same record, R. 20 permitted summary judgment motions to be brought before an associate judge and contained no similar restriction to that found in r. 19.04(3.1)(b). Lastly, as the associate judge was neither a judge nor a registrar in bankruptcy, there was no jurisdiction or authority to make any declaration under s. 178(1)(d) of the (CAN) <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nieltech" p2="Wasero" post.rptr="1724" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63ee2f005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nieltech v. Wasero">Nieltech v. Wasero, 2022 ONSC 1724, 2022 CarswellOnt 3458 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Personal liability pursuant to s. 13 depends on an objective analysis as to what a reasonable person ought to know, and does not require dishonesty, personal benefit, or a subjective awareness of the Act's trust provisions. All that is required is participation of such a degree as to at least put a reasonable person on inquiry as to whether there was a breach of trust. Here, the personal defendant was directly involved in collecting trust funds from construction projects and disbursing those trust funds, making her aware of the receipt of trust funds and aware that those funds were not disbursed in accordance with the corporate defendant's trust obligations. She directly negotiated the terms of the resolution agreement on behalf of the corporate defendant and personally directed when cheques could be negotiated and who was involved in collecting funds. She permitted the comingling of funds and did not set up a proper accounting system. She assented to or acquiesced in conduct that she knew or reasonably ought to have known amounted to a breach of trust by the corporate defendant and was therefore personally liable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Central Lumber Limited" p2="Gentile" post.rptr="20728" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ee2f015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Central Lumber Limited v. Gentile">Central Lumber Limited v. Gentile, 2019 CarswellOnt 20728, 2019 ONSC 7413 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2020 CarswellOnt 19837, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 253 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In an elaborate scheme, the defendant homeowner obscured his identity in dealings with the plaintiff subcontractor that provided lumber for the construction of his home, in order to evade payment. The subcontractor dealt only with an individual, determined to be the owner, who acted on behalf of a shell company contractor set up by the owner and which the latter controlled. The owner drew on his own funds to prepare a bank draft that he faxed to the subcontractor under the contractor's name as evidence to the subcontractor that payment had been received from the owner, and deposited those funds with a paralegal firm, and then directed payment of those funds, at least in part, back to his own numbered company. The court found that the funds provided to the paralegal for deposit in his trust account constituted monies received by the shell company on account of its contract price related to the construction of the owner's home, and were trust funds under s. 8(1)(a) the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. The homeowner was personally liable for breach of trust pursuant to s. 13, as he was a person with effective control of the shell contractor or its relevant activities. In providing the copy of the bank draft to the subcontractor representing the funds owed to it, but then failing to ever provide the latter with those funds, he engaged in conduct that he knew or reasonably ought to have known amounted to a breach of trust by the shell contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gurkal Transport" p2="Grittani" post.rptr="89" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ee2f025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gurkal Transport v. Grittani">Gurkal Transport v. Grittani, 2019 ONSC 89, 2019 CarswellOnt 451, 97 C.L.R. (4th) 154 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although s. 13(1)(a) and (b) are separated by the word ‘and’, it seems clear that the sections are to be read disjunctively. That is, an individual could be liable either because of their status as an officer <ital>or</ital> because of their status as an employee with effective control, so long as they assented or acquiesced in conduct that they knew amounted to a breach of trust. Here, despite her denials, the court found that the individual defendant knew that she was an officer of the corporation, and had effective control of the latter's finances. By writing cheques and using funds received from contractors for things other than paying the plaintiffs, she either assented to or acquiesced in the corporation's breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cooper" p2="2208011 Ontario Limited et al." post.rptr="5512" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63ee56105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cooper v. 2208011 Ontario Limited et al.">Cooper v. 2208011 Ontario Limited et al., 2018 ONSC 5512, 2018 CarswellOnt 15443, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 89 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2019 CarswellOnt 9374, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 191 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The record was clear that one defendant director had signed the rental contract, and was aware of the delivery of the rental equipment, and the fact that the invoices were not paid. The court was satisfied that he had assented or acquiesced in the non-payment for equipment supplied, knowing that the defendants had received funds for the projects which were impressed with a trust in favour of the plaintiff.
