However, the fact of being a director, standing alone, does not prove this level of knowledge and where there was no evidence about the knowledge of the other directors, other than the fact of them being directors, they were not found to have assented to or acquiesced in the conduct at issue.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1705371 Ontario Ltd." p2="Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc." post.rptr="7423" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63ee56115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1705371 Ontario Ltd. v. Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc.">1705371 Ontario Ltd. v. Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc., 2018 ONSC 7423, 2018 CarswellOnt 21112, 85 C.L.R. (4th) 132, 27 C.P.C. (8th) 34 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 480 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff demonstrated that the individual defendant was a director that actively participated in the day-to-day operations of the defendant company. He was the latter's operating mind and would have been in control of funds received and disbursed by the company. He was liable for the breach of trust by the company under s. 13(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sawh" p2="Par-Tek Construction Services Inc." post.rptr="12658" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63ee56125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sawh v. Par-Tek Construction Services Inc.">Sawh v. Par-Tek Construction Services Inc., 2017 CarswellOnt 12658 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The personal defendant, as the officer and director of the corporate defendant, had effective control of the latter at all material times and was personally liable for the corporate defendant's breach of trust provisions. He was personally liable jointly with the corporate defendant for its breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Campoli Electric Ltd." p2="Georgian Clairlea Inc." post.rptr="2784" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63ee56135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Campoli Electric Ltd. v. Georgian Clairlea Inc.">Campoli Electric Ltd. v. Georgian Clairlea Inc., 2017 ONSC 2784, 2017 CarswellOnt 8873, 77 C.L.R. (4th) 70 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2017 CarswellOnt 12734 (Ont. Gregory Dimitriou</ital>, 2018 ONSC 2008, 2018 CarswellOnt 5336, 77 C.L.R. (4th) 139 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In a complicated litigation, the plaintiff trades sought to lift stays of proceedings instituted by virtue of s. 69.1 of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, in order to permit them to pursue their action for breach of trust against the insolvent individual defendants. One defendant sought a re-instatement of a stay that had been lifted on consent, while all the individual defendants sought summary judgment dismissing the actions if the stays were lifted. In denying the motion to lift the stays, the master determined that the moving parties had failed to establish any misapplication of funds for which the individual defendants were responsible, or wrongdoing on the part of the defendants to permit a s. 13 debt to survive their bankruptcy. Viewed as a whole, the evidence the plaintiffs filed was contradictory, lacked documentary support and did not carry sufficient weight to support their assertions that money received in relation to the project was received by anyone who was not within the protected entities that were entitled to be paid without a breach of trust liability arising. While individuals do have liability for misuse of monies that ought to have been applied to pay down debts owing for the construction of a project, simply because a project has lost money does not turn the principals or officers of directors of a corporation into guarantors of the liabilities of a corporation. As well, the date when the alleged breaches of trust could have been discovered fell outside the 2-year period preceding the commencement of the actions. The stays would have no adverse impact on the trades if they proved entitlement to participate in the proposal without the necessity of establishing a violation of s. 13. Summary judgment was granted for the defendant for whom the stay had been previously lifted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="S.G.J. Northland Steel Manufacturing Inc." p2="Local Decor Designs Inc." post.rptr="3262" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63ee7d205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="S.G.J. Northland Steel Manufacturing Inc. v. The plaintiff was not aware of the active role of the officer until shortly before the motion was brought, but the notice of motion to add her as a party was issued within the two-year limitation period in any event.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Forest City Fire Protection Ltd." p2="1099516 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2346" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63eea4325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forest City Fire Protection Ltd. v. 1099516 Ontario Inc.">Forest City Fire Protection Ltd. v. 1099516 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2346, 2015 CarswellOnt 6364, 49 C.L.R. The “three fundamental aspects” of an action on the case were:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(a)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">duty owed by the defendant to the plaintiffs;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(b)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">breach of that duty by the defendant; and</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(c)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">damage suffered by the plaintiff as a result of the breach of duty owed to him by the defendant.</para.text></para></list.item></list><para.text date.updated="0">Here, pursuant to s. 13 of the Act, the defendants owed a duty to the subcontractors (the plaintiffs in their subrogated capacity); there was an allegation of a breach of the duty and a claim for damages.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada" p2="Matthews" post.rptr="1629" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63efb5a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada v. Matthews">Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada v. Matthews (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1629, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 18 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—An action for breach of trust taken pursuant to s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is remedial, not penal, in nature. Section 13 does not declare the directors and officers to be trustees nor does it deem them to be such. It does not make the directors and officers trustees. It imposes liability on directors and officers for breaches of trust committed by the corporation and only if it is found that the directors and officers assented to, or acquiesced in, conduct by the corporation that they reasonably ought to have known amounted to breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="1379691 Ontario Ltd." p2="Appugliesi" post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63efb5a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1379691 Ontario Ltd. v. Appugliesi">1379691 Ontario Ltd. v. Appugliesi (2005), 46 C.L.R. (3d) 302, 2005 CarswellOnt 4684 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 9210 (Ont. S.C.J.); varied (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6580 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where the defendant subcontractor, through its president, knew that the plaintiff sub-subcontractor had not been paid, and failed to account to the plaintiff for trust funds that it received on the project, it was in breach of trust. The defendant's principal was therefore personally liable under s. 13(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Dicola Drywall (London) Inc." p2="Zebcon Construction" post.rptr="256" pre.rptr="52" ref.id="I63efb5a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dicola Drywall (London) Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A principal who, while not dishonest, failed to pay proper attention to the bookkeeping, was held liable under s. 13, but the failure to account did not amount to a level of misconduct such that the debt should survive the bankruptcy under s. 178 of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Forest Trim & Doors" p2="Azor Woodworking Ltd." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I63efb5a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forest Trim & Doors v. Azor Woodworking Ltd.">Forest Trim & Doors v. Azor Woodworking Ltd. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 26, 2005 CarswellOnt 50 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff, a supplier of construction materials, sought the balance due for materials that it supplied for the corporate defendant's construction projects, and claimed against the individual defendant for breach of trust as the corporate defendant's sole officer, director, and controlling mind. In granting summary judgment against both defendants, the court found that there was no genuine issue for trial. The individual defendant did not segregate the monies it received from the projects into separate trust accounts; rather, one bank account was used for all purposes. Payments were made from that account to labourers, subcontractors and suppliers, and the account was also used for general corporate uses, including withdrawals by the individual defendant. While the latter had control over the accounts, he did not keep any books or ledgers to assist him in tracing funds from the account.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Con Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. Secinar Investments Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1585, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 174 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The personal defendants had effective control of the corporate defendants, including cheque signing authority, and breached the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> by using the proceeds from the financing or sale of the project to pay their own bonuses and overhead, knowing that the corporate defendant company owed money to the plaintiff for work that their engineers had approved. As a consequence, the personal defendants were also liable to the plaintiffs for the claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Wolfedale Electric Ltd." p2="R.P.M.'s Systems Automation & Design Quality in Motion Inc." post.rptr="4663" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63efdcb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wolfedale Electric Ltd. v. No. 4663, 2004 CarswellOnt 2956, 47 B.L.R. (3d) 1 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It was not contested that the individual defendant was the director and officer and operating mind of the corporate defendant and that he acted on the construction contract. As set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc." p2="Momat Developments Inc." post.rptr="270" pre.rptr="59" ref.id="I63efdcb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc.">Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc. (2002), 59 O.R. (3d) 270, 2002 CarswellOnt 2284, 19 C.L.R. (3d) 40 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite> the onus was upon the defendant to satisfy that its trust obligations had been complied with. The defendant failed to satisfy its onus and failed to perform its trust obligation. While the debt to the plaintiff was acknowledged, no payment was ever made. The individual defendant acquiesced in the conduct that he knew or ought to have known, by any reasonable standard, amounted to a breach under s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The plaintiff was therefore entitled to judgment against the individual personally.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Dicroce, Re" post.rptr="1742" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63f003c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dicroce, Re">Dicroce, Re (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1742, 2004 CarswellOnt 1673, 33 C.L.R. (3d) 59</ref></cite> (S.C.J.)—The claimant supplied materials to homes built and sold by the owner. The bankrupt was the owner's sole officer, director and shareholder. The claimant obtained unopposed judgment as against the bankrupt, which declared that the owner and bankrupt had committed a breach of trust and misappropriated and caused a defalcation in a fiduciary capacity. The judgment also declared that the defendants were constructive trustees of the funds received by them from the sale of homes to which the claimant supplied materials, and were liable for breach of trust to the claimant both at common law and under the provisions of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. In bankruptcy proceedings, the claimant successfully obtained a declaration that the judgment survive the bankruptcy of the bankrupt and that it was not released by his discharge. Although the earlier judgment was ultimately unopposed, there was an adjudication on the merits. Even if the court were not bound by that judgment, s. 178(1)(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> provided that a discharge did not relieve a bankrupt from “any debt or liability arising out of … misappropriation or defalcation while acting in a fiduciary capacity”. Although simple inadvertence, negligence or incompetence was insufficient to bring the conduct into the embrace of s. 178(1)(d), the bankruptcy court was satisfied that, here, the debt fell within the s. 178(1)(d) exception. The bankrupt was acting in a fiduciary capacity and there was improper conduct by him that constituted a misappropriation or defalcation within the meaning of that subsection.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20030625" p1="Dick Engineering Inc." p2="Thermo Tech Waste Systems Inc." post.rptr="5132" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63f003c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dick Engineering Inc. v. Thermo Tech Waste Systems Inc.">Dick Engineering Inc. v. Thermo Tech Waste Systems Inc. (June 25, 2003), Doc. 02-6071, [2003] O.J. No. 5132 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court declined to appoint a receiver for the owner landlord under the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There were a number of debts owed by the landlord, including a large tax bill. Among the factors considered in reaching this decision were: a) the existence of a dispute as to the claim of lien itself, which was in question; b) the existing tenant had obligations under the lease to pay taxes and preserve the grounds and equipment; c) the nature of the landlord's business involved procuring and holding a tenant in a very complex and specialized endeavour. In light of this, the landlord had not demonstrated irresponsible management, and as the number of tenants for such a specialized endeavour would be few, the appointment of a receiver would be intrusive; d) the preservation of the property did not require the intervention of a trustee; e) the existence of a large list of debts was meaningless in regards to real impecuniosity, as good business reasons for the debts might exist.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Superior Crane (Canada) Inc." p2="Justan Consulting Ltd." post.rptr="4591" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90c454c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Superior Crane (Canada) Inc. v. Justan Consulting Ltd.">Superior Crane (Canada) Inc. v. Justan Consulting Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 4591, [2003] O.J. No. 4717, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 21, 49 C.B.R. (4th) 295 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 169, 40 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—A finding under s. 13 does not necessarily lead to a finding of a common law breach of trust. What separates the s. 13 statutory trust from a common law breach of trust is the degree of knowledge required to find liability. To establish that a stranger to a trust is liable for common law breach of trust, one must establish that the stranger knowingly participated in the breach of trust, either through knowing receipt or knowing assistance. In this case, the defendant had the requisite knowledge to establish a common law breach. As a result, the judgment survived the proposal in bankruptcy under s. 178(1)(d) of the BIA.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Di Iacovo, Re" post.rptr="1307" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63f02ad15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Iacovo, Re">Di Iacovo, Re (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 1307, 2003 CarswellOnt 1781 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The bankrupt made payments from receivables for items such as overhead and his own draws, without paying the suppliers of materials to the jobs from whence the receivables arose. His subsequent application for discharge was opposed by his creditors, who consisted primarily of those suppliers. They argued that the bankrupt's actions amounted to a breach of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and that such a breach, having precipitated his bankruptcy, amounted to culpable neglect under s. 173(1)(e) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>. In granting a conditional discharge, the Court found that even if this supported a finding of a breach of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, that was not what was meant by “culpable neglect” as found in s. 173(1)(e). The phrase “culpable neglect” must be read in conjunction with the other activities in that subsection, all of which have a speculative nature to them. A mere technical breach of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not have the necessary degree of speculation to fall within the subsection. While it is possible that a breach of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> might be culpable neglect, the summary nature of a discharge hearing precluded the Court from entering into the type of inquiry necessary to determine if any such alleged breach was sufficiently morally blameworthy or speculative to fall within s. 173(1)(e).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="802798 Ontario Ltd." p2="McConnery" post.rptr="3282" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63f02ad25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="802798 Ontario Ltd. v. McConnery">802798 Ontario Ltd. v. McConnery (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 3282, 2003 CarswellOnt 3212, 31 C.L.R. (3d) 316 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The corporate owner and construction manager entered into a standard management agreement which amounted to a contracting out of the owner's overhead to the manager. The personal defendant was a director of both corporate bodies, and as a result, the management contract was not at arm's length. In the circumstances, the payment of monies towards the management contract was a breach of the trust provisions of the Act. The three individual defendants all fell within the definition of s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and were, accordingly, liable for the breach, as they reasonably ought to have known that their conduct amounted to a breach of trust created by s. 8 of the Act. Evidence that the defendants thought they were making a profit until they realized that they were dealing with a shortfall was not a defence to a breach of trust claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Malcolm Group Contracting Inc." p2="842879 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="46" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63f051e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Malcolm Group Contracting Inc. v. 842879 Ontario Inc.">Malcolm Group Contracting Inc. v. 842879 Ontario Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 46, 2003 CarswellOnt 41, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 241 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant corporation was originally incorporated by the two personal defendants, who were spouses of each other. The wife resigned two weeks after incorporation, and never regained her status as a director. The husband remained as a director and president. The corporation was involved as general contractor in two construction projects. During the period that trust funds in question were received and payable to subcontractors, the husband was hospitalized, and the wife, although never appointed as an officer, signed a statutory declaration as president of the corporation in order to obtain payment on the second project. She testified that she had signed the statutory declaration in the capacity of president on behalf of the husband because she had his general power of attorney over property. However, her testimony that her role with the company was merely secretarial and that she did not act as a manager or bookkeeper, nor did she exercise any independent judgment with the company was contradicted by other witnesses, and the evidence showed that she took an active role in the affairs of the business. Although she was technically neither a director nor an officer of the general contractor when the plaintiff performed the work and invoiced in respect of the projects, she looked after financial matters for the contractor, was the depositor of the trust monies received, and her statutory declaration triggered their delivery. She and her husband were personally liable for breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc." p2="ESD Industries Inc." post.rptr="290" pre.rptr="60" ref.id="I63f051e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. ESD Industries Inc.">Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. ESD Industries Inc. (2002), 60 O.R. (3d) 290, 2002 CarswellOnt 2286, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 227 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff obtained default judgment against the corporate defendant. It was conceded that the plaintiff was entitled to a finding under s. 13 of the Act against the individual defendant. The issue was whether the form and content of the judgment should be a declaration that the individual defendant was in breach of trust and that the judgment against him was by reason of his own breach of trust, or whether the judgment should recite that the corporation was in breach of its trust, and that the defendant was statutorily liable for the corporate breach of trust by operation of the Act. Judgment issued that the personal defendant was liable to pay by reason of liability imposed under s. 13(1). Section 13 is not a restatement of the common law but rather the creation of a separate and independent statutory scheme for the imposition of liability on certain persons. The breach of trust referred to in s. 13(1) is a breach of trust on the part of the corporation. In order to pass that liability upon officers, directors or persons with effective control, at common law it is necessary to demonstrate that those persons are constructive trustees. Under the statutory provisions of s. 13, however, it is not necessary to obtain that level of proof. It is sufficient to demonstrate that persons are within the defined group, and that their conduct falls within the conduct contemplated. The legislature does not require constructive trusteeship to impose liability. The bare statutory statement that certain persons may be held liable for the conduct of others is sufficient.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc." p2="Momat Developments Inc." post.rptr="270" pre.rptr="59" ref.id="I63f078f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc.">Maintemp Heating & Air Conditioning Inc. v. Momat Developments Inc. (2002), 59 O.R. (3d) 270, 2002 CarswellOnt 2284, 19 C.L.R. (3d) 40 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff entered into a contract with the defendant contractor to supply and install heating and air conditioning systems in seven townhouses being built by the defendant owner. One individual defendant was the president of the owner, while his brother, the second individual defendant, was both its general manager and the president of the defendant contractor. All sums paid for the project were paid by cheques drawn on the owner's bank account. After the relationship between the parties broke down, the plaintiff remained unpaid for part of its work. The plaintiff successfully alleged breach of the statutory trust under s. 13 on the part of the two individual defendants. The company had made no effort at all to segregate trust funds or to ascertain whether the disbursement of trust funds was consistent with the Act. Both individual defendants assented to or acquiesced in the breach of trust and were personally liable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works" p2="4701 Steeles Holdings Inc." post.rptr="250" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63f078f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. 4701 Steeles Holdings Inc.">Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. 4701 Steeles Holdings Inc. (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 250, 2002 CarswellOnt 1268 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Funds from sales of units in various projects were transferred to subsidiary housing corporations instead of being held in trust for the contractor. The defendant argued that the plaintiff had not proven that any loss had been caused by the breach. The Court held that regardless of whether the plaintiff proved that a loss has been caused by a violation of s. 13, the director was personally liable for the breach of trust, which he knowingly authorized.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Amherst Crane Rentals Ltd." p2="Perring" post.rptr="31" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63f078f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Amherst Crane Rentals Ltd. v. (4th) 1 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where the applicant claimed against the respondent estate for indebtedness arising by reason of the deceased's liability as a director of a contractor under s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, it could not claim the proceeds of the RRSP paid to the designated beneficiary on the death of the owner. On death, the RRSP vested in the designated third parties, not in the estate of the deceased. Death terminated the creditor's right to claim the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="ABCO Construction Inc." post.rptr="294" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63f0a0005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. ABCO Construction Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. ABCO Construction Inc. (2000), 5 C.L.R. (3d) 294 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The fact that a contractor did not realize a profit on a project and did not profit from the alleged breach of trust does not of itself affect its liability for damages for breach of trust. A contractor is not permitted to simply deduct the total payments to beneficiaries from the total trust funds received in order to determine its damages. The only way to reduce liability for statutory trust funds is to avail oneself of the statutorily permissible payment schemes in ss. 10, 11 and 12. Payments which do not qualify for a s. 11 defence because they were made in respect of another project cannot reduce the contractor's liability for damages. The fact that all of the claimants on the other project have subsequently been paid means that the contractor no longer has any liability in damages to trust beneficiaries on that project, but it has no impact of the assessment of damages for breach of trust in respect of unpaid beneficiaries of the trust on the project upon which the trust arose.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Structural Contracting Ltd." p2="Westcola Holdings Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63f0a0015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc.">Structural Contracting Ltd. v. Westcola Holdings Inc. (2000), 48 O.R. (3d) 417 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A trial was not required to establish that a sole director assented to or acquiesced in conduct that he knew or reasonably ought to have known amounted to a breach of trust. As the sole officer, director, controlling mind, and signing officer of the corporation, and as the person who signed all of the cheques in question, it was beyond argument that he reasonably ought to have known that he had effective control of the activities of the corporation. Section 35 of the <ital>Trustee Act</ital>, which allows a court to relieve a trustee acting honestly and reasonably either wholly or partly from personal liability for breach of trust, had no application. In this case, even if the director acted honestly, it was beyond argument that he did not act reasonably. What happened could not be described as a “technical breach of trust”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="L.D. Caest Constructions (Eastern) Ltd.">L.D. Contracting & Management Ltd. v. Caest Constructions (Eastern) Ltd. (2000), 3 C.L.R. (3d) 103 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In an action commenced as a standard action for collection of the outstanding account, rather than under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the principal of the defendant was held personally liable under the provisions of s. 13. Trust funds were improperly directed for company overhead, wages, legal fees and general company operating expenses rather than to payment of the beneficiary sub-trades.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Toro Aluminum Ltd." p2="Revah" post.rptr="4825" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I90c4f100f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Toro Aluminum Ltd. v. Revah">Toro Aluminum Ltd. v. Revah (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 4825, 3 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—A finding of liability under the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> will not automatically constitute a liability falling within s. 178(1)(d) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, which provides that a discharge does not relieve a bankrupt from “any debt or liability arising out of fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation or defalcation while acting in a fiduciary capacity”. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Simone" p2="Daley" post.rptr="511" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63f0c7115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simone v. Daley">Simone v. Daley (1999), 43 O.R. (3d) 511 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, the Court of Appeal required some element of wrongdoing or improper conduct on the part of the fiduciary such as failure to account properly for monies or inappropriate dealing with trust property. Under this test, the payment of funds to third parties due to inadvertence or an accounting error might not bring the matter within s. 178(d), while the deliberate misappropriation by a trustee of trust money for his or her own use, so as to defeat the claim of beneficiary, would activate s. 178(d). In the present case, monies were impressed with a trust, and the trustee failed to provide any proper accounting as to his dealings with the trust money, and substantial amounts of the trust fund were deposited directly into the trustee's personal bank account. This activity constituted a clear misappropriation of trust funds for personal benefit and created the kind of liability that should not be extinguished by bankruptcy. Note: The reasoning in this case was adopted in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Zumbo, Re" post.rptr="297" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I63f0c7125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Zumbo, Re">Zumbo, Re (2000), 2 C.L.R. (3d) 297 (Ont. Bktcy)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Pro Caissons Ltd." p2="M&M Contracting Co." post.rptr="13" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I63f0ee205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pro Caissons Ltd. v. M&M Contracting Co.">Pro Caissons Ltd. v. M&M Contracting Co. (1998), [1999] O.J. No. 13, 1998 CarswellOnt 5118 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—It is now well established that overhead expenses are not deductible from trust funds, and there is an obligation on the part of a defendant in an action alleging such a deduction, when faced with a motion for summary judgment, to put its “best foot forward” in order to establish that there is a genuine issue for trial. Photocopies of cheques which conceivably could be related to legitimate expenses of the company presented on their face and without any explanation did not meet that test.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19990927" p1="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates" p2="Bradsil (1967) Ltd." post.rptr="70" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I63f0ee215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. CA C31530 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where on motion for summary judgment there was a genuine issue for trial as to whether a contractor was in breach of the trust provisions of s. 8 of the Act, then summary judgment could not be granted against the director of that contractor under s. 13.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd." p2="Pier One Masonry Inc." post.rptr="3424" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63f0ee225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc.">Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3424, 1998 CarswellOnt 3379 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 87 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In a remarkable, perhaps unique case on its facts, involving the self interested 100 per cent prepayment of a 2,239,759 contract price, and the subsequent expenditure of that sum by the non-arm's length contractor so as to defeat, for all practical surpasses, a mason's lien. The court held that where an owner has prepaid a contractor to the foreseeable prejudice of the trades, equity demands no less than that the owner's obligations be not limited to the 10 per cent holdback and the full liens should be recoverable against the owner. The statutory frame of reference for such an order is found in ss. 8 and 13, the trust sections of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="G.V.B.S. Inc." p2="Hydro Guard Inc." post.rptr="3615" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63f115305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.V.B.S. Inc. v. Hydro Guard Inc.">G.V.B.S. Inc. v. Hydro Guard Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3615, 1998 CarswellOnt 3872 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Neither mistake of fact nor an indirect ordering process could insulate a contractor from the trust provisions of the Act. The contractor ordered supplies from one company, which then obtained approval for the order from the plaintiff supplier. The first company delivered the materials to the contractor and rendered an invoice to the plaintiff for the delivery, which the plaintiff would pay within 30 days. The plaintiff then invoiced the contractor who was to pay the invoice within 60 days. When the contractor defaulted on the payments, the plaintiff successfully sued the defendant corporation and two of its directors personally. The principal of the defendant knew or ought to have known that by refusing to make payments to the plaintiff, he was in breach of the trust imposed on him and his company by the terms of the Act. This case is quoted with approval in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Tam-Kal Ltd." p2="Stock Mechanical Inc." post.rptr="4577" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63f115315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tam-Kal Ltd. v. Stock Mechanical Inc.">Tam-Kal Ltd. v. Stock Mechanical Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 4577, 1998 CarswellOnt 4346 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1999), 50 C.L.R. (2d) 224 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Don Park Inc." p2="S.E. Mechanical Engineering Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63f115325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Don Park Inc. v. S.E. Mechanical Engineering Ltd.">Don Park Inc. v. S.E. Mechanical Engineering Ltd. (1997), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 7 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The personal defendants were found liable both under s. 13 and in tort on the authority of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Air Canada" p2="M & L Travel Ltd." post.rptr="592" pre.rptr="108" ref.id="I63f115335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Air Canada v. M & L Travel Ltd.">Air Canada v. M & L Travel Ltd. (1993), 108 D.L.R. (4th) 592, 15 O.R. (3d) 804 (note), 67 O.A.C. 1 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Commonwealth Brick Ltd." p2="Paron" post.rptr="1196" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63f13c405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Commonwealth Brick Ltd. v. Paron">Commonwealth Brick Ltd. v. Paron (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 1196, 1998 CarswellOnt 1202 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A close examination of the evidence before the lower court did not support the finding that the personal defendant participated in the day to day operations of the company, and did not show that she assented to or acquiesced in conduct that she knew or reasonably ought to have known amounted to a breach of trust. She was not liable under s. 13(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of)" p2="Acro Capital Inc." post.rptr="1038" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63f13c415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc.">700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1038, 2004 CarswellOnt 986, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 47 (S.C.J. [Commercial List]); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 1796 (S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The defendant solicitors acted for the developer owner, and after the sale of certain condominiums was completed, the proceeds were received by the solicitors and a sum paid out of them to the defendant company. The plaintiff was subsequently appointed trustee under s. 68 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to act as receiver and manager of the developer owner's assets, property and undertakings. The Plaintiff claimed against the defendants on the basis that the payment out of the proceeds was a breach of trust for which the solicitors were liable. The latter unsuccessfully moved under Ont. R. 21 to strike out the Statement of Claim against them and dismiss the action as showing no reasonable cause of action. A construction lien trustee had the authority to claim against the defendant solicitors for alleged breaches of the Act's trust provisions when it was not the bankrupt, but the contractor, who was the beneficiary of those trusts. Part II of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> declared how the trusts came into effect and were discharged by payment and declared who are the beneficiaries, but did nothing to alter the law as to the general nature of the trust and the normal right and duties of the trustee. The Act contained no definition of “trust” or “trustee” and it was to be assumed that these terms were to be read in their normal meaning in law, that is, as carrying the rights and obligations of a trustee under the common law. Under ordinary trust law, the trustee was the legal owner of the <ital>corpus</ital> of the trust and had the right to sue any one who deprived the trust of its property or who damages the trust property in any way. The trustee could sell the <ital>corpus</ital> and give good title to it to a <ital>bona fide</ital> purchaser for value without notice, even though he lacked an actual power to sell. Equity took the view that one with title, who contracted in his own name, had full capacity to act. The right of the beneficiary was generally a personal one, to compel the Trustee to properly discharge his duties as trustee. In addition, the trustee may also bring an action on behalf of the trust to recover the trust property, except as against a <ital>bona fide</ital> purchaser for value. This may be regarded as a beneficiary's remedy, or as a trustee's remedy, which the beneficiary is permitted to bring on behalf of the trust in particular circumstances. But the evolution of this remedy has not deprived the trustee of the rights of ownership.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Canard Valley Builders Inc." p2="Jelco Inc." post.rptr="190" pre.rptr="[1997]" ref.id="I63f163505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canard Valley Builders Inc. v. Jelco Inc.">Canard Valley Builders Inc. v. Jelco Inc. (1997), [1997] O.J. No. 190, 1997 CarswellOnt 231 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the defendants had made no pay-out of trust monies to themselves, their rights of set-off with respect to amounts owing to them by the plaintiff claimant were preserved. Such a situation is distinguishable from those cases where defendants paid to themselves out of trust funds amounts they deemed owing to them, claiming their set-off rights to do so, which was contrary to the decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Datasphere Sales Ltd." p2="Universal Light & Power Corp." post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63f163515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp.">Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Arborform Countertops Inc." p2="Stellato" post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63f163525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato">Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 25, 29 O.R. (3d) 129 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. However, the failure to segregate the funds for the specific protection of a beneficiary is a serious breach of a defendant's trust obligations. Merely including an account payable to the plaintiff as an entry on an unaudited financial statement hardly created a segregated, discrete fund, impressed with a trust, which would protect the plaintiff's right to be paid. Where a blanket mortgage was exposed to other creditors who were not entitled to the protection of the Act, it was a corporate asset that was comingled with all the other corporate assets. The least the defendants should have done was to assign the mortgage to a trustee to be held pending the resolution of the dispute between the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="J. (Jim) Quinn Plumbing Ltd." p2="Avtec Engineering Inc." post.rptr="1775" pre.rptr="[1997]" ref.id="I63f18a605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. (Jim) Quinn Plumbing Ltd. v. Avtec Engineering Inc.">J. (Jim) Quinn Plumbing Ltd. v. Avtec Engineering Inc. (1997), [1997] O.J. No. 1775, 1997 CarswellOnt 1461 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendants unsuccessfully argued that since over six years had passed since the completion of the construction contracts in dispute, the <ital>Statute of Limitations</ital> applied to block the plaintiff's claim for breach of trust under s. 13(1). The court held that since the plaintiff had pleaded breach of trust in his pleadings and advised the defendants at discoveries in 1994 that he would rely on the Act, the defendants were not caught by surprise, and the <ital>Rules of Civil Practice</ital> had to be given a wide interpretation. The plaintiff could therefore rely on the Act. However, while s. 13(1) of the Act is onerous, it does not impose strict liability for directors or officers, and the action against a director who was not an operating mind of the company and played no part in the decision-making process, was to be dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="St. Mary's Cement Corp." p2="Construc Ltd." post.rptr="939" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I55e531c0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Construc Ltd.">St. Mary's Cement Corp. v. Construc Ltd. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 939, 32 O.R. (3d) 595, 33 C.L.R. (2d) 234 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In addition to personal liability under s. 13(1), there may also be personal liability at common law under the principles enunciated in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1958" p1="Scott" p2="Riehl" post.rptr="525" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I63f18a625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scott v. Riehl">Scott v. Riehl (1958), 25 W.W.R. 525, [1959] 15 D.L.R. (2d) 67 (B.C. S.C.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Air Canada" p2="M & L Travel Ltd." post.rptr="184" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I63f18a635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Air Canada v. M & L Travel Ltd.">Air Canada v. M & L Travel Ltd. (1991), 2 O.R. (3d) 184, 77 D.L.R. (4th) 536, 43 O.A.C. 215 (C.A.); affirmed [1993] 3 S.C.R. 787, 108 D.L.R. (4th) 592, 50 E.T.R. 225, 159 N.R. 1, 67 O.A.C. 1 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>. This is a most significant development in Ontario's law of personal liability for corporate breach of statutory trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Arborform Countertops Inc." p2="Stellato" post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63f1b1705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato">Arborform Countertops Inc. v. Stellato (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 25, 29 O.R. (3d) 129 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied countertops to the defendant's company for improvements to commercial and residential properties. After the plaintiff obtained default judgement for breach of contract against the company, the company ceased to carry on business and commenced an identical business with the defendants as principals. The plaintiff subsequently brought an action against the individual defendants for breach of trust pursuant to s. 13 of the Act, and the defendants unsuccessfully pleaded <ital>res judicata</ital>. The trust section of the Act created a distinct cause of action such that, where a supplier obtained a judgment in a contract against a contractor, he is not barred from suing another entity under the trust provisions. The action against the personal defendants was based upon entirely different facts which were of little or no relevance to the breach of contract. The action was based simply upon the defendant's failure to abide by the statutory requirements set out under the trust provisions of the Act. As to those requirements, the court held, following <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Datasphere Sales Ltd." p2="Universal Light & Power Corp." post.rptr="25" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I63f1b1715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp.">Datasphere Sales Ltd. v. Universal Light & Power Corp. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Trilec" p2="Bastion" post.rptr="766" pre.rptr="135" ref.id="I63f1b1725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trilec v. Bastion">Trilec v. Bastion (1982), 135 D.L.R. (3d) 766 (B.C. C.A.)</ref></cite>, that the simple act of depositing trust monies into a corporate trustee; general bank account, thereby exposing the funds to being used for non trust-related purposes, or to seizure or removal by others than the beneficiaries of the trust, is sufficient to support a finding of breach of trust against the corporated officers or directors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Dawten Steel Ltd." p2="Vaughan Steel Ltd." post.rptr="2627" pre.rptr="[1996]" ref.id="I63f1b1735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dawten Steel Ltd. v. Vaughan Steel Ltd.">Dawten Steel Ltd. v. Vaughan Steel Ltd. (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 2627, 1996 CarswellOnt 2427 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 3989 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Section 13 does not place a duty on a claimant to advise a defendant that it will rely on the trust provisions of the Act. Where, after materials were sold by the plaintiff to the defendant company that in turn sold it to a third party, and the individual defendant transferred a portion of the payment money from the company and spent it, both defendants were held liable. The individual defendant not only acquiesced in the breach of trust, he personally received the money.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Dietrich Steel Ltd." p2="Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd." post.rptr="475" pre.rptr="170" ref.id="I63f1d8805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dietrich Steel Ltd. v. Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd.">Dietrich Steel Ltd. v. Shar-Dee Towers (1987) Ltd. (1999), 170 D.L.R. (4th) 475 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Section 35 of the <ital>Trustee Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. T.23 may apply, but not in this case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Francisco, Re" post.rptr="77" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63f1d8815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Francisco, Re">Francisco, Re (1996), 40 C.B.R. (3d) 77 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A breach of trust claim pursuant to s. 13(1) survives personal bankruptcy.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd." p2="Fahuki Construction Inc." post.rptr="3286" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I55e5a6f0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd. v. Fahuki Construction Inc.">Shield Sprinkler & Fire System Ltd. v. Fahuki Construction Inc. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 3286, 30 C.L.R. (2d) 156 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the principals of a contractor were well educated and well experienced in the construction field and in dealing with subcontractors and payments to subcontractors, the court concluded that they either knew or ought to have known that the payment out of all of the funds received from the owner and the application of a part of those funds toward the contractor's own overhead and expenses constituted a breach of trust under s. 8 of the Act. Accordingly, the principals were jointly and severally liable for such breach of trust.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction Co." p2="S.I. Guttman Ltd. (1996), 29 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.); appeal dismissed (1997), 104 O.A.C. 232 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—This conscious appropriation of trust funds by secured creditors is sufficient to take them out of s. 35 of the <ital>Trustee Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Heritage Masonry Ltd." p2="Building Team Ltd." post.rptr="1226" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I63f1ff915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heritage Masonry Ltd. v. Div.)</ref></cite>—No special <ital>mens rea</ital> or evil intent is required. The standard is a simple test of reasonableness.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Francisco, Re" post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="19" ref.id="I63f1ff925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Francisco, Re">Francisco, Re (1995), 19 C.L.R. (2d) 146, 32 C.B.R. (3d) 29 (Ont. Bktcy.); affirmed (1996), 40 C.B.R. (3d) 77 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—B Ltd. commenced an action against C Ltd. and F, a director of C Ltd., for amounts owed and for breach of trust pursuant to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Subsequently, B Ltd. was unable to collect its judgment against C Ltd., and its action against F was stayed by F's bankruptcy. B Ltd.'s application for leave to continue the action against F was dismissed by the Registrar in Bankruptcy, and B Ltd.'s appeal was allowed. By alleging that F was director of C Ltd. and had assented to or acquiesced in conduct he knew or should have known amounted to breach of trust by C Ltd., B Ltd. had pleaded enough facts to relieve against the automatic stay of proceedings provided by <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>. It was reasonably arguable that a director acts in a fiduciary capacity with respect to the beneficiaries of the trust relationship. The fact that there had been no finding of fraud or misrepresentation against C Ltd. was not material to issue before the Registrar.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="St. Mary's Cement Co." p2="MacDonald" post.rptr="2179" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I63f226a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="St. Mary's Cement Co. v. MacDonald">St. Mary's Cement Co. v. MacDonald (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 2179 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The successful lien claimant pursued a second action against the debtor corporation and its officer. The issues of quantum decided in the lien proceeding were held binding on the same parties in the subsequent trust proceeding. The corporate officer was found jointly and severally liable with the debtor corporation. Subsection 13(1) does not require that direct contact or dealing be established between the parties to prove liability.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref court="Ont. Gen. Div." fjur="Ontario" jur="Canada" norm.rptr="carsont" p1="Home Depot Inc." p2="Fieder Painting Inc." post.rptr="4514" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I2688e02001a911efa7fea76a6b7cbe8e" title="Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc.">Home Depot Inc. v. Fieder Painting Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 4514 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—There is no justification for reading into s. 13 any kind of extra <ital>mens rea</ital> standard of liability. Subsection 13(1) creates its own standard with the phrase “he or she knows or ought reasonably to know” and it is unreasonable to burden this standard with an illegitimate gloss.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd." p2="Stowe Nut & Bolt Co." post.rptr="115" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I63f24db05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Stowe Nut & Bolt Co.">Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Stowe Nut & Bolt Co. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 115, 1988 CarswellOnt 770 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An element of conscious wrongdoing or “<ital>mens rea</ital>” must be shown on the part of the director against whom personal liability is claimed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Main Line Construction Ltd." p2="Nicolini" post.rptr="2815" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I63f24db15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini">Main Line Construction Ltd. v. Nicolini (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 2815 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant N Ltd., which disputed the allegation that it was the general contractor, received $25,000.00 on account of a renovation project, with $5,000.00 received as a deposit and the balance by way of Minutes of Settlement. In finding N Ltd. to be the general contractor, the court held that the $25,000 constituted a trust fund pursuant to s. 8(1), that N Ltd. was a trustee of the monies pursuant to s. 8(2), and that it was improper for N Ltd. to keep the balance of the monies received. As the trust money went into the hands of N, as N Ltd.'s President, and as a Director of the company, and as N knowingly kept the money and did not pay the subcontractor supervising the construction, nor those subtrades the subcontractor had paid, N was held personally liable under s. 13 of the Act for his failure to pay those entitled to the trust funds.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Van Arnhem" p2="Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc." post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63f24db25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Van Arnhem v. Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc.">Van Arnhem v. Lornewood Tanning Salon Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 54 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The contractor was hired by S to design a system that would give adequate heating and cooling to a tanning salon. The contractor asked S if he had funds set aside for the project, and S replied that he did. The contractor asked which of S's companies would be paying for the work, and S said that he did not know yet. The contractor completed a substantial amount of the work, including the rough-in and unit installation. The contractor then had to stop for the drywaller to do its work. The contractor was never called back to complete its work. The contractor subsequently made efforts to have its bill paid, but such efforts were unsuccessful. The contractor brought an action against the company that owned the salon for breach of statutory trust and against S as president of the company for assenting to or acquiescing in the breach of trust. In the circumstances, it was appropriate to interpret the word “received” in s. 7(1) as including “receivable.” Where the principal of the company controlled both the finance of the project and its ownership and construction, including when, if ever, the designated funds would be “received” by the owner, it was necessary to protect the beneficiaries of the trust funds from such an unscrupulous principal. The trust existed, and it was a breach of trust to fail to fund the owner in order to allow the proper payments to be made from the trust to the beneficiaries. Moreover, it was clear that S assented to and acquiesced in the breach. He was the person whose statement formed the evidence that the fund existed. He advised the contractor that cheques had been drawn up to pay the invoices and then failed to make the cheques available. Further, he told the contractor that the funds had been diverted to other uses until the project in question was completed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Emco Supply" p2="D.E. Witmer Plumbing & Heating Ltd." post.rptr="129" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63f274c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Supply v. D.E. Witmer Plumbing & Heating Ltd.">Emco Supply v. D.E. Witmer Plumbing & Heating Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 129 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff unsuccessfully applied to amend its statement of claim to add K, the defendant company's bookkeeper. An extensive cross-examination had been conducted of K, during which she stated that she was the bookkeeper without responsibility for the affairs of the defendant. K's cross-examination clearly revealed that she had no effective control of the defendant company or its relevant activities, a precondition to liability under s. 13. Moreover, to require K to become a defendant at this late stage of the proceedings, would be prejudiced to her and would not compensate her for the costs that she would incur.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Great Lake Brick & Stone Ltd." p2="837004 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="104" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I63f274c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Great Lake Brick & Stone Ltd. v. 837004 Ontario Ltd.">Great Lake Brick & Stone Ltd. v. 837004 Ontario Ltd. (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 104 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied bricks and related masonry supplies to the corporate defendant, a general contractor, in connection with the construction of a custom-built residence. The corporate defendant received contract moneys from the owners but it did not distribute any of these moneys to the plaintiff. Instead, the corporate defendant paid the moneys in a selective and preferred manner to certain creditors. The plaintiff had been awarded judgment against the corporate defendant. The personal defendant, who was the operating mind of the corporate defendant, a general contractor, was also held to be liable to the plaintiff. He was the operating mind of the corporate defendant, and was in control of the funds received and disbursed by the corporation. He was unable to account for the funds provided by the owners to the corporate defendant, his explanations were very vague and showed a preference for certain creditors. Although there was no evidence that the funds were converted by the personal defendant to his own use, the funds were disbursed by him in a manner that was inconsistent with the concept of a trust. This called for equitable redress. Accordingly, the personal defendant was also liable to the plaintiff, because he either acquiesced in or directed the breach of trust by the corporation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Patrick Harrison & Co." p2="Devran Petroleum Ltd." post.rptr="478" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I63f274c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Patrick Harrison & Co. v. Devran Petroleum Ltd.">Patrick Harrison & Co. v. Devran Petroleum Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 478, 22 C.P.C. (3d) 285 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sought leave to add the directors of a defendant company, D Ltd., as parties in an action alleging breach of trust by failing to pay monies allegedly owing pursuant to a contract for work and materials. More than seven years passed since the completion of the contract which gave rise to the action, and D Ltd. claimed that all the monies owed had been paid out. The motion was dismissed. There was nothing new about the claims, and nothing in the affidavit in support of the motion validated the position that the deponent believed that D Ltd. had appropriated or converted to its own use part of the monies received to finance the project. The provisions of s. 13 did not make the directors trustees but rather made them liable for any breach of trust in the same manner as the trustee corporation would be liable, and for the same damages. The directors were not trustees, and the motion was barred by the <ital>Limitation Act</ital> (Ontario).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="West York Construction (1984) Ltd." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="2980" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I63f311005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="West York Construction (1984) Ltd. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">West York Construction (1984) Ltd. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1993), [1993] O.J. No. 2980 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The trial was at hand. The plaintiff moved for summary judgment on a breach of trust claim, including a breach of trust claim against individual defendants. These named individual defendants defended on the ground that the company of which they were officers had a defence set-off pursuant to s. 12. The court held that the justification for persons included in the provisions of s. 13 to raise s. 12 is a matter of evidence, in this case justifying the dismissal of a motion for summary judgment. By relying on s. 12, the individual defendants admitted the monies in issue were trust monies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc." p2="Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd." post.rptr="6" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63f311015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd.">Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 6 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The bank which put a contractor into receivership, and the company appointed as receiver and manager of that contractor were both liable to the plaintiff subcontractors for any breach of trust created by s. 8.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Emco Supply" p2="Gueguen" post.rptr="229" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I63f311025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Supply v. Gueguen">Emco Supply v. Gueguen (1987), 25 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied materials and services to a number of projects for the defendant E Ltd. for which the defendant G was the sole officer, director and shareholder. E Ltd. became solvent and the plaintiff sought payment from G personally of amounts owing on all projects and claiming that E Ltd. breached the trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> as it did not maintain a separate trust account for each project, but placed all funds received in its general account from which it paid subcontractors, suppliers and its own overhead. The court found that E Ltd. was in breach of the trust provisions of the Act, and that G knew or reasonably ought to have known that by doing so the corporate defendant was in breach of trust. As sole shareholder of E Ltd., G was found liable under s. 13(1) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Wormald Fire Systems Inc." p2="Coopers & Lybrand Ltd." post.rptr="77" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63f338105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wormald Fire Systems Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand Ltd.">Wormald Fire Systems Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand Ltd. (1985), 11 C.L.R. 77 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff claimed for construction work which it performed for the defendant M Ltd., which filed a proposal pursuant to the provisions of the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital>. The defendant CL Ltd. was named trustee under the proposal, and interim receiver and manager of M Ltd. The plaintiff then instituted an action for an accounting of trust moneys and for damages pursuant to the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. CL Ltd. and M Ltd. moved to strike out the statement of claim on the ground that it disclosed no reasonable cause of action and on the further ground that leave to proceed ought to have been applied for pursuant to ss. 49 and 186 of the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital>. The motion was dismissed. The trustee was potentially liable pursuant to s. 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> as a person having effective control of a corporation or its relevant activities. Although s. 186 of the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital> normally required leave to proceed against a trustee with respect to any action taken pursuant to that Act, in this case the act or omission in respect of the proported trust moneys did not constitute an action taken pursuant to the <ital>Bankruptcy Act</ital>, and leave was not required to institute this action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="R." p2="Rosen" post.rptr="91" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63f338115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R. v. Rosen">R. v. Rosen (1985), 12 C.L.R. 91 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—The accused was a builder of residential dwellings and commercial buildings in Ontario and Quebec utilizing a number of corporate vehicles for this purpose. These corporate vehicles were actively and fully controlled by the accused and were financially intertwined. Utilizing one of the corporate vehicles, the accused arranged for the development of a condominium project and the financing for same. In the course of receiving the financing for the project through a particular corporate entity, the accused diverted the financing to his related corporate entities. The accused was charged with fraud, theft and with, being a trustee of funds for the use or benefit of workmen and suppliers of materials, converting with intent to defraud and in violation of the trust, the said funds to a use not authorized by the trust. At trial, the accused was convicted on all three charges, and his appeal to the Ontario Court of Appeal was dismissed. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, the conviction for breach of trust was quashed, but the convictions for theft and fraud were upheld. The accused was not a trustee so that the conviction upon this ground could not be supported. However, the accused did not need to be a trustee to commit the offence of breach of trust. By causing the trustee company to commit a breach of trust, the accused could have committed the offence as an “aider and abettor” under the <ital>Criminal Code</ital>, but the accused was not charged with that offence in that way but with breach of trust “being a trustee”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="R." p2="Sager" post.rptr="1364" pre.rptr="[1990]" ref.id="I63f35f205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R. v. Sager">R. v. Sager (1990), [1990] O.J. No. 1364 (D.C.)</ref></cite>—A criminal conviction for fraud was entered on one of two counts of fraud over $1,000, contrary to s. 338(1)(a) of the <ital>Criminal Code</ital>. By explicitly directing his solicitor to pay a trade on one project from monies held in a segregated trust account for another project, and counselling the beneficiary of the direction to remain silent about the fact, the accused had committed a fraud. A conditional discharge was granted on terms requiring a period of probation, restitution over the period of probation, and 500 hours of community service.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 13(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Cogemar Srl. Marble & Granite" p2="Stone Top Factory Inc." post.rptr="1479" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I63f35f215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cogemar Srl. Marble & Granite v. Stone Top Factory Inc.">Cogemar Srl. Marble & Granite v. Stone Top Factory Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 1479, 2003 CarswellOnt 1437, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 218 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—For the purposes of subs. 13(2), it is not always a corporation's formal corporate documents filed with the Ministry of Consumer and Business Services that govern the issue of control of the corporation, irrespective of the factual evidence as to actual control. The court found the individual defendant liable for breach of trust where he held himself out as an officer of the defendant corporation, with the consent of the president, who acquiesced in, or authorized, the individual defendant making whatever representations were necessary in purchasing materials for the corporation; where he represented to the defendant's bank that he was the Secretary of the corporation, enabling him to have signing authority; where he was understood by the plaintiff supplier to be the owner of the corporation; and where he was the only individual the supplier dealt with in respect of the corporation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co." p2="Caravaggio" post.rptr="178" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63f386305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co. v. Caravaggio">Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co. v. Caravaggio (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 178, 2002 CarswellOnt 2379 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The three individuals operating the construction business to which the plaintiff provided services had seven business entities, the names of which they appeared to have used without any regard to specific job sites, contracts, payments or directions, instructions or control of the work performed. The plaintiff was at no time notified that it was dealing with any specific company or business entity and that at all times the three individual defendants held themselves out as carrying on business directly with the plaintiff without reference to any one of their corporate or business entities as might exist. All of the defendants acting as one received monies for the relevant construction projects at a time when monies were due and owing to the plaintiff for services rendered on those projects and those monies were otherwise disbursed by the defendants for other purposes not consistent with the trust imposed by s. 8 of the Act. To permit the defendant to hide behind the name of an unsued corporate entity would constitute a travesty of justice. Each of the defendants was in breach of the trust imposed upon them pursuant to s. 8 of the Act by reason of the manner in which they carried on business.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 13(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc." p2="ESD Industries Inc." post.rptr="290" pre.rptr="60" ref.id="I63f386315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. ESD Industries Inc.">Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. ESD Industries Inc. (2002), 60 O.R. (3d) 290, 2002 CarswellOnt 2286, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 227 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Whether an individual defendant was in breach of trust or whether the corporate defendant was in breach of its trust, and the individual defendant was statutorily liable for the corporate breach of trust by operation of the Act, was irrelevant to their joint and several liability. It is not essential for the imposition of joint and several liability under s. 13(3) that the defendants all be trustees as such. Joint and several liability arises as a consequence of the straightforward operation of the subsection. Put in simple terms, the legislature's declaration that such persons are jointly and severally liable ends the matter.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13.12:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.12.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.12:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jamrik" p2="2688126 Ont. Inc." post.rptr="2854" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6743dfc03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc.">Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 11019, 2024 ONSC 2854, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3654 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The court provided some guidance on the process to be followed by adjudicators. Adjudicators are bound to follow decisions of the Divisional Court and the Court of Appeal, and would be well advised to consider persuasive authorities, including decisions of Justices and Associate Justices of the Superior Court. An adjudicator has no jurisdiction where none is granted by the Act. Adjudicators must be correct in finding a legal basis for their jurisdiction; their findings of fact in connection with their jurisdictional determinations are entitled to deference. It is a matter of discretion whether to address alternative theories of a point under decision. However, it is often a service to the parties and to the administration of justice to make factual findings in respect to alternative arguments, so that a reviewing court will have the necessary factual findings to assess and decide all available arguments. Here, if the adjudicator had also gone on to make the necessary factual findings about whether any contract work remained for completion and its value, the court might have been able to dispose of this matter on a final basis, rather than sending it back for a fresh determination. While it is open to an adjudicator to decide a point on a basis not raised before him by the parties, the adjudicator must give the parties notice of their concerns and give the parties an opportunity to address them both as a matter of procedural fairness, and to ensure that the adjudicator has the benefit of the parties' submissions on material points. Had additional submissions been sought in this case, the parties might well have persuaded the adjudicator that his proposed analysis was in error.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
