C.30, s. 13.13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.13:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pasqualino" p2="MGW-Homes Design Inc." post.rptr="5632" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I67442de03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc.">Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc., 2022 ONSC 5632, 2022 CarswellOnt 14177, 35 C.L.R. (5th) 453 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—Allowing an adjudicator's decision under s. 13.13 to remain after a lien has been bonded off and security posted does not undermine the purpose and effectiveness of s. 44. Permitting an owner to seek a reduction of the security posted in court by the amount paid pursuant to an adjudicator's decision demonstrated how the two processes work harmoniously together.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13.18:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.18.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.18:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" date.trace="20250528" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gay Co. Ltd." p2="Sayers Foods Ltd." post.rptr="17084" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6744f1303b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Gay Co. Ltd. v. Sayers Foods Ltd.">Gay Co. Ltd. v. Sayers Foods Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 17084, 2024 ONSC 6123 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> Notice to the Attorney General is mandatory in applications for judicial review of prompt payment determinations under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, and the application here was adjourned until that notice was given. The Ontario Dispute Adjudication for Construction Contracts (“ODACC”) was entitled to notice as well, and the court would consider whether ODACC was entitled to be heard on such applications. Since the court required notice to ODACC in this case, it might consider concerns raised in prior decisions that adjudication decisions are not receiving neutral citations and are not being released to reporting services. The court might inquire into and decide whether ODACC should be required to devise and implement a policy for public release of adjudication decisions in the future.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 13.18(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc." p2="Flow-Rite Inc." post.rptr="2928" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6744f1313b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc. v. Flow-Rite Inc.">Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc. v. Flow-Rite Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 2928, 2023 ONSC 1291, 15 Admin. L.R. (7th) 167, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 418 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace>—The interim nature of an adjudicator's adjudication is fundamental to the prompt payment scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> and is designed to secure a reasonable interim payment direction, following a fast and informal process, without prejudice to the parties revisiting their substantive disagreements in litigation or private arbitration. Leave to apply for judicial review of such an interim decision will be granted rarely. Where leave to apply for judicial review is granted, the standard of review is reasonableness. While procedural unfairness could be a ground for review, such an issue will be reviewed through the lens of the prompt and informal process envisioned for these adjudications and the limited impact of the adjudicator's decision on the final disposition of issues between the parties. The focus of the Divisional Court will be on whether the moving party had a fair opportunity to be heard in the adjudication process. Given this context, the “fairly arguable case” test for leave to bring an application for judicial review, as stated in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Raincoast Conservation Foundation" p2="Canada (Attorney General)" post.rptr="224" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I8d9e1720ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Raincoast Conservation Foundation v. Canada (Attorney General)">Raincoast Conservation Foundation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FCA 224 (F.C.A.); leave to appeal refused <ital>Olivier Adkin-Kaya, et al. v. Attorney General of Canada, et al.</ital>, 2020 CarswellNat 609 (S.C.C.); leave to appeal refused <ital>Federation of British Columbia Naturalists carrying on business as BC Nature v. Attorney General of Canada, et al.</ital>, 2020 CarswellNat 605 (S.C.C.); leave to appeal refused <ital>Tsleil-Waututh Nation v. Attorney General of Canada, et al.</ital>, 2020 CarswellNat 607 (S.C.C.); leave to appeal refused <ital>Squamish Nation v. Attorney General of Canada, et al.</ital>, 2020 CarswellNat 727 (S.C.C.); leave to appeal refused <ital>Raincoast Conservation Foundation, et al. v. Attorney General of Canada, et al.</ital>, 2020 CarswellNat 611 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, does not apply to motions for leave to bring an application for judicial review under the prompt payment provisions of the <ital>Construction Act.</ital></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pasqualino" p2="MGW-Homes Design Inc." post.rptr="14177" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I674518403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc.">Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc., 2022 ONSC 5632, 2022 CarswellOnt 14177, 35 C.L.R. (5th) 453 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The parties entered into a fixed price contract for renovations to the owner's home, and a claim for lien was subsequently registered before being vacated by the owner by the posting of security in court. The contractor then filed a notice of adjudication, and the adjudicator ordered payment of a significant part of the funds alleged owing. No issue was raised by the owner as to the adjudicator's jurisdiction before or at the adjudication. The owner unsuccessfully applied for leave for judicial review under s. 13.18 on the basis that a) the contract was invalid or had ceased to exist having been abandoned or terminated prior to the notice to adjudicate; or b) the determination was of a matter that may not be the subject of adjudication as, inter alia, s. 13.18(5)(2) does not apply after a lien is registered and bonded off. In denying leave, the Divisional Court held that any challenge to the jurisdiction of the adjudicator should have first been raised before the adjudicator. There was no merit to the submission that the <ital>Construction Act</ital> compelled the owner to agree to the adjudication. While acknowledging that the <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not set out a test for a motion for leave for judicial review under s. 13.18(1), the court declined to decide what the appropriate test for leave for judicial review of an adjudicator's decision was. It was satisfied that the owner here failed to demonstrate that he had a reasonably or fairly arguable case in the circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="SOTA Dental Studio Inc." p2="Andrid Group Ltd." post.rptr="2254" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63f5d0215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="SOTA Dental Studio Inc. v. Andrid Group Ltd.">SOTA Dental Studio Inc. v. Andrid Group Ltd., 2022 ONSC 2254, 2022 CarswellOnt 4937 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—On application for judicial review of the adjudicator's decision under the prompt payment provisions of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, the Divisional Court suggested the following principles be borne in mind on applications for judicial review: (a) prompt payment is integral to the scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>; (b) failure to pay in accordance with the prompt payment requirements may lead the court to refuse leave for judicial review. Where leave is granted, an applicant must obtain a stay or must make payment, failing which the court may dismiss the application on motion to quash or at the hearing of the application.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 13.18(5)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Blackstone Paving and Construction Ltd." p2="Barrie (City of)" post.rptr="4556" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67453f503b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Blackstone Paving and Construction Ltd. v. Barrie (City of)">Blackstone Paving and Construction Ltd. v. Barrie (City of), 2024 CarswellOnt 12800, 2024 ONSC 4556, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4340 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The requirements of procedural fairness are assessed on a “correctness” or “fairness” standard, applying the conjunctive statutory test set out in s.13.18(5). Here, in denying the application for judicial review, the court found that both adjudicators implicitly accepted the municipality's characterization that it did no more than “elaborate” the reasons it gave, under s. 6.4(2), for non-payment in the Notices of Non-Payment, rather than raise new reasons. As well, even if certain typographical errors amounted to non-compliance with s.6.4(2) of the Act, no prejudice arose from this non-compliance. Finally, the adjudicators' decisions not to permit reply submissions were not inconsistent with the process prescribed by the Act or with the process agreed by the parties with the adjudicators. Therefore, the plaintiff had not met the first branch of the conjunctive statutory test for procedural unfairness prescribed by s.13.18(5)5.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Caledon (Town)" p2="2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction" post.rptr="4555" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67453f513b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Caledon (Town) v. 2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction">Caledon (Town) v. 2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction, 2024 ONSC 4555, 2024 CarswellOnt 12799 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>. The adjudicator erred in failing to find that the contract was in respect to two improvements, not one, and that, as per the transitional provisions of s. 87.3, different versions of the Act therefore applied to claims arising from the two different improvements. One improvement was excluded from adjudication by the transitional provisions of the Act, and the other was not. In the former case, the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applied, and that Act made no provision for adjudication. The adjudicator's determination was varied to exclude claims in respect to one of the two improvements. The court noted that an argument that an adjudicator's decision was substantively unreasonable is not a basis for the court to set aside the determination, as the court will not recharacterize non-procedural arguments as procedural arguments to expand the scope of judicial review prescribed in s.13.18(5). The bases on which the court may intervene on an application for judicial review reflect the nature of the award made by an adjudicator: it is an interim award, without prejudice to the parties, and is to be made swiftly following a prescribed prompt process. The court affords a high degree of deference to an adjudicator's decision and will intervene only in limited circumstances. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also cases under s. 87.3, setting out the <ital>Construction Act</ital>'s transitional provisions. Here, neither side addressed before the adjudicator the issue of how to apply the Act's transitional provisions in respect of multiple improvements, and the court directed the parties on the review to provide supplementary submissions to address what emerged as the central jurisdictional issue in this case.]</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jamrik" p2="2688126 Ont. Inc." post.rptr="2854" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I674566603b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc.">Jamrik v. 2688126 Ont. Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 11019, 2024 ONSC 2854, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3654 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An adjudicator must be correct, in law, on jurisdictional issues, but will be afforded deference on findings of fact related to their jurisdictional analysis. Here, the adjudicator erred in finding that the contract was not “completed” within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> because more than 1% of the contract price was owing and unpaid. The “price of completion” in s. 2(3) of the Act refers to the value of uncompleted work, and not the quantum of disputed payment claims. In coming to a contrary conclusion, the arbitrator misconstrued the plain meaning of the Act, failed to apply settled and longstanding jurisprudence on the meaning of deemed “contract completion” under the Act, and misconceived the scheme of the prompt payment adjudication provisions of the Act. As well, the adjudicator did not make factual findings on the two key issues argued before him respecting the jurisdictional issue. Without those findings, the court could not dispose of the jurisdictional issue on a final basis and sent it back for a fresh determination. In light of the errors in process and principle below, the entire decision was to be regarded as unsafe, all issues were referred back for a fresh determination before a different adjudicator.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ledore Investments" p2="Dixin Construction" post.rptr="931" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I674566613b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Ledore Investments v. Dixin Construction">Ledore Investments v. Dixin Construction, 2024 CarswellOnt 931, 2024 ONSC 598 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The adjudicator concluded that the contractor was not required to pay the subcontractor's invoices pursuant to the prompt payment provisions of the Act, but his reasoning turned on a point neither party had raised. He found that, because the subcontractor had not delivered to the owner a “proper invoice” as defined in the Act, the Act's prompt payment provisions did not apply. The adjudicator's decision breached procedural fairness and should be set aside under s. 13.18(5)5. The subcontractor was not given an opportunity to be heard on the key issue that determined the outcome. Although the Act contemplates a speedy and targeted adjudication process, fundamental procedural fairness demanded an opportunity for the parties to provide at least written submissions on the key issue that would determine the adjudication. The matter was to be remitted to the adjudicator so he would have the opportunity to make a determination on that issue after having received the parties' submissions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc." p2="Flow-Rite Inc." post.rptr="2928" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I67458d703b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc. v. Flow-Rite Inc.">Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc. v. Flow-Rite Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 2928, 2023 ONSC 1291, 15 Admin. L.R. (7th) 167, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 418 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace>—It is in the jurisdiction of an adjudicator to decide whether a claim is properly brought under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Thus, an argument that services or materials provided by a claimant are not lienable, that a claim for lien is out of time, or that the contract in issue “is invalid” or has “ceased to exist”, are within the jurisdiction of an adjudicator to decide, and an adjudicator's decision on these issues is reviewed in this court on a standard of reasonableness. An adjudicator does not “lose jurisdiction” if they “err” on these points. Only where an adjudicator's decision is “unreasonable” would the Divisional Court intervene.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pasqualino" p2="MGW-Homes Design Inc." post.rptr="5632" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I67458d713b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc.">Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc., 2022 ONSC 5632, 2022 CarswellOnt 14177, 35 C.L.R. (5th) 453 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The adjudication process was not intended to require an adjudicator to delve into making factual and legal determinations on whether a contract was abandoned or terminated. The simplified and expeditious process of adjudication would be defeated if the adjudicator was required to consider and decide such issues. Adjudication was also not intended to be only available “while construction proceeds.” The legislature chose not to use words such as the contract is “terminated” or “abandoned”. Instead, the legislature chose to use the words “cease to exist”. If a contract is determined to be abandoned or terminated, even if amounting to repudiation, that did not mean the contract ceased to exist. If either party could allege a termination or abandonment of their construction contract and that allegation were to result in the construction contract “ceasing to exist”, adjudication could be easily avoided and there would be a return to the prior lengthy and expensive legal process with the likelihood that the flow of funds down the construction pyramid would be delayed. Essentially, the adjudication provisions in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> would be gutted.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 13.18(7)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sayers Foods Ltd." p2="Gay Company Limited" post.rptr="13308" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6745b4803b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Sayers Foods Ltd. v. Gay Company Limited">Sayers Foods Ltd. v. Gay Company Limited, 2024 CarswellOnt 13308, 2024 ONSC 4832 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The applicant's motion for a stay of the adjudicator's decision ordering prompt payment to the respondent pending the hearing of an application for judicial review from the adjudicator's decision was granted, on condition that the full amount of the impugned determination was paid into court. It was beyond dispute that the applicant would be required to pay most or all of the adjudicator's determination to the respondent's subcontractors, and the payment should not have to await the extended litigation that might be required to decide the lien claims between the applicant and respondent. Any issue about the proper application of the funds, reduction in lien security upon payment of those funds, and related issues, could be addressed by the application panel.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Accurate Railroad Construction Ltd." p2="Sierra Infrastructure Inc." post.rptr="9781" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6745b4813b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Accurate Railroad Construction Ltd. v. Sierra Infrastructure Inc.">Accurate Railroad Construction Ltd. v. Sierra Infrastructure Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 9781, 2024 ONSC 3722, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3419 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The applicant sought leave to bring an application for judicial review of an adjudication that required repayment of significant funds to the respondent, and also sought a stay of the requirement to pay, pending the hearing of its leave motion. The applicant alleged that the respondent misled the adjudicator by filing a summary chart that contained deliberate errors. The court concluded that the just and expeditious outcome was to neither put money in the respondent's hands in face of the allegations of fraud nor allow the applicant a way around the “pay-as-you-play” regime. Rather, the applicant was to pay the funds into court pending further order of the court, with the respondent prohibited from taking further steps to enforce the adjudicator's order. The leave motion was to be expedited and heard as soon as practically possible.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc." p2="Flow-Rite Inc." post.rptr="2928" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6745b4823b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc. v. Flow-Rite Inc.">Anatolia Tile & Stone Inc. v. Flow-Rite Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 2928, 2023 ONSC 1291, 15 Admin. L.R. (7th) 167, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 418 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace>—It is in the discretion of a case management judge to stipulate whether a stay motion shall be argued (i) before the leave motion is decided, (ii) together with the leave motion, in writing, or (iii) by way of a separately argued motion after the leave motion is decided (if leave is granted). If the case management judge directs that the stay motion be heard in writing by the leave panel, then the leave panel may decide the stay motion in writing or give directions respecting how the stay motion will be heard. As well, it is in the discretion of a case management judge to direct payment into court as a condition precedent to permitting a stay motion and/or a leave motion to be brought while the moving party is in breach of the payment order. A stay will not be granted as a matter of course when leave to apply for judicial review is granted and that where a stay is granted, securing the disputed payment will be a common term of a stay order. The Legislature's goal was, clearly, “prompt payment” and not just “prompt adjudication”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Okkin Construction Inc." p2="Apostolopoulos" post.rptr="6367" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63f5f7305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Okkin Construction Inc. v. Apostolopoulos">Okkin Construction Inc. v. Apostolopoulos, 2022 ONSC 6367, 2022 CarswellOnt 16273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Absent a stay, which was not sought here, an adjudication order must be paid even if it means that someone will have to pay twice in the short term. This allows the contractor to ensure that funds flow. It was possible under the Act to subsequently seek a reduction in the amount of security posted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="SOTA Dental Studio Inc." p2="Andrid Group Ltd." post.rptr="2254" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63f5f7315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="SOTA Dental Studio Inc. v. Andrid Group Ltd.">SOTA Dental Studio Inc. v. Andrid Group Ltd., 2022 ONSC 2254, 2022 CarswellOnt 4937 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—On application for judicial review of the adjudicator's decision under the prompt payment provisions of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, the Divisional Court rejected the applicant's argument that the absence of a stay did no more than enable the respondent to continue enforcement steps but did not preclude an application for judicial review where an applicant has met the high bar for leave. Failure to pay in accordance with the prompt payment requirements may lead the court to refuse leave for judicial review. Where leave is granted, an applicant must obtain a stay or must make payment, failing which the court may dismiss the application on motion to quash or at the hearing of the application. Here, the court dismissed the application without considering the underlying merits of the application. If an owner/payer was insolvent, it should not be permitted to run up costs and delays through recourse to litigation in the face of the adjudicator's order below and the prompt payment provisions of the Act. If there were circumstances that should lead the court to grant a stay, in all of these circumstances, these must be established on proper evidence in the context of a motion for a stay.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13.19:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.19.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.19:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 13.19(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Okkin Construction Inc." p2="Apostolopoulos" post.rptr="6367" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63f61e405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Okkin Construction Inc. v. Apostolopoulos">Okkin Construction Inc. v. Apostolopoulos, 2022 ONSC 6367, 2022 CarswellOnt 16273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the owner terminated the project on account of cost overruns, the contractor filed a Notice of Adjudication. Before the adjudication could be heard, the subcontractor, which was not a party to the adjudication, registered a construction lien against title to the owner's property. The contractor subsequently registered its own lien and the adjudicator eventually ordered the owner to pay a portion of the value of various invoices. The owner did not seek judicial review but moved for directions regarding whether he should pay the adjudication award in the face of a perfected lien registered by the subcontractor and the holdback requirements of the Act, and sought to pay the funds into trust. In essence, the owner was concerned he would be called upon to pay the required holdback twice. The court found that neither s. 51 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> nor r. 59.06 granted it the necessary authority to give the directions sought. In <ital>obiter</ital> comments, the court stated that even if such jurisdiction existed, it would not have provided directions to maintain the funds in escrow. Absent a stay, which was not sought here, an adjudication order must be paid even if it means that someone will have to pay twice in the short term. This allows the contractor to ensure that funds flow. It was then possible under the Act to seek a reduction in the amount of security posted. However, when payment of the order was made, the contractor would become a trustee for the subcontractor with respect to the amounts owing to the latter, and the owner would be credited for this payment. Directing that the proceeds of the adjudicator's order continue to be held in trust would defeat the purpose of the prompt payment provisions of the Act and create a path for delay.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13.20:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.20.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.20:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MGW Homes Design Inc." p2="Pasqualino" post.rptr="8261" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I674677d03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="MGW Homes Design Inc. v. Pasqualino">MGW Homes Design Inc. v. Pasqualino, 2024 CarswellOnt 8261, 2024 ONSC 2852, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2729 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff registered an adjudicator's determination, thereby rendering it enforceable as a court order, but failed to give notice within ten days of filing the determination with the court. The motion judge found that the plaintiff had not complied with the clear language of the Act, voided enforcement steps taken pursuant to the order and ordered that the plaintiff could not enforce the adjudicator's award. In varying this order, the Divisional Court noted that the Act was silent on the consequences of non-compliance with the notice requirement, which placed that issue within the discretion of a motion judge. In this case, the motion judge's order precluding enforcement of the adjudicator's determination was disproportionate to the plaintiff's non-compliance. To provide guidance on this issue, the Divisional Court opined that where there is evidence of actual prejudice, where there is no reasonable explanation for the failure to give notice, or where there are other circumstances that commend a more significant sanction, the court could consider voiding pre-notice enforcement steps, suspending interest for the period of non-compliance, an order for costs, or other sanctions that are proportional to the harm resulting from the failure to comply with the notice requirement. However, it was difficult to imagine any circumstance that would justify an order so draconian as to disentitle a party to ever enforce an adjudicator's payment determination as a consequence of failure to provide notice.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13.23:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.23.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.23:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Westport Insurance" p2="BDA Inc." post.rptr="15030" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67469ee03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Westport Insurance v. BDA Inc.">Westport Insurance v. BDA Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 15030, 2024 ONSC 5450 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was the novel question of whether a surety may assert a security interest on funds awarded in an adjudication<ital>.</ital> In holding that it could, the court noted that the applicant surety was only entitled to losses as defined in the indemnity agreement, and as a result, the disputed funds were to be paid into court pending the outcome of the related proceedings being litigated. Here, the contractor required the subcontractor to provide performance security, and the surety delivered bonds naming the contractor as the obligee, and the subcontractor as the principal, and then registered its security interest under the Ont. <ital>Personal Property Security Act</ital>. Subsequently, following a dispute, the contractor terminated the subcontract and made a claim against the bonds. On an interim basis, the surety entered into a mitigation agreement and paid the contractor various advances, and pursuant to s. 13.5(1), a determination was made awarding payment to the subcontractor. The subcontractor opposed the surety's attempt to assert its security interest in that payment. The clear and unambiguous wording of the indemnity agreement included all funds to which the subcontractor might be entitled or which were awarded in its favour, and provided that all funds due or to become due under the subcontract, constituted trust funds for the benefit of the surety. The court noted that the aim of prompt payment and adjudication, to ensure that funds flow down the construction pyramid, was not defeated by upholding a surety's security interest, as the surety regime ensures that progress continues on construction projects, and that downstream subcontractors and workers are paid. If contractors were able to gain the benefit and protection of surety bonds to secure public contracts but were then permitted to circumvent their indemnity obligations when a claim is made, there could be a chilling effect on the willingness of bonding companies to provide surety bonds. Neither Part XI and Part XI.1 of the Act gave a contractor priority over a surety's security interest where there was a determination in the subcontractor's favour.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
13.23:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 13.23.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">13.23:2</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As of October 1, 2019, the Act will provide for targeted, interim adjudication.</para.text></para><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Adjudication must be conducted in accordance with the adjudication procedures set out in the Act and the regulations</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Adjudication procedures set out in a contract or subcontract apply only to the extent that they do not conflict with the Act and the regulations</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Act sets out minimums for adjudication. The parties may agree to more, but the statutory minimums must be met</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Adjudication in the form introduced in Ontario is designed to tackle discrete issues with respect to the following matters:</para.text></para><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The valuation of services or materials provided under the contract.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Payment under the contract, including in respect of a change order, whether approved or not, or a proposed change order.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Disputes that are the subject of a notice of non-payment under Part I.1.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Amounts retained under section 12 (set-off by trustee) or under subsection 17(3) (lien set-off).</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Payment of a holdback under section 26.1 or 26.2.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Non-payment of holdback under section 27.1.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Any other matter that the parties to the adjudication agree to, or that may be prescribed</para.text></para></list.item></list></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Trigger for obligation to pay under new prompt payment regime is delivery of a “proper invoice”</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Adjudicator's determination is binding on an <ital>interim</ital> basis.</para.text></para><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Determination is binding on the parties to the adjudication until a determination of the matter by a court, a determination of the matter by way of an arbitration conducted under the <ital>Arbitration Act, 1991</ital>, or a written agreement between the parties respecting the matter.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Nothing in the Act prevents a party from commencing proceedings in court or before an arbitrator to finally determine the matter at any time. All the Act does is to keep the money flowing while that process takes place</para.text></para></list.item></list></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Adjudicators' determinations are enforceable as an order of the court.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">There is no need to go to court to obtain judgment on a determination; the determination is akin to a judgment, albeit an <ital>interim</ital> one.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See <ital>Conduct of Lien, Trust and Adjudication Proceedings</ital>, chapter 10.</para.text></para></list.item></list></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
