C.30, s. 14.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">14:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The legislation which created the construction lien in Ontario, <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27, s. 1 stated:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Every mechanic, machinist, builder, miner, contractor, and other person doing work upon, or furnishing materials to be used in the construction, alteration or repair of any building or erection, or erecting, furnishing or placing machinery of any kind, in, upon, or in connection with any building, erection, or mine at the instance or request of the owner thereof, and upon credit given to him, shall have a lien or charge, unless there is an express agreement to the contrary, for the price or value of such work, materials or machinery upon such building or erection, and the land occupied thereby, and usually enjoyed therewith, subject to the provisions of this Act, and limited to the estate or interest in such land of the person at whose request, and upon whose credit such work is done, materials furnished, or machinery erected, and limited to such amount as shall be justly due to the person entitled to such lien.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section was amended by <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1874</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.), to expand the concept of the lien to include “Labourer”. The enactment of this lien legislation was not without its detractors. In 1876 an unattributed article published at (1876), 12 <ital>Canada Law Journal</ital> 300, referred to the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> as “that most absurd and hurtful of all illogical legislation”. A year later another unattributed article published at (1877), 13 <ital>Canada Law Journal</ital> 8, states:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The enactment is in itself unnecessary and illogical, the wording is obscure and its provisions unintelligible and contradictory.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">By 1897, specific categories of potential lien claimants were replaced by the words “any person” (<ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153). There were several alterations to the language of this section over time, including listing types of improvements, but the essence of the section remained unchanged until the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The present version is identical to the 1983 version. The definitions in the Provincial and Territorial legislation differ in detail and wording, but essentially conform to the Ontario definition.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This much litigated section creates the lien remedy. The key words used to create the lien are defined by statute. It is important to note that the lien remedy arises upon the mere supply of lienable services or materials. A lien that has arisen but is not yet preserved is often referred to as a “subsisting lien”. The lien is a purely statutory creation, and does not exist at common law. Efforts in Ontario to establish a lien in equity have been unsuccessful.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">While interest on a debt may be claimed by personal action against the defaulter, there is no lien for interest (s. 14(2)). Interest itself does not increase the inherent value or “price” or services or materials supplied to an improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">While s. 14(2) provides that there is no lien for interest, the subsection preserves the right to recover interest in a personal judgment, which may be obtained against the defaulting payor in the lien action. The Court may refer to the interest provisions of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> to determine the amount of, and entitlement to, interest in a lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The key words used to create a lien itself, namely “services or materials”; “supply of services”; “materials”; “improvement”; “owner”; “contractor”; “subcontractor”; “interest … in the premises”; and “price”, are all terms defined in s. 1(1) of the Act. The word “person” is not specifically defined in the Act, but includes “contractor”, “subcontractor” and “worker”. The definition of “contractor” and “subcontractor” also include material suppliers and lessors of equipment either with or without operator. Certain design professionals, including architects, holders of certificates of practice under the <ital>Architects Act</ital>, and their employees under contract made on or after November 28, 1997 are also “persons” who may be entitled to a lien in some circumstances. It has been held under this section that construction managers are not “persons” that are entitled to a lien. The <ital>Interpretation Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.11 defines “person” in s. 29(1) to include “a corporation and the heirs, executors, administrators or other legal representatives of a person to whom the concept can apply according to law”. The “person” referred to in this section is only one who actually contracted to supply services or materials to the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It is important and often overlooked that liens arise upon the mere supply of lienable services or materials. A lien that has arisen but is not yet preserved is referred to as a “subsisting” lien.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
14:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 14.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">14:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chesney et al." p2="Malamis et al." post.rptr="3477" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8d9f4fa0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Chesney et al. v. Malamis et al.">Chesney et al. v. Malamis et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 3477, 2023 ONSC 1742 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs included either non-lienable services and materials or clearly inflated the value of other lienable services, such that the action was a lost profit/lost opportunity claim for equitable relief masquerading as a construction lien. In the result, the security posted in respect of the plaintiffs' lien was significantly reduced pursuant to s. 44(5)(b). <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="1353025 Ontario Inc." p2="Walden Group Canada Ltd." post.rptr="2583" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I90ca4830f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd.">1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2583, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, was distinguished in that there, the absence of cross-examinations in the face of conflicting affidavits as to the nature of the agreement and the consulting services allegedly provided by the lien claimant led to the court's dismissal of the defendant's motion to vacate the lien. In this case, in contrast, there were cross-examinations, where the plaintiffs were tested on their claims in the invoice and they gave undertakings to provide documentation and receipts in support of the disputed claims. However, no such documentation was provided. An affidavit based on information and belief that merely asserts on a conclusory basis the truth of the claim for the total lien amount cannot logically raise a triable issue as to the quantum of the lien. The plaintiffs offered no sworn evidence in support of their bald statement in court that there was an agreement that they would be paid their share of the total value of the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RJ Concrete" p2="Eco Depot LTD." post.rptr="1759" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63f6e1905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RJ Concrete v. Eco Depot LTD.">RJ Concrete v. Eco Depot LTD., 2022 ONSC 1759, 2022 CarswellOnt 3636 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved under s. 47 to discharge a lien and vacate the related claim for lien and certificate of action, on the basis that the claim for lien was an abuse of process and the amount of the lien was willfully exaggerated. The parties had agreed on a contract price, but the relationship broke down before the contract was completed. At issue was whether the amount of the lien should have been based on the actual market value of the services and materials provided or on the parties' agreement, or whether the claimant was entitled to register its lien based on the value the agreement attributed to the services and materials provided. The court concluded that the price of the services and materials provided, and therefore the amount of the lien, was to be measured with reference to the parties' agreement. It was evident both from the amount of the lien and communications between the parties that the lien was based on the full contract amount, less the amount paid by the plaintiff, rather than on the completed milestones set out in the contract. Although the plaintiff subsequently acknowledged the lien amount was inadvertently calculated at too high an amount, and had attempted to reduce the lien on consent, the lien was not wilfully exaggerated nor an abuse of process. The proper remedy was to reduce the amount of the lien pursuant to s. 35(2) to the amount determined by the court to be still outstanding.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Voutour" p2="MVG Investments Inc." post.rptr="1610" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I63f708a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Voutour v. MVG Investments Inc.">Voutour v. MVG Investments Inc., 2022 ONSC 1610, 2022 CarswellOnt 3246 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2022 CarswellOnt 7810 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There is nothing in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> that denies lien rights to those who supply services and materials to an improvement under an oral contract. An oral contract is as enforceable at law as a written contract. While the (ON) <ital>Statute of Frauds</ital> may apply on its face to construction liens arising from oral contracts and while the <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not expressly exclude the application of s. 4 of the <ital>Statute of Frauds</ital>, the <ital>Construction Act</ital> is of specific application to liens arising from construction work and construction contracts and is a complete code concerning construction liens. If s. 4 of the <ital>Statute of Frauds</ital> applied to construction liens, the effect would be to deprive those with oral construction contracts of the lien rights the <ital>Construction Act</ital> otherwise provided. The <ital>Construction Act</ital> as it applies to oral contracts is an exception to the s. 4 of the <ital>Statute of Frauds</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1140676 Ontario Inc." p2="2650997 Ontario Inc. et al" post.rptr="8176" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I63f708a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al">1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al, 2020 ONSC 8176, 2020 CarswellOnt 19368, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 352 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 143, 2021 CarswellOnt 89, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 359 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An agreement allowing the plaintiff to extract aggregate and wood from the defendant's land was not an agreement to improve the defendant's lands, and therefore not lienable. Any improvements to the defendant's lands were entirely incidental to the agreement, and while the defendant may have benefitted by the construction of a road on to the lands and the stripping back of topsoil to access aggregate, whatever construction was done was wholly for the benefit of the plaintiff's extraction operation. There was no payment made to the plaintiff, and the only consideration flowing from the agreement was payment to the defendant of a percentage of the sale proceeds of the material that was extracted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dominus Construction Corporation" p2="H&W Development Corp." post.rptr="20638" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63f708a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominus Construction Corporation v. H&W Development Corp.">Dominus Construction Corporation v. H&W Development Corp., 2019 CarswellOnt 20638, 2019 ONSC 7235 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff provided management services to the project, with the contract providing that the parties would share in any net savings on an equal basis. The cost savings were held to be lienable to the benefit of the plaintiff. Cost savings provisions are not analogous to profit-sharing provisions, but are integrally linked to the “service” provided for in s. 14, and the service is reflected in the contractor's proficiency in bringing a project to completion under budget. On the other hand, profit-sharing is a system in which the interested party receives a direct share of the profits realized, and were not lienable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sco-Terra" p2="The Corporation of the Town of Mono" post.rptr="669" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63f72fb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sco-Terra v. The Corporation of the Town of Mono">Sco-Terra v. The Corporation of the Town of Mono, 2019 ONSC 669, 2019 CarswellOnt 987, 97 C.L.R. (4th) 285 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CNL. Related proceeding. ONSC 1725, 2019 CarswellOnt 3953, 99 C.L.R. (4th) 90 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The liened land was partially developed, and included a residential development, vacant commercial lands, and other roadways and improvements. The plaintiff argued that the work it performed was for the benefit of the entire parcel of land. The plaintiff's own contractual agreements stated that the liened lands were excluded from its scope of work. If certain lands are excluded from the scope of work, it was not reasonable to then argue that those lands were improved by that work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HMI Construction Inc." p2="Index Energy Mills Road Corp." post.rptr="4075" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63f72fb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp.">HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp., 2017 ONSC 4075, 2017 CarswellOnt 10314, 81 C.L.R. (4th) 88 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In a fixed price context, a contractor cannot include in a claim for lien extra charges beyond the stipulated price without a proper breakdown of expenses. The contractor had simply liened for its project costs and added profit, but had not provided an itemized claim showing (i) contract accounting plus (ii) extras (with amounts claimed for each extra, including the basis on which those claims were calculated), less (iii) credits for contract work not done, and less (iv) acknowledged deficiencies (if any), plus (v) any other claims (such as delay costs). Instead, it provided an accounting of its total costs for the project. That, the court held, completely ignored the nature of the contract. Applied to a fixed price contract, therefore, the statement in <ital>Biotechnik</ital> that resort to <ital>quantum meruit</ital> was necessary to recover “the actual value of the work done” does not mean actual cost of the work done, but rather value as measured by the contract between contractual performance milestones.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chijindu" p2="2153801 Ontario" post.rptr="638" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63f72fb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Chijindu v. 2153801 Ontario">Chijindu v. 2153801 Ontario, 2017 ONSC 638, 2017 CarswellOnt 966, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 248 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 14 entitles a person who provides services or materials to an improvement to a lien on the owner's interest in the premises. The appellants argued that the use of the word “person” in s. 14 meant that only the principal of the numbered company was entitled to the lien, and not the numbered company itself, as the company was not a “person”. The judge found that the word “person” in s. 14 includes a corporation. Section 87 of the <ital>Legislation Act</ital>, S.O. 2006 c. 21 schedule F states that “person” includes a corporation unless the context requires otherwise. The regime created under the Act, and its <ital>raison d'être</ital>, do not support a narrow reading of the section that would exclude corporations. The numbered corporation was a “person” for the purposes of the Act and s. 14 applied. As such, the respondent had properly preserved and perfected its lien under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="N.K.P. Painting" p2="Burnac Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="6902" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63f72fb35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="N.K.P. Painting v. Burnac Holdings Ltd.">N.K.P. Painting v. Burnac Holdings Ltd., 2010 ONSC 6902, 2010 CarswellOnt 9568, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 116 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the contract between an owner and a contractor predates condominium registration by which the parcel register is divided into multiple parcels, but the claim for lien is registered after condominium registration, the contractor is not precluded from claiming a lien against some or all of the units retained by the owner for all of the services and materials supplied under the contract, including services and materials supplied to units already conveyed to individual unit purchasers. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: As the Master found the lien to be out of time and therefore invalid, the above finding was obiter to the judgment.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="SIPGP No. 1 Inc." p2="Eastern Construction Co." post.rptr="2414" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63f756c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="SIPGP No. 1 Inc. v. Eastern Construction Co.">SIPGP No. 1 Inc. v. Eastern Construction Co., 2010 CarswellOnt 2414 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 2962, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 284 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—While a limited partnership cannot register a claim for lien on title, the general partner can. The authority of a general partner to act for a partnership is defined by the limited partnership agreement, and there was no evidence here that the general partner did not in its own name have authority to carry out the subcontract and to register the claim for lien under the limited partnership agreement. The burden of proof in that respect was on the defendants and they adduced no evidence as to the ambit of the limited partnership agreement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Surnoskie" p2="Soderberg" post.rptr="8582" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63f756c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Surnoskie v. Soderberg">Surnoskie v. Soderberg (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 8582 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 1965 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The litigation involved a dispute as to the ownership and management of an apartment building. Despite having a counterclaim in the action, the defendant registered a claim for lien against the title to the apartment building and then commenced an action by statement of claim. The defendant, who claimed to be 50 per cent shareholder of the company, was held not to have a lienable claim. A party could not be a lien claimant, a plaintiff, and also a defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="1353025 Ontario Inc." p2="Walden Group Canada Ltd." post.rptr="2583" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I90cb59a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd.">1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2583, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The issue of whether a claimant was entitled to a lien as the result of the provision of financial consulting services for the purpose of preparation, presentation and liaison with brokers and lenders in order to obtain a construction loan should be decided at trial and not on motion for an order vacating the claim for lien. Though on the facts of the case the judge tended towards a view that the type of services rendered should not be entitled to lien, the appropriate place for decision was at trial, where the truth and reliability of the allegations can be tested for trustworthiness and the witnesses' credibility might be properly evaluated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="940691 Ontario Inc." p2="Philip Services Inc." post.rptr="204" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63f77dd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="940691 Ontario Inc. v. Philip Services Inc.">940691 Ontario Inc. v. Philip Services Inc. (2006), 50 C.L.R. (3d) 204, 2006 CarswellOnt 2046 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 7061, 59 C.L.R. (3d) 223 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where the services performed consist only of the transportation of waste materials from various construction sites to designated transfer stations, and where a claimant performs no other services on the site or in respect of the activities taking place there, the services are not lienable pursuant to s. 14 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Biotechnik Inc." p2="O'Shanter Development Co." post.rptr="4691" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I63f77dd15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co.">Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 4691, 15 C.L.R. (3d) 283 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 5713, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 45 (Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 5714, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 49 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Defendant moved under R. 21 to determine as a question of law whether a lien claim could be maintained where it was based on <ital>quantum meruit</ital>. The motions Judge had held that it could not and that plaintiff had to continue the action as a breach of contract case. In the Divisional Court, defendant attempted to distinguish the Supreme Court of Canada decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Alkok" p2="Grymek" post.rptr="452" pre.rptr="[1968]" ref.id="I63f77dd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alkok v. Grymek">Alkok v. Grymek, [1968] S.C.R. 452</ref></cite>, which had allowed a lien claim based on <ital>quantum meruit</ital> where payment was based on architect's certificates and the contract had been terminated between two certificates. Defendant argued that the contract in <ital>Biotechnik</ital> was a fixed price, performance based contract, and that in such circumstances, there could be no <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim for work already done. The Divisional Court disagreed and held that it was far from plain and obvious that plaintiff could not succeed in its lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Graham Mining Ltd." p2="Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc." post.rptr="291" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I63f77dd35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc.">Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc. (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 291 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 3774 (Div. Ct.); affirmed in the Court of Appeal at (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 1549, 2002 CarswellOnt 1502 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—This case concerned an attempt to lien a limited partnership's contingent future interest in a provincial water power lease. A reading of the definition sections of the Act, together with a reading of s. 76, supports the conclusion that the interest of an owner which is lienable by virtue of s. 14 of the Act is, has always been and will remain an “interest in land”. An interest in personalty, or an interest in an improvement by itself without an attached “interest in land” cannot constitute a lienable interest. The long standing authority to this effect of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pankka" p2="Butchart" post.rptr="837" pre.rptr="[1956]" ref.id="I63f77dd45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pankka v. Butchart">Pankka v. Butchart, [1956] O.R. 837 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, decided under the former <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>, remains good law, as does the authority of the Divisional Court decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63f7a4e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, decided under the present <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Stucor Construction Ltd." p2="Brock University" post.rptr="3678" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I90cba7c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Stucor Construction Ltd. v. Brock University">Stucor Construction Ltd. v. Brock University (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 3678, 13 C.L.R. (3d) 201, [2001] O.J. No. 4060 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2001 CarswellOnt 4601 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A lien does not secure general damages suffered as a result of a tort or breach of contract since such a recovery does not form part of the “price” of the services and materials supplied to the improvement. However, damages which can be equated to compensation for the value of supply of services or materials to an improvement may support a lien. Here, the plaintiff delivered a demand for monies owing over and above the contract price as a result of alleged construction delays. In its demand, the plaintiff described its own claim as a delay claim and sought a “lump sum claim for all additional costs incurred due to the delays throughout the progress of construction”. Even where the plaintiff itself had characterized its claim as being partly for damages, if its allegations regarding the owner's delay were found to be valid, and its claim was subsequently determined to have added value to the improvement, then the lien was enforceable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90cba7c1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A lien claim is a right to claim security in a property or a fund. A construction lien is a creature of statute. The lien attaches to the interest of the owner in the premises improved by the claimant's work or material. The premises thereby become a term of security for payment of the debt owing by the owner to the claimant. In this context, it must be remembered that, because of the duties imposed by the C.L.A., there may be “debts” owed to a lien claimant by various levels of the construction pyramid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1979" p1="K-Line Maintenance & Construction Ltd." p2="Toronto (Metropolitan)" post.rptr="210" pre.rptr="1979" ref.id="I63f7cbf15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K-Line Maintenance & Construction Ltd. v. Toronto (Metropolitan)">K-Line Maintenance & Construction Ltd. v. Toronto (Metropolitan) (1979), 1979 CarswellOnt 210, 30 C.B.R. (N.S.) 261 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varied (1980), 1980 CarswellOnt 1383, 116 D.L.R. (3d) 566 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In a classic and still authoritative case decided under the former <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, a contractor argued that it was entitled to be paid money in addition to the contract price, because of delays caused by the owner. The classic case on such claims generally is <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1974" p1="Marentette Brothers Ltd." p2="Sudbury (City)" post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I63f7cbf25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Marentette Brothers Ltd. v. Sudbury (City)">Marentette Brothers Ltd. v. Sudbury (City) (1974), 3 O.R. (2d) 305, 1974 CarswellOnt 808 (C.A.)</ref></cite>. The question in <ital>K-Line</ital> was whether such a claim was properly included in a lien claim. The Court held that it was. The claim in question in that particular case could properly be described as a claim for the “value of work done, services performed and material supplied”. As a result, the earlier decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1973" p1="Alros Products Ltd." p2="Dalecore Construction Ltd." post.rptr="312" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I63f7cbf35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alros Products Ltd. v. Dalecore Construction Ltd.">Alros Products Ltd. v. Dalecore Construction Ltd. (1973), 2 O.R. (2d) 312, 1973 CarswellOnt 908 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> must be read and applied carefully. See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Power Contracting Inc." p2="Deemar Investments Ltd." post.rptr="119" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I63f7cbf45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Power Contracting Inc. v. Deemar Investments Ltd.">Power Contracting Inc. v. Deemar Investments Ltd. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 119, 1992 CarswellOnt 875 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
14:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 14.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">14:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 14(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Walsh Construction" p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="7974" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I674873a03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Walsh Construction v. Toronto Transit Commission">Walsh Construction v. Toronto Transit Commission, 2024 CarswellOnt 7974, 2024 ONSC 2782, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2772 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant transit commission (“TTC”) and plaintiff entered into a contract for the construction of a subway station. At the conclusion of the trial of the action, the court found, inter alia, that the plaintiff was entitled to a lien against the estate, title and interest of the TTC, the City of Toronto, the Regional Municipality of York, and York University in the lands and premises upon which the Project was constructed. Work was done and materials supplied by the plaintiff for the TTC, making the latter an owner under the Act. While the City of Toronto, the Regional Municipality of York and York University did not have a contract with the plaintiff, they were also owners under the Act as they benefitted from the work and materials and all had an estate or interest in the premises. The court rejected the argument that York University was no longer an owner of the lands because following registration of the claim for lien, certain lands had their PINs (Property Identifier Numbers) changed. When the claim for lien was registered against the lands identified in the Certificate of Substantial Performance issued by the TTC, the Certificate included lands then owned by York University. An <ital>ex post facto</ital> reshuffling of ownership of lands, through the registration of different PINs, did not absolve a one-time owner of liability for a lien claim. Leaving aside the question of whether this was an effective remedy and whether there was a market for the sale of a used subway station, it was an appropriate remedy where there was a valid lien on title.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DNR Restoration Inc." p2="Trac Developments Inc." post.rptr="3680" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8da06110ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc.">DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 3680, 2023 ONSC 1849 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It is well established that “pure construction managers” who provide only services, have lien rights along with all the other parties who provide services and materials to the improvement. In so concluding the Associate Justice relied on <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc." p2="Project 801 Inc." post.rptr="4169" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8da06111ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc.">B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc., 2011 ONSC 4169 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> at para. 25, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20020529" p1="Marino" p2="Bay-Walsh Ltd." post.rptr="2211" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I8da06112ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd.">Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd. (May 29, 2002), Zelinski J., [2002] O.J. No. 2211 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> at para. 111. If construction managers with contracts with the owner, such as here, have lien rights, they surely are “contractors” with “contracts” for the purpose of section 87.3(1)(a). [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: A distinction may be drawn between construction management services provided pre-construction, and those provided during construction. See for example <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tamma Construction Co." p2="Brault" post.rptr="953" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90cbf5e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault">Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 953, 25 O.R. (3d) 472, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 124 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, in which pre-construction services were found to be non-lienable. <ital>Tamma</ital> was differentiated on that ground in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc." p2="Project 801 Inc." post.rptr="4169" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8da08821ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc.">B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc., 2011 ONSC 4169 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. In <ital>Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd.,</ital> the court differentiated the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90cc1cf0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 69 O.R. (2d) 334, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, on the basis that on the facts of that case, the offsite, non-construction related services in question were not “related to the improvement”.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd." p2="Edge on Triangle Park Inc." post.rptr="783" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63f7f3005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Edge on Triangle Park Inc.">Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Edge on Triangle Park Inc., 2017 ONSC 783, 2017 CarswellOnt 1080, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 265 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2016 ONSC 5461, 2016 CarswellOnt 13669, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 256 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 ONSC 7012, 2016 CarswellOnt 18025, 73 C.L.R. (4th) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant was owed monies for goods and services supplied to the defendant's condominium project. The respondent was also owed monies for goods and services supplied to the project, and when the condominium was registered, purchased 2 units in satisfaction of the debt. At the time of closing, the respondent had no knowledge or notice of the lien claim. Subsequently, the claimant registered a claim for lien against various units in the building, including those owned by the respondent, with the last day of work listed as after the respondent's purchase. The statement of claim did not list the respondent as a defendant. The respondent's motion under s. 47 to discharge the claim for lien and certificate of action as against its units was granted. It was not an “owner” because it did not contract with the claimant for the supply of goods and services to its units, nor were improvements made to the premises on its credit, with its privity or consent, or for its direct benefit. The contract was with the defendant owner, and it was entered into before the respondent became an owner of the units and before the condominium was registered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2283624 Ontario Limited" p2="Performance Painting & Floor Coating Ltd." post.rptr="2553" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63f7f3015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2283624 Ontario Limited v. Performance Painting & Floor Coating Ltd.">2283624 Ontario Limited v. Performance Painting & Floor Coating Ltd., 2017 ONSC 2553, 2017 CarswellOnt 11230 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2017 ONSC 4010, 2017 CarswellOnt 11229, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 345 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the parties were never <ital>ad idem</ital> on the issue of a contract to rent certain painting equipment, it was in no way a proper matter for the filing of a construction lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Const. Inc." p2="Unimac-United Mgmt. Corp." post.rptr="4491" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63f7f3025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Const. Inc. v. Unimac-United Mgmt. Corp.">Trenchline Const. Inc. v. Unimac-United Mgmt. Corp., 2017 ONSC 4491, 2017 CarswellOnt 11632, 82 C.L.R. (4th) 127 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 975, 2018 CarswellOnt 2089, 82 C.L.R. (4th) 141 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the subcontractor's seven claims for “stand-by charges” were recoverable in the lien action and/or in the bond action. Over the course of the project, there were myriad delays which the contractor blamed on the owner. The subcontractor claimed recovery for standby costs from the contractor. The master declined to review any arguments on standby costs and lien rights, as the subcontractor failed to prove the alleged standby costs. Standby costs must be proven as a pre-condition to lien entitlement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Toronto Dominion Bank" p2="450477 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4908" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63f81a105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Dominion Bank v. 450477 Ontario Ltd.">Toronto Dominion Bank v. 450477 Ontario Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4908, 2016 CarswellOnt 12434, 65 C.L.R. (4th) 329 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—Repair materials and services, including giant tire repair and replacement services, were held to be lienable where the construction parties, particularly the owner, considered the subject services necessary for the completion of the project and where the services benefitted the majority of the contractors and subcontractors. Reference to the <ital>Ontario Repair and Storage Liens Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. R.25 (“<ital>RSLA</ital>”) did not automatically take repair services and equipment out of the ambit of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The <ital>RSLA</ital> and the <ital>CLA</ital> contemplate the co-existence of rights under those two statutes for the supply of repair services and materials that have a close nexus with a construction project. Only the assertion of rights for unpaid repair services and materials under the <ital>RSLA</ital>, either by way of possessory or non-possessory claims, would amount to an election not to proceed under the <ital>CLA</ital> that the court should enforce. This election applies only to those repaired articles against which the claimant has actually asserted its <ital>RSLA</ital> possessory or non-possessory claims, not to the other articles, despite the fact that these other articles have been supplied under the same contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Toronto Zenith Contracting Ltd." p2="Fermar Paving Ltd." post.rptr="4696" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63f81a115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Zenith Contracting Ltd. v. Fermar Paving Ltd.">Toronto Zenith Contracting Ltd. v. Fermar Paving Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4696, 2016 CarswellOnt 11566, 66 C.L.R. (4th) 278 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The offsite work performed by the plaintiff during the winter shut-down period, which was intended to become part of the improvement, was held to be lienable. This work included: submission of documentation and shop drawings; use of the temporary shoring system which had been installed by the plaintiff's subcontractor to shore and support roadways; communications for the purposes of preparing shop drawings for the shoring system; concrete forms installed earlier which were eventually used when concrete was poured; rubber bearings manufactured earlier and picked up by the contractor during the shut-down; ongoing communications between representatives of the contractor and representatives of the plaintiff regarding the latter's ongoing responsibilities.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Selectra Inc." p2="Penetanguishene (Town)" post.rptr="2293" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63f841205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Selectra Inc. v. Penetanguishene (Town)">Selectra Inc. v. Penetanguishene (Town), 2016 ONSC 2293, 2016 CarswellOnt 5132, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 335 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 8195 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A lien is limited to the amount a contractor is owed. If there is a fixed price contract, in the absence of approved change orders, the contractor cannot include in its claim for lien extra labour or materials charges for work described in the fixed price contract simply because those costs were more than usual or anticipated when the fixed price contract (or change orders) were agreed to. Some amount of risk of a cost escalation is assumed by the contractor. Expenses incurred with respect to the purchase and repair of equipment that is not for the exclusive use of the subject property and merely adds to or maintains a person's equipment to be used by that person on future projects is also not lienable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="U.S. Steel Canada Inc., Re" post.rptr="12275" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63f841215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="U.S. Steel Canada Inc., Re">U.S. Steel Canada Inc., Re, 2016 CarswellOnt 12275 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the materials and services provided were provided to an “improvement” within the definition of the Act, and whether they could therefore be the subject of a lien. The court found the following to be lienable supply of goods or services to an improvement: (i) supply and installation of garden soil and 15 flower plants (if intended to alter and/or add to the land by planting flowers the nursery's supply of flowers would amount to a supply of materials for the improvement and give rise to a lien in no different manner than the supply of lumber for the construction of a building on the land); (ii) labour and material to spray for vegetation control; (iii) labour and material to remove vegetation inside compounds, remove and clean dirt and debris and install landscape cloth and spread gravel; (iv) grounds keeping (the court differentiated a service such as snow ploughing, and addressing vegetation and accumulation of dirt. Although snow would melt of its own accord, vegetation and dirt would not). [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I90cc6b10f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 138 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3385 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3338, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 5 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5779, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5521, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, under s. 1(1) “Improvement”.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Structform International Ltd." p2="Ashcroft Homes Construction Inc." post.rptr="4544" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63f841235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structform International Ltd. v. Ashcroft Homes Construction Inc.">Structform International Ltd. v. Ashcroft Homes Construction Inc., 2013 ONSC 4544, 2013 CarswellOnt 9208, 26 C.L.R. (4th) 13 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 14280 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Not all aspects of a delay claim may be lienable. To properly be the subject of a lien, the claim must be reflective of the value of the work done on the improvement. It must come within the definition of “services or materials supplied to the improvement” and is limited to the “amount owing to the lien claimant in relation to the improvement”. Additional expenses incurred because the project takes longer than anticipated such as labour costs, equipment rental and similar costs of remaining on the job will form the basis for a valid lien. Damages at large, however, such as lost opportunity costs, loss of profits or aggravated damages will not. Additional costs incurred offsite such as administrative overhead or lost profit and even onsite office overhead costs are not lienable. If a portion of the lien claim is attributable to damages that properly the subject of a lien, then the security should be reduced to take that into account.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Butko" p2="Ratayeva" post.rptr="1102" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63f868305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Butko v. Ratayeva">Butko v. Ratayeva, 2015 ONSC 1102, 2015 CarswellOnt 8388, 47 C.L.R. (4th) 344 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Loaning money is not a lienable claim under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Luxterior Design Corp." p2="Gelfand" post.rptr="6539" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63f868315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Luxterior Design Corp. v. Gelfand">Luxterior Design Corp. v. Gelfand, 2014 ONSC 6539, 2014 CarswellOnt 15921, 39 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 CarswellOnt 18880, 39 C.L.R. (4th) 62 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Lien rights do not encompass price for services and materials not supplied. This is one feature that distinguishes lien claims from contract damages claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prochazka" p2="44 Bond Street West Development Inc." post.rptr="3678" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63f88f405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Prochazka v. 44 Bond Street West Development Inc.">Prochazka v. 44 Bond Street West Development Inc., 2014 ONSC 3678, 2014 CarswellOnt 8159, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 131 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contractor contracted with the plaintiff's numbered company for drywall services in respect of the project, but the plaintiff brought the lien action in his personal capacity. The plaintiff's characterization of the contract as being made between himself personally and the contractor was nothing more than a failed attempt to circumvent the contractual obligations to pay union dues binding on his numbered company. Accordingly, the plaintiff was not the proper party to claim the lien and issue the claim. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Bayan Construction Ltd." p2="Cusimano" post.rptr="2210" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I90cc9220f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Bayan Construction Ltd. v. Cusimano">Bayan Construction Ltd. v. Cusimano (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2210, 70 C.L.R. (3d) 123 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, discussed under s. 6, <ital>supra</ital>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd." p2="OHL Construction Canada" post.rptr="7505" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63f88f425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada">Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada, 2013 ONSC 7505, 2013 CarswellOnt 18456, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 213 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 3763, 2014 CarswellOnt 8361, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 223 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—TTC contracted for construction services related to a subway extension to York University. OHL subcontracted with ACT to provide excavation monitoring and ground support for a building under which the extension was being constructed. Documentation noted that on completion, TTC would own, operate, and maintain the new subway line, although the university was the only owner or relevant entity registered on title with respect to any interest in the land. The university granted a temporary construction licence to permit TTC and its agents to enter upon the university lands to carry out their subway construction activities, including the compensation grouting for building support and excavation monitoring work. The licence did not constitute any form of property interest in, or gift or dedication of, university lands. After being ordered off the site following the collapse of a drilling rig, ACT claimed against OHL for delay due to unforeseen or changed soil conditions, improper termination of the contract, and loss of profit. ACT, along with another claimant, brought lien actions for monies alleged owing and to assert security against title, and in its statement of claim alleged that YU was an “owner” within the meaning of the Act. It gave a copy of its lien only to various university officials. OHL obtained an order vacating the registration of the claim for lien upon the posting of security. It then moved to have the lien discharged and the lien action dismissed, <ital>inter alia</ital>, on the basis that neither TTC nor YU were owners as contemplated by s. 14, and hence no lien rights arose. It argued that since TTC, not YU, requested the work in issue, and that as TTC did not have any property interest in the YU lands, was not named as an “owner” in ACT's lien claim, and was not named as a defendant in ACT's Statement of Claim, no enforceable lien rights were available to ACT. In holding that YU was in fact an “owner” the Master found that the object of the construction was to establish a subway station for YU, and ACT's work was done to protect a university building from damage or collapse during excavation operations. As per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1976" p1="Cipriani" p2="Hamilton (City)" post.rptr="409" pre.rptr="1976" ref.id="I63f88f435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cipriani v. Hamilton (City)">Cipriani v. Hamilton (City) (1976), 1976 CarswellOnt 409, 1976 CarswellOnt 409F, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 169 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, an owner's request that the improvement to the property be made, may be by express request or implied by the conduct of the owner; direct dealings between the owner and the contractor are not required. There was no question that YU had an interest in the lands improved, and a sufficient “request” by the owner of the subject lands had been established.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bradhill Masonry Inc." p2="Simcoe County District School Board" post.rptr="4708" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63f88f445fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bradhill Masonry Inc. v. Simcoe County District School Board">Bradhill Masonry Inc. v. Simcoe County District School Board, 2013 ONSC 4708, 2013 CarswellOnt 9684, 24 C.L.R. (4th) 253 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 12638, 24 C.L.R. (4th) 277 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2015 CarswellOnt 8852, 47 C.L.R. (4th) 300 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—When a sub-trade has done work for which it had not been paid, it has a potential lien for “the price of those services or material” under s. 14 of the Act, regardless if whether, under a technical interpretation of the contract, nothing was owing and payable to the sub-trade as of the date the lien was registered. To hold otherwise would mean that the contract terms for the timing of payment would take precedence over the legislation, and that if a sub-trade filed a claim for lien at the wrong time, its lien would be worthless even though the tradesperson has not been fully paid for their work and materials supplied to the job.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Inside Outside Home Services Inc." p2="Einstein Design" post.rptr="1039" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63f8b6505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Inside Outside Home Services Inc. v. Einstein Design">Inside Outside Home Services Inc. v. Einstein Design, 2013 ONSC 1039, 2013 CarswellOnt 3056 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 5946 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant challenged whether the Act applied to leased premises, but, in the absence of evidence that the tenant was required to return the premises to the landlord in a base building condition, and given that the scope of the work performed by the plaintiff appeared to be an “improvement” to the property within the meaning of the Act, the lien was found to be valid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vanezi" p2="1648380 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4878" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63f8b6515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vanezi v. 1648380 Ontario Inc.">Vanezi v. 1648380 Ontario Inc., 2011 ONSC 4878, 2011 CarswellOnt 9449 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Following the approach in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Metron Construction Inc." p2="Belleville Racetrack Development Corp." post.rptr="987" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63f8b6525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Metron Construction Inc. v. Belleville Racetrack Development Corp.">Metron Construction Inc. v. Belleville Racetrack Development Corp., 2011 ONSC 987, 2011 CarswellOnt 1716, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 26 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 3212, 1 C.L.R. (4th) 181 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, it was arguable and therefore a triable issue whether or not the services performed by the plaintiff were capable of supporting a lien. Here, the plaintiff oversaw the construction of eight additional apartments in the defendant's building over a five-year period, although the defendant paid for the project. The plaintiff's work included obtaining city approval, hiring and supervising trades, hiring and supervising day labour, ordering and in some cases picking up materials and delivering them to the site and attending at the site on an almost daily basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gokdenz Construction Ltd." p2="Dalakis" post.rptr="7135" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63f8dd605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gokdenz Construction Ltd. v. Dalakis">Gokdenz Construction Ltd. v. Dalakis, 2011 ONSC 7135, 2011 CarswellOnt 13395 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the lien was registered by a corporate entity that had no contractual relationship with the property owner, and services and materials were supplied by the individual plaintiff, the construction lien was held not to be preserved or perfected as required by the Act by the party entitled to claim a lien. On that basis it was discharged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc." p2="Project 801 Inc." post.rptr="4169" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63f8dd615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc.">B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc., 2011 ONSC 4169, 2011 CarswellOnt 6581, 6 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Construction management services are lienable with respect to the construction phase of a project (as opposed to the pre-construction phase), if, on the facts, they fall within the parameters of s. 14. Div.)</ref></cite>—Certain sprinkler, plumbing and structural design work done by a contractor did not in themselves benefit the land and therefore liens could not be claimed in respect of them. However, landscaping plans that were site specific and not dependent on a specific structure which might be built were lienable items.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Oaks Precast" p2="G.L. Trenching Ltd." post.rptr="312" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I63fa15e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oaks Precast v. G.L. Trenching Ltd.">Oaks Precast v. G.L. Trenching Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 312 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplier provided materials to the defendant's construction site on an ongoing basis. The court found that a continuing contract for the duration of the project existed where: there was no written agreement setting out any terms prior to individual orders being made; credit terms were established and payments monitored to ensure that the credit was never exceeded; payments were made monthly or more frequently if the credit limit had to be paid down; a delivery ticket was generated for each delivery followed by an invoice; the price was established according to the price list prepared by the supplier for the project and the defendants did not inquire about a new price with each order; the defendant ordered supplies on an as-needed basis; all of the materials were supplied to the project site; the last delivery coincided with the completion by the defendant of its work at the site.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Trans Eastern Lumber Corp." p2="Kingston Municipal Non-Profit Housing Corp." post.rptr="230" pre.rptr="26" ref.id="I63fa15e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trans Eastern Lumber Corp. v. Kingston Municipal Non-Profit Housing Corp.">Trans Eastern Lumber Corp. v. Kingston Municipal Non-Profit Housing Corp. (1996), 26 C.L.R. (2d) 230, 27 O.R. (3d) 84 (Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 1511 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant worked on 15 projects and received unallocated lump sum payments until the payor became insolvent. The lien claimant relied upon the rule in <ital>Clayton's Case</ital> to allocate payments so as to maximize the amount of its one remaining lien. This was disallowed. The rule in <ital>Clayton's Case</ital> is supplanted by the trust provisions of Part II of the <ital>Act</ital>. In the absence of any compelling evidence to the contrary, the court exercised its discretion to allocate on a rateable basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Southdale Towers Ltd." p2="Carlton Management Group Inc." post.rptr="233" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I63fa3cf05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southdale Towers Ltd. v. Carlton Management Group Inc.">Southdale Towers Ltd. v. Carlton Management Group Inc. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 233 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The applicant and the respondent entered into a property management contract pursuant to which the applicant authorized the respondent to lease, manage, repair and maintain the respondent's premises, and appointed the respondent “a sole and exclusive agent.” The court, in dismissing a motion to vacate the respondent's registration of a claim for lien against the applicant's property, held that the respondent was a contractor within the meaning of the Act. The fact that the property management agreement between the applicant and the respondent provided that the respondent was the applicant's agent did not alter that fact. In fulfilling its maintenance obligations pursuant to the contract, the respondent supplied services or materials to an improvement as such term is defined in the Act, and was entitled to claim a lien for the price of those services and materials in accordance with s. 14. The respondent's supervision of repair work was also a service in respect of improving or repairing the premises and it was entitled to claim a lien for its fee related to such supervisory work. The respondent's services in renting units, enforcing leases and purchasing and supplying appliances for the units could not be categorized as the supply of services to an improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Smith & Smith Kingston Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="234" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63fa3cf15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Smith & Smith Kingston Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">Smith & Smith Kingston Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 234 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Whether or not a lien attaches on behalf of a surveyor depends on the particular facts and the nature of the actual work performed. The caselaw is clear that if the services performed relate to the actual improvement, then the lien attaches. If the nature of the work done by a surveyor is such that there is no improvement, then the lien would not attach. An example of the latter would be where a surveyor determines a boundary between two parties and does nothing more. In these cases, the services provided related directly to the lands to be liened and were not notional in nature. The work performed was for the direct purpose of enabling the owner to proceed with construction. All aspects of the plaintiff's work were directly related to the construction process, and the plaintiff was expected to do a complete job, which it did, and the full amount of the work done is what the court must consider.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc." p2="Denamer Homes Inc." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63fa3cf25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc.">L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The proposition that a “home buyer” has a responsibility to protect himself if a lien is registered before his conveyance is registered does not reflect the reality of the “home buyer” exemption in s. 14(1)—that it is the vendor/builder and not the “home buyer” who is financing the construction.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I63fa64005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 14 of the Act makes clear that a lien is upon the interest of the owner and, of course, this interest can be subject to the giving of a mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Big Creek Construction Ltd." p2="York-Trillium Development Group Ltd." post.rptr="285" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I63fa64015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd.">Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd. (1993), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 285, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 331 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 138 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the beneficial holders of a construction project were also the officers, directors, and controlling shareholders of the general contractor, which described itself as “owner” of the project in its dealings with the trades, but was not shown as a general contractor on any of the statutory declarations, it was inappropriate to allow liens to be placed on the property on behalf of that contractor. The identification was sufficiently close to run afoul of the concept that an owner cannot lien its own property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd." p2="Valley Ridge Inc." post.rptr="139" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I63fa64025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc.">M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc. (1993), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 139 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A security service could have a valid claim for lien, applying the reasoning of the Alberta Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1980" p1="Alberta Gas Ethylene Co. Ltd." p2="Noyle" post.rptr="179" pre.rptr="108" ref.id="I63fa64035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alberta Gas Ethylene Co. Ltd. v. Noyle">Alberta Gas Ethylene Co. Ltd. v. Noyle (1980), 108 D.L.R. (3d) 179 (Alta. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Barkey" p2="Maier" post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I63fa8b105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barkey v. Maier">Barkey v. Maier (1991), 46 C.L.R. 138 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A plaintiff's oral contract to provide construction services, and his right to claim a lien which arose from it, was not invalid merely because the plaintiff did not have a certificate under the provisions of the <ital>Apprenticeship and Tradesmen's Qualification Act</ital>. The plaintiff had retained the services of a qualified technician to do the electrical work and, in any event, the plaintiff had not acted in a capacity greater than a labourer. The plaintiff was not required to be certified to perform work as a lather or plasterer.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Favot Construction Ltd." p2="Maplecrest Developments Inc." post.rptr="34" pre.rptr="42" ref.id="I63fa8b115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Favot Construction Ltd. v. Maplecrest Developments Inc.">Favot Construction Ltd. v. Maplecrest Developments Inc. (1990), 42 C.L.R. 34 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—No distinction is made in this provision between services or materials supplied as part of a contract or as extras thereto.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd." p2="Villa Nova Construction Inc." post.rptr="227" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63fa8b125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc.">Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc. (1989), 33 C.L.R. 227, 1989 CarswellOnt 690 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The purchaser of a home in a new subdivision was a “home buyer” within the meaning of the Act and was excluded from the statutory definition of “owner”. At the time of closing, there was a preserved lien registered by P Ltd. on title, which the vendor's solicitor undertook to discharge. Before the solicitor was able to do this, P Ltd. registered another lien, contending that the second lien took priority over the conveyance by virtue of s. 80(1) of the Act. The purchaser successfully brought a motion to discharge and vacate P Ltd.'s claim for lien and certificate of action. Section 14 makes it plain that a lien is created when services or materials are supplied “to an improvement for an owner, contractor or subcontractor …” and since the purchaser was none of those listed in the section P Ltd. did not have a valid claim against her. The purchaser obtained title prior to the registration of P Ltd.'s lien claim and that title was free of any unregistered construction lien claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90ce8df0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 69 O.R. (2d) 334, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff performed construction management services for the defendant by making permit applications, negotiating with various building trades and assisting site supervisors, but did not do any site work at the property liened and did not superintend any of the construction at that project. The plaintiff's action was accordingly dismissed, as was the plaintiff's appeal. Section 14 of the Act determined whether a claim properly fell within the scope of the Act. Here, work performed by the plaintiff was not directly related to the construction of the improvement so as to entitle the plaintiff to a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tamma Construction Co." p2="Brault" post.rptr="953" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90ceb500f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault">Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 953, 25 O.R. (3d) 472, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 124 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—With respect to project management fees and site supervision fees, the cases cited by the defendants, namely, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I90ceb501f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 69 O.R. (2d) 334, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Franro Property Development Ltd." p2="Heritage Glen North Ltd." post.rptr="2572" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I63fab2235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Franro Property Development Ltd. v. Heritage Glen North Ltd.">Franro Property Development Ltd. v. Heritage Glen North Ltd., 1993 CarswellOnt 2572, Kirsh's C.L.C.F. 47.15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, establish that that aspect of the claim is not the proper subject of a lien claim. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20020529" p1="Marino" p2="Bay-Walsh Ltd." post.rptr="2211" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I63fab2245fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd.">Marino v. Bay-Walsh Ltd. (May 29, 2002), Doc. 98-0469, [2002] O.J. No. 2211 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc." p2="Project 801 Inc." post.rptr="4169" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63fab2255fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc.">B.I.L.D.O.N. Construction (801) Inc. v. Project 801 Inc., 2011 ONSC 4169, 2011 CarswellOnt 6581, 6 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, for a different view of the lienability of construction management services.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Paintronic Systems Inc." p2="Nova-Link Ltd." post.rptr="298" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I63fad9305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paintronic Systems Inc. v. Nova-Link Ltd.">Paintronic Systems Inc. v. Nova-Link Ltd. (1989), 43 C.L.R. 298 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant was a tenant that purchased an oven and air circulation unit from the plaintiff, which the plaintiff installed on the leasehold premises. The plaintiff registered a lien against the land on the basis that it had supplied services and materials to an improvement of the land. The defendant brought a motion to discharge the lien and vacate the certificate of action on the grounds that the items supplied by the plaintiff were movables rather than improvements and were not affixed to the realty. The defendant's motion was dismissed, as it was not patently demonstrable from the pleadings that no lien existed. In fact, the evidence appeared to indicate that the items supplied by the plaintiff were indeed improvements to the land for which a lien could be registered against. A determination of the exact nature of the materials supplied could only be made at trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="C. Battison & Sons Inc." p2="Mauti" post.rptr="298" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I63fad9315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="C. Battison & Sons Inc. v. Mauti">C. Battison & Sons Inc. v. Mauti (1986), 25 C.L.R. 298, 34 D.L.R. (4th) 700 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (1985), 50 O.R. (2d) 599, 11 C.L.R. 173 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—A general contractor, entered into an oral contract with the owner to perform certain works. The contractor was licensed under the provisions of the relevant by-law of the Municipality of Metropolitan Toronto, which required that all work done by a building renovator must be in accordance with a written contract. The Master held that the relevant section of the by-law was <ital>ultra vires</ital> and was severable from the balance of the by-law and therefore it did not invalidate the contract. On appeal, the General Division refused to confirm the Master's report, finding that the oral contract was unenforceable because of the illegality. The Divisional Court, in overruling the judge, found that the oral contract was enforceable and confirmed the report of the Master. The only sanction arising out of a breach of the by-law was the penalty set out by the by-law. The failure to place a contract in a particular or written form, that is otherwise enforceable, does not, by the wording of the by-law, render the contract unenforceable. The enabling legislation did not confer any such authority on the municipality. The modern approach to similar problems is that the court will not attribute a legislative intent to authorize a municipality to affect a contractual obligation for failure to contract in a particular form.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Co." p2="499812 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="306" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63fad9325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. 499812 Ontario Ltd.">Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. 499812 Ontario Ltd. (1985), 17 C.L.R. 306 <point>at 322</point> (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Delivery charges are lienable. The pertinent jurisprudence makes a distinction between a claim by a carrier for simple transport or delivery of goods of another, and the sale and delivery of the claimant's goods to the purchaser which are incorporated into buildings. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Oliver" p2="Muer Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63fb00405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd.">Oliver v. Muer Construction Ltd. (1985), 12 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Legal services performed by the plaintiff did not have the degree of <ital>nexus</ital> with an improvement required to fall within the scope of the definition of “supply of services”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Landis & Gyr Powers Ltd." p2="Megatech Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="3183" pre.rptr="1992" ref.id="I55ef9200fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Landis & Gyr Powers Ltd. v. Megatech Contracting Ltd.">Landis & Gyr Powers Ltd. v. Megatech Contracting Ltd. (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 3183 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—As a general principle, a lien does not include a claim for damages.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
