14:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 14.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">14:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 14(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="D'Urzo Demolition Inc." p2="Damaris Developments Inc." post.rptr="3938" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63fb00425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc.">D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc., 2012 ONSC 3938, 2012 CarswellOnt 8750, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 229 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Applying the decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Carter Tile Contractors Inc." p2="Ben-Zvi" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63fb27505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi">Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 61, 2005 CarswellOnt 6608 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the master applied security in the form of a letter of credit posted on behalf of the defendant in lieu of the property in satisfaction of the interest and costs ordered payable by the defendant. There was no reason to treat the security posted in the form of a letter of credit differently from security posted in the form of cash. It would not be unfair for the court to see to it that the defendant satisfy the court's award, including interest and costs, from monies in court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Carter Tile Contractors Inc." p2="Ben-Zvi" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I63fb27515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi">Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 61, 2005 CarswellOnt 6608 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—After recovery there was a surplus in the amount posted as security for the lien, but a deficiency in the amount owing for security for the costs. The master applied the surplus monies for the security for the lien to cover the deficiency in the security for the costs, leaving a small surplus which was applied to pre-judgment interest. The circumstances were distinguishable from <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd." p2="York Humber Ltd." post.rptr="185" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fb27525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd.">Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 185, 1994 CarswellOnt 944 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, because all the money was provided personally by the defendant to “bond off” the lien rather than by way of a bond of a bonding company or a bank letter of credit. It was not unfair for the court to see to it that the defendant's money in court was used to pay amounts the court had found to be owing by him to the plaintiff, including costs and interest in addition to the lien claim itself.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Tan-Jen Ltd." p2="Lax" post.rptr="2082" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I63fb27535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tan-Jen Ltd. v. Lax">Tan-Jen Ltd. v. Lax (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 2082, 2002 CarswellOnt 1733 (Master)</ref></cite>—Non-lienable prejudgment interest in a lien action ran from the date when the claim for lien was filed, which was when the cause of action arose, rather than from the date of the issuance of the statement of claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="James Dick Construction Ltd." p2="Durham Board of Education" post.rptr="308" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63fb27545fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education">James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education (2000), 50 O.R. (3d) 308, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 256 (Div. Ct.); affirming (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 36 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 14(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> denies a lien for interest on an amount owed for services or materials supplied. There is no merit in the argument that s. 14(2) does not address interest that would have accrued if a contractor had paid its holdback liability into court in the form of cash.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90cf5140f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A claimant cannot look to either the premises or to the bond which replaced them for satisfaction of a claim for interest. This was a case of a subcontractor's lien bonded off by a general contractor, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Barber-Colman of Canada Ltd." p2="Scarborough (City)" post.rptr="627" pre.rptr="[1987]" ref.id="I63fb4e615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barber-Colman of Canada Ltd. v. Scarborough (City)">Barber-Colman of Canada Ltd. v. Scarborough (City) (1987), [1987] O.J. No. 627</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd." p2="Roko Construction Ltd." post.rptr="268" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I90cf7850f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd.">M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 268, 26 O.R. (3d) 516 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Roboak Developments Ltd." p2="Lehndorff Corp." post.rptr="194" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I63fb4e635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Roboak Developments Ltd. v. Lehndorff Corp.">Roboak Developments Ltd. v. Lehndorff Corp. (1986), 39 R.P.R. 194 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite> are all considered and approved; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Francon" p2="L. Nicolini Construction Ltd." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63fb75705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Francon v. L. Nicolini Construction Ltd.">Francon v. L. Nicolini Construction Ltd. (1988), 33 C.L.R. 107, 1988 CarswellOnt 777 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite> is distinguished and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I63fb75715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> is over-ruled to the extent that it conflicts with this decision. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Northern Air" p2="York" post.rptr="201" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I63fb75725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northern Air v. York">Northern Air v. York (1985), 50 O.R. (2d) 201</ref></cite> is considered and confined to its facts. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd." p2="York Humber Ltd." post.rptr="185" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fb75735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd.">Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 185, 1994 CarswellOnt 944 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> is considered on the issue of costs, and approved. Note: for a re-evaluation of the decision in <ital>P & D Holdings</ital> and its effect on payments into and out of court, see: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd." p2="Roche Ltée" post.rptr="2851" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I55f00730fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée">M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2851, 39 C.L.R. (2d) 251 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd." p2="Roko Construction Ltd." post.rptr="268" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I90cf9f60f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd.">M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 268, 26 O.R. (3d) 516 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 14(2) does not prevent a claim for interest, it simply provides that the claimant has to pursue the claim otherwise than under the lien. Although interest accruing from the date of the registration of a lien could be recoverable as a personal judgment, it was not recoverable as a lienable claim. Therefore, a lien bond could be the source for only the allowable amount of the lien liability plus costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Smith & Smith Kingston Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="234" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63fb9c805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Smith & Smith Kingston Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">Smith & Smith Kingston Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 234 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the court's authority to award pre-judgment interest in a construction lien matter was disputed, the court ruled that s. 130 of the Ontario <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> reserves the court's discretion whether it will allow pre-judgment interest and discretion as to what rate of interest it will allow.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd." p2="York Humber Ltd." post.rptr="185" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fb9c815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd.">Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 185, 1994 CarswellOnt 944 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Interest is not a lienable claim pursuant to s. 14(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (Ont.).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63fb9c825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 14(2) of the Act states that a lien does not arise with respect to interest. In determining priority pursuant to s. 78(2) of the Act between lien claimants and a mortgagee, the lien claimants' right to interest did not have priority over the mortgagee, as s. 14 must govern. The lien claimants were entitled to their claim for interest against the owner, but not in priority to the mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I55f05550fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Interest should not be awarded to lien claimants on the holdback deficiency sum or the other lien priority sums in the same way that interest must accrue under a mortgage. This does not mean that lien claimants would not be entitled to judgment interest on sums owing to each by a defaulting general contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Ben Plastering Ltd." p2="Mollenhauer Residential Ltd." post.rptr="102" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I63fbc3915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ben Plastering Ltd. v. Mollenhauer Residential Ltd.">Ben Plastering Ltd. v. Mollenhauer Residential Ltd. (1993), 12 C.L.R. (2d) 102, 15 O.R. (3d) 418 (Gen. Div.); affirmed (1997), 33 O.R. (3d) 477 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—A claim for lien was registered and vacated upon posting of a lien bond. The claimant commenced a separate trust action against the contractor, its officers, directors and “persons in control”. A consent order was made that the lien bond would also stand to the credit of the trust action and the trust action would be dismissed against the personal defendants. The lien was released. The plaintiff recovered judgment for a principal amount and pre-judgment interest. On application, the court held that the lien bond must respond to the interest component of the judgment. Although by the terms of s. 14(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> a lien bond can only respond to a judgment for principal and costs, the action before the court proceeded as a breach of trust action. The word “<ital>judgment</ital>” has consistently been held to include the component of prejudgment interest. It was clear that leaving the bond in place to “stand credit for any judgment in this action” was the consideration for the removal of the personal defendants from the action, thus ending their personal liability. The bond thus became the security for the final judgment, to which the plaintiff must now look for satisfaction. To order otherwise, in these circumstances, would be manifestly unjust and inequitable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="126" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63fbc3925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 126 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee appealed a judgment which awarded lien claimants priority over the mortgage in respect of pre-judgment interest on the lien claims. It was accepted that there was a deficiency in the holdback and that the trial judge correctly awarded the lien claimants priority over the mortgage to the extent of such deficiency in respect of principal amounts of the claims. The issue on the appeal related to the subsequent decision of the trial judge which awarded interest to the lienholders under the provisions of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. The appeal was allowed. The lien claimants were not entitled to personal judgments against the mortgagee. The mortgagee was not a “payer” as defined in the Act. There was no privity of contract between the lien claimants and the mortgagee. In the absence of any personal judgment against the mortgagee, the lien claimants had no right to claim interest from the mortgagee under the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
15:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 15.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">15:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="0" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A similar section was first proclaimed in s. 2 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1937</ital>, S.O. 1937, c. 41, which repealed s. 7(3) of the then statute and replaced it in part with the following:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"> (a) The time at which the first lien arose shall be deemed to be the time at which the first work or service is performed or first materials furnished, irrespective of whether a claim for lien in respect thereof is registered or enforced, and whether or not such lien is before the court.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.trace="0" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section later became s. 7(4) of the Act, and later s. 8(4). The wording remained substantially unchanged until the enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983 c. 6.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="0" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section establishes the time at which a lien arises. The definition of when materials are supplied is set out in s. 1(2), and when that definition and s. 15 herein are read together, it is clear that the lien arises at the commencement of the first work or when the first materials were furnished. Under this section of the Act, the lien not only “arises”, as referred to in the Commentary under s. 14 above, but also “takes effect” forthwith upon first supply. The term “takes effect” appears only in this section of the Act. The section is important in calculating the date the first lien arose for the purposes of determining priorities under s. 78 below of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
15:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 15.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">15:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="13245" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I674d07803b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 15 provides that “[a] person's lien arises and takes effect when the person first supplies services or materials to the improvement.” Nothing in this language provides that a lien arises on a subcontract-by-subcontract basis. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This decision was decided under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
16:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 16.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">16:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A number of amendments were made pursuant to <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1975</ital>, S.O. 1975, c. 43, to specifically bind the Crown, including the addition of the Crown as the statutory “owner”. The section that prohibited the attachment of a lien to the interest of the Crown in a premise became s. 6(2) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. The Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> stated that the attachment of a lien to Crown land was theoretically absurd and unnecessary. Section 26 of the <ital>Proceedings Against the Crown Act</ital> requires the Crown to pay all final judgments against it. The proclamation of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 resulted in the adoption of s. 16, in its present form.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Although the Act applies to the Crown (see s. 3), a construction lien can not attach to the interest of the Crown in a premise. Provincial construction lien legislation is not competent to affect the title of the Crown in the Right of Canada for constitutional reasons. A practical reason was expressed by Assistant Master Marriott in the case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bain" p2="Canada (Director, Veterans' Land Act)" post.rptr="917" pre.rptr="[1947]" ref.id="I63fc11b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bain v. Canada (Director, Veterans' Land Act)">Bain v. Canada (Director, Veterans' Land Act), [1947] O.W.N. 917 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> at p. 918:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The substance of the enactment (<ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>) is the sale of the land: per Meredith C.J. C.P. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1907" p1="Crawford" p2="Tilden" post.rptr="572" pre.rptr="14" ref.id="I63fc11b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Crawford v. Tilden">Crawford v. Tilden (1907), 14 O.L.R. 572 <point>at 577</point> (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. How can that relief be enforced as against the Dominion Crown? The Ontario Courts have no power to order the sale of property owned by the Crown, and I have found the Director to be an emanation or agent of the Crown.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> specifically extends to the Crown in Right of Ontario, but a lien does not attach to the interest of the Crown in a premise. The Act protects the lien claimants who supply services or materials to the Crown, however, by providing for a charge under s. 21 on amounts required to be retained as holdbacks under Part IV. Subsection 16(3) creates a system of charges equivalent in most material ways to a lien remedy. Where s. 16(3) applies, a claim for lien need not be registered against the premises. A lien can attach to the interests of a third party, with whom the Crown holds a joint interest in premises.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 16(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Dirm Inc." p2="Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3479" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I63fc38c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd.">Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3479, 37 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Master)</ref></cite>—A community college of applied arts and technology and its Board of Governors are Crown agents under s. 2(4) of the Ontario <ital>Colleges of Applied Arts and Technology Act, 2002</ital> and, if necessary, under the <ital>Crown Agency Act</ital>. Where the main contract is with a college, a lien does not attach to the premises and preservation is governed by s. 34(1)(b) of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 16(3)(a)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Atlas Dewatering Corporation" p2="Harvie Construction Inc." post.rptr="4294" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I674d55a03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Atlas Dewatering Corporation v. Harvie Construction Inc.">Atlas Dewatering Corporation v. Harvie Construction Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 4294, 2024 ONSC 1775, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1427 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 6605 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 7440 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the subcontractor lien claimant provided “de-watering” services to a project involving the reconstruction and realignment of a municipal roadway. The work consisted of the installation of a system of well points, pumps and pipes to assist in lowering the groundwater table on the construction site, and subsequent removal of that equipment. The defendant argued that the claimant was required to preserve its lien by registering a claim for lien against the title to the lands in question but erroneously gave it to the municipality. However, the court noted that very purpose of dewatering was to reduce the groundwater on the land requiring the construction or improvement, those premises were an existing highway, and the work done was integral to its alteration and restoration. Section 16(3) applied, and the claimant was not required to register its claim for lien on title, but followed the correct procedure by giving its claim for lien to the municipal clerk as required by (then) s. 34(2) (now s. 34(3.1)).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Simpson" p2="Gateman-Milloy Landscape Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="734" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I63fc38c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simpson v. Gateman-Milloy Landscape Contractors Ltd.">Simpson v. Gateman-Milloy Landscape Contractors Ltd. (1986), 54 O.R. (2d) 734 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contracted with the plaintiff subcontractor for the installation of paving stones on the walkways in a public municipal park. Following the defendant's default on its contract with the plaintiff, the plaintiff served a claim for lien on it and on the municipality, but did not register it, and the defendant brought an application for a declaration that the lien was not preserved. The application was granted. If the walkways were a public street or highway, the procedure followed by the plaintiff would have been correct under ss. 16(3)(a), 34(1)(b) and (2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. However, in modern usage, “<ital>street</ital>” and “<ital>highway</ital>” refer to a thoroughfare for the use of public vehicular traffic. A path in a public park does not fall within that definition. Hence, the plaintiff should have registered his lien in order to preserve it.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
17:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 17.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">17:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amenments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 17(3) was amended to the effect that set-off must now be related to the improvement unless contractor or subcontractor becomes insolvent, in which case set-off continues to be possible whether or not related to the improvement (see also s. 12)</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 17(1) is a consolidation of concepts found in three separate sections of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, namely sections 6, 10 and 11. Sections 10 and 11 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 were both derived from s. 3 of <ital>The Mechanics Lien Act of 1874</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.). The language of <ital>The Mechanics and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35 broadened the language of section 10 (then section 9):</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Save as herein provided where the lien is claimed by any other person than the contractor, the amount which may be claimed in respect thereof shall be limited to the amount owing to the contractor or sub-contractor or other person for whom the work or service has been done or the materials have been placed or furnished.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 9 remained unchanged and s. 10 remained virtually unchanged until they were both incorporated into s. 17 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. Section 17(4) deals with the liability of a municipality in respect of improvements made to land designated as a public street or highway. This subsection was derived from s. 6(2) of the <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, the history of which is discussed above under s. 16 (Interest of Crown).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subject only to the overriding statutory holdback obligation in Part IV of the Act, no lien can attach in value for more than is owed to a payer for the payer's portion of the work. The lien, therefore, does not create “price” or value where there is none, nor does it interfere in any way with the consequences of an improvident bargain by any contractor or subcontractor in the construction pyramid. This provision is necessary because of the pyramidal nature of the construction relationship, where the total value of liens registered against a property can exceed the total owed by an owner to the contractor for that work. Subsection 17(2) extends the limitation of s. 17(1) to the whole “class” of lien claimants, namely to all claimants having the same degree of privity of contract with a given payer. This prevents individual liens from aggregating more than the amount owed to the payer of a given class. Persons who supply services or materials to the same contractor or subcontractor are limited to the amount owed to that contractor or subcontractor. Subsection 17(3) sets the value of any lien claim at the net amount owing after all the respective claims, debts and damages as between the parties have been set off whether or not related to the improvement. Liability for holdback is not affected by this limitation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Advisory Committee on the Draft Construction Lien Act explained the purpose of s. 17(4) as being designed to address <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="George Wimpey Canada Ltd." p2="Peelton Hills Ltd." post.rptr="787" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63fc86e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="George Wimpey Canada Ltd. v. Peelton Hills Ltd.">George Wimpey Canada Ltd. v. Peelton Hills Ltd. (1982), 35 O.R. (2d) 787 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1982), 23 R.P.R. 123 (note) (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subdivision agreements may require a developer to dedicate land to the municipality for public streets and highways and to build those streets and highways to the municipality specifications, but at the developer's expense. Subsection 17(4) makes the municipality liable to the extent that the municipality would have been liable for deficiencies in holdbacks had the improvements been done at its expense. The procedure for enforcing the claim is the same as that in respect of public streets and highways under s. 16(3)(a).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 17(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd." p2="Time Development Construction Inc." post.rptr="7617" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63fc86e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd. v. Time Development Construction Inc.">A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd. v. Time Development Construction Inc., 2015 ONSC 7617, 2015 CarswellOnt 18600, 55 C.L.R. (4th) 231 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2017 ONSC 560, 2017 CarswellOnt 836, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 253 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor successfully moved for summary judgment on its claim for payment of its contract and extras. The defendant contractor had brought a counterclaim for deficiencies. The lien claim and counterclaim were to proceed to trial, as there were issues remaining with respect to the validity of lien and the proof of deficiencies. The subcontractor had also brought another action in relation to a different project, in which a counterclaim had been made. The court held that the counterclaim in the separate action could not be set off against the plaintiff's claim in this action. The separate claim involved a different project, and the only party common to both actions was the plaintiff. There was no nexus by way of privity of contract. Section 17(3) was not so broad as to capture these circumstances. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In affirming the lower court judgment, the Divisional Court declined to make any finding on whether s. 17(3) allows setoff of related claims among related parties and did not comment on the adequacy of the defendant's plea of setoff and equitable setoff.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="LaFarge Canada Inc." p2="B. Gottardo Construction Ltd." post.rptr="6856" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63fc86e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="LaFarge Canada Inc. v. B. Gottardo Construction Ltd.">LaFarge Canada Inc. v. B. Gottardo Construction Ltd., 2015 ONSC 6856, 2015 CarswellOnt 16971, 55 C.L.R. (4th) 275 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There can be no legal basis for requiring an owner to post, as security, an amount to reflect the subcontractor's lien claims where they exceed the contractual amount that might be found owing as between the owner and the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac Group Ltd." p2="Mount Albert United Church (Trustee of)" post.rptr="5624" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I63fc86e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Unimac Group Ltd. v. Mount Albert United Church (Trustee of)">Unimac Group Ltd. v. Mount Albert United Church (Trustee of), 2013 ONSC 5624, 2013 CarswellOnt 13536 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 15243 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff general contractor unsuccessfully argued that in order to obtain an order vacating a construction lien, the defendant owner should have to pay into court as security not only the plaintiff's outstanding lien claim, but also the outstanding lien claims of the various subcontractors. Pursuant to subs. 17(1) and (2), the maximum entitlement of a subcontractor claiming directly through a contractor is restricted to the amount owed by the owner to the contractor, unless an owner failed to comply with its holdback obligations. Here, there was no suggestion that the defendant did not comply with its holdback obligations and there was simply no privity of contract between the subcontractors and the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Reliance Electric Ltd." p2="G.N.S. Contractors Inc." post.rptr="310" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63fcadf05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc.">Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 310, 70 O.R. (2d) 364, 1989 CarswellOnt 705 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Nothing in s. 44(6) affects the operation of ss. 17(1) and (2) of the Act. Accordingly, the value of a lien remains the same after the posting of a bond as it was before the posting.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Cedar Rent All Ltd." p2="Canada Packers Inc." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="59" ref.id="I63fcadf15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cedar Rent All Ltd. v. Canada Packers Inc.">Cedar Rent All Ltd. v. Canada Packers Inc. (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 523, 27 C.L.R. 49 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—It would be contrary to the purpose and intent of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to allow what would otherwise be a valid claim to be defeated by a barter arrangement wherein the parties failed to value the services of the contractor.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 17(3)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sjostrom Sheet Metal Ltd." p2="Geo A. Kelson Company Limited" post.rptr="13584" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I674df1e03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Sjostrom Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Geo A. Kelson Company Limited">Sjostrom Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Geo A. Kelson Company Limited, 2023 CarswellOnt 13584, 2023 ONSC 4959 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 8263, 2024 ONSC 3183, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2810 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—At issue was whether subcontractor K entered into a direct contract with sub-sub-subcontractor S to supply sheet metal labour when issues arose between K and its sheet metal sub-subcontractor A, and whether a change order removed all remaining sheet metal labour from sub-subcontractor A's scope of work. The character of K's payments to S hinged on those determinations, namely whether the payments were made under a direct subcontract with S or made to S as A's sub-subcontractor in accordance with a direct payment provision of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. In its statement of defence, K pleaded and relied on ss. 17(3) and 35, but not s. 28. The right to assert set-off under s. 17(3) required privity of contract between the lien claimant and the party claiming set-off. Pleading and relying on s. 17(3) further supported that K was admitting it had privity of contract with S.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc." p2="Sutton Forming Inc." post.rptr="6751" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I674df1e13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc. v. Sutton Forming Inc.">Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc. v. Sutton Forming Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 6751, 2023 ONSC 2628, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 20 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2022 ONSC 1309, 2022 CarswellOnt 3103 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The combined effect of ss. 21 and 17(3) is that subcontractor liens are a charge against the whole of the amount owed by the owner to the contractor under the contract; however, the owner is entitled to set off claims against the contractor in calculating the overall obligation, provided, however, that set-off claims cannot be applied to reduce the owner's obligation below the amount of the basic holdback created in s. 22(1). As found by the motion judge here, the holdback is based on the contract price as the services are provided. It is not based on the total contract price, or the amounts actually paid. As well, a deficiency claim by an owner against a contractor does not impede payments from the basic holdback to any subcontractors and their suppliers in the absence of parallel deficiency claims at each applicable rung of the construction ladder.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lacroix" p2="Dompierre" post.rptr="3873" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63fcadf25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lacroix v. Dompierre">Lacroix v. Dompierre, 2016 ONSC 3873, 2016 CarswellOnt 9637, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2016 CarswellOnt 17664, 2016 ONSC 6931, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="C & A Steel (1983) Ltd." p2="Tesc Contracting Co." post.rptr="2330" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I90d0d7e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="C & A Steel (1983) Ltd. v. Tesc Contracting Co.">C & A Steel (1983) Ltd. v. Tesc Contracting Co. (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2330, 39 O.R. (3d) 155, 38 C.L.R. (2d) 166 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, the court concluded that the defendant was generally entitled to claim set-off. However, as the evidence in support of those claims was hearsay, the court allowed set-offs only for those items where the plaintiff sub-subcontractor admitted that he did not complete the work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Total Electrical Systems Inc." p2="Collège Boréal d'Arts appliqués & de technologies" post.rptr="4586" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I63fcd5015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Total Electrical Systems Inc. v. Collège Boréal d'Arts appliqués & de technologies">Total Electrical Systems Inc. v. Collège Boréal d'Arts appliqués & de technologies, 2011 ONSC 4586, 2011 CarswellOnt 7779, 107 O.R. (3d) 27, 8 C.L.R. (4th) 129 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2011 CarswellOnt 12641, 8 C.L.R. (4th) 144 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff successfully moved under s. 67(2) for leave to bring a motion for summary judgment, even where the defendant's set-off claim under s. 17(3), advanced in relation to an unrelated construction contract, raised a triable issue. Since the defendant's claim was insufficiently supported, and the defendant did not meet its obligation to “put its best foot forward” in that regard, the plaintiff was granted summary judgment, and the court declined to stay the judgment pending the trial on the set off claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Protosteel Industries Ltd." p2="1355902 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="9675" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I63fcd5025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Protosteel Industries Ltd. v. 1355902 Ontario Ltd.">Protosteel Industries Ltd. v. 1355902 Ontario Ltd., 2009 CarswellOnt 9675, [2009] O.J. No. 3697 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was approached by the contractor to provide work on the improvement and an agreement was entered into between the owner of the project, the plaintiff, and the contractor to ensure a joint cheque program was initiated, as the plaintiff feared that the contractor would default. The plaintiff brought an action against, <ital>inter alia</ital>, the owner in respect of outstanding invoices and for release of the holdback retained by the latter. The plaintiff was entitled to judgment as against the owner for the amount of the holdback. The effect of making rights of set-off in s. 17(3) of “subject to Part IV” suggested the holdback could not be applied in satisfaction of a claim of the payer against the person in default after receipt of a notice of lien. The owner could not withhold funds against any subtrades because of its claims against the contractor and could not set off its claims against the contractor by claiming against the holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="8127" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I63fcd5035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2009 CarswellOnt 8127, 91 C.L.R. (3d) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The combined effect of ss. 21 and 17(3) is such that subcontractor liens are a charge against the whole of the amount owed by the owner to the contractor under the contract. However, the owner is entitled to set-off claims against the contractor in calculating the overall obligation, provided, however, that set-off claims cannot be applied to reduce the owner's obligation below the amount of the basic holdback created in s. 22(1). Thus owner's minimum liability to the subcontractors in this case was therefore the lesser of the basic holdback and the aggregate of all valid and subsisting subcontractor lien claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." p2="Thunder Bay Regional Hospital" post.rptr="145" pre.rptr="75" ref.id="I63fcfc105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital">Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital (2008), 75 C.L.R. (3d) 145, 2008 CarswellOnt 5697 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 6553 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed on other grounds (2009), 82 C.L.R. (3d) 221, 2009 CarswellOnt 4488 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant hospital, when drafting its pleadings in several related lien actions, made a choice not to pursue or to plead set-off for damages for breach of contract and/or negligence. Notwithstanding an initial decision not to plead set-off in the lien actions, the hospital subsequently changed its mind and unsuccessfully brought a motion to consolidate its civil action with the lien actions or, alternatively, to assert a counterclaim pleading the same relief as contained in the civil action. For the hospital to raise a possible set-off as a defence to a motion by the plaintiff for partial summary judgment in light of the decision in the earlier motion would allow it to do indirectly that which it had been directly prevented from doing by judicial order. The joinder of the claims was <ital>res judicata</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="C & A Steel (1983) Ltd." p2="Tesc Contracting Co." post.rptr="2330" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I90d12600f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="C & A Steel (1983) Ltd. v. Tesc Contracting Co.">C & A Steel (1983) Ltd. v. Tesc Contracting Co. (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2330, 39 O.R. (3d) 155, 38 C.L.R. (2d) 166 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The language of s. 17(3) creates a right of set-off broader than equitable set-off and quoting McGuinness, <ital>Construction Lien Remedies in Ontario</ital>, 2d ed., “is intended to furnish the provision with sufficient scope to enable it to deal with the multi-level contractual nature of many construction projects”.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 17(4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd." p2="846539 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="230" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I63fcfc125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd.">Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 230 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4717 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The trust provisions of s. 7(1) expressly exclude amounts received by municipalities from the statutory trust. In dismissing by summary judgment a contractor's claim against a developer's bank and a municipality, the court observed that the lien claimant could not reasonably expect more than the value of holdbacks under Part IV. The relevant letters of credit were not in any event intended to secure contractors against non-payment by the developer (citing: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Parr" p2="Old Carriage Road Developments Ltd." post.rptr="247" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I63fd23205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parr v. Old Carriage Road Developments Ltd.">Parr v. Old Carriage Road Developments Ltd. (1985), 11 C.L.R. 247, 49 O.R. (2d) 234, 7 O.A.C. 268 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
18:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 18.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">18:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section replaced s. 7 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which dealt with an improvement made to the land of a married woman. The original version of the section dealing with improvements to the lands of a married woman was set out in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, which remained virtually unchanged until <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30 was proclaimed on May 8, 1923. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 amended this section by deleting “or services are performed” and making some grammatical changes. The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 deleted the phrase “or an inchoate right of dower”. The section remained unchanged until it was eliminated entirely and s. 18 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 was proclaimed in its place in a form identical to the present version.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision accommodates liens upon interests in land that are held jointly or in common. Since an improvement will be beneficial to all owners, they will in general be held liable to lien claimants for the costs of the improvement. It is only necessary that an owner know or ought to know that the improvement is being made for a lien to attach to the interest of that owner, unless the contractor receives actual notice from the owner to the contrary before the supply of services or materials.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="J. Lepera Contracting Inc." p2="Royal Timbers Inc." post.rptr="271" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63fd23215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. Lepera Contracting Inc. v. Royal Timbers Inc.">J. Lepera Contracting Inc. v. Royal Timbers Inc., 2012 ONSC 271, 2012 CarswellOnt 4196, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 5 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner of land signed a contract to sell a piece of land to a hotel developer which, in anticipation of acquiring title to that land, contracted with the plaintiff to construct and install all the necessary services for its hotel. The owner's only involvement in the latter project was to convey the land to the developer, and to wait for the deal to close. The court found that, on the execution of that agreement of purchase and sale, the equitable interest then acquired by the developer did not co-exist with the legal interest of the land owner in a joint or common capacity such that it was liable as an owner to the plaintiff. The developer was not in possession of the land in circumstances where it could exercise power and control over it at its pleasure, to the exclusion of all others. The purchase agreement only created an equitable interest in favour of the developer, not an ownership interest which would only follow with the completion of its purchase. Until then, the developer's equitable interest was inferior to the legal interest of the defendant owner such that the two could not be considered to co-exist as owners jointly or in common. The owner was not also found not to be an owner within the meaning of s. 1(1) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd." p2="Schleiss Development Co." post.rptr="5504" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I63fd4a305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd. v. Schleiss Development Co.">Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd. v. Schleiss Development Co. (2001), [2001] O.J. No. 5504, 2001 CarswellOnt 4906, 15 C.L.R. (3d) 10 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lands against which liens were registered were owned by a corporate partnership. The partnership had signed an agreement of purchase and sale with a corporate developer who intended to construct an ice rink facility. At one point in the negotiations, the owners agreed in writing to be an equity partner in the rink project and take back common shares as part of the purchase price, although the final agreement did not include such terms. The developer engaged in preliminary preparation for construction on the land using the general contractor and subcontractors, including some excavation and the partial delivery of a pre-fabricated building. The principal of one of the owner-partners had actual knowledge that work was being carried out on the lands, attended on a regular basis to inspect the progress of the work, and although he was not aware and did not consent in any way to the partial delivery of the prefabricated structure, was aware of it almost immediately following its delivery. Subsequently, after the developer failed to obtain necessary zoning changes, the project was cancelled and the agreement of purchase and sale was terminated by mutual consent. In the circumstances, the developer had an equitable interest in the lands which could be liened. Case law held that an agreement of purchase and sale provided the purchaser with an equitable interest in the property under s. 1(1)(b) of the Act, the developer was an owner having an interest in a premises on whose behalf an improvement was made. Similarly, the partnership was an owner within the meaning of s. 1(1)(c) and (d) of the Act as the improvements were made with their “privity or consent” or for their “benefit”. The request of the owner for work to be carried out on its property could be inferred or implied by the actions or inaction of the partnership.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Grand Pre Construction Inc." p2="132305 Canada Inc." post.rptr="2512" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63fd4a315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Grand Pre Construction Inc. v. 132305 Canada Inc.">Grand Pre Construction Inc. v. 132305 Canada Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2512, 1998 CarswellOnt 2481 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where there was an issue of fact as to corporate ownership of closely held private companies, a motion to vacate without security was premature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Can-Tech Construction Co." p2="Relocatable Homes Ltd." post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="19" ref.id="I63fd71405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Can-Tech Construction Co. v. Relocatable Homes Ltd.">Can-Tech Construction Co. v. Relocatable Homes Ltd. (1995), 19 C.L.R. (2d) 317 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Can-Tech did work for Axiom. Axiom, in turn, had an agreement of purchase and sale with Relocatable upon which a deposit had been paid. Relocatable saw Axiom's plans and permitted Axiom to commence work, in anticipation of closing. Relocatable had no direct contact with Can-Tech other than to caution them, prior to work commencing, not to look to Relocatable for payment. Can-Tech registered a lien and sued Relocatable. The court held that as Relocatable knew, in advance, that Can-Tech was going to do work on its land it had a duty to give Can-Tech actual notice before work started that it assumed no responsibility for the improvements to be made, which duty it had discharged. The plaintiff's claim was dismissed.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
19:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 19.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">19:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amenments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 19(1) of the Act was amended to provide that if the interest of the owner to which a lien attaches is leasehold, and if payment for all or part of the improvement is accounted for under the terms of the lease or any renewal of it, or under any agreement to which the landlord is a party that is connected to the lease, the landlord's interest is also subject to the lien, to the extent of 10 percent of the amount of such payment. A subsection 19(5) was added to the Act to confirm that a landlord may still be considered an owner of a premises for the purposes of the Act if he or she meets the criteria set out in the definition of “owner” in subsection 1(1) of the Act.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Corresponding amendments were made to section 39 of the Act, which sets out information that must be provided on request in specified circumstances, in order to expressly address information that must be provided by a landlord to whom subsection 19(1) applies.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27, the liability of an owner of a leasehold interest required the signature of such owner upon the statement of claim at the time of the registering of the lien, duly verified. This provision was amended in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153 to deal with the claim for lien, not the statement of claim. Major revisions to this section were made in <ital>The Mechanics and Wage-Earners Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1914, c. 140, requiring notice in writing, by registered letter or personal service, referring to the section, to the owner or his agent of the work to be done or material to be furnished. It was also provided that no forfeiture or attempted forfeiture of the lease on the part of the landlord or cancellation or attempted cancellation of the lease except for non-payment of rent should deprive any person of a lien. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1958</ital>, S.O. 1958, c. 57, deleted the reference to “registered letter”. The final revisions to this section before the enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was made in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, when both subsections were revised to change the notice period from 10 to 15 days and require the owner's notice to be in writing. The Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> redrafted this section “for the purposes of both clarification and in an effort to bring the terminology in this section in line with that used elsewhere in the Committee Draft”.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 19 governs the attachment of liens to leasehold interests. Under s. 19(1), where the “owner”, as defined in the Act, is a tenant, the interest of the landlord will also be subject to the lien if: (a) the contractor gives the landlord written notice of the improvement before it is made and (b) the landlord fails, within 15 days of receipt of that notice, to provide written notice to the contractor that the landlord assumes no responsibility for the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The liability of the landlord is not affected by the forfeiture or termination of the lease for any reason other than non-payment of rent (s. 19(2)). Pursuant to s. 19(3) and (4), if a landlord intends to terminate a lease for non-payment of rent, written notice of the proposed termination and amount of unpaid rent must be provided to all registered lien claimants, who may pay the arrears within 10 days' notice and add that amount to their lien claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Although the use of the statutory form (O. Reg. 175, s. 2(2)) is not mandatory, it is strongly recommended that Form 2 be adopted and used whenever possible.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vestacon Limited" p2="ARC Productions Ltd." post.rptr="5366" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I63fd98505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd.">Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd., 2018 ONSC 5366, 2018 CarswellOnt 15345, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 38 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant general contractor performed renovations for the tenant renting two properties owned by separate holding corporations, who were in turn owned by a parent company. The tenant subsequently went bankrupt. Section 19 landlord notices had been given pursuant to the parent's construction manual by the lien claimant to the parent company in an email package of start-up documents. At issue was whether the notices and their delivery complied with the Act. S. 87 provided that notices were to be served in the manner permitted by the rules of court or, alternatively, by certified or registered mail. Ont. Rule 16.01(4)(b)(iv) provided that a document may be given by email with consent of the parties. The court found that service on the parent company constituted service on the holding companies, which were wholly owned by the former, had no employees or bank accounts, and had the same business address as the parent. Likewise, the notice properly named the parent. The complex ownership structure should not be available to nominee corporations sheltering under the parent to defeat the rights of lien claimants on technicalities. Also, by providing email addresses in its construction manual, the parent company implicitly consented and expected the contractor to communicate via email. Additionally, on the facts of the case, the s. 19 notices were not buried or overshadowed in a document delivered for some other purpose. The fact that the construction manual provided that all such work was at the sole cost of the tenant and that the tenant was required to clear title of all lien claims did not preemptively constitute compliance with a landlord's obligation to deliver a Form 3 notice to avoid lien liability. Lastly, on the issue of whether the content of the notices was sufficient, the parent was directly involved in the tenant improvements referred to in the s. 19 notices, and specified how the project was to be carried out and listed multiple obligations to which the contractor was required to adhere. The parent was fully informed as to the nature of the construction project and the tenant improvements and the notice was sufficient.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 19(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dean's Standard Inc." p2="Siljub Toronto Ltd." post.rptr="5254" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I63fdbf605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dean's Standard Inc. v. Siljub Toronto Ltd.">Dean's Standard Inc. v. Siljub Toronto Ltd., 2016 ONSC 5254, 2016 CarswellOnt 13317, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 285 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff met with two individuals (“the pending owners”) who identified themselves as the pending owners of a hotel premises owned by the defendant, and entered into a contract under which plaintiff would supply services and materials to renovate a sample hotel room as a mock up for anticipated renovations of more rooms. The sale of the hotel did not proceed. The plaintiff did not name either pending owner in its subsequent lien claim. In the absence of written notice to the defendant of the proposed improvement and the price of the work, together with an opportunity for the defendant to deny liability for it, the plaintiff was not entitled to a lien claim. More importantly, the owner never contracted with the plaintiff and the pending owners did not have actual, implied or ostensible authority to contract as agents of the owner. When a claim is made under the Act, regard must be given to the policy underlying the statutory entitlement to encumber another's property with a lien claim. A claim that an owner is obligated to pay for renovations contracted for by another party requires actual notice to the owner before the owner can be bound.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Industrial Refrigerated Systems Inc." p2="Quality Meat Packers Ltd." post.rptr="4545" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63fdbf615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Industrial Refrigerated Systems Inc. v. Quality Meat Packers Ltd.">Industrial Refrigerated Systems Inc. v. Quality Meat Packers Ltd., 2015 ONSC 4545, 2015 CarswellOnt 10645, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 203 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 13123, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 235 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Summarizing the law in regard to a s. 19 notice, the court noted that: 1) the notice under s. 19 must be in writing: 2) the notice must be sufficiently distinct and memorable to signify to the landlord its potential liability and for it to know when the 15-day period within which it may deny liability begins; 3) the notice cannot be buried or overshadowed in a document delivered for some other purpose and 4) the notice must be given before the contractor begins work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Flexible Contractors Inc." p2="1408023 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5837" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I63fde6705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Flexible Contractors Inc. v. 1408023 Ontario Inc.">Flexible Contractors Inc. v. 1408023 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 5837, 2012 CarswellOnt 12912 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The same individual was president of both the defendant tenant who contracted with the plaintiff contractor, and the defendant landlord who owned the property. No written notice was provided to the landlord, as required by s. 19(1), and any constructive notice that may have been given because of the managerial overlap was insufficient and inconsistent with the requirement that notice be in writing. The claim for lien was vacated as against the defendant landlord, the action against it dismissed and the registration of the claim for lien and certificate of action discharged from the owners' interest in the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="1276761 Ontario Ltd." p2="2748355 Canada Inc." post.rptr="3018" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I63fde6715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1276761 Ontario Ltd. v. 2748355 Canada Inc.">1276761 Ontario Ltd. v. 2748355 Canada Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3018, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2006 CarswellOnt 5392, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 54 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Ontario Divisional Court held that the test set forth in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Venneri Engineering Ltd." p2="Zonenward Leasex Management Inc." post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fde6725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc.">Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 141 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, was too stringent and held that the proper test was that set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pinehurst Woodworking Co." p2="Rocco" post.rptr="669" pre.rptr="1986" ref.id="I63fde6735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pinehurst Woodworking Co. v. Rocco">Pinehurst Woodworking Co. v. Rocco, 1986 CarswellOnt 669, 38 R.P.R. 116, 13 O.A.C. 121 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, which merely required that the notice had to be sufficiently distinct and memorable to allow the landlord to know when the 15-day period in which it could deny liability began. The Divisional Court emphasized that so-called “notice events” such as the landlord's attendance at meetings, its review of plans or its awareness of the work being done, in and of themselves are not enough to constitute sufficient notice under s. 19(1). The Court held that any notice must clearly signal a potential liability to the landlord.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams & Prior Ltd." p2="Taskon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="474" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90d1e950f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd.">Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 474, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2003] O.J. No. 498 (Master)</ref></cite>—Subsection 19(1) of the Act clearly differentiates between the interest of an “owner” and the interest of a “landlord” on the premises. Even if a landlord is not an “owner” within the statutory definition in s. 1(1), its interest can also be subject to the lien if the contractor gives the landlord a special written notice as described in s. 19(1). So the landlord can be held liable as an “owner” under s. 1(1) or liable as a “landlord” under s. 19(1). The following cases make this clear: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Venneri Engineering Ltd." p2="Zonenward Leasex Management Inc." post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fe0d805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc.">Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 141 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Lark Manufacturing Inc." post.rptr="113" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63fe0d815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Lark Manufacturing Inc.">D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Lark Manufacturing Inc. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 113 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Sloot Construction-Design Ltd." p2="North Maple Mall Ltd." post.rptr="4174" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I63fe0d825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sloot Construction-Design Ltd. v. North Maple Mall Ltd.">Sloot Construction-Design Ltd. v. North Maple Mall Ltd. (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 4174, 50 C.L.R. (2d) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, all the cases cited in these cases.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Therefore, it further follows from all of the above that s. 34(5)(a), in specifying that the “name and address of the owner of the premises” must be set out, requires that where a lien claimant claims a lien <ital>against a tenant's interest</ital> in a landlord's land and building, the <ital>name and address of this tenant must</ital> be set out, and where the lien claimant also claims a lien <ital>against the landlord's interest</ital> in the land and building, the name and address of the landlord <ital>must also</ital> be set out.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Sloot Construction-Design Ltd." p2="North Maple Mall Ltd." post.rptr="4174" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I63fe0d835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sloot Construction-Design Ltd. v. North Maple Mall Ltd.">Sloot Construction-Design Ltd. v. North Maple Mall Ltd. (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 4174, 50 C.L.R. (2d) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant mall owners leased space to the defendant grocery chain, which in turn subleased space within its stores to the defendant bakery for stand-alone kiosk operations used for the baking and sale of bagels. The bakery entered into a series of agreements with the plaintiff contractor for the construction of these bakery kiosks, and with the bakery becoming insolvent, the plaintiff registered liens and sought to recover its unpaid account for the construction of the kiosks from the grocer and the mall owners. Subsequent to the registration of the Plaintiff's claims for lien, the grocer obtained orders vacating their registration and that of their related certificates of action, by posting security with the court under s. 44 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Because the plaintiff did not provide the grocer with notice pursuant to s. 19(1), it could not hold the grocer liable for the lien that the plaintiff had against the baker.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19980528" p1="Royal Tile Flooring Ltd." p2="Rannoch Developments Ltd." ref.id="I63fe34905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Tile Flooring Ltd. v. Rannoch Developments Ltd.">Royal Tile Flooring Ltd. v. Rannoch Developments Ltd. (May 28, 1998), Doc. 100/97 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The contractor did not give the landlord any written notice in the form of a letter. The only indication the landlord had was the actual written lease, which required the tenant to make improvements and stipulated that the tenant would do so at its own expense. The landlord argued that based on Master Sandler's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Venneri Engineering Ltd." p2="Zonenward Leasex Management Inc." post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fe34915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc.">Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 141 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the lease could not possibly constitute a notice under s. 19(1). Justice Walters disagreed, holding that the plain wording of s. 19(1) only stipulates written notice. No further particulars are delineated. Even Regulation 175 does not mandate the use of Form 2, it says “may”, while other forms under the Act use the word “shall”. The lease was held to be sufficient notice. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case would appear to be difficult to reconcile with the wording and purpose of s. 19. It should be treated as restricted to its facts.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Grand Pre Construction Inc." p2="132305 Canada Inc." post.rptr="2512" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I63fe34925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Grand Pre Construction Inc. v. 132305 Canada Inc.">Grand Pre Construction Inc. v. 132305 Canada Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2512, 1998 CarswellOnt 2481 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The same individual was the guiding mind of the corporate owner of the liened premises, as well as of the property management company on whose behalf the renovations were undertaken. The court declined to vacate the lien against the property on the technical basis that the corporate owner had not been notified pursuant to s. 19(1). In the circumstances, it would have been premature, inappropriate and unjust to vacate the lien before trial of the lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Southern Plumbing Ltd." p2="Quality Craft Interiors Ltd." post.rptr="195" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I63fe5ba05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southern Plumbing Ltd. v.
