Quality Craft Interiors Ltd.">Southern Plumbing Ltd. v. Quality Craft Interiors Ltd. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 195 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The following “notice” events, taken singly or cumulatively, were not sufficient to amount to notice to a landlord under s. 19(1): (a) Receipt of copies of the mechanical plumbing plans showing the plaintiff as the plumbing contractor. Owners of large buildings have tenants frequently coming and going, effecting renovations, and it would be an unfair burden on the owners to require them to assess their legal position every time they were asked to approve a plan for a tenant's renovations; (b) Delivery of mechanical plumbing plans to the municipal authority, in the absence of evidence that renovation plans had also been delivered directly to the landlord; (c) Viewing by the landlord of the plaintiff's bid to do plumbing work and approval by the landlord of the plaintiff; (d) Presentation by the general contractor to the landlord of copies of the plaintiff's invoices, provided when the contractor sought advances. By the time the general contractor had sought the first advance, much work had been done, and it would have been too late for the 15-day response period under s. 19(1) to have been useful to the landlord.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Venneri Engineering Ltd." p2="Zonenward Leasex Management Inc." post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I63fe5ba15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc.">Venneri Engineering Ltd. v. Zonenward Leasex Management Inc. (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 141 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Although the contractor notified the landlord by letter that improvements were being made, the alleged “notice” was not a notice as required by s. 19(1). The wording of the “notice” was not sufficiently “arresting” or “attention getting” or “sufficiently distinct and memorable” to the landlord that he, or, at least, his land was being looked to as a surety for any money owing by his tenant to the contractor in question.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Lark Manufacturing Inc." post.rptr="113" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I63fe5ba25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Lark Manufacturing Inc.">D.B.M. Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Lark Manufacturing Inc. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 113 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff admitted giving no written notice of an improvement to be made to the leasehold premises as required under s. 19(1) of the Act, and the landlord was found not to be an “owner” pursuant to s. 1(1), the court held that there was no lien against the defendant landlord.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="K.G. Baird General Contracting Ltd." p2="800001 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="316" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I63fe5ba35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K.G. Baird General Contracting Ltd. v. 800001 Ontario Inc.">K.G. Baird General Contracting Ltd. v. 800001 Ontario Inc. (1990), 40 C.L.R. 316 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The question as to whether there has been compliance with s. 19(1) of the Act should be left to the trial judge, rather than being dealt with on a motion for summary judgment.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 19(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Winnen Construction Group Conditioning Ltd." p2="Oxford MRC Inc." post.rptr="129" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I63fe5ba45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Winnen Construction Group Conditioning Ltd. v. Oxford MRC Inc.">Winnen Construction Group Conditioning Ltd. v. Oxford MRC Inc. (2002), 21 C.L.R. (3d) 129, 2002 CarswellOnt 3593 (Master)</ref></cite>—The policy behind s. 19(2) and (3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is to provide some degree of protection to a lien claimant from having the security for its lien taken away by the acts of either the tenant or the landlord which, if taken, would bring an end to the leasehold interest. Leases can, by their provisions, be terminated or forfeited for many different reasons. The most important and common reason for termination or forfeiture by a landlord, or forfeiture by a tenant, is for non-payment of rent. Subsection 19(2) seeks to give some protection to a lien claimant with a lien only against a leasehold interest by providing that, except for non-payment of rent, no forfeiture of the lease to the landlord or termination of the lease by the landlord for any other reason deprives a valid lienholder of its lien against the leasehold premises. This provision is a policy choice that says that protecting the lienholder overrides the interest of a landlord to terminate or forfeit the lease for any reason other than non-payment of rent. To always chose the interest of a lienholder on leasehold property over a landlord, even where the landlord has not been paid rent, was seen to be unfair to the landlord which led to the exception in s. 19(2) for the non-payment of rent. Subsection 19(3) attempts to reach a further comprise between the interests of a landlord and those of the lien claimant in the situation where rent has not been paid, and where the landlord wishes to terminate the lease and mitigate its damages by re-leasing the premises to another tenant (who will hopefully pay the rent). Subsection 19(3) has certain similarities to the right of a second mortgagee or other subsequent encumbrancer to keep a first mortgage in good standing upon default by the mortgagor, by making the mortgage payments and thereby protecting the equity in the property and preventing the first mortgagee from foreclosing subsequent interests. If the property has sufficient equity, the second mortgagee will opt for an immediate sale, either by the first mortgagee or, sometimes, by exercising its own power of sale, while keeping the first mortgagee up-to-date with the mortgage payments. Or, it may keep the first mortgage in good standing to await an improved market. Subsection 19(3) creates a similar regime. The landlord must give the lien claimant written notice of its intention to enforce forfeiture or terminate a lease because of non-payment of rent and must set out the amount of the unpaid rent. Under subsection 19(4), a lien claimant, on receiving such notice, may, within 10 days, pay the landlord the amount of such unpaid rent and the amount paid may be added to the lien claimant's lien claim. A lien claimant would only do this where it thinks that the leasehold interest has, or may well have, a value on the open market if sold, so that any net sale proceeds would reimburse it for such rent payments made plus provide a source of payment for all or at least part of its proper lien claim. This regime provides some assistance to lien claimants to protect their security, although the valuation and sale of a leasehold interest is difficult and risky. If further rent accrues and remains unpaid, after the first notice is given, the landlord can give a further notice or notices which would then oblige the lien claimant to make further payments, in effect requiring the lien claimant to keep the lease up to date.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 20.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">20:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The predecessor of the present section was <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30, s. 33(2). That section read:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">33.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(2)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">Where an owner enters into an entire contract for the supply of material to be used in several buildings the person supplying such material may ask to have his lien follow the form of the contract and that it be for an entire sum upon all the buildings, but in case the owner has sold one or more of such buildings, the Judge or officer shall have jurisdiction equitably to apportion against the respective buildings the amount included in the claim for lien under the entire contract.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section remained virtually unchanged, with the exception of some grammatical amendments in the 1968–69 version of the statute, until the proclamation of s. 20 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. The present section is identical to the 1983 version of the Act. The Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> explained the expansion of this general lien section to include all suppliers of services or materials to assist all suppliers of services or materials to subdivisions by avoiding the problem of allocating the total supply of services or materials generally to each of the individual buildings in a subdivision. Either a contractor or a subcontractor may claim a general lien, provided that the contract or subcontract of the person claiming the lien provided for the general supply of services or materials to more than one premise.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A general lien is designed to assist suppliers of services or materials to subdivisions, or multiple location projects, and avoids the problem of allocating the total supply generally to each of the individual buildings in a subdivision at the time of preservation of a lien. This provision applies only where the work on multiple premises is done under single contract, but may be claimed by either a contractor or subcontractor. It is open to an owner to exclude this subsection by providing in the contract or subcontract that liens arise and expire on a lot-by-lot basis (s. 20(2)). The priority of general liens in relation to other liens is set out in s. 82 of the Act.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 20(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="TACC Construction Ltd." p2="Ajax Audley Developments Limited" post.rptr="5143" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I63fea9c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="TACC Construction Ltd. v. Ajax Audley Developments Limited">TACC Construction Ltd. v. Ajax Audley Developments Limited, 2017 ONSC 5143, 2017 CarswellOnt 15445, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 372 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 1110, 2018 CarswellOnt 2353, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 380 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether there were five contracts, rather than one. If there were five contracts, the plaintiff's lien was not registered in time and the defendant was entitled to an order discharging the lien and a release to it of the remainder of the funds it paid into court. The court found that the administration of payments and holdbacks for the work completed by the plaintiff corresponded to five contracts. Certain of the provisions in the general conditions and supplementary general conditions, mainly those governing payment of holdbacks, were consistent with an interpretation that there were five contracts, not one. As well, the explicit provisions of the contractual materials were clear, and there was no reason to look beyond the plain wording. If there had been but one agreement, the existence of five agreements, each with their own defined scope of work, made little sense. The relief sought by the defendant was granted because the lien was registered out of time. Section 20 had no application here, where the plaintiff registered a lien on premises in respect of which it had no contract and supplied no work or materials, with the exception of the lien registered against certain lots which were invalidated by the late registration.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="N.K.P. Painting" p2="Burnac Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="6902" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I63fea9c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="N.K.P. Painting v. Burnac Holdings Ltd.">N.K.P. Painting v. Burnac Holdings Ltd., 2010 ONSC 6902, 2010 CarswellOnt 9568, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 116 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—It would not be possible to apply the general lien provisions to a condominium project. Construction contracts, by their very nature, predate condominium registration. The preconditions necessary to invoke the general lien provisions cannot apply. A general lien requires that the owner have more than one premises at the time of the contract. In the case of a development project that is ultimately registered as a condominium, the condominium declaration cannot be registered until construction is near completion and ready for occupancy. The construction contracts, in most or all cases, are entered into before the premises is divided into separate parcels by registering the condominium declaration, since the construction work is required to ready the premises for occupancy. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: As the Master found the lien to be out of time and therefore invalid, the above finding was obiter to the judgment.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co." p2="1707583 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I63fed0d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc.">Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc., 80 C.L.R. (3d) 143, 2009 CarswellOnt 2805 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at 2009 CarswellOnt 8879, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Three criteria are required to register a general lien: (a) all of the premises for which the lien claimant seeks payment must be under the same ownership at the time of supply; (b) all of the work must be performed under a single contract and (c) there is no provision in the contract with the owner providing that liens arise and expire on a lot-by-lot basis. Here, the claimant included in its lien an unpaid amount for site supervision services for lots other than the ones in issue. The liens did not state that they were general liens, nor did they refer to services provided to any property other than the one against which each of the liens is registered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The master was not satisfied that the three criteria for a general lien were met. Applying the rationale in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd." p2="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="575" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90d2d3b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)">Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 575, 38 C.B.R. (3d) 250 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1996), 206 N.R. 315 (note), [1996] S.C.C.A. No. 214 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, the master held that to allow general liens to continue in the amounts attributable to services provided to the specific lots would be to allow lien claimants to ignore the scheme of section 20 and encourage the improper registration of liens. Instead, the master treated the liens as exaggerated liens under s. 35 and allowed them to continue in the appropriate amounts. The master then exercised her discretion under subsection 47 of the Act to vacate the liens and certificates of action from title without the posting of security, leaving the remedies available under the Act for the trial judge to determine.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Ledcor Construction Ltd." p2="Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc." post.rptr="9199" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I63fed0d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc.">Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9199 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Whether the claimant was entitled to a general lien under section 20 could not be determined on a motion. Genuine issues were involved and a trial was required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="300016 Ontario Ltd." p2="176419 Canada Ltd." post.rptr="5" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I63fed0d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="300016 Ontario Ltd. v. 176419 Canada Ltd.">300016 Ontario Ltd. v. 176419 Canada Ltd. (1996), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 5, 33 O.R. (3d) 154 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff installed gas furnaces on nine units of a project owned by the defendant, under a contract that did not stipulate that lien rights were to be on a lot-by-lot basis. When its account was not paid, the plaintiff registered a general lien against four of the nine units, for work done on all nine units. After the owner obtained a building mortgage on the four units, the mortgagee took possession of the project and then advanced funds to the trades working on the units, including the plaintiff, without retaining the statutory holdback. In allowing the plaintiff's appeal, the court held that the plaintiff's general lien was valid, and pursuant to s. 34(7), covered all the lots upon which services and materials had been supplied. It attached to units 1, 2, 4 and 9, even though the amount of money received by the plaintiff was said to cover the amount of money expended on those units.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Gillies Lumber Inc." p2="Kubassek Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="2692" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I63fef7e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd.">Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 2692, 1999 CarswellOnt 2160 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1997), 32 O.R. (3d) 475 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There were four separate projects and technically four separate owners at the time of registration of a general lien covering all four projects. The general lien was not allowed, as a single owner was required. The Divisional Court had held that where a general lien has been filed and disallowed, the lien claimant may still have a specific lien on each of the respective properties described in the general lien, following <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1910" p1="Ontario Lime Assn." p2="Grimwood" post.rptr="17" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I63fef7e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Lime Assn. v. Grimwood">Ontario Lime Assn. v. Grimwood (1910), 22 O.L.R. 17 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Rockwell Electric Ltd." p2="Welsford Development Corp." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I63fef7e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rockwell Electric Ltd. v. Welsford Development Corp.">Rockwell Electric Ltd. v. Welsford Development Corp. (1989), 33 C.L.R. 1, 89 N.S.R. (2d) 159 (N.S. C.A.)</ref></cite>. The Court of Appeal overturned this decision and disallowed the lien. The Act does not enable the court to amend or rectify a claim for a general lien that is not available to a lien claimant under s. 20(1). The failure of a general lien can not be “corrected” by s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-Haven Homes Inc." p2="O'Neill" post.rptr="249" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I63ff1ef05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill">Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill (1991), 44 C.L.R. 249 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee held building mortgages over six parcels of land which were being developed, and the plaintiff lien claimants filed a lien claim against all six parcels. After some of the parcels were sold, and discharges were registered, two parcels remained encumbered by the claim. The mortgagee brought a motion to vacate the liens and certificate of action upon payment into court of a reasonable amount. The lien claimants were entitled to a general lien in respect of the two encumbered parcels. As there remained an unadvanced holdback in the hands of the mortgagee in respect of three parts, the full amount was to be paid into court even though only two parts remained encumbered. Accordingly, an order to vacate the liens would be granted upon payment into court of that amount.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 20(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc." p2="Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd." post.rptr="5655" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I63ff1ef15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc. v. Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd.">Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc. v. Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd., 2014 ONSC 5655, 2014 CarswellOnt 15009, 45 C.L.R. (4th) 275, 328 O.A.C. 189 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 6825, 2014 CarswellOnt 16757, 45 C.L.R. (4th) 287 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2016 ONCA 305, 2016 CarswellOnt 6411, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 1, 398 D.L.R. (4th) 251 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—When the contract between the owner and contractor states that liens shall arise and expire on a lot by lot basis, s. 20(2) extinguishes all general lien holder rights for the contractor and all subcontractors under or in respect of that contract. This is so despite the fact that s. 20(2) makes no reference to a subcontract. To conclude otherwise would create in a subcontractor an independent right to a general lien that cannot be waived. It would undermine the ability of contractors and owners to make provision in their contract to allow the owner to release the holdback on a lot-by-lot basis, and that would considerably undermine the benefit of contracting out under s. 20(2). Because the right to a general lien can only arise under s. 20(1) in the contract between the contractor and the owner, a subcontract cannot create that right. Therefore, the fact that a subcontract is silent on the issue cannot have any effect.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Monaco Electric Ltd." p2="Empire Myers Road Inc." post.rptr="713" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I63ff1ef25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Monaco Electric Ltd. v. Empire Myers Road Inc.">Monaco Electric Ltd. v. Empire Myers Road Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 713, 2004 CarswellOnt 773, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 270 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contracts stated that any liens that might arise under the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> were to arise on a lot-by-lot basis. The clauses were not exclusionary clauses and the provisions of s. 20 applied. Where the contract did not allow for a general lien, by specifically stating that liens could only arise on a lot-by-lot basis, there could be no general lien. The contract only determined the manner in which the lien(s) were to be registered, and did not deprive the claimant of a right to a construction lien by virtue of the written agreement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="595997 Ontario Inc." p2="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I63ff1ef35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="595997 Ontario Inc. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)">595997 Ontario Inc. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 61 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A landscape contractor registered a general lien for the full amount of its claim on each of several lots in a townhouse development, even though the contract provided that liens would arise and expire on a lot-by-lot basis and would be apportioned to reflect the actual services and materials provided to each lot. The landscape contractor brought an action against the developer and purchasers of one of the townhouses. The purchasers of the townhouse paid the full amount of the general lien into trust and successfully moved to dismiss the lien action against them, by obtaining a declaration that they were “home buyers” under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The trust funds were paid out to them. The orders were upheld on appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd." p2="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="575" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90d348e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)">Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 575, 38 C.B.R. (3d) 250 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1996), 206 N.R. 315 (note), [1996] S.C.C.A. No. 214 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—A term of a contract providing that liens arose and expired on a lot-by-lot basis was not an exclusionary clause that could be avoided by fundamental breach. It was also held, with a dissent on this point, that a lien claimant cannot convert a lot specific lien to a general lien as this would be to ignore the scheme of s. 20.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd." p2="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="575" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90d348e1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)">Leo P. Abrams & Son Ltd. v. MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 575, 38 C.B.R. (3d) 250 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1996), 206 N.R. 315 (note), [1996] S.C.C.A. No. 214 (S.C.C.); affirming (1995), 35 C.B.R. (3d) 277 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to its contract with the builder, the lien claimant should have liened the lots it provided services to on a lot-by-lot basis, but did not do so because of its own negligence. The general lien that was registered should not be treated as a lien on the lot in question for the work done on that lot. That would permit the claimant to take advantage of its own negligence to the detriment of the other creditors.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
21:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 21.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">21:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35 first expressed the concept of the lien as a charge stating that “the liens created by this Act shall be a charge upon the amounts directed to be retained”. <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, s. 11 expanded this to be a charge upon the amounts directed to be retained by this section in favour of sub-contractors whose liens are derived under persons to whom such moneys so required to be retained are respectively payable. This concept became s. 12(3) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69. The reference to “subcontractors” was replaced by “lienholders” in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30 (see s. 12(3)). No further changes were made until <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, which amendment was short-lived as <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1975</ital>, S.O. 1975, c. 43 repealed the section in its entirety and replaced it with a phrase that was almost identical to the 1923 version. No further revisions were made until the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 was proclaimed. The present s. 21 is identical to the 1983 version.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Even prior to preservation or perfection, the lien is said to be a charge on the holdback and all amounts owed to a claimant's payer on a project, but it is then a mere unperfected and inchoate interest.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc." p2="Sutton Forming Inc." post.rptr="6751" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6750b1003b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc. v. Sutton Forming Inc.">Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc. v. Sutton Forming Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 6751, 2023 ONSC 2628, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 20 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2022 ONSC 1309, 2022 CarswellOnt 3103 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The Act creates two holdback obligations. The first, the “basic holdback”, set out under s. 22, amounts to 10 per cent of the value of the services or materials supplied under a contract or subcontract required to be withheld from payment by Part IV. Section 21 of the Act provides that the lien of a person is a charge upon the holdbacks required to be retained under Part IV, and, subject to subs. 17(3), any additional amount owed by the payor to the contractor on the contract. The lien is a charge against the basic holdback, and also against “any additional amount owed” on the contract. This second aspect of the charge is sometimes referred to as the “additional holdback”. The charge created by s. 21 is subject to s.17(3) in respect to the additional holdback, but is not subject to s.17(3) in respect to the basic holdback. The combined effect of ss.21 and 17(3) is that subcontractor liens are a charge against the whole of the amount owed by the owner to the contractor under the contract; however, the owner is entitled to set off claims against the contractor in calculating the overall obligation, provided, however, that set-off claims cannot be applied to reduce the owner's obligation below the amount of the basic holdback created in s. 22(1). As found by the motion judge here, the holdback is based on the contract price as the services are provided. It is not based on the total contract price, or the amounts actually paid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Khalimov" p2="Hogarth" post.rptr="6244" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I63ff6d105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khalimov v. Hogarth">Khalimov v. Hogarth, 2015 ONSC 6244, 2015 CarswellOnt 15551, 56 C.L.R. (4th) 167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Once a lien is discharged all lien claims expire, including a lien claim asserted as a charge against the holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="8127" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I63ff6d115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2009 CarswellOnt 8127, 91 C.L.R. (3d) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The combined effect of ss. 21 and 17(3) is such that subcontractor liens are a charge against the whole of the amount owed by the owner to the contractor under the contract. However, the owner is entitled to set-off claims against the contractor in calculating the overall obligation, provided, however, that set-off claims cannot be applied to reduce the owner's obligation below the amount of the basic holdback created in s. 22(1). Thus owner's minimum liability to the subcontractors in this case was the lesser of the basic holdback and the aggregate of all valid and subsisting subcontractor lien claims.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A new subsection 22(4) was added to the Act to specify the various forms in which a holdback may be held under the Act</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Holdback may now be retained in cash, of letter of credit in prescribed form, or demand-worded holdback payment bond in prescribed form</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Expert Review found that holdback in the form of cash only simply did not accord with notion of a modernized Act</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This also avoids the obligation of certain owners to maintain cash in circumstances where that might otherwise be administratively cumbersome</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27 did not require the retention of a percentage holdback of the price of all services and materials provided. It was not until March 10, 1882 when <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15 received Royal Assent, that a statutory holdback scheme was established in this Province. Section 5 of that statute read:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">5.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">In case of there being such a contract, as aforesaid, if any person other than the contractor has performed labour or supplied materials on or for the execution of the contract, the owner shall, in the absence of a stipulation to the contrary, be entitled to retain, for a period of thirty days after the completion of the contract, ten per centum of the price to be paid to the contractor.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The obligation to retain a 10 per cent holdback applied only to the owner under the 1882 version of the <ital>Act</ital>. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1887, c. 126 obliged the owner, in the absence of a stipulation to the contrary, to retain for a period of 30 days after the completion of the contract, 10 per cent of the price to be paid to the contractor. <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, required the owner to retain a holdback of 20 per cent of the “value of the work, service and materials actually done, placed or furnished”, but where the contract exceeded $15,000.00, 15 per cent was to be retained. <ital>An Act to amend the Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1897, c. 24 reworded the section to apply to “the person primarily liable upon any contract under or by virtue of which a lien may arise”. Despite the passage of several statutes which amended various sections of the Act over time, in was not until 1952, when <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1953</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 61 was proclaimed in force, that the concept of statutory holdbacks was substantially revisited by the legislature. The time for retention of the holdbacks was increased to 37 days from 30 days. Additional subsections were added to address the certification of payments by an architect, engineer or “other person upon whose certificates payments are to be made”. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1957</ital>, S.O. 1957, c. 68, addressed an apparent inconsistency in the reference to holdback percentages. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1958</ital>, S.O. 1958, c. 57, assented to March 27, 1958, increased the value of the contracts which qualified for the 15 per cent holdback from $15,000.00 to $25,000.00. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 reduced the quantum of the holdback to 15 per cent, irrespective of the value of the contract. Apart from a reorganization of the section in 1975, no substantial changes were made until January 27, 1983 when the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 was proclaimed. The new holdback section was a major departure from s. 12(1) of the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. For the first time, the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> included “Holdback” as a defined term meaning the 10 per cent of the value of the services or materials supplied under a contract or subcontract required to be withheld from payment by Part IV. The holdback scheme outlined in the 1983 version of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is identical to the present scheme, including two types of holdbacks, “Basic Holdback” and “Holdback for Finishing Work”. The provision for holdback for finishing work ensured for the first time that the appropriate holdback would not be released before the finishing trades could exercise their lien rights under the Act. The time period for retaining the holdback was increased to 45 days.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section of the statute governs all others which are enacted expressly “subject to” its application. In the pyramidal structure of construction projects, persons contract to supply services and materials knowing that those services and materials will usually be supplied by persons with whom they have no direct contractual relationship. Suppliers of services and materials also know that payment ultimately comes from a land owner with whom they may have no direct contractual relationship. Part IV is therefore designed to accommodate this reality, and to protect those on lower rungs of the ladder from the insolvency or default of those above.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The result of this holdback scheme should be the withholding of an equal percentage all the way down the line, notionally aggregating the “profit” component of the contract with the owner. As each level of privity with the contractor bears the same proportionate burden, no one should suffer a financial hardship as a result of having a holdback retained from it, as they must retain a proportionate amount from those below.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 22 provides for two different holdbacks. Subsection 22(1) mandates the retention of 10 per cent of the price of services or materials as they are actually supplied until all lien rights have been satisfied, discharged or have expired. Section 26 provides for the release of the basic holdback, and Part V of the Act deals with the expiry, preservation and perfection of lien claims. Section 22(2) creates a second holdback, designed to protect the finishing trades, of 10 per cent of services and materials supplied from the day the contract was certified or declared to be substantially performed until all lien rights have been satisfied, discharged or have expired. The release of holdback for finishing work is provided for in s. 27. It is irrelevant, under s. 22(3) in either situation as to whether the contract calls for partial payments or payment in full upon completion, and hence the holdback must be retained as the work is done, not paid for. The owner is therefore still liable to other suppliers for the holdback, even where the contract calls for payment on completion and the contractor defaults before completion.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
22:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 22.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">22:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 22(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc." p2="Sutton Forming Inc." post.rptr="6751" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I675126303b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc. v. Sutton Forming Inc.">Homes by DeSantis (Lake) Inc. v. Sutton Forming Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 6751, 2023 ONSC 2628, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 20 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2022 ONSC 1309, 2022 CarswellOnt 3103 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The Act creates two holdback obligations. The first, the “basic holdback”, set out under s. 22 amounts to 10 per cent of the value of the services or materials supplied under a contract or subcontract required to be withheld from payment by Part IV. Section 21 of the Act provides that the lien of a person is a charge upon the holdbacks required to be retained under Part IV, and, subject to subs. 17(3), any additional amount owed by the payor to the contractor on the contract. The lien is a charge against the basic holdback, and also against “any additional amount owed” on the contract. This second aspect of the charge is sometimes referred to as the “additional holdback”. The charge created by s. 21 is subject to s.17(3) in respect to the additional holdback, but is not subject to s.17(3) in respect to the basic holdback. As found by the motion judge, the holdback is based on the contract price as the services are provided. It is not based on the total contract price, or the amounts actually paid. As well, a deficiency claim by owner against contractor does not impede payments from the basic holdback to any subcontractors and their suppliers in the absence of parallel deficiency claims at each applicable rung of the construction ladder.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc." p2="AVN Plumbing Limited et al." post.rptr="16272" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I8da8c581ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc. v. AVN Plumbing Limited et al.">Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc. v. AVN Plumbing Limited et al., 2020 CarswellOnt 16272, 2020 ONSC 6728, 16 C.L.R. (5th) 267 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed in part <ital>Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc. v. 690 King Street Corporation</ital>, 2022 CarswellOnt 19707, 2022 ONSC 6439 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—After the defendant contractor withdrew from the condominium construction project, still owing monies to the plaintiff subcontractor, the owner entered into a termination agreement with the contractor, in which it agreed to “arrange payment for outstanding obligations” of the contractor to specified subcontractors and suppliers with respect to the project site once certain materials were returned to the site. At issue was whether the owner was liable to pay the plaintiff supplier directly or indemnify the contractor in respect of the supplier's claim. The owner argued its obligations to the contractor's subcontractors and suppliers was limited to payment of the holdback required to be maintained by it under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Upon a review of the agreement as a whole, the phrase “will arrange payment for outstanding obligations” was not capable of referring merely to the obligation of the owner to retain the statutory holdback in respect of the subcontractors. S. 22 did not contemplate a payer unilaterally determining that its obligation to maintain a holdback is restricted to responding to claims of certain suppliers and subcontractors and not to others and only in reference to invoices issued by a specific date. A payor's holdback must be retained until all liens that may be claimed against it have expired, satisfied, or discharged. In the termination agreement, the owner undertook to arrange payment for “outstanding obligations” to the named suppliers and sub-consultants once material was returned to the site by a specified time. To suggest that the owner simply agreed to pay the holdback in respect of its contract with the contractor to certain suppliers once materials were returned to site was inconsistent with the owner's holdback obligation. The amount was to be paid to the plaintiff from the security in court posted by the owner. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The Divisional Court substantively affirmed all the motion judge's conclusions in the earlier judgment, while allowing the owner's appeal only with respect to the quantum of interest payable by the owner.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thompson" p2="Carleton University" post.rptr="4336" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I63ffe2415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thompson v. Carleton University">Thompson v. Carleton University, 2019 ONSC 4336, 2019 CarswellOnt 11566, 92 C.L.R. (4th) 33 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 7633 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The liens in question were registered by the workers' union trust fund on behalf of carpenters employed by the subcontractor. At issue was the general contractor's liability to the union trust fund for holdback, and the amount of that holdback, which depended on the value of the work performed under the sub-contract at the time the lien was filed. The subcontractor was insolvent and did not actively defend or participate in the proceeding. The court rejected the contractor's position that its contract with the subsequently insolvent subcontractor was amended to a labour only contract, such that the value of the subcontractor's work would not include the material or equipment rental and the basic holdback would be only 10% of a greatly reduced amount. The court also found that there was no “over certification”. Although the parties were not bound by the payment certification made at the time of progress payments, there was a significant onus on a party wishing to show that the certificate was in error, and that onus was not met here.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Construction Inc." p2="Unimac" post.rptr="8183" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I640009505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac">Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac, 2016 ONSC 8183, 2016 CarswellOnt 21034, 73 C.L.R. (4th) 258 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the owner was at risk of paying prejudgment interest on the holdback under s. 128(1) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43 and, as such, was required to post security for prejudgement interest. For such a risk to exist, the obligation of holdback would have to be a payment obligation. The master found that holdback is a retention obligation, not a payment obligation. Holdback must be retained by the payer under ss. 22 and 24. Basic and finishing holdback may only be paid by the payer once all liens have expired, been satisfied, discharged, or provided for under s. 44. A payer may elect to post the holdback with the court under s. 44 in order to obtain an order vacating a lien, but a payer is not required to do so. It is also permissible for an owner to pay notice holdback directly to a notice giver under s. 28, but, once again, no payer is required to do so. If the payer decides to post the holdback with the court, or to pay the holdback into an interest bearing bank account, as in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Co." p2="JJ's Hospitality Ltd." post.rptr="4471" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90d40c30f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd.">Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 4471, 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101, [1993] O.J. No. 1171, 12 O.R. (3d) 351 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, interest will accumulate and be owed. However, this does not affect the nature of the obligation, and the payer's only obligation is to retain holdback. As such, the owner was not at risk of paying prejudgment interest and was not required to post security for prejudgement interest.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I640009525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Multiple lien claimants contracted directly with the defendant owner in respect of the construction of various townhouses, and after the owner abandoned the project and the defendant mortgagee stepped into shoes of the owner. The Master erred when, contrary to the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I640009535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, he calculated the deficiency in the holdback by adding up and determining the sum of all of the lien claims and setting that value against a pooling of all of the holdbacks and the relative value he inferred. The effect was to treat each of the lien claimants as if they were subcontractors instead of suppliers each with their own privity of contract with the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Villa Nicolini Inc." post.rptr="5444" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640009545fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc.">Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc., 2012 ONSC 5444, 2012 CarswellOnt 12496, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 36 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 ONSC 6616, 2012 CarswellOnt 15361, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 37 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although the Act does not mention HST as a component of the basic holdback, if the holdback does not include a component for value added taxes, then the amount actually available for the party entitled to the holdback will not equal 10% of the value of those services. As a practical matter, the payment of value added taxes should be held back by payers along with the required 10% of the value of services provided, until the holdback is released under the terms of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Simpson" p2="Bridgewater Bank" post.rptr="714" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640030605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simpson v. Bridgewater Bank">Simpson v. Bridgewater Bank, 2012 ONSC 714, 2012 CarswellOnt 1420, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 243 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 5054, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff general contractor entered into construction contract with the owner for construction of a home, and the defendant bank provided mortgage financing. The bank's solicitor held back 10 per cent from each of construction advances, and, after the contractor eventually obtained judgment in its lien action against the owner, the bank completed a sale of the property under power of sale pursuant to the mortgage. The contractor brought action for a declaration that the monies held back by the bank were trust funds held for his benefit. Although the funds were ultimately held by the court to be trust funds, the bank was under no obligation under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, as a mortgagee, to maintain a holdback described in s. 22(1). The Bank was not a “payer” within the meaning of the <ital>Act</ital>, and was not “the owner, contractor or subcontractor who is liable to pay for the materials or services supplied to an improvement under a contract or subcontract.” [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See the digest of this case under s. 7(1). See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Vecero" p2="C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc." post.rptr="903" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90d43340f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc.">Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 903, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 74 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> at paras. 15–17, under ss. 1, 7(1) and s. 78.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Selyan's Flooring Inc." p2="2182537 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2922" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640030625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Selyan's Flooring Inc. v. 2182537 Ontario Inc.">Selyan's Flooring Inc. v. 2182537 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 2922, 2012 CarswellOnt 6287, 19 C.L.R. (4th) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff argued that the defendant unduly delayed the calculation and payment of the holdback funds, for the purpose of preventing the sub-trades from discovering that it had not, in fact, complied with its holdback obligations. On the record now before it, the Court was unable to draw that inference and was not of the view that failing to set aside and withhold 10% of the contract price in cash was improper, given that in practice the holdback is more often merely a stacked series of claims upon a final draw by the contractor on the owner's funds, rather than cash held back at each level.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="8127" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I640057705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2009 CarswellOnt 8127, 91 C.L.R. (3d) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The onus lies on the owner to establish that its holdback obligation is less than the total quantum of valid and subsisting subcontractor liens.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Funrooms.ca Inc." p2="Wong" post.rptr="9440" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I640057715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Funrooms.ca Inc. v. Wong">Funrooms.ca Inc. v. Wong (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9440 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The statutory holdback scheme supplants any claim for payment by a subcontractor against an owner on a quantum meruit basis. The statute specifically limits the liability of an owner to a subcontractor to the 10 per cent holdback. In the absence of a contract directly with the plaintiff subcontractor, where the owner already paid the holdback, its obligation to the subcontractor was fulfilled. The lien claim filed by the subcontractor against title to the property was dismissed, the lien discharged and moneys paid into court by the owner were ordered to be paid out to the owner with interest.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Dawson Construction & Haulage Ltd." p2="747877 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="7229" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I640057725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dawson Construction & Haulage Ltd. v. 747877 Ontario Inc.">Dawson Construction & Haulage Ltd. v. 747877 Ontario Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 7229 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 68 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor provided excavation work on the lot in question, but a dispute arose between the developers of the property and the owners of the lot as to who was responsible for payment. As there was no contractual relationship between the owners and contractor, the court held the developer responsible for the full amount of the lien claim and the owners jointly responsible for an amount equal to the 10 per cent holdback they were required to retain under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd." p2="One Shaftesbury Community Assn." post.rptr="5995" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I640057735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn.">Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5995, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 184 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A project for a residential retirement community utilized a right-to-occupy or life-lease legal structure. The property in question was purchased and the title was transferred to a non-profit community association, which entered into a construction and development agreement with a for-profit numbered company that was to assume the role of construction manager. When construction costs escalated, and some units did not sell or could not be sold because of title problems, there was a shortfall in the mortgage money required to pay the general contractor and five trades. The Master found that the numbered company was not a “payer upon a contract under which a lien may arise…” as provided for in s. 22(1) of the Act. The association was not “liable to pay” anything to the numbered company, but instead at best had entered into a profit sharing arrangement which was not a “payment for the price of services or materials as they are actually supplied”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Crownwood Construction Ltd." p2="Omartech Construction Inc." post.rptr="1337" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I64007e805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Crownwood Construction Ltd. v. Omartech Construction Inc.">Crownwood Construction Ltd. v. Omartech Construction Inc. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 1337, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 86 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3715, [2006] O.J. No. 2466, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 134 (Ont. Master); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 8076, 57 C.L.R. (3d) 138 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Master held that an owner's holdback liability to the general contractor is calculated on the value of all contracts, not just the contract of the lien-claiming sub-contractor, relying on the Master's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19930322" p1="Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Kemp" post.rptr="539" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I64007e815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp">Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp (1992), 9 O.R. (3d) 539, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 161, Master; reversed (March 22, 1993)</ref></cite>. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The Master's decision in <ital>Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp</ital> was reversed by a single judge of the Divisional Court, relying on the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I64007e825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd." p2="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." post.rptr="892" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I64007e835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc.">H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 892, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 305 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor was an engineering firm that provided engineering services to the contractor in respect of the construction of a hospital. The plaintiff subcontractor, a second subcontractor and a sub-subcontractor all registered liens against the lands and premises. At issue was the amount of the holdback properly retained by the owner hospital. At the time of the settlement meeting, the sum of $774,446.40 remained owing to the plaintiff. The owner had paid the contractor $14,878,000.00 relating to the project, and the plaintiff argued that the ten percent holdback was therefore $1,487,800.00, less a payment of $260,114.49 made to the sub-subcontractor which all parties agreed should be deducted, resulting in a holdback obligation of $1,227,685.60. The hospital claimed that it was only liable to the plaintiff for $319,071, which was calculated as the $774,446 agreed to be owing less $216,114 paid to sub-subcontractor and $195,261 previously paid to the plaintiff for which a release was given. The hospital also claimed that payments made to the contractor in trust to be paid to other contractors should have been deducted from its holdback liability and that the plaintiff was estopped from arguing that the hospital should not be given any credit towards the holdback. In rejecting the defendant hospital's arguments, the court held that the holdback was to be based upon the value of the contract confirmed in the settlement meeting being $14,703,183.00. The total required holdback as of the date of the statement of settlement was therefore $1,487,800.00, less the payment of $260,114.49 made to the sub-subcontractor, resulting in a holdback obligation of $1,227,685.60. Estoppel could not arise in circumstances where a statute provided mandatory terms. The legal relationship in matters involving construction contracts was governed not only by the contract between the parties, but also by operation of statute. While estoppel might apply on those parts of the contract, which were not effected by the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, they could not apply to permit waiver out of the statutory provisions. The payments made, while they could certainly be applied towards any amount outstanding between the parties, could not be considered to be a reduction in the amount of holdback required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="1023436 Ontario Ltd." p2="Noblestar Properties (Central) Ltd." post.rptr="2900" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I6400a5905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1023436 Ontario Ltd. v. Noblestar Properties (Central) Ltd.">1023436 Ontario Ltd. v. Noblestar Properties (Central) Ltd. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 2900, 2004 CarswellOnt 2781, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 206 (Master)</ref></cite>—The contract provided that the general contractor was to arrange for a 50 per cent performance bond to be supplied by major subcontractors, and to make up the difference between those subtrade bonds and 50 per cent, but the cost of bonding was to be borne by the owner. Bonding became an issue because the bonds were not in place when the first progress draw was requested and the bonds were still not completely in place when that progress draw was paid. The bonding requirement was a condition of financing without which the owner would not be advanced funds by the bank. Once the bonding issue came to light, the work was relatively advanced. The cost consultant retained by the project financier authorized additional progress draws but the project consultant was directed to hold back a “deficiency holdback” in lieu of the requisite bonds in addition to the statutory holdback as a term of continued financing. The court noted that deficiency holdback was not a form of holdback recognized or authorized by the Act but under the circumstances holding back the additional funds was a reasonable, moderate and practical response. While it was true that at the time of the holdback the majority of the work that was to be secured by bonding had been completed, the amount held back was only a fraction of the amount that was supposed to be protected by bonding. The court did not condone this form of self help or sanction a unilateral increase in holdback as the correct legal response to the situation, but it was not prepared to visit the owner with any extraordinary consequences. The task was to calculate what, if anything, was owing to plaintiff, and the additional holdback was simply part of the calculation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="TCG Asphalt & Construction Inc." p2="Newport Properties Ltd." post.rptr="413" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I6400a5915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="TCG Asphalt & Construction Inc. v. Newport Properties Ltd.">TCG Asphalt & Construction Inc. v. Newport Properties Ltd. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 413, 2003 CarswellOnt 626, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 297 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4142 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1030, [2005] O.J. No. 1050, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 203 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—As part of the construction of a subdivision, various contracts were entered into over ten years in order to create the streets and complete the various improvements on and under those streets. Many of those contracts were completed years or months before the plaintiff entered into a contract with the developer to perform a number of services. Disagreement arose as to the quantum of the holdback required to be retained by the owner city. The plaintiff argued the holdback should be 10 per cent of the value of all work performed up to the present pursuant to the original subdivision agreement, while the city submitted that the holdback liability should be limited to 10 per cent of the contract price for the work performed by the plaintiff for the developer. This was one of those rare cases where a substantial part of the improvement had been completed more than 45 days prior to the commencement of the plaintiff's work. In such a case the Plaintiff's contract was the total value of the “improvement”. The holdback amount applicable was therefore 10 per cent of the plaintiff's account for services rendered, not of the total value of all work performed over the ten-year period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd." p2="Sargeant" post.rptr="8583" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I6400a5925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd. v. Sargeant">Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd. v. Sargeant (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 8583, [2002] O.J. No. 2198 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 2197, 2002 CarswellOnt 7436 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 1043, 207 O.A.C. 264, 51 C.L.R. (3d) 10, 264 D.L.R. (4th) 352 (Ont. C.A.); additional reasons 2008 CarswellOnt 1242, 2008 ONCA 166, 67 C.L.R. (3d) 163 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 8183 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The holdback must be based on the services or materials as they are supplied under the contract, not on the improved value of the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="G.M.
