Sernas & Associates Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd. (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 3161, 48 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Each lien claimant is entitled to priority to the extent of a deficiency in the holdback required to be retained by the owner on each contract. The reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6400cca15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> was adopted, concluding that the contract of each lien claimant stood on its own with a separate holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd." p2="Pier One Masonry Inc." post.rptr="3424" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I6400cca25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc.">Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3424, 1998 CarswellOnt 3379 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 3998 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a remarkable, perhaps unique case on its facts, involving the self interested 100 per cent prepayment of a 2,239,759 contract price, and the subsequent expenditure of that sum by the non-arm's length contractor so as to defeat, for all practical purposes, a mason's lien. The Court held that where an owner has prepaid a contractor to the foreseeable prejudice of the trades, equity demands no less than that the owner's obligations be not limited to the 10 per cent holdback and the full liens should be recoverable against the owner. The statutory frame of reference for such an order is found in ss. 8 and 13, the trust sections of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Ellmac Contracting Inc." p2="Hydin Ltd." post.rptr="2935" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I6400f3b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ellmac Contracting Inc. v. Hydin Ltd.">Ellmac Contracting Inc. v. Hydin Ltd. (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 2935 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Divisional Court followed the decision of Fortier J. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6400f3b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and the judgment of Justice Montgomery, sitting as a single judge of the Divisional Court in <ital>Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp</ital>, Kirsh's Construction Lien Case Finder, No. 22.6. This was not a case where there was a separate contract between the owner and each subcontractor/supplier.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Di Mario" p2="Schuster" post.rptr="140" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I6400f3b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Mario v. Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owners entered into an agreement for the purchase of a new home to be constructed by L Inc. The agreement provided for the owners to pay a sum of $25,000 upon acceptance of the offer, a further $25,000 at the rough framing stage and a further $25,000 at the drywall boarding stage. Although the agreement between the owners and L Inc. indicated that the sum of $75,000 was a deposit, both of the parties anticipated that the monies would be used to fund the purchase of the lot and construction of the house. While the first payment of $25,000 to L Inc. was a payment required under the “contract”, the actual construction did not begin until later, and it could not be said to be a payment for the price of services or materials actually supplied, rather, it was intended to act as a deposit towards the land purchase portion of the contract and was not an advance or payment made to L Inc. on a construction portion of the contract. However, the contract consisted of two parts: the transfer of the land and the construction of the home. With respect to the remaining payments, it was a reasonable inference that the value of the services and material on the premises was in excess of $50,000, and the payments were therefore made in compliance with the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Co." p2="JJ's Hospitality Ltd." post.rptr="4471" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90d51da0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd.">Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 4471, 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101, [1993] O.J. No. 1171, 12 O.R. (3d) 351 (Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101 <point>at 122</point> (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1995), 21 O.R. (3d) 788, 19 C.L.R. (2d) 47, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Solo Mill & Lumber Co. v. J.J.'s Hospitality Ltd.)</ital> 79 O.A.C. 281 (Div. Ct.); affirmed (1996), 30 O.R. (3d) 96, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. J.J.'s Hospitality Ltd.)</ital> 93 O.A.C. 159 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs claimed interest on the holdback, arguing that they were entitled to interest equivalent to what the final holdback would have earned had it been paid into court, as they argued the owner should have done. The owner did not pay the holdback into court, but rather into an interest bearing account, earning interest at 9.3 per cent. Had the holdback been paid into court, it would have earned 9.8 per cent. The difference was not great. Had the plaintiffs been prepared to release the owner, the owner would have released the holdback. The plaintiffs were aware of the amount of the holdback that the owner admitted to being liable for even before the statement of claim was issued. Therefore, it was inappropriate to order costs against the owner. Those costs could be set off against the holdback payable to the plaintiffs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd." p2="Valley Ridge Inc." post.rptr="139" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I64011ac05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc.">M.W.M. Construction of Kitchener Ltd. v. Valley Ridge Inc. (1993), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 139 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 25 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Construction of a residential project was halted after a number of claims for lien and several certificates of action had been registered, and the owner, general contractor, and one mortgagee were noted in default. The trial judge, in deciding whether there should be one holdback amount to which all claimants would have access or whether there should be a separate holdback in respect of the contract between the owner and a subcontractor who had supplied security services, found that it would be inequitable to limit the first mortgagee's liability to the subcontractor, by virtue of its direct contract with the owner, to 10 per cent and ruled in favour of a global holdback. On appeal, the court found that, by virtue of ss. 1(1) and 22 of the Act, an owner is only required to hold back 10 per cent of the price of services supplied under the contract. Therefore, all the subcontractor was entitled to was 10 per cent of the contract price.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Dufferin Concrete Products" p2="Waterbrooke Development Ltd." post.rptr="132" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I64011ac15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dufferin Concrete Products v. Waterbrooke Development Ltd.">Dufferin Concrete Products v. Waterbrooke Development Ltd. (1992), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 132 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was a supplier of concrete materials and delivered concrete to an improvement financed with a building mortgage. The plaintiff supplied concrete in the amount of $218,258.67 and there remained $25,926.45 due and owing to the plaintiff for the materials supplied. The plaintiff registered a claim for lien in the amount of $25,926.45 against the lands and premises comprising the improvement. The plaintiff had been paid in full for those invoices which were paid, and consequently the holdback by the defendant was paid prematurely. The plaintiff applied for summary judgment in the amount of $21,817.33. The court held that the failure to retain the 10 per cent holdback deprived those claiming under the plaintiff, not the plaintiff itself. Consequently, the holdback collectable by the plaintiff from the mortgagee was 10 per cent of the unpaid contracts, or $2,592.65.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I64011ac25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial performance issued by the project architect stated that “the contract for the following improvement; Princess Gardens, Phase I, basic shell to the above premises was substantially performed”, even though the architect acknowledged there was no such improvement as a basic shell. As well, the certificate was further deficient in that the name of the contractor was shown as “c/o owner”, and the address for service was left blank. The court found that these irregularities were significant, and not minor ones curable under s. 6 of the Act. Accordingly, the holdback was not properly released pursuant to the certificate.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I640141d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner of a project for the construction of 36 houses on 36 single-family lots became insolvent and stopped paying trades, professionals, and suppliers to the project after all but five of the houses had been completed and sold to third party purchasers. A mortgage in excess of $5,000,000 had been obtained to secure the financing of the entire project, and while the parties agreed that s. 78(2) applied and that the liens had priority over the mortgage to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner, they could not agree on the amount of the holdback. The lien claimants argued that the holdback should be 10 per cent of the value of the whole improvement which would ensure a payout to all lien claimants of 100 per cent. The mortgagee claimed that the lien claimants were entitled to priority only for the deficiency in the holdback on each of their contracts. Held, each lien claimant was entitled only to priority to the extent of a deficiency in the holdback required to be retained by the owner on each of their contracts. It would not be rational under s. 22(1) of the Act to allow a contract, which was completed at the beginning of the project and on which the owner paid out the holdback pursuant to s. 31 at the expiration of the 45-day period for the registration of liens, to be revived for purposes of computing the holdback in the present action. “Improvement” is also defined in the Act and, if it was intended that the holdback be 10 per cent of the “improvement,” that term would have been used in s. 22(1), but instead the word “contract” was used. The interpretation suggested by the lien claimants would cause great confusion in the construction industry and would result in delay in the release of holdbacks when work was done and the lien period expired. Therefore, in the circumstances of the present case, the contract of each lien claimant stood on its own and had a separate holdback to which the lien claimant might look for payment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>But See</ital>:</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Forte Aluminum Ltd." p2="Frank Plastina Investments Ltd." post.rptr="167" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I640141d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forte Aluminum Ltd. v. Frank Plastina Investments Ltd.">Forte Aluminum Ltd. v. Frank Plastina Investments Ltd. (1988), 29 C.L.R. 167 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—This case was decided prior to the amendment to add s. 23(3)(b) and therefore now stands solely for the proposition that the burden of establishing holdback is on the owner. The proper amount of holdback was held to be 10 per cent of the value of the improvement. There will be circumstances where, because the most substantial part of the improvement has been completed more than 45 days prior to the commencement of some new or additional work, the particular contract will be equal to the total value of the improvement, in most istances, as here, the holdback will be 10 per cent of all of the subcontracts on the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19930322" p1="Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Kemp" post.rptr="539" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I640141d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp">Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp (1992), 9 O.R. (3d) 539, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 161, Master; reversed (March 22, 1993)</ref></cite>, Kirsh's Construction Lien Case Finder No. 22.6, Montgomery J.—An owner defaulted on payments to its contractors, and an issue arose as to the priorities between the mortgagee and the seven lien claimants. The parties were in agreement that s. 78(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (Ont.) applied and that the lien claimants had priority to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV of the Act. At the pre-trial motion, the Master was asked to determine the value of the owner's holdback. Held, s. 23(1) determines what holdbacks the owner must retain to protect the lien claimants who are contractors retained by the owner. Therefore, the holdbacks to be retained by the owner for the benefit of the lien claimants, here the contractors, was 10 per cent of the value of the services and materials supplied to the improvement, and not just of the value of each contract. The 10 per cent holdback applied to all contracts for improvement, not only to those for which liens have been filed. The 1990 amendment to s. 23 did not alter the meaning of s. 23(1) as it was prior to the amendment. A single judge of the Divisional Court reversed the Master's decision a year later, relying on the reasoning of Fortier J. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I640141d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Core Developments Ltd." p2="Jerry's Asphalt Paving Ltd." post.rptr="927" pre.rptr="[1990]" ref.id="I640168e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Core Developments Ltd. v. Jerry's Asphalt Paving Ltd.">Core Developments Ltd. v. Jerry's Asphalt Paving Ltd. (1990), [1990] O.J. No. 927 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The court found that, that pursuant to s. 23(1) of the Act, the lien claimants could look to the holdback being retained by the owner in respect to its contract with its contractor rather than just the amount of the holdback that the general contractor would retain in respect to its contract with the claimant. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Section 23 was amended following this case, and subss. (3) and (4) added.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Anron Mechanical Ltd." p2="Valantori Construction Ltd." post.rptr="220" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I640168e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anron Mechanical Ltd. v. Valantori Construction Ltd.">Anron Mechanical Ltd. v. Valantori Construction Ltd. (1990), 43 C.L.R. 220 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The owner's holdback as found in s. 22(1) of the Act is “equal to 10 per cent of the price of the remaining services or materials as they are actually supplied under the contract.” This is not a reference to market value but to the value of materials supplied and work done. It is not necessary to consider what payments were made or where they were applied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1958" p1="Len Ariss & Co." p2="Peloso" post.rptr="121" pre.rptr="1958" ref.id="I90d592d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Len Ariss & Co. v. Peloso">Len Ariss & Co. v. Peloso (1958), 1958 CarswellOnt 121, [1958] O.R. 643 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>: Where a fixed price contract is involved, the holdback is not to be calculated on the actual value of the work, service and materials furnished but upon a value for such work arrived at “on the basis of the contract price”. This does not mean that a percentage of the contract price is to be taken but that the value of the work done or materials furnished is to be calculated with the contract price as a basis of value.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
