C.30, s. 22.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">22:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 22(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Di Mario" p2="Schuster" post.rptr="140" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I64018ff05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di Mario v. Schuster">Di Mario v. Schuster (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Act does not require an owner to hold back 10 per cent of each payment made to the general contractor. The concept of the holdback under the Act is a global concept that looks at the value of the contract and the services and materials that are actually supplied on premises. As long as an owner holds back 10 per cent of the price of the services and materials that have actually been supplied under the contract at the time the contract is either completed or abandoned, the owner has complied with the Act and the lien holders are limited to looking to the holdback for any immediate payments on their liens.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I64018ff15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Following the Master's decision in <ital>Forte Aluminum</ital>, the court held that once the plaintiff has pleaded an amount as a lien, the burden of establishing that the holdback is something less than this amount shifts to the owner.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
23:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 23.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">23:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, s. 23, was the first Ontario lien legislation to outline the personal liability of the owner. An owner is personally liable to those lien claimants who have valid liens to the extent of the holdbacks required to be retained under this Part. Section 23 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 was repealed and replaced by <ital>Construction Lien Amendment Act, 1990</ital>, S.O. 1990, c. 17 which received Royal Assent on June 28, 1990. As presently worded, this section clearly limits the personal liability of owners to lien claimants where the defaulting payer is the contractor or a subcontractor.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In order to permit the enforcement of holdbacks against owners, this section renders an owner personally liable to the extent of the holdbacks that it is required to retain, and lien claimants are entitled to obtain personal judgment against the owner in the event of but only to the extent of the failure to adequately retain holdback funds. The limit of the owner's liability is set out in subss. (2) and (3). In order to protect owners from a multiplicity of proceedings, an owner's liability under this section can only be determined in an action under the Act (subs. (5)). Such an action is a creature of statute and is a form of class action, as will be discussed below.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As many owners fail to maintain a cash holdback, the holdback scheme is strengthened by the inclusion of this provision. In order to protect owners from a multiplicity of proceedings, the liability of the owner under this section can only be determined under the Act.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 23(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Khalimov" p2="Hogarth" post.rptr="6244" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6401de105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khalimov v. Hogarth">Khalimov v. Hogarth, 2015 ONSC 6244, 2015 CarswellOnt 15551, 56 C.L.R. (4th) 167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master found that once the subcontractor discharged its first claim for lien, it was irrevocably precluded by s. 48 from claiming a lien for services and materials supplied prior to the date it registered its first claim for lien, including a lien claim asserted as a charge against the owner's holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd." p2="Pier One Masonry Inc." post.rptr="3424" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I6401de115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc.">Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3424, 1998 CarswellOnt 3379 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1999), 50 C.L.R. (2d) 224 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In a remarkable, perhaps unique case on its facts, involving the self interested 100 per cent prepayment of a $2,239,759 contract price, and the subsequent expenditure of that sum by the non-arm's length contractor so as to defeat, for all practical purposes, a mason's lien. The court held that where an owner has prepaid a contractor to the foreseeable prejudice of the trades, equity demands no less than that the owner's obligations be not limited to the 10 per cent holdback and the full liens should be recoverable against the owner. The statutory frame of reference for such an order is found in ss. 8 and 13, the trust sections of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Dominion Bridge-Ontario" p2="Stephen Sura (Canada) Ltd." post.rptr="2329" pre.rptr="1997" ref.id="I90d5e0f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Dominion Bridge-Ontario v. Stephen Sura (Canada) Ltd.">Dominion Bridge-Ontario v. Stephen Sura (Canada) Ltd. (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 2329, 35 C.L.R. (2d) 1, [1997] O.J. No. 3023 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 3122 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Once the lien claim has been vacated by a lien bond of the general contractor, the owner is under no liability to a plaintiff with respect to the construction lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19951024" p1="P.A.S.A. Enterprises Ltd." p2="Pallas" ref.id="I6401de135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="P.A.S.A. Enterprises Ltd. v. Pallas">P.A.S.A. Enterprises Ltd. v. Pallas (October 24, 1995), File No. 94-CQ-48241, Gibson J. (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner in a construction lien action failed to defend and was noted in default. Notwithstanding this noting in default, as there was no evidence before the court as to what was the value of the contract between the plaintiff and the contractor, and since the owner's responsibility under the Act to a subcontractor is limited to a hold-back of 10 per cent of the contract value, there was no basis in law upon which the court could grant summary judgment for the plaintiff against the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Kemp" post.rptr="539" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I6401de145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp">Lansing Building Supply (Ontario) Ltd. v. Kemp (1992), 9 O.R. (3d) 539, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 161 (Master)</ref></cite>—An owner defaulted on payments to its contractors, and an issue arose as to the priorities between the mortgagee and the seven lien claimants. The parties were in agreement that s. 78(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (Ont.) applied and that the lien claimants had priority to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV of the Act. At the pretrial motion, the Master was asked to determine the value of the owner's holdback. Subsection 23(1) determines what holdbacks the owner must retain to protect the lien claimants who are contractors retained by the owner. Therefore, the holdbacks to be retained by the owner for the benefit of the lien claimants, here the contractors, was 10 per cent of the value of the services and materials supplied to the improvement, and not just of the value of each contract. The 10 per cent holdback applied to all contracts for improvement, not only to those for which liens have been filed. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: For a contrary view, see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I640205205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Forte Aluminum Ltd." p2="Frank Plastina Investments Ltd." post.rptr="167" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I640205215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forte Aluminum Ltd. v. Frank Plastina Investments Ltd.">Forte Aluminum Ltd. v. Frank Plastina Investments Ltd. (1988), 29 C.L.R. 167 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—This case was decided prior to the amendment to add s. 23(3)(b) and therefore now stands solely for the the proposition that the burden of establishing holdback is on the owner. The proper amount of holdback was held to be 10 per cent of the value of the improvement. There will be circumstances where, because the most substantial part of the improvement has been completed more than 45 days prior to the commencement of some new or additional work, the particular contract will be equal to the total value of the improvement, in most instances, as here, the holdback will be 10 per cent of all of the subcontracts on the improvement. Once the plaintiff has pleaded an amount as a lien, the burden of establishing that the holdback is something less than this amount shifts to the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Core Developments Ltd." p2="Jerry's Asphalt Paving Ltd." post.rptr="927" pre.rptr="[1990]" ref.id="I640205225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Core Developments Ltd. v. Jerry's Asphalt Paving Ltd.">Core Developments Ltd. v. Jerry's Asphalt Paving Ltd. (1990), [1990] O.J. No. 927 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The court found that, pursuant to s. 23(1) of the Act, the lien claimants could look to the holdback being retained by the owner in respect to its contract with its contractor rather than just the amount of the holdback that the general contractor would retain in respect to its contract with the claimant. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Section 23 was amended following this case, and subss. (3) and (4) added.]</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 23(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc." p2="Plati" post.rptr="6319" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I64022c305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati">King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati, 2017 ONSC 6319, 2017 CarswellOnt 16276, 77 C.L.R. (4th) 165 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—If an owner complies with the Act and retains the basic holdback until the time limit for registration of the lien expires, the scheme of the Act, and in particular s. 23(2), ensures that the owner will only have to pay the basic holdback once. Following a lien action, the owner will pay the holdback to the successful subcontractor lien holder rather than to the defaulting contractor, with that amount set-off from the owner's obligation to the contractor. Although the holdback was money that the owner was contractually obliged to pay the contractor, such funds are held in trust to pay the subcontractor if the contractor defaults. It would be absurd to suggest that an owner that complied with its obligations to retain the holdback and, following a lien action, paid the holdback to the successful subcontractor, should still be responsible for paying that same amount to the defaulting contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anlane General Contracting Ltd." p2="Lochner" post.rptr="6521" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I64022c315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anlane General Contracting Ltd. v. Lochner">Anlane General Contracting Ltd. v. Lochner, 2010 ONSC 6521, 2010 CarswellOnt 9905, 97 C.L.R. (3d) 303 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor performed work at a home for the defendants, all of whom were family members. The home was owned by a brother, occupied by another brother and his wife, with the improvements being a gift from the mother. A lien was filed after the parties disagreed as to contract price, who was responsible for payment, and allowances for alleged deficiencies. As the mother was the contracting party she was solely liable for payment of the full amount. There was no privity of contract between the plaintiff and the other defendants. Without a direct contractual relationship to the supplier, the owner-brother's liability was at best limited to the amount of the holdbacks provided for in s. 22 of that Act, with said holdbacks only required to be maintained by each payer on a contract or subcontract. As the mother was the sole payer, the owner had no liability to the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Don Fry Scaffold Service Inc." p2="Ontario" post.rptr="310" pre.rptr="65" ref.id="I64022c325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Don Fry Scaffold Service Inc. v. Ontario">Don Fry Scaffold Service Inc. v. Ontario (2007), 65 C.L.R. (3d) 310, 2007 CarswellOnt 5092 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2008), 67 C.L.R. (3d) 4, 2008 CarswellOnt 531 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Applying the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Base Controls Ltd." p2="Bennett + Wright Group Inc." post.rptr="258" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I64022c335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Base Controls Ltd. v. Bennett + Wright Group Inc.">Base Controls Ltd. v. Bennett + Wright Group Inc. (2002), 20 C.L.R. (3d) 258, 2002 CarswellOnt 3682 (Ont. Master); affirmed (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 1350, 24 C.L.R. (3d) 95, [2003] O.J. No. 1313 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the imposition of a fiduciary duty or duty of care between owners and subcontractors is inappropriate. The Court of Appeal further noted that, in this case, the pleadings failed to assert material facts concerning the relationship between the owner and the subcontractor sufficient to ground a duty of care or a fiduciary duty owed by the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd." p2="Sargeant" post.rptr="8583" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I64022c345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd. v. Sargeant">Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd. v. Sargeant (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 8583, [2002] O.J. No. 2198 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 2197, 2002 CarswellOnt 7436 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 1043, 207 O.A.C. 264, 51 C.L.R. (3d) 10, 264 D.L.R. (4th) 352 (Ont. C.A.); additional reasons 2008 CarswellOnt 1242, 2008 ONCA 166, 67 C.L.R. (3d) 163 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 8183 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—This was a house building case. The argument was over holdback. The owner argued for holdback liability based on the value of the agreed contract. The plaintiff subcontractors argued that as virtually the whole contract price had been advanced, even though the house was only 68 per cent complete, the contract price could be “grossed up” to ascertain a final value, and take 10 per cent of that holdback. The court rejected this suggestion. The owners had advanced payment as if 90 per cent of the services had been supplied, when in fact the actual figure was only 89.01 per cent. The plaintiff subcontractor had argued that, because almost all of the contract price other than the holdback had been advanced by the owners to the general contractor, even though a substantial amount of work had yet to be completed, the owners were still liable for holdbacks with respect to the work as it was done. The court held, however, that while the owners were responsible for the 0.99 per cent of the materials upon which they over-advanced, this was the extent of their liability.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Base Controls Ltd." p2="Bennett + Wright Group Inc." post.rptr="258" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I640253405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Base Controls Ltd. v. Bennett + Wright Group Inc.">Base Controls Ltd. v. Bennett + Wright Group Inc. (2002), 20 C.L.R. (3d) 258, 2002 CarswellOnt 3682 (Master); affirmed (2003), 24 C.L.R. (3d) 95, 2003 CarswellOnt 1350, [2003] O.J. No. 1313 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The general contractor was in bankruptcy and the total owed to the lien claimants greatly exceeded the amount held by the owner. The plaintiff lien claimant moved to assert a fiduciary claim against the owner in tort, on the basis that it was in a position of vulnerability if the owner agreed with the general contractor that bonding was not required and failed to inform sub-contractors such as itself. There was no cause of action against the owner for breach of fiduciary duty, but if there was it would not be a legitimate charge against the funds held by it. The scheme of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and of the tendering process itself was predicated on the concept of privity of contract. The owner had no contract with its sub-contractors, and the owner's liability to the latter under the Act was limited to holdback.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 23(3)(b)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The amendments here effectively disposed the <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Forte Aluminum Ltd." p2="Frank Plastina Investments Ltd." post.rptr="167" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I640253415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Forte Aluminum Ltd. v. Frank Plastina Investments Ltd.">Forte Aluminum Ltd. v. Frank Plastina Investments Ltd. (1988), 29 C.L.R. 167 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and the owner's personal liability is no longer enlarged by <ital>Forte Aluminum</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 23(4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Bradstone & York Brick" p2="Uxland Development (East) Inc." post.rptr="256" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I640253425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bradstone & York Brick v. Uxland Development (East) Inc.">Bradstone & York Brick v. Uxland Development (East) Inc. (1994), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 256 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The corporate defendant, which was solely controlled by the individual defendants, it entered into a contract with the plaintiff for the purchase of architectural stone to be incorporated into the individual defendants' residence. When the plaintiff was not paid for most of the stone, it sued both the corporate defendant and the individual defendants. In finding the individual defendants liable on the basis of unjust enrichment, the court rejected the argument that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> limited the liability of the individual defendants as owners to 10 per cent of the amount in question and that equity could not override the provisions of the Act. The plaintiff's action was not brought pursuant to the Act and the liability of the individual defendants was not to be restricted by the provisions of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
24:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 24.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">24:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Specific statutory authority to make payments other than holdback in the absence of written notice of a lien did not appear in the statute that first established the holdback scheme, <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1887, c. 126 in s. 9, specifically referred to payments up to ninety per cent operating as a discharge <ital>pro tanto</ital> of the lien. Subsequent amendments to the 1887 Act altered the percentage to reflect the varying holdback percentages of 20 per cent and 15 per cent respectively. The discharge <ital>pro tanto</ital> was carried through in the various Acts, see s. 12(2) of the 1980 <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. The proclamation of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 led to s. 24 in its present form.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section permits a payer on a contract or subcontract to pay out money that is owing other than holdback if no written notice of lien has been received by that payer. If the payer has received written notice of a lien, the payer must retain an amount sufficient to satisfy that lien in addition to statutory holdback, but is permitted to pay the balance of any money then payable. See: Catherine E. Willson, “Notice Holdback: Section 24 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>: (2001) 8 C.L.R. (3d) 94”. It is important to note, as referenced by Justice LaForme, as he then was, in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd." p2="Shell Canada Products Ltd." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I6402a1605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd.">Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 15, 1996 CarswellOnt 2065 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, that the statutory definition of “written notice of a lien” added to the Act in 1983 is less onerous than the judicial definition of a similar phrase in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I90d6a440f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> under the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 24(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sjostrom Sheet Metal Ltd." p2="Geo A. Kelson Company Limited" post.rptr="13584" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6754a8a03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Sjostrom Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Geo A. Kelson Company Limited">Sjostrom Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Geo A. Kelson Company Limited, 2023 CarswellOnt 13584, 2023 ONSC 4959 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 8263, 2024 ONSC 3183, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2810 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—At issue was whether subcontractor K entered into a direct contract with sub-sub-subcontractor S to supply sheet metal labour when issues arose between K and its sheet metal sub-subcontractor A, and whether a change order removed all remaining sheet metal labour from sub-subcontractor A's scope of work. The character of K's payments to S hinged on those determinations, namely whether the payments were made under a direct subcontract with S or made to S as A's sub-subcontractor in accordance with a direct payment provision of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Pursuant to s. 24, a payer may only make payments on a subcontract of up to 90% of the price of services and materials supplied under that subcontract, which ensures statutory holdback is retained until it may be released in accordance with other provisions. Where a lien has been registered, a payer is required to retain an amount sufficient to satisfy the lien. However, where subcontractor K entered into a direct contract with sub-sub-subcontractor S, it thereby had separate holdback obligations under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for each subcontract with both subcontractors A and S. The preservation of a lien by sub-sub-subcontractor S thereby did not trigger any additional notice holdback obligation on K under s. 24 with respect to A's separate subcontract. There was accordingly no contractual or legislative basis to withhold payment by reason of S's lien, and K breached the sub-subcontract with A by non-payment when the holdback was due to be paid to A under the contract and when final payment to A was due.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Construction Inc." p2="Unimac-United Management Corp." post.rptr="6136" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6402a1625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp.">Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp., 2016 ONSC 6136, 2016 CarswellOnt 15025, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 17928, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master addressed several issues relating to the application of s. 24. First, in determining whether ten written notices provided by the subcontractor to the owner constituted “written notices of lien” that been “received” under s. 24, he found that a written notice under the section must contain a warning that the dispute has reached “the stage where the lien claimant is not satisfied with the <ital>status quo</ital> flow of funds and wants it interrupted”. This is so despite the fact that s. 1(1) makes no reference to a warning or a statement of intention. The requirement flows from the master's reading of the word “notice” and the purpose of such notice, which is to stop the recipient from paying the payee without holding back funds to preserve the lien. The notice could take any form as long as it contained the four elements in s. 1(1) and indicated the claimant's present desire to interrupt the flow of funds. The notice was not required to actually contain the word “lien”, as long as the intention of the claimant was clear. In addition, the master ruled that a “receipt” under s. 24 was not limited to the rules governing how notices are to be “given” under s. 87(1). The definition of a “written notice of lien” in s. 1(1) includes notices that are “given”. However, s. 24 specifically said “received” and not “given”. Had the legislature wanted the rules in s. 87(1) to govern “receipt” under s. 24, it would have used the word “given”, as it did elsewhere in the Act. Tellingly, the previous legislation, the <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>, required a written notice of lien to be “given”. The legislature's decision not to import that language into s. 24 was not without significance. Furthermore, written notices of lien were often given in real time by non-lawyers and a requirement for formal service goes against the spirit of that process. The master noted that the ability of a passive action, receiving a document, to trigger legal consequences is unique to s. 24. Here, a written notice of lien emailed by the subcontractor to the owner had been “received” by the owner as required under s. 24. Finally, the master addressed whether payments made to the subcontractor by the contractor from funds paid to the contractor by the owner reduced the owner's notice holdback liability. The Act treats notice holdback as being tethered to the claim of the notice giver, with the payer being allowed to reduce its notice holdback obligation by paying the notice giver directly. On the other hand, the statute conceives of basic and finishing holdback as belonging to all lien claimants on the improvement. A written notice of lien is first, and foremost, security for the notice giver, and if the notice giver is paid directly by the payer from notice holdback, the statute expressly provides that the notice holdback liability is reduced accordingly. The result should be the same if the notice giver is paid indirectly through an impugned payment, and in that situation the payer's notice holdback liability will be reduced. The “jeopardy” of a payer referred to in s. 24 is not a “crystallized” one fixed for all lien claimants at the time of payment. It is the risk of having an impugned payment not used by the payee to pay the notice giver. In the end, the position of other lien claimants is simply that of residual beneficiaries of notice holdback that is available for distribution with basic and finishing holdback at trial. This end result is a function of the class nature of the proceeding. If other lien claimants wish to enhance their positions, it is incumbent on them to serve their own written notices of lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd." p2="Sargeant" post.rptr="1043" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I6402c8705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd. v. Sargeant">Aiken Bros. Hardware Ltd. v. Sargeant (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 1043, 207 O.A.C. 264, 51 C.L.R. (3d) 10, 264 D.L.R. (4th) 352 (Ont. C.A.); additional reasons 2008 CarswellOnt 1242, 2008 ONCA 166, 67 C.L.R. (3d) 163 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 8183 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An overpayment contrary to s. 24(1) puts an owner at risk of having to make a further payment to subcontractors, but s. 24(1) does not give the subcontractors a cause of action against the owner to recover an amount in excess of the owner's statutory holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Bestdoor Co." p2="Toronto Economic Development Corp." post.rptr="2561" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I6402c8715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bestdoor Co. v. Toronto Economic Development Corp.">Bestdoor Co. v. Toronto Economic Development Corp. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 2561, 2004 CarswellOnt 2426, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 70 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The written notice of lien in this case satisfied the more stringent test laid out in the <ital>Mechanics' Line Act</ital> and, therefore, the less stringent definition in s. 1(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Peterborough (City)" p2="General Accident Assurance Co." post.rptr="1-3083" pre.rptr="[1994]" ref.id="I6402c8725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Peterborough (City) v. General Accident Assurance Co.">Peterborough (City) v. General Accident Assurance Co., [1994] I.L.R. 1-3083 (Ont. Gen. Div.); appeal dismissed (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 84, 108 O.A.C. 361 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The city had an “errors and omissions liability” policy with the respondent insurer. Lien claimants in certain court actions against the city claimed that the city breached s. 24 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> by making payments on a contract at a time when the city had written notice of liens. Since it was open to find that the city was, or was not, liable to pay the lien claimants the amounts owing to them that the lien claimants alleged were contractual payments wrongfully made by the city, and liability imposed for the alleged wrongful payments made by the city would fall within the policy's terminology of “compensatory damages.” Furthermore, any payments the city might be required to make to lien claimants would not come within the para. 7 exclusion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="AFG Glass Inc." p2="Glaxo Canada Inc." post.rptr="215" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I6402ef805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="AFG Glass Inc. v. Glaxo Canada Inc.">AFG Glass Inc. v. Glaxo Canada Inc. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 215 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Due to a faulty fax communication, the solicitor for the plaintiff subcontractor filed and registered a lien for $25,000, when in fact the amount owing was $118,045.22. There were seven lien claimants in total and the owner offered to pay each 72 per cent of its claim out of the holdback. Four lien claimants accepted the offer, but when the plaintiff was about to accept the offer, the error was discovered, and the plaintiff brought a motion to amend the statement of claim and the claim for lien to increase the claim from $25,000 to $118,045.22. The motion was opposed by the owner and the two lien claimants who had not yet accepted the owner's offer. The Master dismissed the motion to amend the actual lien, although the motion to amend the statement of claim was allowed in part. Based on the authorities and on the wording of s. 31(1) and (3)(a) of the Act and on the policy underlying s. 24 of the Act, the court had no power to make the order requested. However, the court did permit the plaintiff to amend the statement of claim so as to increase the prayer for relief and the dollar amount pleaded.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 24(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thompson" p2="Carleton University" post.rptr="4336" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I6402ef815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thompson v. Carleton University">Thompson v. Carleton University, 2019 ONSC 4336, 2019 CarswellOnt 11566, 92 C.L.R. (4th) 33 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 7633 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The liens in question were registered by the workers' union trust fund on behalf of carpenters employed by the subcontractor. At issue was the general contractor's liability to the union trust fund for holdback, and the amount of that holdback, which depended on the value of the work performed under the sub-contract at the time the lien was filed. A notice holdback attaches to any funds due to a subcontractor at the date the lien was registered, and here the union argued that any payments made by the contractor to suppliers after the liens were registered were payments that were improperly made out of the contract monies because they ignored the priority to be given to workers' liens. However, the evidence readily demonstrated that the contractor incurred completion costs and remedial costs which exceeded any amount it might have owed to the subcontractor and accordingly, there was no notice holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc." p2="Plati" post.rptr="557" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6402ef825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati">King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati, 2017 ONSC 557, 2017 CarswellOnt 1712, 64 C.L.R. (4th) 102 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The total contract price for all work done including extras was $184,624, providing a basic holdback of $18,462 by the owner. At the time the owners received notice of the subcontractor's lien, $78,824 was still to be paid by the owner to the contractor, but was never paid. The basic holdback was not retained, although the notice holdback was. Following <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6402ef835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, and pursuant to s. 24(2), the holdback was calculated as 10 per cent of the price of the contract plus the amount retained. Accordingly, the subcontractor held security against the owner's interest in the land to the extent of its lien to a maximum of $97,287, to be divided pro rata with other registered lien claimants. Judgment was also granted in favour of the contractor against the owners in the sum of $78,824. Subsequently, as reported in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc." p2="Plati" post.rptr="6319" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I640316905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati">King Road Paving and Landscaping Inc. v. Plati, 2017 ONSC 6319, 2017 CarswellOnt 16276, 77 C.L.R. (4th) 165 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, at issue was whether, in implementing the above order, the owners had to pay the money twice: once to the subcontractors as holdback money, and again to the contractor as money owed in contract pursuant to the judgment. The court noted that if an owner complies with the Act and retains the basic holdback until the time limit for registration of the lien expires, the scheme of the Act, and in particular s. 23(2), ensures that the owner will only have to pay the basic holdback once. Following a lien action, the owner will pay the holdback to the successful subcontractor lien holder rather than to the defaulting contractor, with that amount set-off from the owner's obligation to the contractor. Although the holdback was money that the owner was contractually obliged to pay the contractor, such funds are held in trust to pay the subcontractor if the contractor defaults. It would be absurd to suggest that an owner that complied with its obligations to retain the holdback and, following a lien action, paid the holdback to the successful subcontractor, should still be responsible for paying that same amount to the defaulting contractor. An owner is liable to pay the holdback twice only if it fails to comply with its obligation to retain the holdback. The same analysis applies to the “notice holdback”. In the present case the owners did retain the notice holdback and were not required to pay that same amount twice. Once the notice holdback was paid to the subcontractors it was to be credited on the judgment owing to the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640316915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In a novel case, the mortgagee bank financed a construction project under a building mortgage, and the subcontractors registered construction liens against the owner's property for amounts owed by the general contractor. The total amount the owner owed to the general contractor under the building contract far exceeded the amount that the owner was required to withhold for the benefit of the subcontractors pursuant to section 22 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. In order to permit the building project to continue, the bank paid into court funds as security for the subcontractors' claims. Ultimately, the property owner was placed in receivership and the property was sold. The proceeds were not sufficient to satisfy the full amount due to the bank under the building mortgage, and the court held that, by paying money into court and vacating the lien, the bank did not lose the priority it would otherwise have had as mortgagee under subsection 78(2) of the Act, since under subsection 44(6), the amount paid into court took the place of the property, and the lien claimants' rights went beyond a charge against the holdback deficiency. After the lien was vacated, the respective priority interests of the mortgagee and lien claimants did not change and continued to be governed by subsection 78(2), with the liens having priority over a building mortgage “to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV” of that statute. The amount of that deficiency in this case was the full amount of the holdback required under subsection 22(1). The Divisional Court subsequently upheld the motions judge's reasoning, noting that the case was distinguished from prior precedents in that the owner's holdback obligation was not necessarily limited to the basic 10% holdback, as it owed much more than that to the contractor and never made payment to the contractor. Under s. 24 of the Act, lien claimants could look to that additional unpaid amount as further security for their liens by giving written notice to the owner, and once given, the lien claimant had security against the owner's interest in the land to the full extent of the amount the owner, as payer, owes to the general contractor. To extend that obligation to a mortgagee would effectively enlarge the statutory definition of “payer”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Base Controls Ltd." p2="Bennett + Wright Group Inc." post.rptr="258" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I640316925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Base Controls Ltd. v. Bennett + Wright Group Inc.">Base Controls Ltd. v. Bennett + Wright Group Inc. (2002), 20 C.L.R. (3d) 258, 2002 CarswellOnt 3682 (Master); affirmed (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 1313, 24 C.L.R. (3d) 95, 2003 CarswellOnt 1350 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant subcontractor moved to assert a fiduciary claim against the owner in tort, and the owner took the position that if any such liability was asserted and ultimately upheld, it was entitled to set it off against the amounts owing to the general contractor in excess of the statutory holdback. The general contractor was in bankruptcy and the total owed to the lien claimants greatly exceeded the amount held by the owner. If there was a cause of action against the owner for breach of fiduciary duty, it would not be a legitimate charge against the funds held by it. If the owner had assumed a fiduciary duty to the sub-contractors and if it had breached that duty, it would be inappropriate to charge the consequences of its own breach of duty to the only pool of money available to the lien claimants as a class.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="L.I.U.N.A. Employee Benefit Trust, Local 506 (Trustee of)" p2="Bayview Hospital" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I64033da05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.I.U.N.A. Employee Benefit Trust, Local 506 (Trustee of) v. Bayview Hospital">L.I.U.N.A. Employee Benefit Trust, Local 506 (Trustee of) v. Bayview Hospital (2000), 1 C.L.R. (3d) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Under the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, a payer, after receiving written notice of a lien, could set-off any costs incurred on the project caused by a contractor's or subcontractor's breach, against any sums over and above the statutory holdback, notwithstanding a written notice of a lien, <ital>provided</ital> the payer did not pay any amounts to such contractor or subcontractor after it received notice in writing of the lien, except amounts owing over and above the statutory holdback, plus the amount claimed in the notice. When the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> replaced the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, it effected no change in this situation, and did not alter the law relating to set-offs by payers against the “statutory holdback” and “notice holdback”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="James Dick Construction Ltd." p2="Durham Board of Education" post.rptr="2817" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I64033da15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education">James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2817, 1998 CarswellOnt 2928 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (2000), 4 C.L.R. (3d) 256 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A contractor bonded off the lien of a lien under its subtrade and, retaining, in addition to the statutory holdback the amount of the said lien and others, used the funds in its hands to complete abandoned work. During completion further liens claiming through the abandoned subcontractor were registered. Following Misener J. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Reliance Electric Ltd." p2="G.N.S. Contractors Inc." post.rptr="310" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I64033da25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc.">Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 310, 70 O.R. (2d) 364, 1989 CarswellOnt 705 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>, the contractor's conduct was approved.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Hal Mann Tiles Inc." p2="Palmer" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I64033da35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer">Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer (1995), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 61 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The constructive notice rising from the registration on title of a claim for lien does not satisfy the requirement that “written notice of a lien” be “received”. The plain meaning of the word “received”, is actual, physical receipt. While some statutes and rules of practice expand the meaning of “received” by deeming that a document has been received in certain circumstances, that is not the case with s. 24(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd." p2="Shell Canada Products Ltd." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I640364b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd.">Andrew Paving & Engineering Ltd. v. Shell Canada Products Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 15 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A letter from the plaintiff subcontractor to the defendant contractor, allegedly faxed to the owner, stated that the plaintiff intended to proceed with a lien registration, but gave the contractor a further deadline within which to resolve the dispute. This letter did not amount to notice for the purposes of s. 24(2). The omission of the amount owed to the Plaintiff was fatal to the written notice. There can be no deviation from the requirement that however and by whatever means notice is given, it must, at a minimum, contain: (a) an identification of the payer and the premises, and (b) the amount that the person has not been paid and is owed to the person by the payer. The decision of Master Saunders is <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I90d76790f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> is referred to for the “four ingredients” of notice in writing of a claim for lien. However, the court in <ital>Andrew Paving</ital> noted that, if anything, the definition of “written notice of a lien” in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is less onerous than the judicial definition of “notice in writing of the lien” as discussed in <ital>Mutic</ital> under <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I640364b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 950, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 28 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Here a group of lien claimants argued that registration of the first claim for lien operated as “written notice of a lien” within the meaning of this subsection. The court found the reasoning of the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Town-N-Country Plumbing and Heating (1985) Ltd." p2="Schmidt" post.rptr="716" pre.rptr="86" ref.id="I640364b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Town-N-Country Plumbing and Heating (1985) Ltd. v. Schmidt">Town-N-Country Plumbing and Heating (1985) Ltd. v. Schmidt (1991), 86 D.L.R. (4th) 716</ref></cite> to be persuasive and noted a similar result in the Ontario case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Hal Mann Tiles Inc." p2="Palmer" post.rptr="93" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I64038bc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer">Hal Mann Tiles Inc. v. Palmer (1995), 24 O.R. (3d) 93, Master</ref></cite>, in coming to its conclusion that only written notice served on the owner in advance of payment will satisfy the subsection, and then only to the extent of the amount claimed in the notice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I90d78ea0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A drywall subcontractor wrote to a mortgagee to block a final advance. The premises and the parties were identified and the amount owing was stated. No lien was claimed. The mortgagee responded requiring a written direction from the mortgagor. The court followed <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1969" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="Mountview Construction Ltd." post.rptr="515" pre.rptr="67" ref.id="I64038bc25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. Mountview Construction Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. Mountview Construction Ltd. (1969), 67 W.W.R. 515, 4 D.L.R. (3d) 203 (Alta. T.D.)</ref></cite> in holding that the notice should contain at least the following four ingredients: an indication of the supply of services or materials to the contractor; a statement that there is an account owed to the subcontractor by the contractor; a statement that the subcontractor is claiming a lien and perhaps will register it unless payment is made, and; the amount that the lien will claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The requirement to actually claim a lien in the written notice is supported by <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Anglin & Co." p2="Simmons" post.rptr="136" pre.rptr="[1933]" ref.id="I64038bc35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Anglin & Co. v. Simmons">Anglin & Co. v. Simmons, [1933] O.W.N. 136, [1933] 2 D.L.R. 794 (C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1923" p1="Sanderson Pearcy & Co." p2="Foster" post.rptr="519" pre.rptr="53" ref.id="I6403b2d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sanderson Pearcy & Co. v. Foster">Sanderson Pearcy & Co. v. Foster (1923), 53 O.L.R. 519 (C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1900" p1="Craig" p2="Cromwell" post.rptr="585" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I6403b2d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Craig v. Cromwell">Craig v. Cromwell (1900), 27 O.A.R. 585</ref></cite>; and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1943" p1="Dziadus" p2="Sloan" post.rptr="449" pre.rptr="[1943] 3" ref.id="I90d7b5b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Dziadus v. Sloan">Dziadus v. Sloan (1943), [1943] 3 W.W.R. 449, 51 Man. R. 236, [1944] 1 D.L.R. 65 (C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
25:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 25.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">25:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As noted under s. 22 above, the statutory holdback scheme was created by <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15. Section 5 of that statute referred only to contracts and not to subcontracts as we know them. Accordingly, the section did not allow for the reduction of the holdback in circumstances where a subcontractor's work has been certified as complete. It was not until <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 54, assented to on April 10th, 1952, that this concept was adopted. Subsection 11(3) of that Act was amended to read:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In the case of a contract that is under the supervision of an architect, engineer or other person upon whose certificates payments are to be made, where thirty-seven days have elapsed after a certificate issued by that architect, engineer or other person to the effect that the subcontract has been completed to his satisfaction has been given to the person primarily liable upon that contract and to the person who became a subcontractor by a subcontract made directly under that contract, the amount to be retained by the person primarily liable upon that contract shall be reduced by 15 per cent of the subcontract price or, if there is no specific subcontract price, by 15 per cent of the actual value of the work, service performed or materials furnished or placed under that subcontract, but this subsection shall not operate if and so long as any lien derived under that subcontract is preserved by anything done under this Act.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Graduated holdback percentages were adopted in the 1957 version of the amending legislation <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1957</ital>, S.O. 1957, c. 68. Graduated percentages were then eliminated in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 and the language in s. 11(3) was accordingly amended, but the conceptual essence remained. This holdback scheme was continued in s. 25 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 provided a remedy in s. 11(4) for the situation where an architect, engineer, or other person upon whose certificate payments were made, neglected or refused to issue and deliver a certificate of completion of a subcontract. The remedy was to apply to the Court for an order that “the work or materials to which the certificate would have related has been done or placed or furnished” and establish that a certificate should have been issued and delivered. The <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 removed the Court application remedy and replaced it in subs. 33(1) with the remedy of the owner and the contractor jointly determining whether a subcontract has been completed and certify completion in the prescribed form.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section allows the early release of the holdback retained on a subcontract <ital>which has been certified complete under s. 33</ital>, to avoid requiring the subcontractor to wait until 60 days after publication of the certificate substantial performance of the head contract.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Villa Nicolini Inc." post.rptr="5444" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6403d9e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc.">Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc., 2012 ONSC 5444, 2012 CarswellOnt 12496, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 36 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 ONSC 6616, 2012 CarswellOnt 15361, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 37 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contractor released significant holdback funds to sub-contractors whose contracts were certified complete as the project went along, and the lender, which had assumed the contractor's holdback obligations following the contractor's default, sought to claim those funds to reduce the holdback. The lien claimants alleged irregularities in the payments. The Certificates of Completion were issued by the architect payment certifier as an after-the-fact attempt to cure payments improperly made to sub-contractors before the certificates were issued, and were made in violation of s. 25 of the Act. The contractor violated s. 25 by prematurely releasing the funds, and as section 25 requires strict compliance with subs. 33(1), the release was fatal, and there was no mechanism in the Act to cure the violation.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
26:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 26.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">26:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Sections 26 and 27 were amended so that the payment of the basic holdback (under section 26) and of the holdback for finishing work (under section 27) is mandatory rather than permissive</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Old wording of the sections stated that a payer “may, without jeopardy”, make payment of the holdbacks.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">New Act replaced “may, without jeopardy” with “shall”</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15 did not specifically provide that the payment of the holdback could be made without liability where no liens have been preserved. This was rectified in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897 c. 153, which provided in s. 11(3):</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Payment of the percentage required to be retained under subsection 1 may be validly made so as to discharge all liens or charges under this Act in respect thereof after the expiration of the said period of thirty days mentioned in subs. 1 unless in the meantime proceedings shall have been commenced under this Act to enforce any lien or charge against such percentage as provided by ss. s 23 and 24 of this Act.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace.deleted date.trace="20250528"/>The payment of holdback into court as a means to discharge liens was introduced in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30. This concept was preserved in subsequent Ontario construction lien legislation, until the enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section specifies the conditions under which payment of the basic holdback required under s. 22(1) <trace date.trace="20250528">must</trace> be made, so as to discharge all claims in respect of that holdback. This section must be read in conjunction with Part V of the Act. A payer under a contract or subcontract <trace date.trace="20250528">must</trace> release the holdback retained once all liens under that contract or subcontract have expired or have been satisfied, discharged or otherwise vacated from title. The section is silent as to whom the payment may be made. The use of the words “all claims” appears not to distinguish between trust claims and lien claims or between subsisting liens and preserved liens.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clearwater Structures" p2="614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction" post.rptr="5601" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I640400f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clearwater Structures v. 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction">Clearwater Structures v. 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction, 2021 ONSC 5601, 2021 CarswellOnt 12375, 70 E.T.R. (4th) 202 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 7565, 2021 CarswellOnt 16601 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The suggestion that the failure to release trust funds when they become due and owing cannot constitute a breach of trust would serve to completely undermine the purpose and effect of the trust provisions of the Act. The decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Susin" p2="Genstar Development Co." post.rptr="4650" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I90d803d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Susin v. Genstar Development Co.">Susin v. Genstar Development Co. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 4650, 14 C.L.R. (3d) 292 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 4980, 27 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, does not stand for the immutable proposition that a failure to pay out trust funds received and owing on a sub-contract can never constitute a breach of trust. Allowing the contractor to conduct its business in this way would lead to the absurd situation wherein a contractor could retain funds owing to a subcontractor arbitrarily and indefinitely without concern for its obligations under the Act. Such conduct would create commercial chaos and allow a contractor to hold off paying a subcontractor for any number of bogus or flimsy reasons or for any number of ulterior purposes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ziebarth Electrical Contractors Ltd. and 2461476 Ontario Inc. et al" post.rptr="3360" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I640428005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ziebarth Electrical Contractors Ltd. and 2461476 Ontario Inc. et al">Ziebarth Electrical Contractors Ltd. and 2461476 Ontario Inc. et al, 2021 ONSC 3360, 2021 CarswellOnt 6872 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor successfully moved for an order directing payment to it from the landlord/owner's statutory holdback. Three other subcontractors who provided labour and materials on project discharged their liens pursuant to a trust agreement entered into with the owner, and the effect of discharges was that these subcontractors' lien rights under Act were extinguished, with no application to their entitlement. The landlord had agreed to substitute for the statutory framework, an agreement that contractually increased its liability from what it might otherwise under Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="614128 Ontario Ltd. (Trisan Construction)" p2="Toronto (City)" post.rptr="18296" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I640428015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="614128 Ontario Ltd. (Trisan Construction) v. Toronto (City)">614128 Ontario Ltd. (Trisan Construction) v. Toronto (City), 2020 CarswellOnt 18296, 2020 ONCA 803 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The applicant/appellant unsuccessfully sought a declaration that the respondent pay to it a construction holdback on two contracts signed before the parties entered into a settlement agreement. The parties entered into a full and complete settlement of all claims that were outstanding between them, and the applicant was fully aware of the monies that the respondent had held back. If the applicant had intended that the holdback funds were to be paid over and above the settlement amount, it could easily have so stipulated in the settlement agreement, but did not. The applicant could not subsequently come forward and advance a claim for additional funds in light of the unambiguous terms of the settlement agreement and release.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Susin" p2="Genstar Development Co." post.rptr="4650" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I90d82ae0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Susin v. Genstar Development Co.">Susin v. Genstar Development Co. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 4650, 14 C.L.R. (3d) 292 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 4980, 27 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff claimed monies due under a contract for a construction project completed in 1974 made between the plaintiff's bankrupt predecessor and a predecessor of the defendant. The monies included the outstanding balance of the holdback and extras allegedly due and owing to the plaintiff's predecessor. The plaintiff argued that the defendant's predecessor breached the trust provisions of the Ontario former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> by failing to pay the balance of the holdback, and that the defendant was answerable for the breach. In dismissing the action, the court ruled that failure to pay the holdback did not, in itself, amount to a breach of trust, even if the holdback balance constituted a trust fund. As well, due to the passage of time, the defendant was no longer in a position to answer the plaintiff's claims respecting the status or disposition of the holdback.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
26.2:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 26.2.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">26.2:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Sections 26.1 and 26.2 were added to the Act to provide for the payment of basic holdbacks on an annual and on a phased basis, respectively.</para.text></para></list.item></list></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
