date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Sections 26 and 27 were amended so that the payment of the basic holdback (under section 26) and of the holdback for finishing work (under section 27) is mandatory rather than permissive</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Old wording of the sections stated that a payer “may, without jeopardy”, make payment of the holdbacks.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">New Act replaced “may, without jeopardy” with “shall”</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The provision for retaining and paying holdback funds for finishing work was not set out in the Ontario construction lien legislation until the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section corresponds to s. 26, but applies only to the holdbacks retained in respect of services or materials supplied in the period between the date the contract has been certified or declared to be substantially performed (in accordance with s. 32) and the date of completion of the contract.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
27.1:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 27.1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">27.1:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This new section provides that an owner may refuse to pay some or all of a holdback amount if prior compliant notice is given in accordance with Regulation 304/18.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Contractor may refuse to pay the amount of holdback withheld by the owner if the contractor gives notice to the applicable subcontractors that the amount is not being paid.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As of October 1, 2019, contractor will have to refer the matter to adjudication.</para.text></para></list.item></list></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
28:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 28.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">28:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, s. 11, outlined the concept of direct payment as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">11.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">In case an owner or contractor chooses to make payments to any persons referred to in the fifth section of this Act for or on account of any debts justly due to them for work or service done or for materials placed or furnished to be used as therein mentioned, and shall within three days afterwards give, by letter or otherwise, written notice of such payment to the contractor or his agent, or to the sub-contractor or his agent, as the case may be, such payments shall, as between the owner and the contractor or as between the contractor and the sub-contractor, as the case may be, be deemed to be payments to the contractor or sub-contractor, as the case may be, on his contract generally, but not so as to affect the percentage to be retained by the owner, as provided by s. 10 of this Act.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The essence of this section remained with minor variations to the wording, in subsequent amending statutes. The 1910 version of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69 expanded the category of who were entitled to make payments to include sub-contractors. No substantive alterations were made to this section until the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The 1983 rewrite of s. 28 is identical to the present version. The substantive difference between the earlier legislation and the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not define a timetable for the written notice of payments made. The earlier versions did not provide for the notice of the intention to pay, which is contemplated in the present statute.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1958" p1="Len Ariss & Co." p2="Peloso" post.rptr="121" pre.rptr="1958" ref.id="I55fb51d0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Len Ariss & Co. v. Peloso">Len Ariss & Co. v. Peloso (1958), 1958 CarswellOnt 121, [1958] O.R. 643 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> discussed the issue of payments made “in good faith” by an owner to a contractor under the 1950 version of the Act. At page 650 of the majority decision, McGillivray J.A. stated:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The purpose of having this phrase included in the subsection is obviously to protect a lienholder where the owner sets up a contractor who is little more than a man of straw with the intention of securing improvements to his land without paying for them. It is true an owner might find himself liable for such amounts if he had given a subcontractor a personal undertaking to pay his account or a guarantee that his account would be paid but the trial Judge has made no finding of any such agreements being made or guarantees given by the Pelosos here.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Court of Appeal in this case acknowledged that it would require “very strong evidence” (p. 650) that supports an allegation of bad faith as the “obvious result of such a finding would, in most cases, be to require the owner to pay a portion of the contract price twice over”. The Alberta <ital>Builders' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.A. 1980, c. B-12, in s. 29(1)(a) expands the category of payers to permit an “owner, mortgagee, contractor or subcontractor” to make a direct payment as long as written notice of the intention to make the payment is given to “(i) the person liable on the contract or his agent, and (ii) the persons liable on any intervening contracts of their agent”. The Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not require notice to all intermediate parties in the construction pyramid.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section permits a payer to make a direct payment to a subcontractor with whom the payer has no direct contractual relationship. The amount of the payment may be withheld by the payer from the person who was supposed to pay the claimant. Such a payment does not reduce the amount of the holdback required to be retained by the payer, nor does it reduce the additional amount that must be retained in response to a written notice of lien. Notice of such a payment must be given to the proper payer of the person to be paid, and this notice can be given either before or after the payment is made. This section ensures that the flow of funds will not be unduly impeded by the temporary or permanent incapacity of any given payee.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Demikon Construction Ltd." p2="Oakleigh Holdings Inc." post.rptr="19539" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I675767c03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Demikon Construction Ltd. v. Oakleigh Holdings Inc.">Demikon Construction Ltd. v. Oakleigh Holdings Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 19539, 2024 ONSC 6261 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2024 CarswellOnt 5369, 2024 ONSC 2151, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1738 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversing additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 12204, 2024 ONSC 4472 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Properly interpreted, s. 28 applies to direct payments to a “person having a lien” relating to “any amount owing to that person for services or materials supplied to the improvement”. The motion judge erred in interpreting s. 28 more broadly, so as to include payments to other subcontractors who were not persons “having a lien”. Limiting the scope of s. 28 payments to persons having a lien accords with the statutory scheme and the purpose of the Act. A person having a lien has an interest in the owner's premises and in the holdbacks, and owners have an interest in seeing liens resolved because their lands can be tied up and because they have holdback obligations. This interest, however, disappears once the liens expire or are resolved. Once the liens expire, there is no practical reason under the Act to allow payors to ‘jump the rung’ to avoid privity of contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Construction Inc." p2="Unimac-United Management Corp." post.rptr="6136" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6404c4415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp.">Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp., 2016 ONSC 6136, 2016 CarswellOnt 15025, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 17928, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Payments made to the subcontractor by the contractor from funds paid to the contractor by the owner were held to have reduced the owner's notice holdback liability. The Act treats notice holdback as being tethered to the claim of the notice giver, with the payer being allowed to reduce its notice holdback obligation by paying the notice giver directly. Conversely, basic and finishing holdbacks belong to all lien claimants on the improvement. Under s. 28, the only section that addresses payment of notice holdback directly, a direct payment made by the payer to a lien claimant on notice to the lien claimant's proper payer does reduce the payer's liability for notice holdback to the notice giver who has been paid. Other liens against that holdback do not need to have been discharged, released or vacated for the reduction to occur. However, a payer cannot assert set-off claims against notice holdback liability if it has not retained the funds. Section 24 makes it necessary to “retain” the notice holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd." p2="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." post.rptr="892" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I6404eb505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc.">H.H. Angus & Associates Ltd. v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 892, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 305 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where there is a direct payment by an owner to a subtrade which it has no contractual obligation to pay, s. 28 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not apply so as to permit such a payment to reduce the amount of holdback required to be maintained with respect to the recipient of the funds. The payments made, while they may certainly be applied towards any amount outstanding between the parties, cannot be considered to be a reduction in the amount of holdback required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="James Dick Construction Ltd." p2="Durham Board of Education" post.rptr="308" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I6404eb515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education">James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education (2000), 50 O.R. (3d) 308, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 256 (Div. Ct.); affirming (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 36 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A sub-subcontractor registered a lien against a property and sent notice of same to the general contractor, who bonded off the lien. Subsequently, the contractor received a written direction from its subcontractor to pay the sub-subcontractor. The contractor paid its subcontractor but withheld funds representing the lien amount. In finding that the direction was not binding, the court held that while s. 28 of the Act permits a contractor to make a payment directly to a subcontractor, there is no obligation to do so. The direction given to the contractor did not provide for the removal for the sub-subcontractor's notice of lien. The contractor was therefore at liberty to post security and obtain an order vacating the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Oram" p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="190" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I6404eb525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission">Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 190 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A holdback had to be quantified before any payment out of holdback could be ordered. Where the general contractor was involved in litigation against the co-defendant transit company, and the holdbacks could not be quantified until the litigation was completed, funds could not be distributed.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
29:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 29.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">29:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Earlier Ontario lien statutes provided that payment may validly be made to discharge the liens, but they did not expressly state that these liens were discharged on a dollar by dollar basis as the holdback was paid. The <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 in s. 29 made that concept clear. This section remains unchanged in the present statute.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 29 makes it clear that payments made in accordance with Part IV discharge liens on a dollar by dollar basis. The concept of “discharge” is particularly powerful in this statute and the <ital>Southridge</ital> case, recorded under s. 47(1)(6) below, should be referred to.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
30:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 30.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">30:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This prohibition against set-offs on holdbacks originated with s. 3(7) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 54, assented to on April 10, 1952. The wording of this section varied only slightly in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 to add the words “required to be retained”. No further amendments were made. The present wording was adopted in s. 30 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">There is no right to set off against the holdback fund. The inviolable nature of the holdbacks survives as long as the holdback can be characterized as such. This characterization terminates when all the lien rights against that holdback have expired, or have been satisfied, discharged, or vacated from title. As long as the lien rights subsist, the owner or person primarily liable can not defray the cost of completion or of rectifying deficiencies by claiming a set-off against the holdback fund. When the holdback can no longer be considered holdback, s. 17(3) of the Act would apply and the owner or person primarily liable would be entitled to use the funds of the defaulting contractor or subcontractor for set-off purposes.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Landry Mechanical Services Ltd." p2="J.C. Sulpher Construction Ltd." post.rptr="301" pre.rptr="51" ref.id="I640539705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landry Mechanical Services Ltd. v. J.C. Sulpher Construction Ltd.">Landry Mechanical Services Ltd. v. J.C. Sulpher Construction Ltd. (2005), 51 C.L.R. (3d) 301, 2005 CarswellOnt 7238 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 230 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant city made a liquidated damages claim against the contractor for delays in completing the project, and claimed a right of set-off against the contractor and various subcontractor lien claimants as a result of their failure to complete their work in a timely manner. In its statement of defence, the contractor specifically pleaded a right of set-off against the other lien claimants. A claimant's motion for payment of its <ital>pro rata</ital> share of the city's holdback was denied and the city was directed to pay the amount of the statutory holdback into an account of the solicitors of the subcontractor or the contractor. There were no lien claimants below the subcontractors that had registered claims for liens and while the city could not set-off its delay claims against holdback, as those funds were for the benefit of the subtrades, the contractor as payer could do so since there was no one below for whom funds were required to be held back.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="James Dick Construction Ltd." p2="Durham Board of Education" post.rptr="2817" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I640539715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education">James Dick Construction Ltd. v. Durham Board of Education (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2817, 1998 CarswellOnt 2928 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (2000), 4 C.L.R. (3d) 256 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A contractor bonded off the lien of a lien under its subtrade and, retaining, in addition to the statutory holdback the amount of the said lien and others, used the funds in its hands to complete abandoned work. During completion further liens claiming through the abandoned subcontractor were registered. Following Misener J. in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Reliance Electric Ltd." p2="G.N.S. Contractors Inc." post.rptr="310" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I640539725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc.">Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 310, 70 O.R. (2d) 364, 1989 CarswellOnt 705 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>, the contractor's conduct was approved. A payer does not jeopardize its position by relying on s. 30.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Oram" p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="190" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I640539735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission">Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 190 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Various lien claimants had entered into conditional minutes of settlement that left open the possibility that the amount settled upon could be reduced by future set-offs, depending on the results of litigation between the defendant general contractor and the defendant transit company. In such circumstances, the general contractor's right to set-off could not be determined until the litigation between the defendants was completed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="West York Construction (1984) Ltd." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="32" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I640539745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="West York Construction (1984) Ltd. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">West York Construction (1984) Ltd. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 32 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The completion of a residential/church facility construction project was postponed by several delays on the part of the owner and the contractor. The owner withheld part of the holdback for interest costs but later released the funds, and the contractor successfully sought interest on the holdback. While owner was entitled to assert a claim for damages, by the terms of the construction contract it could not exercise a set-off.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Amendments were made to section 31 of the Act in order to extend the timelines for the expiry of liens from 45 days to 60 days.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The section was also amended to make express reference to the termination of a contract as a factor in whether or not a lien is expired.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A new subsection (2.1) was added to specifically address the expiry of a lien of the trustee of a workers' trust fund.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 31(5) was new to the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. Sections 31(1) to 31(4) have their roots in s. 4 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27, which read:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">4.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Such lien shall absolutely cease to exist within ninety days after such work shall have been completed, or materials or machinery furnished or the expiry of the period of credit, unless in the meantime proceedings shall have been instituted to realize such a claim under the provisions hereinafter contained, and a certificate of <ital>lis pendens</ital> thereof, be registered in the proper registry office, which certificate may be granted by the Judge or Court before whom the proceedings are instituted.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The enactment of s. 14 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1874</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.), reduced the time period to thirty days. The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15 made minor amendments of form. Further detail was added with the proclamation of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1887, c. 120 and <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35. In 1923 s. 22(1) was amended by <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30, to state that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">A claim for lien by a contractor or sub-contractor in cases not otherwise provided for, may be registered before or during the performance of the contract; or of the subcontract or within thirty days after the completion or abandonment of the contract or of the sub-contract as the case may be.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The three other subsections were not changed at that time. In 1952, <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 54 increased the time period in each of the subsections from 30 days to 37 days. The final amendments to this section, prior to the enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 were merely some grammatical changes to ss. 21(2) and 21(4).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 31 sets out a complete code for the expiration of liens arising from the supply of services and materials to an improvement. The policy behind the section is that time should run against a lien claimant only from a date that can be readily ascertained by that claimant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The section refers to the publication of either a certificate or a declaration of substantial performance of a “contract”. In this sense, the word “declaration” refers to a court order declaring a contract to be substantially performed, under s. 32(1) Rule 7, and not a “declaration in prescribed form” under s. 32(5).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 31(2) deals with the expiry of contractors' liens. Subsection 31(2)(a) deals with those cases where the contract has been certified as substantially performed, and provides for expiration of lien rights against the holdback 60 days after the earlier of: (i) publication of the certificate of substantial performance; or (ii) completion, termination, or abandonment of the contract. Subsection 31(2)(b) applies where there is no certification or declaration of substantial performance; lien rights expire 60 days after the earlier of completion of the contract or its abandonment or termination. Generally, the release of the holdback to a contractor will coincide with the expiry of the contractor's lien on a given improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The expiration of the liens of persons other than the contractor is dealt with in s. 31(3). Where there is certification or declaration of substantial performance of contract (<ital>i.e.</ital> the contract with the owner), s. 31(3)(a) provides that such liens expire 60 days after the earliest of: (i) publication of the certificate of substantial performance or (ii) the date on which the person last supplies services or materials or (iii) the date the contract is completed, abandoned, or terminated, or (iv) the date a subcontract is certified to be completed under s. 33. Under s. 31(3)(b), in the absence of certification or declaration of substantial performance, liens expire 60 days after: (i) the last supply of services or materials or (ii) the date the contract is completed, abandoned, or terminated, or (iii) the date the subcontract is certified to be completed under s. 33.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 31(4) saves the lien rights of persons who supply services or materials after the date certified or declared to be the date of substantial performance but only to the extent of services or materials supplied after that date.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 31(5) provides for a declaration of last supply by persons under a contractor, fixing the date so declared as against the person making the declaration. A subcontractor can thereby start its own lien expiration period, with certainty.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">With regard to expiration dates falling on holidays see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Goldyear Construction Inc." p2="Oriental Ocean Seafood Restaurant Ltd." post.rptr="1910" pre.rptr="1988" ref.id="I6405d5b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Goldyear Construction Inc. v. Oriental Ocean Seafood Restaurant Ltd.">Goldyear Construction Inc. v. Oriental Ocean Seafood Restaurant Ltd., 1988 CarswellOnt 1910 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pan Abode Buildings Ltd." p2="Duguay" post.rptr="188" pre.rptr="1979" ref.id="I6405d5b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pan Abode Buildings Ltd. v. Duguay">Pan Abode Buildings Ltd. v. Duguay, 1979 CarswellOnt 188, 30 C.B.R. (N.S.) 50 (Ont. Bktcy.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Argus Steel Construction Ltd." p2="Burns Transport Ltd." post.rptr="56" pre.rptr="1961" ref.id="I6405d5b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Argus Steel Construction Ltd. v. Burns Transport Ltd.">Argus Steel Construction Ltd. v. Burns Transport Ltd., 1961 CarswellOnt 56, [1962] O.W.N. 153 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="13245" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I675963903b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The trial judge was held to have erred in law in finding that separate claims for lien must be registered in respect to separate subcontracts between the same parties for the same improvement. Absent certification of substantial performance or completion, it matters not whether a subcontractor provides its services or materials under one subcontract or multiple subcontracts. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990 c. C.30].</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Rafat General Contractor Inc." p2="1015734 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="7519" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90d9ffa1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.">Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 7519, 81 O.R. (3d) 798, 52 C.L.R. (3d) 63, [2005] O.T.C. 1107, [2005] O.J. No. 5526 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor did not register a claim for lien but instead brought an action for payment of its invoice. It then moved to register a certificate of pending litigation against the lands of the owner, which were the same lands against which it could have registered a claim for lien. The motion was dismissed. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides a comprehensive code as to how liens are to be preserved, and by supplying labour and material, a lien arose in favour of the contractor pursuant to the Act. Having failed to preserve a lien in the subject property, the plaintiff could not then look to the trust provisions in the Act to later assert an interest in the same land.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Delview Construction Ltd." p2="Meringolo" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="71" ref.id="I640623d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo">Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo (2004), 71 O.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was not an existing corporation at the time its lien was registered and the action commenced, but was later revived. During the time of dissolution, the lien had expired under s. 31(1). The court held that the plaintiff could not rely on s. 241(5) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. B.16, which provided that “upon revival, the corporation, subject to […] the rights, if any, acquired by any person during the period of dissolution, shall be deemed for all purposes to have never been dissolved”, because the defendant had acquired “rights” by virtue of the passage of the time limits in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The claim for lien and the certificate of action were vacated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="AFG Glass Inc." p2="Glaxo Canada Inc." post.rptr="215" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I640623d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="AFG Glass Inc. v. Glaxo Canada Inc.">AFG Glass Inc. v. Glaxo Canada Inc. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 215 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Due to a faulty fax communication, the solicitor for the plaintiff subcontractor filed and registered a lien for $25,000, when in fact the amount owing was $118,045.22. There were seven lien claimants in total and the owner offered to pay each 72 per cent of its claim out of the holdback. Four lien claimants accepted the offer, but when the plaintiff was about to accept the offer, the error was discovered, and the plaintiff brought a motion to amend the statement of claim and the claim for lien to increase the claim from $25,000 to $118,045.22. The motion was opposed by the owner and the two lien claimants who had not yet accepted the owner's offer. The Master dismissed the motion to amend the actual lien, although the motion to amend the statement of claim was allowed in part. Based on the authorities and on the wording of s. 31(1) and (3)(a) of the Act and on the policy underlying s. 24 of the Act, the court had no power to make the order requested. However, the court did permit the plaintiff to amend the statement of claim so as to increase the prayer for relief and the dollar amount pleaded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Michelin Group Inc." p2="Forsan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I640623d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd.">Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 523, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 202 (Gen. Div.); affirmed (1995), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 215 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—It was not appropriate to allow the plaintiff to amend its statement of claim and by implication its claim for lien to allege that work continued to a date later than set out in the claim for lien, because one of the cornerstones of the Act is the concept of notice to others. Furthermore, one consistency in the case law was that the sections prescribing the time periods for preserving and perfecting liens were to be strictly construed. However, the Divisional Court was prepared to amend the claim for lien if the plaintiff's subcontractor could have demonstrated that it had, in fact, performed work between the date of last supply as set out in the claim for lien and the date on which the affidavit verifying the lien was sworn.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">[<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case has to be read in light of the Court of Appeal decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Gillies Lumber Inc." p2="Kubassek Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="2692" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I640623d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd.">Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 2692, 1999 CarswellOnt 2160 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1997), 32 O.R. (3d) 475 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, which held that claims for lien could not be amended.]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions)" p2="Deltro Electric Ltd." post.rptr="8182" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I640623d45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions) v. Deltro Electric Ltd.">9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions) v. Deltro Electric Ltd., 2021 ONSC 8182, 2021 CarswellOnt 19273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At the time the lien was purported to be preserved and perfected, the corporate lien claimant was dissolved due to a missed fee payment, but was subsequently revived upon its general manager filing the appropriate fee and form pursuant the <ital>Canadian Business Corporations Act</ital>. Since it was formally dissolved at the time it preserved and perfected the lien, it was not a legal entity entitled to do so, and did not comply with the required timelines set out in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Bound by the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90da4dc0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the court had no discretion in equity to permit the lien action to continue. The medical issues of the general manager, including legal blindness in one eye, did not deter him from operating a business and arranging for the preserving and perfecting of the lien, and were not an excuse not to keep the company books and records in good standing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd." p2="Carnello Civil Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4877" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I64064ae15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd. v. Carnello Civil Construction Ltd.">Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd. v. Carnello Civil Construction Ltd., 2014 ONSC 4877, 2014 CarswellOnt 11416, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 97 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 CarswellOnt 17069, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 116 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As repair work does not extend lien rights (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates" p2="161975 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3928" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I64064ae25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. 161975 Ontario Inc.">Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. 161975 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 3928, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>) the work performed here did not extend the plaintiff's lien rights and the claim for lien was declared expired under s. 45.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates" p2="161975 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3928" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640671f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. 161975 Ontario Inc.">Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. 161975 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 3928, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The 45-day lien period does not extend if the work that is done is to repair deficiencies. The court cited, in support of this proposition, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90da4dc1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219, 1993 CarswellOnt 833, [1993] O.J. No. 2985 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Micon Interiors General Contractors Inc." p2="D'Abbondanza Enterprises Inc." post.rptr="6156" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I90da4dc2f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Micon Interiors General Contractors Inc. v. D'Abbondanza Enterprises Inc.">Micon Interiors General Contractors Inc. v. D'Abbondanza Enterprises Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 6156, 76 C.L.R. (3d) 289, [2008] O.J. No. 4132 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Arcon Group Inc." p2="Jelco Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4154" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I640671f35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Arcon Group Inc. v. Jelco Construction Ltd.">Arcon Group Inc. v. Jelco Construction Ltd. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 4154, [2001] O.J. No. 4661 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc." p2="Baun Construction Inc." post.rptr="307" pre.rptr="85" ref.id="I640671f45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc.">Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc. (2009), 85 C.L.R. (3d) 307, 2009 CarswellOnt 7122 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vaughan-Scape Landscape Contractors Inc." p2="Watermark Developments Ltd." post.rptr="1219" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640671f55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vaughan-Scape Landscape Contractors Inc. v. Watermark Developments Ltd.">Vaughan-Scape Landscape Contractors Inc. v. Watermark Developments Ltd., 2010 CarswellOnt 1219, [2010] O.J. No. 853 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This jurisprudence was also cited in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vaughan-Scape Landscape Contractors Inc." p2="Watermark Developments Ltd." post.rptr="1219" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640699005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vaughan-Scape Landscape Contractors Inc. v. Watermark Developments Ltd.">Vaughan-Scape Landscape Contractors Inc. v. Watermark Developments Ltd., 2010 CarswellOnt 1219 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1951" p1="T.D. Swan Construction (1951)" p2="Blanc" post.rptr="240" pre.rptr="68" ref.id="I640699015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="T.D. Swan Construction (1951) v. Blanc">T.D. Swan Construction (1951) v. Blanc (2008), 68 C.L.R. (3d) 240, 2008 CarswellOnt 888 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff corporation purported to register its claim for lien while its charter was dissolved. Notwithstanding the subsequent revival of the plaintiff more than one year later, the claim was held not preserved in law within the requisite 45-day period. Subsection 241(5) of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital> made subsequent revival subject to rights acquired by any person during the period of dissolution. The expiry of the 45-day lien preservation period between the time of the plaintiff's dissolution and its revival was a post-dissolution right that could be relied on to defeat the statute-barred claim. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I640699025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Delview Construction Ltd." p2="Meringolo" post.rptr="2245" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I640699035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo">Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2245, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 48 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—A revived corporation cannot proceed with a construction lien action, where the time limits under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for preserving and perfecting the claim for lien have expired while the corporation was dissolved. Here, the appellant had registered a construction lien against the respondent's property and then commenced an action claiming payment of the balance owing under a construction contract and enforcement of its claim for lien. Following completion of examinations for discovery, the respondent successfully moved for an order dismissing the appellant's action and vacating the appellant's claim for lien on the grounds that the appellant was not an existing corporation at the time the lien was registered and the action commenced. The appellant then unsuccessfully moved for an order permitting it to amend its statement of claim and claim for lien by substituting the name “826744 Ontario Limited carrying on business as Delview Construction” for the name “Delview Construction Limited.” “Delview Construction Limited” was incorporated approximately three months after the appellant's lien was registered and its action commenced. The Divisional Court dismissed the appellant's appeal from the motion judge's order which vacated the appellant's claim for lien and certificate of action. In addition, the Divisional Court allowed the respondent's cross-appeal from the motion judge's order permitting the appellant's contract claim to continue, and dismissed the appellant's action. Assuming, without deciding, that naming Delview Construction Limited as the lien claimant in the claim for lien was a misnomer that could be corrected by s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the Ontario Court of Appeal concluded that the appellant could not rely on the provisions of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporation Act</ital> to revive its action, because the time periods stipulated in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for registering and perfecting its lien expired prior to the revival of 826744 Ontario Limited. The appellant's breach of contract action should not be dismissed because the limitation period for that action had not expired, but the order in this regard was, <ital>inter alia</ital>, without prejudice to any defences that might be raised with respect to rights acquired during the period in which 826744 was dissolved.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90da9be0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The lien action was called for trial for the October 2002 sittings. On September 30, 2002, the defendant's counsel notified the claimant's counsel that the latter's corporate charter had been cancelled on March 14, 1973. The claimant's charter was revived October 1, 2002. The defendant moved for an order discharging the lien, cancelling the bond posted, dismissing the lien action, and for costs on a substantial indemnity basis on the grounds, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that the lien claimant's charter was cancelled at the time the lien was preserved and perfected and not revived until the time limitations contained in ss. 31(2), 36(2) and 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had expired. The claimant motion was for an order declaring its charter was revived for the purposes of the action effective November 1, 1978. In the alternative, the claimant sought an order declaring that the revival of its charter on October 1, 2002 retroactively validated the preservation and perfection of its lien, or an order extending the time within which to preserve and perfect the lien to October 1, 2002. While the Divisional Court reversed the motions judge's holding that the Articles of Revival of October 1, 2002 did not effectively retroactively validate all actions taken by the claimant subsequent to its corporate dissolution, including the preservation and perfection of its claim of lien, it upheld her ruling that the lapse of limitation period between the claimant's dissolution and its revival was an acquired legal right of the defendant upon which the latter was entitled to rely. The time limits within which to preserve and perfect claims for lien under the Act could not be extended by the exercise of judicial discretion, and that in any event, no special circumstances existed to warrant such extension. The time limits set out in the Act were to be strictly interpreted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1960" p1="Lambton (County)" p2="Canadian Comstock Co." post.rptr="689" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I6406c0115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lambton (County) v. Canadian Comstock Co.">Lambton (County) v. Canadian Comstock Co. (1960), 21 D.L.R. (2d) 689 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—Completion means what it says. Time does not begin to run until it can be said that the contractor or sub-contractor has done all that has been promised to be done and is entitled to maintain an action for the full amount.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">[<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The section of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> considered here permitted the sub-contractor to register a lien within 37 days after completion or abandonment of the subcontract, which is no longer correct under the present statute.]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(2)(a)(i)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2019" p1="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc." p2="2603774 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5278" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I90dac2f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc.">Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc. (2019), 2019 ONSC 5278, 2019 CarswellOnt 14629, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2020 CarswellOnt 9830, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 182 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Under s. 31 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, a lien expires at “the earlier of” 45 days after publication or 45 days after the contract is completed. A contract can be completed even though a certificate or declaration of substantial performance of the contract is never published. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> the time period for expiration of a lien has been extended to 60 days after publication or after the contract is completed].</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="J.D. Strachan Construction Limited" p2="Egan Holding Inc." post.rptr="522" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I6406e7205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J.D. Strachan Construction Limited v. Egan Holding Inc.">J.D. Strachan Construction Limited v. Egan Holding Inc., 2019 ONSC 522, 2019 CarswellOnt 658, 98 C.L.R. (4th) 95 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2021 ONSC 6425, 2021 CarswellOnt 13640 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Plaintiff registered its certificate of action after the period prescribed under s. 31(2)(a)(i), and failed to perfect its lien in timely fashion. Citing promissory estoppel, the plaintiff unsuccessfully argued that the defendants were estopped from relying on that limitation period. In this case, the defendants made a promise to pay without any further requests or representations regarding the limitation period, which was not discussed or addressed. The parties were sophisticated business entities who were able to look after their own interests, and the plaintiff was well aware of its earlier challenges in obtaining payment from the defendants that originally led it to preserve its lien. The plaintiff had ample time and opportunity to perfect its lien within the prescribed period. It made a business decision not to do so. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In <ital>obiter</ital> comments, the Divisional Court noted that the decision did not signal that promissory estoppel can arise to defeat the deadlines in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, (or presumably, the successor <ital>Construction Act</ital>. It suggested, without ruling on the issue, that s. 4 might not permit promissory estoppel to operate to defeat deadlines stipulated in the Act.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="570 South Service Road Inc." p2="Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd." post.rptr="6978" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I6406e7215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="570 South Service Road Inc. v. Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd.">570 South Service Road Inc. v. Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd., 2010 ONSC 6978, 2010 CarswellOnt 9631, 97 C.L.R. (3d) 285 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2011 CarswellOnt 5996, 3 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In publishing a certificate of substantial performance, a party could not at once claim to be the owner, the contractor, and the payment certifier. In so doing, the party did not comply with the requirements of the Act concerning certification or declaration of substantial performance. As a result, the contract was not completed until subsequent to the certificate's publication. The motion by the builder for a declaration that the lien had expired therefore failed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="7972" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I64070e305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 7972, 2 C.L.R. (4th) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A motion brought by the mortgagee under s. 47 to have the lien discharged and the action dismissed as against the mortgagee on the basis that the lien was not preserved in time was dismissed where the validity of the certificate of substantial performance was a triable issue. The registered owner and the alleged contractor purported to sign the certificate and arrange for publication, yet evidence suggested that they were managed by the same person, and thus may have both been the “owner” under s. 1(1). In that case, the plaintiff would have become the contractor, and its signature on the certificate would have been required in order for the 45 day period to have commenced running.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Demik Construction Ltd." p2="Royal Crest Lifecare Group Inc." post.rptr="114" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I64070e315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Demik Construction Ltd. v. Royal Crest Lifecare Group Inc.">Demik Construction Ltd. v. Royal Crest Lifecare Group Inc. (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 114 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Two defendants brought parallel motions pursuant to s. 45 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (Ont.) seeking an order vacating the registration of the claim for lien and the certificate of action. The moving parties filed no affidavit material. They relied, instead, on the contents of the claim for lien, the affidavit of verification of the lien claim, and on the assertions made by the contractor in its statement of claim. The contractor had registered its claim for lien 44 days after publication of the certificate of substantial performance, and 49 days after the date of substantial performance identified therein. The affidavit on behalf of the lien claimant did not state explicitly that the contract was completed, and simply affirmed that the facts cited in the claim for lien were true. The determination of the proper completion date was held to be a matter for trial. In the result, it was concluded that the moving parties had failed to prove that the lien had not been preserved within the time allowed.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(2)(a)(ii)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3161" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64070e325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 3161, 2012 CarswellOnt 6816, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 67 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2013 CarswellOnt 7357, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 9258, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In determining whether the plaintiff's lien was preserved within 45 days after the date the contract was completed, the master found that the work last performed by the plaintiff was work that had to be completed after all the other trades had finished their work, and that it was not thereby reduced to mere touch-ups or rectification of deficiencies. The latter would be relevant to the plaintiff's completion date only if it pertained to rectifying its own work, but here it was rectifying deficiencies caused by other trades. The contract was therefore not substantially complete when the work was carried out, and the lien was preserved in time. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="7972" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I64070e335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 7972, 2 C.L.R. (4th) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, under s. 31(2)(a)(i), <ital>supra</ital>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="D'Urzo Demolition Inc." p2="Damaris Developments Inc." post.rptr="1912" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64070e345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc.">D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc., 2012 ONSC 1912, 2012 CarswellOnt 3535, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 210 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 8750, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 229 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Abandonment requires a cessation of work and an intention not to complete the contract, and a claimant must register its lien within 45 days of forming the intention not to continue the contract work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Edgecon Construction Inc." p2="746136 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="6347" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I64070e355fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgecon Construction Inc. v. 746136 Ontario Ltd.">Edgecon Construction Inc. v. 746136 Ontario Ltd., 2010 ONSC 6347, 2010 CarswellOnt 8853, 97 C.L.R. (3d) 133 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 9802, 97 C.L.R. (3d) 143 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Attendance on site by the construction manager with his millwork sub-contractor unannounced and unscheduled, during which no actual work was performed, was a futile attempt to revive an expired lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Paris Construction Co." p2="JAV Residences Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I640735405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paris Construction Co. v. JAV Residences Ltd.">Paris Construction Co. v. JAV Residences Ltd. (1985), 11 C.L.R. 1, 30 A.C.W.S. (2d) 287 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Cessation of work and abandonment are not necessarily co-existent. In order to constitute abandonment, a cessation of work would have to be permanent in the sense that it was not intended to carry the project to completion. While work on the project in question ceased before completion, the evidence at trial was clear that it was intended that work would be resumed when the financial problems had been overcome. It was likely that those problems would be overcome because the cost of completion was more than offset by the funds remaining to be advanced on the mortgage.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Warner et al.">JP Reno Inc. v. Warner et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 7776, 2024 ONSC 2935, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2549 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Distinguishing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Baeumler Quality Construction Inc." p2="Pirraglia" post.rptr="7610" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I675a75013b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Baeumler Quality Construction Inc. v. Pirraglia">Baeumler Quality Construction Inc. v. Pirraglia, 2018 ONSC 7610, 2018 CarswellOnt 21580, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 358 (Ont. S.C.J.), additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 4864 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nigeco Contracting Ltd." p2="Aizenstros" post.rptr="3364" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I675a75023b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Nigeco Contracting Ltd. v. Aizenstros">Nigeco Contracting Ltd. v. Aizenstros, 2019 ONSC 3364, 2019 CarswellOnt 8696, 99 C.L.R. (4th) 348 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> below, the contract was found to be terminated or abandoned after a heated meeting, the date of termination being such that the preserved lien was not perfected in a timely fashion. Among the facts that the court considered were: the defendants obtained quotes from other contractors; the plaintiff stormed off and the defendants changed the locks on the doors; the plaintiff called the police in order to enter the house to retrieve its tools; the plaintiff removed the building permit off the front door and contacted the company from which it had rented a portable toilet and requested its removal; no further substantive work was done on the property by the plaintiff after that date. There was no satisfactory evidence of any subsequent communication by the plaintiff in furtherance of continuing the renovations and no ongoing discussions about payment of invoices.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Osmi Homes Inc." p2="Kumar" post.rptr="6045" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64075c505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Osmi Homes Inc. v. Kumar">Osmi Homes Inc. v. Kumar, 2020 CarswellOnt 6045, 2020 ONSC 2712, 14 C.L.R. (5th) 85 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 12741, 2020 ONSC 5334, 14 C.L.R. (5th) 179 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master determined that the building contract was not abandoned by the claimant and was not completed more than 45 days prior to registration of the claim for lien, as set out in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The lien was therefore timely.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Scepter Industries Ltd." p2="Georgian Custom Renovations Inc." post.rptr="7515" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64075c515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Ct.); reversing 2018 ONSC 988, 2018 CarswellOnt 1901, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 174 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motions judge determined that the owner's notice of termination of the contract triggered the running of the deadline for filing of the claim for lien, holding that a payer terminating the contract constituted “abandonment” of the contract for the purposes of the Act. In reversing the judge's ruling that the lien was registered out of time, the Divisional Court stated that where parties have reached an impasse in their discussions aimed at resolving their conflict, then the contract may be considered to have been abandoned by the contractor, but this was not equivalent to saying that the owner may, itself, force abandonment by sending a notice of termination of the contract. In this case, the contractor relied upon the text of s. 31(2) and longstanding practice under the Act to continue settlement discussions, and did not register its claim for lien until the parties were at an impasse. On the motions judge's findings of fact, the contractor's conduct was objectively reasonable. In all these circumstances, the contract had not been abandoned. The motion judge's <ital>obiter</ital> comment that where a lien has expired, a litigant might secure a claim through a certificate of pending litigation, an interim preservation order, or an injunction, were wrong. A lien claimant, as such, has no interest in the land, other than its claim for lien. The Act provides a complete code for securing the price of services and materials provided to an improvement, and the alternative remedies proposed were not available to a lien claimant if its lien has expired.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Reno Rescue" p2="Ashton and Vilis" post.rptr="5339" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64075c525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reno Rescue v. Ashton and Vilis">Reno Rescue v. Ashton and Vilis, 2019 ONCS 5339, 2019 CarswellOnt 14960, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 361 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Abandonment occurs when there has been both a cessation of work and an intention not to complete the contract. Here, the defendant homeowners argued that the contractor abandoned the project when it removed its sign and equipment from the premises and returned the homeowners' keys, even though the contractor continued to work on the project after receiving a payment from them. The contractor successfully argued that the earliest possible date the project could be considered to have been abandoned was the day the homeowners refused to give the contractor's worker access to the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nigeco Contracting Ltd." p2="Aizenstros" post.rptr="3364" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64075c535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nigeco Contracting Ltd. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—If the parties continue to discuss payment and the completion of the project, the contractor is maintaining its intention to return to complete a contract and the contract is not abandoned. Whether a contract is terminated is to be determined by the intentions of the parties. Here, the conduct of the defendant was not consistent with a terminated contract, but rather was indicative of him trying to have it both ways by trying to start the clock on the plaintiff's lien rights with a letter of termination while still negotiating to complete the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Baeumler Quality Construction Inc." p2="Pirraglia" post.rptr="7610" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64075c545fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baeumler Quality Construction Inc. v. Pirraglia">Baeumler Quality Construction Inc. v. Pirraglia, 2018 ONSC 7610, 2018 CarswellOnt 21580, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 358 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 4864 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The question of abandonment of a contract is one of fact, and here, unlike the facts in both <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Scepter Industries Ltd." p2="Georgian Custom Renovations Inc." post.rptr="7515" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64075c555fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Georgian Custom Renovations Inc.">Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Georgian Custom Renovations Inc., 2019 ONSC 7515, 2019 CarswellOnt 20917 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2018 ONSC 988, 2018 CarswellOnt 1901, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 174 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Homewood Development Inc." p2="2010999 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4441" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64075c565fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Homewood Development Inc. v. 2010999 Ontario Inc.">Homewood Development Inc. v. 2010999 Ontario Inc., 2013 ONSC 4441, 2013 CarswellOnt 8867, 22 C.L.R. (4th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 ONSC 5337, 2013 CarswellOnt 12133, 32 C.L.R. (4th) 156 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the defendants never hired a lawyer and never advised the contractor expressly, through a lawyer or not, that the contract was terminated. It is not good policy to encourage the frantic filings of liens by contractors at the first sign of any trouble with their customers, and where the triggering event for the 45-day window for preservation of a construction lien is argued to be abandonment on the basis of termination of the contract, it is not too much to insist upon some solid evidence of same.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Romanov Romanov Architects Incorporated" p2="Cardillo Capital Corp." post.rptr="6628" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640783605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Romanov Romanov Architects Incorporated v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Discussing with the owner potential work and the use of a third party subcontractor, and the attendance by the plaintiff architect at the property on his own initiative, did not constitute a supply of services to an improvement for the purposes of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gem in Niagara Homes Inc." p2="Dewling et al" post.rptr="3500" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640783615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gem in Niagara Homes Inc. v. Here, a letter from the defendant's counsel informed the plaintiff that the defendants wished to terminate the contract, the defendant called police to remove the plaintiff from the job site, the plaintiff left with project's blue prints after police were called but before they arrived, and the portable washroom in use by workers was removed from the site. (4th) 326 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 17510 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In dismissing the defendant's motion for summary judgment, the court concluded that the contract was not abandoned more than 45 days before the lien was registered. Discussions took place between the parties within the registration window, and while there was a cessation of work, there was not an abandonment. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien was preserved and perfected within the time prescribed by the Act, the action set down for trial also within the time prescribed, and therefore the challenge to the timeliness of the lien claim failed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Martin Creek Construction Ltd." p2="Emelko" post.rptr="485" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I6407aa725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Martin Creek Construction Ltd. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In rejecting the contention that the contractor's lien was not preserved and perfected in time, the Master found that the plaintiff maintained its intention to complete the project until discussions over payment broke down. Abandonment required a cessation of work coupled with an intention not to return. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Attendance at the work site to clean up some concrete splashes that had been caused during earlier work was a remedial effort that did not extend the time limits for filing a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lido Cabinet Ltd." p2="Joy" post.rptr="5058" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6407d1805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lido Cabinet Ltd. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The principle that repair or deficiency work will not extend the forty-five day period is a broad one, and applies to s. 31(2)(b). Repair or deficiency work is not included in the last provision of services or the completion of a contract for services.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Mammoth Erection" p2="Vann Niagara Ltd." post.rptr="3434" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I6407d1845fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mammoth Erection v. The labour of loading the scaffolding onto trucks and removing it from the property at a later date did not extend the time for registering the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Larochelle Group Corp." p2="Cabral" post.rptr="1473" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I6407f8905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Larochelle Group Corp. v.
