The principles applicable to prevenient arrangements in this case entitled them to protect their lien rights to all of their services furnished on each of the premises in question, so long as their claim for liens were registered within 45 days of their last provision of services under the arrangement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Ron Robinson Ltd." p2="Rhodes Tanks Ltd." post.rptr="261" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I6407f8915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ron Robinson Ltd. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the time for making a lien claim had expired in 1996, after the plaintiff had abandoned the job, the plaintiff could not re-activate the claim by alleging that work it did subsequently was part of the original agreement between the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd." p2="Schleiss Development Co." post.rptr="5504" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I90dbd460f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Melloul-Blamey Construction Ltd. v. The lands were owned by a corporate partnership, which had signed an agreement of purchase and sale with a corporate developer intending to construct an ice rink facility thereon. The developer, who had initiated the delivery of supplies and dealt directly with the contractor, explored a variety of avenues to obtain financing and to achieve timely re-zoning. When it became apparent that the development was in jeopardy, the contractor and its building supplier arranged for a small delivery of building components to the lands in December 1997, under the calculated but mistaken belief that the delivery would allow the contractor to register a construction lien within 45 days of the delivery. Nevertheless, despite these attempts to circumvent the Act, the court concluded that it was not until the contractor finally reached the conclusion that the developer was not being realistic with respect to access to funding that the former had “abandoned” the “lands” within the meaning of s. 31(2)(b)(ii) of the Act. The attendances by representatives of the contractor after that date were merely to retrieve salvage and equipment. This was not a situation similar to that in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd." p2="Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd." post.rptr="1325" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I64081fa15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Eng" post.rptr="2839" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I90dbfb70f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd. v. Eng">Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd. v. As a result, in the <ital>Wood Lumber</ital> case, the time periods set out in s. 31 and s. 36 of the Act do not commence until the last materials were supplied to the project.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="LDR Contracting Inc." p2="Filion" post.rptr="16" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I64081fa45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="LDR Contracting Inc. v. Before work was completed, the owner instructed the contractor to leave the site, and the contractor subsequently sent the account to the insurer and, approximately 17 days later, to the owner. In determining whether the contractor's lien had been perfected in a timely manner, the court found the date of abandonment to be the date the account was sent to the owner, not the date it had been sent to the insurer.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Southdale Towers Ltd." p2="Carlton Management Group Inc." post.rptr="233" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I640846b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southdale Towers Ltd. v. The initial one-year term of the contract expired May 31, 1993 and was renewed for a further one-year term subject to the parties' respective rights of termination. The property management contract between the applicant and the respondent was terminated January 28, 1994, and the respondent registered its claim for lien on February 28, 1994. The court held that the property management contract should be considered one entire contract, with the result that the respondent's lien rights have not expired. The property management agreement provided that the expenses incurred could be paid out of the account maintained for the deposit of rent receipts, however, the expense burden could not be covered with the cash flows generated by the premises. Pursuant to the contract, the applicant remained responsible for the liabilities incurred by the respondent at the termination of the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Economark Renovations Ltd." p2="Hecht-Kugelmass" post.rptr="2986" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I640846b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Economark Renovations Ltd. v. Hecht-Kugelmass">Economark Renovations Ltd. v. Hecht-Kugelmass (1993), [1993] O.J. No. 2986, 1993 CarswellOnt 3143 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—An “abandonment” by a contractor, within the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, can come about through the blameworthy acts of “repudiation” or “breach”, or by the non-blameworthy, <ital>i.e.</ital>, innocent acts of acceptance of an owner's repudiation, and the resulting rescission or termination of the contract, or by mutual agreement, or, possibly, even by frustration of the contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="D'Andrea Developments Inc." p2="Farnham Development Corp." post.rptr="289" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I640846b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D'Andrea Developments Inc. v. Farnham Development Corp.">D'Andrea Developments Inc. v. Farnham Development Corp. (1992), 9 C.L.R. (2d) 289 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In October 1989, the owner entered into an agreement with the contractor to build a small plaza and gas bar. In late November or early December 1989, the owner asked contractors to stop work on the project because the owner did not want to incur the cost of winter construction. In April 1990, the contractor again started work on the project, but was told by the owner that the owner was in financial trouble and work on the project should stop. On June 6, 1990, the contractor registered a lien on title. At the trial of the construction lien action, the action was allowed in part. The owner had a continuing intention to complete the project until the first week of May 1990 when it instructed the contractor to cease work. The contract was therefore not abandoned until the first week of May. Since the lien was registered on June 6, 1990, it was properly registered within the 45-day period prescribed by s. 31(2)(b) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Landac Developments Ltd." p2="Kerry T. Howe Ltd." post.rptr="12" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I64086dc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landac Developments Ltd. v. Kerry T. Howe Ltd.">Landac Developments Ltd. v. Kerry T. Howe Ltd. (1990), 38 C.L.R. 12, 72 O.R. (2d) 760 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—When s. 31(2) refers to “the contract”, it must mean the contract of that particular contractor, not a different contract of a different contractor. This must be so even if the services supplied by a contractor also relate to the completion of a contract of another contractor. If follows, then, that survival of a contractor's lien is not tied to the certificate of a different contractor. In this case, the claimant, which supplied engineering work and construction supervision, was not required to register its lien within 45 days of the publication of the certificate of substantial completion of the contract of the construction contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd." p2="Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd." post.rptr="1325" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I64086dc15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd.">Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 1325, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 184 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Four plaintiffs sought payment for equipment supplied and delivered to a remote mining location in Northwestern Ontario. The mining program was to have proceeded in a series of stages, but a cessation of work halted the program indefinitely. The Court relied on the definition of “abandonment” set forth in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1974" p1="Dieleman Planer Co." p2="Elizabeth Townhouses Ltd." post.rptr="449" pre.rptr="[1975] 2" ref.id="I64086dc25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dieleman Planer Co. v. Elizabeth Townhouses Ltd.">Dieleman Planer Co. v. Elizabeth Townhouses Ltd. (1974), [1975] 2 S.C.R. 449, [1975] 2 W.W.R. 752, 1974 CarswellBC 8 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>. In determining whether the project had been abandoned for the purposes of s. 31(2)(b)(ii), the court found that while active pursuit of the mining program at the site ceased on or about May 2, 1993, the program was not abandoned at that point either in fact or in law. Not only did the defendant fail to advise any of the plaintiffs that the project was at an end, several expressions about the imminent resumption of work on the project were made. In the circumstances, abandonment occurred at the point when reasonable people ought to have concluded that the project was at an end, in the legal sense of having been “abandoned”. That point was set at September 30, 1993, after which the plaintiffs had 45 days to preserve their lien.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:7: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(2)(b)(ii)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="S31 Inc." p2="Ecolomondo Environmental (Hawkesbury) Inc." post.rptr="5071" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I675b86703b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="S31 Inc. v. Ecolomondo Environmental (Hawkesbury) Inc.">S31 Inc. v. Ecolomondo Environmental (Hawkesbury) Inc., 2023 ONSC 5071, 2023 CarswellOnt 13766 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not define abandonment, but this has been determined to occur when there is a cessation of work and either an intention not to complete the contract or a refusal to complete the contract. As indicated by the Divisional Court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Scepter Industries Ltd." p2="Georgian Custom Renovations Inc." post.rptr="7515" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I8db45e40ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Georgian Custom Renovations Inc.">Scepter Industries Ltd. v. Georgian Custom Renovations Inc., 2019 ONSC 7515, 2019 CarswellOnt 20917 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2018 ONSC 988, 2018 CarswellOnt 1901, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 174 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, subjective abandonment by the lien claimant is sufficient to establish abandonment, but when abandonment is denied by the lien claimant, all relevant circumstances may be considered to determine whether a contract was abandoned. Further, also as indicated in <ital>Scepter</ital>, although considering both the subjective intentions of the parties and the objective relevant circumstances, the focus should still be on the contractor as it is necessary that the lien claimant be the person to abandon the contract. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: <ital>Scepter Industries</ital> was decided under the <ital>Construction Lien Act.</ital> Subsections 31(2)(a)(ii) and s. 31(2)(b)(ii) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> were amended subsequent to that decision to add “<ital>or terminated”</ital> (emphasis added). In <ital>S31</ital>, the defendant initially argued termination of the contract as well, but by the time of the motion only abandonment was argued.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2280092 Ontario Inc." p2="Collins" post.rptr="4365" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64086dc35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2280092 Ontario Inc. v. Collins">2280092 Ontario Inc. v. Collins, 2021 ONSC 4365, 2021 CarswellOnt 8894 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff, via counsel, advised the defendants that it did not intend to continue with the contract unless arrangements for payment of outstanding amounts were made; the defendants declined to make any such payment arrangements. The defendants' subsequent termination letter only served to recognize the plaintiff's earlier abandonment of the contract. The evidence as a whole established that the tools and minor items delivered or collected from the project were insufficient to constitute the supply of services under the Act. The plaintiff's lien rights expired before registration of the lien.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:8: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:8</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Quality General Contractor's Inc." p2="Wu" post.rptr="2909" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I675bad803b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Quality General Contractor's Inc. v. Wu">Quality General Contractor's Inc. v. Wu, 2024 CarswellOnt 7523, 2024 ONSC 2909, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2528 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 14677, 2024 ONSC 5318 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In an action under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the plaintiff lien claimant failed to meet its onus of proving the timeliness of its claim for lien, which expired on account of its failure to have it preserved. The invoices provided to the court to support the last day of supply were found to be generated to construct an inaccurate narrative after the fact and did not accord with the evidence. The plaintiff's site diary entries also lacked credibility, and the plaintiff failed to produce timesheet entries that would have been critical evidence to show attendance at the site.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="13245" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I675bd4903b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Subcontractor lien claims do not expire on a subcontract-by-subcontract basis under s. 31(3)(ii) of the Act, but persist until 45 days (now 60 days) after last supply “to the improvement”. Any owner or contractor wishing to terminate a subcontractor's lien rights in respect to one of several subcontracts may have recourse to s. 31(3)(iii) of the Act, which would require certification of completion of the subcontract pursuant to s. 33, although that was not done in this case. Aside from cases involving prevenient arrangements, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1955" p1="Menzies & Herbert Ltd." p2="Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590" post.rptr="74" pre.rptr="1954" ref.id="I675bd4913b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590">Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590, 1954 CarswellAlta 74, [1955] 1 D.L.R. 161, [1954] S.C.R. 589 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> does not apply to the expiry of subcontractor lien claims, and no Ontario court has followed <ital>Rocky Mountain</ital> to find expiry of subcontracts on a subcontract-by-subcontract basis since enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> in 1983. Here, the trial judge erred in law in finding that separate claims for lien must be registered in respect to separate subcontracts between the same parties for the same improvement. Absent certification of substantial performance or completion, it matters not whether a subcontractor provides its services or materials under one subcontract or multiple subcontracts. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990 c. C.30].</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Parma General Contractors Inc." p2="Pulcini" post.rptr="1948" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I640894d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini">Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini, 2014 ONSC 1948, 2014 CarswellOnt 3833 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 CarswellOnt 11228 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Various persons entered into a joint venture agreement for the purpose of purchasing, severing and redeveloping residential lots, and sharing in the profits realized. The principal of the plaintiff was the son of RM, one of the participants in the joint venture. The plaintiff subcontractor performed framing and related work, registered lien claims against three properties, and purported to perfect them by bringing three lien actions, as well as an action for breach of contract, relating to unpaid invoices. The Master found that the plaintiff did not, as it alleged, extend the time of last supply by hiring and paying for finishing trim work by a subcontractor and by providing paving quotes to the joint venture. The trim work was held not to be the work of the plaintiff, as it was not sensible to conclude that a contractor would approach its framing subcontractor to finish the much later work of its trim subcontractor. As well, none of the quotes ended up in work being done on site and did not give rise to lien rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R." p2="1431633 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I2d5f2ca0f65111ee9732e3e835885970" title="R. v. 1431633 Ontario Inc.">R. v. 1431633 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 161, 2010 ONSC 266, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 263, 250 C.C.C. (3d) 354 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The supplier sold lumber used to construct a house owned by an accused against whom the Crown had obtained and registered a restraint order under the <ital>Criminal Code</ital>. Subsequent to that registration, and unaware of the restraint order, the supplier filed a claim for lien and brought an action to enforce it without giving notice to the Crown or obtaining a prior court order, contrary to the provisions of the restraint order. The supplier successfully applied under s. 462.42 of <ital>Criminal Code</ital> for relief from forfeiture. The supplier would have had a valid interest in the property under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> but for provision of the restraint order declaring it void, and it was appropriate to vary the order <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> to allow the registration of the lien claim and the action to enforce it. It was not consistent with purpose of forfeiture provisions to punish innocent third parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dirm Inc." p2="Bennington Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4171" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640894d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dirm Inc. v. Bennington Construction Ltd.">Dirm Inc. v. Bennington Construction Ltd., 2010 CarswellOnt 4171, 96 C.L.R. (3d) 102 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's failure to produce time sheets for services rendered at the work site within the lien period allowed the court to draw an adverse inference. The lien was not registered within the time provided by s. 31(3).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc." p2="Baun Construction Inc." post.rptr="307" pre.rptr="85" ref.id="I6408bbe05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc.">Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc. (2009), 85 C.L.R. (3d) 307, 2009 CarswellOnt 7122 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Applying the rulings in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90dc97b1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219, 1993 CarswellOnt 833 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Blockwall Masonry Ltd." p2="Arcaio Design" post.rptr="155" pre.rptr="66" ref.id="I6408bbe25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design">Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design (2007), 66 C.L.R. (3d) 155, 2007 CarswellOnt 5451 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1434 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the court held that a trivial amount of work performed or services supplied after completion of a contract will not serve to extend the time within which a claim for lien must be registered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Ramer Builders Supplies (Toronto) Ltd." p2="Roitman" post.rptr="2857" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I6408bbe35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ramer Builders Supplies (Toronto) Ltd. v. Roitman">Ramer Builders Supplies (Toronto) Ltd. v. Roitman (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 2857, 2004 CarswellOnt 2707 (Master)</ref></cite>—A drywall supplier argued “prevenient arrangement” to string or tie together a supply within the 45-day period to supplies outside the 45-day period. Citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1954" p1="Menzies & Herbert Ltd." p2="Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590" post.rptr="74" pre.rptr="1954" ref.id="I90dc97b2f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590">Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590 (1954), 1954 CarswellAlta 74, [1955] 1 D.L.R. 161, [1954] S.C.R. 589 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Dufferin Concrete Products" p2="Waterbrooke Development Ltd." post.rptr="132" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I6408e2f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dufferin Concrete Products v. Waterbrooke Development Ltd.">Dufferin Concrete Products v. Waterbrooke Development Ltd. (1992), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 132, 1992 CarswellOnt 881 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Oaks Precast" p2="G.L. Trenching Ltd." post.rptr="312" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I6408e2f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oaks Precast v. G.L. Trenching Ltd.">Oaks Precast v. G.L. Trenching Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 312, 1996 CarswellOnt 2767 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Dominion Lumber Winnipeg Ltd." p2="A & S Builders Ltd." post.rptr="303" pre.rptr="45" ref.id="I6408e2f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Lumber Winnipeg Ltd. v. A & S Builders Ltd.">Dominion Lumber Winnipeg Ltd. v. A & S Builders Ltd. (1999), 45 C.L.R. (2d) 303, 1999 CarswellMan 285 (Q.B.)</ref></cite>; and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Eng" post.rptr="2839" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I90dcbec0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd. v. Eng">Wood Lumber Co. (Ontario) Ltd. v. Eng (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 2839, 48 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 45 O.R. (3d) 795, [1999] O.J. No. 3404 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the Master found that in all cases there was, at the beginning, at least an informed understanding that the supplier would furnish all the labour or materials for a particular improvement and that the purchaser would order all required labour or material for the particular improvement from the supplier, so that a series of otherwise separate contracts would be linked together by a preceding, previous, anticipatory or expectant (prevenient) arrangement. It is crucial that only one project be involved.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Greycor Industrial Coatings" p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="4975" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I64090a005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Greycor Industrial Coatings v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Greycor Industrial Coatings v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd. (2001), [2001] O.J. No. 4975, 2001 CarswellOnt 4427 (Master)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant must prove the timeliness of its lien on a balance of probabilities. Although the claimant failed to do so, personal judgment was granted under s. 63.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of)" p2="Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality)" post.rptr="191" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I64090a015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of) v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality)">I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 (Trustees of) v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality) (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 191 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial performance, issued by the contractor on December 29, 1995 and published on January 3, 1996, did not contain a description of the lot and plan number. The claimant, which was not aware of the publication until February 29, 1996, registered a lien against the contractor on February 22, 1996, after instructing its solicitors to conduct a title search on the property on January 22, 1996. The claimant argued that the 45-day time limit set out in s. 31(3) had not expired because the contractor's certificate was not in compliance with the Act. The Master held that the certificate of substantial performance was valid under s. 6 of the Act, reserving until trial the issue of whether the plaintiff has been prejudiced on or after January 22, 1996 by the certificate's omissions. Subcontractor argued that its supplier's lien was invalid as the parties had a separate contract for cash delivery of supplies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Oaks Precast" p2="G.L. Trenching Ltd." post.rptr="312" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I64090a025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oaks Precast v. G.L. Trenching Ltd.">Oaks Precast v. G.L. Trenching Ltd. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 312 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—All that is needed to be found as a fact to support prevenient arrangement for material supply is an informal understanding which serves to link together the subsequent series of transactions into one continuing contact or open account. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The law involving prevenient arrangements is reviewed in detail in this case.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Re Don Crichton as Trustee for U.A. Local Union 853, Ontario Sprinkler Industry Benefit Trust Fund" p1.pp="Re" post.rptr="19" pre.rptr="26" ref.id="I64090a035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Re Don Crichton as Trustee for U.A. Local Union 853, Ontario Sprinkler Industry Benefit Trust Fund">Re Don Crichton as Trustee for U.A. Local Union 853, Ontario Sprinkler Industry Benefit Trust Fund (1995), 26 C.L.R. (2d) 19 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A subcontractor, by prior agreement, advanced monies to the Trustee in Bankruptcy of a bankrupt sprinkler installer, for the purpose of paying tradesmen to continue their work. The installer abandoned its work, but the subcontractor continued. The installer's tradesmen liened. Some returned to work for one day, a month later. The trades took the position they had actually been employed by the subcontractor, whose money had been used to pay them, and who was still on the job, thereby rendering their liens timely. The subcontractor argued that the tradesmen's lien rights dated from the date of the installer's abandonment, whether or not they later returned, and had expired before they were preserved. The subcontractor's argument prevailed. The tradesmen's liens were removed, with a possible order of solicitor and client costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd." p2="951034 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2064" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I90dce5d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc.">L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. 2064 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor entered into a contract with the defendant contractor to supply and install electrical services and equipment at the project. A certificate of substantial performance was issued on November 18, 1992, but finishing work continued until February 18 of the next year. The holdback on the building mortgage was released by the mortgagee on February 28, 1993 at a time when the plaintiff was still entitled to register a claim for lien. The court found the certificate to be defective, and accordingly held that the lien had priority over the mortgage. Work performed by the plaintiff on a variety of dates following the issuance of the certificate did not create separate lien expiry dates prior to that of the finishing work in the main contract. The plaintiff was hired to do the electrical work in connection with the building. During this contract changes were made to the scope of work and the price on seven occasions before November 16, 1992 and on three occasions thereafter. The circumstances of the case were consistent with a prevenient contract for the supply of electrical work as required, and all of the work performed by the plaintiff is governed by one contract. This case was distinguished from other decisions such as <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd." p2="Preston Heights Estates Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I640931105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd.">G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd. (1992), 1 C.L.R. (2d) 157 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, on its facts. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Caution should be used when applying this case, as the court used. s. 31(2) rather than 31(3) in determining when the subcontractor's lien rights would expire.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd." p2="Canadian Glass" post.rptr="833" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90dd0ce0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass">Canadian Rogers Eastern Ltd. v. Canadian Glass (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 833, 12 C.L.R. (2d) 219 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff a subcontractor, contracted to provide doors, which were delivered to the job site on March 19, 1993. The plaintiff re-attended on June 8 to repair some defects, and registered its lien on July 23. The defendant subcontractor successfully moved to dismiss the lien action on the ground that the claim for lien was registered too late. Remedial work done by a supplier of services or materials to remedy a defect in the work or materials originally supplied does not extend the time for registering a lien where more than 45 days have elapsed since the services or materials under the original contract were last supplied. Since the repair work did not extend the time for filing a lien, the “last supply” of materials was on March 19. Accordingly, the plaintiff's lien was registered outside the 45-day period provided by s. 31(3)(b)(i).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I5601e180fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 171, 1994 CarswellOnt 956 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 486, 40 O.R. (3d) 543, 1998 CarswellOnt 2653 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Replacing two by fours warped by weather, before the drywall is put up, is part of preparing a house for drywall and not a repair. A lien filed within 45 days of the performance of such work was held to be timely and valid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd." p2="Preston Heights Estates Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I640931135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd.">G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd. (1992), 1 C.L.R. (2d) 157 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claim was made by a subcontractor which supplied patio doors and screens for the entire project. The claimant's completion certificate was dated November 5, 1989, but the claimant was forced to reattend on the site on March 26, 1990, to replace items which had been damaged or removed from the site during the winter. In this case, the re-attendance did not extend the 45-day period for filing the claim for lien. Accordingly, the claimant was given judgment for the full amount owing, but its lien was limited to the amount owing on the invoices for the last attendance on the site.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Extender Products Ltd." p2="Patrick Harrison & Co." post.rptr="8" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I640958205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Extender Products Ltd. v. Patrick Harrison & Co.">Extender Products Ltd. v. Patrick Harrison & Co. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 8 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff leased certain trucks to a contractor, who removed the vehicles from the construction site on February 4, 1989. A lien filed on June 5, 1989, was held to be out of time. Where the contract is not certified or declared substantially performed, the lien time for all services or materials supplied to the improvement commences to run on the date on which the defendant last supplied services or materials to the improvement as per s. 31(3)(a)(ii). Accordingly, since that date in the present case was February 4, 1989, the claim for lien was capable of being preserved only until March 22, 1989.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:9: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:9</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(3)(b)(i)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Infinite Construction Development Ltd." p2="Chen" post.rptr="3929" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I675c97e03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Infinite Construction Development Ltd. v. Chen">Infinite Construction Development Ltd. v. Chen, 2022 ONSC 3929, 2022 CarswellOnt 9316, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 386 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2023 CarswellOnt 8169, 2023 ONSC 2627, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 409 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 5721, 2022 CarswellOnt 14512 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The lien claimant subcontractor alleged that it, not the original contractor, had performed all of the work required under a renovation contract, and that the contract was equitably assigned to it by contractor through an oral agreement. No written assignment agreement was executed until over two years later after the claimant had registered both of its claims for lien against the property. The claimant was held to be a “subcontractor” under the Act and its lien rights were found to have been expired when its claims were registered, based on last supply of services or materials. While nothing in the Act prevented a general contractor, who has been contracted by the owner, from subcontracting with a second general contractor to perform the full scope of the first general contractor's work, absent a contract with the owner or its agent, the second general contractor would still fall within the definition of a “subcontractor” under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Its services and materials would be supplied under an agreement with the first general contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="3458" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I675c97e13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069 (Ont. S.C.J.); varied on other grounds, 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace>—The supply of chair dollies and brackets, valued at $5,500, was not “trivial” or an artificial attempt to extend the plaintiff's lien rights. While the amount did not reflect a substantial percentage of the overall value of the work, it could not be characterized as “trivial”. The plaintiff's work had proceeded in fits and spurts over a number of months, and it was unlike the situation in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Wildberry Homes Inc." p2="Prosperity One Credit Union Ltd." post.rptr="8314" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I90dd33f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Wildberry Homes Inc. v. Prosperity One Credit Union Ltd.">Wildberry Homes Inc. v. Prosperity One Credit Union Ltd. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 8314, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 109 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, (see Subsection 31(2)(b), above), where the contractor attended two-and-a-half months after its last supply and installed a handrail in an obvious attempt to extend its lien rights. The plaintiff had been puttering away at the work for months. Accordingly, in so far as the lien related to certain work, it was registered in a timely fashion. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990 c. C.30].</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Frattaroli" p2="Ricci" post.rptr="2765" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64097f305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Frattaroli v. Ricci">Frattaroli v. Ricci, 2018 ONSC 2765, 2018 CarswellOnt 6915, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Employees of the claimant attended the site in mid-November for periods of 8.5 and 9.5 hours respectively, ostensibly to complete parging and patching, claiming that the work had been deferred to a date when the temperature was appropriate. The claimant also took pictures of the workmen. The court concluded that the work done was a deliberate attempt to bootstrap the claimant's earlier lien rights beyond expiry.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ken Tulloch Construction Ltd." p2="1684567 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2071" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64097f315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ken Tulloch Construction Ltd. v. 1684567 Ontario Inc.">Ken Tulloch Construction Ltd. v. 1684567 Ontario Inc., 2018 ONSC 2071, 2018 CarswellOnt 5007, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 121 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The fact that the claimant had invoiced the owner for work earlier than the date specified for last supply did not mean that the contract had been completed at the time of the invoice. Many contracts call for payment “up front”. The relevant date under the Act is not the date of invoicing but rather the date on which the contract work was completed. Invoicing is only one of many factors to consider when determining the date a contract is completed for purposes of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pollard Windows" p2="1459855 Ontario Limited et al" post.rptr="558" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64097f325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pollard Windows v. 1459855 Ontario Limited et al">Pollard Windows v. 1459855 Ontario Limited et al, 2018 ONSC 558, 2018 CarswellOnt 802, 88 C.L.R. (4th) 103 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant delivered all required windows and doors to the construction site but did not deliver screens for same, and invoiced for everything, including the screens, on the next day. The motions judge properly considered whether the screens added value to the project, that the screens were not separately invoiced, that there was no valid reason why they could not have been delivered sooner, and that the appellant intentionally kept the screens to attempt to extend an otherwise expired lien. The motions judge made no reviewable error in concluding that the appellant failed to register its lien within the required time period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2349914 Ontario Inc. o/a Antares Construction Group" p2="Oleg Mazlov" post.rptr="339" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64097f335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2349914 Ontario Inc. o/a Antares Construction Group v. Oleg Mazlov">2349914 Ontario Inc. o/a Antares Construction Group v. Oleg Mazlov, 2018 ONSC 339, 2018 CarswellOnt 332, 88 C.L.R. (4th) 366 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—All of the items listed as work carried out to extend the start of the lien claim period were either deficiency rectification or adjustments to work already completed. This type of work does not qualify as new work sufficient to revive an otherwise expired claim for lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cos Shore Inc." p2="Unimac-United Mgmt. Corp." post.rptr="4813" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6409a6405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cos Shore Inc. v. Unimac-United Mgmt. Corp.">Cos Shore Inc. v. Unimac-United Mgmt. Corp., 2017 ONSC 4813, 2017 CarswellOnt 12357, 80 C.L.R. (4th) 336 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Applying the factual analysis set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarkway Construction Ltd." p2="2247129 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3991" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6409a6415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkway Construction Ltd. v. 2247129 Ontario Inc.">Clarkway Construction Ltd. v. 2247129 Ontario Inc., 2016 ONSC 3991, 2016 CarswellOnt 9626, 68 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the master concluded that the sub-contract equipment rental provider's claim for a lien was not registered in time. The claimant had relied on a last supply of services taking place after termination of the general contract. Although unlike in <ital>Clarkway</ital>, the claimant was a “pure” equipment renter that did not provide a labour component, there was more than enough other evidence that the claimant was made fully aware of the contract's termination at an earlier date which invalidated the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cohen" p2="Brin" post.rptr="1302" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6409a6425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cohen v. Brin">Cohen v. Brin, 2013 ONSC 1302, 2013 CarswellOnt 2307 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A contractor cannot revive an expired lien by performing a minimal amount of work after the date of completion, abandonment or last supply.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Roe" p2="Elgaard Developments Inc." post.rptr="7831" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6409a6435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Roe v. Elgaard Developments Inc.">Roe v. Elgaard Developments Inc., 2016 ONSC 7831, 2016 CarswellOnt 19639, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 77 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In determining the date on which the person last supplied services or materials to the improvement, the courts have drawn a distinction between substantive work performed under the terms of the contract and remedial or trivial work. Work will be remedial or trivial where it relates to a minor deficiency or rectification of work already completed or where the service performed does not add to the value of the improvement. While the distinction between the two is at times fine, the courts are on guard against permitting the performance of a minor or trivial amount of work to artificially extend the time for filing a lien. Here, there were concerns that the claimant may have engaged in an <ital>ex-post</ital> bootstrapping exercise to artificially extend the time frames for preserving his lien. The court was not satisfied that the date of the final service allowed for a validly preserved and perfected lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarkway Construction Ltd." p2="2247129 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3991" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6409a6445fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkway Construction Ltd. v. 2247129 Ontario Inc.">Clarkway Construction Ltd. v. 2247129 Ontario Inc., 2016 ONSC 3991, 2016 CarswellOnt 9626, 68 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether a subcontractor's lien rights against an owner could continue to accrue after the contract between the owner and the general contractor ended. The subcontractor argued that because the owner did not give it notice of termination of the main contract, those lien rights continued at least until the owner instructed the subcontractor to remove a water tank which the latter had supplied. In rejecting this argument, the Master noted that there was no direct contractual relationship between the owner and subcontractor, and that the claimant, having supplied rental equipment to the contractor, had a responsibility to keep itself informed as to the status of the project, particularly when arrears in rental payments accrued. A case of equipment rental was no different from a case of the supply of labour. A subcontractors “preservation clock” should run only from a date that can be readily ascertained by that claimant. However, in this case, the date of the contractor's abandonment of the general contract was readily ascertainable had the subcontractor made the appropriate inquiries on an ongoing basis, particularly in view of ongoing and increasing rental arrears for its equipment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Toronto Zenith Contracting Ltd." p2="Fermar Paving Ltd." post.rptr="4696" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6409cd505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Zenith Contracting Ltd. v. Fermar Paving Ltd.">Toronto Zenith Contracting Ltd. v. Fermar Paving Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4696, 2016 CarswellOnt 11566, 66 C.L.R. (4th) 278 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although the plaintiff's lien was registered more than 45 days after the latest date that its forces were physically on site, the lien was timely, because it was served within 45 days of the date of the alleged termination of the subcontract agreement, and while it continued to perform its ongoing off-site subcontract responsibilities in relation to the improvement. Applying <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc." p2="Baun Construction Inc." post.rptr="307" pre.rptr="85" ref.id="I6409cd515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc.">Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc. (2009), 85 C.L.R. (3d) 307, 2009 CarswellOnt 7122, [2009] O.J. No. 4845 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the court held that the last legitimate supply of services or materials under the contract was the trigger that started the 45-day period to run.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarkway Construction Ltd." p2="2247129 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3991" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6409cd525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkway Construction Ltd. v. 2247129 Ontario Inc.">Clarkway Construction Ltd. v. 2247129 Ontario Inc., 2016 ONSC 3991, 2016 CarswellOnt 9626, 68 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the date of last supply of the subcontractor to the general contractor could extend beyond the date on which the contract between the contractor and owner ended. It was held that the time for a subcontractor to preserve a lien claim starts to run when the general contractor with whom the subcontractor had contracted abandons or terminates its contract with the owner. While a subcontractor's “preservation clock” should begin to run only from a date that can be readily ascertained by that claimant, in this case the date of the contractor's abandonment of the general contract was readily ascertainable to the subcontractor, had it made the appropriate inquiries on an ongoing basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Khalimov" p2="Hogarth" post.rptr="6244" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6409f4605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khalimov v. Hogarth">Khalimov v. Hogarth, 2015 ONSC 6244, 2015 CarswellOnt 15551, 56 C.L.R. (4th) 167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owners entered into a contract for renovation of their home and paid the contractor's invoices without retaining holdback. Following a dispute over payments and scope of work, work on the project stopped for several months, after the contractor and plaintiff subcontractor left the site. The contractor advised the owners by email that the contract had been terminated “some time ago” and informed them that they could pay out the holdback after 45 days. Subsequently, there was a brief attendance by the subcontractor to retrieve tools and equipment. The subcontractor then registered a claim for lien, citing the date of last supply as the date work originally stopped. The lien was subsequently discharged following execution of a document titled “Amendment to Contract”, which provided a scope of work, a method of verifying that the work was performed, and a contract price. Work under the amending document began and then subsequently stopped; after the subcontractor registered a second claim for lien, the owners terminated the contract. Citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Blockwall Masonry Ltd." p2="Arcaio Design" post.rptr="155" pre.rptr="66" ref.id="I6409f4615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design">Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design (2007), 66 C.L.R. (3d) 155, 2007 CarswellOnt 5451 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1434 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, it was held that the subcontractor had taken a hiatus from work, and its lien rights, including its right to claim holdback against the owners, expired 45 days after the last work prior to the hiatus. Upon discharging the first lien claim, all lien rights arising from the services and materials supplied prior to the hiatus, including the right to claim holdback from the owners, were extinguished.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Provincial Partitions Ltd." p2="Toronto (City)" post.rptr="2839" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6409f4625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Provincial Partitions Ltd. v. Toronto (City)">Provincial Partitions Ltd. v. Toronto (City), 2015 ONSC 2839, 2015 CarswellOnt 6264, 48 C.L.R. (4th) 158 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Minor amounts of outstanding deficiency repair work for which the subcontractor is not entitled to be paid an additional amount does not qualify as the last supply of services and materials for purposes of counting the 45 day lien claim period. In determining the date of last supply, the Master characterized the installation of panels as being for the purpose of completing the work required pursuant to the contract, either within the contract's original scope of work or as a required extra, rather than as the completion of deficiency repair work, even given a one year delay in returning to the site. The motion to discharge the lien therefore failed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc." p2="Baun Construction Inc." post.rptr="307" pre.rptr="85" ref.id="I6409f4635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc.">Applewood Glass & Mirror Inc. v. Baun Construction Inc. (2009), 85 C.L.R. (3d) 307, 2009 CarswellOnt 7122, [2009] O.J. No. 4845 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Each lapse of time during the currency of a subcontract does not cause the 45-day period to run. Rather, it is the last legitimate supply of services or materials under the contract that does. If a subcontract called for material and/or services to be provided over the span of a year, and material and services could not be supplied for a 60-day period during the year because intervening work had to be performed by the contractor, the subcontractor would still have a claim for lien for material and services supplied before and after the 60-day period providing the claim for lien was registered within the 45-day next following the “last supplied services or materials” pursuant to the subcontract. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This is contrary to a strict reading of the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Blockwall Masonry Ltd." p2="Arcaio Design" post.rptr="155" pre.rptr="66" ref.id="I6409f4645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design">Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design (2007), 66 C.L.R. (3d) 155, 2007 CarswellOnt 5451 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1434 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="1442968 Ontario Ltd." p2="Houston Engineering & Drafting Inc." post.rptr="2155" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I640a1b705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1442968 Ontario Ltd. v. Houston Engineering & Drafting Inc.">1442968 Ontario Ltd. v. Houston Engineering & Drafting Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2155, 71 C.L.R. (3d) 165 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2774, 70 C.L.R. (3d) 268 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant was subcontracted to construct a fire escape on a renovation project, and construction was completed in August 2007. In December 2007, the claimant registered a claim for lien alleging it was owed monies for services or materials supplied on the project to the general contractor and the owner between 2004 and November 30, 2007. The claimant alleged that it inspected the fire escape and site, and reviewed structural steel work for compliance with plans in October and November 2007, pursuant to a written commitment that the owner asserted was a fraud. The owner's motion to vacate the lien was granted. When the lien claimant allegedly visited the site in October and November 2007, he spoke with no one, did not check in with the site foreman or otherwise tell the owner or anyone that he was there, and made no reports or field notes. He simply reviewed the site, which he had no authority to enter at that time. Even if the lien claimant did this “work”, which the court believed it did not, it was not lienable work and added absolutely no value to the improvement, as the claimant's earlier work had been previously certified by it and approved by the municipality, and the claimant had been paid for it.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Blockwall Masonry Ltd." p2="Arcaio Design" post.rptr="155" pre.rptr="66" ref.id="I640a1b715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design">Blockwall Masonry Ltd. v. Arcaio Design (2007), 66 C.L.R. (3d) 155, 2007 CarswellOnt 5451 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1434 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Minor masonry work was performed more than 45 days after the subcontractor's main work was completed. While legitimate, the work was an attempt on the subcontractor's part to bootstrap lien rights which had already expired and was an attempt to keep those rights alive. Work performed on that day was minor, added no value to improvement, was not intended to prepare the exterior for further work, and did not constitute the kind of work that could revive an expired lien. Section 31(3)(b)(i) provides a rigid calendar test for subcontractor liens that does not exist for contractors. Unlike a contractor, a subcontractor cannot take a hiatus or holiday from work, and a period of 45 days elapses when the subcontractor is not working on the job.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353" p2="779857 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2528" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I640a1b725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 v. 779857 Ontario Inc.">I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 v. 779857 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2528, 36 C.L.R. (3d) 48 (Master)</ref></cite>—Liens were filed after the electrical contractor failed to pay both its suppliers and, for several weeks of work, its unionized workers. The workers' claim for lien was registered on February 10, 2003, and for its timely preservation, the “supply of services” had to be last supplied on or after December 28, 2002. However, the job site was closed at the end of the day on December 20, 2002 and was reopened on January 2, 2003 with the result that no services were or could have been supplied between December 21 and January 1. Following that hiatus, the owner terminated the contractor's contract, a process that was started on January 2, 2003 and finalized on January 3, 2003. At least 20 of the workers named in the claim for lien and the statement of claim had returned to the job site on January 2, 2003, and although no actual physical electrical work was performed, the workers prepared for the work day, and packed up when the foreman advised that the job site would be closed. It was argued that the “supply of services” required that some actual physical electrical work be performed on the improvement that advanced the scope of the work in the contract. The Master ruled that attending to hear their foreman assign the work for the day, and readying their tools and equipment for the day's work, and cleaning up and packing up their tools and equipment and job boxes was “work done” and, therefore, a “supply of services”. As a result, the lien was preserved in a timely manner. If a different conclusion was reached, it would have the effect of shortening the workers' lien period from 45 days to 33 days. When the workers finished work on December 20th, they anticipated returning to work on January 2, 2003, and that their lien rights would not be affected by the intervening 12-day holiday period. The Act should not be construed and applied in such a way that, through no fault or neglect of theirs, the workers would lose some of the rights given to them.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Cambareri Construction Inc." p2="Nanometrics Inc." post.rptr="3095" pre.rptr="[1997]" ref.id="I640a1b735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cambareri Construction Inc. v. Nanometrics Inc.">Cambareri Construction Inc. v. Nanometrics Inc. (1997), [1997] O.J. No. 3095, 1997 CarswellOnt 3395 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The work contract between the plaintiff drywall contractor and defendant construction contractor was terminated by the defendant because of the plaintiff's failure to complete the job in a timely manner. In determining the date of the last work performed on the premises by the plaintiff, the court held that work performed by the plaintiff's subcontractor, hired by the defendant directly to complete the job, could not be used to extend the time within which the plaintiff contractor could register a lien where the plaintiff was terminated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="182" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I640a42805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. (1994), 22 C.L.R. (2d) 182, 1994 CarswellOnt 1108 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—When the plaintiff falsely prepared a document to obtain release of the holdback, it raised grave concerns over the reliability of the time sheets put forward by the plaintiff to support its position with respect to the date of completion of the contract. The court declined to rely on those time sheets.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:10: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:10</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(3)(b)(ii)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lacroix" p2="Dompierre" post.rptr="3873" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I640a42815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lacroix v. Dompierre">Lacroix v. Dompierre, 2016 ONSC 3873, 2016 CarswellOnt 9637, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2016 CarswellOnt 17664, 2016 ONSC 6931, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 325 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The billing for holdback can be evidence that the lien period has expired and the contractor or owner can release holdback funds because the work is complete and other sub-trades cannot lien. Here, the sub-subcontractor lien claimant's final invoice for the holdback was a strong piece of evidence that the work under the contract was 100% complete at a date which would render the lien expired. The claimant was attempting to bootstrap its claim against the subcontractor by relying on the contractor's contractual right to take possession of the subcontractor's work, but there was no evidence that the contractor did so. The lien was declared expired and the lien bond was cancelled.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="81" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640a42825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2012 ONSC 81, 2012 CarswellOnt 462, 10 C.L.R. (4th) 203 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor's attendance at the work site to finish imperfections in the surface of concrete was part of the contract work, not rectification of a deficiency. While it would have been a “deficiency” to leave these imperfections unfinished, it was not a “deficiency” that they occurred in the first place, as this was a normal and expected part of the work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Any-Wall Concrete Forming Inc." p2="Bloomfield" post.rptr="2374" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640a42835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Any-Wall Concrete Forming Inc. v. Bloomfield">Any-Wall Concrete Forming Inc. v. Bloomfield, 2012 ONSC 2374, 2012 CarswellOnt 7139, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 275 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—If work amounts to rectification of deficient or improper work, it does not extend the time for preserving the claim for lien. Rather, it amounts to bootstrapping.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3161" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640a69905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 3161, 2012 CarswellOnt 6816, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 67 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2013 CarswellOnt 7357, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 9258, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff's last site visit included work that a cabinet and millwork contractor must complete after all the other trades have finished their work, such items were not mere touch-ups or rectification of deficiencies. The latter would be relevant to the completion date only if it pertained to rectifying the plaintiff's work. In this case the plaintiff was rectifying deficiencies caused by other trades, including repainting areas where other trades had caused scratches and chipped paint, and the work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Metron Construction Inc." p2="Belleville Racetrack Development Corp." post.rptr="987" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I640a69915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Metron Construction Inc. v. Belleville Racetrack Development Corp.">Metron Construction Inc. v. Belleville Racetrack Development Corp., 2011 ONSC 987, 2011 CarswellOnt 1716, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 26 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 3212, 1 C.L.R. (4th) 181 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—On motion by the defendants for an order to vacate and discharge the plaintiff's construction lien as out of time, the question of whether there was “abandonment” of the work was one of mixed fact and law and there was a triable issue as to whether the lien was in time.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Geoffrey Kendall Architect Inc." p2="1317621 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3814" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I640a69925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Geoffrey Kendall Architect Inc. v. 1317621 Ontario Inc.">Geoffrey Kendall Architect Inc. v. 1317621 Ontario Inc. (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 3814, 2002 CarswellOnt 3287 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—It is a pure question of fact whether a contract is a new contract or an amendment to an existing contract for the purposes of subs. 1(1) of the Act. The judgment of Master Clark in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Ravell Investments Ltd." p2="DCLC Developments Ltd." post.rptr="863" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I640a69935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravell Investments Ltd. v. DCLC Developments Ltd.">Ravell Investments Ltd. v. DCLC Developments Ltd. (1995), 24 O.R. (3d) 863, 1995 CarswellOnt 833, 23 C.L.R. (2d) 304 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, does not go so far as to say that no new contract can ever arise in law so long as there was, at some earlier point in time, a prior and separate contract for similar work, whether completed or not.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Ravell Investments Ltd." p2="DCLC Developments Ltd." post.rptr="863" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I640a90a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravell Investments Ltd. v. DCLC Developments Ltd.">Ravell Investments Ltd. v. DCLC Developments Ltd. (1995), 24 O.R. (3d) 863, 1995 CarswellOnt 833, 23 C.L.R. (2d) 304 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the main subcontract had been augmented by a contract for extras, both involving the same kind of work, the subcontracts were held to have melded into one another for the purposes of calculating the last day on which work was done. The time for registration of the lien was to be based on the last day that work was done under either the subcontract or the extras contract.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:11: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:11</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(4)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Carosi Construction Ltd." p2="Barrie & District Assn. for People with Special Needs" post.rptr="275" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I640a90a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carosi Construction Ltd. v. Barrie & District Assn. for People with Special Needs">Carosi Construction Ltd. v. Barrie & District Assn. for People with Special Needs (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 275 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 31(4) clearly provides that if a person supplies materials and services both before and after the certificate publication date, that person's lien for pre-publication work expires without affecting any lien that person may have for the supply of services after that date. Publication of a certificate of substantial performance is notice to all suppliers of materials and services that lien periods have started to run, irrespective of what stage the work is at, but only with regard to materials and services supplied prior to publication. There is no expiry of lien rights regarding materials and services supplied after the date in the published certificate. A plaintiff that continued to contractually supply materials and services after publication is not required to register a further claim for lien and certificate of action where its lien claim also includes work supplied prior to publication.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Co." p2="JJ's Hospitality Ltd." post.rptr="96" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I640a90a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd.">Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. JJ's Hospitality Ltd. (1996), 30 O.R. (3d) 96, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. J.J.'s Hospitality Ltd.)</ital> 93 O.A.C. 159 (C.A.); affirming (1995), 21 O.R. (3d) 788, 19 C.L.R. (2d) 47, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Soo Mill & Lumber Co. v. J.J.'s Hospitality Ltd.)</ital> 79 O.A.C. 281 (Div. Ct.); affirming (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101, 12 O.R. (3d) 351 (Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101 <point>at 122</point> (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, should be referred to.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Landac Developments Ltd." p2="Kerry T. Howe Ltd." post.rptr="12" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I640a90a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landac Developments Ltd. v. Kerry T. Howe Ltd.">Landac Developments Ltd. v. Kerry T. Howe Ltd. (1990), 38 C.L.R. 12, 72 O.R. (2d) 760 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—Read in context with the section as a whole, s. 31(4) is intended simply to preserve lien rights for materials or services supplied after the date certified to be the date of substantial performance. The preservation of lien rights is not tied to the certificate of substantial completion, if the supplier is another contractor. The actual expiry mechanisms are spelled out in subss. (2) and (3).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
31:12: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 31.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">31:12</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 31(5)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Tamarack North Holdings Ltd." p2="Hallisey" post.rptr="92" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I640ab7b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tamarack North Holdings Ltd. v. Hallisey">Tamarack North Holdings Ltd. v. Hallisey (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 92, 59 C.L.R. (3d) 316 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where, at a relatively advanced stage in the proceedings prior to trial, the evidence before the court did not unambiguously support the contention that a number of contracts were completed more than 45 days prior to the filing of the lien, the lien was not to be struck nor should it be reduced because portions of the work had been completed more than 45 days prior to the filing of the lien. Unless such a finding could be made on material filed by the plaintiff itself, the issue must be left to the trial judge.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
32:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 32.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">32:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 32(2)(e) and (f) of the Act were amended to provide for changes in the information that must be included in certificates or declarations of substantial performance.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The new Act incorporates the Expert Review's recommendation that the legal description, including PINs and specific municipal address(es); and in the case of a lien to be given (i.e. where the lien does not attach to the land), the name and address of the person(s) to whom a claim for lien must be given, be included in the certificate.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The concept of substantial performance was first incorporated into the Ontario legislation in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65. Subsections 1(3) and (4) of that Act stated:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1.
