(3)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">For the purposes of this Act, a contract shall be deemed to be substantially performed,</stat.text><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(a)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">when the work or a substantial part thereof is ready for use or is being used for the purpose intended; and</stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(b)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">when the work to be done under the contract is capable of completion or correction at a cost of not more than,</stat.text><stat.subpara sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(i)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">3 per cent of the first $250,000 of the contract price,</stat.text></stat.subpara><stat.subpara sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(ii)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">2 per cent of the next $250,000 of the contract price, and</stat.text></stat.subpara><stat.subpara sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(iii)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">1 per cent of the balance of the contract price.</stat.text></stat.subpara></stat.para></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1. (4)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">For the purposes of this Act, where the work or a substantial part thereof is ready for use or is being used for the purpose intended and where the work cannot be completed expeditiously for reasons beyond the control of the contractor, the value of the work to be completed shall be deducted from the contract price in determining substantial performance.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section did not change until the enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. Subsection 2(1) of the Act sets out the revised formula. Prior to the inclusion of the concept of substantial performance, the Ontario lien legislation did not provide for the release of holdback until “the completion of the Contract”. Refer to the Legislative History for s. 22 above for more detail on the history of this concept.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 32(1) sets out 10 rules for the certification or declaration of substantial performance of a contract. The term “payment certifier” is defined in ss. 1(1) of the Act. The procedure is outlined in mandatory language, thereby compelling the payment certifier to follow the statutory procedure if the contractor applies for certification and declaration. The procedure was succinctly stated by The Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital>:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The date of substantial performance is to be determined by either the payment certifier on the contract, or where there is no payment certifier, by the owner and the contractor jointly. That date must be set out in a formal certificate of substantial performance. The date set out in the certificate is conclusively presumed to be the date of substantial performance. This will normally be the date the contractor applied for certification. The contractor is required to publish a copy of this certificate once, in a construction trade newspaper. Should he fail or refuse to do so, a copy of the certificate may be published by any other interested person, such as the owner or a subcontractor. The newspaper is required to publish these certificates in accordance with the regulations.</para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The 45-day lien period provided for in clause 31(2)(a) begins to run from the date of publication. Under Part VI of the Act, all persons are provided with a right to require the contractor to inform them in writing of the date of publication and the name of the construction trade newspaper in which the certificate was published. If there is no publication, the lien period will not begin to run until the completion or the abandonment of the contract. At the end of the lien period, the basic holdback retained under s. 22(1) of the Act may be released, provided that all liens that may be claimed against that holdback have expired or have been satisfied, discharged or provided for under s. 44 (payment into court).</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As the object of the substantial performance concept is to expedite the release of the holdback, it is crucial that the date of substantial performance be readily and objectively ascertainable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 32(2) prescribes the necessary contents of a certificate of substantial performance.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsections 32(3) and 32(4) assign liability for failure to comply with the provisions of the section.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 32(5) specifies the manner of publication of a certificate of substantial performance.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Note that ss. 32(2) and (5) are among the sections to which the so-called curative section, s. 6, applies.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Interborough Electric Inc." p2="724352 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="5591" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I640b2ce05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Interborough Electric Inc. v. 724352 Ontario Ltd.">Interborough Electric Inc. v. 724352 Ontario Ltd., 2015 ONSC 5591, 2015 CarswellOnt 14676, 53 C.L.R. (4th) 214 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 2440 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not provide for substantial performance of a subcontract, and therefore the concept of substantial performance applies only to a contractor, not a subcontractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Bank" p2="Penex Metropolis Ltd." post.rptr="464" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640b2ce15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Bank v. Penex Metropolis Ltd.">Royal Bank v. Penex Metropolis Ltd., 2010 CarswellOnt 464, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 199 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—There is nothing limiting the time for a motion to the court under s. 32 to declare a contract substantially complete. Therefore, where the Receiver for the contractor undertook a sale process as approved by various orders of the court, a sale agreement was entered into and a motion for approval of the transaction scheduled, it was appropriate for the court to grant a declaration of substantial completion <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> as of the date of request for a declaration, and prior to the approval of a distribution of the proceeds of the sale.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd." p2="951034 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2064" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I90dee1a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc.">L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. 2064 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor entered into a contract with the defendant contractor to supply and install electrical services and equipment at the project. A certificate of substantial performance was issued on November 18, 1992, but finishing work continued until February 18 of the next year. The plaintiff registered its lien on March 16 and its certificate of action on May 3, 1993. In ruling that the plaintiff's lien was registered within the proper time limit, the court held the certificate of substantial performance to be defective. Its form differed significantly from that of Form 6, and omitted significant pieces of required information such as the description of the improvement, the name or address of either the owner or general contractor, the name of the payment certifier, and the proper identification of the premises. Although publication of the certificate contained some of the information originally missing from the certificate itself, the publication was significantly defective in that it failed to provide a legal and concise description containing a reference to lot and plan or instrument registration number sufficient to identify the premises and it identified as the payment certifier a corporate entity whereas the party purporting to certify substantial completion was an individual. These irregularities were not minor or clerical irregularities that could be “cured” by s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 32(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vestacon Limited" p2="ARC Productions Ltd." post.rptr="5366" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640b2ce35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd.">Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd., 2018 ONSC 5366, 2018 CarswellOnt 15345, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 38 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant general contractor performed renovations for the tenant renting two properties owned by separate holding corporations, who were in turn owned by a parent company. The tenant subsequently went bankrupt. The contractor sought declarations that a) three issued certificates of substantial performance were invalid, in order to extend the time period for expiration of the lien, and that b) the lien claim was registered in time. The contractor had not applied for the first two CSPs, but had sent all three to a trade newspaper for publication. The Master found that, as a matter of law, the first two CSPs were invalid because the contract had not been substantially performed when the payment certifier certified substantial performance, having considered only the portion of the contract work relating to one of the premises without taking into account the remaining contract work. The contract had been improperly severed for the purposes of certifying substantial performance in CSP #1 and CSP #2, rendering the CSPs invalid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="For-Con Construction Ltd." p2="1120062 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="20" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I640b2ce45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="For-Con Construction Ltd. v. 1120062 Ontario Inc.">For-Con Construction Ltd. v. 1120062 Ontario Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 20, 1998 CarswellOnt 3644 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Failure to comply with s. 32(1), R. 4, is not necessarily fatal to the validity of a certificate of substantial performance. The drafters of the Act envisaged that failures to strictly comply with the mandatory contents of a certificate of substantial performance, or in its publication, may occur and so there is an express reference to ss. 32(2) and 32(5) in s. 6. But where the error is the failure to give a copy of the certificate to the contractor, as required by s. 32(1) rule 4, which is not referred to in s. 6, no relief is possible. The purpose of s. 32(1) rule 4, in the context of all the rules in s. 32(1), is to ensure that the contractor gets a copy of the certificate in a timely way, so it can arrange for publication. Even if the contractor is not given a copy and someone else, such as the owner or payment certifier, arranges publication, the contractor is not prejudiced. The contractor still has the opportunity, like every other lien claimant, to see and read the publication in Daily Commercial News and act accordingly if it wishes to register a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="SNC Services Inc." p2="Peel Resource Recovery" post.rptr="254" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I640b53f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="SNC Services Inc. v. Peel Resource Recovery">SNC Services Inc. v. Peel Resource Recovery (1992), 6 C.L.R. (2d) 254 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Subsection 32(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not use the term “motion”, but rather the word “apply”. The process contemplated by s. 32(1) to obtain from the court a declaration that a contract is substantially performed is an application. Masters have no application jurisdiction because applications are governed by R. 38 of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. In addition, the issue contemplated by s. 32(1) deals with substantive rights and is not procedural. A statute cannot validly delegate s. 96 (<ital>Constitution Act, 1867</ital>) power to a court that is not a s. 96 court. The statute would be constitutionally valid, as it should be presumed to be, if the word “apply” means to apply by way of application. Accordingly, a Master has no jurisdiction to hear a dispute under the procedure contemplated by s. 32(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-City Flooring Co." p2="Quatrosense Environmental Ltd." post.rptr="744" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I640b53f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd.">Tri-City Flooring Co. v. Quatrosense Environmental Ltd. (1991), 3 O.R. (3d) 744, 49 C.L.R. 319 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A contractor's claim for lien was disputed because more than 45 days had elapsed between the publishing of the certificate of substantial performance and the filing of the lien. However, the certificate did not use Form 6 as required by the regulations to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, 1983 and omitted the names and addresses of the owner and contractor and the street address and legal description of the premises. As well, notification of the substantial completion was not made by publication of a copy of the actual certificate, as required by the Act, but by publication of a certificate which included the missing details except for the legal description of the premises. On application by the contractor, the certificate of substantial performance and publication thereof were held to be invalid. The omissions were not minor or clerical irregularities to be “cured” by s. 6 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The contractor had not published a copy of the actual certificate but had created a largely different one by adding most of the missing details. Consequently, the contractor was entitled to judgment in the amount of the lien. <ital>Tri-City Flooring</ital> was cited with approval and applied in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd." p2="951034 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2064" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I90df08b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc.">L.A. Legault Electric Ltd. v. 951034 Ontario Inc. (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 2064 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. The irregularities in the certificate and its publication were found not to be minor or clerical irregularities. The integrity of the system was protected.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 32(1)7</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Torbear Contracting Inc." p2="Haldimand (County)" post.rptr="5785" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I640b7b005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Torbear Contracting Inc. v. Haldimand (County)">Torbear Contracting Inc. v. Haldimand (County) (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5785, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 273 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6206, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor entered into a contract with the county for the redevelopment of a long-term care facility, with the work to occur in four phases so that existing services could be maintained. The contractor completed the first two phases in April 2006, which represented 92 percent of the total work, with the last two phases expected to be completed by December 2006. In May 2006, the contractor asked the consultant to issue the certificate of substantial performance and requested release of the holdback. When the consultant denied the request on the grounds that substantial performance of the entire project had not been achieved, the contractor unsuccessfully applied for an order declaring that a portion of work was substantially performed to allow release of holdback funds after expiration of the lien period. The consultant considered the request for a certificate of substantial performance as to phases 1 and 2 and did properly review the criteria in s. 2(2). There was no evidence to suggest the consultant, the decision-maker in the first instance, was anything but a well-qualified architect firm. Adopting the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Cityscape Richmond Corp." p2="Vanbots Construction Corp." post.rptr="517" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I640b7b015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cityscape Richmond Corp. v. Vanbots Construction Corp.">Cityscape Richmond Corp. v. Vanbots Construction Corp. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 517, 8 C.L.R. (3d) 196 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, there was no basis to overturn the architect's decision.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Cityscape Richmond Corp." p2="Vanbots Construction Corp." post.rptr="517" pre.rptr="2001" ref.id="I640b7b025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cityscape Richmond Corp. v. Vanbots Construction Corp.">Cityscape Richmond Corp. v. Vanbots Construction Corp. (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 517, 8 C.L.R. (3d) 196 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Absent a showing of fundamental error by the payment certifier, the court should decline to grant relief under s. 32 of the Act. This section is not intended to permit a reconsideration <ital>de novo</ital> each time a person feels aggrieved by a rejection of an application for a certificate of substantial performance. It would be an improper step for the court on summary application to substitute its view for that of an expert who was contractually selected by the parties to perform this very task. A showing of significant error, legal or factual, is required to warrant the relief in such a case.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 32(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vestacon Limited" p2="ARC Productions Ltd." post.rptr="5366" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640b7b035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd.">Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd., 2018 ONSC 5366, 2018 CarswellOnt 15345, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 38 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant general contractor performed renovations for the tenant renting two properties owned by separate holding corporations, who were in turn owned by a parent company. The tenant subsequently went bankrupt. The contractor sought declarations that a) three issued certificates of substantial performance were invalid, in order to extend the time period for expiration of the lien, and that b) the lien claim was registered in time. The contractor had not applied for the first two CSPs, but had sent all three to a trade newspaper for publication. All three certificates identified and described the lands only by municipal address and not by legal description, and the contract had not been substantially performed by any of the publication dates. The omission of a proper legal description in CSP #1, CSP #2 and CSP #3 was serious, not a minor irregularity that could be cured by s. 6 of the Act, and prejudiced the contractor. In the absence of valid CSPs the 45 day period began to run from the date the contract was completed, which resulted in the timely preservation of the claim for lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="570 South Service Road Inc." p2="Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd." post.rptr="6978" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640ba2105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="570 South Service Road Inc. v. S.C.J.); affirmed 2011 CarswellOnt 5996, 3 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In publishing a certificate of substantial performance, a party could not at once claim to be the owner, the contractor and the payment certifier. A certificate so structured was not in compliance with the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I640ba2115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial performance issued by the project architect stated that “the contract for the following improvement; Princess Gardens, Phase I, basic shell to the above premises was substantially performed …”, even though the architect acknowledged there was no such improvement as a basic shell. As well, the certificate was further deficient in that the name of the contractor was shown as “c/o owner”, and the address for service was left blank. The court found that these irregularities were significant, and not minor ones curable under s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd." p2="F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma)" post.rptr="162" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I640ba2125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd. v. F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma)">Bob Dionisi & Sons Ltd. v. F.J. Davey Home for the Aged (Algoma) (1992), 3 C.L.R. (2d) 162 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A certificate of substantial completion as published failed to comply with the following statutory requirements under s. 32(2): The name of the owner was present but his address for service was not included; the name of the contractor was present, but there was no address for service; it did not describe the payment certifier; it did not state the date on which the contract was substantially performed; and there was no legal description of the property upon which the construction was done. Nevertheless, the defects were curable pursuant to s. 6, as there was no evidence that anyone was prejudiced by these deficiencies or omissions. The architect, contractor and the owner and their addresses were well known.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 32(2)(c)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Kappeler Masonry Corp." p2="Winston Hall Nursing Homes Ltd." post.rptr="65" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I640ba2135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kappeler Masonry Corp. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 32(2)(c) requires that a certificate of substantial performance must include a short description of the work. Where the project phase name and the words “ground floor”, “second, third & forth floors” and “basement, level 5 & level 6” were inserted by the payment certifier in the description, they sufficiently described the improvement regardless of whether they were defined terms or activities in the contract distinct from any other construction activities.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
33:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 33.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">33:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The predecessors to s. 33(2) of the Act were adopted into s. 11 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1952</ital>, S.O. 1952, c. 54 as the following:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Where a certificate issued by an architect, engineer or other person to the effect that a subcontract by which a subcontractor became a subcontractor has been completed to the satisfaction of the architect, engineer or other person has been given to that subcontractor, then for the purposes of subsections 1, 2 and 3 of section 21 and section 23 that subcontract and any materials furnished or placed or to be furnished or placed thereunder and any work or services performed or to be performed thereunder shall, so far as concerns any lien thereunder of that subcontractor, be deemed to have been completed or furnished or placed not later than the time at which the certificate was so given.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This subsection eventually evolved into s. 12(3) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. Subsequent changes to this subsection were for the most part grammatical and numerical (as well as the deletion of the reference to services) until the subsection was replaced entirely in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The concept of substantial performance does not apply to subcontracts. Section 33 provides for a voluntary system for the certification of the completion of subcontracts in order to expedite the release of holdbacks to subcontractors, particularly those involved in the early stages of a major project.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Villa Nicolini Inc." post.rptr="5444" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I640bf0305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc.">Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc., 2012 ONSC 5444, 2012 CarswellOnt 12496, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 36 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 ONSC 6616, 2012 CarswellOnt 15361, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 37 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 33 is to be strictly construed, as a party's lien rights, and the time in which to preserve them, may be directly affected by the issuance of a Certificate of Completion. Applying that principle, failure of the architect to set out the dates of the sub-contracts certified as complete, where no actual prejudice was involved, did not invalidate the impugned Certificates of Completion at issue, and the default could be cured by s. 6 of the Act. The court did not determine whether the architect's non-compliance with subs. 33(4) was fatal in the circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd." p2="Redesco Inc." post.rptr="844" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I640bf0315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd. v. Redesco Inc.">Omega Trim Carpentry Ltd. v. Redesco Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 844, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 148 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the architect/payment certifier did not certify completion in the prescribed form and did not, within seven days of the date of certification, give a copy to the subcontractor whose subcontract had been certified as completed, the owner was required to pay again monies it had already paid out of the statutory holdback. The words, “certifying payment for work completed during this period, the certificate certifies payment […] representing the holdback for the following subtrades which are now completed”, in the architect's letter merely communicated to the owner that it was to disburse the holdback and could not be construed as an attempt to comply with s. 33.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
33.1:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 33.1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">33.1:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Prior to registration of a condominium, the land is owned by the developer or other owner, and the usual law regarding liens applies. After registration, however, every unit must be liened in order to lien the common elements, because the common elements are owned collectively by all unit owners as tenants in common. The need to lien every unit, which requires searching the Property Identification Numbers associated with each unit to learn the owner's name, makes the remedy of the lien prohibitively expensive for many small contractors. To assist lien claimants in avoiding these costs, the <ital>Open for Business Act, 2010</ital> added this new s. 33.1, which requires developers of condominiums, before registering the condominium declaration, to publish a notice of the intended registration in a construction trade newspaper (The Daily Commercial News) at least five and not more than 15 days before the description is submitted. Contractors will therefore receive sufficient notice of pending registration to preserve their liens before it becomes prohibitively cumbersome and expensive to do so. An owner who fails to comply with this section is liable to any person entitled to a lien who suffers damages as a result.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 34.34:12018 Amendments, Legislative History, and Commentary2018 Amendmentssubsection 34(5) of the Act was amended to provide for changes in the information that must be included in a claim for lien with respect to a claim on behalf of a workers' trust fund.person who preserves a lien that relates to an improvement to the common elements of a condominium must give notice of the lien's preservation to specified persons to the condo corporation and the owner of the unitextension of the times for a lien's expiry if the matter that is the subject of the lien is also the subject of an adjudication under the new Part II.1 of the Act, but only for the purposes of section 34Legislative HistoryThe six subsections of this section are consolidations and replacements of diverse sections of the Mechanics' Lien Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, with the exception of ss. 34(4), which was introduced for the first time with the Construction Lien Act, 1983, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The Mechanics' Lien Act sections from which the six present sections were derived or relate to are as follows:Construction Lien ActMechanics' Lien Actsubsection 34(1)subsections 17(1), 24(1) and 25;subsections 34(2)(3)subsections 23(3)(4);subsection 34(4)new (subsection 17(3) was substantially different)subsection 34(5)subsection 17(1);subsection 34(6)subsection 17(2); andsubsections 34(7)(8)subsection 18(1).
Section 17 in the 1980 version of the Mechanics' Lien Act originated from s. 2 of The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873, S.O. 1873, c. 27. Originally no affidavit of verification was required, nor was there any provision in respect of liens against railways. The concept of the affidavit of verification was incorporated into s. 4 of The Mechanics' Lien Act, R.S.O. 1877, c. 120. The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882, S.O. 1882, c. 15, set out criteria regarding the statement of claim and affidavit of verification in ss. 8, 9 and 10. An Act to Amend the Mechanics' Lien Acts, S.O. 1884, c. 18, added further requirements to these documents in ss. 2 and 3. The term “claim of lien” was incorporated into s. 16 of The Mechanics' Lien Act, R.S.O. 1877, c. 120. The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, included a provision relating to a claim for lien against railways. Subsection 24(1) in the 1980 version of the Mechanics' Lien Act put in an expiration period.24. (1)Every lien for which a claim is not registered ceases to exist on the expiration of the time limited in s. 22 for the registration thereof.The sections dealing with cesser of lien in The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873, S.O. 1873 c. 27 and The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1874, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.), namely s. 4 and 14 respectively, are discussed in the Legislative History of s. 31 above. By the proclamation of The Mechanics' Lien Act, R.S.O. 1877, c. 120, the concept of preservation was expanded. Specific reference to “thirty days” was eliminated by 1887, and the concept of claim for lien was incorporated into the 1910 version, the section was not drastically revised until The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 was enacted in the same format as the 1980 version outlined above. The requirement for an affidavit of verification was deleted by S.O. 2010, c. 16, Sch. B., s. 2(9).CommentaryA lien will expire unless the specified steps are taken to preserve it. The preservation of a claim for lien in the prescribed form is effected in most cases by the registration of a lien on the title of premises improved, and in certain clearly defined cases, by service of the lien on a designated person. An expired lien cannot be revived.Under s. 34(1), the procedure for preserving a lien will vary depending upon whether or not the lien attaches to the premises. Liens attaching to the premises are preserved by registration in the appropriate registry office of a duly executed claim for lien, while those not attaching to the premises are preserved by giving to the owner copy of such claim. Subsections (3)-(4) set out the particular service requirements of a lien claim where Crown premises, municipal premises or railways right-of-ways are involved. The contents of lien claim are prescribed by subs. (5). The claim for lien is limited to services and materials that have actually been supplied to the improvement and cannot be used to secure payment for future supply.The preservation of general liens described by s. 20 is provided for in s. 34(7). The uniting of the liens of several persons in one lien claim is to be approached cautiously, but is expressly authorized by s. 34(8).

Chijindu">RVL Masonry Ltd. v. Chijindu, 2014 ONSC 7153, 2014 CarswellOnt 17271, 46 C.L.R. (4th) 140 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2016 CarswellOnt 14486, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 60 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The court held that the lien claim was preserved within the requirements of the Act and that the plaintiff perfected the lien with its subsequent certificate of action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Logger Town Homes Ltd." p2="Sadeghian" post.rptr="6056" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I640c8c715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Logger Town Homes Ltd. v. Sadeghian">Logger Town Homes Ltd. v. Sadeghian, 2013 ONSC 6056, 2013 CarswellOnt 13518, 30 C.L.R. (4th) 164 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 11 of the <ital>Limitations Act</ital> (ON) (limitation period not running during attempts at alternative resolution) does not apply to the time period for preserving a lien under section 34. A construction lien is not a “claim” for purposes of the <ital>Limitations Act</ital> nor is it “pursued in court proceedings,” and the fact that sections 31 and 36 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> are referenced in the schedule pursuant to s. 19 of the <ital>Limitations Act</ital> is not conclusive evidence of an intention that section 11 should apply. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> represents a complete code in respect of construction lien actions. Therefore, application of s. 11 to the <ital>Limitations Act</ital> would be contrary to the policy of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Namely, that a party holding holdback monies pertaining to a project be in a position to pay out such monies without risk within a reasonable period of time after the last work on a project is completed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R." p2="1431633 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I90e04130f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R. v. 1431633 Ontario Inc.">R. v. 1431633 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 161, 2010 ONSC 266, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 263, 250 C.C.C. (3d) 354 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied lumber used to construct a house owned by the accused. Prior to preservation of the plaintiff's lien, the Crown registered a restraint order against the property under s. 462.33 of the <ital>Criminal Code</ital>, said order containing a prohibition against any person encumbering the property or the commencement of any proceedings in respect of the property without a prior order of the Court. Subsequently, the plaintiff's solicitors, overlooking the registration of the restraint order, took the appropriate steps under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to preserve its lien by filing its claim for lien on title within the required 45 day period, and then moved to perfect its lien claim by commencing an action to enforce its claim under the Act within the prescribed time. At issue was whether the plaintiff had a valid lien claim under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> in these circumstances and, if not, if there was some other basis upon which it could claim an interest in the property. The plaintiff successfully applied under s. 462.42 of <ital>Criminal Code</ital> for relief from forfeiture. The plaintiff would have had valid interest in the property under <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> but for provision of the restraint order declaring it void and it was appropriate to vary the restraint order <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> to allow the registration of the lien claim and the action to enforce it. The Crown had notice of the plaintiff's claim prior to the forfeiture order and was not prejudiced by the plaintiff's delay in applying. Alternatively, the plaintiff had established an interest in property pursuant to the equitable principle of unjust enrichment, and there was no reason to exercise the court's discretion not to grant the relief sought, as the plaintiff's interest in the property was not obtained from the proceeds of crime, and was inconsistent with the purpose of the <ital>Criminal Code</ital>'s forfeiture provisions to punish innocent third parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Simpson" p2="Gateman-Milloy Landscape Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="734" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I640cb3805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simpson v. Gateman-Milloy Landscape Contractors Ltd.">Simpson v. Gateman-Milloy Landscape Contractors Ltd. (1986), 54 O.R. (2d) 734 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contracted with the plaintiff subcontractor for the installation of paving stones on the walkways in a public municipal park. Following the defendant's default on its contract with the plaintiff, the plaintiff served a claim for lien on it and on the municipality, but did not register it, and the defendant brought an application for a declaration that the lien was not preserved. The application was granted. If the walkways were a public street or highway, the procedure followed by the plaintiff would have been correct under ss. 16(3)(a), 34(1)(b) and (2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. However, in modern usage, “street” and “highway” refer to a thoroughfare for the use of public vehicular traffic. A path in a public park does not fall within that definition. Hence, the plaintiff should have registered his lien in order to preserve it.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 34.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">34:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 34(1)(b)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Dirm Inc." p2="Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3479" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I640cb3815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd.">Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3479, 37 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Master)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant entered into a contract with the general contractor to perform concrete work for a construction project on lands owned by the owner college of applied arts and technology. The claimant's solicitor electronically registered a claim for lien and also sent a letter to the College, addressed to “The Board of Governors”, following which the lien was vacated on the posting of security by the general contractor under s. 44(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The statement of claim named only the general contractor since, by s. 44(6), the lien ceased to attach to the premises and to the holdbacks and other amounts subject to a charge under s. 21, and became instead a charge upon the security. The general contractor successfully obtained a discharge of the lien on the basis that preservation was improper because the claimant had registered its lien in the land registry office under s. 34(1)(a) rather than “give” a copy of the claim for lien and affidavit of verification to the owner under s. 34(1)(b) and s. 34(3), by mailing them to the “office of the president of the college”. Both the College and its Board of Governors were Crown agents under s. 2(4) of the Ontario <ital>Colleges of Applied Arts and Technology Act, 2002</ital> and, if necessary, under the <ital>Crown Agency Act</ital>. The “Crown” was the owner of the premises within s. 16(3) and s. 16(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the lien did not attach to the premises, and preservation was governed by s. 34(1)(b). Under O. Reg. 175, s. 1.3, where the “contract” is with a college of applied arts and technology, the copy of the claim for lien and the affidavit of verification must be given to “the office of the president of the college”. “Contract” meant the contract between the owner and the contractor and did not refer to the sub-contract. Here, the envelope containing the claim for lien and affidavit of verification, and the covering letter, were misaddressed, not to the “office of the president of the college” but to “The Board of Governors of the College”. Strict compliance with the terms of the statute was required and the lien was therefore not properly preserved.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Harvie Construction Inc.">Atlas Dewatering Corporation v. Harvie Construction Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 4294, 2024 ONSC 1775, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1427 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 6605 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 7440 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the subcontractor lien claimant provided “de-watering” services to a project involving the reconstruction and realignment of a municipal roadway. The work consisted of the installation of a system of well points, pumps and pipes to assist in lowering the groundwater table on the construction site, and subsequent removal of that equipment. The defendant argued that the claimant was required to preserve its lien by registering a claim for lien against the title to the lands in question but erroneously gave it to the municipality. However, the court noted that very purpose of dewatering was to reduce the groundwater on the land requiring the construction or improvement, those premises were an existing highway, and the work done was integral to its alteration and restoration. Section 16(3) applied, and the claimant was not required to register its claim for lien on title, but followed the correct procedure by giving its claim for lien to the municipal clerk as required by (then) s. 34(2). [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Before its repeal, s. 34(2) governed the preservation of claims for lien specifically in respect of a public street or highway owned by a municipality, providing that the copy of the claim for lien was to be given to the clerk of the municipality. Current s. 34(3.1) more generally applies to any premises owned by a municipality.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lavis Contracting Co." p2="Coores Construction Inc." post.rptr="5479" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I640cda905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lavis Contracting Co. v. Coores Construction Inc.">Lavis Contracting Co. v. Coores Construction Inc., 2014 ONSC 5479, 2014 CarswellOnt 12941, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 204, 29 M.P.L.R. (5th) 158 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is nothing in s. 34(2) requiring that delivery to the Clerk be made by the lien claimant himself. Where a copy of the claim for lien was given in a timely manner to the Deputy Clerk, who then delivered it to the Clerk, the subsection was complied with. The purpose of service is to provide actual notice of the claim for lien to the Clerk, and that was clearly accomplished. Alternatively, s. 228(2) of the Ontario <ital>Municipal Act, 2001</ital>, served to delegate all of the powers and duties of the Clerk of a municipality to the Deputy Clerk, under the <ital>Municipal Act</ital> and “any other Act”. This included delegation of the power and duty to receive notices of claims for lien under s. 34(2) of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Ct.)</ref></cite>—Strict compliance is required under ss. 34(1)(b) and 34(3), and an affidavit is required when the owner is a Crown agency. As well, the master was entitled to engage s. 67 in order to make a summary determination with respect to compliance with s. 34(1)(b) and (3).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Current s. 34(3.1) more generally applies to any premises owned by a municipality.]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
34:7: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 34.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block date.trace="20250528" toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">34:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 34(5)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Beta Construction Inc." p2="Chiu" post.rptr="5288" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I640cda925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beta Construction Inc. v. Chiu">Beta Construction Inc. v. Chiu, 2015 ONSC 5288, 2015 CarswellOnt 12694, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 100 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 ONSC 5353, 2015 CarswellOnt 12959, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 133 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the lien claimant was the contracting party. The master declined to allow the defendants to rely on a technicality to avoid paying the contractor that supplied services and materials to their home renovation, in the face of clear evidence that they were dealing with the corporate plaintiff throughout the renovation, rather than another unincorporated business owned by the corporate plaintiff's principal. Although the written contracts identified the contractor on the first page and the signing page as the unincorporated entity, the defendants believed that they had contracted with the principal's incorporated entity, and the intention of the parties was that the contracting party be the corporate defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Govan Brown & Associates Ltd." p2="Equinox 199 Bay Street Co." post.rptr="3924" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I640cda935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Govan Brown & Associates Ltd. v. Equinox 199 Bay Street Co.">Govan Brown & Associates Ltd. v. Equinox 199 Bay Street Co., 2014 ONSC 3924, 2014 CarswellOnt 8856, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 78 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A lien claim that fails to comply with the requirements of s. 34(5) of the Act is invalid. But if it is merely a failure to “strictly” comply then, absent prejudice, s. 6 operates to maintain the claim's validity unless the court determines that it is invalid due to prejudice. The test is one of degree. When the electronic form required to be used to register a claim for lien merged (i) the name of the owner, (ii) the person to whom services and materials were supplied, and (iii) the description of what was supplied, into one section called “statements”, an owner ought to reasonably be informed that a claim is made against its interest in the property, absent evidence of prejudice. Inserting the owner's name in the wrong part of the statements is a failure to “strictly” comply with the requirements of s. 34(5) of the Act, but not so serious an error as to take it outside of the application of s. 6 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Engineered Construction Ltd." p2="Arena Entertainment Corp." post.rptr="8685" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I640cda945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Engineered Construction Ltd. v. Arena Entertainment Corp.">Engineered Construction Ltd. v. Arena Entertainment Corp. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 8685 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—There is no provision in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> providing for the amendment of a claim for lien. If it is found that a claim for lien has a minor irregularity it is not invalidated; rather the statement of claim can, if need be, be amended to correct the minor irregularity and the claim for lien can proceed to trial on that basis. Here, the plaintiff by cross-motion sought leave to amend its claim for lien by making a change in the legal name of the lien claimant, by adding the defendant as a tenant and an owner, and by changing the amount claimed for lien from $1,793,000 to $3,500,000. The first amendment was minor, and as the statement of claim was delivered with the change in place no amendment was necessary. The failure to name an “owner” in the claim for lien, however, was a fundamental error, as was the significant understating of the amount claimed for lien. It was not a case of transposing figures or misplacing a decimal, rather it was a substantial and real error on the part of the plaintiff. The claim for lien failed to meet the requirements of s. 34(5) by naming an owner as defined in the Act; consequently, the Master discharged the lien, vacated the certificate of action and dismissed the action without prejudice to the plaintiff commencing a non-lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Braun" p2="974850 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="6257" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I640d01a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Braun v. 974850 Ontario Inc.">Braun v. 974850 Ontario Inc. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6257, 60 C.L.R. (3d) 121 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A variance in the monetary amount contained in the lien claim filed on title and the statement of claim was not significant or fatal to the claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Ambler-Courtney Inc." p2="CAAG Land Development Ltd." post.rptr="58" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I640d01a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ambler-Courtney Inc. v. CAAG Land Development Ltd.">Ambler-Courtney Inc. v. CAAG Land Development Ltd. (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 58 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant inadvertently registered its lien in the Land Registry system, when it had previously been transferred into Land Titles. There were further irregularities in the description itself, both in the Claim for Lien, Document General, and Certificate of Action, apparently contrary to s. 34(5). The defendant owner moved under ss. 45 and 47 to discharge and vacate the lien. The issue of the proper registry office was resolved in favour of the lien claimant as in the relevant jurisdiction, the offices were in the same building. This was “the proper land registry office”. The irregularities in legal description in form were cured under s. 6.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Southside Construction (London) Ltd." p2="Emco Ltd." post.rptr="73" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I640d28b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southside Construction (London) Ltd. v. Emco Ltd.">Southside Construction (London) Ltd. v. Emco Ltd. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 73 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner applied for a declaration that E Ltd.'s lien was expired, arguing that it was not validly sheltered because there was no indication that the lien was “in respect of the same improvement” as the lien under which it purported to shelter. The court dismissed the application, stating that perfection through sheltering is a question of fact. Subsection 34(5) of the Act requires a description of the premises appropriate for registration, not identification of “the same improvement”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I640d28b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207, 52 O.A.C. 107 (Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Claims for liens and certificates of action which wrongly named lands that had previously been conveyed and which no longer formed part of the defendant's leasehold property were ordered to be discharged. The discretionary power of the court under s. 6 does not extend to permit a court to validate a claim for lien where wrong lands are named under s. 34(5)(e). The setting out of the wrong lands is a fatal flaw which is not empowered under the Act to correct.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Irving Oil Ltd." p2="M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I640d28b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Irving Oil Ltd. v. M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd.">Irving Oil Ltd. v. M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd. (1985), 20 C.L.R. 26 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor supplied bulldozers and operators to a road reconstruction job for which N was the general contractor for the defendant township. After receiving a NSF cheque, the plaintiff was advised by P, an employee of the township, to report its problems with N by registered mail before the end of the month to the township, the Ministry of Transport and the township's consulting engineers. The plaintiff was also advised that it had 45 days after completion to make its claim. In a further telephone conversation in late October between D and P, D was told that N's work was finished on October 11, 1984, and that D had 45 days from that date to register its claim. D was further advised to send a registered letter to the township by the end of the week. D sent a registered letter to the township dated November 2, 1984, which was received by the township on November 7, 1984. On November 5, 1984, P advised D to contact a lawyer. On November 14, 1984, D delivered to the township its formal claim for lien. At trial, the court held, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that D's letter of November 2 was an invalid claim for lien, and D was not entitled to share in the holdback fund. In addition, its claim for lien served on November 14, 1984 was not validated by reason of promissory estoppel. D's letter of November 2, 1984, failed to meet all of the requirements of s. 34(5) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (Ontario) for a valid claim for lien. In addition, there was no verifying affidavit accompanying the letter as required by s. 34(6). Although s. 6 relieves against failure to comply strictly with s. 34(5), there is no similar provision relating to s. 34(6). The letter of November 2, 1984, was not “given” to the township within the time allowed by the Act or by the Rules. Promissory estoppel, as it relates to a lien registered out of time was personal to the parties and would not affect the rights of any third parties. Accordingly, such an estoppel would not extend to those with valid lien claims. It followed that D was not entitled to share in the holdback.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
34:8: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 34.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block date.trace="20250528" toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">34:8</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 34(5)(a)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters Benefit Trust Funds (Trustee of)" p2="RES Canada Construction (Ontario) L.P." post.rptr="2854" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I640d28b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters Benefit Trust Funds (Trustee of) v. RES Canada Construction (Ontario) L.P.">Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters Benefit Trust Funds (Trustee of) v. RES Canada Construction (Ontario) L.P., 2016 ONSC 2854, 2016 CarswellOnt 6661, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 122 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 ONSC 6705, 2016 CarswellOnt 16634, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 134 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is varying practice in Ontario regarding claims for liens involving union members, with some lawyers listing the actual names of the workers on the claim for lien or on an attached schedule, and others referring only to the person claiming the lien as “agent for the affected members” of the particular union. Here, the defendants argued that the claim for lien did not comply with the requirements of s. 34(5) because the claim for lien did not contain the names and addresses of the Carpenters Union members who actually did the work. The court held that the phrase “the person claiming the lien” in Section 34(5)(a) was not defined, and that showing the person claiming the lien as a specified individual as “the Trustee of the Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters Benefit Trust Funds and as agent for all affected members of the Carpenters Union and its locals” adequately identified the group of workers involved for anyone reading the claim for lien and provided an address for service for the person claiming the lien. The motion vacating the lien and dismissing the action was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams & Prior Ltd." p2="Taskon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="474" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90e0dd70f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd.">Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 474, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2003] O.J. No. 498 (Master)</ref></cite>—In specifying that the “name and address of the owner of the premises” must be set out, s. 34(5)(a) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> requires that where a lien claimant claims a lien against a tenant's interest in a landlord's land and building, the name and address of this tenant must be set out, and where the lien claimant also claims a lien against the landlord's interest in the land and building, the name and address of this landlord must also be set out.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
34:9: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 34.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block date.trace="20250528" toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">34:9</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 34(6)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Wildberry Homes Inc." p2="Prosperity One Credit Union Ltd." post.rptr="8314" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I640d4fc15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wildberry Homes Inc. v. Prosperity One Credit Union Ltd.">Wildberry Homes Inc. v. Prosperity One Credit Union Ltd. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 8314, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 109 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Applying the rulings in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Petroff Partnership Architects" p2="Mobius Corp." post.rptr="2260" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I640d4fc25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp.">Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2260, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 277, 65 O.R. (3d) 118 (Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="1230027 Ontario Inc." p2="Jones" post.rptr="232" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I640d4fc35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1230027 Ontario Inc. v. Jones">1230027 Ontario Inc. v. Jones (2005), 54 C.L.R. (3d) 232, 2005 CarswellOnt 8677 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 8686, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 63 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, s. 24 of the <ital>Land Registration Reform Act</ital> permits e-registration using the electronic Construction Lien form which contains an “affirmation of facts” section with language that is substantially similar to that used in the suggested affidavit under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> Regulations.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="1230027 Ontario Inc." p2="Jones" post.rptr="232" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I640d4fc45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1230027 Ontario Inc. v. Jones">1230027 Ontario Inc. v. Jones (2005), 54 C.L.R. (3d) 232, 2005 CarswellOnt 8677 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 8686, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 63 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Under s. 24 of the <ital>Land Registration Reform Act</ital> (LRRA), when a document is submitted electronically, the supporting evidence is also to be in electronic format, and is deemed to comply with a requirement to submit an affidavit despite the fact that the evidence is not in writing and has not been signed by the parties. Sections 34(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and ss. 24(1) and (2) of LRRA can logically and rationally work together and are not in conflict with one another. Subsections 24(1) and (2) of LRRA support the contention that electronic “affirmation of facts” is equivalent to a formal written affidavit and that it meets the requirement for an affidavit of verification under s. 34(6).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Petroff Partnership Architects" p2="Mobius Corp." post.rptr="2260" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I640d76d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp.">Petroff Partnership Architects v. Mobius Corp. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2260, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 277, 65 O.R. (3d) 118 (Master)</ref></cite>—An electronically registered lien is valid in the absence of a sworn paper affidavit of verification. The plaintiff registered a construction lien electronically and followed the electronic registration requirements, which did not include an affidavit of verification as contemplated by s. 34(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and Form 9 under Reg. 175, R.R.O. 1990. Section 24 of the <ital>Land Registration Reform Act</ital> provides in subsection (1) that: “If a document is submitted in an electronic format and is required under any Act to include an affidavit, a declaration, a statement or other written evidence, the evidence shall be in an electronic format approved by the Director and shall be included in a manner approved by the Director”. Subsection (2) of s. 24 provides that: “If an electronic document includes evidence in an electronic format in accordance with this section, the evidence shall be deemed to comply with the requirement to submit the affidavit, declaration, statement or other written evidence under the applicable Act despite the fact that the evidence is not in writing and has not been signed by the parties required to provide the evidence.” The defendants moved for an order discharging the lien and vacating its registration, arguing that the affidavit of verification should have been electronically scanned into the claim for lien. Master Sandler dismissed the motion, holding that “in my view, s. 24(1) requires the ‘evidence’ […] to be in an electronic format, as was done in this case, and s. 24(2) ‘deems’ that ‘evidence’ to comply with the requirement to submit an affidavit of verification under the C.L.A. No additional paper affidavit is required. Mr. Gillott's suggestion (noted in para. 10 above) was based on an ‘abundance of caution’ so as to avoid the very issue that arose in this case. Now that it has [been] raised, and rejected by a court ruling, perhaps those in the profession who have adopted this practice will use slightly less caution. (But probably, some will await the ruling of an appellate court before changing their practice)”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Haflidson" p2="Salandy" post.rptr="284" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I640d76d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haflidson v. Salandy">Haflidson v. Salandy (2002), 16 C.L.R. (3d) 284, 2002 CarswellOnt 1698 (Master)</ref></cite>—Form 9 under the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> requires a deponent to select one of three options, A, B or C, to identify the deponent's relationship to the lien claimant. Option A is for the lien claimant, option B is for the agent of the lien claimant and option C is for a trustee of a workers' trust fund named as a lien claimant. Here, the plaintiff/deponent inadvertently failed to cross out parts B and C of the affidavit of verification and accordingly failed to identify himself as the personal lien claimant. The defect in the affidavit of verification was only a matter of form, not substance, and there was no evidence that it gave rise to prejudice. The plaintiff had sworn that the facts were true, but merely failed to clearly identify himself as the personal lien claimant. It would be perverse to say an essential element of the affidavit is missing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Zemelman" p2="Feder" post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I640d9de05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Zemelman v. Feder">Zemelman v. Feder (2001), 54 O.R. (3d) 15, 13 C.L.R. (3d) 84, 2001 CarswellOnt 1684 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The absence of a signed jurat to an Affidavit of Verification does not invalidate the registration of a claim for lien. There is a distinction to be made between the Affidavit of Verification itself, as required under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and the jurat, which provides evidential proof of the proper completion of the affidavit.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Graham Mining Ltd." p2="Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc." post.rptr="279" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I640d9de15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc.">Graham Mining Ltd. v. Rapid-Eau Technologies Inc. (2000), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 300 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Lien not valid by reason of Affidavit of Verification being sworn by “agent” of the solicitor of the lien claimant. An “agent or assignee of the claimant” includes an agent of a solicitor of the lien claimant, who, as the sub-agent of the lien claimant, otherwise makes the necessary averments under s. 34(6). Thus, there would seem to be no practical limit on the number of removes that a deponent may be from first hand knowledge of the facts set out in the claim for lien, nor any real limitation on the number of degrees of hearsay that may be put forward in an affidavit of verification, as long as the essential averment is made in the form of affidavit itself.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="573521 Ontario Inc." p2="Waldman" post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I640d9de25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="573521 Ontario Inc. v. Waldman">573521 Ontario Inc. v. Waldman (1996), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 305 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—There is an onus on a participant to a contract who seeks to avoid personal liability and to shelter under the limited liability of a corporation, to establish that the other participant to the contract was aware at the time of contracting that it was dealing with a limited company. Where a contractor did not advise the owners that they were contracting with the plaintiff numbered company, and the contracts referred to a non-entity, the plaintiff's principal personally was found to be the contracting party. The affidavit of verification contradicted the lien claim in that the numbered company, rather than its principal, was the lien claimant. Since the wrong form had been completed, and the affidavit did not contain the sworn statement that the affiant was an agent who was informed of the truth of the facts stated in the claim, the affidavit of verification was defective and incurable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Edgecon Construction Inc." p2="All Saints Church Homes for Tomorrow Society" post.rptr="3501" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90e152a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Edgecon Construction Inc. v. All Saints Church Homes for Tomorrow Society">Edgecon Construction Inc. v. All Saints Church Homes for Tomorrow Society (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 3501, [1995] O.J. No. 2209, 18 C.L.R. (3d) 254 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—On this motion, one of a series relating to the liens and lands of a closely held group of corporations, the court considered an Affidavit of Verification upon which Forms B and C had been deleted. Form A is appropriate to the lien of an individual. Following <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Carlo's Electric Ltd." p2="Metropolitan Separate School Board" post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I640d9de45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carlo's Electric Ltd. v. Metropolitan Separate School Board">Carlo's Electric Ltd. v. Metropolitan Separate School Board (1990), 40 C.L.R. 26, Master</ref></cite>, the court held that O. Reg. 175/90, Form 9, is permissive, not mandatory and therefore as long as the essential averments were stated, it did not matter how they were expressed. The motion on this point was dismissed. The second argument was that the facts deposed to in the affidavit were untrue and that the deponent did not have sufficient knowledge to make the averment that they were true. The court considered, carefully, the decision of the Master in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Accent Design Inc." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="33" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I640d9de55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1994), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 33 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and, approving <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Total Crane Erection" p2="Canada Life Assurance Co." ref.id="I640d9de65fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Total Crane Erection v. Canada Life Assurance Co.">Total Crane Erection v. Canada Life Assurance Co., Toronto CLA 93-CQ-46492, Master, unreported</ref></cite>, held that such deficiencies as there were could be cured by s. 6 and that the affidavit otherwise complied with s. 34(6). The motion was dismissed on this ground as well.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Accent Design Inc." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="33" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I640dc4f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1994), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 33 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—After security was posted under s. 44, a lien was discharged and the certificate of action vacated. Following the pre-trial, the defendant moved to dismiss the action and surrender the bond on the basis that the plaintiff failed to comply with the requirement of an affidavit of verification. The deponent swore that the lien claimant was D Inc. when the lien claimant was actually an unincorporated partnership. The motion was allowed and the action was dismissed. In the affidavit of verification, the deponent swore to facts which were incorrect. In such circumstances, there was no valid affidavit of verification and the lien was invalid from the start.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Michelin Group Inc." p2="Forsan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I640dc4f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd.">Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 523, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 202 (Gen. Div.); affirmed (1995), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 215 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—One of the cornerstones of the Act is the concept of notice to others. The Act requires lien claimants to tell the world at large, by registration, of the intention to pursue a claim for lien. The lien claimant is further required to tell the world at large of the intention to continue the pursuit for claim for lien by the commencement of an action and the registration of a certificate of action. These requirements are designed to permit others involved in the construction projects, large or small, to organize their affairs in the light of the actions taken by other participants in the project. If a lien claimant swears in the affidavit required by the Act that certain services were performed to and including a specific date, other interested parties should be able to rely on that date; to find otherwise would require the point to be litigated in every instance to establish the last date work was performed or materials delivered. In Ontario, it is clear if subsequent services are performed, a further lien can be registered for those services, but all subject to the same requirements for preservation and perfection.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="891178 Ontario" p2="Humphrey" post.rptr="253" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I640dc4f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="891178 Ontario v. Humphrey">891178 Ontario v. Humphrey (1992), 6 C.L.R. (2d) 253 (Ont.
