Master)</ref></cite>—The illegibility of the signature of the commissioner does not render an affidavit of verification a nullity so as to totally invalidate a plaintiff's lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Sefri Construction International Ltd." p2="Jaltas Inc." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I640dec005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sefri Construction International Ltd. v. Jaltas Inc.">Sefri Construction International Ltd. v. Jaltas Inc. (1990), 38 C.L.R. 15 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A claim for lien registered in the registry office, which contained an affidavit of verification that was unsigned by a Commissioner of Oaths, was invalid, although it was conceded by all parties that the error was by pure inadvertence. Section 34(1) provided that a lien must be registered on title according to provisions of ss. 34 and 34(6), provided that any claim for lien shall be verified by an affidavit of the person claiming the lien. The respondent's claim for lien was, thus, not complete. Furthermore, recent case law held that the court had no power to cure such error and, accordingly, the respondent's lien was ordered discharged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Carlo's Electric Ltd." p2="Metropolitan Separate School Board" post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I640dec015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carlo's Electric Ltd. v. Metropolitan Separate School Board">Carlo's Electric Ltd. v. Metropolitan Separate School Board (1990), 40 C.L.R. 26 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant, C Ltd., registered a claim for lien together with an affidavit of verification sworn by CF indicating that he was the lien claimant. CF was not the lien claimant as C Ltd. was the proper lien claimant. The general contractor brought a motion to vacate the claim for lien because the lien claimant had not complied with s. 34(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, as there was an error in the affidavit of verification. The motion was dismissed. The deponent in the affidavit incorrectly used Part A, rather than Part B. stating that he was the agent or assignee of the lien claimant. Since the lien claimant was a limited company, it could not swear an affidavit of verification. Thus, the only error within the affidavit of verification, as sworn, was that it did not state that the deponent was the agent of the lien claimant. This defect was a matter of form only and not a matter of substance. Since the moving party had not claimed that it had been misled, or proved that it had been misled by the deviation, the affidavit of verification complied with the requirements of s. 34(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Venditti" p2="Petriglia" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I640dec025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Venditti v. Petriglia">Venditti v. Petriglia (1989), 33 C.L.R. 1, 33 O.A.C. 76 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Section 34(6) is mandatory, and where the lien claimant is the person claiming the lien, there must be an affidavit by the claimant swearing that the facts stated in the claim for lien are true. This is clear from the concluding words of the subsection which deal with an affidavit by an agent or assignee and which require that the agent or assignee “state that he believes those facts [<ital>i.e.</ital>, the facts set out in the claim] to be true”. Subsection 2(9) of O. Reg. 159/83 is permissive, hence the affidavit of verification need not comply with Form 9. It must, however, contain the essential averment that the facts stated in the claim for lien are true, regardless of the way in which that averment is expressed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Gallaway" p2="Gary Eddie Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="14" ref.id="I640dec035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gallaway v. Gary Eddie Construction Ltd.">Gallaway v. Gary Eddie Construction Ltd. (1985), 14 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The failure to file the affidavit of verification was a mere slip or inadvertence which the court had discretion to relieve against where no prejudice was alleged or proven. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court, in reaching its conclusion in this case, relied in part upon an earlier decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. Subsequent cases have held that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not permit the court to relieve against the failure to file the affidavit of verification under s. 34(6).]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
34:10: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 34.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block date.trace="20250528" toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">34:10</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 34(8)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Interested readers are referred to: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1954" p1="Menzies & Herbert Ltd." p2="Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590" post.rptr="74" pre.rptr="1954" ref.id="I90e1a0c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590">Menzies & Herbert Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House School District No. 2590 (1954), 1954 CarswellAlta 74, [1955] 1 D.L.R. 161, [1954] S.C.R. 589 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Fulton Hardware Co." p2="Mitchell" post.rptr="1205" pre.rptr="[1923] 4" ref.id="I640e13105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Fulton Hardware Co. v. Mitchell">Fulton Hardware Co. v. Mitchell, [1923] 4 D.L.R. 1205 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1960" p1="McColl-Frontenac Oil Co." p2="Blakeny Concrete Products" post.rptr="507" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I640e13115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="McColl-Frontenac Oil Co. v. Blakeny Concrete Products">McColl-Frontenac Oil Co. v. Blakeny Concrete Products (1960), 27 D.L.R. (2d) 507 (N.B. C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Perimeter Concrete Ltd." p2="Tomar Enterprises Inc." post.rptr="69" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I640e13125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Perimeter Concrete Ltd. v. Tomar Enterprises Inc.">Perimeter Concrete Ltd. v. Tomar Enterprises Inc. (1983), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 69 (Man. Q.B.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19981125" p1="Wabco Standard Trane Inc." p2="Inter Wide Mechanical & Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I640e13135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wabco Standard Trane Inc. v. Inter Wide Mechanical & Contracting Ltd.">Wabco Standard Trane Inc. v. Inter Wide Mechanical & Contracting Ltd. (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 143 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 1831 (Ont. Master); appeal dismissed (November 25, 1998), unreported, Lederman J. (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The case contains an interesting and detailed discussion of circumstances in which multiple lien claimants can unite in a single claim for lien. The Act does not require a separate affidavit for each claimant, as long as the affiant is agent of each of the claimants who have united in claim for lien and says so in the supporting affidavit.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
35:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 35.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">35:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 35 was amended to replace the concept of “grossly inflated” liens with the concept of “willfully exaggerated” liens, which the Expert Review suggested would focus the threshold at a more sensitive level</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A new subsection (2) was added to give the court authority to, on motion, reduce a lien amount by any exaggerated portion, as long as it finds that the person who preserved the lien or gave notice acted in good faith.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 35 is an entirely new provision enacted by the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The intent of the section is to provide for a statutory remedy for all those who may be injured as a result of an exaggerated claim for lien, not just the registered owner who would have an action in slander of title in such circumstances.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision is designed to deter preservation of negligently or intentionally exaggerated lien claims, expired lien claims or non-lienable claims and applies where either a lien claim is preserved or written notice of a lien given. It is notable in that it creates a direct right of action between or among non-privies.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tony's Touch Plumbing Ltd." p2="Hatcho Nersesian" post.rptr="4418" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640e3a205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tony's Touch Plumbing Ltd. v. Hatcho Nersesian">Tony's Touch Plumbing Ltd. v. Hatcho Nersesian, 2018 ONSC 4418, 2018 CarswellOnt 11910, 93 C.L.R. (4th) 52 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A defendant must provide any evidence of having suffered damages in order to make a claim under s. 35.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dominion Drywall Systems Limited" p2="Volta Lofts Inc." post.rptr="1918" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640e3a215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Drywall Systems Limited v. Volta Lofts Inc.">Dominion Drywall Systems Limited v. Volta Lofts Inc., 2018 ONSC 1918, 2018 CarswellOnt 4355, 90 C.L.R. (4th) 243 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The usual practice when a construction contractor is not paid for services and materials supplied is to register a claim for lien for the amount owing. In this case, the claimant genuinely believed that it was entitled to be paid the amounts invoiced and it registered a claim for lien for the unpaid balance of amounts invoiced. It did not “knowingly” register a grossly excessive lien claim, and recovered almost 75 percent of the lien amount claimed. It did not recover more of its claim because of its poor bookkeeping and administration of the contract. The section 35 threshold test was not met.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cornelis Grey Construction Inc." p2="Folz" post.rptr="647" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I640e61305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cornelis Grey Construction Inc. v. Folz">Cornelis Grey Construction Inc. v. Folz, 2018 ONSC 647, 2018 CarswellOnt 1909, 81 C.L.R. (4th) 307 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It was improper for a contractor to register a lien for the full price of completing a contract when the contractor has abandoned the job and has no intention of returning. However, here the lien was not grossly inflated or based on imaginary claims, and the homeowners failed to prove damage flowing from the lien registration.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ravenda Homes Ltd." p2="1372708" post.rptr="834" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I640e61315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708">Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708, 2017 ONCA 834, 2017 CarswellOnt 16988, 78 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendant claimed damages under s. 35 for the additional amounts it incurred to maintain a letter of credit to vacate the plaintiff's construction lien because the appropriate amount had not been calculated and claimed in the lien action. After having obtained expert evidence, the plaintiff had reduced the value of its lien as pleaded by approximately 23%. The Court of Appeal held that the correct test under s. 35 required the motion judge to consider whether the plaintiff's lien claim was “grossly in excess” of what was ultimately proven to be owed under the lien, not merely “excessive”, as the motions judge found here. As well, the motion judge erred in making any a determination under s. 35 where the amount of the lien had not been determined but was one of the issues that the motion judge had referred to trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ramey" p2="Winkleigh Co-operative Housing Corp." post.rptr="4676" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640e61325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ramey v. Winkleigh Co-operative Housing Corp.">Ramey v. Winkleigh Co-operative Housing Corp., 2010 ONSC 4676, 2010 CarswellOnt 6357 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In seeking damages under s. 35, the defendant claimed that the registration of the lien affected both its credit and created losses flowing from the vacancy of rental units caused when necessary repairs to the units were stalled due to lack of funds caused by the registered lien. In rejecting the s. 35 claim as unsupported by the evidence, the court indicated that entitlement to claim damages under s. 35 of the Act was not subject to an obligation on the part of an owner to file a bond with the court and have the lien removed from title.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Frank & Sons Painting & Decorating Ltd." p2="M2 Group" post.rptr="4359" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I640e61335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Frank & Sons Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. M2 Group">Frank & Sons Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. M2 Group, 2010 CarswellOnt 4359, 94 C.L.R. (3d) 120 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 6812, 94 C.L.R. (3d) 152 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contractor was awarded $900 in compensation where the plaintiff's lien was registered out of time and the defendant incurred legal expenses to have the lien discharged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co." p2="1707583 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I640e88405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc.">Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc., 80 C.L.R. (3d) 143, 2009 CarswellOnt 2805 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at 2009 CarswellOnt 8879, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Liens registered against several lots in a real estate development were found to be invalid as general liens. Instead, the master treated the liens as exaggerated liens under s. 35 and allowed them to continue in the appropriate amounts. The master exercised her discretion under section 47 of the Act to vacate the liens and certificates of action from title without the posting of security, leaving the remedies available under the Act for the trial judge to determine.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Landmark II Inc." p2="1535709 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4814" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I640e88415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landmark II Inc. v. 1535709 Ontario Ltd.">Landmark II Inc. v. 1535709 Ontario Ltd., 2008 CarswellOnt 4814, [2008] O.J. No. 3189, 75 C.L.R. (3d) 157 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2009 CarswellOnt 2858 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The proper measure of the defendant's damages under s. 35, after the plaintiff registered a claim for lien that it ought to have known was grossly in excess of the amount it was owed by the defendant, was held to be equal to the interest paid by the defendant to borrow the funds which were paid into court to discharge the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Pickering Harbour Co." p2="Barton" post.rptr="6762" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I640e88425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pickering Harbour Co. v. Barton">Pickering Harbour Co. v. Barton (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 6762, 39 C.P.C. (6th) 293, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 201 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 874, 85 O.R. (3d) 526 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff paid monies into court to clear title to the subject property, in order that the defendants might deal with the property. Subsequently, the defendants moved for leave to issue a third party claim. The plaintiff argued that it had lost the use of those monies for approximately two years, and the delay that potentially would be occasioned by the granting of leave would result in a further loss for an indeterminate period of time. In granting the motion, the court held that, if it was established at trial that the plaintiff was wrongfully deprived of the use of the monies, it could be compensated by virtue of s. 35 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The fact of having to pay money into court did not amount to prejudice of the sort that should defeat the defendant's motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Scepter Industries Ltd." p2="MacIntosh" post.rptr="8925" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I640e88435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scepter Industries Ltd. v. MacIntosh">Scepter Industries Ltd. v. MacIntosh (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 8925 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's claim for delay damages in addition to the balance owing on the amended construction contract was unreasonable, and the plaintiff knew or ought to have known that it could not recover damages for delay based on a wrongful demand for payment without holdback. Elements of those damages were already included in the extras forming part of the fixed price, and this claim should have been an alternative to the claim for breach of contract and not in addition to it. If the defendants had simply paid the entire balance of the amended price without any deduction, it would not have exceeded $103,000.00, making a lien for $225,490 excessive. The defendant was entitled to damages under s. 35 of the Act for the balance. In the absence of evidence of specific damages caused by the registration of the inflated lien, the measure of damages was the cost of over-securing the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="JDM Developments Inc." p2="J. Stollar Construction Ltd." post.rptr="6486" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I640e88445fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd.">JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 6486, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 296 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 817, 51 C.L.R. (3d) 293 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6081, 63 C.L.R. (3d) 163 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff builder alleged the existence of an oral agreement with the defendant developer which authorized the builder to erect houses on lots owned by the developer and defer the payment of purchase monies for each lot until construction was completed and each house was sold. The court vacated the liens registered by the builder against the lots in subsequent actions, and found that the builder had mischaracterized its claims as lien claims when they were grounded in a breach of the alleged oral agreement and the dispute really concerned the sale of lots by the developer and the appropriate purchase price in respect of those lots. Section 35 applied in this case, because the plaintiff knew or ought to have known that it did not have a lien, but there was no award of compensatory or non-compensatory damages as there was no evidence of damages pursuant to s. 35. Although the defendant sought costs on a substantial indemnity scale pursuant to s. 35, s. 86 was held to be the proper provision to be relied upon.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of)" p2="974040 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2076" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I640eaf505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) v. 974040 Ontario Inc.">MacDonald Homes Inc. (Trustee of) v. 974040 Ontario Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2076, 1998 CarswellOnt 2232 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Although not specifically referred to, it appears that damages, including costs, were assessed as a result of registrations of liens that should never have been made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Disal Contracting Ltd." p2="J. Salamon Holdings Inc." post.rptr="200" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I640eaf515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Disal Contracting Ltd. v. J. Salamon Holdings Inc.">Disal Contracting Ltd. v. J. Salamon Holdings Inc. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 200 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4275 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4274 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Burdens of proof were determinative of an issue involving the registration of an untimely series of liens. The burden of proving failure to mitigate is on the lien claimant and not on the person who alleges a cause of action under s. 35. The court in this case went further and ruled that the use of the phrase “is liable” in this section removed any residual discretion to disallow damage claims proven by an owner in the face of an untimely lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Garrett" p2="Ayr Ventures Inc." post.rptr="407" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I640eaf525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Garrett v. Ayr Ventures Inc.">Garrett v. Ayr Ventures Inc. (1995), 21 O.R. (3d) 407, 18 C.L.R. (2d) 300, 44 R.P.R. (2d) 215 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The statutory tort created by s. 35 is similar in many respects to a claim for slander of title and requires proof of elements of lack of justification, intent and malice. A lien claimant placed a general lien on all the lots in a subdivision notwithstanding that work was performed on one lot only, causing the purchaser of a different lot within the subdivision to refuse to close. As the registration was carried out in error, without malice, the claimant was not liable under s. 35.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Rideau Valley Constructors Ltd." p2="Visa Construction Co." post.rptr="1801" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I640eaf535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rideau Valley Constructors Ltd. v. Visa Construction Co.">Rideau Valley Constructors Ltd. v. Visa Construction Co. (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 1801 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Rideau registered a lien on June 3, 1993, for $105,834.55, failing to take into account a payment of $51,632.20 paid to it the day before. Rideau pursued a lien action; Visa counterclaimed for damages under s. 35. The court held that while there was no doubt that the preservation of a lien before payment is due can cause financial loss to the payer, this is an unavoidable risk of the statutory scheme. The court concluded further that the word “owed” in s. 35 and the word “owing” in the Affidavit of Verification mean that the contractor has supplied the services and material and has not yet been paid, but do not mean that the amount is already due and payable under the contract. The court cited with approval <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Classic Masonry Contracting Ltd." p2="Southside Construction London Ltd." post.rptr="1997" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I640eaf545fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Classic Masonry Contracting Ltd. v. Southside Construction London Ltd.">Classic Masonry Contracting Ltd. v. Southside Construction London Ltd. (1993), [1993] O.J. No. 1997 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> to hold that s. 35 is only concerned with exaggerated claims, not claims for which an amount was not yet due or payable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It is sufficient to establish liability under s. 35 if negligence is proven. There is no need to prove malice. It would not be a defence to establish that the defendant was acting in good faith with the intent to protect what he negligently believed were his rights. In this case, counterclaim under s. 35 was allowed, however for lack of probative evidence no award of compensatory damages were made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Johnston & Associates Co." p2="Wade" post.rptr="6898" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I5607ade0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade">Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 6898 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—As part of the overall factual background, the deposition of the affidavit of documents was considered by the court in awarding solicitor and client costs of the action against the deponent.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Yorkdale Drywall Co." p2="Schulberg" post.rptr="851" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90e26410f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Yorkdale Drywall Co. v. Schulberg">Yorkdale Drywall Co. v. Schulberg (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 851, [1993] O.J. No. 137, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 100 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A substantial assessment of punitive damages and solicitor and client costs was made against a defendant contractor. Although s. 35 is not addressed, the liability is analogous. See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Johnston & Associates Co." p2="Wade" post.rptr="6898" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I5607ade1fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade">Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 6898 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 35(1)1</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tenoes Construction" p2="Pinto" post.rptr="14014" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6761ef103b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Tenoes Construction v. Pinto">Tenoes Construction v. Pinto, 2024 CarswellOnt 14014, 2024 ONSC 5119 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court concluded that the plaintiff's lien was not timely and wilfully exaggerated. The plaintiff was accordingly liable for any damages that the owners suffered as a result of the invalid lien. Those damages included fees and disbursement costs associated with the loan obtained to vacate the lien. However, the owners did not meet their evidentiary onus of demonstrating that discharge of a first and second mortgages on title was required by reason of the lien, and the costs associated with those discharges and the subsequent mortgage were not recoverable as s. 35 damages.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1593095 Ontario Ltd. (Northwood Window and Door Centre)" p2="McCann" post.rptr="163" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I676216203b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="1593095 Ontario Ltd. (Northwood Window and Door Centre) v. McCann">1593095 Ontario Ltd. (Northwood Window and Door Centre) v. McCann, 2024 CarswellOnt 207, 2024 ONSC 163, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3229 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the increased amount in the lien was the result of an accounting error or an oversight, and no prejudice was suffered by the defendants, the court declined to hold the plaintiff liable, or to void the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2002759 Ontario Inc." p2="Koropeski et al." post.rptr="3651" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I640ed6635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2002759 Ontario Inc. v. Koropeski et al.">2002759 Ontario Inc. v. Koropeski et al., 2022 ONSC 3651, 2022 CarswellOnt 9791 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The appropriate time to claim formal damages under s. 35 is at trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RJ Concrete" p2="Eco Depot LTD." post.rptr="1759" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I640ed6645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RJ Concrete v. Eco Depot LTD.">RJ Concrete v. Eco Depot LTD., 2022 ONSC 1759, 2022 CarswellOnt 3636 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved under s. 47 to discharge a lien and vacate the related claim for lien and certificate of action, on the basis that the claim for lien was an abuse of process and the amount of the lien was willfully exaggerated. The parties had agreed on a contract price, but the relationship broke down before the contract was completed. At issue was whether the amount of the lien should have been based on the actual market value of the services and materials provided, or whether the claimant was entitled to register its lien based on the value the agreement attributed to the services and materials provided. The court concluded that the price of the services and materials provided, and therefore the amount of the lien, was to be measured with reference to the parties' agreement. It was evident both from the amount of the lien and communications between the parties that the lien was based on the full contract amount, less the amount paid by the plaintiff. Although the plaintiff subsequently acknowledged the lien amount was inadvertently calculated at too high an amount, and had attempted to reduce the lien on consent, the lien was not wilfully exaggerated nor an abuse of process. The proper remedy was to reduce the amount of the lien pursuant to s. 35(2) to the amount determined by the court to be still outstanding.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Crawford" p2="Standard Building Contractors Limited" post.rptr="166" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I640efd705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Crawford v. Standard Building Contractors Limited">Crawford v. Standard Building Contractors Limited, 2021 ONSC 166, 2021 CarswellOnt 108, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 353 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 CarswellOnt 1099 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contractor and his related companies contracted to rebuild the plaintiff's house, but after 20 months had failed to advance the project beyond some initial excavation work. The principal engaged in deceptive and fraudulent conduct both personally and through his companies, such as utilizing a forged engineer's stamp, and registered a lien against the property. He also contacted the plaintiff's insurer and purported to assert a trust over the remaining insurance proceeds available under the plaintiff's policy. That communication constituted “written notice of a lien”, within the meaning of s. 35, and that the notice was given without a legal basis and in bad faith. The exaggerated lien interfered with the plaintiff's economic relations and delayed their efforts to rebuild their house. Damages of $7,500 were awarded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="McLarty" p2="2210961 Ontario Limited et al." post.rptr="7435" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I640efd715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="McLarty v. 2210961 Ontario Limited et al.">McLarty v. 2210961 Ontario Limited et al., 2020 CarswellOnt 7435, 2020 ONSC 1865, 14 C.L.R. (5th) 49 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 7436, 2020 ONSC 2838 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> A.K. Mitchell J.—At its highest, the value of the plaintiff's lien claim was $124,300, not $203,400 as registered, and the claim was therefore exaggerated. However, unlike the defendant in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Landmark II Inc." p2="1535709 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="567" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I640efd725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landmark II Inc. v. 1535709 Ontario Ltd.">Landmark II Inc. v. 1535709 Ontario Ltd., 2011 ONCA 567, 2011 CarswellOnt 8789, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 1, 283 O.A.C. 239 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, the defendant did not file any evidence to prove it suffered damages as a result of the exaggerated lien claim registered by the plaintiff. Accordingly, the s. 35 claim was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="London Eco-Roof Manufacturing Inc." p2="Syson" post.rptr="3014" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I640efd735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="London Eco-Roof Manufacturing Inc. v. Syson">London Eco-Roof Manufacturing Inc. v. Syson, 2020 CarswellOnt 3014, 2020 ONSC 1338, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 6931, 2020 ONSC 3101, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 173 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The roofing contractor registered a lien for $15,000 against the owner's property and named the owner's bank as an additional co-defendant to the proceeding, but later withdrew the claim against the bank. The latter charged the owner, by way of a debit to his line of credit account, a fee representing litigation fees and disbursements. Although the proper amount of the lien was determined to be $10,000, and the lien was therefore registered in an amount in excess of the amount owed, s. 35 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not apply so as to allow the owner to be reimbursed for the fee. A claimant seeking recovery of damages pursuant to section 35(1)1 must establish not only the existence of a wilfully exaggerated lien, but that the damages being claimed were occasioned “as a result” of the lien amount being exaggerated. Here, it was not demonstrated that the charge had anything to do with the exaggerated amount of the lien, and had the plaintiff registered a lien for the proper amount, it likely would have added the bank as an additional defendant to address the possibility of a priority dispute with a mortgagee.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Kalogon Spar Ltd." p2="Papageorge" post.rptr="1884" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I640f24805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kalogon Spar Ltd. v. Papageorge">Kalogon Spar Ltd. v. Papageorge, 2020 CarswellOnt 1884, 2020 ONSC 710, 6 C.L.R. (5th) 245 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2020 CarswellOnt 7344, 2020 ONSC 3234, 6 C.L.R. (5th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff registered a lien in the amount of $300,000, whereas the court confirmed the right to a lien in the amount of $155,339. However, there was no evidence that the plaintiff was aware of any deficiencies claims when it registered the lien, nor whether it took certain loans from the defendant into account in his calculations. The evidence fell short of showing that the plaintiff wilfully exaggerated the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9585800 Canada Inc." p2="JP Gravel Construction et al." post.rptr="3396" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I640f24815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction et al.">9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction et al., 2019 ONSC 3396, 2019 CarswellOnt 8917, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 29 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed 2019 CarswellOnt 19773, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 38 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor registered and then discharged a construction lien against the construction project, and then immediately registered a second construction lien after that discharge, for the same amount and using substantially the same information as contained in the first lien. The first lien was allegedly discharged due to an error in the time of delivery of services which listed the incorrect year, an error corrected in the second lien, and the plaintiff denied any intention of discharging its entitlement to a lien against the defendant contractor. The court rejected the defendant's argument that the claimant registered a lien that it knew or ought to have known was grossly in excess of the amount owed. Both affiants contradicted each other's evidence, and there was no clear evidence one way or the other.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="JMCC Ltd." p2="Buttcon Ltd." post.rptr="3202" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I640f24825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="JMCC Ltd. v. Buttcon Ltd.">JMCC Ltd. v. Buttcon Ltd., 2016 ONSC 3202, 2016 CarswellOnt 8079, 57 C.L.R. (4th) 153 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Had the defendant pleaded s. 35, it would not have succeeded because the plaintiff believed it had a valid claim for a lien in the amount claimed, based on recovery for what it characterized as extras. Although the plaintiff did not have the evidence it needed to prove its entitlement to extras at trial, the court would not have awarded s. 35 damages because the test for such damages had not been met.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Landmark II Inc." p2="1535709 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="567" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I640f24835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landmark II Inc. v. 1535709 Ontario Ltd.">Landmark II Inc. v. 1535709 Ontario Ltd., 2011 ONCA 567, 2011 CarswellOnt 8789, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 1, 283 O.A.C. 239 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was liable under s. 35 for registering a lien for three remaining instalment payments on a construction job where the lien was registered two and half months after it had abandoned job, and the claimant had no intention of completing the contract. A claimant cannot register a lien for unpaid balance when it has left the job and does not intend to finish it. As well, in this case the affidavit in support of the lien was signed by a person with no knowledge of how much of the job had been completed, and who took no steps to find out.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="MHA Contracting Inc." p2="Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="713" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I640f24845fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MHA Contracting Inc. v. Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd.">MHA Contracting Inc. v. Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 713, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 35(a) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides that “any person who preserves a claim for lien or who gives written notice of a lien … for an amount which the person knows or ought to know is grossly in excess of the amount which the person is owed…” is liable to any person who suffers damages as a result. Here, the “person” to whom the money was said to be owing was a corporate plaintiff. “Person” could not logically be given different meanings in the same paragraph and hence s. 35 does not extend so far as to fix an individual with personal liability for an excessive lien he has caused to be filed by a corporation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20030509" p1="Power Lift Equipment Ltd." p2="KGM Holdings (Ontario) Ltd." post.rptr="5345" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I640f4b905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Power Lift Equipment Ltd. v. KGM Holdings (Ontario) Ltd.">Power Lift Equipment Ltd. v. KGM Holdings (Ontario) Ltd. (May 9, 2003), Doc. 00-BN-3634, [2003] O.J. No. 5345 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sued for $1,995, being the amount owing for the rental of equipment used for the installation by the defendant of a security system on a customer's premises. The defendant counterclaimed for damages in the amount of $25,000 for the loss of future business as a result of the plaintiff placing a construction lien against the customer's property. The court dismissed the plaintiff's claim and assessed damages of $10,000 on the counterclaim. The plaintiff was entitled to put a lien on the subject property where the equipment was; however, to do so for the small amount owing, knowing full well what effect it would have on the defendant's relationship with his client, verged on mean-spirited.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Markborough Properties Inc." p2="841202 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="77" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I640f4b915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Markborough Properties Inc. v. 841202 Ontario Inc.">Markborough Properties Inc. v. 841202 Ontario Inc. (1996), 28 C.L.R. (2d) 77 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the defendants did not expend any money directly or indirectly as a result of the grossly excessive face amount of the lien, the claim was for compensation and there was no loss, the court made no award for damages.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Kelton and Ferracuti Consultants Ltd." p2="588147 Ontario Inc." ref.id="I640f4b925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kelton and Ferracuti Consultants Ltd. v. 588147 Ontario Inc.">Kelton and Ferracuti Consultants Ltd. v. 588147 Ontario Inc. (1993), C.L.C.F. 35.6 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Reimbursement allowed for expenditures made due to grossly excess lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Concord Construction Inc." p2="Camara" post.rptr="263" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I640f4b935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Concord Construction Inc. v. Camara">Concord Construction Inc. v. Camara (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 263 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—By issuing inflated invoices and by obtaining falsified back-up documents, the plaintiff was found to have breached its obligations to the defendants. The plaintiff was therefore liable to the defendants for overpayments and for damages arising from the registration of an excessive or improper lien. In addition, the president and sole director of the plaintiff company was personally liable for damages assessed against the plaintiff because he was the directing mind and will of the plaintiff in terms of causing it to issue inflated invoices to the defendants and in causing the plaintiff to obtain falsified invoices from subcontractors. The defendants' claim for punitive damages was rejected.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="G.B. Mécanique Ltée." p2="Roche Ltée" post.rptr="16" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I640f4b945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.B. Mécanique Ltée. v. Roche Ltée">G.B. Mécanique Ltée. v. Roche Ltée (1996), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 16 (Ont. Gen. Div.); supplementary reasons at (1996), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 16 (note) (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff lien claimant obtained summary judgment for a portion of the moneys claimed and the defendant moved for a partial stay of execution of that summary judgment. The defendant argued that the plaintiff's lien was exaggerated within the meaning of s. 35, and counterclaimed for premiums paid on the bond posted to secure and vacate the lien. In granting a partial stay of execution pursuant to R. 20.08 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, the court noted that the fact the plaintiff liened an amount $3,796,904.20 more than the unpaid total of the invoices it submitted provided some basis to support that the lien was excessive and the defendant's position was therefore arguable or tenable. However, the fact that invoices may not have been submitted for the full amount claimed did not mean that materials and services in that amount were not supplied, and a contractor could quite reasonably be expected to claim its lien on the whole amount of the materials and services supplied, and not just on those for which invoices had been submitted and denied or defaulted upon.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="LDR Contracting Inc." p2="Filion" post.rptr="2768" pre.rptr="[1996]" ref.id="I640f72a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="LDR Contracting Inc. v. Filion">LDR Contracting Inc. v. Filion (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 2768, 1996 CarswellOnt 2874 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A claim for lien that included extras outside the contract was held to be grossly excessive, and damages were awarded to reflect the cost of obtaining an expert witness, including legal fees involved in retaining and instructing the expert.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 35(1)2</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Haas Homes Ltd." p2="March Road Gym & Health Club Inc." post.rptr="2847" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I640f72a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc.">Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2847, 2003 CarswellOnt 2687, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 243 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An offer to lease was made on behalf of the tenant and accepted by the landlord of the strip mall development where the construction work was performed. The offer set out the respective scope of the work required by the landlord and the tenant to renovate the upper floor of the property as a health club. The lien claimant submitted a quotation to the tenant and commenced its work without a written construction contract, and there was never a written contract entered into by the claimant with the tenants. Liens were subsequently filed. Within months of completion of the improvements to the tenant's demised premises, the tenant stopped paying rent, abandoned the premises and subsequently went bankrupt. The landlord asserted a counterclaim against the lien claimant under s. 35 for damages for preserving claims for lien where he knew or ought to have known that it did not have a lien, with the result that the landlord was unable to obtain a final advance under its construction mortgage and lost a more favourable interest rate on the permanent financing of the development. As well, its payments to its own general contractor were delayed. A motion was taken by the landlord to oppose confirmation of the Master's report, which upheld the lien and concluded in the alternative that if the landlord was not a statutory owner under the Act, the lien claimant would be entitled to recover the amount of its claim against it on the ground of <ital>quantum meruit</ital> or implied contract. The court declined to confirm the report, and rejected the validity of the lien and the alternative damage claims. It also rejected the counterclaim as being without merit. There was insufficient evidence to satisfy the test set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I640f99b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 171, 1994 CarswellOnt 956 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, that the lien claimant and his lawyer believed that the liens were invalid when they registered them or that they acted with malice or intent to injure the landlord.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Ron Robinson Ltd." p2="Rhodes Tanks Ltd." post.rptr="261" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I640f99b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ron Robinson Ltd. v. Rhodes Tanks Ltd.">Ron Robinson Ltd. v. Rhodes Tanks Ltd. (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In order to establish slander of title, the defendant must prove that the registration of a claim for lien was effected with the intent of causing damage. This element of proof was missing in this case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Sintra Ont. Inc." p2="Metric Contracting Services Corp." post.rptr="1798" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I640f99b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sintra Ont. Inc. v. Metric Contracting Services Corp.">Sintra Ont. Inc. v. Metric Contracting Services Corp. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 1798, 1999 CarswellOnt 1272 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sought to determine if the certificate of substantial performance had been published, and therefore whether it had a valid lien, by requesting that information from the contractor by letter pursuant to s. 39(4) of the Act. The defendant failed to give the proper information and therefore was estopped from claiming damages under s. 35(b). In effect, the defendant could not rely on its own failure to give the information to recover damages under s. 35(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Chute Construction Ltd." p2="Bican Construction Corp." post.rptr="175" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I640f99b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Chute Construction Ltd. v. Bican Construction Corp.">Chute Construction Ltd. v. Bican Construction Corp. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 175 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Each phase of a construction project was the subject of a separate construction contract, and the evidence indicated that the lien claimants had been paid for the first phase. The defendant argued that the claimants knew, or ought to have known, that they had no general lien claim or other commitment from the defendant with respect to the first phase that would allow them to register a lien against that phase. In dismissing the defendant's counterclaim pursuant to s. 35 of the Act, the court stated that while s. 35(b) appears to set mere negligence as the threshold of liability, the law may require even more than negligence or recklessness to slander a title. As it was not unreasonable for the claimants to believe that they had an agreement for an ongoing, two-phase, ten-unit project, there was no breach of s. 35(b) of the Act and no slander of title.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd." p2="Sarcevich" post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I640f99b45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich">Woodmere (Credit Valley) Ltd. v. Sarcevich (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 171, 1994 CarswellOnt 956 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The court was satisfied that both the lien claimant and its lawyer believed there was a valid lien both in fact and in law. As it was more the existence of the lien rather than its amount, which had been inflated by errors, including a typographical error, that was complained of this was an answer to a claim under s. 35.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I640fc0c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Subsequent to the registration of his lien, a contractor realized that he had understated the amount owing, and instructed his solicitors to register a new lien and release the previous lien claim so as not to unduly encumber the title to the owner's property. The owner then successfully moved to discharge the contractor's lien, to vacate the registration of the lien and certificate of action, and to dismiss the contractor's lien action. The court held, and the appeal court concurred, that the discharge of the contractor's first lien was irrevocable and terminated all of the contractor's lien rights in respect of the work done by the contractor during this period of time. The lien could not be revived. Accordingly, the lien asserted in the second claim for lien, being for the same work during the same period of time, albeit claiming a larger amount of money, could not, in law, be asserted. An acceptable alternative, <ital>inter alia</ital>, would have been to register a second lien for the correct full amount of the plaintiff's claim, again assuming it could be done in time, and then move, under s. 47(1)(b), on notice, for an order vacating the registration of the first lien, so as to avoid any liability under s. 35 of the Act for “exaggerated claims”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Franro Property Development Ltd." p2="Heritage Glen North Ltd." post.rptr="2572" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90e34e70f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Franro Property Development Ltd. v. Heritage Glen North Ltd.">Franro Property Development Ltd. v. Heritage Glen North Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 2572, [1993] O.J. No. 2396 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—This case confirms the result in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I640fc0c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> without referring to that case. Once discharged by a release, a lien cannot be revived. Also, while s. 35 provides for damages in the case of exaggerated lien, it does not preclude a court from discharging a lien under s. 47 where the lien claimant has manifestly acted in bad faith.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(2) of the Act was amended to extend the timeline for the perfection of a preserved lien from 45 days to 90 days.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section derives from ss. 26 and 27 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 26 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> was derived from s. 4 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">4.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">Such lien shall absolutely cease to exist within ninety days after such work shall have been completed, or materials or machinery furnished or the expiry of the period of credit, unless in the meantime proceedings shall have been instituted to realize such a claim under the provisions hereinafter contained, and a certificate of <ital>lis pendens</ital> thereof, be registered in the proper registry office, which certificate may be granted may be granted by the Judge or Court before whom the proceedings are instituted.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 14 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1874</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.) reduced the time period to 90 days (see discussion under Legislative History of s. 31 above) and introduced the concept of the expiration of a lien unless proceedings were instituted and a Certificate of Action was registered. The time period of 90 days was reinstated in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1877, c. 120, s. 21. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1975</ital>, S.O. 1975, c. 43, dealt with the expiration of liens against Crowns and municipalities. The section remained substantially unchanged until the enactment of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The 1983 version of what is now s. 36(6) dealing with the situation where a period of credit has been extended, was originally excluded and later amended by the <ital>Construction Lien Amendment Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 77, to include the current provision.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A subsisting lien that has been “preserved” under s. 34 must be “perfected” under s. 36 before it expires under ss. 36(2). Only liens that have been preserved may be perfected. The time limitations set out in s. 31 discussed above must be strictly adhered to. Liens must be perfected before the end of the 90-day period following the last day on which they could have been preserved or else they expire and cannot be revived. Accordingly, once the time period for preservation begins to run, there is a maximum of 150 days for the lien claimant to preserve and perfect its lien claim. If the lien is preserved before the end of the initial 60-day period, the remaining days are effectively added to the 90-day perfection period. For example, if a lien is preserved on the 10th day after publication of a certificate of substantial performance, that lien could be perfected at any time during the balance of the preservation period, namely 50 days in the example, plus the 90 days prescribed by ss. 36(2) for perfection.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(3)(a) provides that where a lien has been preserved by registration, it becomes perfected when the lien claimant both commences an action to enforce the lien, and registers a certificate of action against title to the premises. If the lien is one which is not preserved by registration, then it is perfected by the mere timely issuance of a Statement of Claim. “Action” is defined in ss. 1(1) of the Act. If an order vacating the registration of a lien has been obtained under s. 44 of the Act, the requirement for registering a certificate of action against the premises is dispensed with. Actions must be brought, and Certificates of Action must be registered in the jurisdiction in which the lands are situated (see ss. 53(1)). Note that although recent amendments to the Rules of Civil Procedure enable lien claimants to bring motions in any jurisdiction, ss. 53(1) applies in respect of actions and Certificates of Action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(4) provides for the perfection of a preserved claim for lien by “sheltering” under an action commenced in respect of the lien of another claimant. The doctrine of sheltering is complex. The rules regarding sheltering are set out in the four subsections of s. 36(4). The concept of sheltering was developed to avoid a multiplicity of actions relating to the same improvement and to simplify the procedure required to perfect small liens, but it is rarely used for this purpose today. The sheltering of a preserved lien under the perfected lien of another claimant is fraught with danger. The consequences can be fatal to the lien itself or to the jurisdiction of the Court over the lien, or both. Sheltering should therefore be looked upon in practice as a saving provision only, and not as an acceptable method of avoiding the cost of a lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Under s. 36(4.1), a preserved lien is sheltered under another lien if that other lien is both subsisting and perfected at the time the sheltered lien is preserved, or if that other lien becomes perfected before the sheltered lien would expire under s. 36(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(4.2) protects the sheltered lien from flaws in the sheltering lien, because a sheltered lien claimant cannot realistically be expected to explore the validity of the sheltering lien claim in the short time given. If, however, a sheltering claim fails to name a necessary party, the sheltered claim may be defeated notwithstanding the protection of this subsection.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(4.3) shelters a lien claimant only as to the named defendants and “nature of relief” claimed in the sheltering action. A party wishing to advance different claims, or claims against different parties must bring a separate action and deliver separate pleadings.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(4.4) ensures that a defendant may obtain sufficient particulars to prepare a defence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The reader is referred to Reynolds and Pattison “Sheltering, Consolidation and Trial Together: The Constructions Lien Action as a Class Action” (1996), 29 C.L.R. (2d) 214.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The perfection of preserved general liens is provided for in ss. 36(5). A claimant having a general lien has an election to make at the time of perfection, as it must be perfect against each lot it desires to affect with its lien. Caution should be exercised in this regard as well (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Gillies Lumber Inc." p2="Kubassek Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="334" pre.rptr="176" ref.id="I64100ee05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd.">Gillies Lumber Inc. v. Kubassek Holdings Ltd. (1999), 176 D.L.R. (4th) 334, 47 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 36(6) ensures that persons who have preserved a lien, but who have given extended payment terms, can perfect their lien while waiting for payment in accordance with those terms. Under the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> the time for commencement of an action was extended by a period of time equal to any period of credit. This concept has been abandoned, but the misconception that a period of credit extends the time for perfection still persists.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R." p2="1431633 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I90e39c90f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R. v. 1431633 Ontario Inc.">R. v. 1431633 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 161, 2010 ONSC 266, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 263, 250 C.C.C. (3d) 354 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The supplier sold lumber used to construct a house owned by accused, against whom the Crown obtained and registered a restraint order under the <ital>Criminal Code</ital>. Subsequent to that registration, and unaware of the restraint order, the supplier filed a claim for lien and brought an action to enforce it without giving notice to the Crown or obtaining a prior court order, contrary to the provisions of the restraint order. The supplier successfully applied under s. 462.42 of <ital>Criminal Code</ital> for relief from forfeiture. The supplier would have had a valid interest in the property under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> but for provision of the restraint order declaring it void, and it was appropriate to vary the order nunc pro tunc to allow the registration of the lien claim and the action to enforce it. Failure to commence the action within 90 days of completion means that the plaintiff has failed to perfect its lien, despite the payment of security into court, and notwithstanding the fact that a defendant has subsequently delivered a statement of defence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd." p2="Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board" post.rptr="1228" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I5609d0c0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd. v. Quebecor World Inc.">State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc., 2013 ONSC 2277, 2013 CarswellOnt 4462, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 164 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>: The contractor sought an order declaring that the claim for lien under which it purported to shelter was a valid sheltering lien and properly perfected in relation to the subject improvement. In determining whether perfected liens under which a subject lien purports to shelter relates to the “same improvement”, the Master noted that the performance of work on the same land does not necessarily make the work of the “same improvement,” but that once a lien has been established as having been properly preserved, the court should liberally interpret the sheltering requirements in favour of the lien claimant. The question of “same improvement” is largely a question of fact, with the governing principle being the establishment of some nexus between the work done by the lien claimants in question that makes it a common effort. The same improvement can have one “contract” or many “contracts,” but what makes it an improvement is the coordination of the contract work toward a common purpose or goal. Here, because the contractor supervised the work of the lien claimants under whose liens it purported to shelter, it could not be said to be doing its work on anything other than the same improvement. To rule otherwise would lead to the rather bizarre conclusion that the supervision of the work was somehow divorced from the work that was supervised to such an extent as to render them separate improvements.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Buttcon Ltd." p2="Beaver Construction Services Corp." post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="51" ref.id="I6410d2345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Buttcon Ltd. v.
