S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court rejected the proposition that a contractor's lien could not be perfected by “reverse vertical sheltering” (<ital>i.e.</ital> sheltering under the properly perfected lien of its own subcontractor). No case law was provided that supported the position that “reverse vertical sheltering” was not available under s. 36.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Sesco Ltd." p2="Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax)" post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I6410f9405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sesco Ltd. v. Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax)">Sesco Ltd. v. Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax) (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 66, 37 O.R. (3d) 764, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Metric Masonry Amalgamated Ltd. v. Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax))</ital> 37 O.R. (3d) 764, 163 D.L.R. (4th) 317, 107 O.A.C. 258, 38 C.L.R. (2d) 66 (Ont. Div. Ct.); leave to appeal refused (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 1430 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—It was concluded on appeal, after an exhaustive review of the authorities, that the sheltering provisions form part of the enforcement provisions of the Act and should therefore be given a liberal interpretation on the authority of the Supreme Court of Canada decision in <ital>Ace Lumber Ltd. v. Clarkson Co.</ital> The Act must be given a strict interpretation in determining whether any lien claimant is entitled to a lien, but if a person passes that threshold and is found to be entitled to claim a lien, then the statute should be liberally interpreted with respect to the rights conferred upon the lien claimant. Once the existence of a valid lien is established, the sheltering provisions set out in the Act should be given a liberal interpretation. When relief such as the enforcement of a lien has been claimed in a Statement of Claim by a party commencing an action, then others claiming the enforcement of lien rights should be able to shelter under the existing claim. The sheltered claims do not need to be for the same services and materials as are included in the perfected actions. Moreover, it was held, on appeal, that the requirements of R. 25.06(1) requiring specification of the “nature of the relief claimed” cannot be read into R. 3 of s. 36(4). The words “nature of the relief claimed” entail only the remedies sought and not the substance of the claim. The case is now authority for what has come to be called “horizontal” as opposed to “vertical sheltering” under the Act. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The lower court decision in Sescso case generated a great deal of controversy and debate. It led to uncertainty as to whether the sheltering claim must plead a description of services and materials that could reasonably be said to include the scope of services and materials claimed in the lien seeking shelter. A number of decisions had been reserved pending the outcome of this appeal. This liberal reading of the section should resolve the doubt in most, if not all such cases, in favour of the lien claimant.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Chute Construction Ltd." p2="Bican Construction Corp." post.rptr="175" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I6410f9415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Chute Construction Ltd. v. Bican Construction Corp.">Chute Construction Ltd. v. Bican Construction Corp. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 175 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A construction lien action is something akin to a class action. Once one contractor or subcontractor commences an action, a process is created whereby the defendant owner can know all claims being made against it and an adjudication process is available. Claimants, often small contractors with small claims, are enabled to come to court with whatever records they have and prove their claims, as was done in this case. When relief such as the enforcement of a lien has been claimed in a statement of claim by a party commencing an action, then others claiming the enforcement of lien rights should be able to shelter under the existing claim. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court in this decision was not prepared to follow the reasoning in either <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tri-Haven Homes Inc." p2="O'Neill" post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="23" ref.id="I641120505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill">Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill (1995), 23 O.R. (3d) 205, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 105 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Sesco Ltd." p2="Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax)" post.rptr="230" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I641120515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sesco Ltd. v. Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax)">Sesco Ltd. v. Life Centre Non-Profit Housing Corp. (Ajax) (1996), 30 C.L.R. (2d) 230, 30 O.R. (3d) 449, 139 D.L.R. (4th) 751 (Gen. Div.); reversed (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 66, 37 O.R. (3d) 764 (Ont. Div. Ct.); leave to appeal refused (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 1430 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. The <ital>Sesco</ital> case appeal to the Divisional Court was heard September 19, and October 27, 1997, and reserved. In several other instances, motions dealing with this issue have been adjourned <ital>sine die</ital> pending guidance from the Divisional Court in <ital>Sesco</ital>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="M & S Roofing & Sheet Metal Ltd." p2="Arthur J. Fish Ltd." post.rptr="148" pre.rptr="32" ref.id="I641120525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M & S Roofing & Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Arthur J. Fish Ltd.">M & S Roofing & Sheet Metal Ltd. v. Arthur J. Fish Ltd. (1988), 32 C.L.R. 148 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A subcontractor filed a lien claim subsequent to that of another subcontractor, IF Inc., and moved to set aside an order determining that its lien had expired and to set aside an order for the delivering up of the bond filed by the general contractor. The subcontractor had not commenced an action to enforce its lien, although it purported to shelter its claim under that of IF Inc., which had issued a statement of claim and commenced an action against the general contractor. The motion was dismissed. The fact that the subcontractor had not commenced an action meant that the only way it could perfect its lien would be to shelter it under that of IF Inc. pursuant to s. 36(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. IF Inc., however, had not commenced an action to enforce its lien pursuant to s. 36(3)(a) of the Act and had only claimed against the general contractor and not against the owner. Therefore, the subcontractor's sheltered lien was only against the contractor and, as no lien action can exist without an owner, the subcontractor's lien was not perfected. The fact that IF Inc. could still add the owner as a party in its action did not alter the subcontractor's position. The motion to set aside had to be considered and determined according to the facts existing at the time of the proceedings and the court could not speculate upon future actions or added parties which could possibly effect the subcontractor's lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tri-Haven Homes Inc." p2="O'Neill" post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="23" ref.id="I641120535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill">Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill (1995), 23 O.R. (3d) 205, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 105 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Rule 3 under s. 36(4) has the effect of confining the perfection of “sheltered” lien claims to work done or materials supplied within the ambit of the relief claimed in the statement of claim under which it seeks sheltering. For example, if the statement of claim in question relates to work or materials of an electrical contractor, then a lien claim for the work or material of a plumbing contractor or supplier would not be sheltered. On the other hand, if the statement of claim in question was by a general contractor for an entire project, then anyone who provided work or materials could “shelter” under the claim of the general contractor, whether or not they did work or supplied the materials under a contract with the general contractor, provided that they were engaged on “the same improvement”, <ital>i.e.</ital> the same building or the same aspect of construction within a building.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
37:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 37.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">37:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The concept of expunging lien actions registered for 2 years or more and not brought to trial was established in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1932</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(2)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">Where a certificate of action has been registered for two years or more in the registry office or land titles office as the case may be, and no appointment has been taken out for the trial of such action, any interested part may apply <ital>ex parte</ital> to a judge or officer who has jurisdiction to try the action who may make an order vacating such certificate of action.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1933</ital>, S.O. 1933, c. 30, s. 2 added the words “and discharging all liens depending thereon” to this section. Changes to this section subsequent to the 1933 amendment dealt mainly with references to Masters. The present version of the statute derives from the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The present version makes it clear that a lien claimant is required to <ital>either</ital> obtain an order for trial, or get the action down for trial, not both. The <ital>Statute Law Amendment Act</ital>, S.O. 1994, c. 27, s. 42 amended s. 37 to its present form. Note that the language under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> was permissive, while the language in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is mandatory. The Court has no discretion whatsoever under the current section.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section contains a crucial and often overlooked expiration period. Every perfected lien expires two years after commencement of the action which perfected that lien unless one of the two steps provided for in s. 37(1) is taken. Note that the period commences with the action that perfects any given lien, and if that lien has been perfected by sheltering under s. 36(4) it is the action under which the lien is sheltered that is relevant. The section was amended by S.O. 1994, c. 27, s. 4, to resolve any doubt as to the alternative nature of these steps and the taking of only one step is required. Section 37(1).1 and .2 provide alternative routes for causing the trial of an action to realize a lien. Where a lien has expired under subs. (1), the proper course is for a motion without notice under s. 46 requesting that the lien be discharged, all security returned to the person or party that posted it, all relevant registrations vacated, and, subject to the cases discussed below, the action dismissed. The court has no residual discretion under this section.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Section 37—General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Envirofix Corporation" p2="Faber" post.rptr="20397" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I676460103b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Envirofix Corporation v. Faber">Envirofix Corporation v. Faber, 2023 CarswellOnt 20397, 2023 ONSC 7197, 2023 A.C.W.S. 6454 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lawyer failed to set the action down for trial within two years as required by s. 37 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and the plaintiff lost the ability to enforce the lien against the property. The property was sold without any payment to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff did not recover the monies owed by the owner of the property. Had the lien been valid and enforceable, the plaintiff would have had the opportunity to at least negotiate for the recovery of some of the amount outstanding on the lien or would have received some, if not all, of the amount owing on the lien following a sale. Damages were awarded on that basis, and were not nominal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="MacKenzie Group Inc." p2="Hobby Jewellery Ltd." post.rptr="3489" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I641147605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MacKenzie Group Inc. v. Hobby Jewellery Ltd.">MacKenzie Group Inc. v. Hobby Jewellery Ltd. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 3489 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On facts similar to those in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19940927" p1="UMA Engineering Ltd." p2="P.O.L. Developments Inc." ref.id="I641147615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="UMA Engineering Ltd. v. P.O.L. Developments Inc.">UMA Engineering Ltd. v. P.O.L. Developments Inc. (September 27, 1994), Eberhard J.</ref></cite> (unreported), the plaintiff's lien was to expire on February 15, 2007 unless an order was made for the trial of an action in which its lien could be enforced, or unless an action in which the lien could be enforced was set down for trial. The court clerk date-stamped the trial record for February 15, 2007, but the defendant/applicant actually received the record on February 16, 2007. The defendant was denied an order that the plaintiff's construction lien action had expired and dismissing action. The plaintiff successfully argued that R. 2 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> provided relief where the failure to comply with rules was an irregularity and did not render a proceeding or a step, document or order in a proceeding a nullity. When reasonable and positive efforts were made to comply with the legislation, and no prejudice flowed from an irregularity, relief ought to be granted pursuant to Rr. 2.01(1)(a) and 2.03 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. A court can look at all circumstances including the efforts made by a lien claimant to set the action down for trial. The plaintiff's non-compliance was a minor irregularity that did not prejudice the defendant. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court noted the decision in <ital>UMA Engineering</ital> and expressed the view that it did not correspond with the reasoning of the Divisional Court in <ital>Beaver Engineering Ltd.</ital> in subs. 37(1)2, below.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19940927" p1="UMA Engineering Ltd." p2="P.O.L. Developments Inc." ref.id="I64116e705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="UMA Engineering Ltd. v. P.O.L. Developments Inc.">UMA Engineering Ltd. v. P.O.L. Developments Inc. (September 27, 1994), Eberhard J.</ref></cite> (unreported)—A trial record was filed, with proof of service, on the last possible day. Service under R. 16.06(2), however, was not then effective and the two-year period under s. 37 passed before it became effective. The liens had expired. Rule 2 did not assist. An appeal was taken but the case settled before the appeal was heard.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 37(1)—General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions)" p2="Deltro Electric Ltd." post.rptr="8182" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64116e715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions) v. Deltro Electric Ltd.">9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions) v. Deltro Electric Ltd., 2021 ONSC 8182, 2021 CarswellOnt 19273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At the time the lien was purported to be preserved and perfected, the corporate lien claimant was dissolved due to a missed fee payment, but was subsequently revived upon its general manager filing the appropriate fee and form pursuant the <ital>Canadian Business Corporations Act</ital>. Since it was formally dissolved at the time it preserved and perfected the lien, it was not a legal entity entitled to do so, and did not comply with the required timelines set out in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Bound by the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90e52330f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the court had no discretion in equity to permit the lien action to continue. The medical issues of the general manager, including legal blindness in one eye, did not deter him from operating a business and arranging for the preserving and perfecting of the lien, and were not an excuse not to keep the company books and records in good standing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="QH Renovation & Construction Corp." p2="2460500 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3237" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64116e735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="QH Renovation & Construction Corp. v. 2460500 Ontario Ltd.">QH Renovation & Construction Corp. v. 2460500 Ontario Ltd., 2019 ONSC 3237, 2019 CarswellOnt 8577, 1 C.L.R. (5th) 76 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 10988 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is simply no authority for the proposition that the parties may, through mutual agreement or by a consent court order, agree to extend the mandatory time period set out in s. 37 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Rather, the provisions of sections 37 and 46 are mandatory.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lee" p2="Chiarella" post.rptr="7374" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64116e745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lee v. Chiarella">Lee v. Chiarella, 2018 ONSC 7374, 2018 CarswellOnt 21402, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 351 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the requirements of s. 37 of the Act have not been complied with the court “shall declare that the lien has expired and dismiss the lien action.” The Court does not have discretion to allow the lien to remain if the criteria set out in s. 37(1) are not satisfied. This is consistent with the purpose of the Act, which is to ensure that construction lien claims are dealt with in an expeditious manner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="M. Fuda Contracting Inc." p2="1291609 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4663" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641195805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M. Fuda Contracting Inc. v. 1291609 Ontario Ltd.">M. Fuda Contracting Inc. v. 1291609 Ontario Ltd., 2018 ONSC 4663, 2018 CarswellOnt 13069, 94 C.L.R. (4th) 64 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, and the relevant provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> support the conclusion that lien actions are intended to be prosecuted diligently and expeditiously, in this case a delay of 5 years in bringing a lien action to trial was not sufficient, in the specific circumstances of the case, to dismiss the plaintiff's action for delay. No lien action cases were cited here where actions were dismissed and/or liens vacated for delay, notwithstanding compliance with s. 37(1). This case was in the “grey zone” between clearly acceptable and clearly unacceptable. A careful and nuanced look at all of the prevailing circumstances, such as complexity of the matter, prejudice suffered by the parties, and the plaintiff's explanation for the delay, resulted in a closely considered decision by the court to deny the defendant's motion to dismiss the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Krypton Steel Inc." p2="Maystar General Contractors Inc." post.rptr="3836" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641195815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Krypton Steel Inc. v. Maystar General Contractors Inc.">Krypton Steel Inc. v. Maystar General Contractors Inc., 2018 ONSC 3836, 2018 CarswellOnt 9955, 92 C.L.R. (4th) 88 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 15885 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—On appeal from an order of the Master dismissing a lien claim but allowing the underlying action to continue, the court noted, in dismissing the appeal, that a specific trial date must set for the two year time period to stop running. This is “the” trial which is referred to in s. 37(1) rather than “a” trial which is not. The preconditions to an order under section 60(1) of setting the date, time and place for trial or for the holding of a settlement meeting had not been met at the time the order of the court was made. The fact that the parties advised the judge, through their consent to the order, that the conditions in s. 37(1) had been satisfied does not change the fact that they had not been.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rockhill Construction Ltd." p2="Ottens" post.rptr="2814" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641195825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rockhill Construction Ltd. v. Ottens">Rockhill Construction Ltd. v. Ottens, 2018 ONSC 2814, 2018 CarswellOnt 6911, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 262 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was which date “the commencement of the action that perfected the lien”, as provided for in s. 37, was to be calculated from: a) the date the statement of claim was issued, being October 1, 2015 or; b) the date when the statement of claim was amended to include reference to the lien registered on the property, namely October 6, 2015. In holding that the relevant date was the former, the court noted that the original statement of claim specifically pleaded that the plaintiff was entitled to a claim for a lien on the defendants' property under the Act. The addition of the registration number of the lien in the amended claim was not a new cause of action, but, rather, it simply provided particulars of an allegation already pled. There was no authority to support the position that the statement of claim had to expressly reference the registration number of the lien in order to commence the lien action. The plaintiff therefore failed to meet the deadline imposed by s. 37(1), and the defendants were entitled to an order under s. 46(1) declaring that the plaintiff's lien has expired, and an order dismissing the action to enforce the lien and vacating the registration of the claim for lien on the defendants' property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Built-Con Contracting Ltd." p2="Lisgar Construction Co." post.rptr="1720" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I641195835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Built-Con Contracting Ltd. v. Lisgar Construction Co.">Built-Con Contracting Ltd. v. Lisgar Construction Co., 2016 ONSC 1720, 2016 CarswellOnt 3494, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The default judgment obtained from a registrar over the counter was not sufficient to meet the requirements of s. 37, which requires that a perfected lien be set down for trial within two years after the action is commenced.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Delview Construction Ltd." p2="Meringolo" post.rptr="2245" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I6411bc905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo">Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2245, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 48 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—A revived corporation cannot proceed with a construction lien action, where the time limits under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for preserving and perfecting the claim for lien have expired while the corporation was dissolved.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90e57150f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved for an order discharging the claimant's lien, cancelling the bond posted, dismissing the lien action, and for costs on a substantial indemnity basis on the grounds, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that the lien claimant's charter was cancelled at the time the lien was preserved and perfected and not revived until the time limitations contained in ss. 31(2), 36(2) and 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had expired. The motions judge ordered the claimant's lien be discharged on the grounds first, that the claimant's company charter was cancelled at the time its lien was preserved and perfected, and that the charter could not be retroactively revived to validate its claim for lien and, secondly, on the basis that the charter was revived after the time limits in the Act had expired. The Divisional Court reversed the lower court's holding that the Articles of Revival of October 1, 2002 did not effectively retroactively validate all actions taken by the claimant subsequent to its corporate dissolution, including the preservation and perfection of its claim of lien. The cancellation of a charter did not render a company non-existent, nor its acts absolute nullities, but rather a company was in a legal state of limbo capable of restoration by Articles of Revival which have effect for all purposes <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>, save for rights acquired by any person in the interim. The Divisional Court upheld the motions judge's ruling that the lapse of limitation period between the claimant's dissolution and its revival was an acquired legal right of the defendant upon which the latter was entitled to rely.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Haflidson" p2="Salandy" post.rptr="284" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I6411bc925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haflidson v. Salandy">Haflidson v. Salandy (2002), 16 C.L.R. (3d) 284, 2002 CarswellOnt 1698 (Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien for services and materials provided to a renovation was perfected in 1997 when the claim was issued, and the action was set down for trial on the last possible day, preventing the lien from expiring. The plaintiff waited until 2001 to obtain a judgment of reference, and a further three months to obtain a trial date. There was no evidence before the court to explain the plaintiff's lengthy delay in proceeding with this action. However, while the delay was lengthy, there was no evidence that it was intentional. As well, while there was inordinate and inexcusable delay on the part of the plaintiff, the defendants filed no evidence of prejudice, and the evidence presented fell short of identifying any substantial risk that a fair trial could not be conducted. Nor was there any evidence of serious actual prejudice to the defendants such as would arise if a witness or documents were no longer available. In a motion to dismiss for delay, it was not sufficient to assume prejudice by the mere passage of time, and the motion was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90e59860f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—When a lien action is not set down for trial within two years of its commencement, there is, nonetheless, discretion to permit a claim on the contract to continue. The avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings guides the interpretation of s. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d) of the Act. The court has discretion to dismiss an action or to proceed without the lien aspect of the claim, as circumstances dictate. All arguments against denying a defendant the procedures and protections of the usual form of litigation can be answered by court's discretion under s. 47(1)(d) to dismiss the action because the defendant will be prejudiced or because little has transpired in the action that would be duplicated or by imposing conditions for continuance to assure protection of the defendant. The legislature intended more than claims for liens to be litigated in lien actions. That intention is best served by an interpretation of s. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d) that leaves it to the court to monitor the interests of the parties and the procedure to be followed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Jordan Construction Management Inc." p2="Simcoe County Roman Catholic School Board" post.rptr="2535" pre.rptr="[1996]" ref.id="I6411bc945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Jordan Construction Management Inc. v. Simcoe County Roman Catholic School Board">Jordan Construction Management Inc. v. Simcoe County Roman Catholic School Board (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 2535, 1996 CarswellOnt 2631 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff served the defendant with the trial record by facsimile transmission, but no consent for such service was obtained as required by R. 16.05(3.2), compliance with that rule was dispensed with so that service was validated in a timely manner, and there was no breach of s. 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Mohiuddin" p2="Ahmadiyya Movement in Islam (Ontario) Inc." post.rptr="127" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I6411e3a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mohiuddin v. Ahmadiyya Movement in Islam (Ontario) Inc.">Mohiuddin v. Ahmadiyya Movement in Islam (Ontario) Inc. (1995), 24 C.L.R. (2d) 127, [1995] O.J. No. 2641 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—After a series of unsuccessful attempts to cross-examine the plaintiff lien claimant, the defendant successfully moved to dismiss the plaintiff's claim. With new counsel, the plaintiff served a Notice of Appeal, thereby staying the order dismissing its action and the defendant moved to quash arguing that in the meanwhile the lien had expired under s. 37. The appellant relied upon the Court of Appeal's jurisdiction under the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-43, s. 134, to make any interim order it saw fit to prevent prejudice to a party making an appeal. The court discussed the issue but did not decide it, as, it transpired that, due to the appellant's inaction, the appeal had not been perfected until after the two-year period had expired. The plaintiff's appeal was therefore quashed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Sayers & Associates Ltd." p2="United Centre Inc." post.rptr="42" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I6411e3a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sayers & Associates Ltd. v. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 37(1) does not require a lien claimant to both set a trial date as well as set a matter down for trial within the stipulated two year time frame. Instead, it provides that the claimant must obtain a fixed trial date within two years of the date of the commencement of the action or must set the action down for trial within that same period. If either of these conditions are fulfilled, the lien will not expire pursuant to the section. Therefore, s. 37(1)(a) and (b) provide alternative routes for causing the trial of an action to realize a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Creative Design Consultants" p2="Dawson" post.rptr="193" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I6411e3a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Creative Design Consultants v. Div.)</ref></cite>—The actions set out in s. 37(1)1 and 2 should be read disjunctively, so that the taking of either action will preserve the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd." p2="Samet" post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I6411e3a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet">Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet (1991), 46 C.L.R. 317, 4 O.R. (3d) 771, 83 D.L.R. (4th) 574, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Schultz (Benjamin) & Associates Ltd. v. Samet)</ital> 52 O.A.C. 180 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In November 1989, the defendant moved under s. 46 to vacate a lien action on account of the plaintiff's failure to set the action down for trial within the time limits set out in s. 37. Although the action was set down for trial in December 1989, the Master declared the lien expired and ordered registration of the claim for lien to be vacated. The plaintiff's appeal was dismissed. Sections 37(1) and 46 were mandatory and left no room for judicial discretion. The court had no residual discretion to allow a lien action to proceed as an action different from its original form as a construction lien action. Sections 38 and 65, which preserve legal and equitable remedies of the court and allow it to award a personal judgment whether or not a lien is proven, do not render s. 37 and 46 inoperative.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Burnt Hill Developments Ltd." p2="Eglinton Village Ltd." post.rptr="874" pre.rptr="1992" ref.id="I560b5760fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Burnt Hill Developments Ltd. v. Eglinton Village Ltd.">Burnt Hill Developments Ltd. v. Eglinton Village Ltd. (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 874, 5 C.L.R. (2d) 52 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The trial was not formally set down. The plaintiff did manage to obtain an order within the two-year period that “… trial to be expedited: assignment Court September 8/92”, however, the court noted that a formal order was not taken out and that, as it had no discretion in the matter, the lien had to be declared expired and the action dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Rainone Construction Ltd." p2="American Barrick Resources Corp." post.rptr="259" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I64120ab15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rainone Construction Ltd. v. American Barrick Resources Corp.">Rainone Construction Ltd. v. American Barrick Resources Corp. (1991), 43 C.L.R. 259 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claim that was sheltered under the claim of another lien claimant was held to have expired two years from the date of the prior lien's perfection and not from the date of the issuance of its own statement of claim. Accordingly, s. 46 of the Act dictated that the plaintiff's lien action be dismissed and its lien be vacated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co." p2="Iona Corp." post.rptr="266" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I64120ab25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co. v. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully applied for an order dismissing a lien action on the ground that it had not been set down for trial within two years of the commencement of the action. The plaintiff had argued that the defendant was estopped from relying on the limitation period because the defendant was in breach of two court orders requiring it to honour undertakings given at the examination for discovery. Sections 37 and 46 of the Act are mandatory, and the court has no discretion to refuse to dismiss an action if no date for trial is fixed within two years of the date of commencement of the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="U.C.L.
