High Glen Development Ltd.">U.C.L. Underground Construction Ltd. v. High Glen Development Ltd. (1990), 42 C.L.R. 1, 75 O.R. (2d) 603 (Master)</ref></cite>—Section 37 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not discriminate, within the meaning of s. 15(1) of the <ital>Charter of Rights</ital>, against those who pursue actions through the Act as opposed to those who file a general civil claim. Nothing forces a plaintiff to use the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and so it cannot be considered discriminatory. Additionally, if the construction lien action is not set down within the two-year period, what the plaintiff loses is its right to a lien, but it does not lose its right to bring an action in the courts to enforce its claim. By arranging for discovery, a party was not estopped from raising the two-year limitation period under s. 37(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="C.S. Yachts Ltd." post.rptr="192" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I64120ab45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd. (1990), 46 C.L.R. 192 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A court does not have authority to extend or interfere with the two-year limitation period provided under s. 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for setting down an action for trial. In such circumstances, the court is required to dismiss the action to enforce the lien pursuant to s. 46(1) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Ramrock Electric" p2="Lords & Ladies" post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I641231c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ramrock Electric v. Lords & Ladies">Ramrock Electric v. Lords & Ladies (1989), 34 C.L.R. 26 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Section 37 of the Act eliminates any lien from further validity upon the expiry of two years if no date for trial is fixed within two years of the date of commencement of the action. The effect of this section is to invalidate encumbrances to the land of third parties simply by the operation of time.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Section 37(1)1</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Hugomark Services Inc." p2="Ontario" post.rptr="126" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I641231c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hugomark Services Inc. v. Ontario">Hugomark Services Inc. v. Ontario, 2012 ONSC 126, 2012 CarswellOnt 256, 17 C.L.R. (4th) 301 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff brought an application to amend pleadings, but the judgment on the application would not be delivered until after the deadline would have passed to set the action down for trial pursuant to s. 37. Distinguishing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I641231c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the court granted the plaintiff leave to the set action down within the s. 37 deadline based on existing pleadings. The trial record could be filed with the pleadings as they existed and on a “without prejudice” basis to both parties to file whatever materials were necessary. The plaintiff had not engaged in undue delay in seeking the amendment, and the defendant was attempting to obtain a tactical advantage which was not warranted in the circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I641231c35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The “order” contemplated by s. 37(1)1 is a legally valid order made with lawful jurisdiction. An order under s. 60(1) cannot validly be made by a Master unless there is already a judgment of reference under s. 58(1). Where there was no judgment of reference, and the order merely provided for the trial to take place “in the week of October 30, 2000 or such subsequent date as may be agreed to be between counsel or ordered by this court”, such wording was not sufficient to be an “order” within s. 61 and 37(1)1. The lien was held to have expired.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 37(1)2</bold></name></name.block></head><feature.para.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><ital>Authors' Note</ital>:</name></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Regard should be had to changes in Rule 48 regarding setting down, eliminating the previous 15-day period.</para.text></para></feature.para.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Common Ground Architecture Inc." p2="Naccarato" post.rptr="4563" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641258d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Common Ground Architecture Inc. v. Naccarato">Common Ground Architecture Inc. v. Naccarato, 2014 ONSC 4563, 2014 CarswellOnt 13864, 44 C.L.R. (4th) 269 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was perfected, and the action set down for trial six days short of the two-year time limit under s. 37(1)2. It was subsequently struck off the list, having been struck off five times earlier, for various reasons, and at the request of various parties, including the defendants. The plaintiff was then ordered dissolved by the provincial Corporate Tax Branch for tax arrears, although it was later revived. In dismissing the defendants' motion to vacate the lien, the court noted that there was no ambiguity in s. 37(1)2, and no discretion to grant relief from its terms, for delay in proceeding expeditiously after the action was set down for trial. As well, the plaintiff's dissolution did not mean that its lien became a nullity, or that its real or personal property ceased to exist. Additionally, its inchoate property like the chose in action, in support of which the lien was registered, continued to exist. The right under Rule 24.01(e) to have the action dismissed, which the defendant acquired during the plaintiff's dissolution, was not a “right” of the type referred to in s. 242(5) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1475707 Ontario Inc." p2="Foran" post.rptr="6882" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641258d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1475707 Ontario Inc. v. Foran">1475707 Ontario Inc. v. Foran, 2013 ONSC 6882, 2013 CarswellOnt 15238, 117 O.R. (3d) 772, 316 O.A.C. 153 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2014 ONCA 830, 2014 CarswellOnt 16470, 123 O.R. (3d) 1, 36 C.L.R. (4th) 1, 64 C.P.C. (7th) 1, 378 D.L.R. (4th) 548, 328 O.A.C. 201 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—At the time the action was set down for trial, the plaintiff had not yet delivered a defence to counterclaim. The setting down for trial was subsequently vacated by the motions judge, who held that the plaintiff's lien claim had expired because it had not then been properly set down within two years from the commencement of the action. The plaintiff's appeal was allowed and leave was granted to file an amended trial record. Contrary to the suggestion in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ravenda Homes Ltd." p2="1372708 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="250" pre.rptr="90" ref.id="I641258d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc.">Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc., 90 C.L.R. (3d) 250, 2010 CarswellOnt 721 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, a trial record which does not comply with the Rules is not necessarily a nullity. The purpose of s. 37 is to promote a speedy trial of construction lien actions, and there was no reason why the motions judge could not have granted leave to the plaintiff to file an amended record containing the missing defence to the counterclaim and leaving the lien claim alive, given that the trial record was originally filed within two years. There was no reason to believe that an injustice would necessarily result if the original trial record were not struck, a condition mandated by rule 2.01(1)(b) before a step in a proceeding may be set aside. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: It was argued in dissent that s. 37 was an unqualified declaratory provision, and that the Act recognized no allowance for granting relief to those who do not comply with it, regardless of the reason for the non-compliance.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Eurodale Developments Inc." p2="Rimgate Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="13933" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I90e634a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Eurodale Developments Inc. v. Rimgate Holdings Ltd.">Eurodale Developments Inc. v. Rimgate Holdings Ltd., 2012 CarswellOnt 13933, 2012 ONSC 6031 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff successfully moved for leave to conduct examinations for discovery notwithstanding that it had filed a trial record. Whatever the record disclosed in terms of the dispute between counsel for the parties respecting the order and timing of discoveries, there was nothing to suggest the plaintiff was foregoing the process of production and discoveries, and that it only filed a trial record to save its lien claims within the time limit stipulated in s. 37 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Deslaurier Custom Cabinets Inc." p2="6383009 Canada Inc." post.rptr="3350" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64127fe05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Deslaurier Custom Cabinets Inc. v. 6383009 Canada Inc.">Deslaurier Custom Cabinets Inc. v. 6383009 Canada Inc., 2012 ONSC 3350, 2012 CarswellOnt 7205, 21 C.L.R. (4th) 130 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2012 ONSC 5490, 2012 CarswellOnt 12700, 21 C.L.R. (4th) 144 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The requirement under s. 37(1)2 is not that “the action that perfected the lien” be set down for trial or ordered for trial but that “an action” be set down. That action need not be an action in which the lien “will be” or “must be” enforced but an action in which the lien “may be enforced”. The plain wording of s. 37 therefore suggests that it is sufficient if another action in which the lien may be enforced is set down for trial. Though the Act requires specific timely steps to preserve and protect lien rights, it does not require every party to duplicate every step. As an example, the sheltering rules provide that it is only necessary for one lien claimant to commence an action. Similarly any one lien claimant may take the initiative to obtain a trial date. It is not necessary (though it may be prudent) for each of the parties to do so independently. This is not to say that lien claimants may always rely on the actions of other lien claimants to preserve their rights. The actions which perfect liens or protect a perfected lien from expiring must occur within the times set out in the Act. If a particular lien has expired at the time the step is taken, it will not be saved by the actions of the other lien claimant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ravenda Homes Ltd." p2="1372708 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="250" pre.rptr="90" ref.id="I64127fe15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc.">Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc., 90 C.L.R. (3d) 250, 2010 CarswellOnt 721 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a matter involving a technical procedural point, the defendant argued that the liens had expired because the actions that perfected the liens were not set down for trial within two years of their commencement, as required by s. 37(1). Although the plaintiff delivered trial records within the two-year period, the defendant contended that pleadings were still open at the time and did not close until the two years had passed, thereby placing the plaintiff in breach of s. 37(1) because an action could be set down for trial until pleadings were closed. The plaintiff had served a reply and defence to counterclaim in the lien actions, five days before the liens were to expire under s. 37(1), in response to the defendant's statement of defence and counterclaim served almost one year earlier and which itself followed service of the statement of claim by one year. The defendant contended that, in accordance with rule 27.06, it had ten days to deliver a Reply to defence to counterclaim, and that during that ten-day period, pleadings remained open and the lien actions could not be set down for trial. The defendant's argument failed. In a construction-lien action, a reply is a permitted pleading only with leave of the court. The reply served by the plaintiff was therefore a nullity. It followed that the defendant did not have the right to serve a reply to defence to counterclaim, and acquiescence by the defendant to the plaintiff having served a reply could not afford the plaintiff a right available only with leave of the court. Accordingly, when the defendant served its statement of defence and counterclaim, the only permitted pleading remaining was a defence to counterclaim, and pleadings were closed in the lien actions after it was served.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Mueller-Hein Corp." p2="Donar Investments Ltd." post.rptr="2223" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I64127fe25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mueller-Hein Corp. v. Donar Investments Ltd.">Mueller-Hein Corp. v. Donar Investments Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2223, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 143 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant was noted in default, a trial record was filed, the action placed on the Construction Lien trial list and a requisition for trial was completed. However, the requisition and trial record inadvertently noted the incorrect action number, while the Statement of Claim correctly stated it. In the circumstances, the action was held to be set down for trial within the required two-year period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="T.R. Renovations Ltd." p2="Mississauga (City)" post.rptr="873" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I64127fe35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="T.R. Renovations Ltd. v. Mississauga (City)">T.R. Renovations Ltd. v. Mississauga (City) (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 873, 2003 CarswellOnt 843, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 295 (S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 1213 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien action was consolidated with three other construction lien actions into one action and the consolidated action was set down for trial for the purposes of s. 37 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, with the trial record to be set down in due course. Subsequently, the relevant action was severed from the consolidated action on consent order, with the trial record referred to in the consolidation order being served more than two years after the commencement of the action. The limitation period did not run during the time the action was part of the consolidated action. There was nothing in the Act or case law to support the proposition that the effect of s. 37 was somehow undone by the deconsolidation order. The argument that the lien expired pursuant to the provisions of subs. 37(1) and s. 46 of the Act took no account of the time period during which the action was part of the consolidated action for which the limitation period had ceased to run because the action had been ordered to be set down for trial. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="601039 Ontario Ltd." p2="Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd." post.rptr="135" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I64127fe45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="601039 Ontario Ltd. v. Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd.">601039 Ontario Ltd. v. Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 135, 5 O.R. (3d) 26 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, properly construed, supported the argument that the consolidation could impact on the two-year limitation period in s. 37(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Clarkway Construction Co." p2="Stars of Malwa Investments Inc." post.rptr="312" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I64127fe55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarkway Construction Co. v. Stars of Malwa Investments Inc.">Clarkway Construction Co. v. Stars of Malwa Investments Inc. (2001), 7 C.L.R. (3d) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff served and filed the trial record in an effort to ensure compliance with s. 37 of the Act, the defendant argued that pursuant to R. 48.04 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, the plaintiff was no longer entitled to discovery of the defendant. While the court was not persuaded that there was an inconsistency or direct conflict between the Rules and the Act in this case, it did acknowledge tension between the strict requirement of s. 37 and the consequences of setting an action down as prescribed by r. 48.04. It was clear that the plaintiff had been trying to obtain discovery of the defendant and there was no evidence to suggest that the plaintiff was intending to forego the discovery process. Especially in regard to the practice outside of Toronto, construction lien matters may, by necessity, be put on the trial list before they are ready to proceed. Accordingly, it was an appropriate case in which to grant the leave allowed under R. 48.04 for discoveries to proceed, notwithstanding that a trial record had been served and filed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="D.W. Buchanan Construction Ltd." p2="Bruce (Township)" post.rptr="180" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I6412a6f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.W. Buchanan Construction Ltd. v. Bruce (Township)">D.W. Buchanan Construction Ltd. v. Bruce (Township) (1996), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 180 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Buchanan commenced its lien action, then an order for trial was made in another lien action, these two actions and others were consolidated, and all but the Buchanan action settled. The defendant moved successfully under s. 46 the two-year period under s. 37 having expired. It was reasoned that as the Buchanan action was not consolidated when the order for trial was made, it could not rely on the order of trial to stop its own two-year expiration period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Alros Products Ltd. (c.o.b. Polytarp Product)" p2="Cambridge Leaseholds Ltd." post.rptr="265" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I6412a6f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alros Products Ltd. (c.o.b. Polytarp Product) v. Cambridge Leaseholds Ltd.">Alros Products Ltd. (c.o.b. Polytarp Product) v. Cambridge Leaseholds Ltd. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 265 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In Ontario it has been the widely accepted practice to include the text of the claim for lien in the statement of claim, or to attach a copy of the claim for lien as a schedule, the only purpose being to ensure that the lien information is conveyed to the defendant in the fullest and most convenient manner. There is no requirement that the text of the lien be included in that statement of claim or that the lien documents be attached as schedule. The court rejected the defendant's argument that the amended statement of claim was served in a deficient condition, and that the action could not be said to have been set down properly or at all. Apart from the missing Schedule “A”, the statement of claim in the present action was not otherwise not deficient.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="94" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I6412a6f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 94 (Ont. Gen. Div.); supplementary reasons at (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 85 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 1337, 1996 CarswellOnt 1312 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—It is sufficient that the action under which lien claims have been sheltered is set down for trial. It is not necessary that the sheltered lien claimants each take further action to comply with the terms of s. 37. None of the subject lien claimants could have set down their “action” for trial since none had started separate actions of their own. It is also unnecessary that each lien claimant be specifically mentioned in any subsequent order of the court before they are entitled to prove their claim at the trial of the action. Nor is it mandatory that a sheltered claimant participate in any settlement meeting which may be held during the course of the proceedings, although it runs the risk of having an order made against it in its absence at that meeting. On March 20, 1996, an appeal to the Divisional Court unanimously upheld the decision of the trial judge and accepted her reasons.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Beaver Engineering Ltd." p2="Swedlove" post.rptr="54" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I6412ce005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beaver Engineering Ltd. v. Swedlove">Beaver Engineering Ltd. v. Swedlove (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 54, 17 O.R. (3d) 355 (Div. Ct.); reversing (1993), 109 D.L.R. (4th) 557 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimants followed the long-standing local practice, as outlined by the trial co-ordinator at Ottawa, with respect to the setting down of construction lien actions. Unfortunately, the local practice did not comply with the rules, and the motions court judge held that the liens had expired on the grounds that s. 37 of the Act had not been complied with. On appeal, the court found that in the special circumstances of this case, it was in the interests of justice to grant relief to the lien claimants pursuant to Ontario Rr. 2.01(1)(a) and 2.03. If relief were not granted to the lien claimants, their actions against the respondent would be dismissed, a consequence of far greater significance to them than any consequence the respondent might suffer if the relief were granted. Accordingly, compliance with the procedure outlined by the trial co-ordinator at Ottawa was deemed to be sufficient compliance with the Act and R. 48.02(1) in order to satisfy the requirements of s. 37(1) of the Act. In the result, the liens had not expired.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="Bracknell Corp." post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I6412ce015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp. (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 171 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1993), 12 B.L.R. (2d) 113, 110 D.L.R. (4th) 390 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—When a stay of proceedings resulting from the arbitration of the matter potentially threatened the dismissal of the action pursuant to s. 37(1)(b) [now s. 37(1) 2], the parties agreed to a temporary lifting of the stay sufficient to set the action down for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Johnsons Home Centre Inc." p2="Greco" post.rptr="181" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I6412ce025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Johnsons Home Centre Inc. v. Greco">Johnsons Home Centre Inc. v. Greco (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 181 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff registered its lien on April 24, 1990 and its certificate of action on May 24, 1990. When the action was not set down for trial within two years as required by s. 37(1) of the Act, the defendants moved to dismiss the action. Held, the motion was dismissed. The plaintiff had diligently pursued every available means to comply with the requirements of s. 37, but was unable to obtain a date for the trial because the court's administration made it impossible to do so. In such circumstances, the court found that the plaintiff had satisfied the requirements of s. 37(1)(b) [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, ss. 31(1), (2).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19931217" p1="K-W Blair Readymix" p2="Matsias" ref.id="I6412ce035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K-W Blair Readymix v. Matsias">K-W Blair Readymix v. Matsias (December 17, 1993), Doc. Kitchener 3213/90 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—While the entitlement to a lien must be established upon a strict interpretation of the Act, the incidents of that right should be determined on the basis of a liberal interpretation. Following that approach, in interpreting the wording of s. 37(1)(a) and (b), the court held that a perfected lien expires where neither an action has been set down nor a day for trial has been set within the statutory period. Since in this case an action was set down within the required time, the perfected lien continued in force.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Eurocor Ltd." p2="Vernich" post.rptr="631" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I6412f5105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich">Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich (1992), 9 O.R. (3d) 631, 2 C.L.R. (2d) 208 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claim was dismissed where the owners moved under ss. 37(1)(b) and 46 of the Act on the ground that it had not been set down for trial within two years. The court had no discretion under the Act, but the contractor's claim for breach of contract was allowed to continue.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="601039 Ontario Ltd." p2="Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd." post.rptr="135" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I6412f5115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="601039 Ontario Ltd. v. Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd.">601039 Ontario Ltd. v. Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 135, 5 O.R. (3d) 26 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—After three liens were perfected and actions commenced, the court ordered the actions to be consolidated with an action involving a fourth lien. The defendant unsuccessfully moved to have the first three liens dismissed for failure of the actions involving the initial three liens to be set down for trial within the time prescribed in s. 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Subsection 61(2)(a) of the Act allowed the court to consolidate several actions into one action. The actions involving the first three liens were consolidated into the fourth action which was set down within the time prescribed in s. 37(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Graham Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Correct Building Corp." post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I6412f5125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Graham Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Correct Building Corp.">Graham Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Correct Building Corp. (1991), 46 C.L.R. 205 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendants in a lien action brought a motion for an order dismissing the action pursuant to ss. 37 and 46 of the Act on the basis that the perfected lien expired because it was not set down for trial within two years of the date of commencement of the action. The plaintiff claimed that since the defendants engaged in settlement negotiations they were estopped from relying upon the two-year limitation period. The motion was allowed. There existed no basis for applying the doctrine of estoppel by conduct under the circumstances of this case. The defendants had not deliberately misled or deceived the plaintiffs into believing that they were not relying on the limitation period. There were no representations, either express or implied, that the defendants did not intend to rely on the limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Ionion Construction Inc." p2="Christo" post.rptr="135" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I6412f5135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ionion Construction Inc. v. Christo">Ionion Construction Inc. v. Christo (1991), 46 C.L.R. 135 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The steps taken in having a settlement meeting and in scheduling a pre-trial did not constitute setting down the action for trial within the meaning of s. 37(1) of the Act. The plaintiff had fallen short of complying with s. 37 and had not made out a case on estoppel or waiver by the defendants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Dal Bello" p2="Serrani" post.rptr="83" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I6412f5145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dal Bello v. Serrani">Dal Bello v. Serrani (1991), 44 C.L.R. 83 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff registered its claim for lien, issued a statement of claim, served its trial record on the defendants' solicitors, and filed an affidavit of service with the Court Registrar. A settlement meeting was held between the parties, but there was never a formal settlement. The court rejected the defendants' argument that the lien had expired because it had not been set down for trial within the required period. When faced with a procedural ambiguity, the Act directs in s. 69(3) that resort may be had to the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. The plaintiff had complied with R. 48.02(1) by serving the trial record and had, therefore, satisfied s. 37(1)(b) of the Act in setting the construction lien action down for trial within the requisite two-year period. Although the notice of readiness required by R. 48.02(1)(a) was not served and filed, R. 48.02(1)(a) is not mandatory in construction lien actions, and the requirement to serve and file a notice of readiness in construction lien actions should not be followed.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 37(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1351150 Ontario Inc." p2="Chartrand" post.rptr="6980" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I6412f5155fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1351150 Ontario Inc. v. Chartrand">1351150 Ontario Inc. v. Chartrand (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6980 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the defendant's solicitor successfully removed himself from the record, the court found no valid ground to order setting the action down <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> in order to avoid the mandatory provisions of ss. 37 and 46 of the Act. The rationale of the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="5779" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I6412f5165fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5779, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2006] O.J. No. 3817 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, was applicable here. The action would have had to be set down for trial whether or not the defendant's solicitor had brought a motion to be removed as solicitor of record. It was not a case where the evidence disclosed wilful conduct by the former solicitor to mislead the plaintiff's lawyer.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I64131c205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 138 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3385 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3338, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 5 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5779, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In a novel case, the defendants moved to have the plaintiff's lien declared expired for failure to set the matter down for trial within the two-year period stipulated in s. 37(1) of the Act. However, that two-year period expired during a time when the Divisional Court had under reserve the question of whether the supply made by the plaintiffs was “lienable”. The plaintiff asserted a situation of impossibility, arguing that it was contrary to the policy of the Act to be expected to fix a date for the trial of the lien action when the foundation of that claim was being challenged in an appellate court. As such, the plaintiff argued that this case was unlike previous cases where the expiry of the two-year period arose owing to action or inaction between the parties to the litigation themselves, and the reserve period ought to suspend the running of that expiry period because it results from an action of the court, not the parties. The court found, on the authority of the Court of Appeal's <ital>obiter</ital> in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Mohiuddin" p2="Ahmadiyya Movement in Islam (Ontario) Inc." post.rptr="127" pre.rptr="24" ref.id="I64131c215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mohiuddin v. Ahmadiyya Movement in Islam (Ontario) Inc.">Mohiuddin v. Ahmadiyya Movement in Islam (Ontario) Inc. (1995), 24 C.L.R. (2d) 127, 85 O.A.C. 362, 1995 CarswellOnt 954 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, that there may well be circumstances, such as when a matter central to the litigation between the parties is subject to reserve by an appellate court and where the failure to set the matter down for trial within the two-year period does not result from action or inaction of the parties themselves, where relief of the type sought by the plaintiff ought to be granted. However, the court stated that no evidence was advanced by the plaintiff of impossibility, and there was no material before the court to demonstrate that the plaintiff attempted to set the action down for trial within the two-year period and was refused permission to do so by court officials, or that it took any other concrete steps to meet either of the two stipulations set out in s. 37 of the Act. There was no evidence in support of the assertion that to seek to set the matter down for trial during the two-year period, while a fundamental legal issue in the case was subject to appellate review, would have contravened the policy directives that are embodied in the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
38:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 38.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">38:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision was first introduced in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. It has remained unchanged to date.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides lien and trust remedies and a complete code for the enforcement of those remedies, but it does not purport to be, nor is it, an exclusive remedy. It takes nothing away from a creditor's other remedies, such as an action for breach of contract.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Biotechnik" p2="848835 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="6794" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I641343305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Biotechnik v. 848835 Ontario Inc.">Biotechnik v. 848835 Ontario Inc., 2021 ONSC 6794, 2021 CarswellOnt 16675 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed in part <ital>1191650 Ontario Limited v. 848835 Ontario Inc.</ital>, 2022 ONSC 6574, 2022 CarswellOnt 16848 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—While a construction lien is a statutory remedy and therefore not governed by the (ON) <ital>Limitations Act 2002</ital> (“LA 2002”), the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not specify a limitation period applicable to claims for breach of contract joined with actions to enforce claims for lien. Therefore, there is no conflict between the <ital>CLA</ital> and the LA 2002, and pursuant to s. 19 of the LA 2002, the limitation period applied to contractual claims joined with lien claims. Here, the underlying claim was for breach of contract that was joined with an action to enforce a claim for a lien, and the transitional rules of the LA 2002 applied such that there was no limitation period on the lien claimant's right to enforce its lien judgment obtained in 1999.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="EDA Development Group Inc." p2="Zhou et al" post.rptr="6491" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I641343315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="EDA Development Group Inc. v. Zhou et al">EDA Development Group Inc. v. Zhou et al, 2021 ONSC 6491, 2021 CarswellOnt 13617 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff failed to set the matter down for trial within the statutory two-year period, the lien was dismissed and the certificate of action was vacated. The defendant's motion to dismiss the action was dismissed and the matter allowed to proceed as a contract action, to be decided on its merits. A motion judge has discretion to permit a claim on the contract to continue without a lien claim, and here, the defendant showed no evidence of prejudice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd." p2="Kaplan et al" post.rptr="4592" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I641343325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd. v. Kaplan et al">A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd. v. Kaplan et al, 2019 ONSC 4592, 2019 CarswellOnt 13144, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 79 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not contemplate that dismissal of a lien constitutes dismissal of any underlying non-contractual cause of action. While the Act contemplates a dismissal of the “action to enforce the lien” where a lien has expired, the underlying claim is not extinguished by such an order. A plaintiff is still able to proceed against the defendant in relation to the underlying cause.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Edgcumbe" p2="Vicary" post.rptr="2656" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641343335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgcumbe v. Vicary">Edgcumbe v. Vicary, 2018 ONSC 2656, 2018 CarswellOnt 8420, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff's lien was held to have expired pursuant to section 37(1), the court was called upon to determine whether it had discretion to allow the action to continue as a regular action. Referencing, inter alia, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90e74610f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd." p2="Smiley" post.rptr="6037" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64136a405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley">K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley, 2015 ONSC 6037, 2015 CarswellOnt 14820, 54 C.L.R. (4th) 315 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, it concluded that it had discretion to allow the contractual actions to continue.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd." p2="Smiley" post.rptr="6037" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64136a415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley">K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley, 2015 ONSC 6037, 2015 CarswellOnt 14820, 54 C.L.R. (4th) 315, 340 O.A.C. 89 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Summary dismissal of contract claims as a result of expiry of lien rights would significantly affect a plaintiff's legal right to recover on its contract claims, and thus run counter to the express wording of s. 38. The legislature never intended that s. 46(1) be used for mandatory summary dismissal of contract claims without notice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sirro Brothers Cement Finishing & Spray Ltd." p2="Wedgewood Brockville Inc." post.rptr="5389" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64136a425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sirro Brothers Cement Finishing & Spray Ltd. v. Wedgewood Brockville Inc.">Sirro Brothers Cement Finishing & Spray Ltd. v. Wedgewood Brockville Inc., 2012 ONSC 5389, 2012 CarswellOnt 12094 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While the statement of claim was issued in order to perfect a construction lien which was subsequently vacated, wat is not restricted in its terms to an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The order vacating the lien and the certificate of action under the Act did not purport to address the claim in contract. It is settled that a motion to dismiss an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> may allow for the action to continue in breach of contract, there being no other impediments.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Hewitt" p2="Rennie" post.rptr="304" pre.rptr="72" ref.id="I64136a435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hewitt v. Rennie">Hewitt v. Rennie (2008), 72 C.L.R. (3d) 304, 2008 CarswellOnt 1035 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff purchaser initiated a lien action over an aborted purchase and sale agreement after having made pre-closing improvements to the vendor's residence. Following expiration of the lien, the plaintiff consented to an order dismissing the action. The plaintiff then commenced an action for loss of bargain and included a sum with respect to the improvements that had been the subject of the lien action. The defendant sought dismissal of the action on the basis, <ital>inter alia</ital>, of <ital>res judicata</ital>. The court ruled that as the lien action was dismissed on a consent basis without the merits being considered, s. 38 permitted the second action, and the previous order was not a bar to the proceedings. The clear intent of s. 38 was to permit these claims to proceed, particularly when they were not two parallel actions going forward.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Thompson" p2="Sheehan" post.rptr="117" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I64136a445fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thompson v. Sheehan">Thompson v. Sheehan (2000), 5 C.L.R. (3d) 117 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 3775 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 38 does nothing more than preserve the right of a person whose lien has expired to maintain a claim for whatever rights or remedies he or she may otherwise have. It does not purport to alter or extend any applicable limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd." p2="Samet" post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I641391505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet">Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet (1991), 46 C.L.R. 317, 4 O.R. (3d) 771, 83 D.L.R. (4th) 574, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Schultz (Benjamin) & Associates Ltd. v. Samet)</ital> 52 O.A.C. 180 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Sections 38 and 65, which preserve legal and equitable remedies of the court and allow it to award a personal judgment whether or not a lien is proven, do not render ss. 37 and 46 inoperative.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="612354 Ontario Ltd." p2="Tonecraft Corp." post.rptr="799" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I90e76d20f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp.">612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp. (1991), 1991 CarswellOnt 799, 5 O.R. (3d) 764, 47 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The expiry of a claim for lien prior to trial does not oust the jurisdiction of the court to hear an action for personal judgment. The mandatory provisions of s. 46(1) requiring the court to dismiss an action to enforce a claim for lien do not apply to dismissal of actions for personal judgment. Subsection 47(1)(d) applies to such actions and gives the court discretion. This conclusion is supported by s. 38, which keeps the expiration of a lien from affecting any other legal or equitable rights, and the general provisions of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, which are intended to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings and secure the just, most expeditious and least expensive determination of a proceeding on its merits.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 39.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">39:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In addition to being amended to address landlords under subsection 19(1) of the Act, section 39 of the Act was amended to require a “state of accounts” for the purposes of the section (ss. 4.1).</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Paragraph 1 of subsection 39(1) of the Act was amended to add a requirement that an owner or contractor must provide information as to whether the contract provides that it is based on the completion of specified phases or milestones</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A new subsection (4.2) was added to the section regarding information to be provided by a mortgagee in case of mixed purpose mortgages, requiring a breakdown of amounts advanced by purpose</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A statutory right to information first appeared in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35. Section 27 of that Act entitled lien holders to information from the owner as to the terms of the contract or agreement with the contractor in respect of which the work was done or the materials supplied. The right was limited in that it allowed only a lien holder to request from an owner or its agent the terms of the contract with a contractor and the amounts due and unpaid. Section 28 of the 1896 Act provided for the possibility of a summary application for an order by the Court to an owner or its agent to permit any lien holder to inspect the contract. Section 30 of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69, consolidated these two sections into one section under the heading “Information to be given Lien Holder”. Lien holders' rights to information remained virtually unchanged until the <ital>Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30. Section 29(2) of that Act permitted lien holders to demand from mortgagees or unpaid vendors the terms of any mortgage or agreement for the purchase of the lands showing the advances made or the amount owing to the vendor, as well as liability for failing to respond or knowingly falsely stating the terms of the mortgage or the agreement. The subsection entitling the lien holder to inspect a contract was expanded to include the right to production and inspection of the mortgage or agreement with the vendor. Section 32 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 was in substantially the same form as s. 29 of the 1923 Act. Significant changes were introduced in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The Attorney General's Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> stated that the philosophy underlying the new section was to require the disclosure of only that information which facilitated the enforcement of rights under the Act. Consistent with this philosophy, production of the contract was no longer required. These 1983 amendments also, and for the first time, extended the rights to information to beneficiaries of the statutory trust. The 1983 revisions specifically enumerated the type of information that could be requested from an owner, contractor, subcontractor, mortgagee or unpaid vendor. The decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dominion Bridge Co." p2="Marla Construction Co." post.rptr="453" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I6413df705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Bridge Co. v. Marla Construction Co.">Dominion Bridge Co. v. Marla Construction Co., 12 D.L.R. (3d) 453, [1970] 3 O.R. 125 (Ont. Co. Ct.)</ref></cite> which had held that there was no obligation on a trustee of a labour and material payment bond to advise claimants under the bond of the existence of the bond was effectively dealt with by s. 39, which now provides a statutory right to any person “having a lien”, or who is a mortgagee, or who has a trust claim to demand delivery of a copy of any labour and material payment bond.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Part VI creates a procedure to require the disclosure of information which can assist and even enable the enforcement of remedies under the Act. Section 39(1) extends its scope to include demands for information by any person having a subsisting lien, whether or not preserved, any beneficiary of a trust created by the Act, or “a person who is a mortgagee” which term would include the whole holder of a hypothec or charge. Subsection 39(1) deals with the right to information on the part of a lien claimant from an owner, contractor or subcontractor. Subsection (2) applies only to persons having a lien and trust beneficiaries and provides for information from mortgagees or unpaid vendors, which may be significant in determining priorities under s. 78. To protect fringe benefits, which can form a significant part of a worker's compensation, trustees of a workers' trustee fund have the right, under subsection (3), to access employer's payroll records. Pursuant to subsection (4), “any person” may obtain the particulars of the publication of the certificate of substantial performance. Subsections (5) and (6) set out the consequences for the failure to provide the information required under this section, providing for both civil liability in damages and production by court order with a punitive order as to costs.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="35 Mercer Limited" p2="Intact Insurance Company" post.rptr="19544" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67671f303b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="35 Mercer Limited v. Intact Insurance Company">35 Mercer Limited v. Intact Insurance Company, 2024 CarswellOnt 19544, 2024 ONSC 6466 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 39 provides a statutory mechanism by which a lien claimant may obtain information relevant to when a procurement process was commenced or a contract entered into, for the purposes of determining whether, pursuant to the transitional provisions of s. 87.3, a lien is governed by the current <ital>Construction Act</ital> (“<ital>CA</ital>”) or former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (“<ital>CLA</ital>”). Although s. 39 under the <ital>CLA</ital> had a narrower scope that did not include information on the date on which a contract was entered into or a procurement process was commenced for the improvement, making a request for information under s. 39 of the <ital>CA</ital> would elicit a response that relayed the owner's or contractor's position on the application of s. 87.3. A response that the information sought was not properly requested because s. 39 of the <ital>CLA</ital> still applied would relay the contractor or owner's position on the operation of s. 87.3. If an owner or contractor does not respond to the s. 39 request, a lien claimant may simply opt to preserve its lien on the basis that the <ital>CLA</ital> applied or move under s. 39(6) to compel compliance with the unanswered request for information. Alternatively, if the preservation or perfection deadline is missed, then relief could be sought under s. 39(5), which provides that a person failing to provide the information or access to information as required by s. 39(1), or knowingly or negligently misstates that information, is liable for any damages suffered as a result.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Normar Drywall" p2="4241258 Canada Inc. o/a Laurin General Contractor and Dennis Laurin" post.rptr="7873" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dc37970ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Normar Drywall v. 4241258 Canada Inc. o/a Laurin General Contractor and Dennis Laurin">Normar Drywall v. 4241258 Canada Inc. o/a Laurin General Contractor and Dennis Laurin, 2023 CarswellOnt 7873, 2023 ONSC 3106 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Plaintiffs must exercise reasonable diligence to determine if they have a trust claim when they have not been paid. Reasonable diligence with respect to a potential trust claim would include making the appropriate inquiries under s. 39, to obtain information relevant to the potential claim. If the plaintiff believed funds were owed to it after it completed work on the project, it had an obligation to make timely s. 39 requests to confirm if a breach of trust had occurred with respect to the project funds. The plaintiff could not rely on its own failure to act with due diligence to be fully appraised of information relating to project funds to delay the running of the limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jackman Construction Limited" p2="Brown et al." post.rptr="6562" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I8dc37971ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Jackman Construction Limited v. Brown et al.">Jackman Construction Limited v. Brown et al., 2022 ONSC 6562, 2022 CarswellOnt 16886 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2023 CarswellOnt 1817, 2023 ONSC 1126 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant homeowners were ordered to provide all information required of them under s. 39(1) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, including the amount of the applicable holdbacks, if any, that they had retained.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MK General Contractors Incorporated" p2="Egfrost Holdings Limited" post.rptr="4831" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641406815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MK General Contractors Incorporated v. Egfrost Holdings Limited">MK General Contractors Incorporated v. Egfrost Holdings Limited, 2022 ONSC 4831, 2022 CarswellOnt 11861 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the defendant tenant moved for discharge of the plaintiff's lien against its leasehold interest, the plaintiff opted to voluntarily release its lien prior to scheduled cross-examinations on affidavits, with the parties agreeing that the contract claim would continue as an ordinary action. However, they were unable to agree, <ital>inter alia</ital>, on costs of the motion. Although the issue of whether a tenant is obliged to provide lease information under s. 39 was not argued, the tenant's refusal to respond to the request was, in effect, a decision to stonewall the claimant on information that, had it been provided, would have allowed it to assess whether its claim against the landlord was viable and whether to pursue its lien. In the result, substantial indemnity costs for the tenant were not appropriate.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Emco Corporation" p2="Total Air Solutions Inc." post.rptr="1636" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I641406825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Corporation v. Total Air Solutions Inc.">Emco Corporation v. Total Air Solutions Inc., 2019 ONSC 1636, 2019 CarswellOnt 3718, 98 C.L.R. (4th) 374 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There was no evidence that the defendant had appropriated or converted any part of any trust fund(s) to its own use, and if the plaintiff had knowledge of an improvement in respect of which its materials had been supplied, then it could have required information under s. 39 that would have informed whether there had been a breach of trust. The bald assertion of a breach of trust in the statement of claim does not provide a sufficient basis to find that a defendant has, in fact, committed a breach of trust under s. 8.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Coastal Steel Construction Ltd." p2="Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc." post.rptr="3923" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64142d905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Coastal Steel Construction Ltd. v. Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc.">Coastal Steel Construction Ltd. v. Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc., 2015 ONSC 3923, 2015 CarswellOnt 10176, 51 C.L.R. (4th) 346 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor sought to require the defendant to comply with a request by the plaintiff for information made under s. 39(1)2, which the defendant ignored, although the defendant had provided answers to the plaintiff's subsequent requests that covered the information set out in s. 39(1)1. A request pursuant to s. 39(1)2 is to determine information about a subcontract between the contractor and the subcontractor. The plaintiffs in this case appeared to be requesting information that they should have knowledge of. Although there was nothing in s. 39 that prevented this request, there did not appear to be a reason why the plaintiffs would not already have this information. The plaintiff's motion was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd." p2="Trisura Guarantee Insurance Co." post.rptr="5450" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64142d915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Trisura Guarantee Insurance Co.">Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Trisura Guarantee Insurance Co., 2013 ONSC 5450, 2013 CarswellOnt 11796, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 328, [2013] I.L.R. I-5480 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 13878 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In an action arising out of a construction matter, on motion for production of certain documents without redactions, it was held that documents related to the defendant's instructions and procedures regarding responses to demands under s. 39 of <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not have to be produced.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2010" p1="Sunview Doors Ltd." p2="Academy Doors & Windows Ltd." post.rptr="163" pre.rptr="87" ref.id="I90e83070f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Sunview Doors Ltd. v. Academy Doors & Windows Ltd.">Sunview Doors Ltd. v. Academy Doors & Windows Ltd. (2010), 87 C.L.R. (3d) 163, 2010 CarswellOnt 1450 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Provided that a supplier is able to link the material to the improvement for which the subcontractor was owed money or has been paid, the supplier will be entitled to the benefit of s. 8. Here, the link was established because of the corporate defendant's conduct in deliberately frustrating the plaintiff's attempts to obtain the disclosure that would enable it to link its products to the improvements into which they had been incorporated. Under s. 39(6), a person entitled to information under s. 39 can bring a motion to compel disclosure at any time, “whether or not an action has been commenced”. The information obtained by using s. 39 can assist, and even enable, the enforcement of remedies under the Act. The corporate defendant and its principals were the only practical source of information the supplier had to trace the materials it had supplied, and the stance taken by the defendant's principals in their evidence at trial contravened the spirit of disclosure required under the Act or Rule 76.03(1) respecting disclosure of relevant documents.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Comstock Canada Ltd." p2="Durr Systems Inc." post.rptr="1669" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I64142d935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Comstock Canada Ltd. v. Durr Systems Inc.">Comstock Canada Ltd. v. Durr Systems Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 1669, 85 O.R. (3d) 355 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff commenced a lien action and the defendants posted security for the full amount of the claim and costs. The plaintiff then made a demand on the defendants pursuant to s. 39 for information setting out the state of the accounts between the defendants and the owner. The defendants refused to comply, arguing that the information was not relevant as the only claim now was against the security. The defendants were ordered to provide information about the state of accounts between them and the owner within 21 days. The information could very well be relevant to the merits of the claim, and the section was of general application.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc." p2="Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd." post.rptr="6" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I64142d945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd.">Maple Leaf Homes & Cottages Inc. v. Zoellner Windows (1982) Ltd. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 6 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs were suppliers of windows, doors and other building materials to the defendants. The defendants used the materials in the manufacture of products which they supplied under contract directly to owners as improvements in the construction of homes. The plaintiffs did not know to whom the products were sold. The defendants alleged that the materials supplied to them were done so in the ordinary course of business and that the plaintiffs had no entitlement to a trust fund under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The plaintiffs commenced an action to enforce their rights and, <ital>inter alia</ital>, brought a motion to compel the defendants to release information pertaining to the materials. The motion was granted. The plaintiffs were suppliers of materials used in making the various improvements by the defendants to the owner's properties. As suppliers of such materials, the plaintiffs were entitled to the benefit of the trust fund provisions in s. 8 of the Act and to receive the specifically enumerated information set out in s. 39. The plaintiffs otherwise had no way of knowing to whom, where or to what amount the materials were provided.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 39(5)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Sintra Ont. Inc." p2="Metric Contracting Services Corp." post.rptr="1798" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I641454a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sintra Ont. Inc. v. Metric Contracting Services Corp.">Sintra Ont. Inc. v. Metric Contracting Services Corp. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 1798, 1999 CarswellOnt 1272 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In answer to a request under s. 39(4) of the Act, the defendant sent to the plaintiff a certificate of completion rather than a certificate of substantial performance. Neither the plaintiff nor the defendant took further steps in respect of the request for information, and the plaintiff did not read the construction newspaper nor advise the defendant that the wrong document had been sent. The defendant did not knowingly or negligently misstate the information, and in the circumstances, its conduct was not such that would entitle the plaintiff to damages under s. 39(5).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 39(6)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Epoxy Flooring & Painting Inc." p2="Gillam Group Inc." post.rptr="4726" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I641454a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Epoxy Flooring & Painting Inc. v. Gillam Group Inc.">Epoxy Flooring & Painting Inc. v. Gillam Group Inc., 2019 ONSC 4726, 2019 CarswellOnt 12913, 2 C.L.R. (5th) 357 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff received no response from two different counsel, to two faxed written requests for information pursuant to s. 39 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, nor to follow-up letters by fax which also received no response. Counsel for the plaintiff prepared and served the plaintiff's motion record by fax, which both defendants admitted to receiving. Opposing counsel argued that there should be no costs as there was no evidence that the s. 39 written notices were in fact delivered, and that the s. 39(6) motion was, therefore, not necessary or proper. As it made no sense that the two earlier letters containing the written notices that were sent to the same fax numbers, did not get sent, and given the fax conformation form, the conclusion drawn from the evidence was that both opposing counsel lost or ignored the s. 39 written notices. Therefore, the motion was necessary, and defendants were liable for costs.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
40:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 40.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">40:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 40 of the current statute has its origins in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, c. 65, s. 38(10), which became s. 42(10) of the 1980 <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. Section 38(10), for the first time, allowed any party to an action or other interested person, at any time, to apply to a judge or a master for directions, including directions as to the cross-examination of a lien claimant or its agent on the affidavit of verifying the claim for lien. This provision was of limited use in practice because it was believed that the subsection could only be used after an action had been commenced: see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pecco Cranes (Can.) Ltd., Re" post.rptr="737" pre.rptr="[1973] 3" ref.id="I64147bb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pecco Cranes (Can.) Ltd., Re">Pecco Cranes (Can.) Ltd., Re, [1973] 3 O.R. 737 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>. <ital>Pecco Cranes</ital> was distinguished in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Dominion Elevator Ltd." p2="Pittao" post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I64147bb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Elevator Ltd. v. Pittao">Dominion Elevator Ltd. v. Pittao (1982), 28 C.P.C. 317 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>. The ability to cross-examine as of right was added by s. 40 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 and is continued in s. 40 of the current statute.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Open for Business Act, 2010</ital> replaced the right to examine the person who verified a claim for lien by affidavit of verification with a general right to cross-examine a lien claimant, an agent or assignee or a trust fund trustee.</para.text></para><feature.para.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><ital>Authors' Note</ital>:</name></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Act does not specify who is to be cross-examined if the lien claimant is a corporation. It will be interesting to see how the courts will treat requests from the examining party to cross-examine a particular person within the corporation which the corporation objects to producing for cross-examination.</para.text></para></feature.para.block><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">After the abolishment of the affidavit of verification, the lien claimant, an agent or assignee of the lien claimant, or a trust fund trustee may be cross-examined on a claim for lien. This is designed to permit claims to be tested in advance of trial and permit dubious liens to be vacated on reduced security or discharged at an early stage upon proper evidence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Attorney-General's Committee heeded the reasoned decision of the Court in <ital>Dominion Elevator</ital> and stated that the purpose of s. 40 is to provide a means of verifying claims for lien, and allow people named in the claim for lien that have an interest in the premises and also the contractor to obtain information regarding the claim for lien. Leave of the Court is no longer required to cross-examine, nor is it necessary that an action have been commenced. The contractor and the payer of the lien claimant are entitled as of right to participate in the examination. Any person named in the claim for lien as having an interest in the property is also entitled to participate in the examination. Therefore, since the contractor and payer of the lien claimant are specifically named as participants to the cross-examination, a mortgagee's right to participate can only arise if the lien claimant named the mortgagee as a person having an interest in the premises. If the mortgagee is not named as an “owner” in the claim for lien, then presumably the mortgagee is not entitled to participate in that cross-examination. Only one examination may be conducted. Section 40 is also of importance when dealing with a sheltered claim for lien. Since a sheltered lien claimant does not have a pleading, the s. 40 cross-examination may provide defendants their one clear right to ascertain the nature of the sheltered lien in advance of trial.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 40(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Elegant Façade Inc." p2="Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc." post.rptr="6951" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I6414a2c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elegant Façade Inc. v. Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc.">Elegant Façade Inc. v. Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc., 2021 ONSC 6951, 2021 CarswellOnt 14404 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved to quash the plaintiff's appeal against a production order following a s. 40 examination under the Act. Production and disclosure orders are generally interlocutory, and an order for production and/or reattendance for examination made against a corporation's witness is not rendered final because that witness is not a party to the proceedings. Since the appeal was brought by the corporate plaintiff, it had no standing to assert the personal interest of the examinee in the impugned order. If the latter had wished to challenge the order because it finally disposed of her personal interest in making disclosure and providing production, it would have been for her to bring the appeal in her own name, and thus to expose herself personally to the risk for costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GTA Restoration Group Inc." p2="Baillie" post.rptr="5190" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I6414a2c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="GTA Restoration Group Inc. v. Baillie">GTA Restoration Group Inc. v. Baillie, 2020 ONSC 5190, 2020 CarswellOnt 12410, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 89 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2020 CarswellOnt 15469, 2020 ONSC 6327, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 127 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2021 CarswellOnt 2443 (Ont. Div. Ct.); leave to appeal refused 2021 CarswellOnt 2444 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Cross-examinations on a claim for lien are an examination under oath or affirmation and bind the lien claimant. They are the only examination expressly provided in the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Examinations for discovery in a lien action are not contemplated by the Act. While leave for the latter is often granted, it is also common for an order to be made that any cross-examination on the claim for lien stand as discovery evidence with additional examination limited to issues based on the pleadings not already examined upon. During a cross-examination on a claim for lien, an examining party is entitled to full disclosure from the lien claimant regarding all evidence relied upon to substantiate the quantum of the lien, the lienability of claimed services and materials, and timeliness of the lien. There is no distinction between a lien claimant's disclosure obligation during a s. 40 cross-examination and the disclosure obligation during an examination for discovery, where leave for discoveries has been granted. The only difference between the two examinations is one of scope, and questions that are relevant based on the pleadings may not be relevant to the lien and, accordingly, might be properly refused during a s. 40 cross-examination, yet properly asked during an examination for discovery.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Eagle Construction Service, Inc." p2="Royal One 2225 Markham Road Med Centre Ltd." post.rptr="12822" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I90e8a5a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Eagle Construction Service, Inc. v. Royal One 2225 Markham Road Med Centre Ltd.">Eagle Construction Service, Inc. v. Royal One 2225 Markham Road Med Centre Ltd., 2019 CarswellOnt 12822, 2019 ONSC 4629, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 60 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The only issue to be explored at the s. 40 cross-examination was the quantum of the plaintiff's claims for lien. The defendants successfully sought various categories of documents that pertained to the plaintiff's costs concerning its claim for lien, such as subcontracts, purchase orders, invoices, proofs of payments, timesheets and payroll records. The court rejected the plaintiff's argument that the governing contracts between the parties were fixed price contracts, that the defendant retained a payment certifier who certified several payment applications by the plaintiff pursuant to these fixed price contracts, that the plaintiff relied upon these certified draws to establish the quantum of its claim for lien, and that, therefore, the issue of the plaintiff's costs was irrelevant to the quantum issue.
