While the issue of proportionality and summary proceeding under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> were important, it was undisputed that the quantum of the plaintiff was a proper subject matter for the s. 40 cross-examination.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Great Lakes Copper Inc." p2="1623242 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2600" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6414a2c35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Great Lakes Copper Inc. v. 1623242 Ontario Inc.">Great Lakes Copper Inc. v. 1623242 Ontario Inc., 2013 ONSC 2600, 2013 CarswellOnt 7227 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court was unable to conclude from the evidence before it that the plaintiff had not discharged its onus of establishing that the defendant should be deprived of its presumptive right to select the representatives it wished to examine in the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Plaza Electric II Ltd." p2="CMGC Management Inc." post.rptr="306" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I6414c9d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Plaza Electric II Ltd. v. CMGC Management Inc.">Plaza Electric II Ltd. v. CMGC Management Inc. (1996), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 306 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 72 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Evidence obtained pursuant to s. 40 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is not subject to R. 30.1 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="AMCA International Ltd." p2="Ellis-Don Ltd." post.rptr="227" pre.rptr="42" ref.id="I6414c9d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="AMCA International Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd.">AMCA International Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd. (1990), 42 C.L.R. 227 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The object of the examination was to obtain admissions which would reduce the amount of security required to vacate the lien. Where after 13 days of examination there was nothing approaching a clear admission which would assist the defendant, the examination had clearly gone beyond acceptable limits and amounted to an examination for discovery without giving the plaintiff the benefit of a review of documents produced for discovery.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 40(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="1238295 Ontario Inc." p2="2054518 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4642" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I6414c9d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1238295 Ontario Inc. v. 2054518 Ontario Ltd.">1238295 Ontario Inc. v. 2054518 Ontario Ltd. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 4642, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 304 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where counsel for the plaintiff had offered to have his client answer written questions, and some questions had already been answered in prior examinations, the court dismissed the applicant's request for a fourth attendance for cross-examination by a representative of the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Eurocor Ltd." p2="Vernich" post.rptr="2315" pre.rptr="[1995]" ref.id="I6414c9d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich">Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich (1995), [1995] O.J. No. 2315 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—This case was originally reported for its reconciliation of conflicting cases as to whether or not a personal action can survive an expired lien. The original motions court judge, now a Justice of the Court of Appeal, had retained jurisdiction over the costs of the original motion, on which ruling the extent of permissible cross-examination under s. 40(2) came in issue. The section was designed to give all interested parties an early opportunity to obtain more information about the claim. The claim for lien being a creature of statute, the owner would be interested in the date work commenced, the date the contractor last worked on the project, any documents to verify those dates and any other information relevant to the validity of the claim for lien. Other contractors, subcontractors and suppliers, some of whom would be concerned about sheltering under the claim for lien in question would be interested in similar matters. The cross-examination is not intended to be an examination for discovery. There is no right to examination for discovery in lien proceedings; leave must be sought and granted.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 40(4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Eagle Construction Service, Inc." p2="Royal One 2225 Markham Road Med Centre Ltd." post.rptr="12822" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I6414c9d45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eagle Construction Service, Inc. v. Royal One 2225 Markham Road Med Centre Ltd.">Eagle Construction Service, Inc. v. Royal One 2225 Markham Road Med Centre Ltd., 2019 CarswellOnt 12822, 2019 ONSC 4629, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 60 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant sought production of documents pursuant to a s. 40 cross-examination pertaining to the plaintiff's costs concerning its claim for lien, such as subcontracts, purchase orders, invoices, proofs of payments, timesheets, and payroll records. The only issue to be explored at the s. 40 cross-examination was the quantum of the claims for lien. In ordering production, the Master acknowledged that while the cross-examination may well deal with issues that are the proper subject matter of discovery, the overlap could be managed by the court in the lien proceedings. The claims for lien were large and merited careful scrutiny, particularly given what has already been paid to the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Any-Wall Concrete Forming Inc." p2="Bloomfield" post.rptr="2374" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6414f0e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Any-Wall Concrete Forming Inc. v. Bloomfield">Any-Wall Concrete Forming Inc. v. Bloomfield, 2012 ONSC 2374, 2012 CarswellOnt 7139, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 275 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 40 permits a one-time cross-examination on the claim for lien either before or after an action has been commenced to enforce the claim for lien, and the rules of court pertaining to examinations apply with necessary modifications to a section 40 cross-examination. The answers given by the representative of the lien claimant/plaintiff are binding on the lien claimant/claimant and can be relied upon in support of any of the permitted motions. Although a mini summary trial during a reference conducted pursuant to a judgment of reference is not technically a motion, the issue of the timeliness of the lien is no different than that which can be raised on a motion declaring a preserved or perfected lien expired or a motion ordering the discharge of a lien. It would be absurd to state that the lien claimant is bound by the lien claimant's admissions in a s. 40 cross examination on motions brought under the provisions of the Act but not on a mini summary trial deciding the same issue. It would also fly in the face of the policy of the Act that the action be as far as possible of a summary character. With necessary modifications, Rule 31 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> applies to a section 40 cross-examination so as to permit the answers to be read in at trial in the same way as answers given on an examination for discovery.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2183164 Ontario Inc." p2="Gillani" post.rptr="1456" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6414f0e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2183164 Ontario Inc. v. Gillani">2183164 Ontario Inc. v. Gillani, 2013 ONSC 1456, 2013 CarswellOnt 2891, 114 O.R. (3d) 676, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 134 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2012 CarswellOnt 7261, 2012 ONSC 3377, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 8627, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 204 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—As the result of two abortive cross-examinations of the plaintiff, and the Master's view that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> procedures would be inappropriate for achieving a fair, expeditious and least costly resolution of all the issues because of a variety of foreseeable procedural hurdles, the master exercised his discretion and ordered the discharge of the lien, and the vacating of registration of the lien and certificate of action and the dismissal of the lien action. Reversing that decision on appeal, the Divisional Court indicated that the Master should have proceeded with the alternative relief claimed rather than wander beyond the parameters of the motion before him as it had been framed by the defendants. The fact that the actual relief granted by the Master was sought in the Notice of Motion did not resolve the lack of notice, as it was the grounds for that relief that were important. Even if the issue was properly before the Master, which it was not, the Master exceeded his jurisdiction under s. 47(1) and erred in law in striking the lien and dismissing the lien action in the circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Edgecon Construction Inc." p2="All Saints Church Homes for Tomorrow Society" post.rptr="3501" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I641517f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgecon Construction Inc. v. All Saints Church Homes for Tomorrow Society">Edgecon Construction Inc. v. All Saints Church Homes for Tomorrow Society (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 3501, [1995] O.J. No. 2209, 18 C.L.R. (3d) 254 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In considering the sufficiency of an affidavit of verification under s. 34(6), the court, in <ital>obiter</ital>, paused to comment on s. 40 and, particularly, s. 40(4). The Master questioned whether or not a person who is a deponent's source of information and belief could also be cross-examined, referring to <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Mutual Life Assurance Co. of Can." p2="Buffer Investments Inc." post.rptr="335" pre.rptr="52" ref.id="I641517f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mutual Life Assurance Co. of Can. v. Buffer Investments Inc.">Mutual Life Assurance Co. of Can. v. Buffer Investments Inc. (1985), 52 O.R. (2d) 335 (H.C.)</ref></cite>, in order to curb potential abuse with affidavits of verification sworn by “agents or assignees”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="413528 Ontario Ltd." p2="951 Wilson Ave. Inc." post.rptr="472" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I641517f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="413528 Ontario Ltd. v. 951 Wilson Ave. Inc.">413528 Ontario Ltd. v. 951 Wilson Ave. Inc. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 472, 42 C.P.C. (2d) 70, [1989] O.J. No. 2599 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1990), 71 O.R. (2d) 40n (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—This carefully reasoned decision deals exhaustively with the issue of the propriety of communication by counsel with a witness under cross-examination.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
41:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 41.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">41:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 41 of the Act was amended to provide for the registration of a discharge of lien, in the form prescribed by the regulations, in order to discharge a preserved or perfected lien.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A corresponding amendment was made to section 42 of the Act. See O. Reg. 303/18, Form 19.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This was part of the Expert Review's recommendation that separate forms be implemented, one to release a lien, one to discharge a lien or certificate of action, and one to vacate the registration of a claim for lien or certificate of action</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 41 first appeared in 1882. Section 15 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15, provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">A lien for wages may be discharged by a receipt signed by the claimant acknowledging payment, and verified by affidavit and filed. Such receipt shall be numbered and entered by the Registrar, like other instruments, but need not be copied in any book. The fees shall be the same as for registering a statement of claim.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 25(1) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1937, c. 200, allowed for an agent of the lien claimant, authorized in writing, to sign the receipt acknowledging payment. <ital>An Act to amend The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1958, c. 57, s. 5(1) distinguished between acknowledgement of payment by corporations and claimants other than corporations. From 1958 to 1980, the provision remained in that form:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">(1) A lien may be discharged by the registration of a receipt acknowledging payment,</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(a)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">where made by a claimant other than a corporation, signed by the claimant or his agent duly authorized in writing and verified by affidavit;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(b)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">where made by a corporation, bearing its corporate seal.</para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The current version of s. 41 first appeared as s. 41 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section provides a mechanism for discharging preserved or perfected liens, and for withdrawing written notice of liens, without court order. In the case of withdrawal of a written notice of lien, the section goes on to describe the consequence of withdrawal in that a payer in receipt of such a notice of withdrawal is in the same position as if written notice of a lien had never been given.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 41 allows for the discharge of a preserved or perfected lien without a court order by the registration of a release in the prescribed form (see form 14, Release of Lien under s. 41). Form 14 requires that where the lien claimant is a corporation, the release of lien be executed by the lien claimant as well as by a witness. Where the lien claimant is not a corporation, the release of lien must be verified by an affidavit of a subscribing witness.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 41(1)(a)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gay Company Limited" p2="962332 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="16471" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dc4b1f0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Gay Company Limited v. 962332 Ontario Inc.">Gay Company Limited v. 962332 Ontario Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 16471, 2023 ONSC 6023 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In order to be effective, the registration of a claim for lien or application to delete a construction lien under the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital> requires that the instrument must be certified by the Land Registrar and not be withdrawn before it is certified. The <ital>Construction Act</ital>, by using the same word, “registration”, indicates the intention of the drafters to adopt the same meaning of registration under the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital>. Registration under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> therefore means that the instrument must be received, certified and not withdrawn before it is certified. Once an instrument is certified, then the registration is complete. Here, the defendant registered a claim for lien with an error in the claimant's name and sought to correct that error by registering a second claim for lien in the correct name, but in the process mistakenly and prematurely registered an Application to Delete the First Claim for Lien at the same time. The court rejected the plaintiff's argument that upon filing of the purported discharge of the first lien, the claimant's lien rights were irrevocably lost and could not be revived. Because neither the first lien nor the application to delete it had been certified, they were not “registered” within the meaning of either the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital> or the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. The valid second lien remained on title to preserve the claimant's lien rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Kaplin" p2="FCC Mortgage Associates Inc." post.rptr="3791" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I64153f005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kaplin v. FCC Mortgage Associates Inc.">Kaplin v. FCC Mortgage Associates Inc. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 3791, 1999 CarswellOnt 3239 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 4769, 1999 CarswellOnt 3563 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Two claims for lien relating to the same work were registered on title by the lien claimant, one in the Registry Office and one in the Land Titles Office. The lien claimant subsequently agreed to discharge the claim for lien registered in the Registry Office, but argued such release was only in respect to the Registry Office land, and not the land in Land Titles. The Master held that since the liens were for the same work done over the same period of time, what was released was the lien itself, notwithstanding that the description in the first lien included the land in Land Titles, while the release did not include the land in Land Titles. An order was to be made discharging the claim for lien in both Registry and Land Titles.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Meo & Assns." p2="Gottenu Developments Ltd." post.rptr="2582" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I560f00e0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd.">Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2582, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 159 (Ont. Master); reversed (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 4489, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 78 (Ont. Master); affirmed Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 737, 1 C.L.R. (3d) 74, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Meo (R.) & Associates v. Gottenu Developments Ltd.)</ital> 131 O.A.C. 394 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There can be only one lien for the same work even though two claims for lien may be registered. When a release of a lien is registered, the <ital>Act</ital> clearly stipulates that it is the lien that is released and not a piece of paper known as the Claim for Lien. In this case, two claims for lien were registered in respect of the same work, the second claim being registered because of a mis-spelling in the first. After the first lien expired, the plaintiff registered a release of the first lien, which had expired, intending to leave the second preserved and perfected lien intact. Notwithstanding that the plaintiff's intention was to vacate a claim for lien that had long since become a useless piece of paper, the effect of the registration of the release was to discharge the underlying lien rights themselves. The discharged lien was exactly the same lien that was preserved a second time as the subject of the second claim for lien. Accordingly, the court had no choice but to discharge the plaintiff's lien and certificate of action and dismiss the action. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Initially, the Master ruled that the registration of the release of an expired lien did not terminate the plaintiff's rights in respect of the work done during the period of time stated in the lien which was the subject of the second claim for lien. However, while preparing additional reasons for judgment in the matter, the Master developed doubts and invited submissions from counsel as to whether he was entitled to reconsider the issue, given that his earlier reasons had not found their way into a formal order. He concluded that he did in fact have jurisdiction to do so.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I641566105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Subsequent to the registration of his lien, a contractor realized that he had understated the amount owing, and instructed his solicitors to register a new lien and release the previous lien claim so as not to encumber unduly the title to the owner's property. The owner then successfully moved to discharge the contractor's lien, to vacate the registration of the lien and certificate of action, and to dismiss the contractor's lien action. The court held that the discharge of the contractor's first lien was irrevocable and terminated all of the contractor's lien rights in respect of the work done by the contractor during this period of time. The lien could not be revived. Accordingly, the lien asserted in the second claim for lien, being for the same work during the same period of time, albeit claiming a larger amount of money, could not, in law, be asserted. An acceptable alternative, <ital>inter alia</ital>, would have been to register a second lien for the correct full amount of the plaintiff's claim, again assuming it could be done in time, and then move, under s. 47(1)(b), on notice, for an order vacating the registration of the first lien, so as to avoid any liability under s. 35 of the Act for “exaggerated claims”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="94" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I641566115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 94 (Ont. Gen. Div.); supplementary reasons at (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 85 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 1337, 1996 CarswellOnt 1312 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 41(1)(a) is quite clear that registration of a release is necessary before a lien can be said to have been discharged. The execution of a discharge is not sufficient. Accordingly, where a mortgage advance is made after execution of a release of a lien but before registration, all liens arising from the improvement will have priority over the advance, whether they arose before or after the advance is made and whether they were registered or not at the time of the advance. On March 20, 1996, an appeal to the Divisional Court unanimously upheld the decision of the trial judge and accepted his reasons.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 41(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Construction Inc." p2="Unimac-United Management Corp." post.rptr="6136" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I641566125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp.">Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp., 2016 ONSC 6136, 2016 CarswellOnt 15025, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 17928, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether a written notice of lien provided by the subcontractor to the owner under s. 24 had been “withdrawn” under s. 41(2). The court found that while there are no requirements for the contents of a written notice of withdrawal included in s. 42(1), a written notice of withdrawal must clearly state that the notice giver is expunging the recipient of the entirety of the “jeopardy” relating to the original notice of lien. The court reasoned that the purpose of such notice is to put the payer given the notice of withdrawal “in the same position as if the written notice of lien had never been given”. It follows that the notice giver's intention to do so must be clearly expressed. The court also noted that arrangements for the partial payment of outstanding amounts do not expunge the whole of the jeopardy. If the whole of the jeopardy is not expunged, the payer is not placed in the same position as if the original notice had never been given. As such, the two emails sent by the subcontractor setting a deal for payment from the contractor did not constitute withdrawals under s. 41(2).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
42:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 42.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">42:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 41 of the Act was amended to provide for the registration of a discharge of lien, in the form prescribed by the regulations, in order to discharge a preserved or perfected lien.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A complementary amendment was made to section 42 of the Act. See O. Reg. 303/18, Form 19.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The provisions concerning general liens date back to <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30, s. 33(2). This section dealing specifically with the discharge of a general lien is relatively new. The current s. 42 first appeared as s. 42 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section allows a claimant holding a general lien to selectively discharge one or more of the premises affected by that lien. This is usually done in the context of subdivision construction, to assist in the sale of the discharged premises, from the proceeds of which the claimant would be paid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The provision permits a lien claimant who has preserved or perfected a general lien to discharge the general lien against any one or more of the premises that are subject to the lien without affecting the general lien's application to any other premises. The discharge is effective upon the registration of a release in the prescribed form. See Form 19.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Draft Masonry (York) Co." p2="P.A. Restoration Inc." post.rptr="231" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I90e99000f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Draft Masonry (York) Co. v. P.A. Restoration Inc.">Draft Masonry (York) Co. v. P.A. Restoration Inc. (1988), 48 R.P.R. 231, 29 C.L.R. 256 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor entered into an agreement with the contractor to perform certain work in a housing project. The plaintiff filed a mechanics' lien pursuant to the relevant statutory provisions. The registration of the lien would detrimentally affect the progress of the work so the plaintiff's solicitor forwarded to the defendant a discharge of the claim for lien in escrow. It was obvious from the correspondence adduced in evidence that the defendant was required to hold the discharge until certain requirements were fulfilled. The defendant nevertheless registered the discharge which caused the plaintiff's lien to lapse. The defendant later fell upon difficult times and could not fully pay off the plaintiff who had no lien benefit to rely upon. In granting judgment for the plaintiff, that court found the defendant was in breach of trust for registering the discharge. The breach of escrow resulted in a loss to the plaintiff in the amount of the lien for which he ought to be compensated in damages.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
43:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 43.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">43:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 43 is an entirely new provision, introduced as s. 43 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, allowing a lien claimant with a preserved or perfected lien to postpone that lien in favour of the interest of another person in the premises by registering on title a notice of postponement in the prescribed form. See Form 15 for a Notice of Postponement under the Act. The notice of postponement requires the prior registration of the instrument to which the lien is postponed. This section is unique to Ontario.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section permits the postponement of lien claims in favour of other persons, a procedure which may be used to facilitate building mortgage advances in the face of registered liens. A form of postponement is prescribed and the consequences of postponement are dealt with in s. 78(8). Particular care must be taken in practice to avoid discharging a lien in such circumstances (see Commentary to s. 48).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Various amendments were made to section 44 of the Act.</para.text></para><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Clause 44(1)(d) was amended to raise the threshold amount required to be provided as security for costs from $50,000 to $200,000.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection (3.1) was added to address expressly provide for the posting of security to vacate a written notice of lien.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection (5.1) was added to provide that a letter of credit that contains a reference to an international commercial convention is acceptable as security under the section. This reflects the commercial reality that international conventions in letters of credit are essential in a global economy.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In addition, subsections 44(2.1) and (2.2) were added to address the application of clause (1)(a) and subsection (2), which provide for motions to vacate a lien where the lien attaches to a premises in a condominium context.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Corresponding amendments were made to the <ital>Condominium Act, 1998</ital>, by the reenactment of sections 13 and 14 of that Act.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 9 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27, allowed a Court to receive security or payment into Court in lieu of the amount of the lien claim and thereby vacate the registration of the claim for lien:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Upon application to the county court or the judge thereof, in claims under two hundred dollars, and to the Court of Chancery in other cases, such Judge or court may receive security or payment into court in lieu of the amount of such claim, and may thereupon vacate the registry of such lien, or upon any other ground, if the said Judge or court shall think fit, annul said registry; and, in any of said cases, may, nevertheless, proceed to hear and determine the matter of the said lien, and to make such order as the Judge or court may think fit […]</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This much of the section remained unchanged for 50 years. Section 14 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15, incorporated a provision to the effect that where a judgment was given in favour of the lien claimant, the court may add to the judgment the costs of, and incidental to, the registry of the lien, as well as costs of the suit. Section 41 of the <ital>Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, went further and provided that the costs awarded to lien claimants could not exceed, in the aggregate, 25 per cent of the amount of the judgment, excluding disbursements. The costs were in addition to the amount of the judgment and apportioned and borne in such proportions as the court directed. These costs, attendant upon a successful lien claim, prompted later revisions to the payment into court sections. Section 45 of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35 also introduced the concept of payment out of court, however it was of limited value since the language used suggests that it was only payment out of court after judgment that was contemplated. Payment out of court could be made by the judge “where money has been paid into court and the time for payment out arrives” by the judge forwarding a requisition for cheques and a certified copy of the judge's judgment to the Accountant's office.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30, s. 26(4), introduced a change to the effect that at the time of payment into court to vacate the lien, the court had a discretion to fix costs and require that costs be paid into court as well. The Act was also amended so that the money paid into court was subject to the claims of all persons for liens to the same extent as if such money was realized by sale of the property, the genesis of our current “pooling” provisions. The entitlement to costs not to exceed 25 per cent was amended in s. 41 of the same 1923 Act to afford the court a discretion with regard to the value of the actual services rendered by or on behalf of the parties. There was also a change to the method in which the 25 per cent for costs was calculated, from “the total amount awarded” to the “total amount found to have been actually due on the liens at the time of registration thereof”. <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1932</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19, s. 6, introduced the concept of security in the form of bond or other security to vacate a lien. The amendment permitted a “bond or other security for securing the like amount and satisfactory to the judge or officer having jurisdiction”. “Other security” is not specified. Presumably prior to 1932, the security paid into court was always in the form of cash. Section 3 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1937</ital>, S.O. 1937, c. 41, amended the payment into court provision so that the lien that was vacated by the payment into court became a “first charge” upon the money, bond or other security in court. This aspect of the payment in provisions remained unchanged until 1983.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Prior to 1958, where a lien was vacated upon security being paid into court, the lien claimant was still required to register a certificate of action at the time it commenced its action. Subsection 5(2) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1958</ital>, S.O. 1958, c. 57, provided that where the lien was vacated and security paid into court, “the lien shall not cease to exist for the reason that no certificate of action is registered”. Section 3 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1960</ital>, S.O. 1960, c. 65, provided that if, at the time the lien was vacated, a certificate of action was registered, it too could be vacated. There were no payments out of court provisions, except upon judgment, until <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1961–62</ital>, S.O. 1961–62, c. 78. This was enacted for the sole purpose of permitting payment of money out of court or delivery-up of a bond for cancellation upon the consent of all parties and the lien claimants effected. In s. 25(6) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, there was a further amendment to permit the payment of money out of court or delivery-up of the bond for cancellation upon notice to those parties as directed by the court. The provisions for payment into and out of court, so amended, remained unchanged until the sweeping 1983 reforms. The <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, collected the provisions for payment into and out of court that had been scattered throughout the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. In 1983, the idea of a “first charge” was displaced by a new “pooling” concept so that each lien claimant shared rateably with all others. The Act now provides for an absolute right to vacate a lien upon payment into court of cash equivalent to the value of the lien, and 25 per cent of the value of the lien up to a maximum of $50,000.00 for costs, all without notice to the lien claimant.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Some basic principles have emerged from the case law:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">a)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">payment into Court does not enlarge the lien rights of the lien claimant so that:</para.text></para><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">i)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">if the money, bond or other security is paid into Court by the payer of a lien claimant, that class of lien claimant is entitled to be paid the full amount of its lien from the money, bond or other security paid into Court;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">ii)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">if the money, bond or other security is paid into Court by someone who is not the payer of the lien claimant, the lien claimant is only entitled to be paid what is owed by the general contractor to the sub-contractor or the statutory holdback, whichever is greater. This rationale applies, for example, where the owner pays into Court to vacate the lien of a subcontractor (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Reliance Electric Ltd." p2="G.N.S. Contractors Inc." post.rptr="310" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I641602505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc.">Reliance Electric Ltd. v. G.N.S. Contractors Inc. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 310, 70 O.R. (2d) 364 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>);</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">iii)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">if the money, bond or other security is paid into Court by a mortgagee, the mortgagee's priority position is unchanged. The lien claimants must still prove a priority over the mortgagee to claim from the money, bond or other security paid into Court (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I90ea2c40f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1979" p1="P. Michaud Roofing Ltd." p2="National Trust Co." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="103" ref.id="I641629605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="P. Michaud Roofing Ltd. v. National Trust Co.">P. Michaud Roofing Ltd. v. National Trust Co. (1979), 103 D.L.R. (3d) 523 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (1980), 30 O.R. (2d) 620 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>);</para.text></para></list.item></list></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">b)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">payment into Court is not an admission of the amount or validity of the lien that has been vacated (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="313" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I641629615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd. (1990), 40 C.L.R. 313 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">c)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">the money, bond or other security paid into Court cannot be used to pay a claim for costs beyond the $50,000.00 limit (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd." p2="York Humber Ltd." post.rptr="2075" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I90ea2c41f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd.">Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd. (1993), [1993] O.J. No. 2075 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 185, 1994 CarswellOnt 944 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">d)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">where a motion is brought to vacate a lien by paying in the full amount of the claim for lien, the amount of security for costs that is required to be paid into Court is limited to $50,000.00 no matter how big the lien (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="United Dominion Industries Ltd." p2="Ellis-Don Ltd." post.rptr="855" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90ea2c42f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd.">United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 855, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 65 O.A.C. 115 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">e)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">if multiple liens are vacated, the costs limitation applies to each, not to the aggregate value of the group.</para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 44 provides a complete code for the vacating of lien registrations from title or, in the case of unregistered liens, service of the lien itself, together with all associated certificates of action, through payment into court or posting of security. Any security posted takes the place of the land, facilitating the flow of funding on an improvement that is subject to liens.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 44(1) provides an <ital>ex parte</ital> procedure by which the court must vacate a lien if the conditions set out in the subsection concerning security are met. If the person seeking to vacate the lien wishes to post reduced security, or, in practice, security other than cash, they may do so under subss. (2) and (3), upon motion to the court with notice. If there is more than one motion made under these subsections, as for example when two or more lien claims are inter-related, then the motions may be consolidated, and the amount required to be paid in adjusted accordingly (subs. (8)).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Where a general lien is involved, once a motion under subs. (1) has been made, the court has the jurisdiction, on notice, to apportion that lien amongst the premises covered by the motion and any others affected by the lien. This is referred to in subs. (4).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection (5) gives the court jurisdiction, on motion, with notice, to reduce the amount paid into court or posted as security. Such a motion would be appropriate where, for example, a payment has been made to the lien claimant or clear and unequivocal admission is made during cross-examination or discovery is made that a lien was exaggerated or otherwise invalid, in whole or in part.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Once vacated, the lien becomes a charge upon the security and no longer attaches to the premises (subs. (6)) or the holdback (subs. (7)), in the case of unregistered liens. Subsection (9) sets out three rules whereby such security, or the proceeds from the sale of the premises is to be distributed. All funds are pooled and all lien claimants share rateably in accordance with the priorities set out in s. 80.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It is important to note that a lien claimant who has preserved its lien, but has the lien vacated before perfection, must still perfect its lien or it will expire. In perfecting its lien in these circumstances, R. 1 merely removes the necessity for a registered Certificate of Action as part of the perfection process.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The motion to vacate may be brought in any office of the Ontario Court General Division and need not be brought in the jurisdiction in which the land is situate. The practice in the Master's Office in Toronto is to dispense with the requirement for evidence by way of certified copies of abstract pages in favour of a competent, current affidavit deposing to a thorough up to date search of the day books.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">If the full amount of the lien is posted, the result on a motion to vacate is interlocutory and unappealable. If the lien is vacated for less than its face value plus costs, the order is final and appealable (s. 71(2)).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd." p2="Grascan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1028" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I641650705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd. v. Grascan Construction Ltd.">Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd. v. Grascan Construction Ltd., 2017 ONSC 1028, 2017 CarswellOnt 3814, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 151 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Court of Appeal's conclusion in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90ea5350f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> that security for costs could be pooled was not one of general application. Rather, that conclusion was reached on the basis of counsel's agreement as to the effect of (Ont.) No. 43 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—After the general contractor deposited a lien bond for the full amount of the subcontractor's lien claim, it sought an order that the filing of the lien bond satisfied its trust obligations to the subcontractor under the Manitoba <ital>Builders' Liens Act</ital>. The lien bond merely secured the lien claim; it did not satisfy the claim through payment. There may be circumstances where a contractor will choose to maintain double security where there are lien and trust claims for the same work, services, or materials, by acquiring a lien bond while still holding trust funds. However, a contractor can avoid double security by paying cash into court pursuant to s. 55(2) instead of depositing a lien bond. While s. 44(6) provides that upon payment into court the lien ceases to attach to the land and becomes a charge on the amounts paid into court or posted as security, that does not mean that a lien claimant becomes entitled to the entire amount of its claim out of that security. Such payment is restricted to the amount fixed by the Act for a payer's liability and must be shared <ital>pro rata</ital> with other lien claimants. A contractor who has posted security to vacate liens does not make the security available to satisfy the claims of all lien claimants of a class in addition to the 10 per cent statutory holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Robert McAlpine Ltd." p2="Woodbine Place Inc." post.rptr="134" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I641677815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Robert McAlpine Ltd. v. Woodbine Place Inc.">Robert McAlpine Ltd. v. Woodbine Place Inc. (1998), 3 C.L.R. (3d) 134 (Ont. C.A. A return of the letter of credit would have caused irreparable harm, because if the contractor were successful on appeal, it would have no chance of recovery without the letter. It argued that because it was foreclosing and not proceeding under power of sale as an order in the usual form pursuant to s. 44 was not satisfactory. The plaintiff opposed as order under s. 47 but did not oppose the usual form of order under s. 44. In granting an order under s. 44, the Master stated that the mortgagee's draft order would rewrite the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for the purposes of the particular action, on very preliminary material at a very early stage in the proceedings. Gen Div.)</ref></cite>—The surety of a bond posted as security to vacate a lien was required to pay the plaintiff's costs if the defendant failed to do so. At the subsequent construction lien trial, the court ordered that the defendants pay to the plaintiff the judgment and the plaintiff's party-party costs to a specified date, and that plaintiff pay the defendant's solicitor-client costs from that date forward. A creditor took assignment of the account payable by the plaintiff and looked to payment from the surety under the bond. Further, it was doubtful that the surety could assert a right of set-off where there was no mutuality of debts.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="313" pre.rptr="40" ref.id="I6416c5a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tech-Ex Contractors & Associates Inc. v. (1989), 35 C.L.R. 310, 70 O.R. (2d) 364, 1989 CarswellOnt 705 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—A subcontractor failed to meet its contractual obligations to its subcontractors. The general contractor made all payments to the subcontractor except for the holdback amount until it received notice of claims for lien, after which it ceased to make payments. The general contractor then brought a motion for orders vacating the claims for lien upon posting security in the form of a bond. In RE Ltd.'s case, the bond amount was approximately $31,000. The amount held back by ED Ltd. was $11,100, and RE Ltd.'s rateable portion was approximately $4,600. The parties referred a special case to the court for the determination of the issue of whether RE Ltd. was entitled to look to the bond to satisfy all or part of the amount owing over and above the holdback amount. The court held that the lien rights of the subcontractors were limited to $11,100. The relevant statutory provisions, when applied to the facts of the case at hand, did not enlarge the lien rights in question. Section 44 could not be read so as to support the position that, by the posting of security by general contractor, RE Ltd.'s lien was enlarged. The provision did not confer substantive rights upon RE Ltd. The expression “the full amount claimed as owing in the claim for lien” in s. 44(1) was not synonymous with the lien. The posted bond did not become security for the full amount claimed as owing in the claim for lien. It was security only for the lien. Moreover, nothing in s. 44(6) affected the operation of s. 17(1) and (2) of the Act. Accordingly, the value of RE Ltd.'s lien remained the same after the posting of the bond as it was before the posting of the bond. That is not to say that the utilization of s. 44 by a general contractor will never result in additional moneys becoming available to the sub-subcontractors, but it would only have that result if, in fact, after an order under s. 44 is made, the general contractor's subcontractor supplies further services or materials under his contract. In that event, if the general contractor wishes to avoid the risk of a liability greater than his liability to his subcontractor, then he will be obliged to withhold all payments to his subcontractor until the amount in his hands represents an amount equal to the proper holdback at the time of the order, the proper holdback for any additional services or materials supplied, and the value of the lien discharged by the order. At the end of the day, and by virtue of the second and third rules set out in s. 44(9), these three bundles of money become available to satisfy the liens of the subcontractors of the general contractor's subcontractor rateably.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Francon" p2="L. H.C.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Canada Heating Ltd." p2="Brompton Manufacturing Ltd." post.rptr="311" pre.rptr="26" ref.id="I6416ecb55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canada Heating Ltd. v. Brompton Manufacturing Ltd.">Canada Heating Ltd. v. Brompton Manufacturing Ltd. (1987), 26 O.A.C. 311 (Div. Ct.); reversed (1989), 36 C.L.R. 113 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff commenced a lien action against the defendant owners, sub-contractors and the general contractor. The plaintiff had entered into a contract with the defendant B to carry out work on a construction project. The defendant B had subcontracted with the defendant V for similar work and, in turn, the defendant V had subcontracted with the defendant general contractor. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant V was indebted to the defendant B for a holdback. The defendant B chose not to register its own lien, but defended the action. During the course of the action, the defendant V posted security for the lien in the form of a lien bond naming as obligors of the bond the defendant V and a surety. The amount posted under the bond was equal to the total of the full amount claimed for the lien and thus the lien on the land was vacated. Subsequently, the defendant V declared bankruptcy and the claim against it did not proceed. On the day of trial, the surety paid the total amount of the claim to the plaintiff and obtained an assignment and subrogation of the plaintiff's claim. This was not made known to the defendant nor the court until final argument was presented. At the outset of trial, counsel acting on behalf of the surety made an opening statement that the action was proceeding as a contract claim and not a lien claim. At trial, the defendant B was ordered to pay the plaintiff damages. The defendant B appealed to the Divisional Court and the appeal was dismissed. The defendant B appealed to the Court of Appeal, and the appeal was allowed. Nothing in the Act specifically provides for subrogation. This silence is significant because the Act does provide for subrogation to payment on other kinds of bonds. As well, subrogation could only have taken place between the lien group against V Ltd. Since B Ltd. had not filed a lien it was not included in the lien group and thus there could not be any subrogation against it. An order to proceed was required to support the assignment but it would not have made a difference. The scheme of the Act assures that if a subcontractor is paid by the owner, the contractor is relieved of any obligation to the same extent. In these circumstances, the claim was paid in full and thus the lien disappeared.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90eb16a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. C.A.)</ref></cite>. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="United Dominion Industries Ltd." p2="Ellis-Don Ltd." post.rptr="855" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90eb3db0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="United Dominion Industries Ltd. v.
