Karmina Holdings Inc.">TruGrp Inc. v. Karmina Holdings Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 5453, 2024 ONSC 2165 (Ont. S.C.J.) additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 15721, 2024 ONSC 4643 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff moved to set aside an <ital>ex parte</ital> order under s. 44(1) vacating its two claims for lien and certificate of action in favour of the payment of security into court. The core dispute was whether the form of letter of credit commonly used as lien security and approved by the court complied with the scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, and the role of the Accountant as “custodian” as set out in O. Reg. 191/95 under the <ital>Public Guardian and Trustee Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.51. The commonly used form of letter of credit contains a provision permitting the issuing bank to decline renewal of the letter of credit provided that the Accountant is given at least thirty days' notice and is provided with a bank draft for the amount of letter of credit, less any payments already made under it. It was argued that the language of that provision gave rise to a contingency in the security that is at odds with the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Before addressing the substantive issue, the associate judge ordered adjournment of the motion <ital>sine die</ital> pending notice to the Accountant and issuing bank, and service on them of the relevant pleadings, and a further hearing being scheduled, if required, for any submissions that they may wish to make in response. Both the Accountant and the bank later submitted that they would not require further explicit court authorization to accept the bank draft as replacement security for the court-approved letter of credit. Considering this development, TruGrp confirmed that its concerns were satisfied, and the motion was resolved. The issue of the sufficiency of the commonly accepted form of letter of credit as security to vacate a lien has been affirmed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Biotechnik" p2="848835 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="6794" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64173ad05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Biotechnik v. 848835 Ontario Inc.">Biotechnik v. 848835 Ontario Inc., 2021 ONSC 6794, 2021 CarswellOnt 16675 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed in part <ital>1191650 Ontario Limited v. 848835 Ontario Inc.</ital>, 2022 ONSC 6574, 2022 CarswellOnt 16848 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A lien does not secure post-judgment interest, and therefore, on a motion under s. 44, the amount to be paid into court to vacate a lien does not include post-judgment interest.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sundance Development Corporation" p2="Islington Chauncey Residence Corp." post.rptr="241" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64173ad15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sundance Development Corporation v. Islington Chauncey Residence Corp.">Sundance Development Corporation v. Islington Chauncey Residence Corp., 2021 ONSC 241, 2021 CarswellOnt 105, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 350 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master could not grant the defendant's <ital>ex parte</ital> motion to vacate the lien because: 1) a copy of the claim for lien was not submitted. The registered claim for lien, with any schedules, must be available for the court's review in any vacating motion to verify both the claimed amount of the lien and the quantum of required security; 2) the letter of credit submitted for approval as security for the lien was unacceptable, as it made no reference to being issued in respect of the subject premises or the claim for lien, and the language used by the issuing bank differed from the form of letter of credit generally accepted by the court. More importantly, the letter of credit was subject to the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (“UCP”) of the International Chamber of Commerce, which terms were not before the court, absent which the master could not ascertain if there were conditions under which the bank could refuse to honour a demand on the letter of credit contrary to the intent of lien security within the scheme of <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Although the current Act contemplates that a letter of credit containing reference to an international commercial convention may be acceptable security, such a letter of credit is only acceptable where the convention text is written into the terms of the credit and the letter of credit is unconditional and accepted by a Schedule I bank operating in Ontario. It was not clear that the UCP document contained no additional conditions available to the bank not reflected in the text of the letter of credit, and that it was truly unconditional, other than with respect to standard conditions of automatic renewal and cancellation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Man-Shield Construction Inc. et al." p2="1876030 Ontario Inc. et al." post.rptr="5231" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64173ad25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Man-Shield Construction Inc. et al. v. 1876030 Ontario Inc. et al.">Man-Shield Construction Inc. et al. v. 1876030 Ontario Inc. et al., 2018 ONSC 5231, 2018 CarswellOnt 15511, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 30 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants moved for an order for payment of cash out of court, which they posted as security pursuant to s. 44, providing the plaintiff with the amount awarded it, while retaining in court the statutory maximum for costs in the amount of $50,000.00 plus any accrued interest. The plaintiffs took the position that the motion was premature, as there were other claims against the security arising from unresolved issues. The lien dispute was being resolved by way of a private arbitration, and the arbitrator released his decision on a portion of matter involving the basis for the original lien claim, but not the quantum of the defendants' counterclaim against the plaintiffs, awarding the plaintiffs a sum significantly less than the amount in court. He then determined that the costs of the original claim should be deferred until the conclusion of the complete arbitration. In finding that the motion was premature, the court distinguished the decision of Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd." p2="Roche Ltée" post.rptr="2851" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I561123c0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée">M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2851, 39 C.L.R. (2d) 251 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, in that <ital>M. Sullivan</ital> was driven by the fact that the lien claimants were seeking to pool against other security posted for other lien claims. That was not the situation here, which involved a single owner, a single lien claimant, and one global amount of security. Adjudication of the issues of quantum of work and costs of the proceeding were ongoing. This case was therefore more akin to the facts in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="D'Urzo Demolition Inc." p2="Damaris Developments Inc." post.rptr="3938" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64173ad45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc.">D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc., 2012 ONSC 3938, 2012 CarswellOnt 8750, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 229 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Carter Tile Contractors Inc." p2="Ben-Zvi" post.rptr="61" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I90eb64c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi">Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 61, 2005 CarswellOnt 6608 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1954294 Ontario Ltd." p2="Gracegreen Real Estate Development Ltd." post.rptr="6369" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I641761e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1954294 Ontario Ltd. v. Gracegreen Real Estate Development Ltd.">1954294 Ontario Ltd. v. Gracegreen Real Estate Development Ltd., 2017 ONSC 6369, 2017 CarswellOnt 16295, 80 C.L.R. (4th) 297 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The agreement of purchase and sale allowed for its termination where the vendor was unable or unwilling to remove any valid objection to title. A registered mortgage and construction lien did not constitute such defects in title because they could both be discharged at the instance of the vendor, with the lien able to be vacated by a motion without notice to pay money into court pursuant to s. 44(1). Accordingly, the vendor could not rely on the said clause to unilaterally terminate the agreement of purchase and sale by refusing to discharge the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="D'Urzo Demolition Inc." p2="Damaris Developments Inc." post.rptr="3938" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I641761e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc.">D'Urzo Demolition Inc. v. Damaris Developments Inc., 2012 ONSC 3938, 2012 CarswellOnt 8750, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 229 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The Master applied security in the form of a letter of credit posted on behalf of the defendant in lieu of the property in satisfaction of the interest and costs ordered payable by the defendant. There was no reason to treat the security posted in the form of a letter of credit differently from security posted in the form of cash. It would not be unfair for the court to see to it that the defendant satisfy the court's award, including interest and costs. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Master Albert followed the decision of Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Carter Tile Contractors Inc." p2="Ben-Zvi" post.rptr="6608" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I641761e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi">Carter Tile Contractors Inc. v. Ben-Zvi, 2005 CarswellOnt 6608, 49 C.L.R. (3d) 61 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> (see the digest under s. 14(2), <ital>supra</ital>,) but distinguished both <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd." p2="York Humber Ltd." post.rptr="185" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I90eb8bd0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd.">Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd., 16 C.L.R. (2d) 185, 1994 CarswellOnt 944 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="United Dominion Industries Ltd." p2="Ellis-Don Ltd." post.rptr="855" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90eb8bd1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd.">United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 855, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 65 O.A.C. 115 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Naylor Group Inc." p2="Enfinity Canada EPC Inc." post.rptr="4365" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I641761e65fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Naylor Group Inc. v. Enfinity Canada EPC Inc.">Naylor Group Inc. v. Enfinity Canada EPC Inc., 2012 ONSC 4365, 2012 CarswellOnt 9316, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 155 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In an unsuccessful <ital>ex parte</ital> motion brought to substitute a letter of credit for posted cash security, the proposed letter of credit was made subject to ICC Publication 590 of the International Chamber of Commerce. Section 44 of the Act contemplates payment of cash security in lieu of the lands and premises. Section 78(10) contemplates that in lieu of cash a financial guarantee bond or a letter of credit or a guarantee from a bank listed in Schedule I to the <ital>Bank Act</ital> can be posted. Implicit is that any such bond or letter of credit be free of any term or restrictions that potentially could give rise to the issuer/surety refusing to pay. A form of Financial Guarantee Bond is prescribed in Form 23, and while there is no form of letter of credit prescribed, the practice has been that its terms be equivalent. There was potential that the above-noted term in the proposed letter of credit could be invoked to deny payment, thus embroiling the Accountant in a lawsuit. Regardless of the fact that in a lawsuit the Accountant may be successful, the mere fact of the potential of the lawsuit is sufficient to reject the form of the tendered letter of credit. The letter of credit was not equivalent to Form 23 in terms of conditions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="United Dominion Industries Ltd." p2="Ellis-Don Ltd." post.rptr="855" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90eb8bd2f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd.">United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 855, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 65 O.A.C. 115 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 44(1) requires the court to vacate a lien upon the motion of any person who complies with the provisions without giving notice to any other person. There is no discretion in the court to refuse to make the order in accordance with that subsection.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd." p2="York Humber Ltd." post.rptr="3124" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I641788f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd.">Cesan Mechanical Systems (1990) Ltd. v. York Humber Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 3124, [1993] O.J. No. 2075 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (1994), 16 C.L.R. (2d) 185, 1994 CarswellOnt 944 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A plaintiff is only entitled to look to a bond posted under s. 44(1) to satisfy an amount paid as security for costs, because costs are not part of the lien. In this case, therefore, recovery was limited to $50,000, even though the bond was for substantially more.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="666659 Ontario Inc." p2="Foster-Ross Mechanical Ltd." post.rptr="29" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I641788f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="666659 Ontario Inc. v. Foster-Ross Mechanical Ltd.">666659 Ontario Inc. v. Foster-Ross Mechanical Ltd. (1993), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 29, 93 D.T.C. 5515 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A number of liens were registered against a property by sub-contractors of F. Ltd., and then were vacated, by <ital>ex parte</ital> order under s. 44(1), by the general contractor, E. Ltd., upon the payment of security into court. Revenue Canada subsequently delivered to E. Ltd. a requirement to pay issued pursuant to s. 224(1.2) of the <ital>Income Tax Act</ital>. The notice, which was in respect of source deductions, required the contractor to pay to the Receiver General an amount, which would otherwise be payable to F. Ltd., on account of F. Ltd.'s tax liability. Revenue Canada claimed priority over the lien claimants pursuant to s. 224(1.2) of the <ital>Income Tax Act</ital>, and the court concurred. The payment into court had the effect of releasing E. Ltd. from its statutory liability but not its contractual liability. The lien bond stood as security or in place of the property described in the claim for lien; therefore, it did not follow that E. Ltd.'s potential liability either to F. Ltd. or the lien claimants had been discharged by posting the lien bond. Its liability, if any, would be determined following trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Northern Air Construction Ltd." p2="Borough of York Public Library Board" post.rptr="123" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I641788f35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northern Air Construction Ltd. v. Borough of York Public Library Board">Northern Air Construction Ltd. v. Borough of York Public Library Board (1985), 13 C.L.R. 123 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—G, a general contractor hired by the owner O to build a public library building, had ten subcontractors on the project, including B. In turn, B had two subcontractors, N and W. Commencing in early February, 1982, G's insolvency resulted in the registration of liens under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, as follows: (1) On February 23, 1982, N registered a claim for lien for $16,000. G vacated the registration of this lien by posting a bond (the “first bond”) issued by the appellant bonding company (the “bonding company”), on February 26, 1982; (2) On February 26, 1982, B registered a claim for lien for $39,500, which included moneys owed to N and W. G vacated the registration of this lien by posting a bond, (the “second bond”) on March 4, 1982; (3) After making a $29,000 payment to G on March 24, 1982, O paid $108,000 into court, representing the full amount remaining unpaid by O to G, pursuant to s. 12(8) of the Act. Subsequently, nine other liens, all of which were subsisting when the two bonds were posted, were registered. At the trial of the lien action, the bonding company contended that all of the lien claimants, including N and B should be paid out of the moneys in court and that the bonds should be cancelled. It was argued that since N claimed through B, the first bond was unnecessary, and that since B could be paid out of the moneys in court, no recourse to the second bond was necessary. The Master held that: (1) N and B could first look to their respective bonds for payment without regard to the moneys in court. (2) N was to obtain payment of its claim, interest and costs from the first bond, and its carriage costs from the moneys in court. B would receive its claim and costs from the second bond, deducting the value of N's claim. If the first bond was insufficient, N would share in the second bond <ital>pari passu</ital> with W and in priority to B and the other lien claimants. (3) Any surplus in the bonds would be paid to the other lien claimants <ital>pari passu</ital> if their claims had not been paid in full from the moneys in court. Surplus funds would be used to pay interest and thereafter, if any, paid to the surety. (4) N and B could share in the moneys in court should the bonds be insufficient. (5) The other lien claimants could not claim interest out of the moneys in court. The bonding company appealed and the appeal was dismissed. The court agreed with all of the Master's conclusions, save for para. (3), above. The general contractor's money or bond posted to vacate the liens makes available to those lien claimants moneys additional to the sums the owner is responsible for. The Act did not provide that a subsequent payment by an owner allows the contractor to retract his money or security. Where a contractor posts a bond, that security remains available to those lien claimants whose liens have been discharged. This is quite apart from rights had by other lien claimants to the liened land and moneys in court. As to the surplus of the bonds, s. 29(4) accords rights to all claimants with “subsisting” liens. The Master incorrectly held that this meant “registered” liens. Accordingly, all claimants had a right to the surplus, after giving effect to the first charge on the bonds held by N and B respectively. While interest is not a lienable item, the courts have held it to be recoverable as money wrongfully withheld. Accordingly, notwithstanding the strict wording of the bonds, those bonds must meet the requirements of the Act and must secure the payment of interest. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This case was decided under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. The Ontario Court of Appeal has recently placed <ital>Northern Air</ital> in context and has confined it to its facts. See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90ebb2e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(1)(d)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90ebd9f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—In principle, costs do not form part of a lien because they add nothing to the value of the premises in question. As a further matter of principle, in view of the pooling scheme contemplated by the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, there is no reason why the costs portion of the security paid in for a class of lien claimants cannot be pooled to satisfy the otherwise unsecured excess claim of an individual member of that class. This case, however, must be read carefully in light of the subsequent decision of Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd." p2="Roche Ltée" post.rptr="2851" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I561198f0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée">M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2851, 39 C.L.R. (2d) 251 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. The learned Master there rejected an argument for pooling of the unspent portions of other lien claimants' security, and concluded that <ital>P & D Holdings</ital> is not a case of general application, and that it may have proceeded as it did on an erroneous concession of counsel as to the effect of s. 44(9), Rr. 2 and 3.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Central Yonge Development Inc." p2="Armoshep Properties Inc." post.rptr="257" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I6417b0035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Central Yonge Development Inc. v. Armoshep Properties Inc.">Central Yonge Development Inc. v. Armoshep Properties Inc. (1993), 12 C.L.R. (2d) 257 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendants in a construction lien action moved under R. 56.01 for security for costs on the basis that the plaintiff corporation had insufficient assets within the jurisdiction to pay the defendants' costs. An earlier motion for security brought by the defendants had been dismissed, but the trial of the action was taking considerably longer than had been estimated at the time of the first motion. The plaintiff contended that if the order was made, it would be unable to continue with the trial. The plaintiff also argued that <ital>res judicata</ital> and issue estoppel applied since the defendants' application had already been dismissed once. The court rejected the plaintiff's argument respecting issue estoppel or <ital>res judicata</ital>. The rules specifically provided that the amount of security required by order could be increased or decreased at any time. Accordingly, the fact that a “nil” order had been made earlier did not mean that the court could not later increase that “nil” order. However, it was not appropriate at the time to order the plaintiff to provide security for costs. Instead, the court released from the security given by the defendants the total sum that the defendants had lodged with the court for security for costs. In the result, neither the plaintiff nor the defendants had security for their costs. The balance remaining with the court was security for lien and not security for costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Soloway" p2="Falcon Crest Homes Inc." post.rptr="1275" pre.rptr="[1991]" ref.id="I6417d7105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Soloway v. Falcon Crest Homes Inc.">Soloway v. Falcon Crest Homes Inc. (1991), [1991] O.J. No. 1275 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Falcon registered a lien. M bonded the lien of title. A lien judgment followed. Falcon's lien claim was satisfied by setting off against it an award of solicitor and client costs made in favour of M by the trial judge. In order to pay his lawyers, M assigned them his costs order and they, in turn, garnished the bonding company. Remarkably, in some ways, the fact that the lien claim had been satisfied did not deter the court from enforcing the garnishment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="R.E. Clipsham Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="266" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I6417d7115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R.E. Clipsham Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">R.E. Clipsham Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1990), 43 C.L.R. 266 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The security for costs provisions in the Act were intended to prevent prejudice to lien claimants. The amount of security to be posted should be calculated by determining the amount claimed for each lien in the claim and then adding the lesser of $50,000 or 25 per cent of that amount pursuant to s. 44(1)(d).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="4241258 Canada Inc." p2="Diamond Jubilee Hospitality Inc. et al." post.rptr="567" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6417d7125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="4241258 Canada Inc. v. Diamond Jubilee Hospitality Inc. et al.">4241258 Canada Inc. v. Diamond Jubilee Hospitality Inc. et al., 2022 ONSC 567, 2022 CarswellOnt 1148, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 25 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved under subs. 44(2) to pay security into court in an amount less than the full amount of the claim for lien, relying in part on the plaintiff's admission given at an examination for discovery, that the “proper claim for lien amount” was considerably less than the amount claimed. The test to be applied on a s. 44(1) motion was similar to the test on a summary judgment motion, in that the court must be satisfied based on the motion materials that there was no reasonable prospect of the plaintiff proving a lien for the amount it has claimed. However, a motion under s. 44 is not a full-fledged summary judgment motion under Rule 20 and is not a venue for determining complex issues of contested facts going to the merits of the claim. While lienable services can include additional expenses that are incurred because the project takes longer than anticipated, such as labour costs, equipment rental and similar costs of remaining on the job, there was no basis in the materials for the court to find that “stand-by” charges referred to in the plaintiff's factum related to any valid lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cancore Production Ltd." p2="Hau" post.rptr="1027" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I6417d7135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cancore Production Ltd. v. Hau">Cancore Production Ltd. v. Hau, 2021 ONSC 1027, 2021 CarswellOnt 1580, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 137 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant's unjust enrichment claim should not be considered in exercising the court's discretion under s. 44(2). However, since the evidence supported a maximum potential liability of the owners to the contractor that was greater than the amount of the subcontractor's lien, there was no reasonable basis upon which to limit the value of that lien and order a reduction in the security required to vacate it.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="H.I.R.A. Limited" p2="Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823" post.rptr="5931" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I6417d7145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823">H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823, 2018 ONSC 5931, 2018 CarswellOnt 16544, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 153 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 6199, 2018 CarswellOnt 17476 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying <ital>H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium</ital>, 2018 ONSC 1526, 2018 CarswellOnt 3328, 78 C.L.R. (4th) 226 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The owner sought an order pursuant to s. 44(2) to vacate the plaintiff's lien by posting security for $394,954 plus costs, an amount significantly less than the lien claim of $2,744,377. After engaging in a detailed analysis of the lien claim to ascertain what amount of security would be reasonable in the circumstances, the motions judge ordered that the lien would be vacated upon the posting of security for $1,408,905.59 plus $50,000 for costs. On appeal, the Divisional Court upheld the order, while varying it to reflect a mathematical error in providing credit to the owner. A motions judge is entitled to reduce the amount of security required to satisfy the lien if the evidence supporting the calculation fails to establish a “reasonable basis” for the amount claimed (as noted in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HMI Construction Inc." p2="Index Energy Mills Road Corp." post.rptr="4075" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6417fe205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp.">HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp., 2017 ONSC 4075, 2017 CarswellOnt 10314, 81 C.L.R. (4th) 88 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> at para. 25.) Here, the motions judge articulated the correct legal principles and applied them properly. He analyzed both the plaintiff's entitlement to the elements of the lien claim and the quantum that could be supported by the evidence. He held that certain matters could not be resolved on the documentary record and could only be resolved at a trial, and was alive to the requirement that he not resolve complex issues of contested fact on a s. 44(2) motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HMI Construction Inc." p2="Index Energy Mills Road Corp." post.rptr="4075" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6417fe215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="HMI Construction Inc. v. Master)</ref></cite>, do not stand for the proposition that a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim is available for contract work even where there is an agreed contract price. With a fixed price contract, in the absence of approved change orders, a contractor cannot include in a claim for lien extra charges for the work included in the fixed price contract simply because costs were more than usual or anticipated. When a party signs a fixed price contract, the party assumes risks of cost changes. The statement in <ital>Biotechnik</ital> that resort to <ital>quantum meruit</ital> was necessary to recover “the actual value of the work done” did not mean “actual cost of the work done” but rather value between contractual performance milestones, as measured by the contract. Here, the motions judge did not err in significantly reducing the security required to bond liens off title from the amount of the claims for lien. The claimant did not provide an itemized accounting of its claim showing contract accounting, extras, credits for work not done, and acknowledged deficiencies if any. Instead, it provided an accounting of its total costs for the project, ignoring the fact that it was bound by a fixed price contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="LaFarge Canada Inc." p2="B. However, where: the plaintiffs registered a lien for $250,000, but only produced invoices totalling $60,000 with questionable timing; the contract was long from being completed when terminated; and significant financing would have been needed to complete the work; the lien as registered was deemed excessive and allowing it to continue would be abuse of the Act. The master found that in order to vacate a lien against a particular unit, the amount to be posted was an amount attributable to the owner's common interest as specified in the declaration. If all owners of the units in the condominium did so, then the lien claimant would be in the same position as if the lands were not registered as a condominium. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant sought an order vacating registration of a claim for lien and certificate of action without payment into court. The claimant had provided no evidence of the dates that work was performed but unpaid, no evidence of its request for payment, or how it calculated the amount owing. There was also no evidence that the defendant ever notified the claimant of deficiencies in their work until a counterclaim was launched. The purpose of s. 44(2) is not to have a trial before a trial. Here, the issues required a trial which would put all of the evidence before the court. Without a trial, and with insufficient evidence before the Master from both parties, he was unable to conclude whether, after trial, the claimant would be able to prove the amount claimed pursuant to the lien, or whether the setoffs and the claim for liquidated damages claimed by defendant were proper. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As s. 44(2) requires a court to determine what is reasonable in the circumstances to satisfy the lien, the court refused to order that only the holdback be paid as there was no evidence to establish what, if anything, was owed by the owner to the general contractor. Lien liability under s. 44(2) cannot be equated with the holdback liability. This section does not, nor does any other provision of the Act, permit the granting as of right, on motion of an owner, of an order vacating a lien by payment into court of the amount of the statutory holdback. The holdback provisions in the Act do not always operate to limit the value of the lien, but apply only when the “least amount owed” by a payer is less than its holdback obligation. The court held that:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The words “satisfy the lien” at the end of this section means satisfy the lien or liens that can be proven, and not the amounts as claimed;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">2)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The discretion given in s. 44(2) permits the court to look not only at the gross amount claimed as owing under the contract, but also any proper set-offs which the owner might prove.</para.text></para></list.item></list><para.text date.updated="0">On the face of the owner's affidavit, the amounts of $134,413.01, $50,000, and $44,100 should be added to the amount claimed to be owing. When those three amounts were added to the amount that the owner conceded was owing, a possible amount of $585,101.20 was owed by the owner to the general contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Power Contracting Inc." p2="Deemar Investments Ltd." post.rptr="119" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I64189a645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Power Contracting Inc. v. The mortgagee brought a motion to vacate the lien and certificate of action upon payment into court of a reasonable amount. Div.)</ref></cite>—In calculating the amount of security necessary to vacate a lien under this subsection, the court will not consider a bonus amount due under the contract which represents projected savings to the owner by reason of the contractor's efficiency if the contract was completed at under a stated cost. Such an amount is not calculated from the price of materials or services, and is totally contingent on savings being realized by the owner.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:6: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Electrical Equipment Co." p2="General Motors of Canada" post.rptr="2630" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I6418c1725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Electrical Equipment Co. v. General Motors of Canada">Electrical Equipment Co. v. General Motors of Canada (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2630, 1998 CarswellOnt 2603 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was registered against the defendant's head office rather than its truck plant, and accordingly the lien and the certificate vacated and the action dismissed. The plaintiff sought to have the defendant's statutory holdback paid into court pending the plaintiff's review and accounting of funds as between the contractor and the sub-contractor with whom the plaintiff had contracted. The court found that since the lien was registered on the wrong land, there was no holdback, and while allegations of breach of trust and responsibility remained open, those obligations did not support an application for payment into court.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:7: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(5)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="High Tech Power Inc." p2="BDA Inc." post.rptr="11703" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I676c28403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="High Tech Power Inc. v. BDA Inc.">High Tech Power Inc. v. BDA Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 11703, 2024 ONSC 4327 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The parties agreed to reduce the amount of the bond filed with the Accountant of the Superior Court but could not agree on the appropriate quantum for the replacement bond. The plaintiff had obtained an adjudication determination on two invoices; after the defendant paid that amount to its lawyers in trust, part of the funds were released on consent to the plaintiff, and part retained because of a pending preservation order sought by a third party in regard to a separate claim related to enforcement of an indemnity agreement. It was held that the reduction should only be in respect of the funds paid out on consent, as a deposit to counsel's trust account is not payment to the lien claimant, and could not stand as security. The plaintiff was at risk of counsel taking instructions from their client to deal with the funds in a manner contrary to the plaintiff's interests. The fact the payment was to a law firm was of no consequence, as the lawyer was an agent for their client and is required to act on instructions. The <ital>Construction Act</ital> contemplated prompt payment on an adjudication determination to ensure the flow of money on construction projects is protected. Paying funds into a lawyer's trust account fails to achieve this fundamental goal.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Demikon Construction Ltd." p2="Oakleigh Holdings Inc." post.rptr="19539" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I676c28413b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Demikon Construction Ltd. v. Oakleigh Holdings Inc.">Demikon Construction Ltd. v. Oakleigh Holdings Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 19539, 2024 ONSC 6261 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2024 CarswellOnt 5369, 2024 ONSC 2151, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1738 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 12204, 2024 ONSC 4472 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a s. 44(5) motion, the judge reduced the required security by the amount that the defendant developer had paid directly to the plaintiff construction manager's subcontractors and suppliers to satisfy outstanding amounts owed to them, pursuant to s. 28. The Divisional Court held that the motion judge erred in law by, among other things, reducing the posted security by an amount that included payments to subcontractors who did not fall within the statutory definition of a “person having a lien”. Properly interpreted, s. 28 applies to direct payments to a “person having a lien” relating to “any amount owing to that person for services or materials supplied to the improvement.” The motion judge erred in interpreting s. 28 more broadly, so as to include payments to other subcontractors who were not persons “having a lien”. Limiting the scope of s. 28 payments to persons having a lien accords with the statutory scheme and the purpose of the Act. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Demikon Construction" p2="Oakleigh Holdings" post.rptr="992" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I676c28423b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Demikon Construction v. Oakleigh Holdings">Demikon Construction v. Oakleigh Holdings, 2024 CarswellOnt 1829, 2024 ONSC 992 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2024 CarswellOnt 12204 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed 2024 CarswellOnt 19539 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, a precursor motion to the original s. 44(5) application, where the judge denied the plaintiff's request for disclosure of documents involving the settlement between the defendant owner and a subtrade to which the s. 28 payment was made.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Arad Incorporated" p2="Rejali et al." post.rptr="10385" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dc88280ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Arad Incorporated v. Rejali et al.">Arad Incorporated v. Rejali et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 10385, 2023 ONSC 3949 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The determinations of the adjudicator that no monies were owed by the defendants to the plaintiff did not mean that the money paid into court should be returned. The court must be satisfied on the basis of the motion material that there is no reasonable prospect of the lien claimant proving that the lien attracts security per ss. 44(1) or (2). The determinations of an adjudicator alone did not meet the evidentiary threshold required for the court to conclude that the lien claim did not attract need for security. As interim decisions, these determinations do not put an end to the proceeding, which continues between the parties, including that which was subject of the adjudication process. The determinations are not binding upon the court, and the findings and conclusions of an adjudicator set out in the determination is evidence, like any other evidence, that the court may take into consideration in determining whether to exercise its discretion to reduce security “where it is appropriate to do so.” However, an adjudicator's conclusions alone are not determinative on the decision to reduce security.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chesney et al." p2="Malamis et al." post.rptr="3477" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dc88281ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Chesney et al. v. Malamis et al.">Chesney et al. v. Malamis et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 3477, 2023 ONSC 1742 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While acknowledging that the plaintiffs had lienable services and materials, the defendants successfully argued that the plaintiffs included either non-lienable services and materials or clearly inflated the value of other lienable services, such that the action was a lost profit/lost opportunity claim for equitable relief masquerading as a construction lien. The basis for the disputed items in the lien were in the nature of a claim for an equitable interest by way of a share of the value of the subject property, based upon an alleged agreement among the parties and the subsequent work performed by the plaintiffs. However, to properly be the subject of a lien, the claim had to come within the definition of “services or materials supplied to the improvement.” Damages at large, such as lost opportunity costs, loss of profits or aggravated damages will not form the basis for a valid lien. In the result, the security posted in respect of the plaintiffs' lien was significantly reduced pursuant to s. 44(5)(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brook Restoration Ltd." p2="Greatwise Developments Ltd." post.rptr="2778" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I676c28433b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Brook Restoration Ltd. v. Greatwise Developments Ltd.">Brook Restoration Ltd. v. Greatwise Developments Ltd., 2023 CarswellOnt 2778, 2023 ONSC 1118, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 332 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2023 ONSC 4090, 2023 CarswellOnt 10759 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2023 CarswellOnt 4291, 2023 ONSC 1996 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The defendant moved to discharge the plaintiff's lien, or in the alternative reduce the security posted. The nature of the actual agreement between the parties – whether it was a fixed cost or a cost plus agreement - was a highly significant and material factual dispute that was beyond the scope of a s. 44 motion. It was an issue best resolved on a full evidentiary record following a trial. Likewise, whether the plaintiff had abandoned the project was also a triable issue, and the court concluded that the lien claim was not frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process. However, the amount of security was reduced to take into account an overlooked payment by the defendant and certain minor calculation errors and non-lienable items claimed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pasqualino" p2="MGW-Homes Design Inc." post.rptr="5632" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I676c4f503b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc.">Pasqualino v. MGW-Homes Design Inc., 2022 ONSC 5632, 2022 CarswellOnt 14177, 35 C.L.R. (5th) 453 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—Allowing an adjudicator's decision under s. 13.13 to remain after a lien has been bonded off and security posted does not undermine the purpose and effectiveness of s. 44. Permitting an owner to seek a reduction of the security posted in court by the amount paid pursuant to an adjudicator's decision demonstrated how the two processes work harmoniously together.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Elegant Façades Inc." p2="Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc." post.rptr="8336" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I6418e8815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elegant Façades Inc. v. Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc.">Elegant Façades Inc. v. Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc., 2021 ONSC 8336, 2021 CarswellOnt 20736 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons Elegant Façade Inc. v. Broccolini Construction 2022 CarswellOnt 5529 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court was satisfied that a portion of the lien claim was attributable to damages that were not properly the subject of a lien, such as the claim for lost opportunity costs, and that while there were elements of the claim which were properly lienable, they were clearly inflated. A reduction in the amount posted for security was ordered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pentad Construction Inc." p2="2022988 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="824" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I6418e8825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pentad Construction Inc. v. 2022988 Ontario Inc.">Pentad Construction Inc. v. 2022988 Ontario Inc., 2021 ONSC 824, 2021 CarswellOnt 4039, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 164 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Divisional Court's direction in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="H.I.R.A. Limited" p2="Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823" post.rptr="5931" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I6418e8835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823">H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823, 2018 ONSC 5931, 2018 CarswellOnt 16544, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 153 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 17476 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, regarding the proper approach to motions under s. 44(2) is equally applicable to motions under s. 44(5), because both sections serve the same purpose, namely to ensure that an amount of security required to vacate a lien is reasonable. The governing test is that the court is entitled to reduce the amount of the security posted to vacate a lien “if the evidence supporting the calculation of the claim for lien fails to establish a reasonable basis for the amount claimed.” The assessment of the evidence in support of, or contrary to, the amount claimed is to be approached much in the same way that the evidentiary record is approached on a motion for summary judgment, i.e. that the trial judge is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on the basis of the record filed. That was the case here, where the central issue was whether the payment certifier's decisions were final and binding on the parties under the contract. If so, then the amount of the lien was not reasonable, since the position of the payment certifier was that the plaintiff had been overpaid at the time its lien was registered. The court found that the payment certifier's decision was binding, and that there was no evidence the certifier acted in bad faith, fraudulently, failed to be impartial, or knowingly and wilfully disregarded his duty. The security paid into court by the defendant was accordingly ordered to be significantly reduced.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1982" p1="Lennox Snow Fence Co. (1982) Ltd." p2="1187855 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="6060" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64190f905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lennox Snow Fence Co. (1982) Ltd. v. 1187855 Ontario Inc.">Lennox Snow Fence Co. (1982) Ltd. v. 1187855 Ontario Inc., 2016 ONSC 6060, 2016 CarswellOnt 18231 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion under s. 44(5) is not the venue for determining complex issues of contested facts going to the very merits of the claim. Motions to reduce security cannot succeed where there are genuine issues of fact that require a trial to determine whether the entire amount claimed or some lesser amount is appropriate. Only where the evidence clearly and unequivocally proves that the lien as registered is excessive or improper should a Court reduce or release the security at the interlocutory stage. A motion is not a substitute for lien trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Selectra Inc." p2="Penetanguishene (Town)" post.rptr="2293" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64190f915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Selectra Inc. v. Penetanguishene (Town)">Selectra Inc. v. Penetanguishene (Town), 2016 ONSC 2293, 2016 CarswellOnt 5132, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 335 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 8195 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The amount of security to be posted with the court was reduced to reflect the following non-lienable claims: i) the lost opportunity costs for rental of a site trailer and container that were not available for rental elsewhere; ii) notional rental costs for a generator and scissor lift where there was no direct cost to the defendant and the claim sounded more appropriately in damages at large rather than expense incurred in improvement of the property; iii) bonding costs that did not add value to the improvement and did not form a proper part of the claim for lien; iv) permit expenses which were analogous to a building permit expense and part of administrative or onsite office overhead; v) expenses for the provision of temporary services at the site, where there was a fixed price contract and these services and materials were within the original scope of that contract, and did not represent a direct contribution to the improvement of the property. Appropriate costs related to a delay on the project, such as additional attendance by a site supervisor, were not deducted, as it was not possible or necessary for the court to determine whether the claim for lien would succeed, but only whether there was a reasonable possibility of success. It was not possible to determine the cause of the delay at the time of the motion, and the supervisor's time on-site was arguably a service rendered in improvement of the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Totalsiteworks Management" p2="Elite Construction Inc." post.rptr="2809" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I64190f925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Totalsiteworks Management v. Elite Construction Inc.">Totalsiteworks Management v. Elite Construction Inc., 2014 ONSC 2809, 2014 CarswellOnt 6596, 40 C.L.R. (4th) 299 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Four lien actions were commenced for amounts owing by the defendant general contractor to various subcontractors. The defendant unsuccessfully moved under s. 44(5) to reduce the total amount of security posted in all four actions, having proposed to post a new bond for the reduced amount and asking that each of the four previous bonds posted as security in the four actions be delivered up for cancellation. The court was not satisfied that any security posted by the main lien claimant overlapped or duplicated the bonds posted as security for the lien claims of the other lien claimants. The evidence did not satisfy the court, on the balance of probabilities, that there was no triable issue that the rights of any party would be compromised if the amount of security posted was reduced. Also, if an order was made allowing the defendant to post a new lien bond in the place of the four previous lien bonds, one or more of the lien claimants could lose the security posted in one or more of the other actions because an order had not been made consolidating all four lien actions. This could lead to a priority contest under ss. 44(9) and 80 for the benefit of any security posted in the main action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ben-Air Systems Inc." p2="Neilas (799 College St) Inc." post.rptr="7205" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I64190f935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ben-Air Systems Inc. v. Neilas (799 College St) Inc.">Ben-Air Systems Inc. v. Neilas (799 College St) Inc., 2014 ONSC 7205, 2014 CarswellOnt 17576, 45 C.L.R. (4th) 71 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a motion to reduce security under s. 44(5), it is well settled law that the onus of proof the moving party must meet is comparable to that which applies to a motion for summary judgment. The defendant failed to meet that standard in this case. The dismissal of the plaintiff's subcontractor's lien claim, for failure to appoint a lawyer, could not in any way warrant reduction of the contractor's lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Structform International Ltd." p2="Ashcroft Homes Construction Inc." post.rptr="4544" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64190f945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Structform International Ltd. v. Ashcroft Homes Construction Inc.">Structform International Ltd. v. Ashcroft Homes Construction Inc., 2013 ONSC 4544, 2013 CarswellOnt 9208, 26 C.L.R. (4th) 13 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons as to costs at 2013 CarswellOnt 14280, 2013 ONSC 6283, 233 A.C.W.S. (3d) 566 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It will only be appropriate to reduce the security if it can convincingly be demonstrated that the maximum recovery by the lien claimant will be less than the amount it has liened for. The test to be applied on a motion of this type is similar to that on a summary judgment motion, however, it is important to note that a motion under s. 44 of the Act is not a full-fledged summary judgment motion under Rule 20. If a portion of the lien claim is attributable to damages that are not properly the subject of a lien then the security should be reduced to take that into account. Security can also be reduced if there are elements of the claim which are properly lienable but are clearly inflated. Mathematical and addition errors in calculating the lien or other admissions obtained on cross examination may be taken into account in assessing the amount of the security. That said, however, the lien claimant should not be held to a standard of strict mathematical or scientific proof at this early stage of the litigation, and as long as the amount claimed is not grossly excessive it may nevertheless be proper. It is not inherently unreasonable to include amounts in a claim for lien that must be estimated. Here, where an additional claim contained in the claim for lien was for non lienable delay damages or overestimated, the security was reduced by that amount.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1652472 Ontario Inc." p2="Miwel Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4433" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64190f955fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1652472 Ontario Inc. v. Miwel Construction Ltd.">1652472 Ontario Inc. v. Miwel Construction Ltd., 2013 ONSC 4433, 2013 CarswellOnt 9044, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 104 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved for an order reducing the amount of security posted in court as security for the various liens in more than 45 construction lien actions. Under normal circumstances, when numerous liens are registered and all are bonded off, there is likely to be excess security because a number of liens will overlap. The best approach was for the lien claimants to pool the security and to agree on a single bond sufficient to cover off all liens. In the absence of consent, it was difficult to determine which liens should be reduced. The Master ordered all parties to review the amounts properly lienable and the maximum holdback liability to which the liens could attach. Where certain lien claimants conceded that their liens were too high or the same claim for lien was registered on two improvements and bonded off twice, the master reduced the security accordingly.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Ledcor Construction Ltd." p2="Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc." post.rptr="9199" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I641936a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc.">Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9199 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A motion to reduce security under section 44(5) cannot succeed where there are genuine issues of fact that require a trial to determine whether the entire amount claimed or some lesser amount is appropriate. Only where the evidence clearly and unequivocally proves that the lien as registered is excessive or improper should the court reduce or release security at an interlocutory stage. A motion is not a substitute for a lien trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Ashco Paving" p2="Brant Q.E.W. Developments Inc." post.rptr="3163" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I641936a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ashco Paving v. Brant Q.E.W. Developments Inc.">Ashco Paving v. Brant Q.E.W. Developments Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3163, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 281 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The owner sought, pursuant to s. 44(5), to reduce the amount of the security which was posted to vacate all of the liens registered on the property. The owner had settled its claims with a great number of the lien claimants, and the security with respect to those claimants was reduced on consent. The remaining lien claimants vigorously opposed the owner's application. In dismissing the application, the court noted that the holdback belonged to the lien claimants as a class, and the security stood to the credit of all the lien claimants. The owner chose to release portions of the holdback funds to certain lien claimants while others received nothing, thereby undermining the ability of the responding lien claimants to challenge the timelines or quantum of those liens. Further, the remaining lien claimants lost the ability to share prorate in the security that was released to the lien claimants the owner had settled with. Although there was some case law that might suggest a court could take “a good hard look at the lien claims”, it was not appropriate for the court to resolve on affidavits alone, conflicting evidence on outstanding issues involving the work done and amounts owning. Those were issues for a trial judge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Proform Construction Ltd." p2="Noblestar Properties (Central) Inc." post.rptr="4973" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I641936a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Proform Construction Ltd. v. Noblestar Properties (Central) Inc.">Proform Construction Ltd. v. Noblestar Properties (Central) Inc. (2001), [2001] O.J. No. 4973, 2001 CarswellOnt 4414 (Master)</ref></cite>—In an application under s. 44(5) to reduce the amount of security paid into court, the following amounts, <ital>inter alia</ital>, were deducted from the face amount of the registered lien: certain office overheads; certain G.S.T. claims; marketing and research claims; work done on other projects; the costs of an assistant on stand-by at the same time that the engineer supervisor was also on standby; and that portion of administration costs which included the costs of running an offsite office.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Tom Jones Corp." p2="OSBBC Ltd." post.rptr="44" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I641936a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tom Jones Corp. v. OSBBC Ltd.">Tom Jones Corp. v. OSBBC Ltd. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 44 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Although s. 44(5) does not expressly provide for the substitution of lien bonds for cash or <ital>vice versa</ital>, restricting substitution of one type of security for another, under s. 44(5), would be unduly restrictive and perhaps absurd. While there is no difference at law between the posting of a letter of credit and a payment of money into court or, for that matter, the filing of a lien bond in lieu of cash, it would make a difference to the person moving to vacate the lien in that the posting of a lien bond would free up working capital which could be put to better use, and which would facilitate the completion of the project.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="T.R.A.C.S. Construction Ltd." p2="Whitby Hydro-Electric Commission" post.rptr="214" pre.rptr="10" ref.id="I641936a45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="T.R.A.C.S. Construction Ltd. v. Whitby Hydro-Electric Commission">T.R.A.C.S. Construction Ltd. v. Whitby Hydro-Electric Commission (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 214 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien, one of three liens on title, was for $180,008.56. The defendant posted a bond for 100 per cent of all three liens plus 25 per cent for costs, totalling $256,076.32. The liens and the one certificate of action were vacated after the bond was posted, and the other two claims were settled and paid. The defendant applied to reduce the security by posting a fresh bond under the same terms for $225,010.70, which was the total amount claimed in the plaintiff's claim for lien plus 25 per cent for costs. The earlier bond would then be delivered up for cancellation. The Master rejected the plaintiff's objection that it might have a claim against the first bond if it established a claim for lien in excess of $180,008.56 plus 25 per cent for costs, and if interest or awarded costs exceeded 25 per cent. There was only one lien claimant left and its claim could only be established to a maximum of $180,008.56. Under the new bond there would be security of $225,010.70 with the court, so there could be no deficiency. Interest was not lienable and it was doubtful that costs were lienable, and, in any event, there would be security of $45,002.14 for costs. This would surely cover any award of costs to the plaintiff. In the result, the new proposed security was adequate to cover the “lien” of the plaintiff that was permitted by the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Neil Vanderkruk Holdings Inc." p2="Grand Harbour Development Ltd." post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I64195db05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Neil Vanderkruk Holdings Inc. v. Grand Harbour Development Ltd.">Neil Vanderkruk Holdings Inc. v. Grand Harbour Development Ltd. (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 205 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Every lien claimant's lien had been bonded off and secured for 100 per cent plus 25 cents for costs, and the plaintiff had settled with the owner. The parties and one defendant consented to have the action dismissed and the security paid out to the plaintiff and the defendant in some share proportions. Two lien claimants objected on the basis that future lien claims might be made, share in their security and thus reduce it. The Master dismissed the objection, stating that the land stood as security for these future claimants. The possibility of future lien claims did not prevent the plaintiff's motion from being successful.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:8: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:8</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(5.1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sundance Development Corporation" p2="Islington Chauncey Residence Corp." post.rptr="241" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64195db15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sundance Development Corporation v. Islington Chauncey Residence Corp.">Sundance Development Corporation v. Islington Chauncey Residence Corp., 2021 ONSC 241, 2021 CarswellOnt 105, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 350 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master could not grant the defendant's <ital>ex parte</ital> motion to vacate the lien in part because the letter of credit submitted for approval as security for the lien was unacceptable, as it made no reference to being issued in respect of the subject premises or the claim for lien, and the language used by the issuing bank was variant from the form of letter of credit generally accepted by the court. More importantly, the letter of credit was subject to the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (“UCP”) of the International Chamber of Commerce, which terms was not before the court, absent which the master could not ascertain if there were conditions under which the bank could refuse to honour a demand on the letter of credit contrary to the intent of lien security within the scheme of <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Although the current Act contemplates that a letter of credit containing reference to an international commercial convention may be acceptable security, such a letter of credit is only acceptable where the convention text is written into the terms of the credit and the letter of credit is unconditional and accepted by a Schedule I bank operating in Ontario. It was not clear that the UCP document contained no additional conditions available to the bank not reflected in the text of the letter of credit, and that it was truly unconditional, other than with respect to standard conditions of automatic renewal and cancellation. Counsel was referred to Appendix II in <ital>Conduct of Lien, Trust and Adjudication Proceedings</ital> for a draft form of letter of credit commonly accepted by the court.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:9: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:9</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(6)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64195db25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After multiple lien claimants contracted directly with the defendant owner in respect of the construction of various townhouses, the owner abandoned the project and the defendant mortgagee stepped in to complete construction and sales of the remaining units. The mortgagee posted security pursuant to s. 44(1) to vacate the claims for lien registered by the claimants, rather than register security on title pursuant to s. 78(10), or moving under s. 68 to appoint a trustee to complete and sell the properties. Applying both <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I90edd5c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I641984c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the Court confirmed that following the posting of security and an order made pursuant to s. 44, the priority of a lien claimant is limited to any deficiency in the holdback. The legislation did not intend a different priority between lien holders and mortgagees based only on the fact that a mortgagee moved under s. 44 to vacate the liens in order to facilitate a sale. Section 78(2) and the limit it imposes on the priority provided to lien claimants still applied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I641984c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In a novel case, the mortgagee bank financed a construction project under a building mortgage, and the subcontractors registered construction liens against the owner's property for amounts owed by the general contractor. The total amount the owner owed to the general contractor under the building contract far exceeded the amount that the owner was required to withhold for the benefit of the subcontractors pursuant to section 22 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. In order to permit the building project to continue, the bank paid into court funds as security for the subcontractors' claims. Ultimately, the property owner was placed in receivership and the property was sold. The proceeds were not sufficient to satisfy the full amount due to the bank under the building mortgage, and the court held that, by paying money into court and vacating the lien, the bank did not lose the priority it would otherwise have had as mortgagee under subsection 78(2) of the <ital>Act</ital>, since under subsection 44(6), the amount paid into court took the place of the property, and the lien claimants' rights went beyond a charge against the holdback deficiency. After the lien was vacated, the respective priority interests of the mortgagee and lien claimants did not change and continued to be governed by subsection 78(2), with the liens having priority over a building mortgage “to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV” of that statute. The amount of that deficiency in this case was the full amount of the holdback required under subsection 22(1). The Divisional Court subsequently upheld the motions judge's reasoning, noting that the case was distinguished from prior precedents in that the owner's holdback obligation was not necessarily limited to the basic 10% holdback, as it owed much more than that to the contractor and never made payment to the contractor. Under s. 24 of the Act, lien claimants could look to that additional unpaid amount as further security for their liens by giving written notice to the owner, and once given, the lien claimant had security against the owner's interest in the land to the full extent of the amount the owner, as payer, owes to the general contractor. To extend that obligation to a mortgagee would effectively enlarge the statutory definition of “payer”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Ablesystems Mechanical Ltd." p2="AER Comfort Mechanical Services Ltd." post.rptr="236" pre.rptr="78" ref.id="I6419abd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ablesystems Mechanical Ltd. v. AER Comfort Mechanical Services Ltd.">Ablesystems Mechanical Ltd. v. AER Comfort Mechanical Services Ltd. (2009), 78 C.L.R. (3d) 236, 2009 CarswellOnt 6 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Applying <ital>Concord Carriers Ltd. v. Alnet Holdings Ltd.</ital>, the court held that even though s. 47(1) may not technically require the dismissal of any action where a claim for lien has been vacated, an action against an owner or other defendants lacking privity of contract with the plaintiff should be dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Concord Carriers Ltd." p2="Alnet Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="4110" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I6419abd15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Concord Carriers Ltd. v. Alnet Holdings Ltd.">Concord Carriers Ltd. v. Alnet Holdings Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 4110, 15 C.P.C. (6th) 138, 46 C.L.R. (3d) 313 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 9051 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff's claim for lien was vacated from title by virtue of court order, the lien ceased to attach to the premises and ceased to attach to the holdbacks and other amounts subject to a charge under s. 21, and became instead a charge upon the amount paid into court or security posted, and the owner or payer was in the same position as if the lien had not been preserved or written notice of the lien had not been given. Therefore, both the owner and tenant of the property were no longer necessary or proper parties to the action in the absence of privity of contract between the plaintiff and the owner or tenant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Wentworth Condominium Corp. No. 293" p2="Stonehaven Homes Inc." post.rptr="239" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I6419abd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wentworth Condominium Corp. No. 293 v. Stonehaven Homes Inc.">Wentworth Condominium Corp. No. 293 v. Stonehaven Homes Inc. (2005), 47 C.L.R. (3d) 239, 2005 CarswellOnt 4030 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After funds were paid into court in order to vacate a lien in a construction lien action, the plaintiff commenced a second action and sought an order that none of the monies paid into court in the first action be paid out without providing notice to the plaintiff. The plaintiff was not a party to the first action. The court held that litigants in other non-lien actions could not avail themselves of the funds arising from the process of the Act. The purpose of s. 44 of the Act was merely to allow the flow of funding to the construction to resume by vacating the lien so that it is no longer attached to the premises.
