Section 77 of the Act provided that liens have priority over all judgments, executions, assignments, attachments, garnishments and receiving orders except those executed or recovered upon before the time when the first lien arose in respect of the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Benny Haulage Ltd." p2="Carosi Construction Ltd." post.rptr="5238" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I6419abd35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benny Haulage Ltd. v. Carosi Construction Ltd.">Benny Haulage Ltd. v. Carosi Construction Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 5238, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Benny Haulage Ltd. v. Hamilton-Wentworth Roman Catholic)</ital> 33 C.L.R. (2d) 44 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Liens were vacated before any lien action was commenced. The plaintiff then sought an order for leave to discontinue its subsequently commenced action without costs. Master Sandler held that either a stay or an outright dismissal was appropriate, preferring outright dismissal. The court relied upon <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19960626" p1="Bratti Mechanical Inc." p2="Orlando Corp." ref.id="I6419abd45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bratti Mechanical Inc. v. Orlando Corp.">Bratti Mechanical Inc. v. Orlando Corp. (June 26, 1996), Saunders Master (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19930420" p1="Delange Asphalt" p2="W.F. Gallagher Construction" ref.id="I6419abd55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Delange Asphalt v. W.F. Gallagher Construction">Delange Asphalt v. W.F. Gallagher Construction (April 20, 1993), Kirsh's Construction Case Finder No. 4429, Tobias J.</ref></cite> (unreported). For the further progress of this case through the court system, see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Benny Haulage Ltd." p2="Carosi Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2989" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I6419abd65fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benny Haulage Ltd. v. Carosi Construction Ltd.">Benny Haulage Ltd. v. Carosi Construction Ltd. (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2989, 40 C.L.R. (2d) 247 (Ont. C.A.); refusing leave to appeal from (1998), 39 C.L.R. (2d) 175, 1998 CarswellOnt 3036 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varied (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 4114, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Benny Haulage Ltd. v. Hamilton-Wentworth Roman Catholic Separate School Board)</ital> 33 C.L.R. (2d) 47 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Tilar Roofing Ltd." p2="John Boddy Developments Ltd." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I6419abd75fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tilar Roofing Ltd. v. John Boddy Developments Ltd.">Tilar Roofing Ltd. v. John Boddy Developments Ltd. (1986), 20 C.L.R. 161 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Subsection 36(3)(a) makes it clear that, when an order vacating a lien has been obtained, a claimant must still commence an action within the requisite period although the claimant does not file a certificate of action on title. Subsection 44(6) does not alter the effect of s. 36(3)(a) by stating that a lien becomes a charge against the security posted. It does not transform the action from one for a lien to an action to realize a “charge” against moneys, and the section does not provide a separate right of action against such security. Section 44 merely states the obvious, that the lands are free of the charge once security has been posted, it does not provide a different right or procedure after the placing of security.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="Akimov" p2="K-W Housing Co-operative Inc." post.rptr="794" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I6419d2e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Akimov v. K-W Housing Co-operative Inc.">Akimov v. K-W Housing Co-operative Inc. (1984), 47 O.R. (2d) 794, 7 C.L.R. 274, 34 R.P.R. 150 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—Once vacating orders were obtained and registered, the liens so vacated became charges against the security posted, and therefore became “unpreserved”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Supreme Signs Ltd." p2="Chartex Construction Ltd." post.rptr="851" pre.rptr="1992" ref.id="I56143100fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Supreme Signs Ltd. v. Chartex Construction Ltd.">Supreme Signs Ltd. v. Chartex Construction Ltd. (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 851, 2 C.L.R. (2d) 305 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—On account of its counsel's failure to obtain judgment against a defendant, the plaintiff could not collect its judgment out of a bond filed with the court at the time the order was made discharging the lien. The action was dismissed as against the defendant, and the plaintiff applied to set aside the order. The application was allowed. Counsel for the defendants was under no obligation to remind the plaintiff's counsel about a fact which he had forgotten, but he was obliged not to mislead in any way, including by silence, either the court or the plaintiff's counsel. On the evidence, the defendants agreed that the plaintiff could look to the bond for payment and confirmed the plaintiff's counsel's mistaken belief that he could do so even without a judgment against the defendant.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:10: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:10</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(9)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd." p2="Grascan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1028" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6419f9f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd. v. Grascan Construction Ltd.">Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd. v. Grascan Construction Ltd., 2017 ONSC 1028, 2017 CarswellOnt 3814, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 151 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant in a lien action successfully moved to strike the plaintiff's claim, obtain default judgment against the plaintiff on its counterclaim, discharge the plaintiff's lien, and obtain delivery up for cancellation of the lien bond posted by the defendant in relation to the plaintiff's lien. The court rejected the argument of a sub-contractor of the plaintiff that the bond should not be delivered up for cancellation because the sub-contractor had a claim against the plaintiff for interest and costs. Section 44(9) did not entitle the sub-contractor to claim any portion of the bond relating to plaintiff's lien. All of the liens were bonded-off and pooling of security for costs could therefore not take place. The operation of (Ont.) R. 3 was such that where all of the liens were bonded off, there would be no amounts from the sale of the premises or otherwise and accordingly pooling would not take place. The Court of Appeal's conclusion in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90ee4af0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> that security for costs could be pooled was not one of general application. Rather, that conclusion was reached on the basis of counsel's agreement as to the effect of (Ont.) RR. 2 and 3 and without any analysis of the wording of those rules.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="2058007 Ontario Inc." p2="1381794 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5256" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I6419f9f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2058007 Ontario Inc. v. 1381794 Ontario Inc.">2058007 Ontario Inc. v. 1381794 Ontario Inc. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 5256 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The security posted for a lien claim is pooled and available for other claims. To participate in a distribution from the posted security, a person with an unpreserved lien must register a claim for lien. The security stands for all persons entitled to a lien, and is distributed among those who ultimately pursue their lien claims. If the totality of the posted security exceeds that required for all extant claims, then a motion may be brought to reduce security on that basis. However, if there is insufficient equity in the property to pay all valid claims, and one claimant settles, the court will not return the security posted by that claimant on the basis that to do so could result in the settling claimant receiving priority over other claimants, in violation of the principle in ss. 80 and 44(9), Rule 2. It would not be fair for one claimant to settle at a basis more favourable than the other claimants and thereby reduce the security available to all. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court concluded that <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I56145810fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc.">Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc. (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 66, 36 O.R. (3d) 502, 1997 CarswellOnt 4411 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, was incorrectly decided. In <ital>Interhaven</ital>, the learned Master ordered return of the security posted for a lien claim where there were only two claimants; the lien of one had been lost through misconduct rather than settlement, and thus the lien claimant had not achieved any advantage over the remaining claimant as a result. The court here did not agree that these differences should have formed a basis for returning the security in <ital>Interhaven</ital>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Georgian Equipment & Contracting Services Ltd." p2="Ross Clair Contractors" post.rptr="2212" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I6419f9f45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Georgian Equipment & Contracting Services Ltd. v. Ross Clair Contractors">Georgian Equipment & Contracting Services Ltd. v. Ross Clair Contractors (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2212, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A general contractor moved for an order dismissing the action and delivery up of a bond. A subcontractor registered two liens, which the general bonded off. Eight other subcontractors of the same class also liened, but were not bonded off. When the subcontractor which was bonded off was petitioned into bankruptcy, its trustee decided not to proceed with the lien action and did not object to a motion to dismiss the action and for delivery up of the bond. All other lien claimants opposed the motion. The court allowed the motion for delivery up of the bond. It held that the bankrupt subcontractor was in exactly the same position as a lien claimant whose lien had expired. The court held that it would have been illogical in these circumstances to expect the general contractor to provide security for a lien claimant who had no possibility of sharing in the claims of the other lien claimants, since there was no possibility of the other lien claimants unfairly obtaining any priority. The reasoning of Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I90ee4af1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc.">Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc. (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 66, 36 O.R. (3d) 502, 1997 CarswellOnt 4411 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, was adopted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Modern Glass & Mirror Ltd." p2="Chicanda Ltd." post.rptr="5559" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I641a21015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Modern Glass & Mirror Ltd. v. Chicanda Ltd.">Modern Glass & Mirror Ltd. v. Chicanda Ltd. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 5559, 1998 CarswellOnt 5179 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1999), 46 C.L.R. (2d) 316 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Money was paid out of court in one lien action, to the prejudice of a lien claimant in a second lien action involving the same property. The plaintiff in the second action sought to have the money paid back into court to the credit of the second action. In such circumstances, the plaintiff should have brought a motion in the first action under Ont. R. 37.14 as a person affected by an order obtained on an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion, rather than a fresh motion in its action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd." p2="Roche Ltée" post.rptr="2851" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I56147f20fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée">M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Roche Ltée (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2851, 39 C.L.R. (2d) 251 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Defendant settled 21 lien claims of 19 lien claimants, leaving 4 who had not settled. The Defendant moved for a corresponding reduction of security. The case can only be described as a compendium of the law under s. 44, clearly and succinctly stated and applied. <ital>Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd.</ital> was distinguished as there certain liens remained on title. In <ital>M. Sullivan</ital> all were bonded off. The “pooling” rule, R. 3, was held to apply only where money was realized by the sale of the premises, not where all liens are bonded off. Rules 2 or 3 do not require “pooling” where all liens are off title. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90ee7200f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> is confined to its unique facts.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I90ee7201f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc.">Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc. (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 66, 36 O.R. (3d) 502, 1997 CarswellOnt 4411 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The Plaintiff contractor liened and the lien was bonded off title. A completion contractor also liened and was bonded off title. The original contractor essentially abandoned its case and failed to pay costs awarded against it. The owner moved under s. 47 to discharge and dismiss the original contractor's lien and action and for a return of security. Subsection 44(9), Rr. 2 and 3, are not applicable where the lien of a claimant has been lost by procedural misconduct, and there remains only one lien against title, with all other liens having been vacated upon posting security, and where there will never be “a distribution” as between the lien claimant's as contemplated by R. 3 of s. 44(9). The Master allowed the motion which was opposed by the completion contractor. The so-called “pooling provisions” in s. 44(9) Rr. 2 and 3 were argued, unsuccessfully, in opposition. The Master distinguished <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Atlas Corp." p2="617430 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="201" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I641a48125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd.">Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 201 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> on the factual difference that in <ital>Atlas</ital> certain liens remained on title. This case is under appeal motion to quash dismissed at (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2378 (Ont. C.A.).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Grant" p2="Tiercel Digital Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I641a48135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Grant v. Tiercel Digital Ltd.">Grant v. Tiercel Digital Ltd. (1993), 9 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Prior to the signing of an agreement of purchase and sale, it was made clear to the purchasers and his solicitor that there were substantial construction liens registered against the property. The agreements of purchase and sale required the vendors to discharge any liens, charges, and encumbrances affecting the real property on or before completion. The so-called Northern Air doctrine, decided under s. 29 of the repealed <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, established that all moneys a party paid into court to obtain the removal of liens and certificates of action could be used to satisfy all such claims then subsisting, regardless of any limits on the paying party's liability. The vendors believed that their actual liability to the lienholders was $500,000, but that the effect of the doctrine would require them, if they chose to discharge the liens by paying moneys into court, to pay an additional $400,000 into court to discharge the liens. The agreements of purchase and sale were eventually amended to provide that the agreements would automatically be terminated if the vendors were unable to delete all construction liens from title by a specified date. The lien trials were delayed beyond that date, and the vendors refused to close, based on the amending agreement. In December 1989, the vendors resold the land for a higher amount, and the purchasers sued for breach of the agreement of purchase and sale. The court dismissed the purchaser's action. The amending agreement provided that if the lien claims were not removed by the specified date, the transactions would be at an end. The vendors were entitled to rely on this clause and the did so. The vendors' conduct could not be described as reckless or lacking in substantive fairness. The purchaser was unable to rely on the doctrine of estoppel.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Atlas Corp." p2="617430 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="201" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I641a48145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd.">Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 201 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 44(9)2 of the Act, the money paid into court is subject to the claims of all persons having a lien. Pursuant to s. 1(1)18 of the Act, the definition of “person having a lien” includes both a lien claimant and a person with an unpreserved lien. Therefore, the money paid into court stands not only to the credit of those who have proved a lien after a trial, or whose lien has been consented to by the defendant, but is also subject to those lien claimants who have only just filed their lien.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
44:11: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 44.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">44:11</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 44(9)2</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dew Point Insulation Systems Inc." p2="Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="2759" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I641a6f205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dew Point Insulation Systems Inc. v. Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd.">Dew Point Insulation Systems Inc. v. Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd., 2017 ONSC 2759, 2017 CarswellOnt 12707, 83 C.L.R. (4th) 175 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant general contractor G engaged the services of the subcontractor AMC which, in turn, hired the plaintiff sub-subcontractor DPIS. AMC made no payments to DPIS, and subsequently registered a lien against G, which posted security to vacate AMC's lien. AMC did not pursue its lien action. After DPIS registered its own lien and commenced its own action against the G and AMC, G posted security by way of a lien bond pursuant to s. 44(1)(d) to vacate DPIS's lien. Making no recovery from AMC, DPIS claimed judgment against G, for a sum exceeding the amount of security posted by G to vacate DPIS' lien. DPIS sought to apply some of the security that was posted by G to vacate the AMC lien to satisfy the balance owing on its claims, including its claims for pre-judgment interest and costs. Relying on the authority of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90ee9910f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, the court held that the security posted by G to vacate the AMC lien could be used to satisfy DPIS' claims to the extent it exceeded the security posted in connection with its own lien. This included DPIS' claims for costs and interest. Whether an award for interest arises out of a judgment, or is otherwise awarded pursuant to the wider discretion of the court under s. 128 and s. 130 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, the recovery of such an award for interest was not precluded by the <ital>Act</ital>. The treatment of interest and costs in excess of that recoverable under the <ital>Act</ital> should be treated as a collection matter in the absence of competing creditors. The debt, including the lien amount, costs and interest, was accordingly to be paid out of the pooled security held in court. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In reaching its decision, the court adopted the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I90eec020f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. Presumably, on a reading of <ital>P & D Holdings Ltd.</ital>“the pooled security” referenced by the court here refers only to the costs portions of the bonds put as security, not that portion of the bond securing the lien itself.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Morley" p2="Vann" post.rptr="2971" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I641a6f235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Morley v. Vann">Morley v. Vann (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 2971, 63 C.L.R. (3d) 191 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant negotiated the dismissal of the lien action of one of the claimants, and the return of the letter of credit posted as security for that lien claim. A second lien claimant sheltering under the lien argued that the letter of credit should remain in place as security for its lien claim, even though the defendant had posted a separate letter of credit as security for the second lien claim. The first lien action was dismissed and the letter of credit was returned for cancellation. The lien claimant sought security for its lien claim beyond its right to security as set out in the Act. The distribution of funds described in s. 44(9)2 is restricted to the lien claims of the lien claimants, and does not apply to all claims, personal or secured, that any lien claimant may have against the defendant. Therefore, in this case, any right that the second claimant might have had to a share of the security under R. 2 was restricted to the amount of its lien claim, which was the money owing for services and materials provided and 25 per cent for costs. Since the second claimant already had security for this amount, Rule 2 was not engaged. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: A similar case is <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Georgian Equipment & Contracting Services Ltd." p2="Ross Clair Contractors" post.rptr="2212" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I641a96305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Georgian Equipment & Contracting Services Ltd. v. Ross Clair Contractors">Georgian Equipment & Contracting Services Ltd. v. Ross Clair Contractors (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2212, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I2d73ed20f65111ee9732e3e835885970" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—As a claim for interest is not a valid lien claim, a personal judgment for interest in favor of a subcontractor can neither be enforced against the land, nor against the bond posted by the general contractor to remove that subcontractor's lien. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Barber-Colman of Canada Ltd." p2="Scarborough (City)" post.rptr="627" pre.rptr="[1987]" ref.id="I641a96325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barber-Colman of Canada Ltd. v. Scarborough (City)">Barber-Colman of Canada Ltd. v. Scarborough (City) (1987), [1987] O.J. No. 627</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd." p2="Roko Construction Ltd." post.rptr="268" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I90eee730f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd.">M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 268, 26 O.R. (3d) 516 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>; and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Roboak Developments Ltd." p2="Lehndorff Corp." post.rptr="194" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I641a96345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Roboak Developments Ltd. v. Lehndorff Corp.">Roboak Developments Ltd. v. Lehndorff Corp. (1986), 39 R.P.R. 194; affirmed (1987), 47 R.P.R. 274 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> are all considered and approved. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Francon" p2="L. Nicolini Construction Ltd." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I641a96355fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Francon v. L. Nicolini Construction Ltd.">Francon v. L. Nicolini Construction Ltd. (1988), 33 C.L.R. 107, 1988 CarswellOnt 777 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite> is distiguished and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I641abd405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> is overruled to the extent that it conflicts with the Court's decision in <ital>P & D Holdings</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd." p2="Roko Construction Ltd." post.rptr="268" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I90eee731f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd.">M. Alzner Contractors Ltd. v. Roko Construction Ltd. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 268, 26 O.R. (3d) 516 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Nowhere in s. 44 is a claim for interest added on in the same way as a claim for costs was “added on” to a payment in under s. 44, therefore where third party security such as a lien bond or letter of credit is posted, interest may not be claimed from that security.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
45:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 45.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">45:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The provisions regarding the discharge of liens can be traced back to s. 26(4) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(4)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">Where the certificate required by section 22 or section 23 of this Act has not been registered within the time limited, and an application is made to vacate the registration of a lien after the time for registration of the certificate required by section 22 or 23 of this Act, the applicant shall not be required to give notice of the application to the person claiming the lien, and the order vacating the lien may be made <ital>ex parte</ital> upon production of the certificate of the proper registrar certifying the facts entitling the applicant to such order.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision remained in substantially the same format for more than 70 years. In 1968–69, the requirement to produce a “certificate of the proper registrar” was replaced by a requirement to produce documentation under either the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital> or the <ital>Registry Act</ital>; see s. 25(5) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65. This section was introduced in its present form in s. 45 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, replacing s. 29(5) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Where it is evident on the face of the record that a lien has not been preserved or perfected with the time periods allowed under ss. 31 or 36 and has thereby expired, this section permits a motion without notice to have the lien declared expired and vacate its registration from title. Once proof that the lien has expired is presented, the section is mandatory and the court must issue a declaration to that effect and order the registration of the claim for lien to be vacated. The return of any amount paid into court under s. 44 is provided for in subs. (3).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2829785 Ontario Inc." p2="Total Home & Yard Improvement Inc." post.rptr="15772" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dca7e50ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2829785 Ontario Inc. v. Total Home & Yard Improvement Inc.">2829785 Ontario Inc. v. Total Home & Yard Improvement Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 15772, 2023 ONSC 5855 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion to declare a lien expired may be brought without notice to any other person, as set out in s. 45(1)(a). Motions to declare liens expired are commonly brought <ital>ex parte</ital> in Toronto Region. Opposed motions in non-Toronto actions or, if no action has been commenced, dealing with non-Toronto properties cannot be brought in Toronto. Here, the lien claimant's position on the <ital>ex parte</ital> motion needed to be sought, and if the lien claimant ultimately consented or was unopposed to the motion, then it could be brought in Toronto, in writing and with leave. Otherwise, the motion was to be brought on notice to the lien claimant in the jurisdiction where the property was situated or in the court where any action by the lien claimant had been commenced.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Mobilinx Hurontario Contractor" p2="Edge1 Equipment Rentals Inc." post.rptr="5885" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dca7e51ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Mobilinx Hurontario Contractor v. Edge1 Equipment Rentals Inc.">Mobilinx Hurontario Contractor v. Edge1 Equipment Rentals Inc., 2023 ONSC 5885 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The evidentiary requirements for an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion brought under s. 45 are not the same as the evidentiary requirements for an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion brought under s. 44. A motion under s. 44 is brought essentially to change the security for a lien. A vacating motion seeks interlocutory relief that does not prejudice an absent lien claimant; it merely swaps the security interest for another form of security. No determinations are made on the validity of the lien. A motion under s. 45 is not the same. It is a motion seeking a final order. A declaration that a lien has expired is irrevocable. Therefore, evidence on a motion to declare a lien expired must satisfy the court that no additional evidence or argument from the absent lien claimant would reasonably make a difference in disposition of the motion. That is required because the lien claimant has no opportunity to file responding materials or argue against the relief sought. The evidence filed by the moving party must support a clear finding that the subject lien has expired.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Blundell" p2="Frederick Fortune Operating as Home-Works et al." post.rptr="1722" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I641ae4505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Blundell v. Frederick Fortune Operating as Home-Works et al.">Blundell v. Frederick Fortune Operating as Home-Works et al., 2019 ONSC 1722, 2019 CarswellOnt 4727, 99 C.L.R. (4th) 7 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Whether funds paid to counsel in trust can be considered equivalent to funds paid into court for security may be determined according to the context and circumstances of the particular case. Here, the lien claimant registered a lien as the result of unpaid invoices by the subcontractor. The subcontractor alleged the unpaid amounts were set-offs to address deficiencies in the lien claimant's work. The correspondence from the subcontractor enclosing a trust payment to the sub-subcontractor, equal to the lien amount, did not make it clear that the funds were intended to function as a payment of security, nor did it set out any conditions on the trust. However, an agreement by the sub-subcontractor to discharge the lien after receipt of the payment into trust was more consistent with the expectation that the funds would be released to satisfy the unpaid invoices unless a claim in respect of the deficiencies was brought by the subcontractor. The application by the claimant's solicitor to release to his client the funds in his trust account was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Janik" p2="Stillman" post.rptr="1801" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I641b0b605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Janik v. Stillman">Janik v. Stillman, 2016 ONSC 1801, 2016 CarswellOnt 10279, 68 C.L.R. (4th) 201 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 19470 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lawyer was held liable in tort and contract for breach of his duty of reasonable competence and diligence as solicitor of record in a lien action. He neglected to inform the plaintiff of the potential risk of the removal of the lien and possible steps that could be taken to preserve his interest in the property, and consented to the lien being removed from title without getting instructions from the client and without notifying the client once he had done so. Even though the lawyer was of the belief that the construction lien was the wrong remedy, in that the plaintiff was claiming ownership interest in the property, he failed to raise this opinion and failed to offer advice as to alternative remedies to preserve the plaintiff's interest in the property.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="State Group Inc." p2="Quebecor World Inc." post.rptr="2277" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641b0b615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc.">State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc., 2013 ONSC 2277, 2013 CarswellOnt 4462, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 164 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>: A contractor sought an order declaring the claim for lien under which its claimed purported to shelter was a valid sheltering lien and properly perfected in relation to the subject improvement. With respect to the master's jurisdiction to make such an order under sections 45, 46 or 47 of the Act, he proceeded on the basis of his inherent general jurisdiction as a superior court judge, as the motion was being brought within the context of a reference of which he was seized.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Disal Contracting Ltd." p2="J. Salamon Holdings Inc." post.rptr="200" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I641b0b625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Disal Contracting Ltd. v. J. Salamon Holdings Inc.">Disal Contracting Ltd. v. J. Salamon Holdings Inc. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 200 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4275 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4274 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the dates upon which the plaintiffs' work was completed were in dispute, and the plaintiffs failed to call evidence from individuals who could have supplied information respecting the last day of work, or to provide admissible business records supporting their position, it could not be established that the liens in question were filed within prescribed periods. The claims for lien were therefore held to be invalid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Carosi Construction Ltd." p2="Barrie & District Assn. for People with Special Needs" post.rptr="275" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I641b0b635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carosi Construction Ltd. v. Barrie & District Assn. for People with Special Needs">Carosi Construction Ltd. v. Barrie & District Assn. for People with Special Needs (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 275 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Publication of a certificate of substantial completion is notice to all suppliers of materials and services that lien periods have started to run, irrespective of what stage the work is at, but only with regard to materials and services supplied prior to publication. There is no expiry of lien rights regarding materials and services supplied after the date in the published certificate. A plaintiff that continued to contractually supply materials and services after publication is not required to register a further claim for lien and a certificate of action where its lien claim also includes work supplied prior to publication.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="690452 Ontario Ltd." p2="Cataract Plaza Ltd." post.rptr="231" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I641b0b645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="690452 Ontario Ltd. v. Cataract Plaza Ltd.">690452 Ontario Ltd. v. Cataract Plaza Ltd. (1989), 36 C.L.R. 231 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—During discoveries it was determined that the last invoice for work submitted by the plaintiff to the defendant was dated more than 45 days prior to registration of the lien. There were discrepancies in the plaintiff's evidence, which included allegations that a percentage of work was completed after the invoices were submitted. The defendant moved to have the lien set aside because the lien was filed more than 45 days after the last invoice had been submitted, and the motion was dismissed. Pleadings in a construction lien action are succinct and the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> concerning discoveries are normally suspended. In this instance, the defendant merely highlighted the inconsistencies in the plaintiff's evidence. It was not the function of a judge in this instance, to deprive either party of significant remedies afforded by law on the basis of findings of credibility. The evidence was equivocal to what percentage of work was done prior to the date the last invoice was sent. It was, thus, for the trial judge to determine what weight would be given to the plaintiff's statements concerning the amount of work allegedly done after the invoices had been submitted.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 45(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Quality General Contractor's Inc." p2="Wu" post.rptr="2909" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I676e99403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Quality General Contractor's Inc. v. Wu">Quality General Contractor's Inc. v. Wu, 2024 CarswellOnt 7523, 2024 ONSC 2909, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2528 (Ont.S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 14677, 2024 ONSC 5318 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In an action under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the plaintiff lien claimant failed to meet its onus of proving the timeliness of its claim for lien, which expired on account of its failure to have it preserved. The invoices provided to the court to support the last day of supply were found to be generated to construct an inaccurate narrative after the fact and did not accord with the evidence. The plaintiff's site diary entries also lacked credibility, and the plaintiff failed to produce timesheet entries that would have been critical evidence to show attendance at the site. </para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gandhi" p2="Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="1001" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I676e99413b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd.">Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 1691, 2024 ONSC 1001, 2024 A.C.W.S. 686 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A declaration that a lien has expired pursuant to s. 45 is a final order, as the declaration is irrevocable and an expired lien cannot be revived. Likewise, an order releasing funds held in counsel's trust account as an alternative form of security in lieu of a claim for lien is also a final order.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nova Concrete Inc." p2="2035211 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2391" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641b32705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nova Concrete Inc. v. 2035211 Ontario Inc.">Nova Concrete Inc. v. 2035211 Ontario Inc., 2022 ONSC 2391, 2022 CarswellOnt 5224, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 230 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The successor by amalgamation of the original corporate defendant sought to continue the proceeding as defendant, declare the plaintiff's lien expired, pay out security it posted to vacate Nova's lien, and dismiss the action for delay. The plaintiff cross-moved to restore the action to the trial list. In declaring the plaintiff's lien expired and ordering the security posted returned, the court rejected the plaintiff's argument that the defendant's motion should be dismissed because it came to court with unclean hands by failing to serve the vacating order in compliance with its terms and failing to answer an undertaking given on cross-examination. S. 45 was mandatory, and there was no provision of the Act nor any case law supporting a legal or equitable basis on which to deviate from that mandatory language. The court had no ability or discretion to ignore or adjust the time periods set by the legislation. As well, delayed service of the vacating order was not itself sufficient to trigger equitable considerations and the plaintiff had not suffered any prejudice from delayed notice that its lien was vacated.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 45(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2829785 Ontario Inc." p2="Total Home & Yard Improvement Inc." post.rptr="15772" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcaf380ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2829785 Ontario Inc. v. Total Home & Yard Improvement Inc.">2829785 Ontario Inc. v. Total Home & Yard Improvement Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 15772, 2023 ONSC 5855 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion for an order declaring that a lien has expired, the quantum of the lien is not a material factor in deciding whether there is sufficient evidence to support a declaration that the lien has clearly expired. Here, the only evidence tendered in support was a copy of the parties' contract, a statement by the owner that the lien claimant completed work by a specific date, and the fact that a certificate of action had not been registered. There were no other liens, and no issue of sheltering. However, this limited evidence tendered was not enough. Bald and unsubstantiated statements that a contract has been completed (or has been terminated or abandoned) are insufficient to support an ex parte motion to declare a lien expired. Providing “proof” that the lien has clearly expired requires more, such as evidence on whether the lien claimant agreed that the scope of work outlined in the purchase order was the entirety of the contractual scope of work or supporting that the lien claimant did not dispute that it had completed its work. There was a notable absence of any correspondence to or from the lien claimant about the work performed, and the record did not support clear findings on the full contractual scope of work or that all work under the contract has been completed or deemed completed within the meaning of s. 2(3) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. The owner's motion was dismissed without prejudice to moving again on notice to the lien claimant.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 45(3)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nova Concrete Inc." p2="2035211 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2391" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641b32715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nova Concrete Inc. v. 2035211 Ontario Inc.">Nova Concrete Inc. v. 2035211 Ontario Inc., 2022 ONSC 2391, 2022 CarswellOnt 5224, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 230 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The successor by amalgamation of the original corporate defendant sought to continue the proceeding as defendant, declare the plaintiff's lien expired, pay out security it posted to vacate Nova's lien, and dismiss the action for delay. There was no triable issue over timeliness of the plaintiff's lien, in that its lien rights had already expired when the claim for lien was registered. Since the associate judge was satisfied that the lien was not preserved in time, s. 45(3) required that payout be ordered of the funds paid into court to vacate the plaintiff's lien. The plaintiff's action continued as an ordinary action under the Rules.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Slaven" p2="Azadian" post.rptr="7571" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I641b32725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Slaven v. Azadian">Slaven v. Azadian, 2020 ONSC 7571, 2020 CarswellOnt 19676, 21 C.L.R. (5th) 357 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 845, 2021 CarswellOnt 1296, J.R. Henderson J. (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants successfully moved for a declaration that the lien had expired and for an order that the registration of the claim for lien be vacated pursuant to s. 45(1). The parties had entered into a contract for the renovation of the defendants' property, which contract was superseded by a new contract that was eventually abandoned by the plaintiff. Any lien for work done pursuant to the original renovation agreement expired long before the registration of the claim for lien. Based on the last date worked by the plaintiff before abandonment, the lien under the second contract also expired prior to the registration of the claim for lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd." p2="Carnello Civil Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4877" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641b32735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd. v. Carnello Civil Construction Ltd.">Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd. v. Carnello Civil Construction Ltd., 2014 ONSC 4877, 2014 CarswellOnt 11416, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 97 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 CarswellOnt 17069, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 116 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As repair work does not extend lien rights (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates" p2="161975 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3928" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I641b59805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. 161975 Ontario Inc.">Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. 161975 Ontario Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 3928, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>) the work performed here did not extend the plaintiff's lien rights. The court declared the claim for lien expired under s. 45.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Demik Construction Ltd." p2="Royal Crest Lifecare Group Inc." post.rptr="114" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I641b59815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Demik Construction Ltd. v. Royal Crest Lifecare Group Inc.">Demik Construction Ltd. v. Royal Crest Lifecare Group Inc. (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 114 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—It may be argued that a motion under s. 45 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is analogous to a motion for summary judgment under R. 20 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. If so, it is not sufficient for the parties to rely upon the allegations in the pleadings. They must adduce affidavit or other evidence. Subsection 45(1)(b) creates an onus of burden of proof on the moving party to demonstrate that the lien has not been preserved within the time allowed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Landac Developments Ltd." p2="Kerry T. Howe Ltd." post.rptr="12" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I641b59825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Landac Developments Ltd. v. Kerry T. Howe Ltd.">Landac Developments Ltd. v. Kerry T. Howe Ltd. (1990), 38 C.L.R. 12, 72 O.R. (2d) 760 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The owner was developing a residential subdivision and retained the respondent as consulting engineers and planning consultants, to do all of the engineering work and supervision of the sewer, watermain and road construction. The respondent's work had not yet been completed when the construction contractor completed its work, and on November 28, 1988, the respondent published certification that the construction contract was substantially performed. The respondent registered its claim for lien on March 8, 1989, and the owner brought an application for an order that the registration of the respondent's lien claim be vacated on the ground that it was not registered within 45 days of certification publication. The application was dismissed. The respondent was a contractor within the meaning of the definition in the Act. As such, the respondent was subject to the expiry provisions contained in s. 31(2) of the Act, which provided that a contractor's lien expires 45 days after the certificate of substantial performance is published or the contract is completed. Accordingly, the survival of the respondent's lien was not tied to the certificate of substantial completion of another contract. The respondent was, therefore, not required to register its lien claim within the 45-day period following substantial completion publication relating to the work of the construction contractor.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 45(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Southside Construction (London) Ltd." p2="Emco Ltd." post.rptr="73" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I641b59835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southside Construction (London) Ltd. v. Emco Ltd.">Southside Construction (London) Ltd. v. Emco Ltd. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 73 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner applied for a declaration that the lien of E Ltd. was expired, arguing that it was not validly sheltered because there was no indication that the lien was “in respect of the same improvement” as the lien under which it purported to shelter. The court dismissed the application, stating that the perfection through sheltering is a question of fact. Subsection 34(5) of the Act requires a description of the premises appropriate for registration, not identification of “the same improvement”.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 45(3)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="686946 Ontario Inc." p2="A.B.P. Constructors Ltd." post.rptr="5833" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I641b59845fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="686946 Ontario Inc. v. A.B.P. Constructors Ltd.">686946 Ontario Inc. v. A.B.P. Constructors Ltd., 2011 ONSC 5833, 2011 CarswellOnt 11614 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor brought three lien actions against the defendant subcontractor, with the latter initiating a damages action against the plaintiff alleging breach of contract. The plaintiff counterclaimed alleging breach of a joint venture agreement. In each lien action, the respective general contractors posted security by payment into court pursuant to s. 44 of Act, and obtained an order vacating the lien. After more than two years with no substantive steps, the defendant brought three motions for a declaration that the liens had expired, for an order dismissing the actions, and for order that the monies paid into court were to be returned to the general contractors. The plaintiff moved for an order that the monies paid into court in the lien actions were to be held in trust pending disposition of the damages action. On consent in the lien actions, the monies paid into court were ordered paid out to the general contractors, the issues relating to dismissal of the lien actions and costs of the subcontractor motions were adjourned, as was the plaintiff's motion. Any funds received by the defendant subcontractor in respect of the lien actions would be held in trust by its solicitor, pending resolution of the four motions. On consent, the lien actions were dismissed without prejudice to the parties' rights with respect to the damages action, costs were reserved, and certificates of action in lien actions were vacated. The plaintiff's motion was dismissed, as the plaintiff had not shown that Rule 45.02 (where right of party to specific fund is in question, court may order fund paid into court or otherwise secured on terms.) would have application in that the monies were not “profits earned from completing the work under the construction contact”, and reasonably identifiable as earmarked for the litigation in issue. Even assuming that the monies would be paid out by the general contractors to the defendant, there was no evidence which distinguished the monies from any other monies which the defendant may have received or would receive from the general contractors in payment of the goods and services provided.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd." p2="Preston Heights Estates Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="1" ref.id="I641b80905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd.">G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd. (1992), 1 C.L.R. (2d) 157 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The former owner of a property opposed the payment out of court to the first mortgagee of the sum secured by the first mortgage, and brought a cross-motion seeking to have the money paid out to the credit of a separate action that it had brought against the mortgagee in which it claimed a declaration that the first mortgage was void and unenforceable. Alternatively, the former owner requested leave to amend its pleadings in the lien action to claim that the mortgage was void and unenforceable or, alternatively, that the actions be consolidated or tried together. The court dismissed the cross-motion. In its statement of defence, the former owner admitted the validity of the mortgage, and it failed to establish that the admission was made inadvertently; that the solicitor was wrongfully instructed; that the proposed amendment raised a triable issue; or that the admission would not cause injustice to the other parties. What the former really sought was an order preserving the funds so that they could be a source for payment in the event that it was successful in its separate action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Kasper Land Drainage Inc." p2="Spectrum Realty Inc." post.rptr="44" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I641b80915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kasper Land Drainage Inc. v. Spectrum Realty Inc.">Kasper Land Drainage Inc. v. Spectrum Realty Inc. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 44 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's construction lien action was vacated on account of its failure to obtain a trial date, the security which the defendant had posted was cancelled, and the action for recovery of payment continued as provided by s. 38. When the letter of credit was cancelled, the guaranteed investment certificate supporting it as collateral was cashed, and the proceeds were disbursed to various creditors of the defendant. The plaintiff obtained a <ital>Mareva</ital> injunction on the basis that the funds paid out were imposed with a trust pursuant to s. 7(1) Act, and subsequently moved to continue the injunction. Held, the injunction was continued, although it was far from clear that proceeds from the release of the posted security were impressed by a trust under s. 7. Subsection 45(3) provided for the mandatory return of funds paid as security to the payer and did not provide that the funds be subject to the holdback provisions of the Act, although the legislature could have done so. However, it was clear on the evidence that the defendant had not complied with the trust provisions of the Act. The plaintiff had more than a strong <ital>prima facie</ital> case that it would succeed at trial and had met the conditions required to entitle it to a <ital>Mareva</ital> injunction.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
46:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 46.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">46:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 46 was derived from s. 24(3) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which, subject to minor amendments over the years, was introduced to the Ontario lien legislation by way of the amendments of S.O. 1932, c. 19, s. 5. The previous legislation provided that upon an application by any interested person the court may make an order vacating the certificate of action and discharging all the liens depending thereon if the certificate of action had been registered for two or more years and no appointment for the trial of the action had been taken out. In 1975, the amendments of c. 43, s. 11, added what was to become s. 24(4) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which restricted the application of s. 24(3) by making it inapplicable to liens which were not attached to the land. This amendment was seemingly reversed in 1983 with the introduction of s. 46(2), which provides for the dismissal of such liens in such circumstances. Subsection 24(3) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, and its predecessors provided that the motion for dismissal was to be made on an <ital>ex parte</ital> basis. Initially, there was no provision with respect to costs or the release funds or return of security posted with the court. This jurisdiction was found, where necessary in other sections of their early legislation. Subsection 46(4) introduced the mandatory requirement that the court order the release of funds paid into court and return of security posted under s. 44, if the lien action is ordered dismissed. This is a departure from the previous legislation which provided only a general discretionary power to the court to release funds and return security where considered appropriate, as was provided for example in s. 29(6) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 46 provides a complete code as to the consequences of expiration under s. 37. Once a court is satisfied that a lien has expired under s. 37(1), the provisions of s. 46 are mandatory. The court must dismiss the lien action, vacate the registration of the claim and certificate of action, and order the return of any monies paid into court or the cancellation of any security posted under s. 44. The preferred view at the time of writing is that the action itself may continue between the parties to the contract or subcontract as a simple action in debt.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
