C.30, s. 46.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">46:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions)" p2="Deltro Electric Ltd." post.rptr="8182" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I641bceb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions) v. Deltro Electric Ltd.">9727868 Canada Inc. (Plug & Play Solutions) v. Deltro Electric Ltd., 2021 ONSC 8182, 2021 CarswellOnt 19273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At the time the lien was purported to be preserved and perfected, the corporate lien claimant was dissolved due to a missed fee payment, but was subsequently revived upon its general manager filing the appropriate fee and form pursuant the <ital>Canadian Business Corporations Act</ital>. Since it was formally dissolved at the time it preserved and perfected the lien, it was not a legal entity entitled to do so, and did not comply with the required timelines set out in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Bound by the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90eff8a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the court had no discretion in equity to permit the lien action to continue. The medical issues of the general manager, including legal blindness in one eye, did not deter him from operating a business and arranging for the preserving and perfecting of the lien, and were not an excuse not to keep the company books and records in good standing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Associated Paving and Materials Ltd." p2="Pylon Paving 1996 Inc." post.rptr="3718" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641bceb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Associated Paving and Materials Ltd. v. Pylon Paving 1996 Inc.">Associated Paving and Materials Ltd. v. Pylon Paving 1996 Inc., 2014 ONSC 3718, 2014 CarswellOnt 8306, 42 C.L.R. (4th) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's in-house counsel failed to set down for trial the plaintiff's construction lien action for payment for supplied materials within two years of commencement of the action, as required by s. 37, and the defendant obtained an <ital>ex parte</ital> order under s. 46 dismissing the action. The plaintiff brought a motion to set aside a dismissal and permit the claim to continue, on conditions (as per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f01fb0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). The court granted the motion to set aside the dismissal, on the basis that the plaintiff had a viable case, there was no irrevocable prejudice to defendant if the action was restored, and the delays were not so deliberate or egregious as to justify denying a trial on the merits.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="State Group Inc." p2="Quebecor World Inc." post.rptr="2277" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641bceb45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc.">State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc., 2013 ONSC 2277, 2013 CarswellOnt 4462, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 164 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>: A contractor sought an order declaring the claim for lien under which its claimed purported to shelter was a valid sheltering lien and properly perfected in relation to the subject improvement. With respect to the master's jurisdiction to make such an order under sections 45, 46 or 47 of the Act, he proceeded on the basis of his inherent general jurisdiction as a superior court judge, as the motion was being brought within the context of a reference of which he was seized.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sirro Brothers Cement Finishing & Spray Ltd." p2="Wedgewood Brockville Inc." post.rptr="5389" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I641bceb55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sirro Brothers Cement Finishing & Spray Ltd. v. Wedgewood Brockville Inc.">Sirro Brothers Cement Finishing & Spray Ltd. v. Wedgewood Brockville Inc., 2012 ONSC 5389, 2012 CarswellOnt 12094 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While the statement of claim was issued in order to perfect a construction lien which was subsequently vacated, it is not restricted in its terms to an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The order vacating the lien and the certificate of action under the <ital>Act</ital> did not purport to address the claim in contract. It is settled that a motion to dismiss an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> may allow for the action to continue in breach of contract, there being no other impediments.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1339408 Ontario Inc." p2="1579138 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9443" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I90f01fb1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1339408 Ontario Inc. v. 1579138 Ontario Inc.">1339408 Ontario Inc. v. 1579138 Ontario Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 9443, 71 C.L.R. (3d) 13 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.—While the Court of Appeal in <ital>Teepee</ital> held that the guiding principle in interpreting s. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d) was the avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings, the Divisional Court in this case held that with the advent of the <ital>Limitations Act, 2002</ital>, the avoidance of a multiplicity of proceedings was no longer a factor. The court held that if the two-year period for setting the action down for trial has expired, it follows that the two-year limitation period relating to an action in contract will also have expired, thereby precluding any subsequent action in contract. Thus, a plaintiff who sued the defendants within the prescribed limitation period would be denied access to the courts to pursue its claim, if the claims in contract are dismissed under s. 47(1)(d). The Divisional Court allowed the action in contract to proceed based in part on the enormous prejudice if the entire action were dismissed after expiry of the 2-year limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I641bf5c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 138 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3385 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3338, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 5 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5779, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—An order under s. 46 of the Act does not deprive the court of jurisdiction with respect to the parties or other claims that might be advanced under the Act. It merely deprives the court of jurisdiction with respect to the lien claim itself, since s. 46 makes clear that upon the expiry of the two-year period stipulated in s. 37 of the Act, the court shall grant an order vacating the lien and lifting the certificate of action registered against the property alleged to be subject to the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Mueller-Hein Corp." p2="Donar Investments Ltd." post.rptr="2223" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I641bf5c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mueller-Hein Corp. v. Donar Investments Ltd.">Mueller-Hein Corp. v. Donar Investments Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2223, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 143 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 46(3) of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides that a motion for a declaration that a perfected lien has expired under s. 37 may be brought without notice. However, the right to move without notice is not an absolute one. When an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion is presented to the court, the judge or master, as the case may be, must first be assured that the motion falls within one of the notice exceptions. Once a preliminary determination has been made that, indeed, the motion may proceed on an <ital>ex parte</ital> basis, the judge must then consider the matter on its merits. The solicitor having carriage of the motion, as an officer of the court, is under an obligation to ensure that the matter is fully and fairly presented to the court with respect to all material issues. Here, in this case, the non-disclosure was material, and the order was set aside.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="B.R. Davidson Mining & Development Ltd." p2="Lac des Iles Mines Ltd." post.rptr="3966" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I641c1cd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B.R. Davidson Mining & Development Ltd. v. Lac des Iles Mines Ltd.">B.R. Davidson Mining & Development Ltd. v. Lac des Iles Mines Ltd. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 3966, 2003 CarswellOnt 3835, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 175 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It was conceded that the claim for lien expired without being set down for trial before the two years limitation, but the plaintiff argued that the claim in contract that coexisted with the lien action should be allowed to continue, in accordance with the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f046c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. While the lien action had dragged on, the bonding company had commenced a claim against the plaintiff and others as defendants, and in response, the plaintiff had initiated a third party action against, among others, the defendant in the lien action. The claim approximated the allegations in the construction lien action, which was already before the court. In rejecting the plaintiff's argument, the court noted that there was already a second action underway, with pleadings closed, that encompassed the same issues between the same parties in the third party action as in the lien claim. Permitting the contract claim in the lien action to go forward, with the bonding company's claim running parallel, would set up the very multiplicity of proceedings that the Court of Appeal in <ital>Teepee Excavation</ital> sought to avoid. The plaintiff in effect seeks two chances at an adjudication of the same issues. This would be wasteful of costs as between the parties, and wasteful of the court's resources. An order was issued declaring that the plaintiff's lien had expired, ordering the defendant's letter of credit delivered up for cancellation and dismissing the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f06dd0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—When a lien action is not set down for trial within two years of its commencement, there is, nonetheless, discretion to permit a claim on the contract to continue. The avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings guides the interpretation of s. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d) of the Act. The court has discretion to dismiss an action or to proceed without the lien aspect of the claim, as circumstances dictate. All arguments against denying a defendant the procedures and protections of the usual form of litigation can be answered by court's discretion under s. 47(1)(d) to dismiss the action because the defendant will be prejudiced or because little has transpired in the action that would be duplicated or by imposing conditions for continuance to assure protection of the defendant. The legislature intended more than claims for liens to be litigated in lien actions. That intention is best served by an interpretation of s. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d) that leaves it to the court to monitor the interests of the parties and the procedure to be followed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Rentshop Inc." p2="Tekke Thermal Inc." post.rptr="99" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I641c1cd35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rentshop Inc. v. Tekke Thermal Inc.">Rentshop Inc. v. Tekke Thermal Inc. (2001), 6 C.L.R. (3d) 99 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The general provision in s. 54(4) does not take away the power of an owner to move for a declaration and the other relief provided for in s. 46(1) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Park" p2="Metropolitan Separate School Board" post.rptr="202" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I641c43e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Park v. Metropolitan Separate School Board">Park v. Metropolitan Separate School Board (1998), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 202 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The only issue was the timeliness of the plaintiff's lien, and the Master was satisfied from a review of all evidence that the plaintiff would not be able to adduce any further evidence at trial concerning the last day of supply. In granting summary judgment to the plaintiff, and dismissing the defendant's motion under s. 46, the Master relied on the plaintiff's ordinary business records to prove the lien's timeliness on a balance of probabilities.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19931217" p1="K-W Blair Readymix" p2="Matsias" ref.id="I641c43e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K-W Blair Readymix v. Matsias">K-W Blair Readymix v. Matsias (December 17, 1993), Doc. Kitchener 3213/90 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An application by the owners for a declaration under s. 46 that a lien had expired failed where no date was ordered for the trial as required by s. 37(1)(a) Act, although the action was set down within the prescribed time. A perfected lien expires where neither an action has been set down nor a day for trial has been set within the statutory period. Since in this case an action was set down within the required time, the perfected lien continued in force.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Rainone Construction Ltd." p2="American Barrick Resources Corp." post.rptr="259" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I641c43e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rainone Construction Ltd. v. American Barrick Resources Corp.">Rainone Construction Ltd. v. American Barrick Resources Corp. (1991), 43 C.L.R. 259 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claim that was sheltered under the claim of another lien claimant was held to have expired two years from the date of the prior lien's perfection and not from the date of the issuance of its own statement of claim. Accordingly, s. 46 of the Act dictated that the plaintiff's lien action be dismissed and its lien be vacated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd." p2="Samet" post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I641c43e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet">Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet (1991), 46 C.L.R. 317, 4 O.R. (3d) 771, 83 D.L.R. (4th) 574, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Schultz (Benjamin) & Associates Ltd. v. Samet)</ital> 52 O.A.C. 180 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In November 1989, the defendant moved under s. 46 to vacate a lien action on account of the plaintiff's failure to set the action down for trial within the time limits set out in s. 37. Although the action was set down for trial in December 1989, the Master declared the lien expired and ordered registration of the claim for lien to be vacated. The plaintiff's appeal was dismissed. Sections 37(1) and 46 were mandatory and left no room for judicial discretion. The court had no residual discretion to allow a lien action to proceed as an action different from its original form as a construction lien action. Sections 38 and 65, which preserve legal and equitable remedies of the court and allow it to award a personal judgment whether or not a lien is proven, do not render ss. 37 and 46 inoperative.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Graham Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Correct Building Corp." post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I641c43e45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Graham Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Correct Building Corp.">Graham Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Correct Building Corp. (1991), 46 C.L.R. 205 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendants in a lien action brought a motion for an order dismissing the action pursuant to ss. 37 and 46 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> on the basis that the preferred lien expired because it was not set down for trial within two years of the date of commencement of the action. The plaintiff claimed that since the defendants had engaged in settlement negotiations they were estopped from relying upon the two-year limitation period. The motion was allowed. There existed no basis for applying the doctrine of estoppel by conduct under the circumstances of this case. The defendants had not deliberately misled or deceived the plaintiffs into believing that they were not relying on the limitation period. There were no representations, either express or implied that the defendants did not intend to rely on the limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co." p2="Iona Corp." post.rptr="266" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I641c6af05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co. v. Iona Corp.">Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co. v. Iona Corp. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 266 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1993), 12 C.L.R. (2d) 1, 106 D.L.R. (4th) 532 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully applied for an order dismissing a lien action on the ground that it had not been set down for trial within two years of the commencement of the action. The plaintiff had argued that the defendant was estopped from relying on the limitation period because the defendant was in breach of two court orders requiring it to honour undertakings given at the examination for discovery. Sections 37 and 46 of the Act are mandatory, and the court has no discretion to refuse to dismiss an action if no date for trial is fixed within two years of the date of commencement of the action. In addition, there was no evidence that the defendant, either expressly or impliedly, represented it would not move under s. 46. However, the plaintiff's claim in contract was allowed to continue.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19901105" p1="Mast Construction (Ontario) Ltd." p2="Appleton" ref.id="I641c6af15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mast Construction (Ontario) Ltd. v. Appleton">Mast Construction (Ontario) Ltd. v. Appleton (November 5, 1990) (Ont. Div. Ct. [unreported])</ref></cite>—Although there was jurisdiction under s. 46 to dismiss the action to enforce the lien, there was no such jurisdiction under s. 46 to make such an order with respect to the personal contract claim. It is clear from ss. 38, 57 and 65 that a personal contract action is separate from and survives the dismissal of a lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Ionion Construction Inc." p2="Christo" post.rptr="135" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I641c6af25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ionion Construction Inc. v. Christo">Ionion Construction Inc. v. Christo (1991), 46 C.L.R. 135 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The steps taken in having a settlement meeting and in scheduling a pre-trial did not constitute setting down the action for trial within the meaning of s. 37(1) of the Act. The plaintiff had fallen short of complying with s. 37 and had not made out a case on estoppel or waiver by the defendants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Ramrock Electric" p2="Lords & Ladies" post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I641c6af35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ramrock Electric v. Lords & Ladies">Ramrock Electric v. Lords & Ladies (1989), 34 C.L.R. 26 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—Section 46 provides for a mandatory disposition upon the motion of any person. There is no room for judicial discretion.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
46:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 46.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">46:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 46(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Con-Spec Constr. Inc." p2="Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp." post.rptr="20410" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I676ff8d03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Con-Spec Constr. Inc. v. Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp.">Con-Spec Constr. Inc. v. Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp., 2023 CarswellOnt 20410, 2023 ONSC 7229 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Sections 46(1) and 47(1)(d) of the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, when read together, provided the court with the discretion to either dismiss or permit a contract claim to continue without the lien claim. Absent any evidence from the defendant as to its own efforts to move the action forward, it was either complicit in the delay or at least complacent about it. That was a factor militating against dismissal, since the delay was not fairly viewed as being laid solely at the plaintiff's feet. The only prejudice cited by the defendant was additional time and expense, which was “prejudice” inherent in litigation. The contract claim was to be continued as an ordinary action governed by the Rules of Civil Procedure, with costs to the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Whitestone Gate Development Inc." p2="Perpetual Succession For East Toronto Chinese Baptist Church" post.rptr="459" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641c92005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Whitestone Gate Development Inc. v. Perpetual Succession For East Toronto Chinese Baptist Church">Whitestone Gate Development Inc. v. Perpetual Succession For East Toronto Chinese Baptist Church, 2022 ONSC 459, 2022 CarswellOnt 489, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 86 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 46 only provides for mandatory dismissal of the action to enforce the lien, which is distinct from dismissing the action in which enforcement of the lien is pursued. Where an action only seeks to enforce the statutory lien remedy, the entire action may properly be dismissed. Here, however, the action did not only pursue a lien, but also pursued damages for breach of contract. That breach of contract claim was properly joined in the lien action under s. 55(1), and since it was a separate cause of action from enforcement of the lien it was not captured by the mandatory dismissal outlined in s. 46. A motion for dismissal on grounds of a plaintiff's delay in advancing litigation was more appropriately the subject matter of s. 47, which permits a court, upon motion, to dismiss an action on “any proper ground and subject to any terms and conditions that the court considers appropriate in the circumstances.”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd." p2="Kaplan et al" post.rptr="4592" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I641c92015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd. v. Kaplan et al">A.C. Concrete Forming Ltd. v. Kaplan et al, 2019 ONSC 4592, 2019 CarswellOnt 13144, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 79 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not contemplate that dismissal of a lien constitutes dismissal of any underlying non-contractual cause of action. While the Act contemplates a dismissal of the “action to enforce the lien” where a lien has expired, the underlying claim is not extinguished by such an order. A plaintiff is still able to proceed against the defendant in relation to the underlying cause. In this case, the lien had clearly expired, having been set down for trial some five months later than the time limits required. The court retains the discretion to dismiss the claim in its entirety if the circumstances warrant it, and in many cases this may be justified. With that said, there is nothing which mandates such a dismissal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="QH Renovation & Construction Corp." p2="2460500 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3237" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I641c92025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="QH Renovation & Construction Corp. v. 2460500 Ontario Ltd.">QH Renovation & Construction Corp. v. 2460500 Ontario Ltd., 2019 ONSC 3237, 2019 CarswellOnt 8577, 1 C.L.R. (5th) 76 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 10988 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is simply no authority for the proposition that the parties may, through mutual agreement or by a consent court order, agree to extend the mandatory time period set out in s. 37 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Rather, the provisions of sections 37 and 46 are mandatory.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lee" p2="Chiarella" post.rptr="7374" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641c92035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lee v. Chiarella">Lee v. Chiarella, 2018 ONSC 7374, 2018 CarswellOnt 21402, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 351 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—When read together, ss. 46(1) and s. 47(1)(d) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> provide the Court with the discretion to either dismiss or permit a claim on the contract to continue without the lien claim, pursuant to decisions such as <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f0e300f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Edgcumbe" p2="Vicary" post.rptr="2656" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641cb9105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgcumbe v. Vicary">Edgcumbe v. Vicary, 2018 ONSC 2656, 2018 CarswellOnt 8420, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. In exercising this discretion, the Court must consider the prejudice that each of the parties will suffer and the Court's preference to have disputes resolved on their merits. Although the plaintiff did not attend the motion and did nothing to move the matter forward for over three years, and the defendants were prepared to have the counterclaim dismissed with the action, the matter should be heard on its merits and it was appropriate that the plaintiff be given a final opportunity to respond to the motion on terms.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9448616 Canada Ltd." p2="Focal Elements et al." post.rptr="6031" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641cb9115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9448616 Canada Ltd. v. Focal Elements et al.">9448616 Canada Ltd. v. Focal Elements et al., 2018 ONSC 6031, 2018 CarswellOnt 17157, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 237 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 17718 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The perfected lien was found to have expired after an order for the trial of the action was not made, nor was the action set down for trial, within two years of the commencement of the action. In addition, the plaintiff failed to comply with an interlocutory order requiring it to appoint a new lawyer of record.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Edgcumbe" p2="Vicary" post.rptr="2656" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641cb9125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgcumbe v. Vicary">Edgcumbe v. Vicary, 2018 ONSC 2656, 2018 CarswellOnt 8420, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff's lien was held to have expired pursuant to section 37(1), the court was called upon to determine whether it had discretion to allow the action to continue as a regular action. Referencing, inter alia, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f10a10f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd." p2="Smiley" post.rptr="6037" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641cb9145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley">K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley, 2015 ONSC 6037, 2015 CarswellOnt 14820, 54 C.L.R. (4th) 315 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, it concluded that it had discretion to allow the contractual actions to continue. It declined to read the decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="310 Waste Ltd." p2="Casboro Industries Ltd." post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I90f10a11f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd.">310 Waste Ltd. v. Casboro Industries Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 138 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3385 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3338, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 5 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5779, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.); affirmed (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5521, 54 C.L.R. (3d) 204 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, as finding that s. 46 was mandatory. Rather, the court in <ital>310 Waste</ital> merely decided to exercise its discretion in a particular manner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd." p2="Smiley" post.rptr="6037" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641cb9165fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley">K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley, 2015 ONSC 6037, 2015 CarswellOnt 14820, 54 C.L.R. (4th) 315, 340 O.A.C. 89 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff failed to set the action down for trial or to schedule a trial date within two years of commencement of its lien proceeding, as mandated by s. 37(1)2 and its lien expired. After the defendant successfully moved <ital>ex parte</ital> to have the lien removed from title and the action dismissed, the plaintiff successfully appealed on the basis that, although the lien was properly discharged, and the lien claims were properly dismissed, the court should not have dismissed its claims for breach of contract. Summary dismissal of contract claims as a result of expiry of lien rights would affect significantly a plaintiff's legal right to recover on its contract claims, and thus run counter to the express wording of s. 38. The legislature never intended that s. 46(1) be used for mandatory summary dismissal of contract claims without notice. This is especially true given the current two-year limitation period for contract actions. It is a matter of discretion for the court to decide whether the contract claim should proceed under the auspices of the Act, or whether the subsisting contract claims should be transferred to the general civil list of the Superior Court or to the Small Claims Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="21114 Ontario Inc." p2="Stadia Industries Ltd." post.rptr="3221" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641ce0205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="21114 Ontario Inc. v. Stadia Industries Ltd.">21114 Ontario Inc. v. Stadia Industries Ltd., 2014 ONSC 3221, 2014 CarswellOnt 7129, 14 C.B.R. (6th) 1, 32 C.L.R. (4th) 77 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the court allows a contract claim to proceed after a lien claim is dismissed, the court may decide whether the Act's procedures apply. In such a case, the court could transfer the contract action to the Small Claims Court if the claim was under $25,000, or it could direct that it proceed as an ordinary Superior Court action and possibly be governed by the Rule 76 Simplified Procedure if the claim was between $25,000 and $100,000, or it could direct that it proceed as an ordinary action and be governed by the general Rules of Civil Procedure without any reference to the Simplified Procedure if the claim was in excess of $100,000. The court could even direct that the contract claim would continue within the framework of the statement of claim in the now-dismissed lien action, with judgment to be given pursuant to s. 63, and still to be governed by the procedure under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and, in particular, procedural ss. 51–63, 67, and 71.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sandro Steel Fabrication Ltd." p2="Chiesa" post.rptr="658" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641ce0215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sandro Steel Fabrication Ltd. v. Chiesa">Sandro Steel Fabrication Ltd. v. Chiesa, 2013 ONSC 658, 2013 CarswellOnt 1164 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 3458 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2013 CarswellOnt 8520 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff's lien had expired because the action had not been set down within two years, the court exercised its discretion to allow the lien action to continue as an ordinary breach of contract action. The plaintiff had a reasonable explanation for the delay and did not simply sit on its rights, there was no evidence of prejudice by the delay, and a dismissal of the lien action would not end the litigation between the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1339408 Ontario Inc." p2="1579138 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9443" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I90f13120f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1339408 Ontario Inc. v. 1579138 Ontario Inc.">1339408 Ontario Inc. v. 1579138 Ontario Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 9443, 71 C.L.R. (3d) 13 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—If the two-year period for setting the action down for trial has expired, it follows that the two-year limitation period relating to an action in contract under the <ital>Limitations Act, 2002</ital> has also expired, thereby precluding any subsequently commenced action in contract. Where a moving party relies upon the principles established in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f13121f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> to dismiss a lien action under s. 46 for delay, the effect of which would be to effectively dispose of the plaintiff's claim forever, the case law developed under R. 24.01 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> is relevant and the action in contract will not be dismissed unless the delay is intentional or contumelious, or the plaintiff or its counsel are responsible for an inexcusable delay that gives rise to a substantial risk that a fair trial is not possible.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="986506 Ontario Ltd." p2="Pringle" post.rptr="286" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I641d07325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="986506 Ontario Ltd. v. Pringle">986506 Ontario Ltd. v. Pringle (2003), 30 C.L.R. (3d) 286, 2003 CarswellOnt 5603 (Master)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff failed to fix a trial date within two years from issuance of the statement of claim, the defendants moved under s. 46(1) to declare the lien expired. As the plaintiff had released the lien, it was unnecessary to make the declaration, but the lien claim was dismissed and the contract action allowed to continue under the simplified procedure of R. 76.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See also: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I641d07335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> as to when a party may and when a party must bring a s. 46(1) motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Skyaramic Development Inc." p2="Zotalis" post.rptr="323" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I641d07345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Skyaramic Development Inc. v. Zotalis">Skyaramic Development Inc. v. Zotalis (1996), 33 C.L.R. (2d) 323, 19 O.T.C. 388 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved to discharge the plaintiff's lien, vacate the registration of the certificate of action and dismiss the action on the grounds that the plaintiff company had been dissolved more than 10 years before the lien was registered. Substantive steps were not taken to revive the plaintiff until the defendant's motion and, given the plain meaning of s. 241(5) of the <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital> of Ontario, revival would not stop the time requirement within which a construction lien must be preserved and then perfected by a valid entity. Once those time limits were expended, the defendant acquired the protection of not having his property liened for work and materials.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Meo & Assns." p2="Gottenu Developments Ltd." post.rptr="2582" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I56180190fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd.">Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2582, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 159 (Ont. Master); reversed (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 4489, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 78 (Ont. Master); affirmed Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 737, 1 C.L.R. (3d) 74, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Meo (R.) & Associates v. Gottenu Developments Ltd.)</ital> 131 O.A.C. 394 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Meo registered two liens for the same work, the first lien expired, the second lien was perfected, and then the first lien was released. The Defendants moved to discharge the second lien on the basis of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I641d2e405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>. In 1996 Master Clark held that the release of an expired lien had no further effect than to clear title. More than a year later supplementary reasons were released and the Master reconsidered and reversed his original decision discharging the second Meo lien. An appeal to the Divisional Court was dismissed holding that the intentions of the party releasing the lien are irrelevant, and affirming the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I641d2e415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="94" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I641d2e425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 94 (Ont. Gen. Div.); supplementary reasons at (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 85 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 1337, 1996 CarswellOnt 1312 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—It is sufficient that the action under which lien claims have been sheltered is set down for trial. It is not necessary that the sheltered lien claimants each take further action to comply with the terms of s. 37.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Eurocor Ltd." p2="Vernich" post.rptr="631" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I641d55505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich">Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich (1992), 9 O.R. (3d) 631, 2 C.L.R. (2d) 208 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 46(1) does not refer to “an order dismissing the action,” but to “an order dismissing the action to enforce that lien.” Hence, where a lien claim must be dismissed on the ground that it had not been set down for trial within two years, a claim for breach of contract may be allowed to continue. Where a contractor would be required to commence a fresh action, which would result in a multiplicity of proceedings, it was appropriate for the court to exercise its discretion in favour of splitting the action and allowing the claim for breach of contract to continue on its own.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="612354 Ontario Ltd." p2="Tonecraft Corp." post.rptr="799" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I90f17f40f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp.">612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp. (1991), 1991 CarswellOnt 799, 5 O.R. (3d) 764, 47 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—When the plaintiff failed to have its lien action set down within the required two years, the defendant brought a motion pursuant to ss. 37 and 46(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital> to have the action dismissed in its entirety. Documentary discovery and examination for discovery had been ordered and had taken place. The plaintiff sought leave to amend its statement of claim to include a claim for personal judgment for breach of contract. Held, the expiry of a claim for lien prior to trial does not oust the jurisdiction of the court to hear an action for personal judgment. The mandatory provisions of s. 46(1) requiring the court to dismiss an action to enforce a claim for lien do not apply to dismissal of actions for personal judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="C.S. Yachts Ltd." post.rptr="192" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I641d55525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd. (1990), 46 C.L.R. 192 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A court does not have authority to extend or interfere with the two-year limitation period provided under s. 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, 1983 for setting down an action for trial. In such circumstances, the court is required to dismiss the action to enforce the lien pursuant to s. 46(1) of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 46.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">46:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 46(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Burnt Hill Developments Ltd." p2="Eglinton Village Ltd." post.rptr="874" pre.rptr="1992" ref.id="I561828a0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Burnt Hill Developments Ltd. v. Eglinton Village Ltd.">Burnt Hill Developments Ltd. v. Eglinton Village Ltd. (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 874, 5 C.L.R. (2d) 52 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 46(2) gives the court no discretion. Accordingly, where a lien action was not set down for trial, the lien was declared to have expired and the action was dismissed. The defendant, a numbered company, by asserting its right to defend the action, even though it was a successor to the contracting party, did not in any way undertake not to proceed under s. 46(2). Indeed, that was one way of defending the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="601039 Ontario Ltd." p2="Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd." post.rptr="135" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I641d55545fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="601039 Ontario Ltd. v. Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd.">601039 Ontario Ltd. v. Meadowvale Green Phase I Ltd. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 135, 5 O.R. (3d) 26 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—After three liens were perfected and actions commenced, the court ordered the actions to be consolidated with an action involving a fourth lien. The defendant unsuccessfully moved to have the first 3 liens dismissed for failure of the actions involving the initial three liens to be set down for trial within the time prescribed in s. 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. Subsection 61(2)(a) of the Act allowed the court to consolidate several actions into one action. The actions involving the first three liens were consolidated into the fourth action which was set down within the time prescribed in s. 37(1). Accordingly, s. 46 had no application.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
