C.30, s. 46.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">46:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 46(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd." p2="Smiley" post.rptr="6037" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641d7c605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley">K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley, 2015 ONSC 6037, 2015 CarswellOnt 14820, 54 C.L.R. (4th) 315, 340 O.A.C. 89 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff failed to set the action down for trial within two years of commencement of its lien proceeding, and its lien expired, the defendant moved <ital>ex parte</ital> to have the lien removed from title and the action dismissed. The plaintiff successfully appealed on the grounds, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that s. 46(1) was not to be used for mandatory summary dismissal of contract claims without notice. The right to move without notice under s. 46(3) was not an absolute one, and the party bringing the motion had the duties that applied to any party moving without notice to provide full and frank disclosure of all material matters to the court before which the motion is brought. This includes a duty to fully and fairly advise the court of the law.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
46:6: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 46.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">46:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 46(4)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Halton Standard Condominium Corp. No. 472" p2="Tritan Inc." post.rptr="18545" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dccef50ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Halton Standard Condominium Corp. No. 472 v. Tritan Inc.">Halton Standard Condominium Corp. No. 472 v. Tritan Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 18545, 2023 ONSC 6745 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On account of inadequate motion materials, the court declined to grant the applicant's motion for consent orders discharging the respondent's construction liens and directing the return of security paid into court. Among the shortcomings identified by the court, the motion materials failed to address whether there were any other preserved liens that might be sheltering under the respondent's, an issue properly addressed by way of updated parcel registers that included deleted instruments for all properties against which the subject lien was claimed and which had been preserved and perfected. As well, the draft order improperly provided for the “release and disbursement” of the subject security to the parties' respective lawyers. Section 46(4) clearly and expressly mandates that the posted security be returned to the person who posted it. There is no provision for “release and disbursement” to anyone else. Counsel must be punctilious in the drafting of their materials, and in the proper discharge of their duty, attend to each and every drafting task with the highest levels of care and fastidiousness without regard to whether the applicable litigation step is proceeding on consent or is expected to be vigorously opposed. As a result of carelessness, a straightforward consent motion was being sent back to be returned a second time for further consideration by the court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Heinrichs" p2="374427 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="78" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641d7c615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heinrichs v. 374427 Ontario Ltd.">Heinrichs v. 374427 Ontario Ltd., 2018 ONSC 78, 2018 CarswellOnt 25, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 121 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 994, 2018 CarswellOnt 2304 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—As consideration for the discharge of a lien on its property, the owner offered to hold back from the sale proceeds the full amount of the plaintiffs' claim plus 25% for costs, with the owner's lawyers holding the sum in escrow pending receiving a joint direction or, in the alternative, a Court order directing the payment of the same. The lien was then discharged pursuant to that undertaking. Following the release of the lien instruments, the plaintiffs did not take any steps to prosecute the action or set it down for trial, and the defendants moved to dismiss the action for delay or, in the alternative, to direct that the action proceed as an action in contract. In respect of both options, the defendants sought an order directing the release of the escrow funds. The Master ordered the funds be paid out to the defendants, on the basis that the security provided by the undertaking was akin to security for the lien having been posted in court. The appropriate interpretation of the undertaking and the underlying agreement was that the lien would be discharged and that the monies held in trust would not be released until there was a resolution among the parties or a court decided the merits of the claim. There was no intention that those monies would be subject to the operation of sections 37, 44 and 46.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1351150 Ontario Inc." p2="Chartrand" post.rptr="6980" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I641d7c625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1351150 Ontario Inc. v. Chartrand">1351150 Ontario Inc. v. Chartrand (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6980 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An unambiguous direction by a defendant, addressed to the court and providing that in the event that monies paid into court were to be paid out to the defendant, those monies were instead to be paid to a third party, could not trump the clear words of s. 46(4). The Legislature's intent was clearly to avoid having third party claims to the monies dealt with within the confines of motions under s. 46. The language of s. 46(4), providing that “the court <ital>shall</ital> order that any amount that has been paid into court under section 44 in respect of that action be returned to the person who paid the amount into court”, was unequivocal. There were sound policy reasons for preventing third parties, who had no rights under the lien, to assert a claim or interest in the funds paid into court that simply replaced the lien. To permit such a practice would invite a multitude of complex layers of litigation defeating the very purpose of the construction lien regime. The direction signed by the defendant did not grant the third party any prior interest in the funds held in court. The Act required that the funds be paid back to the defendant's law firm in trust for the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Coldmatic Refrigeration of Canada Ltd." p2="1234777 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="532" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I641d7c635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Coldmatic Refrigeration of Canada Ltd. v. 1234777 Ontario Inc.">Coldmatic Refrigeration of Canada Ltd. v. 1234777 Ontario Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 532, 2004 CarswellOnt 474 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court held that all of the funds paid into court, including accrued interest, were available to satisfy the claim and costs. While this action was framed as a construction lien action, the claim was essentially a personal one between the contracting parties which did not involve a payment out which would result in any unfairness or prejudice to a third party potential lien claimant or third party bonding company. The only rights affected were those of the parties themselves who were the ones who entered into the building contract in the first place, and it was not logical to deny the plaintiff access to funds paid into court to lift the lien when the plaintiff and defendant were the only parties who could possibly benefit or be prejudiced, either by the availability or unavailability of the funds and accrued interest. Both costs and prejudgment interest were held to be payable out of the entire fund in court, including accrued interest, whether or not such sums were originally paid in as part of the claim, or costs, or both. The funds in court, including all accrued interest, were ordered paid out first in full payment of the plaintiff's claim, and then in full payment of the plaintiff's costs. The surplus balance was ordered to be paid to the defendant. The judgment reflected the plaintiff's unnecessary concession that pre-judgment interest was not payable out of the funds in court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I90f1cd60f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc.">Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc. (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 66, 36 O.R. (3d) 502, 1997 CarswellOnt 4411 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The lien of a claimant was discharged and its action dismissed in part because of procedural misconduct with respect to discovery. The owner had posted security to vacate the lien claim and brought a motion in order to recover the security. In the interim, however, a second lien claimant had subsequently registered a lien against the owner's land. The second lien action was ongoing at the time of the owner's motion, and the second claimant argued that its lien remained a charge upon the security posted. In granting the owner's motion, the Master ruled that s. 44(9), Rr. 2 and 3, were not applicable where the lien of a claimant has been lost by procedural misconduct, and there remains only one lien against title, all other liens having been vacated upon posting of security, and where there will never be “a distribution” as between the lien claimant's as contemplated by Rr. 3 of s. 44(9). <ital>Note</ital>: The decision in this case is under appeal; motion to quash appeal dismissed at (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2378 (Ont. C.A.).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
47:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 47.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">47:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Amendments, Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Following the Expert Review's recommendation, s. 47(1) now expressly grants the court the power to discharge a lien on the basis that the claim for lien is frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process. This should be read together with the changes to s. 35 of the Act, which now imposes sanctions for “willfully exaggerated” liens.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A new subsection 1.1 was added mirroring former s. 47(1)(b), (2) and (3).</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A similar section can be traced back to the very first Act, <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27, which authorized the Court to “annul the registry” upon proper ground. The power to annul in its early version was regulated in one lengthy section, which also dealt with other matters such as the payment of security into court. The general power to vacate remained in that form until <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, c. 233, separated it into s. 25(2)(b). The power to dismiss the action in ss. 47(1)(c) of the current Act was introduced in s. 25(2)(c) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65 and remained in that form until the 1983 reforms. Subsection 47(1)(c) was enacted in the 1983 amendments and remains in that format.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section gives to the court a wide discretion to discharge liens, vacate registrations and dismiss actions where the circumstances warrant. It endows the court with the flexibility to deal with any number of situations which may arise in the course of a lien action. The legislative committee set up to advise upon the then proposed <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, <ital>1983</ital> was concerned to protect owners from unnecessarily cluttered titles and to curb any abuse of the remedies conferred by the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
47:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 47.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">47:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lazi Ventures Inc." p2="Carter" post.rptr="3111" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641df1905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lazi Ventures Inc. v. Carter">Lazi Ventures Inc. v. Carter, 2022 ONSC 3111, 2022 CarswellOnt 7247 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2023 CarswellOnt 615 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 47 motions are brought by defendants and do not require that the plaintiff to “put its best foot forward”, as per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f1f470f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> at para. 46. They are comparable to motions for summary judgment, with the test to be met being whether the defendant has proven that there is no genuine issue for trial. Keeping in step with the evolving law on motions for summary judgment, the motions judge on a section 47 motion can weigh evidence and draw inferences from the evidence to determine whether there is a genuine issue for trial, as set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1140676 Ontario Inc." p2="2650997 Ontario Inc. et al" post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I641df1925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al">1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al, 2021 ONSC 143, 2021 CarswellOnt 89, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 359 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. In this case, the lien claimant exhibited a pattern of conduct that used deceptive tactics to gain access to work and misrepresentations about practicing law to pressure customers into paying apparently excessive charges, amounting to oppressive and unfair conduct. Allowing the claimant to use the legal process to further its plans grounded in such oppressive and unfair practice would bring the administration of justice into disrepute; the claim for lien was discharged and the entirety of the action dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Infinite Construction Development Ltd." p2="Chen" post.rptr="3929" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I677158603b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Infinite Construction Development Ltd. v. Chen">Infinite Construction Development Ltd. v. Chen, 2022 ONSC 3929, 2022 CarswellOnt 9316, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 386 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2023 CarswellOnt 8169, 2023 ONSC 2627, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 409 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 5721, 2022 CarswellOnt 14512 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The principles set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GTA General Contractors Ltd." p2="2566213 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="20894" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I90f21b80f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="GTA General Contractors Ltd. v. 2566213 Ontario Inc.">GTA General Contractors Ltd. v. 2566213 Ontario Inc., 2019 CarswellOnt 20894, 2019 ONSC 7370 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 8234, 2020 ONSC 3398, 8 C.L.R. (5th) 100 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, still remain applicable in light of the rulings in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments. Inc." p2="2603774 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9830" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f21b81f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments. Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc.">Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments. Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 9830, 2020 ONSC 4308, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 182 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f21b82f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, but as guidance on appropriate considerations for s. 47 motions where discharge or dismissal is sought on the merits. There is no language in s. 47 limiting the court's discretion to assess and decide what is “a proper ground” to discharge a lien or dismiss an action in the particular circumstances of a particular case. In deciding a s. 47 motion, there are times when a genuine issue could be resolved by motion, but it is more fair, just, and appropriate for that issue to be decided at trial. Such a reading of <ital>GTA General Contractors</ital> is consistent with these Divisional Court decisions, and with the statutory mandate in s. 50(3) that procedure in a lien action be as far as possible of a summary character, having regard to the amount and nature of the liens in question.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GH Asset Management Services Inc." p2="Lo" post.rptr="18355" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I67717f703b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="GH Asset Management Services Inc. v. Lo">GH Asset Management Services Inc. v. Lo, 2022 CarswellOnt 18355, 2022 ONSC 7218, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 247 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The defendant owner's property manager, allegedly acting as agent for the owner, contracted with the original lien clamant to perform property maintenance and renovation services at the property. The owner denied any knowledge or authorization of the work. After this action was commenced, the lien was assigned to the property manager, and the owner intended to bring a motion to discharge the lien, return the security posted and dismiss or permanently stay the lien action, on the grounds that the delayed disclosure of this assignment gave rise to an abuse of process. The owner intended to seek relief under s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act,</ital> as well as under Ont. r. 21.01(3)(d) or s. 106 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. It was held that the owner's s. 47 motion could proceed; it was premature to assess the merits of whether this novel ground supported relief under s. 47, since this would amount to importing a leave requirement into s. 47 where one was not prescribed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Whitestone Gate Development Inc." p2="Perpetual Succession For East Toronto Chinese Baptist Church" post.rptr="459" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641e18a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Whitestone Gate Development Inc. v. Perpetual Succession For East Toronto Chinese Baptist Church">Whitestone Gate Development Inc. v. Perpetual Succession For East Toronto Chinese Baptist Church, 2022 ONSC 459, 2022 CarswellOnt 489, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 86 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion for dismissal brought under ss. 45 and 46 on grounds of a plaintiff's delay in advancing litigation was more appropriately the subject matter of s. 47, which permits a court, upon motion, to dismiss an action on “any proper ground and subject to any terms and conditions that the court considers appropriate in the circumstances.” Section 46 only provides for mandatory dismissal of the action to enforce the lien, which is distinct from dismissing the action in which enforcement of the lien is pursued. Where an action only seeks to enforce the statutory lien remedy, the entire action may properly be dismissed. Here, however, the action did not only pursue a lien, but also pursued damages for breach of contract. That breach of contract claim was properly joined in the lien action under s. 55(1), and since it was a separate cause of action from enforcement of the lien it was not captured by the mandatory dismissal outlined in s. 46. Ultimately, this was a case where it would be unjust to grant the ultimate remedy of dismissal without first providing the plaintiff with a final opportunity to proactively advance its claim. A strict timetable and an adverse costs award expressed the court's disapproval of the unrepresented plaintiff's approach thus far in the litigation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Voutour" p2="MVG Investments Inc." post.rptr="1610" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641e3fb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Voutour v. MVG Investments Inc.">Voutour v. MVG Investments Inc., 2022 ONSC 1610, 2022 CarswellOnt 3246 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2022 CarswellOnt 7810 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A claim for unjust enrichment in a claim for lien concerned an alternative remedy that was not the proper subject matter of a motion under s. 47.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1140676 Ontario Inc." p2="2650997 Ontario Inc. et al" post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I641e3fb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al">1140676 Ontario Inc. v. 2650997 Ontario Inc. et al, 2021 ONSC 143, 2021 CarswellOnt 89, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 359 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 ONSC 8176, 2020 CarswellOnt 19368 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The provisions of the new <ital>Construction Act</ital> did not expand the discretion of a motions judge on a s. 47 motion to discharge. However, the traditional test under section 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was articulated in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Beaver Materials Handling Co." p2="Hejna" post.rptr="2803" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90f24290f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna">Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 2803, 45 C.L.R. (3d) 242 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and modified by the later ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Combined Air Mechanical Services Inc." p2="Flesch" post.rptr="744" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641e3fb35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Combined Air Mechanical Services Inc. v. Flesch">Combined Air Mechanical Services Inc. v. Flesch [2014 CarswellOnt 744, 2014 CarswellOnt 745 (S.C.C.)]</ref></cite> by expanding the discretion of a motions judge on a summary judgment motion to, <ital>inter alia</ital>, weigh evidence. The law regarding summary judgment has significantly evolved since the <ital>Beaver Materials</ital> ruling and correspondingly, a motions judge has a greater discretion to discharge a lien if it is patently demonstrable that a party has no right to a lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GTA Restoration Group Inc." p2="Baillie" post.rptr="5190" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I641e3fb45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="GTA Restoration Group Inc. v. Baillie">GTA Restoration Group Inc. v. Baillie, 2020 ONSC 5190, 2020 CarswellOnt 12410, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 89 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 15469, 2020 ONSC 6327, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 127 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2021 CarswellOnt 2443 (Ont. Div. Ct.); leave to appeal refused 2021 CarswellOnt 2444 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The master held that neither <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f269a0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, nor <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc." p2="2603774 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9830" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f269a1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc.">Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 9830, 2020 ONSC 4308, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 182 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> altered the prior case law requiring both the moving party and responding lien claimant to put their best foot forward in s. 47 motions where the court must assess if there are triable issues, such as challenges to timeliness of a lien, quantum of a lien, or lienability of services or materials supplied. Rather, the Divisional Court clarified only that the evidentiary onus extends solely to the bases on which discharge is sought. In <ital>R&V Construction</ital>, in the context of the defendant's motion to discharge the lien, the defendant had no “best foot forward” evidentiary onus to demonstrate triable issues in his own defences. Such a reading was consistent with the Divisional Court's statement that s. 47 did not provide a remedy for a plaintiff to obtain judgment. It is also consistent with the decision in <ital>Maplequest</ital>, in which the Divisional Court held the underlying test on a s. 47 discharge motion to be “whether there is a triable issue in respect to any of the bases on which discharge of the lien is sought”. As s. 47(1)(a) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> adds a specific ground to discharge a lien “on the basis that the claim for the lien is frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process”, it remains an open question whether a moving party must demonstrate that there is no triable issue on an allegation of abuse of process.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Davis" p2="Under Construction Incorporated" post.rptr="7686" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I641e3fb75fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Davis v. Under Construction Incorporated">Davis v. Under Construction Incorporated, 2020 CarswellOnt 7686, 2020 ONSC 3466, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 102 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Declaring a lien expired is significant relief. When a motion for such a declaration is brought <ital>ex parte</ital>, the lien claimant has no opportunity to file responding materials or argue against the relief sought. It follows that the evidence filed by the moving party must support a clear finding that the subject lien has expired. That includes considering if there is sheltering where other liens have been registered. Evidence on a motion to declare a lien expired must satisfy the court that no additional evidence or argument from the absent lien claimant would reasonably make a difference in disposition of the motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f269a2f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part <ital>R & V Construction v. Baradaran</ital>, 2019 ONSC 1551, 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the defendant moved under s. 47 for orders dismissing the action and returning his lien security or, alternatively, reducing his lien security, the master granted summary judgment to the plaintiff, finding that she had jurisdiction to use the “Enhanced Powers” accorded to judges on motions for summary judgment because she was acting in her capacity as a construction lien master to whom an action had been referred for trial under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. On motion by the defendant opposing confirmation of the master's report, the motions judge found that the master did not have jurisdiction to use the Enhanced Powers on a motion for summary judgment and had therefore exceeded her jurisdiction when she granted summary judgment and declined to confirm the master's report. On further appeal to the Divisional Court, the court held that while the motions judge erred in finding master was without jurisdiction to use the enhanced powers on a motion for summary judgment while sitting as a construction lien master on a reference, those powers were not available to the master on the s. 47 motion as it was not a motion for summary judgment. A motion under s. 47 may be brought before a master before or after a construction lien action has been referred to the master for trial. It is a discrete step in construction lien proceedings, used to dispose of liens that are out of time, have been registered against the wrong property, have failed to name a necessary party, or have other fatal defects. Routinely a master's motion, brought before or after a case has been referred to the master for trial, it is not a motion for summary judgment under R. 20. There is no requirement for parties to “put their best foot forward”. And a s. 47 motion is always a defence motion that does not provide a means for a plaintiff to move for judgment. The remedies available under s. 47 do not include granting judgment for the plaintiff. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also the discussion of this case under s. 58(4), below. Note also that in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="4382" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I641e8dd05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran, 2022 ONSC 4382, 2022 CarswellOnt 10736 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the plaintiff's subsequent motion for summary judgment was heard and granted.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Romanov Romanov Architects Incorporated" p2="Cardillo Capital Corp." post.rptr="6628" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641e8dd15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Romanov Romanov Architects Incorporated v. Cardillo Capital Corp.">Romanov Romanov Architects Incorporated v. Cardillo Capital Corp., 2018 ONSC 6628, 2018 CarswellOnt 18439, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 294 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A trial was not required with respect to the timeliness of the lien claim and summary judgment was appropriate. It was possible to gain a full appreciation of all issues on the motion without a trial. The record was not voluminous, was comprised primarily of short affidavits and cross-examination transcripts from 2 witnesses, and most of the material facts were not in dispute. The lien claim was not registered in a timely manner and expired prior to registration, and the lien claim and certificate were to be discharged and the security be returned.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vestacon Limited" p2="ARC Productions Ltd." post.rptr="5366" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I641e8dd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd.">Vestacon Limited v. ARC Productions Ltd., 2018 ONSC 5366, 2018 CarswellOnt 15345, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 38 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motion brought by the owners to declare the subcontractor's lien claim expired and to dismiss the action was akin to a summary judgment motion, and it was dismissed where the evidence relied on was insufficient and there was a genuine issue that required a trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="TACC Construction Ltd." p2="Ajax Audley Developments Limited" post.rptr="5143" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I641e8dd35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="TACC Construction Ltd. v. Ajax Audley Developments Limited">TACC Construction Ltd. v. Ajax Audley Developments Limited, 2017 ONSC 5143, 2017 CarswellOnt 15445, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 372 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 1110, 2018 CarswellOnt 2353, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 380 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved for leave, if required, to move for an order discharging the plaintiff's lien and a release to it of the balance of funds paid in. On the question of leave, s. 47(1) explicitly allowed for a motion seeking the discharge of lien upon any proper grounds. This provision does not import a requirement for leave and stands independently of s. 67(2). As a statutory provision, it trumps R. 48 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> governing the requirement for leave in the prescribed circumstances. Therefore, leave was not required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Diamond Drywall Contracting Inc." p2="Ikram" post.rptr="5411" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I641e8dd45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Diamond Drywall Contracting Inc. v. Ikram">Diamond Drywall Contracting Inc. v. Ikram, 2016 ONSC 5411, 2016 CarswellOnt 13668, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 278 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion brought pursuant to rule 47 is not an actual motion for summary judgment, but is akin to a motion for summary judgment under Ont. R. 20, and is made to “the court”. The Act does not require such motions to be heard by a judge. Moreover, section 67 of the Act requires the court to adopt procedures in an action that are “as far as possible of a summary character, having regard to the amount and nature of the liens in question”. Reading section 47 and 67 together, a master hearing a motion under s. 47 is entitled to import all of the powers available on a motion for summary judgment under Ont. R. 20. This is particularly important in Toronto Region, where the Superior Court of Justice has delegated much of the construction lien work of the court to two masters whose work is devoted in one case exclusively, and in the other case partially, to construction lien matters. On a motion pursuant to s. 47, a Master has the jurisdiction to weigh evidence, make findings of fact and apply the law to the facts. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f2b7c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 2019 ONSC 1551, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc." p2="2603774 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9830" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f2b7c1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc.">Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 9830, 2020 ONSC 4308, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 182 (Ont. Div._Ct.); affirming on other grounds 2019 ONSC 5278, 2019 CarswellOnt 14629, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Walsh Construction/Bondfield Partnership" p2="Chartis Insurance Company of Canada" post.rptr="3985" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I641e8dd75fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Walsh Construction/Bondfield Partnership v. Chartis Insurance Company of Canada">Walsh Construction/Bondfield Partnership v. Chartis Insurance Company of Canada, 2017 ONSC 3985, 2017 CarswellOnt 9972, 78 C.L.R. (4th) 368 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2017 CarswellOnt 15175 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> to the same effect.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Limen Group Ltd." p2="Allform Group Ltd." post.rptr="4344" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I641eb4e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Limen Group Ltd. v. Allform Group Ltd.">Limen Group Ltd. v. Allform Group Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4344, 2016 CarswellOnt 10590, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 164 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion brought pursuant to s. 47 is akin to a summary judgment motion. If there are genuine issues of fact that require a trial then the motion fails. Here, a trial was required to determine whether the lien claimants registered their claims for lien against lands that were not included in the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Northridge Homes Ltd." p2="Travellers Motel (Owen Sound) Ltd." post.rptr="3743" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641eb4e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northridge Homes Ltd. v. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 ONSC 4811, 2015 CarswellOnt 11554, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 281 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion under s. 47(1) is analogous to a motion for summary judgment under Rule 20. If there is a genuine issue of fact for trial, the matter should be left to the trial judge. The court referenced in this regard <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1246798 Ontario Inc." p2="Sterling" post.rptr="4023" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I641eb4e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1246798 Ontario Inc. v. Sterling">1246798 Ontario Inc. v. Sterling, 2000 CarswellOnt 4023, 51 O.R. (3d) 220, 5 C.L.R. (3d) 146 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> at para. 12; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Beaver Materials Handling Co." p2="Hejna" post.rptr="2803" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I641edbf05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna">Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna, 2005 CarswellOnt 2803, 45 C.L.R. (3d) 242, [2005] O.J. No. 2733 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> at para. 24; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="1353025 Ontario Inc." p2="Walden Group Canada Ltd." post.rptr="2583" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I90f2ded0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd.">1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2583, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> at para. 14. Here, the court was not persuaded that the liens ought to be discharged. There were far too many genuine issues of fact that require a trial for their resolution. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court referenced the amendments to Rule 20 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> providing expanded powers on motions for summary judgment, and noted that in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Hryniak" p2="Mauldin" post.rptr="7" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641edbf25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hryniak v. Mauldin">Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, 2014 CarswellOnt 640, 2014 CarswellOnt 641, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, the Supreme Court of Canada stated that there will be no genuine issue requiring trial when the judge is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment. This will be the case when the process (1) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, (2) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and (3) is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Butko" p2="Ratayeva" post.rptr="1102" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641edbf35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Butko v. Ratayeva">Butko v. Ratayeva, 2015 ONSC 1102, 2015 CarswellOnt 8388, 47 C.L.R. (4th) 344 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A case management master exercising discretion as the court but not as the reference master has jurisdiction under s. 47 of the Act to weigh evidence, evaluate credibility and draw reasonable inferences from the evidence in considering whether to dismiss an action. The test that applies to summary judgment motions brought in civil actions under Rule 20.04 is the same as the test to be applied to motions under s. 47. That test is whether there is a genuine issue that requires a trial. Rule 20.04(2.1) empowers the court to weigh evidence, evaluate credibility and draw reasonable inferences from the evidence in considering whether to dismiss an action. The powers available to the court to determine a motion under s. 47 of the Act are not limited in their application to motions heard by a judge. A master may exercise the same powers on a motion under s. 47 of the Act whether or not the master is presiding over a reference or a motion in an action that has not been referred.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="G.C. Rentals & Enterprises Ltd." p2="Advanced Precast Inc." post.rptr="4237" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I641edbf45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. Rentals & Enterprises Ltd. v. Advanced Precast Inc.">G.C. Rentals & Enterprises Ltd. v. Advanced Precast Inc., 2014 ONSC 4237, 2014 CarswellOnt 10733, 44 C.L.R. (4th) 95 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 5373, 2014 CarswellOnt 13537, 44 C.L.R. (4th) 107 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion to discharge a lien under s. 47 is analogous to a motion for summary judgment under Rule 20. As such, if there are genuine issues of fact, the matter should be left to the trial judge. The court in this regard referenced <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1246798 Ontario Inc." p2="Sterling" post.rptr="4023" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I641edbf55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1246798 Ontario Inc. v. Sterling">1246798 Ontario Inc. v. Sterling, 2000 CarswellOnt 4023, 5 C.L.R. (3d) 146 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="1353025 Ontario Inc." p2="Walden Group Canada Ltd." post.rptr="2583" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I90f305e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd.">1353025 Ontario Inc. v. Walden Group Canada Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 2583, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. The court was not prepared to assume that on a s. 47 motion it had the new, expanded powers expressly given to a summary judgment motions judge under rules 20.04(2.1) and (2.2), to weigh the evidence, evaluate credibility of a deponent, draw any reasonable inference from the evidence and order that oral evidence be presented by one or more parties. The trial here would proceed on the issue of breach of contract, with the same witnesses involved in this motion. The goals of timeliness, affordability and proportionality would not be furthered by expanding the motion to hear oral evidence on the facts in dispute, evaluate credibility and draw inferences, even if the court had the discretion to do so by analogy to Rule 20. As a result, the issue of whether there was one continuing contract or two separate contracts was a genuine issue of fact that required a trial. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also on this point <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Northridge Homes Ltd." p2="Travellers Motel (Owen Sound) Ltd." post.rptr="3743" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641f03005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northridge Homes Ltd. v. Travellers Motel (Owen Sound) Ltd.">Northridge Homes Ltd. v. Travellers Motel (Owen Sound) Ltd., 2015 ONSC 3743, 2015 CarswellOnt 8840, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 273 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 ONSC 4811, 2015 CarswellOnt 11554, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 281 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Butko" p2="Ratayeva" post.rptr="1102" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I641f03015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Butko v. Ratayeva">Butko v. Ratayeva, 2015 ONSC 1102, 2015 CarswellOnt 8388, 47 C.L.R. (4th) 344 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd." p2="OHL Construction Canada" post.rptr="7505" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641f03025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada">Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada, 2013 ONSC 7505, 2013 CarswellOnt 18456, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 213 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 3763, 2014 CarswellOnt 8361, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 223 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a complicated piece of litigation, TTC contracted for construction services related to a subway extension to York University. OHL subcontracted with ACT to provide excavation monitoring and ground support for a building under which the extension was being constructed. Documentation noted that on completion, TTC would own, operate and maintain the new subway line, although the university was the only owner or relevant entity registered on title with respect to any interest in the land. The university granted a temporary construction licence to permit TTC and its agents to enter upon university lands to carry out their subway construction activities, including the compensation grouting for building support and excavation monitoring work. The licence did not constitute any form of property interest in, or gift or dedication of, university lands. After being ordered off the site following the collapse of a drilling rig, ACT claimed against OHL for delay due to unforeseen or changed soil conditions, improper termination of the contract, and loss of profit. ACT, along with another claimant, brought lien actions for monies alleged owing and to assert security against title, giving a copy of its lien only to various university officials. OHL obtained an order vacating the registration of the claim for lien upon the posting of security. In the motion here, it moved to have the lien discharged and the lien action dismissed on three main grounds. First, that lien rights were unenforceable on public policy grounds, on the basis that areas under government, government agency, or even private control or supervision relating to the transportation of persons and goods, ought not to be the subject of a construction lien claim. Second, it argued that the work involved a “railway right-of-way” and that the lien claimants ought to have preserved those liens in the manner set out in s. 34(4) of the Act, and that by failing to do so their liens were not properly preserved. Third, it argued that neither TTC nor YU were owners as contemplated by s. 14, and hence no lien rights arose. In rejecting the public policy argument, the Master distinguished <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Big Creek Construction Ltd." p2="York-Trillium Development Group Ltd." post.rptr="285" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I641f2a105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd.">Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd. (1993), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 285, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 331 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 138 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, on the basis that TTC and YU turned their minds to the public policy issue and expressly agreed that there would be no gift or dedication of any portion of the York University lands to the general public or for any public use or purpose. As well, the fact the lien was able to be vacated from title represented an appropriate balancing of interests in the case. There was no request in the statement of claim for sale of the lands, and no evidence that the lands in question formed any part of any future property right that might be transferred to the City of Toronto and/or TTC. On the issue of preservation of the lien in the context of a “railway right-of-way,” the Master engaged in an extensive review of relevant legislation and precedents. Notwithstanding that it could be characterized as a street railway, TTC had no property interest in the project or YU lands on which the liens were registered. It had not right-of-way, either by easement or in fee simple, and in the absence of a right-of-way there could be no “railway right-of-way.” If an order was sought for the sale of the YU premises for failure to pay the amount of any lien proven, the court would have the power to refuse to grant such an order if it elected instead to exercise its power to grant an easement of necessity by way of a partial severance of the portion of the lands on which the TTC was constructing the subway and subway stations. Lastly, YU was an owner within the meaning of the Act. The object of the construction was to establish a subway station for YU, and ACT's work was done to protect a university building from damage or collapse during excavation operations. There was no question that YU had an interest in the lands improved, and a sufficient “request” by the owner of the subject lands had been established.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="State Group Inc." p2="Quebecor World Inc." post.rptr="2277" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641f2a115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc.">State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc., 2013 ONSC 2277, 2013 CarswellOnt 4462, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 164 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>: The contractor sought an order declaring the claim for lien under which its claimed purported to shelter was a valid sheltering lien and properly perfected in relation to the subject improvement. With respect to the master's jurisdiction to make such an order under sections 45, 46 or 47 of the Act, he proceeded on the basis of his inherent general jurisdiction as a superior court judge, as the motion was being brought within the context of a reference of which he was seized.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2183164 Ontario Inc." p2="Gillani" post.rptr="1456" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I641f2a125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2183164 Ontario Inc. v. Gillani">2183164 Ontario Inc. v. Gillani, 2013 ONSC 1456, 2013 CarswellOnt 2891, 114 O.R. (3d) 676, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 134 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2012 CarswellOnt 7261, 2012 ONSC 3377, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 8627, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 204 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—As the result of two abortive cross-examinations of the plaintiff, and the Master's view that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> procedures governing lien actions would be inappropriate for achieving a fair, expeditious and least costly resolution of all the issues because of a variety of foreseeable procedural hurdles, the master exercised his discretion and ordered the discharge of the lien, and the vacating of registration of the lien and certificate of action and the dismissal of the lien action. Reversing that decision on appeal, the Divisional Court indicated that the Master should have proceeded with the alternative relief claimed rather than wander beyond the parameters of the motion before him as it had been framed by the defendants. The fact that the actual relief granted by the Master was sought in the Notice of Motion did not resolve the lack of notice, as it was the grounds for that relief that were important. Even if the issue was properly before the Master, which it was not, the Master exceeded his jurisdiction under s. 47(1) and erred in law in striking the lien and dismissing the lien action in the circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vanezi" p2="1648380 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4878" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I641f2a135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vanezi v. 1648380 Ontario Inc.">Vanezi v. 1648380 Ontario Inc., 2011 ONSC 4878, 2011 CarswellOnt 9449 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff lien claimant was a figurehead officer and director of the defendant company, with no real power within the structure of the defendant, and while he had a named title within the company to allow him to sign documents, all real decisions were dictated by the shareholders located in the United States. Even if it could be argued that an officer and director was precluded from registering a lien, the court was not prepared to do so on a motion under s. 47 in these circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DCL Management Ltd." p2="Zenith Fitness Inc." post.rptr="5915" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I641f51205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="DCL Management Ltd. v. Zenith Fitness Inc.">DCL Management Ltd. v. Zenith Fitness Inc., 2010 ONSC 5915, 2010 CarswellOnt 9524, 97 C.L.R. (3d) 159 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at 2011 CarswellOnt 1730, 97 C.L.R. (3d) 190 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—While a motion under s. 47 is “akin to a motion for summary judgment” and, like a motion under Rule 20, the moving party must show that there is “no genuine issue for trial” it is <ital>not</ital> a motion under Rule 20. By virtue of s. 67(1), new Rule 20 cannot limit the broad power of the court given to it under s. 47 since the current wording of new Rule 20 is inconsistent with the broad general power given to the court under s. 47. The Master also noted that s. 47 only allows the court to discharge a lien (and s. 45 only allows the court to declare a lien expired), and therefore these provisions can only be used to <ital>attack</ital> a lien claim, and cannot be used by a lien claimant to seek summary judgment declaring a lien to be valid and to seek the enforcement of the lien. A lien claimant seeking such a remedy must use Rule 20.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Federated Contractors Inc." p2="Ann-Maura Developments Inc." post.rptr="370" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I641f51215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Federated Contractors Inc. v. Ann-Maura Developments Inc.">Federated Contractors Inc. v. Ann-Maura Developments Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 370 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2010 CarswellOnt 1520 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 47 provides that the court has jurisdiction to determine issues raised under that section. The court includes the master and case management master. Raising a novel point of law does not deprive the master of jurisdiction. Here, the plaintiff served a notice of lien, requiring the owner to hold back the amount for which notice was given in addition to the statutory ten per cent holdback obligation under the Act. Several years later the plaintiff filed a construction lien for the exact amount set out in the notice, a circumstance that would have required the plaintiff to estimate to the penny the fee to which it would be entitled over the several years based on construction that had not yet been done and materials and services that had not yet been provided. In the circumstances, the only explanations were that the lien was substantially out of time or the notice of lien was a sham, intended to defeat or take priority over <ital>bona fide</ital> creditors, and that the plaintiff served notice of lien when it was not entitled to do so. Accordingly, the plaintiff did not come to court with clean hands and forfeited any entitlement to benefit from the extraordinary remedies the Act provided. The court will not be an accomplice to an abuse of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Polsoni Estimating & Construction Co." p2="Algibon Investments Inc." post.rptr="5063" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I641f51225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Polsoni Estimating & Construction Co. v. Algibon Investments Inc.">Polsoni Estimating & Construction Co. v. Algibon Investments Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 5063 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion for discharge of a claim for lien is akin to a motion for summary judgment, and although some proof was tendered in the case at bar that the lien was not registered within the 45 day period, there was other evidence that tended to refute this. As such, a material fact remained in dispute and the defendants' motion was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Beaver Materials Handling Co." p2="Hejna" post.rptr="2803" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I641f51235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna">Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 2803, 45 C.L.R. (3d) 242 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court summarized the case law in respect of s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> as follows: (1) Section 47 of the Act gives the court authority to vacate the registration of the construction lien and certificate of action; declare that the lien has expired, or that written notice of the lien shall no longer bind the person to whom it was given and/or dismiss the action; (2) The motion under s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is akin to a motion for summary judgment and therefore R. 20 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> applies; (3) Therefore the moving party must establish in a s. 47 motion that there is no genuine issue for trial; (4) If there are genuine issues of fact, the matters should be left to be determined by the trial judge; (5) If it is not patently demonstrable on an interlocutory motion that a party has no right to a lien, or unless the court is satisfied that the cause of action could not possibly succeed at trial, then the matter should be left to the trial judge; (6) Assessing credibility, weighing the evidence and drawing inferences are the function of the trial judge, not the motions judge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Dirm Inc." p2="Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3479" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I641f78305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd.">Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3479, 37 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Master)</ref></cite>—The owner, a college of applied arts and technology, and its Board of Governors, were held to be Crown agents under s. 2(4) of the Ontario <ital>Colleges of Applied Arts and Technology Act, 2002</ital> and the <ital>Crown Agency Act</ital>. The lien did not attach to the premises, and preservation was governed by s. 34(1)(b) of the Ontario Act. The general contractor successfully obtained discharge of the lien under s. 47 on the basis that preservation was improper because the claimant had registered its lien in the land registry office under s. 34(1)(a) rather than “give” a copy of the claim for lien and affidavit of verification to the owner college of applied arts and technology under s. 34(1)(b) and s. 34(3), by mailing them to the “office of the president of the college”. In the circumstances, even though there was a factual dispute, factual findings could be made on a s. 47 motion, without a trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90f37b10f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The lien action was called for trial for the October 2002 sittings. On September 30, 2002, the defendant's counsel notified the claimant's counsel that the latter's corporate charter had been cancelled on March 14, 1973. The claimant's charter was revived October 1, 2002. The defendant moved for an order discharging the lien, cancelling the bond posted, dismissing the lien action, and for costs on a substantial indemnity basis on the grounds, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that the lien claimant's charter was cancelled at the time the lien was preserved and perfected and not revived until the time limitations contained in ss. 31(2), 36(2) and 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had expired. The motions judge ordered the lien to be discharged, but granted the claimant leave to proceed with the action as a personal judgment, to add the defendant's sole officer as a party defendant, and to add a trust fund claim. However, the claimant unsuccessfully argued on appeal that the judge erred in failing to order the defendants to post security for the claim, and in failing to order further productions and discoveries in regard to the amended trust fund claim. Here, there was no evidence of a breach of trust before the court. Nor was there any evidence that the corporate defendant would not be in a position to pay any judgment that the claimant might obtain. There was no evidence to suggest that the motions judge's exercise of discretion under s. 47(1) of the act was “clearly wrong”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="G. Wright & Associates Ltd." p2="Vace Investments Inc." post.rptr="2872" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I641f78325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G. Wright & Associates Ltd. v. Vace Investments Inc.">G. Wright & Associates Ltd. v. Vace Investments Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2872, 2003 CarswellOnt 2732, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 239 (S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 3964 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The claimant project manager provided services to the owner for 8 years, those services resulted in a substantial improvement to the lands, and the owner indicated that future revenue would be split among the parties. When such profit sharing did not take place, the claimant was entitled to rely on the provisions of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Profit sharing arrangements, by themselves, do not prohibit a lien claim and justify discharge of a lien. It is only where there are other relevant considerations involved that the discretionary remedy under s. 47(1) of the Act should be invoked.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Coldstream Concrete Ltd." p2="Dacosta Realty Inc." post.rptr="410" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I641f78335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Coldstream Concrete Ltd. v. Dacosta Realty Inc.">Coldstream Concrete Ltd. v. Dacosta Realty Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 410, 2003 CarswellOnt 638, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 304 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—One defendant unsuccessfully moved for an order discharging a lien and vacating the registration of the lien and certificate of action on the grounds that the plaintiff had no lienable interest against the subject property. The moving defendant argued that the plaintiff was not a contractor within the definition of the Act because the main defendant was not an owner within the meaning of the Act. The argument raised substantial credibility issues, the resolution of which required a trial. Genuine issues of fact should be dealt with at trial, where the answers to identified issues were not clear and unequivocal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Dearlove" p2="451019 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4217" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I641f9f405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dearlove v. 451019 Ontario Ltd.">Dearlove v. 451019 Ontario Ltd. (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 4217, 2002 CarswellOnt 3743, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 315 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants argued that they did not receive written notice of any improvements to be made to the premises, while the plaintiff contended that the former had both written and oral notice, although not specifically in accordance with Form 2. In such circumstances, the issue of compliance with s. 19(1) of the Act should be placed before the trial judge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re" post.rptr="262" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I641f9f415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re">A.G. Simpson Automotive Inc., Re (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 262, 2002 CarswellOnt 210, 21 C.L.R. (3d) 50 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a motion brought under s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the onus is on the moving party to satisfy the court that there is no genuine issue for trial (citing the recent decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1972" p1="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd." p2="Modern Tile Supply Co." post.rptr="216" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I641f9f425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co.">Central Supply Co. (1972) Ltd. v. Modern Tile Supply Co. (1998), 43 C.L.R. (2d) 216, 1998 CarswellOnt 4637 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed by (2001), 2001 CarswellOnt 3138, 11 C.L.R. (3d) 1, 55 O.R. (3d) 783 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>). If there are genuine issues of fact, the matter should be left to be determined by the trial judge. Where the lien claimant supplied all material and services necessary to remove and demolish parts of an automotive assembly line and designed, constructed and installed the new assembly line equipment at the plant, the question of whether or not the material supplied came within the definition of “improvement” depended on full understanding of the factual matrix, including ownership of the parts and the length of time it was intended and expected that the assembly line might be in place. A trial was the best place for the determination of both the legal and factual issues.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Alloy Wheels International (Canada) Ltd., Re" post.rptr="173" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I641f9f435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alloy Wheels International (Canada) Ltd., Re">Alloy Wheels International (Canada) Ltd., Re (2002), 31 C.B.R. (4th) 173, 2002 CarswellOnt 567, 15 C.L.R. (3d) 253 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A registrar in bankruptcy derives his or her jurisdiction from s. 192 of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3 and, in a general sense, is confined to matters in bankruptcy. The trustee asked the registrar to read into s. 192(1)(h), the jurisdiction to give effect to the trustee's disallowance of the creditor's lien claim. The registrar refused to do so, holding that it did not have jurisdiction to grant the trustee's motion to vacate a claim for lien and lift the certificates of action under s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Park" p2="Metropolitan Separate School Board" post.rptr="202" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I641fc6505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Park v. Master)</ref></cite>—This case contains a thorough analysis of the nature and quality of evidence required to hold in a lien for material supply. The learned Master also considered relevance and utility of burdens of proof on such motions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I90f3c930f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v.
