Master)</ref></cite>—The court held that this section contemplated the return of security in certain circumstances which include the consent of the parties on a successful motion for summary judgment or similar relief. Such a motion, in any event, must be brought upon notice. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Under appeal. Motion to quash appeal dismissed at [1998] O.J. No. 2378 (Ont. C.A.).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd." p2="J.D.S. Investments Ltd." post.rptr="443" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I641fc6525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. J.D.S. Investments Ltd.">Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. J.D.S. Investments Ltd. (1995), 6 W.D.C.P. (2d) 443</ref></cite>—The first mortgagee moved to post a letter of credit as security and to vacate the registration of a claim for lien using a form of order under s. 47. It argued that because it was foreclosing and not proceeding under power of sale and an order in the usual form pursuant to s. 44 was not satisfactory. The plaintiff opposed the order under s. 47 but did not oppose the usual form of order under s. 44. In granting an order under s. 44, the Master stated that the mortgagee's draft order would rewrite the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for the purposes of the particular action, on very preliminary material at a very early stage in the proceedings. The mortgagee's concern was unfounded, as <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was never intended to displace the priority of the mortgagee, where the mortgagee clears the title pursuant to s. 44.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Accent Design Inc." p2="Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc." post.rptr="33" pre.rptr="15" ref.id="I641fed605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc.">Accent Design Inc. v. Walton Place (Scarborough) Inc. (1994), 15 C.L.R. (2d) 33 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The action was dismissed where the affidavit of verification stated that D Inc. was the lien claimant when it was actually an unincorporated partnership. The affidavit of verification was invalid, and consequently so was the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Big Creek Construction Ltd." p2="York-Trillium Development Group Ltd." post.rptr="285" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I641fed615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd.">Big Creek Construction Ltd. v. York-Trillium Development Group Ltd. (1993), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 285, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 331 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 138 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where the beneficial holders of a construction project were also the officers, directors, and controlling shareholders of the general contractor, which described itself as “owner” of the project in its dealings with the trades, but was not shown as a general contractor on any of the statutory declarations, it was inappropriate to allow liens to be placed on the property on behalf of that contractor. Given that the ultimate beneficiaries of the project had either directly or indirectly given covenants not to have the project liened and given indemnities in this respect, it was an appropriate exercise of the court's discretion under s. 47 to make an order vacating the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Franro Property Development Ltd." p2="Heritage Glen North Ltd." post.rptr="2572" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I642014705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Franro Property Development Ltd. v. Heritage Glen North Ltd.">Franro Property Development Ltd. v. Heritage Glen North Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 2572, [1993] O.J. No. 2396 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The power of a court under s. 47 to discharge a lien manifestly preserved in bad faith is not displaced by s. 35, which provides a remedy in damages.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Sefri Construction International Ltd." p2="Jaltas Inc." post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I642014715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sefri Construction International Ltd. v. Jaltas Inc.">Sefri Construction International Ltd. v. Jaltas Inc. (1990), 38 C.L.R. 15 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The court had no power to cure a claim for lien which contained an affidavit of verification that was unsigned by a Commissioner of Oaths. Accordingly, the lien was ordered discharged pursuant to s. 47.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Melgold Construction Management Ltd." p2="Banton Investments Ltd." post.rptr="216" pre.rptr="32" ref.id="I642014725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Melgold Construction Management Ltd. v. Banton Investments Ltd.">Melgold Construction Management Ltd. v. Banton Investments Ltd. (1988), 32 C.L.R. 216 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff had one corporate shareholder which was equally controlled by M and G, and the defendant B Ltd. was controlled by G. The plaintiff had provided its services as a construction manager for B Ltd., and registered a lien claim against the property, which B Ltd. subsequently vacated. Without a director's resolution authorizing the preservation or perfection of the lien, the plaintiff commenced an action to perfect its lien. The defendant submitted that the plaintiff could not commence any action without authorization of the board of directors and that any lien thus perfected would not be perfected or improperly perfected. The defendant brought a motion to dismiss the plaintiff's action, to cancel and release the security posted in respect of the plaintiff's lien claim and to cancel the plaintiff's lien and extinguish its rights therein. The court dismissed the defendant's motion. In the normal course of business, the plaintiff was a construction manager, which required it to protect its claims to recover debts for its services. The commencement of the action by the plaintiff, without director authorization, was nevertheless within the company's normal course of business, and therefore, the lien was not improperly perfected. Under such circumstances, the indoor management rule applied and it was not necessary for the plaintiff to demonstrate any express authority given by the board of directors to commence an action to protect its lien claim.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
47:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 47.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">47:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 47(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bank-Strox Renovation Inc." p2="Lugano View Limited" post.rptr="4526" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67732d203b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Bank-Strox Renovation Inc. v. Lugano View Limited">Bank-Strox Renovation Inc. v. Lugano View Limited, 2024 CarswellOnt 4526, 2024 ONSC 1901 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner was denied an order lifting a consent stay order and an order under s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> discharging the claim for lien and dismissing the action, on account of delay. The parties had suspended the lien action several years before when they agreed to arbitrate and then later obtained a consent stay of that action to facilitate the arbitration. While a plaintiff usually bears the primary responsibility for the progress of an action and suffers the consequences of delay, this principle does not apply to an arbitration where both parties together agree to arbitrate the case after the commencement of a civil action to perfect a lien. Where, as here, the defendant fails even to plead, either in the lien action or in the arbitration, the defendant bears a greater responsibility to move the arbitration forward to allow for pleadings and the other necessary interlocutory steps. The defendant did nothing to advance the arbitration once the arbitration agreement was in place and did not bring a motion under s. 10 of the <ital>Arbitration Act, 1991</ital>, S.O. 1991, c. 17 to seek a court appointed arbitrator. Although the arbitration agreement was an oral one, it was no less binding.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="S31 Inc." p2="Ecolomondo Environmental (Hawkesbury) Inc." post.rptr="5071" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I67732d213b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="S31 Inc. v. Ecolomondo Environmental (Hawkesbury) Inc.">S31 Inc. v. Ecolomondo Environmental (Hawkesbury) Inc., 2023 ONSC 5071, 2023 CarswellOnt 13766 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The enhanced powers available in R. 20 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> are not available on a s. 47 motion under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Although an analogous test is used under R. 20 and s. 47, these are procedurally different motions. Here, the court could not distinguish the decision of the Divisional Court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc." p2="2603774 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9830" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f3f040f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc.">Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 9830, 2020 ONSC 4308, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 182 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming on other grounds 2019 ONSC 5278, 2019 CarswellOnt 14629, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, where this point was in issue and clearly decided. It was impossible to decide whether the contract in this case was abandoned before the relevant date without weighing the evidence, evaluating the credibility of the parties, and drawing reasonable inferences from the evidence. The defendant's motion for discharge of the lien was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1936230 Ontario Inc." p2="Hari Kaush Developments Inc." post.rptr="12610" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcf6050ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="1936230 Ontario Inc. v. Hari Kaush Developments Inc.">1936230 Ontario Inc. v. Hari Kaush Developments Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 12610, 2023 ONSC 4718 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a s. 47 motion, the moving party must prove that there is no triable issue as to the basis on which the lien is sought to be discharged and both parties must “put their best foot forward” in the evidence to assist the court in making this determination. Here, there remained a triable issue as to whether the plaintiff's lien was timely. The defendant's evidence contained documents that were not introduced or explained by anyone with direct knowledge or experience with the project, and other allegedly supporting reports included hearsay, with no attempt made to qualify them under the business records exception. As well, the defendant was unable to demonstrate that the lien was “frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process”. Referencing the ruling in <trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="XPL Construction Solutions Inc." p2="North Bay Capital Investments Ltd." post.rptr="238" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I677354303b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="XPL Construction Solutions Inc. v. North Bay Capital Investments Ltd.">XPL Construction Solutions Inc. v. North Bay Capital Investments Ltd., 2023 ONSC 238, 2023 CarswellOnt 172, 32 C.L.R. (5th) 277 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>, the court noted that “frivolous” describes an action so highly unlikely to succeed that it is apparently devoid of practical merit; “vexatious” included actions that obviously could not succeed and that are brought for an improper purpose, while “abuse of process” was a flexible doctrine giving the court the inherent power to prevent the misuse of its process. Here, there was simply no clear evidence as to whether either side was correct with respect to the accounting which determined the lien's quantum, and whether extras should be included in the total. The defendant's motion was dismissed. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The Associate Judge also rejected the application of s. 44(5), as the evidence on such a motion was assessed in the same way as on a motion for summary judgment.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Built By Engineers" p2="Coronation Medical Plaza" post.rptr="7446" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcf6052ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Built By Engineers v. Coronation Medical Plaza">Built By Engineers v. Coronation Medical Plaza, 2023 CarswellOnt 7446, 2023 ONSC 2969 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2023 CarswellOnt 10726, 2023 ONSC 4170 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a s. 47 motion to discharge a lien, the court does not have the enhanced powers that would be available on a summary judgment motion. Here, these were disputed factual issues that could not be determined without making findings of credibility, and the s. 47 motion was dismissed. Even if the motion were converted to a summary judgment motion, deciding the issue of the timeliness of the lien would not fully resolve all trial issues, but would only be a partial summary judgment that would risk inconsistent findings regarding the validity of some of the claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Kamlu Engineering Inc." p2="Cadorin Homes" post.rptr="7271" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcf6053ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Kamlu Engineering Inc. v. Cadorin Homes">Kamlu Engineering Inc. v. Cadorin Homes, 2023 CarswellOnt 7271, 2023 ONSC 2940 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Despite delays and certain non-compliance with the Associate Justice's orders in the lien reference, the plaintiff's conduct did not rise to the level of warranting a discharge of its lien and dismissal of this action. The plaintiff's actions included delays in retaining new counsel after a removal order for its previous lawyers; failure to respond to the defendant's attempts to schedule discovery; delay/failure to comply with the court's timetable order; providing service of its outstanding productions as a single digital.pdf file instead of as separate documents; and non-payment of a fairly recent costs award. However, these actions could be fairly compensable in costs and did not warrant dismissal of the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes" p2="Jia Deve" post.rptr="6437" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcf6054ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Deve">2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Deve, 2023 CarswellOnt 6437, 2023 ONSC 2301 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons <ital>2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Deve</ital>, 2023 CarswellOnt 8234, 2023 ONSC 3361 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants successfully brought a motion under s. 47 for an order discharging the claim for lien and vacating the related certificate of action from title, on the basis that the quantum claimed was frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process. There was no evidence that the defendant did any of the work alleged in its claim for lien, and the circumstances indicated that the claim for lien was made for an improper purpose, namely either to force the defendants to agree with the plaintiff's joint venture proposal or as a reprisal for not doing so. As well, the action was dismissed under rule 15.04(6) and (7) on account of the plaintiff's failure to hire a lawyer or get an order granting it leave to be represented by a non-lawyer. That the plaintiff's principal did not appear at the case conference scheduled to determine whether the defendant would retain a lawyer, indicated that the action had been abandoned.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2675076 Ontario Inc." p2="Gilman, et al. / Gilman et al." post.rptr="5822" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcf8760ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2675076 Ontario Inc. v. Gilman, et al. / Gilman et al.">2675076 Ontario Inc. v. Gilman, et al. / Gilman et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 5822, 2023 ONSC 2178 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To obtain an order registering a lien against a property, a lien claimant need only swear a declaration as to the outstanding alleged debt. This preserves the lien claimant's ability to enforce the lien if it is ultimately successful in its action. However, the corollary to this speedy remedy is that the lien claimant is required to act with expediency and move the matter forward summarily, because the property is encumbered by virtue of what is really a pre-judgment remedy. As noted in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GTA Restoration Group Inc." p2="Baillie" post.rptr="5190" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I8dcf8761ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="GTA Restoration Group Inc. v. Baillie">GTA Restoration Group Inc. v. Baillie, 2020 ONSC 5190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 ONSC 6327 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2021 ONSC 1262 (Ont. Div. Ct.); leave to appeal refused 2021 ONSC 1250 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, “ongoing procedural delays contrary to the summary procedure required” by the Act and “non-compliance with court orders” are grounds that justify a discharge of the lien. Here, the court discharged the plaintiff's lien, vacated the Certificate of Action and dismissed the <ital>Construction Lien Action</ital> on account of the plaintiff's failure to proceed expeditiously. Specifically, the plaintiff failed to provide the documents necessary to substantiate its claim for lien, or to adduce evidence that it was seeking to obtain that information in a diligent manner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DNR Restoration Inc." p2="Trac Developments Inc." post.rptr="3680" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcf8762ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc.">DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 3680, 2023 ONSC 1849 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The owner failed to meet its onus of proving that there was no triable issue concerning the timeliness of the subcontractor's claim for lien, or that the latter had abandoned the project at an earlier date such that the lien was out of time. Although the claimant served the owner with a formal notice of “suspension” of the work due to the failure by the parties to agree to on new pricing, the notion of “suspension” of work was not the same as an intention not to complete the contract work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brook Restoration Ltd." p2="Greatwise Developments Ltd." post.rptr="2778" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I67737b403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Brook Restoration Ltd. v. Greatwise Developments Ltd.">Brook Restoration Ltd. v. Greatwise Developments Ltd., 2023 CarswellOnt 2778, 2023 ONSC 1118, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 332 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2023 ONSC 4090, 2023 CarswellOnt 10759 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2023 CarswellOnt 4291, 2023 ONSC 1996, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 351 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The defendant moved to discharge the plaintiff's lien, or in the alternative reduce the security posted. The nature of the actual agreement between the parties – whether it was a fixed cost or a cost plus agreement - was a highly significant and material factual dispute that was beyond the scope of a s. 44 motion. It was an issue best resolved on a full evidentiary record following a trial. Likewise, whether the plaintiff had abandoned the project was also a triable issue, and the court concluded that the lien claim was not frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process. However, the amount of security was reduced to take into account an overlooked payment by the defendant and certain calculation errors and non-lienable items claimed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RA Crete-Scape Ltd." p2="Minhas" post.rptr="1086" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dcfae70ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="RA Crete-Scape Ltd. v. Minhas">RA Crete-Scape Ltd. v. Minhas, 2023 CarswellOnt 1086, 2023 ONSC 796 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Despite the plaintiff doing very little of any merit to advance its claim over seven years and purporting to engage in fruitless efforts to transfer the lien action to Small Claims Court, the Associate Justice declined to grant the defendant's motion to dismiss the action for delay and discharge the lien. The defendant, although unsuccessful, was granted its costs of the motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lazi Ventures Inc." p2="Carter" post.rptr="615" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I67737b413b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Lazi Ventures Inc. v. Carter">Lazi Ventures Inc. v. Carter, 2023 CarswellOnt 615, 2023 ONSC 578, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 23 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2022 CarswellOnt 7247, 2022 ONSC 3111, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 13 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—A proceeding can be vexatious even where there is originally a good cause of action. The existence of a good cause of action originally does not, after considering the whole history of the matter, preclude a proceeding from being found vexatious. The Court here found no fault with the Associate Justice's conclusion that the lien claimant's use of the court's process was the final step in a scheme grounded in oppressive and unfair practices and that the action was brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of other parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2369119 Ontario Inc." p2="Kondazi" post.rptr="303" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6773a2503b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="2369119 Ontario Inc. v. Kondazi">2369119 Ontario Inc. v. Kondazi, 2023 CarswellOnt 303, 2023 ONSC 305, 34 C.L.R. (5th) 355 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—In a matter decided under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the court declined, pursuant to s. 47, to dismiss the action on the basis that delay on the plaintiff's part was inordinate, inexcusable, intentional and abusive. That delay was in part the result of the plaintiff's attempts to obtain new representation following the removal of its previous counsel. There was no evidence that a fair trial was not possible. As well, there was no clear and cogent evidence as to when the contract was terminated and therefore abandoned, such as to render the lien registered out of time. There was a genuine issue for trial concerning the date of abandonment on the evidence proffered by the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="XPL Construction Solutions Inc." p2="North Bay Capital Investments Ltd." post.rptr="238" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6773a2513b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="XPL Construction Solutions Inc. v. While there may be circumstances in which a party's conduct can be such an affront to the integrity of the court that it constitutes an abuse of process, and the failure to obey court orders may be one such example, courts are generally reluctant to dismiss a claim for a failure to answer undertakings, even where compelled to do so by court order, and particularly where there is a legitimate excuse for the non-compliance. Here, the plaintiff's principal was incarcerated after the original compliance order, and unable to respond to counsel. There was an overwhelming preference for claims to be determined on their merits.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GH Asset Management Services Inc." p2="Lo" post.rptr="18355" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6773a2523b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="GH Asset Management Services Inc. v. After the action was commenced, the claim between the claimant and the property manager was settled, and the claim was assigned to the property manager. The owners subsequently sought to permanently stay the lien action on the basis of inadequate disclosure of the litigation agreement. In dismissing the owners' motion, the associate judge held that the settlement and lien assignment between the original plaintiff and the property manager was not a settlement that triggered the immediate disclosure requirement. Rather, it arises when the settlement “changes entirely the landscape of the litigation in a way that significantly alters the adversarial relationship among the parties to the litigation or the ‘dynamics of the litigation’”. The delineation between which services support a claim for lien and which do not and in particular the allocation of the price created a genuine issue for trial best determined by the trial judge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Tamarack North Holdings Ltd." p2="Hallisey" post.rptr="92" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I6420fed15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tamarack North Holdings Ltd. v. Hallisey">Tamarack North Holdings Ltd. v. Hallisey (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 92, 59 C.L.R. (3d) 316 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff corporation carried on business as “Tamarack North Ltd.” Although the correct name of the corporation was “Tamarack North Holdings Ltd.”, the two construction contracts in question were signed using the former name, although there was no such corporate legal entity and it was not a registered trade name within the meaning of the <ital>Business Names Act</ital>. The defendants sought an order discharging the lien and dismissing the action on the ground that the contracting party was not the lien claimant or in fact a legal entity. The court declined to give the order, as there was never a time when the defendants were not aware of the fact that they were dealing with a corporation. There was no reason for depriving the plaintiff of its substantive rights under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> on such narrow technical grounds. All negotiations in connection with both contracts and all interaction throughout the construction occurred between the defendants and the same representative of the plaintiffs. There was nothing in the evidence to suggest that the defendants did not know that they were dealing with a limited company or that they were prejudiced in any way by the fact that Tamarack North Holdings Ltd. held itself out as Tamarack North Ltd. The proper legal entity adopted the contracts and acted throughout as the signatory to them. While the use of the name without registration was a technical violation of the <ital>Business Names Act</ital>, a principal purpose of that Act was to ensure that members of the public know with whom they are dealing and whether a business using a separate name was incorporated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Buttcon Ltd." p2="Beaver Construction Services Corp." post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="51" ref.id="I6420fed25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Buttcon Ltd. v. Beaver Construction Services Corp.">Buttcon Ltd. v. Beaver Construction Services Corp. (2006), 51 C.L.R. (3d) 150, 2006 CarswellOnt 171 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the claimant contractor failed to pay the costs ordered against it, and failed to be properly represented and respond to the motion, it was appropriate to declare that its sheltered liens, which had been preserved but nor perfected, had expired and were to be discharged, and that the defendant's security was to be returned to it for cancellation. The claimant continued to have right of action in contract against the defendant but its right to proceed under the Act was extinguished.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Beaver Materials Handling Co." p2="Hejna" post.rptr="2803" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I642125e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna">Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 2803, 45 C.L.R. (3d) 242 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff provided materials and installation for four boat storage module units for the marina owned by the defendant. The marina was situated on both the east and west sides of a provincial highway, with each portion of the divided property owned by a different numbered company controlled by the same individual. The defendant argued that the lien claimant was retained by one numbered company to provide materials and services for the construction of boat storage modules on the west side of the highway, but incorrectly registered the claim for lien and certificate of action on the land and premises owned by the other numbered company. The court found that the marina was an integrated operation on both sides of the highway, with no separate or distinct business name used to designate the lands to the west of the highway. The two parcels of land had a common function, and enjoyed each with the other as provided in the statute. Accordingly, the plaintiff's claim supported the claim for a lien on the property and was reasonable in the circumstances. The lien could only be vacated and the certificate of action discharged upon payment into court, or the posting of security.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Edelstein" p2="1411151 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4104" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I642125e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edelstein v. 1411151 Ontario Inc.">Edelstein v. 1411151 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4104, 37 C.L.R. (3d) 212 (Master); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 4501 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff builder approached the defendant, his brother-in-law, to finance the building of two houses, and the latter incorporated a company to purchase property. The building was eventually completed but the terms of the agreement between the parties were oral only. The defendant alleged that the parties were equal partners and would share in any profits from the sale of the properties. The plaintiff claimed to be a salaried employee of the company, and registered construction liens on the properties, as well as bringing an action for his construction services. The company made payment into court and the liens were discharged. The master ruled that the plaintiff failed to prove a charge under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> on the security in court under s. 44(6). The money in court was to be paid out to the defendant after confirmation of the formal report.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Monaco Electric Ltd." p2="Empire Myers Road Inc." post.rptr="713" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I642125e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Monaco Electric Ltd. v. Empire Myers Road Inc.">Monaco Electric Ltd. v. Empire Myers Road Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 713, 2004 CarswellOnt 773, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 270 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The applicant owners argued that as a result of the express terms of the written contract, the lien claimant had no right to a general lien on the properties in question. They sought orders, <ital>inter alia</ital>: declaring that the claimant's general claims for lien were invalid and discharging them; dismissing the actions to enforce the liens; and ordering payment out of court of the security posted to the credit of the actions. The court viewed the motion as akin to a motion for summary judgment under Ont. R. 20. Given that, it was up to the claimant to provide evidence from which it could be concluded that there was a genuine issue regarding its entitlement to a general lien. In this case, such evidence was unsatisfactory and the relief was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="W. Robert Hutcheson Sand & Gravel Ltd." p2="Taylor" post.rptr="292" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I642125e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="W. Robert Hutcheson Sand & Gravel Ltd. v. Taylor">W. Robert Hutcheson Sand & Gravel Ltd. v. Taylor (1999), 48 C.L.R. (2d) 292 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff vacated its construction lien as part of what it believed was a binding settlement, in exchange for a mortgage in a lesser amount. On the grounds that there was no consensus between the parties as to the terms of their agreement, the minutes of settlement were set aside. The court held that, in the circumstances, it would be unfair for the plaintiff to be left without security for its full claim, and unfair to the defendants for the plaintiff to have a mortgage or their lands that was not subject to the basic enforceability requirement of a construction lien, namely, success at trial. Therefore, the defendants were to provide security to the plaintiff by way of bond, letter of credit or other form of irrevocable security that would abide the outcome of the action and be available to satisfy the plaintiff's claim, if successful. Once security was furnished, the plaintiff was to execute a discharge of the mortgage on the defendants' lands.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
47:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 47.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">47:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 47(1.1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Con-Spec Constr. Inc." p2="Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp." post.rptr="20410" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I6774b3c03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Con-Spec Constr. Inc. v. Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp.">Con-Spec Constr. Inc. v. Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp., 2023 CarswellOnt 20410, 2023 ONSC 7229 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Sections 46(1) and 47(1)(d) of the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, when read together, provided the court with the discretion to either dismiss or permit a contract claim to continue without the lien claim. Absent any evidence from the defendant as to its own efforts to move the action forward, it was either complicit in the delay or at least complacent about it. That was a factor militating against dismissal, since the delay was not fairly viewed as being laid solely at the plaintiff's feet. The only prejudice cited by the defendant was additional time and expense, which was “prejudice” inherent in litigation. The contract claim was to be continued as an ordinary action governed by the Rules of Civil Procedure, with costs to the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="In the Matter of the Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c.C.30 Sierra General Contracting Inc." p1.pp="In the Matter of" post.rptr="11729" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dd0bfe0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="In the Matter of the Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c.C.30 Sierra General Contracting Inc.">In the Matter of the Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c.C.30 Sierra General Contracting Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 11729, 2023 ONSC 4482 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To help facilitate re-financing of the property in question, the general contractor moved <ital>ex parte</ital> for an order vacating the registration of its liens without prejudice to liens “that have arisen or may arise in relation to the lands and premises”. The order was sought because the financing bank had required title to the property to be clear of all liens before any financing was approved. In declining to grant the order, the court was concerned that such wording would preserve any and all rights the contractor enjoyed by way of formal registration of its existing liens on title, despite the liens being formally vacated from title to the property. The bank, and possibly other parties considering registering further liens or other charges against title, arguably would have their rights compromised by or subordinated to the ongoing rights created by the liens the contractor had registered, without the former having any knowledge or notice, via formal registration of liens on title to the property, of any potential concerns and/or legal issues in that regard. The requested relief should not be granted without those parties being provided with notice of the motion and an opportunity to be heard.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc." p2="2603774 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9830" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f576e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc.">Maplequest (Vaughan) Developments Inc. v. 2603774 Ontario Inc. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 9830, 2020 ONSC 4308, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 182 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming on other grounds 2019 ONSC 5278, 2019 CarswellOnt 14629, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Divisional Court upheld the motion judge's ruling, under a s. 47 motion, discharging the claim for lien and vacating the certificate of action, on the basis that the claim for lien was registered out of time. However, the motions judge erred in categorizing a s. 47 motion as being the same as a motion for summary judgment. While a motion under s. 47 is analogous to a motion for summary judgment and the underlying test—whether there is a triable issue in respect to any of the bases on which discharge of the lien is sought—is the correct test to apply, the two kinds of motions are procedurally different things. The Court referenced the recent decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90f59df0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 2019 ONSC 1551, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, (see General, above, and s. 58(3) and (4), below).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lee" p2="Chiarella" post.rptr="7374" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64214cf25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lee v. Chiarella">Lee v. Chiarella, 2018 ONSC 7374, 2018 CarswellOnt 21402, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 351 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—When read together, ss. 46(1) and (then) s. 47(1)(d) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> provide the Court with the discretion to either dismiss or permit a claim on the contract to continue without the lien claim, pursuant to decisions such as <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f59df1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Edgcumbe" p2="Vicary" post.rptr="2656" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642174015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgcumbe v. Vicary">Edgcumbe v. Vicary, 2018 ONSC 2656, 2018 CarswellOnt 8420, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Edgcumbe" p2="Vicary" post.rptr="2656" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642174025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Edgcumbe v. Vicary">Edgcumbe v. Vicary, 2018 ONSC 2656, 2018 CarswellOnt 8420, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. In exercising this discretion, the Court must consider the prejudice that each of the parties will suffer and the Court's preference to have disputes resolved on their merits. Although the plaintiff did not attend the motion and did nothing to move the matter forward for over three years, and the defendants were prepared to have the counterclaim dismissed with the action, the matter should be heard on its merits and it was appropriate that the plaintiff be given a final opportunity to respond to the motion on terms.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 47(1.1)1</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sco-Terra" p2="The Corporation of the Town of Mono" post.rptr="669" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I642174035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sco-Terra v. The Corporation of the Town of Mono">Sco-Terra v. The Corporation of the Town of Mono, 2019 ONSC 669, 2019 CarswellOnt 987, 97 C.L.R. (4th) 285 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CNL. Related proceeding. ONSC 1725, 2019 CarswellOnt 3953, 99 C.L.R. (4th) 90 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While the question of what is, and is not, a lienable service can be a genuine issue for trial, here the work that the plaintiff carried out was related to contract administration, final clearances and the completion of paperwork. A trial was not necessary to determine what the plaintiff was doing in the last few weeks before the liens were placed on the property, and what was done were not lienable services. In the result, the lien was not properly registered against the lands, and the lien was discharged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brock Contracting" p2="Kozikowski" post.rptr="7618" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642174045fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brock Contracting v. Kozikowski">Brock Contracting v. Kozikowski, 2018 ONSC 7618, 2018 CarswellOnt 21555, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor carried on business as a sole proprietorship using the original business name. She later incorporated a numbered company, and, after the last supply of services and materials to the defendant's property, registered the subsequent business name, and cancelled the original business name's registration. The new corporation then commenced a lien action under the subsequent business name. Pursuant to s. 73, the corporation did not have the right to register a lien, since it was not a party to the contract and supplied no services or materials to the project. The defendants were entitled to an order under s. 47(1) discharging the plaintiff's claim for lien and vacating the plaintiff's certificate of action. The plaintiff's contract claim against the defendants was unaffected, as the ruling did not address the question of whether any other contractual rights were assigned or transferred outside of s. 73.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Ablesystems Mechanical Ltd." p2="AER Comfort Mechanical Services Ltd." post.rptr="236" pre.rptr="78" ref.id="I642174055fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ablesystems Mechanical Ltd. v. AER Comfort Mechanical Services Ltd.">Ablesystems Mechanical Ltd. v. AER Comfort Mechanical Services Ltd. (2009), 78 C.L.R. (3d) 236, 2009 CarswellOnt 6 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Generally, once registration of a lien has been vacated upon payment of security into court under s. 44(6), the action against the owners or other defendants lacking privity of contract with the plaintiff should be dismissed, as they are no longer necessary or proper parties. This is so even though s. 47(1) may not technically require the dismissal of any action where a claim for lien has been vacated. Here, the ground relied on by the defendants was a “proper ground” and the action was dismissed as against the owner and general contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gordon Ridgely Architects & Associates Inc." p2="Glowinsky" post.rptr="269" pre.rptr="78" ref.id="I64219b105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gordon Ridgely Architects & Associates Inc. v. Glowinsky">Gordon Ridgely Architects & Associates Inc. v. Glowinsky, 78 C.L.R. (3d) 269, 2009 CarswellOnt 853 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The general test applicable to a section 47(1) motion, as summarized in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Beaver Materials Handling Co." p2="Hejna" post.rptr="2803" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I64219b115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna">Beaver Materials Handling Co. v. Hejna (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 2803, 45 C.L.R. (3d) 242 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, is similar to that applicable to a motion for summary judgment: the defendant as the moving party must establish that there is no genuine issue for trial. It is not for the judge or master hearing the motion to weigh evidence and decide timeliness; that is the jurisdiction of the trial judge. Instead, the question is whether there are genuine issues for trial to be left to be determined by the trial judge or if there is a judgment of reference to be determined by the master seized of the reference. The onus is on the defendants to establish that a claim for lien was not timely and that there are no genuine issues for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="King Carrier Ltd." p2="Trifield Construction Co." post.rptr="2447" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I64219b125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="King Carrier Ltd. v. Trifield Construction Co.">King Carrier Ltd. v. Trifield Construction Co. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 2447, 89 C.L.R. (3d) 237 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants obtained orders discharging the claims for lien and certificates of action registered by the plaintiffs where there was clear evidence that the plaintiffs inadvertently liened lands they did not supply services to.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="JDM Developments Inc." p2="J. Stollar Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3942" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I64219b135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd.">JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3942, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 198 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff builder alleged the existence of an oral agreement with the defendant developer which authorized the builder to erect houses on lots owned by the developer and defer the payment of purchase monies for each lot until construction was completed and each house was sold. The court vacated the liens registered by the builder against the lots in subsequent actions, and found that the builder had mischaracterized its claims as lien claims when they were grounded in a breach of the alleged oral agreement, and the dispute really concerned the sale of lots by the developer and the appropriate purchase price in respect of those lots.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="1246798 Ontario Inc." p2="Sterling" post.rptr="2962" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I90f5ec10f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="1246798 Ontario Inc. v. Sterling">1246798 Ontario Inc. v. Sterling (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 2962, 46 O.R. (3d) 72, [1999] O.J. 3513 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed (2000), 5 C.L.R. (3d) 146 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The onus is on the moving party under s. 47(1) to establish the invalidity of the lien, but not on a straight balance-of-probabilities. The court must be satisfied that a determination of the validity of the lien does not require a trial. A litigant will not be too quickly deprived of the right to prove a claim for lien at trial and the court will limit itself to deciding whether there is a genuine issue for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Meo & Assns." p2="Gottenu Developments Ltd." post.rptr="2582" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I6421c2215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd.">Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2582, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 159 (Ont. Master); reversed (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 4489, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 78 (Ont. Master); affirmed (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 737, 1 C.L.R. (3d) 74, 131 O.A.C. 394 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There can be only one lien for the same work even though two claims for lien may be registered. When a release of a lien is registered, the <ital>Act</ital> clearly stipulates that it is the lien that is released and not a piece of paper known as the claim for lien. In this case, two claims for lien were registered in respect of the same work, the second claim being registered because of a misspelling in the first. After the first lien expired, the plaintiff registered a release of the first lien, which had expired, intending to leave the second preserved and perfected lien intact. Notwithstanding that the plaintiff's intention was to vacate a claim for lien that had long since become a useless piece of paper, the effect of the registration of the release was to discharge the lien itself. The discharged lien was exactly the same lien that was preserved a second time as the subject of the second claim for lien. Accordingly, the court had no choice but to discharge the plaintiff's lien and certificate of action and dismiss the action. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Initially, the Master ruled that the registration of the release of an expired lien did not terminate the plaintiff's rights in respect of the work done during the period of time stated in the lien which was the subject of the second claim for lien. However, while preparing additional reasons for judgment in the matter, the Master developed doubts, and invited submissions from counsel as to whether he was entitled to reconsider the issue, given that his earlier reasons had not found their way into a formal order. He concluded that he did in fact have jurisdiction to do so and reversed himself, discharging the plaintiff's second, perfected lien. (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 78 (Master). This decision was appealed to the Divisional Court and the appeal was dismissed (2000), 1 C.L.R. (3d) 74 (Ont. Div. Ct.).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I6421c2225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Subsequent to the registration of his lien, a contractor realized that he had understated the amount owing, and instructed his solicitors to register a new lien and release the previous lien claim so as not to encumber unduly the title to the owner's property. The owner then successfully moved to discharge the contractor's lien, to vacate the registration of the lien and certificate of action, and to dismiss the contractor's lien action. The court held that the discharge of the contractor's first lien was irrevocable and terminated all of the contractor's lien rights in respect of the work done by the contractor during this period of time. The lien could not be revived. Accordingly, the lien asserted in the second claim for lien, being for the same work during the same period of time, albeit claiming a larger amount of money, could not, in law, be asserted. An acceptable alternative, <ital>inter alia</ital>, would have been to register a second lien for the correct full amount of the plaintiff's claim, again assuming it could be done in time, and then move, under s. 47(1)(b), on notice, for an order vacating the registration of the first lien, so as to avoid any liability under s. 35 of the Act for “exaggerated claims”.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 47(1.1.)2</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Atlantic Construction Group Inc." p2="2567616 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9152" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I6421e9305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlantic Construction Group Inc. v. 2567616 Ontario Inc.">Atlantic Construction Group Inc. v. 2567616 Ontario Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 9152, 2020 ONSC 3992, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 317 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On <ital>ex parte</ital> motions by the owner landlord for declarations that the liens of the plaintiff had expired, the master noted the onus placed on a party so moving on an <ital>ex parte</ital> basis as outlined in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Davis" p2="Under Construction Incorporated" post.rptr="7686" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I6421e9315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Davis v. Under Construction Incorporated">Davis v. Under Construction Incorporated, 2020 CarswellOnt 7686, 2020 ONSC 3466, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 102 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. The master then concluded that on the material before him, he was unable to make a finding with respect to the date of completion and could also not determine with certainty that the liens in question were perfected out of time. There was insufficient evidence on which to find that the contracts were completed or abandoned prior to the relevant date. The landlord had not met the evidentiary onus, and fairness dictated that contractor be afforded an opportunity to defend timeliness of its liens.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 47(1.1)3</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Con-Spec Constr. Inc." p2="Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp." post.rptr="20410" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I677528f03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Con-Spec Constr. Inc. v. Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp.">Con-Spec Constr. Inc. v. Marquee St. Clair West GP Corp., 2023 CarswellOnt 20410, 2023 ONSC 7229 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Sections 46(1) and 47(1)(d) of the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, when read together, provided the court with the discretion to either dismiss or permit a contract claim to continue without the lien claim. There was no dispute that the plaintiff's lien had expired or that the defendant was entitled to a declaration of expiry, vacating the registrations of the claim for lien and certificate of action, and dismissal of the action insofar as enforcement of the lien was concerned. The sole dispute was whether the plaintiff's joined contract claim was properly dismissed. There was nothing in the record to support that the defendant had taken any steps to move the action forward, and the court concluded that the defendant had previously intended to pursue its own counterclaim regardless of whether the plaintiff pursued its lien and contract claims. Absent any evidence from the defendant as to its own efforts to move the action forward, it was either complicit in the delay or at least complacent about it. That was a factor militating against dismissal, since the delay was not fairly viewed as being laid solely at the plaintiff's feet. The only prejudice cited by the defendant was additional time and expense, which was “prejudice” inherent in litigation. The contract claim was to be continued as an ordinary action governed by the Rules of Civil Procedure, with costs to the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1814219 Ont. Inc." p2="2332574 Ont. Ltd." post.rptr="21112" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I6421e9325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1814219 Ont. Inc. v. 2332574 Ont. Ltd.">1814219 Ont. Inc. v. 2332574 Ont. Ltd., 2019 CarswellOnt 21112, 2019 ONSC 7468 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff's business name registration inadvertently expired, it continued to conduct business under the same unregistered name, in contravention of s. 2(1) of the (Ont.) <ital>Business Names Act</ital> for a period of approximately three years. It was during this time period that the two construction contracts at issue were executed, consisting of an initial contract with one corporate defendant and a second contract with a related corporate defendant that replaced the first agreement. The defendants argued that they contracted with the plaintiff's principal in his personal capacity when both the initial contract and the replacement contract were executed and relied on the expired business name registration and on s. 2 of the <ital>Business Names Act</ital>. The defendants' motion under s. 47(1)(d) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (now s. 47(1.1)3 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>) was dismissed. The record contained contradictory evidence and provided support for both parties' positions on the issues in dispute. While it was sufficient for the judge to familiarize himself with the evidence of the parties, that was not the same as fully appreciating the evidence in a way that permitted a fair and just adjudication of the issues. As well, dismissal of the plaintiff's contractual claims would not dispose of its alternative claim for damages based on <ital>quantum meruit</ital>. The Ontario Court of Appeal, in the context of Rule 20.04 summary judgment motions, has repeatedly cautioned against granting partial summary judgment where there is a risk of inconsistent or duplicative findings at trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="21114 Ontario Inc." p2="Stadia Industries Ltd." post.rptr="3221" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I6421e9335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="21114 Ontario Inc. v. Stadia Industries Ltd.">21114 Ontario Inc. v. Stadia Industries Ltd., 2014 ONSC 3221, 2014 CarswellOnt 7129, 14 C.B.R. (6th) 1, 32 C.L.R. (4th) 77 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the court allows a contract claim to proceed after a lien claim is dismissed, the court may decide whether the Act's procedures apply. In such a case, the court could transfer the contract action to the Small Claims Court if the claim was under $25,000, or it could direct that it proceed as an ordinary Superior Court action and possibly be governed by the Rule 76 Simplified Procedure if the claim was between $25,000 and $100,000, or it could direct that it proceed as an ordinary action and be governed by the general Rules of Civil Procedure without any reference to the Simplified Procedure if the claim was in excess of $100,000. The court could even direct that the contract claim would continue within the framework of the statement of claim in the now-dismissed lien action, with judgment to be given pursuant to s. 63, and still to be governed by the procedure under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and, in particular, procedural ss. 51–63, 67, and 71.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1339408 Ontario Inc." p2="1579138 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9443" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I6421e9345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1339408 Ontario Inc. v. 1579138 Ontario Inc.">1339408 Ontario Inc. v. 1579138 Ontario Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 9443, 71 C.L.R. (3d) 13 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 518 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the court should exercise its discretion under s. 47(1) and allow the action to continue after the lien action has been dismissed on consent. The motions judge found the conduct of the plaintiff had been one of undue delay, without valid reason, and dismissed the action. The registration of the claim for lien and the certificate of action were vacated. The ruling was reversed on appeal. The motions judge did not refer to the fact that the defendants were more than five months late delivering the statement of defence, that examinations for discovery had been held, and that plaintiff would suffer enormous prejudice if entire action was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">If the two-year period for setting the action down for trial has expired, it follows that the two-year limitation period relating to an action in contract under the <ital>Limitations Act, 2002</ital> has also expired, thereby precluding any subsequently commenced action in contract. Where a moving party relies upon the principles established in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd." p2="Niran Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2335" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I90f63a30f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd.">Teepee Excavation & Grading Ltd. v. Niran Construction Ltd. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 2335, 189 D.L.R. (4th) 210, 49 O.R. (3d) 612, 4 C.L.R. (3d) 193, [2000] O.J. No. 2554 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> to dismiss a lien action under s. 46 for delay, the effect of which would be to effectively dispose of the plaintiff's claim forever, the case law developed under R. 24.01 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> is relevant and the action in contract will not be dismissed unless the delay is intentional or contumelious, or the plaintiff or its counsel are responsible for an inexcusable delay that gives rise to a substantial risk that a fair trial is not possible.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I642210415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In reviewing the file in preparation for the first construction lien pre-trial, the Master noted a number of procedural irregularities which were fatal to the lien claim. Although there was no formal written notice of motion served by the defendants, nor any supporting material, the Master exercised his discretion under s. 47(1)(d) and dismissed both the lien action and the personal contract action of the plaintiff. Subsection 67(6) of the Act provided that any motion may be made in the manner provided by the rules of court for the making of motions. Subsection 67(3) provided that except where inconsistent with the Act, the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, and the rules of court, applied to proceedings under the Act. Subsection 37(2) and s. 46(1), used the term “motion”. The facts to attract the operation of ss. 37 and 46 were all part of the court file and no further evidence was required. Rule 37.07(1) requires notice of a motion to be served on all affected parties. Pursuant to Ont. Rule 2.03, the Master, in the highly unusual circumstances of the case, dispensed with service of a formal written notice of motion on the plaintiff under ss. 46(1) and 47(1)(d).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="612354 Ontario Ltd." p2="Tonecraft Corp." post.rptr="799" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I90f63a31f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp.">612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp. (1991), 1991 CarswellOnt 799, 5 O.R. (3d) 764, 47 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In an action to enforce a claim for lien, the plaintiff failed to have the action set down within two years of its commencement. The defendant brought a motion pursuant to ss. 37 and 46(1) of the Act to have the action dismissed in its entirety. Documentary discovery and examination for discovery had been ordered and had taken place. The plaintiff sought leave to amend its statement of claim to include a claim for personal judgment for breach of contract. The expiry of a claim for lien prior to trial does not oust the jurisdiction of the court to hear an action for personal judgment. The mandatory provisions of s. 46(1) requiring the court to dismiss an action to enforce a claim for lien do not apply to dismissal of actions for personal judgment. Subsection 47(1)(d) applies to such actions and gives the court discretion. This conclusion is supported by s. 38, which keeps the expiry of a lien from affecting any other legal or equitable rights, and the general provisions of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, which are intended to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings and secure the just, most expeditious and least expensive determination of a proceeding on its merits. As discoveries had taken place, it could not be argued that the defendant had been deprived of the usual rights of trial. Considering all the circumstances, an order was to be issued vacating the lien and dismissing the action to enforce the lien. The motion to dismiss the action for personal judgment was dismissed, and the plaintiff was granted leave to amend its statement of claim to add specifically a claim for breach of contract so as to clarify the personal judgment claim.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
47:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 47.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">47:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 47(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Entablature Frieze & Pillars Inc." p2="Serio" post.rptr="716" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I642237515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Entablature Frieze & Pillars Inc. v. Serio">Entablature Frieze & Pillars Inc. v. Serio (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 716 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the length of the inaction was not great and the defendants did not suffer any discernable prejudice, the court exercised its discretion and allowed the balance of the plaintiff's claim and the defendants' counterclaim to continue under the Simplified Procedure Rules and proceed to trial.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
48:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 48.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">48:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Prior lien legislation did not address the irrevocable nature of the discharge of a lien. As stated by the Master in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I642237525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177, 11 O.R. (3d) 56 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the addition of s. 48 was to affirm the result arrived in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1966" p1="Reisman" p2="Laworand Properties Ltd." post.rptr="190" pre.rptr="10" ref.id="I642237535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reisman v. Laworand Properties Ltd.">Reisman v. Laworand Properties Ltd. (1966), 10 C.B.R. (N.S.) 190 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>, and to prevent the result arrived in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Esquire Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd." p2="Hoffman" post.rptr="184" pre.rptr="56" ref.id="I642237545fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Esquire Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Hoffman">Esquire Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Hoffman, 56 A.R. 184, [1984] 6 W.W.R. 730 (Alta. Master)</ref></cite>. The intention that a discharged lien cannot be revived is clear, both within the section and within the case law that the section is said to affirm. The Advisory Committee reported that this section is intended to provide that which is not possible under the prior legislation by taking into consideration that an individual may claim more than one lien with respect to an improvement. This section can be applied provided that each lien claim is with respect to different services or materials that have been supplied. The Advisory Committee thought that claims for lien should more accurately reflect the unpaid price of services or materials that have been supplied to the time of the claim.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Although the discharge of a lien is irrevocable, a claimant has the right to claim a lien for services or materials supplied after registration of the discharged lien. A person could, for example, preserve a new lien for each progress advance carefully discharging any prior lien on payment for those services.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The certification of the registration of the release is necessary before a lien can be said to have been “discharged” for the purposes of s. 48. Execution of the release alone is insufficient. Registration alone is insufficient. See the debate on this point by Harvey Kirsh, “Breathing Life into Lost Lien Rights” and Andrew Gurlesky, “Not Certified Dead”, both published in (2004) 5:68 <ital>Construction Law Update</ital> 1 and 3.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gay Company Limited" p2="962332 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="16471" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dd1aa40ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Gay Company Limited v. 962332 Ontario Inc.">Gay Company Limited v. 962332 Ontario Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 16471, 2023 ONSC 6023 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant's claim for lien was held not to be discharged when the defendant purported to “register” an application to delete the construction lien. In order to be effective, the registration of a claim for lien or application to delete a construction lien under the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital> requires that the instrument must be certified by the Land Registrar and not be withdrawn before it is certified. The <ital>Construction Act</ital>, by using the same word, “registration”, indicates the intention of the drafters to adopt the same meaning of registration under the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital>. Registration under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> therefore means that the instrument must be received, certified and not withdrawn before it is certified. Once an instrument is certified, then the registration is complete. Here, the defendant registered a claim for lien with an error in the claimant's name and sought to correct that error by registering a second claim for lien in the correct name, but in the process mistakenly and prematurely registered an Application to Delete the First Claim for Lien at the same time. The court rejected the plaintiff's argument that upon filing of the purported discharge of the first lien, the claimant's lien rights were irrevocably lost and could not be revived. Because neither the first lien nor the application to delete it had been certified, they were not “registered” within the meaning of either the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital> or the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. The valid second lien remained on title to preserve the claimant's lien rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9585800 Canada Inc." p2="JP Gravel Construction et al." post.rptr="3396" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64225e605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction et al.">9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction et al., 2019 ONSC 3396, 2019 CarswellOnt 8917, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 29 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversed 2019 CarswellOnt 19773, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 38 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor registered and then discharged a construction lien against the construction project, and then immediately registered a second construction lien after that discharge, for the same amount and using substantially the same information as contained in the first lien. The first lien was allegedly discharged due to an error in the time of delivery of services which listed the incorrect year, an error corrected in the second lien, and the plaintiff denied any intention of discharging its entitlement to a lien against the defendant contractor. The court found the first lien to be a nullity since it was a lien for non-existent work, and as a result, the second lien was appropriate and s. 48 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not apply.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ben Air Systems Inc." p2="Toronto Transit Commission et al." post.rptr="2375" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64225e615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ben Air Systems Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission et al.">Ben Air Systems Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission et al., 2018 ONSC 2375, 2018 CarswellOnt 5959, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 239 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 48 makes it clear that the discharge of a lien means that the claimant cannot lien again for the services performed and materials supplied before the date of the perfection of the first, discharged lien. A claimant can lien for the unpaid balance of the contract only if it stays on the job and intends to finish the job. By logical extension, where a party terminates the contract because he or she accepts the breach by the other party, the party may lien only for services and goods delivered to the time of the termination. In this case, there was no basis to conclude that a second lien was purely duplicative of the first lien, which had been discharged. The dollar values claimed were slightly different, and the second lien was valid on its face.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Khalimov" p2="Hogarth" post.rptr="6244" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642285705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khalimov v. Hogarth">Khalimov v. Hogarth, 2015 ONSC 6244, 2015 CarswellOnt 15551, 56 C.L.R. (4th) 167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master found that once the subcontractor discharged its first claim for lien it was irrevocably precluded by s. 48 from claiming a lien for services and materials supplied prior to the date it registered its first claim for lien, including a lien claim asserted as a charge against the owner's holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="JDM Developments Inc." p2="J. Stollar Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3942" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I642285715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd.">JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3942, 58 C.L.R. (3d) 198 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant failed to seek a stay of proceeding or request any form of injunctive relief restraining the registration of the orders. After the registration of the discharge, the lien claimant sought leave to appeal to set aside the orders. The court held that under s. 48 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and s. 78(4) of the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital>, once the lien was discharged and the orders were embodied in the register upon registration, there was no jurisdiction in any appellate court to revive the lien. The appeal was therefore held to be moot.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Mueller-Hein Corp." p2="Donar Investments Ltd." post.rptr="2223" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I642285725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Mueller-Hein Corp. v. Donar Investments Ltd.">Mueller-Hein Corp. v. Donar Investments Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 2223, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 143 (Ont.
