S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the order discharging a lien and vacating the registration of the lien and a Certificate of Action is improperly obtained, the discharge is not irrevocable under s. 48 of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Here, given material non-disclosure on an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion under s. 46(3), the order was set aside.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Carpenters Local 27 Benefit Trust Funds (Trustee of)" p2="Embee Properties Ltd." post.rptr="1647" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I642285735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carpenters Local 27 Benefit Trust Funds (Trustee of) v. Embee Properties Ltd.">Carpenters Local 27 Benefit Trust Funds (Trustee of) v. Embee Properties Ltd. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 1647, 2003 CarswellOnt 5535 (Master)</ref></cite>—The first lien registered on title was for work done from September 7th to September 20th, 2001, and was discharged. The second lien was for exactly the same amount of money as set out in the first lien, and was for the work done from August 23, 2001 to September 20, 2001. The court held that discharge of the first lien included the work done by the workers prior to September 7, 2001, and the second lien was not valid for the period August 23, 2001 to September 7, 2001. While s. 48 stated that “no discharge affects the right of the person whose lien was discharged to claim a lien in respect of services or materials supplied by the person subsequent to the preservation of the discharged lien,” this did not refer to liens that were prior to the preservation of the discharged lien. The decision of Master Sandler in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I642285745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, is followed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Northway Developments Inc." p2="1200946 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3082" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I642285755fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northway Developments Inc. v. 1200946 Ontario Inc.">Northway Developments Inc. v. 1200946 Ontario Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3082, 1998 CarswellOnt 3048 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A form entitled “Release of Lien” used language that referred only to vacation of the lien. Nevertheless the legal consequence was discharge in accordance with <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I6422ac805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Meo & Assns." p2="Gottenu Developments Ltd." post.rptr="2582" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I6422ac815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd.">Meo & Assns. v. Gottenu Developments Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2582, 28 C.L.R. (2d) 159 (Ont. Master); reversed (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 4489, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 78 (Ont. Master); affirmed (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 737, 1 C.L.R. (3d) 74, 131 O.A.C. 394 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Meo registered two liens for the same work, the first lien expired, the second lien was perfected, and then the first lien was released. The Defendants moved to discharge the second lien on the basis of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I6422ac825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>. In 1996 Master Clark held that the release of an expired lien had no further effect than to clear title. More than a year later supplementary reasons were released and the Master reconsidered and reversed his original decision discharging the second Meo lien. An appeal to the Divisional Court was dismissed holding that the intentions of the party releasing the lien are irrelevant, and affirming the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I6422d3905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="N.K.P. Painting" p2="Polygrand Developments Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I90f6d670f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="N.K.P. Painting v. Polygrand Developments Inc.">N.K.P. Painting v. Polygrand Developments Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 417, [1995] O.J. No. 1070, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 31 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff painting subcontractor agreed to discharge its lien in exchange for payment of the contract balance less the holdback amount, but subsequently claimed further tough up work and registered a second lien. Under s. 48, the discharge of the first lien was irrevocable and the discharged lien could not be revived. The second lien could only be valid if it related to work subsequent to the discharged first lien and no such work was shown to have been performed. The plaintiff was only entitled to claim the holdback amount.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Southridge Construction Group Inc." p2="667293 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="177" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I6422d3925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd.">Southridge Construction Group Inc. v. 667293 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 177 (Ont. Master); affirmed (1993), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 12 O.R. (3d) 223 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Subsequent to the registration of his lien, a contractor realized that he had understated the amount owing, and instructed his solicitors to register a new lien and release the previous lien claim so as not to encumber unduly the title to the owner's property. The owner then successfully moved to discharge the contractor's lien, to vacate the registration of the lien and certificate of action, and to dismiss the contractor's lien action. The court held, and the appeal court concurred, that the discharge of the contractor's first lien was irrevocable and terminated all of the contractor's lien rights in respect of the work done by the contractor during this period of time. There was no requirement that the claimant receive payment, as under the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> for s. 48 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, to apply. The lien could not be revived.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Southridge</ital> has since been applied in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="N.K.P. Painting" p2="Polygrand Developments Inc." post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I6422d3935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="N.K.P. Painting v. Polygrand Developments Inc.">N.K.P. Painting v. Polygrand Developments Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 417, [1995] O.J. No. 1070, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 31 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> referring also to <ital>Starevic v. Halton Hills Dev.</ital>, (Gen. Div.) (unreported), see Kirsh's Construction Lien Case Finder, pp. 48.1, 48.2, and also in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Four Valleys Excavating Grading Ltd." p2="Forsan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I6422d3945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Four Valleys Excavating Grading Ltd. v. Forsan Construction Ltd.">Four Valleys Excavating Grading Ltd. v. Forsan Construction Ltd. (1994), 21 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
49:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 49.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">49:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section came into existence with the 1966, c. 84, s. 1 amendment to then s. 25 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, c. 233, and was carried through into s. 29(7) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. There were no amendments or changes to this provision through to the 1980 Act. The 1980 Act referred to an “order or a certificate thereof, under the seal of the Court”. The 1983 amendments referred to a “certified copy of the order”. The contents of the order to be registered as set out in the 1980 legislation remained unchanged. The Advisory Committee did however recommend changing the requirement for registration of such an order from mandatory to discretionary. Under the previous legislation, it was mandatory that the order discharging or vacating be registered. The 1983 amendments changed this provision, allowing that such an order “may” be registered.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section sets out the requirements for the registration of court orders declaring a lien expired, discharging a lien or vacating a lien or certificate of action from title and the registration requirements thereof.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
50:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 50.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">50:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments and Legislative History</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 50(1) remains substantially unchanged.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 50(2) used to provide that a trust and a lien claim could not be joined. That provision was removed from the Act in its entirety and not replaced elsewhere. As to whether a plaintiff can now join any claim with a lien claim, see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="6628842 Canada Inc." p2="Topyurek" post.rptr="253" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6422faa05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek">6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek, 2022 ONSC 253, 2022 CarswellOnt 132 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> <trace date.trace="20250528">and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Devlan Construction Ltd." p2="SRK Woodworking Inc." post.rptr="7622" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I677661703b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc.">Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 7622, 2023 ONSC 3035, 167 O.R. (3d) 704, 29 C.L.R. (5th) 27 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace> under s. 3(2) of O. Reg. 302/18.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The new section 50(2) is the former s. 67(3).</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 50(3) used to provide for the joinder of any number of lien claimants in the same action. That provision was moved to section 3 of O. Reg. 302/18.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The new section 50(3) is the former section 67(1)</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The current wording of s. 50(1) did not appear in the initial <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27. A claim for lien was initially enforceable through the county of division courts if the amount was within those courts' jurisdictions. All other claims for lien were enforceable in the Court of Chancery. As the court structure changed, the provisions of the Act were amended accordingly. Today a claim for lien is enforceable in an action in the Superior Court of Justice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 50(2), the former s. 67(3), dates back to the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968-69</ital>, S.O. 1968-69, c. 65, which provided for the first time that the Rules of Practice applied to proceedings under the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 50(3), the former s. 67(1), was first introduced in substance by s. 47 of <ital>The Mechanics' and wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
50:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 50.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">50:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 50(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Refplus Inc." p2="2073427 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="8195" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I642321b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Refplus Inc. v. 2073427 Ontario Inc.">Refplus Inc. v. 2073427 Ontario Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 8195, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 121 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff brought a motion seeking an order transferring the action from Peterborough to Toronto on the basis that two of the parties had agreed to settle on terms that included the plaintiff bringing the transfer motion. The master found that the motion, on the material before him, amounted to an attempt by two parties to the action to transfer the action for their convenience without regard to the other named party or any other potential parties. An abstract of title together with an execution search against the owner would have identified if there were any other affected parties but no such searches were provided. The plaintiff did not satisfy its burden to demonstrate why the action should be transferred to Toronto having regard to the terms of the Act and Ont. Rule 13.1.02(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Glencoe Insulation Co." p2="3170497 Canada Inc." post.rptr="6310" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90f74ba0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc.">Glencoe Insulation Co. v. 3170497 Canada Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 6310, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 238, [2003] O.J. No. 5834 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved for an order discharging the claimant's lien, cancelling the bond posted, dismissing the lien action, and for costs on a substantial indemnity basis on the grounds, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that the lien clamant's charter was cancelled at the time the lien was preserved and perfected and not revived until the time limitations contained in ss. 31(2), 36(2) and 37(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had expired. The motions judge ordered the claimant's lien to be discharged on the grounds first, that the claimant's company charter was cancelled at the time its lien was preserved and perfected, and that the charter could not be retroactively revived to validate its claim for lien and, secondly, on the basis that the charter was revived after the time limits in the Act had expired. The Divisional Court reversed the lower court's holding that the Articles of Revival of October 1, 2002 did not effectively retroactively validate all actions taken by the claimant subsequent to its corporate dissolution, including the preservation and perfection of its claim of lien. The cancellation of a charter did not render a company non-existent, nor its acts absolute nullities, but rather a company was in a legal state of limbo capable of restoration by Articles of Revival which have effect for all purposes <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>, save for rights acquired by any person in the interim. The Divisional Court upheld the motions judge's ruling that the lapse of limitation period between the claimant's dissolution and its revival was an acquired legal right of the defendant upon which the latter was entitled to rely. The claimant had preserved and perfected its lien during the time that it was dissolved. For this reason, the claim was in abeyance, albeit one that could be retroactively revived by the application of s. 241(5) of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>. However, the statutory period for preserving and perfecting a construction lien expired before the company had been revived. As a matter of law, the claimant failed to preserve and perfect its lien within the statutory time period. It was at this point in time that the defendant acquired its right to rely upon the expiration of the limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Bauer" p2="Sadrieh" post.rptr="521" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I642348c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bauer v. Sadrieh">Bauer v. Sadrieh (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 521, 2003 CarswellOnt 510, 26 C.L.R. (3d) 310 (Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff had been in possession of a contractor's and renovator's licence which had expired. The court drew a distinction between a contract which was inherently illegal, as, for example a contract to commit a crime, and a contract which was illegal only in its performance. To uphold a plea of illegality, the defendant would have to prove that the plaintiff intended to enter into an illegal agreement, that the plaintiff lacked the requirements which would have been necessary to obtain a license and that the by-law which was apparently violated intended to interfere with contractual relations. In the circumstances, the court declined to hold the contract illegal. See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Morrell" p2="Cserzy" post.rptr="94" pre.rptr="14" ref.id="I642348c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Morrell v. Cserzy">Morrell v. Cserzy (2002), 14 C.L.R. (3d) 94, 2002 CarswellOnt 658 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Agasi" p2="Wai" post.rptr="101" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I642348c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Agasi v. Wai">Agasi v. Wai (2000), 4 C.L.R. (3d) 101 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, to the same effect.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Vinpat Construction Ltd." p2="Henze Holdings Inc." post.rptr="2274" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I642348c35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Vinpat Construction Ltd. v. Henze Holdings Inc.">Vinpat Construction Ltd. v. Henze Holdings Inc. (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 2274, 18 C.L.R. (3d) 307 (Master)</ref></cite>—Held, in the case of a pre-incorporation contract that the corporate plaintiff had no status to maintain the lien action; thus the lien action and counterclaim had to be dismissed, and the lien discharged (citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Sherwood Design Services Inc." p2="872935 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="576" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I642348c45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sherwood Design Services Inc. v. 872935 Ontario Ltd.">Sherwood Design Services Inc. v. 872935 Ontario Ltd. (1998), 39 O.R. (3d) 576 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Netmar Inc." p2="Aquilina" post.rptr="133" pre.rptr="93" ref.id="I642348c55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Netmar Inc. v. Aquilina">Netmar Inc. v. Aquilina (1999), 93 O.T.C. 133 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, s. 21(2) <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. B.16).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="688558 Ontario Ltd." p2="Morgan" post.rptr="463" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I642348c65fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="688558 Ontario Ltd. v. Morgan">688558 Ontario Ltd. v. Morgan (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 463, 21 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The construction lien action of plaintiff interior design company was dismissed where the plaintiff was carrying on business as a building renovator without a licence contrary by-law. The prohibition in the by-law was against doing “building renovations”, which would include both work and material, and the contract was illegal and therefore unenforceable.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
50:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 50.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">50:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 50(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Praxy Cladding Corp." p2="Stone Lamina Inc." post.rptr="1209" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6776af903b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Praxy Cladding Corp. v. Stone Lamina Inc.">Praxy Cladding Corp. v. Stone Lamina Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 1209, 2024 ONSC 727 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 50(2) provides that the rules of court apply in lien actions, except to the extent that they are inconsistent with the Act. Discovery rules in the Rules of Civil Procedure thereby applied to the parties' examinations for discovery. Where leave is granted for discoveries, as in this case, both the parties and the court must take seriously the summary nature of lien proceedings. Proportionality is not assessed in a vacuum, though. Only the party being asked to provide the answer can reasonably explain why a request is unreasonable because of logistical difficulties in accessing the information, its overall volume, or other reasons. It is incumbent on the objecting party to put their concerns and the reasons for them before the court.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Insite Construction Management Inc." p2="Ambient Mechanical Ltd." post.rptr="457" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6776af913b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Insite Construction Management Inc. v. Ambient Mechanical Ltd.">Insite Construction Management Inc. v. Ambient Mechanical Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 518, 2024 ONSC 457 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The documentary discovery rules in the Rules of Civil Procedure must be read purposively with regard to the scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, in that procedure in lien actions should be, as far as possible, of a summary character, having regard to the amount and nature of the liens in question. Relevance for discovery purposes is grounded in the pleadings, not an expert's opinion, and here, project costing was not raised in the current pleadings. Baldly pleading <ital>quantum meruit</ital> and unjust enrichment in a lien action does not itself open the door to full production of project costing. There must be some additional particularization that makes costing relevant to assessing the value of services and materials on a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> basis. A vague reference to the prime contract was not enough.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Alfa Mechanical Inc." p2="Chang" post.rptr="19916" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dd2bbb0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Alfa Mechanical Inc. v. Chang">Alfa Mechanical Inc. v. Chang, 2023 CarswellOnt 19916, 2023 ONSC 7167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's motion for default judgment, which was brought on notice to the defendants, resulted a consent order setting aside the defendants' noting in default and allowing the defendants to deliver a defence. The plaintiff's motion had sought a declaration of entitlement to a lien against the defendants' interest in their property, as well as personal judgment for the same amount. In obiter comments delivered on a ruling as to costs, the court suggested without deciding that default judgment may be available to validate a lien under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. The Associate Judge noted that the legislation did not indicate that default judgment was available only on a joined contract claim. As well, requiring a trial to prove a lien in all cases, including where the defendant has been noted in default, would seem contrary to the requirement in s. 50(3), that procedures be of a summary character. While there is no procedure outlined in the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, there were established procedures for default judgment set out in the Rules of Court. Whether an associate judge had jurisdiction to validate a lien by way of a motion for default judgment remained an open question.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Praxy Cladding Corp." p2="Stone Lamina Inc." post.rptr="14517" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dd2bbb1ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Praxy Cladding Corp. v. Stone Lamina Inc.">Praxy Cladding Corp. v. Stone Lamina Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 14517, 2023 ONSC 5288 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is no prescribed process for amending a pleading in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> and regulations. Ont. r. 26.01 provides that leave to amend shall be granted unless the responding party would suffer non-compensable prejudice, but that is a step in a lien action requiring leave of the court. Here, leave was granted for the motion to amend to be brought, where the plaintiff was alleged to have made a binding admission on what comprised the contract documents. Whether or not the plaintiff is able to rely on the quotation would impact remaining steps and the ultimate trial. It was both necessary and would expedite resolution of issues in dispute to have the disputed issue addressed at this stage of the proceeding.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Leblon Carpentry Inc." p2="QH Renovation & Construction Corp." post.rptr="8011" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dd2bbb2ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Leblon Carpentry Inc. v. QH Renovation & Construction Corp.">Leblon Carpentry Inc. v. QH Renovation & Construction Corp., 2023 CarswellOnt 8011, 2023 ONSC 3182 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was denied an order granting it leave to extend an ordered deadline to provide answers to undertakings from its examination for discovery. Lien actions are statutorily prescribed to be as far as possible of a summary character, and the plaintiff gave only a modest number of straightforward undertakings when examined. It failed to provide a proper explanation for its inability to meet the court-ordered deadline for answering those undertakings, and the record did not support that it made honest and meaningful efforts to provide responsive answers in a timely fashion, particularly given the specific undertakings. Parties that do not take their litigation obligations seriously cannot expect the court to excuse breaches of court orders, including timetable orders, particularly in the context of summary lien proceedings. The plaintiff was not entitled to rely at trial on any information or evidence not given or produced prior to the ordered deadline.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Adapt. The plaintiff's motion seeking a Certificate of Pending Litigation against the property failed.<trace.deleted date.trace="20250528"/></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jackman Construction Limited" p2="Brown et al." post.rptr="6562" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I8dd2e2c2ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Jackman Construction Limited v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The defendants moved for partial summary judgment seeking a determination on whether the (ON) <ital>Consumer Protection Act, 2002</ital> applied to their residential construction contract, and if so, an order requiring the plaintiff to pay damages under that Act equal to the amounts paid in excess of the listed amounts for various items in Schedule B to the construction contract. Nothing in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> expressly excludes the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital> from applying to the supply of services and materials that give rise to lien and other rights under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There was also no proper basis to hold, as a general proposition, that the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital> cannot and does not apply to costs-plus contracts concerning residential construction and renovation of premises. In this case, the plaintiff was constructing a custom residential house for use by the defendants' family, and not for any commercial or industrial purpose. The plaintiff's operations and supply of services fit within the definition of “supplier” in the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital>. The construction contract was an agreement between the parties in which the plaintiff agreed to supply services and materials for the construction work at the premises for payment. The parties' contract was accordingly a “consumer agreement” within the meaning of the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital>. There were, however, triable issues on whether the Schedule B items were “estimates” within the meaning of the <ital>Consumer Protection Act</ital> and, if so, whether changes to the scope of work were agreed, expressly or impliedly.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Reid" p2="Xiao" post.rptr="4524" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I64236fd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Reid v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—In an action to which the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applied, the plaintiff moved before an associate judge to, <ital>inter alia</ital>, strike the statement of defence, note the defendants in default, and obtain judgment on its breach of trust claim against them under (ON) rule 19.05. However, that rule expressly required a motion to a judge, and an associate judge had no jurisdiction to grant default judgment under it outside a lien reference. An associate judge's jurisdiction to grant default judgment under the Rules was found in r. 19.04(3.1)(b), which only permits a motion for default judgment to be brought to “the court” if it concerns one of the claims outlined in subrule 19.04(1).The plaintiff's breach of trust claim, as pleaded, did not fall within the types of claims outlined in subrule 19.04(1), and therefore default judgment on it could not be made. While it might seem inconsistent for an associate judge to be precluded from granting default judgment for an unliquidated sum, yet still be entitled to grant summary judgment on the same record, R. 20 permitted summary judgment motions to be brought before an associate judge and contained no similar restriction to that found in r. 19.04(3.1)(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="4241258 Canada Inc." p2="Diamond Jubilee Hospitality Inc. et al." post.rptr="567" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I642396e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="4241258 Canada Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, to conclude that, in the construction context, the limitation period on an invoice, issued for the supply of goods and services in accordance with a contract commences after a “reasonable” period of time has passed for the invoice to be issued and a “reasonable” period of time has passed for the invoice to be paid. There was only one construction lien action arising from the construction, brought by a subcontractor, and because that lien had been bonded off, the provisions of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> as to how and when the holdback monies were to be paid out, to protect subcontractors, appeared to no longer apply. Rather, the holdback monies became monies that would otherwise be payable to the plaintiff under the contract between the plaintiff contractor and the defendant owner municipality. The application was held to be duplicative of the contractor's main action, and was dismissed as an abuse of process under rule 25.11(c).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bernach" p2="Makepeace" post.rptr="1289" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I642433215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bernach v. R. 24.01(1)(c) permits a defendant to seek dismissal for delay by reason of a plaintiff failing to set an action down for trial within six months after the close of pleadings. However, that Rule is inconsistent with the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and inapplicable in lien actions, as set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Smith" p2="Hudson's Bay Company" post.rptr="2348" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64245a305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Smith v. There are no prescribed procedural deadlines in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for lien actions after close of pleadings until the two-year requirement in s. 37. Documentary and oral discovery are interlocutory steps not expressly contemplated by the Act, which require leave pursuant to s. 67(2). The discharge of a lien and dismissal of a lien action for delay within two years of perfection with pleadings closed is not supported by case law. Delay in setting the action down for trial, when the time to comply with s. 37 has not yet expired, does not warrant discharge of the lien and dismissal of the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Earth Boring Company Limited" p2="Groupe CRH Canada Inc." post.rptr="18471" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64245a315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Earth Boring Company Limited v. Given the potential for inconsistent findings, and the fact that the City of Mississauga was also a party, by way of the third-party proceeding, there would likely be greater convenience to the parties, witnesses, and the court that the action be heard where the project and work was performed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Van Geel" p2="Pennha" post.rptr="16833" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64245a325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Van Geel v. Subsection 67(3) provides that, except where inconsistent with the Act and subject to s. 67(2), the Rules of Court apply to pleadings and proceedings under this Act. Section 37 provides for the expiry of a perfected lien and for a motion under s. 46 to order that the lien has expired, that the action is dismissed and that the lien and certificate of action are vacated. In a prior proceeding the defendant was ordered to answer specified refusals within 60 days. On motion to strike the statement of defence, the court held that the defendants' conduct undermined the purpose of the Rules and the Act and caused unnecessary delay and unnecessary costs. Rather than striking the defendants' pleading and precluding them from presenting a defence, the court ordered the defendants to post security in the same fashion as required to vacate a lien. The purpose of the security was to ensure there were assets available to pay the claim and to pay future unnecessary costs the plaintiff might incur.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Yellow Brick Masonry" p2="Lima" post.rptr="3245" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I64262ef25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yellow Brick Masonry v. Lima">Yellow Brick Masonry v. Lima (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3245, 57 C.L.R. (3d) 155 (Ont. Div. Ct); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 3189 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—On appeal, the defendant's motion to set aside a default judgment was granted. The defendant was being sued as an officer or director of the non-party corporations under ss. 8(1), (2) and 13 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The plaintiff was dissolved in 1994. When the statement of claim was issued and served in November 1995, the plaintiff corporation was not a legal entity. Accordingly, the statement of claim was a nullity and not capable of creating any obligation on the part of the defendant. It was immaterial that the defendant did not know of the plaintiff's lack of capacity to sue him at the time. Revival of the corporation later, after judgment was signed may have breathed new life into the statement of claim by virtue of s. 241(5) of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital>, but the unilateral act of the plaintiff in re-creating itself should not, by itself, create an obligation on the part of the defendant of which he was unaware. Section 241(5) specifically preserves rights of other parties which arise during the dormancy of the corporation and should not be defeated by the signing of default judgment, particularly when that judgment was defective at the time. It may be that in this case, involving a trust claim under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, there was no applicable <ital>Limitations Act</ital> defence. However, the <ital>Limitations Act</ital> was not the only reason a defendant should have an opportunity to have the rights or obligations of the parties determined on the merits.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="1508270 Ontario Ltd." p2="Laudervest Developments Ltd." post.rptr="5066" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I642656005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1508270 Ontario Ltd. v. Laudervest Developments Ltd.">1508270 Ontario Ltd. v. Laudervest Developments Ltd. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5066, 59 C.L.R. (3d) 120 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> contains no provision expressly dealing with an abandoned motion. Subsection 67(3) provides that except where inconsistent with the Act and subject to the s. 67(2) limitation on interlocutory steps, the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> and <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> apply to pleadings and proceedings under the Act. Ont. R. 37.09 deals with abandoned motions, and applies to a motion pursuant to s. 44(5)(a) abandoned by a party.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Rafat General Contractor Inc." p2="1015734 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="7519" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90fa58e0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd.">Rafat General Contractor Inc. v. 1015734 Ontario Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 7519, 81 O.R. (3d) 798, 52 C.L.R. (3d) 63, [2005] O.T.C. 1107, [2005] O.J. No. 5526 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor did not register a claim for lien but instead brought an action for payment of its invoice. It then moved to register a certificate of pending litigation against the lands of the owner, which were the same lands against which it could have registered a claim for lien. The motion was dismissed. To obtain a Certificate of Pending Litigation, a party must have a reasonable claim to an interest in land pursuant to s. 103 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides a comprehensive code as to how liens are to be preserved, and by supplying labour and material, a lien arose in favour of the contractor pursuant to the Act. Having failed to preserve its lien in the subject property created by the Act, the plaintiff could not then look to the trust provisions in the Act to later assert an interest in the same land.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="John Bianchi Grading Ltd." p2="Eastern Construction Co." post.rptr="111" pre.rptr="51" ref.id="I642656025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="John Bianchi Grading Ltd. v. Eastern Construction Co.">John Bianchi Grading Ltd. v. Eastern Construction Co. (2005), 51 C.L.R. (3d) 111, 2005 CarswellOnt 5276 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In the context of a s. 47 motion, the master was entitled to engage s. 67 in order to make a summary determination with respect to compliance with s. 34(1)(b) and (3).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Heyday Homes Ltd." p2="Gunraj" post.rptr="3061" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I90fa58e1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunraj">Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunraj (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3061, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 169, [2005] O.J. No. 2986 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 429, 2004 CarswellOnt 254, 31 C.L.R. (3d) 66 (Master)</ref></cite>. The case law about the standard of review under Rule 54.09 of a Master's decision on a reference is consistent with the recent case law that highlights the scope of appellate review of a trial judgment. That case law establishes that trial judgments should be upheld by appellate courts unless there is a “palpable and overriding error”: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Housen" p2="Nikolaisen" post.rptr="178" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I90fa58e2f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Housen v. Nikolaisen">Housen v. Nikolaisen (2002), 2002 CarswellSask 178, 2002 CarswellSask 179, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Waxman" p2="Waxman" post.rptr="165" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I642656055fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Waxman v. Waxman">Waxman v. Waxman (2004), 44 B.L.R. (3d) 165, 2004 CarswellOnt 1715 (C.A.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3955 (C.A.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4941 (C.A.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3956 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1217, 2005 CarswellOnt 1218 (S.C.C.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 6554 (C.A.)</ref></cite>. A “palpable error” is one that is obvious, plain to see or clear. An “overriding error” of fact is an error that is sufficiently significant to vitiate the challenged finding of fact. The appellant must demonstrate that the error goes to the root of the challenged finding of fact such that the fact cannot safely stand in the face of that error: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Waxman" p2="Waxman" post.rptr="165" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I64267d105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Waxman v. Waxman">Waxman v. Waxman (2004), 44 B.L.R. (3d) 165, 2004 CarswellOnt 1715 (C.A.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3955 (C.A.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4941 (C.A.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3956 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1217, 2005 CarswellOnt 1218 (S.C.C.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 6554 (C.A.) 297</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Firenze Exteriors Inc." p2="Westwing Construction Group Inc." post.rptr="934" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I64267d115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Firenze Exteriors Inc. v. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractors provided construction materials and services to the defendant general contractor and claimed breach of trust against both it and its principals. The plaintiffs sought an accounting and a tracing order, and obtained an interim certificate of pending litigation against the principals' residence. On a preliminary motion with respect to burden of proof, the court ruled that the defendant was required to establish the essential elements necessary to remove the certificate. In the absence of evidence as to the source of funds the court was entitled to draw an adverse inference.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="1379691 Ontario Ltd." p2="Appugliesi" post.rptr="3799" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I64267d125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1379691 Ontario Ltd. v. Appugliesi">1379691 Ontario Ltd. v. Appugliesi (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3799, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 62 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sub-subcontractor unsuccessfully sought an order requiring the defendant school board and defendant contractor to pay into court separate sums equal to or in excess of its principal claim, interest and costs, pending the outcome of the action. The funds sought to be paid by the board formed part of the holdback from the contract price to be paid to a second defendant contractor. The funds sought from the defendant contractor were being held in its solicitor's trust account. As there was a real risk of removal of the solicitor's funds that would serve to deprive the plaintiff of any meaningful remedy if its claims were upheld at trial, preservation of those funds by maintaining them intact in the trust account pending resolution of the matter was an appropriate disposition of that part of the plaintiff's motion. Although it could be argued that the board's holdback funds, which were well in excess of the plaintiff's claim, were subject to trust obligations imposed by s. 7 and s. 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, there was no evidence that there was any danger that either defendant contractor planned to remove from the jurisdiction those funds if and when received from the board, or to otherwise thwart the plaintiff's efforts to obtain a remedy. The plaintiff did not, at any time, file or deliver either a notice of lien or lien to pursue its claims in that way.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Rock Construction & Management Ltd." p2="Ganatra Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="1137" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I64267d135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rock Construction & Management Ltd. v. Ganatra Holdings Ltd.">Rock Construction & Management Ltd. v. Ganatra Holdings Ltd. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1137, 2004 CarswellOnt 1095 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Rules 25.06(8) and 25.07(4) of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> require a party to plead fraud, misrepresentation, breach of trust, malice or intent. Collusion was not pleaded here and arose for the first time at trial, when the appellant argued that the payment certificates issued by the defendant's architect were tainted and inflated as a result of collusion. The parties were bound by the certificates, even if they had errors, unless there was conduct on the part of the owner or the payment certifier that would make it inequitable to rely on the certificates. An adverse inference was drawn against the defendant due to the fact that its architect was not called as a witness.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Alex Repairs & Construction Ltd." p2="Loureiro" post.rptr="2898" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I6426a4205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alex Repairs & Construction Ltd. v. (3d) 160 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor registered and perfected its lien, and then issued a statement of claim against the owners. A judgment on consent of the parties referred the action to the Master for trial, and at the first pre-trial the Master directed the plaintiff to provide details of the value of the work performed and ordered the parties to exchange documents. By the date of the second pre-trial, the plaintiff had not provided the details of the value of its work nor had it exchanged documents with the defendants. The defendants provided their documents just before entering the courtroom at the pre-trial, and the Master found that the plaintiff had failed to provide the defendants with details of the work and documents and failed to prove a valid lien. He discharged the lien, dismissed the action and ordered that the monies paid into court by the defendants be paid out to them. He also ordered that the plaintiff pay costs. The plaintiff moved under Ont. R. 54.09(5) for an order opposing confirmation of a report on a reference. In dismissing the motion and confirming the report of the Master, the appeal judge was not satisfied that there was an error in principle or an absence of jurisdiction such that he should interfere with the Master's decision. It was not for the appeal court to substitute its exercise of discretion for that of the Master.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Base Controls Ltd." p2="Bennett + Wright Group Inc." post.rptr="432" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I6426a4215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Base Controls Ltd. v. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Master dismissed the plaintiff lien claimant's motion to amend its statement of claim to assert a fiduciary claim against the owner in tort. The general contractor was in bankruptcy and the total owed to the lien claimants greatly exceeded the amount held by the owner. The Registrar dismissed the plaintiff's appeal for delay while the parties were attempting to settle the form of the Master's order. The Divisional Court granted the plaintiff's further motion to extend the time for perfecting its appeal. The court rejected the respondent's unique argument that it would be prejudiced by the extension because the longer the appeal was outstanding and the monies held under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> kept from the parties, the more likely it was that the Canada Customs and Revenue Agency would exercise its so-called “super priority” to seize the monies owing by the bankrupt. This was a somewhat speculative kind of prejudice that ought not to deter the court from exercising a discretion to set aside the order of the Registrar and to permit the appellant to proceed with its appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="McKee" p2="Thistlethwaite" post.rptr="264" pre.rptr="29" ref.id="I6426a4225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="McKee v. Thistlethwaite">McKee v. Thistlethwaite (2003), 29 C.L.R. (3d) 264, 2003 CarswellOnt 2681 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor commenced a construction lien action and contract claim against the owners, who, in addition to a counterclaim, launched a separate action against nine defendants, including the claimant. The owners alleged, <ital>inter alia</ital>, negligent misrepresentation and conspiracy on the part of the claimant. The owners unsuccessfully moved that the construction lien action and their second action be tried together. It was clear from the statement of defence and counterclaim in the lien action that the owners were pointing to issues involving deficient repair work, failure to carry out proper repairs, deliberate misleading or misrepresentation with respect to the repair work necessary to rectify the condition of the structure in question. Those issues, as between the claimant and owners, were to proceed to trial, at the conclusion of which the trial judge would deal with the contract claim made by the plaintiff as well as the defences and the counterclaim raised by the owners. While the main conspiracy claim as against the remaining defendants was to proceed through the civil justice system in as timely a basis as possible, the lien action should dispose of all issues as between the claimant and owners. The claimant ought not to be forced to wait to have his day in court, particularly when most of the issues involving the three parties, in both actions, were quite similar.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="1067833 Ontario Ltd." p2="1274123 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="325" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I6426a4235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1067833 Ontario Ltd. v. 1274123 Ontario Ltd.">1067833 Ontario Ltd. v. 1274123 Ontario Ltd. (2001), 31 C.L.R. (3d) 325, 2001 CarswellOnt 5901 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The word “action” is defined to mean an action under Part VIII, which restricts its meaning to lien claims. Rule 76.01(1) is intended to prevent claims which are enforceable under Part VIII from being brought under the simplified procedure. Here, the defendant was permitted to amend the defence and file a counterclaim, which could be brought under the simplified procedures, because the counterclaim was not an action within the meaning of the R. 76.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Bangs" p2="Angle" post.rptr="5092" pre.rptr="[2002]" ref.id="I6426cb305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bangs v. No. 5092, 2002 CarswellOnt 4486 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A credibility issue was raised between the plaintiff and the defendants as to whether the defendants ordered a latch lock and whether the installation by the plaintiff was done in good faith. The defendants' motion for summary judgment was granted and the construction lien filed on the defendants' property was removed. There was not a genuine issue to proceed to trial, as the issue of credibility did not amount to a genuine issue of credibility within the meaning of R. 20.04(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co." p2="Caravaggio" post.rptr="178" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I6426cb315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Con Concrete Finishing Co. v. (3d) 178, 2002 CarswellOnt 2379 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Rules are procedural and do not abolish the discretion the court has to permit a plaintiff to utilize the discovery transcript of one defendant as against another defendant. The circumstances here were such that to permit an individual defendant to restrict his examination on discovery to himself personally under circumstances where he, along with the other defendants, has engaged in conduct that has deprived the plaintiff of the documentary evidence necessary to implicate the other defendants, would be a gross travesty of justice. (3d) 182 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The owner applied for an order appointing a project mediator pursuant to the construction management agreement and for an order under the <ital>Arbitration Act</ital> (Ont.) staying the lien action commenced by the contractor. In granting the application, the court held that the relevant provision of the agreement constituted an arbitration agreement within the meaning of that expression in the <ital>Arbitration Act</ital>. It was not an abuse of process to initiate a separate proceeding to stay the construction lien action. It would be improper to require both a motion for a stay brought within the construction lien action and a second application for the order appointing the project mediator. Rule 2.02 was not applicable in the circumstances. At issue was a substantive dispute over whether or not the dispute resolution process in the contract should take precedence over the construction lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Newstruc Ltd." p2="Sherway Automotive Corp." post.rptr="21" pre.rptr="27" ref.id="I6426f2415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Newstruc Ltd. v.
