Wilkinson">2259964 Ontario Inc. v. Wilkinson, 2021 ONSC 4006, 2021 CarswellOnt 7962 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The calculation of delay in an action is measured from the commencement of the action to the motion to dismiss. In this case, that was a span of over nine years, and in over seven of those years, the claimant did nothing to advance the action. The lien here was modest in size and the proceeding was not complicated. The delay was inordinate and inexcusable and prejudiced the defendants' ability to defend the action. The action was dismissed for delay, and the claim for lien and certificate of action discharged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Schindler Elevator Corporation" p2="Walsh Construction Company of Canada" post.rptr="20714" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I642719505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schindler Elevator Corporation v. Walsh Construction Company of Canada">Schindler Elevator Corporation v. Walsh Construction Company of Canada, 2019 CarswellOnt 20714, 2019 ONSC 7392 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 279, 2020 ONSC 252, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 120 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Settlement privilege is subject to being overridden “when the justice of the case requires it”. Here, the plaintiff's motion for disclosure of fully unredacted minutes of settlement between the defendants and another lien claimant was brought within a consolidated reference which subsumed three proceedings, including a third party claim against the plaintiff by the defendants arising out of yet another settled lien claim. It was a term of that latter settlement that the claimant there would cooperate with the defendants and share in their recovery against the plaintiff above a certain amount. While alleging concurrent delays caused by the plaintiff and the other claimants, following the above settlements the defendants were proceeding to trial only against the plaintiff. The plaintiff argued that concerns of procedural fairness, over-compensation and double recovery were engaged, and sought access to the unredacted settlement minutes. It was held that, although the specific settlement amounts should remain protected by privilege the plaintiff was entitled to review and assess other redacted information in order to properly prepare for trial, including the opportunity before trial to consider its position on how allocation of settlement amounts might impact a potential damages award in favour of the defendants against the plaintiff. It was both inefficient and contrary to subsection 67(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (now s. 50(3) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>) to disclose the complete minutes of settlement and entertain submissions from the plaintiff only <ital>after</ital> liability had been determined in circumstances where there would be no bifurcation of liability and damages at trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Concord Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Canadian Tire Real Estate Limited" post.rptr="6361" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642719515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Concord Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Canadian Tire Real Estate Limited">Concord Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Canadian Tire Real Estate Limited, 2018 ONSC 6361, 2018 CarswellOnt 17840, 94 C.L.R. (4th) 178 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sought partial summary judgment against the defendant contractor within a construction lien action that included a lien claim against the defendant owner's interest in the property on which a retail store was being built. The latter lien claim was an alternative claim to provide security against the property in the event that the plaintiff could not collect from the defendant contractor. In the main action, the owner advanced claims for deficiencies relating to work completed by the plaintiff, and the court acknowledged that the plaintiff's claim was impacted by a larger disagreement between the contractor and owner that went beyond the scope of its work. Because of that, it was clear that the issues involved in the litigation were complex and intertwined, and that the litigation would involve determinations relating to the certain deficiencies alleged by the owner against the plaintiff, and there was a clear risk of inconsistent and contradictory findings. This risk was sufficient to foreclose the suitability of partial summary judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dean's Standard Inc." p2="Siljub Toronto Ltd." post.rptr="5254" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I642740605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dean's Standard Inc. v. Siljub Toronto Ltd.">Dean's Standard Inc. v. Siljub Toronto Ltd., 2016 ONSC 5254, 2016 CarswellOnt 13317, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 285 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff met with two individuals (“the pending owners”) who identified themselves as the pending owners of a hotel premises owned by the defendant, and entered into a contract under which plaintiff would supply services and materials to renovate a sample hotel room as a mock up for anticipated renovations of more rooms. The sale of the hotel did not proceed. The plaintiff did not name either pending owner in its subsequent lien claim against the defendant. The requirement in s. 67 to resolve construction lien claims expeditiously overrides the broad discretion in Ont. R. 26 to grant leave to amend pleadings in almost every case. Here, leave to amend the statement of claim to add a claim for unjust enrichment after having adduced all trial evidence was denied. Such an amendment would have changed nature of the case considerably, and would have been prejudicial to the defendant in a way that could not have been overcome by costs or an adjournment of the trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Southwestern Sales Corp." p2="Spurr Bros. Ltd." post.rptr="590" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I642740615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Southwestern Sales Corp. v. Spurr Bros. Ltd.">Southwestern Sales Corp. v. Spurr Bros. Ltd., 2016 ONCA 590, 2016 CarswellOnt 11687, 55 C.L.R. (4th) 23 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—After the appellant commenced six lien actions and filed its trial record, it commenced a breach of trust action. Periods of activity were followed by long periods of inactivity, and the trial was set for September 2009, but did not proceed. In 2012, the actions were struck from the trial list, and the actions were dismissed at a status hearing. Counsel for the appellant had surrendered his licence about two months before the status hearing. In upholding the dismissal, the Court of Appeal agreed with the master that if a lien claimant wants to take advantage of the provisions of Act, and tie up title to a defendant's property, it ought to proceed expeditiously to have its claim determined. Similarly, if a lien claimant wants to take advantage of the Act's trust provisions, it ought to be prepared to proceed expeditiously to have its claim determined. A lien claimant ought not to be entitled to sit back and allow years to pass while the defendant's property or money is held hostage. As part of its obligation to move its construction lien actions along, the appellant was required to take reasonable steps to supervise its counsel's work to ensure there would be an expeditious determination of the actions on their merits. On a motion to set aside a dismissal order, one would expect a commercial plaintiff like the appellant to file concrete evidence describing the steps it had taken to supervise its counsel's handling of its actions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Total Meter Services Inc." p2="Aplus General Contractors Corp." post.rptr="3830" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642740625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Total Meter Services Inc. v. Aplus General Contractors Corp.">Total Meter Services Inc. v. Aplus General Contractors Corp., 2015 ONSC 3830, 2015 CarswellOnt 9059, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 290 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 10651, 50 C.L.R. (4th) 303 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was granted leave, pursuant to s. 67(2), to bring a motion for partial summary judgment. Summary judgment is by definition, a step that is “of a summary character”, and is entirely in keeping with s. 67(1). In the result, the court awarded the plaintiff partial judgment and ordered trial of an issue with respect to certain of its claims against the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="485" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I642740635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2013 ONSC 485, 2013 CarswellOnt 549, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 13 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 4792, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 87 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2015 CarswellOnt 2329, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Construction lien references are subject to a form of case management through the hearing for directions process pursuant to Ont. Rule 55 and section 67 of the Act. The purpose is to narrow the issues and limit the scope of the reference trial. Rule 55 provides that a referee may dispense with any procedure ordinarily taken that the referee considers unnecessary, or adopt a procedure different from that ordinarily taken. As a matter of pre-trial practice for references in Toronto, the parties attend “pre-trial hearings for directions” in which the reference master gives directions for the conduct of the reference prior to conducting the evidentiary portion of the reference trial. Usually in a simple reference one or two pretrial hearings for directions are convened. (In this case, twelve such hearings were required.). The master here directed the parties to call evidence in chief by affidavit where witnesses were co-operative and imposed time restrictions on <ital>viva voce</ital> evidence of all witnesses. Procedural orders that incorporated procedures similar to Rule 76 summary trial procedures were issued.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5144" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I642767705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2011 ONSC 5144, 2011 CarswellOnt 8835 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff registered construction liens and issued lien claims against ten properties for amounts owing for elevator maintenance services, and subsequently and successfully moved to strike the defence of set-off and counterclaim on the grounds that the defendant had repeatedly breached court orders. It was court's responsibility to ensure the effective administration of justice, and the repeated failures by the defendant to comply with six court orders, including at least three “last chance” orders led the court to dismiss its claim for set-off and counterclaim that related to lost revenue, reduction in property value and overpayment. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The master distinguished the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Starland Contracting Inc." p2="1581518 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3431" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I642767715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Starland Contracting Inc. v. 1581518 Ontario Ltd.">Starland Contracting Inc. v. 1581518 Ontario Ltd. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 3431, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9126 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, on the basis that, by the time the <ital>Starland</ital> motion was before her, the party in breach had remedied the breach and complied with the court's orders. Here, the defendant had not cured the breach before the date the motion was before the court. She also noted the similarity between this case and that of <ital>Elevator Corp. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.</ital>, with the only difference being the claim for set-off.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1510610 Ontario Inc." p2="Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc." post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I642767725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1510610 Ontario Inc. v. Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc.">1510610 Ontario Inc. v. Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc., 2012 ONSC 302, 2012 CarswellOnt 1395, 22 C.L.R. (4th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While there is an emphasis on summary proceedings in the Act, motions are controlled by the requirement for leave as set out by section 67(2). Accordingly, parties bringing motions in lien cases, other than for routine consent matters, should carefully consider the fluid nature of most construction disputes, particularly as they relate to changing fact situations, and act in a cautious manner. Here, the defendant's adjournment request on its motion for an order requiring a sub-contractor to post security to replace security previously posted by general contractor in a related construction lien action, was denied. If a party takes such a significant interlocutory step, the jurisprudence governing civil cases indicates that a moving party should be prepared to “lead trump or risk losing,” and a similar approach applied for construction lien matters where partial summary judgment or injunctive relief was sought.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="International Wall Systems Ltd." p2="English Lane Residential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="5209" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I642767735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="International Wall Systems Ltd. v. English Lane Residential Developments Ltd.">International Wall Systems Ltd. v. English Lane Residential Developments Ltd., 2010 ONSC 5209, 2010 CarswellOnt 7272, 99 C.L.R. (3d) 168 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A purchase order contained a clause requiring the plaintiff vendor to indemnify the defendant purchaser in the event that the purchaser incurred costs by reason of any act, omission or representation of the vendor as the result of the supply of the materials. On the basis of this condition the defendant asserted that the plaintiff was obligated to reimburse it for legal and other costs attributable to a lien bond relating to the subcontractor's claim for lien. In rejecting this claim, the Master noted that the plaintiff made no attempt to ascertain whether the claim was subsumed in the plaintiff's claim (it was), which would have resulted in the only security posted being that for the plaintiff's claim. Thereafter, the purchaser should have followed up to have the security reduced but failed to do so. This failure flew in the face of the summary procedures mandated by s. 67(1) of the Act, and to award such costs would have been to condone the payment of unnecessary costs consequential to the failure to ascertain the appropriate amount of security to be posted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1508270 Ontario Ltd." p2="Prusky" post.rptr="4781" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I642767745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1508270 Ontario Ltd. v. Prusky">1508270 Ontario Ltd. v. Prusky, 2010 CarswellOnt 4781 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2010 CarswellOnt 6066 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Compensation was not awarded with respect to deficiencies in regard to the colour of inserts in file drawers as the claim was so minor and petty as to not warrant the preparation and trial time devoted to it. To allow compensation would only encourage parties to advance complaints that are grossly disproportionate to the cost of litigating the issue, contrary to s. 67.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Schindler Elevator Corp." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="8876" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I64278e805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schindler Elevator Corp. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Schindler Elevator Corp. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 8876 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Parties responding to pleadings are entitled to know the case they must meet. Section 67 requires the court to apply as summary a procedure as possible. It is incumbent on the party seeking an amendment to minimize delay by providing sufficient particulars so that a motion for particulars will not be required. Here, the proposed pleading was so lacking in material facts and particulars that if permitted in the form proposed, it would lead to a motion for particulars. When the motion was argued, the proceeding was already over three years old, and it was vague and improper. Nevertheless, the master granted the defendant a final opportunity to deliver a Fresh As Amended Statement of Defence incorporating the findings and rulings made in her reasons, provided that the costs ordered were paid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Barne Building & Construction Inc." p2="Young" post.rptr="142" pre.rptr="78" ref.id="I64278e815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barne Building & Construction Inc. v. Young">Barne Building & Construction Inc. v. Young (2009), 78 C.L.R. (3d) 142, 2009 CarswellOnt 1 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a motion for an order allowing for discoveries, where the amount in issue was modest, it was important that the parties not be forced to undergo a lengthy and expensive discovery process. To balance the competing interests of conducting discoveries and maintaining cost-effective litigation, it was appropriate that the parties define more closely the documents that they would be relying upon in support of their respective claims, and that there be time-limited discovery focusing on those issues most important to the parties. The court ordered that documents be exchanged within 60 days, limited the discovery of each party to three hours, and ordered that discoveries take place notwithstanding that the matter may be set down for trial in the meantime.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Starland Contracting Inc." p2="1581518 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3431" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I6427b5905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Starland Contracting Inc. v. 1581518 Ontario Ltd.">Starland Contracting Inc. v. 1581518 Ontario Ltd. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 3431, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9126 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where an order is made by a court on a “last chance” basis, the defaulting party is given fair warning as to the possible consequences of a failure to comply with its terms. However, the fact that an order has been described as a “last chance” order is not determinative where a party seeks to strike the other party's pleadings. In each case the discretion of the master or judge must be exercised having regard to the circumstances prevailing at the time the matter is brought back to court, including whether and to what extent the party remains in default of the order in question. Here, the master's conclusion that there was “borderline compliance at best” was not consistent with the record, and the master erred in striking the pleadings.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Schindler Elevator Co." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="110" pre.rptr="65" ref.id="I6427b5915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schindler Elevator Co. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Schindler Elevator Co. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc. (2007), 65 C.L.R. (3d) 110, 2007 CarswellOnt 6253 (Ont. Master); affirmed (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 5796, 76 C.L.R. (3d) 123 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, claims must be conducted efficiently and expeditiously. Where the defendant owner did not comply with orders for particulars and production of documents, it was appropriate to dismiss its counterclaim considering its repeated failures to comply with court orders.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." p2="Thunder Bay Regional Hospital" post.rptr="7471" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I6427b5925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital">Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 7471, 60 C.L.R. (3d) 219 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 1018 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Courts should avoid a multiplicity of actions and must be concerned with the matters proceeding in an expeditious and cost efficient manner. Permitting a defendant to add a counterclaim, which, while based on the same factual background, would significantly broaden the scope of the lien actions, does not foster the policy of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to expedite the claim in a summary fashion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Dirm Inc." p2="Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3479" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I6427b5935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd.">Dirm Inc. v. Dalton Engineering & Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3479, 37 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Master)</ref></cite>—The general contractor successfully obtained a discharge of the lien under s. 47 on the basis that preservation was improper because the claimant had registered its lien in the land registry office under s. 34(1)(a) rather than “give” a copy of the claim for lien and affidavit of verification to the owner college under s. 34(1)(b) and s. 34(3), by mailing them to the “office of the president of the college”. In the circumstances, even though there was a factual dispute, factual findings could be made on a s. 47 motion, without a trial. The master relied on s. 67(1), which directed him to proceed in as summary a way as possible, having regard to, <ital>inter alia</ital>, the nature of the liens in question.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Park" p2="Metropolitan Separate School Board" post.rptr="202" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I6427b5945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Park v. Metropolitan Separate School Board">Park v. Metropolitan Separate School Board (1998), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 202 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—This case arose in rather unusual circumstances in which two bonding companies sought a ruling on the validity of a material supplier's lien, to determine if there was liability and whose liability it was. The Plaintiff brought a two tier motion for summary judgment under R. 20. The motion was successful and the liens were declared proven and timely.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Bruce-Grey Roman Catholic Separate School Board" p2="Carosi Construction Ltd." post.rptr="75" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I6427b5955fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bruce-Grey Roman Catholic Separate School Board v. Carosi Construction Ltd.">Bruce-Grey Roman Catholic Separate School Board v. Carosi Construction Ltd. (1998), 39 C.L.R. (2d) 75 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The combined effects of s. 67(1) and (2) of the Act and s. 108(2)6 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> do not operate so as to make the issuance of a jury notice irregular in a lien proceeding. Where a counterclaim, focussing on allegations of negotiations and bad faith on the part of the plaintiff, is consolidated with lien actions, it is not somehow transmuted into the relief sought in any of the construction lien actions, namely, the “sale and distribution of the proceeds of property are subject to any lien or charge”, as stated in s. 108(2)6. A consolidation order is a procedural mechanism whose purpose is to assist in the orderly and expeditious trial processing of the disputes between the parties, and does not operate to change the essential character of the parties' claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Michaels Engineering Consultants Canada Inc." p2="961111 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="221" pre.rptr="91" ref.id="I6427b5965fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Michaels Engineering Consultants Canada Inc. v. 961111 Ontario Ltd.">Michaels Engineering Consultants Canada Inc. v. 961111 Ontario Ltd. (1996), 91 O.A.C. 221, 29 O.R. (3d) 273 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There is no reason, in principle, why a motion for summary judgment may not proceed in a construction lien action. As motions for summary judgment, in general, are not inconsistent with the Act, they are sanctioned by s. 67(3). Indeed, because the purpose of R. 20 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> is to dispose of claims, or defences, which do not raise a genuine issue for trial early in a proceeding, a motion for summary judgment advances the intention of the legislature as found in s. 67(1). The Divisional Court refers, with approval, to <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Hamilton Landscaping & Paving" p2="603893 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="127" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I6427dca05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hamilton Landscaping & Paving v. 603893 Ontario Inc.">Hamilton Landscaping & Paving v. 603893 Ontario Inc. (1988), 30 C.L.R. 127 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="St. Clair Roofing & Tinsmithing Inc." p2="Davidson" post.rptr="275" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I6427dca15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="St. Clair Roofing & Tinsmithing Inc. v. Davidson">St. Clair Roofing & Tinsmithing Inc. v. Davidson (1992), 50 C.L.R. 275, 7 C.P.C. (3d) 240, 8 O.R. (3d) 578 (Master)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
51:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 51.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">51:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section remains substantially unaltered, the changes in the wording reflect the changes to the reference provisions.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section dates back to s. 33 of the 1896 <ital>Act Respecting Liens of Mechanics, Wage-Earners and Others</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, providing that once a date for trial was fixed the judge or officer was to proceed to try the action, and all questions arising therein, or which were necessary to be tried, to completely dispose of the action and to adjust the rights and liabilities of the persons before him, and that said judge or officer was to make all inquiries, and give all directions, and do all things necessary to try and finally dispose of the action and all questions, matters and accounts arising from the action. The provision was carried through substantially unchanged to s. 35(4) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1950, c. 227, which read as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(4)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">The judge or officer shall try the action and all questions which arise therein or which are necessary to be tried in order to completely dispose of the action and to adjust the rights and liabilities of the persons appearing before him or upon whom the notice of trial has been served, and shall take all accounts, make all inquiries, give all directions and do all other things necessary to finally dispose of the action and of all matters, questions and accounts arising therein or at the trial, and to adjust the rights and liabilities of and give all necessary relief to all parties to the action and all persons who have been served with the notice of trial and shall embody the results in a judgment (Form 7), which judgment may direct payment forthwith by the person or persons primarily liable to pay the amount of the claims and costs as ascertained by the judgment and execution may be issued therefore forthwith.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The current section was introduced by the <ital>Statute Law Amendment Act</ital>, S.O. 1994, c. 27, s. 42, and amended by the <ital>Courts Improvement Act</ital>, S.O. 1996, c. 25, s. 4(1). The reference to the “case management master” was inserted by S.O. 1996, c. 25, s. 4(1). This section was drafted with regard to the fundamental objective of the Act, <ital>i.e.</ital>, to try lien actions as expeditiously as possible. To that effect, the judge or master is given powers that are more reminiscent of those of a civil law judge.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section requires the court to deal with all pleaded claims and all “issues that arise therein” and, more significantly, to adjust the rights and liabilities of all persons appearing before it, including any person served with Notice of Trial. The limits of this section, particularly s. 51(b) have not been fully explored. Section 51(b), for example, requires a court to “make all inquiries” and to “give all directions” and to do “all things necessary” to adjust all rights and liabilities of and “give all necessary relief” to all parties. For an interesting and creative example of efficiency in the conduct of two related references before the Master, see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Greycor Industrial Coatings" p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="4975" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I64282ac05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Greycor Industrial Coatings v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Greycor Industrial Coatings v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd. (2001), [2001] O.J. No. 4975, 2001 CarswellOnt 4427 (Master)</ref></cite>. The references were conducted with full, detailed Scott Schedules, on the basis of affidavit evidence in chief and <ital>viva voce</ital> cross examinations only where required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The nature of Scott Schedules was outlined in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="8127" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I64282ac15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2009 CarswellOnt 8127, 91 C.L.R. (3d) 145, [2009] O.J. No. 5531 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> at paras. 14–19, where the court characterized them as “a standard tool for organizing construction lien cases … In Scott Schedules, the parties list each of the disputed factual issues concerning claims, counterclaims, and defences, and then summarize their positions on each of those issues. Although neither the [<ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>] nor the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> provide for Scott Schedules, experienced construction law counsel know that the court will expect them to prepare and exchange these documents in any lien proceeding involving multiple parties and numerous issues … In large construction projects Scott Schedules are generally organized in the following fashion. First, the parties set out their positions on what the contracts say (identifying the parties in privity, the contract price(s), and their respective positions on the extent to which the contract has been performed) and the contract accounting. Second, the parties set out their positions on “extras” to the contract, that is, work that was performed outside the scope of the contract, and the amounts claimed and/or paid in respect to such work. Third, the parties set out their positions in respect to alleged “deficiencies” in the work performed (these are defects in work actually performed, rather than work that has not yet been performed), including the alleged costs to remedy these deficiencies. Fourth, the parties set out their positions respecting the cost to complete the contract work. Fifth, the parties set out their positions respecting ancillary claims (such as damages for delay, alleged set-off claims arising from matters other than the construction of the project at issue, and anything else that is alleged to affect the quantum claimed). Finally, a comprehensive Scott Schedule may also include a chart of the parties' positions respecting technical issues such as the formal validity and timeliness of liens … The Scott Schedules should be a detailed map to the claims asserted and defences raised, on an issue-by-issue basis, among all the parties. This map then becomes the outline for the evidence at trial and for the court's judgment itself … Each of the parties is required to set out in the Scott Schedules its position on each issue affecting its interests.”</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Central Welding" p2="HPN et al." post.rptr="2253" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I677af5503b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Central Welding v. HPN et al.">Central Welding v. HPN et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 2253, 2024 ONSC 1141 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Here, the test for striking pleadings was met and the statement of claim against the Attorney General of Canada was struck in its entirety. While the <ital>Construction Act</ital> did not apply to the federal Crown, the statement of claim also claimed compensation for unjust enrichment and <ital>quantum meruit</ital>. Because the allegations against the Attorney General arose out of contract within the construction project, the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tremblar" p2="1839563 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1316" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I677af5513b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario Ltd.">Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario Ltd., 2020 ONSC 1316, 2020 CarswellOnt 15015, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 275 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2020 CarswellOnt 15163 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> applied, in that the <ital>Construction Act</ital>'s scheme of liens and trusts was among the juristic reasons to eliminate the plaintiff's unjust enrichment claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Okkin Construction Inc." p2="Apostolopoulos" post.rptr="6367" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I64282ac25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Okkin Construction Inc. v. Apostolopoulos">Okkin Construction Inc. v. Apostolopoulos, 2022 ONSC 6367, 2022 CarswellOnt 16273 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the owner terminated the project on account of cost overruns, the contractor filed a notice of adjudication. Before the adjudication could be heard, the subcontractor, which was not a party to the adjudication, registered a construction lien against title to the owner's property. The contractor subsequently registered its own lien and the adjudicator eventually ordered the owner to pay a portion of the value of various invoices. The owner did not seek judicial review but moved for directions regarding whether he should pay the adjudication award in the face of a perfected lien registered by the subcontractor and the holdback requirements of the Act, and sought to pay the funds into trust. In essence, the owner was concerned he would be called upon to pay the required holdback twice. The court found that neither s. 51 nor r. 59.06 granted it the necessary authority to give the directions sought. The owner was essentially seeking a stay of the adjudicator's order, which only the Divisional Court could order, and to provide for the proceeds of the adjudicator's order to be held in trust. Rule 59.06 did not assist the owner because once filed, the adjudicator's order became an order in a different and separate proceeding.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Tremblar" p2="1839563 Ontario" post.rptr="15015" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90fc0690f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario">Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15015, 2020 ONSC 1316, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 275 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15163, 2020 ONSC 6302 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 20127 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master allowed the defendant owner's motion for summary judgment and dismissed the plaintiff subcontractor's claim against it for breach of trust and unjust enrichment. With respect to the issue of unjust enrichment, the master noted that the remedy required an absence of juristic reason for the enrichment, and a contract between an owner and a contractor constituted a juristic reason. As well, the existence of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was in effect the juristic reason for any unjust enrichment by the owner that a subcontractor may otherwise be able to establish. The <ital>Act</ital> provided subcontractors with specific <ital>in personam</ital> remedies against owners which turn on the concepts of lien and holdback. To give subcontractors the added non-statutory remedy of restitutionary <ital>quantum meruit</ital> when the statutory remedies fail would undermine the statute.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Kovacs" p2="Sparkes" post.rptr="938" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I64282ac45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kovacs v. Sparkes">Kovacs v. Sparkes, 2017 ONSC 938, 2017 CarswellOnt 7375, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 248 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the Plaintiff was awarded a default judgment on his counterclaim against a corporate defendant in a construction lien action, he brought a subsequent action alleging that the personal defendants misrepresented and concealed information and stripped the corporate defendant of its assets to make it judgment proof. The court rejected the personal defendants' motion to strike portions of the claim on the basis that it sought to re-litigate the default judgment. The claims were not made against the personal defendants in the counterclaim, nor could they have been made there, and could not be made against those defendants until after plaintiff obtained judgment in the lien action. The issues against the personal defendants had not been adjudicated by the Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1318847 Ontario Ltd." p2="Laval Tool & Mould Ltd." post.rptr="2664" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642851d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1318847 Ontario Ltd. v. Laval Tool & Mould Ltd.">1318847 Ontario Ltd. v. Laval Tool & Mould Ltd., 2015 ONSC 2664, 2015 CarswellOnt 8283 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Unlike the conclusion reached in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Juddav Designs Inc." p2="Cosgriffe" post.rptr="6597" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I642851d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Juddav Designs Inc. v. Cosgriffe">Juddav Designs Inc. v. Cosgriffe, 2010 ONSC 6597, 2010 CarswellOnt 8955, 99 C.L.R. (3d) 137 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6493, 2012 CarswellOnt 14470, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 140 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, it was not appropriate to allow a corporate plaintiff to advance an unjust enrichment claim founded in the services supplied by its principal in his personal capacity. The circumstances of this case were distinguished from those in <ital>Juddav Designs</ital> because, <ital>inter alia</ital>: i) the plaintiffs failed to prove that a contract ever existed; ii) no windfall benefit would have enured to the defendants as a result of a mere “technicality”; iii) the party who actually supplied the services was before the court asserting his own remedial claim for unjust enrichment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="5773" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I642851d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2013 ONSC 5773, 2013 CarswellOnt 12696, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 173 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant terminated its construction contract with the plaintiff on account of alleged delays, and at the date of termination, various sub-trades who had not received payment filed claims for lien. The plaintiff also brought an action claiming payment under the contract and the defendant counterclaimed for its costs incurred in arranging for completion of the outstanding work. When the defendant did not complete its evidence as of the date the trial of the matter went into recess, it sought an order under Ont. Rule 31.11(1) that the evidence provided by the sub-trades at their examinations for discovery be admitted into evidence at the trial, as the subcontractors, as lien claimants, were parties for purpose of the liability phase of the trial, and as such, were adverse in interest to the defendant, and under sections 57 and 59 could be treated as parties to the action. As well, under ss. 51 and 67, the trial judge was to completely dispose of the action in a procedure that was as far as possible summary in character. In dismissing the motion, the court held that discovery evidence could not be read in against any party other than party who gave it; neither defendant nor plaintiff could read in the discovery evidence of the lien claimants. The word “the” in Rule 31.11 on its face restricts read-in evidence on discovery for use against the party who gave the evidence and not against “an” adverse party.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Villa Nicolini Inc." post.rptr="5444" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I642851d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc.">Wellington Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Villa Nicolini Inc., 2012 ONSC 5444, 2012 CarswellOnt 12496, 20 C.L.R. (4th) 36 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 ONSC 6616, 2012 CarswellOnt 15361, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 37 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant contractor released significant holdback funds to sub-contractors whose contracts were certified complete as the project went along, and the lender, which had assumed the contractor's holdback obligations following the contractor's default, sought to claim those funds to reduce the holdback. The lien claimants alleged irregularities in the payments, and on the issue of standing, the court found that as statutory parties, the lien claimants had the right to raise and/or participate in arguments surrounding the calculation of the basic holdback. As well, the lien claimants had standing at common law because they were directly affected by the outcome of the decision.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2011" p1="Voka Steel Inc." p2="Edgecon Construction Inc." post.rptr="4051" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I90fc2da0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Voka Steel Inc. v. Edgecon Construction Inc.">Voka Steel Inc. v. Edgecon Construction Inc. (2011), 2011 CarswellOnt 4051, 2011 ONSC 3231 (Ont. Master); additional reasons (2011), 2011 CarswellOnt 4051 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Following a dispute between the general contractor and subcontractor regarding a delay in payments, the subcontractor left the job site before completing the work. The contractor relied on a provision in the contract stipulating that payments did not have to be made to the subcontractor until the contractor received payments from the project owner. The subcontractor's action against the contractor for amounts owing was allowed in part, but the court deducted allowable completion costs and overhead and profit. The contractor's pleading that the subcontractor had breached the contract was sufficient for awarding completion costs by way of set off, as the contractor had provided particulars of the set-off claim so subcontractor was not prejudiced. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was designed to protect contractors' accounts in these circumstances while allowing a construction project to proceed. A contractor engaged in a payment dispute has lien rights and remedies with payment of amounts owing secured by the lands. The subcontractor's proper course of action if its payment dispute could not be resolved was to register a lien and continue the work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Juddav Designs Inc." p2="Cosgriffe" post.rptr="6597" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I642878e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Juddav Designs Inc. v. Cosgriffe">Juddav Designs Inc. v. Cosgriffe, 2010 ONSC 6597, 2010 CarswellOnt 8955, 99 C.L.R. (3d) 137 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6493, 2012 CarswellOnt 14470, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 140 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 55(1) generally precludes a plaintiff in a lien action from joining a claim for unjust enrichment because it is not based on the contract between the parties for the supply of services and materials. However, where the unjust enrichment claim is put forward because the contract relied on has, for some reason, been struck down, then s. 51 of the Act allows the judge or reference master to nevertheless determine the claim on the basis of unjust enrichment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="David J. Cupido Construction Ltd." p2="Humphrey Funeral Home & Chapel Ltd." post.rptr="238" pre.rptr="73" ref.id="I642878e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="David J. Cupido Construction Ltd. v. Humphrey Funeral Home & Chapel Ltd.">David J. Cupido Construction Ltd. v. Humphrey Funeral Home & Chapel Ltd. (2008), 73 C.L.R. (3d) 238, 2008 CarswellOnt 4382 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Notwithstanding that the claim for lien stated that the date of last supply was earlier than it may in fact have been, the lien claim could be amended at trial if the court was satisfied that the evidence proved that materials or services were supplied on or after the date referenced in the claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Summers" p2="Harrower" post.rptr="303" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I642878e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Summers v. Harrower">Summers v. Harrower (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 303, 2005 CarswellOnt 7953 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 674 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The nature and scope of a trial under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is broad and comprehensive and permits a court to award damages on a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> basis, although such a claim was not pleaded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Partridge" p2="Villa Lathing & Drywall Co." post.rptr="3005" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I64289ff05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Partridge v. Villa Lathing & Drywall Co.">Partridge v. Villa Lathing & Drywall Co. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 3005, 2003 CarswellOnt 2865 (Master)</ref></cite>—In rejecting the defendant's counterclaim for breach of contract, the court held that the issue in respect of deficiencies was not how much was completed but rather what deficiencies, if any, existed in the work which was completed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Haas Homes Ltd." p2="March Road Gym & Health Club Inc." post.rptr="2847" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I64289ff15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc.">Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2847, 2003 CarswellOnt 2687, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 243 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An offer to lease set out the respective scope of the landlord's and the tenant's work required to renovate the upper floor of the property as a health club. The lien claimant quoted to the tenants, never entered into a written contract, and dealt with the tenants for payment, claims for extras and credits for approval. Liens were filed, and shortly after the improvements were completed to the tenants' premises, the tenants stopped paying rent, abandoned the premises and subsequently went bankrupt. The construction lien trial before the Master was converted into a reference and his reasons for judgment were converted into a report. A motion was taken by the landlord to oppose confirmation of the Master's report, which concluded in the alternative that if the landlord was not a statutory owner under the Act, the lien claimant would be entitled to recover the amount of its claim against it on the ground of <ital>quantum meruit</ital> or implied contract. The court declined to confirm the report, and rejected the alternative damage claims. A <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim was usually allowed only where one person had supplied goods or services to another person outside the scope of their contract as to price, and the claimant asks the court to establish a reasonable value for the goods and services. Such claims may arise under the Ontario Act as a result of the definition of “price” in s. 1(1), which, in the alternative, means the “agreed price” or the “actual value” of the services or materials supplied to the improvement under the contract. Here, however, the amount claimed was not the “actual value” of services and materials supplied, but was the balance of the “agreed price” under its contract with the tenants. Consequently, a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> recovery did not apply. There was insufficient evidence of any special relationship arising from the indirect involvement in the construction process of the non-contracting owner, so as to give the supplier a claim based on unjust enrichment against the landlord. In any event, the landlord was deprived of any real benefit from the improvements by reason of subsequent events involving the tenants and the major expenses incurred in refitting the demised premises for alternative use as office space.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Riddell Contracting Ltd." p2="2004778 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3819" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I90fc54b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Riddell Contracting Ltd. v. 2004778 Ontario Inc.">Riddell Contracting Ltd. v. 2004778 Ontario Inc. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 3819, 31 C.L.R. (3d) 209, [2003] O.J. No. 3916 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The property was owned by the first defendant and at all material times occupied by the second defendant, at whose request the plaintiff performed work. The court found that the relationship between the two was not at arm's length, but was a sham designed to shield the second defendant from judgments and financial obligations. The evidence established that the second defendant's principal controlled all aspects of the business, including signing the name of the first defendant's principal on cheques. Accordingly, the plaintiff's claim based on <ital>quantum meruit</ital> should succeed. The second defendant benefited from the plaintiff's work, which meant that the first defendant also benefited.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19990927" p1="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates" p2="Bradsil (1967) Ltd." post.rptr="70" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I64289ff35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. Bradsil (1967) Ltd.">Nortown Electrical Contractors Associates v. Bradsil (1967) Ltd. (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 70, 1999 CarswellOnt 39 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (September 27, 1999), Doc. CA C31530 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where the debt that a defendant was seeking to set-off against the plaintiff was contingent on its success as plaintiff in another, unrelated action, the debt did not have sufficient “maturity” to be capable of being raised as a defence of set-off.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19951206" p1="Fibre Free Technology Co." p2="1062869 Ontario Ltd." ref.id="I64289ff45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Fibre Free Technology Co. v. 1062869 Ontario Ltd.">Fibre Free Technology Co. v. 1062869 Ontario Ltd. (December 6, 1995), Court File No. CLA-94-CQ-53275, Master Sandler (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner terminated the demolition contract for failure of the plaintiff contractor to meet the required time deadlines. After the plaintiff was removed from the job site, a new contractor completed the project. The plaintiff subsequently commenced a lien action for the balance owing on the contract including and for items such as tools left on the premises, recyclable materials from the demolition site, and a fence constructed around the site. In dismissing the plaintiff's claim, the master noted that time was of the essence in the contract, and that the commercial nature of the contract was undermined by the plaintiff failing to meet the deadline. The claim for the “recyclables”, was not a lienable item, as their retail value, when taken off the premises, did not constitute an improvement to the lands. It was the intention of the parties that the fence was being supplied and sold to the owner and that its value was included in the contract price.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Komorowski" p2="Van Weel" post.rptr="856" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I90fc7bc0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Komorowski v. Van Weel">Komorowski v. Van Weel (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 856, 12 O.R. (3d) 444, 9 C.L.R. (2d) 39 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The contractor agreed to renovate the owners' residential property, and work continued until the owners refused to pay sums which were not immediately due under the terms of the contract. Eventually, the contractor left the site, and sued the owners, who counterclaimed against the contractor. The matter was referred to a Master who, after applying a set-off, awarded the owners a judgment plus costs. The contractor opposed confirmation of the Master's report and requested that its damages be determined on a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> basis, notwithstanding that it had not raised the issue of a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim at any time during the trial. In view of the contractor's unwarranted insistence upon “concessions” in the matter of the timing of payments and in view of the serious deficiencies brought to light after the contractor had withdrawn its forces, the owners were entitled to treat the contractor's withdrawal of services as a repudiation of the contract. Moreover, the absence of any indication at trial that a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim was being made in the alternative and, more importantly, the fact that the contractor did not seek to keep completion costs separate from the costs of remedying deficiencies provided a strong secondary reason for dismissing the motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="W.D. Lester Construction" p2="Purdy" post.rptr="2421" pre.rptr="1992" ref.id="I6428ee105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="W.D. Lester Construction v. Purdy">W.D. Lester Construction v. Purdy (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 2421, [1992] O.J. No. 2774 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Following the evidence at trial, the trial judge reduced the plaintiff's claim by an amount in respect of deficient workmanship and materials even though this was not pleaded in the statement of defence and there was no counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc." p2="Lombardo" post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I6428ee115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo">Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo (1991), 49 C.L.R. 141 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant entered a defence to a lien action and counterclaimed for $250,000. The action was placed on the trial list for construction lien claims, and shortly before trial, the defendant successfully moved for an order requiring the plaintiff to post security for costs and allowing the defendant to amend its statement of defence and counterclaim to include allegations of misrepresentation, negligence and breach of contract, as well as damages in the amount of $527,500. Before commencement of the trial, the plaintiff moved under R. 23.01(1)(b) to discontinue the lien action. The defendant consented to the discontinuance but brought a counter-motion to continue its counterclaim as a separate action. The plaintiff's motion was allowed, but the defendant's motion was dismissed. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> authorizes an abridged proceeding which may severely limit parties' rights available in the ordinary course of litigation. The defendant, by its counterclaim in negligence, had adopted a procedure with the effect, for monetary or lack of security reasons, of depriving the plaintiff of the right to a trial by jury in a negligence action. By waiting until the eve of trial to bring a motion for security for costs, for an amount greater than the plaintiff's lien, and to amend its statement of defence and counterclaim, the defendant had in effect defeated the purposes of the Act, namely, the provision of security for work done and materials supplied and an expeditious and cheap manner to proceed to trial. The plaintiff was therefore allowed to discontinue its lien action on the payment of costs to the defendant on a party and party basis, those costs to include the costs of the counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Wharton Enterprises Ltd." p2="Brompton Financial Corp." post.rptr="121" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I6428ee125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wharton Enterprises Ltd. v. Brompton Financial Corp.">Wharton Enterprises Ltd. v. Brompton Financial Corp. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 121, 71 O.R. (2d) 463, 40 C.P.C. (2d) 51, 67 D.L.R. (4th) 119 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner in a construction lien action commenced a separate action against the related company of the plaintiff contractor as guarantor of the performance of the contract by the plaintiff. The court dismissed the defendant's motion to add the related company as a defendant by counterclaim. An action brought under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is a statutory action and the authority of the court to deal with it is derived under the relevant legislation. That legislation makes no provision for claiming against a non-party as a defendant by counterclaim. The broad scope of s. 51 is limited by s. 55(2) to persons appearing before the court or upon whom notice of trial has been served. As well, on the principle <ital>expressio unius est exclusio alterius</ital>, the court was obliged to hold that the necessary authority could not be found by implication. This reasoning is followed by the Master in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Metric Excavating Ltd." p2="Ghods Builders Inc." post.rptr="4380" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I56237340fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Metric Excavating Ltd. v. Ghods Builders Inc.">Metric Excavating Ltd. v. Ghods Builders Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 4380 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, to the effect that except in the case of a general lien, the use of the word “contract” or “subcontract” in the Act, as defined terms, limits the plaintiff's claims to a single improvement. For procedural reasons relating to the jurisdiction conferred upon the Master by the judgment of reference, the pleading could not be struck in this case.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 51(a)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Deep Foundations Contractors Inc." p2="B. Gottardo Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4875" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6428ee145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Deep Foundations Contractors Inc. v. B. Gottardo Construction Ltd.">Deep Foundations Contractors Inc. v. B. Gottardo Construction Ltd., 2015 ONSC 4875, 2015 CarswellOnt 11732, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 267 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 5964, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 288 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motion to dismiss the defendant's counterclaim was granted, as construction lien actions are intended to be of a summary character, and heard within a reasonable period of time after the completion of the work. Almost six years had elapsed after the plaintiff's work was completed, the matter has been set down for trial on four different dates, and the defendant's actions were calculated to deliberately delay the trial of the counterclaim. There are circumstances where the interests of justice are seen to be perverted because of the deliberate and flagrant actions of one party who does its utmost to avoid a determination on the merits. This conduct amounts to an abuse of the litigation process.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pre-Con Inc." p2="Carosi Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4431" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I642915205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pre-Con Inc. v. Carosi Construction Ltd.">Pre-Con Inc. v. Carosi Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4431, 38 C.L.R. (3d) 65 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor rendered its invoice for supply and installation of pre-cast concrete double tees, less 10 per cent statutory holdback required under the Act. The contractor submitted its application for payment to the owner municipality, which included monies for the double tees but not the full amount of the subcontractor's invoice. A payment certificate was issued to the contractor, and the subcontractor brought an action for damages with respect to its unpaid invoice. Pursuant to minutes of settlement, the parties agreed that if the court found that the contractor received funds from the municipality, which were owing to the subcontractor, the subcontractor was entitled to judgment, including a declaration against the contractor for breach of trust under the Act. The subcontractor's action was allowed. The contractor's liability for breach of trust extended to the full amount of the invoice, and not only the amount allocated in the contractor's application for payment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="1150402 Ontario Inc." p2="Delfino" post.rptr="768" pre.rptr="62" ref.id="I642915215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1150402 Ontario Inc. v. Delfino">1150402 Ontario Inc. v. Delfino (2003), 62 O.R. (3d) 768, 23 C.L.R. (3d) 277, 2003 CarswellOnt 87 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Court awarded punitive damages against the defendants in the amount of $15,000 arising from their involvement in a blatant breach of trust, “accomplished by forgery and attempted to be justified by fraud”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Michelin Group Inc." p2="Forsan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I642915225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd.">Michelin Group Inc. v. Forsan Construction Ltd. (1994), 18 O.R. (3d) 523, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 202 (Gen. Div.); affirmed (1995), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 215 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A distinction must be made between an amendment to the statement of claim and an amendment to the claim for lien in construction lien matters.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Melgold Construction Management Ltd." p2="Banton Investments Ltd." post.rptr="216" pre.rptr="32" ref.id="I642915235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Melgold Construction Management Ltd. v. Banton Investments Ltd.">Melgold Construction Management Ltd. v. Banton Investments Ltd. (1988), 32 C.L.R. 216 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A master has jurisdiction pursuant to the Rules of Practice to entertain a motion which raises the sufficiency of a solicitor's authority to commence an action, and need to resort to any powers given the master by the judgment of reference.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 51(b)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="One Source Fire and Life Safety Inc." p2="Prica Group Construction Management Inc." post.rptr="653" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64293c305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="One Source Fire and Life Safety Inc. v. Prica Group Construction Management Inc.">One Source Fire and Life Safety Inc. v. Prica Group Construction Management Inc., 2021 ONSC 653, 2021 CarswellOnt 988 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Earlier procedural rulings in the lien claim ordered, <ital>inter alia</ital>, the exchange of Scott schedules and that certain further items be included in those Scott schedules (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="One Source" p2="Prica" post.rptr="4329" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64293c315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="One Source v. Prica">One Source v. Prica, 2019 ONSC 4329, 2019 CarswellOnt 11470 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>). In support of its counterclaim, the defendant was required to identify separately all deficiencies, incomplete work and work that was omitted by agreement, with a detailed description and a reference number, but its Scott schedule failed to do this. The parties were permitted to amend their Scott schedules after examination for discovery, but the plaintiff was not satisfied with the particulars in the defendant's Scott schedule with respect to deficiencies in the work that were remedied by the contractor who replaced it. The remedy successfully sought by the plaintiff was an order amending the earlier order to provide that any amendment to the Scott schedule would not advance new claims relating to the plaintiff, or new claims for work done by the replacement contractor, without leave of the court.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

The section is unique to Ontario. Section 52 in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, first appeared in substantially the same form replacing s. 42(9) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which provided that an action or reference under the Act could be tried by any judge or officer having jurisdiction to try the action or reference notwithstanding that the time and place for the trial was appointed and fixed by another judge or officer. The reference to the case management master was inserted by the <ital>Courts Improvement Act, 1996</ital>, S.O. 1996, c. 25, s. 4(2). Effective September 1, 2021 the title of Case Management Master has been changed to Associate Judge by the <ital>Accelerating Access to Justice Act, 2021</ital>, 2021, S.O. 2021, c. 4, Sch 3, s. 20(1).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Act creates new procedures, such as the settlement meeting and motion to fix trial dates, and a judge or Associate Judge (formerly called a case management master) does not acquire exclusive jurisdiction as a result of participation in these events.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
