58:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 58.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">58:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 58 was amended to provide for a reference of the action to the Small Claims Court for claims under $25,000.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In the Act of 1873, claims for lien were to be enforced, depending on the amount at stake, in the county or division courts or the Court of Chancery. The Act of 1896 provided that an action to enforce a lien may be tried by the Master Ordinary, a local master of the High Court, an official referee, or a judge of the County or High Court, S.O. 1896, c. 35, s. 31. Provisions to that effect remained in the Acts until 1916, when <ital>An Act to amend The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1916, c. 30, s. 1, repealed the corresponding provision in the 1914 Act and replaced it with a provision differentiating between actions commenced in the County of York and those commenced outside that county, the prior to be tried before the Master Ordinary or the Assistant Master, and the latter to be tried before a judge of the county or district court. The 1923 Act, S.O. 1923, c. 30, s. 32(2), introduced a new provision to the effect that an application could be made by any party to the action to have the action tried before a judge of the Supreme Court at the regular sittings of the High Court. Notwithstanding some changes in the wording, this section remained substantially intact until the Revised Statutes of 1950. Subsection 31(1) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1950, c. 227, provided as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(1)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">The action shall be tried in the county or district in which the land is situate before a judge of the county or district court, provided that where the land is situate in the County of York the action shall be tried before a Master of the Supreme Court or an Assistant Master.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1959" p1="Ontario (Attorney General)" p2="Victoria Medical Building Ltd." post.rptr="32" pre.rptr="[1960]" ref.id="I6429b1605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario (Attorney General) v. Victoria Medical Building Ltd.">Ontario (Attorney General) v. Victoria Medical Building Ltd. (1959), [1960] S.C.R. 32, 21 D.L.R. (2d) 97 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, the Supreme Court of Canada held that the appointment of the Master under s. 31(1) was unconstitutional under s. 96 of the B.N.A. Act due to the nature of the jurisdiction conferred upon the Master, and the fact that the Master was given the power of final adjudication. In response to this decision, the reference model in s. 31(3) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, was introduced. This section was substantially changed in 1983 and again in 1990, before being introduced in its current form the 1994 <ital>Statute Law Amendment Act</ital>, S.O. 1994, c. 27, s. 42(5). The 1994 statute amended the section to allow for a reference to a Master or “to a person agreed on by the parties”. In Toronto, it has been common practice for more than 50 years to have lien actions conducted by reference to masters. The reference to case management masters was inserted by S.O. 1996, c. 25, s. 4(3). Effective September 1, 2021 the title of Case Management Master has been changed to Associate Judge by the <ital>Accelerating Access to Justice Act, 2021</ital>, 2021, S.O. 2021, c. 4, Sch 3, s. 20(2).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 58 empowers associate judges, who have a recognized expertise in complex construction lien matters, to conduct these actions by means of a reference of the entire action or any part of it to an associate judge (s. 58(1)(a)), or a person agreed to by the parties (s. 58(1)(b)), or the Small Claims Court (s. 58(1)(c) for trial. The motion for a reference is made to a judge with notice at the close of pleadings. In addition to reference by order at the close of pleadings, a judge at the trial may direct a reference to the appropriate associate judge or a person agreed upon by the parties. Parties added subsequent to the reference order are provided with an opportunity under subs. (5) to set it aside, failing which they are bound by the results (subs. (6)). The broad powers of the associate judge or the consensual third party on the reference are contained in subss. (4) and (4.1). Essentially, such person exercises all of the powers of the court.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I56243690fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 2019 ONSC 1551, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not create a process called a “summary trial”. There is nothing in the <ital>Act</ital> that prescribes the summary nature of construction lien proceedings, other than the provisions in s. 67. The one provision that prescribes “summary process” does not refer to a trial, but to the “procedure in an action”. While it is true that construction lien masters have developed a process for summary construction lien trials, generally used where proportionality so recommends, that is a practice that has been developed in reliance on the general authority conferred on masters under s. 58. The summary trial is one solution developed by construction lien masters to exercise their jurisdiction under the Act.</para.text></para><feature.para.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><ital>Authors' Note</ital>:</name></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="4382" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6429d8715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran, 2022 ONSC 4382, 2022 CarswellOnt 10736 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the plaintiff's subsequent motion for summary judgment was heard and granted.</para.text></para></feature.para.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="PCR Contractors Inc." p2="Wilson Station Development Corp." post.rptr="6319" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6429d8725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="PCR Contractors Inc. v. Wilson Station Development Corp.">PCR Contractors Inc. v. Wilson Station Development Corp., 2015 ONSC 6319, 2015 CarswellOnt 15810, 55 C.L.R. (4th) 304 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 16811 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A party to a construction lien action is not entitled, at law, to have an action referred to a master. Rather, such a referral is at the discretion of the judge. It is not a pre-condition to exercise of the court's discretion that the parties consent to such a referral nor is it required that there be credible evidence that the Court's time will be “bogged down with tedious documentary or accounting matters”. Section 55(1) of the Act provides that a plaintiff in an action may join with a lien claim a claim for breach of contract or subcontract. A counterclaim on a reference to a master is not limited to breach of contract and need not be related to the making of the improvement. Accordingly, the Act clearly contemplates that a master may adjudicate a claim for breach of contract as part of a construction lien reference, and its provisions do not support the view that such matters would be too complex for a master to determine. Here, the plaintiff's motion to refer the construction lien action to a master was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac-United Management Corp." p2="St. Clare's-Monaco Place" post.rptr="4760" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6429ff805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Unimac-United Management Corp. v. St. Clare's-Monaco Place">Unimac-United Management Corp. v. St. Clare's-Monaco Place, 2015 ONSC 4760, 2015 CarswellOnt 11914, 53 C.L.R. (4th) 63 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2015 ONSC 4874, 2016 CarswellOnt 12249, 66 C.L.R. (4th) 273 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The applicant unsuccessfully sought judicial review of the case management Master's refusal to recuse herself from further hearing of a lien action on the grounds of bias. The adverse consequences of delay outweighed the possible hardship to the applicant by not determining the bias issue before the completion of the lien reference. The Act provided for full appeals on the merits as a corollary to the restrictive approach to interlocutory appeals, and it would be open to the applicant to raise the issue of bias in any subsequent appeal. The motion was premature. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="4361814 Canada Inc." p2="Dalcor Inc." post.rptr="1481" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6429ff815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="4361814 Canada Inc. v. Dalcor Inc.">4361814 Canada Inc. v. Dalcor Inc., 2015 ONSC 1481, 2015 CarswellOnt 3046, 24 C.B.R. (6th) 171, 40 C.L.R. (4th) 4 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 5431, 40 C.L.R. Master)</ref></cite>—Rule 37.03(2) of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, the place-of-hearing rule, could apply as much to motions in construction lien cases as to any other type of action. Section 58 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (Ont.) does not override the rule requirement that motions are to be returnable where the solicitor for the responding party practises law. The order of reference is irrelevant. However, once a reference has been directed, then R. 54, governing references, applies. Rule 54.05(1) provides that the referee “shall hear and dispose of any motion made in connection with the reference”, and R. 54.05(2) specifically provides that R. 37.03(2) does not apply to a motion under R. 54.05(1). Because of s. 58 of the Act, a motion to add a defendant and amend pleadings is a “motion made in connection with the reference”. Thus, R. 54.05 applies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Res-Com Excavating" p2="Commonwealth Richmond Properties Inc." post.rptr="207" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I642a4da15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Res-Com Excavating v. Groomes">Justwork Construction Ltd. v. Groomes (1991), 48 C.L.R. 183 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—After the parties to a construction lien action had consented to an order referring the trial to a master, a second contractor commenced an action against the owner, one which was not under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The owner brought a motion to consolidate the actions, which the first plaintiff opposed on the grounds that it should not be deprived of the summary procedure and rights of the Act to accommodate the interests of the defendant, and secondly, that the pre-trial of the lien action had been scheduled and an early trial date was expected. The motion was allowed. The court had the jurisdiction to provide the relief requested and to vary the consent order. Although there was some prejudice to the original contractor in the form of delay, there was no reason why the second action should not be able to proceed through examinations for discovery and be ready for trial in a short period of time, and it was proper for the matters to be tried one after the other. The lien action was to continue under the Act to preserve the rights of the original contractor, but was to be tried by a judge. The plaintiffs were to hold one examination for discovery of the defendant (if discovery was desired) and share the cost of that examination, but the defendant was not to be entitled to object to overlapping questions by counsel for each plaintiff unless such questioning became oppressive or vexatious.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 58(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Voutour" p2="MVG Investments" post.rptr="4911" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I642a4da35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Voutour v. Here, the court exercised that discretion to refer the action for trial by an Associate Judge because: 1) the defendants had already availed themselves of the court in an unsuccessful motion to an Associate Judge under s. 47 to discharge the plaintiff's claim for lien; 2) the defendants had paid the amount in dispute into the court and would require an order of the court for these funds to be paid out to the successful party; 3) the plaintiff tendered evidence from the Associate Judge's construction lien registrar that a two-day trial in this action could be scheduled expeditiously, while a referral for trial to the Small Claims Court would result in a longer delay; 4) the Associate Judge has broad powers under s. 58(4) to direct and manage the trial of this action in an efficient manner proportionate to the amounts in issue.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 58(4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Pylon Paving (1996) Inc." p2="Beaucon Building Services Inc." post.rptr="3282" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I677cf1203b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Pylon Paving (1996) Inc. v. The defendant subcontractor sought an order transferring the action brought against it in Newmarket to Toronto, assigning that action to the Master for trial and to have the action tried concurrently with, or immediately after, other lien and bond claims that had been referred to the Master. The plaintiff had also commenced action in Newmarket against the owner of the project, but later consented to it being transferred to Toronto. The motion was granted in part, the Master ruling that he had jurisdiction under Ont. R. 13.1.02 to order the change of venue but did not have jurisdiction to assign or refer the action, once moved, or to order it heard with other claims. That portion of the motion had to be adjourned for hearing in front of a judge. On the substantive issue, the Master ordered the venue moved to Toronto. While the action did not deal with the lien or bond claims, it had common issues with those claims, and a change of venue would promote economy, efficiency, and justice by avoiding inconsistent findings of fact. The plaintiff was unable to establish a rational connection between its chosen jurisdiction and the cause of action, or the parties, which was sufficient to warrant deference to its choice. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The matter of assignment or reference of the action to be heard with other claims, which was beyond the Master's jurisdiction, was subsequently brought for hearing before a judge in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac-United Management Corp." p2="Cobra Power Inc." post.rptr="208" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642a74b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Unimac-United Management Corp. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, where it was held that the transfer of this action to the construction lien list, to be heard before the Master together with the other cases which he was case managing that arose from the project here, or to be heard seriatim, was the most efficient and expeditious means of proceeding with the case and would ensure that there would not be inconsistent findings of fact or law.]</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 58(4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Li" p2="Zhu" post.rptr="18" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dd92450ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Li v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sought orders, <ital>inter alia</ital>, dismissing the claim and striking the defence to counterclaim in a lien action, and striking certain defences in a related civil action. The ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90fe0260f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 18748, 2019 ONSC 6590, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 193 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> was held not to apply. First, the jurisdictions under which the motions were brought expressly authorized the court to grant “judgments” as per s. 54(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Most importantly, there was a good reason for allowing the court, even one acting under a judgment of reference such as this one, to issue “judgments” on motions for default judgment. By the nature of these motions, there is no opposition, the opposing party is not entitled to participate any further and is bound by deemed admissions. The purpose of the motion is to determine whether the deemed admissions plus any evidence in “support” of the deemed admissions justify a judgment that can be immediately enforced. These were not, in the court's view, the “findings” contemplated by the judgment or order of reference. The “findings” contemplated by a judgment of reference are those that arise from contested proceedings, such as with the contested motion to enforce a settlement in <ital>Prasher</ital>. As the defaulting party is not entitled to participate in the proceedings, there can be no motion to oppose confirmation of a report.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90fe2970f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 18748, 2019 ONSC 6590, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 193 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Master had jurisdiction to hear a motion to enforce a settlement under R. 49 or for summary judgment under R. 20. An order for a construction lien reference was made in 2013. No judgment or reference report was issued prior to the motion before the Master, so the case was still before him on a construction lien reference at the time of the motion. In this situation, the Master had “all the powers of a judge” to hear and decide the case, including the power to decide a motion under R. 49 or under R. 20. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90fe2971f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 2019 ONSC 1551, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>].</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Yuanda Canada Enterprises Ltd." p2="Walsh Construction/Bondfield Partnership" post.rptr="19791" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I642a9bc25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yuanda Canada Enterprises Ltd. v. Walsh Construction/Bondfield Partnership">Yuanda Canada Enterprises Ltd. v. Walsh Construction/Bondfield Partnership, 2019 CarswellOnt 19791, 2019 ONSC 6988, 49 C.P.C. (8th) 364 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—When conducting a reference pursuant to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, a reference master does not acquire greater discretion or authority than the court would otherwise have. Consequently, since the court lacks discretion to authorize a non-licensee to conduct examinations at trial, a reference master under the Act also lacks discretion to permit a non-licensee to conduct such examinations. A reference master appointed under Ont. R. Rule 54 would similarly lack that discretion. Neither the (Ont.) <ital>Law Society Act</ital> nor applicable by-laws under that Act provided any statutory exemption for foreign lawyers. As a result, the motion by a party to a consolidated reference, for an order authorizing an American attorney to conduct the examination and cross-examination of two American-based experts intended to be called at the pending trial in reference, was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90fe2972f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 2019 ONSC 1551, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the defendant moved under s. 47 for orders dismissing the action and returning his lien security or, alternatively, reducing his lien security, the master granted summary judgment to the plaintiff, finding that she had jurisdiction to use the “Enhanced Powers” accorded to judges on motions for summary judgment because she was acting in her capacity as a construction lien master to whom an action had been referred for trial under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. On motion by the defendant opposing confirmation of the master's report, the motions judge found that the master did not have jurisdiction to use the Enhanced Powers, and had therefore exceeded her jurisdiction when she granted summary judgment, and declined to confirm the Master's report. On further appeal to the Divisional Court, the Court ruled that, in ordinary civil litigation, a master does not have the Enhanced Powers on a motion for summary judgment. However, in this case the master was a referee to whom a construction lien action had been referred for trial. In this capacity, a master has all the powers of a construction lien referee and is not confined to the jurisdiction conferred on masters in ordinary civil litigation. The procedural powers of a construction lien referee include the full range of powers accorded to a judge under the (Ont.) Rules of Civil Procedure. These, in turn, include the Enhanced Powers that may be used on a motion for summary judgment. Motions under Ont. Rules 20 and 21 may be brought before a master, if leave is granted, in cases referred to the master for trial under the Act. Where a R.20 motion is brought in such a case, the master may use the Enhanced Powers. However, while the motions judge erred in finding that the master acted without jurisdiction, the master did not have a motion for summary judgment for the plaintiff before her. Rather, it was a s. 47 motion brought by the defendant. In proceeding as if she did, she deprived the self-represented defendant of procedural fairness, and her report could not be confirmed. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The Divisional Court emphasized that “in judicial regions with masters (including Toronto), construction lien cases are referred routinely to a master for trial. The jurisdiction of a master to conduct these trials, with all the power accorded to construction lien referees under the [<ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>], was an important aspect of maintaining the efficient specialized court that masters have become for the adjudication of construction lien cases.” Note also that in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="4382" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I642ac2d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran, 2022 ONSC 4382, 2022 CarswellOnt 10736 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the plaintiff's subsequent motion for summary judgment was heard and granted.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642ac2d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Having all the “… jurisdiction, powers and authority of the court …” as set out in the s. 58(4) of the Act does not have the effect of making the referee a judge of the Superior Court of Ontario. Subsection 58(4) does nothing other than provide for the conduct of the reference, and does not change the position of the referee within the judicial structure. The Master continues to have the status and place that comes from being a Master. The Master does not, for the purposes of the reference, obtain the standing of or become a judge. On this basis, he or she would be bound to follow the decision of a single judge of the Superior Court. In this case, the Master expressly declined to follow the rulings in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1109" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I90fe5080f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 1109, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 203 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I642ae9e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2101641 Ontario Corp." p2="Suvarna" post.rptr="7247" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I642ae9e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2101641 Ontario Corp. v. Suvarna">2101641 Ontario Corp. v. Suvarna, 2013 ONSC 7247, 2013 CarswellOnt 15897 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the lien action was referred to the master for trial, the plaintiff agreed to post security for costs and executed a consent to judgment dismissing its lien claim and its action in the event that it failed to comply with that agreement. Following the plaintiff's failure to post security, the defendant's motion for judgment on the basis of the consent to judgment, was granted. Under s. 58, the reference master had all the powers of the court, including the hearing of a motion for judgment in the circumstances here. While the court had discretion even in the face of a consent to judgment; due to factors such as the plaintiff's conduct throughout the reference in breaching court orders, the consent to judgment, and the defendant's willingness to discontinue its counterclaim if the plaintiff's claim was dismissed; it was appropriate to grant judgment and dismiss the plaintiff's claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="International Wall Systems Ltd." p2="English Lane Residential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="6920" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I642ae9e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="International Wall Systems Ltd. v. English Lane Residential Developments Ltd.">International Wall Systems Ltd. v. English Lane Residential Developments Ltd., 2011 ONSC 6920, 2011 CarswellOnt 14415 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 2889, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 234 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Noting the lack of case law on the point, the court found that it is acceptable for a master, seized and intimately familiar with the details of a lengthy and complex construction lien reference and trial, to intervene in the questioning of witnesses more often than a judge in a civil trial. However, it is imperative when doing so that the master not create an impression, through the questioning process, of having adopted a position on the facts, issues or credibility. Here, bearing in mind the high threshold of establishing a reasonable apprehension of bias based on undue intervention, together with the unique role of a master in a construction lien trial, the court was not persuaded that the interventions of the master during the trial, though numerous and sometimes pointed, created a reasonable apprehension that he was biased such that the defendant was denied the appearance of a fair trial. The master was very familiar with the facts and issues by the time the trial began, and in the context of the entire record, his questions of the various witnesses for the defendant were directed to specific areas and issues that he perceived had to be clarified in order for him to arrive at a comprehensive and reasoned decision. While many of his interventions were out of context with the area of examination being conducted at a particular time, they were directed at issues that he knew to be relevant and wanted clarified at that time.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Rebelo" p2="Borody" post.rptr="1694" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I642ae9e35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rebelo v. Borody">Rebelo v. Borody (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 1694, 61 C.L.R. (3d) 154 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A case management Master to whom a reference has been directed has jurisdiction under s. 58(4) to hear a motion for an order striking out a cross-claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd." p2="Ding" post.rptr="2319" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I90fe7790f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding">Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2319, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Master); affirmed 2004 CarswellOnt 4167 (S.C.J.); leave to appeal denied (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 5401, 39 C.L.R. (3d) 150, 193 O.A.C. 145 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The owners did not retain any holdback funds, which would have covered the lien claim, but instead paid the entire amount to a general contractor. The plaintiff subcontractor registered a claim for lien of $15,242.15 and commenced an action. The issue of liability was settled prior to a motion for summary judgment but the issue of costs was unresolved. The Master held that the successful subcontractor was not precluded from recovering costs that exceeded the amount of the lien claim. The owners had breached their statutory obligation to retain holdback funds, and should have paid the subcontractor immediately, as they were fully liable. Had the owners complied with their holdback obligation under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, very little of the significant costs incurred by the claimant would have been necessary. All of the costs experienced after the first pretrial could have been avoided. This was an appropriate case for costs on a partial indemnity scale for the period up to and including the first pretrial, and on a full indemnity scale for the period after the first pretrial. The owners unsuccessfully sought an order denying confirmation of the report or setting aside or varying it. The Master had broad powers to award costs under ss. 86 and 58(4) and her award should only be set aside if it was plainly wrong. She was entitled to hold that action would have ended at the outset if the owners had admitted liability and paid the amount owing into court. The Master was in the best position to decide the facts and to determine bad faith on the part of the owners since she was involved on a continuous basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Biotechnik Inc." p2="O'Shanter Development Co." post.rptr="1895" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I642b10f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co.">Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 1895, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 52 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 58(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, a master on a reference has the “powers and authority” of a single judge of the Superior Court of Justice and is not bound to follow a judgment of another judge of co-ordinate jurisdiction although such decision is to be considered persuasive and is to be given much respect. The Master on a reference can treat rulings on matters of law by other single judges of the Superior Court just as a judge could under the law of <ital>stare decisis</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Snowmont Investments Corp." p2="Elliott" post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="153" ref.id="I642b10f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott">Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott (1997), 153 D.L.R. (4th) 305, 1997 CarswellOnt 4333, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 240 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In supplementary reasons following the removal of a reference from a Master upon grounds of reasonable apprehension of bias, upon the test set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1976" p1="Committee for Justice & Liberty" p2="Canada (National Energy Board) (1976)" post.rptr="369" pre.rptr="[1978] 1" ref.id="I642b10f35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Committee for Justice & Liberty v. Canada (National Energy Board) (1976)">Committee for Justice & Liberty v. Canada (National Energy Board) (1976), [1978] 1 S.C.R. 369, 68 D.L.R. (3d) 716 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, the court confirmed its jurisdiction to make such a ruling, including its jurisdiction under s. 58(4).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction" p2="Stern" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I642b10f45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern">Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern (1997), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—There is no inconsistency between rule 59.06 of the Rules of Civil Procedure and the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Therefore, a master who has heard a reference under the <ital>Act</ital>, and who has signed the report, has jurisdiction to hear a motion under R. 59.06. Rule 52, dealing with the situation where one party fails to attend at a trial applies to references trials, and the reports thereon, whether confirmed or unconfirmed. Rr. 59.06(1) and (2), Rules 1.03 and 1.04(2), and s. 58(4) of the <ital>Act</ital> give jurisdiction to a Master to correct accidental slips or omissions in a Report, whether issued or not.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Metric Excavating Ltd." p2="Ghods Builders Inc." post.rptr="4380" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I56256f10fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Metric Excavating Ltd. v. Ghods Builders Inc.">Metric Excavating Ltd. v. Ghods Builders Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 4380 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor provided excavation services to the defendant builder G. on eight separate, and unconnected, properties owned by different owners. The plaintiff registered a lien on the property owned by the defendant A, for the total balance owing by the defendant G. on all eight properties, and commenced an action against G. for the full amount and against A., claiming a general lien on his land. No attack was made by the defendant G. on the joinder of these claims, <ital>i.e.</ital>, the balances owing on the eight projects, and the plaintiff proceeded with a motion under s. 60(1) of the Act to have the action referred to the Master for trial. On a preliminary motion, the Master held that the joinder of claims by the plaintiff against G. for the payment of amounts owing in relation to the excavating work done at the other sites were not proper. Nevertheless, because G. had not opposed the joinder prior to the judgment of reference, nor sought to set the judgment aside, the plaintiff's claim was allowed to stand for the full amount. While s. 58(4) referred to making the making of amendments to pleadings, what was before the court was not an attempt by G. to amend a pleading, but to strike out a part of the plaintiff's pleading, which was not even contemplated by the section.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="821952 Ontario Ltd." p2="1002476 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3175" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I642b38005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="821952 Ontario Ltd. v. 1002476 Ontario Inc.">821952 Ontario Ltd. v. 1002476 Ontario Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 3175, [1995] O.J. No. 3283 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff failed to prove a lien but succeeded in its claim for personal judgment against one defendant. As the Master had all the jurisdiction, power and authority of the court to try and completely dispose of the action and all matters and questions arising in connection with the action, he advised counsel that “it would be constructive” in the circumstances of the case to refer issues of quantum and prejudgment interest and costs to the A.D.R. Centre for an attempt at settlement through mediation before embarking for trial.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

62:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 62.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">62:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 62 was amended to reflect the changes to the reference section (s. 58), but remains otherwise substantially unchanged.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>References and the Introduction of the Report</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Under <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, a judge, master or official referee was empowered to try an action to enforce a claim for lien and to otherwise completely dispose of the action. Under s. 35 of the 1897 Act, the master or official referee was empowered to grant judgment in the form prescribed. The decision of the master or official referee could only be challenged through the appeal processes, which applied to judgments. The requirement that a master or official referee issue a ‘Report’ that needed confirmation prior to judgment, was introduced under <ital>The Mechanics Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, by 1969. The Report automatically became confirmed 15 days following its issue unless a motion was brought to oppose the motion. The provision to that effect in s. 62(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was repealed by 1999, c. 12, Sched. B, s. 3; the procedure for confirmation of a Report is now governed by R. 54.09 of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. In 1994, s. 62 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was amended by S.O. 1994, c. 27, to allow the parties to agree to refer the action to a person agreed to by the parties. The person agreed to by the parties has the same powers on a reference as does an associate judge. (See s. 58, above, on reference practice).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Form of Judgment</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 35 of the 1897 Act provided for only one form of judgment to be rendered by each of the master, official referee, or judge. The Act did not provide specifically for variants of the forms. In 1923, the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> was amended to allow the prescribed form of judgment to be varied. This ability to vary the form of judgment has been retained in the present Act, allowing the trier of fact to vary the form to meet the particular circumstances of each case.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>The Right to Sell Materials</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 35 of the 1897 Act provided specifically for the sale of the estate or interest charged with the lien, and also for the sale of any materials located on the subject premises. Further, s. 53 of the 1897 Act authorized the judge, master, or official referee to order the removal of any materials from the subject premises. An order directing the sale or removal of materials is no longer available in the present Act. The requirement that a master or referee's report be confirmed is consistent with similar requirements in Rr. 54 and 55 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. These Rules apply to all references directed under a statute, subject to the provisions of the statute. These Rules also govern procedure on a reference and on motions to oppose confirmations. A party may oppose the confirmation of the Report by motion. Pursuant to s. 70, a party may appeal an order made on a motion opposing the confirmation of a Report in the same manner as a party may appeal from a judgment. On a motion to oppose a confirmation a moving party may not simply ask that the matter be re-tried on its facts. The leading case on the standard of review on such motions is <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Jordan" p2="McKenzie" post.rptr="573" pre.rptr="1987" ref.id="I5625bd30fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Jordan v. McKenzie">Jordan v. McKenzie (1987), 1987 CarswellOnt 573, 26 C.P.C. (2d) 193 (Ont. H.C.); affirmed (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 453, 39 C.P.C. (2d) 217 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. In this case it was held that a judge hearing the motion should not interfere with the findings in the Report unless there has been an error in principle, a jurisdictional error, or a “patent misapprehension of the evidence”. The distinction between a Judgment and a Report is discussed in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19940509" p1="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works" p2="Di Iorio" ref.id="I642b86215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio">Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio (May 9, 1994), Doc. CLA45704/89 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. The relationship between the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> and the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> with respect to references and reports is complicated. Care should be taken to read the Rules and the Act in conjunction with one another. For a discussion of the complicated inter-relationship between s. 62(3) and Rr. 54 and 55, see Master Sandler's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction" p2="Stern" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I642bad305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern">Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern (1997), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>. Master Sandler's decision also offers a detailed analysis of the historical development of Rr. 54 and 55 in conjunction with s. 62(3) and its predecessors.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Order for Sale (s. 62(5))</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It was recognized early in the history of Ontario lien legislation that attaching lien rights to <ital>materials</ital> located on the subject premises created some difficulty. Holmested, writing in <cite finder="legacy" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="If4f67b805dfc11ee9244de2abbdb9a85" short="y"><ital>The Mechanics' Lien Acts of Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia</ital> (Toronto: Dudley & Burns, 1899), at page 156</ref></cite>, stated that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Notwithstanding the generality of the words ‘any materials’, materials which are not subject to the claim of the lien holder, could not be ordered to be sold or removed under this section. Neither is it probable that the jurisdiction hereby conferred would be exercised, except in cases where it would be for the general benefit of all parties interested that the materials should be sold apart from the land.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The present Act no longer allows for the sale or removal of materials from the subject premises. While this may appear to be reasonable given the inherent difficulties noted by Holmested, above, it is noted that other jurisdictions do allow for the sale of materials.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>s. 62(6) Persons Who May Be Let In</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">By operation of ss. 57 and 60 of the present Act, everyone who registers a claim for lien against a premises is a party to an action commenced to enforce any other claim for lien registered against those premises. As the Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> recognized in its Report (annexed as an Appendix herein), this can lead to a situation where a lien claimant does not prove its claim for lien in an action to which it is deemed to be a party. The solution to this problem is to ‘let in’ a claimant to prove its claim for lien after judgment. The first lien act to so allow a lien claimant to be ‘let in’ was <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, s. 35(4). Subsection 62(6) of the present legislation gives the court the authority to allow a lien claimant to be ‘let in’ to prove his claim at any time before the amount(s) realized in the action are distributed. Where the lien claimant proves its claim, the judgment or report is varied accordingly.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 62 sets out a mandatory practice for the entry and enforcement of judgments and reports following trial. Unless a notice of a motion to oppose confirmation is served in the meantime, a report is deemed confirmed pursuant to Ont. R. 54.09, following the 15-day period after notice of filing of the report is given. The judgment or report will generally provide for the payment of the monies deemed owing as a debt or personal judgment, a declaration of holdback liability, an order as to payment of holdback by the owner, and an order that if such payment is not forthcoming the lands will be sold. The terms of such a judicial sale are referred to and approved by the Master, and all proceeds distributed in accordance with s. 65. As outlined above, where individuals with perfected liens do not participate in the trial of a lien because they had not been served with a trial notice, or because an arbitration order had stayed their actions, these individuals may be “let in” under ss. (6) to prove their claim before distribution of any proceeds realized pursuant to the judgment. After distribution there is no remedy.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
62:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 62.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">62:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 62(1)(b)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Li" p2="Zhu" post.rptr="18" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dda0eb0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Li v. Zhu">Li v. Zhu, 2023 CarswellOnt 18, 2023 ONSC 17, 32 C.L.R. (5th) 83 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sought orders, inter alia, dismissing the claim and striking the defence to counterclaim in a lien action, and striking certain defences in a related civil action. The ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90ff13d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 18748, 2019 ONSC 6590, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 193 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> was held not to apply. First, the jurisdictions under which the motions were brought expressly authorized the court to grant “judgments” as per s. 54(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Most importantly, there was a good reason for allowing the court, even one acting under a judgment of reference such as this one, to issue “judgments” on motions for default judgment. By the nature of these motions, there is no opposition, the opposing party is not entitled to participate any further and is bound by deemed admissions. The purpose of the motion is to determine whether the deemed admissions plus any evidence in “support” of the deemed admissions justify a judgment that can be immediately enforced. These were not, in the court's view, the “findings” contemplated by the judgment or order of reference. The “findings” contemplated by a judgment of reference are those that arise from contested proceedings, such as with the contested motion to enforce a settlement in <ital>Prasher</ital>. As the defaulting party is not entitled to participate in the proceedings, there can be no motion to oppose confirmation of a report.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Mount Royal Painting Inc." p2="Unifor Canada Inc." post.rptr="6316" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I677e29a03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Mount Royal Painting Inc. v. Unifor Canada Inc.">Mount Royal Painting Inc. v. Unifor Canada Inc., 2022 ONSC 6316, 2022 CarswellOnt 16269, 32 C.L.R. (5th) 296 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—On motion to oppose a <ital>Construction Act</ital> reference pursuant to (ON) r. 54.09 the court was to give the decision below considerable deference. This is particularly the case where, as here, the reference involved live evidence. The report should be confirmed unless the associate justice made an error in principle, exceeded his jurisdiction, patently misapprehended the evidence, or if the court found the award to be unsatisfactory on all of the evidence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Construction Industries Inc." p2="Festival Hall Dev. Limited" post.rptr="3974" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I642bd4415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Construction Industries Inc. v. Festival Hall Dev. Limited">Ontario Construction Industries Inc. v. Festival Hall Dev. Limited, 2021 ONSC 3974, 2021 CarswellOnt 8403 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were deemed to admit the allegations of fact in the statement of claim by operation of s. 54(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and the master had no difficulty granting entitlement to a default judgment to the plaintiff. However, given the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90ff3ae0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the master could not sign a judgment in the motion, which took place within a reference, but was required to write and deliver a report.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I90ff3ae1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 18748, 2019 ONSC 6590, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 193 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While the Master had jurisdiction to hear a motion to enforce a settlement under R. 49 or for summary judgment under R. 20, the Master was required to embody his findings in a report rather than in a judgment. As a construction lien reference master, the Master was required to embody his findings in a report, which would then be subject to confirmation in the Superior Court pursuant to the Ont. Rules. The distinction between a judgment and a report determines the routes by which the Master's decision may be reviewed and appealed. In particular, once a master issues a report, it is for an objecting party to move before a single judge of the Superior Court to oppose confirmation of the report. The judge's decision on the motion to oppose confirmation is then subject to appeal to a panel of the Divisional Court. An appeal from a final order granted by the Master is to a single judge of the Divisional Court, and thereafter to the Court of Appeal, with leave.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642bfb505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Master, in order to arrive at a decision he found appropriate and in line with his perception of a just result, chose not to follow the cases that were binding on him in issuing the Report on a construction lien reference. It was not right for a decision-maker to attempt to bend the facts and reshape the law to fit a particular result, as judges and masters are bound to go where precedent and other proper emanations of the law direct, having regard to the facts. To do what the Master did was an error in principle.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3015" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I642bfb515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2013 ONSC 3015, 2013 CarswellOnt 7357, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 ONSC 4646, 2013 CarswellOnt 9258, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2014 ONSC 7143, 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Master had held that a defendant's admission as to date on which mortgage funds were advanced was an admission of fact and refused leave to allow its withdrawal. On motion to set aside the report of the Master, the defendant argued that the admission was properly classified as a request for an admission with respect to a legal conclusion, and that when the request to admit is asking for a conclusion of law, one is inherently barred from making an admission of fact. In dismissing the motion, the court noted that the Master gave very detailed reasons as to why leave to withdraw the admission was denied, yet the notice of motion to set aside did not deal with alleged errors of law arising from the refusal to grant leave to withdraw the admission. By virtue of failing to include the Master's reasons for denying their motion in their motion record or referring to these reasons in their subsequent argument, the defendant was requesting that the court set aside the report as a result of error of law in certain <ital>obiter</ital> comments. There was no legal basis to grant the relief requested. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3161" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I642c22605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 3161, 2012 CarswellOnt 6816, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 67 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2013 CarswellOnt 7357, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 9258, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, discussed under s. 78(4).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd." p2="Hyde Park Residences Inc." post.rptr="8015" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I642c22615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc.">X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc., 2013 ONSC 8015, 2013 CarswellOnt 18442 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were the developers of a residential project against which various lien claims were registered. The parties reached an agreement to resolve the claims, under which consent to judgment for the balance of the original lien claims was signed by the defendants to be held in escrow and used in the event of default. The lien claimants agreed to take partial payment and defer the balance of their claims for the time being in order to lift the liens in exchange for a second mortgage and to return to work on the basis that funds to pay them for that additional work would be deposited in trust in advance of performance. In the event of default, the lien claimants were to be entitled to judgment and to enforce their remedies. The agreement was unequivocal, there was no evidence that the lien claimants caused the defendants to default, and the latter gave up their rights to challenge the lien claims. Once the funds stopped flowing, the lien claimants were entitled to leave the job and to enforce their pre-existing liens by signing judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I642c22625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A party desiring the trial of an action to be heard by a judge should set the action down for trial under Ontario Rules 48.01 and 48.02. A party seeking the usual procedure, which is to have a master hear the case, must obtain a judgment of reference under s. 58(1) of the Act to a Toronto master or case management master. Subsection 58(1) and s. 67(6) detail how the motion for this judgment of reference is to be made. Either all parties must consent or notice of the motion must be given to any defending party, which does not consent. Subsection 54(4) deals with non-defending parties who have been noted in default. Ont. Reg. 175, R.R.O. 1990 mandates the form of this judgment of reference in s. 2(16) and Form 16. This Regulation provides that the judgment under s. 58 “shall be in Form 16”. Form 16 contains four specific paragraphs, the most important of which provides that “… this action be referred to the master at Toronto … for trial” who is to issue a report that must then be confirmed. In this regard, reference should be had to s. 62(1)(b) and Ont. Rr. 54.07(1) and 54.09(1). Once the judgment of reference has been obtained, then a party must make a motion to the master without notice, to have a date, time and place fixed for the trial of the action. It is generally the party obtaining that judgment who makes this routine motion. However, in order to validly make this order, there must be a judgment of reference under s. 58(1). The date so fixed is called the “first construction lien pre-trial” but is really the first day of the trial. Once this order has been obtained, the party who obtained it must serve a properly worded notice of trial and a copy of the order on all persons described in s. 60(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Heyday Homes Ltd." p2="Gunraj" post.rptr="429" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I90ff8900f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunraj">Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunraj (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 429, 2004 CarswellOnt 254, 31 C.L.R. (3d) 66 (Master); affirmed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3061, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 169, [2005] O.J. No. 2986 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a detailed examination of the facts, the plaintiff was found to be in fundamental breach of the construction contract by claiming money that it was not entitled to, and by registering unjustified liens, and by failing to proceed with the work. An interim Report was therefore issued providing that the plaintiff had not proved any lien under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, discharging its lien and registration thereof and vacating the certificate of action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Oram" p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="190" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I642c49705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission">Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 190 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and the Rules as to references, (r. 55.02(19)), contemplate only one report from the referee delivered at the conclusion of the hearing. The issuance of an interim report is therefore purely discretionary, to be exercised in rare circumstances including circumstances where one or more liens are challenged as to validity or where all necessary parties agree to payment of a specific sum to an entitled class.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Chartex Construction Ltd.">Supreme Signs Ltd. v. Chartex Construction Ltd. (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 851, 2 C.L.R. (2d) 305 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A necessary defendant was dropped from an action prior to trial under somewhat dubious circumstances. After trial, it became evident that this former defendant was a necessary party if the bond filed to vacate the plaintiff's lien was to be called upon. On appeal, the Divisional Court had no difficulty setting aside the order, dismissing the action against the necessary party, and ordering the trial to continue against that party, on terms.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 62.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">62:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 62(4)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc." p2="ESD Industries Inc." post.rptr="290" pre.rptr="60" ref.id="I642c49725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. ESD Industries Inc.">Baltimore Aircoil of Canada Inc. v. ESD Industries Inc. (2002), 60 O.R. (3d) 290, 2002 CarswellOnt 2286, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 227 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Considerations as to whether or not a person found liable under s. 13 can be obliged to make payment on a judgment or whether they can avoid payment by reason of the operation of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> (“BIA”) are inappropriate considerations for the interpretation of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The scheme set out by the legislature leads to a method by which liability can be imposed upon a corporation for breach of trust and liability can be imposed upon persons in a defined group by reason of their conduct falling within the definition set out in s. 13. The Act deals with issues of the creation of trust and the imposition of liability and not with issues related to the collectability of the judgments or the effect of the BIA. These issues should be left to the Bankruptcy Court in a proceeding brought under that statute.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="York Marble, Tile & Terrazzo Ltd." p2="Exim Group of Canada Inc." post.rptr="110" pre.rptr="41" ref.id="I642c49735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="York Marble, Tile & Terrazzo Ltd. v. Exim Group of Canada Inc.">York Marble, Tile & Terrazzo Ltd. v. Exim Group of Canada Inc. (1998), 41 C.L.R. (2d) 110, [1998] O.J. No. 3828, 1998 CarswellOnt 3730 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A procedural objection was taken to an admitted liability, as found in an interim Master's report. The court's policy to support the efficacy of the long established pre-trial procedure is clearly stated, referring to <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.A. Robinson" p2="Dunwoodco" post.rptr="826" pre.rptr="[1968] 2" ref.id="I642c70805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B.A. Robinson v. Dunwoodco">B.A. Robinson v. Dunwoodco, [1968] 2 O.R. 826</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1973" p1="Kennedy Glass Ltd." p2="Jeskay Construction Ltd." post.rptr="527" pre.rptr="1973" ref.id="I56268080fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Kennedy Glass Ltd. v. Jeskay Construction Ltd.">Kennedy Glass Ltd. v. Jeskay Construction Ltd. (1973), 1973 CarswellOnt 527, [1973] 3 O.R. 493 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction" p2="Stern" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I642c70825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern">Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern (1997), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>. The motion to oppose confirmation of the Master's interim report was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Oram" p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="190" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I642c70835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission">Oram v. Toronto Transit Commission (1997), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 190 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where the general contractor was involved in litigation against the co-defendant transit company, the Master's report requiring the general contractor to pay the lien claims could not be made while litigation was on-going.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19940509" p1="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works" p2="Di Iorio" ref.id="I642c70845fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio">Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio (May 9, 1994), Doc. CLA 45704/89 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In seeking terms on the adjournment of a motion to oppose the confirmation of the Master's report, the plaintiff requested the right to issue and file writs of seizure and sale, that a letter of credit be reduced to the extent of the judgment and that the preparation of the transcript of the evidence be expedited. The request was denied. The Act clearly differentiated between a trial decision and a Master's report, not just the formalities of the manner in which a decision is rendered. To treat the report as having the same effect as a judgment would fly in the face of the provisions of that section, and the court was not prepared to give the plaintiff permission to issue and file writs of seizure and sale. Furthermore, payment should be made after confirmation of the report, not before, and hence no order should be made with respect to the letter of credit. Lastly, there was no indication that counsel for the defendants has not moved promptly, with respect to the transcript, and there was no need to order that it be expedited.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd.">Lake of the Woods Electric (Kenora) Ltd. v. Kenora Prospectors & Miners Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 3820, 31 C.L.R. (2d) 148 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Claimants, for liens in respect of a mill that was being built to process ore from various mining claims of the owner, sought to have the owner's abutting lands included in the judgment, arguing that if they were not, the sale could not comply with the <ital>Planning Act</ital> (Ont.). In holding that the judgments reflected valid liens against the abutting lands, the court noted that there is nothing to prevent the owner from using the several parcels of land as through they constituted one parcel. Additionally, the facts indicated that the work at the parcel containing the mill was merely part of one project, and the mining programme was clearly intended to benefit the entire holding. The owner demonstrated a strong will to bring all of the claims into production, and the intended use was cohesive.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Stucor Construction Ltd.">Brock University v. Stucor Construction Ltd. (2002), [2002] O.J. No. 2300, 2002 CarswellOnt 5728, 33 C.L.R. (3d) 182 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where parties to a lien action have agreed to have disputes arbitrated, an application for an order directing the parties to proceed with the arbitration should succeed and the arbitral issues incorporated into the lien action will likely be otherwise stayed until the completion of the arbitration. See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Cityscape Richmond Corp." p2="Vanbots Construction Corp." post.rptr="196" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I642c97925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cityscape Richmond Corp. v. Vanbots Construction Corp.">Cityscape Richmond Corp. v. Vanbots Construction Corp. (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 196, 2001 CarswellOnt 517 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="Bracknell Corp." post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I642c97935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp. (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 171 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1993), 12 B.L.R. (2d) 113, 110 D.L.R. (4th) 390 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—It is clear that the Act not only anticipates that some issues will be resolved by arbitration, but, in addition, expressly accommodates such resolutions. As a matter of principle, it is difficult to see why, in the context of the Act, any distinction should be drawn between domestic and international arbitration or, for that matter, between domestic and interprovincial arbitration. Accordingly, where an agreement between a contractor and subcontractor provided that any claims arising under it would be arbitrated and that such arbitration would be held in Missouri in accordance with Missouri law, the parties should be held to their agreement and the courts should defer to the arbitrators. Accordingly, the subcontractor's action was stayed as against the contractor, but not as against the owner, who was not party to the agreement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="E.S. Fox Ltd." post.rptr="165" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I642cbea05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. E.S. Fox Ltd.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. E.S. Fox Ltd. (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 165 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1993), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 165 <point>at 168</point> (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Given that parties to a subcontract on an Ontario construction project can agree to arbitrate disputes where the <ital>International Commercial Arbitration Act</ital> applies [see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Automatic Systems Inc." p2="Bracknell Corp." post.rptr="171" pre.rptr="13" ref.id="I642cbea15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp.">Automatic Systems Inc. v. Bracknell Corp. (1994), 13 C.L.R. (2d) 171 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (1993), 12 B.L.R. (2d) 113, 110 D.L.R. (4th) 390</ref></cite>], the matter of whether a binding arbitration agreement in fact existed was to be sent back for disposition by the Ontario Court of Justice.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
