Kilic">Demir v. Kilic, 2018 ONSC 7279, 2018 CarswellOnt 20717, 97 C.L.R. (4th) 191 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2018 ONSC 949, 2018 CarswellOnt 1891, 90 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The standard of review on a contested confirmation of a report from a reference is that on a true appeal and not on the basis of a hearing <ital>de novo</ital>. The result should not be interfered with unless there has been some error in principle demonstrated by the Master's reasons, some absence or excess of jurisdiction, or some patent misapprehension of the evidence. Here, the Motions Judge treated the motion as a <ital>de novo</ital> hearing, in which he substituted his own view of the merits of the case for that of the Master. He found that there was no contract, assessed the case on a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> basis, re-weighed the evidence, and awarded the amount which he thought the plaintiff should receive. This constituted an error of law.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Silver Streams Homes Inc. (Re)" post.rptr="5490" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642cbea35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Silver Streams Homes Inc. (Re)">Silver Streams Homes Inc. (Re), 2018 ONSC 5490, 2018 CarswellOnt 15581, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 80 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The test on an opposition to the confirmation of a referee's report requires considerable deference. In this case, the third party bank made a claim for costs attributable to a reference on full indemnity basis; the referee concluded that bank's participation in the lien claimant litigation contributed little to the litigation and was unnecessary. He limited the bank's recovery to a partial indemnity basis. The lien claimants had brought the bank into the litigation and kept them in it, and for the most part, the bank simply supported the priority position taken by the lien claimants. The referee was a highly experienced expert in this type of litigation and had carriage of the reference to the point of the settlements, and had the costs submissions of both parties before him. He was in a significantly better position than the Court to understand and assess the circumstances in an informed manner notwithstanding the fact that the reference did not proceed to a trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Turano's Home Improvement" p2="Zittell" post.rptr="4428" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642ce5b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Turano's Home Improvement v. Zittell">Turano's Home Improvement v. Zittell, 2018 ONSC 4428, 2018 CarswellOnt 15100, 90 C.L.R. (4th) 42 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 17814 (Ont. S.C.J.); refusing leave to appeal <ital>Turano's Home Improvement Inc. v. Stern</ital>, 2018 ONSC 201, 2018 CarswellOnt 60, 90 C.L.R. (4th) 14 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The standard of review on a contested confirmation of a report from a reference is as an appeal, and not a trial <ital>de novo</ital>. A court hearing a motion opposing confirmation of a construction lien reference report ought not to interfere with the results unless there is an error in principle, an absence of jurisdiction or a patent misapprehension of evidence. The court cited in this regard <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Jordan" p2="McKenzie" post.rptr="573" pre.rptr="1987" ref.id="I5626cea0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Jordan v. McKenzie">Jordan v. McKenzie (1987), 1987 CarswellOnt 573, 26 C.P.C. (2d) 193 (Ont. H.C.); affirmed (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 453, 39 C.P.C. (2d) 217 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="D & M Steel Ltd." p2="51 Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2171" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642ce5b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D & M Steel Ltd. v. 51 Construction Ltd.">D & M Steel Ltd. v. 51 Construction Ltd., 2018 ONSC 2171, 2018 CarswellOnt 5226, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 140 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 8844, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 166 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="D & M Steel Ltd." p2="51 Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2171" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642ce5b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D & M Steel Ltd. v. 51 Construction Ltd.">D & M Steel Ltd. v. 51 Construction Ltd., 2018 ONSC 2171, 2018 CarswellOnt 5226, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 140 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 8844, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 166 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Rule 54.09 permits a party to a reference to oppose the confirmation of the Master's report. The case law establishes that the review of the decision or report is in the nature of an appeal with the onus on the party opposing confirmation to demonstrate that the Master's decision is wrong. The court hearing a motion to oppose the confirmation of a report on a reference ought not to interfere with the results unless there has been some error in principle demonstrated by the Master's reasons, some absence or excess of jurisdiction, or some patent misapprehension of the evidence, and the award should not be disturbed unless it appears to be unsatisfactory on all the evidence. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court cited in support of the above proposition: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Luxterior Design Corp." p2="Gelfand" post.rptr="1621" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I642ce5b45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Luxterior Design Corp. v. (4th) 321 (Ont. Pulcini">Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini, 2016 ONSC 5193, 2016 CarswellOnt 13045, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 56 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Although the motions judge did not formally confirm the report when she dismissed the plaintiff's motion to oppose its confirmation, that confirmation was implicit in the motion judge's rejection of the motion to oppose. Rule 54.09 simply suspends the 15-day confirmation period until any motion to oppose confirmation of the report is filed and determined. Once any such motion is dismissed, the suspension of the 15-day period is automatically lifted and the report is then confirmed by operation of the rule. No other interpretation would be consistent with the practical realities or with common sense.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Parma General Contractors Inc." p2="Aloe" post.rptr="6229" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642d33d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Aloe">Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Aloe, 2015 ONSC 6229, 2015 CarswellOnt 15646, 55 C.L.R. (4th) 316 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court declined to oppose confirmation of the master's report refusing the contractor's request that judgment be satisfied from lien security or, in alternative, for order directing new trial on reference. The allegations of error on the part of the Master centred on matters of fact, weighing of evidence and analyzing credibility, and the Court would not interfere with factual conclusions based on a difference of opinion over the weight to be assigned to evidence and underlying facts, nor would it differently assess the credibility of witnesses. There was no palpable or overriding error that would permit this Court to interfere with the careful analysis and conclusions of the Master.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">[<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Subsection 62(3), which set out the process for confirmation of the Master's Report, was repealed by 1999, c. 12, Sched. B, s. 3.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Men At Work General Contractors Ltd." p2="MacDonald" post.rptr="3413" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642d5ae05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Men At Work General Contractors Ltd. v. MacDonald">Men At Work General Contractors Ltd. v. MacDonald, 2015 ONSC 3413, 2015 CarswellOnt 8545, 49 C.L.R. (4th) 309 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2013 ONSC 4211, 2013 CarswellOnt 8616 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The decision of an experienced construction lien Master is entitled to deference on a motion to oppose confirmation of his Report. Here, the court set aside the decision of the motion judge and substituted in its place an order confirming the Master's Report, subject to a minor correction of an arithmetical error.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Xhebraj" p2="Bassi" post.rptr="2781" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642d5ae15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Xhebraj v. Bassi">Xhebraj v. Bassi, 2015 ONSC 2781, 2015 CarswellOnt 6301 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 12406 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2016 CarswellOnt 2608 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—On a motion to oppose confirmation of a report on a reference, the results should not be interfered with unless there has been an error in principle, an absence or excess of jurisdiction, or some patent misapprehension of the evidence. Unless it seems unsatisfactory on all of the evidence, the award should not be disturbed. Further, the onus of proof is on the party opposing confirmation, and where questions of fact are involved and the Master has seen and heard the witnesses, the conclusions of the Master will not be readily interfered with.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="503" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642d5ae25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 503, 2015 CarswellOnt 2329, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2013 ONSC 485, 2013 CarswellOnt 549, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 13 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion or cross-motion brought pursuant to Rule 54.09 is to be dealt with substantially as an appeal from the Report. The matter is not to be retried. The Master's Report will not be interfered with unless there had been some error of principle demonstrated by the Master's reasons, some absence or excess of jurisdiction or some patent misapprehension of the evidence. The award should not be disturbed unless it appears to be unsatisfactory on all of the evidence. Here, considering all of the record, there was no patent misapprehension of the evidence on the part of the Master which would permit the court to interfere with her decision.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pegah Construction Ltd." p2="Panterra Mansions Joint Venture Corp." post.rptr="3966" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I642d5ae35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pegah Construction Ltd. v. Panterra Mansions Joint Venture Corp.">Pegah Construction Ltd. v. Panterra Mansions Joint Venture Corp., 2014 ONSC 3966, 2014 CarswellOnt 8889, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 58 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List]); affirming 2013 ONSC 3226, 2013 CarswellOnt 7268, 21 C.L.R. (4th) 175 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 ONSC 6719, 2013 CarswellOnt 14956, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 227 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The standard of review applicable upon a motion to oppose the confirmation of a report of a master of a trial of a reference is that on a true appeal and not on the basis of a hearing <ital>de novo</ital>. The result should not be interfered with unless there has been some error in principle demonstrated by the master's reasons, some absence or excess of jurisdiction, or some patent misapprehension of the evidence. Where the decision under review involves the interpretation of a contract, the fact-finding functions involved in such an exercise, such as the determination of the factual context in which the contract was negotiated and considerations of extrinsic evidence, are to be addressed from the palpable and overriding error perspective. In its other aspects, the contractual interpretation exercise is essentially a legal one attracting a standard of review closer to the “correctness” end of the spectrum. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="International Wall Systems Ltd." p2="English Lane Residential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="14415" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I642d5ae45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="International Wall Systems Ltd. v. English Lane Residential Developments Ltd.">International Wall Systems Ltd. v. English Lane Residential Developments Ltd., 2011 CarswellOnt 14415 (Ont. S.C.J.) <point>at paras. 39-40</point>; additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 2889, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 234 (Ont. Economical Insurance Group">Zeitoun v. Economical Insurance Group, 2008 CarswellOnt 2576 (Ont. Div. Ct.) <point>at para. 34</point>; additional reasons 2008 CarswellOnt 3734 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2009 CarswellOnt 2665 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Jordan" p2="McKenzie" post.rptr="573" pre.rptr="1987" ref.id="I562743d0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Jordan v. McKenzie">Jordan v. McKenzie (1987), 1987 CarswellOnt 573, 26 C.P.C. (2d) 193 (Ont. H.C.); affirmed (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 453, 39 C.P.C. (2d) 217 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd." p2="Ding" post.rptr="2319" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I91009a70f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding">Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2319, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Master); affirmed 2004 CarswellOnt 4167 (S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 5401, 39 C.L.R. (3d) 150, 193 O.A.C. 145 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The owners unsuccessfully sought an order denying confirmation of the Report or setting aside or varying it. The Master had broad powers to award costs under ss. 86 and 58(4) and her award should only be set aside if it was plainly wrong. She was entitled to hold that the action would have ended at the outset if the owners had admitted liability and paid the amount owing into court. The Master was in the best position to decide the facts and to determine bad faith on the part of the owners since she was involved on a continuous basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Ontario Electrical Construction" p2="Stern" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I642d81f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern">Ontario Electrical Construction v. Stern (1997), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The intention of the drafters of s. 62(3) was merely to provide for confirmation in whatever manner was provided by the prevailing rule of court. If this rule changes, then s. 62(3) must be read and understood as providing for confirmation at the expiration of the 15-day period next following the date that is to be considered the “trigger date” by whatever process is then contemplated by the prevailing rule of court. The prevailing rule, as of 1985, provided for service of a copy of the report and the filing of another copy of the report with proof of service, as a prelude to confirmation by the expiry of the fifteen-day time period. Therefore, the 15-day time period in which to serve a motion to oppose confirmation commences to run from the time of the giving of notice of the process contemplated by rule 54.09(1)(b), namely, a copy of the report itself. This interpretation provides for the same procedure for the confirmation of reports in both lien and non-lien references.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works" p2="Di Iorio" post.rptr="295" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I642da9005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio">Dominion Sheet Metal & Roofing Works v. Di Iorio (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 295 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The standard of review in opposing confirmation of a Master's report is well settled: it is one of error in principle, excess or absence of jurisdiction or patent misapprehension of the evidence. The court in this case, citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Jordan" p2="McKenzie" post.rptr="573" pre.rptr="1987" ref.id="I56276ae0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Jordan v. McKenzie">Jordan v. McKenzie (1987), 1987 CarswellOnt 573, 26 C.P.C. (2d) 193 (Ont. H.C.); affirmed (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 453, 39 C.P.C. (2d) 217 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, affirmed these principles on a motion to oppose confirmation under r. 54.09. It is a relevant consideration that the Master carefully deliberated on the evidence as a whole (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19931130" p1="Regan" p2="Regan-Graham Ltd." post.rptr="2877" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I642da9025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Regan v. Regan-Graham Ltd.">Regan v. Regan-Graham Ltd. (November 30, 1993), Doc. RE 994/89, [1993] O.J. No. 2877 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (September 16, 1994), Doc CA C17426 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Dorsam Investments Ltd." p2="Counsel Trust Co." post.rptr="76" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I642da9035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dorsam Investments Ltd. v. Counsel Trust Co.">Dorsam Investments Ltd. v. Counsel Trust Co. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 76 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A prior mortgagee paid $13,000 to settle certain lien claims, and added that amount to the mortgage debt pursuant to a clause in the mortgage. A subsequent mortgagee, whose mortgage was registered prior to the registration of the liens, contested the matter before the master on the basis that it had priority over the liens. The subsequent mortgagee knew nothing of the settlement when it was made and had not been given notice of the informal settlement meeting convened by the mortgagee. The Master approved the prior mortgagee's actions, but the chambers judge refused to approve that part of the Master's report, and the prior mortgagee's appeal was dismissed. There was no evidence before the Master that any of these liens had any actual value. The lien claimants might have grossly exaggerated their claims, and there was no evidence on which the master could have held that the settlement was proper in the circumstances. The Master made an error in principle, and the chambers judge reached the correct result.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Haas Homes Ltd." p2="March Road Gym & Health Club Inc." post.rptr="2847" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I642da9045fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc.">Haas Homes Ltd. v. March Road Gym & Health Club Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 2847, 2003 CarswellOnt 2687, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 243 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As a result of a retroactive order made in the exercise of the court's inherent powers, a construction lien trial before the Master was transmogrified into a reference and his reasons for judgment into a report. A motion was subsequently taken by the applicant to oppose confirmation of the Master's report on a reference under R. 54.09 of the Ont. <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. A motion to oppose confirmation of a master's report was not a rehearing, but rather was in the nature of an appeal. The court was not to interfere with the result unless there has been some error in principle demonstrated by the Master's reasons, some absence or excess or jurisdiction, or some patent misapprehension of the evidence. Here, the report was not confirmed as the Master made an error in law in concluding that the applicant was a statutory owner within the meaning of s. 1(1) of the Act.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 63.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">63:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The issue of personal judgment where a claimant fails to prove its lien dates back to s. 48 of <ital>An Act Respecting Liens of Mechanics, Wage-Earners and Others</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35. This same provision was included in the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, s. 44. Pursuant to these prior Acts, a personal judgment was allowed where a lien claimant failed to prove its lien. The present <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, s. 55, allows a lien claimant to combine certain breach of contract claims with a lien claim. As a consequence s. 63 now allows for personal judgment whether or not the lien claimant proves its lien (see the Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital>, annexed herein).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Under s. 63, a lien claimant may acquire personal judgment “upon any ground relating to the claim that is disclosed by the evidence against any party to the action that may be due to the claimant and that the claimant might have recovered in a proceeding against that party”. On a strict reading, this might include a personal judgment for breach of trust under the Act (as opposed to a judgment <ital>in rem</ital>) notwithstanding that a party may not join a breach of trust claim with a lien action pursuant to s. 50(2). It might also include a personal judgment for amounts owed on a contract not described by s. 55(1) of the Act. The scope of the judgment available under s. 63 has not been fully explored in the case law. The discretion of the judge, master or referee to award a personal judgment is considerable and has been expanded since s. 63 came into force. It was originally thought that the principles to be applied in determining if personal judgment should be granted were not affected by the amendments allowing a personal judgment, whether or not the lien claimant failed to prove its lien. Master Sandler stated the original principle substantially as follows in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="EMCO Supply" p2="Anduhyaun Inc." post.rptr="91" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I642dd0105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc.">EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc. (1998), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 91 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>: personal judgment could only be granted where all of the evidence had been tendered as at the time it was determined that the claimant did not have a valid claim for lien. The decisions of Master Sischy in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Tilar Roofing Ltd." p2="John Boddy Developments Ltd." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I642dd0115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tilar Roofing Ltd. v. John Boddy Developments Ltd.">Tilar Roofing Ltd. v. John Boddy Developments Ltd. (1986), 20 C.L.R. 161 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite> and the Divisional Court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd." p2="Samet" post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I642dd0125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet">Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet (1991), 46 C.L.R. 317, 4 O.R. (3d) 771, 83 D.L.R. (4th) 574, 52 O.A.C. 180 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> have held that the court has no discretion to allow a claim in contract to continue where the lien action had been dismissed. Subsequent cases, however, have recognized some discretion in granting a personal judgment (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="612354 Ontario Ltd." p2="Tonecraft Corp." post.rptr="799" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I9100e890f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp.">612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp. (1991), 1991 CarswellOnt 799, 5 O.R. (3d) 764, 47 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Eurocor Ltd." p2="Vernich" post.rptr="208" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I642df7215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich">Eurocor Ltd. v. Vernich (1992), O.R. (3d) 631, 2 C.L.R. (2d) 208 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co." p2="Iona Corp." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="12" ref.id="I91010fa0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co. v. Iona Corp.">Golden City Ceramic & Tile Co. v. Iona Corp. (1993), 12 C.L.R. (2d) 1, 106 D.L.R. (4th) 532 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>). Master Sandler has concluded that the current practice is as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Once a lien claimant is found to not have an enforceable claim for lien, the trier of fact has the discretion to split the action and allow the claimant to continue with its contract claim. Alternatively, the trier of fact may refuse to so split the action, and may require the claimant to commence a subsequent action to perfect its claim.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Master Sandler followed this practice in <ital>EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc.</ital> and refused to exercise discretion to grant personal judgment where the claimant had failed to prove its lien and had the right to commence an independent action for breach of the trust under the Act. The reader is also referred to the broad jurisdiction conferred upon the lien court by s. 57 and the consequences of a motion under s. 46.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="13245" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I677ffe603b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Pre-Eng Contracting Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 13245, 2024 ONSC 4772, 2024 A.C.W.S. 4526, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.); varying 2022 ONSC 3458, 2022 CarswellOnt 8320, 36 C.L.R. (5th) 190 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2022 ONSC 6627, 2022 CarswellOnt 17069 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Divisional Court held that the trial judge erred in law in finding that separate claims for lien must be registered in respect to separate subcontracts between the same parties for the same improvement. A single claim for lien could preserve the plaintiff's lien rights arising from two separate contracts relating to the same property. The trial judge had then found the main contract to be out of time, but held the court had jurisdiction to award a personal judgment on the plaintiff's breach of contract claim for that unpreserved portion of the claim, pursuant to s. 63. The Divisional Court held that, despite being in error as to expiration of the plaintiff's lien, the trial judge had correctly applied s. 63, even though that issue ceased to have force in light of the conclusion that the plaintiff was entitled to enforce its lien and was not restricted to a “personal judgment” in any event. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This decision was decided under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Strada Aggregates Inc." p2="YSL Residences Inc." post.rptr="16984" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I642df7265fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc.">Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 16984, 2020 ONSC 7034, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motion of the plaintiff subcontractor in a lien action, brought an <ital>ex parte</ital> for an order that the defendant contractors and owner be noted in default, and for default judgment against them, was granted in part. The plaintiff sought personal judgment for the unpaid amounts claimed as owing for its supply of aggregates to the subject improvement. The defendants were operated commonly by the same individual, and there were contracts between the plaintiff and contractors, but no privity of contract with the registered owner of the premises. The claims for personal judgment against the contractors as pleaded were claims for breach of contract contemplated by s. 3(2) of O. Reg. 302/18 and properly joined in the lien action. However, the owner's liability to the subcontractor was limited to the holdbacks that the owner was required to retain, and such liability was further limited only to proven valid liens against the owner's interest in the premises. Absent any pleaded contract between the plaintiff and owner, or any pleading of the mutual control and domination argued on the motion, the statement of claim did not support any claim against the owner permitted by s. 3(2) of O. Reg. 302/18, in addition to claimed holdback liability. Although the plaintiff asserted a general claim of unjust enrichment against all the defendants, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tremblar" p2="1839563" post.rptr="6302" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I642e1e305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tremblar v. 1839563">Tremblar v. 1839563, 2020 ONSC 6302, 2020 CarswellOnt 15163 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> had recently confirmed that a subcontractor had no claim of unjust enrichment as against an owner. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See s. 51 the Divisional Court ruling in <ital>Tremblar v. 1839563 Ontario</ital>, which noted that unjust enrichment required, inter alia, the absence of a “juristic reason” for the enrichment.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="W.S. Nicholls Construction Inc." p2="Barton-Malow Canada, Inc." post.rptr="5082" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I642e1e315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="W.S. Nicholls Construction Inc. v. Barton-Malow Canada, Inc.">W.S. Nicholls Construction Inc. v. Barton-Malow Canada, Inc., 2019 ONSC 5082, 2019 CarswellOnt 14068, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 153 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 15656 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To suggest that s. 63 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> permits claims based on unjust enrichment and <ital>quantum meruit</ital> in the circumstances of this action would be contrary to the plain reading of section 55(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and the decision of the Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc." p2="Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd." post.rptr="305" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I642e45405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc. v. Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd.">Yorkwest Plumbing Supply Inc. v. Nortown Plumbing (1998) Ltd., 2016 ONCA 305, 2016 CarswellOnt 6411, 131 O.R. (3d) 149, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 1, 398 D.L.R. (4th) 251, 348 O.A.C. 47 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: Former section 55(1) was repealed without substitution by 2017, c. 24, s. 42(2), such that a lien claim under the current <ital>Construction Act</ital> can be joined with any claim whatsoever.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dew Point Insulation Systems Inc." p2="Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="2759" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I642e45415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dew Point Insulation Systems Inc. v. Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd.">Dew Point Insulation Systems Inc. v. Aqua Mechanical Contracting Ltd., 2017 ONSC 2759, 2017 CarswellOnt 12707, 83 C.L.R. (4th) 175 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The grounds upon which a lien claimant may make a claim for interest are found in the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, and in sections 55 and 63 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Whether an award for interest arises out of a judgment, or is otherwise awarded pursuant to the wider discretion of the court under s. 128 and s. 130 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, the recovery of such an award for interest is not precluded by the <ital>Act</ital>. The treatment of interest and costs in excess of that recoverable under the <ital>Act</ital> should be treated as a collection matter in the absence of competing creditors. The debt, including the lien amount, costs and interest, was accordingly to be paid out of the pooled security held in court. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In reaching its decision, the court adopted the reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="P & D Holdings Ltd." p2="Alta Surety Co." post.rptr="2937" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I910136b1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co.">P & D Holdings Ltd. v. Alta Surety Co. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 2937, 29 C.L.R. (2d) 60, 30 O.R. (3d) 97, 92 O.A.C. 203, 138 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. Presumably, on a reading of <ital>P & D Holdings Ltd.</ital> “the pooled security” referenced by the court here refers only to the costs portions of the bonds put as security, not that portion of the bond securing the lien itself.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="N.K.P. Painting Inc." p2="Boyko" post.rptr="3016" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I642e45435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="N.K.P. Painting Inc. v. Boyko">N.K.P. Painting Inc. v. Boyko, 2016 ONSC 3016, 2016 CarswellOnt 7332, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 344 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 8953 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor's claim against the owner for unjust enrichment was allowed on appeal, where the owner retained the 10% holdback but received 100% of the benefit of the improvement. The ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc." p2="Country Cottage Living Inc." post.rptr="2289" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I642e45445fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc. v. Country Cottage Living Inc.">Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc. v. Country Cottage Living Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 2289, 93 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 2783, 93 C.L.R. (3d) 166 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, was distinguished in that there, the general contractor liened the owner's property while the subcontractor did not, and specifically extricated itself from the general contractor's main action. The resolution in <ital>Barrie Trim</ital> presupposed a valid claim for lien having been made under the Act. Here, the general contractor did not lien and was in fact bankrupt.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Essa Carpentry Inc." p2="Falconwin Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="2989" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I642e45455fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Essa Carpentry Inc. v. Falconwin Holdings Ltd.">Essa Carpentry Inc. v. Falconwin Holdings Ltd., 2014 ONSC 2989, 2014 CarswellOnt 6361, 36 C.L.R. (4th) 142 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The action having proceeded as a civil action pursuant to s. 63, the plaintiff's motion to strike the defendant's pleadings was granted in part. The defendant's repeated breaches of court orders and failure to provide a reasonable explanation for failing to produce the documents required promptly or at all, must attract significant sanctions. Otherwise reference orders under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, which provide a form of case management, would be ineffectual and the mandate of the Act to provide an expeditious summary disposition of construction disputes, would be defeated.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Butko" p2="Ratayeva" post.rptr="1102" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642e45465fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Butko v. Ratayeva">Butko v. Ratayeva, 2015 ONSC 1102, 2015 CarswellOnt 8388, 47 C.L.R. (4th) 344 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—This provision is useful when a lien claim is preserved or perfected out of time but there is a chance of success on the claim as a personal judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dean Construction Co." p2="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4629" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I642e45475fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd.">Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd., 2011 ONSC 4629, 2011 CarswellOnt 8977, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 240 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2011 CarswellOnt 8862 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A claim for standby charges for men and equipment required to be kept on the site as a consequence of the differences in soil conditions from those represented by the owner is no different than charges for the supply of materials, men and equipment for actual work necessitated by the differences in soil conditions or rental equipment kept on site, and can be recovered in a lien action, without recourse to a personal action under s. 63.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc." p2="Country Cottage Living Inc." post.rptr="2289" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I642e6c505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc. v. Country Cottage Living Inc.">Barrie Trim & Mouldings Inc. v. Country Cottage Living Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 2289, 93 C.L.R. (3d) 161 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at 2010 CarswellOnt 2783, 93 C.L.R. (3d) 166 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A supplier of goods or materials who chooses not to shelter under a valid lien cannot seek a remedy against the owner directly on the basis of unjust enrichment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Coldmatic Refrigeration of Canada Ltd." p2="1234777 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="532" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I642e93605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Coldmatic Refrigeration of Canada Ltd. v. 1234777 Ontario Inc.">Coldmatic Refrigeration of Canada Ltd. v. 1234777 Ontario Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 532, 2004 CarswellOnt 474 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> permitted “personal” claims to be annexed to the liened claim, and both costs and prejudgment interest would therefore be payable out of the entire fund in court, including accrued interest, whether or not such sums were originally paid in as part of the claim, or costs, or both. Here, the plaintiff was the contracting builder and the defendant was the contracting owner, and payment out would not result in any unfairness or prejudice to a third party potential lien claimant or third party bonding company. Nevertheless, the plaintiff unnecessarily conceded that pre-judgment interest was not payable out of the funds in court, although the court would have likely reached a different conclusion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="EMCO Supply" p2="Anduhyaun Inc." post.rptr="91" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I642e93615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc.">EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc. (1998), 36 C.L.R. (2d) 91 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The definition of “lien claimant” within the meaning of s. 63 only requires the “person” to have what purports to be a preserved lien, that is, a claim for lien that has been registered, and does not require that lien to be validly or properly preserved. A non-plaintiff but validly sheltering lien claimant, whose lien is ultimately found to be out of time, and thus improperly preserved, can, as a matter of law, still seek to obtain personal judgment on its contract claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd." p2="Samet" post.rptr="317" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I642e93625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet">Benjamin Schultz & Associates Ltd. v. Samet (1991), 46 C.L.R. 317, 4 O.R. (3d) 771, 83 D.L.R. (4th) 574, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>Schultz (Benjamin) & Associates Ltd. v. Samet)</ital> 52 O.A.C. 180 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Sections 38 and 63, which preserve legal and equitable remedies of the court and allow it to award a personal judgment whether or not a lien is proven, do not render ss. 37 and 46 inoperative.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="612354 Ontario Ltd." p2="Tonecraft Corp." post.rptr="799" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I910184d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp.">612354 Ontario Ltd. v. Tonecraft Corp. (1991), 1991 CarswellOnt 799, 5 O.R. (3d) 764, 47 C.L.R. 229 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The expiry of a claim for lien prior to trial does not oust the jurisdiction of the court to hear an action for personal judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Favot Construction Ltd." p2="Maplecrest Developments Inc." post.rptr="34" pre.rptr="42" ref.id="I642e93645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Favot Construction Ltd. v. Maplecrest Developments Inc.">Favot Construction Ltd. v. Maplecrest Developments Inc. (1990), 42 C.L.R. 34 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff filed a lien claim against the defendant in respect of a construction project, and subsequently issued a statement of claim for the same amount. In pre-trial proceedings, the plaintiff's president admitted that the construction of bulkheads was a “freebie” and would not be claimed as an extra under the contract. Upon realizing that the defendant intended to pursue its counterclaim for damages against the plaintiff in respect of deficiencies in the construction of the bulkheads, the plaintiff applied for leave to amend its statement of claim to allege extras in respect of the bulkheads, thereby increasing the claim. Held, the motion was adjourned <ital>sine die</ital> to allow the plaintiff to amend its motion. The court has no jurisdiction under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to increase the amount of the lien claim. However, the court may award personal judgment to the extent the amount claimed in the statement of claim exceeds the lien claim. The plaintiff could amend its motion to seek an alternative personal claim and judgment in respect of the extras. No distinction is made in this provision between services or materials supplied as part of a contract or as extras thereto.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Tilar Roofing Ltd." p2="John Boddy Developments Ltd." post.rptr="161" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I642e93655fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tilar Roofing Ltd. v. John Boddy Developments Ltd.">Tilar Roofing Ltd. v. John Boddy Developments Ltd. (1986), 20 C.L.R. 161 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Although s. 63 allows the court to give personal judgment to a lien claimant whether he proves his lien or not, this is not so where it is established in advance of trial that a lien has expired for failure to perfect it.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Irving Oil Ltd." p2="M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I642e93665fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Irving Oil Ltd. v. M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd.">Irving Oil Ltd. v. M.D.G. Holdings (Bay) Ltd. (1985), 20 C.L.R. 26 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—If s. 63 is interpreted to restrict recovery to a “lien claimant”, <ital>i.e.</ital>, a person with a preserved or perfected lien, that result would not be consonant with s. 51. If ss. 51 and 63 are read together, and some meaning is assigned to the words “whether he proves his lien or not” in s. 63, the apparent conflict between those words and “lien claimant” may be resolved in one of two ways in order to permit a claimant whose lien has failed to claim under s. 63. First, a party to the trial of an action is a “lien claimant” until the court decides that it is not. Accordingly, it is entitled, in an action, to assert its claim to a personal judgment “whether [it] proves [its] lien or not”. Second, bearing in mind the extent of the powers described in s. 51 and the words, “whether he proves his lien or not” in s. 63 it follows that the Legislature intended that the words “lien claimant” in s. 63 be given their normal meaning, that is, a person asserting a right to a lien, rather than the definition in s. 1(1).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
64:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 64.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">64:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section is substantially similar to s. 45 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which was first introduced in identical form in s. 39 of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69. The section is made necessary by the combination of ss. 57, 60(2) and 60(4) of the present Act. These sections combine to make anyone who has a claim for lien against, or registered interest in, the subject premises, and all execution creditors of the owner, parties to the action. Section 64 recognizes that amounts owed to a lien holder may not have become due or payable prior to the trial of the action or distribution of the proceeds of sale. Newfoundland and Labrador's s. 39 is to similar effect.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section permits an individual who has a perfected lien claim to participate in the proceeds of sale even if the debt was not, strictly speaking, payable at the time of sale or distribution. Such a situation might arise when a particularly long payment period is provided for in the contract or where there are multiple head contracts and finishing trade liens well after the initial trades. Unless that individual's claim is dealt with at the same time as the other claimants, lien rights could be lost. Given the length of time it takes to bring a lien claim to trial, this section rarely has application in practice.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
65:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 65.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">65:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 65(1) first appeared in virtually identical form as s. 37(2) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30. Subsections 62(2) to (5) can be traced back to s. 33(5) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, 1896, S.O. 1896, c. 35. The provision was first enacted as a separate section in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69, s. 38.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 65 invests the lien court with the necessary authority to close a judicial sale in multi-party litigation and to deal with the proceeds of that sale. Subsections (2)–(5) set out the rules regulating the administration of the proceeds of sale. If the proceeds are insufficient to satisfy the judgment and costs, a personal judgment will be given against any defendants found to be liable. This places the responsibility of a falling market upon an owner to the extent of any judgment against it for holdback, even if the judgment is in favour of a party with whom the owner had no privity of contract.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
