C.30, s. 67.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">67:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 67 was repealed and moved as follows:</para.text></para><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Former s. 67(1) (summary procedure) is now found in s. 50(3), unchanged.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Former s. 67(2) (interlocutory steps) is now found in s. 13 of O. Reg. 302/18.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Former s. 67(3) (application of rules of court) is now found in s. 50(2).</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Former s. 67(4) (technical assistance) is now found in s. 14 of O. Reg. 302/18.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Former ss. 67(5) (representation) and 67(6) (manner of making motion) were repealed without replacement</para.text></para></list.item></list></list.item></list></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
68:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 68.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">68:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">By the early 1930s it had become apparent that lien legislation in Ontario should deal with the possibility that the value of the premises might depreciate in value notwithstanding the work, service and materials supplied by lien holders. Where a project had been abandoned, for example, the interests of lien claimants could be better protected in some cases if some party took control of the premises and performed necessary improvements to preserve and enhance the market value of the premises. Accordingly, by s. 8 of <ital>An Act to Amend the Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19, persons having an interest in the subject premises were permitted to apply to appoint a receiver or trustee to collect rents or profits and manage, sell or lease the premises. The 1932 legislation is substantially similar to s. 68 of the present Act, with the exception that the present Act does not specifically refer to the collection of rents and profits. The right of the trustee to collect rents and profits is part of the receiver's powers as referred to in s. 68(2) of the Act. In addition, the present Act contemplates that a trustee be appointed, and that the trustee would perform the duties of a receiver. The prior legislation allowed for either a receiver or a trustee to be appointed such that, in some circumstances, the management of the premises could become complicated. It has been established that, as at common law, a trustee appointed under this section will have the onus of satisfying the Court that his efforts and resulting charges were justified (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Dufferin-Custom Concrete" p2="Carling/Maplehurst Developments Inc." post.rptr="2306" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I91022110f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Dufferin-Custom Concrete v. Carling/Maplehurst Developments Inc.">Dufferin-Custom Concrete v. Carling/Maplehurst Developments Inc. (1993), [1993] O.J. No. 2306, 1993 CarswellOnt 239 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section provides for the appointment of a trustee, on motion, to manage, sell or lease the premises, complete the improvement, or take other appropriate action. Such motions are granted on terms appropriate to the given case. A trustee appointed under this section will require the leave of the court to sell, lease or mortgage a property, or to take any other steps not enumerated in the section (subs. (2)). The court is authorized to make any order that is necessary to facilitate those actions (subs. (5)). A sale is subject to any encumbrances that the court directs (subs. (4)) and any disposition of the premises must comply with the provisions of the <ital>Planning Act</ital>. Pursuant to subs. (3), any liens on a property are also a charge on the net rents and proceeds received by the trustee, after normal management expenses have been deducted. These proceeds should be paid into court and treated in the same manner as proceeds of sale under s. 65. Any person having a lien or an interest in the property may apply for the order. The remedy is available at any stage of the project, from the date the first liens arise to the sale of the completed project. Evidence that a lien claimant's interest will be at risk appears to be a precondition to the application of a receiver under this section (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Royaledge Industries Inc." p2="Perma-Roof Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="160" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I642f2fa15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royaledge Industries Inc. v. Perma-Roof Ontario Ltd.">Royaledge Industries Inc. v. Perma-Roof Ontario Ltd. (1991), 44 C.L.R. 160, 2 O.R. (3d) 488 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). Once appointed, however, the courts may be reluctant to interfere with the discretion of a trustee to implement the order of the Court (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19890405" p1="Dinacon Construction Ltd." p2="743189 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="548" pre.rptr="[1989]" ref.id="I642f2fa25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dinacon Construction Ltd. v. 743189 Ontario Ltd.">Dinacon Construction Ltd. v. 743189 Ontario Ltd. (April 5, 1989), Doc. 11917/89, 11747/88, 11624/88, 11626/88, 12148/89, 11948/89, 12284/89, [1989] O.J. No. 548 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 68(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="144 Park Ltd., Re" post.rptr="6735" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I642f2fa35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="144 Park Ltd., Re">144 Park Ltd., Re, 2015 ONSC 6735, 2015 CarswellOnt 16684, 32 C.B.R. (6th) 113, 48 C.L.R. (4th) 212 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List]); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 18697 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—In seeking to terminate the purchase agreements of certain pre-sales and parking units that had not yet closed on a condominium development, a trustee appointed under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had to take into account the equitable situation of all stakeholders. In all of the circumstances, the trustee's request to terminate the purchase agreements was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Romspen Investment Corp." p2="6711162 Canada Inc." post.rptr="2781" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I642f56b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Romspen Investment Corp. v. 6711162 Canada Inc.">Romspen Investment Corp. v. 6711162 Canada Inc., 2014 ONSC 2781, 2014 CarswellOnt 5836, 13 C.B.R. (6th) 136, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 167 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List]); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 3480, 2014 CarswellOnt 7939, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 193 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—At issue was the control of the development and/or realization of a partially completed condominium project, where the plaintiff's loan to the respondent had matured and not been repaid. On application by the plaintiff, the court ordered the appointment of a receiver and construction lien trustee over the respondents under s. 243(1) of the <ital>Bankrupcty and Insolvency Act</ital>, s. 101 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> and s. 68 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The making of an initial order under s. 11.02 of the <ital>Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act</ital> was denied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of)" p2="Acro Capital Inc." post.rptr="1038" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I642f56b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc.">700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1038, 2004 CarswellOnt 986, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 47 (S.C.J. [Commercial List]); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 1796 (S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The defendant solicitors acted for the developer owner, and after the sale of certain condominiums was completed, the proceeds were received by the solicitors and a sum paid out of them to the defendant company. The plaintiff was subsequently appointed trustee under s. 68 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to act as receiver and manager of the developer owner's assets, property and undertakings. The Plaintiff claimed against the defendants on the basis that the payment out of the proceeds was a breach of trust for which the solicitors were liable. The latter unsuccessfully moved under Ont. R. 21 to strike out the Statement of Claim against them and dismiss the action as showing no reasonable cause of action. A construction lien trustee had the authority to claim against the defendant solicitors for alleged breaches of the Act's trust provisions when it was not the bankrupt, but the contractor, who was the beneficiary of those trusts. Part II of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> declared how the trusts came into effect and were discharged by payment and declared who are the beneficiaries, but did nothing to alter the law as to the general nature of the trust and the normal right and duties of the trustee. The Act contained no definition of “trust” or “trustee” and it was to be assumed that these terms were to be read in their normal meaning in law, that is, as carrying the rights and obligations of a trustee under the common law. Under ordinary trust law, the trustee was the legal owner of the <ital>corpus</ital> of the trust and had the right to sue any one who deprived the trust of its property or who damages the trust property in any way. The trustee could sell the <ital>corpus</ital> and give good title to it to a <ital>bona fide</ital> purchaser for value without notice, even though he lacked an actual power to sell. Equity took the view that one with title, who contracted in his own name, had full capacity to act. The right of the beneficiary was generally a personal one, to compel the Trustee to properly discharge his duties as trustee. In addition, the trustee may also bring an action on behalf of the trust to recover the trust property, except as against a <ital>bona fide</ital> purchaser for value. This may be regarded as a beneficiary's remedy, or as a trustee's remedy, which the beneficiary is permitted to bring on behalf of the trust in particular circumstances. But the evolution of this remedy has not deprived the trustee of the rights of ownership.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20030625" p1="Dick Engineering Inc." p2="Thermo Tech Waste Systems Inc." post.rptr="5132" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I642f56b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dick Engineering Inc. v. Thermo Tech Waste Systems Inc.">Dick Engineering Inc. v. Thermo Tech Waste Systems Inc. (June 25, 2003), Doc. 02-6071, [2003] O.J. No. 5132 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court declined to appoint a receiver for the owner landlord under the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There were a number of debts owed by the landlord, including a large tax bill. Among the factors considered in reaching this decision were: a) the existence of a dispute as to the claim of lien itself, which was in question; b) the existing tenant had obligations under the lease to pay taxes and preserve the grounds and equipment; c) the nature of the landlord's business involved procuring and holding a tenant in a very complex and specialized endeavour. In light of this, the landlord had not demonstrated irresponsible management, and as the number of tenants for such a specialized endeavour would be few, the appointment of a receiver would be intrusive; d) the preservation of the property did not require the intervention of a trustee; e) the existence of a large list of debts was meaningless in regards to real impecuniosity, as good business reasons for the debts might exist.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd." p2="One Shaftesbury Community Assn." post.rptr="210" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I642f56b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn.">Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 210, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 279 (Master)</ref></cite>—It is unclear whether a master has jurisdiction to make an order appointing a trustee under s. 68 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. An order flowing from a motion to appoint a trustee in a construction lien action, whether granted or refused, has been held to be an interlocutory order, and under s. 71(3) of the Act, no appeal lies from an interlocutory order made by the court. Therefore, the question should be decided by way of stated case in the Divisional Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Avenue Structures Inc." p2="Pacific Empire Development Inc." post.rptr="128" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I642f7dc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc.">Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc. (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee bank, which had advanced non-building loans, sought an order declaring that expenses it incurred for the preservation and protection of the premises had priority over the claims of lien claimants in respect of proceeds derived from the sale or other disposition of the property. The lien claimants had previously conceded that the mortgages were not building mortgages under s. 78(2) of the Act. The expenses for which the Bank claimed priority included: realty taxes; penalties and bailiff's costs; winter protection costs; hydro bills; insurance premiums; replacement of stolen electrical cable for electrical heaters; architect's fees relating to dealings with municipal authorities over a demolition order; legal fees regarding the prevention of demolition; city inspection fees; and a payment to the municipality under a letter of credit provided by the bank for the insolvent owner-developer. In dismissing the bank's motion with respect to all expenses except realty taxes, the Master noted that the bank ought to have applied for the appointment of a trustee under s. 68(1). The court may then have authorized the sale of the property as contemplated by s. 68(2)(a), thereby avoiding many of the expenses that were incurred. Even if a sale was not appropriate at that time, a trustee could have taken “appropriate steps for preservation of the premises” under s. 68(2)(c), and could have sought court approval for “such other steps that are appropriate” under s. 68(2)(d). Section 68 gave the mortgagee Bank the remedy it required to protect itself, but it failed to use that remedy and instead resorted to self-help. The expenses for penalties, interest and bailiff's costs were not absolutely necessary since these could all have been avoided by the Bank by paying the taxes on time after obtaining an agreed priority for such payment, or again by the application for the appointment of a trustee under s. 68, who could then have sought court approval for a borrowing to pay the taxes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Ru-Ko Inc." p2="Croatia (Republic)" post.rptr="269" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I642fa4d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ru-Ko Inc. v. Croatia (Republic)">Ru-Ko Inc. v. Croatia (Republic) (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 269 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The words in s. 68(2) “… or any other person having an interest in the premises…” does not include a lien claimant whose lien has been vacated pursuant to s. 44 by court order, following payment into court by the defendant. Rather, it refers to a party such as an owner, a mortgagee, or someone having an interest other than an interest as a lien claimant. In this case, the claimant had sought the appointment of a trustee to manage the sale of the property in question, and a direction that the trustee hold the proceeds of the sale in trust pending further court order. The lien claimant had thereby attempted to defeat the defendant's special diplomatic status by ensuring that the sale funds would not come into the latter's possession (<ital>Note</ital>: see s. 1(1), definition of “premises”).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Atlas-Gest Inc." p2="Brownstones Building Corp." post.rptr="275" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I642fa4d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas-Gest Inc. v. Brownstones Building Corp.">Atlas-Gest Inc. v. Brownstones Building Corp. (1992), 2 C.L.R. (2d) 275, 26 R.P.R. (2d) 233 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A condominium development required approximately $200,000 to render it into a state of completion that would permit the many remaining condominium units to be offered for sale. Several of the units were sold and had undergone the first phase of closing, known as occupancy closing, but the general contractor had left the site, and the parties were engaged in extensive litigation. As a result of this deadlock, the units which had already sold could not proceed to final closing, new sales could not be completed, the interests of construction lien claimants were being jeopardized, and interest was accruing on the mortgage. On motion by the mortgagee under s. 68, the court found that in order to protect the interests of innocent parties from eroding any further, it was just and convenient in all of the circumstances to appoint a trustee of the land and a receiver/manager of the registered owner. The court rejected the procedural argument that the proceeding should have been brought by way of application, not motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Toronto Dominion Bank" p2="General Glass & Aluminum Co." post.rptr="31" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I642fa4d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Dominion Bank v. General Glass & Aluminum Co.">Toronto Dominion Bank v. General Glass & Aluminum Co. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 31 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—This was an application for directions under s. 68. As to the distribution of funds received by the Bank from its customer, the defendant counsel had agreed that there were no credibility issues and that the matter could be determined on the basis of affidavit evidence filed. The court disposed of trust issues in a summary fashion under this section.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd." p2="Preston Heights Estates Ltd." post.rptr="293" pre.rptr="45" ref.id="I642fa4d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd.">G.C. McDonald Supply Ltd. v. Preston Heights Estates Ltd. (1991), 45 C.L.R. 293 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A motion was made seeking court approval of an offer of sale of a construction property, which was supported by all the lien claimants, and by the mortgagee, provided that its mortgage was paid out in full. The court found that the mortgagee would suffer no prejudice by a sale, and such a sale would be in the best interests of all the competing litigants. However, instead of a court-approved sale, a trustee was appointed under s. 70 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, as that course would offer the best protection for all parties. There was no appraisal filed with the court as to the value of the property, and a number of prospective purchasers had been reluctant to bid on the property so long as it was bogged down with legal matters.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Royaledge Industries Inc." p2="Perma-Roof Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="160" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I642fa4d45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royaledge Industries Inc. v. Perma-Roof Ontario Ltd.">Royaledge Industries Inc. v. Perma-Roof Ontario Ltd. (1991), 44 C.L.R. 160, 2 O.R. (3d) 488 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The applicant was the developer and first mortgagee of certain lands for which it had draft approval of a subdivision plan, and which it had sold the lands to the respondent owner. The applicant applied for the appointment of a trustee under s. 70 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital> [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 68] on the basis of a lien registered against the lands respecting the services installation for which it was responsible. The lien claimant had created an impasse between itself, the respondent owner and second mortgagee whereby the respondents refused to sign a subdivision agreement, because of the impasse, the applicant argued, the project was no longer being managed appropriately. The application was dismissed. The intervention of a trustee was not required in order to preserve the property. Section 68 of the Act is primarily intended to protect the interests of lien claimants, and accordingly had no application to the circumstances of the case. It was not appropriate under the facts of this case to remove control of the property from the owners simply because there existed a contractual dispute holding up development of the property. There was no evidence to indicate that any lien claimants were at risk.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce" p2="Acchione Construction Co." post.rptr="144" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I642fcbe05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Acchione Construction Co.">Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Acchione Construction Co. (1989), 36 C.L.R. 144 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—An order appointing a receiver-manager as trustee under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provided that “all of the receipts, income, costs, disbursements, expenses and claims received or expended pursuant to this Order be kept and are separate as between the properties described in Schedule ‘A’ and in Schedule ‘B’”. The receiver-manager-trustee appointed solicitors to carry out certain responsibilities and the respondents argued that the dockets were exorbitant if calculated on a per-lot basis and that the fees were not kept separate as stipulated in the order. In the result, the fees were assessed and approved. The evidence supported the inference that the trustee and counsel carried out the requirements as directed by the court and no evidence was brought forward to suggest that what was done was superfluous incompetent or incomplete. Furthermore, although the trustees and counsel failed to follow the stipulation that they were required to apportion the fees, which could not be specifically identified as applicable to one sub-division or the other, the respondents failed to prove any prejudice resulting from such failure and thus failed to show why compensation would be justified. The trustee must satisfy the court that the efforts expended and the resulting charges were justified, and had done so.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Dufferin-Custom Concrete" p2="Carling/Maplehurst Developments Inc." post.rptr="2306" pre.rptr="[1993]" ref.id="I91029640f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Dufferin-Custom Concrete v. Carling/Maplehurst Developments Inc.">Dufferin-Custom Concrete v. Carling/Maplehurst Developments Inc. (1993), [1993] O.J. No. 2306, 1993 CarswellOnt 239 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 69(1) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> is quite clear and all actions are stayed until further order of the court including an application by lien claimants to appoint a trustee under s. 68 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19890405" p1="Dinacon Construction Ltd." p2="743189 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="548" pre.rptr="[1989]" ref.id="I642fcbe25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dinacon Construction Ltd. v. 743189 Ontario Ltd.">Dinacon Construction Ltd. v. 743189 Ontario Ltd. (April 5, 1989), Doc. 11917/89, 11747/88, 11624/88, 11626/88. 12148/89, 11949/89, 11948/89, 11284/89, [1989] O.J. No. 548 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—This is an early example of the approach of a court to the appointment of a trustee and the reluctance of the court to unduly inhibit a trustee once appointed.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 68(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc." post.rptr="57" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I642fcbe35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc.">Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc. (2005), 50 C.L.R. (3d) 57, 19 C.B.R. (5th) 267, 2005 CarswellOnt 8022 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff registered a claim for lien against the defendant's property, the property was destroyed by fire and a trustee was appointed to oversee its sale. The trustee set a six week deadline for the sale. After receiving a timely satisfactory offer, the trustee received an additional offer six months after the deadline, which the plaintiff alleged was substantially better than the earlier offer. In dismissing the plaintiff's motion for an order directing the trustee to consider the late offer, or in the alternative, to re-advertise the property and recommence sale proceedings, the court noted that the trustee had acted appropriately in conducting the initial sale, and had obtained appraisals, solicited offers and protected the interests of the lien claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of)" p2="Acro Capital Inc." post.rptr="1038" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I642ff2f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc.">700 King Street (1997) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Acro Capital Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1038, 2004 CarswellOnt 986, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 47 (S.C.J. [Commercial List]); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 1796 (S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The Legislature has not used the word “trustee” rather than “receiver and manager” in s. 68 without any apparent reason. The Act appoints a trustee and also allows that appointee to function as receiver and manager. This added function does not derogate from the appointment as a “trustee”, nor the broad powers allowed a trustee under the common law.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Toronto Dominion Bank" p2="Crosswinds Golf & Country Club Ltd." post.rptr="1149" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I642ff2f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Dominion Bank v. Crosswinds Golf & Country Club Ltd.">Toronto Dominion Bank v. Crosswinds Golf & Country Club Ltd. (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 1149, 21 C.L.R. (3d) 38 (S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The lien holders opposed approval of the sale of a golf course property by the receiver, alleging that the fiduciary duties owed to the lien claimants were not met with respect to: notice of the proceeding; the disclosure of information; the lack of opportunity for the lien claimants to be informed and to participate in the legal process. As well, they alleged that the sale price was improvident, and pointed to the existence of a significantly higher second offer to purchase. The court held that, pursuant to the principles laid down in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Royal Bank" p2="Soundair Corp." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I642ff2f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Bank v. Soundair Corp.">Royal Bank v. Soundair Corp. (1991), 4 O.R. (3d) 1, 1991 CarswellOnt 205 (C.A.)</ref></cite>, a court, when reviewing a receiver's decision should: 1) consider whether the receiver has made a sufficient effort to get the best price and has not acted improvidently; 2) consider the interests of all parties; 3) consider the efficacy and integrity of the process by which offers are obtained; 4) consider whether there has been unfairness in the working out of the process. The law was clear that so long as the receiver meets those criteria, offers received late in the day, after the method stipulated by the receiver has been followed, are generally to be discouraged. Here, however, serious concerns had been raised that militated against approval of the sale. Notice of the proceedings was a fundamental prerequisite to ensure that participants had an opportunity to satisfy themselves as to the fairness and impartiality of the process. Also of particular concern was the 28-day time limit for the sale of a golf course in the middle of winter. Lastly, the significantly larger second offer was an indication that the price in the first offer, on its face, may have been improvident. In the result, the motion for approval of the sale was adjourned to permit the parties to file further materials.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Metropolitan Toronto Condominium Corp. No. 1175" p2="Irving A. Burton Ltd." post.rptr="268" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I642ff2f35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Metropolitan Toronto Condominium Corp. No. 1175 v. Irving A. Burton Ltd.">Metropolitan Toronto Condominium Corp. No. 1175 v. Irving A. Burton Ltd. (1999), 25 R.P.R. (3d) 268 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 49(3) of the <ital>Condominium Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.26, although a lien trustee was appointed over certain condominium units owned by the original condominium developer, the condominium corporation was still entitled to be paid out of the rental proceeds on those units the amount owed to it for arrears in common element expenses. The lien trustee argued unsuccessfully that s. 49 is nothing more than a garnishment section which could give no higher right to the corporation than any creditor would have if it instituted garnishment proceedings. The court found that the section provided a particular form of protection to a condominium corporation while at the same time protecting the tenant's position under the lease. The section ensures that the condominium corporation could recover amounts due for common expenses, attributable to the owner of a unit, which is being leased, from the tenant of the unit. Other creditors, including the lien trustee, are only entitled to claim those monies that are paid to, and come into the hands of, the landlord as rents. Section 49 permits the condominium corporation to direct a tenant to pay a portion of the rent to it in advance of any rent being paid to the landlord.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 69.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">69:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 69 was repealed and replaced with a new s. 85.2. The provisions governing labour and material payment bonds remain substantially unchanged.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Provisions regarding performance bonds were added.</para.text></para></list.item></list></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
70:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 70.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">70:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Consistent with the principle that lien actions proceed in a summary fashion, the ability of a court to refer a question of law to a higher court was first introduced into Ontario's lien legislation by <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1927, c. 173, s. 39. Section 39 provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(1)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">If in the course of proceedings to enforce a lien a question of law arises, the judge or officer trying the case may, at the request of any party, state the question in the form of a stated case for the opinion of the court and the stated case shall thereupon be set down to be heard before a Divisional Court and notice of hearing shall be served by the party setting down upon all parties concerned.</stat.text></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(2)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">The stated case shall set forth the facts material for the determination of the question raised and all papers necessary for the hearing of the appeal shall be transmitted to the registrar of the Appellate Division.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection (1) remained identical until the 1983 reforms. Subsection 42(2) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, introduced a change in that documents for the hearing no longer had to be submitted to the Registrar of the Appellate Division, but to the Registrar of the Supreme Court. Aside from that change, the 1923 version remained unchanged until 1983 as well. Section 72 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital> dropped the requirement for a “request by any party” in subs. (1) and deleted the second part of subs. (2). Section 70 of the present Act allows “the Court” to refer any question of law which arises “in the course of an action”. Accordingly, the present Act allows for the reference to occur at any stage of the proceedings.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 70 provides that a question of law arising during the course of an action may be dealt with by means of a stated case to the Divisional Court. This section appears to have been rarely used. This is most likely because lien claims, by their very nature, are dependant on factual determinations, such as the last day of work, the price of work or services, and the preservation and perfection of the claims for lien.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd." p2="One Shaftesbury Community Assn." post.rptr="210" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I643041105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn.">Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 210, 25 C.L.R. (3d) 279 (Master)</ref></cite>—The Master stated the following question of law for the opinion of the Divisional Court: “Does a Master (or case management Master) hearing a construction lien action under a judgment of reference under subs. 58(1) of the Act have the jurisdiction to hear a motion seeking an order under s. 68 appointing a trustee?”</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
71:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 71.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">71:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The blanket prohibition of appeals from interlocutory orders was replaced with the possibility of appealing such orders with leave of the Divisional Court. The Expert Review's reasoning was as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As construction lien matters have grown more complex since 1983, the ability to appeal interlocutory orders would allow for procedural precedents to be promulgated from the senior echelons of the court, and would allow parties in complex litigation to exercise rights that are otherwise available in civil actions. Extending the right to appeal from interlocutory orders must be balanced with the objective of summary procedure under the Act. Therefore, leave of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice should be required to avoid unnecessary protracted litigation and ensure that only meritorious appeals are heard.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Where the amount claimed is $10,000 or less, however, appeals remain precluded.</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Lien legislation in Ontario has always limited rights of appeal where the amount of the lien or liens in issue exceeded a certain threshold. Sections 38 to 40 of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">38.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">In all actions where the amount recovered by the judgment is $100 or less, the said judgment will be final, binding, and without appeal, except that upon application within fourteen days after judgment is pronounced, to the judge or officer who tried the same, he may grant a new trial.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">39.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">In all actions where the amount recovered by the judgment is more than $100 but not more than $200, any party affected thereby may appeal therefrom to a divisional court, whose judgment shall be final and binding, and no appeal shall lie therefrom.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">40.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">In all other cases the same right to appeal shall exist as is given in actions tried without a jury in the High Court.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">By 1914, the Court of Appeal limit had risen to $500, s. 40(2) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1914, c. 140. The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1958</ital>, S.O. 1958, c. 57, s. 9 provided that all judgments up to a value of $200 were to be final, and that in all other cases, an appeal could be had to the same extent as from the decision of a Supreme Court judge. That section was repealed in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1960</ital>, which for the first time introduced a section similar to the form that prevailed until the 1983 reforms. Section 43 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, expressly provided that an appeal was to go to the Court of Appeal, which was changed in 1980 to the effect that an appeal from judgments over $200 was to lie to the Divisional Court. Under s. 71 of the present Act, no appeal lies from a judgment or report where the amount claimed is $1,000.00 or less. Subsection 71(3), which provides that no appeal lies from an interlocutory order of the court, was introduced in s. 73(3)(b) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6 and merely codified established principles of common law.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 71 limits the rights of appeal under the Act and describes the court to which an appeal will lie. It has been held that s. 71 takes priority over the provisions of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> in relation to appeals (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="C.S. Yachts Ltd." post.rptr="225" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I643068205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 225, 38 O.A.C. 147 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>) It is also noted that where in an interlocutory proceeding a final determination of a party's rights is made, an appeal may be brought (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19980414" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="2378" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I64308f305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc.">Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc. (April 14, 1998), Doc. 873/97, [1998] O.J. No. 2378 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="52" ref.id="I64308f315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reason to (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207, 52 O.A.C. 107 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
71:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 71.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">71:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Robert McAlpine Ltd." p2="Woodbine Place Inc." post.rptr="134" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I64308f325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Robert McAlpine Ltd. v. Woodbine Place Inc.">Robert McAlpine Ltd. v. Woodbine Place Inc. (1998), 3 C.L.R. (3d) 134 (Ont. C.A. [In Chambers])</ref></cite>—The owner posted a letter of credit to vacate a lien and the property was sold. The contractor sued to have the lien enforced, the owner counterclaimed for damages. Both the action and the counterclaim were allowed, the lien claim was set off against the damages awarded to the owner. The contractor was ordered to return the letter of credit to the owner. The contractor moved for an order directing the delivery of the letter of credit stayed pending an appeal. The motion was granted in part. While the stay pending appeal rule, R. 63.01, only applies to orders directing the payment of money and consequently did not apply in this case, the order had immediate and significant monetary implications that justified an order under the discretionary provisions of R. 63.02. A return of the letter of credit would have caused irreparable harm, because if the contractor were successful on appeal, it would have no chance of recovery without the letter. The delivery was stayed on the condition that the contractor pays the costs for maintaining the letter of credit.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
71:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 71.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">71:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 71(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1995636 Ontario Inc. C.O.B. 2B Developments" p2="5010729 Ontario Inc. C.O.B. as Astute Capital Corp." post.rptr="19763" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678221403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="1995636 Ontario Inc. C.O.B. 2B Developments v. 5010729 Ontario Inc. C.O.B. as Astute Capital Corp.">1995636 Ontario Inc. C.O.B. 2B Developments v. 5010729 Ontario Inc. C.O.B. as Astute Capital Corp., 2024 CarswellOnt 19763, 2024 ONSC 7089 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2025 CarswellOnt 624 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The court granted the lien claimant's motion for a stay of the judgment dismissing its action, discharging its lien and awarding damages to the defendant. The appeal raised a serious question to be tried, and although the plaintiff could still proceed against the defendant on a non-lien judgment, a refusal to stay the discharge of the lien would cause irreparable harm that could not be compensated with costs. The plaintiff's statutory lien rights would be lost, as the discharge of a lien was irrevocable, and once gone, could not in any way be reversed by the court, even on appeal. Even though the registered lien had been found to be exaggerated, and there were serious findings of bad faith on the part of the plaintiff, the grounds of appeal were not frivolous and those findings did not militate against the exercise of discretion to stay the appeal.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MGW-Homes Design Inc." p2="Pasqualino" post.rptr="7537" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678221413b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="MGW-Homes Design Inc. v. Pasqualino">MGW-Homes Design Inc. v. Pasqualino, 2024 CarswellOnt 7537, 2024 ONCA 422, 172 O.R. (3d) 770, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2555 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—On appeal by the contractor from an order vacating a writ of enforcement issued in connection with the adjudicator's determination, the Court of Appeal held that adjudication under Part II.1 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> is a “proceeding under the Act” and the motion judge's order on the enforceability of the adjudicator's determination is a “judgment … under [the] Act”. The appeal therefore lay to the Divisional Court.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Arcamm Electrical Services Ltd." p2="Avison Young Real Estate Management Services LP" post.rptr="4999" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678221423b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Arcamm Electrical Services Ltd. v. Avison Young Real Estate Management Services LP">Arcamm Electrical Services Ltd. v. Avison Young Real Estate Management Services LP, 2024 CarswellOnt 4999, 2024 ONCA 251, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1620 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The fact that a claim is styled as a proceeding under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not mean that the <ital>Construction Act</ital> automatically governs the appeal route. Rather, the jurisdiction of the court is governed by the substance of the order made. Here, after the defendant appealed the granting of summary judgment to the plaintiff, the plaintiff unsuccessfully sought to quash the appeal for want of jurisdiction, on the basis that the judgment was a final order, and therefore appealable to the Divisional Court. The judgment was not made under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>; instead, the source of the motion judge's jurisdiction was r. 20. The relief granted was based on a claim for damages in contract for unpaid invoices, a non-statutory cause of action, and the primary ground for appeal was the defence of contributory negligence. These issues were not matters governed by the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, but were specific to the application of the test under r. 20.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dal Bianco" p2="Deem Management Services Limited" post.rptr="13345" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64308f335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services Limited">Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services Limited, 2020 CarswellOnt 13345, 2020 ONCA 585, 82 C.B.R. (6th) 161, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 196 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Here, the order under appeal, ruling that certain construction lien claimants had priority over a mortgagee in the sale proceeds of a debtor's property under s. 78 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, was granted at least partly in reliance on jurisdiction under the (Can.) <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>. The substance of the order was in proceedings authorized by the <ital>BIA</ital> and responded to a motion for the court's directions brought under s. 249 of the <ital>BIA</ital> to help the receiver distribute the remaining funds in the receivership. Section 249 of the <ital>BIA</ital> was thus a source of jurisdiction for the court's order. This established, under the principle of federal paramountcy, that the appeal route was to the Court of Appeal rather than to the Divisional Court by virtue of s. 71(1) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="9585800 Canada Inc." p2="JP Gravel Construction Inc." post.rptr="19773" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I6430b6405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction Inc.">9585800 Canada Inc. v. JP Gravel Construction Inc., 2019 CarswellOnt 19773, 2019 ONSC 7022, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 38 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 8917, 2019 ONSC 3396, 3 C.L.R. (5th) 29 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor registered and then discharged a construction lien against the construction project, and then immediately registered a second construction lien after that discharge, for the same amount and using substantially the same information as contained in the first lien. The first lien was allegedly discharged due to an error in the time of delivery of services which listed the incorrect year, an error corrected in the second lien. The motions judge refused to vacate the second lien and found it was valid. The declaration of the validity with respect to the second lien made the order final, and the motions judge's reasons made it apparent that she was resolving the validity issue. Accordingly, the Divisional Court had jurisdiction to hear the appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Demir" p2="Kilic" post.rptr="7279" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I6430b6415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Demir v. Kilic">Demir v. Kilic, 2018 ONSC 7279, 2018 CarswellOnt 20717, 97 C.L.R. (4th) 191 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2018 ONSC 949, 2018 CarswellOnt 1891, 90 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Under s. 71(1), an appeal lies to the Divisional Court from a judgment or an order on a motion to oppose confirmation of a report under that statute. The standard of review of an appeal from a judge's decision is set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Housen" p2="Nikolaisen" post.rptr="178" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I91035990f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Housen v. Nikolaisen">Housen v. Nikolaisen (2002), 2002 CarswellSask 178, 2002 CarswellSask 179, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>. On questions of law, the standard is correctness, on questions of fact, the standard is palpable and overriding error, and on questions of mixed fact and law, there is a spectrum. Where there is an extricable legal principle, the standard of review is correctness. However, with respect to the application of the correct legal principles to the evidence, the standard is palpable and overriding error.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Heinrichs" p2="374427 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="78" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I6430dd505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heinrichs v. 374427 Ontario Ltd.">Heinrichs v. 374427 Ontario Ltd., 2018 ONSC 78, 2018 CarswellOnt 25, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 121 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 994, 2018 CarswellOnt 2304 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was discharged pursuant to an undertaking by the defendant's' lawyers to hold sufficient funds from sale of the property in escrow under certain terms. Following the release of the lien instruments, the plaintiffs did not take any steps to prosecute the action or set it down for trial, and the defendants moved to dismiss the action for delay or, in the alternative, to direct that the action proceed as an action in contract. In respect of both options, the defendants sought an order directing the release of the escrow funds. The Master directed the action to proceed as a contract action and ordered the funds be paid out to the defendants, on the basis that the security provided by the undertaking was akin to security for the lien having been posted in court. On the plaintiff's appeal to the Divisional Court, the word “judgment” in s. 71(1) was held to apply to any decision by which the rights of a party are finally disposed of, and although the Master allowed the breach of contract action to continue, her interpretation of the undertaking and the parties' intention concerning the action was the basis of her order to release the security. That disposition was final in nature in that it finally determines those issues. Accordingly, an appeal from the order to the Divisional Court was not prohibited by s. 71(3)(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dircam Electric" p2="Am-Stat Corp." post.rptr="3421" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6430dd515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dircam Electric v. Am-Stat Corp.">Dircam Electric v. Am-Stat Corp., 2017 ONSC 3421, 2017 CarswellOnt 8300, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 256 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Lien claimants appealed the ruling that the respondent's mortgage had priority over their construction liens. The ruling was a “judgment” within the meaning of s. 71, as it finally decided the question of priorities and had the effect of deciding that the remaining equity in the property will not be available to satisfy the claims of the lien claimants. This was a final order, not an interlocutory order, and could be appealed to the Divisional Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Imperial Trim Supply Ltd." p2="Am-Stat Corp." post.rptr="734" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6430dd525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Imperial Trim Supply Ltd. v. Am-Stat Corp.">Imperial Trim Supply Ltd. v. Am-Stat Corp., 2017 ONSC 734, 2017 CarswellOnt 1035, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 120 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The moving parties were four lien claimants who sought an extension of time to appeal an order that determined, among other things, that a mortgage had priority over the lien claimants. The Divisional Court found it had jurisdiction to hear the appeal. The decision in question finally disposed of the issue of priority as between the respondent and the lien claimants and effectively precluded any likelihood of recovery by the lien claimants. The decision therefore constituted a “judgment” as that term was commonly understood.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Airex Inc." p2="Ben Air Systems Inc." post.rptr="6450" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6430dd535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Airex Inc. v. Ben Air Systems Inc.">Airex Inc. v. Ben Air Systems Inc., 2016 ONSC 6450, 2016 CarswellOnt 16241, 67 C.L.R. (4th) 116 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendants appealed to the Divisional Court from a summary judgment and a finding that they were in breach of trust provisions of the Act. This action involved a claim for monies owed on unpaid invoices for goods sold and delivered, along with monies due under a guarantee and was commenced in the normal course in the Superior Court of Justice. No lien was claimed. The Divisional Court declined jurisdiction to hear the appeal, on the basis that s. 71 did not extend to cover the circumstances of this case. This was not a proceeding under the Act and could not reasonably be held to have led to a judgment under that Act. Unlike a lien claim, a trust claim was not a special proceeding under the Act. The proceeding was instead governed by the general appeal routes found in s. 6 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. Breach of trust claims under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> have been traditionally appealed to the Court of Appeal, likely because those claims were often joined with non-statutory causes of actions. The court did not determine whether a breach of trust claim would be properly appealable to the Divisional Court if it stood alone. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd." p2="Pier One Masonry Inc." post.rptr="76" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I643104605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc.">Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc. (2001), 54 O.R. (3d) 76 (C.A.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="TRS Components Ltd." p2="Devlan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="294" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643104615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="TRS Components Ltd. v. Devlan Construction Ltd.">TRS Components Ltd. v. Devlan Construction Ltd., 2015 ONCA 294, 2015 CarswellOnt 6142, 125 O.R. (3d) 161, 42 C.L.R. (4th) 169 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A “judgment … under this Act” in s. 71 includes a judgment granted in an action commenced and continued under Part VIII of the Act, including any counterclaim, cross-claim or third party claim, unless the action or any part of the action is removed from the construction lien proceeding, and directed to proceed under the Rules. In the absence of an order directing that the proceeding is to continue as an ordinary action, the appeal of a judgment in a construction lien proceeding, whether or not in respect of a lien claim, and including any counterclaim, is subject to s. 71(1) of the Act. Accordingly, the Divisional Court has exclusive jurisdiction over the appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Starland Contracting Inc." p2="1581518 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3431" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I643104625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Starland Contracting Inc. v. 1581518 Ontario Ltd.">Starland Contracting Inc. v. 1581518 Ontario Ltd. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 3431, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 1 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9126 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Although the appeal in this case from the decision of the master striking the statement of defence and counterclaim for failure to comply with court orders was heard by a panel of the Divisional Court, any appeal of a master's final order should be heard by a single judge of the Divisional Court. This approach is consistent both with the practice of the Court regarding appeals from the master, and with the objective of s. 67(1) to promote prompt resolution in construction lien matters.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Gryphon Building Solutions Inc." p2="Danforth Estates Management Inc." post.rptr="4324" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I64312b705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gryphon Building Solutions Inc. v. Danforth Estates Management Inc.">Gryphon Building Solutions Inc. v. Danforth Estates Management Inc. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 4324 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 4741 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Divisional Court has no jurisdiction to hear an appeal under s. 71(l) from the decisions of a Master where the master's report has not been confirmed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="D.J. Venasse Construction Ltd." p2="MVD Properties Inc." post.rptr="3487" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I64312b715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.J. Venasse Construction Ltd. v. MVD Properties Inc.">D.J. Venasse Construction Ltd. v. MVD Properties Inc. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 3487, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 243 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The test for reviewing the decision of the motions judge on a summary judgment motion is the standard of correctness.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd." p2="Pier One Masonry Inc." post.rptr="76" pre.rptr="54" ref.id="I64312b725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc.">Villa Verde L.M. Masonry Ltd. v. Pier One Masonry Inc. (2001), 54 O.R. (3d) 76 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 71(1) of the Act applies to appeals concerning lien claims under Part III as well as appeals concerning trust claims under Part II of the Act. There is no basis for giving the word “judgment” a restrictive meaning so that it relates only to a judgment on a lien claim. Accordingly, appeals concerning trust claims under Part II of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> should be heard by the Divisional Court rather than the Court of Appeal. There are rare circumstances when the Court of Appeal could take jurisdiction over the lien and trust claims by constituting itself as the Divisional Court, but this is an option generally only resorted to in cases where the jurisdictional issue is noticed after the appeal has been argued and when it is necessary so as to save the parties the expense and inconvenience of having to re-list and re-argue the appeal. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court makes reference to counsel's suggestion that the reason appeals concerning trust claims have traditionally come to the Court of Appeal is that they are often joined with non-statutory causes of actions. In such cases the Court of Appeal may have taken jurisdiction under s. 6(2) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. Subsection 6(2) provides that the Court of Appeal has jurisdiction to hear and determine an appeal that lies to the Divisional Court “if an appeal in the same proceeding lies to and is taken to the Court of Appeal”. Where a judgment concerns claims only under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the appeal is to the Divisional Court and not to the Court of Appeal for Ontario.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="United Dominion Industries Ltd." p2="Ellis-Don Ltd." post.rptr="855" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I9103a7b0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd.">United Dominion Industries Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Ltd. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 855, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 184, 65 O.A.C. 115 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The Master dismissed the plaintiff's cross-motion for an order under s. 44(2) of the Act requiring the defendant to post security, not only for the full amount of the liens but for an amount of 25 per cent in excess thereof as security for costs because of the complexity and anticipated length of the trial proceedings. The court quashed the plaintiff's appeal. Orders for security for costs do not determine the real matter in dispute between the parties. They are incidental thereto. Here the real matter was the validity and quantum of the lien. Costs in a construction lien action as in an ordinary civil action are in the discretion of the court. Even if costs were properly part of the lien, an order for interim security was interlocutory in nature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Bird Construction Co." p2="C.S. Yachts Ltd." post.rptr="225" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I64312b745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd.">Bird Construction Co. v. C.S. Yachts Ltd. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 225, 38 O.A.C. 147 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendants brought a motion <ital>ex parte</ital> and received an order declaring that the plaintiff's claim for a lien had expired. The order provided, further, that the certificate of action was vacated and the entire action was dismissed without costs. The plaintiff's motion to set aside the order was dismissed and the earlier order was confirmed. The issue to be determined was whether the appeal was to the Divisional Court pursuant to the provisions of s. 73(1) [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 71(1)] of the Act or to the Court of Appeal, pursuant to the provisions of s. 17(1)(c) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. Held, the appeal was to the Divisional Court. Subsection 73(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides that an appeal lies to the Divisional Court from a judgment under the Act. The order constituted a final judgment of the court notwithstanding that it was referred to as an order or that it was made without a trial having taken place. The order purporting to confirm the earlier order dismissed the plaintiff's action and finally disposed of his rights. This constituted a judgment within the meaning of the words used in s. 73(1). Furthermore, the provisions of s. 73(1), with respect to appeals, are provisions under a special Act dealing with construction liens and, therefore, take precedence over the provision of s. 17(1)(c) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act, 1984</ital>, which is a general provision merely providing that an appeal from a final order of a local judge of the High Court lies to the Court of Appeal.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

C.30, s. 71.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">71:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 71(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gandhi" p2="Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="1001" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6782bd803b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd.">Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 1691, 2024 ONSC 1001, 2024 A.C.W.S. 686 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Due to inadvertence by his former counsel, the lien claimant missed the 15-day deadline under s. 71(2) of the Act for delivering a notice of appeal from a judgment finding that the lien claim had expired. In granting an extension of time to file the appeal, the court was satisfied that the claimant had a good faith intention to appeal the judgment within the prescribed period, and provided a compelling explanation for the delay in bringing the appeal, namely the inadvertence of his former counsel. The delay in serving the notice of appeal did not prejudice the defendant in the sense contemplated under the analysis for an extension of time. The relevant consideration was not prejudice from the progress of the appeal as of right, but rather prejudice from the delay in delivering the notice of appeal. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gandhi" p2="Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="5490" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6782bd813b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd.">Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 5490, 2024 ONSC 2184, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3698 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons at 2024 CarswellOnt 8126, 2024 ONSC 3095, (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, allowing the claimant's appeal.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="690 King Street Corp." p2="Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc." post.rptr="1050" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I643152805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="690 King Street Corp. v. Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc.">690 King Street Corp. v. Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc., 2021 ONSC 1050, 2021 CarswellOnt 1516 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The applicant formed an intention to appeal within the 15-day appeal period, but there was a delay of 14 days after the expiry of the appeal period resulting from the inadvertence of counsel. The <ital>Construction Act</ital> provides that a judge may extend the time where an “appropriate case” is made out for doing so. Comparable to Ont. Rule 3.02, this is an umbrella factor that encompasses fairness, balance, and a contextual consideration of other relevant factors. An appeal the applicant was entitled to, and wanted to pursue, should not be defeated because of a mistake by its lawyer, where there was no real prejudice to the other side.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Parma General Contractors Inc." p2="Pulcini" post.rptr="5193" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I643152815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini">Parma General Contractors Inc. v. Pulcini, 2016 ONSC 5193, 2016 CarswellOnt 13045, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 56 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In refusing to grant leave to the plaintiff to appeal the dismissal of its motion to oppose confirmation of the master's final report, the court accepted that the plaintiff had an intention to appeal and an explanation for its significant delay in doing so. However, there was an element of prejudice to the defendants if an extension was granted involving both the lack of finality of a matter that had been ongoing for eight years, and the possibility that the defendant might be required to repay the monies into court. The defendant was no longer an active business and had used the monies it obtained out of court to pay its liabilities. More importantly, the merits of the appeal were wanting. The plaintiff was essentially attacking findings of fact made by the Master, and those attacks were carefully considered by the motions judge and found to be lacking.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DiBella Construction Ltd." p2="Cloud" post.rptr="4300" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I643152825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="DiBella Construction Ltd. v. Cloud">DiBella Construction Ltd. v. Cloud, 2016 ONSC 4300, 2016 CarswellOnt 10429, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 344 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A costs judgment is a separate, collateral determination rather than part of the main merits proceeding, and the time for the appeal of the merits judgment runs from the date it is released and not the date that the costs judgment is released. Where there is inadequate evidence of an intention to appeal and no real explanation as to why the appeal was not even mentioned to the plaintiff's lawyer until after the costs decision in the matter was released, the plaintiff's motion to quash the appeal within the time requirements of s. 71(2) was allowed. The defendant's motion for an order extending the time for service of the notice of appeal was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Men at Work General Contractors Ltd." p2="MacDonald" post.rptr="860" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643179905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Men at Work General Contractors Ltd. v. MacDonald">Men at Work General Contractors Ltd. v. MacDonald, 2015 ONSC 860, 2015 CarswellOnt 1706, 42 C.L.R. (4th) 33 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Extension of time to appeal an order denying confirmation of the Master's Report was granted where the moving parties formed an intention to appeal within the prescribed period, were actively attempting to obtain clarification of the motions judge's unusually brief decision, and were engaging in settlement discussions. A significant portion of the delay was due to the motions judge's retirement. There was a reasonable explanation for the delay. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also the related ruling of Morawetz R.S.J. at <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Men at Work General Contractors Ltd." p2="MacDonald" post.rptr="4176" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I643179915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Men at Work General Contractors Ltd. v. MacDonald">Men at Work General Contractors Ltd. v. MacDonald, 2014 ONSC 4176, 2014 CarswellOnt 9827, 42 C.L.R. (4th) 241 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2015 ONSC 383, 2015 CarswellOnt 599 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 7665 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, in which he held that the intended purpose of s. 123 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> was to provide guidance where a judge dies, retires or otherwise becomes incapacitated while still having outstanding work. It did not seek to address concerns a litigant might have with the content of a decision that had been rendered. The remedy that the moving parties were seeking was in the nature of an appeal.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Birkshire Group Inc." p2="Wilkes" post.rptr="4408" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I643179925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Birkshire Group Inc. v. Wilkes">Birkshire Group Inc. v. Wilkes, 2014 ONSC 4408, 2014 CarswellOnt 10146, 44 C.L.R. (4th) 89 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff brought both a lien and contract action in relation to the same transaction, and were directed to be tried together.
