Both actions were disposed of in part by one set of reasons, although no lien findings were made and no lien relief was granted by the trial judge. The appellants' Divisional Court appeal was dismissed by way of administrative error based on the misapprehension that no transcript was required. Both parties agreed that the matter was to return before the trial judge in regards to his findings and reasons for relief sought under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. In the interests of justice, the court extended the time for appeal of the contract action until 30 days after the further reasons and decision of the trial judge, and set aside any administrative dismissal of the appeal while the motion was pending.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="3925308 Manitoba Inc." p2="Hoffer" post.rptr="1964" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I643179935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="3925308 Manitoba Inc. v. Hoffer">3925308 Manitoba Inc. v. Hoffer, 2011 ONSC 1964, 2011 CarswellOnt 2060 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendants successfully moved for an order extending the time to file a notice of appeal of judgment and costs granted in a construction lien case, where the failure to file the notice of appeal was the result of a slip by out-of-province counsel which had not prejudiced the plaintiff. While society has an interest in having cases finally resolved with certainty, the courts recognize that a slip of counsel may jeopardize the rights of the client. The appellants' solicitor deposed he received instructions to appeal a few days after the release of the judgment, and the failure to serve and file a notice of appeal was attributable to the ignorance of counsel that a shortened appeal period is prescribed in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. As well, counsel misapprehended the time from which the appeal period started to run under Ontario law, which differed from the practice in Manitoba.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Bob Seabrook Construction Ltd." p2="Kenaidan Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="6730" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I6431a0a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bob Seabrook Construction Ltd. v. Kenaidan Contracting Ltd.">Bob Seabrook Construction Ltd. v. Kenaidan Contracting Ltd. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 6730, 85 C.L.R. (3d) 179 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Even if, under s. 71(2), a judge may extend the time for serving and filing a Notice of Appeal <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>, the applicant would still be required to show: (a) a <ital>bona fide</ital> intention to appeal within the 15 day period; (b) an explanation for the delay; (c) that there is no prejudice to other parties; and (d) that the proposed appeal had merit. Those conditions were not met, and the plaintiff's motion to extend was denied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Deman Construction Corp." p2="1429036 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4430" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I6431a0a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Deman Construction Corp. v. 1429036 Ontario Inc.">Deman Construction Corp. v. 1429036 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4430, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 235 (Div. Ct.); leave to appeal allowed (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1320, [2005] O.J. No. 1987 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendants launched their appeal to the wrong court 29 days after the judgment of the motions judge. The time for appeal prescribed under s. 71(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is 15 days. The defendants did not bring a motion seeking an extension of the time to serve and file their notice of appeal. The appeal was brought out of time and should be dismissed. On further appeal to the Court of Appeal, however, the appeal was allowed to proceed without a discussion of s. 71(2), based on the fact that the appellant had initially taken some steps to oppose the judgment. See (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 4214, 2005 CarswellOnt 4859 (Ont. C.A.); additional reasons at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2196 (Ont. C.A.).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="20030627" p1="Cornell Pump Co." p2="York (Regional Municipality)" post.rptr="3655" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I6431a0a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cornell Pump Co. v. York (Regional Municipality)">Cornell Pump Co. v. York (Regional Municipality) (June 27, 2003), Doc. 240/03, [2003] O.J. No. 3655 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Where the moving party had a firm intention to appeal and potential settlement discussions offered a reasonable explanation for the delay, the motion to extend time to perfect the appeal was granted, while a concurrent motion for a stay of the judgment was denied. The Court of Appeal's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Frey" p2="MacDonald" post.rptr="13" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I6431c7b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Frey v. MacDonald">Frey v. MacDonald (1989), 33 C.P.C. (2d) 13, 1989 CarswellOnt 343 (C.A.)</ref></cite> did not add a third proposition in regards to the merits of the appeal, but merely stated that an extension may be granted in any event if an extension is warranted on the “justice of the case”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Verly Construction Group Inc." p2="Gregmen Construction Ltd." post.rptr="2376" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I6431c7b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Verly Construction Group Inc. v. Gregmen Construction Ltd.">Verly Construction Group Inc. v. Gregmen Construction Ltd. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 2376 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where it was not demonstrated that any lasting prejudice was suffered by the inadvertence of the appellant, a 12-day extension of time to perfect an appeal was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Plaza Electric II Ltd." p2="CMGC Management Inc." post.rptr="2708" pre.rptr="[1997]" ref.id="I6431c7b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Plaza Electric II Ltd. v. CMGC Management Inc.">Plaza Electric II Ltd. v. CMGC Management Inc. (1997), [1997] O.J. No. 2708 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Where no indication of any intention to appeal was given during the statutory 15-day period, the appeal period expired and the sale of the land in question had proceeded, it was inappropriate under the circumstances to allow the appeal to proceed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Solomon Rothbart Goodman" p2="Davidovits" post.rptr="314" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I6431c7b35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Solomon Rothbart Goodman v. Davidovits">Solomon Rothbart Goodman v. Davidovits (1996), 46 C.P.C. (3d) 314 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A motion to oppose confirmation of a Master's Report is in the nature of an appeal and therefore new evidence, in this case by affidavit, is inadmissible unless it would otherwise meet the tests for new evidence on appeal. In this case the tendered affidavit was struck from the record.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Zenon Devs. Ltd." p2="Barna" post.rptr="2964" pre.rptr="1986" ref.id="I6431eec05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Zenon Devs. Ltd. v. Barna">Zenon Devs. Ltd. v. Barna (1986), 1986 CarswellOnt 2964, [1986] O.J. No. 1300 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—There is no requirement that the party objecting to confirmation of the Master's report must obtain a transcript of the trial evidence; that is a matter of choice by the moving party. If any party intends to refer to the transcripts, however, it must be filed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HMI Construction Inc." p2="Index Energy Mills Road Corp." post.rptr="4075" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I6431eec15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp.">HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp., 2017 ONSC 4075, 2017 CarswellOnt 10314, 81 C.L.R. (4th) 88 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An order reducing the security required to discharge a lien from title pursuant to s. 44(2) of the Act is final and may be appealed to the Divisional Court. It is a final order in that it determines, on a final basis, the maximum amount of the lien claim.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
71:5: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 71.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">71:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 71(3)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trillium Masonry Group Inc." p2="Marydel Homes (Beaverton) Inc." post.rptr="5668" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678359c03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Trillium Masonry Group Inc. v. Marydel Homes (Beaverton) Inc.">Trillium Masonry Group Inc. v. Marydel Homes (Beaverton) Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 16003, 2024 ONSC 5668 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff provided masonry services and materials for a residential subdivision being developed by the defendant. After the plaintiff registered a claim for lien a subdivision lot, the claim for lien was vacated by court order upon payment of funds into court as security. On subsequent motion, the motion judge reduced the amount of security that the defendant had been required to pay into court. As per <ital>H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823</ital>, below, the Divisional Court had jurisdiction to hear the appeal, as the order was a final order. The motion judge erred in law by providing deficient reasons that prevented meaningful appellate review of the decision. The matter was remitted for redetermination by a different judge.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gandhi" p2="Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="1001" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678359c13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd.">Gandhi v. Mayfield Arcadeium Holdings Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 1691, 2024 ONSC 1001, 2024 A.C.W.S. 686 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A declaration that a lien has expired pursuant to s. 45 is a final order, as the declaration is irrevocable and an expired lien cannot be revived. Likewise, an order releasing funds held in counsel's trust account as an alternative form of security in lieu of a claim for lien is also a final order.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Soo Mill & Lumber Company Ltd." p2="Pozzebon" post.rptr="16827" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678359c23b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Soo Mill & Lumber Company Ltd. v. Pozzebon">Soo Mill & Lumber Company Ltd. v. Pozzebon, 2024 CarswellOnt 16827, 2024 ONSC 5950 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff supplied building materials used to construct houses in a subdivision, and sought a declaration that all amounts paid or owing to the defendants, in relation to that house construction, were held in trust for it, and for damages for breach of trust. When the sale of a home in the subdivision was pending, the plaintiff moved under Ont. r. 45.02 for an order that the proceeds of sale be held in court as security for its claim. The motion judge ordered that only a part, of the proceeds would be retained in court as security for the plaintiff's claims. On the hearing of the plaintiff's appeal, the court reserved on the jurisdictional issue and heard argument on the merits of the appeal. It concluded for several reasons that the order was an interlocutory order from which no appeal lay, and quashed the appeal. The motion judge was not asked to make a final determination of the scope of the trust, but found, for the purposes of deciding the motion, that there was a serious issue to be tried only in relation to the amount owing to the plaintiff for materials supplied to the individual house sale. The question of whether the entire proceeds of sale were trust funds for the plaintiff's benefit was not finally determined by the order under appeal. If the motion had been dismissed in its entirety on its initial return date, it would clearly have been interlocutory because it would have had no effect on the claims or defences. The action would have proceeded as it would have, had the motion not been made. The fact that an interim order was made or that the motion was allowed in part could not be relied on to argue that the order as made was final. As well, orders made on interlocutory motions were presumed to be interlocutory.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Elegant Façade Inc." p2="Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc." post.rptr="6951" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I6431eec25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elegant Façade Inc. v. Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc.">Elegant Façade Inc. v. Broccolini Construction (Toronto) Inc., 2021 ONSC 6951, 2021 CarswellOnt 14404 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved to quash the plaintiff's appeal against a production order following a s. 40 examination under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Production and disclosure orders are generally interlocutory, and an order for production and/or reattendance for examination made against a corporation's witness is not rendered final because that witness is not a party to the proceedings. However, where a production or disclosure order is directed against a “stranger to the litigation”, the order is final, in respect to that person. Here, the plaintiff's representative was directed to provide production and disclosure in her capacity as a representative of and witness for the plaintiff, but she had no role in the proceeding other than in that capacity. There was no basis to distinguish her role from the role of the plaintiff, for the purposes of examination and production. She was not a true stranger to the litigation, and the wording of the order, directed as it was to the individual examinee, did not transform an interlocutory order against the plaintiff into a final order against her personally. As well, since the appeal was brought by the corporate plaintiff, it had no standing to assert the personal interest of the examinee in the impugned order. If the latter had wished to challenge the order because it finally disposed of her personal interest in making disclosure and providing production, it would have been for her to bring the appeal in her own name, and thus to expose herself personally to the risk for costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc." p2="AGC Flat Glass North America Ltd." post.rptr="3993" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I643215d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc. v. AGC Flat Glass North America Ltd.">Man-Shield (NWO) Construction Inc. v. AGC Flat Glass North America Ltd., 2019 ONSC 3993, 2019 CarswellOnt 10537 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An order refusing a stay of a summary judgment is procedural and therefore interlocutory. Here, the Divisional Court therefore had no jurisdiction, under s. 71(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, to hear the matter.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="H.I.R.A. Limited" p2="Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823" post.rptr="3661" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I643215d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823">H.I.R.A. Limited v. Middlesex Standard Condominium Corporation No. 823, 2018 ONSC 3661, 2018 CarswellOnt 9729, 78 C.L.R. (4th) 248 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Any reduction in the quantum of security required to bond liens off title has the effect of altering the legal rights and remedies of a lien claimant, as the lien claimant loses a certain amount of security for its claim. As set out in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HMI Construction Inc." p2="Index Energy Mills Road Corp." post.rptr="4075" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I643215d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp.">HMI Construction Inc. v. Index Energy Mills Road Corp., 2017 ONSC 4075, 2017 CarswellOnt 10314, 81 C.L.R. (4th) 88 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, such an order is a final order in that it determines, on a final basis, the maximum amount of the lien claim, and can be appealed. A motion brought by the plaintiff for an order pursuant to Rule 63.02(b) staying an order vacating the lien from title by posting security of just slightly more than half of the amount claimed, pending the final determination of the appeal of the order, was therefore a final order and appealable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Stubbes Precast" p2="King & Columbia" post.rptr="6539" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I643215d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Stubbes Precast v. King & Columbia">Stubbes Precast v. King & Columbia, 2018 ONSC 6539, 2018 CarswellOnt 18402, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 281 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2018 ONSC 3062, 2018 CarswellOnt 8086, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 275 (Ont. Div. Ct.); quashing appeal 2018 ONSC 995, 2018 CarswellOnt 2163, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 270 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In filing two separate construction liens against the defendant's property, the plaintiff's lawyer incorrectly set out a portion of the plaintiff's corporate name as <ital>Ltd.</ital> instead of the correct <ital>Inc.</ital> On motion by the defendant to discharge the liens, the lower court exercised its discretion under the curative provision of s. 6 and amended the style of cause accordingly. When the defendant appealed that decision to the Divisional Court, the plaintiff moved to quash the appeal before the Divisional Court on the basis that s. 71(3) prohibited any appeal from an interlocutory order. The motions judge then ruled that the effect of the lower court order was to preclude the defendant from raising a defence which would have ended the lien action and enabled it to return of its posted security, and that the order was therefore final. On further motion by the plaintiff to set aside that order, the full court found that the lower court reasons were made for purposes of the motion only. They did not preclude the defendant from raising the misnomer defence at trial, where the plaintiff would have the onus of proving that it had valid liens, and that it was the proper lien claimant. In the result, the lower court order was interlocutory, and not subject to appeal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Heinrichs" p2="374427 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="78" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I64323ce05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heinrichs v. 374427 Ontario Ltd.">Heinrichs v. 374427 Ontario Ltd., 2018 ONSC 78, 2018 CarswellOnt 25, 86 C.L.R. (4th) 121 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 994, 2018 CarswellOnt 2304 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was discharged pursuant to an undertaking by the defendant's' lawyers to hold sufficient funds from sale of the property in escrow under certain terms. Following the release of the lien instruments, the plaintiffs did not take any steps to prosecute the action or set it down for trial, and the defendants moved to dismiss the action for delay or, in the alternative, to direct that the action proceed as an action in contract. In respect of both options, the defendants sought an order directing the release of the escrow funds. The Master directed the action to proceed as a contract action and ordered the funds be paid out to the defendants, on the basis that the security provided by the undertaking was akin to security for the lien having been posted in court. On the plaintiff's appeal to the Divisional Court, the word “judgment” in s. 71(1) was held to apply to any decision by which the rights of a party are finally disposed of, and although the Master allowed the breach of contract action to continue, her interpretation of the undertaking and the parties' intention concerning the action was the basis of her order to release the security. That disposition was final in nature in that it finally determines those issues. Accordingly, an appeal from the order to the Divisional Court was not prohibited by s. 71(3)(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pflanzer" p2="Laari Construction Ltd. et al." post.rptr="4877" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I64323ce15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pflanzer v. Laari Construction Ltd. et al.">Pflanzer v. Laari Construction Ltd. et al., 2017 ONSC 4877, 2017 CarswellOnt 12724, 84 C.L.R. (4th) 267 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Two subcontractors appealed the dismissal of their motion seeking the dismissal of the palintiff's lien claim, having argued that the information in the lien registration documents did not comply with the requirements of the Act. In allowing the plaintiff's motion for an order quashing the appeal, the Divisional Court held that the motion was interlocutory rather than final and, pursuant to s. 71(3), no appeal lay from it. The dismissal of the dismissal motion allowed the action to survive, but did not relieve the plaintiff of having to prove the claim for lien. It did not preclude the subcontractors from arguing at trial that the lien had expired.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urbacon Building Groups Corp." p2="Guelph (City)" post.rptr="3840" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I64323ce25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City)">Urbacon Building Groups Corp. v. Guelph (City), 2014 ONSC 3840, 2014 CarswellOnt 8577, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 287, 327 O.A.C. 6 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Given the extensive evidence and costs associated with proving the claim and the counterclaim, counsel obtained a bifurcation of the liability and damages phases of the trial so that only one of the parties would have to prove damages. After the parties were advised that the trial judge had determined the issue of liability in favour of the lien claimants, the City issued a notice of appeal and moved to stay the proceedings pending a determination of its appeal by the Divisional Court. The court held that the order arising from the judge's reasons did not constitute a “judgment” as they did not finally dispose of the actions in the case. They only made a finding of liability, and until the issue of damages and costs were determined, the actions were not finally disposed of on their merits. An order arising from the determination on the liability phase of the trial was an interlocutory order which could not be appealed until after the damages phase of the trial was completed. In any event, the court would not have exercised its discretion to stay the proceedings.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trifield Construction Co." p2="HC Matcon Inc." post.rptr="6514" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I643263f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trifield Construction Co. v. HC Matcon Inc.">Trifield Construction Co. v. HC Matcon Inc., 2013 ONSC 6514, 2013 CarswellOnt 15048 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 15767 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved to quash the plaintiff's appeal to the Divisional Court on the ground that the appeal was from an interlocutory rather than final order. At a pre-trial meeting, the Master had noted in her procedure book that the defendant's counterclaim was capped at a lesser amount, prompting the defendant to move at the next pre-trial to vary this note on the ground that it arose from a misunderstanding. The Master agreed and noted in her procedure book that the counterclaim was not to exceed a revised, larger amount, and it was from the second note that the plaintiff sought to appeal. The court held that the merits of the case remained to be determined, and the order was clearly interlocutory. A report of a Master had no effect until it has been confirmed, and here, the Master has not issued a report or an interim report. An appeal did not lie to the Divisional Court in an unconfirmed report of a Master in these circumstances.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5144" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I643263f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2011 ONSC 5144, 2011 CarswellOnt 8835 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—An adjournment was not necessary merely because the master's decision to refuse to recuse herself from the matter was still under appeal. Section 71(3)(b) provided that there was no appeal from an interlocutory order of the court, and a recusal motion was an interlocutory motion. Because an appeal from the disposition of the recusal motion was not available, the fact that an appeal was launched did not justify adjourning the motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="570 South Service Road Inc." p2="Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd." post.rptr="3410" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I643263f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="570 South Service Road Inc. v. Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd.">570 South Service Road Inc. v. Lawrence-Paine & Associates Ltd., 2011 ONSC 3410, 2011 CarswellOnt 5996, 3 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The dismissal of a motion for an order discharging a construction lien is an interlocutory order. It is analogous to a motion for summary judgment, which is a final order if judgment is granted, but if summary judgment is refused, it is interlocutory, and the case proceeds to trial, where the plaintiff must prove its case. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The court declined to distinguish this case from the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Teperman & Sons Inc." p2="Alros Products Ltd." post.rptr="957" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I9104b920f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teperman & Sons Inc. v. Alros Products Ltd.">Teperman & Sons Inc. v. Alros Products Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 957, 18 C.L.R. (2d) 228 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, on the basis that the motions judge made a positive ruling that the lien had not expired and thereby did more than simply refuse to order that the lien had expired.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ravenda Homes Ltd." p2="1372708 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="6338" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I643263f45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc.">Ravenda Homes Ltd. v. 1372708 Ontario Inc., 2010 ONSC 6338, 2010 CarswellOnt 8745, 95 C.L.R. (3d) 190 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant sought an order declaring that the construction liens had expired, vacating the certificates of action and dismissing two actions, on the basis that the plaintiff could not set the action down for trial when it purported to do so, because pleadings remained open after the plaintiff had delivered a reply and defence to counterclaim, after which the defendant had filed an amended defence and counterclaim. The orders dismissing the defendant's motion were held to be interlocutory, and the appeal of those orders were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. No substantive rights of the parties had been finally disposed of, and the real matters in dispute remained to be determined. The judge's order that a reply in a lien action may be filed only with leave of the court, and was a nullity, only rendered the amended defence as filed a nullity as well, but did not strike it out. Any defences raised in the amended pleadings remained available to the defendant to assert, if it wished to take steps to do so under Rule 26.01.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Tabrco Management Ltd. Estate (Trustee of)" p2="Sundial Homes (Bronte) Ltd." post.rptr="81" pre.rptr="79" ref.id="I64328b005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tabrco Management Ltd. Estate (Trustee of) v. Sundial Homes (Bronte) Ltd.">Tabrco Management Ltd. Estate (Trustee of) v. Sundial Homes (Bronte) Ltd. (2009), 79 C.L.R. (3d) 81, 2009 CarswellOnt 2639 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An order impacting the scheduling of two lien actions was an interlocutory order from which there was no appeal under s. 71(3)(b).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="V. Gibbons Contracting Ltd." p2="Losani Homes (1998) Ltd." post.rptr="242" pre.rptr="77" ref.id="I64328b015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="V. Gibbons Contracting Ltd. v. Losani Homes (1998) Ltd.">V. Gibbons Contracting Ltd. v. Losani Homes (1998) Ltd. (2008), 77 C.L.R. (3d) 242, 2008 CarswellOnt 5787 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2008), 77 C.L.R. (3d) 77, 2008 CarswellOnt 6091 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the defendant was denied leave to bring a motion seeking answers to outstanding undertakings and refusals, permission to amend the statement of defence and counterclaim, and costs, the order was final. Denial of leave effectively precluded the defendant from raising any defence it wished to assert and it deprived it of its substantive rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="I.C.I. Construction Ltd." p2="Altavista Properties Inc." post.rptr="613" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I64328b025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.C.I. Construction Ltd. v. Altavista Properties Inc.">I.C.I. Construction Ltd. v. Altavista Properties Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 613 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An order denying a party leave to bring a motion for security for costs is interlocutory. It does not dispose of any aspect of the real matter in dispute between the parties or even dispose of the right or potential right to costs. It merely deprives the party of the opportunity to get security for any costs it might ultimately recover. Subsection 71(3)(b) of the Act clearly states that there is no appeal from an interlocutory order and there is no jurisdiction in the court to hear it.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="John Bianchi Grading Ltd." p2="Belrock Design Build Inc." post.rptr="3034" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I64328b035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="John Bianchi Grading Ltd. v. Belrock Design Build Inc.">John Bianchi Grading Ltd. v. Belrock Design Build Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3034, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 198 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In the absence of authority for the proposition, the court declined to treat an order setting a trial date as being an interlocutory order within the meaning of the term used in s. 71(3)(b). An order setting a trial date or an order adjourning a trial date, though not finally disposing of the matter in dispute, was more of an administrative nature than an adjudicative nature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="McGowan Construction of Ravenna Ltd." p2="Cedar Highland Ski Club" post.rptr="5832" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I6432b2105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="McGowan Construction of Ravenna Ltd. v. Cedar Highland Ski Club">McGowan Construction of Ravenna Ltd. v. Cedar Highland Ski Club (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 5832, 194 O.A.C. 309 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—At issue was whether the order of the Master sought to be appealed from was final or interlocutory. Subsection 17(1)(c) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> provided that an appeal from an interlocutory order of a master was to a single judge of the Superior Court rather than to the Divisional Court. The law was clear that an order setting aside a default judgment was an interlocutory order. Accordingly, the Master, in setting aside a default judgment on terms which included the payment into court of the amount claimed in the lien action, did not finally determine a substantive right of the defendants. While the effect of this was, for practical purposes, to vacate the lien in that the security of the lien for the amount claimed was replaced by the security of the payment into court, it did not preclude the defendants from raising, by way of motion pursuant to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> or the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> or in the action itself, any defence it might wish to assert as to the validity of the plaintiff's claim, the amount of the claim, the entitlement of the plaintiff to a lien for such amount or any other defence. No substantive right to the defendants had been finally determined by the order of the Master and it was therefore interlocutory. The appeal was quashed as being improperly brought before the Divisional Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19980414" p1="Interhaven Development Corp." p2="Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc." post.rptr="2378" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I6432b2115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc.">Interhaven Development Corp. v. Slovak Village Non-Profit Housing Inc. (April 14, 1998), Doc. 873/97, [1998] O.J. No. 2378 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A motion to quash an appeal from a Master's order providing for cancellation of a letter of credit was dismissed. The taking away of a right granted by statute is the final determination of that right, and an appeal lies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Atlas Construction Inc." p2="Brownstones Ltd." post.rptr="67" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I6432b2125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas Construction Inc. v. Brownstones Ltd.">Atlas Construction Inc. v. Brownstones Ltd. (1996), 46 C.P.C. (3d) 67, 31 C.L.R. (2d) 89 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An order denying a request to plead a new defence was a final order and therefore the appeal was not barred by s. 71(3)(b) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. As the outcome of the appeal could greatly affect the continuation of the trial, an adjournment of the trial was required pending its hearing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc." p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="4408" pre.rptr="[1996]" ref.id="I6432b2135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission">Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 4408, 1996 CarswellOnt 4831 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1997), 1997 CarswellOnt 347 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 71(3) was not applicable where the relevant action was not commenced under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, but was a separate action commenced in the usual way which was ordered tried with related construction lien actions, and the claims included claims in tort, in contract and others which were beyond the traditional jurisdiction of a Master in construction lien matters. (<ital>Note</ital>: application for judicial review of Master's decision dismissed at (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3986, 1998 CarswellOnt 3844 (Ont. Gen. Div.).)</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Teperman & Sons Inc." p2="Alros Products Ltd." post.rptr="957" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I91050740f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Teperman & Sons Inc. v. Alros Products Ltd.">Teperman & Sons Inc. v. Alros Products Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 957, 18 C.L.R. (2d) 228 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 17(a) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, which provides for an appeal to a judge from an interlocutory order of a master does not override s. 71(3)(b) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Bravo Cement" p2="University of Toronto" post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="52" ref.id="I6432d9205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto">Bravo Cement v. University of Toronto (1991), 52 O.A.C. 107 <point>at 110</point> (Div. Ct.); additional reasons to (1991), 46 C.L.R. 207, 52 O.A.C. 107 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—An order under appeal that is final with respect to the lienability of lands in question is not an interlocutory order, and, accordingly, an appeal lies to the Divisional Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Alpa Lumber Inc." p2="786366 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="220" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I6432d9215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alpa Lumber Inc. v. 786366 Ontario Ltd.">Alpa Lumber Inc. v. 786366 Ontario Ltd. (1991), 48 C.L.R. 220, 6 O.R. (3d) 496 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The trustee accepted an offer to purchase in respect of a building project, subject to approval by the court. The trustee in good faith applied to the court for approval of the offer but before the application was heard, the trustee received another higher offer, and eventually recommended that the court accept the higher offer. The court did approve the higher offer, but recognizing that the applicant had expended certain funds to improve the property and make it safe during the winter months, the court, based on an affidavit by the president of the applicant indicating that the money expended in winterizing the premises was $50,000, directed that $50,000 be paid to the applicant out of the proceeds of purchase and sale. The Divisional Court quashed an application by the first, would-be purchaser to set aside the court order. The real matter in dispute was the disposition of the construction lien between the parties to the lien action. The order under appeal did not dispose of the issues to be determined in the main action, which remained outstanding. The order under appeal was therefore interlocutory in nature, and since there was no evidence that the order under appeal was an improvident order, the court had no jurisdiction to intervene.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd." p2="Davis" post.rptr="66" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I6432d9225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Davis">Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Davis (1990), 43 C.L.R. 66 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff brought an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for the value of goods sold and rented to the defendant for construction purposes. The defendant counterclaimed for goods alleged to have been wrongfully seized from him and brought a motion for an order for the return of the goods. The defendant appealed dismissal of the motion, and the plaintiff successfully moved to quash on the basis that there was no right of appeal. Subsection 73(3)(b) of the Act provides that there is no appeal from an interlocutory order made by the court. While the counterclaim was a separate action, it was governed by the provisions of the Act. The order in question being an interlocutory order, there was no right of appeal.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
72:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 72.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">72:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, s. 14(2), stipulated that “every wage earner shall be entitled to enforce a lien in respect of the contract not completely fulfilled”. That wording was amended in 1914 to the format still found in 1980, with the exception that the “wage-earner” was replaced by a “workman” in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, s. 15(2). Section 72 of the current statute replaces s. 14 and s. 16(2) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. Section 14 had provided that every subcontractor was entitled to enforce a lien notwithstanding the non-completion or abandonment of the contract by any contractor or subcontractor under whom he claimed. An identical provision first appeared in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30, s. 13(2). Subsection 16(2) entitled every workman to enforce a lien in respect of any contract or subcontract that had not been completed, and allowed the workman to serve a notice of motion on the proper persons. With the exception of making the text gender neutral, the provision as it appears today is identical to the one introduced in the 1983 revisions.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section creates another exception to the general rule that an owner is not liable for more than it owes to the contractor. A lien claimant may enforce a lien, despite the noncompletion or abandonment of any contract or subcontract. Thus, an owner could be liable for the amount of holdback on the value of the work done or an abandoned contract where as a result of the abandonment no monies are owed by the owner to the contractor.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Partridge" p2="Villa Lathing & Drywall Co." post.rptr="3005" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I643300305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Partridge v. Villa Lathing & Drywall Co.">Partridge v. Villa Lathing & Drywall Co. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 3005, 2003 CarswellOnt 2865 (Master)</ref></cite>—The contract between the parties had no express terms providing for a completion date or milestones or required progress by set dates. Absent such terms in the contract, the actions of the defendant's representatives directing the plaintiff and his forces to leave the job was a breach of their contract, not a repudiation of the contract by the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="U.A.W. Local Union 853 Ontario Sprinkler Industry Benefit Trust Fund" p2="Metro Sprinkler & Fire System Co." post.rptr="19" pre.rptr="26" ref.id="I643300315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="U.A.W. Local Union 853 Ontario Sprinkler Industry Benefit Trust Fund v. Metro Sprinkler & Fire System Co.">U.A.W. Local Union 853 Ontario Sprinkler Industry Benefit Trust Fund v. Metro Sprinkler & Fire System Co. (1995), 26 C.L.R. (2d) 19 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The right of an individual worker to enforce a lien in the face of an abandonment, as provided in s. 72 of the Act, must be exercised within the confines of ss. 31 and 34. The lien right of a worker cannot be exercised independently of the time horizons established by the contract in respect of which the individual has supplied her or his services. While the individual person's right to enforce a lien is not lost when the employer abandons the project, the act of abandonment sets the preservation clock ticking for the employer's workers.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
73:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 73.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">73:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act of 1874</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20 (2nd Sess.), s. 12, which first amended the original Act of 1873, provided that “in the event of the death of the lien holder his right of lien shall pass to his personal representatives, and the right of a lien holder may be assigned by an instrument in writing”. A general right of assignment was introduced in s. 26 of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69. Aside from minor changes to the wording, that section remained substantially identical until today.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The right to a lien, like other choses in action, may be assigned. Personal liens pass to a deceased's personal representative and may also be seized in execution, as personal property.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brock Contracting" p2="Kozikowski" post.rptr="7618" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I643327405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brock Contracting v. Kozikowski">Brock Contracting v. Kozikowski, 2018 ONSC 7618, 2018 CarswellOnt 21555, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The contractor carried on business as a sole proprietorship using the original business name. She later incorporated a numbered company, and, after the last supply of services and materials to the defendant's property, registered the subsequent business name, and cancelled the original business name's registration. The new corporation then commenced a lien action under the subsequent business name. Pursuant to s. 73, the corporation did not have the right to register a lien, since it was not a party to the contract and supplied no services or materials to the project. The ordinary grammatical meaning of s. 73 is that any assignment of lien rights must be in writing. The permissive “may” in that section applies to the words “be assigned”, not the words “by an instrument in writing”. The court has no discretion to authorize an assignment that is not in writing. While the change from sole proprietorship to corporation might have been a “technicality”, it was a technicality with important legal consequences.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
74:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 74.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">74:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section was introduced in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, s. 76, replacing s. 37 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which had provided that where an owner entered into an entire contract for the supply of materials to various buildings, the supplier could ask to have its lien follow the form of the contract and that it be for the entire amount for all the buildings. In case one or more of the buildings were sold, the judge could apportion against the respective buildings the amount included in the claim for lien under the entire contract.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A general lien is not diminished by the sale or release of one of the properties to which it relates, although the lien cannot be enforced against the property or properties which have been sold. Hence, where materials are supplied to many units in a subdivision, the sale of several of those units will not affect the supplier's right to realize the lien for the total amount remaining unpaid on the unsold units. This section should be read in conjunction with s. 44(4), dealing with the apportionment of a general lien, and s. 82, dealing with the subordination of the general lien to other lien claimants. As outlined by the Attorney General's Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital>, s. 82 may, in certain circumstances, postpone recovery by a general lien claimant against a premise to the recovery of non-general lien claimants against the same premise.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 74(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-Haven Homes Inc." p2="O'Neill" post.rptr="249" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I64334e505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill">Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill (1991), 44 C.L.R. 249 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee held building mortgages over six parcels of land which were being developed, and the plaintiff lien claimants filed a lien claim against all six parcels. After some of the parcels were sold, and discharges were registered, two parcels remained encumbered by the claim. The mortgagee brought a motion to vacate the liens and certificate of action upon payment into court of a reasonable amount. The court found that the lien claimants were entitled to a general lien in respect of the two encumbered parcels.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
75:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 75.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">75:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 26(5) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, first stipulated that certain acts were not to prejudice a claimant's right to enforce a lien. Subsection 26(5) read as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The taking of any security for, or the acceptance of any promissory note for, or the taking of any other acknowledgement of the claim, or the giving of time for the payment of the claim, or the taking of any proceedings for the recovery of the claim or the recovery of any personal judgment for the claim, shall not merge, waive, pay, satisfy, prejudice or destroy any lien created by this Act, unless the lien-holder agrees in writing that it shall have that effect; provided, however, that a person who has extended the time for payment of any claim for which he has a lien under this Act to obtain the benefit of this sub-section shall commence an action to enforce such lien within the time limited by this Act, and register a certificate as required by sections 22 or 23 of this Act, but no further proceedings shall be taken in the action until the expiration of such extension of time; provided further, that notwithstanding such extension of time, such person may, where an action is commenced by any other person to enforce a lien against the same property, prove and obtain payment of his claim in such action, as if no such extension had been given.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The section first appeared under the heading of “effect of taking security or extending time”, and in a format substantially identical to its 1980 counterpart in ss. 28(1) to (3) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1914, c. 140. Today's version is a slightly amended version, which dates back to the 1983 revisions. Throughout the various <ital>Mechanics' Lien Acts</ital>, the section had contained four subsections. The fourth subsection provided that anybody extending the time for payment for which he or she had a claim for lien in order to obtain the benefit of that section had to commence the action to enforce the claim within the time prescribed by the Act. As explained by the Attorney General's Advisory Committee, that subsection was deleted, as the extending of a period of credit does not extend the time for commencing an action.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Pursuant to subs. (1), a lien cannot be satisfied other than by payment for the services or materials supplied, although a lien claimant can of course choose at any time to register a release and discharge the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A lien claimant may enforce a lien even if payment has been made by means of a promissory note or bill of exchange of which it is still the holder at the time the claimant proves the claim. The taking of security does not extend the time limits set out in the Act for preservation or perfection of a lien under ss. 31 and 36 (subs. (3)).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
76:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 76.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">76:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision can be traced back to the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1873, c. 27. The last sentence of s. 2 of that Act reads as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">And when so registered the person entitled to said lien shall be deemed a purchaser <ital>pro tanto</ital>, and within the provisions of the <ital>Registry Act</ital>.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The provision became a section in its own right with the Revised Statutes of 1887, R.S.O. 1887, c. 126, s. 19. Aside from the inclusion of a reference to the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital> in addition to the <ital>Registry Act</ital> in S.O. 1910, c. 69, s. 21, the section remained unchanged until 1983, when it appeared in its current wording, still substantially unchanged.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section, in conjunction with ss. 77 and 78, serves to protect the priority of a lien claim as against other interests in a property. A registered lien will obtain priority over ensuring interests in the premises, with the exception of other liens relating to the same improvement.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I64339c705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The owner of a project for the construction of 36 houses on 36 single-family lots became insolvent and stopped paying trades, professionals, and suppliers to the project after all but five of the houses had been completed and sold to third party purchasers. A mortgage in excess of $5,000,000 had been obtained to secure the financing of the entire project, and while the parties agreed that s. 78(2) applied and that the liens had priority over the mortgage to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner, they could not agree on the amount of the holdback. The lien claimants argued that the holdback should be 10 per cent of the value of the whole improvement which would ensure a payout to all lien claimants of 100 per cent. The mortgagee claimed that the lien claimants were entitled to priority only for the deficiency in the holdback on each of their contracts. Held, each lien claimant was entitled only to priority to the extent of a deficiency in the holdback required to be retained by the owner on each of their contracts. It would not be rational under s. 22(1) of the Act to allow a contract, which was completed at the beginning of the project and on which the owner paid out the holdback pursuant to s. 31 at the expiration of the 45-day period for the registration of liens, to be revived for purposes of computing the holdback in the present action. “Improvement” is also defined in the Act and, if it was intended that the holdback be 10 per cent, of the “improvement,” that term would have been used in s. 22(1), but instead the word “contract” was used. The interpretation suggested by the lien claimants would cause great confusion in the construction industry and would result in delay in the release of holdbacks when work was done and the lien period expired. Therefore, in the circumstances of the present case, the contract of each lien claimant stood on its own and had a separate holdback to which the lien claimant might look for payment.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
77:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 77.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">77:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section was introduced in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, s. 79. It replaced s. 15(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which had been the source of some confusion. Former s. 15(1) read as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(1)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">The lien has priority over all judgments, executions, assignments, attachments, garnishments and receiving orders recovered, issued or made after the lien arises, and over all payments or advances made on account of any conveyance or mortgage after notice in writing of the lien has been given to the person making such payments or after registration of a claim for the lien as hereinafter provided, and, in the absence of such notice in writing or the registration of a claim for lien, all such payments or advances have priority over any such lien.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The section dates back to <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, s. 12(1). The last part of the section, dealing with the absence of written notice or registration, was added in <ital>An Act to Amend The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19, s. 3. The section remained unchanged until the 1983 reforms.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A comment on the then new mechanics' lien legislation in the January 1877 <ital>Canada Law Journal</ital> laments that the “wording is obscure, and its provisions unintelligible”. More than 100 years later, s. 15(1) (now s. 77) fell into the same category. As noted by the Attorney General's Advisory Committee, both the purpose and the effect of this section had always remained cryptic. The new section is intended to and does clarify the purpose of the Act, ensuring that suppliers of services or materials toward an improvement shall have priority to the owner's general creditors. A construction lien enjoys priority over the general creditors from the date the first lien arises. In other words, there is no priority over judgments executed or recovered upon before the time when the first lien arose. In those cases an execution or judgment creditor will indeed have priority over the lien. The underlying theory appears to be that any increase in value after the time the first lien arose is likely due in whole or in part to the supply of services or materials by lien claimants.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DBDC Spadina Ltd." p2="Walton" post.rptr="2550" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6433c3805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="DBDC Spadina Ltd. v. Walton">DBDC Spadina Ltd. v. Walton, 2015 ONSC 2550, 2015 CarswellOnt 5706, 24 C.B.R. (6th) 34, 45 C.L.R. (4th) 313 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The order appointing the manager provided for two super-priority charges to secure its fees and disbursements, and other various amounts. The lien claimants unsuccessfully contended that there was no authority for the court to make such an order in light of provisions of s. 77, given that the liens arose before the appointment of the Manager. Although the lien claimants were notified of the appointment and the super-priority, they took no steps to vary or set aside the order or challenge the court's jurisdiction to grant priority until the Manager's mandate with respect to the property, which benefited all parties including the lienholders, was essentially complete. It would not be equitable for the lien claimants to challenge the Manager's charges at the late date of the latter's motion to approve its fees.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R." p2="Morvai" post.rptr="279" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I6433c3815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R. v. Morvai">R. v. Morvai, 2010 ONSC 279, 2010 CarswellOnt 190 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The applicant worker successfully applied under s. 462.42 of the <ital>Criminal Code</ital> for relief from forfeiture, and while he did not acquire a right to an interest in property by operation of statute, he had an equitable interest pursuant to the principle of unjust enrichment. There was no juristic reason for the Crown to be enriched by a worker's labour that enhanced the value of the property. The worker's interest, however, was declared to rank below that of any secured creditors and parties with valid registered liens. As a matter of public policy, contractors who ignored the requirements of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> should not be entitled to share in the proceeds of sale on an equal footing with those who did comply with the <ital>Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Wentworth Condominium Corp. No. 293" p2="Stonehaven Homes Inc." post.rptr="239" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I6433c3825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wentworth Condominium Corp. No. 293 v. Stonehaven Homes Inc.">Wentworth Condominium Corp. No. 293 v. Stonehaven Homes Inc. (2005), 47 C.L.R. (3d) 239, 2005 CarswellOnt 4030 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After funds were paid into court in order to vacate a lien in a construction lien action, the plaintiff in a second action unsuccessfully sought an order that none of the monies paid into court in the first action be paid out without providing notice to the plaintiff. The plaintiff was not a party to the first action. The court held that litigants in non-lien actions could not avail themselves of the funds arising from the process of the Act. The purpose of s. 44 of the Act was merely to allow the flow of funding to the construction to resume by vacating the lien so that it is no longer attached to the premises. Section 77 of the Act provided that liens have priority over all judgments, executions, assignments, attachments, garnishments and receiving orders except those executed or recovered upon before the time when the first lien arose in respect of the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Di-Mar Construction Ltd." p2="Wellington Business Centre Inc." post.rptr="68" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6433c3835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Di-Mar Construction Ltd. v. Wellington Business Centre Inc.">Di-Mar Construction Ltd. v. Wellington Business Centre Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 68 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—W. Ltd. constructed a building with financing obtained from P. Ltd. After initial construction, it was decided to enclose the ground floor area, and a new mortgagee agreed to provide a mortgage to W. Ltd. to pay off the P. Ltd. mortgage, to assist with the cost of enclosure, and to allow the balance to be used by W. Ltd. for investments purposes. The mortgagee advanced the entire sum to W. Ltd., part of which was deposited into an interest-bearing money market fund held in trust for W. Ltd. The balance of the mortgage proceeds were used to pay off P. Ltd.'s mortgage, rather than to complete the enclosure. Two liens were subsequently registered against the property, and the moneys in the money market fund were seized by the mortgagee and applied to reduce the outstanding balance of the mortgage. The court found that the liens had priority over this assignment, and that the lien claimants were entitled to recover the amount of their respective liens from the mortgagee. The increase in the new mortgage was obtained to pay for the enclosure of the ground floor. When the mortgagee appropriated the trust funds in the bank account held for W. Ltd., there was nothing left to pay the subtrades. The reassignment of those funds to the mortgagee was made to deprive lien claimants from recovering sums owed to them.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1975" p1="Baxter Student Housing Ltd." p2="College Housing Co-operative Ltd." post.rptr="85" pre.rptr="1975" ref.id="I6433ea905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Baxter Student Housing Ltd. v. College Housing Co-operative Ltd.">Baxter Student Housing Ltd. v. College Housing Co-operative Ltd. (1975), 1975 CarswellMan 85, 1975 CarswellMan 3, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 475 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—An order appointing a receiver and providing priority to money paid to the receiver over “any and all other charges or encumbrances… affecting the lands” was invalidly made as it conflicted with rights of lien holders under s. 11 of the Manitoba <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
78:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">78:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section first appeared in similar form as s. 80 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, replacing ss. 8(3), 8(5), 8(6) and 15(1) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. The scope and legislative history of s. 15(1) has been outlined under s. 77. Sections dealing with prior mortgages, first appeared in substantially the same form as s. 8(3) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30. Sections relating to priority over future advances were added 14 years later as s. 2 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1937</ital>, S.O. 1937, c. 41, which repealed and substituted subs. (3) of s. 7 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1927, c. 173, as re-enacted by s. 2 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1932</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19. Provisions concerning registered agreements for sale and purchase of land have the longest history in this group, dating back to 1896. Subsection 12(2) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In case of an agreement for the purchase of land, and the purchase money or part thereof is unpaid, and no conveyance made to the purchaser, the purchaser shall, for the purposes of this Act and within the meaning thereof, be deemed a mortgagor and the seller a mortgagee.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The section remained basically unchanged until 1969, when s. 7(6) of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, amended it to read as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A registered agreement for the sale and purchase of land and any moneys <ital>bona fide</ital> secured or payable thereunder has the same priority over a lien as is provided for a mortgage and mortgage moneys in subsections 3 and 5, and for the purposes of this Act the seller shall be deemed to be a mortgagee, and any moneys <ital>bona fide</ital> secured and payable under such agreement shall be deemed to be mortgage moneys <ital>bona fide</ital> secured or advanced.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The subsection remained in that format until the changes in 1983. Subsection (5) of the current Act was inserted by the Advisory Committee in 1983 to redress what it believes to be a major inequity in the law resulting from the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dorbern Investments Ltd." p2="Provincial Bank of Canada" post.rptr="459" pre.rptr="[1981] 1" ref.id="I643438b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dorbern Investments Ltd. v. Provincial Bank of Canada">Dorbern Investments Ltd. v. Provincial Bank of Canada, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 459 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> (see comments below). As it appears today, it originates from 1983, c. 77, s. 9(1). Subsection (6) corresponds to the former s. 15(1), the scope and history of which was discussed under s. 77. Subsection (7) is based on s. 38(2) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. It can be traced back to 1932, when <ital>An Act to amend The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19, s. 8, amended s. 32 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1927, c. 173 by adding the passage in similar format. Subsection (8) is a relatively new provision, having been inserted in the 1983 revisions which, as outlined by the Advisory Committee, responds to numerous recommendations to the effect that provision should be made for the registration of a “conditional discharge”. The Committee did not believe a conditional discharge to be a workable concept, and found the giving of a postponement preferable to the registration of a discharge, since it continues the lien as an interest in the premises. Subsection (9) dates back to 1983. Subsection (10) in its current version first appeared in the <ital>Red Tape Reduction Act</ital>, S.O. 1997, c. 19, s. 30, and subs. (11) as it reads today was introduced in s. 9(2) of <ital>An Act to amend the Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 77.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 78 sets out the general relative priorities of construction liens and other secured interests on a property. A key component of this scheme is protection of the holdback. This is achieved by giving the lien priority over any “building mortgage” or any mortgage registered after work commences on the improvement to the extent of any deficiency on holdback. This scheme is an attempt to balance the interests of the various parties and ensure a fair allocation of risk and benefit in the construction process. It recognizes the fact that construction is financed both by morgagees and unpaid trades. Mortgagees are generally in the best position to assess the risk relating to a construction project in advance of work being done. Without the subordination of mortgage advances provided in this section, a mortgagee faced with an insolvent owner and unpaid suppliers would obtain both the property under a power of sale and the benefit of the unpaid suppliers' services and materials.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 78(1) grants construction liens a general priority over registered interests affecting the premises. Subsection 78(2) gives a lien priority, to the extent of any deficiency in the holdback, over mortgages taken to secure the financing of an improvement, regardless of whether the mortgage is registered before or after work is first done on the improvement. It is the intention of the mortgagee which is decisive in determining whether a mortgage has been advanced to secure improvements and is, therefore, a “building mortgage”.
