There is an argument to be made that when a contractor, having privity with the owner, gives written notice of lien to the owner, its building mortgage priority is equal to its entire lien since the use of the plural of “holdback” may refer to both the statutory and notice holdbacks of Part IV of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Pursuant to subs. (3), all conveyances, non-building mortgages and other encumbrances which have been registered prior to the date when the first services or materials are supplied to the improvement have priority over the lien. That priority is limited to the lesser of the value of premises at the time the first lien arose or the total amounts advanced before the first lien arose. Subsection 78(4) provides that a conveyance, non-building mortgage or other agreement which has been registered before the first lien arises has additional priority with respect to any advances made in the absence of a preserved lien or actual written notice of a lien. Subsection 78(6) sets out similar parallel priority rules for mortgage advances made on mortgages registered after the first lien arose. The key element from the lien claimant's perspective is to fix a mortgage lender with written notice of a lien at the earliest opportunity.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection (5) overturns previous case law under the Act's predecessor, the <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>, which permitted a subsequently registered collateral mortgage to take priority over liens that had not been preserved or concerning which actual written notice of lien had not been given. The subsection gives liens priority over all subsequently registered mortgages to the extent of any deficiency in the owner's holdback amount. However, neither subs. (5) nor subs. (2) applies to a mortgage given or assumed by a home buyer, and neither subsection is retroactive to the coming into force of the Act which, as of the date of writing, is largely academic.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Where a trustee appointed under Part IX gives a mortgage or other interest, it is given free of liens pursuant to subs. (7)(a). Any monies advanced under that mortgage are not subject to any existing liens (subs. (7)(b)), as those monies are used to complete the improvement and are administered by the court appointed trustee for that purpose.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 78(8) allows a mortgagee to make an advance in the face of a postponed lien and not be concerned about liens that have not at that time been preserved or with respect to which no actual written notice has been given. The general priority that liens receive under subss. (2) and (5) is not affected by this section.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 78(10) facilitates conveyance by power of sale contained in a mortgage. A purchaser takes title from a mortgagee free of liens where a financial guarantee bond in prescribed form is registered against the title to the premises. In that case, the financial guarantee bond would take the place of the priorities created by subss. (2) and (5), and lien claimants would have a right of action against the bond surety.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
78:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">78:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Peoples Trust Company et al." p2="Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al." post.rptr="6648" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678555903b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Peoples Trust Company et al. v. Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al.">Peoples Trust Company et al. v. Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 18855, 2024 ONSC 6648 (Ont. S.C.J. [Comm. List])</ref></cite>—The lien priority regime established by s. 78 is an exception to the general priority scheme established by s. 93(3) of the <ital>Land Titles Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990 c. L.5. That subsection provides that, when registered, a mortgage takes priority over all unregistered interest in the land, which would include an equitable lien. It follows that, at its highest, the claim by the lien claimants here to an equitable lien would be a claim to an unregistered interest. There is nothing in the language of s. 93(3) that permits an unregistered equitable lien to override its provisions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Simpson" p2="Bridgewater Bank" post.rptr="714" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64345fc05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simpson v. Bridgewater Bank">Simpson v. Bridgewater Bank, 2012 ONSC 714, 2012 CarswellOnt 1420, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 243 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 5054, 18 C.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff general contractor entered into a construction contract with the owner for construction of a home, and the defendant bank provided mortgage financing. The Bank's solicitor held back 10% from each advance and, after the contractor eventually obtained judgment in its lien action against the owner, the bank completed a sale of the property under power of sale pursuant to the mortgage. The contractor brought action for a declaration that the monies held back by the bank were trust funds held for his benefit. Although the court ultimately found that the funds were indeed held in trust for the contractor, it found that s. 78(5) of the <ital>Act</ital> did not oblige the bank, as mortgagee, to maintain a holdback. The only obligation to maintain a holdback is found in s. 22, and s. 78(5) deals only with the loss of priority for the mortgagee where the owner has failed to maintain a holdback. As this was a “building mortgage”, s. 78(2) applied, and provided only for a limited priority of a lien over the mortgage to the extent of any deficiencies in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Vecero" p2="C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc." post.rptr="903" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I910666d0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc.">Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 903, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 74 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> at paras. 15–17, under ss. 1, 7(1) and s. 78.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2183164 Ontario Inc." p2="Gillani" post.rptr="1456" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I643486d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2183164 Ontario Inc. v. Gillani">2183164 Ontario Inc. v. Gillani, 2013 ONSC 1456, 2013 CarswellOnt 2891, 114 O.R. (3d) 676, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 134 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2012 CarswellOnt 7261, 2012 ONSC 3377, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 8627, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 204 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—On account of the plaintiff's repeated failure to attend for cross-examination, and the Master's view that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> procedures would be inappropriate for achieving a fair, expeditious and least costly resolution of all the issues in the specific circumstances, the Master ordered the discharge of the lien, the vacating of registration of the lien and certificate of action and the dismissal of the lien action, and ruled that this also ended a claim for priority over the mortgagee as such claim could only be asserted, under s. 78, in a lien action. The Divisional Court reversed that decision on appeal, indicating that the Master should have proceeded with the alternative relief claimed rather than wander beyond the parameters of the motion before him as it had been framed by the defendants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Peter Lombardi Construction Inc." p2="Colonnade Investments Inc." post.rptr="4874" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I562d1030fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Peter Lombardi Construction Inc. v. Colonnade Investments Inc.">Peter Lombardi Construction Inc. v. Colonnade Investments Inc. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 4874, 6 C.L.R. (3d) 244 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor successfully moved to add the mortgagee as a party defendant with a view to claiming priority under s. 78 on the basis that no mortgage funds were ever advanced. Service was effected. The mortgagee did not defend, and pleadings were noted closed against it, bringing into operation s. 54(3) and (4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Since there was a deemed admission that no mortgage funds were ever advanced by the mortgagee, the plaintiff's judgment and writ of execution had priority over the mortgage. When the plaintiff's lien was subsequently found to be registered out of time, s. 78 of the Act could not apply.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd." p2="846539 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="230" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I643486d35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd.">Con-Drain Co. (1983) Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 230 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4717 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A bank financed a developer's subdivision project and, during the currency of the loan, relaxed various preconditions to the advance of funds. The bank became aware of cost overruns and required the developers to inject further equity but took no steps to inform the contractors. The bank continued to make advances until the first notice from the contractors that they were not being paid. After the developer became bankrupt, the bank sold the lots and paid down the loan. A group of unpaid contractors then brought action against the bank. The court found that the bank was under no duty to inquire about the shortfalls, and did not owe a duty to the trades not to relax the loan conditions or advise contractors of the shortfalls. The <ital>Mortgages Act</ital> (R.S.O. 1990, c. M-40) and s. 78 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> govern the relationship among mortgagees, lien holders and subsequent encumbrancers. It would impose undesirable costs and commercial uncertainty to add a common law duty.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Vecero" p2="C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc." post.rptr="903" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I910666d1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc.">Vecero v. C. Wood Inns Marketing Inc. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 903, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 74 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Where a mortgagee was held to be neither an owner nor payer, mortgage moneys retained by it did not constitute a holdback under the Act, as only a payer was required to hold back. And as funds were not impressed with a trust until received by a payer, the funds held by the mortgagee were not trust funds. Hence, where the lands in question were sold, the lien claimants were not entitled to resort to the mortgagee for payment of the amounts retained, but were restricted to the proceeds of sale, in which they had priority to the extent of the holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc." p2="Denamer Homes Inc." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I643486d55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc.">L.D. Ducharme Systems Inc. v. Denamer Homes Inc. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 78 reflects the responsibility on a mortgagee who has chosen to finance a construction to protect itself once a lien is registered. Section 78 does not impose these responsibilities on a “home buyer” and the priorities addressed in this section do not apply in the case of a “home buyer” who is not an “owner” within the meaning of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Dorsam Investments Ltd." p2="Counsel Trust Co." post.rptr="76" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I643486d65fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dorsam Investments Ltd. v. Counsel Trust Co.">Dorsam Investments Ltd. v. Counsel Trust Co. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 76 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 78 does not alter the need for some showing that liens are valid as to amount and that the facts necessary to establish priority exist.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Barkey" p2="Maier" post.rptr="138" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I6434ade05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Barkey v. Maier">Barkey v. Maier (1991), 46 C.L.R. 138 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Liens registered before a mortgage and a conveyance of the property in favour of a third party were given priority over both the mortgage and the conveyance by virtue of the provision of s. 78.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Bernard J. Kamin Ltd." p2="Blue Mountain Capital Corp." post.rptr="264" pre.rptr="72" ref.id="I6434ade15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bernard J. Kamin Ltd. v. Blue Mountain Capital Corp.">Bernard J. Kamin Ltd. v. Blue Mountain Capital Corp. (1990), 72 O.R. (2d) 264, 43 C.L.R. 100 (Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A mortgagee, seeking to sell lands to a purchaser pursuant to a power of sale, sought a declaration under the <ital>Vendors and Purchasers Act</ital>, that the purchaser's requisition that certain claims for lien and certificates of action be vacated prior to closing, was an invalid objection to title. The court dismissed the application. A mortgagee was required under the <ital>Mortgages Act</ital> to provide notice to all persons having a prior interest in the subject lands of its purported exercise of its power of sale, and that if service was made and a statutory declaration obtained, the mortgagee could convey valid title to a purchaser. However, s. 80(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, provided that all liens arising from an improvement of land had priority over any mortgages on the property. The purposes under each Act were different: under the <ital>Mortgages Act</ital>, procedural rules provide for the giving of good and valid title, while the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides lien claimants with substantive protection of their investments by way of a system of priorities. In this case, the issue respecting priorities was to be determined in the various lien actions prior to the applicant being in a position to convey good title. Accordingly, the matter could not be determined by summary procedure by way of a vendor and purchaser application to deal with objections to title.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Kovacs" p2="812828 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="91" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I6434ade25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kovacs v. 812828 Ontario Inc.">Kovacs v. 812828 Ontario Inc. (1989), 34 C.L.R. 91 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs entered into two separate agreements of purchase and sale to purchase several properties, but neither transaction was ever completed. Subsequently, after the plaintiffs commenced work on the buildings situate on the properties, a certificate of default judgment for immediate foreclosure respecting all of the said properties was registered in favour of J, in trust. A deed of land was then registered from J, in trust, to the defendant numbered company, 812828. A mortgage from 812828 to H and E was then registered. Subsequently, a claim for lien against 812828 H, E and other defendants was registered. A motion for an order dismissing the lien claim against 812828, H, E was granted. The plaintiffs did not plead that written notice of the lien had been given to the defendants. There was no lien registered against the moving defendants until after they had an interest in the property, and the plaintiffs had not supplied any services or materials to the defendants. Therefore, by operation of s. 80(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78(6)] no valid lien existed against the moving defendants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="Norwon Electric Sault Co." p2="Ross" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I6434d4f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Norwon Electric Sault Co. v. Ross">Norwon Electric Sault Co. v. Ross (1984), 7 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—A mortgagee has an obligation to pay interest on the amount of the holdback, where interest was awardable pursuant to s. 36 of the <ital>Judicature Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 223, and by exercise of judicial discretion. If the amount of the holdback had been paid into court, interest would have accrued thereon. Alternatively, if the amount had been paid into an interest-bearing account by the mortgagee bank, interest would have accrued. There was no reason to deprive the claimants of the interest receivable by virtue of s. 36 of the said Act [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="126" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6434d4f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 126</ref></cite>, the Divisional Court held that with respect to this point, <ital>Norwon Electric Sault Co.</ital> is not good law. See cases under s. 14(2).]</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
78:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">78:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 78(1)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="James Lathem Excavating Limited" p2="Mansteel New Liskeard Inc." post.rptr="5304" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I6434d4f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="James Lathem Excavating Limited v. Mansteel New Liskeard Inc.">James Lathem Excavating Limited v. Mansteel New Liskeard Inc., 2018 ONSC 5304, 2018 CarswellOnt 14981, 94 C.L.R. (4th) 258 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff claimed priority of its lien over the mortgage that the defendant registered against the subject properties. The mortgagee did not provide any evidence that its mortgage fell within any exceptions in s. 78, such that the plaintiff's lien would not have priority.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="David Schaeffer Engineering Ltd." p2="D.T.A. Investments Inc." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I6434d4f35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="David Schaeffer Engineering Ltd. v. D.T.A. Investments Inc.">David Schaeffer Engineering Ltd. v. D.T.A. Investments Inc. (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 26 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—On consent, an interim report was issued fixing a threshold price over which a lien claimant would have priority over a prior registered mortgage. Before the deduction of the mortgagee's expenses there was a surplus, after deduction there was none. The mortgagee was entitled to deduct its expenses.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="O'Byrne" p2="1085043 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="252" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I6434d4f45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="O'Byrne v. 1085043 Ontario Inc.">O'Byrne v. 1085043 Ontario Inc. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 252 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Liens registered under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> have priority over an unregistered vendor's lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I562d5e50fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 78(1) is the overarching principle of the new regime of the Act for the determination of priorities. It necessarily implies that, in cases of conflict, as here, the burden must be on the mortgagee to persuade the court that it somehow falls clearly within a specified exception to the generalized priority of the liens.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd." p2="Villa Nova Construction Inc." post.rptr="227" pre.rptr="33" ref.id="I6434fc005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc.">Paolo's Painting & Decorating Ltd. v. Villa Nova Construction Inc. (1989), 33 C.L.R. 227, 1989 CarswellOnt 690 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The purchaser of a home in a new subdivision was a “home buyer” within the meaning of the Act and was excluded from the statutory definition of “owner”. At the time of closing, there was a preserved lien registered by P Ltd. on title, which the vendor's solicitor undertook to discharge. Before the solicitor was able to do this, P Ltd. registered another lien, contending that the second lien took priority over the conveyance by virtue of s. 80(1) of the Act. The purchaser successfully brought a motion to discharge and vacate P. Ltd.'s claim for lien and certificate of action. The priorities adressed in s. 80 do not apply in the case of a purchaser who is a “home buyer” and who is thereby not an “owner” under the Act. Section 14 makes it plain that a lien is created when services or materials are supplied “to an improvement for an owner, contractor or subcontractor” and since the purchaser was none of those listed in the section P Ltd. did not have a valid claim against her. The purchaser obtained title prior to the registration of P Ltd.'s lien claim and that title was free of any unregistered construction lien claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="Norwon Electric Sault Co." p2="Ross" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I6434fc015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Norwon Electric Sault Co. v. Ross">Norwon Electric Sault Co. v. Ross (1984), 7 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—A reasonable interpretation of s. 80(1) [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78(1)] leads one to the conclusion that if, at the time a mortgage advance is made, there is a lien registered against the premises, all liens “arising from the improvement” have priority to all advances made subsequent to the registration of the first lien. Section 80 distinguishes between “liens arising from the improvement” and liens “preserved or perfected” against the premises. The former deals with work and service performed, the latter with registration. Section 80 creates a priority of all valid liens over mortgage advances made subsequent to any registered lien. Once there is a lien registered against the premises the payer such as the mortgagee is at risk of losing priority if it makes an advance in the face of one or more registered liens. The risk is that he will also lose priority over other liens arising and subsequently registered. One obvious solution is to maintain the proper holdback and arrange for the removal of the registered lien by payment direct or into court.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
78:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">78:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 78(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Kingsett Mortgage Corporation" p2="Mapleview Developments Ltd." post.rptr="18276" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678618e03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Kingsett Mortgage Corporation v. Mapleview Developments Ltd.">Kingsett Mortgage Corporation v. Mapleview Developments Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 18276, 2024 ONSC 6477 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee registered two mortgages against the lands, and made advances under them. Subsequently, the mortgages were discharged and replaced with a single consolidated mortgage, but no further advances were made. At the times of the advances secured by the consolidated mortgage, there were no preserved or perfected liens against the lands. The construction liens subsequently registered did not have priority over the consolidated mortgage for their full amounts and did not constitute “priority payables” under a land sale agreement approved by the court. Rather, the mortgage had priority over the construction liens except to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained. As held in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dal Bianco" p2="Deem Management Services et al." post.rptr="3530" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I678618e13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services et al.">Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services et al., 2020 CarswellOnt 3530, 2020 ONSC 1500, 16 R.P.R. (6th) 244 (Ont. S.C.J.), affirmed 2021 CarswellOnt 18071, 28 C.L.R. (5th) 30 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>, s. 78(2) is a statutory exception to the general rule in s. 78(1), and where the statutory requirement in s. 78(2) is satisfied, the effect is to restrict the priority of the lien claims solely to any deficiency in the holdback amount, and not over the mortgage generally. Section 78(2) does not operate so as to preserve the general lien priority in s. 78(1) and then grant a special priority to liens to the extent of a deficiency in the holdbacks. The court then distinguished <ital>Dal Bianco</ital> in that there, the mortgage was registered to secure previously unsecured financing of an improvement that had already been made through prior advances, whereas in this case, the original mortgages were taken with the intention to secure the financing of an improvement, which financing would then be made through advances secured by registered mortgages. All advances were made by the mortgagee with this intention, which operated prospectively when the original mortgages were taken and continued to the time when the consolidated mortgage was registered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="BCIMC Construction Fund Corp. et al." p2="33 Yorkville Residences Inc. et al." post.rptr="2326" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I678618e23b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="BCIMC Construction Fund Corp. et al. v. 33 Yorkville Residences Inc. et al.">BCIMC Construction Fund Corp. et al. v. 33 Yorkville Residences Inc. et al., 2022 ONSC 2326, 2022 CarswellOnt 6142, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 218 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List]); affirmed <ital>BCIMC Construction Fund Corporation v. 33 Yorkville Residences Inc.</ital>, 2023 ONCA 1, 2023 CarswellOnt 2, 32 C.L.R. (5th) 1 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite></trace>—When, as here, there was more than one building mortgage taken with the intention to secure the financing of the improvement, the liens had priority to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner over all building mortgages combined, rather than each lien claimant having priority over each building mortgage to the extent of the deficiency in the holdback. The lien claimants unsuccessfully argued they were, under the language of s. 78(2), entitled to a priority of, in effect, 20%, rather that the holdback required under s. 22 of 10%, because there were two building mortgagees against which they could assert their priority. Whether there was one building mortgage or two, or three, was irrelevant. The key principle was that the lien claimant receives priority only to the extent of any deficiency in the owner's holdback.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dal Bianco" p2="Deem Management Services et al." post.rptr="3530" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643523115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services et al.">Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services et al., 2020 CarswellOnt 3530, 2020 ONSC 1500, 16 R.P.R. (6th) 244 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2021 CarswellOnt 18071 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The Receiver moved to determine competing priorities under s. 78 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> between registered lien claimants and a registered third mortgage, which secured amounts that were all advanced prior to registration and without security having been registered. The mortgage was registered after the time when the first lien arose and was therefore a “subsequent mortgage” within the meaning of the <ital>Act</ital>. In granting priority to the lien claimants, the court found that the mortgage did not fit into the exclusion of a “subsequent mortgage” as the mortgage did not secure advances, which were already made. Nor was the mortgage a “building mortgage” such that the mortgagee would lose priority only to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks. While the <ital>Act</ital> does not contain a definition for the term “building mortgage”, the section denotes a future intention on the part of a mortgagee, namely an intention to secure financing, and should be taken to mean that the mortgage is registered and then funds advanced in the normal course. What happened in this case was the reverse and was not intended by 78(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Hogg Fuel" p2="Historic Royal Wales" post.rptr="6106" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I643523125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hogg Fuel v. Historic Royal Wales">Hogg Fuel v. Historic Royal Wales, 2018 ONSC 6106, 2018 CarswellOnt 17242, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 244 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 CarswellOnt 20880 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The holdback required by s. 22 was not retained. The lien claimants unsuccessfully argued the words “the liens <ital>arising</ital> from the improvement have priority over that mortgage …” in s. 78(2) meant that that preservation of their liens was not required for there to be priority over the mortgage up to the amount of the basic holdback. The advance by the mortgagee was made at a time when there were no preserved or perfected liens against the property. A lien expires 45 days after publication of the certificate of completion. Only lien claimants with properly preserved and perfected liens are entitled to make a claim against a deficiency in the holdbacks. There were no preserved or perfected liens against the properties within 45 days after the publication of the certificate and therefore, those lien rights expired in relation to a claim against the basic holdback. If liens have been registered and the required holdback was not maintained or the advance was made notwithstanding, then the lien claimants would have been entitled to priority over the mortgage up to the amount of the deficiency in the holdback or the amount of the advance. The reasoning in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I91070310f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed 1995 CarswellOnt 244, 18 C.L.R. (2d) 255 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> would apply if the mortgagee had paid off the construction mortgage in the face of a preserved or perfected lien without retaining a holdback. In theses circumstances, however, the lien claimants were entitled to have their liens satisfied from the finishing holdback only.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Trenchline Construction Inc." p2="Unimac-United Management Corp." post.rptr="6136" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64354a215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp.">Trenchline Construction Inc. v. Unimac-United Management Corp., 2016 ONSC 6136, 2016 CarswellOnt 15025, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 279 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 17928, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master declined to apply the rules of priority found in s. 78 to notice holdback liability. The rules govern disputes between mortgagees and lien claimants, establishing how security in the land is to be allocated between creditors. This function is best served by establishing clear and fixed rules. The policy considerations underpinning notice holdback liability are much broader. At its core, notice holdback liability establishes the extent to which the owner should police payment issues between contractors and subcontractors, which requires a more flexible approach.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I91070311f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Act does not intend to effect a different priority between lienholders and mortgagees as set out in s. 78(2) based only on the fact a mortgagee moves under s. 44 to vacate all liens in order to expedite a sale pursuant to its power of sale under the mortgage. In the present case, there was no allegation that the mortgagee used s. 44 to affect the lien claimants' interest in any surplus on the sale, as there was in fact no surplus. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also in this regard the recent rulings in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I64354a235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite> <ital>and</ital> <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64354a245fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Wealth Management Corp." p2="1713515 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="6503" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64354a255fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd.">Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd., 2013 ONSC 6503, 2013 CarswellOnt 18879 (Ont. S.C.J.); extension of time to appeal and leave to appeal denied 2014 ONCA 500, 2014 CarswellOnt 8586, 17 C.B.R. (6th) 91, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 191, 323 O.A.C. 101 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A receiver/trustee was appointed for the defendant owner pursuant to several statutes, including s. 68(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. At the time the receiver was appointed, the defendant owned a property under renovation for use as a boutique hotel. Various liens had been registered and subsequently vacated or discharged. The renovations were not completed and the receiver sold the property. Prior to that sale, the applicant OW held a first mortgage that secured principal financing and made various advances to the defendant, with the initial advance applied to re-finance a prior first mortgage held by CCL. After the advances were made, the lien claimant registered its construction lien, and claimed priority under ss. 78(1), (2) and (5) over the OW advances, to the amount of the deficiencies in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner. It argued that the CCL advance was obtained to finance the same improvement for which the OW mortgage was obtained and that the work done both prior to and post the lien claimant's involvement was all in respect of the same improvement. In rejecting the lien claimant's claim to priority, the court noted that when OW made its advances, prior construction liens had been vacated or discharged. It found that the OW advance to pay out the CCL mortgage was for the land portion of the mortgage and not improvements, and was therefore not a building mortgage. Section 78(3) was the applicable provision and under it the OW advance took priority over any lien claim. The improvements undertaken by the claimant did not relate to the same contract, but rather were stand-alone improvements disconnected from the prior lien claimants' interests that were discharged or vacated prior to OW's financing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643571305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After multiple lien claimants contracted directly with the defendant owner in respect of the construction of various townhouses, the owner abandoned the project and the defendant mortgagee stepped in to complete construction and sales of the remaining units. The mortgagee posted security pursuant to s. 44(1) to vacate the claims for lien registered by the claimants, rather than register security on title pursuant to s. 78(10), or moving under s. 68 to appoint a trustee to complete and sell the properties. Applying both <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I91072a20f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I643571325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the court confirmed that following the posting of security and an order made pursuant to s. 44, the priority of a lien claimant is limited to any deficiency in the holdback. The legislation did not intend a different priority between lien holders and mortgagees based only on the fact that a mortgagee moved under s. 44 to vacate the liens in order to facilitate a sale. Section 78(2) and the limit it imposes on the priority provided to lien claimants still applied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Basic Drywall Inc." p2="1539304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="1155" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I643598405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc.">Basic Drywall Inc. v. 1539304 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 1155, 2012 CarswellOnt 2566 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2012 ONSC 6391, 2012 CarswellOnt 16493, 114 O.R. (3d) 219, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 321 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee bank financed a construction project under a building mortgage, and the subcontractors registered construction liens against the owner's property for amounts owed by the general contractor. The total amount the owner owed to the general contractor under the building contract far exceeded the amount that the owner was required to withhold for the benefit of the subcontractors pursuant to section 22 of the <ital>Act</ital>. In order to permit the building project to continue, the bank paid into court funds drawn down under letters of credit, as security for the subcontractors' claims. Ultimately, the property owner was placed in receivership and the property was sold. The proceeds were not sufficient to satisfy the full amount due to the bank under the building mortgage, and the court, in a novel case, was required to determine the priority between the bank and the construction lien claimants with respect to the amount paid into court. The subcontractors argued that the amount due for distribution to them was $276,072.42, the minimum amount the property owner owed to the general contractor for unpaid work certified as complete. The amount paid into court was in excess of that amount, and the bank argued that the correct amount due for distribution to the lien claimants was $50,696.98, the amount of the statutory holdback required under s. 22 of the <ital>Act</ital>. This amount was 10% of the total amount certified as complete under the building contract between the owner and the general contractor. In accepting the bank's argument, the court found that, by paying money into court and vacating the lien, the bank did not lose the priority it would otherwise have had as mortgagee under s. 78(2) of the <ital>Act</ital>, since under s. 44(6), the amount paid into court took the place of the property, and the lien claimants' rights went beyond a charge against the holdback deficiency. After the lien was vacated, the respective priority interests of the mortgagee and lien claimants did not change and continued to be governed by s. 78(2), with the liens having priority over a building mortgage “to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV” of that statute. The amount of that deficiency in this case was the full amount of the holdback required under subsection 22(1), which is included in Part IV of that statute. The Divisional Court subsequently upheld the motions judge's reasoning, noting that the case was distinguished from prior precedents in that the owner's holdback obligation was not necessarily limited to the basic 10% holdback, as it owed much more than that to the contractor and never made payment to the contractor. Under s. 24 of the <ital>Act</ital> lien claimants could look to that additional unpaid amount as further security for their liens by giving written notice to the owner, and once given, the lien claimant had security against the owner's interest in the land to the full extent of the amount the owner, as payer, owes to the general contractor. To extend that obligation to a mortgagee would effectively enlarge the statutory definition of “payer”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd." p2="One Shaftesbury Community Assn." post.rptr="5995" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I643598415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn.">Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn. (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 5995, 55 C.L.R. (3d) 184 (Ont. Master); additional reasons as to costs at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 3684, 72 C.L.R. (3d) 71 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A project for a residential retirement community used a right-to-occupy or life-lease legal structure. The property in question was purchased and the title was transferred to a non-profit community association, which entered into a construction and development agreement with a for-profit numbered company that was to assume the role of construction manager. When construction costs escalated, and some units did not sell or could not be sold because of title problems, there was shortfall in the mortgage money required to pay the general contractor and five trades. There was not enough available money or realizable assets to pay off the six lien claimants, whose lien claims totalled $416,197, and to pay the mortgagee. Subsection 78(2) provided that a building mortgage was subject to the priority of any liens “to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV, irrespective of when the mortgage was registered”. In this case, the mortgage was a “building mortgage” and s. 78(2) applied to the priority claims as between the lien claimants and the mortgagee. The size of the priority of the lien claimants over that of the mortgagee depended upon whether the lien claimants had contracted with the association, or whether they had contracted with the numbered company as contractor and the lien claimants as sub-contractors. If the lien claimants contracted with the association, then they were “contractors” and the holdbacks to be retained (following the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I643598425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>) were 10 per cent of each of their six separate contracts which produced a maximum priority of $122,113.12 to cover the lien claims. If they contracted with the numbered company, as general contractor, who, in turn, contracted with the association to build the entire project, the holdback to be retained was 10 per cent of the Association's “contract” with the numbered company, which priority would cover 100 per cent of the lien claims of $416,197.75. The Master found that both the association and numbered companies were owners within the meaning of the Act, that the numbered company was not a contractor, and that, as a result, the holdbacks required to be retained under Part IV of the Act were 10 per cent of the contract price of each of the contracts entered into with the lien claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="78" ref.id="I643598435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc.">Parkland Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Minaki Lodge Resort 2002 Inc. (2009), 78 C.L.R. (3d) 1, 2009 CarswellOnt 1522 (Ont. C.A.); reversing (2007), 76 C.L.R. (3d) 259, 2007 CarswellOnt 9547, 74 R.P.R. (4th) 296 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing (2006), 54 C.L.R. (3d) 142, 2006 CarswellOnt 2801 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>. The trial judge found that the mortgagee which sought priority over the lien claimants acted in a commercially irresponsible manner by engaging in acts such as continuously advancing funds to an owner which made no payments and which did not have fire insurance in place. Its failure in this regard was a decision of an “owner” and the judge pierced the corporate veil to give the lienholders priority over the second mortgage. In upholding the trial judge's reasoning, the Court of Appeal noted that the absence of direct dealings between the person said to be an owner under the Act and construction suppliers was not determinative, and was only one factor to consider in examining the relationship between the parties. Otherwise, a developer could easily escape its obligations to suppliers by the simple device of arranging for an associated or related company to directly engage suppliers for the provision of services or materials, which would defeat the intended protection provided to lienholders under the Act. For this reason, a “request” for work to be done may be inferred from the totality of the circumstances, viewed in light of the substance of the relationship between the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Northway Developments Inc." p2="1200946 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3082" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I6435bf505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Northway Developments Inc. v. 1200946 Ontario Inc.">Northway Developments Inc. v. 1200946 Ontario Inc. (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3082, 1998 CarswellOnt 3048 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The law is clear that it is the mortgagee's intention, not the mortgagor's that is relevant in determining whether a mortgage is a building mortgage within the meaning of s. 78(2), citing <ital>Salazar v. Bond Towers Ltd.</ital>, Kirsch's C.L.C.F. and the 1982 Attorney General's Committee Report, p. 180 (See Appendix to this volume).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Atlas-Gest Inc." p2="Brownstones Building Corp." post.rptr="757" pre.rptr="[1996]" ref.id="I6435bf515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas-Gest Inc. v. Brownstones Building Corp.">Atlas-Gest Inc. v. Brownstones Building Corp. (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 757, 1996 CarswellOnt 758 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed on other grounds (1996), 46 C.P.C. (3d) 366 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee sought unsuccessfully to amend its defence to allege deficiencies in the work done. The action, which involved numerous lien claims, had been subject to much delay and many of the statements of claim had been issued over five years earlier. There were no complaints against most of the contractors and subcontractors, yet they could not get paid until all lien claims relating to the improvement were finalized. Such finalization would be further delayed if the mortgagee's motion was allowed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Marsil Mechanical" p2="A Reissing-Reissing Enterprise Ltd." post.rptr="301" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I6435bf525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Marsil Mechanical v. A Reissing-Reissing Enterprise Ltd.">Marsil Mechanical v. A Reissing-Reissing Enterprise Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 301, 26 C.L.R. (2d) 148 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—For the purposes of the Act, an “advance” is made when the owner, or the owner's delegate, acquires actual control of the money. The date the morgagee releases funds from its own accounts should not be taken as the date of the advance, because the transfer of the funds will not be completed unless the conditions set out by the mortgagee are fulfilled. The release of funds from the mortgagee's own account to its solicitors is merely one step in the process of advancing the money, but it does not in itself constitute a completed advance. The parties are still free, however, to agree between themselves on some other date for the commencement of interest. When, prior to the discharge of a third party lien, a mortgagee delivered funds to its solicitors to be held in escrow until verification that the mortgagee had a first charge, the mortgagee was deemed not to have advanced the funds before discharge of the lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Royal Bank" p2="Lawton Developments Inc." post.rptr="212" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I6435bf535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Bank v. Lawton Developments Inc.">Royal Bank v. Lawton Developments Inc. (1994), 36 R.P.R. (2d) 212, 16 O.R. (3d) 450, 13 C.L.R. (2d) 74 (Gen. Div.); set aside (1996), 27 O.R. (3d) 417 (C.A.)</ref></cite>—The bank agreed to finance the acquisition of land and the subsequent construction of a condominium project. A first mortgage was registered, and an advance made upon closing. The construction was then begun and construction liens were registered on the property. The lands and buildings were subsequently sold for a price that was less than the purchase price paid by the developer. The lien claimants claimed priority over the interests of the bank, on the basis that the mortgage was a building mortgage that was covered by s. 78(2). In line with the general principle that the rights of the lien claimants begin when they begin to add value, it made sense that, where a mortgagee agrees to take a mortgage with the dual intentions of financing the acquisition of the land and, thereafter, financing the erection of a building upon it, s. 78(2) should be interpreted in a way that is consistent with convenient commercial practice, so as to allow the mortgagee to take a single mortgage for more than one purpose. In this case, the mortgage had three purposes: to assist in the purchase of the property, to provide loans for construction, and to provide a guarantee in accordance with the Ontario New Home Warranty Program. Since the first purpose involved the acquisition of the land, the first advance was not a building mortgage and s. 78(2) did not apply. In the result, the bank had priority over the lien claimants. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: On appeal, the Court of Appeal allowed a motion to admit further documentation and to set aside the lower court order. The court remitted for determination the issues of (1) when the first valid lien arose; (2) the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained, and; (3) whether credit should be given against the deficiency for the proceeds of a letter of credit posted by the respondent on account of the liens. The Court of Appeal did not hear submissions and made no decision regarding the application of s. 78(2) of the Act, with the intention that, depending on the disposition of the issues set out above, the appellants would have the right to pursue their appeal with regard to the application of s. 78(2).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Dufferin Concrete Products" p2="Waterbrooke Development Ltd." post.rptr="132" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I6435e6605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dufferin Concrete Products v. Waterbrooke Development Ltd.">Dufferin Concrete Products v. Waterbrooke Development Ltd. (1992), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 132 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was a supplier of concrete materials and delivered concrete to an improvement financed with a building mortgage. The plaintiff supplied concrete in the amount of $218,258.67 and there remained $25,926.45 due and owing to the plaintiff for the materials supplied. The plaintiff registered a claim for lien in the amount of $25,926.45 against the lands and premises comprising the improvement. The plaintiff had been paid in full for those invoices which were paid, and consequently the holdback by the defendant was paid prematurely. The plaintiff applied for summary judgment in the amount of $21,817.33. The court held that the failure to retain the 10 per cent holdback deprived those claiming under the plaintiff, not the plaintiff itself. Consequently, the holdback collectable by the plaintiff from the mortgagee was 10 per cent of the unpaid contracts, or $2,592.65.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd." p2="Halton Hills Development Corp." post.rptr="23" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6435e6615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp.">Lindsay Brothers Construction Ltd. v. Halton Hills Development Corp. (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 23, 4 C.L.R. (2d) 168, 1992 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 1 of the Act refers to the holdback as 10 per cent of the value of the services or materials under a contract, in the singular. Therefore, each lien claimant is entitled to priority to the extent of a deficiency in the required holdback retained by the owner on each contract. This reasoning was adopted in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="G.M. Sernas & Associates Ltd." p2="846539 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3161" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I562e48b0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="G.M. Sernas & Associates Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd.">G.M. Sernas & Associates Ltd. v. 846539 Ontario Ltd. (1999), 1999 CarswellOnt 3161, 48 C.L.R. (2d) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I64360d715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner acquired title to a parcel of land and entered into a loan agreement with the mortgagee for $2 million, for construction of condominiums on the land. The mortgagee advanced moneys to the defendants' mutual solicitor, to be held in trust until 45 days after construction was completed. The mortgage was discharged and a new mortgage was obtained in favour of a third party. The defendant mortgagee then gave the owner a second mortgage for $1,687,000. A large part of the construction project was destroyed or damaged by fire. The principal lien claimant commenced an action to determine, <ital>inter alia</ital>, whether the lien claimants had priority over the mortgagee with respect to the moneys advanced to the solicitor totalling $515,000. Subsection 78(2) of the Act gave liens arising from an improvement priority over a mortgage intended to secure the financing of such improvement. Subsection 78(5) affirmed this priority to the extent of any deficiency in the holdback required to be retained by the owner. The court held that the lien claimants were therefore entitled to their respective lien claims against the land and had the right to sell the property if the money was not paid. They had priority over the mortgages to the extent of the deficiency in the holdback and further had priority over two advances totalling $515,000.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Tri-Haven Homes Inc." p2="O'Neill" post.rptr="249" pre.rptr="44" ref.id="I64360d725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill">Tri-Haven Homes Inc. v. O'Neill (1991), 44 C.L.R. 249 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee held building mortgages over six parcels of land which were being developed, and the plaintiff lien claimants filed a lien claim against all six parcels. After some of the parcels were sold, and discharges were registered, two parcels remained encumbered by the claim. The mortgagee brought a motion to vacate the liens and certificate of action upon payment into court of a reasonable amount. The mortgagee, which had held back funds on three parcels, contended that the proper holdback amount was 10 per cent of the contract price for the improvements on the two remaining encumbered parcels of land. The court accepted the plaintiff's argument that the amount to be paid into court was fixed at an amount equal to the total of the holdbacks retained on three parcels. The lien claimants were entitled to a general lien in respect of the two encumbered parcels. As there remained an unadvanced holdback in the hands of the mortgagee in respect of three parts, the full amount was to be paid into court even though only two parts remained encumbered. Accordingly, an order to vacate the liens would be granted upon payment into court of that amount.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

List])</ref></cite>—<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Wealth Management Corp." p2="1713515 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="6503" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I678703403b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd.">Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd., 2013 ONSC 6503, 2013 CarswellOnt 18879 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> is not authority for the general proposition that, where services and materials for the same project were previously supplied under an earlier contract (for example, pre-construction development), services or materials supplied under a new contract (for example, for construction work), should be treated as being in respect of a separate improvement. Here, pre-construction architectural work carried out before the mortgage was registered and giving rise to liens, was in respect of the same project as the subsequent construction work carried out after the mortgage was registered. Ultimately, the project was a townhouse development consisting of five residential buildings, two commercial buildings and a below-grade parking structure. The mortgage at issue was found to be registered after the time when the first lien arose, and s. 78(3) of the Act was held not to apply. Rather, the mortgage was a subsequent mortgage governed by ss. 78(5) and 78(6).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pollard Windows Inc." p2="1736106 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4859" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64360d735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pollard Windows Inc. v. 1736106 Ontario Inc.">Pollard Windows Inc. v. 1736106 Ontario Inc., 2019 ONSC 4859, 2019 CarswellOnt 13133, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 58 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 17956 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2018 ONSC 7567, 2018 CarswellOnt 22765 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Subsections 78(3) and (4) limit a mortgagee's priority to the amount advanced under the mortgage prior to the lien arising. Where the mortgagee failed to prove on the balance of probabilities that any amounts had ever been advanced under the mortgage prior to the supplier's lien arising, the lien rights of the supplier had priority to the proceeds of sale of the property. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The motions judge found a strong inference that the mortgage transaction was part of a scheme to defeat creditors.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Scott, Pichelli & Easter Limited" p2="Dupont Developments Ltd." post.rptr="6579" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64360d745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scott, Pichelli & Easter Limited v.
