Ct.); reversing 2019 ONSC 4555, 2019 CarswellOnt 12914, 90 C.L.R. (4th) 191 (Ont. S.C.J.); reconsideration / rehearing refused 2019 ONSC 6789, 2019 CarswellOnt 18782 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 21891 (Ont. S.C.J.); reversing in part 2018 ONSC 3126, 2018 CarswellOnt 7904, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 248 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2022 CarswellOnt 15905 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—At issue here was whether the prior vendor-take-back mortgage, which was in default, had priority over the registered liens with respect to arrears in interest, fees, charges and expenses that related to the mortgage. Ultimately, the Divisional Court reversed the motion judge's variation of the master's original report, and held that the mortgage did have priority. In the report, the master had found that the vendor take-back mortgage (“VTB”) was fully advanced to fund the purchase price, with an additional cash payment making up the balance. The property was sold by way of power of sale and the net proceeds of sale were paid into Court in place of the lien claimants' security, pursuant to a vesting order. However, there were no monies remaining to pay to the lien claimants after payment of the VTB and the fees, charges and expenses approved by the vesting order. For the purposes of s. 78(3), a VTB was the same as an institutional mortgage, and not equivalent to a collateral mortgage. The mortgagee's interest therefore had priority over the lien claimants' interests and the mortgagee was entitled to the funds held in court. The applicable measure of the actual value of a premises at the time when a lien arises is the price at which a willing buyer would buy and a willing seller would sell a property. The test was not what a “prudent” purchaser would do. It was not appropriate to discount the value of the property to account for the cost of any remediation. In this case the property could continue its commercial and light industrial uses without remediation, and there was no evidence that the purchasers were unaware of the contamination and failed to take the cost of remediation into account in making its offer, or that remediation was in fact required. However, on appeal, the motions judge reversed a portion of that judgment, finding that the defendant mortgagee's priority ended with the funds advanced under the mortgage. While property taxes and legal expenses relating to the sale of the property stood in priority to the liens, the lien claimants were held to have priority over the deduction for arrears of interest, fees, charges and expenses calculated as part of the “net proceeds” in the vesting order and thus should have access to the funds paid into Court. In reversing the motion judge's ruling, and restoring the report's conclusion, the Divisional Court held that once the motions judge concluded that the VTB had priority over the lien claimants, the analysis should have ended. The nature and purpose of a prior mortgage is not altered or changed by the registration of a lien, and the mortgage encompasses obligations and terms that the mortgagee and mortgagor are responsible for and that are secured by the mortgagor's interest in the lands and premises. This includes any interest due and any reasonable expenses or charges incurred that directly relate to the mortgage or enforcement of the mortgage, if the mortgage is in default. Therefore, the whole of the mortgage had priority, and this included interest and reasonable charges to enforce the mortgage. In this case, it was not within the realm of a determination of priorities for the motions judge to separately determine that arears in interest or reasonable expenses incurred on the VTB did not have priority over the lien claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Wealth Management Corp." p2="1713515 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="6503" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I643634805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd.">Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd., 2013 ONSC 6503, 2013 CarswellOnt 18879 (Ont. S.C.J.); extension of time to appeal and leave to appeal denied 2014 ONCA 500, 2014 CarswellOnt 8586, 17 C.B.R. (6th) 91, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 191, 323 O.A.C. 101 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—A receiver/trustee was appointed for the defendant owner pursuant to several statutes, including s. 68(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. At the time the receiver was appointed, the defendant owned a property under renovation for use as a boutique hotel. Various liens had been registered and subsequently vacated or discharged. The renovations were not completed and the receiver sold the property. Prior to that sale, the applicant OW held a first mortgage that secured principal financing and made various advances to the defendant, with the initial advance applied to re-finance a prior first mortgage held by CCL. After the advances were made, the lien claimant registered its construction lien, and claimed priority under ss. 78(1), (2) and (5) over the OW advances, to the amount of the deficiencies in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner. It argued that the CCL advance was obtained to finance the same improvement for which the OW mortgage was obtained, and that the work done both prior to and post the lien claimant's involvement was all in respect of the same improvement. In rejecting the lien claimant's claim to priority, the court noted that when OW made its advances, prior construction liens had been vacated or discharged. It found that the OW advance to pay out the CCL mortgage was for the land portion of the mortgage and not improvements, and was therefore not a building mortgage. Section 78(3) was the applicable provision, and under it the OW advance took priority over any lien claim. The improvements undertaken by the claimant did not relate to the same contract, but rather were stand-alone improvements disconnected from the prior lien claimants' interests that were discharged or vacated prior to OW's financing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Haflidson" p2="Salandy" post.rptr="284" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I643634815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haflidson v. Salandy">Haflidson v. Salandy (2002), 16 C.L.R. (3d) 284, 2002 CarswellOnt 1698 (Master)</ref></cite>—Section 78 of the Ontario <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> gives rise to the presumption that a lien claim has priority over a mortgage, but the presumption is rebuttable where the mortgage was registered prior in time to when the first lien arose, but only to the lesser of the actual value of the premises at the time the first lien arose, and the total of all amounts that prior to that time were advanced under the mortgage. Here, the mortgage was registered prior in time to when the lien arose, and there was no evidence before the court to counter the evidence of property value in the request to admit and in the moving party's supplementary affidavit. The mortgagee therefore had a priority over the lien claim to the full extent of the mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Avenue Structures Inc." p2="Pacific Empire Development Inc." post.rptr="128" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I643634825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc.">Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc. (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee bank, which had advanced non-building loans, sought an order declaring that expenses it incurred for the preservation and protection of the premises had priority over the claims of lien claimants in respect of proceeds derived from the sale or other disposition of the property. The lien claimants had previously conceded that the mortgages were not building mortgages under s. 78(2) of the Act. The expenses for which the Bank claimed priority included: realty taxes; penalties and bailiff's costs; winter protection costs; hydro bills; insurance premiums; replacement of stolen electrical cable for electrical heaters; architect's fees relating to dealings with municipal authorities over a demolition order; legal fees regarding the prevention of demolition; city inspection fees; and a payment to the municipality under a letter of credit provided by the bank for the insolvent owner-developer. In dismissing the bank's motion with respect to all expenses except realty taxes, the Master noted that the bank ought to have applied for the appointment of a trustee under s. 68(1). The court may then have authorized the sale of the property as contemplated by s. 68(2)(a), thereby avoiding many of the expenses that were been incurred. Even if a sale was not appropriate at that time, a trustee could have taken “appropriate steps for preservation of the premises” under s. 68(2)(c), and could have sought court approval for “such other steps that are appropriate” under s. 68(2)(d). Section 68 gave the mortgagee Bank the remedy it required to protect itself, but it failed to use that remedy and instead resorted to self-help. The expenses for penalties, interest and bailiff's costs were not absolutely necessary since these could all have been avoided by the Bank by paying the taxes on time after obtaining an agreed priority for such payment, or again by the application for the appointment of a trustee under s. 68, who could then have sought court approval for a borrowing to pay the taxes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Avenue Structures Inc." p2="Pacific Empire Development Inc." post.rptr="42" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I64365b905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc.">Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc. (2000), 4 C.L.R. (3d) 42 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—“Actual value” means “market value”, which means the most probable price that a property would bring in a competitive and open market, under all conditions requisite to a fair sale, the buyer and seller each acting prudently and knowledgeably. In determining market value, the master took into account that a higher legal zoning density which had been obtained for the property could allow for future expansion when purchaser/tenant demand would justify such expansion, and made the property more valuable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="561861 Ontario Ltd." p2="1085043 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2935" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I64365b915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc.">561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc. (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2935, 66 O.T.C. 305, [1998] O.J. No. 2925 (Ont. Bktcy.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee registered a first mortgage as security for a loan made to her brother for the purchase of interest in land to be sold to a golf course development company. On the closing of the transaction, the mortgagee agreed to discharge the original mortgage, and a new first mortgage was granted to a third party and a second mortgage to the mortgagee. A new first mortgage was eventually arranged and the mortgagee signed a postponement agreement on the understanding she would receive payment from the monies her brother would be given on the sale of the land. Construction liens were subsequently registered against the land, and the mortgagee consented to a vesting order, which discharged all encumbrances including her second mortgage. In an application to determine the priorities, the mortgagee was unsuccessful in arguing that her mortgage was a registered instrument providing notice to all persons and took priority over the liens pursuant to s. 78(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. By discharging the first mortgage and taking a second mortgage, the prior mortgage debt against which all monies had been advanced, had been discharged. No funds were advanced against the second mortgage as required by s. 78(3) of the Act so to create priority over the lien claimants. Equitable relief for unjust enrichment was unavailable, since the first mortgage had not been discharged in error.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="O'Byrne" p2="1085043 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="252" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I64365b925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="O'Byrne v. 1085043 Ontario Inc.">O'Byrne v. 1085043 Ontario Inc. (1997), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 252 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The Plaintiff sued to enforce a vendor's lien. In somewhat dubious circumstances, a golf course developer purchased a farm property and constructed a golf course on it, notwithstanding that the original vendor of the land, a farmer, never received the vendor take back mortgage he was promised. There were many liens. There was no evidence that any lien claimant had any notice of the unregistered vendor take back mortgage. Relying on the <ital>Registry Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. R-20, providing that no equitable interest is valid against a registered instrument, the covenants implied by the <ital>Land Registry Reform Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. L-4, s. 5(1) and the conclusiveness of the statement of consideration, as provided for by s. 7 of the <ital>Conveyancing & Law of Property Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-34, the court had no alternative but to grant the construction lien claimants priority over the unregistered vendor's lien. Once the priority of a mortgagee is established under s. 78(3), then the party with carriage of the sale will be entitled to have the reasonable “fees and actual disbursements” in connection with the sale deducted from the gross proceeds, and reimbursement allowed accordingly. This position is in accordance with the common practice of the court in all sorts of proceedings where the sale of land is ordered. Where the mortgagee conducts the sale, the sale expenses are not “advances” under the mortgage within s. 78(3), but rather, are to be allowed by the court under its powers regarding costs in ss. 59, 62(5), 65, 58(4), 84, and 86. Note that in the related case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="561861 Ontario Ltd." p2="1085043 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2935" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I643682a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc.">561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc. (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 2935, 66 O.T.C. 305, [1998] O.J. No. 2925 (Ont. Bktcy.)</ref></cite>, a motion was heard as to the status of O'Byrne as a mortgagee following a vesting order that did not mention, for obvious reasons, a previously discharged mortgage. The argument, based on equitable principles failed and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Central Guaranty Trust Company" p2="Dixdale Mortgage Investment Corp." post.rptr="137" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I643682a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Central Guaranty Trust Company v. Dixdale Mortgage Investment Corp.">Central Guaranty Trust Company v. Dixdale Mortgage Investment Corp. (1994), 43 R.P.R. (2d) 137 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> was distinguished.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Beaver Lumber Co." p2="Archview Developments Ltd." post.rptr="242" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I643682a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Beaver Lumber Co. v. Archview Developments Ltd.">Beaver Lumber Co. v. Archview Developments Ltd. (1997), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 242 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The court in this case pursued a sound analysis of a conventional fact situation. Advances were deemed made when the owner acquired actual control of the money (citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Marsil Mechanical" p2="A Reissing-Reissing Enterprise Ltd." post.rptr="301" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I643682a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Marsil Mechanical v. A Reissing-Reissing Enterprise Ltd.">Marsil Mechanical v. A Reissing-Reissing Enterprise Ltd. (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 301, 26 C.L.R. (2d) 148 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Park Contractors Inc." p2="Royal Bank of Canada" post.rptr="255" pre.rptr="38" ref.id="I643682a45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Park Contractors Inc. v. Royal Bank of Canada">Park Contractors Inc. v. Royal Bank of Canada (1998), 38 C.L.R. (2d) 255, 38 O.R. (3d) 290 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—An interesting argument was made by a lien claimant who had removed contaminated soil. The argument was that the environmental contamination of a site rendered its value nil for the purposes of a priority fight with a prior registered mortgagee. “Value in use” was inappropriate as the land was not in use. A market value approach was taken. It was held that no reasonable purchaser would have purchased the contaminated property without first deducting the cost of making it right. Under s. 78(3), actual value means the market value that would likely result from negotiations between a willing vendor and a willing purchaser. At the time when the lien arose, the cleanup costs were unknown, and a would be purchaser of the property would not have made an offer until clean up costs were quantified. Accordingly, at the time when the environmental clean up commenced, the property had no actual value.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Plaza Electric II Ltd." p2="CMGC Management Inc." post.rptr="306" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I6436a9b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Plaza Electric II Ltd. v. Master)</ref></cite>—For the purposes of s. 78(3), the actual value of the land was found to be the amount set out in the purchase and sale agreement, even though it was the same as the mortgage amount advanced.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Rinaldis" p2="Landmark Development (North Bay) Ltd." post.rptr="137" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I6436a9b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rinaldis v. Landmark Development (North Bay) Ltd.">Rinaldis v. Landmark Development (North Bay) Ltd. (1995), 21 C.L.R. (2d) 137, 32 C.B.R. (3d) 291, 124 D.L.R. (4th) 279, 23 O.R. (3d) 564 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A trustee in bankruptcy brought an action to set aside a fraudulent conveyance of certain premises to L Ltd. and filed certificates of pending litigation. After lien claims arose following the registration of the certificates of pending litigation, the Trustee successfully appealed a judgment granting the lien claimants priority over the Trustee's interest and payment of their judgment amounts out of the funds held in trust in priority to the Trustee's claim. The registration of a certificate of pending litigation is the means provided for a plaintiff to protect his or her interests and to give notice to other parties that he or she claimed an interest in the property and was seeking to enforce his or her rights by action. Such registration operates as notice to all parties who are or may become interested in the property. If the conveyance to L Ltd. was fraudulent, then L Ltd. could not encumber the premises in priority to the Trustee whether by mortgage or lien or in any other way. The Trustee therefore had priority over the lien claimants, but its claim was limited to the value of the property at the time the first lien arose.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I6436a9b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsections 78(3) and (4) make it clear that all building mortgages registered prior to the time when the first lien arises in respect of an improvement have priority over the lien arising therefrom unless the lien was preserved or perfected at the time of a subsequent advance or unless the mortgagee had received written notice. Thus, if a property is sold by judicial sale or simply sold by the mortgagee to a willing buyer on the understanding that all proceeds would be paid into court, the mortgagee would have priority over the general contractor and its sub-trades for the full extent of the moneys owing to it pursuant to its mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="W.A. Hassan (1993), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 93 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The “actual value” of the property at the time the first lien arose was the price that would likely result from negotiations between a willing vendor and a willing purchaser. Such price was the purchase price paid by the owner less the extra cost of excavating caused by the unusual soil conditions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="D'Andrea Developments Inc." p2="Farnham Development Corp." post.rptr="289" pre.rptr="9" ref.id="I6436d0c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D'Andrea Developments Inc. v. Farnham Development Corp.">D'Andrea Developments Inc. v. Farnham Development Corp. (1992), 9 C.L.R. (2d) 289 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—To finance a construction project, the owner obtained $68,000 from the defendant DF, secured by a mortgage for $275,000 which DF assigned to a holding company. When the owner abandoned the project, the contractor named the owner, DF, and the mortgagee as defendants to the lien action. At the trial of the construction lien action, the defendants claimed that the mortgage had priority over the lien. DF advanced the $68,000 as trustee for a group of investors. DF was therefore not an owner, and the mortgage was a valid and subsisting mortgage on the property. However, only $68,000 had been advanced before the registration of the lien. Accordingly, pursuant to s. 78(3), the mortgage had priority to the extent of $68,000 plus accrued interest.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al.">Peoples Trust Company et al. v. Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 18855, 2024 ONSC 6648 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—There was no issue that for the purposes of s. 78(5) each of the liens arose before the mortgage was registered, nor that for the purposes of s. 78(6)(a), at the time the advance under the mortgage was made, neither lien was preserved or perfected. The court reiterated that where a lien has arisen before an advance under the mortgage, but the lien has not been perfected or preserved and the mortgagee has no notice of the lien, the mortgage has priority over the lien. It was unreasonable to conclude here that either the mortgagee had constructive knowledge of unpaid liens or that it ought to have conducted any further inquiries about the probability of unpaid liens. The fact that in a very significant multiunit residential project involving multiple trades, two liens had been previously registered and almost immediately thereafter discharged could equally have supported the opposite conclusion or inference, namely that the borrower was dealing with its trades in the ordinary course and where disputes arose, it was settling them promptly. It would be entirely inconsistent with the clear statutory regime to impose a duty of inquiry on a lender arising from the simple observation of a trade on the building site. Each of the lien claimants elected to wait for months to exercise the rights which had arisen long before the mortgage was registered and before the funds were advanced. That was not the circumstance the statutory regime is designed to protect.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="RSG Mechanical Inc." p2="1398796 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2070" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6436d0c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc.">RSG Mechanical Inc. v. 1398796 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2070, 2015 CarswellOnt 7504, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 124 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2014 ONSC 3936, 2014 CarswellOnt 8905, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirming 2014 ONSC 4692, 2014 CarswellOnt 11094, 38 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.); varying 2013 CarswellOnt 2982 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Funds that are transferred so that they can be posted as security to replace liens which will, as a result, be vacated, are not an advance that is protected by the posted security. This is a “circularity”. The lien claimants are protected by the security that has been posted, but they have no further claim in priority to the mortgagee. This is so in regard to the repayment of the money used to post the security through the realization that came with the subsequent sale of the remaining townhouses or otherwise.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd." p2="Hyde Park Residences Inc." post.rptr="8015" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6436d0c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc.">X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc., 2013 ONSC 8015, 2013 CarswellOnt 18442 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were the developers of a residential project against which various lien claims were registered. The parties reached an agreement to resolve the claims under which consent to judgment for the balance of the original lien claims was signed by the defendants to be held in escrow and used in the event of default. Under the agreement, the first mortgagee was to advance funds towards the project and the defendants were to arrange the balance of funding necessary to complete it. The defendants could not arrange the balance of financing and the lien claimants were granted judgment. The first mortgagee sought return of the funds held in trust on the basis that those funds were earmarked to pay for work packages that did not proceed, and to permit the lien claimants to realize against borrowed funds defeated its priority claim. The mortgagee was not permitted to claw back the funds already advanced. The mortgagee was fully aware of the terms of the agreement and therefore knew of the potential consequences when it agreed to advance the funds on behalf of the defendants. Secondly the lien claimants had served notice of default under the agreement and claimed the funds before the first mortgagee had itself declared default under its mortgage; unless the funds had been advanced subject to an understanding that they remained the property of the mortgagee then the fund was an asset available for the benefit of the lien claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rosedale Kitchens Inc." p2="2114281 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="3161" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6436f7d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc.">Rosedale Kitchens Inc. v. 2114281 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 3161, 2012 CarswellOnt 6816, 15 C.L.R. (4th) 67 (Ont. Master); affirmed 2013 CarswellOnt 7357, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 312 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 CarswellOnt 9258, 33 C.L.R. (4th) 319 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Whether mortgage funds have been advanced is a question of fact; funds are advanced when control shifts from the mortgagee to mortgagor. Here, control was held not to shift when the mortgagee delivered an uncertified cheque to the mortgagor, but only when the cheque was subsequently certified by the latter. Until the cheque was certified, the mortgagee could have stopped payment or cleared out the account. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The mortgagee's motion challenging confirmation of the Master's Report was dismissed on other grounds by the Superior Court of Justice and, on further appeal, the Divisional Court (See 2014 ONSC 7143, 2014 CarswellOnt 17327, 43 C.L.R. (4th) 159 (Ont. Div. Ct.). See as well the discussion of that decision under subs. 62(1)(b), <ital>supra</ital>). However, the Divisional Court expressly noted that it was not approving the principle applied by the Master, described as <ital>obiter</ital>, that the owner did not have control over the building mortgage funds until it had certified the cheque. Absent a demonstrated concern about whether sufficient funds existed to cover the cheque, such a principle would place control over the priority of those funds in the hands of the owner/mortgagor, thereby exposing such funds to subsequently filed lien claims, a result which seems contrary to the policy of s. 78.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="255" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I6436f7d15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1995), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 255, 21 O.R. (3d) 771, 122 D.L.R. (4th) 596, 77 O.A.C. 276 (C.A.); affirming (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A mortgagee choosing to make an advance when a lien is registered on title, loses priority for that advance, whether the amount may be, as against all liens “arising from the improvement” and not just against prior registered liens. Where, subsequent to a fourth advance on a mortgage, a registered lien was vacated under the Act, the mortgagee lost priority for its fourth advance as against all liens arising from the improvement and not just against prior registered liens. As a mortgagee's priority for mortgage advances is tied to individual advances, each advance is to be treated separately. When the faulty advance was made, the order of priority was crytallized so that the amount of the faulty advance kept its place in the order of priorities. It remained there for benefit of all potential liens arising from the improvement and subsequent advances are ranked after the faulty advance.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="94" pre.rptr="17" ref.id="I6436f7d25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 17 C.L.R. (2d) 94 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The priorities established by s. 78(4) of the Act mean that a mortgagee can safely make advances under the mortgage, subject to the holdback provisions, only if no lien is registered against title or if he has received no written notice of a lien. However, when a lien remains preserved or perfected by registration, the mortgagee makes any advance at its peril, since all liens arising from the improvement will have priority over the advance, whether they arose before or after the advance is made and whether they were registered or not at the time of the advance. However, a mortgagee which meets the conditions set out in s. 78(4) with respect to a series of advances establishes a priority to the extent of each of those advances. That priority is crystallized in time and is not lost by reason of a further advance by the mortgagee made subsequent to the perfection of a lien against the premises.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Boehmers" p2="794561 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="821" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I562f5a20fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc.">Boehmers v. 794561 Ontario Inc. (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 821, 14 O.R. (3d) 781, 11 C.L.R. (2d) 99, 105 D.L.R. (4th) 473 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 78(4) deals with the priorities of a mortgagee on an advance-by-advance basis and not otherwise. If the mortgagee loses priority for an advance, that loss is permanent, not temporary, and the later advances cannot percolate or bubble upwards but, rather, must always remain below the priority sum gained by the liens. To hold otherwise is to fail to recognize the re-ordering of priorities reflected in the scheme propounded under s. 78 generally. Hence, a mortgagee was not entitled to the same priority over liens for advance Nos. 5–9 and 12–13 as it had for advance Nos. 1–3 because, at the time of those later advances, the title had been cleared of liens. Section 78 only provides priority for a mortgage as an exception rather than as a general rule and that the mortgagee's priorities are tied to individual advances and not to the mortgage as a whole. If an individual advance is bad because of an outstanding lien, then the result must be that the liens have a fixed priority for the amount of the bad advance in the same way that they have a fixed priority for a holdback deficiency.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="830889 Ontario Inc." p2="607643 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="181" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I64371ee05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="830889 Ontario Inc. v. 607643 Ontario Inc.">830889 Ontario Inc. v. 607643 Ontario Inc. (1990), 43 C.L.R. 181 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Principal and interest are equally secured under a mortgage, and “advances” or “money advanced” includes interest. Hence, interest payments with respect to two mortgages were held to have priority over a construction lien. The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd." p2="Rideau Carleton Raceway Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="2" pre.rptr="[1971]" ref.id="I64371ee15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Rideau Carleton Raceway Holdings Ltd.">M. Sullivan & Son Ltd. v. Rideau Carleton Raceway Holdings Ltd., [1971] S.C.R. 2</ref></cite>, is followed.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
78:7: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">78:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 78(5)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS" p1.pp="In the Matter of" post.rptr="12454" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6787eda03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS">IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS, 2024 CarswellOnt 12454, 2024 ONSC 4625 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—Pre-construction architectural work carried out before the mortgage was registered gave rise to certain liens, and was held to be in respect of the same project as subsequent construction work carried out after the mortgage was registered. The mortgage was accordingly found to be registered after the first lien arose, and s. 78(3) of the Act was held not to apply. Rather, the mortgage was a subsequent mortgage governed by ss. 78(5) and 78(6). The question was whether the mortgage was a vendor-take-back mortgage given in partial payment of the purchase price for the conveyance of the beneficial ownership of the property, governed by s. 78(6), or whether it was a collateral mortgage in respect of which no advance was made, as contemplated by s. 78(5). There was no reason, in principle, why a mortgage must secure a guarantee of existing indebtedness to qualify as a “true” collateral mortgage. The significant factor is that the mortgage secures the guarantee given by the mortgagor of indebtedness owed by another entity, the principal debtor. In such circumstances, the advance is made to the principal debtor, not to the guarantor. The court concluded here that mortgage was a collateral mortgage that was given by the guarantor to secure its obligation as guarantor of the indebtedness of the purchaser to the mortgagee to pay part of the purchase price for purchased securities. There was no advance made in respect of the mortgage within the meaning of s. 78(6) of the Act. The mortgage did not have priority over the claimant's lien or other liens under s. 78(6) of the Act. Instead, under s. 78(5), the liens would have priority over the mortgage to the extent of the deficiency in the statutory holdbacks that should have been retained by the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Wealth Management Corp." p2="1713515 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="6503" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64371ee25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd.">Ontario Wealth Management Corp. v. 1713515 Ontario Ltd., 2013 ONSC 6503, 2013 CarswellOnt 18879 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A receiver/trustee was appointed for the defendant owner pursuant to several statutes, including s. 68(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. At the time the receiver was appointed, the defendant owned a property under renovation for use as a boutique hotel. Various liens had been registered and subsequently vacated or discharged. The renovations were not completed and the receiver sold the property. Prior to that sale, the applicant OW held a first mortgage that secured principal financing and made various advances to the defendant, with the initial advance applied to re-finance a prior first mortgage held by CCL. After the advances were made, the lien claimant registered its construction lien, and claimed priority under ss. 78(1), (2) and (5) over the OW advances, to the amount of the deficiencies in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner. It argued that the CCL advance was obtained to finance the same improvement for which the OW mortgage was obtained and that the work done both prior to and post the lien claimant's involvement was all in respect of the same improvement. In rejecting the lien claimant's claim to priority, the court noted that when OW made its advances, prior construction liens had been vacated or discharged. It found that the OW advance to pay out the CCL mortgage was for the land portion of the mortgage and not improvements, and was therefore not a building mortgage. Section 78(3) was the applicable provision, and under it the OW advance took priority over any lien claim. The improvements undertaken by the claimant did not relate to the same contract, but rather were stand-alone improvements disconnected from the prior lien claimants' interests that were discharged or vacated prior to OW's financing.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Royal Bank" p2="Lawton Developments Inc." post.rptr="212" pre.rptr="36" ref.id="I64371ee35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Bank v. Lawton Developments Inc.">Royal Bank v. Lawton Developments Inc. (1994), 36 R.P.R. (2d) 212, 16 O.R. (3d) 450 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The bank agreed to finance the acquisition of land and the subsequent construction of a condominium project. A first mortgage was registered, and an advance made upon closing. The construction was then begun and construction liens were registered on the property. The lands and buildings were subsequently sold for a price that was less than the purchase price paid by the developer. The lien claimants claimed priority over the interests of the bank, on the basis that the first lien arose prior to the closing, based on the existence, and the inclusion in the transaction, of architectural, engineering, mechanical, and electrical drawings. However, the court rejected the argument that the existence of these drawings, and the lien which arose in respect of their creation, brought into play the provisions of s. 78(5) of the Act. The plans and drawings that were the subject of the transaction in February 1990 did not include plans and drawings in respect of which any lien was created and, accordingly, it could not be said that the mortgage in question was one which was affected by s. 78(5). This matter was then appealed to the Ontario Court of Appeal, which allowed a motion to admit further documentation, set aside the underlying order, and to revisit the issues of when the first lien arose, the extent of the deficiency in holdbacks, and credit for proceeds of a letter of credit. See 27 O.R. (3d) 417.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1983" p1="Seltor Holdings Ltd." p2="Kettles" post.rptr="659" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I643745f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Seltor Holdings Ltd. v. Kettles">Seltor Holdings Ltd. v. Kettles (1983), 43 O.R. (2d) 659, 29 R.P.R. 214, 3 C.L.R. 259, 2 D.L.R. (4th) 373 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—It is a valid requisition for a purchaser of a house being built according to plans to require the vendor to prove that he has complied with the holdback provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, on the ground that the mortgagee financing the purchase refuses to advance the funds without such proof. Although the purchaser would normally not be entitled to make the requisition in that the conveyance to him would take priority over any liens under s. 80(6) [now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 80(6)] of the Act, unless at the time of the conveyance there was a preserved or perfected lien, or he had received actual written notice of the lien, a mortgagee under a mortgage registered after the first lien arises takes subsequent in priority to any liens to the extent of any deficiency in the holdback under s. 80(5). The latter section applies not only to a mortgage given by an owner, such as a vendor, but to any mortgage registered after the first lien arose. Moreover, since unregistered liens have priority over the mortgage under the section, the requisition was a proper one.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
