Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al.">Peoples Trust Company et al. v. Vandyk-Backyard Queensview Limited et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 18855, 2024 ONSC 6648 (Ont. S.C.J. [Comm. List])</ref></cite>—The court rejected the submission that the lien claims had priority over the first mortgage because the funds advanced under the loan and secured by the mortgage did not constitute an “advance made in respect of that … mortgage” as required by s. 78(6). The mortgage here was not a collateral mortgage, and the loan was advanced to the borrower in a single transaction, at the same time the mortgage was registered. Nothing in the language of s. 78(6) requires the mortgagee to establish not only that the loan monies were advanced to the mortgagor, as was done, but also that they were applied to the improvement of the land. The fact that the borrower then dispersed those funds, or at least some of them, to creditors in respect of other projects did not invalidate the priority of the mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Kingsett Mortgage Corporation" p2="Mapleview Developments Ltd." post.rptr="18276" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678814b13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Kingsett Mortgage Corporation v. Mapleview Developments Ltd.">Kingsett Mortgage Corporation v. Mapleview Developments Ltd., 2024 CarswellOnt 18276, 2024 ONSC 6477 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The mortgagee registered two mortgages against the lands, and made advances under them. The mortgages were discharged and replaced with a single consolidated mortgage, but no further advances were made. As the latter mortgage was registered after the date when the first lien arose, it was a subsequent mortgage. At the times of the advances secured by the consolidated mortgage, there were no preserved or perfected liens against the lands. The exception in s. 78(6) applied such that, subject to subsections (2) and (5), the consolidated mortgage had priority over the liens of the lien claimants. <ital>XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd.</ital> and <ital>Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re</ital>, which involved collateral mortgages, were distinguishable in that the mortgage in each of those cases secured a guarantee given by the mortgagor to the mortgagee of indebtedness owed by a separate entity. In those cases, no advance was made to the mortgagor/guarantor at any time. Here, the original mortgages were taken with the intention to secure the financing of an improvement, which financing would then be made through advances secured by registered mortgages. All advances were made by the mortgagee with this intention, which operated prospectively when the original mortgages were taken and continued to the time when the consolidated mortgage was registered.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS" p1.pp="In the Matter of" post.rptr="12454" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I67883bc03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS">IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT AND A PLAN OF COMPROMISE OR ARRANGEMENT OF CLARKSON ROAD DEVELOPMENTS GP INC. AND OTHERS, 2024 CarswellOnt 12454, 2024 ONSC 4625 (Ont. S.C.J. [Comm. List])</ref></cite>—Pre-construction architectural work carried out before the mortgage was registered gave rise to certain liens, and was held to be in respect of the same project as subsequent construction work carried out after the mortgage was registered. The mortgage was accordingly found to be registered after the time when the first lien arose, and s. 78(3) of the Act was held not to apply. Rather, the mortgage was a subsequent mortgage governed by ss. 78(5) and 78(6). The question was whether the mortgage was a vendor-take-back mortgage given in partial payment of the purchase price for the conveyance of the beneficial ownership of the property, governed by s. 78(6), or whether it was a collateral mortgage in respect of which no advance was made, as contemplated by s. 78(5). There was no reason, in principle, why a mortgage must secure a guarantee of existing indebtedness to qualify as a “true” collateral mortgage. The significant factor is that the mortgage secures the guarantee given by the mortgagor of indebtedness owed by another entity, the principal debtor. In such circumstances, the advance is made to the principal debtor, not to the guarantor. The court concluded here that mortgage was a collateral mortgage that was given by the guarantor to secure its obligation as guarantor of the indebtedness of the purchaser to the mortgagee to pay part of the purchase price for purchased securities. There was no advance made in respect of the mortgage within the meaning of s. 78(6) of the Act. The mortgage did not have priority over the claimant's lien or other liens under s. 78(6) of the Act. Instead, under s. 78(5), the liens would have priority over the mortgage to the extent of the deficiency in the statutory holdbacks that should have been retained by the owner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dal Bianco" p2="Deem Management Services et al." post.rptr="3530" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643745f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services et al.">Dal Bianco v. Deem Management Services et al., 2020 CarswellOnt 3530, 2020 ONSC 1500, 16 R.P.R. (6th) 244 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2021 CarswellOnt 18071 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The Receiver moved to determine competing priorities under s. 78 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> between registered lien claimants and a registered third mortgage, which secured amounts that were all advanced prior to registration and without security having been registered. The mortgage was registered after the time when the first lien arose and was therefore a “subsequent mortgage” within the meaning of the <ital>Act</ital>. In granting priority to the lien claimants, the court found that the mortgage did not fit into the exclusion of a “subsequent mortgage” as the mortgage did not secure advances, which were already made. S. 78(6) contemplated a mortgage registered after a project has commenced, and the only way in which a mortgagee could gain priority over lien claimants under the subsection was if the advances were made “in respect of that mortgage,” there were no preserved or protected liens at the time of the advance, and the mortgagee has had written notice of any lien at the time of the advance. The last two conditions did not apply to this case. Particularly in large projects, sub trades must be able to adequately assess their risk before undertaking work. If mortgagees are entitled to “lie in the weeds” while advancing funds for the project and then attempt to gain priority later by registering mortgages after liens arise, this would be unfair to lien claimants and contrary to the overall protection intended by the <ital>Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re" post.rptr="7125" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64376d005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re">Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re, 2016 ONSC 7125, 2016 CarswellOnt 19127, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Dircam Electric v. Am-Stat Corp.</ital>, 2017 ONSC 3421, 2017 CarswellOnt 8300, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 256 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In a matter that raised several interesting issues, the developer of a condominium project granted: a first mortgage to a bank securing credit facilities; a second mortgage made jointly to the developer and another company and advanced to third party recipients; and a collateral mortgage in favour of the first mortgagee, to secure the developer's guarantee for a loan made by the bank to another entity. There were no registered or perfected liens against the lands secured by the mortgages at the time the mortgage advances at issue were made, although the mortgagees were aware that construction was underway. In such a situation, the mortgagees did not have an obligation to make inquiries to determine if any work was unpaid at that time before advancing funds. Section 78(6) provides for priority of a mortgage provided the conditions in paragraphs (a) and (b) are satisfied. There was no basis for implying a further condition, particularly a condition which would render paragraphs (a) and (b) redundant. As well, the phrase “advance made in respect of that mortgage” does not require proof not only that monies advanced have been advanced to the mortgagor, but also that they have been applied toward the improvement of the lands under construction. An advance made under a loan agreement between a lender and a borrower is not “an advance in respect of” a collateral mortgage given to secure the obligations of a guarantor under a guarantee of the borrower's obligation under the loan agreement. In determining priorities, the court found that professional fees owed on the first mortgage were entitled to benefit of priority in s. 78(6) of Act to the extent that they were contractual obligations under the terms of the credit facilities. All of the monies advanced under the second mortgage represented an advance in respect of the mortgage for the purposes of s. 78(6), and had priority over the lien claimants to extent of the money secured under the mortgage. Lastly, the lien claimants had priority over the collateral mortgage to the extent they had registered and perfected liens over the land subject to that mortgage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="755055 Ontario Ltd." p2="McIntyre" post.rptr="1694" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I64376d015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="755055 Ontario Ltd. v. McIntyre">755055 Ontario Ltd. v. McIntyre, 2011 ONSC 1694, 2011 CarswellOnt 5995 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Correspondence from the claimant's solicitor to the lawyer representing both the owner and mortgagee bank did not constitute a written notice of lien to the bank. The letter was not intended to be written notice of a lien but rather, it was a letter to the owners' lawyer setting out the terms of an agreement that the plaintiff and defendants had entered into. No reasonable person reading the letter would conclude that the plaintiff intended to file a lien or claim a lien. To the contrary, the letter appeared to confirm that the agreement that the plaintiff had entered into with the owners necessitated the bank advancing mortgage funds.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Schwegel" p2="Nelson" post.rptr="5605" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I64376d025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schwegel v. Nelson">Schwegel v. Nelson, 2003 CarswellOnt 5605, 37 C.L.R. (3d) 76 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at 2003 CarswellOnt 5445 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Written notice, in order to comply with s. 78(6)(b) must: (1) contain the identity of the trade or supplier; (2) contain a statement that work has been done or materials supplied with respect to improvements; (3) indicate the specified premises; (4) state that an account is owing and has not been paid; (5) state the specific amount owing which forms the basis for the lien; (6) identify the owner or other person who owes the amount claimed; and (7) be authored or sent by or on behalf of the person who possesses the lien. (See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1978" p1="354628 Ontario Ltd." p2="Mutic" post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="1978" ref.id="I562fa840fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic">354628 Ontario Ltd. v. Mutic (1978), 1978 CarswellOnt 198, 20 O.R. (2d) 581, 29 C.B.R. (N.S.) 88, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 442 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, decided under the former <ital>Mechanics Lien Act</ital>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="XDG Ltd." p2="1099606 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4535" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I64376d045fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd.">XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd. (2002), 2002 CarswellOnt 4535, 23 C.L.R. (3d) 67 (S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 1316 (S.C.J.); affirmed (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 1581, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 78 refers to amounts advanced, not amounts secured. Here, the mortgage was given by the owner as <ital>collateral security</ital> with respect to the prior indebtedness of its related lessee, and no advance was made to the owner, nor did the owner benefit in any manner whatsoever. Because there was no advance under the mortgage, the lien claimants had priority pursuant to s. 78(6). In reaching this conclusion, the court was influenced in large part by the failure of the mortgagee to perform a customary due diligence investigation with respect to the owner. Failure to do so could be construed as an attempt to obtain additional security for a customer it knew was on the edge of failure. It was unconscionable and inequitable to allow the mortgagee to obtain priority based upon its wilful blindness or negligence, when a due diligence investigation would likely have led the mortgagee to decide against the mortgage security.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="300016 Ontario Ltd." p2="176419 Canada Ltd." post.rptr="5" pre.rptr="34" ref.id="I643794105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="300016 Ontario Ltd. v. 176419 Canada Ltd.">300016 Ontario Ltd. v. 176419 Canada Ltd. (1996), 34 C.L.R. (2d) 5, 33 O.R. (3d) 154 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff installed gas furnaces on nine units of a project owned by the defendant, under a contract that did not stipulate that lien rights were to be on a lot-by-lot basis. When its account was not paid, the plaintiff registered a general lien against four of the nine units, for work done on all units. After the owner obtained a building mortgage on the four units, the mortgagee took possession of the project, and then advanced funds to the trades working on the units, including the plaintiff, without retaining the statutory holdback. In allowing the plaintiff's appeal, the court held that, even though the mortgaged money was paid out to the trades and not to the mortgagors, those payments were advances under the mortgage. The plaintiff's lien therefore had priority over the mortgage to the extent of the statutory holdback and to the extent of the mortgage advances made after registration of the plaintiff's lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Garrett" p2="Ayr Ventures Inc." post.rptr="407" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I643794115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Garrett v. Ayr Ventures Inc.">Garrett v. Ayr Ventures Inc. (1995), 21 O.R. (3d) 407, 18 C.L.R. (2d) 300, 44 R.P.R. (2d) 215 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant placed a general lien in the amount of $1,700 on all the lots in a subdivision notwithstanding that work was performed on one lot only. The purchaser of a different lot within the subdivision refused to close, and the vendor was held entitled to a declaration that the deposit was forfeited. The vendor's solicitor had undertaken at closing to remove the lien and the certificate of action, and it was clear from the evidence that the property was a speculative venture for the purchaser, who intended resell before taking title. It was also clear that, because of a downturn in the real estate market, the purchaser was seeking a way to avoid the transaction. In such circumstances, it was unreasonable, capricious, and arbitrary for the purchaser to refuse to cooperate with the vendor and reject the offered undertaking or agree to postpone closing to permit the vendor to remove the lien from title.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Ron Miller Realty Ltd." p2="Honeywell, Wotherspoon" post.rptr="239" pre.rptr="46" ref.id="I643794125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ron Miller Realty Ltd. v. Honeywell, Wotherspoon">Ron Miller Realty Ltd. v. Honeywell, Wotherspoon (1991), 46 C.L.R. 239, 4 O.R. (3d) 492, 1 C.P.C. (3d) 134 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In authorizing the payment of a mortgage advance before the discharge of a lien registered against title, thereby subordinating the advance to subsequent perfected liens, a solicitor did not meet the standard of care and skill required of solicitors, that of reasonable competence and diligence. Further, the solicitor was not acting in accord with the prevailing practice of solicitors in the area at the time when it allowed the funds to be advanced before discharging the existing lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1986" p1="Carpet-Trend (Eastern) Inc." p2="519583 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="307" pre.rptr="43" ref.id="I643794135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carpet-Trend (Eastern) Inc. v. 519583 Ontario Inc.">Carpet-Trend (Eastern) Inc. v. 519583 Ontario Inc. (1986), 43 C.L.R. 307 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant developer sold 17 condominium units. Prior to the registration of the transfers, two liens were registered on title. Sales of 11 units (“group 1”) were then closed and transfers were registered after undertakings to discharge the liens were given by the solicitors for the vendor. The two liens were discharged by registration of releases and the six remaining transfers (“group 2”) were registered at a time when no liens and no certificates of title were registered. Other liens were later registered and continued to form a cloud on title, and the court was called upon to rule on the question of priorities. Under s. 80(6), conveyances registered after the time the first lien arose in respect to the improvement have priority over the liens to the extent of any advance made in respect of that conveyance, unless a preserved or perfected lien was registered against the premises at the time of the advance. A preserved lien is one which is registered, and it becomes perfected when a certificate of action is registered within the time and the manner specified in the Act. When the first 11 sales were registered, two liens had been preserved by registration, and hence the Group was second in priority to the liens subsequently registered. With respect to the second group of six sales, those registered at a time when no preserved or perfected liens were on title, the grantees would take in priority to unregistered liens arising from the improvement to the extent of advances made under those conveyances. The resale of one of the 11 conveyances in the first group should be treated in the same manner as the six sales in Group 2, as releases of the prior liens had been registered and no other liens had been preserved or perfected at the time of the registration of this resale. The resale was therefore not subject to lien claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1985" p1="Paris Construction Co." p2="JAV Residences Ltd." post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I910925f0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Paris Construction Co. v. JAV Residences Ltd.">Paris Construction Co. v. JAV Residences Ltd. (1985), 11 C.L.R. 1, 30 A.C.W.S. (2d) 287 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>—A bank advanced the sum of $200,000 under a building mortgage, and the deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained was $131,000. At the time when the bank made its advance, there were no preserved or perfected liens against the subject lands and the bank had received no written notice of lien. The lien holders argued that they had priority over the mortgage advance to the full extent of the valid liens, arguing that the legislation is remedial and that the intention of the Legislature was to prevent the mortgagee from having an unjust advantage against the lien claimants whose efforts have improved the value of the lands. The court ruled that the mortgage advance had priority. That mortgage moneys advanced pursuant to a registered mortgage have priority over the liens to the extent of the advance made where the liens were not preserved or perfected and the mortgagee did not have written notice of a lien at the time of the advance of the mortgage money.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
78:9: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 78.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">78:9</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 78(10)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Naylor Group Inc." p2="Enfinity Canada EPC Inc." post.rptr="4365" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6437bb215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Naylor Group Inc. v. Enfinity Canada EPC Inc.">Naylor Group Inc. v. Enfinity Canada EPC Inc., 2012 ONSC 4365, 2012 CarswellOnt 9316, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 155 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—In an unsuccessful ex parte motion brought to substitute a letter of credit for posted cash security, the proposed letter of credit was made subject to ICC Publication 590 of the International Chamber of Commerce. Section 44 of the Act contemplates payment of cash security in lieu of the lands and premises. Section 78(10) contemplates that in lieu of cash a financial guarantee bond or a letter of credit or a guarantee from a bank listed in Schedule I to the <ital>Bank Act</ital> can be posted. Implicit is that any such bond or letter of credit be free of any term or restrictions that potentially could give rise to the issuer/surety refusing to pay. A form of Financial Guarantee Bond is prescribed in Form 23, and while there is no form of letter of credit prescribed, the practice has been that its terms be equivalent. There was potential that the above-noted term in the proposed letter of credit could be invoked to deny payment, thus embroiling the Accountant in a lawsuit. Regardless of the fact that in a lawsuit the Accountant may be successful, the mere fact of the potential of the lawsuit is sufficient to reject the form of the tendered letter of credit. The letter of credit was not equivalent to Form 23 in terms of conditions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd." p2="Kinalea Development Corp." post.rptr="85" pre.rptr="18" ref.id="I6437bb225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp.">J. Sousa Contractor Ltd. v. Kinalea Development Corp. (1994), 18 C.L.R. (2d) 85 (Ont. Gen. Div.); affirmed (1996), [1996] O.J. No. 1337 (Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Where a mortgagee had obtained a financial guarantee bond prior to a sale under a power of sale, the subsequent purchaser took title free of the priority of the liens created by s. 78(2) with respect to holdback deficiencies.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I6437bb235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 950, 17 C.L.R. (2d) 187 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 78(10) does not provide for the vacating of liens, such as pursuant to s. 44, and responds only to liens arising from an improvement which have a priority over the mortgage to the extent of any deficiency in the holdbacks required to be retained by the owner under Part IV.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
79:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 79.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">79:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The section was first introduced in the 1983 revisions. It has remained unchanged since.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section defines a concept that is central to the operation of the statute. Essentially, all persons supplying services or materials to a payer comprise a class. A person may belong to more than one class.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
80:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 80.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">80:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section replaces s. 15(2) and (3) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. Subsection 15(2), dealing with the priority among lien holders, can first be found in substantially the same format in s. 12(3) of the <ital>Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35. Subsection 15(3), which was replaced by what is now s. 80(2), was added as s. 13(3) in s. 4 of <ital>An Act to amend The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1932, c. 19. It remained unchanged until the revisions of 1983.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section addresses the issue of priorities among classes of lien claimants. Certain fundamental proportions are set out in subs. (a), (b) and (c). Distributions are rateable among members of a class and each class has priority, as a class, over its payer. In every sense, claims are paid from “the bottom up”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection (2) precludes a lien claimant from circumventing the priority scheme set out in subs. (1) by obtaining additional security on the premises, although other forms of security not related to the premises, such as a personal guarantee, may be obtained.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re" post.rptr="7125" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I643809405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re">Jade-Kennedy Development Corp., Re, 2016 ONSC 7125, 2016 CarswellOnt 19127, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 236 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Dircam Electric v. Am-Stat Corp.</ital>, 2017 CarswellOnt 8300, 72 C.L.R. (4th) 256 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A procedure order of the court provided, among other things, that if a lien claimant did not deliver a responding affidavit by the bar date, it was barred from asserting a claim against the property for an amount in excess of the basic holdback, in priority to the mortgages registered against it. In making the order, it was not the intention of the court that a lien claimant who failed to file an affidavit in the proceeding would be denied its claim even if such claim was validly registered and perfected, and notwithstanding the provisions of s. 80. The Court did not intend to require a lien claimant to file an affidavit unless it asserted a priority over other lien claimants with whom it would otherwise be in the same class for the purposes of s. 80. A lien claimant who did not assert such a claim was nevertheless at liberty to participate in the proceedings contemplated by the procedure order, including attending cross-examinations and filing a factum, to the extent it wished to do so. The Court further was only prepared to proceed to a determination of the issues if it was satisfied that none of the parties would be relying on the absence of an affidavit from any lien claimant to assert a priority over such lien claimant for that reason alone.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 80(1)(a)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Direct Equipment Ltd." p2="Metrolinx et al." post.rptr="347" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I643809415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Direct Equipment Ltd. v. Metrolinx et al.">Direct Equipment Ltd. v. Metrolinx et al., 2018 ONSC 347, 2018 CarswellOnt 331, 87 C.L.R. (4th) 324 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Agreement was reached by the parties concerning distribution of the holdback ordered to be posted by the owner. The issue before the master was whether the amount allocated to one party, T, as a subcontractor to the general contractor and as a subcontractor to another subcontractor, was to be divided equally with its own subcontractor, DEL, in accordance with an agreement between them. A default judgment had been granted to T against the defendant general contractor, and a consent order had been granted to DEL as against T. DEL also brought a claim of breach of contract and unjust enrichment as against the owner as an alternative claim to its lien claim. The master determined that the distribution question was to be determined at the trial of the unjust enrichment action. However, he found that the agreement between T and DEL did not purport to change the priority rules of section 80. It simply specifies that any recovery through the T lien from the holdback was to be divided equally. It did not purport to render the lien superior in priority to that of the DEL lien. In addition, the priority rules did not deny a party entitled to holdback funds the freedom to distribute the received holdback through an agreement such as the one in question, subject to statutory or other trust rights.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Atlas Corp." p2="617430 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="201" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I643809425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd.">Atlas Corp. v. 617430 Ontario Ltd. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 201 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendants moved, with the plaintiff's consent, for payment out of court of the moneys paid to vacate the plaintiff's lien. It was learned that there were five other liens registered on title in addition to the plaintiff's, and three of the five lien claimants objected to the payment out of court. The motion was dismissed. The court reasoned, <ital>inter alia</ital>, that if the money paid into court to vacate this lien is paid out to the plaintiffs, and the other lien claimants were successful at trial and sell the property, the proceeds of sale may be less than the amount of their proven claims, which would mean that the plaintiffs in this action would have been given a priority contrary to s. 80(1)(a).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 80(1)(c)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="X-L-Air Energy Systems Ltd." p2="Hyde Park Residences Inc." post.rptr="5117" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I643830505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="X-L-Air Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc.">X-L-Air Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc., 2014 ONSC 5117, 2014 CarswellOnt 12104, 37 C.L.R. (4th) 243 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2015 ONSC 2019, 2015 CarswellOnt 6201, 42 C.L.R. (4th) 40 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—After various lien claims were registered against a residential project in 2012, the parties reached agreement in 2013 to resolve the claims. A subtrade who was not part of the original agreement registered additional liens in 2013 and 2014, as did its payer in the construction chain, and the two parties reached their own agreement based on that earlier, larger agreement. The Master finding that the subtrade did not contract out of its lien rights for work done after 2012 was upheld on appeal. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd." p2="Hyde Park Residences Inc." post.rptr="8015" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I643830515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc.">X-L-AIR Energy Systems Ltd. v. Hyde Park Residences Inc., 2013 ONSC 8015, 2013 CarswellOnt 18442 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, under ss. 62(1)(b) and 78(4).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="George & Asmussen Ltd." p2="MCM Projects Inc." post.rptr="254" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I643830525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Projects Inc.">George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Projects Inc. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 254, <ital>(</ital>sub nom. <ital>George & Asmussen Ltd. v. MCM Holdings Inc.)</ital> 6 O.R. (3d) 645 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 80(1)(c) of the Act is clearly an attempt to ensure that a subcontractor is paid in priority to the contractor hiring him. There is nothing in the legislation to suggest that the subcontractor's rights are dependent upon its payer filing a lien. Such an interpretation would leave the subcontractor at the mercy of an unscrupulous contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Neil Vanderkruk Holdings Inc." p2="Grand Harbour Development Ltd." post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I643830535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Neil Vanderkruk Holdings Inc. v. Grand Harbour Development Ltd.">Neil Vanderkruk Holdings Inc. v. Grand Harbour Development Ltd. (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 205 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Every lien claimant's lien had been bonded off and secured for 100 per cent plus 25 per cent for costs, and the plaintiff had settled with the owner. The parties and one defendant consented to have the action dismissed and the security paid out to the plaintiff and the defendant in some share proportions. Two lien claimants objected on the basis that future lien claims might be made, share in their security and thus reduce it. The Master dismissed the objection, stating that the land stood as security for these future claimants. The possibility of future lien claims did not prevent the plaintiff's motion from being successful.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 80(2)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd." p2="Edge on Triangle Park Inc." post.rptr="783" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I643857605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Edge on Triangle Park Inc.">Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Edge on Triangle Park Inc., 2017 ONSC 783, 2017 CarswellOnt 1080, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 265 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming 2016 ONSC 5461, 2016 CarswellOnt 13669, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 256 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 ONSC 7012, 2016 CarswellOnt 18025, 73 C.L.R. (4th) 145 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimant was owed monies for goods and services supplied to the defendant's condominium project. The respondent was also owed monies for goods and services supplied to the project, and when the condominium was registered, purchased 2 units in satisfaction of the debt. At the time of closing, the respondent had no knowledge or notice of the lien claim. Subsequently, the claimant registered a claim for lien against various units in the building, including those owned by the respondent, with the last day of work listed as after the respondent's purchase. The statement of claim did not list the respondent as a defendant, and the lien was discharged as against the respondent's units. The lien claimant unsuccessfully argued that the conveyance from the developer to the respondent was void by operation of s. 80(2). Section 80 is designed to protect members of a class of lien claimants from receiving priority by the transfer of property at the expense of other members of the same class. The respondent was not a lien claimant, and the claimant and respondent were not members of the same class. Section 80(2) did not apply.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
