C.30, s. 81.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">81:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The concept of a worker's priority for 30 days' wages was first introduced in the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1882</ital>, S.O. 1882, c. 15, s. 2, s. 4:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">In case of there being a contract for the construction, alteration, repair, erecting or placing aforesaid, the said lien for wages shall, to the extent of 10 per cent of the price to be paid to the contractor, have priority over all other liens under the said Act, and over any claim by the owner against the contractor for, or in consequence of, the failure of the latter to complete his contract.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>An Act to further facilitate the enforcement of the just rights of Wage-Earners and Sub-contractors</ital>, S.O. 1893, c. 24, first provided that every device to defeat that priority should be void:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Preamble</para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Whereas it is just and reasonable that the wages of wage-earners for the thirty days provided by <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> should have priority over all other claims not having a superior equity, and should be easily recoverable and promptly paid; […]</para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Ontario, enacts as follows:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Every device by any owner or contractor which shall be adopted in order to defeat the priority of wage-earners for their wages under the several Acts relating to mechanics' liens shall, as respects such wage-earners, be null and void.</para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The preamble was transformed into s. 13(1) of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, which remained in substantially the same form until the 1983 amendments. Section 1 of the 1893 Act remained virtually unchanged until the 1983 reforms. The current s. (2) was introduced in 1983. Its purpose, as explained by the Attorney General's Advisory Committee, was to meet a new development within the field of labour relations, <ital>i.e.</ital>, the development of trusts for workers' benefits. The main change in the 1983 revisions was an extension from 30 days' wages to 40 regular-time working days, making it clear that the priority is limited to the extent of the worker's normal wages.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Act gives construction workers a special priority to the extent of 40 regular workings days wages over other non-worker members of the same class.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In order to protect funds in a trust set up for workers' benefits, such as vacation pay and health insurance, subs. (2) provides for the subrogation of the trust fund to the workers' rights to the extent of the money owed to the fund. The trustee of the fund must make the claim for any monies owed to it, and the workers' individual lien claims are disallowed to that extent. Subsection (3) makes it clear that the priority given to workers cannot be evaded.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thompson" p2="Carleton University" post.rptr="4336" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64387e705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Thompson v. Carleton University">Thompson v. Carleton University, 2019 ONSC 4336, 2019 CarswellOnt 11566, 92 C.L.R. (4th) 33 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2020 CarswellOnt 7633 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A contractor cannot artificially reduce its statutory holdback by seeking to amend the contract after the lien rights have arisen. A contractor and subcontractor cannot collude to reduce the holdback liability after the fact. This is particularly the case with a worker's lien protected under the provisions of s. 81(3). Here, the contractor unsuccessfully argued, for the purposes of calculating its holdback obligations, that its contract with the subsequently insolvent subcontractor was amended to a labour only contract, such that the value of the subcontractor's work would not include the material or equipment rental and the basic holdback would be only 10% of a greatly reduced amount. Rather than amending the contract to a labour only contract, the evidence showed that the parties decided to continue with the original contract and to provide credits against progress draws.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353" p2="779857 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2528" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I64387e715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 v. 779857 Ontario Inc.">I.B.E.W. Trust Fund, Local 353 v. 779857 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 2528, 36 C.L.R. (3d) 48 (Master)</ref></cite>—Liens were filed after the electrical contractor failed to pay both its suppliers and, for several weeks of work, its unionized workers. Subsection 81(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> gave the lien of a worker priority over the lien of any other person of the same class to the extent of the amount of 40 regular time working days' wages. The supplier lien claimants challenged the workers claim for lien on the basis that it was not preserved within the requisite 45-day period. The workers' claim for lien was registered on February 10, 2003, and for its timely preservation, the “supply of services” had to be last supplied on or after December 28, 2002. However, the job site was closed at the end of the day on December 20, 2002 and was reopened on January 2, 2003 with the result that no services were or could have been supplied between December 21 and January 1. Following that hiatus, the owner terminated the contractor's contract, a process that was started on January 2, 2003 and finalized on January 3, 2003. At least 20 of the workers named in the claim for lien and the statement of claim had returned to the job site on January 2, 2003, and although no actual physical electrical work was performed, the workers prepared for the work day, and packed up when the foreman advised that the job site would be closed. It was argued that the “supply of services” required that some actual physical electrical work be performed on the improvement that advanced the scope of the work in the contract. The Master ruled that attending to hear their foreman assign the work for the day, and readying their tools and equipment for the day's work, and cleaning up and packing up their tools and equipment and job boxes was “work done” and, therefore, a “supply of services”. As a result, the lien was preserved in a timely manner and the workers' and union trustee's lien claim had priority under s. 81(1) over the lien claims of the suppliers and the agent for the trustees of the Local only entitled to the proper amount for the “monetary supplementary benefits” portion.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
82:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 82.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">82:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision first came into existence as s. 84 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, and has remained unchanged since.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision prevents the general lien provisions of the Act from working to the detriment of lien claimants who have supplied services or materials only to the premises against which the general lien claim is enforced. General lien claims are postponed in favour of those single premises lien claimants in so far as the general lien does not relate to that particular premises. A formula by which that postponement is to be calculated is set out in the section.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
83:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 83.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">83:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section replaces s. 9 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. As a number of changes were made, it is worth providing the wording of s. 9:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Where any of the property upon which a lien attaches is wholly or partly destroyed by fire, any money received by reason of any insurance thereon by an owner or prior mortgagee or chargee shall take the place of the property so destroyed and is, after satisfying any prior mortgage or charge in the manner and to the extent set out in subsection 8(3), subject to the claims of all persons for liens to the same extent as if the money had been realized by a sale of the property in an action to enforce the lien.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">That provision had been part of the various Acts in substantially the same format since its introduction in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, s. 7:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Where any of the property upon which a lien is given by this Act is wholly or partly destroyed by fire, any money received by reason of any insurance thereon by an owner or prior mortgagee or chargee shall take the place of the property so destroyed, and shall be subject to the claims of all persons for liens to the same extent as if such moneys were realized by a sale of such property in an action to enforce a lien.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The main change introduced in the 1983 revisions was the extension of the section's application from fire insurance only in 1980 to all insurance in 1983.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section provides for the distribution of insurance proceeds in the hands of either the owner or the mortgagee to be dealt with under the priority provision of the Act in the event that a premises is destroyed before lien claims are settled.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="A. Topazzini Construction Inc." p2="National Frontier Insurance Co." post.rptr="11" pre.rptr="20" ref.id="I6438cc905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A. Topazzini Construction Inc. v. National Frontier Insurance Co.">A. Topazzini Construction Inc. v. National Frontier Insurance Co. (1995), 20 C.L.R. (2d) 11 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Section 83 has no application if at the time of the fire there are no liens on the premises.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Riverside Glass Ltd." p2="Charron's Quality Market Ltd." post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6438cc915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd.">Riverside Glass Ltd. v. Charron's Quality Market Ltd. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 150 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Where a lien and certificate of action were registered, but the building under construction burned to the ground before the plaintiff completed its contracted work on the windows and doors, the doctrine of frustration was held not to apply. Pursuant to s. 83 of the Act, insurance is to be distributed according to the priorities set out in the Act where a building subject to a lien has been destroyed. There was insurance on the building; the proof of loss claim included loss for the windows and the door, and the plaintiff was not paid. Therefore, the doctrine of frustration did not apply, and the plaintiff was entitled to judgment.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Trus Joist Canada Ltd." p2="Princess Gardens Inc." post.rptr="146" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I6438cc925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc.">Trus Joist Canada Ltd. v. Princess Gardens Inc. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 146 (Ont. Gen. Div.); varied (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 126 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner acquired title to a parcel of land and entered into a loan agreement with the mortgagee for $2 million for construction of condominiums on the land. Prior to completion, a large part of the construction project was destroyed or damaged by fire, and the principal lien claimant commenced an action to determine, <ital>inter alia</ital>, whether the lien claimants had priority over the mortgagee with respect to the moneys advanced by the mortgagee. The court held that the lien claimants were entitled to their respective lien claims against the land and had the right to sell the property if the money was not paid. In the event of a deficiency from the proceeds of a sale of the property, the lien claimants had the right to claim against any insurance moneys on the premises destroyed or damaged by fire received by the owner or mortgagee as provided under s. 83.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
84:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 84.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">84:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This provision first appeared in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>. It codifies a practice, which had evolved under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, resulting from the incorporation by reference of s. 43 of the Act into s. 38(4) of the Act. Subsection 43(1) provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(1)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">Where a sale is had, the moneys arising therefrom shall be paid into court to the credit of the action, and the judge or officer before whom the action was tried shall direct to whom the moneys in court shall be paid and may add to the claim of the person conducting the action his fees and actual disbursements incurred in connection with the sale, and, where sufficient to satisfy the judgment and costs is not realized from the sale, he shall certify the amount of the deficiency and the names of the persons who are entitled to recover the same, showing the amount that each is entitled to recover and the persons adjudged to pay the same, giving credit for payments made, if any, under subsection 42(4), and the persons so entitled may enforce payment of the amounts so found to be due by execution or otherwise.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 38(4) read as follows:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(4)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">The proceeds of any sale made by a trustee or trustees under subsection (2) shall be paid into court and are subject to the claims of all lien claimants, mortgagees or other persons interested in the property so sold as their respective rights are determined, and, in so far as applicable, section 43 applies.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section pools all monies received on sale or lease of liened premises with all money or security in court for the purpose of distribution under the Act.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pollard Windows Inc." p2="1736106 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="7567" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I6438f3a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pollard Windows Inc. v. 1736106 Ontario Inc.">Pollard Windows Inc. v. 1736106 Ontario Inc., 2018 ONSC 7567, 2018 CarswellOnt 22765 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 1348 (Ont. S.C.J.); appeal quashed 2019 CarswellOnt 14848 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2019 ONSC 4859, 2019 CarswellOnt 13133, 91 C.L.R. (4th) 58 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 17956 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A notice of sale by a mortgagee under the <ital>Mortgages Act</ital> did not defeat the priorities set out in s. 78(3) and (4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, following a court ordered sale, where the court doubted the <ital>bona fides</ital> and the validity of the notice. It was given between parties who were not at arm's length and it was not proven that the mortgage was in default, nor that the notice was signed when it was issued.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="David Schaeffer Engineering Ltd." p2="D.T.A. Investments Inc." post.rptr="26" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I6438f3a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="David Schaeffer Engineering Ltd. v. D.T.A. Investments Inc.">David Schaeffer Engineering Ltd. v. D.T.A. Investments Inc. (1998), 37 C.L.R. (2d) 26 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Once the priority of a mortgagee is established under s. 78(3), then the party with carriage of the sale will be entitled to have the reasonable fees and actual disbursements in connection with the sale deducted from the gross proceeds and reimbursement allowed accordingly. This position is in accordance with the common practice of the court in all sorts of proceedings where the sale of land is ordered. Where the mortgagee conducts the sale, the sale expenses are not “advances” under the mortgage within s. 78(3), but rather, are to be allowed by the court under its powers regarding costs in ss. 59, 62(5), 65, 58(4), 84, and 86.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
85:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 85.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">85:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section was first introduced in 1983. No similar provision existed under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The insolvency of a payer is dealt with here. Insolvency may occur well before bankruptcy and can be assumed to be a necessary article of proof in any application to appoint a trustee of a project under s. 68. In such a case, the Act mandates that all funds be paid first in satisfaction of beneficiaries of the trust that have proven liens, again by class, and rateably within the class.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Re: North House Foods Ltd. Proposal" post.rptr="3567" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6789e9703b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Re: North House Foods Ltd. Proposal">Re: North House Foods Ltd. Proposal, 2024 CarswellOnt 9252, 2024 ONSC 3567, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3255 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On an application pursuant to s. 50.1(4) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital> to revise the proposed value of a subcontractor's security, at issue was whether the sub-trade lien claimant was to be treated as secured creditor, an unsecured creditor or a partially secured creditor. The claimant had registered a construction lien against the debtor's leasehold interest, and the trustee had valued the security at $0, which ranked the claimant with other unsecured creditors in the proposal. In denying the application, the court noted that the registration of a lien gives the successful lien claimant priority over subsequent encumbrancers of the interest in land, but it is a contingent form of security with contingent enforcement through a court process. There are no private rights of enforcement available to lien claimants, and the lien claimant here could not seize and sell the leasehold interest to determine its actual value. Because the objective was for the debtor to keep operating, the Trustee would also not do so during a proposal. Hence, the exercise of determining the value of the claimant's security was theoretical in nature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="CJK Goodmen Inc." p2="SRR Stables Inc." post.rptr="6713" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I64391ab05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="CJK Goodmen Inc. v. SRR Stables Inc.">CJK Goodmen Inc. v. SRR Stables Inc., 2013 ONSC 6713, 2013 CarswellOnt 15101 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Monies paid into court by a property insurer following a fire was not paid out to the lien claimant or the second mortgagee where there was insufficient evidence before the court that a valid, timely lien existed, or that the second mortgage would hold up to scrutiny. A trial of the issue was required.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="561861 Ontario Ltd." p2="1085043 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I64391ab15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc.">561861 Ontario Ltd. v. 1085043 Ontario Inc. (1999), 49 C.L.R. (2d) 143, 15 C.B.R. (4th) 146, 1999 CarswellOnt 2227 (Ont. Bktcy.)</ref></cite>—Where an owner has made a proposal in bankruptcy, lien claimants who have registered and perfected their liens in accordance with the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> are secured creditors within the meaning of s. 2(1) of the <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>. As secured creditors, they stand separate and apart from, and do not have a commonality of interest with, the unsecured creditors.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd." p2="Stowe Nut & Bolt Co." post.rptr="115" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I64391ab35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Stowe Nut & Bolt Co.">Steeplejack Services (Sarnia) Ltd. v. Stowe Nut & Bolt Co. (1988), 31 C.L.R. 115, 1988 CarswellOnt 770 (Ont. Dist. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The trust provisions imposed upon a payer are inapplicable to the Crown. Under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> a contractor is at liberty to disburse progress payments to suppliers in the ordinary course of business, as he sees fit. The statutory rules of distribution under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> only apply on insolvency. In other words, during the course of construction, the trustee is permitted to discriminate between various beneficiaries. The trust funds need not be set aside by the trustee, nor is the trustee obligated to keep separate books relating to them.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
85.2:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 85.2.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">85.2:1</designator><name date.updated="0">2018 Amendments, Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>2018 Amendments</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This new Part XI.1 governs surety bonds. Section 85.1 is a new provision dealing with public contracts. Section 85.2 replaces the former s. 69. The provisions governing labour and material payment bonds remain substantially unchanged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Provisions regarding performance bonds were added.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section was one of the innovations of the 1983 reforms. The provision was introduced in s. 71 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, and has remained unchanged since. A virtually identical provision can be found in s. 81 of the Saskatchewan Act.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Most commercial construction of any size is performed by bonded contractors and, often, bonded subcontractors. One of the bond forms most commonly required is the “Trustee Form” Labour and Material Payment Bond. Such bonds are mandatory on most public construction projects. Although each of these bonds contains express language entitling unnamed beneficiaries to sue on it and recover judgment, the enactment of S. 85.2(5) (formerly s. 69(3)) leaves no doubt about the subject. Subsection 85.2(3) (formerly s. 69(2)) makes it clear that the statutory right of action granted by s. 85.2(1) (formerly s. 69(1)) has no substantive effect on the penal sum limitation expressed by the bond, a limitation of fundamental importance to the surety. Subsection 85.2(3) codifies the well established common law right of subrogation.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Westport Insurance" p2="BDA Inc." post.rptr="15030" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678a5ea03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Westport Insurance v. BDA Inc.">Westport Insurance v. BDA Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 15030, 2024 ONSC 5450 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At issue was the novel question of whether a surety may assert a security interest on funds awarded pursuant to an adjudication determination<ital>.</ital> In holding that it could, the court noted that the applicant surety was only entitled to losses as defined in the indemnity agreement, and as a result, the disputed funds were to be paid into court pending the outcome of the related proceedings being litigated. Here, the contractor required the subcontractor to provide performance security, and the surety delivered bonds naming the contractor as the obligee, and the subcontractor as the principal, and then registered its security interest under the <ital>Personal Property Security Act</ital>. Subsequently, following a dispute, the contractor terminated the subcontract and made a claim against the bonds. On an interim basis, the surety entered into a mitigation agreement and paid the contractor various advances, and pursuant to s. 13.5(1), a determination was made awarding payment to the subcontractor. The subcontractor opposed the surety's attempt to assert its security interest in that payment. The clear and unambiguous wording of the indemnity agreement included all funds to which the subcontractor might be entitled or which were awarded in its favour, and provided that all funds due or to become due under the subcontract, constituted trust funds for the benefit of the surety. The court noted that the aim of prompt payment and adjudication, to ensure that funds flow down the construction pyramid, was not defeated by upholding a surety's security interest, as the surety regime ensures that progress continues on construction projects, and that downstream subcontractors and workers are paid. If contractors were able to gain the benefit and protection of surety bonds to secure public contracts but are then permitted to circumvent their indemnity obligations when a claim is made, there could be a chilling effect on the willingness of bonding companies to provide surety bonds. Neither Part XI and Part XI.1 of the Act gave a contractor priority over a surety's security interest where there was a determination in the subcontractor's favour.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Don Fry Scaffold Service Inc." p2="Ontario" post.rptr="310" pre.rptr="65" ref.id="I643968d05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Don Fry Scaffold Service Inc. v. Ontario">Don Fry Scaffold Service Inc. v. Ontario (2007), 65 C.L.R. (3d) 310, 2007 CarswellOnt 5092 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2008), 67 C.L.R. (3d) 4, 2008 CarswellOnt 531 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The owner entered into a renovation agreement with the contractor, who provided a labour and materials payment bond to ensure that subcontractors were paid for their services. After the contractor declared bankruptcy, the subcontractor commenced a lien action claiming from the contractor's receiver and an action against the company that provided the bond. The judgment for the full amount owed plus interest was not satisfied, and the company that provided the bond was found not to be licensed to sell insurance or to do business in Ontario. The subcontractor then commenced an action against the owner alleging that the owner had breached its duty to the subcontractor to ensure that the company that provided the bond was properly licensed. On motion by the owner, the statement of claim was struck without leave to amend. The law of tort was not central to determining the rights and obligations, and the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applied. The imposition of a fiduciary duty or duty of care between the owners and subcontractors was inappropriate. In upholding the ruling, the court held that the pleading failed to assert any material facts concerning the relationship between owner and subcontractor sufficient to ground a duty of care or fiduciary duty owed by the owner.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 85.2(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Urban Mechanical Contracting Ltd. et al." p2="Zurich Insurance Company Ltd." post.rptr="2535" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64398fe05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Urban Mechanical Contracting Ltd. et al. v. Zurich Insurance Company Ltd.">Urban Mechanical Contracting Ltd. et al. v. Zurich Insurance Company Ltd., 2021 ONSC 2535, 2021 CarswellOnt 5043, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>Urban Mechanical Contracting Ltd. v. Zurich Insurance Company Ltd.</ital>, 2022 CarswellOnt 11581, 24 C.L.R. (5th) 26 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Rescission is available as a matter of law on a construction bond where there has been fraud and collusion in the procurement process, even where the rights of innocent third parties are engaged. The court rejected the argument that s. 85.2(1) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> provides a clear right of action for claims under a labour and material bond such that equitable doctrines do not apply. The legislature cannot have intended that the liability of a surety be absolute, and common law and equitable remedies are still available. Otherwise, the section would stipulate that the surety's liability arose upon execution of the bond rather than when the bond was “in effect.” Here, the surety commenced a rescission action as soon as it learned of the fraud, and if the payment bond was rescinded <ital>ab initio</ital>, it would not be “in effect” as required by the section. In affirming the lower court's ruling, the Ontario Court of Appeal stated that prejudice to the rights of third parties may be, but is not always, a bar to rescission, particularly in the case of fraudulent misrepresentation and in cases where it is possible to provide restitution in other ways. The issue of rescission was to proceed to trial on a full factual record so that the court might consider all the circumstances and equities of the case. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not explicitly address the trades' right of action on the payment bond when the bond agreement was founded on fraud. Nor is there anything in the legislative record to show whether the legislature specifically intended former s. 69 to sustain the bond even in the face of fraud. It was therefore not appropriate to foreclose this argument without hearing full submissions on this issue. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The reported version of this case references s. 85(1), but this appears to be a typographical error, as the discussion in the judgement make it clear that the court is referencing s. 85.2(1).]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lopes Limited" p2="Guarantee Company of North America" post.rptr="804" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64398fe15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lopes Limited v. Guarantee Company of North America">Lopes Limited v. Guarantee Company of North America, 2019 ONSC 804, 2019 CarswellOnt 1371, 89 B.L.R. (5th) 339, 98 C.L.R. (4th) 250 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2019 CarswellOnt 17373, 98 C.L.R. (4th) 261 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff moved for summary judgment on its claim under a labour and materials payment bond issued by the defendant insurer. The claim under the payment bond was for the aggregate amount of unpaid invoices that it issued under a subcontract with the defendant general contractor for a construction project. After failing to pay the invoices, the general contractor walked away from the project and a replacement general contractor was selected to complete the project. The replacement general contractor then entered into a new subcontract with the plaintiff for the completion of the work that remained to be performed under the original subcontract. The court concluded that the plaintiff did not mitigate its damages for non-payment of its invoices by entering into the new subcontract, and that it was entitled to be paid the amount of its claim under the payment bond. The opportunity for the plaintiff to bid for and profit from the new subcontract did not arise from non-payment of its invoices, but rather as a result of the abandonment of the project by general contractor after liens were filed by subcontractors, including the plaintiff, and after the solicitation of bids by the completion general contractor. The opportunity for the plaintiff to earn a profit from the new subcontract was separate from and collateral to the breach of contract by the general contractor through non-payment of the invoices.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ozz Electric Inc." p2="Zurich Insurance Co." post.rptr="6331" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64398fe25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ozz Electric Inc. v. Zurich Insurance Co.">Ozz Electric Inc. v. Zurich Insurance Co., 2016 ONSC 6331, 2016 CarswellOnt 15865, 70 C.L.R. (4th) 323 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 CarswellOnt 16542 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff was denied leave to amend its statement of claim in order to advance various claims against the municipality/owner of the construction project, including pleading that the defendants were liable for payment under a labour and material payment bond for all amounts outstanding. The proposed amendment did not merely purport to require the municipality to enforce the trust for the benefit of the plaintiff, as such a step was unnecessary given the provisions of s. 69(1). Rather, the proposed amendment asserted that the municipality was liable for all amounts owed to the plaintiff under the bond. There was no basis for such a claim under the terms of the bond, and no jurisprudence supported the claim. The bond only provided that a claimant was to indemnify and save harmless the obligee against all costs, charges, and expenses or liabilities incurred thereon, and any loss or damage resulting to the obligee by reason of any proceeding commenced against the obligee by a claimant to enforce the bond.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 85.2(5)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada" p2="Matthews" post.rptr="1629" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I6439b6f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada v. Matthews">Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada v. Matthews (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1629, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 18, 254 D.L.R. (4th) 97 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were officers and directors of the general contractor, to which labour and material payment bonds were issued by the plaintiff insurer to guarantee payment in respect of any default by the company in paying its subcontractors. After the general contractor was petitioned into bankruptcy, the plaintiff's bonds were called upon, and the plaintiff became subrogated to the subcontractors' rights against the general contractor. Based on those subrogated rights, the plaintiff commenced an action against the appellants for breach of the trust provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. For the purposes of the subrogated action, the plaintiff stood in the shoes of the subcontractors. Accordingly, the defendants' claim of improvident underwriting was not a tenable defence at law to the subrogated action for breach of trust under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1975" p1="AXA Pacific Insurance Co." p2="R.J.B. Nicol Construction (1975) Ltd." post.rptr="18" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I6439b6f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="AXA Pacific Insurance Co. v. R.J.B. Nicol Construction (1975) Ltd.">AXA Pacific Insurance Co. v. R.J.B. Nicol Construction (1975) Ltd. (1998), 39 C.L.R. (2d) 18 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff issued lien bonds on behalf of the defendant contractor, who subsequently became bankrupt. After settling the claims of various subcontractors, the plaintiff commenced a subrogated action claiming that trust funds received by the defendant contractor from the owners of the construction projects, were improperly converted and paid to the defendant bank. The court rejected various amendments to the defence, based on voluntary assumption of risk, mitigation, and consent and acquiescence. The court stated that while the surety takes on the risk of non-payment or non-performance by its principal, the contractor, it does not thereby preclude or relinquish recovery against a contractor or other party who acts improperly with respect to the financial operations of the contractor. With respect to mitigation, a duty arises only if a defendant has been held liable to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff could have taken reasonable steps to avoid loss caused by the defendant's wrongdoing, which was not the case here. Lastly, there was nothing untoward in providing a bond to a contractor in shaky financial circumstances. In fact, such a bond only benefits the subcontractors or owners who are thereby granted a new source of recovery.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Brant Community Place Homes (Trustees)" p2="Halifax Insurance Co." post.rptr="1124" pre.rptr="[1994]" ref.id="I6439b6f25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Brant Community Place Homes (Trustees) v. Halifax Insurance Co.">Brant Community Place Homes (Trustees) v. Halifax Insurance Co. (1994), [1994] O.J. No. 1124 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In this case the owner had paid holdback into court. The payment bond surety had settled with the lien claimants for less than the face value of the vetting committee's recommended value. The surety subrogated to the lien claimants pursuant to s. 69(3) claimed the holdback. The lien claimants resisted, claiming an amount in excess of their settlements, up to the lien committee totals, plus costs. It was held that s. 69(3) set out a complete code and, on payment by the surety of the settlement amount offered by the lien claimants, it became subrogated to their rights by statute and, if necessary, at common law. The appeal settled and this decision stands.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
86:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 86.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">86:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section replaces ss. 49 and 47(4) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. The provisions were consolidated in the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, s. 88. That section contained a ss. (3), which provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(3)</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0">Except where otherwise ordered by the court hearing an appeal, the costs of an appeal shall be on the scale of costs allowed in county court appeals where the amount involved is within the proper competence of the county court and where it exceeds that amount shall be on the Supreme Court scale.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">That subsection was repealed by s. 165(32) of S.O. 1984, c. 11. Subsection (1) was amended in S.O. 1996, c. 25, s. 4(10) to include a reference to the case management master. The current ss. (2) dates back to the 1893 <ital>Act to further facilitate the enforcement of the just rights of Wage-Earners and Sub-contractors</ital>, S.O. 1893, c. 24, s. 15:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In case the least expensive course is not taken by a plaintiff under this Act or the other <ital>Mechanics' Lien Acts</ital>, the costs allowed to the solicitor shall in no case exceed what would have been incurred if the least expensive course had been taken.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 86(1) can be traced back to ss. 41 and 42 of <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, which provided that the costs awarded to the plaintiffs and successful lien holders or, if such be the case, against the plaintiff or other persons claiming the lien, were not to exceed an amount in the aggregate equal to 25 per cent of the amount of the judgment or claim. This rather inflexible approach prevailed until 1983 when this limitation was removed in favour of the current scheme. The 25 per cent limitation survives only in s. 44 as one of the upper limits of costs on motions to post security to vacate liens.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section gives to the court significant discretion with respect to the levying of costs against claimants and their solicitors, where those individuals have put forward groundless or excessive claims, or have prejudiced or delayed the lien action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 86(2) ensures that parties who fail to follow the most expeditious claim route will not thereby benefit from taking that more expensive route when costs are awarded.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
86:2: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 86.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">86:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 86(1)(a)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Quality General Contractor's Inc." p2="Wu" post.rptr="14677" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678ad3d03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Quality General Contractor's Inc. v. Wu">Quality General Contractor's Inc. v. Wu, 2024 CarswellOnt 14677, 2024 ONSC 5318 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons to 2024 CarswellOnt 7523, 2024 ONSC 2909, 2024 A.C.W.S. 2528 (Ont.S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's principal essentially fabricated the key invoices and his own diary entries to create the false narrative that the defendants had entered into a contract of guarantee with the plaintiff and that the claim for lien was timely when the lien had in fact expired. He used Quality's key witnesses as his mouthpieces and did not produce the key time sheets that his own employees said existed. This was abusive conduct of the kind contemplated by s. 86(1) as meriting an award of substantial indemnity costs. </para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2449442 Ontario Inc." p2="Cambridge Drywall Services LTD." post.rptr="9680" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678ad3d13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="2449442 Ontario Inc. v. Cambridge Drywall Services LTD.">2449442 Ontario Inc. v. Cambridge Drywall Services LTD., 2024 CarswellOnt 9680, 2024 ONSC 3673, 2024 A.C.W.S. 3328 (Ont.S.C.J.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cambridge Drywall Services Ltd." p2="2449442 Ontario Inc." ref.id="I678ad3d23b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Cambridge Drywall Services Ltd. v. 2449442 Ontario Inc.">Cambridge Drywall Services Ltd. v. 2449442 Ontario Inc.; leave to appeal refused 2024 CarswellOnt 16852 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Costs penalties were not imposed on the plaintiff because it did not proceed under the simplified procedure under r. 76.01(6). Rule 76.13(2) does not apply to an action commenced under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, and as the action here was brought under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> and the plaintiff did not advance any trust claims, there was to be no reduction of the plaintiff's costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Alfa Mechanical Inc." p2="Chang" post.rptr="19916" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8de643b0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Alfa Mechanical Inc. v. Chang">Alfa Mechanical Inc. v. Chang, 2023 CarswellOnt 19916, 2023 ONSC 7167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's motion for default judgment, which was brought on notice to the defendants, resulted an order setting aside the defendants' noting in default and allowing the defendants to deliver a defence. The plaintiff's motion had sought a declaration of entitlement to a lien against the defendants' interest in their property, as well as personal judgment for the same amount. In declining to award costs of the motion, the court noted that considerations for deciding costs under s. 86 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> and r. 57.01 generally flow from having determined rights on a motion. As that was not done here, it was not appropriate to hypothetically consider what might have been the result of the motion in the absence of any argument from either party on the motion itself. The plaintiff was only entitled to its costs thrown away from the noting in default.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bellsam Contracting Limited" p2="Torgerson" post.rptr="15300" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8de66ac0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Bellsam Contracting Limited v. Torgerson">Bellsam Contracting Limited v. Torgerson, 2023 CarswellOnt 15300, 2023 ONSC 5652 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Ultimately, costs awards in lien actions are discretionary and as with non-lien civil actions, should reflect what the court views as a fair and reasonable amount that should be paid by the unsuccessful party, having regard to the expectations of the parties concerning the quantum of costs, rather than any exact measure of the actual costs of the successful litigant. Here, the trial was not a trial of all issues in the claim and counterclaim but was limited to determining whether there was a contract between the parties and, if so, the parties to the contract and the terms of the contract. The successful defendants were found not to have taken the least expensive course of action in preparing their case for this trial of an issue, and opted to use a team of four lawyers, three clerks, five students-at-law, and an eDiscovery specialist, all of whom expended significant time preparing for and conducting the trial. The defendants' success at the trial did not mean that the plaintiff was liable to pay those costs. The time spent by the defendants' counsel was not reasonable and proportionate to the proceeding. There was no clear correlation between the costs expended on the trial, $501,941 of which were sought here, and litigating the remaining issues. However, given the defendant's success at trial and its creative offers to settle, substantial indemnity costs from the date of the offers were warranted in the circumstances, and costs of the trial in the total amount of $285,000 was awarded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd" p2="BWK Construction Company Limited and Peel District School Board" post.rptr="8786" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I678afae03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd v. BWK Construction Company Limited and Peel District School Board">Prasher Steel Ltd v. BWK Construction Company Limited and Peel District School Board, 2023 CarswellOnt 8786, 2023 ONSC 3494, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 204 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="B.W.K. Construction Company Ltd." post.rptr="1427" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678afae13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. B.W.K. Construction Company Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. B.W.K. Construction Company Ltd.; affirmed 2024 CarswellOnt 3255, 2024 ONSC 1427 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace>—In the present case, the lien amount exceeded the maximum adjusted contract value, the plaintiff proceeded through to trial in the absence of documentary evidence, and a portion of the lien amount was abandoned during closing arguments. There was a sufficient basis for the defendant to receive a substantial indemnity of their costs throughout this proceeding. Otherwise, the plaintiff would have been permitted to advance a claim through trial, with the defendant's funds being tied up in court for ten years, with the intent of leveraging a settlement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rowe" p2="Fred Hageman's Holdings Limited" post.rptr="7015" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I8de66ac2ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Rowe v. The Act provides that the fees and disbursements of the “party having carriage of the action” may be added to the lien claimant's claim, although the general practice is that carriage costs are payable first from the trust monies recovered and thereafter, the balance of the monies are distributed <ital>pari passu</ital> to the lien claimants. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd." p2="Edge on Triangle Park Inc." post.rptr="7012" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I8de72e15ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Dolvin Mechanical Contractors Ltd. v. Ct.)</ref></cite>—While an award of substantial indemnity costs under the Rules is rare, it is a tool available under the Act to discourage improper registration of construction liens. The policy underlying the broad discretion for the court to award costs on a substantial indemnity basis is that the Act creates the extraordinary entitlement of a lien claimant to encumber another person's property. That entitlement must be exercised reasonably and responsibly and when it is not, the court should take such conduct into account in awarding costs to compensate the property owner for an improperly placed construction lien. In this case the lien claimant registered a large claim for lien against property in circumstances where there had been no contract between the claimant and the property owner and the claim for lien was never perfected as against the property owner. When asked to release the lien as against the respondent's units, it refused to do so. This was an appropriate case in which to exercise the court's discretion under s. 86 of the Act and award costs on a substantial indemnity basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Segreto" p2="Maatouk" post.rptr="4899" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I8de75520ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Segreto v. Therefore the usual factors set out in rule 57 apply except that the proportionality doctrine ought to be tempered by the consideration that plaintiffs who are forced to sue for relatively small amounts and who are successful ought not to be punished by an unrealistically low costs award.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac-United Management Corp." p2="St. Clare's-Monaco Place" post.rptr="4874" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I8de75521ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Unimac-United Management Corp. v. A “case management master” has all of the jurisdiction of a “master” conferred “under the rules of court” and jurisdiction specifically conferred on a case management master under a statute such as the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Case management masters are not constituted as assessment officers under the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> because s. 90(2) only refers to masters. This was an intentional policy choice made when the new office was created and is the only case in which the jurisdiction of a case management master is narrower than the jurisdiction of a master.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac-United Management Corp." p2="Cobra Power Inc." post.rptr="3827" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I8de75523ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Unimac-United Management Corp. v. As the successful parties, their claim for partial indemnity costs was within reasonable expectation of what the plaintiff should expect to pay. In an assessment of the appropriate costs award, the residential property owners were not guilty of misconduct in failing to pay the full amounts of the claims of the subtrades until the end of trial. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The stipulation in s. 44(1)(d) that a moving party pay 25 percent of the amount claimed in the lien for costs, does not establish an objective measure of what a losing party in a lien action is reasonably expected to pay in costs, especially when a full trial is held and a substantial counterclaim advanced.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2452" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I8de7a343ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2013 ONSC 2452, 2013 CarswellOnt 4792, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 87 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the unsuccessful party has forced a long and expensive proceeding, proportionality should not normally result in reduced costs. Here the plaintiff sought costs of $119,947.23, including disbursements of $12,495.40, in proceedings where the total amount claimed was originally $223,397.92 but reduced to $122,810.30 before trial, after crediting the owner with payments made after liens were registered. The amount recovered was $122,810.30. The owner forced a long and protracted proceeding, both at the pretrial and at the trial stages. The plaintiff did not over-resource the case, but responded to the tactical threats continuously raised by the owner, and in these circumstances the costs claimed were reasonable and not disproportionate to the claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2011" p1="Voka Steel Inc." p2="Edgecon Construction Inc." post.rptr="4051" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I910d1d90f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Voka Steel Inc. v. Edgecon Construction Inc.">Voka Steel Inc. v. Edgecon Construction Inc. (2011), 2011 CarswellOnt 4051, 2011 ONSC 3231 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff sought costs on a substantial indemnity scale for the entire action based on the conduct of the defendant which gave rise to unnecessary steps, delays and increased costs. Although substantial indemnity costs could be awarded for conduct related reasons in extreme cases, it was more appropriate in this case to compensate the plaintiff for time spent that might otherwise be considered excessive in a case of this nature, recognizing that the defendant's conduct caused the plaintiff to incur additional legal time and expense. However, the plaintiff was entitled to costs on a substantial indemnity scale from the date of its offer to settle.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lomoth" p2="Maslo" post.rptr="1074" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8de7a345ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Lomoth v.
