S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—the master was not persuaded that the defence was so devoid of merit as to warrant an award of substantial indemnity costs as was the case in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd." p2="Ding" post.rptr="2319" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I8de7a346ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding">Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding, 2004 CarswellOnt 2319, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2004 CarswellOnt 4167 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused (2004), 39 C.L.R. (3d) 150, 193 O.A.C. 145, 2004 CarswellOnt 5401 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wo-Built Inc." p2="Sangster" post.rptr="3554" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8de7ca50ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Wo-Built Inc. v. Sangster">Wo-Built Inc. v. Sangster, 2011 ONSC 3554, 2011 CarswellOnt 5213, 4 C.L.R. (4th) 286 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Offers to settle are in keeping with the policy of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to bring about a complete end to a lien proceeding in as far as possible a summary manner having regard to amount and nature of the lien in issue. It would be impossible in most Toronto lien actions to make settlement offers before the commencement of the pre-trial for directions. Section 62(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> states that <ital>“The results of the trial</ital> [not the reference] <ital>shall be embodied … in a report … where the trial is conducted on a reference by a … case management master.”</ital> The Act thus contemplates that a reference includes both hearings for directions or other proceedings <ital>plus</ital> a trial, and therefore delivery of an offer to settle which provides it is “open for acceptance until the commencement of trial” in the context of a reference complies with the requirements of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and Rule 49. The reference had a specific, evidentiary portion, the trial, which followed directions, all given with a view to preparing the action, and making it ready for trial, to receive the evidence commencing at a specific date and time. On the basis of its settlement offer, the plaintiff here was entitled to costs fixed on the basis of partial indemnity to the date of the offer, and substantial indemnity thereafter.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dean Construction Co." p2="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="5125" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8de7ca51ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd.">Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd., 2011 ONSC 5125, 2011 CarswellOnt 8856, 12 C.L.R. (4th) 61 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2011 ONSC 4629, 2011 CarswellOnt 8977, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2011 ONSC 5104, 2011 CarswellOnt 8862 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master summarized the following general principles governing the award of costs in a reference under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(i)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The costs to be awarded in an action brought under the ordinary procedure pursuant to the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> are governed by section 131(1) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. Section 131(1) provides that costs are in the discretion of the court, and that the court may determine by whom and to what extent the costs shall be paid;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(ii)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> set out a non-exhaustive list of factors which the Court may consider in exercising its discretion, in addition to the result in the action and any offer to settle made in writing. Rule 1.04(1.1) provides that in applying the rules the court shall make orders that are proportionate to the importance and complexity of the issues and the amounts involved. As a rule of general application, it has a direct bearing on cost orders;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(iii)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In a lien action brought under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the court's authority to award costs is set out in section 86. Costs are in the court's discretion, and a costs order may be made on a substantial indemnity basis subject to the limitation set out in s. 86(2), namely, where the least expensive course is not taken by a party, the costs allowed to a party shall not exceed what would have been incurred had the least expensive course been taken;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(iv)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 67(3) provides that, except where inconsistent with the Act, the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> and the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> apply to pleadings and proceedings under the Act. As rule 57.01(1) is discretionary and not mandatory, and therefore not inconsistent with the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and that the non-mandatory and non-exhaustive conditions set out therein may be considered in fixing costs in a lien action. Rule 1.04(1.1) is mandatory, and as such is inconsistent with section 86 of as it impinges on the court's discretion set out therein. However, its contents relating to proportionality is consistent with the object of s. 67(1). Proportionality is a non-binding factor which can be considered by the court in exercising its discretion as to costs in a lien action, very much akin, although not alike, the limitation set out in s. 86(2);</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">(v)</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Established principles applicable to fixing costs are that: the court should not engage in a purely mathematical calculation of hours times rate, but instead the costs award should reflect a fair and reasonable amount; in coming to that amount, the court should consider the reasonable expectation of the parties as to costs of the proceeding in issue.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">(The master reiterated these principles in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="State Group Inc." p2="Quebecor World Inc." post.rptr="3891" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I8de7f160ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc.">State Group Inc. v. Quebecor World Inc., 2012 ONCS 3891, 2012 CarswellOnt 8398, 19 C.L.R. (4th) 126 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>). A court, in dealing with costs in an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, can in the exercise of its discretion as to costs take into consideration an offer to settle, but is not bound to make a specific order otherwise, as contemplated by rule 49.10(1).</para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="SIPGP No. 1 Inc." p2="Eastern Construction Co." post.rptr="2695" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de7f161ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="SIPGP No. 1 Inc. v. Eastern Construction Co.">SIPGP No. 1 Inc. v. Eastern Construction Co., 2010 ONSC 2695, 2010 CarswellOnt 2962, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The non-mandatory and non-exhaustive conditions set out in Rule 57.01(1) may be considered in fixing costs in a lien action. Rule 1.04(1.1), however, to the extent that it is mandatory, is inconsistent with s. 86 in that it impinges on the court's discretion set out in s. 86. Proportionality is a non-binding factor which can be considered by the court in exercising its discretion as to costs, very much akin, although not alike, the limitation set out in s. 86(2). Here, the plaintiff sought costs throughout on a substantial indemnity basis, particularly on the basis that the defendants advanced an unmeritorious defence and had good reason to know it was unmeritorious. Although on the evidence there appeared to be good suspicion that such was the case, particularly in relation to the counterclaim, the appropriate scale of costs was partial indemnity until the plaintiff delivered an offer to settle and on a substantial indemnity basis thereafter. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: This approach was reiterated by the Master in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc." p2="Toronto Catholic District School Board" post.rptr="3400" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de7f162ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc. v. Toronto Catholic District School Board">Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc. v. Toronto Catholic District School Board, 2010 CarswellOnt 3400 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Federated Contractors Inc." p2="Ann-Maura Developments Inc." post.rptr="1664" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de7f163ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Federated Contractors Inc. v. Ann-Maura Developments Inc.">Federated Contractors Inc. v. Ann-Maura Developments Inc., 2010 ONSC 1664, 2010 CarswellOnt 1520 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Generally an award of substantial indemnity costs requires misconduct in the conduct of the motion. Success on a motion does not invite costs on a substantial indemnity scale. If that were the case then that scale would be the norm, not the exception. The fact that the lien here was found to be improperly registered was simply the result of the motion, and although the master found that the only two possible reasons for the lien being out of time pointed to misconduct by the plaintiff, that did not go to the conduct of the motion but rather to the plaintiff's conduct in registering the lien. It did not justify costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity scale.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Hull Enterprises" p2="924920 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="892" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de7f164ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Hull Enterprises v. 924920 Ontario Inc.">Hull Enterprises v. 924920 Ontario Inc., 2010 ONSC 892, 2010 CarswellOnt 1324 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court must consider whether the fees claimed are proportional to the amount in issue and the success of the case. Where the fees were less than one-third of the total recovery, the costs claimed were reasonable and proportionate to the amount recovered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="821962 Ontario Ltd." p2="Sterling of York Ltd." post.rptr="1119" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de81870ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="821962 Ontario Ltd. v. Sterling of York Ltd.">821962 Ontario Ltd. v. Sterling of York Ltd., 2010 ONSC 1119, 2010 CarswellOnt 953 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where a lien action was dismissed without costs, it was improper for the defendant to attempt to recover those costs by a counterclaim in a subsequent action. The defendant's claim for costs of the lien action was disposed of and was final.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1508270 Ontario Ltd." p2="Prusky" post.rptr="4484" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de81871ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="1508270 Ontario Ltd. v. Prusky">1508270 Ontario Ltd. v. Prusky, 2010 ONSC 4484, 2010 CarswellOnt 6066 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A disbursement claim for property searches was properly recoverable in the costs award, as searches are required to ensure that all parties entitled to notice of trial are served. Here, a law firm was retained to conduct the search and their fee charged as a disbursement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chris Nash Building Inc." p2="Buckland" post.rptr="7076" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I8de81872ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Chris Nash Building Inc. v. Buckland">Chris Nash Building Inc. v. Buckland, 2010 ONSC 7076, 2010 CarswellOnt 10009, 98 C.L.R. (3d) 157 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The former mechanics lien legislation included a bar to the unsuccessful plaintiff paying more than 25 percent of its claim in costs, and while the provision was not carried forward directly, the current legislation provides that a claim for lien may be vacated on providing security for the full amount plus 25 percent for costs. However, a 25 percent rule does not apply simply because the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is invoked, and costs orders must be primarily based on the general principles set out in Ontario Rule 57.01(1). The proportionality principle is not a <ital>percentage</ital> principle, and it may very well be that a party will necessarily incur costs that exceed the amounts in issue and that fact in and of itself does not result in an automatic reduction of a cost award. Rule 57.01(1)(0.a) first refers to the principle of indemnity and that principle is not abrogated by Rule 1.04(1.1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Ledcor Construction Ltd." p2="Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc." post.rptr="269" pre.rptr="79" ref.id="I8de81873ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc.">Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Canalfa Liberty Village Homes Inc. (2009), 79 C.L.R. (3d) 269, 2009 CarswellOnt 1475 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The mandatory imposition of substantial indemnity costs provided for in Rule 20.06 does not apply to an unsuccessful motion brought under ss. 44(2), 44(5) and 47. However, substantial indemnity was appropriate in the circumstances of this case, and the court looked to Rule 20.06 as analogous in determining the rationale for imposing cost consequences.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Elegant Design Kitchen Renovations & Contracting Inc." p2="Ojero" post.rptr="4877" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I910d92c0f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Elegant Design Kitchen Renovations & Contracting Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the plaintiff filed a lien for an exaggerated amount, did nothing to move the case forward for two years, and then, on the eve of the statutory expiry of the lien, withdrew it, this conduct amounted to an abuse of process. Substantial indemnity costs were awarded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ryan's Masonry Inc." p2="Craigleith Meadows Inc." post.rptr="9109" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I8de81875ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Ryan's Masonry Inc. v. Craigleith Meadows Inc.">Ryan's Masonry Inc. v. Craigleith Meadows Inc., 2008 CarswellOnt 9109 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court rejected the defendant's argument that where judgment was for approximately $7,500, costs should be assessed within the jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. The provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> had no monetary limits and contained a greater array of available rights. The plaintiff should not be penalized for exercising rights given it by the Legislature.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1442968 Ontario Ltd." p2="Houston Engineering & Drafting Inc." post.rptr="2774" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I8de83f80ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="1442968 Ontario Ltd. v. Houston Engineering & Drafting Inc.">1442968 Ontario Ltd. v. Houston Engineering & Drafting Inc., 2008 CarswellOnt 2774, 70 C.L.R. (3d) 268, [2008] O.J. No. 1926 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In determining the quantum of costs, the overarching principles of fairness and reasonableness apply, so that even a party that is “overwhelmingly successful” on a motion to vacate liens for various reasons cannot recover for unreasonable legal fees.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Vector Construction Ltd." p2="Finn Way General Contractor Inc." post.rptr="653" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I8de83f81ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Vector Construction Ltd. v. Finn Way General Contractor Inc.">Vector Construction Ltd. v. Finn Way General Contractor Inc., 2008 CarswellOnt 653 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court erroneously granted an order, on a motion by the defendant without notice, “vacating and discharging” the registration of the plaintiff's claim for lien. Subsection 44(1) of the Act under which the <ital>ex parte</ital> order was granted, authorized the vacating of the registration of the claim for lien but not the discharge of the claim for lien. The matter was remedied by a consent order revoking the discharge of the claim for lien, <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>. As the plaintiff bore no responsibility for the error and although the defendant was co-operative, the latter's own attempts to remedy the matter were not sufficient and the plaintiff had to incur expense to obtain the consent order. Costs were fixed at $1,500.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Dawson Construction & Haulage Ltd." p2="747877 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="68" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I910d92c1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Dawson Construction & Haulage Ltd. v. 747877 Ontario Inc.">Dawson Construction & Haulage Ltd. v. 747877 Ontario Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 68 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court declined to exercise its discretion to decrease the amount of costs award to the plaintiff because of the small amount at stake in the action. As a construction lien action, the matter brought a certain level of complexity to the courtroom. Here the costs sought amounted to only about one-third of the damages awarded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd." p2="One Shaftesbury Community Assn." post.rptr="3684" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I8de83f83ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn.">Celebrity Flooring Systems Ltd. v. One Shaftesbury Community Assn., 2008 CarswellOnt 3684, 72 C.L.R. (3d) 73 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a complex and lengthy lien action involving the mortgagee's priorities, success was divided. The mortgagee won on the main “Phase 1” issue of the quantum of the holdback deficiency and on the critical issue of whether the developer was the general contractor to the owner association. It also exceeded its offer to lien claimants to settle, which was subject to its right to argue certain other “Phase 2” issues. However, the mortgagee lost on the “Phase 1” issue of whether the liens of two claimants were preserved in time. The lien claimants should not recover any costs from the mortgagee. The lien claimants were successful on the “Phase 2” issues, and it was fair to set off the lien claimants' costs for their partial success in Phase 1 and complete success in Phase 2 against the mortgagee's costs for its win and lien claimants' loss in Phase 1.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Centrum Renovations & Repair Inc." p2="Ditta" post.rptr="2992" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I8de86690ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Centrum Renovations & Repair Inc. v. Ditta">Centrum Renovations & Repair Inc. v. Ditta, 2007 CarswellOnt 2992, 67 C.L.R. (3d) 137 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although the claim for lien overreached the judgment by some $40,000, this circumstance should not deprive the successful parties of their presumptive entitlement to substantial indemnity costs under R. 49. Nothing in s. 86 would support this proposition.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="JDM Developments Inc." p2="J. Stollar Construction Ltd." post.rptr="6486" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I56339fe0fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd.">JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 6486, 48 C.L.R. (3d) 296 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 817, 51 C.L.R. (3d) 293 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6081, 63 C.L.R. (3d) 163 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 35 was held to apply in this case, because the plaintiff knew or ought to have known that it did not have a lien, but there was no award of compensatory or non-compensatory damages as there was no evidence of damages pursuant to s. 35. Although the defendant sought, in place of damages, costs on a substantial indemnity scale pursuant to s. 35, s. 86 was held to be the proper provision to be relied upon.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Bestdoor Co." p2="Toronto Economic Development Corp." post.rptr="1708" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I910db9d1f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Bestdoor Co. v. Toronto Economic Development Corp.">Bestdoor Co. v. Toronto Economic Development Corp. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 1708, 43 C.L.R. (3d) 315 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff argued that the Master erred in principle in fixing costs at $16,072.02 when the total amount claimed by the plaintiff was $25,881.70, given that there were very few documents, the trial lasted less than one full day and there were no examinations for discovery. In upholding the costs award, the appeal judge held that the Master specifically considered the amount of the costs awarded, in relation to the amount in issue, and determined that the amount was not unjust. While another court might have awarded a lesser amount of costs, the Master's cost award was entitled to deference.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Kennedy Electric Ltd." p2="Rumble Automation Inc." post.rptr="5301" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I910db9d2f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Kennedy Electric Ltd. v. S.C.J.); affirmed on other grounds 2006 CarswellOnt 1491, 50 C.L.R. (3d) 283 (Ont. Div. Ct.); additional reasons 2006 CarswellOnt 3129 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirmed 2007 CarswellOnt 6120, 2007 ONCA 664, 64 C.L.R. (3d) 33, 229 O.A.C. 156, 285 D.L.R. (4th) 466 (Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal refused 2008 CarswellOnt 1079, 2008 CarswellOnt 1080 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff and its several subtrades started a construction lien action after registering lien claims against the automotive plant property of the defendant owner. The lien claim was unsuccessful and the work done by the claimant was held not to be an “improvement” under the Act. The construction lien action was converted into a contract action for damages as between the general contractor and its major subtrade. Costs were assessed in favour of the contractor with respect to the lien action, and the parties sought a determination as to when those costs should be paid. In the result, the costs awarded to the general contractor in the lien action were not to be paid until the contract action had been tried or otherwise disposed of.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd." p2="Ding" post.rptr="2319" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I8de86694ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding">Bellissimo Excavating Ltd. v. Ding, 2004 CarswellOnt 2319, 34 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2004 CarswellOnt 4167 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused (2004), 39 C.L.R. (3d) 150, 193 O.A.C. 145, 2004 CarswellOnt 5401 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The owners did not retain any holdback funds, which would have covered the lien claim, but instead paid the entire amount to the general contractor. The plaintiff subcontractor registered a claim for lien of $15,242.15 and commenced an action. The issue of liability was settled prior to a motion for summary judgment but the issue of costs was unresolved. The Master held that the successful subcontractor was not precluded from recovering costs that exceeded the amount of the lien claim. The owners had breached their statutory obligation to retain holdback funds, and should have paid the subcontractor immediately, as they were fully liable. Had the owners complied with their holdback obligation under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, very little of the significant costs incurred by the claimant would have been necessary. All of the costs experienced after the first pretrial could have been avoided. This was an appropriate case for costs on a partial indemnity scale for the period up to and including the first pretrial, and on a full indemnity scale for the period after the first pretrial. Costs were fixed at $30,825.42.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="XDG Ltd." p2="1099606 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1555" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I8de88da0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd.">XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd., [2003] O.J. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A lien claimant is entitled to have its counsel participate in the proceedings even where carriage of the action is granted to another claimant. That does not necessarily mean it is entitled to its costs on the same basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Biotechnik Inc." p2="O'Shanter Development Co." post.rptr="1895" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I8de88da1ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co.">Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co., 2003 CarswellOnt 1895, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 52 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is silent on the subject of whether there is a lien for costs. But, even if a plaintiff's costs award is not lienable against the land in the situation where the lien itself has not been “bonded-off”, if the land were ultimately to be sold to enforce the lien, the net sale proceeds would be paid into court for distribution to the plaintiff for its claim and, presumably, for its costs. If the lien part of the judgment were paid by the defendant to avoid a court sale of its property but the costs were not, the plaintiff could issue a writ of execution and register it against the land and then take enforcement proceedings under R. 60.07(17), (18) and (19).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="M.S. Electric Co." p2="Canada Brick Ltd." post.rptr="2525" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I8de88da2ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="M.S. Electric Co. v. Canada Brick Ltd.">M.S. Electric Co. v. Canada Brick Ltd., [2003] O.J. No. 2525, 2003 CarswellOnt 2426, 29 C.L.R. (3d) 261 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Carriage or “salvage” costs may be awarded, in effect, for the management of the action by a claimant on behalf of the other lien claimants and itself. Such an award reflects the reality that a construction lien action is akin to a class action and the carriage party may be entitled to receive a special award of costs for the extra work performed on behalf of the lien claimants at large. Although the Act does not specifically refer to “salvage” costs, the practice of awarding salvage costs was approved of as long ago as 1968 in the decision of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="B.A. Robinson Plumbing & Heating Ltd." p2="Dunwoodco Ltd. (Trustee of)" post.rptr="826" pre.rptr="[1968] 2" ref.id="I8de88da3ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="B.A. Robinson Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Dunwoodco Ltd. (Trustee of)">B.A. Robinson Plumbing & Heating Ltd. v. Dunwoodco Ltd. (Trustee of), [1968] 2 O.R. 826, 1968 CarswellOnt 219 (Ont. S.C.)</ref></cite>. Salvage costs are payable out of the lien fund in priority to the claims and costs of the other lien claimants. They may be awarded in “pretrial” hearings where issues in the action are resolved prior to trial. Here, interim salvage costs were held to be appropriate as the issues had been agreed upon and settled.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Avenue Structures Inc." p2="Pacific Empire Development Inc." post.rptr="128" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I8de88da4ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc.">Avenue Structures Inc. v. Pacific Empire Development Inc. (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In most, if not all construction lien trials and references, costs are decided when all other issues have been adjudicated upon and the proceeding is complete (see ss. 58(4) and 62(1) of the Act.). Where lien proceedings are still in progress, it is premature to rule on any question of costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="All About Construction Ltd." p2="1336555 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="4896" pre.rptr="[2001]" ref.id="I8de8b4b0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="All About Construction Ltd. v. 1336555 Ontario Ltd.">All About Construction Ltd. v. 1336555 Ontario Ltd., [2001] O.J. Additionally, the principal of the defendant engaged in numerous episodes of misbehaviour during the course of the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Marble Trend Ltd." p2="Sir Wynne - Highlands Inc." post.rptr="129" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I8de8b4b1ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Marble Trend Ltd. v. Una Power Heating & Air Conditioning Inc.">Nekison Engineering & Contractors Ltd. v. Una Power Heating & Air Conditioning Inc., 1998 CarswellOnt 1558 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff abandoned a motion for summary judgment after the defendant served and filed its responding material. As it ought to have been apparent from the plaintiff's investigation that there was a genuine issue for trial before the motion was brought, the bringing of the motion was held to be unreasonable, and costs were awarded on a solicitor and client basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="950" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I910e2f00f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc. Div.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is a protective statute, not meant to penalize lien claimants by putting them at risk of paying costs of all other lien claimants.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Belmar Sheet Metal Co." p2="849539 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="297" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I8de8dbc0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc.">Belmar Sheet Metal Co. v. 849539 Ontario Inc., 1996 CarswellOnt 297 (Ont. A “Sanderson” order was made, awarding successful plaintiffs their costs against unsuccessful defendants jointly and severally. Had the court made a “Bullock” order, it would not have done so jointly and severally as the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is a protective statute, not meant to put lien claimants at risk of paying costs of other lien claims.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="caseparser" type="case"><ref case.id="1996443361" court="Ont. Div.); additional reasons (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 101 at 122 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</cite>—The plaintiffs claimed interest on the holdback, arguing that they were entitled to interest equivalent to what the final holdback would have earned had it been paid into court, as they argued the owner should have done. The owner did not pay the holdback into court. The owner paid the holdback into an interest-bearing account, earning interest at 9.3 per cent. Had the holdback been paid into court, it would have earned 9.8 per cent. The difference was not great. Had the plaintiffs been prepared to release the owner, the owner would have released the holdback. The plaintiffs were aware of the amount of the holdback that the owner admitted to being liable for even before the statement of claim was issued. Therefore, it would be inappropriate to order costs against the owner. Those costs could be set off against the holdback payable to the plaintiffs. Since this proceeding was caused by the default of the contractor, the plaintiffs should recover their costs on a party and party basis, including costs paid to the owner, against the contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thomas Fuller Construction Co. Greatwise Developments Corp.">Thomas Fuller Construction Co. (1958) Ltd. v. Greatwise Developments Corp., 1992 CarswellOnt 3631 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A general contractor is to be awarded solicitor and client costs if an owner's conduct borders on being scandalous and is an abuse of the process of the court. In addition, the Goods and Services Tax is included in the calculation of such costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1984" p1="Norwon Electric Sault Co." p2="Ross" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="7" ref.id="I8de8dbc3ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Norwon Electric Sault Co. v. Ross">Norwon Electric Sault Co. v. Ross (1984), 7 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien was registered under the regime of the former <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, and the liens of the two other claimants were registered under the new Act. The court considered it to be a reasonable exercise of its attributed and inherent discretion to award costs on the basis of either the High Court scale pursuant to s. 86 of the new Act, or s. 49(2) of the old Act, whichever was the higher. Section 86(1) confers a broad discretion on the court as to the costs in an action, application, motion or settlement meeting.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Gilvesy Construction" p2="810941 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1109" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I910e5610f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd.">Gilvesy Construction v. 810941 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 1109, 22 C.L.R. (2d) 203 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Following a settlement offer by the defendant mortgagee to the general contractor plaintiff, the parties submitted a stated case to the Divisional Court, which rules in the mortgagee's favour on the main issue. However, because the mortgagee had kept alive central elements of the action long after it became clear that its position on those issues was untenable, the general contractor was entitled to its party-and-party costs of the action against the mortgagee down to the date of the offer. The mortgagee was entitled to its costs of the stated case.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chown, Cairns" p2="601039 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3809" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I8de902d0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Chown, Cairns v. 601039 Ontario Ltd.">Chown, Cairns v. 601039 Ontario Ltd., 1994 CarswellOnt 3809, [1994] O.J. No. 2982 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—On a motion to oppose confirmation of an Assessment Officer report dealing with salvage costs arising out of the disposition of 15 lien claims. The practice of awarding salvage costs was affirmed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Tamma Construction Co." p2="Brault" post.rptr="953" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I910e5611f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault">Tamma Construction Co. v. Brault (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 953, 25 O.R. (3d) 472, 24 C.L.R. (2d) 124 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The portion of a lien claim relating to amounts allegedly owing to the subtrades was shown to be unsupported and inaccurate, and the remaining portion dealing with management fees was held not to be the proper subject of a lien claim. The court, in granting the defendant's motion to discharge the lien and dismiss the action, invoked s. 86 and awarded substantial solicitor and client costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Johnston & Associates Co." p2="Wade" post.rptr="6898" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I56343c20fe1b11ee8837faf0ac1888bb" title="Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade">Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 6898 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Solicitor and client costs of a trial were awarded against the deponent of the affidavit of verification of an inflated lien, personally.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
86:3: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 86.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">86:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 86(1)(b)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes" p2="Jia Development Inc" post.rptr="3671" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678d92f03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Development Inc">2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Development Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 3671, 2024 ONSC 1608 (Ont.S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>JIA Development Inc. v. 2708320 Ontario Ltd. (Viceroy Homes)</ital>, 2024 CarswellOnt 18367 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—A lawyer for a lien claimant has a “gatekeeping” function. Given the powerful remedy of a claim for lien and its ability to be used without immediate judicial oversight, a lawyer for a lien claimant has a duty outside of the lawyer's duty to the client, a duty to the court and those who may be adversely affected, not to participate in allowing the remedy to be abused. Nevertheless, while a lawyer in a lien case has a gatekeeper function, this function must be melded with the lawyer's first duty to his or her client. Applying the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co." p2="1707583 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I678dba003b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc.">Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc., 80 C.L.R. (3d) 143, 2009 CarswellOnt 2805 (Ont. S.C.J.), additional reasons 2009 CarswellOnt 8879, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, below, the court found that liability for costs under s. 86(1)(b)(i) requires a finding that the representative subjectively knew of the baselessness of the claim for lien when it was registered and perfected. Such actual knowledge was an “essential precondition” to a costs order against a lawyer. Negligence, which involves an objective test, is not sufficient. However, liability for costs under s. 86(1)(b)(i) includes recklessness and willful blindness. Statutory interpretation is one reason for this conclusion. Section 86(1)(b)(i) captures situations where the representative does not have actual knowledge of the baselessness of the claim but knowledge of a “clear probability” that it is baseless and fails to act or inquire. Where the lawyer's knowledge has reached that of a “clear probability” of the claim's baselessness, the lawyer's duty to the court, the property owner and others who may be adversely affected should supersede the lawyer's duty to the client, and the lawyer should investigate or refuse to participate.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1917196 Ontario Ltd." p2="Kazmi" post.rptr="20398" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I678dba013b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="1917196 Ontario Ltd. v. Kazmi">1917196 Ontario Ltd. v. Kazmi, 2023 CarswellOnt 20398, 2023 ONSC 7284 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons to 2023 CarswellOnt 529, 2023 ONSC 384 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where the corporate plaintiff's principal solely caused the plaintiff to engage in extortionary activity by causing the company to render an improper invoice for the extra based on a revised contract price to make up for the company losses; causing the company to stop work when that invoice was not paid, leaving the defendants with an unfinished project; and causing the company to register the claim for lien, personal liability for costs was ordered on a substantial indemnity basis.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes" p2="Jia Development Inc." post.rptr="8234" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8de902d3ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Development Inc.">2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Development Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 8234, 2023 ONSC 3361 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons <ital>2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Deve</ital>, 2023 CarswellOnt 6437, 2023 ONSC 2301 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Having found that the corporate plaintiff had concocted a large claim for lien to frustrate the efforts of the defendant owners to sell the subject property, and after granting an order discharging the claim for lien on the grounds, inter alia, that it was frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process, the highest scale of full indemnity costs was awarded to each of the defendants. Those costs were significant. It was also an appropriate case to pierce the corporate veil to make the plaintiff's principal liable for the costs sought by one of the defendants. There was no doubt that the principal dominated the corporate plaintiff at the relevant times and caused it to register and perpetuate a totally groundless claim for lien for extortionary purposes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2018" p1="Marcos" p2="Lad" post.rptr="4900" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I8de902d4ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Marcos v. Lad">Marcos v. Lad, 2021 ONSC 4900, 2021 CarswellOnt 10207 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming <ital>Marcos Limited Building Design Consultants v. Lad</ital> (2018), 143 O.R. (3d) 665 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons <ital>Marcos Limited Building Design Consultants v. Lad</ital>, 2018 ONSC 3273, 2018 CarswellOnt 8618, 82 C.L.R. (4th) 57 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a lien action, the plaintiff's principal, a non-party, was found, <ital>inter alia</ital>, to have engaged in behaviour that included findings of “fabricated or deceptively manipulated” evidence, false paper trails and false and altered documents, and multiple deliberate lies. As well, the plaintiff engaged in unreasonable tactics in the conduct of the case, such as last-minute productions contrary to the court ordered timeline, and failing to admit uncontroverted facts, thereby necessitating the calling of witnesses and unnecessarily extending trial time. The trial judge awarded costs against the plaintiff and the non-party, fixed on full indemnity basis in amount of $579,000 payable jointly and severally. The trial judge properly interpreted and applied her inherent jurisdiction to order costs against a non-party who had committed abuse of process. The argument that had non-party received notice of defendants' intention to seek costs before trial he might not have lied to court or presented fraudulent documents was without merit and lacked common sense.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Archdekin" p2="Ko" post.rptr="1255" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I8de929e0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Archdekin v. Ko">Archdekin v. Ko, 2021 ONSC 1255, 2021 CarswellOnt 2845, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 179 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 1472, 2021 CarswellOnt 2838 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Full indemnity costs were awarded where it was clear that the defence request for a conference to deal with “serious conduct/ethical issue” on the eve of trial was an abuse of the court's process used as a tactic to adjourn the trial by alleging that the plaintiff's current and previous lawyers “knew” that the lien claim was invalid, the last invoice was fraudulent, the amount of the lien was exaggerated and that the claim for lien was a forgery.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2222028 Ontario Inc." p2="Adams and Nguyen" post.rptr="3113" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I8de929e1ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2222028 Ontario Inc. v. Adams and Nguyen">2222028 Ontario Inc. v. Adams and Nguyen, 2017 ONSC 3113, 2017 CarswellOnt 9362 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Two defendants, solicitors for a project owner and general contractor being sued for the misappropriation of funds from a trust fund under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, were awarded partial indemnity costs after the claim against them was dismissed as lacking any factual foundation, and as a vexatious abuse of process. The judge found that the plaintiff's claims that the solicitors had knowingly assisted their clients in dishonest activities were unsubstantiated. The defendants' request for costs under s. 86(1)(b)(ii) against the plaintiff's agent for prejudicing or delaying the action was denied as the matter had proceeded in a timely fashion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Petrelli Construction & Renovation Inc." p2="Phillips" post.rptr="8159" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I8de929e2ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Petrelli Construction & Renovation Inc. v. Phillips">Petrelli Construction & Renovation Inc. v. Phillips, 2016 ONSC 8159, 2016 CarswellOnt 21042, 73 C.L.R. (4th) 275 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's principal allowed the lien action to drift, and did not voluntarily discharge the lien, post ordered security for costs or provide disclosure as ordered. He did not instruct his lawyer to set the action down for trial and instead required the defendants to bring the motions to dismiss the action. The costs to be paid by the plaintiff were also awarded against the principal in his personal capacity. However, plaintiff's counsel was not held liable for costs or damages. The evidence did not support a finding that the latter knew or ought to have known the lien was “without foundation” or for a “grossly excessive amount.” To the contrary, the information he was provided by his client was to the effect that the amount owing had been properly invoiced and could be proven.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co." p2="1707583 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="143" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I8de929e3ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc.">Brian T. Fletcher Construction Co. v. 1707583 Ontario Inc., 80 C.L.R. (3d) 143, 2009 CarswellOnt 2805 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2009 CarswellOnt 8879, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where a motion raises a distinct issue, isolated from the remainder of the case, and a different judicial officer will conduct the trial, it is preferable for the judicial officer hearing the motions to determine costs. As well, parties who unsuccessfully bring or resist interlocutory motions ought to pay for the position taken before proceeding to trial. The underlying policy is to discourage frivolous motions or unreasonable resistance to valid motions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Torty" p2="Gilina" post.rptr="2211" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I910ea430f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="Torty v. Gilina">Torty v. Gilina (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2211 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the self-represented defendant had been ordered to pay monies into court as security for the plaintiff's claims for liens, the Master heard the matter, dismissed both the claim and the counterclaim and ordered that each party bear their own costs. The defendant served a motion to oppose confirmation of the report and then brought an <ital>ex parte</ital> motion before a judge and secured an order directing payment out to her of the monies posted for security in the action, together with accrued interest. Subsequently, it moved for an order for costs against the law firm that represented the opposing party at trial. The court held that where a party has initiated a motion to oppose confirmation of the Master's report, it is premature for that party to bring a motion for costs, particularly when costs are sought against the law firm that represented the opposing party at trial. As well, the Rules made it clear that a party who attends before the court on an <ital>ex parte</ital> basis must make full and fair disclosure of all material facts and all relevant information. In this case, the defendant had not advised the judge of her outstanding motion to oppose the report, and on cross-motion the order for payment out was set aside.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="JDM Developments Inc." p2="J. Stollar Construction Ltd." post.rptr="293" pre.rptr="51" ref.id="I8de950f0ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd.">JDM Developments Inc. v. J. Stollar Construction Ltd. (2006), 51 C.L.R. (3d) 293, 2006 CarswellOnt 817 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2007 CarswellOnt 6081, 63 C.L.R. (3d) 163 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff builder alleged the existence of an oral agreement with the defendant developer which authorized the builder to erect houses on lots owned by the developer and defer the payment of purchase monies for each lot until construction was completed and each house was sold. The court vacated the liens registered by the builder against the lots in subsequent actions, and found that the builder had mischaracterized its claims as lien claims when they were grounded in a breach of the alleged oral agreement and the dispute really concerned the sale of lots by the developer and the appropriate purchase price in respect of those lots. The court awarded costs on a substantial indemnity basis, but did not award costs on a solicitor-client basis against the plaintiff's solicitor personally. On the evidence, the court was not persuaded that he knowingly participated in the lien proceedings where it was clear that the claims were without foundation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="MHA Contracting Inc." p2="Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="713" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I910ecb40f58711eeb783edad15548364" title="MHA Contracting Inc. v. Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd.">MHA Contracting Inc. v. Christie Mechanical Contractors Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 713, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 185 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 86(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides that in appropriate circumstances an order for costs may be made against an agent who has “knowingly participated in the preservation or perfection of a lien”. Subsection 34(6) of the Act provides that a claim for lien “shall be verified by an affidavit of the person claiming the lien … or of an agent or assignee of the claimant who is informed of the facts set out in the claim and the affidavit of the agent or assignee shall state that the agent or assignee believes those facts to be true”. Here, the principal of the plaintiff corporation identified himself as agent of the lien claimant in each of the five affidavits of verification of lien claim, and that he believed the facts stated in the claim for lien were true. “Agent” in s. 86(1) included a person like the principal who had effective control of the plaintiff and signed the claims for lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="3239" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I8de950f2ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc., [2004] O.J. No. 3239, 2004 CarswellOnt 3189 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Pineau supplied and installed steam, water and air systems to Kretschmar's smokehouse. Pineau's contract was terminated. He registered a claim for lien and issued a statement of claim on June 18, 1999. All defendants defended. Pleadings were completed by August, 1999. Pineau's counsel served s. 39 demands. Two of the defendants responded, two did not. Pineau's lawyer encountered problems scheduling discoveries and served a motion asking the Toronto construction lien master to order a settlement meeting. Lien masters in Toronto do not, as a matter of practice, order settlement meetings under s. 60(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The first “lien pre-trial”, supervised by the lien master, is considered a more effective procedure than an unsupervised settlement meeting under s. 61. The parties then asked the master to fix a day for trial, without first obtaining a judgment of reference. Next, the solicitors brought another motion asking for a settlement meeting, although such relief had been refused earlier. Later, the solicitors filed pre-trial memoranda and briefs, neither of which are appropriate to Toronto lien actions. While all this was going on, the lien expired under s. 37.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The issue was whether costs should be awarded against the solicitors personally. The Master held that the various plaintiffs' solicitors' conduct fell within s. 86(1)(b)(ii). Their conduct “prejudiced” and “delayed” the conduct of this action in fact, even though that was not their intention. The Master held that an order under s. 86(1)(b)(ii) does not require proof of an element of intention to prejudice or delay an action, or reprehensible conduct, or bad faith, or a finding of encouraging prejudice or delay. All that is required is a finding that, because of the solicitors' actions, the conduct of the action was prejudiced or delayed or the opposite parties were prejudiced or delayed. Simple negligence is enough. It is an objective rather than a subjective test. Importantly, the Master also held that s. 86(1)(b)(i) and (ii) and R. 57.07(1) are not inconsistent. They mutually reinforce one another. They stand together to cover all the different scenarios that can arise in the problematic conduct of a lien action. Rule 57.07(1)(c) was also applied to the facts of this case, giving the court discretion to order the various former solicitors to pay the costs to which the defendants were found to be entitled.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="986506 Ontario Ltd." p2="Pringle" post.rptr="286" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I8de97800ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="986506 Ontario Ltd. v. Pringle">986506 Ontario Ltd. v. Pringle (2003), 30 C.L.R. (3d) 286, 2003 CarswellOnt 5603 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the plaintiff failed to fix a trial date within two years from issuance of the statement of claim, the defendants moved under s. 46(1) to declare the lien expired. As the plaintiff had released the lien, it was unnecessary to make the declaration, but the lien claim was dismissed and the contract action allowed to continue under the simplified procedure of R. 76. The plaintiff's former solicitor, who allowed the lien to expire, was ordered to pay costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19920316" p1="Wayne & Harold Smith Construction Ltd." p2="Dedi-Care Centres Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3130" pre.rptr="[1992]" ref.id="I8de97801ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Wayne & Harold Smith Construction Ltd. v. Dedi-Care Centres Ontario Ltd.">Wayne & Harold Smith Construction Ltd. v. Dedi-Care Centres Ontario Ltd. (March 16, 1992), Doc. S.C.O. 3873, [1992] O.J. No. 3130 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In this unusual case, a law firm was required by agreement to hold certain proceeds of sale to be paid by its client, the purchaser of lands upon which the plaintiff's lien was registered. At trial, the court awarded costs against the law firm, even though it scrupulously performed the agreement. The court held that the law firm was subject to a transmitted fiduciary obligation which superseded the agreement and required them to act affirmatively to interplead the money in question.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
86:4: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 86.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">86:4</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Subsection 86(2)</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Monalt Environmental Inc." p2="BDA Inc." post.rptr="4703" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678e2f303b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Monalt Environmental Inc. v. BDA Inc.">Monalt Environmental Inc. v. BDA Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 4703, 2024 ONSC 1417, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1061 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Ultimately, costs awards in lien actions are discretionary, and should reflect what the court views as a fair and reasonable amount that should be paid by the unsuccessful party, having regard to the expectations of the parties concerning the quantum of costs, rather than any exact measure of the actual costs of the successful litigant. Here, the costs claims of both parties were extremely reasonable and commensurate with the summary nature of lien proceedings and in the spirit of s. 86(2), which is a costs provision intended to encourage parties in a lien action to take the least expensive course of action.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Deltro Electric" p2="Coldbox Builders" post.rptr="3677" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678e2f313b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Deltro Electric v. Coldbox Builders">Deltro Electric v. Coldbox Builders, 2024 CarswellOnt 3677, 2024 ONSC 1556, 2024 A.C.W.S. 1218 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The court acknowledged that as the “prompt payment regime” under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> was relatively new and unsettled, the court would not conclude that the applicant's conduct throughout was manifestly unreasonable.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes" p2="Jia Development Inc." post.rptr="8234" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8de97802ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Development Inc.">2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Development Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 8234, 2023 ONSC 3361 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons <ital>2708320 Ontario Ltd. cob Viceroy Homes v. Jia Deve</ital>, 2023 CarswellOnt 6437, 2023 ONSC 2301 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Having found that the corporate plaintiff had concocted a large claim for lien to frustrate the efforts of the defendant owners to sell the subject property, and after granting an order discharging the claim for lien on the grounds, inter alia, that it was frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process, the highest scale of full indemnity costs was awarded to each of the defendants. Those costs were significant. In addressing s. 86(2), the court noted that the fact that the plaintiff had hired experienced construction lawyers from a reputable, downtown Toronto law firm to preserve and perfect the lien sent the message that, while the claim for lien appeared to have no merit and while it appeared to have been registered for an improper purpose, the plaintiff would defend its claim for lien vigorously and must have evidence that would allow its claim for lien to pass the “triable issue” test on a s. 47 motion. In addition, the lien was a significant impediment to the sale of the property, and with a potential sale finally being negotiated, it was not unreasonable for the defendant to apply all available resources, including senior and junior counsel, extensive research, a detailed cross-examination, and the preparation of detailed affidavits and factum, to move as quickly as possible and attack the claim for lien as thoroughly as possible.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MK General Contractors Incorporated" p2="Egfrost Holdings Limited" post.rptr="4831" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I8de97803ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="MK General Contractors Incorporated v. Egfrost Holdings Limited">MK General Contractors Incorporated v. Egfrost Holdings Limited, 2022 ONSC 4831, 2022 CarswellOnt 11861 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After the defendant tenant moved for discharge of the plaintiff's lien against its leasehold interest, the plaintiff opted to voluntarily release its lien prior to scheduled cross-examinations on affidavits, with the parties agreeing that the contract claim would continue as an ordinary action. However, they were unable to agree, <ital>inter alia</ital>, on costs of the motion. Costs awards should reflect what the court views as a fair and reasonable amount that should be paid by the unsuccessful party rather than any exact measure of the actual costs to the successful litigant, as held in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Davies" p2="Clarington (Municipality)" post.rptr="722" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I8de97804ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Davies v. Clarington (Municipality)">Davies v. Clarington (Municipality), 2009 ONCA 722, 2009 CarswellOnt 6185 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>. Here, substantial indemnity costs for the tenant were not appropriate. Proportionality and reasonable expectations were factors to be considered, particularly given the statutory directive in s. 86(2) that, where the least expensive course is not taken by a party, the costs allowed shall not exceed what would have been incurred had the least expensive course been taken. Although the issue of whether a tenant is obliged to provide lease information under s. 39 was not argued, the tenant's refusal to respond to the request was, in effect, a decision to stonewall the claimant on information that, had it been provided, would have allowed it to assess whether its claim against the landlord was viable and whether to pursue its lien.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Reid" p2="Xiao" post.rptr="4524" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I8de99f10ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Reid v. Xiao">Reid v. Xiao, 2022 ONSC 4524, 2022 CarswellOnt 10930 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The willingness of a party to explore reasonable pre-trial resolution of a lien action is a factor that falls within the ambit of s. 86(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Silver Streams Homes Inc. (Re)" post.rptr="5490" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I8de99f11ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Silver Streams Homes Inc. (Re)">Silver Streams Homes Inc. (Re), 2018 ONSC 5490, 2018 CarswellOnt 15581, 95 C.L.R. (4th) 80 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—The bank moved to oppose confirmation of the referee's report, on the basis that, in determining costs, the referee erred in concluding that the former's participation in lien claimant litigation contributed little to that litigation and was unnecessary. The referee found that the bank's cost recovery should be on partial indemnity basis and fixed those costs at $50,000. As the bank had consented to the settlements with the lien claimants on a no-costs basis, the referee considered that the only costs that could be awarded were costs related to facilitating the settlements, being “salvage costs”, taking into consideration s. 86. The referee concluded that, if the bank's counsel had taken the “least expensive course” in respect of their participation in the settlements, the resulting costs would have approximated one-half of the partial indemnity expectation of $85,000. The motion's judge reiterated that a court hearing a motion to oppose the confirmation of a report on a reference ought not to interfere with the results unless there has been some error in principle demonstrated by the reasons, some absence or excess of jurisdiction, or some patent misapprehension of the evidence, and the award should not be disturbed unless it appears to be unsatisfactory on all the evidence. In dismissing the motion, he noted that the referee was a highly experienced expert in this type of litigation and had carriage of the reference to the point of the settlements. He was, therefore, in a significantly better position than the court to understand and assess the circumstances in an informed manner notwithstanding the fact that the reference did not proceed to a trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd." p2="Johnstone" post.rptr="1818" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I8de99f12ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd. v. Johnstone">Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd. v. Johnstone, 2015 ONSC 1818, 2015 CarswellOnt 3851, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 239 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 ONSC 768, 2015 CarswellOnt 1250, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 199 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Both parties acted in a manner that was highly adversarial, and when conducting litigation in this manner, they were presumed to be prepared to pay for it. The plaintiff over-prepared its case and asserted an unwinnable “quid pro quo” claim, while the defendant advanced and then reduced a large counterclaim made up of many unwinnable items. In awarding costs, the Master distinguished his decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2452" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I8de99f13ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2013 ONSC 2452, 2013 CarswellOnt 4792, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 87 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> because there the lien claimant was almost 100 per cent successful and the owner's conduct had caused costs to escalate. Here, the plaintiff was only 33 per cent successful, and the conduct of both parties caused costs to escalate. The plaintiffs had not done everything reasonable to streamline the cases and reduce costs. A significant reduction from the partial indemnity costs incurred was warranted on the basis of proportionality.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Luxterior Design Corp." p2="Gelfand" post.rptr="990" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I8de99f14ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Luxterior Design Corp. v. Gelfand">Luxterior Design Corp. v. Gelfand, 2014 ONSC 990, 2014 CarswellOnt 18880, 39 C.L.R. (4th) 62 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 6539, 2014 CarswellOnt 15921, 39 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The expressed limitation on the court's discretion in s. 86(2), namely the requirement to award only costs of the “least expensive course” of action that could have been takes, is akin to the factor of proportionality (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dean Construction Co." p2="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4629" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8de99f15ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd.">Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd., 2011 ONSC 4629, 2011 CarswellOnt 8977, 5 C.L.R. (4th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2011 ONSC 5104, 2011 CarswellOnt 8862 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2011 ONSC 5125, 2011 CarswellOnt 8856 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>). This makes sense, as the least expensive course would be the course that is appropriate to the importance and complexity of the issues and the amount involved in the case, which is the definition of the proportionality in Rule 1.04. The principles of proportionality and the reasonable expectation of the parties are, to a degree, also related.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd." p2="Carnello Civil Construction Ltd." post.rptr="7020" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I8de9c620ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd. v. Carnello Civil Construction Ltd.">Sub-Terrain Directional Drilling Ltd. v. Carnello Civil Construction Ltd., 2014 ONSC 7020, 2014 CarswellOnt 17069, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 116 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 4877, 2014 CarswellOnt 11416, 41 C.L.R. (4th) 97 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In setting costs, the master declined to penalize the claimant for not pursuing the matter in a Small Claims Court action instead of a lien proceeding, as that required a finding that it had no reasonable grounds for believing that its extra claim was valid, which was not the case. Once a claim for lien is preserved in good faith, there are limited options open to a party. Perfection of a construction lien can only be done in the Superior Court. After perfection, the established procedure to follow in Toronto to avoid the Act's automatic lien expiration provisions was to get a judgment of reference and an order for trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Above All Emergency Services Inc." p2="Reuter" post.rptr="4381" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I8de9c621ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Above All Emergency Services Inc. v. Reuter">Above All Emergency Services Inc. v. Reuter, 2012 ONSC 4381, 2012 CarswellOnt 9327 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff knew or ought to have known that its claim for lien was out of time, and that it had little chance of making out its claim for remedial services within the monetary limit of the court. The plaintiff knew or ought to have known that there was no basis for its unilateral claim to storage costs. In all of those circumstances, the plaintiff knew or ought to have known that both in terms of proportionality and in terms of s. 86, the least expensive course would have been to bring its claim in Small Claims Court. The Master therefore awarded those costs which would have been incurred had the claim been brought in Small Claims Court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5144" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I8de9c622ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Thyssenkrupp Elevator (Canada) Ltd. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2011 ONSC 5144, 2011 CarswellOnt 8835 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The principle of proportionality should not normally result in reduced costs where the unsuccessful party has forced a long and expensive proceeding. Any disproportion in this case was caused by the defendant's repeated breach of court orders.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Toddglen Construction Ltd." p2="Concord Adex Developments Corp." post.rptr="7309" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I8de9c623ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Toddglen Construction Ltd. v. Concord Adex Developments Corp.">Toddglen Construction Ltd. v. Concord Adex Developments Corp., 2005 CarswellOnt 7309, 52 C.L.R. (3d) 259 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The services of three lawyers were not needed to bring a motion to court and time spent on research and preparation was not justified by the complexity of the motion. The least expensive course would have been for one lawyer to prepare and argue the simple motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="XDG Ltd." p2="1099606 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="1555" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I8de9ed30ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd.">XDG Ltd. v. 1099606 Ontario Ltd., [2003] O.J. No. 1555, 2003 CarswellOnt 1316 (Ont. S.C.J.); varied 2004 CarswellOnt 1581, 35 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—There were a multitude of proceedings involving the parties, including insolvency proceedings by the mortgagee against the owner and its related companies. These proceedings necessitated the involvement of the lien claimants to protect their interests in the property. A mortgage was provided by the owner as collateral security with respect to the prior indebtedness of its related lessee, and the lien claimants were held at trial to have priority pursuant to s. 78(6) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The mortgagee had failed to perform a customary due diligence investigation with respect to the owner before the mortgage was entered into, and was negligent or wilfully blind to the obvious improvements occurring to the property. A due diligence investigation would have led the mortgagee to decide against the mortgage security. The lien claimants were entitled to an award of costs on a substantial indemnity scale for the action and had they sought costs on a full indemnity basis, the court would have been inclined to so order, as the result of the conduct of the mortgagee.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
87:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 87.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">87:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section first appeared in a similar format in the 1983 revisions, and in its current wording was included in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. C. 30. The section replaced s. 51 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, which merely provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0">Except where otherwise directed by the judge having jurisdiction to try the action or, in the Judicial District of York, the master, all documents relating to an action under this Act, other than statements of claim and notices of trial, are sufficiently served upon the intended recipient if sent by registered mail addressed to the intended recipient at his address for service.</stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.structure></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">That provision had come into existence as s. 47 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65. It was amended to include a reference to the master in s. 47 of <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section provides the rules for service of documents required to be given under the Act and the date of their deemed receipt.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tenoes Construction" p2="Pinto" post.rptr="9725" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dea1440ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="Tenoes Construction v. Pinto">Tenoes Construction v. Pinto, 2023 CarswellOnt 9725, 2023 ONSC 3787 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants sought an order, <ital>inter alia</ital>, dismissing the plaintiff's claim and discharging the plaintiff's lien. The unrepresented plaintiff did not appear at the motion hearing. The defendants had served their motion record on the plaintiff by courier to his last known address. They also served the plaintiff's former lawyer, but only after being served with the order removing him as lawyer of record. Neither constituted valid service on the plaintiff, as courier was not the same as certified or registered mail and was not a valid form of service on an unrepresented party under Ont. r. 16.01(4)(b). On motion for an order validating service, the defendant provided a courier delivery receipt confirming that the package was delivered to the front door of the plaintiff's last known address.
