While the court did not condone invalid forms of service, lien actions are to be as far as possible of a summary character, and the Associate Justice was prepared to validate courier service of the motion record.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Quadform Ltd." p2="Rock Con Forming Ltd." post.rptr="7903" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643dae915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Quadform Ltd. v. Rock Con Forming Ltd.">Quadform Ltd. v. Rock Con Forming Ltd., 2020 ONSC 7903, 2020 CarswellOnt 18729, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 118 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2021 ONSC 3379, 2021 CarswellOnt 6559 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Section 87(1) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> permits service by registered mail, but that provision must be read along with s. 87(2), which provides for “evidence to the contrary” that a document has not been received. Here, where the mail tracking history of a claim indicated that the defendant never retrieved the registered mail containing the statement of claim and certificate of action, it amounted to evidence to the contrary. The court rejected the view that once delivery notices are left at a party's address, any documents contained in the registered mail, which remain under the control of Canada Post, are “received” by that party. Such an interpretation would strain the plain meaning of these provisions past their breaking point. “Receipt” when it comes to a document, means actual physical receipt of it.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Epoxy Flooring & Painting Inc." p2="Gillam Group Inc." post.rptr="4726" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I643dd5a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Epoxy Flooring & Painting Inc. v. Gillam Group Inc.">Epoxy Flooring & Painting Inc. v. Gillam Group Inc., 2019 ONSC 4726, 2019 CarswellOnt 12913, 2 C.L.R. (5th) 357 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff received no response from two different counsel to two faxed written requests for information pursuant to s. 39 of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, nor to follow-up letters by fax which also received no response. Counsel for the plaintiff prepared and served the plaintiff's motion record by fax, which both defendants admitted to receiving. Opposing counsel argued that there should be no costs as there was no evidence that the s. 39 written notices were in fact delivered, and that the s. 39(6) motion was, therefore, not necessary or proper. Counsel also argued that the faxing of the written notice was not consistent with s. 87 which specifies that all notices that need to be given under the <ital>Act</ital> can be served pursuant to the service rules of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> or by registered or certified mail. They argued that faxing was only allowed by the <ital>Rules</ital> for service on lawyers of record, and there were no lawyers of record at the time in question. However, Ont. Rule 16.08 allows the court to validate service that was not otherwise consistent with the rules, where the court was satisfied that the document came to the notice of the person being served. The court was satisfied that the written requests came to the notice of both opposing counsel, and service was deemed valid.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Canada-Wide Reinforcing Steel Co. (1987) Ltd." p2="ABCO One Corp." post.rptr="1044" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I643dd5a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canada-Wide Reinforcing Steel Co. (1987) Ltd. v. ABCO One Corp.">Canada-Wide Reinforcing Steel Co. (1987) Ltd. v. ABCO One Corp., 2014 ONSC 1044, 2014 CarswellOnt 1853, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 297 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Service of the statement of claim by registered mail to the recipient's last known mailing address, in the manner authorized by section 87, was valid service whether or not it complied with the Rules. Where the Act and the Rules conflict, s. 67 of the Act provides that the Act prevails, and consequently service in the manner provided for by section 87 of the Act is valid service.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Select Acoustic Supply Inc." p2="College of Physicians & Surgeons (Ontario)" post.rptr="3284" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I643dd5a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Select Acoustic Supply Inc. v. College of Physicians & Surgeons (Ontario)">Select Acoustic Supply Inc. v. College of Physicians & Surgeons (Ontario) (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 3284, 70 C.L.R. (3d) 118 (Ont. Div. Ct.); affirming (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 9387 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The individual defendant was served at the address shown for him in the corporation profile report for the corporate defendant, which the plaintiff's solicitors obtained from the Ministry of Consumer and Business Services at or just before the date of service. The claim was also sent to him at the address of the corporate defendant of which the defendant was one of the two principals. The Master held that there was not proper service under either s. 87 or under the Rules, but was satisfied that notice of the claim likely did come to the defendant's attention. Although no formal motion was made under Ont. R. 16.08 to validate service and notwithstanding the master's comment as to lack of compliance with the method of service, the Divisional Court found that an order validating service was unnecessary because the plaintiff complied with s. 87 of the Act. The statement of claim was sent by registered mail to the last address for the defendant in the possession of the plaintiff at the time of mailing. This was not a case of failure to comply with the method of service provided by the Rules or with an alternative method of service permitted by statute, and accordingly the defendant was not entitled to have the default judgment set aside as of right as a nullity.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
87.3:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 87.3.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">87.3:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="35 Mercer Limited" p2="Intact Insurance Company" post.rptr="19544" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678f19903b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="35 Mercer Limited v. Intact Insurance Company">35 Mercer Limited v. Intact Insurance Company, 2024 CarswellOnt 19544, 2024 ONSC 6466 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The transition provisions in s. 87.3 operate such that all liens arising from contracts and subcontracts in respect of the same “improvement” are subject to the same version of the <ital>Construction Act.</ital> The date of a subcontract has no relevance in determining which version of the legislation applies, and the lien claimant bears the obligation to seek out the facts relevant to s. 87.3 as they relate to timely preservation and perfection of liens, as a contractor and owner often cannot reasonably know every subtrade and supplier who performs work or supplies materials on a project, particularly on larger construction projects where there are multiple tiers of contract and subcontract streams. Section 39 provided a statutory mechanism by which a lien claimant may obtain that information itself. A response that the information sought was not properly requested because s. 39 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> still applied would relay the contractor or owner's position on the operation of s. 87.3. If an owner or contractor does not respond to the s. 39 request, a lien claimant may simply opt to preserve its lien on the basis that the <ital>CLA</ital> applied or move under s. 39(6) to compel compliance with the unanswered request for information. Alternatively, if the preservation or perfection deadline is missed, then relief could be sought under s. 39(5), which provides that a person failing to provide the information or access to information as required by s. 39(1), or knowingly or negligently misstates that information, is liable for any damages suffered as a result. A lien claimant's actual knowledge of the date of a procurement process or a contract for the improvement is not material in assessing operation of s. 87.3. As well, nothing in the language of s. 87.3 permits the court to consider delays between an initial procurement process and contracts being entered into or prejudice to an owner, contractor, subcontractor, or other person. Here, by operation of s. 87.3(1)(b) of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was held to apply.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc." p2="Global HVAC & Automation Inc." post.rptr="16009" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678f40a03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc. v. Global HVAC & Automation Inc.">HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc. v. Global HVAC & Automation Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 16009, 2024 ONSC 5752 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused <ital>KCL Group Limited v. HVAC Depot & Metal Mfg. Inc.</ital>, 2025 CarswellOnt 6184 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimants registered their respective claims for lien against title to the property on the 56th day following their last supply to the project, rendering the liens timely under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, but out of time under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. However, the corporate entities who initiated the purchase of the land in question, and sought a preliminary proposal and quote for the project design prior to July 1, 2018, had nothing more than an interest in the shares of its subsidiaries or closely held corporations that ultimately obtained ownership of the land. They were legally distinct and separate corporate entities, and they had no rights or interest in the assets of the ultimate corporate owner. Because neither were owners at any time prior to July 1, 2018, any agreements, contracts or dealings they engaged in or entered into in respect of the project could not have been “contracts” for the purpose of the transition provisions. And since these entities were not owners, they could not have commenced a procurement process before July 2018, which would have served to maintain the lien preservation timelines in the former Act.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Caledon (Town)" p2="2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction" post.rptr="4555" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I678f40a13b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Caledon (Town) v. 2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction">Caledon (Town) v. 2220742 Ont. Ltd. o/a Bronte Construction, 2024 ONSC 4555, 2024 CarswellOnt 12799 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—As noted in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors" p2="Form & Build Supply (Toronto) Inc." post.rptr="3396" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I678f40a23b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors v. Form & Build Supply (Toronto) Inc.">Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors v. Form & Build Supply (Toronto) Inc., 2021 ONSC 3396, 2021 CarswellOnt 6564, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 143 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DNR Restoration Inc." p2="Trac Developments Inc." post.rptr="1849" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I678f40a33b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc.">DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc., 2023 ONSC 1849, 2023 CarswellOnt 3680 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, below, the transitional provisions have the effect of providing that contracts in respect to the same “improvement” are subject to the same version of the Act. The scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> practically requires this result, with the proceedings being a distinct form of class proceeding where competing claims of different classes of claimants are adjudicated in respect to claims secured against specific lands (lien claims), specific funds (trust claims) and in respect to which specific remedies may be available (including appointment of a receiver). If a single contract in respect to multiple improvements requires a single claims process, this could have a cascading effect of grouping stakeholders in an over-broad process of unnecessary scope and complexity. In this case, the adjudicator erred in failing to find that the contract was in respect to two improvements, not one, and that different versions of the Act therefore applied to claims arising from the two different improvements. One improvement was excluded from adjudication by the transitional provisions of the Act, and the other was not. The adjudicator's determination was varied to exclude claims in respect to one of the two improvements.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Mobilinx Hurontario Contractor" p2="Edge1 Equipment Rentals Inc." post.rptr="5885" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I678f67b03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Mobilinx Hurontario Contractor v. Edge1 Equipment Rentals Inc.">Mobilinx Hurontario Contractor v. Edge1 Equipment Rentals Inc., 2023 ONSC 5885, 2023 CarswellOnt 16055 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—To find that a lien had clearly expired, the court had to be satisfied that the procurement process for the improvement was commenced prior to July 1, 2018. The evidence tendered was insufficient to meet that high evidentiary burden. A law clerk's affidavit in that respect was sworn entirely on information and belief based on a review of Infrastructure Ontario's website for the project. Various information had been extracted from the website and included as exhibits. While on its face, that evidence supported that the procurement process was commenced prior to July 1, 2018, it amounted to unverifiable hearsay and no argument had been advanced on the reliability of the evidence. No factum has been tendered, so there was no legal argument on why the court should accept that the information from Infrastructure Ontario's website was reliable or subject to a hearsay exception. No evidence has been tendered from those who would reasonably have direct evidence on the timing of the procurement process. The decision on the transition provisions was significant. It was not interlocutory in nature, like a vacating motion, but would finally dispose of the claimant's lien rights. Before finding on an <ital>ex parte</ital> basis that the <ital>CLA</ital> clearly continued to apply to the improvement, the court had to be satisfied that the record contained properly admissible and reliable evidence on the timing of procurement and, further, that the evidence was not reasonably challengeable. The court was not satisfied from the evidence tendered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DNR Restoration Inc." p2="Trac Developments Inc." post.rptr="3680" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I8dea6261ed8711ee8f7c9f534f68fef7" title="DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc.">DNR Restoration Inc. v. Trac Developments Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 3680, 2023 ONSC 1849 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—If the earliest “contract” predates July 1, 2018, all contracts on the improvement fall under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> regardless of the dates of those contracts. This applies to subcontracts as well. The <ital>Construction Act</ital> does not confine the concept of “contract” to the provision of “services and materials.” The court rejected the argument that the contract between the owner and the “pure” construction manager was not “a contract for the improvement” under section 87.3(1)(a) as it concerned the provision of services only. If construction managers with contracts with the owner, such as here, have lien rights, they surely are “contractors” with “contracts” for the purpose of section 87.3(1)(a). A “contract” can encompass the entire improvement or, such as in this case, a part of it. Where a contract is narrower than the scope of the improvement, and there are other contracts for the improvement, the only logical interpretation to be given to section 87.3(1)(a) is that the first contract will determine which version of the Act will apply to all contracts for the improvement, subject to any evidence of procurement if all the contracts are dated after July 1, 2018. The transition rule of section 87.3(1)(a) applied to subcontracts, and subcontracts dated after July 1, 2018 were not governed by the new <ital>Construction Act</ital> if the date of the main contract was prior to July 1, 2018. Throughout the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, including in section 87.3, the concept of improvement is not tied to and limited by the concept of “contract.” Indeed, it is the contrary, in that an improvement can be broader in scope than a contract. Section 87.3 does not change that definition.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Devlan Construction Ltd." p2="SRK Woodworking Inc." post.rptr="7622" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I678f8ec03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc.">Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 7622, 2023 ONSC 3035, 167 O.R. (3d) 704, 29 C.L.R. (5th) 27 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing <ital>SRK Woodworking Inc. v. Devlan Construction Ltd. et al.</ital>, 2022 ONSC 1038, 2022 CarswellOnt 2371, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 375 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The plaintiff sought to amend its pleadings by adding parties who were officers and directors of the defendant and claim breach of trust within a lien action under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Although mindful of the rulings in <ital>Damasio Drywall Inc. v. 2444825 Ontario Limited</ital> and <ital>6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek</ital>, the court found that, based in part on the application of the transitional provisions of the new Act, there was no reason why the trust and lien claims could not be part of the same action in this case. Reversing this ruling, the Divisional Court concluded that O. Reg. 302/18 precludes joinder of claims in a construction lien proceeding, other than contract and subcontract claims. When the amendments reflected in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> came into effect, joinder of any claims appeared to be governed by the principle of joinder reflected in the Rules of Civil Procedure - and a contested issue of joinder was to be addressed pursuant to those Rules. When O. Reg. 302/18 came into effect, however, the situation changed. By expressly permitting joinder of contract and subcontract claims, by implication the Regulation precludes joinder of other claims, and this provision ousts the application of the Rules of Civil Procedure in respect to joinder of claims, given the express language of s.50(2) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors" p2="Form & Build Supply (Toronto) Inc." post.rptr="3396" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I643e23c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors v. Form & Build Supply (Toronto) Inc.">Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors v. Form & Build Supply (Toronto) Inc., 2021 ONSC 3396, 2021 CarswellOnt 6564, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 143 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor lien claimant unsuccessfully argued that s. 87.3 was not intended to apply to subcontracts and that, since both of its subcontracts were entered into after July 1, 2018, it was statutorily entitled to the longer 60-day lien preservation period provided in the current version of the legislation. However, the court concluded that the intended effect of the language used in s. 87.3 is that the same legislative scheme for rights, obligations, and remedies provided in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> applies consistently to all persons involved in the same improvement. The purpose of s. 87.3(2) is only to clarify that the date of a subcontract has no relevance in determining which version of the legislation applies to an improvement. Accordingly, the claimant had 45 days from its last supply to preserve its liens, both liens had expired when the claims were registered and the defendants were entitled to orders declaring both liens expired and to return of the security posted to vacate them.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Strada Aggregates Inc." p2="YSL Residences Inc." post.rptr="16984" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643e23c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc.">Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 16984, 2020 ONSC 7034, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motion of the plaintiff subcontractor in a lien action, brought <ital>ex parte</ital> for an order that the defendant contractors and owner be noted in default, and for default judgment against them, was granted in part. YSL was the registered owner of the premises and pleaded as the statutory owner. Since neither contractor was pleaded to be a statutory “owner”, it followed in determining whether the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> or <ital>Construction Act</ital> applied, that the plaintiff must thereby be a “subcontractor”. The date of a subcontract was not relevant to the transition provisions. There was no substantive difference between the relevant provisions as they read in the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and as they now read in O Reg 302/18. Accordingly, in the absence of evidence that the prime contract for the subject improvement was entered into prior to July 1, 2018, or a procurement process occurred prior to that date, the amended provisions of the <ital>Construction</ital> applied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Atlantic Construction Group Inc." p2="2567616 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="9152" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643e23c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlantic Construction Group Inc. v. 2567616 Ontario Inc.">Atlantic Construction Group Inc. v. 2567616 Ontario Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 9152, 2020 ONSC 3992, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 317 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—For premises subject to a lease agreement entered into prior to July 1, 2018, but where the prime contract for an improvement is entered into (or procurement process is commenced) between July 1, 2018 and December 6, 2018, the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> still apply. The <ital>Construction Act</ital> and its regulations otherwise apply in respect of an improvement to leased premises if the prime contract was entered into or procurement process commenced after December 6, 2018.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
88:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Construction Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30, s. 88.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">88:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The current wording of this section was introduced in the revisions of 1983. It replaced s. 53 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, which, in that form, had been introduced in <ital>An Act to amend The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1975, c. 43, s. 14. That section still provided for regulations requiring the posting of notices on building sites. The earliest version of this section was introduced in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, s. 49.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The main change is the deletion of the provision concerning notes to be posted on building sites. This was deleted in 1983 because the Attorney General's Advisory Committee found that the requirements under the old Acts were rarely complied with and were difficult to enforce.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Devlan Construction Ltd." p2="SRK Woodworking Inc." post.rptr="7622" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I678fdce03b9611f0b5ec9cc9d9ad4a87" title="Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc.">Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 7622, 2023 ONSC 3035, 167 O.R. (3d) 704, 29 C.L.R. (5th) 27 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing <ital>SRK Woodworking Inc. v. Devlan Construction Ltd. et al.</ital>, 2022 ONSC 1038, 2022 CarswellOnt 2371, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 375 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—In determining whether the plaintiff could join a trust claim with its lien action, the motions judge held nothing in s.88 gave authority to pass by regulation a provision that dictates what actions may be brought, which was a matter of fundamental importance which should be dealt with in the statute. The Divisional Court disagreed. The Act contemplated that Regulations may be promulgated “governing procedures that apply to [construction lien] actions” and joinder rules are squarely within that mandate. In authorizing such Regulations, the Legislature conferred legislative authority on the Lieutenant Governor in Council in respect to matters of procedure. The legislature retains the authority to establish procedures, and to the extent that it does so, the Lieutenant Governor in Council may not enact a Regulation inconsistent with the Act. Although the Act was now silent on joinder of claims, the joinder provision in the Regulation was not inconsistent with that silence.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA1:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA1.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA1:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The first provisions substantially corresponding to the current ss. 1(1) and (2) appeared in the Act of 1896, S.O. 1896, c. 35, s. 29(2) and (3), according to which an action was to be commenced by filing in the proper office a statement of claim, verified by affidavit. The statement of claim was to be served within one month after it was filed. As is the case today, the judge or officer could extend that period. In the first Act of 1873, it was provided that proceedings to recover the claim were to be taken according to the usual procedure of the respective courts. These provisions remained substantially the same from 1896 until the Revised Statutes of 1980. Subsection (1) is now in substantially the same form as s. 33(2) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261 and ss. (2) corresponds to s. 33(3) of that Act. The main change is the extension of the time period to 90 days as opposed to the 30 days provided for in s. 33(3). The Attorney General's Advisory Committee recommended the extension of the time for service of the Statement of Claim to 90 days. It was believed to be nearly impossible in many cases to serve a statement of claim within 30 days on the many defendants to a standard lien claim. On the other hand, the Committee thought that any period longer than 90 days, such as the 12 months provided for service of a writ of summons formerly provided under the <ital>Judicature Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 223, would unduly delay the process. Section 1(3) dates back to the revisions of 1983, which introduced express provisions regulating counterclaims, cross-claims, and third party proceedings.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 1 corresponds to former s. 53(1) and (2) and remains substantially unchanged.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>General</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19960328" p1="Don Park Inc." p2="Windsor Western Hospital Inc." ref.id="I643e71e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Don Park Inc. v. Windsor Western Hospital Inc.">Don Park Inc. v. Windsor Western Hospital Inc. (March 28, 1996), Borins J.</ref></cite> (unreported)—The land was situate and lien actions commenced in Windsor. A motion was returned at Toronto by and among Toronto counsel. The court held that R. 37.03(1) did not apply and adjourned all motions to Windsor. See also <cite finder="legacy" type="periodical"><ref normalpub="lr" ref.id="If4fdce805dfc11ee9244de2abbdb9a85" reftext="Shafir and Roberts-Logan, “Proper Venue for a Motion in a Construction Lien Action or Proceeding”">Shafir and Roberts-Logan, “Proper Venue for a Motion in a Construction Lien Action or Proceeding” (1997), 27 C.L.R. (2d) 183</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1623242 Ontario Inc." p2="Great Lakes Copper Inc." post.rptr="2548" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I643e71e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1623242 Ontario Inc. v. Great Lakes Copper Inc.">1623242 Ontario Inc. v. Great Lakes Copper Inc., 2013 ONSC 2548, 2013 CarswellOnt 7148 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2013 ONSC 7935, 2013 CarswellOnt 18057 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A fraud action against various related entities, including GLC and 3N, was brought in Guelph, alleging conspiracy to induce the plaintiff to purchase property at inflated price by not disclosing contamination and then charging it for clean-up with a view to repossessing the property. GLC brought two construction lien actions against the plaintiff, also in Guelph, for failure to pay for the clean-up it undertook. 3N commenced a foreclosure action against the plaintiff in London based on the latter's failure to continue to make mortgage payments to it. The plaintiff successfully moved to join the fraud action with the foreclosure action and the construction lien actions. There were common issues of fact or law in the actions, the relief claimed in the fraud action arose out of the same transaction of purchase and sale in which the mortgage was given, and the lien claimant pleaded that the mortgage was for the purpose of improvements, including the clean-up that was the basis for the construction lien claim. A trial of the actions together avoided a multiplicity of proceedings. The foreclosure action was to be tried with the other actions following common examinations for discovery and a single pre-trial conference for all of the actions. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also the related ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="3072453 Nova Scotia Co." p2="1623242 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2105" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643e98f05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="3072453 Nova Scotia Co. v. 1623242 Ontario Inc.">3072453 Nova Scotia Co. v. 1623242 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2105, 2015 CarswellOnt 6947 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 12801 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, where the plaintiff obtained leave to pay/redeem the mortgage in the foreclosure action, and to have it assigned to another company.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I643e98f15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The Master provided an excellent summary of the proper procedure for processing a Toronto construction lien claim to trial. If the premises are situate within the legal limits of the City of Toronto, the action must be commenced by the issuing of a statement of claim in the Toronto office of the Superior Court of Justice, pursuant to s. 53(1). The statement of claim must then be served, within 90 days, subject to any extension, pursuant to s. 53(2). The exchange of pleadings is governed by ss. 53(3), 54(1), 55 and 56. Noting in default is provided by s. 54(2). At this point, a decision must be made as to whether the case is to be tried by a judge or by a master. Although the election is usually made by the plaintiff it can, in fact, be made as well by any defending party. If any party wants a judge to hear the case, it should set the action down for trial under Ontario Rr. 48.01 and 48.02, but cannot initiate or continue any form of discovery or any motions except with leave of the court: R. 48.04. Discovery or other interlocutory proceeding must therefore be proceeded with first. Such leave is dealt with by the Toronto construction lien motions master on Mondays. [See also ss. 60, 62 and 67.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Williams & Prior Ltd." p2="Taskon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="474" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I91bd0ca0f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd.">Williams & Prior Ltd. v. Taskon Construction Ltd. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 474, 22 C.L.R. (3d) 1, [2003] O.J. No. 498 (Master)</ref></cite>—A lien action had been commenced and a certificate of action had been registered within the 45-day time limit in s. 36(2) and (3)(a) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, but one of the defendants was not yet named as a defendant to the action. Neither subss. 36(2) and (3), nor subs. 53(1) required the statement of claim to name every person alleged to be an owner, within the 45-day time limit. In fact, s. 57(2) allowed the court “at any time” to add or join any person as a party. This followed the ruling in the case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Hudson Electric Ltd." p2="Wilson & Cousins Inc." post.rptr="534" pre.rptr="60" ref.id="I643ec0005fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hudson Electric Ltd. v. Wilson & Cousins Inc.">Hudson Electric Ltd. v. Wilson & Cousins Inc. (1987), 60 O.R. (2d) 534, 1987 CarswellOnt 1002 (Master)</ref></cite> which had been cited in several subsequent cases without criticism. As well, s. 34(5)(a) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, in specifying that the “name and address of the owner of the premises” must be set out, requires that where a lien claimant claims a lien against a tenant's interest in a landlord's land and building, the name and address of this tenant must be set out, and where the lien claimant also claims a lien against the landlord's interest in the land and building, the name and address of this landlord must also be set out.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd." p2="Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board" post.rptr="1228" pre.rptr="1996" ref.id="I5451e790fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd. v. Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board">Simcoe Block (1979) Ltd. v. Simcoe County Roman Catholic Separate School Board (1996), 1996 CarswellOnt 1228, 28 O.R. (3d) 380, 27 C.L.R. (2d) 296 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The failure to commence an action in the proper court office, pursuant to s. 53(1), does not nullify the otherwise proper perfection of a lien. Subsection 53(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not seek to control transfer of actions, only their commencement, in this, it is not inconsistent with s. 110 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> and Rr. 1.04 and 2.01 which permit transfer of actions from the wrong court or before the wrong officer and the correction of irregular procedural matters in the interests of justice. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is remedial legislation enacted by the legislature to provide an effective right for the workman or supplier in good faith to claim and obtain for payment for work and materials. Section 50 provides the General Division with jurisdiction to hear lien actions, the Act's procedures should be interpreted in that spirit where there is no real prejudice to others. The omission of s. 53(1) from the curative provision of s. 6 means nothing more than that the details of the action were left to Part VIII and the rules of court. Section 6 addresses only defects in the claim for lien, not the proceedings to enforce lien rights. In the end, this is an issue more akin to the days of the forms of action where procedure was to entrap rather than assist parties. The case contains an exhaustive review of the historical basis of the courts' jurisdiction over liens.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Alros Products Ltd. (c.o.b. Polytarp Product)" p2="Cambridge Leaseholds Ltd." post.rptr="265" pre.rptr="25" ref.id="I643ec0025fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Alros Products Ltd. (c.o.b. Polytarp Product) v. Cambridge Leaseholds Ltd.">Alros Products Ltd. (c.o.b. Polytarp Product) v. Cambridge Leaseholds Ltd. (1995), 25 C.L.R. (2d) 265, [1995] O.J. No. 3608 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Here a defendant sought to set aside a listing for trial and to discharge a lien and dismiss an action under s. 37 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. In this context, the Master held that although the Statement of Claim is an important instrument, the <ital>Act</ital> does not specify any particular form, leaving that to the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. Although it is widely accepted practice in Ontario to include the text of the claim for lien, or to attach a copy, there is no requirement for this to be done.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19950417" p1="Geralina Construction Ltd." p2="Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park" ref.id="I643ec0035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Geralina Construction Ltd. v. Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park">Geralina Construction Ltd. v. Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park (April 17, 1995), Doc. 15381/90 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The failure to commence a lien action in the area in which the premises or part thereof are situate, contrary to s. 53(1) is an irregularity only, and the action to be transferred, rather than dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19930611" p1="DMF Holdings Ltd." p2="Dicenzo Construction Co." ref.id="I643ec0045fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="DMF Holdings Ltd. v. Dicenzo Construction Co.">DMF Holdings Ltd. v. Dicenzo Construction Co. (June 11, 1993), Stayshyn J. (unreported)</ref></cite>—In light of s. 110 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> and s. 10 of the <ital>Interpretation Act</ital> (Ont.) and despite the reasoning of the court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="878104 Canada Inc." p2="Dupont Canada Inc." post.rptr="196" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I643ec0055fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="878104 Canada Inc. v. Dupont Canada Inc.">878104 Canada Inc. v. Dupont Canada Inc. (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 196 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, the court was of the view that non-compliance with s. 53(1) should be treated as an irregularity, and relieved against on that basis. The proceedings should be transferred to the appropriate court office.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="878104 Canada Inc." p2="Dupont Canada Inc." post.rptr="196" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I643ee7105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="878104 Canada Inc. v. Dupont Canada Inc.">878104 Canada Inc. v. Dupont Canada Inc. (1992), 4 C.L.R. (2d) 196 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully applied to have a lien action dismissed on the ground that the action was commenced in the office of the local registrar of the wrong county. Section 53 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> requires that an action be commenced in the area in which “the premises or a part thereof are situate.” In this case, the action was commenced in a county in which the lands were not situate. Accordingly, the action had to be dismissed. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In reaching the above-noted decision, the court did not comment on two earlier decisions, namely <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prestressed Developments Inc." p2="Expervest Properties Inc." ref.id="I643ee7115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Prestressed Developments Inc. v. Expervest Properties Inc.">Prestressed Developments Inc. v. Expervest Properties Inc. (November 5, 1990 (unreported))</ref></cite>, a decision of Oulette J., and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Stahlkran Inc." p2="Olympic Gear & Manufacturing Inc." ref.id="I643ee7125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Stahlkran Inc. v. Olympic Gear & Manufacturing Inc.">Stahlkran Inc. v. Olympic Gear & Manufacturing Inc. (April 4, 1986 (unreported))</ref></cite>, a decision of Dandie J. Both of these decisions treated the failure to adhere to s. 53(1) as an irregularity and relieved against it. Subsequent case law has followed the <ital>Prestressed Developments Inc.</ital> and <ital>Stahlkran</ital> line of reasoning. See, for example, <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19950417" p1="Geralina Construction Ltd." p2="Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park" ref.id="I643ee7135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Geralina Construction Ltd. v. Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park">Geralina Construction Ltd. v. Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park (April 17, 1995), Doc. 15381/90 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="B. Gerlach & Son Enterprises Inc." p2="Peterborough (City)" post.rptr="2892" pre.rptr="[1992]" ref.id="I643ee7145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="B. Gerlach & Son Enterprises Inc. v. Peterborough (City)">B. Gerlach & Son Enterprises Inc. v. Peterborough (City) (1992), [1992] O.J. No. 2892, 1992 CarswellOnt 3479 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, in s. 53(1), does not contemplate convenience and requires the statement of claim to be issued from the office of the court “for the area in which the premises are situate”. Where the plaintiff failed to do so, the error was procedural only, and could be remedied under s. 110 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital> (Ont.) and s. 67(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act. Simcoe Block</ital> is approved.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsections 1(2) and (3)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Fox Contracting Ltd." p2="133 King Street East Inc." post.rptr="8313" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I643ee7155fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Fox Contracting Ltd. v. 133 King Street East Inc.">Fox Contracting Ltd. v. 133 King Street East Inc., 2021 ONSC 8313, 2021 CarswellOnt 19274 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It is well established that the factors to be considered on a motion to extend the 90-day time for service of the statement of claim in construction lien actions are: the length of the delay and whether a limitation period has expired; the explanation for the delay in serving the statement of claim and in bringing the motion to extend; and whether the defendants have been prejudiced by the delay in service. Although the delay here was lengthy, being just over 11 months from the end of the 90-day time service period, the plaintiff's action in holding back on the lien enforcement to allow the defendant tenant time to obtain the wherewithal to pay the acknowledged debt during the very challenging time of the pandemic was consistent with the philosophy underlying the Act as expressed in s. 86(2). Extension of time to serve the claim was granted, both in respect of the defendant tenant and the defendant landlord, even though the latter had made none of the arrangements with and representations to the plaintiff that the tenant had made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Atlantic Construction Group Inc." p2="2567616 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2658" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I643f0e205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlantic Construction Group Inc. v. 2567616 Ontario Inc.">Atlantic Construction Group Inc. v. 2567616 Ontario Inc., 2021 ONSC 2658, 2021 CarswellOnt 4873, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 325 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 4118, 2021 CarswellOnt 8169, 12 C.L.R. (5th) 345 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master granted the plaintiff's motion for order extending time for service of its statement of claims in two lien actions. This was so even though the plaintiff contractor failed to put forward any adequate or acceptable explanation for its failure to make any efforts to serve the statements of claim within the 90-day service period, and failed to adequately explain its failure to move sooner to extend the time for service and seek validation of a manner of service that did not comply with either the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> or the Ont. Rules of Civil procedure. On the totality of the evidence, the period of delay was not overly inordinate taking into consideration its overlap with the ongoing pandemic. Combined with the lack of any demonstrable prejudice to the defendant arising from the delay, as it had actual notice of the liens, the latter's complacency in defending the claims, and concerns about the lack of forthrightness in the defendant's evidence, this was an appropriate case to grant the extensions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Diamond Drywall Contracting Inc." p2="Elderberry Enterprises Ltd." post.rptr="1068" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I643f0e215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Diamond Drywall Contracting Inc. v. Elderberry Enterprises Ltd.">Diamond Drywall Contracting Inc. v. Elderberry Enterprises Ltd., 2021 ONSC 1068, 2021 CarswellOnt 1586 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In granting the plaintiff's motion for an order extending time for serving statement of claim, the master was more forgiving on the issue of the adequacy of the explanation for the delay because of the consequences of the Covid-19 pandemic. While the explanation, involving difficulties receiving instructions from the client and raising retainer monies, was “borderline”, the nine months to get service underway was half the 18 months of service delay in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MGI Construction Corp." p2="2273865 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4716" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643f0e225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MGI Construction Corp. v. 2273865 Ontario Inc.">MGI Construction Corp. v. 2273865 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 4716, 2015 CarswellOnt 11221, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 340 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, and was not egregious. As well, the existence of the claim for lien itself was insufficient evidence of the prejudice required to deny the extension of the 90-day service period. However, the plaintiff's counsel, having assumed the responsibility of a lawyer of record, should have taken steps to serve the statement of claim in a timely way. Waiting for a retainer cheque, even during the pandemic did not justify this failure.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Petrasso" p2="Fuller" post.rptr="18482" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643f0e235fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Petrasso v. Fuller">Petrasso v. Fuller, 2020 CarswellOnt 18482, 2020 ONSC 7915, 19 C.L.R. (5th) 296 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The assessment on a motion to extend the time for service of a statement of claim in an action governed by the <ital>Construction Act</ital> has different considerations than in an action governed by the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. However, they are not completely dissimilar. Given the scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, tolerance for delay and assessment of prejudice in a lien action are viewed through a different lens, having particular regard to the requirement in s. 50(3) that lien actions be as far as possible of a summary character. The 90-day service deadline is not of the same character as the mandatory deadlines in ss. 31, 36, and 37. It is a deadline that the legislation expressly contemplates may be extended by the court. Unlike in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MGI Construction Corp." p2="2273865 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4716" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643f0e245fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MGI Construction Corp. v. 2273865 Ontario Inc.">MGI Construction Corp. v. 2273865 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 4716, 2015 CarswellOnt 11221, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 340 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the delay here between expiry of the 90-day service period and bringing of the motion was not inordinate, at approximately six weeks. The Master was satisfied that the failure to serve within 90 days was not intentional, and that the delay between expiry of the service period and bringing of the motion had not given rise to any prejudice that would not already have been present had the claim been served in time. The deadline for service of the statement of claim was extended.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Strada Aggregates Inc." p2="YSL Residences Inc." post.rptr="16984" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643f0e255fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc.">Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 16984, 2020 ONSC 7034, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a lien action, s. 50(3) mandates that the court is to apply procedures that are, as far as possible, of a summary character taking into account the amount and nature of the liens in question. In this case, the defendant contractors and owner were operated commonly by the same individual. The master accepted that service on the contractors by registered mail was delivered, and by virtue of the common director and officer, a reasonable inference followed that the owner, even if not directly served, ought to have had notice of the claim at or around the same time. Given the particular circumstances of a common principal of the defendants, the quantum in dispute, and the application of summary procedures, the master exercised his discretion to extend the time for service on the owner <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Goldribbon Homes Ltd." p2="Kessler" post.rptr="987" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I643f35305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Goldribbon Homes Ltd. v. Kessler">Goldribbon Homes Ltd. v. Kessler, 2018 ONSC 987, 2018 CarswellOnt 2170, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 278 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2018 ONSC 1503, 2018 CarswellOnt 3517 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Master found that: a) the plaintiff had not proven that the defendant was evading service, and there was no basis to grant an Order dispensing with service and the attendant relief; b) the plaintiff's reasons for extending the time for service of the statement of claim for the lien claim were insufficient to justify granting an extension, as the plaintiff had not rebutted the presumption that it was prejudicial to the defendant to have posted security for the lien claim in order to clear the title to his property. On appeal, the court held that the Master had made no error based on the record before her and her decision was affirmed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="SNS Construction Contracting Ltd." p2="Dougall Cabana Inc." post.rptr="21725" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I643f35315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="SNS Construction Contracting Ltd. v. Dougall Cabana Inc.">SNS Construction Contracting Ltd. v. Dougall Cabana Inc., 2016 CarswellOnt 21725, 68 C.L.R. (4th) 354 (Ont. S.C.J.), Justice Patterson</ref></cite>—Where the default was not intentional, where the delay had not been inordinate, and where the delay did not affect the hearing of a fair trial, courts may extend time for service or order that service was made “<ital>nunc pro tunc</ital>” to comply with s. 53(2) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MGI Construction Corp." p2="2273865 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4716" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I643f35325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MGI Construction Corp. v. 2273865 Ontario Inc.">MGI Construction Corp. v. 2273865 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 4716, 2015 CarswellOnt 11221, 52 C.L.R. (4th) 340 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The Act provides a procedural code for construction lien claims, with truncated limitation periods that are intended to expedite the resolution of lien actions. It bestows rights on a lien claimant that exceed the rights of an ordinary plaintiff in a civil action, but the trade-off is that lien claims are to proceed expeditiously and many of the procedures permitted in an ordinary action are not permitted, or are only permitted with leave. It follows that compliance with the 90 day period within which to serve the statement of claim is required to meet the objective of the Act to achieve an expedited resolution of the claim. While the court has discretion to extend this limitation period, to exercise that discretion, compelling reasons are required. Here, the delay from issuance of the claim and service was one and a half years. The only explanation offered was that there was miscommunication between the plaintiff and its lawyers. It was not appropriate to extend the time to serve the statement of claim regarding the lien claim action although it was appropriate to extend time to serve the statement of claim, to the extent that it claimed relief as a civil action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Abbotsford Group Inc." p2="Rea" post.rptr="3251" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I643f35335fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Abbotsford Group Inc. v. Rea">Abbotsford Group Inc. v. Rea, 2012 ONSC 3251, 2012 CarswellOnt 6856, 16 C.L.R. (4th) 316 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff failed to give full, frank and complete disclosure of all material facts that the <ital>ex parte</ital> motions judge might have considered in exercising his discretion to grant the extension of the time for service under s. 53(2). This lack of disclosure weighed against the exercise of any discretion in his favour. While a party's right to adjudication on the merits of a claim is a guiding principle of civil litigation, that right in construction lien claims is clearly balanced by requirements to preserve liens, perfect those liens by issuing claims within truncated limitation periods, and to serve originating processes within a shorter time frame than under the ordinary rules. By flouting the full disclosure requirement while it sought <ital>ex parte</ital> discretionary relief from the court under s. 53(2), the plaintiff effectively tipped the discretionary balance in favour of a strict application of the timelines in the <ital>Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="An-Dell Electric Ltd." p2="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4047" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I643f35345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="An-Dell Electric Ltd. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd.">An-Dell Electric Ltd. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4047, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 255 (Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's' lien was registered on title on September 7, 2002, and the statement of claim was issued on November 4, 2002, in which the last day on which services or materials where performed or provided was stated to be August 16, 2001. On the face of the claim, the lien had therefore expired on October 31, 2001. On November 23, 2002 a copy of the statement of claim was sent by ordinary mail to the defendant's solicitor, who never accepted service as per R. 16.03(2) There was no further service attempted until August 13, 2004 when the plaintiff wrote to the defendant's solicitor requesting a defense, which was not forthcoming. The statement of claim was amended on August 16, 2004 to change the date upon which the last work or services were performed or materials supplied, from August 16, 2001 to August 16, 2002. The court denied the plaintiff an order extending time for service of the statement of claim, or, in the alternative, validating service on the defendant's solicitor as of November 23, 2002. For the purpose of establishing service, an amended statement of claim for lien is a new statement of claim. The time limits set out in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> were not observed and there was no basis offered to the court on which service of the statement of claim could be either validated or extended. The plaintiff did not provide any evidence of compelling reasons for not executing proper service of the statement of claim within 90 days of its issuance. Further, prejudice to the defendant in respect of the expense and inconvenience of having to remove a lien and post security could not be ignored.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Haflidson" p2="Salandy" post.rptr="284" pre.rptr="16" ref.id="I643f5c405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Haflidson v. Salandy">Haflidson v. Salandy (2002), 16 C.L.R. (3d) 284, 2002 CarswellOnt 1698 (Master)</ref></cite>—In a motion to dismiss for delay it was not sufficient to assume prejudice by the mere passage of time. Accordingly, where there was inordinate and inexcusable delay on the part of the plaintiff, but the defendants filed no evidence of prejudice, and the evidence presented fell short of identifying any substantial risk that a fair trial could not be conducted, the motion to dismiss was denied. There was no evidence of serious actual prejudice to the defendants such as would arise if a witness or documents were no longer available.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA2:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA2.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA2:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Statute Law Amendment Act, 1939</ital>, S.O. 1939, c. 47, s. 19, granted the court powers with respect to the trial of “all questions of set-off and counterclaim arising under the building contract…”. Cases decided before that amendment had held counterclaims in a lien action to be impermissible (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Neri" p2="Benham" post.rptr="192" pre.rptr="[1934]" ref.id="I643f5c415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Neri v. Benham">Neri v. Benham, [1934] O.W.N. 192 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>). Counterclaims not arising under the building contract, now expressly provided for in s. 55(2), were not specifically provided for under earlier <ital>Mechanics' Lien Acts</ital>, but had been held to be permissible in certain circumstances. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1980" p1="Chicago Vitreous (Can.) Ltd." p2="Clark" post.rptr="283" pre.rptr="28" ref.id="I643f83505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Chicago Vitreous (Can.) Ltd. v. Clark">Chicago Vitreous (Can.) Ltd. v. Clark (1980), 28 O.R. (2d) 283 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>, the permissibility of such claims under the Act was considered. The Court found that while the Act then in force, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, did not expressly create a right to counterclaim, the Act when read as a whole allowed such a claim only where the claim arose out of the building contract itself, the work done, or the materials furnished to the property against which the lien was registered. Section 57 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, first provided for the joining of counterclaims arising otherwise than from the improvement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Timing of defence provision were introduced for the first time in the 1983 revisions. It replaces s. 33(4) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which provided that the time for delivering a statement of defence was the same as for entering an appearance in an action in the then Supreme Court. A provision to that effect can first be found in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, s. 31(3), which provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">(3) The statement of claim shall be served within one month after it is filed, but a Judge or other officer having power to try the action may extend the time for service thereof, and the time for delivering a statement of defence (Forms 7 and 8) shall be the same as for entering an appearance in an action in the High Court.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The 1897 provisions remained unchanged until The <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968-69</ital>, S.O. 1968-69, c. 65, s. 29, which separated the provisions regarding statements of claim and defence into s. 29(3) and (4) which remained unchanged until s. 56 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, brought the provisions into substantially the same form as they are found today. Under the old Acts, a practice had evolved to substantially delay service of statements of defence, prejudicing the plaintiff and complicating the settlement process. The new default provisions, including severe cost implications were thought likely to promote timely response.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><list list.item.desig="bull" list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(1) corresponds to former s. 55(2).</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Sections 2(2), (3) and (4) were formerly s. 53(3).</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 2(5) corresponds to former s. 54(1).</para.text></para></list.item></list><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 2(1)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Backyard XP Inc." p2="Cesario-Valela" post.rptr="17248" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I4dfe7230dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Backyard XP Inc. v. Cesario-Valela">Backyard XP Inc. v. Cesario-Valela, 2023 CarswellOnt 17248, 2023 ONSC 6312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Despite the potential for judicial economies, the scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> and its regulations does not permit a non-party to be added by way of counterclaim or by way of third party claim other than a claim for contribution or indemnity. Hence, leave was denied to the defendant owners under O Reg 302/18, subss. 4(2) and (3) to issue a third-party claim against the corporate entity alleged by the owners to be the plaintiff's alter ego, agent, and the de facto plaintiff. In addition, parties cannot be added to a lien action by way of counterclaim, and O Reg 302/18, s. 2(1)(a) limits the scope of a counterclaim, by only authorizing a defendant to “counterclaim against the person who named the defendant as a defendant in respect of any claim that the defendant may be entitled to make against that person, whether or not that claim is related to the making of the improvement”. While the owners could counterclaim against the plaintiff for any claim that they have against it, they were not entitled advance their counterclaim against other parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Sedia Inc." p2="Athena Donair Distributors Ltd." post.rptr="900" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I643f83515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Sedia Inc. v. Athena Donair Distributors Ltd.">Sedia Inc. v. Athena Donair Distributors Ltd., 2021 ONSC 900, 2021 CarswellOnt 1325 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 1457, 2021 CarswellOnt 2440 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—S. 55(2)(a) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> does not permit a non-party to be added by way of counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pentad Construction Inc." p2="2022988 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2669" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I643f83525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pentad Construction Inc. v. 2022988 Ontario Inc.">Pentad Construction Inc. v. 2022988 Ontario Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 2669, 2020 ONSC 1227, 14 C.L.R. (5th) 277 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants sought consolidation of a lien action with a claim by the defendant against the performance bond surety. Both actions had questions of law and fact in common, with the defendant alleging that the lien claimant failed to satisfy its obligations with respect to the work it was performing on the project, and the surety potentially liable under the performance bond for any of the plaintiff's defaults under the contract. Given that the consolidation power under s. 59(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was limited to lien actions and did permit the consolidation of lien and non-lien actions, and that the surety could not be added to the construction lien action as a defendant by way of counterclaim, by virtue of the limitations on counterclaims set out of s. 55(2), hearing the cases at the same time or one immediately after the other was the legally sound procedural step. The defendant could only counterclaim against the lien claimant, not make the surety a party to that action by counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Aqua Pools Ltd." p2="Hanna" post.rptr="850" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I643faa605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aqua Pools Ltd. v. Hanna">Aqua Pools Ltd. v. Hanna, 2019 ONSC 850, 2019 CarswellOnt 1496, 97 C.L.R. (4th) 245 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Two related companies with almost identical names—Aqua Pools Ltd. and Aqua Pool Ltd.—had been incorporated several years apart by the same principal. The construction contract was executed in the name of Aqua Pools Ltd., on Aqua Pool letterhead. The corporate plaintiff styled itself in the lien claim as “Aqua Pools Ltd. also known as Aqua Pool Ltd.”, although there was no such business name registered. The defendant sought to add the principal and Aqua Pool Ltd. as plaintiffs in the lien action and in its counterclaim. The court found that the general jurisdiction in s. 57(2) to add or join parties to a lien action did not give the court jurisdiction to add the original corporate plaintiff's principal and a related company as plaintiffs in a lien action commenced by corporate plaintiff, given the specific limitations in s. 55(2). If the jurisdiction in s. 57(2) was that broad, there would have been no need for the strict limitations in s. 55(2) [now s. 2(1) of Ont. Reg. 302/18]. Even if all of the potential parties were contracting parties with the defendants for the construction work, only the original corporate defendant was the entity who registered the claim for lien and was entitled to maintain the lien action as plaintiff. As well, the court had no jurisdiction in the lien action to permit the counterclaim to be amended to add as plaintiffs the related company as a separated corporate entity and the original plaintiff's principal.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Webb & Lashbrook Inc." p2="Sorbara" post.rptr="7278" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I643faa615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Webb & Lashbrook Inc. v. Sorbara">Webb & Lashbrook Inc. v. Sorbara, 2013 ONSC 7278, 2013 CarswellOnt 16011, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 313 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor carried out renovations on two properties owned by the defendant, but brought a lien action in respect of only one of those properties. The defendant counterclaimed, asking for an accounting of all amounts charged, paid and owing in respect of the renovation of both properties, and then moved to add her spouse, who was the co-owner of the unliened property, as plaintiff to the counterclaim to assert a claim for overpayments in respect of that latter property. The spouse was not an owner of liened property and not a party to that contract. The plaintiff cross-moved, <ital>inter alia</ital>, to sever those portions of the counterclaim that pertained to the unliened property. Both motions were denied. The court noted that construction lien proceedings were summary in nature and streamlined to provide for the expeditious resolution of construction lien claims. Because the spouse was not named as a defendant in the construction lien action, and because the restrictions on joinder in subs. 55(1) prevented the plaintiff from adding him as a defendant, subs. 55(2) precluded him from being added as a plaintiff by counterclaim. On the question of severance, however, subs. 55(1), which deals with the types of claims that a lien claimant may join with a lien claim, is clearly restrictive, while subs. 55(2), which deals with the scope of permissible counterclaims in a lien claim action, is not. The limitation in a counterclaim to a lien claim action is that it is confined to claims made against the party who named the defendant as a party to the litigation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subs. 55(2) allowed the defendant to assert a counterclaim in contract against the party that named her as a defendant, where the two contracts in issue were between the same parties for the supply of renovation services and materials, but in respect of different properties. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: In reaching these conclusions, the Master distinguished <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Clarke's Electrical Service Ltd." p2="Gottardo Construction Ltd." ref.id="I643faa625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Clarke's Electrical Service Ltd. v. Gottardo Construction Ltd.">Clarke's Electrical Service Ltd. v. Gottardo Construction Ltd.</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc." p2="Lombardo" ref.id="I643faa635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo">Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo</ref></cite>, noting in the latter case that if the plaintiff were to abandon its lien claim then Progressive Drywall would apply and the court would have to consider whether it would be an abuse of process to permit the defendant to proceed with her counterclaim as a summary claim under the Act. See also the discussion of this case under subsection 55(1) for the court's reasoning with respect to the application of that subsection.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1997" p1="Disal Contracting Ltd." p2="J. Salamon Holdings Inc." post.rptr="200" pre.rptr="35" ref.id="I643faa645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Disal Contracting Ltd. v. J. Salamon Holdings Inc.">Disal Contracting Ltd. v. J. Salamon Holdings Inc. (1997), 35 C.L.R. (2d) 200 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4275 (Ont. Gen. Div.); additional reasons at (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt 4274 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Burdens of proof were determinative of an issue involving the registration of an untimely series of liens. The burden of proving failure to mitigate is on the lien claimant and not on the person who alleges a cause of action under s. 35. The court in this case went further and ruled that the use of the phrase “is liable” in this section removed any residual discretion to disallow damage claims proven by an owner in the face of an untimely lien. The owner posted lien bond security following registration of construction liens on its property, and was required to pay premiums to obtain and maintain the lien bond. After an order vacated the liens as out of time, the defendants' successfully counterclaimed for recovery of those premiums. The lien claimants were liable for the damages resulting from their wrongful lien registration. The burden of adducing evidence to prove a failure of mitigation on the part of an owner is upon the lien claimant and not upon the owner. Additionally, there is no reason why an owner faced with the registration of construction liens on his residence should not be entitled to avail himself of the remedies of posting lien bond security as provided for in the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc." p2="Lombardo" post.rptr="141" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I643fd1705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo">Progressive Drywall & Interior Systems Inc. v. Lombardo (1991), 49 C.L.R. 141 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The defendant entered a defence to a lien action and counterclaimed for $250,000. The action was placed on the trial list for construction lien claims, and shortly before trial, the defendant successfully moved for an order requiring the plaintiff to post security for costs and allowing the defendant to amend its statement of defence and counterclaim to include allegations of misrepresentation, negligence and breach of contract, as well as damages in the amount of $527,500. Before commencement of the trial, the plaintiff moved under R. 23.01(1)(b) to discontinue the lien action. The defendant consented to the discontinuance but brought a counter-motion to continue its counterclaim as a separate action. The plaintiff's motion was allowed, but the defendant's motion was dismissed. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> authorizes an abridged proceeding which may severely limit parties' rights available in the ordinary course of litigation. The defendant, by its counterclaim in negligence, had adopted a procedure with the effect, for monetary or lack of security reasons, of depriving the plaintiff of the right to a trial by jury in a negligence action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Wharton Enterprises Ltd." p2="Brompton Financial Corp." post.rptr="121" pre.rptr="37" ref.id="I643fd1715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wharton Enterprises Ltd. v. Brompton Financial Corp.">Wharton Enterprises Ltd. v. Brompton Financial Corp. (1990), 37 C.L.R. 121, 71 O.R. (2d) 463, 40 C.P.C. (2d) 51, 67 D.L.R. (4th) 119 (H.C.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner in a construction lien action commenced a separate action against the related company of the plaintiff contractor as guarantor of the performance of the contract by the plaintiff. The court dismissed the defendant's motion to add the related company as a defendant by counterclaim. The defendant's counterclaim could not be asserted against a non-party. The specific wording regulating counterclaims in s. 55(2) of the Act limited the broad scope of s. 51. Subsection 55(2) only specifically provided that a defendant in an action may counterclaim against the person who named him as a defendant in respect of any claim under the Act.
