This decision was relied on by both the trial and appeal courts in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="Bay City Carpentry Inc." p2="Matushovsky" post.rptr="506" pre.rptr="[1999]" ref.id="I643fd1725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bay City Carpentry Inc. v. Matushovsky">Bay City Carpentry Inc. v. Matushovsky (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 506, 1999 CarswellOnt 482 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc." p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="172" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I643fd1735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission">Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission (1998), 39 C.L.R. (2d) 172, 1998 CarswellOnt 1539 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Various individual subcontractors started separate lien actions against the plaintiff general contractor and the defendant owner. These various actions were consolidated into two actions and referred to the Master in the ordinary way for trial. The plaintiff general contractor did not lien the property but began its own separate action against the defendant for the amount due under its two contracts, for damages for delay, breach of trust and economic loss. All actions were ordered to be tried together. The owner unsuccessfully challenged the Master for apprehended bias, and then moved for judicial review on the basis that the Master did not have jurisdiction to deal with the issues raised in the non-lien action. The Divisional Court dismissed the application for judicial review. All claims in the non-lien action related to contracts entered into between the plaintiff and the owner for the making of improvements to the property. As those claims related to the making of improvements, they were permissible under s. 55(2)(b) and could be advanced in a construction lien action. Even if the court had the power to question the conduct of a Master by way of judicial review, such an application should not be entertained in the middle of a lengthy trial except in the most exceptional circumstances, which circumstances did not here exist. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The fact that the owner allowed 106 hearing days to go by without challenging the master's jurisdiction figured prominently in this decision.] The issue of bias was heard <ital>de novo</ital>, (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc." p2="Toronto Transit Commission" post.rptr="3986" pre.rptr="[1998]" ref.id="I643fd1745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission">Bemar Construction (Ontario) Inc. v. Toronto Transit Commission (1998), [1998] O.J. No. 3986, 1998 CarswellOnt 3844 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>). The defendant's claim was found to be without merit.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Four Valleys Excavating Grading Ltd." p2="Forsan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="107" pre.rptr="21" ref.id="I643fd1755fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Four Valleys Excavating Grading Ltd. v. Forsan Construction Ltd.">Four Valleys Excavating Grading Ltd. v. Forsan Construction Ltd. (1994), 21 C.L.R. (2d) 107 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Here, a defendant sought to add a crossclaim against an owner who had not defended the action and had been noted in default. As s. 55(2)(b) specifically provides for a crossclaim, s. 67(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> renders the definition of “crossclaim” in R. 26 irrelevant. As s. 55(2)(b) is silent on time periods, however, resort to the rules is permitted by s. 67(3). In order to prevent a fresh proceedings in a non-lien forum and the possibility of inconsistent verdicts, the crossclaim was allowed, but on strict terms.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Yorkdale Drywall Co." p2="Schulberg" post.rptr="851" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I643fd1765fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yorkdale Drywall Co. v. Schulberg">Yorkdale Drywall Co. v. Schulberg (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 851, [1993] O.J. No. 137, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 100 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A crossclaim was allowed against a contractor both corporately and personally, in a lien action brought by an unpaid subtrade, including a substantial award of punitive damages and costs on a solicitor and client scale.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1994" p1="Johnston & Associates Co." p2="Wade" post.rptr="6898" pre.rptr="1994" ref.id="I54567b70fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade">Johnston & Associates Co. v. Wade (1994), 1994 CarswellOnt 6898 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The jurisdiction to award punitive damages in a counterclaim in a lien action is affirmed, citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Yorkdale Drywall Co." p2="Schulberg" post.rptr="851" pre.rptr="1993" ref.id="I643ff8815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yorkdale Drywall Co. v. Schulberg">Yorkdale Drywall Co. v. Schulberg (1993), 1993 CarswellOnt 851, [1993] O.J. No. 137, 8 C.L.R. (2d) 100 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>. However, the court dealt with the issue by making an award of solicitor and client costs of the trial against the deponent of the affidavit of verification, personally.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsections (2), (3) and (4)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Shaaravi" p2="Kreshtopova" post.rptr="1061" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I643ff8825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Shaaravi v. Kreshtopova">Shaaravi v. Kreshtopova (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1061, 73 C.L.R. (3d) 116 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The mandatory test of R. 26.01, which provides that the court must grant leave to amend a pleading if no prejudice would result that could not be compensated by costs or an adjournment, does not apply to counterclaims under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Rule 26.01 is inconsistent with s. 53(3), and s. 67(3) gives priority to s. 53(3). See also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." p2="Thunder Bay Regional Hospital" post.rptr="7471" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I643ff8835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital">Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 7471, 60 C.L.R. (3d) 219 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 1018 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Rebelo" p2="Borody" post.rptr="1694" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I64401f905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rebelo v. Borody">Rebelo v. Borody (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 1694, 61 C.L.R. (3d) 154 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Co-defendants purchased a property to renovate and sell for a profit, and hired the plaintiff to carry out the renovations. The plaintiff registered a construction lien against the property and subsequently issued a claim against the defendants. Ten months prior to issuing a cross-claim against his co-defendant, the defendant settled an application initiated against him by the co-defendant by paying part of the proceeds of sale into court to vacate the lien, but did not assert any claim against the co-defendant. Since the defendant could have raised the issues referred to in its cross-claim at that time, it was precluded from subsequently doing so by reason of the doctrine of <ital>res judicata</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2006" p1="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." p2="Thunder Bay Regional Hospital" post.rptr="7471" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I64401f915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital">Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. v. Thunder Bay Regional Hospital (2006), 2006 CarswellOnt 7471, 60 C.L.R. (3d) 219 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 1018 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff architect firm entered into a consulting contract with the defendant hospital to build an acute care facility. When certain payment issues could not be resolved by mutual agreement, the plaintiff registered and perfected two separate liens. After pre-trials in the lien actions, the plaintiff unsuccessfully moved pursuant to Rule 26 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> to amend its statement of defence to add a counterclaim of $1.5 million within the construction lien proceedings. R. 26.01 states that, on motion at any stage of an action, the court shall grant leave to amend a pleading on such terms as are just, unless prejudice would result that could not be compensated for by costs or an adjournment. The court held that the mandatory provisions of R. 26.01 must be read in terms of the permissive wording of s. 53(3). The test to be applied should be the permissive test in the Act rather than the mandatory aspect of the Rules. Permitting the amendment sought to be made would mean that the construction lien litigation would be dwarfed by a much broader, expansive claim against many more parties, which would not foster the policy of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to expedite the claim in a summary fashion. The plaintiff would also then be in a position of having to follow the procedures in s. 56(2) and R. 29, requiring them to seek leave to add third parties. Such leave would not necessarily be granted, and in the event it were, the proceeding of the lien actions would be further complicated. There was therefore prejudice to the plaintiff beyond that which could be compensated for by costs or an adjournment. The defendant therefore was not permitted to amend its pleadings by adding a counterclaim.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Subsection 2(5)</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Martin" p2="Mazza" post.rptr="5093" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I64401f925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Martin v. Mazza">Martin v. Mazza (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 5093 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 54(1) is mandatory. Thus, the moving parties should have filed a statement of defence and counterclaim within the time provided. The plaintiff's decision not to waive the mandatory filing date did not amount to sharp practice. Rather, the plaintiff's lawyer was standing by his client's rights to have a statement of defence filed within 20 days. In moving to set aside the default, the defendant acted in a timely manner and stated its defence in a full and complete manner. Therefore, leave was granted to set aside the default judgment and allowing the moving party to file the statement of defence and counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." p2="Hakim Optical Laboratory Ltd." post.rptr="144" pre.rptr="79" ref.id="I64401f935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd. v. Hakim Optical Laboratory Ltd.">M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd. v. Hakim Optical Laboratory Ltd. (2009), 79 C.L.R. (3d) 144, 2009 CarswellOnt 1671 (Ont. Master); additional reasons at (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 2666 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant failed to deliver its statement of defence within the time mandated by s. 54(1), and default judgment was entered nine days later. Although the defendants moved promptly to set aside the default judgment and noting in default, they did not adequately explain the delay in failing to deliver the defence, and in essence had unilaterally purported to amend time prescribed under the Act for delivery of a defence to an unspecified length of time. Any order in their favour would amount to a reward for ignoring the provisions of the Act without explanation. The Master dismissed the motion to set aside the noting in default and any enforcement procedures.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="1191226 Ontario Ltd." p2="Niagara College of Applied Arts & Technology" post.rptr="1358" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I64401f945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1191226 Ontario Ltd. v. Niagara College of Applied Arts & Technology">1191226 Ontario Ltd. v. Niagara College of Applied Arts & Technology (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1358, 71 C.L.R. (3d) 282 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant in a construction lien action sought to amend its pleadings during the trial to allege that a sub-trade of the plaintiff was responsible for certain on-site water damage. The defendant had, in 2005, obtained leave to amend its defence but had not done so. In denying the amendment at trial, the court noted that the defendant had 20 days to file a statement of defence pursuant to s. 54(1) and also, presumably, 20 days after leave to amend was granted in 2005. However, granting the amendment would result in great prejudice to the plaintiff that could not be cured by costs or adjournment.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

SRK Woodworking Inc.">Devlan Construction Ltd. v. SRK Woodworking Inc., 2023 CarswellOnt 7622, 2023 ONSC 3035, 167 O.R. (3d) 704, 29 C.L.R. (5th) 27 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing <ital>SRK Woodworking Inc. v. Devlan Construction Ltd. et al.</ital>, 2022 ONSC 1038, 2022 CarswellOnt 2371, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 375 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The plaintiff sought to amend its pleadings by adding parties who were officers and directors of the defendant and claim breach of trust within a lien action under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. Although mindful of the rulings in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Damasio Drywall Inc." p2="2444825 Ontario Limited" post.rptr="8398" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I4e013151dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Damasio Drywall Inc. v. 2444825 Ontario Limited">Damasio Drywall Inc. v. 2444825 Ontario Limited, 2021 ONSC 8398, 2021 CarswellOnt 19408 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="6628842 Canada Inc." p2="Topyurek" post.rptr="253" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I4e015860dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek">6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek, 2022 ONSC 253, 2022 CarswellOnt 132 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the court found that, based in part on the application of the transitional provisions of the new Act, there was no reason why the trust and lien claims could not be part of the same action in this case. Reversing this ruling, the Divisional Court concluded that O. Reg. 302/18 precludes joinder of claims in a construction lien proceeding, other than contract and subcontract claims. When the amendments reflected in the <ital>Construction Act</ital> came into effect, joinder of any claims appeared to be governed by the principle of joinder reflected in the Rules of Civil Procedure—and a contested issue of joinder was to be addressed pursuant to those Rules. When O. Reg. 302/18 came into effect, however, the situation changed. By expressly permitting joinder of contract and subcontract claims, by implication the Regulation precludes joinder of other claims, and this provision ousts the application of the Rules of Civil Procedure in respect to joinder of claims, given the express language of s.50(2) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="6628842 Canada Inc." p2="Topyurek" post.rptr="253" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I644046a45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek">6628842 Canada Inc. v. Topyurek, 2022 ONSC 253, 2022 CarswellOnt 132 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The former s. 55(1) was originally omitted from the new Act but reintroduced in 2019 as s. 3(2) of the Regulation. To the Associate Justice, this indicated that the Legislature had a change of mind with respect to the issue of joining trust claims with lien claims, despite the fact that the former s. 50(2), which expressly prohibited such joinder, was not reintroduced, with the result that the joinder of trust claims with lien claims is once again prohibited.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Damasio Drywall Inc." p2="2444825 Ontario Limited" post.rptr="8398" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644046a55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Damasio Drywall Inc. v. 2444825 Ontario Limited">Damasio Drywall Inc. v. 2444825 Ontario Limited, 2021 ONSC 8398, 2021 CarswellOnt 19408 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff unsuccessfully sought an order granting it leave to amend its statement of claim to add a corporate party and its principal as defendants, and by adding allegations of breach of the statutory trust under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> against those added parties. Although the previous explicit prohibition against the joinder of trust claims with lien claims in s. 50(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was not returned to the statute, a trust claim could not pass the test of O. Reg. 302/18 section 3(2) as that section had been historically interpreted. A trust claim was an entirely different cause of action than a breach of contract claim, and involved tracing and potential collateral remedies against officers and directors of a corporate trustee. The new Act maintained in s. 50(3) the mandate that the procedure of a lien action must be “as far as possible of a summary character.” If the Legislature intended to allow trust claims to be joined with lien claims, it should have stated so explicitly, given this mandate and the nature and complexity of a trust claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="MGL Construction Inc." p2="Boutet" post.rptr="4477" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64406db05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="MGL Construction Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The lien claimants did not meet the onus of proof concerning the timeliness of their claims for lien, which expired for not having been preserved in a timely way. In rejecting the plaintiff's claim in restitutionary <ital>quantum meruit</ital>, the court held that such claims fell outside the ambit of what was allowed under s. 55(1). There is consistent authority for the proposition that claims in restitutionary <ital>quantum meruit</ital> by subcontractors against owners should not be allowed because to do so would circumvent and undermine the scheme established by the Act. The Act provides subcontractors with specific <ital>in personam</ital> remedies against owners which turn on the concepts of lien and holdback. To give subcontractors the added non-statutory remedy of restitutionary <ital>quantum meruit</ital> when the statutory remedies fail would undermine the statute. In reaching this conclusion, the Master distinguished the decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd." p2="Johnstone" post.rptr="768" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64406db15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd. v. (4th) 239 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, on the grounds that there was no contract in that case, while here there was no dispute as to the existence of binding contracts between all of the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd." p2="Johnstone" post.rptr="768" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I64406db25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cleanol Integrated Services Ltd. v. The plaintiff moved to sever that portion of counterclaim that dealt with the unliened property, or, in the alternative, to add a claim for monies owing for that renovation, and to add the defendant's spouse, who was the co-owner of the unliened property, as a defendant in the construction lien action. The plaintiff registered a lien on the property owned by the defendant A, for the total balance owing by the defendant G. on all eight properties, and commenced an action against G. for the full amount and against A., claiming a general lien on his land. No attack was made by the defendant G. on the joinder of these claims, <ital>i.e.</ital> the balances owing on the eight projects, and the plaintiff proceeded with a motion under s. 60(1) of the Act to have the action referred to the Master for trial. The plaintiff subsequently conceded that it could not succeed on its claim against A. for work that did not relate to the A.'s property, but proceeded with its contract claims against the defendant G., for the full amount owing as between G. and the plaintiff. G. contended that the plaintiff could only assert, against it, a claim for a maximum of the work done on A.'s property, and as to the other claims, the plaintiff would have to pursue G. in an ordinary contract action. Held, the legislature had made express provision for joinder of claims under s. 55(1), which limited joinder to claims for breach of a “contract” or a “subcontract” as defined in s. 1(1) of the Act. The claims by the plaintiff against G. for the payment of amounts owing in relation to the excavating work done at the other sites were not claims under an agreement relating to supply of services to the improvement in question, being A.'s property. If the plaintiff's claim for a general lien under s. 20 had been proper, so that the one owner could be liable for all the plaintiff's work at all the lots, then the joinder, <ital>vis-à-vis</ital> G., would have been proper. Nevertheless, because G. had not opposed the joinder prior to the judgment of reference, nor sought to set the judgment aside, the plaintiff's claim was allowed to stand for the full amount.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Taylor" p2="Georgina (Town)" post.rptr="3791" pre.rptr="1992" ref.id="I91c76ce0f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="Taylor v. Georgina (Town)">Taylor v. Georgina (Town) (1992), 1992 CarswellOnt 3791, [1992] O.J. No. 1240 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—There were three actions commenced by a plaintiff: a lien action, an action for negligent misrepresentation including a third party proceeding, and an action in contract. The fact that the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> did not permit claims in the second action to be joined with a lien claim does not deprive the court of jurisdiction over its own process. It was ordered that all three actions be heard together in such fashion as the trial judge may direct.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="V.K. Mason Construction Ltd." p2="Strasscorp Holdings Inc." post.rptr="779" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I91c793f0f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. v. Strasscorp Holdings Inc.">V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. v. Strasscorp Holdings Inc. (1991), 1991 CarswellOnt 779, 45 C.L.R. 101 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 55(1), a plaintiff in an action may join with his lien claim a claim for breach of his contract or his subcontract. Therefore, claims other than for breach of contract cannot be included in the claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="697470 Ontario Ltd." p2="Presidential Developments Ltd." post.rptr="698" pre.rptr="1989" ref.id="I91c793f1f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd.">697470 Ontario Ltd. v. Presidential Developments Ltd. (1989), 1989 CarswellOnt 698, 34 C.L.R. 224 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's lien action was dismissed on the basis that the work performed by the plaintiff was not directly related to the construction of the improvement so as to entitle the plaintiff to a lien. On appeal, the Divisional Court upheld the lower court's ruling, and rejected the plaintiff's argument that, by virtue of s. 55(1) of the Act, the action in <ital>personam</ital> should proceed. Once the lien claim failed, there was nothing to join with, and the contractual claim could not proceed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Canada Heating Ltd." p2="Brompton Manufacturing Ltd." post.rptr="776" pre.rptr="1987" ref.id="I644131035fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canada Heating Ltd. v. Brompton Manufacturing Ltd.">Canada Heating Ltd. v. Brompton Manufacturing Ltd., 1987 CarswellOnt 776, 26 O.A.C. 311 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversed 1989 CarswellOnt 707 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Where a party with an unquestioned right to assert a claim <ital>on</ital> its own behalf for a lien chooses not to do so, does not file a lien or take any step to protect its position as a lien claimant under the Act, it cannot rely upon the provisions of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> in an action which proceeded as a contract action only.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA4:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA4.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA4:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Third party proceedings were not permitted under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261. The section first appeared as s. 58 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. Third party proceedings were not permitted under <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act, 1968–69</ital>, S.O. 1968–69, c. 65, because it was thought to have been unjust to deprive a third party of rights to discovery, production and trial by a judge of the Supreme Court, which it would otherwise enjoy in a non-lien action (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1971" p1="Caruso" p2="Campanile" post.rptr="437" pre.rptr="[1972] 1" ref.id="I644158105fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Caruso v. Campanile">Caruso v. Campanile (1971), [1972] 1 O.R. 437 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1998" p1="EMCO Supply" p2="Anduhyaun Inc." post.rptr="80" pre.rptr="1998" ref.id="I86ac5fb0144411ef8eadf16a00232d13" title="EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc.">EMCO Supply v. Anduhyaun Inc. (1998), 1998 CarswellOnt. 80, 36 C.L.R. (2d) 91 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Attorney General's Advisory Committee on the <ital>Draft Construction Lien Act</ital> had contemplated the possibility of such proceedings without leave, but the Committee argued that the primary purpose of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was the resolution of lien claims and that access to third party proceedings should be restricted.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 4 essentially mirrors former s. 56.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section provides three “rules” under which a third party claim will be permitted to proceed. There may be situations where a third party claim for indemnity or contribution is closely linked to the circumstances of the lien claim. Leave is required to be obtained on motion with notice not only to the owner, but to all persons having subsisting preserved or perfected liens at the time of the motion. An affidavit is required as to possible prejudice to the third party claimant, any lien claimant or defendant, and as to delay or complication of the main action. Other aspects of possible prejudice to the plaintiff in an action in which third party proceedings are contemplated are not a factor. The court is given an unlimited discretion as to terms.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Backyard XP Inc." p2="Cesario-Valela" post.rptr="17248" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I4e04b3c0dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Backyard XP Inc. v. Cesario-Valela">Backyard XP Inc. v. Cesario-Valela, 2023 CarswellOnt 17248, 2023 ONSC 6312 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Despite the potential for judicial economies, the scheme of the <ital>Construction Act</ital> and its regulations does not permit a non-party to be added by way of counterclaim or by way of third party claim other than a claim for contribution or indemnity. Hence, leave was denied to the defendant owners under O Reg 302/18, subss. 4(2) and (3) to issue a third party claim against the corporate entity alleged by the owners to be the plaintiff's alter ego, agent, and the de facto plaintiff. In addition, parties cannot be added to a lien action by way of counterclaim, and O Reg 302/18, s. 2(1)(a), limits the scope of a counterclaim, by only authorizing a defendant to “counterclaim against the person who named the defendant as a defendant in respect of any claim that the defendant may be entitled to make against that person, whether or not that claim is related to the making of the improvement”. While the owners could counterclaim against the plaintiff for any claim that they have against it, they were not entitled advance their counterclaim against other parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Magil Construction Canada" p2="JBelli Holdings" post.rptr="3652" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I4e04dad0dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Magil Construction Canada v. JBelli Holdings">Magil Construction Canada v. JBelli Holdings, 2023 CarswellOnt 3652, 2023 ONSC 1837 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The applicable test on a motion for leave under (then) s. 56 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (now s. 4 of O. Reg. 302/18) requires that the proposed joinder (1) does not unduly prejudice the ability of the proposed third party, the lien claimant or the defendant to prosecute a claim or conduct a defence; and (2) does not unduly delay or complicate the resolution of the lien action. The court referenced <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ekarte" p2="GUPM" post.rptr="2203" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I4e04dad1dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Ekarte v. GUPM">Ekarte v. GUPM, 2021 ONSC 2203, 2021 CarswellOnt 4036 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed <ital>1159337 Ontario Ltd. v. Saplys</ital>, 2021 ONSC 7909, 2021 CarswellOnt 18456 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ekarte" p2="GUPM" post.rptr="2203" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644158125fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ekarte v. GUPM">Ekarte v. GUPM, 2021 ONSC 2203, 2021 CarswellOnt 4036 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2021 ONSC 7909, 2021 CarswellOnt 18456 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Leave to convert a construction lien third party claim into a separate action in the ordinary civil case stream was sought for the first time after the expiry of the limitation period for commencing the third party claim. The motion judge did not have the authority to convert the claim, as the statutory requirement for leave to convert a third party claim commenced under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> required the leave motion to be brought before the expiry of the limitation period.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lomax Realty Development Group Inc." p2="New Foundation Development Co-operative Corp." post.rptr="6276" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I644158135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lomax Realty Development Group Inc. v. New Foundation Development Co-operative Corp.">Lomax Realty Development Group Inc. v. New Foundation Development Co-operative Corp., 2016 ONSC 6276, 2016 CarswellOnt 15861, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 92 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner unsuccessfully sought leave under s. 56 to join <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> two officers and directors of the plaintiff as third parties in two related lien actions, claiming contribution and indemnity for having sworn statutory declarations allegedly fraudulently or negligently. A defendant is prohibited from joining third parties for claims that are not strictly claims for contribution and indemnity concerning the plaintiff's lien claim. Such prohibited claims include separate claims for damages against the third parties, such as contract or tort damages. In this case, it was difficult to see how the allegedly false statutory declarations could have caused or contributed to any non-payment of subtrades. The statutory declarations were after the fact statements as to what was paid. As well, the proposed third party claims were tantamount to trust claims, which were expressly prohibited by s. 50(2) from being joined with lien claims. The defendant appeared to be concerned about the inconvenience and loss to it (such as the payment of holdback) and the expense to it (such as higher bond premium, legal costs and financing costs) that arise from unpaid subtrades. While these may justify third party actions under Rule 29.01, they did not amount to a true claim for “contribution and indemnity” under s. 56.1.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Wilson Cartage Ltd." p2="Carlisle" post.rptr="1154" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I64417f205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Wilson Cartage Ltd. v. Carlisle">Wilson Cartage Ltd. v. Carlisle, 2011 ONSC 1154, 2011 CarswellOnt 1081 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Ontario Rule 29.01, dealing with third parties, is inconsistent with s. 56 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> and, therefore, did not apply to the defendant's motion to add a municipality and district health unit as third parties to a construction lien claim. Section 56 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> applies even where security has been posted for the full amount of the claim for lien and the lien has been vacated as a result. Section 44(6) provides that where security is posted and an order is obtained vacating the lien, it does not transform the action from a lien claim to some other type of claim. Here, the true nature of the proposed third party claim was not for contribution and indemnity, as required by s. 56, but rather it was a separate claim for damages by way of tort for alleged negligence by the health unit. As well, the allegations and issues of negligence as against the health unit would unduly complicate resolution of the Plaintiff's lien claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Hobbs Miller Maat Inc." p2="UPI Inc." post.rptr="126" pre.rptr="80" ref.id="I64417f215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hobbs Miller Maat Inc. v. UPI Inc.">Hobbs Miller Maat Inc. v. UPI Inc. (2009), 80 C.L.R. (3d) 126, 2009 CarswellOnt 2093 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Notwithstanding that the words “contribution and indemnity” were used in a proposed third party claim, the true nature of the claim against was for damages for negligence and breach of statutory duty larger in scope than the claims made in the statement of claim and counterclaim in the related construction lien action. The motion for leave to join the third parties was denied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Domus Development Corp." p2="York Condominium Corp. No. 82" post.rptr="228" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I64417f225fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Domus Development Corp. v. York Condominium Corp. No. 82">Domus Development Corp. v. York Condominium Corp. No. 82 (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 228 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—As the contractor failed to remedy alleged defaults within the time frame required by the owner's architectural consultant, the consultant terminated the construction contract. In the ensuing lien action the contractor pleaded wrongful termination and the owner sought to join the consultant as a third party. Rule 29.01 of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> was found to be inconsistent with the more restrictive terms of s. 56.1 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and therefore R. 29.01 did not apply, and only the more restricted third party proceedings authorized by the Act were permitted. The third party claim, however, with the exception of certain paragraphs, came within s. 56.1. A contribution or indemnity claim can arise in either contract or tort even though the main claim is only permitted to be in contract or is a lien claim. Granting leave would not unduly prejudice the ability of the consultant to conduct its defence, nor would it unduly delay or complicate the resolution of the lien actions. In choosing not to follow the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="V.K. Mason Construction Ltd." p2="Strasscorp Holdings Inc." post.rptr="779" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I91c8a560f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. v. Strasscorp Holdings Inc.">V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. v. Strasscorp Holdings Inc. (1991), 1991 Carswell Ont 779, 45 C.L.R. 101 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, the master also distinguished it on the basis that the proposed third party claim there was only in tort, while here there was privity of contract between the owner and contractor.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1999" p1="BMR Golf International Ltd." p2="Forgehill Equities Inc." post.rptr="240" pre.rptr="48" ref.id="I6441a6315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="BMR Golf International Ltd. v. Forgehill Equities Inc.">BMR Golf International Ltd. v. Forgehill Equities Inc. (1999), 48 C.L.R. (2d) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The provisions of s. 56 constitute a complete code and it is inappropriate to refer to the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, specifically R. 29 and the case law thereunder. The proper construction of the words “that claim” in para. 1 of the section is that such words relate to the claim by a plaintiff in a main action or by a plaintiff by counterclaim in a main action, in respect of which claim or counter-claim contribution or indemnity is being sought from the proposed third party. A claim for damages rather than contribution or indemnity would not fall within the parameters of the section (see also: <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Atlas Construction Inc." p2="Brownstones Ltd." post.rptr="97" pre.rptr="26" ref.id="I6441a6325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas Construction Inc. v. Brownstones Ltd.">Atlas Construction Inc. v. Brownstones Ltd. (1996), 26 C.L.R. (2d) 97 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="V.K. Mason Construction Ltd." p2="Strasscorp Holdings Inc." post.rptr="779" pre.rptr="1991" ref.id="I91c8f380f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. v. Strasscorp Holdings Inc.">V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. v. Strasscorp Holdings Inc. (1991), 1991 Carswell Ont 779, 45 C.L.R. 101 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Pursuant to s. 56(1), third party claims must be for the purpose of contribution and indemnity. Hence, a claim against an architect based on professional negligence was not properly determined in a lien action. Such a claim was based in tort and could not properly be included in a lien action based in contract. For the same reasons, a claim against a subcontractor could stand as being an action claim grounded in contract.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19901224" p1="Cana Construction Co." p2="North York Branson Hospital" ref.id="I6441a6345fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Cana Construction Co. v. North York Branson Hospital">Cana Construction Co. v. North York Branson Hospital (December 24, 1990), Doc. CLA 46740/90 (unreported)</ref></cite>—A motion by the defendant hospital to add the architects as third parties was dismissed where substantial issues of negligence not giving rise to indemnity and contribution would be canvassed, which would unnecessarily complicate the trial. The mischief of possible conflicting decisions were outweighed by the prejudice to the proposed third party of having a professional negligence action tried in a summary manner of lien trials and without the benefit of appealing interlocutory decisions and the need to seek leave for all interlocutory steps.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1989" p1="Gregman Construction Ltd." p2="Kensett Corp. Ltd." post.rptr="1076" pre.rptr="[1989]" ref.id="I6441a6355fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gregman Construction Ltd. v. Kensett Corp. Ltd.">Gregman Construction Ltd. v. Kensett Corp. Ltd. (1989), [1989] O.J. No. 1076 (L.J.S.C.O.)</ref></cite>—The Ontario Court General Division has no jurisdiction to deal with a third party claim against the federal Crown, even if leave has been granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bentivoglio" p2="Groupe Brigil Construction" post.rptr="1237" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I6441a6365fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bentivoglio v. Groupe Brigil Construction">Bentivoglio v. Groupe Brigil Construction, 2016 ONSC 1237, 2016 CarswellOnt 3318, 57 C.L.R. (4th) 82 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2016 ONSC 2307, 2016 CarswellOnt 6220, 57 C.L.R. (4th) 87, W.D. Newton J. (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2017 ONCA 413, 2017 CarswellOnt 7511, 64 C.L.R. (4th) 177 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—The defendant added a third party without leave and the third party claim was not limited to contribution and indemnity, but included other claims. The third party added the plaintiff and M as fourth parties without leave, but the fourth party claim was limited to contribution and indemnity. Between these two events, the plaintiff's statement of claim and claim for lien were dismissed by an order that also provided that the third party claim survived and the third party could move to bring a fourth party claim against the plaintiff. The third party moved to either strike the third party claim against it or, alternatively, leave to continue the fourth party claim against M. Although not condoning the conduct of the third party in attempting to shelter the fourth party claim under the original order, the motions judge ruled it was appropriate to grant leave <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> to issue the fourth party claim. The fourth party action was commenced within the limitation period, and while the action was technically still under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, what was intended at the time of the original order was that the action was to continue under the ordinary track. If the court did not have the power to grant leave <ital>nunc pro tunc</ital> to permit the fourth party claim, it ordered that the action be converted to the “ordinary track” as of the date of the original order, to therefore validate the fourth party claim. The Court of Appeal, in affirming the ruling, noted that since only claims for contribution and indemnity are permitted under s. 56, the third party claim here could only “<ital>survive</ital>” in proceedings on the ordinary track. Accordingly, the motions judge adopted the only reasonable interpretation that could be given to the original order.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Interborough Electric Inc." p2="Walsh Construction Co. Canada" post.rptr="3037" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6441cd405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Interborough Electric Inc. v. Walsh Construction Co. Canada">Interborough Electric Inc. v. Walsh Construction Co. Canada, 2015 ONSC 3037, 2015 CarswellOnt 6968 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff subcontractor purported to perfect its lien by commencing an action naming only the defendant contractor, which had also commenced an action against the owner to increase the contract price. The defendant successfully sought leave to add the owner as a third party under s. 56. The onus was on the moving party to establish the grounds for leave, firstly that the proposed third party claim was for contribution and indemnity in respect of the claim of the plaintiff. Despite the owner's arguments to the contrary, the pleading was ultimately subject to the prayer for relief, which was only for contribution and indemnity, interest and costs. As well, the owner was not unduly prejudiced, either by being deprived of the dispute resolution provisions of the construction contract, by having the issues in the contractor's claim determined in the lien action, or by unduly delaying or complicating the resolution of the claim. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: The ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd." p2="OHL Construction Canada" post.rptr="7505" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6441cd415fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada">Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada, 2013 ONSC 7505, 2013 CarswellOnt 18456, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 213 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 3763, 2014 CarswellOnt 8361, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 223 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, was distinguished on its facts.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd." p2="OHL Construction Canada" post.rptr="7505" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6441cd425fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada">Advanced Construction Techniques Ltd. v. OHL Construction Canada, 2013 ONSC 7505, 2013 CarswellOnt 18456, 27 C.L.R. (4th) 213 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 ONSC 3763, 2014 CarswellOnt 8361, 35 C.L.R. (4th) 223 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—In a complicated action, TTC contracted for construction services related to a subway extension to York University. OHL subcontracted with ACT to provide excavation monitoring and ground support for a building under which the extension was being constructed. Documentation noted that on completion, TTC would own, operate, and maintain the new subway line, although the university was the only owner or relevant entity registered on title with respect to any interest in the land. The university granted a temporary construction licence to permit TTC and its agents to enter upon the university lands to carry out their subway construction activities, including the compensation grouting for building support and excavation monitoring work. The licence did not constitute any form of property interest in, or gift or dedication of, university lands. After being ordered off the site following the collapse of a drilling rig, ACT claimed against OHL for delay due to unforeseen or changed soil conditions, improper termination of the contract, and loss of profit. ACT, along with another claimant, brought lien actions for monies alleged owing and to assert security against title, giving a copy of its lien only to various university officials. OHL obtained an order vacating the registration of the claim for lien upon the posting of security, and, <ital>inter alia</ital>, moved to add TTC as a third party to the lien proceeding on the basis that the construction requirements imposed by TTC caused or contributed to ACT's alleged damages. In denying the defendant's third party motion, the Master noted that the series of issues between the defendant and TTC were complex, and to add the TTC Third Party claims in this case would unduly prejudice the lien claimant's ability to prosecute its claim and unduly delay or complicate the resolution of the lien action. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also discussions of this matter under, <ital>inter alia</ital>: s. 4 (stay of lien action granted to permit the lien issues to be arbitrated). The Master was guided in part by the fact that the parties agreed to a summary, simplified arbitration to resolve the lien claim issues, and TTC was not party to the arbitration agreement.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Art Nouveau Inc." p2="Razumenko" post.rptr="420" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I6441cd435fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Art Nouveau Inc. v. Razumenko">Art Nouveau Inc. v. Razumenko, 2011 ONSC 420, 2011 CarswellOnt 905 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Leave was granted where the applicant would be initiating a claim against the proposed third parties in any event, and that action would in all likelihood be consolidated with the existing action, since the third party was a principal of the lien claimant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Dean Construction Co." p2="M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd." post.rptr="485" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I6441cd445fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd.">Dean Construction Co. v. M.J. Dixon Construction Ltd. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 485, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 56 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Section 56.2 contemplates that a court is to consider what stage the lien proceedings are at when leave is sought, and what interlocutory steps have already been taken.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Stensca/Procon Ltd." p2="York University" post.rptr="13" pre.rptr="10" ref.id="I6441cd455fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Stensca/Procon Ltd. v. York University">Stensca/Procon Ltd. v. York University (1993), 10 C.L.R. (2d) 13 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff brought a construction lien action against the defendant. The defence was delivered in December 1991. The pre-trial was held on July 3, 1992 and at least one day of discoveries had already been conducted. On November 4, 1992, the defendant's solicitors raised the question of a third party claim, seeking contribution against two third parties. The defendant subsequently brought a motion under s. 56 for leave to join the two proposed third parties. However, the court was not satisfied that the proposed third party claim would not unduly delay or complicate the plaintiff's action. If the defendant lost, it would still have all its rights against the two third parties to seek contribution in a second action.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA5:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA5.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA5:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Commentary and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 5 corresponds to former ss. 54(2) to (4).</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="DMD Building Systems Corp." p2="2665408 Ontario Inc. et al." post.rptr="15012" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I655333503b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="DMD Building Systems Corp. v. 2665408 Ontario Inc. et al.">DMD Building Systems Corp. v. 2665408 Ontario Inc. et al., 2024 CarswellOnt 15012, 2024 ONSC 5425 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is nothing in r. 19 that conflicts with s. 5 of Ont. Reg. 302/18. Thus, on a motion for default judgment under r. 19, the Court has jurisdiction to grant judgment based on deemed admissions arising from the allegations in the statement of claim. However, as per r. 19.06, deemed admissions on their own may not necessarily provide the court with the necessary evidentiary basis to grant the relief requested by the plaintiff. The court has a legal obligation to only grant judgment where the deemed admissions and/or admissible evidence provide the necessary facts that permits the court to grant the relief sought by the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Alfa Mechanical Inc." p2="Chang" post.rptr="19916" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I4e06d6a0dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Alfa Mechanical Inc. v. Chang">Alfa Mechanical Inc. v. Chang, 2023 CarswellOnt 19916, 2023 ONSC 7167 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff's motion for default judgment, which was brought on notice to the defendants, resulted a consent order setting aside the defendants' noting in default and allowing the defendants to deliver a defence. The plaintiff's motion had sought a declaration of entitlement to a lien against the defendants' interest in their property, as well as personal judgment for the same amount. In <ital>obiter</ital> comments delivered on a ruling as to costs, the court suggested without deciding that default judgment may be available to validate a lien under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. The Associate Judge noted that the legislation did not indicate that default judgment was available only on a joined contract claim. As well, requiring a trial to prove a lien in all cases, including where the defendant has been noted in default, would seem contrary to the requirement in s. 50(3), that procedures be of a summary character. While there is no procedure outlined in the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, there were established procedures for default judgment set out in the Rules of Court. Whether an associate judge had jurisdiction to validate a lien by way of a motion for default judgment remained an open question.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Li" p2="Zhu" post.rptr="18" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I65535a603b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Li v. Zhu">Li v. Zhu, 2023 CarswellOnt 18, 2023 ONSC 17, 2023 CarswellOnt 18, 32 C.L.R. (5th) 83 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The plaintiff sought orders, <ital>inter alia</ital>, dismissing the claim and striking the defence to counterclaim in a lien action, and striking certain defences in a related civil action. The ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I91ca04f0f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing 2019 CarswellOnt 18748, 2019 ONSC 6590, 96 C.L.R. (4th) 193 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite> was held not to apply. First, the jurisdictions under which the motions were brought expressly authorized the court to grant “judgments” as per s. 54(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Most importantly, there was a good reason for allowing the court, even one acting under a judgment of reference such as this one, to issue “judgments” on motions for default judgment. By the nature of these motions, there is no opposition, the opposing party is not entitled to participate any further and is bound by deemed admissions. The purpose of the motion is to determine whether the deemed admissions plus any evidence in “support” of the deemed admissions justify a judgment that can be immediately enforced. These are not, in my view, the “findings” contemplated by the judgment or order of reference. The “findings” contemplated by a judgment of reference are those that arise from contested proceedings, such as with the contested motion to enforce a settlement in <ital>Prasher</ital>. As the defaulting party is not entitled to participate in the proceedings, there can be no motion to oppose confirmation of a report.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nova Concrete Inc." p2="2035211 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2391" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6441f4505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Nova Concrete Inc. v. 2035211 Ontario Inc.">Nova Concrete Inc. v. 2035211 Ontario Inc., 2022 ONSC 2391, 2022 CarswellOnt 5224, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 230 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Fixing a static “test” for setting aside a noting in default under s. 54(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> would amount to a procedural requirement that ignores the summary nature of lien proceedings or the amount or nature of the lien in question. By failing to take any active steps to seek judgment, the plaintiff here left the door open for the defendant to step in and defend. Given that the defendant demonstrated a meritorious defence, and the prejudice to it from denying it the opportunity to defend itself was greater than the prejudice to the plaintiff, the associate judge set aside the noting in default, on terms that the statement of defence be delivered within 15 days.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Quadform Ltd." p2="Rock Con Forming Ltd." post.rptr="7903" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64421b605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Quadform Ltd. v. Rock Con Forming Ltd.">Quadform Ltd. v. Rock Con Forming Ltd., 2020 ONSC 7903, 2020 CarswellOnt 18729, 18 C.L.R. (5th) 118 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2021 ONSC 3379, 2021 CarswellOnt 6559 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—In the context of claims under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, a party seeking to set aside a default judgment under O. Reg. 302/18, s. 5(3) must demonstrate facts, through evidence, that provide it with an arguable defence to the claim. The defence must have an air of reality.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ontario Construction Industries Inc." p2="Festival Hall Dev. Limited" post.rptr="3974" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64421b615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ontario Construction Industries Inc. v. Festival Hall Dev. Limited">Ontario Construction Industries Inc. v. Festival Hall Dev. Limited, 2021 ONSC 3974, 2021 CarswellOnt 8403 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were deemed to admit the allegations of fact in the statement of claim by operation of s. 54(4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and the master had no difficulty granting entitlement to a default judgment the plaintiff. However, given the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Maystar General Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="15646" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I91ca7a20f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd.">Prasher Steel Ltd. v. Maystar General Contractors Ltd. (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 15646, 2020 ONSC 6598, 10 C.L.R. (5th) 238 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>, the master could not sign a judgment in the motion, which took place within a reference, but was required to write and deliver a report.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Eco-Power Electrical Co." p2="Under the Sun Home Renovations Inc." post.rptr="3653" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64421b635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Eco-Power Electrical Co. v. Under the Sun Home Renovations Inc.">Eco-Power Electrical Co. v. Under the Sun Home Renovations Inc., 2021 ONSC 3653, 2021 CarswellOnt 7202 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—It would be unjust to grant summary judgment in terms which would affect the rights of the defendant homeowners without first affording them an opportunity to advance their motion to set aside the noting of default and, if successful, to be heard and to contest the amount claimed under the subcontract. This was so even though the defendants had not yet filed a motion record or a draft defence. The matter was adjourned and a deadline set for the homeowners to deliver their motion record and draft statement of defence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Carreiro" p2="Skrzeczkowska" post.rptr="3614" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64421b645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Carreiro v. Skrzeczkowska">Carreiro v. Skrzeczkowska, 2021 ONSC 3614, 2021 CarswellOnt 7109 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 CarswellOnt 9903 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Noting of default was set aside where 1) the motion was brought expeditiously; 2) there was an adequate, albeit imperfect, explanation for the delay which included the lengthy hospitalization of the defendant abroad after contracting COVID-19; 3) the existence of an air of reality to the defence, which was not a high threshold.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ekarte" p2="GUPM" post.rptr="2203" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64421b655fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ekarte v. GUPM">Ekarte v. GUPM, 2021 ONSC 2203, 2021 CarswellOnt 4036 (Ont. S.C.J.); affirmed 2021 ONSC 7909, 2021 CarswellOnt 18456 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The motion judge articulated the correct legal test for setting aside a noting in default under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. There was no error with respect to the legal test, and no palpable and overriding error in the application of that test to the facts. All the facts found by the motion judge were open to her on the evidence. There was no reason to interfere with the motion judge's finding that service was not effective, and that the noting in default should be set aside.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Halton Electric" p2="Beaucon Building" post.rptr="163" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644242705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Halton Electric v. Beaucon Building">Halton Electric v. Beaucon Building, 2021 ONSC 163, 2021 CarswellOnt 1181, 22 C.L.R. (5th) 172 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved to set aside the noting in default and personal default judgment against him as a director of defendant, under s. 13(1). The court noted that the defendant was not required to put his best foot forward, as in a summary judgment motion, but simply to show that his defence has an air of reality. As well, two of the invoices in dispute post-dated the defendant's resignation from the corporate defendant. There was no evidence that the plaintiff would suffer prejudice in respect of pursuing its claim if the motion was allowed. Given the impact of the pandemic on the Court's operations, the action would not have been heard at that point even if the defendant had filed his defence in a timely manner.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Strada Aggregates Inc." p2="YSL Residences Inc." post.rptr="16984" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I644242715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc.">Strada Aggregates Inc. v. YSL Residences Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 16984, 2020 ONSC 7034, 17 C.L.R. (5th) 240 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The motion of the plaintiff subcontractor in a lien action, brought <ital>ex parte</ital> for an order that the defendant contractor and owner be noted in default, and for default judgment against them, was granted in part. Although noting in default is addressed in s. 5 of O Reg 302/18 under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, no procedure is provided for obtaining default judgment. Accordingly, the processes for obtaining default judgment in Ont. R. 19 apply to lien actions, except to the extent of any inconsistency with provisions of the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. There are two aspects of inconsistency between the procedures for default judgment in Ont. R. 19 and the <ital>Construction Act</ital>. First, s. 63 affords “the court” with authority to grant a personal judgment “upon any ground relating to the claim” and “for any amount that may be due to the claimant and that the claimant might have recovered in a proceeding”, which is authority to grant judgment for claims beyond the claims listed in Ont. R. 19.04(1). That means a motion to a judge is not necessarily required to obtain personal judgment for such claims, even though only a judge or s. 58 referee has authority to declare a lien valid under the <ital>Construction Act</ital> (as distinct from the court's authority to declare a lien invalid pursuant to various provisions of the Act). Second, default judgment is not properly granted for “any claim” advanced by a lien claimant, since the only additional claim properly joined with a lien claim in a lien action is a claim for breach of contract. Here, the defendants were operated commonly by the same individual, and there were contracts between the plaintiff and contractors, but no privity of contract with the registered owner of the premises. The claims for personal judgment against the contractors as pleaded were claims for breach of contract contemplated by s. 3(2) of O Reg 302/18 and properly joined in the lien action. However, the owner's liability to the subcontractor was limited to the holdbacks that the owner was required to retain, and such liability was further limited only to proven valid liens against the owner's interest in the premises. Absent any pleaded contract between the plaintiff and owner, or any pleading of the mutual control and domination argued on the motion, the statement of claim did not support any claim against the owner permitted by s. 3(2) of O Reg 302/18, in addition to claimed holdback liability.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Architecture Unfolded Inc." p2="Fortress Charlotte 2014 Inc." post.rptr="6885" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I644242725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Architecture Unfolded Inc. v. Fortress Charlotte 2014 Inc.">Architecture Unfolded Inc. v. Fortress Charlotte 2014 Inc., 2019 ONSC 6885, 2019 CarswellOnt 19621 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The assessment of the merits is generally not a relevant consideration on a motion to set aside the noting in default of defendants, and delay caused by the proof of the plaintiff's claim does not amount to prejudice <ital>per se</ital>. Here, the Master erred in principle in exercising his discretion solely based on delay, even if deliberate, without considering: the speed of the action once the defendants were served with the default judgment motion; the relative prejudice (of which none was suffered by the plaintiff) and, most particularly, the policy adopted by the Court of Appeal that consent should be given to set aside technical defaults.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1705371 Ontario Ltd." p2="Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc." post.rptr="7423" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="I644242735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1705371 Ontario Ltd. v. Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc.">1705371 Ontario Ltd. v. Leeds Contracting Restoration Inc., 2018 ONSC 7423, 2018 CarswellOnt 21112, 85 C.L.R. (4th) 132, 27 C.P.C. (8th) 34 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2019 CarswellOnt 480 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The test to set aside a default judgment requires the defendant to put forward actual evidence in support of their defence. This does not make the motion to set aside a default judgment akin to a summary judgment motion that requires the responding party to put its best foot forward. Where the defendant was cross-examined on his affidavit but not asked questions about the proposed statement of defence and counterclaim, this did not mean that the statement of defence and counterclaim stood uncontested, such that the court was required to accept it as an arguable defence. It was not incumbent on the plaintiff to elicit evidence on a defendant's cross-examination with respect to payments alleged to have been made by the corporate defendant to the plaintiff. The facts establish whether a defendant has an arguable defence on the merits, and those facts must be proven by evidence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Deman Construction Corp." p2="1429036 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="4430" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I644269805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Deman Construction Corp. v. 1429036 Ontario Inc.">Deman Construction Corp. v. 1429036 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 4430, 41 C.L.R. (3d) 235 (Div. Ct.); varied on other grounds (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 4859, 203 O.A.C. 117 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>—Under s. 54(2) and (3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the defendants, having failed to file a statement of defence within the required statutory time limit, could be noted in default and were not allowed to file a statement of defence “except with the leave of the court, to be given only where the court is satisfied that there is evidence to support a defence”. Under R. 19.04(1)(a) of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, the claim must be for “a debt or liquidated demand in money” in order to clothe the registrar with jurisdiction to sign default judgment. Here, evidence of a signed contract, invoices, the registered liens, a “Change Order” and the defendants' admissions established that the plaintiff's claim was for a debt or liquidated demand in money. The claim fell within R. 19.04(1)(a) and thus, the registrar had jurisdiction to sign default judgment. The motions judge did not err in refusing to set aside the noting of default and default judgment. The motions judge correctly assessed the evidence on the written record before him and found that the defendants contracted for, and acknowledged receipt of the invoiced goods and services. The motions judge found the plaintiff to be credible and the defendants not to be credible. The motions judge found the counterclaim was so bereft of particularity that it could not be considered a statement of material facts. The motions judge did not accept the allegations of the defendants and was not satisfied that there was evidence to support a defence. There was no basis in law, mixed law and fact or in fact to reverse the order of the motions judge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Derbtile Construction Inc." p2="E-Sun International Inc." post.rptr="4963" pre.rptr="[2003]" ref.id="I644269815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Derbtile Construction Inc. v. E-Sun International Inc.">Derbtile Construction Inc. v. E-Sun International Inc. (2003), [2003] O.J. No. 4963, 2003 CarswellOnt 4698, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 102 (S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 185 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 54 of the Ontario Act puts a greater onus with respect to providing evidence of a defence on a defendant seeking to set aside a noting of default in a construction lien action than under the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> in other actions. However, neither the statute nor the case law is intended to negate the long-standing principle that lawyers are entitled to rely on their counterparts' undertakings, especially where such reliance causes the lawyers to change their client's position to the detriment of the client. Therefore, where the defendant in a default motion alleged a breach of a promise contained in a letter to the defendant, to the effect that at least twenty days notice to provide the statement of defence would be given, the defendant's motion to set aside a noting of default was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1988" p1="Hamilton Landscaping & Paving" p2="603893 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="127" pre.rptr="30" ref.id="I644269825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hamilton Landscaping & Paving v. 603893 Ontario Inc.">Hamilton Landscaping & Paving v. 603893 Ontario Inc. (1988), 30 C.L.R. 127 (Ont. H.C.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff had obtained default judgment against the defendants in an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> which was not appealed. The defendants brought a motion to set aside the judgment and note pleadings not closed on the grounds that the procedural sections of the Act read together lead to the conclusion that the Act contemplates judgment only after trial, that the default was due to solicitor's error and that the defendants had a defence on the merits. The motion was allowed, but on the basis of the merits of the defendant's defence. The procedural sections contained in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, 1983 are not inconsistent with Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> R. 19 concerning default proceedings. Under the circumstances in this case, it was appropriate to utilize default proceeding. In a review of the evidence provided by both sides on the motion, however, triable issues were raised and, therefore, the defendants did demonstrate a defence on merits.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Canada Building Materials Company" p2="Pitts Construction" post.rptr="5792" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I644269835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canada Building Materials Company v. Pitts Construction">Canada Building Materials Company v. Pitts Construction, 2017 ONSC 5792, 2017 CarswellOnt 15441, 82 C.L.R. (4th) 239 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the test to set aside a Noting in Default under section 54(3) is more onerous than the test under the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, in that the moving party must show that there is a “meritorious defence.” However, the test for setting aside a default judgment is similar under the Act and the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. The test governing the exercise of discretion to set aside a default judgment involves the following five factors: i. Whether the facts establish an arguable defence; ii. Whether there is a plausible excuse or explanation for the defendant's default in complying with the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>; iii. Whether the motion to set aside was brought promptly; iv. What are the competing potential prejudices to the parties of granting or refusing to set aside the default judgment; and, v. What is the effect of any order on the overall integrity of the administration of justice. Although the delay in bringing the motion was concerning, the remaining four factors weighed in favour of granting the motion. [Authors' note: For further authority on the test for setting aside a default judgment, see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Peterbilt of Ontario Inc." p2="1565627 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="333" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I644290905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Peterbilt of Ontario Inc. v. 1565627 Ontario Ltd.">Peterbilt of Ontario Inc. v. 1565627 Ontario Ltd., 2007 ONCA 333, 2007 CarswellOnt 2713 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="420-450 Britannia Road East Ltd." p2="Kennedy Transportation Network Ltd." post.rptr="1791" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I644290915fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="420-450 Britannia Road East Ltd. v. Kennedy Transportation Network Ltd.">420-450 Britannia Road East Ltd. v. Kennedy Transportation Network Ltd., 2015 ONSC 1791, 2015 CarswellOnt 3838 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 5358 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Swanson" p2="Vogrin" post.rptr="1413" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I644290925fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Swanson v. Vogrin">Swanson v. Vogrin, 2017 ONSC 1413, 2017 CarswellOnt 2859, 76 C.L.R. (4th) 328 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To have a noting in default set aside under s. 54(3), a defendant must demonstrate to the court that there is evidence to support a defence. A defendant must also show that it moved promptly to cure the defect. The evidence provided must have substance beyond mere unsupported allegations or statements. The contractor's counsel had noted the owner in default after the owner had requested several extensions, but did so without informing the owner's counsel. Once the owner's counsel learned that a noting in default had been filed, they quickly acted to have the noting set aside and provided the court with an affidavit with attached exhibits, including emails between the parties. The motion judge found that the owner had met the requirements under s. 54(3) and granted the motion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Built-Con Contracting Ltd." p2="Lisgar Construction Co." post.rptr="1720" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I644290935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Built-Con Contracting Ltd. v. Lisgar Construction Co.">Built-Con Contracting Ltd. v. Lisgar Construction Co., 2016 ONSC 1720, 2016 CarswellOnt 3494, 63 C.L.R. (4th) 163 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff would not be significantly prejudiced by an order setting aside the Registrar's default judgment other than the additional costs and time of having to prove its claim, because the Registrar had no jurisdiction to issue default judgments for lien remedies.
