The wording of the default judgment here only referred to a “debt or liquidated demand for money” with no reference to a lien judgment. The plaintiff should have moved before a judge for default judgment on both the contract and lien actions, and the provisions of s. 37 would have been met. However, this lack of prejudice did not justify an order to set aside the default judgment where the defendant generally failed to meet the various heads of test for setting aside a default judgment, as recently outlined by the Ontario Court of Appeal in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Intact Insurance Co." p2="Kisel" post.rptr="4011" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I644290945fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Intact Insurance Co. v. Kisel">Intact Insurance Co. v. Kisel, 2015 CarswellOnt 4011, [2015] O.J. No. 1473 (Ont. C.A.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1987" p1="Canada-Wide Reinforcing Steel Co. (1987) Ltd." p2="ABCO One Corp." post.rptr="1044" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I6442b7a05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Canada-Wide Reinforcing Steel Co. (1987) Ltd. v. ABCO One Corp.">Canada-Wide Reinforcing Steel Co. (1987) Ltd. v. ABCO One Corp., 2014 ONSC 1044, 2014 CarswellOnt 1853, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 297 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A party seeking equitable relief from the court must put their best foot forward and present their best evidence. A defendant in default who fails to provide evidence of a meritorious defence should not be permitted to drag construction lien proceedings out unnecessarily. Where a defendant noted in default did not adequately explain its failure to deliver a statement of defence, did not display a continuous intention to defend, and its proposed statement of defence filed with the motion materials was merely a bald denial, the test for setting aside a noting in default under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> was not met.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Oxy Teknologies Inc." p2="Du-Mor Construction Ltd." post.rptr="1185" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6442b7a15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Oxy Teknologies Inc. v. Du-Mor Construction Ltd.">Oxy Teknologies Inc. v. Du-Mor Construction Ltd., 2013 ONSC 1185, 2013 CarswellOnt 2132 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant successfully moved to set aside a default judgment made against it in a construction lien action for environmental remediation work, and was given leave to deliver a statement of defence within 10 days. There would have been considerable prejudice to the defendant had the order not been granted, and the motion record provided evidence of a defence that could not be prosecuted if the motion had been denied. Any prejudice to the plaintiff from setting aside the default could be compensated by a costs award.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="William Hannah Heating and Cooling Inc." p2="Evans Estate" post.rptr="517" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6442b7a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="William Hannah Heating and Cooling Inc. v. Evans Estate">William Hannah Heating and Cooling Inc. v. Evans Estate, 2013 ONSC 517, 2013 CarswellOnt 524 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The default judgment and noting in default was set aside and the defendants given 15 days to file their defence. The motion was brought promptly, there was always an intent to defend that was known to the plaintiff, the defendant demonstrated that it had a viable defence, and there was little prejudice to the plaintiff because the full amount of lien plus 25% for security for costs had been paid into court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Peoples Trust Co." p2="Rose of Sharon (Ontario) Retirement Community" post.rptr="7319" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6442b7a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Peoples Trust Co. v. Rose of Sharon (Ontario) Retirement Community">Peoples Trust Co. v. Rose of Sharon (Ontario) Retirement Community, 2012 ONSC 7319, 2012 CarswellOnt 16827, 97 C.B.R. (5th) 303, 19 C.L.R. (4th) 1 (Ont. S.C.J. [Commercial List])</ref></cite>—After the general contractor began proceedings against the defendant condominium, a receiver was appointed over the defendant and proceedings were stayed pursuant to the federal <ital>Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act</ital>. Default judgment having been granted in favour of the contrattor, the latter moved to set the stay aside as the lien claim would expire if the stay was not lifted, but opposed the receiver's condition that the default judgment be set aside. The Court had authority to determine all matters touching on receivership, and as the default judgment was likely made without knowledge of the appointment and was in contravention of its terms, and there was evidence of a reasonable explanation by the receiver about why it did not take steps at the time in the lien action, the receiver met the test for setting aside the default under s. 54(3) of the Act, and the default and noting in default were set aside.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Metaldoor Hardware & Installations Ltd." p2="York Region District School Board" post.rptr="3067" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6442b7a45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Metaldoor Hardware & Installations Ltd. v. York Region District School Board">Metaldoor Hardware & Installations Ltd. v. York Region District School Board, 2012 ONSC 3067, 2012 CarswellOnt 7143, 25 C.L.R. (4th) 21 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Service of the statement claim in the lien action, although in accordance with the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, was made in a manner that would almost certainly result in the defendant being noted in default because of the address it was sent to was not the defendant's place of business. The defendant moved to set aside the subsequent noting in default and default judgment. The court noted that although rule 19.03 allowed for a noting in default to be set aside “on such terms as are just”, the rule conflicts with s. 54(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, which requires a moving party to show evidence to support a defence. Accordingly cases decided under rule 19.03 should be approached with some caution. Nevertheless, cases considering the setting aside of a default judgment under Rule 19.08(1) are applicable to construction lien matters, although evidence supporting a defence must be provided in a construction lien matter, rather than just an outline or theory of a defence with a consideration of issues of prejudice as in the normal case, the cases considering the first two criteria under rule 19.08(1) are useable and applicable in a construction lien matter. Applying those criteria, the court found that the defendant's delay in bringing this motion was not unreasonable in the circumstances, and even if it were, the defendant's reliance upon the courtesy of counsel not to take steps against his client without some sort of notice was a reasonable excuse for that delay. In addition, the defendant adequately explained its default in appearance as the result of the manner of service, and had shown that there was evidence to support a defence. Such evidence need not be admissible at a trial, but only show that there is evidence of the defence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Schindler Elevator Corp." p2="1147335 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="505" pre.rptr="2012" ref.id="I6442b7a55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Schindler Elevator Corp. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc.">Schindler Elevator Corp. v. 1147335 Ontario Inc., 2012 ONSC 505, 2012 CarswellOnt 609, 11 C.L.R. (4th) 132 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The judgment of reference required the reference master to “determine all questions arising in this action on the reference and all questions arising under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>”. The question of whether the parties in an action have reached a settlement agreement is a question arising in the action and on the reference and as such it is a question that the reference master is required to decide.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc." p2="Toronto Catholic District School Board" post.rptr="2376" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I6442deb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc. v. Toronto Catholic District School Board">Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc. v. Toronto Catholic District School Board, 2010 CarswellOnt 2376 (Ont. Master); additional reasons 2010 CarswellOnt 3400 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant made an assignment in bankruptcy and the surety to the lien bond and its indemnifiers sought to be added as a party and to suspend the operation of the Interim Report on the basis that the plaintiff was obligated to give them notice that it was seeking a judgment against the lien bond that had been posted. The trustee in bankruptcy elected not to defend the action and was noted in default. The master held that once the bond was issued, the surety could be called upon. There was no obligation on the plaintiff at any time to give notice of any steps in the action. If the surety wanted to move to step into the shoes of the defendant at any time, it was its obligation to monitor the action. When a lien bond is posted, the surety is on notice by its very terms that it may be called by the Accountant of the Superior Court for payment and that it has no right to question the merit of the demand despite any objection by the principal. It is up to the surety to keep itself informed of the progress of the action and the financial health of its principal and if it wishes to intervene to seek leave in a timely fashion.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Khatachadourian" p2="Roopchand" post.rptr="6408" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I6442deb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khatachadourian v. Roopchand">Khatachadourian v. Roopchand, 2009 CarswellOnt 6408, 94 C.L.R. (3d) 179 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—By its wording, the heading, its placement and the context of the section, s. 54(3) applies to the delivery of pleadings only where under s. 54(2) “a person defaults in the delivery of a defence to that claim” and not where pleadings have been delivered but subsequently struck. Even if s. 54(3) applied where the defence has been struck, the language of the section does not remove the judicial discretion to refuse leave where the motion is an abuse of process. The language of s. 54(3) sets out a precondition for the granting of leave—“to be given only where the court is satisfied that there is evidence to support a defence”—but does not make leave mandatory if that precondition is met.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Glasstech Inc." p2="Belle View Construction Corp." post.rptr="5189" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I6442deb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Glasstech Inc. v. Belle View Construction Corp.">Glasstech Inc. v. Belle View Construction Corp. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 5189 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 5069 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant provided a draft statement of defence, crossclaim and counterclaim. The case had not been adjudicated on its merits, and there were issues of deficiencies and monies paid yet to be determined and verified. In the circumstances, the defendant had put forth sufficient facts to support an arguable case on its merits. Default judgment was set aside.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="A1 Equipment Rental Ltd." p2="Borkowski" post.rptr="1717" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I6442deb35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="A1 Equipment Rental Ltd. v. Borkowski">A1 Equipment Rental Ltd. v. Borkowski (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 1717, 70 C.L.R. (3d) 274 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a motion to set aside a default judgment and the noting in default that preceded it, promptness demonstrated in bringing the motion remains relevant, in addition to the existence of evidence to support a defence, even where the action is brought under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. This is not a circumstance where the Act is inconsistent with the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Emco Corp." p2="Ontario Trenchless Construction Ltd." post.rptr="33" pre.rptr="65" ref.id="I644305c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Emco Corp. v. Ontario Trenchless Construction Ltd.">Emco Corp. v. Ontario Trenchless Construction Ltd. (2007), 65 C.L.R. (3d) 33, 2007 CarswellOnt 3628 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 5093 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Default judgment was set aside on terms where the motion to set aside the judgment was timely and there was a plausible, albeit very weak, explanation for the default. The defendant had not yet shown a defence on the merits because it had not provided details of how payments were used and instead simply denied that he breached the Act. Because a breach of trust was a serious allegation, the defendant should at least have the opportunity to show that the use of the funds was permissible.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Walker Brothers Quarries Ltd." p2="1276304 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="5085" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I644305c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Walker Brothers Quarries Ltd. v. 1276304 Ontario Inc.">Walker Brothers Quarries Ltd. v. 1276304 Ontario Inc. (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 5085 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The test under s. 54 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> to set aside the noting in default is more stringent than that set out in the Rules as it is more akin to the test to set aside a default judgment under the Rules. To be successful in a motion to set aside the noting in default a party must show (a) promptness, and (b) evidence of a good defence.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Van Horne Construction Ltd." p2="Ldask MBC Corp." post.rptr="1790" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I644305c25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Van Horne Construction Ltd. v. Ldask MBC Corp.">Van Horne Construction Ltd. v. Ldask MBC Corp. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 1790, 2004 CarswellOnt 1690 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Subsection 54(3) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> provides that where a defendant has been noted in default, the defendant shall only be permitted to contest the claim of the plaintiff and to file a Statement of Defence if leave of the court is given, such leave to be given only where the court is satisfied that there is evidence to support a defence. The test to set aside a noting of default is more restrictive under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> than under the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. Here, the defendant established that the Statement of Claim did not come to its attention until after it had been noted in default, and the plaintiff's counsel at no time advised the defendant's solicitor that the plaintiff had instructed him to note the defendant in default. Counsel should not have caused any default or dismissal to be entered without first notifying opposing counsel. As well, the defendant raised a number of facts and allegations supporting its position that it had a good defence on the merits.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1991" p1="Twin City Mechanical" p2="Chicapee Park Centre Ltd." post.rptr="4" pre.rptr="47" ref.id="I644305c35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Twin City Mechanical v. Chicapee Park Centre Ltd.">Twin City Mechanical v. Chicapee Park Centre Ltd. (1991), 47 C.L.R. 4 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—In applications to set aside a default judgment in a <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> case, the Act is more restrictive than the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. Accordingly, where neither the affidavit in support of the motion nor the examination for discovery indicates that there is a valid defence to the claim of the plaintiff, an order setting aside the default judgment or directing repayment into court cannot be made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Paragon Building Ltd." p2="Bleta Estate" post.rptr="383" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I644305c45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Paragon Building Ltd. v. Bleta Estate">Paragon Building Ltd. v. Bleta Estate, 2014 ONSC 383, 2014 CarswellOnt 689, 9 C.B.R. (6th) 25, 29 C.L.R. (4th) 284 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2014 CarswellOnt 2376, 32 C.L.R. (4th) 139 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants were noted in default and took no steps to set the defaults aside. They were deemed to admit the allegations in the statement of claim and the plaintiff was granted personal judgment on its claim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Lucas" p2="Marin" post.rptr="9435" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I644305c55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lucas v. Marin">Lucas v. Marin (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 9435 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant paid money into court to vacate a lien. After the lien claimant requisitioned the court to note the defendant in default, the local registrar signed default judgment. The lien claimant then sought payment out of court of the money paid in by the defendant. The motion was refused. Money paid into court to vacate a lien is money held by the court as a substitute for the interest claimed by a lien claimant in the defendant's land. Such money is not held pursuant to a claim in contract for a liquidated sum. The registrar's default judgment was limited to a claim in contract for a liquidated sum. A registrar's default judgment is not a basis upon which to order that money paid into court as a substitute for a claim to an interest in land be paid out of court to satisfy a judgment for a liquidated sum. The money paid into court was available to all persons entitled to notice under section 60 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> who claimed and could prove a lien against the lands. Consequently the moneys could not be ordered paid out of court to the plaintiff on the basis of a registrar's default judgment. If the plaintiff sought judgment on the lien portion of the claim, the proper procedure was to bring a motion for judgment returnable before a judge in the region where the lands were situate, on notice to all those entitled to notice under section 60 of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Peter Lombardi Construction Inc." p2="Colonnade Investments Inc." post.rptr="4874" pre.rptr="2000" ref.id="I545e91c0fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Peter Lombardi Construction Inc. v. Colonnade Investments Inc.">Peter Lombardi Construction Inc. v. Colonnade Investments Inc. (2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 4874, 6 C.L.R. (3d) 244 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff contractor successfully moved to add the mortgagee as a party defendant with a view to claiming priority over it under s. 78, on the basis that no mortgage funds were ever advanced. Service was effected but the mortgagee did not defend, and pleadings were noted closed against it, bringing into operation s. 54(3) and (4) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Since there was a deemed admission that no mortgage funds were ever advanced by the mortgagee, the plaintiff's judgment and writ of execution had priority over the mortgage. When the plaintiff's lien was subsequently found to be registered out of time, s. 78 of the Act could no longer apply.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="Rentshop Inc." p2="Tekke Thermal Inc." post.rptr="99" pre.rptr="6" ref.id="I64432cd15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rentshop Inc. v. Tekke Thermal Inc.">Rentshop Inc. v. Tekke Thermal Inc. (2001), 6 C.L.R. (3d) 99 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The general provision in s. 54(4) does not take away the power of an owner to move for a declaration and the other relief provided for in s. 46(1) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="St. Clair Roofing & Tinsmithing Inc." p2="Davidson" post.rptr="275" pre.rptr="50" ref.id="I64432cd25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="St. Clair Roofing & Tinsmithing Inc. v. Davidson">St. Clair Roofing & Tinsmithing Inc. v. Davidson (1992), 50 C.L.R. 275, 7 C.P.C. (3d) 240, 8 O.R. (3d) 578 (Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff roofing contractor registered a lien against the defendants' house, and commenced a construction lien action against the defendants. A statement of defence was not filed, and the plaintiff signed a default judgment on the debt claim only. A writ of seizure and sale was filed, and when the plaintiff instructed the sheriff to seize the defendants' bank account, the defendants applied for an order setting aside the noting in default and the default judgment and lifting the writ of seizure and sale. The application was allowed but on terms that the defendants pay the full amount of the claim plus costs and interest into court within 60 days. The plaintiff was entitled to sign default judgment under R. 19.04 of the Ontario <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>, since the plaintiff was looking to the primary debtor for payment on the debt, and nothing more. The default judgment did not prejudice the position of any other lien claimants, since it did not affect the plaintiff's rights as a lien claimant. However, the defendants did have a potentially meritorious defence in their argument that the invoice price was too high. The plaintiff could not produce any written contract, nor could it produce any written quotation or estimate approved by the defendants, and the price charged might be subject to review under a <ital>quantum meruit</ital> claim if the plaintiff could not establish an oral contract. Accordingly, it was appropriate to allow the application, but only if the defendants paid the full amount of the claim plus costs and interest into court within 60 days of the date of pronouncement of the order.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Pet Valu Inc." p2="Whitlock" post.rptr="233" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I64432cd35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pet Valu Inc. v. Whitlock">Pet Valu Inc. v. Whitlock (1992), 8 C.L.R. (2d) 233 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Allegation of facts deemed to be admissions in a prior lien action were not deemed admissions in a subsequent action, where the current action was between different parties dealing with different issues and the property in question was in a different county.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA6:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA6.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA6:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Subsection 29(4) of The <ital>Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act, 1896</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, provided that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It shall not be necessary to make any lienholders parties defendant to the action, but all lienholders served with the notice of trial shall for all purposes be treated as if they were parties to the action.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">With the exception of a change from “shall for all purposes be treated as if they were parties” to “shall be deemed parties” in <ital>The Mechanics' and Wage-Earners' Lien Act</ital>, S.O. 1910, c. 69, s. 31(4) and a change from “shall not be necessary” to “is not necessary” in <ital>The Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1960, c. 233, s. 29(3), the provision remained unchanged until the 1983 amendments when s. 59 was introduced in a form identical to the present s. 57. Subsection 57(1) replaced s. 33(5) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1980, c. 261, which had provided that it was not necessary to make any lien claimants parties defendant to the action, but all lien claimants served with the notice of trial were for all purposes deemed to be parties to the action. The section in its present form originated in the 1983 amendments.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 6 mirrors former s. 57.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section identifies the parties to a lien action. It is significant and often over-looked that “all persons” served with the notice of trial are parties to the action. As the lien remedy is a remedy <ital>in rem</ital>, it is important to have all interested parties before the court. Execution creditors, for example, could and should be made parties if the lien remains registered against the premises. Although s. 6(2) would appear to confer a broad jurisdiction on the court to have all persons added as parties who have an interest in the outcome, lien bond sureties have enjoyed little success and been subject to strict terms in seeking to be added as parties, even when the party who posted their lien bond has failed to defend. Added parties have enjoyed little success in participating in the hearing of lien proceedings or their merits.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ozz Electric Inc." p2="Bondfield Construction Company Limited" post.rptr="2861" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I644353e05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ozz Electric Inc. v. Bondfield Construction Company Limited">Ozz Electric Inc. v. Bondfield Construction Company Limited, 2022 ONSC 2861, 2022 CarswellOnt 6812 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant's bonding company successfully moved to be added as a party in order to have the lien claims vetted as quickly as possible by a vetting committee that included it, with a view to reaching a consensus on the distribution of the agreed upon holdback. The intervention issue was not subject to a s. 67(2) leave requirement as s. 57(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, which governed this case, expressly authorized the court to add or join any person to a lien action at any time subject only to s. 54. However, s. 67(2) leave would be required to strike a vetting committee. The court must be guided by s. 57(2) on issues of joinder of parties to lien actions, and not (ON) rule 13.01. However, the court can be guided by the provisions of r. 13.01.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pryers Construction Ltd." p2="MVMB Holdings Inc." post.rptr="6135" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I644353e15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pryers Construction Ltd. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant R was the tenant on lands owned by the defendant MVMB, and the individual defendant was the principal of both these defendant corporations. The plaintiff performed renovation work for R, pursuant to an oral agreement with the individual defendant, and subsequently registered a claim for lien on the property, naming MVMB as owner and the individual defendant as the person to whom the lien claimant supplied services or materials. The plaintiff initially did not register a claim for lien against R's leasehold interest, or advance a claim against R in contract, but at the commencement of the trial, successfully moved to add R as a party defendant. The trial judge then found both R and MVMB to be “owners” within the meaning of s. 1 and granted judgment to the plaintiff enforcing its claim for lien against the interest of MVMB in the property. In granting judgment against R, the trial judge held that although the plaintiff had not commenced an action against R within that 90-day period in the Act, the doctrine of “special circumstances” operated to extend the time, and that the two-year limitation period under s. 4 of the <ital>Limitations Act, 2002 (“LA2002”)</ital> was superseded by the terms of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (“CLA”). In reversing the trial ruling, the Divisional Court found that it did not follow from the mere fact of common governance and ownership, that in requesting the improvement upon behalf of R, the individual defendant was also requesting the improvement upon behalf of MVMB, and upon its credit, or privity or consent. The trial judge erred in law in piercing the corporate veil of MVMB, which was a distinct legal entity, even though the individual defendant was the sole officer, director and shareholder of both corporate defendants. In respect of the judgment against R, the “special circumstances” doctrine did not apply in actions under the <ital>CLA</ital> to enforce a lien. The <ital>CLA</ital> did not contain a limitation period applicable to claims for breach of contract joined with actions to enforce claims for lien, and there was no conflict between the provisions of the <ital>CLA</ital> and the <ital>LA2002</ital> in relation to such claims. Accordingly, the two-year limitation period under the <ital>LA2002</ital> applied to contractual claims joined with lien claims and that limitation period had expired approximately eight months before the motion to add R was made.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Aqua Pools Ltd." p2="Hanna" post.rptr="850" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I644353e25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Aqua Pools Ltd. v. If the jurisdiction in s. 57(2) was that broad, there would have been no need for the strict limitations in s. 55(2) [now s. 2(1) of Ont. Reg. 302/18]. It was also held that s. 57 appears to create such “statutory parties” without any limitation on their rights of participation and that the bank had standing to participate at trial in the determination of issues under s. 14 (the lien) and s. 17 (limitation on value of the lien). Master)</ref></cite>—The court has jurisdiction under s. 57(2) to add parties to a construction lien action where an assignment in bankruptcy is made by a defendant and the party seeking to be added is the surety to the lien bond posted as security in lieu of the land by the bankrupt defendant to vacate the lien. The right to be added is subject to the provisions of s. 54 of the Act. This right to be added is not limited to a surety under a lien bond, and an indemnifier of the surety, a director, a shareholder or a creditor of the bankrupt defendant would be in no different position. Such addition would be on terms which limit the rights of the added party in the action to those of the defendant. In addition, the party seeking to be added, depending on the stage of the action, must demonstrate that it can carry on with the action. If the action is at the stage of discovery, leave having been granted for discovery, the added party must provide discovery as if it were the defendant; that is, have access to the documents and to someone knowledgeable who can be examined for discovery. The party seeking to be added must agree to be personally bound to pay the costs. In this case, the trustee had been noted in default, and therefore the moving parties needed leave to file a statement of defence pursuant to s. 54(3). PA7:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA7.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA7:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Act to Amend the Mechanics' Lien Act of 1873</ital>, S.O. 1874, c. 20, s. 13, first provided that any number of lien holders may join in one suit. All suits brought by a lien holder shall be taken to be brought on behalf of all the lien holders in the same class. A provision for the carriage of proceedings appeared in the 1890 <ital>Act to Simplify the Procedure for Enforcing Mechanics' Liens</ital>, S.O. 1890, c. 37, s. 26, allowing any lien holder entitled to the benefit of the action to apply for carriage of the proceedings. These two provisions appeared together in 1896 in the <ital>Act respecting Liens of Mechanics, Wage-Earners and Others</ital>, S.O. 1896, c. 35, ss. 35 and 36. Section 35 allowed any party to an action to realize liens in respect of the same property to make an application to a judge or officer having power to try such actions to consolidate all actions into one action, and to give the conduct of the consolidated action to any plaintiff to whom, in his discretion, he saw fit. Section 36 entitled any lien holder entitled to the benefit of the action to apply for carriage, which, if granted, made that lien holder the plaintiff of the action. These sections remained in their 1896 format until the Revised Statutes of 1980. The provision first appeared in its current form in s. 61 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, when the prerequisite of an application by a party or any other interested person was dropped. As lien actions are to be disposed of in as summary a manner as possible, and as lien actions have now been recognized as a kind of class proceeding, most acts contain provisions similar to those in Ontario.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 7 mirrors former s. 59(1).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Lien actions often involve many lien claimants of different degrees of privity of contract with the owner. In order to permit the orderly conduct of such actions the statute creates a kind of class proceeding. This scheme is carried into effect through “consolidation.” The right to conduct of a consolidated action is called “carriage.” The special costs usually payable by the group to the solicitor having carriage are called “salvage costs.” The section is silent as to who may bring a motion for carriage and consolidation, but it is clear that carriage may only be awarded to a person who “has a perfected lien”. One party may undertake responsibility for the progress of all actions to trial, and this section provides for that eventuality.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA8:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA8.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA8:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Commentary and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 8 mirrors former s. 59(2)</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Pentad Construction Inc." p2="2022988 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2669" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I644417305fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pentad Construction Inc. v. 2022988 Ontario Inc.">Pentad Construction Inc. v. 2022988 Ontario Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 2669, 2020 ONSC 1227, 14 C.L.R. (5th) 277 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants sought consolidation of a lien action with a claim by the defendant against the performance bond surety. Both actions had questions of law and fact in common, with the defendant alleging that the lien claimant failed to satisfy its obligations with respect to the work it was performing on the project, and the surety potentially liable under the performance bond for any of the plaintiff's defaults under the contract. Given that the consolidation power under s. 59(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (now s. 8 of Ont. Reg. 302/18) was limited to lien actions, and did not permit the consolidation of lien and non-lien actions, and that the surety could not be added to the construction lien action as a defendant by way of counterclaim, by virtue of the limitations on counterclaims set out of s. 55(2) (now s.2(1) of Ont. Reg. 302/18), hearing the cases at the same time or one immediately after the other was the legally sound procedural step.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1652472 Ontario Inc." p2="Miwel Construction Ltd." post.rptr="4433" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I644417315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1652472 Ontario Inc. v. Miwel Construction Ltd.">1652472 Ontario Inc. v. Miwel Construction Ltd., 2013 ONSC 4433, 2013 CarswellOnt 9044, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 104 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff moved for an order for transfer to Ottawa and consolidation of various lien proceedings affecting more than 45 construction lien actions commenced in Ottawa, Brockville and Picton. A true consolidation would likely result in a confusing amalgamated proceeding and require costs to be run up unnecessarily on pleading amendments. Instead, it was more efficient to keep the separate actions and designate the “main action” in which notice of trial would be served. The other actions were to be stayed for the time being but if several liens were settled prior to trial then the individual actions could be dismissed and those lien claimants let out of the main action. The court files in relation to the subsidiary actions would not be active and would be left as bookmarks to ensure all of the issues were ultimately dealt with. It was also not necessary to transfer each of the sub-trade lien actions to Ottawa, as they would be subsumed in the main actions, and no purpose was served by imposing the administrative burden and cost of multiple transfers on either the Ministry or on the parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Country Cottage Living Inc." p2="Heath" post.rptr="2766" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I644417325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Country Cottage Living Inc. v. Heath">Country Cottage Living Inc. v. Heath (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 2766, 72 C.L.R. (3d) 301 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The consolidation power under s. 59(2) is limited to lien actions and does not apply to “regular” actions. Subsection 107(2) of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>, which provides that an action can only be consolidated on consent of the plaintiff, was therefore not inconsistent with the general consolidation power provided for in s. 59(2).</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA9:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA9.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA9:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The provisions regarding an application to fix a date for trial and those regarding the notice of trial to be given by the party which obtained the appointment can be traced back to the <ital>Act Respecting Liens of Mechanics, Wage-Earners and Others</ital>, R.S.O. 1897, c. 153, ss. 35 and 36. The notice period was extended from eight to ten days in 1927. As early as 1892, the Master Ordinary, then interpreting the Act of 1890, held that the notice period stipulated was not to be enforced strictly (<cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1892" p1="Orr" p2="Davie" post.rptr="430" pre.rptr="22" ref.id="I64443e405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Orr v. Davie">Orr v. Davie (1892), 22 O.R. 430 (Ont. Ch.)</ref></cite>). The request for identification of all other persons having liens was introduced in 1983. This section replaced s. 42(1), (2) and (3) of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>. It was introduced in its current form in s. 62 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6. The major change was to give the party an option between a motion to obtain an appointment for the trial of the action, a motion to have the date fixed for the holding of the settlement meeting, or both. The group of persons to be served changed with the amendments in 1983. Under the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital>, that group consisted of solicitors of defendants who were represented by counsel, the defendants appearing in person personally, all the lien holders who registered their claims as required by the Act or of whose claims the party obtaining the appointment had notice, and finally of all other persons having any charge, encumbrance, or claim on the land subsequent in priority to the lien, who were not parties. Service was to be personal unless otherwise directed by the court. Service now has to be effected to all persons who are or would be entitled to notice of a settlement meeting under ss. (2). While in other parts of the province, courts will not fix a date for trial until a settlement meeting has taken place, practice in Toronto is different due to the fact that settlement meetings there are replaced by pre-trials (see comments under s. 61). In Toronto, dates for trial are normally set at the end of pre-trial.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 9 corresponds to former s. 60 and remains substantially unchanged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section and s. 10 of this Regulation contain a complete code for setting a trial date or a date for holding a settlement meeting, which procedure is unique to the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Subsection (1) provides parties with the flexibility to concurrently fix a trial date and provide for a settlement meeting, or to take either step separately. In some cases, it will be helpful to hold a settlement meeting before a trial date has been set. The persons to whom notice of a settlement meeting must be provided, and the requirements for service on them, are set forth in subs. (2). These are the same persons who must be served with the notice of trial. Although an individual who has been noted in default is not entitled to a notice for trial or a settlement meeting in his or her capacity as a defendant, he or she may be entitled to notice under one of the other heads set out in subs. (2). The person or persons to whom notice of a settlement meeting must be given reflects the <ital>in rem</ital> nature of the remedy, providing, as it does ultimately, for the judicial sale of land.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Refplus Inc." p2="2073427 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="8195" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I644465505fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Refplus Inc. v. 2073427 Ontario Inc.">Refplus Inc. v. 2073427 Ontario Inc. (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 8195, 83 C.L.R. (3d) 121 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff brought a motion seeking an order transferring the action from Peterborough to Toronto on the basis that two of the parties had agreed to settle on terms that included the plaintiff bringing the transfer motion. The master found that the motion, on the material before him, amounted to an attempt by two parties to the action to transfer the action for their convenience without regard to the other named party or any other potential parties. An abstract of title together with an execution search against the owner would have identified if there were any other affected parties but no such searches were provided. The plaintiff did not satisfy its burden to demonstrate why the action should be transferred to Toronto having regard to the terms of the Act and Ont. Rule 13.1.02(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="Atlas Construction Inc." p2="Brownstones Ltd." post.rptr="97" pre.rptr="26" ref.id="I644465515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Atlas Construction Inc. v. Brownstones Ltd.">Atlas Construction Inc. v. Brownstones Ltd. (1996), 26 C.L.R. (2d) 97, 27 O.R. (3d) 711 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A person made a statutory party by virtue of s. 60 and s. 57 has the standing to participate at trial in the determination of issues under s. 14 and s. 17 (including issues of deficiencies or uncompleted work) which issues involve parties with whom the person has no contract. This participation includes the right to question witnesses, call evidence and make submissions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="Pineau" p2="Kretschmar Inc." post.rptr="396" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I644465525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc.">Pineau v. Kretschmar Inc. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 396, 2004 CarswellOnt 548 (Master); additional reasons at (2004), 2004 CarswellOnt 3189, [2004] O.J. No. 3239 (Master); further additional reasons at (2004), 42 C.L.R. (3d) 56, 2004 CarswellOnt 6072 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—An order under s. 60(1) cannot validly be made by a Master unless there is already a judgment of reference under s. 58(1). Where, as here, there was no judgment of reference, and the order merely provided for the trial to take place “in the week of October 30, 2000 or such subsequent date as may be agreed to be between counsel or ordered by this court”, such wording was not sufficient to be an “order” within s. 61 and 37(1)1, and the lien was held to have expired. Once a judgment of reference has been obtained, then a party must make a motion to the master without notice, to have a date, time and place fixed for the trial of the action. However, in order to validly make this order, there must be a judgment of reference under s. 58(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. It is generally the party obtaining that judgment who makes this routine motion. The date so fixed is called, the “first construction lien pre-trial”, but is really the first day of the trial. Once this order has been obtained, the party who obtained it must serve a properly worded notice of trial and a copy of the order on all persons described in s. 60(2), generally all other lien claimants, if any. A notice of trial, which is a critical document, may be in Form 17 but it must be served, and the person serving it and all persons served with it, are “parties to the action” as per s. 57(1). Once a master conducts the first “pre-trial”, he or she is seized of the reference (trial), but is not so seized by reason only of having appointed the day, time and place for the trial (first “pre-trial”) under s. 60(1). As a matter of practice, Toronto construction lien masters do not order settlement meetings to take place, under s. 60(1), in Toronto lien actions, because the first “pre-trial”, which is supervised by the master, is a more effective procedure than an unsupervised settlement meeting under s. 61. Sometimes, the trial master may establish a vetting committee to scrutinize the various lien claims and report back but this is a totally different procedure than a settlement meeting under s. 61. Outside of Toronto, in some jurisdictions, settlement meetings are often ordered. The practice varies across the Province.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="F.T. Construction Inc." p2="Woodcrest Homes Ltd." post.rptr="201" pre.rptr="3" ref.id="I644465535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="F.T. Construction Inc. v. Woodcrest Homes Ltd.">F.T. Construction Inc. v. Woodcrest Homes Ltd. (1992), 3 C.L.R. (2d) 201 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiff commenced an action under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, 1983. The trial judge ordered that the matter be placed on the trial list, with a trial date to be confirmed at pre-trial. The defendants contended that the above order failed to meet the requirements of s. 62(1) [now R.S.O. 1990, s. 60(1)] of the Act, in that it failed to specify a day, a time, and place fixed for trial of the action, and moved for a declaration that the plaintiff's lien had expired and for a resultant dismissal of the claim. The motion was dismissed. One meaning of the word “fix” was “to make definite arrangements about.” The trial judge's order substantially complied with s. 62(1) [now R.S.O. 1990, s. 60(1)], in that it was sufficiently clear in “fixing” a day, time, and place for trial to have complied with this definition. Further, such order conformed with the practice of the court.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA10:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA10.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA10:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As far back as 1916, the Assistant Master in Ordinary in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1916" p1="Elliott" p2="Rowell" post.rptr="203" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I64448c605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elliott v. Rowell">Elliott v. Rowell (1916), 11 O.W.N. 203 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, had held that “[t]he plaintiff must prove his claim in open court and submit it to full investigation and to any contest which the lien-holders and subsequent encumbrancers may choose to make against it”. Under the various early <ital>Mechanics' Lien Acts</ital> in Ontario, a practice grew of conducting a pre-trial hearing to allow the multiple parties to meet, discuss, and evaluate the various issues and their respective positions. While widely adopted and sanctioned in other jurisdictions (see <ital>Builders' Lien Act</ital> of Alberta, R.S.A. 1970, c. 35, s. 39(3)), and although often resulting in settlements, the practice was not formally sanctioned. Thus, the Divisional Court in 1973, while recognizing the benefits of the procedure, and recognizing that it would cause delays and add to the costs of proceedings should it be abolished, ruled that such proceedings could not be considered a “trial” within the meaning of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Act</ital> (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1973" p1="Kennedy Glass Ltd." p2="Jeskay Construction Ltd." post.rptr="527" pre.rptr="1973" ref.id="I546325a0fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Kennedy Glass Ltd. v. Jeskay Construction Ltd.">Kennedy Glass Ltd. v. Jeskay Construction Ltd. (1973), 1973 CarswellOnt 527, [1973] 3 O.R. 493 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>). The concept of a formal, structured settlement meeting was introduced by s. 63 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, which was carried over as s. 61 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. It should be noted that in Toronto, the long-standing practice continues to override the express wording of the Act to the effect that pre-trials are still held in lieu of a settlement meeting. No corresponding provisions on settlement meetings are to be found in the other provinces.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 10 corresponds to former s. 61 and remains substantially unchanged.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The settlement procedure as contemplated in the Act is not a pre-trial conference as contemplated in the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. Consequently, as was the case under the former rules of court, R. 50 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> does not apply to an action under the Act. The objectives of the pre-trial conference as set forth in the Rules, <ital>i.e.</ital>, the canvassing of all reasonable avenues for the resolution of the conflict, the narrowing down of the relevant issues, the presentation and evaluation of evidence, are the objectives that the settlement meeting is enacted to achieve. Section 10 sets out the mandatory rules for the conduct of a settlement meeting. There exists a wide regional variation in practice, much of which has now been affected by Practice Directions. Following the meeting, the results are formally set out in a Statement of Settlement, which is filed with the court and becomes part of the court record. The settlement, which is binding on a defendant who has been noted in default, may be varied or set aside by the court, subject to the terms of s. 5 dealing with the effect of a default in the delivery of a defence. The court is given broad powers to make whatever orders are necessary as the result of the meeting. In some jurisdictions judges are scheduled to be available for this purpose.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1990" p1="Heritage Contracting & Design London Ltd." p2="Bayley-Hay" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="39" ref.id="I6444b3705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Heritage Contracting & Design London Ltd. v. Bayley-Hay">Heritage Contracting & Design London Ltd. v. Bayley-Hay (1990), 39 C.L.R. 1 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The parties held a settlement meeting. Those in attendance prepared a statement of settlement and appeared before the court requesting judgment in that amount. A party did not appear before the court, and judgment was handed down for the amount which appeared in the statement of settlement. The absent party brought a motion to set aside the judgment, indicating that its written notice of acceptance of the offer was different from the amount indicated in the judgment. Section 61 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, provides that settlement results shall be binding upon all persons served with notice, and the court declined to exercise its discretion to vary or set aside the statement of settlement or the judgment which flowed therefrom.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="Kuch Stephenson Gibson Malo Architects & Engineers" p2="Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc." post.rptr="892" pre.rptr="[2005]" ref.id="I6444b3715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Kuch Stephenson Gibson Malo Architects & Engineers v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc.">Kuch Stephenson Gibson Malo Architects & Engineers v. Salter Farrow Pilon Architects Inc. (2005), [2005] O.J. No. 892, 2005 CarswellOnt 894, 42 C.L.R. (3d) 258 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved to discharge and vacate a claim for lien registered against the defendant's property. The plaintiff preserved a lien in the amount of $43,992.52 and then commenced an action to enforce a lien in the amount of $341,284.53. A settlement meeting was held in relation to this lien, and others, and, as a result of the meeting, a Statement of Settlement was filed. It was agreed therein that the parties had no dispute with respect to the timeliness, quantum or lienability of the liens. The defendant challenged the settlement and argued that perfection of the lien pursuant to s. 36(3) of the Ontario Act required commencement of an action to enforce the lien in the amount of $43,992.52. The court held that even though the defendant did not specifically acknowledge the validity of this lien in the Statement of Settlement, there was sufficient acknowledgement of the lien that it should not be invalidated. Further, the defendant had conceded that there was no prejudice.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1993" p1="Dorsam Investments Ltd." p2="Counsel Trust Co." post.rptr="76" pre.rptr="11" ref.id="I6444b3725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dorsam Investments Ltd. v. Counsel Trust Co.">Dorsam Investments Ltd. v. Counsel Trust Co. (1993), 11 C.L.R. (2d) 76 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—Where a settlement of a lien claim has been made without notice to, or the concurrence of, an affected party, the settling party must be prepared to establish by evidence that the settlement made was reasonable, if such settlement is to be approved in the mortgage accounts. That would involve evidence sufficient to show the Master that the lien had priority over the party objecting to the settlement, that it was worth at least what was paid and that it was reasonable, in the circumstances, to make the settlement.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Moffatt & Powell Ltd." p2="682901 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="205" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I6444b3735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Moffatt & Powell Ltd. v. 682901 Ontario Ltd.">Moffatt & Powell Ltd. v. 682901 Ontario Ltd. (1992), 49 C.L.R. 205 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—After negotiations between the mortgagee and the lien claimants, a construction lien action was continued as claims by 16 lien claimants for their proper <ital>pro rata</ital> share to a sum of money being held in court. A settlement meeting was subsequently held and the court later made an order validating the settlement meeting and ordering the trustee to prepare a report to the court with respect to the quantum and validity of all of the outstanding liens. The trustee's report expressed complete satisfaction with the validity of the liens of 14 of the 16 claimants, but questioned whether the liens of the other two claimants had expired before their claims for lien were registered. The plaintiff in the action then brought an application for summary judgment on behalf of the 14 lien claimants whose liens had been endorsed by the trustee. The two claimants who did not receive approval opposed the application. Held, the application was granted. Subsections 63(5)(b) and (c) [now R.S.O. 1990, s. 61(5)(b) and (c)] of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, clothed the court with the necessary jurisdiction to grant the application. The trustee had prepared his report pursuant to an order of the court made under s. 63(5)(b). Subsection 63(5)(c) authorized the court “to make an order that is necessary in order to give effect to any judgment … of the court under clause (a) or (b)”, therefore, the court could grant the relief sought.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA11:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA11.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA11:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 11 concerns the manner of giving the notice of motion for a reference to a person agreed to by the parties or to the Small Claims Court.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
PA12:1: <editorial.commentary.section date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="annotated.statute"><value>See Ont. Reg. 302/18, O. Reg. 302/18, s. PA12.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA12:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History, Commentary, and Case Law</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section, which is unique to Ontario, was added by the <ital>Construction Lien Act, 1983</ital>, S.O. 1983, c. 6, to allow those holding funds in relation to a project to obtain directions in regard to how they are to be dispersed in circumstances where several interests may be in conflict.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 12 mirrors former s. 66.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Modern land development requires many obligations to be secured before and during development. Lot levies are paid, security in the form of cash is lodged with municipal authorities and utilities, financing commitments often provide for contingency reserves, taxation statutes such as GST can give rise to refunds and some mechanism was required to permit such third parties to obtain directions in the event of competing claims, one of which, at least, is a trust claim under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. Section 12 allows this.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Case Law</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2001" p1="LeBrun Northern Contracting Ltd., Re" post.rptr="150" pre.rptr="8" ref.id="I6444da805fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="LeBrun Northern Contracting Ltd., Re">LeBrun Northern Contracting Ltd., Re (2001), 8 C.L.R. (3d) 150 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—As a result of disputes surrounding invoicing and purchase orders submitted for payment, the owner (who was a joint venture partner in the general contractor, and a subcontractor in its own right) ceased to approve any further payments to the plaintiff (who was also a joint venture partner in the general contractor and a subcontractor). The owner effected various set-offs for its benefit as a subcontractor. Additionally, the owner withheld from later certificates of payment to the general contractor holdback amounts that had been paid as cash advances on earlier certificates. The plaintiff subcontractor argued that the owner ought to have applied to the court under s. 66 for directions in respect of the set-offs. In these circumstances, the plaintiff's application for the appointment of a receiver/manager under s. 248 of the Ontario <ital>Business Corporations Act</ital> and R. 45.02 was rejected by the court. Ultimately, the issues required determination by a trial judge, and the appointment of a receiver/manager to deal with the set-offs would not materially advance the matter.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1992" p1="Toronto Dominion Bank" p2="General Glass & Aluminum Co." post.rptr="31" pre.rptr="5" ref.id="I644501905fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Toronto Dominion Bank v. General Glass & Aluminum Co.">Toronto Dominion Bank v. General Glass & Aluminum Co. (1992), 5 C.L.R. (2d) 31 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—The subcontractor deposited a cheque from the general contractor at its bank, and the bank applied the funds to eliminate the subcontractor's indebtedness to the bank. The trust claimants obtained a declaration that the funds were impressed with a trust in their favour pursuant to s. 8 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The bank had intimate knowledge of the nature of the subcontractor's business since it had a banking relationship with the subcontractor for 15 years, and was also aware that the subcontractor's accounts receivable were subject to holdbacks. The bank was therefore under a duty to inquire as to whether the cheque was subject to a trust in favour of the trust claimants. Furthermore, a trust arises on the date that funds are received by the bank for subcontractor obligations that commenced prior to receipt of the funds but were completed afterwards. Therefore, the entire amount was subject to a trust in favour of the trust claimants. That portion of the total funds representing payment for the Goods and Services Tax was to be held in trust by the bank in favour of Revenue Canada, if it chose to advance such a claim.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

PA13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA13:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This section was introduced in substance by s. 47 of the <ital>Mechanics' and Wage Earners' Lien Act, 1923</ital>, S.O. 1923, c. 30.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 13 corresponds to former s. 67(2) and remains unchanged.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
