PA13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA13:2</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>General</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gowing Contractors Ltd" p2="Walsh Construction Company Canada" post.rptr="11621" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I655aad603b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Gowing Contractors Ltd v. Walsh Construction Company Canada">Gowing Contractors Ltd v. Walsh Construction Company Canada, 2023 CarswellOnt 11621, 2023 ONSC 4407, 2023 A.C.W.S. 3843 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On motion under the former <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> for further and better production from the defendants and for leave to amend the pleadings, leave under s. 67(2) was not required. The production motion pertained at least in part to several other related actions, neither of which were governed by the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>. The amendments motion was not governed by s. 67(2) at all, as those amendments pertained to the related civil actions. As well, the production motion as it pertained to the lien action was a natural part of the leave granted at a trial management conference for the parties to exchange affidavits of documents and productions.</para.text></para><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Symtech Innovations Ltd." p2="Siemens Canada Limited" post.rptr="15908" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I655aad613b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Symtech Innovations Ltd. v. Siemens Canada Limited">Symtech Innovations Ltd. v. Siemens Canada Limited, 2023 CarswellOnt 15908, 2023 ONSC 5795 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Partial summary judgment may be appropriate if (i) dividing the determination of the case into several parts will prove cheaper for the parties; (ii) it will get the parties' case in and out of the court system more quickly; and (iii) it will not result in inconsistent findings by the multiple judges who touch the divided case. However, partial summary judgment may be inappropriate where it is possible that the trial judge will develop a fuller appreciation of the relationships and the transactional context than the motions judge, which could risk inconsistent findings and substantive injustice. Where, as here, the motion has been brought within a reference under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, the associate judge is seized of all motions and other interlocutory steps in the action, as well as the ultimate trial, thereby mitigating many of the concerns raised in the case law about partial summary judgment. Granting summary judgment on the plaintiff's prolongation claim by dismissing it for failure to follow notice requirements, and directing a trial of the balance of the claim, which would be a much shorter and more focused trial, achieved the objectives of proportionate, timely, and affordable justice and met the statutory mandate in s. 67(1) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (now s. 50(3))<ital/> that lien actions be as far as possible of a summary character.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Nelco Mechanical Limited" p2="2335213 Ontario Inc et al." post.rptr="2781" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I655ad4703b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Nelco Mechanical Limited v. 2335213 Ontario Inc et al.">Nelco Mechanical Limited v. 2335213 Ontario Inc et al., 2023 CarswellOnt 2781, 2023 ONSC 1521, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 29 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—Proportionality is a governing principle as it relates to the production of documents in an action, especially under the <ital>Construction Act.</ital> Here<ital>,</ital> as one of the main issues for trial was whether the s. 7 trust provisions applied to the defendants and, if so, to what extent, documents relating to the receipt, deposit and transfer of funds used to finance the project appeared to be relevant. Any certificates of payment were relevant to the issues, even those in the hands of third parties. A party has an obligation to list all relevant documents in their affidavit of documents and to produce every document relevant to the matters in issue in the proceeding. To the extent there are relevant documents within the possession of a non-party, such documents are still producible whether through the party obtaining a copy of them or through a r. 30.10 motion. The defendants could not simply refuse to produce the certificates on the basis that they do not possess them, but were required make reasonable efforts to obtain any certificates of payment from any third party that may have them and produce them to the plaintiff.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc." p2="690 King Street Corporation" post.rptr="19707" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I655ad4713b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc. v. 690 King Street Corporation">Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc. v. 690 King Street Corporation, 2022 CarswellOnt 19707, 2022 ONSC 6439, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 349 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part <ital>Desco Plumbing and Heating Supply Inc. v. AVN Plumbing Limited et al.</ital>, 2020 CarswellOnt 16272, 2020 ONSC 6728, 16 C.L.R. (5th) 267 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The defendant owner raised the issue of failure by the plaintiffs to seek leave to bring an interlocutory motion. The court noted that the issue should have been raised early in the motion proceedings and should not have been raised for the first time on appeal. If the issue had been raised in a timely manner, the moving parties would have added a request for leave to their motion, and the motion judge surely would have granted it. The judgment was amended to include a paragraph adding leave to bring the motions for summary judgment that were adjudicated by the motions judge.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Green Scene Landscaping" p2="Singh" post.rptr="4701" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I655afb803b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Green Scene Landscaping v. Singh">Green Scene Landscaping v. Singh, 2022 ONSC 4701, 2022 CarswellOnt 11503, 27 C.L.R. (5th) 57 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—Leave was granted for the defendants to move to amend their statement of defence and counterclaim and to substitute the affidavit evidence of a new expert witness for one who died after preparing his report. This relief was sought after affidavits for trial had been exchanged but before the trial had taken place. The determination of the motion was necessary to deal with the concerns raised by the death of the original expert, the alleged discovery of further claims against the plaintiff regarding the quality of its work that arose from the second expert report, and the problems that arose from the original amended statement of defence and counterclaim.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Leblon Drywall Inc." p2="King Station Facility" post.rptr="3181" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I655afb813b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Leblon Drywall Inc. v. King Station Facility">Leblon Drywall Inc. v. King Station Facility, 2022 ONSC 3181, 2022 CarswellOnt 7336, 29 C.L.R. (5th) 316 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—On a motion for summary judgment to vacate/discharge the claim for lien, the onus is on the defendant to establish that, based on the evidence before the court on the motion, the court can, with or without its enhanced fact-finding powers under the Rules, make a fair and just determination without requiring a trial. In this case, there were serious credibility issues and conflicting evidence on facts going to the heart of the two issues to be decided, which did not allow the court to make a fair and just determination without a trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ozz Electric Inc." p2="Bondfield Construction Company Limited" post.rptr="2861" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I644501935fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Ozz Electric Inc. v. Bondfield Construction Company Limited">Ozz Electric Inc. v. Bondfield Construction Company Limited, 2022 ONSC 2861, 2022 CarswellOnt 6812 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant's bonding company successfully moved to be added as a party in order to have the lien claims vetted as quickly as possible by a vetting committee that included it, with a view to reaching a consensus on the distribution of the agreed upon holdback. The intervention issue was not subject to a s. 67(2) leave requirement as s. 57(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> expressly authorized the court to add or join any person to a lien action at any time subject only to s. 54. However, s. 67(2) leave would be required to strike a vetting committee. The court must be guided by s. 57(2) on issues of joinder of parties to lien actions, and not (ON) rule 13.01. However, the court can be guided by the provisions of r. 13.01.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="The Fifth Wall Corp." p2="Tonelli" post.rptr="599" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I655b22903b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="The Fifth Wall Corp. v. Tonelli">The Fifth Wall Corp. v. Tonelli, 2022 ONSC 599, 2022 CarswellOnt 838, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 259 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—The threshold for assessing leave for a summary judgment motion under s. 67(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> should not be considered “low”, nor should it be viewed differently than for other interlocutory steps requiring leave. Determining whether a step is necessary or whether it will expedite resolution of issues in dispute is a case-specific exercise, requiring the court to consider the specific circumstances of the specific case in the context of the overall scheme of the Act. It would be contrary to the Act to apply a general “one size fits all” approach on the appropriateness of summary judgment motions, including partial summary judgment, in all lien actions. Here, the proposed motion for partial summary judgment essentially addressed whether and how the (ON) <ital>Consumer Protection Act, 2002</ital> applied to the construction contract. It was clearly not necessary, and the issues to be addressed were as readily addressed at trial, but it would genuinely expedite resolution of issues in dispute between the parties, and leave was granted. [Authors' Note: See also <trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="The Fifth Wall Corp." p2="Tonelli" post.rptr="6590" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I655b22913b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="The Fifth Wall Corp. v. Tonelli">The Fifth Wall Corp. v. Tonelli, 2022 ONSC 6590, 2022 CarswellOnt 16879, 37 C.L.R. (5th) 267 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>, in which the <ital>Consumer Protection Act, 2002</ital> was held to apply to the construction contract.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="GH Asset Management Services Inc." p2="Lo" post.rptr="506" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I644528a25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="GH Asset Management Services Inc. v. Lo">GH Asset Management Services Inc. v. Lo, 2022 ONSC 506, 2022 CarswellOnt 612, 21 C.L.R. (5th) 50 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant owner's property manager, allegedly acting as agent for the owner, contracted with the original lien clamant to perform property maintenance and renovation services at the property. The owner denied any knowledge or authorization of the work. After the action was commenced, the lien was assigned to the property manager, and the owner intended to bring a motion to discharge the lien, return the security posted and dismiss or permanently stay the lien action, on the grounds that the delayed disclosure of this assignment gave rise to an abuse of process. The owner intended to seek relief under s. 47 of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, as well as under Ont. rule 21.01(3)(d) or s. 106 of the <ital>Courts of Justice Act</ital>. It was held that the owner's s. 47 motion could proceed; it was premature to assess the merits of whether this novel ground supported relief under s. 47, since this would amount to importing a leave requirement into s. 47 where one was not prescribed. However, motions for disposition without trial, namely motions seeking a final order, that are not provided for in the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> were still “interlocutory steps” to which the leave requirement in s. 67(2) applied. Accordingly, the proposed motion for relief under r. 21.01(3)(d) and s. 106 of the CJA required consent of the court before it could be brought. If successful, it would fully and finally resolve the lien and contract claims in the lien action, and a dismissal or permanent stay of the lien proceeding would have the effect of preventing the property manager from taking further steps to enforce the lien. In these circumstances, the motion, if successful, would expedite resolution of the issues in dispute in this lien action, and leave to proceed with it was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gowing Contractors Ltd." p2="Walsh Construction Company Canada" post.rptr="7683" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644528a35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gowing Contractors Ltd. v. Walsh Construction Company Canada">Gowing Contractors Ltd. v. Walsh Construction Company Canada, 2021 ONSC 7683, 2021 CarswellOnt 17066 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved for security for costs, but first sought to compel answers to questions refused during the cross-examination of the plaintiff's principal on her responding affidavit. The security motion, being interlocutory, required leave of the court, and the refusals motion was, essentially, an interlocutory motion within that interlocutory motion, also requiring leave. While there may be a case where leave is properly denied for a refusals motion arising from cross-examinations for a pending interlocutory motion, in this case the defendant connected each of its questions to issues to be decided on the security for costs motion. Assessing whether they were proper questions and, if so, ought not to have been refused, was necessary to ensuring that procedural cross-examination rights were not diminished in construction lien actions. Leave was granted on the refusals motion, and answers to four of the refused questions was ordered.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="PBW High Voltage Ltd." p2="Metrolinx" post.rptr="6715" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644528a45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="PBW High Voltage Ltd. v. Metrolinx">PBW High Voltage Ltd. v. Metrolinx, 2021 ONSC 6715, 2021 CarswellOnt 14035 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Although adding new issues at trial did not expedite resolution of the parties' dispute, the court granted leave to the plaintiff to amend its statement of claim to seek prejudgment and post-judgement interest. The motion was necessary, and an injustice might arise if the plaintiff was precluded from pursuing recovery of contractual interest to which it may be entitled purely by reason of a pleading omission, particularly where the applicable subcontract terms and conditions was already a live issue. There was also no non-compensable prejudice to the defendant.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1917196 Ontario Ltd." p2="Kazmi" post.rptr="6132" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64454fb05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1917196 Ontario Ltd. v. Kazmi">1917196 Ontario Ltd. v. Kazmi, 2021 ONSC 6132, 2021 CarswellOnt 12734 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The claimant successfully sought leave to amend its statement of claim to add a claim in breach of contract damages for “additional construction costs,” and a claim that the defendant was a “builder” or “vendor” under the <ital>New Home Warranties Plan Act</ital>, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.31 (“ONHWPA”) but misrepresented himself as an owner, thereby inducing the claimant to enter into the contract and assume the responsibility of a “builder” under <ital>ONHWPA</ital> including the statutory warranties and expenses required of a “builder” by Tarion. Leave was granted notwithstanding that the proposed amendments were poorly drafted and unclear, as the court must read pleadings generously when determining whether they disclose a reasonable claim or defence. Here, whether the defendant was a pure project manager or a contractor was a real issue that needed to be determined, and several issues turned on this determination, such as the timeliness of the claim for lien and applicable lien period, and identification of the person liable to pay the claimant. The court distinguished <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Becerra" p2="Ronchin" post.rptr="4232" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64454fb15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Becerra v. Ronchin">Becerra v. Ronchin, 2016 ONSC 4232, 2016 CarswellOnt 10274, 69 C.L.R. (4th) 152 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, where the claims were either statute barred or incapable of being joined.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="5197" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I64454fb25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran, 2021 ONSC 5197, 2021 CarswellOnt 10694 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master concluded that further disclosure from the plaintiff regarding a bank account transaction record would not assist in the determination of any outstanding issues in the lien action, as the plaintiff's use of money paid by the defendant was not an issue in dispute in this lien action. Rather, it was an issue in the defendant's related non-lien action, misappropriation of those funds by the plaintiff's principal was expressly pleaded. Leave under (then) s. 67(2) was denied. However, leave was granted to the plaintiff to bring a motion for summary judgment, which, although not necessary, would expedite resolution of the issues in dispute. The master disagreed that the evidentiary record from the defendant's earlier s. 47 motion, (see <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2020" p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="7064" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I91d305a0f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran (2020), 2020 CarswellOnt 7064, 2020 ONSC 3111, 13 C.L.R. (5th) 355, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 91 (Ont. Div. Ct.); reversing in part 2019 ONSC 1551, 2019 CarswellOnt 3825, 145 O.R. (3d) 625, 89 C.L.R. (4th) 96, 32 C.P.C. (8th) 197 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>) which included lengthy affidavit evidence from both sides on which cross-examination had already occurred, was sufficiently complete for the court to decide the case. In the prior motion, the defendant was the moving party and had a different evidentiary onus than as the responding party to a summary judgment motion. Had he known there was a risk that judgment might be granted against him, he may have tendered different or further evidence. He was entitled to tender further evidence on the summary judgment motion, if needed. [Authors' Note: In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R&V Construction Management Inc." p2="Baradaran" post.rptr="4382" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I644576c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran">R&V Construction Management Inc. v. Baradaran, 2022 ONSC 4382, 2022 CarswellOnt 10736 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the plaintiff's subsequent motion for summary judgment was heard and granted.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Quad Pro Construction Inc." p2="Canadian Leaseback (GP) Inc." post.rptr="4740" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644576c15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Quad Pro Construction Inc. v. Canadian Leaseback (GP) Inc.">Quad Pro Construction Inc. v. Canadian Leaseback (GP) Inc., 2021 ONSC 4740, 2021 CarswellOnt 9728 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Leave was granted to the plaintiff to bring a motion for partial summary judgment leading to an interim report ordering that the defendants pay the “undisputed monies” that formed a part of its claim for lien. As per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="4 Star Drywall (99) Ltd." p2="Nanak Homes Inc." post.rptr="2006" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I91d32cb0f58711eeab02e3aac0249471" title="4 Star Drywall (99) Ltd. v. Nanak Homes Inc.">4 Star Drywall (99) Ltd. v. Nanak Homes Inc. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 2006, 82 C.L.R. (3d) 260 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, (then) s. 67(2) under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> should not be used to allow only interlocutory steps that resolve all of the issues in a case. The test is meant to avoid unnecessary motions or motions that do not advance the resolution of any of the issues in dispute.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Hobson" p2="Turner" post.rptr="4407" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644576c35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Hobson v. Turner">Hobson v. Turner, 2021 ONSC 4407, 2021 CarswellOnt 8847 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Ont. R. 26.01 specifies that the court “shall” grant leave to amend on such terms as are just unless prejudice would result that cannot be compensated for by costs or an adjournment. If this test can be met, the court should be hesitant to deny leave for the motion under the <ital>Construction Act</ital>, Ontario Reg. 302/18 s. 13, for the simple reason that there is a necessity to put all issues between the parties properly before the court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Archdekin" p2="Ko" post.rptr="1255" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I644576c45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Archdekin v. Ko">Archdekin v. Ko, 2021 ONSC 1255, 2021 CarswellOnt 2845, 23 C.L.R. (5th) 179 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2021 ONSC 1472, 2021 CarswellOnt 2838 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—At the pre-trial of the action, the defendants sought to bring a motion to challenge the authenticity of the lien claim, but the motion was not properly scheduled and did not proceed. The motion was not rescheduled, but days before the exit pre-trial and the trial itself, counsel for the defendants alleged to the court that the plaintiff's current and previous lawyers “knew” that the lien claim was invalid, the last invoice was fraudulent, the amount of the lien was exaggerated and that the claim for lien was a forgery. The defendants' counsel sought to both adjourn the trial and have the plaintiff's counsel removed. As the trial could not proceed, the adjournment was achieved de facto, and the defendants' counsel unsuccessfully sought leave to challenge the validity of the claim for lien and amend the statement of defence. No supporting evidence was filed with the motion, and the defendants did not move to remove plaintiff's counsel despite the very serious allegations. The supporting material served and filed on the morning of the motion showed that allegations against the plaintiff's counsel were mere speculation aimed at derailing the trial.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="NDF Financial Inc." p2="Tomas" post.rptr="5594" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I644576c55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="NDF Financial Inc. v. Tomas">NDF Financial Inc. v. Tomas, 2020 ONSC 5594, 2020 CarswellOnt 13249, 26 R.P.R. (6th) 157 (Ont. Together, they require the court to impose a procedure that is as expeditious and cost-efficient as is suitable to meet the needs of the case. The parties are to narrow the documents required for trial and deliver them in advance of trial in the form of a document book. Joint document books are encouraged. When a trial is conducted as a summary trial with affidavit evidence in chief, documents attached as exhibits to such affidavit evidence need not also be included in the document book. Documents that are not required for trial, and multiple copies of the same documents, should not clutter up the trial record. An affidavit of documents is not appropriately an exhibit at trial in a construction lien reference trial. Here, leave for the defendant to tender as evidence the plaintiff's affidavit of documents was denied where all but one of the documents were already before the court.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dalcor Inc." p2="Unimac Group Ltd." post.rptr="4662" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64463a135fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Dalcor Inc. v. Unimac Group Ltd.">Dalcor Inc. v. Unimac Group Ltd., 2016 ONSC 4662, 2016 CarswellOnt 12099, 71 C.L.R. (4th) 333 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The plaintiffs registered construction liens against an existing apartment building where each provided services and materials to the construction of an addition. The applicant was the surety for the defendant general contractor on the project. Where the motion brought by the applicant was to set aside a charging order that was obtained by the contractor's former lawyers without notice, it was not an interlocutory step that was directly part of the construction lien proceeding. It was a step dealing with legal costs owed as between the law firm and its former client, and did not deal with either of the plaintiffs in the proceedings nor the (discontinued) defendant. Leave under s. 67(2) was therefore not required. However, a motion brought by the applicant for exoneration and payment out of the bond posted with the Accountant did require leave, which was not granted, as it would not reduce costs, or simplify or expedite the lien actions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Limen Structures Ltd." p2="Brookfield Multiplex Construction Canada Ltd." post.rptr="5107" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64463a145fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Limen Structures Ltd. v. Whether or not the plaintiff would appeal an unsuccessful outcome of the summary judgment motion was not a factor that the court should consider in applying the test for leave to bring an interlocutory motion under the Act. The likelihood of success on the merits of the motion was also not relevant to whether the statutory test for leave was met.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Becerra" p2="Ronchin" post.rptr="4232" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I64463a155fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Becerra v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court denied leave to the plaintiff to issue a fresh as amended statement of claim to increase the quantum of the claim, add new grounds of recovery and join with his construction lien claim a claim for recovery in respect of construction services provided to renovate a property other than the defendants' property. Counsel erroneously assumed that because the court granted leave to conduct further examinations for discovery on the amendments, the court must have found that a motion under Rule 34.14 was necessary or would expedite the resolution of the issues in dispute. There was no basis for that assumption. Even if, by allowing additional discoveries, the court was acknowledging that discovery was necessary, it did not follow that a motion for directions under Rule 34.14 was necessary, and the Rule 34.14 motion failed the test for leave and was dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lecompte Electric Inc." p2="Doran (Residential) Contractors Ltd." post.rptr="6290" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I6446fd635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lecompte Electric Inc. v. Doran (Residential) Contractors Ltd.">Lecompte Electric Inc. v. Doran (Residential) Contractors Ltd., 2010 ONSC 6290, 2010 CarswellOnt 8715, 100 C.L.R. (3d) 228 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Discoveries or even an affidavit of documents are not automatic and the Act intends that the parties will obtain direction from the court before engaging in costly interlocutory procedures. Discovery planning is now required in all actions pursuant to Rule 29.1. This requirement also applies in lien actions if leave for discovery is granted. If the parties are convinced that affidavits of documents and discoveries are necessary then they are directed to use their best efforts to agree on a plan. If they have legitimate issues that require court direction then they may seek a case conference or if there are factual issues in dispute, they may bring the matter back by motion for directions. It is not appropriate to proceed without a plan and then to launch a motion that implies the other party is in breach of the rules or is doing its production improperly. That is the purpose of the limitation in Rule 29.1.05.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="6007325 Canada Inc." p2="LPQ 18 Yorkville Avenue Inc." post.rptr="3356" pre.rptr="2010" ref.id="I6446fd645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="6007325 Canada Inc. v. LPQ 18 Yorkville Avenue Inc.">6007325 Canada Inc. v. LPQ 18 Yorkville Avenue Inc., 2010 CarswellOnt 3356, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 100 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—On a motion for summary judgment, once the plaintiff had proved that there was no triable issue, the defendant was required to adduce specific facts demonstrating that there was a genuine issue requiring a trial. The master found that there was no genuine issue for trial and the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment succeeded.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Scott Morris Architects Inc." p2="Blu Skye Medical Inc." post.rptr="279" pre.rptr="90" ref.id="I6446fd655fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Scott Morris Architects Inc. v. Blu Skye Medical Inc.">Scott Morris Architects Inc. v. Blu Skye Medical Inc., 90 C.L.R. (3d) 279, 2010 CarswellOnt 865 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendant moved to amend the statement of defence and counterclaim to seek significant additional damages, while the plaintiff brought a cross-motion seeking severance of the counterclaim if the amendments were permitted. The defendant was ordered to file and serve an affidavit of documents together with documents supporting the claim for additional damages, and to provide particulars in respect of each head of damages claimed. The materials were to be served on the plaintiff within 30 days, allowing the plaintiff to assess potential prejudice to be caused to the plaintiff if the amendments were permitted. The parties were to attend again to make additional submissions on the matter within 60 days.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="4 Star Drywall (99) Ltd." p2="Nanak Homes Inc." post.rptr="2006" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I644724705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="4 Star Drywall (99) Ltd. v. Nanak Homes Inc.">4 Star Drywall (99) Ltd. v. Nanak Homes Inc. (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 2006, 82 C.L.R. (3d) 260 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 67(2) does not limit consent to situations where <ital>all</ital> issues between the parties would be resolved by the proposed interlocutory step. The purpose of s. 67(2) is to avoid unnecessary motions or motions which would not advance the resolution or determination of the issues in dispute. Where the Court is satisfied that either the motion is: a) necessary to advance the litigation between the parties; or b) significant issues would likely be resolved by hearing the motion, by bringing about the resolution or determination of some issues in dispute, achieve cost savings to the parties, shortened the trial, or promote the possibility of settling the entire action, consent should be granted by the court. Where these conditions are met to the satisfaction of the court, the proposed interlocutory step would not defeat the summary nature of construction lien actions but rather promote the efficient resolution of such actions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2009" p1="Elegant Design Kitchen Renovations & Contracting Inc." p2="Ojero" post.rptr="4877" pre.rptr="2009" ref.id="I644724715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Elegant Design Kitchen Renovations & Contracting Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A motion to dismiss the action and discharge the lien under s. 47 may be akin to a motion for summary judgment, but it is still a motion to dismiss an action under s. 47 of the Act. As such it is an interlocutory step provided for in the Act. Subsection 67(2) of the Act only requires leave to take an interlocutory step “other than those provided for in this Act.” It may proceed when production and discovery have not taken place.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="1351150 Ontario Inc." p2="Chartrand" post.rptr="6980" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I644724725fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1351150 Ontario Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—There is no requirement that leave be obtained for a motion for payment of money in or out of court under the Act. Such motions are specifically permitted by other sections of the Act and they are therefore not interlocutory motions intended to be covered by s. 67(2). A third party seeking to be added as an intervener must obtain leave.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Rooftek Canada Inc." p2="614730 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="7319" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I644724735fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rooftek Canada Inc. v. 614730 Ontario Inc.">Rooftek Canada Inc. v. 614730 Ontario Inc. Master)</ref></cite>—In order to grant any interlocutory order including a pleading amendment, the court must be mindful of the requirement in s. 67 that the procedure in lien matters should so far as possible be of a summary character, and that additional interlocutory steps be permitted only on being satisfied that the steps are necessary or would expedite the resolution of the matters in dispute. A proposed counterclaim brought beyond the limitation period after the action has been set down for trial, following a pre-trial and that, <ital>inter alia</ital>, would significantly delay the proceeding, was denied.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Tamarack North Holdings Ltd." p2="Hallisey" post.rptr="92" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I644724745fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Tamarack North Holdings Ltd. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The defendants sought leave to conduct examinations for discovery in a case based primarily upon a time and materials contract. The <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is designed to be a summary procedure to reduce costs and simplify proceedings as much as possible. Therefore leave to conduct examinations for discovery is required. Here, the construction was complicated. The design of the buildings and their details developed and changed on an almost daily basis as the work progressed. The success of both the plaintiff and the defendant was dependant upon how the evidence of the many meetings between the parties would be received. It was therefore appropriate that the minutiae of the parties' dealings be examined at discovery rather than before the judge at trial, and leave to conduct examinations for discovery was granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Brantford Engineering & Construction Ltd." p2="1562772 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2655" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I546ac6c0fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Brantford Engineering & Construction Ltd. v. 1562772 Ontario Inc.">Brantford Engineering & Construction Ltd. v. 1562772 Ontario Inc. (3d) 271 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Following pleadings, the plaintiff lien claimant moved pursuant to s. 67(2) for leave to bring a motion for summary judgment under the provisions of R. 20 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. The court was not satisfied, at this stage of the action, that the criteria for summary judgment could be met, as there appeared to be a genuine issue for trial. The allegations of fraud could not be said to be “spurious” or “extraneous” defences which should not proceed to trial. Subsection 67(2) puts an onus on the moving party to prove that the interlocutory step is either necessary or would expedite the resolution of the issues in dispute. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant was self-represented at the time the plaintiff brought a motion for leave for summary judgment. The motion was served by giving it to a courier, a method of service not provided for in the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> for service of a person appearing in person. The lands and premises to which the improvement is supplied stand as security for any claim for lien, and the registering of a construction lien against the lands and premises thus affects the owner. The court should consent to an interlocutory step only if the requisite proof of its necessity is furnished. PA13.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA13:3</designator><name date.updated="0">Case Law<sep/>Security for Costs</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20250528" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2388208 Ontario Inc., operating as Ronen Management Services" p2="Silver Seven Executive Storage Inc." post.rptr="5657" pre.rptr="2024" ref.id="I6560a0d03b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="2388208 Ontario Inc., operating as Ronen Management Services v. Silver Seven Executive Storage Inc.">2388208 Ontario Inc., operating as Ronen Management Services v. Silver Seven Executive Storage Inc., 2024 CarswellOnt 5657, 2024 ONSC 2298 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Security for costs was ordered where the plaintiff's claim for a construction lien for allegedly negotiating a rebate on the capital and construction costs for various parking spaces, was found to be frivolous and vexatious. The construction of the parking spaces was completed in 2014, long before the plaintiff's attempts in 2022 to negotiate the rebate, and there was no evidence the latter was responsible for creating any improvement within the time limit to register a lien. As well, there was good reason to believe that the plaintiff did not have sufficient assets in Ontario to pay the anticipated legal costs of completing the proceeding.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tricott Developments" p2="Sunvest Development Corp. et al." post.rptr="18765" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6560c7e03b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="Tricott Developments v. Sunvest Development Corp. et al.">Tricott Developments v. Sunvest Development Corp. et al., 2022 CarswellOnt 18765, 2022 ONSC 7319, 33 C.L.R. (5th) 431 (Ont. S.C.J.); leave to appeal refused 2023 ONSC 2727, 2023 CarswellOnt 7230 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite></trace>—The test for leave where security for costs is sought is effectively the same as the threshold test under the Rules for an order for security for costs: the moving party must make out a prima facie case of one of the justifications for an order for security for costs set out in r. 56 (in this case, that the plaintiff has insufficient assets in Ontario to pay the costs of the defendant). The burden on the moving party is not onerous and is a lighter onus than proof on a balance of probabilities. Once that threshold has been met, the onus then shifts to the plaintiff to show either that it does have sufficient assets to satisfy a costs award or that an order for security for costs would be unjust. In this case, there was evidence that the company which became the plaintiff contractor was incorporated as a numbered company, sat dormant for roughly 13 years, and that prior to entering into the contract and taking on the project had never conducted any business. When the project came to an end, the plaintiff had no other work, closed its offices, and had only two employees. There was no evidence that it has any assets, nor that it had earned any income since the project was terminated. In all these circumstances, the moving parties had demonstrated that there was good reason to believe that the plaintiff has insufficient assets in Ontario to pay the defendants' costs. While the existence of the latter's counterclaim might be relevant on a motion for security for costs, it did not preclude the granting of the relief sought here.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Probert Construction Inc." p2="Trez MR Holdings (Ontario)Ltd." post.rptr="2766" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I4e15cac1dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="Probert Construction Inc. v. Trez MR Holdings (Ontario)Ltd.">Probert Construction Inc. v. Trez MR Holdings (Ontario)Ltd., 2023 CarswellOnt 2766, 2023 ONSC 1490, 30 C.L.R. (5th) 263 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where it is shown that there is good reason to believe that a corporate plaintiff does not have sufficient assets in Ontario to pay the defendant's costs, the defendant has met the test of “necessity” for leave under s. 13 of O. Reg. 302/18. However, the fact that there are lien claims registered against a plaintiff is not, in and of itself, evidence of insufficient funds. There can be valid reasons for contractors and subcontractors to disagree on payment and for lien claims to be filed. In the result, the defendant did not meet its onus to show that there was “good reason to believe” that the plaintiff had insufficient assets to satisfy a costs order.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="10760919 Canada Inc. dba Harbels Construction Ontario" p2="Crosslinx Transit Solutions Constructors" post.rptr="1271" pre.rptr="2023" ref.id="I4e15cac2dab911ee81eeeb29d9a41c1c" title="10760919 Canada Inc. dba Harbels Construction Ontario v. (5th) 86 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite><ital>—</ital>The court reiterated that the test of necessity under s. 67(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> (now s. 13 of O. Reg. 302/18) is demonstrated in a security for costs motion when the moving party meets its threshold onus by showing that there is “good reason to believe” that a plaintiff has insufficient assets in Ontario to pay the defendant's costs. Here, the defendant met that threshold onus where the plaintiff had ceased business operations, no longer leased office space and no longer had any employees; had significant unpaid debts to the Canada Revenue Agency, the Workplace Safety and Insurance Board, and its subcontractors and suppliers; did not own any real property in the area; failed to make mandatory annual corporate filings in recent years and had not held an annual general meeting in several years. Distinguishing the facts of this case from those in <ital>Gowing Contractors Ltd. v. Walsh Construction Company Canada,</ital> below, the Associate Judge declined to consider the plaintiff's earned and unpaid holdback amounts. Unlike in <ital>Gowing</ital>, here there were subcontractor lien claimants which had first priority claims to any additional holdbacks that the defendant was required to retain. The evidence did not support a strong claim for proving an additional holdback obligation that exceeded the unpaid amounts owing to the plaintiff's subcontractors, and those holdback funds were not properly considered an “asset” for security for costs purposes.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><trace date.trace="20250528"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="SRK Woodworking Inc." p2="Devlan Construction Ltd. et al." post.rptr="6229" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6560eef03b9611f09c42d605d1c8dfb5" title="SRK Woodworking Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite></trace>—Adopting the analysis in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Compass Mechanical Contracting Inc." p2="AIM Recycling Hamilton et al." post.rptr="4656" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6447c0b05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Compass Mechanical Contracting Inc. v. AIM Recycling Hamilton et al.">Compass Mechanical Contracting Inc. v. AIM Recycling Hamilton et al., 2022 ONSC 4656, 2022 CarswellOnt 11376 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the court found that the test of necessity in s. 13 had been met, and that the plaintiff did not have the ability to pay a costs award. The plaintiff had not met its obligation to make full financial disclosure which would include disclosure of the amount and source of all income; a description of its assets (including values); a list of liabilities and other significant expenses; an indication of the extent of the ability of the plaintiff to borrow funds; and details of any assets disposed of or encumbered since the cause of action arose.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Abtrex Contractors Inc." p2="Stewart" post.rptr="4708" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6447c0b15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Abtrex Contractors Inc. v. Stewart">Abtrex Contractors Inc. v. Stewart, 2022 ONSC 4708, 2022 CarswellOnt 11575 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—On a motion for security for costs, it was well established that the defendants have the initial onus to show that there is “good reason to believe” a plaintiff has insufficient assets in Ontario to pay costs. Only when the defendants have met this initial onus does the onus shift to the plaintiff to show either that it has sufficient assets to pay costs or that it does not and that its claim has merit thereby requiring the court to deny the security for costs motion as a matter of justice. Here, the plaintiff conceded that the defendants had met their initial onus. The test for leave under s. 67(2) of the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital> is met when the defendant meets its initial onus under (ON) rule 56.01(1)(d). By conceding the initial onus point under r. 56.01(1)(d), the plaintiff here had also conceded the leave point.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Compass Mechanical Contracting Inc." p2="AIM Recycling Hamilton et al." post.rptr="4656" pre.rptr="2022" ref.id="I6447c0b25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Compass Mechanical Contracting Inc. v. In the circumstances, the test of necessity was met. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Security for costs was ordered where the plaintiff had not adduced any evidence of impecuniosity, did not argue such an order would result in any injustice, and the defendant had posted security for costs into court to vacate the lien. It was fair in the circumstances to require the plaintiff to have a stake in the litigation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2280092 Ontario Inc." p2="Collins" post.rptr="4365" pre.rptr="2021" ref.id="I6447e7c05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2280092 Ontario Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—A corporate plaintiff who claims impecuniosity must demonstrate that it cannot raise security for costs from its shareholders and associates. This requires substantial evidence about the personal means and abilities of its shareholders and others who have or might have an interest in the litigation to post security. Bare assertions are not sufficient. Otherwise, shareholders and others with an interest in the action would be able to take the benefits of an action without being exposed to the consequences of an unsuccessful action. Because the plaintiff had not established that it was impecunious, it was not necessary to embark on an analysis of whether the main action was not clearly devoid of merit, or on an analysis of why it might be unjust to order security for costs under Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Both a related lien action and a bond action arose out of the same construction project and raised many of the same issues. At issue on this motion was whether the defendant should be awarded further amounts for security for its costs when a previous security for costs order was made in its favour in the lien action. The lien action and the bond action were substantively duplicative, and the defendant's delay in bringing the later motion was tactical, based on the result in the lien motion. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Supposition based on an unsubstantiated suspicion that a lack of finances was the reason that the plaintiff elected to represent himself and had not taken steps since the close of pleadings, was insufficient to suggest the claimant was impecunious. The proposed motion, if brought and successful, would not expedite the resolution of the issues in dispute, and would result in adjournment of the scheduled long motion. Although the plaintiff had raised issues of trust funds under s. 7(2) and set off under s. 12, which were potentially relevant to the issue of security for costs, the Master preferred to first hear argument and decide the trust argument. If he ultimately accepted the plaintiff's position on those issues, but was unable to fairly resolve the motion on the existing record without further submissions or evidence, he had the discretion to require either or both. That was a more timely, cost-effective, and proportionate way to proceed in all the circumstances, and was consistent with the summary process required by the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Lancaster Group Inc." p2="Kenaidan Contracting Ltd." post.rptr="3896" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I6447e7c45fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Lancaster Group Inc. v. Kenaidan Contracting Ltd.">Lancaster Group Inc. v. Kenaidan Contracting Ltd., 2020 CarswellOnt 3896, 2020 ONSC 1653, 6 C.L.R. (5th) 146 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—To obtain leave for a motion for security for costs, the defendant must demonstrate that there is good reason to believe that the plaintiff has insufficient assets in Ontario to pay the former's costs. If the defendant meets its burden, the onus shifts to the plaintiff to show that it has sufficient assets or that the order is unjust. The court is to consider all the circumstances of the case and look at the overall justness of the order. Here, the defendant met its burden, the plaintiff did not show sufficient assets, and the overall justice of the case favoured a security for costs order.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Bolton Mechanical" p2="EBC Inc." post.rptr="7437" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I6447e7c55fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Bolton Mechanical v. EBC Inc.">Bolton Mechanical v. EBC Inc., 2020 CarswellOnt 7437, 2020 ONSC 3407, 11 C.L.R. (5th) 254 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—After granting leave to bring the motion, the master awarded security for costs to the defendant after the defendant failed to meet its onus to show that it had sufficient assets in Ontario to pay for the defendant's costs. She held that the posting of security for the lien and for the plaintiff's costs was a factor to be considered in favour of an order for security for costs to achieve procedural fairness and justice to both parties. The existence of the defendant's counterclaim did not preclude the court from making an order for security for costs, as the defendant's counterclaim was separate from its defence. The existence of a counterclaim could, however, factor in the quantum of the security.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="2232117 Ontario Inc." p2="Somasundaram" post.rptr="3193" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64480ed05fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="2232117 Ontario Inc. v. Somasundaram">2232117 Ontario Inc. v. Somasundaram, 2020 CarswellOnt 3193, 2020 ONSC 1434, 5 C.L.R. (5th) 249 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The master granted the owners' motion and ordered the plaintiff to post, on a staged basis, security for costs on a partial indemnity basis. The master noted that, in assessing if the threshold onus on such a motion has been satisfied, a court may consider all evidence filed on a motion. However, that does not equate to an evidentiary onus on the plaintiff at the first stage. Accordingly, since a plaintiff has no evidentiary onus unless the defendant's threshold onus has been met, a failure by a plaintiff to provide any evidence of its assets would not generally, in and of itself, support a reasonable inference regarding that plaintiff's financial circumstances at the first stage of the analysis. At the second stage of the analysis, the onus is on a plaintiff to establish that it either has sufficient assets in Ontario to satisfy a costs order or that an order for security for costs would be unjust. There can be procedural unfairness between a lien claimant having security for its claim either in the lands or posted in court and, on the other hand, a defendant having no security for costs of defending the claim. Referencing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Yuanda Canada Enterprises Ltd." p2="Pier 27 Toronto Inc." post.rptr="1892" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I64480ed15fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Yuanda Canada Enterprises Ltd. v. Pier 27 Toronto Inc.">Yuanda Canada Enterprises Ltd. v. Pier 27 Toronto Inc., 2017 ONSC 1892, 2017 CarswellOnt 3791, 78 C.L.R. (4th) 181 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, the imbalance becomes acute with evidence that the plaintiff corporation does not have sufficient assets to pay the defendant's costs, and the defendant has posted security, including security for costs, for the plaintiff's claim. That was precisely the case here.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Prasher Steel Ltd." p2="Gateman-Milloy Inc." post.rptr="2503" pre.rptr="2020" ref.id="I64480ed25fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Prasher Steel Ltd. v. However, the defendant apparently received payment from the owner for the plaintiff's work on the job as certified by the architect, but had not released those funds to the plaintiff, presumably because the defendant had decided to counterclaim against the plaintiff for alleged deficiencies in the work and had decided to retain those amounts in contemplation of its counterclaim. In the circumstances, an order for security for costs was neither appropriate or necessary.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Gatti Group Corp." p2="Zuccarini" post.rptr="3393" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I64480ed35fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Gatti Group Corp. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Motions for security for costs have a two-step process, the first step, placing the onus on the moving party to establish that the case falls into one of the enumerated categories (in this case Ont. Rule 56.01(1)(d)), and the second step, where the moving party has met that initial onus, placing on the respondent the onus of showing that it would be unjust to order security for costs or that the security should be reduced. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Where there was good reason to believe that the plaintiff subcontractor had insufficient assets in Ontario to satisfy an award of costs, leave to bring a motion for security for costs was granted. While there was reason to believe that the subcontractor would succeed in proving that contractor breached the subcontract, it did not establish a good chance of success as to the entirety of the quantum of its claim, and its behaviour evidenced a propensity to act without fair and proper notice, and to engage in unnecessary activity to avoid the consequences of the motion for security for costs. What was “necessary” for the purpose of s. 67(2) in such motions was similar to the threshold for the determination of whether “there is good reason to believe” that the plaintiff corporation did not have sufficient assets in Ontario to pay the defendant's cost. As articulated in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="City Commercial Realty (Canada) Ltd." p2="Bakich" post.rptr="10512" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I644884015fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="City Commercial Realty (Canada) Ltd. v. [In Chambers])</ref></cite>, the defendant did not have to establish that the plaintiff corporation in fact had insufficient assets to pay costs, but did have to establish a “belief of insufficiency that goes beyond mere conjecture, hunch, or speculation.” The moving party had to show “indicia of insolvency” or “instability,” such as a failure to make corporate filings, unpaid judgments or liabilities, a temporary dissolution, a significant disposition of assets, or the plaintiff as a single purpose entity, namely a shell company. Here, there was no evidence on the motion that the plaintiff was insolvent and unstable. The contractor was an insolvent corporation that was pursuing litigation on behalf of solvent corporations that were not parties to litigation and therefore not subject to any award of costs. R. 56.01(d) in this situation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc." p2="Devlan Construction Ltd." post.rptr="3" pre.rptr="2014" ref.id="I6448ab115fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Royal Windsor Mechanical Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="1652472 Ontario Inc." p2="Black & McDonald Ltd." post.rptr="4560" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6448ab155fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1652472 Ontario Inc. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—While leave will not automatically be granted in every instance, a motion for security for costs may generally be justified as a necessary step to doing justice between the parties, and because it may shorten the proceeding by ensuring the plaintiff cannot proceed with risk free litigation. The court will not refrain from ordering security just because the defendant caused the plaintiff's poverty by wrongfully withholding funds. It should not be taken as a given that security for costs will be unjust in this situation. The court must also have regard to the injustice that will result if the plaintiff fails to prove its case and the defendant is unable to collect its costs. On the questions of delay in bringing the motion, and the existence of a counterclaim, the Master adopted the analysis in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac-United Management Corp." p2="Canadian National Railway" post.rptr="2372" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6448ab165fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Unimac-United Management Corp. v. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, to hold that: a) that the defendant was not disentitled from bringing the motion simply because a trial date had been set; and b) this was not a case in which the counterclaim introduced new issues or was likely to generate costs unrelated to the main action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Unimac-United Management Corp." p2="Canadian National Railway" post.rptr="2372" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6448ab175fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Unimac-United Management Corp. v. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2015 CarswellOnt 10177, 48 C.L.R. (4th) 98 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The security for costs rules are designed to achieve procedural fairness and justice between the parties. The process for leave under s. 67(2) parallels the general process under Rule 56.01. First, it is on the defendant to establish whether the matter falls under one of the six enumerated categories in the Rule. The onus is then on the plaintiff to show that an order for security for costs is unjust. Where there is an unjustified multiplicity of proceedings by the plaintiff, it is a matter of procedural fairness that the defendant should, at minimum, have its costs secured by the plaintiff. On an application for leave to bring a motion for security of costs under s. 67(2), if it appears that there are two or more proceedings for the same relief, the motion is “necessary” and leave follows. The onus then shifts to the plaintiff to show that the multiplicity of proceedings is justified or not unfair. Motions for security are usually not brought until at least the pleadings and productions are done, because it is difficult before that point to decipher what the issues and the costs of the action will be. There should be no hard and fast rule about when such motions should be initiated, and the courts give defendants latitude to move through the initial stages of a proceeding before requiring that they bring motions for security for costs. Lastly, citing <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="European Flooring Contract Services Ltd." p2="Toddglen ILofts Ltd." post.rptr="6445" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6448d2205fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="European Flooring Contract Services Ltd. v. Toddglen ILofts Ltd.">European Flooring Contract Services Ltd. v. Toddglen ILofts Ltd., 2013 ONSC 6445, 2013 CarswellOnt 14289, 31 C.L.R. (4th) 141 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, where there is a counterclaim and the facts on which the counterclaim are based in large part on the same facts and circumstances raised in the plaintiff's claim, this militates against an order for security for costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Simpson's Fence (Chatham) Inc." p2="1187855 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="2430" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I6448d2215fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Simpson's Fence (Chatham) Inc. v. 1187855 Ontario Inc.">Simpson's Fence (Chatham) Inc. v. 1187855 Ontario Inc., 2015 ONSC 2430, 2015 CarswellOnt 5242, 47 C.L.R. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>, where there is some evidence that the plaintiff may not have sufficient assets in Ontario to pay the defendant's costs should the defendant be successful, there is a “necessity” for the motion as required by s. 67(2). On the question of quantum, procedural fairness dictates that an order for security for costs should be proportionate not only to the amount of the lien claim but also to the notionally off-setting security posted by the defendant when it elected to have the lien on the project property vacated. The legislation employs a formula for calculating the amount of costs that must form part of the bond posted in order to obtain the order vacating the lien, and this approach is helpful to the court in determining the quantum of security to be posted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="European Flooring Contract Services Ltd." p2="Toddglen ILofts Ltd." post.rptr="6445" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I6448f9315fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="European Flooring Contract Services Ltd. v. Here, on the hearing of the motion on its merits, security for costs was denied on account of the defendants' delay in bringing the motion, their breach of a court order and the existence of counterclaims. Where the counterclaim in an action is based in large part on the same facts and circumstances raised in the plaintiff's claim, this militates against an order for security for costs, as per <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Better Business Bureau of Metropolitan Toronto Inc." p2="Tuz" post.rptr="1069" pre.rptr="1999" ref.id="I6448f9325fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Better Business Bureau of Metropolitan Toronto Inc. v. Catan Canada Inc.">2016637 Ontario Inc. v. Catan Canada Inc., 2012 ONSC 2055, 2012 CarswellOnt 5997, 23 C.L.R. (4th) 157 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons 2012 CarswellOnt 5983, 24 C.L.R. (4th) 162 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The two prongs of the test in s. 67(2) are distinct, as exemplified by the disjunctive “or” between them. The second prong focuses on the policy in favour of expediting the resolution of the issues on their merits. The first prong can encompass broader issues including the question of procedural fairness. The purpose of s. 67(2) should be viewed in the context of the entire section, including s. 67(1). Section 67(1) recognizes that there may be a broad spectrum of lien actions, involving from the simplest home renovation project to the most complex commercial, industrial or institutional mega-project. The degree to which the procedure is “summary” will vary with “the amount and nature of the liens in question” and will be summary only “as far as possible.” The requirement for leave for interlocutory steps in s. 67(2) is the mechanism by which the Courts acts as gate-keeper to ensure that the process is as “summary” as it should be in the circumstances. The intent of s. 67(2) is not to eliminate considerations of procedural fairness by application of the rules governing security for costs, or other rules of civil procedure. Its purpose is to permit the court to consider the degree to which a particular lien action should be summary in nature, having regard to the amount and nature of the liens in question, and in that context, to determine whether an interlocutory step is “necessary” to achieve procedural fairness, or would “expedite the resolution of the issues in dispute.” Where, as here, impecuniosity has been shown, a plaintiff need only demonstrate that the claim is not plainly devoid of merit. As the plaintiffs had met that low threshold, it was not “necessary” to order that the plaintiffs post security for costs, in order to achieve procedural fairness. To order security for costs would effectively stop the actions.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Melco Construction Inc." p2="Jack Frost Sparkling Springs Co." post.rptr="2197" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I644920405fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Melco Construction Inc. v. (2009), 80 C.L.R. (3d) 135, 2009 CarswellOnt 2294 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons at (2009), 2009 CarswellOnt 3231 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Section 67(2) was intended to cover interlocutory motions leading to trial only and not interlocutory matters involving appeals, which are governed by the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>. The section is intended to ensure that actions do not get delayed through extensive interlocutory motions unless the interlocutory motions meet the threshold test. The same policy considerations do not apply to an appeal, which the parties may have as of right. There are very few interlocutory motions available to either party pending an appeal, and they do not normally delay the hearing of the appeal, as the appeal date has already been set. Thus, s. 67(2) does not apply to a motion for security for costs on appeal, and no leave is required to bring this motion under Rule 61.06 of the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Brian T.
