Master); additional reasons at 2009 CarswellOnt 8879, 92 C.L.R. (3d) 128 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—A motion to discharge or vacate a lien upon proper grounds is specifically provided for under section 47 of the Act. As such leave is not required. Motions not provided for under the Act where leave is required would be motions for interlocutory relief such as security for costs or for discovery or to compel answers to questions refused at discovery.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2008" p1="Khatachadourian" p2="Roopchand" post.rptr="3909" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I644947515fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Khatachadourian v. Roopchand">Khatachadourian v. Roopchand (2008), 2008 CarswellOnt 3909 (Ont. Div. Ct.)</ref></cite>—The order of the master giving leave to move to strike the pleadings satisfied the requirement of s. 67(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="I.I.C.I. Construction Ltd." p2="Altavista Properties Inc." post.rptr="6995" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I644947525fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="I.I.C.I. Construction Ltd. v. Altavista Properties Inc.">I.I.C.I. Construction Ltd. v. Altavista Properties Inc. (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6995 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—Leave pursuant to s. 67 of the Act to bring a motion for an order for security for costs was denied. <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="GTA Structural Steel Ltd." p2="20 Ashtonbee Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I644947535fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="GTA Structural Steel Ltd. v. 20 Ashtonbee Holdings Ltd.">GTA Structural Steel Ltd. v. 20 Ashtonbee Holdings Ltd. (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 157, 2005 CarswellOnt 6820 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, was distinguished. Here, the claim was not being advanced by a secured creditor, the action had been settled to the extent possible and a trial date had been set. An order for security for costs would not encourage a settlement between the plaintiff and the moving defendant. [<ital>Authors' Note</ital>: See also the Divisional Court's ruling, under s. 71(3)(b) of the Act, below, to the effect that there was no jurisdiction in the court to hear an appeal of this interlocutory ruling.]</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2007" p1="Englelake Ltd." p2="Simons" post.rptr="45" pre.rptr="67" ref.id="I64496e605fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Englelake Ltd. v. Simons">Englelake Ltd. v. Simons (2007), 67 C.L.R. (3d) 45, 2007 CarswellOnt 5179 (Ont. S.C.J.); additional reasons (2007), 2007 CarswellOnt 6948 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—Leave to bring a motion for security for costs was granted, the motion was denied. The defendants acknowledged that they had no information that the plaintiff had insufficient assets to pay the defendants' costs of defending the action.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="1049086 Ontario Ltd." p2="Torbear Contracting Inc." post.rptr="204" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I64496e615fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="1049086 Ontario Ltd. v. Torbear Contracting Inc.">1049086 Ontario Ltd. v. Torbear Contracting Inc. (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 204, 2005 CarswellOnt 7322 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The policy underlying R. 56.01 is to provide a mechanism to preserve the procedural balance between the parties. Where the defendant had already been put to the expense of providing security for costs under the Act, the court imposed a similar obligation on the plaintiff to “level the playing field”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="GTA Structural Steel Ltd." p2="20 Ashtonbee Holdings Ltd." post.rptr="157" pre.rptr="49" ref.id="I64496e625fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="GTA Structural Steel Ltd. v. 20 Ashtonbee Holdings Ltd.">GTA Structural Steel Ltd. v. 20 Ashtonbee Holdings Ltd. (2005), 49 C.L.R. (3d) 157, 2005 CarswellOnt 6820 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—For leave to be granted to bring an interlocutory step, including a motion for security for costs, the moving party must satisfy the court that at a minimum one of the conditions precedent set out in s. 67(2) has been met, namely that the interlocutory step is necessary or would expedite the resolution of the issues in dispute. It follows that the moving party will have to adduce the basis upon which the condition precedent is satisfied and the evidence in support thereof. On the facts before the Master, a successful motion for security for costs would ensure that if the plaintiff failed in the action the defendant would not be left without a source to pay its costs, and would encourage a settlement of the issues between the parties. In this case, the findings did support the second prong of the test, in that the resolution of the issues in dispute would be expedited. On that basis leave was given pursuant to s. 67(2) to bring the motion for security for costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2005" p1="John Bianchi Grading Ltd." p2="Belrock Design Build Inc." post.rptr="3034" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I64496e635fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="John Bianchi Grading Ltd. v. Belrock Design Build Inc.">John Bianchi Grading Ltd. v. Belrock Design Build Inc. (2005), 2005 CarswellOnt 3034, 44 C.L.R. (3d) 198 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—The court followed the ruling of the Master in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Biotechnik Inc." p2="O'Shanter Development Co." post.rptr="1895" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I64496e645fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co.">Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 1895, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 52 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>, and held that the security for costs regime set out in the <ital>Rules of Civil Procedure</ital> was “necessary” rather than interlocutory.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2004" p1="D.M.S. Concrete Forming Inc." p2="Eastern Construction Co. Ltd." post.rptr="3145" pre.rptr="[2004]" ref.id="I64496e655fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.M.S. Concrete Forming Inc. v. Eastern Construction Co. Ltd.">D.M.S. Concrete Forming Inc. v. Eastern Construction Co. Ltd. (2004), [2004] O.J. No. 3145, 2004 CarswellOnt 3124, 36 C.L.R. (3d) 153 (Master)</ref></cite>—An interesting example of creativity in the structuring of security for costs. The court has, and will exercise, wide discretion as to the terms imposed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2003" p1="Biotechnik Inc." p2="O'Shanter Development Co." post.rptr="1895" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I64496e665fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co.">Biotechnik Inc. v. O'Shanter Development Co. (2003), 2003 CarswellOnt 1895, 30 C.L.R. (3d) 52 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—When faced with conflicting rulings of the Superior Court in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Global Design & Building Inc." p2="1289193 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="271" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I64496e675fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Global Design & Building Inc. v. 1289193 Ontario Inc.">Global Design & Building Inc. v. 1289193 Ontario Inc. (2000), 2 C.L.R. (3d) 271, 2000 CarswellOnt 1216 (S.C.J.)</ref></cite> and <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co." p2="Windigo Community Development Corp." post.rptr="111" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I64496e685fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp.">D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp. (1996), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 111, 1996 CarswellOnt 4798 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, the Master chose to follow the ruling in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co." p2="Windigo Community Development Corp." post.rptr="111" pre.rptr="31" ref.id="I64496e695fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp.">D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp. (1996), 31 C.L.R. (2d) 111, 1996 CarswellOnt 4798 (Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>, and ruled that consent (or leave) to bring a motion for security for costs under s. 67(2) can be granted if such a motion is necessary to do procedural justice to both parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2000" p1="Global Design & Building Inc." p2="1289193 Ontario Inc." post.rptr="271" pre.rptr="2" ref.id="I644995705fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Global Design & Building Inc. v. 1289193 Ontario Inc.">Global Design & Building Inc. v. 1289193 Ontario Inc. (2000), 2 C.L.R. (3d) 271 (Ont. S.C.J.)</ref></cite>—An order for security for costs in a construction lien action is not “necessary” within the meaning of that word in s. 67(2).</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1996" p1="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co." p2="Windigo Community Development Corp." post.rptr="198" pre.rptr="4" ref.id="I644995715fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp.">D.E. & J.C. Hutchison Contracting Co. v. Windigo Community Development Corp. (1996), 4 C.P.C. (4th) 198, 31 C.L.R. (2d) 111 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Security for costs has been ordered, in appropriate cases, under the <ital>Construction Lien Act</ital>, and it was too late for a party to argue that such motions were not within the contemplation of the legislation. Leave to bring a motion for security for costs was therefore granted.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Snowmont Investments Corp." p2="Elliott" post.rptr="4670" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I54704500fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott">Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 4670 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—A motion for security for costs was made by a defendant in an 9<fraction style="shilling"><numerator>1</numerator><denominator>2</denominator></fraction>-year-old construction lien action, after four adjournments of the trial itself, each at the instance of the defendant. Leave to bring the motion was denied and, notwithstanding that leave to bring the motion was denied, the motion was also dismissed in its entirety.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="Snowmont Investments Corp." p2="Elliott" post.rptr="4670" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I54704501fe1b11ee86bacfd15eb09fa9" title="Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott">Snowmont Investments Corp. v. Elliott (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 4670 (Ont. Gen. Div.)</ref></cite>—Dealing with the alternative ground for leave that the step would be necessary, it was argued that the “necessity” of a motion for security for costs was that it was needed to allow a defendant to collect its costs if it was successful in the defence and counterclaim and, generally, that it was necessary to do justice in a procedural sense. The motion was brought during a court ordered stay in a trial slightly more than one month prior to the resumption of the trial in a case that was ten years old. The court held that although delay was not a major consideration in a motion for security for costs, it was the opposite of “expedite” and, the court reasoned, delay can therefore be a factor in granting leave under s. 67(2) of the Act.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="19950123" p1="Buttcon Ltd." p2="Bolton Village Crossroads Inc." ref.id="I6449bc815fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Buttcon Ltd. v. Bolton Village Crossroads Inc.">Buttcon Ltd. v. Bolton Village Crossroads Inc. (January 23, 1995), Kirsh's Construction Case Finder No. 67.38, Master</ref></cite>—Due to the consolidation of five lien proceedings, Buttcon was styled as plaintiff, however, in fact, they were defendant and moved for security for costs without seeking leave. The Master interpreted a “necessary step” as one allowing the trial to be heard as the litigation moved along. Where leave is not sought, or if sought, the test in the Act cannot be met, the motion should be dismissed.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rock Construction & Management Ltd." p2="Arosan Enterprises Ltd." post.rptr="464" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I6449bc825fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="Rock Construction & Management Ltd. v. Arosan Enterprises Ltd.">Rock Construction & Management Ltd. v. Arosan Enterprises Ltd., 1995 CarswellOnt 464, [1995] O.J. No. 1438, 21 C.L.R. (2d) 173 (Ont. Master)</ref></cite>—The defendant Arosan moved for an order from security for costs. The notice of motion did not seek leave under s. 67(2). Taken altogether, the various subsections of s. 67 are intended to reduce costs and delay in construction lien litigation by giving the court the opportunity to assess, in advance, the likely value and impact of an intended interlocutory motion. As there was no material before the court to satisfy the subsection, the motion was dismissed with costs.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="1995" p1="816855 Ontario Ltd." p2="953225 Ontario Ltd." post.rptr="3656" pre.rptr="1995" ref.id="I6449bc835fd911ee863d9b592332bce9" title="816855 Ontario Ltd. v. 953225 Ontario Ltd.">816855 Ontario Ltd. v. 953225 Ontario Ltd. (1995), 1995 CarswellOnt 3656, [1995] O.J. No. 1767 (Master)</ref></cite>—A different approach was adopted by the Master in this case. Having heard and disposed of the defendant's motion on undertakings and refusals, he heard argument on the merits of the defendant's motion for security for costs and reserved the issue of leave. The Master concluded that the test for granting security for costs had been met and for that reason alone granted leave.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>

PA14.</value></metadata></metadata.block><editorial.commentary.section.front date.updated="0"><editorial.outline.name.block toc.include="n" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">PA14:1</designator><name date.updated="0">Legislative History and Commentary</name></editorial.outline.name.block></editorial.commentary.section.front><editorial.commentary.section.body date.updated="0"><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Legislative History</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The first predecessor of s. 14 came into force in s. 5 of the <ital>Mechanics' Lien Amendment Act, 1937</ital>, S.O. 1937, c. 41 in a version substantially identical to today's section.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Commentary</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Section 14 corresponds to former s. 67(4) and remains substantially unchanged, but for the provision allowing the parties to make submissions as to the remuneration of the expert.</para.text></para></editorial.commentary.section.body></editorial.commentary.section>
